en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Vinayālaṅkāra Commentary on the Vinaya Piṭaka (First Part)
The Introduction to the Composition:
Verses on the Muttahāra and Other Methods He who is the world and the lord of the world, the most excellent among others, the king of kings, the noble elephant-knower;
He whose form is like space, who delights in supreme bliss, the God of gods, the peerless Vajra-holder;
the essence of the worthless cycle of existence, honored by the best of men, the destroyer of Māra, the sovereign within the realms;
the creator of the world’s adornment, possessed of exceeding wisdom and conduct, whose delight is in steadfast heroism.
I bow to that Fully Enlightened One, the possessor of excellent qualities, who has crushed the wheel of saṃsāra, whose mind is perfectly serene,
and who has taught the path that is so difficult to see. I pay homage to the Lion among Men.
The verse on the Turning of the Waters of Anotatta:
By whom evils were destroyed, by whom fears were extinguished,
by whom the worlds emerged [from suffering]— to him I bow.
Verses on the Wheel-Turning Monarch of the Four Continents:
I pay homage to the Saṅgha, together with its members, who have vomited forth the most excellent Dhamma;
who abide in the fruits of the path’s progression, who are well-praised, and whose minds are beautiful.
I pay homage to the Vinaya, which is the essence of discipline; to the Saṅgaha, which effects a compendium; to the Cariyā, which is conduct;
and to the Parama, the supreme learning—this verse, beginning with the four feet, is a *yamaka* (chime) that does not lose its integrity.
A verse with interlocking yamakas at the beginning and end of each of its four quarters:
To you who are manifold in your modes, the ocean of virtues, the ocean itself— To my venerable teacher, my teacher, I pay homage; I bow down, I prostrate deeply.
Having abandoned all calamities through the reverential homage I have performed toward the three teachers who composed the treatises,
may the wise ones who desire training and carry out the Conqueror’s dispensation [attain success].
At the respectful request of the monks who are experts in the Vinaya,
I shall explain this compendium of the Vinaya, which increases joy, according to my own ability and strength,
for the sake of those monks who are seekers of discipline.
Although there exists a commentary composed by the ancients,
it does not fulfill one's desires because of its extreme brevity.
Therefore, having carefully extracted the essence from various treatises, [I shall compose this].
I shall provide an exposition of the meaning that is neither too concise nor too prolix.
May all virtuous ones properly uphold this treatise, named *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which brings joy to those who are well-behaved.
Commentary on the Introduction to the Book:
This work is endowed with various distinguished methods; it is capable of effecting the discipline of body and speech; it dispels the doubts of bhikkhus who are modest and refined;
it brings about the purification of virtue for individuals who are practitioners of yoga; and it serves as a cause for the increase of the Conqueror’s Dispensation.
Desiring to begin this treatise, this bull among teachers first spoke the words “Having paid homage to the Triple Gem,” and so forth,

in order to demonstrate the homage, the state of being worthy of homage, the subject matter, the purpose, the cause, the manner of composition, the title of the work, the motive, and the benefit. For here,
by the phrase “having paid homage to the Triple Gem,” the homage to the Three Jewels is expressed, because it demonstrates both the object of homage and the act of homage itself.
"Refuge for all living beings": by this, the state of being worthy of salutation is shown through the demonstration of the reason for that salutation.

"A commentary on the meaning apart from the text": this is the subject matter, because it constitutes the meaning of this treatise. "Scattered in many places": this is the instrumental cause, because the treatise was composed for that very reason.
"Having gathered together in one place, I shall show it without confusion": this is the manner of the action, performed in that way.
Because of the composition of this treatise (*pakaraṇa*). The designation "treatise" (*pakaraṇa*), however, is shown by the power of the word "compiling" (*samāharita*);
for it is precisely through the act of compiling [the material] that this treatise receives the name *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
As for the cause (*nimitta*), it is twofold: internal and external. Among these, the internal is compassion (*karuṇā*); that—
It is shown by virtue of its capacity for the act of seeing, because in its absence there would be no act of seeing. "The external" refers to the assembly of listeners;

it belongs to the bhikkhus who are practitioners of yoga because they constitute the objective support for that compassion. Furthermore, the purpose (payojana) is twofold, by way of the purpose of the salutation and the purpose of the treatise.
Therein, the purpose of the salutation consists of the dispelling of obstacles, the generation of confidence, and so forth.
The phrase "to him, the refuge of all living beings" is shown by way of its functional power (*sāmatthiya*), because when the cause exists, the fruit is invariably present (*avinābhāva*).

For it has been said by the commentator on the Abhidhamma: "One who possesses distinguished qualities is worthy of salutation; and a salutation offered to one worthy of salutation brings about the accomplishment of the stated purpose.
The purpose of the treatise (*pakaraṇa-payojana*) is also twofold, according to the primary and the secondary.

Among these, the primary purpose (*mukhyapayojana*) consists of the penetration and exposition of the meaning in accordance with the phrasing, and the recitation and instruction of the phrasing in accordance with the meaning;
this is what is expressed by the phrase "for the sake of proficiency in the Vinaya.

The secondary purpose (*anusaṅgikapayojana*) is the goal beginning with virtue (*sīla*) and ending in final Nibbāna through non-clinging; having gathered that together, they will demonstrate it as being in one place for this [work].

When there is a demonstration that brings together in one place what has been shown by way of their respective capacities, the purpose is that the goal may be accomplished without obstacle for one who has applied themselves through the study and interrogation of those [teachings].
But for what purpose were the homage to the Triple Gem and so forth performed here by the Teacher? Is it not the commencement of the intended treatise itself?
"Should it be done? It is said: here, the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of completing the composition without effort by removing obstacles that might arise from it.
The statement regarding the state of being worthy of homage is for the purpose of showing that one has acted appropriately and fittingly;
that is for the purpose of pleasing the wise; that is for the purpose of the wise taking up this treatise; and that is for the purpose of bringing about every form of excellence.
The statement of the subject matter is for the purpose of enabling the wise to engage with a text whose subject matter is already known, by means of learning, memorizing, and so forth.
The statement of the cause of composition is for the purpose of precluding effort that is fruitless when directed toward what is not the true cause.
The statement of the manner of composition is for the purpose of generating interest in listeners for the learning and other activities concerning a text whose manner of composition is already known.
The mention of the title is for the sake of ease in conventional usage. The statement of the sign (the subject matter) is for the sake of showing the proximate cause.
The statement of the purpose is for the sake of generating enthusiasm in listeners who desire the two-fold purpose.
Furthermore, the teachers explain the purpose of the homage to the Triple Gem in many ways; that [explanation] is found therein.
In that case, it should be understood according to the method already stated.
Here, however, for the sake of releasing the burden of the text, we have explained only the purpose intended by the teachers of the *Aṭṭhakathā*. For it was said by the teacher of the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"Of this act of reverential salutation..."
"By the power of his devotion to the Three Jewels,
having dried up all obstacles without exception."
This is the meaning of the whole here; this, however, is the meaning of the parts: "I pay homage to the Triple Gem, which is the refuge and that which has become the refuge for all living beings.

Having paid homage, I shall—having collected in one place the various meanings scattered throughout the canonical texts and their commentaries, and having rendered them free from confusion—show, I shall show, the *Pāḷimuttakavinicchaya* for the sake of proficiency in the Vinaya for bhikkhus who are practitioners of yoga. This is the construction.
In this context, *vatthu* means "that which dwells here. What is that? It is the jewel of the Buddha and so forth.

For, because good persons who have gone for refuge, being endowed with the act of going for refuge, take the jewel of the Buddha and so forth as their object (*ārammaṇa*) and dwell, abide, and reside upon that object;
therefore it is called a "basis" (*vatthu*). For the object is the support (*ādhāra*), and that which possesses the object is the supported (*ādheyya*).

Beyond this, other explanations of the meaning and so forth of the word *vatthu* have been stated by the teachers; these too should be understood according to the method explained in their respective places.
However, it should be understood that only this much has been stated here for the purpose of avoiding excessive bulk in the text.
*Tayaṃ* means "a collection of three"; or, it is *tayaṃ* because it possesses three parts (*aṃsa*) or components (*avayava*). What is that?
A collection. "The triad of bases" (*vatthuttaya*) refers to the three bases; what is that? It is the Triple Gem beginning with the Buddha.

Regarding the words "having paid homage" (*namassitvā*) and "having bowed down" (*anamitvā*): when the mind arises having made the Triple Gem beginning with the Buddha its object, the suffix *-tvā* pertains to the present time.
Therefore, the first analysis was performed according to the *Pāḷimuttaka-vinicchaya*.
In one instance, at the time of seeing [the Buddha], it is past-tense; therefore, the second analysis is formed.
For that very reason, in the application of the meaning as well, the construction is made according to the present tense and the past tense.

It is a refuge (*saraṇa*) because it remembers (*sarati*) and because it protects (*hiṃsati*). What is it? It is the Triple Gem beginning with the Buddha. For that [Gem] belongs to those good persons who have gone for refuge.
It remembers, protects, and destroys fear, terror, suffering, rebirth in the states of woe, and defilement;
therefore it is called "refuge" (*saraṇa*). For it was said by the Blessed One:
"Mahānāma, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, on that occasion his mind is not overwhelmed by lust," and so forth.
“Thus for those who remember the Buddha,
the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, O bhikkhus,
fear or trepidation— ”
And [it is said]: "He shall not be one with body-hair.

Since, however, this word *saraṇa* is a synonym for the word *nātha*—a term whose name is purified by its root—and is not merely a word for the root itself, the meaning of the verbal root is included within it.
For it is stated that *sara* has the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsā*); thus, it is a word signifying injury.

Having grasped [the meaning] as "having paid homage to the Three Refuges, which are the refuge for all living beings," it is appropriate only when understood as "having paid homage to the Three Refuges, which have become the refuge and the protector for all living beings," because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence [of the refuges being limited].
For that very reason, the same construction was made even in the explanation of the meaning (*atthayojanā*). The word *sabba* expresses the sense of "without remainder."

This is a compound noun (*sabbanāmapada*). When it is formed as *sabbo*—meaning "that which exists together with life"—it becomes a compound noun expressing a collective whole, similar to the word *sakala*.

"Those who possess breath" (*pāṇino*) are so called because they have breath (*pāṇo*); here, "breath" refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). "All living beings" (*sabbapāṇino*) means all those who possess breath;
[the phrase] "of them, of all living beings" (*tesaṃ sabbapāṇīnaṃ*) follows. Up to this point, the state of the Triple Gem being the refuge for the entire world has been established.

And by this very [verse], he demonstrates his own state of being worthy of veneration, the fact that the act of veneration performed toward those worthy of veneration brings about the accomplishment of the intended purpose,
and the fact that his own action has become a "field" (khetta).
Having thus demonstrated the homage to the Triple Gem along with its cause, he now states the primary purpose of undertaking this treatise together with its motive.

To show this, he said: "For the sake of proficiency in the Vinaya, for bhikkhus who are practitioners of yoga. Here, "for the sake of proficiency in the Vinaya" is the statement of the primary purpose;
by stating that, the incidental purpose is also clearly revealed, since when the cause is accomplished, the effect is necessarily achieved.
"For bhikkhus who are practitioners of yoga" is the indication of the external persons concerned.
When that [external sign] has been shown, the internal sign is also thereby demonstrated, because when the object is known, the subject who possesses that object must also be known.

In this context, *vinaya* means "that in which various methods (*naya*) exist"; the meaning is that various and manifold methods—such as the two types of *Pātimokkha*, the two types of *Vibhaṅga*, the fivefold recitation of the *Pātimokkha*, the five aggregates of offenses, and the seven aggregates of offenses—exist herein. Alternatively, *vinaya* means "that in which specific methods exist."
The meaning is that there are specific methods (naya) here, such as the method of subsequent ordinances (anupaññatti), which serve the purpose of strengthening or relaxing the disciplinary rules.
Alternatively, it is called *vinaya* because it "leads" (*vineti*). It leads the body and speech; thus, it is *vinaya* because it leads the body and speech.
For it is said in the Commentary:
“Because it possesses various specific characteristics,
and because it disciplines both body and speech,
this [Dhamma] is called ‘Vinaya’ by those who know the meaning of Vinaya.”
"Discipline is called 'discipline'.
What is that? It is the Vinaya Piṭaka. In that discipline, "paṭu" means one who moves forward or attains a state of proficiency.
Who is that? The wise person. The state of being paṭu is "pāṭava. What is that? Knowledge. The meaning is that it exists in accordance with its cause.
What is it? It is the purpose (*payojana*). Skillfulness itself is the object; "for the sake of that object of skill" means for the purpose of the knowledge of skill regarding the Vinaya Piṭaka.
Application is *yoga*, which is the attention (*manasikāra*) to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). They move within it, thus they are "movers" (*avacarā*);
movers in yoga are "yogāvacaras," namely, the monks who practice meditation subjects. They see fear in saṃsāra, thus they are "bhikkhus"; [they are] yogāvacaras.
"And those monks" means those monks who are practitioners of yoga (*yogāvacara*); [the phrase] "of those monks who are practitioners of yoga" is used.

By this, it is shown that proficiency in the Vinaya is intended for monks alone, and not for householders, ascetics, wanderers, and so forth. Furthermore, among monks, it is intended only for those monks who are modest and devoted to their meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and not for shameless monks who have abandoned their meditation subjects. This is the meaning demonstrated.

Having thus shown the purpose along with its sign for the commencement of this treatise, he now says, "Scattered in many places, a detailed exposition apart from the canonical text," in order to show the subject matter together with its cause.

Therein, by the phrase "scattered in many places," he shows the cause for the commencement of the treatise, because it is a qualification of that which possesses the cause; for it is precisely because this [subject] is scattered in many places.
The teacher’s undertaking concerns [the material] that is not scattered; for he will say: "Having gathered it together, I shall show it in one place.
By the phrase "exposition apart from the text" (*pāḷimuttavinicchaya*), the title of this treatise is indicated. In this context, that which is scattered (*kiṇṇa*) is that which is dispersed;
that which is scattered in various ways is *pakiṇṇa*; that which is scattered in manifold ways is *vippakiṇṇa*. What is that? It is the exposition apart from the text; that is what is scattered.
Regarding the term *anekattha*: here, the word *eka* is a pronoun denoting number, meaning "not one" (*na eko*), i.e., "many" (*aneke*).
The word *aneka* denotes the sense of "many. Furthermore, although the word *eka* is invariably singular, because it is joined with the indeclinable particle *na*, it becomes plural.
In this context, *anekattha* means "in many [places]," that is, "in many treatises such as the *Pārājika-khandha-aṭṭhakathā* and others."
This has been stated. However, in the *Porāṇaṭīkā*, the meaning of "in many meanings" (*anekattha*) is shown as "in many sections of the training rules" (*sikkhāpada-padesesu*);

and since this is the case, because it will be said later, "having gathered together those that have a single meaning," these words—"scattered in many meanings" and "having gathered them together in a single meaning"—function as a correlative pair, [meaning] "scattered in many sections of the training rules."
The meaning would be "having collected [them] in one portion of a training rule," but that meaning is incorrect. Why?
Because we have stated that the meaning is "having collected in one treatise what was scattered across many treatises.
However, by alternatively interpreting the word *ekatthā* as "together" (*ekato*), [one might suggest it refers to] many portions of training rules.
"Having gathered together what was scattered" means one should grasp the meaning; that meaning would be appropriate. *Pāḷi* is the "lineage" (*āḷi*) of excellent [teachings];

the meaning is the sequence of the supreme words. Alternatively, it is called *pāḷi* because it protects (*pāleti*) and guards the meaning divided into self-interest, the interest of others, and so forth;
there is no distinction between *pāḷi* and *laḷi*. What is it? It is the Vinaya-treasury. One who is liberated is "liberated" (*mutto*).

“Free from the text” means released from the canonical text (*pāḷi*). That by which something is cut is a “cutting” (*chayo*); having extracted [the meaning] from that, it is a “separation” (*nicchayo*);

a separation in a specific manner is a “detailed analysis” (*vinicchayo*). It refers to the method of words and the method of meanings that proceeds in the manner of crushing the obstructions (*khila*).

Being both free from the text and a detailed analysis, it is called “the detailed analysis free from the text” (*pāḷimuttavinicchaya*); that is, the *pāḷimuttavinicchaya*. And this—“O homeless ones... [and so forth].
This is stated according to the method of majority (yebhuyyanaya), as seen in such passages as "the Khadira forest," since the term *pāḷivinicchaya* is also observed in some instances.

However, in the Ancient Commentary (*Porāṇaṭīkā*), it should be understood that this was stated either by way of a single-remainder compound (*ekadesasarūpekasesa*)— namely, that both the "exegesis of the text" (*pāḷivinicchaya*) and the "exegesis apart from the text" (*pāḷimuttavinicchaya*) are referred to as "exegesis" (*vinicchaya*)— and thus a second method is also mentioned.

This being the case, since there is no exposition other than the exposition of the Pāḷi and the exposition based on the Pāḷi (pāḷimutta), what is the use of this cumbersome inclusion of the term "based on the Pāḷi" (pāḷimutta)? For a qualification is meaningful only when both possibility and deviation exist;
thus, the first method alone is to be preferred.
Having thus shown the subject matter together with its cause, he now shows the manner of composition by means of the words beginning with “having collected.
Here, the manner of composition is twofold, by way of collecting things that have a single purpose and by way of making [the work] free from confusion.
Because the treatise was composed in those two ways, it is called the “manner of composition. In this context, “having collected” means “I shall collect.”
The word *saṃ* has the sense of "conciseness" (*saṅkhepa*); therefore, the meaning is: "I shall bring it forth by way of abbreviation.
Because it is co-temporal with the word "shall show" (*dassayissaṃ*), which is in the future tense, the suffix *-tvā* here is stated as being in the future tense.
"In one place" (*ekattha*) means in this single treatise on the compendium of the Vinaya. Alternatively, "in one place" (*ekattha*) means together (*ekato*). "Shall show" (*dassayissaṃ*)...

"I shall show" means "I shall make known. One who is agitated or thoroughly agitated is *ākula*; one who is not agitated is *anākula*, which refers to a commentary on the text that is free from the confusion of preceding and following sections.

Furthermore, *anākula* is a neuter abstract noun (*bhāvanapuṃsaka*); therefore, it should be construed with the act of showing by connecting it with the word *katvā*, which is derived from the verbal root *kṛ*.
Having thus shown the preliminary practice beginning with the salutation to the Triple Gem, he now says, "In this regard,

here is the table of contents," establishing the *mātikā* (table of contents) for the sake of providing the sequential order for those who wish to see the analysis (*vinicchaya*) that is independent of the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
For in the absence of a table of contents, the analyses already shown would become scattered and dispersed, like flowers not held together by a string.
However, when the analysis is presented by means of a matrix (mātikā), it does not scatter or disintegrate, just like flowers gathered together by a string.
Those who wish to know various meanings can proceed according to the matrix, reach whichever specific analysis they desire, and thereby come to know those respective meanings;
therefore, the matrix has been established for the purpose of easy comprehension. In this regard:
In this context, "therein" means in that exposition independent of the canonical text (*pāḷi*). "This" refers to what is about to be spoken by me.
It is called a "matrix" (*mātikā*) because it is like a mother. For just as children originate from a mother, so too do the words of the exposition originate from the enumeration (*uddesa*);
therefore, the enumeration is like a matrix and is thus called a "matrix."

Regarding the phrase "on the daytime rest" (*divāseyyā*) and so forth: the construction is as follows—"daytime rest" refers to the discussion on the determination of daytime rest; "requisites" (*parikkhāra*) refers to the discussion on the determination of requisites... [and so on] ...
"miscellaneous matters" (*pakiṇṇaka*) refers to the discussion on the determination of miscellaneous matters.

For this very reason, he will say: "The discussion on the determination of daytime resting is finished," and so forth. The word *iti* has the sense of "this," or the sense of "illustration," or the sense of "conclusion. Among these—
In what sense is this "iti"? It is in the sense of "thus" [referring to] daytime sleeping... up to ... miscellaneous topics. How is it in the sense of "illustration"?
It is in the sense that daytime sleeping... up to ... miscellaneous topics are to be regarded as such. In the sense of "completion," how complete is it?

The meaning is that it is completed by just this much: daytime sleeping... up to ... miscellaneous topics. Now, regarding the grammatical analysis (*vākyaviggaha*) of these words beginning with "daytime sleeping":
If these matters were explained here [in this work], there would be excessive prolixity, and it would be difficult for the listeners to grasp;
therefore, we shall explain each one as appropriate at the very beginning of its respective exposition.
The commentary on the introductory discourse of the treatise is concluded.
1. Discussion on the Determination of Sleeping During the Day.

Having thus established the table of contents for the explanations detached from the canonical text (*pāḷimutta-vinicchaya-kathā*), he now proceeds to explain them according to the sequence of that established table of contents, saying:
"In this regard, 'sleeping during the day' means lying down during the day," and so forth. Therein, "in this regard" (*tattha*) refers to those entries in the table of contents.
The construction is as follows: for one who is firmly attached [to the practice], the meaning of the term *divāseyyā* should be understood as "lying down during the day.

In this context, the word *divā* is an indeclinable particle ending in *-ā* that denotes "day. For it is said in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*: "In the sense of conformity, *saddhañca*; in the sense of night, *doso*;
and in the sense of day, *divā*. Lying down is *seyyā*. It is the upward [movement] of the material forms belonging to the body born of karma (*karajakāya*).
The specific posture (iriyāpatha) characterized by proceeding in detail over a long distance is called "walking.
"Day-laying" (divāseyyā) refers to lying down during the daytime; it is the performance of the reclining posture during the period from sunrise until sunset.
Therefore, he said: "The meaning is 'lying down during the day.'"

The construction is as follows: "Therein" means that this explanation which is about to be stated should be understood regarding that daytime resting place. The passage beginning with "I allow... [and so on]...
because of the statement" is an indicative text spoken by the Blessed One among the cases of legal procedure (*vinītavatthu*) for the first *pārājika* training rule.
In that context, "by one who reclines during the day" means by one who lies down during the day. "Having closed the door... [and so on].
“To retire into seclusion” means to lie down after closing the door. “One should not lie down during the day... [and so on] is a general instruction.
Anticipating the objection, “Is it not the case that no specific offense is mentioned in the Canon? Then how is an offense to be understood here? he says, “And herein, although... and so forth.
In this context, “herein” refers to this lying down during the day. The word *ca* (and) [indicates inclusion].
The particle *kiñcāpi* is a compound of indeclinables (*nipāta*) that indicates the commencement of a sentence;

its meaning is "even though" or "although. Although it is not explicitly stated in the Canon (*pāḷi*) that this is a specific offense, nevertheless, because the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) states that there is an act of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who lies down without having restrained himself, the construction [of the sentence] is:
"therefore, an offense is understood here. Even so, in the absence of [a specific rule] from the Blessed One...
Regarding the statement, "How could it be said in the Commentary? he says: "Because, having opened... it was permitted.
By this, he shows that even the Blessed One’s permission becomes a cause for an offense for one who does not act accordingly.
In this context, "when the matter has arisen" means "when the matter of a woman's misconduct has occurred," according to the *Vimativinodanī*.

It is stated [thus]; however, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is said, "when the matter of sexual intercourse has arisen," and the ancient commentary (*porāṇaṭīkā*) also adopts that very same reading, saying, "when the matter of sexual intercourse has arisen. This must be investigated, because the characteristic of sexual intercourse (*methunalakkhaṇa*) is absent [in this case].
Is it not the domain of the Buddha alone to lay down the training rules (*sikkhāpada*); then why is there a "wrong-doing" (*dukkaṭa*) mentioned in the commentary?
He said "of the Blessed One" and so forth to show that it was spoken. The commentaries were not established by the Elder Upāli and others alone;

rather, they were spoken by the Buddha, the Blessed One, both according to the text and according to the meaning. For there is no canonical passage (*tantipada*) that was left unexplained by the Blessed One;
the meaning of all of them has been told. Therefore, by the Fully Enlightened One himself, [the meaning] of the three Piṭakas...

It should be understood that the sequence of the commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*) has also been spoken. For it is precisely those occasional teachings (*pakiṇṇakadesanā*) delivered by the Blessed One here and there that constitute the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Now, as to this matter:

is this incurrence of an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭāpatti*) for one who lies down without closing the door during the day established solely because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, or is it established by other means as well?
To this he says: "The implication of the meaning" (*atthāpatti*), and so forth. This incurrence of an offense of wrong-doing...

The construction is as follows: this is established not only because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, but rather it is also established by this passage from the *Parivāra*: “There is an offense that one commits during the day, but not at night.
In what matter, then, was this training rule (sikkhāpada) spoken? “Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu in Vesālī, in the Great Wood...”
Having gone to the Gabled Hall for his midday rest, he opened the door and lay down. His limbs became stiffened by wind.
Now at that time, a number of women, taking perfumes and garlands, came to the monastery to see the vihāra. Then those women, seeing that bhikkhu...
Having sat down upon the sexual organ, having performed their purpose to their heart’s content, and having said, “What a bull among men he is!”, they offered scents and garlands and departed.
When the monks saw it soiled, they reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, for five reasons the sexual organ becomes functional: through passion, through feces, through urine, [through wind, and through semen].”
By wind, or by being bitten by a centipede or a scorpion. In these five ways, monks, the sexual organ becomes functional.
It is impossible, monks, it cannot happen, that the sexual organ of that monk should become functional through lust;
for that monk, monks, is an arahant, and there is no offense for that monk. I allow [this].
It should be understood that this was said in reference to the following matter: "Monks, one who seeks seclusion during the day should close the door before entering seclusion.
Now, in order to show the specific type of door, he said, "Of what kind? and so forth. In that context, "only a revolving door" means:
It is simply a door suitable for turning back and forth by means of closing and opening.
"Tree-stake-thorn door" refers to both a tree-stake door and a thorn door; or rather, the reading is "tree-stake-door-and-thorn-door.
This is [a door] where two or three tree-stakes have been driven into tree-posts sunk on both sides and pierced therein, with two or three tree-stakes in the middle.
Having inserted [a bolt], they close it; this is called a "tree-thorn door" (*rukkhasūcidvāra*).
A "thorn door" (*kaṇṭakadvāra*) is made from one or many thorny branches that are removed at the time of entering or exiting and are suitable for bolting.

For the purpose of closing a village gate, a door-panel (*kavāṭa*) is made of earth or thorny branches and the like; because it lacks a mortar-block (*udukkhala*) and a crossbar (*pāsaka*), it is closed by one person.
For a door that cannot be closed or opened by hand, they attach a single wheel beneath it;
with reference to that by which the revolving door-panel becomes easy to open and close, it is said: “a door fitted with a wheel.

For the wheel itself—because it must be taken hold of in the sense of being grasped for the purpose of closing and opening—is called a *cakkalaka*; and the door-panel joined with that [wheel] is likewise so designated.
“Cakkalaka” means a wheel; thus, a door fitted with that is a “cakkalakayuttadvāra.
Regarding the large doors, however, he says “on the panels,” etc., because two or three wheels are fitted there.

“Kiṭikāsu” refers to the latticed windows made of bamboo strips and the like, or thorny branches and the like. “Saṃsaraṇakiṭikadvāraṃ” means a large door fitted with a movable lattice window by means of a wheeled mechanism.
"Having woven" means having spun, or having tied with ropes. "Only one cloth-and-cane door" includes here even a mat-and-cane door.
However, in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, it is stated: "A cloth-door and a cane-door constitute a 'cloth-and-cane door.
By including everything mentioned as cloth-canes, mat-canes, and so forth under the single category of 'cloth-and-cane,' it is said thus because they are of the same nature."
"It is said 'one way'"—thus it was stated. 3.
Having thus shown the distinction of the doors, he now says "by how much," etc., in order to show the measure by which a door is secured.
Therein, "needle" refers to one inserted after making a hole in the middle. "Lid" refers to that on top...
[The rule] has been applied. Now, in order to show the procedure to be followed where it is not possible to lie down after closing the door, it is said: "If it is a place used by many," and so forth.

Even in a place not used by many, it is still permissible to lie down after having asked permission from one person. Then, as for the passage beginning "the bhikkhus... were seated," this refers to that situation.
This was stated for the purpose of showing that monks are present there, not for the purpose of precluding their being engaged in other postures;
therefore, it is permissible to exercise mindfulness even while lying down. However, it is not permissible to exercise mindfulness while lying down and falling asleep.
Because they stand on the side of those who are not [laypeople], the closing of the door for women is like sitting in private with them.
He said, "It was permitted for the purpose of preventing entry," in the passage beginning with "only a bhikkhunī" and so forth.
And here, that is appropriate; likewise, in all instances, whichever Elder’s opinion or Commentary’s opinion is stated later must be accepted as the authority.
This [statement] of the Master exceeds the words of the Commentary.
[This is] the statement. The preceding and following statements here are indeed the words of the Aṭṭhakathā.
In that context, "that is logical" means that the statement uttered by the masters of the Aṭṭhakathā—namely, "But in the Kurundi-aṭṭhakathā...
[it] is not tenable"—is logical. Thus... it should be accepted; for just as the statement spoken in the Kurundi is logical in this instance, so too is it in all cases.
In the *Vinicchaya*, whatever is stated later—whether it be the word of the Elders (*theravāda*) or the word of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathāvāda*)—that alone should be accepted as authoritative;
the intention is that what was stated earlier, whether the word of the Elders or the word of the commentaries, should not be accepted as authoritative.
This statement appears as if spoken out of place. How so? That which was stated [earlier] is indeed appropriate.

In this determination regarding the formal request (*āpucchana*) and the making of an effort (*ābhogakaraṇa*), it is impossible to assert the opinion of another who is unsuitable, whether that be the *Aṭṭhakathā* school or the *Theravāda*, because there is no such thing [in our tradition].
For in the preceding statement, the restriction "only monks" (*bhikkhū eva*) was not made;
rather, by way of proximity or by way of sequence, it refers precisely to "the monks [performing] the robe-work" (*bhikkhū cīvarakammaṃ*), and so forth.
It has been stated. As for what was also stated, beginning with “In this way, in all cases,” etc., that too lacks an opportunity [for refutation].
In this exposition, because no other commentary position or teacher’s position is mentioned, neither priority nor posteriority is seen;
thus, it must be accepted that “this is authoritative,” and that “this is not to be accepted” is the state of what ought to be said.
Furthermore, in the answer to the question "Who is liberated and who is not liberated?
three commentarial traditions are recorded: the Mahāpaccarī tradition, the Kurundi tradition, and the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā tradition; there is also the tradition of the Elder Mahāpaduma.
Therefore, it is precisely therein that one should determine what is appropriate and inappropriate, what is authoritative and non-authoritative, and what is to be accepted and what is to be rejected.
Since it is seen [in the text], it should have been stated in that very place;

however, because it was stated by the teacher Ācariya Asabha—who is endowed with perfectly pure and vast analytical wisdom—in a place where it should not have been stated, it ought to have been stated after the words "spoken by Mahāpaduma Thera at the conclusion of the reconciliation of the Aṭṭhakathā and the Vāda," which appear later; that [omission] was made by the scribes later on.
It may have been written by transposition; for this statement is found in the *Aṭṭhakathā* on the *Pārājika-khaṇḍa*.
It is not mentioned at this point in the *Ṭīkā*, but is mentioned further above in the passage:
"He who is possessed by a *yakkha*, and he who is laid down after being bound. Since it follows that latter part of the *Aṭṭhakathā* discourse, that alone should be accepted as authoritative.
And thus he will say: "In all cases, whatever the commentary's opinion or the Elder’s opinion is stated later, that alone should be regarded as authoritative.
Therefore, this must be understood here after due consideration.
Now, in order to show that it is permissible to lie down even without having restrained oneself when there is an obstacle to the restraint of the doors [of the senses]:
He said, “Now, regarding the door,” and so forth. “Having raised the ladder” means having raised it to the upper floor, then dismantled it and set it down on the ground;
or, having discarded it, it is permissible to lie down. This is stated because [the ladder] is fixed in one place.
“Both doors must be maintained” means that here, if there is no door-panel at one of the two doors, [one should maintain it] according to the method explained below.
If it is impossible to close it, it is permissible to lie down without closing the other door.
"To the doorkeeper" means to one who stands at the gatehouse, at the main entrance, or at the base of the ladder, and who is responsible for looking after the door.
"The burden of the latter" is said with reference to those who come along as a continuous chain. This should be construed as: "in the inner chamber where the door is not closed."
"It blows from the interior to the exterior. Regarding the statement, "Even at the time of lying down...

it is indeed permissible," they say that since the one who guards the door is dependent on him [the monk], it is indeed permissible for him to direct his attention there even without considering whether [the person] is present or absent at that time.
Regarding the phrase "enclosed by anything whatsoever," here the measurement of the enclosure's height is exactly the same as that stated for what is sufficient for sleeping together.
For it is said in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "That lodging which is entirely covered above by five roofs or by any other means is called 'completely covered'... [omission] ...but that which..."
A lodging that is enclosed by a wall or by anything else— even just a cloth— starting from the ground up to the roof-covering,
is called a "completely covered" bed. Even if it does not reach the roof-covering,
if it is enclosed by a wall or similar structure at least one and a half cubits high, it is also considered "completely covered."

"It is stated in the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*. "It is one and a half cubits high and should be grasped with the carpenter’s cubit (*vaḍḍhakihattha*)"—this is stated in both the *Sāratthadīpanī* and the *Vimativinodanī*. "Mahāpariveṇa" means a large courtyard.
By this, he indicates a place frequented by many people. Therefore, he says "the Great Bodhi," and so forth.
"He rises when the dawn has broken": there is no offense because he lay down with a pure mind during a night that constitutes a "field of non-offense.

"Having woken up, he sleeps again": this is an offense if, having woken up at the rising of the dawn—whether he recognizes the rising of the dawn or not—he sleeps while his continuum of consciousness remains in a state of lying down without rising; or if, having risen, he fails to perform what ought to be done, such as securing the doors.

Because it has not been done, there is an offense arising from non-action, since the act of lying down was performed in a place where it is not an offense. This offense should be understood as follows:
in such a case, it is non-action; at the moment of lying down after leaving the door unsecured during the day, it is both action-and-non-action and is without mental involvement (*acittaka*).
This remains so even for one who wakes up before dawn and continues to sleep until sunrise.
It is indeed an offense according to the previous method.
Regarding the statement, "If one thinks, 'I will rise when the dawn has broken'... [and so on] ...it is indeed an offense," it may be asked:

when does this become an offense? It is said: not during the night; because it is stated that "one incurs it by day, not at night," one is not exempt from the *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) for disrespect.
Furthermore, the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) mentioned here is not merely an offense of wrong-doing for sleeping during the day;

it is specifically an offense of wrong-doing due to disrespect (*anādariya-dukkaṭa*). Regarding this, the *Vimativinodanī* states: "It should be understood that at the rising of the sun, one incurs an offense that is unintentional (*acittaka*) and originated by non-action (*akiriyasamuṭṭhāna*).
The *Sāratthadīpanī* also says: "'He emerges exactly according to the limit' means he rises only when the sun has actually risen."
"His offense": because he lay down with an impure mind, even while sleeping, when the sun has risen, there is an offense rooted in daytime seclusion (*divāpaṭisallāna*).

Since it is stated, "One who lies down in this manner is not exempt from the *dukkaṭa* of disrespect," one who lies down with an impure mind incurs the offense at the very moment of lying down, whether they rise before sunrise or do not rise.
It is stated: "One incurs a *dukkaṭa* for disrespect, but one incurs the *dukkaṭa* rooted in daytime seclusion at dawn itself.
Therefore, it should be understood that two *dukkaṭas* are incurred by one who lies down in this manner.
If, however, one closes the door and lies down thinking, "I will rise when dawn has broken," and [the door] is opened by others at the time of dawn—
Even when it is open, there is no offense for him, because there is no distinction between the day and night portions regarding the burning of the door.
It should be understood that only a distinction in time is required for the incurrence of an offense, not for its avoidance;

for it is said: "Having closed the door, he lies down at night. For one who has closed [the door] during the day and lies down, there is likewise no offense even if the door is opened by someone else.

They say that even if one does not personally attend to it, there is no offense provided the requisite conditions are present and [the time] has opened up; this too is stated precisely in the *Vimativinodanī*.
"He emerges exactly according to the limit" means he emerges only when the dawn has risen;

"there is indeed an offense" is said with reference to the root-offense (*mūlāpatti*). However, the offense of disrespect (*anādariya*) occurs for him even if he has emerged before the dawn; [this refers to] the *dukkaṭa*.

Because it is stated, "he is not released from the *dukkaṭa*. Regarding the phrase "he is not released from the *dukkaṭa*," the intended meaning is that even if one has been released from the root offense (*mūlāpatti*) by rising before dawn, one is still not released from the *dukkaṭa* for disrespect.
5. "He lies down on account of sleep" means that, being overcome by drowsiness, he lies down on one side. "He lies down on account of sleep"—so it is said.
This was stated by way of conventional usage; however, because the feet have not been released from the ground, it is said that there is no offense for one who is merely "lying down.
Regarding "sleeping without having supported [the body]": this refers to sleeping while not allowing even a small portion of the area above the hip bone (kaṭiṭṭhi) and the spine to touch the ground.
But for one who allows the hip bone to touch the ground, it is considered lying down.

There is no offense. For lying down, characterized by stretching out the back, is long; and even in acts such as prostration, because the vertebrae are stretched out horizontally, it is indeed "lying down," so one must avoid the offense. For even prostration is described as "lying down" in such passages as "he lies down at the foot of the feet.
"He rises suddenly" means he rises suddenly like one who has stumbled and fallen; for him too...
There is no offense at the moment of falling because it was not within one's range, and because one rose up suddenly once the range had been reached.

However, for one who, due to unconsciousness, remains outside the range even afterwards, there is likewise no offense, just as at the moment of falling. By the phrase "he lies right there and does not rise," he shows that there is no action even when within the range;
for that very reason, it is stated that an offense occurs [only] in that case.
Now, in order to reconcile the explanations found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), he says: "Who is liberated? Who is not liberated? and so forth.
Regarding the phrases "in the Mahāpaccarī," etc., the word *paccarī* refers to a raft; because [the work] was composed while sitting upon one, it received that very name.
There is a monastery called Kurundivallivihāra; because [the work] was composed there, it received the name Kurundī.
The *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* is the commentary on the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas as recorded in the three councils;
it was brought to the island of Tambapaṇṇi by the Elder Mahāmahinda and subsequently translated into the Sinhalese language by the Elders of Tambapaṇṇi.
"With one side" means with one flank, without lifting the foot from the ground.
"It is said that he lay down after breaking his body. However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is connected with the statement made by the Elder Mahāpaduma.
By this, he indicates that "this" is the opinion of the Elder Mahāpaduma as recorded in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
The Elder stated: "Because he fell in a swoon and [the act] was not within his conscious control, no offense is seen. But the Teachers say...

Just as one possessed by a *yakkha*, having been bound and laid down, is under the control of another, so too, because he is not in control of himself, they say there is no offense in the case where, being deluded and fallen, he lies down after knowing [the time] for a short while;
however, when he is unconscious (*visaññita*), there is indeed no offense.

The passage beginning with "two people" and so forth is a statement from the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* itself; since that alone was stated later, it is the authoritative source. By the very mention of "one possessed by a *yakkha*,"...

And here, one who has lost consciousness is also included; however, it should be understood that one who lies down on only one side is indeed released from the offense because he has not fully lain down.

Furthermore, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, regarding the statement in the commentary, "both he who is possessed by a spirit and he who is made to lie down after being bound," the latter alone should be accepted as the authoritative standard; and so he will say.
“Wherever a statement from the *aṭṭhakathā* is mentioned later on, that very same one must be accepted as the authoritative standard.

Since this reading from the *aṭṭhakathā* has been introduced at this point, it is our conviction that this same passage should also be stated at this very place in the present work, the *Vinayasaṅgaha*. And here, [the text says]: “Having opened the door at night...”

Because of such statements as, "If one who has lain down rises when the dawn has broken, there is no offense," the discourse on the dawn must be explained for the purpose of dispelling doubts regarding the breaking of dawn.
In this regard, it is said:
"What is this that is called 'dawn'?"
By what means does he become ruddy?
Of what kind is his color?
What would his shape be like?
“At what time and in what place does the dawn arise?
Is this established through direct perception, or rather through inference?

Regarding that, as for the question “What is this so-called dawn?”—here, this thing called dawn is a particular radiance of the sun. For it has been said in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*: [“Dawn is the light of the sun...”]
“Before the rising of the sun, the ray that has already arisen may be called ‘dawn’ (aruṇa). And in its commentary: “The ray that has arisen prior to the rising of the sun is what is called dawn.
And in the Vinaya commentary titled *Vimativinodanī*: “And here, ‘dawn’ refers to the specific radiance that precedes the emergence of the sun, which is thick with redness and increasing.”
It is said, "it should be seen"; therefore, it should be understood that what is called *aruṇa* (dawn) is simply the radiance of the sun, and nothing else.

As for the question, "By what does that become *aruṇa*?"—here, *aruṇa* means "that which has the color of dawn" (*aruṇo vaṇṇo assa*), the sense being that it is endowed with the color of a little redness.
Alternatively, it is *aruṇa* because it goes toward redness (*arati gacchati*) and proceeds by way of having a red color. For this has been stated in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā-ṭīkā*: [text follows].
“Because it goes toward a dawn-colored state (*aruṇa-vaṇṇatā*), it is called ‘dawn’ (*aruṇo*).
As for the question, “What is its color?”—its color would be a slightly reddish hue. For it is said in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*: “Dawn (*aruṇo*) is somewhat red. And in its commentary:
“Dawn is called that which is slightly red, a slightly reddish hue, like the eye of a fish. And in the *Vimativinodanī*...

Regarding the phrase “the specific radiance that increases the thick redness,” it should be understood that for the sun, the dawn is so called only because of its red radiance, and not because of its white radiance and so forth.
If this is so, how is one to reconcile this with what is stated in the *Vimativinodanī* commentary on the *Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhaka*:
“In the Canon, however, ‘with a joyful face’ means having a face that is joyful due to facing the direction of the white quarter”?

"It would be fitting" means it is not unfitting. For in that context, at the time of sunrise, it is the state of the eastern quarter being white by the light of dawn that is stated, not the whiteness of the light of dawn itself. Indeed, this is said in the *Udāna-aṭṭhakathā*:
"‘With a joyful face’ means with a face made joyful by the night because the dawn has risen, [the night] which causes beings who subsist on the light of the sun to rejoice."
The meaning is: "to one who has been born and is trembling.
And in the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*:
"In the night when hunger arises, when the dawn has broken..."
"She who is seen with the most excellent form and beauty—
O deity, she appeared to me as such.
Tell me, which goddess is she?"
In the commentary on the meaning of this verse, it says: "Therein, 'the final watch of the night' means the end of the night;
'when dawn has risen' means when the sun has appeared. 'She goes' refers to the eastern direction, which appears as if bearing a supreme form due to its crimson hue.
Thus, the crimson color of the eastern direction at the time of sunrise is described; therefore:
At that time, because dawn has arisen, the dark portion of the eastern direction is perceived as being covered by the light of the sun, while the remaining directions appear white.
As for its shape: there is no separate shape for dawn itself, as it consists merely of rays of light.
To whatever extent it pervades a region, its shape should be understood as corresponding to that extent. Alternatively, it has the shape of the eastern direction;
for it is said in the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*: "The eastern direction appears, possessing a red color and bearing a sublime form.
And at what time and in what place does the dawn arise? Herein, this dawn occurs prior to the rising of the sun.
At that time, it rises in the eastern direction. For this is said in the Udāna-aṭṭhakathā:
“When the dawn has risen means when the dawn has appeared; ‘dawn’ is the light that arises in the eastern direction even prior to the rising of the sun.
And in the Abhidhānappadīpikā: “The rays that arise before the rising of the sun.”
Is this established through direct perception (*paccakkha*) or through inference (*anumāna*)? In this regard, this [light] called *aruṇa* is established only by direct perception, not by inference.
If it is asked why this is known, it is because it exists as a sphere of visible form (*vaṇṇāyatana*) within the range of visual consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*).
"Direct" (*paccakkha*) means "in front of the eye" (*akkhassa pati*); visual consciousness has come into its objective range by way of being directly present before the eye and the visible forms.
It exists. For this was said by the Blessed One: “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises.
Therefore, this dawn-colored [light], being known by seeing with the eye, is established through direct perception (*paccakkha-siddha*) itself;
it is not established through repeated reflection by means of inference (*anumāna*), such as “if this were so, then that would be so. This is the answer to the question.
Having carefully taken this to heart, the wise should understand and observe that it is indeed the dawn-light that is called "dawn.
But why is the discussion of dawn mentioned in this place? Because this discussion of dawn has a vast scope. How so?
Laymen and laywomen observing the Uposatha, not knowing the true nature of the rising of dawn, [might think it has risen] even when it has not yet risen.
If, with the perception that dawn has broken, they eat solid food or consume soft food, or wear garlands, scents, and the like, their virtue is then broken.
Novices likewise reach the destruction of their virtue by eating at the improper time.
Bhikkhus who are undergoing dependence, being outside the boundary without their teachers or preceptors...
While traveling, they reach the point where the dependence [on a teacher] is suspended; monks going outside the precinct boundary during the rainy season incur a breach of the rains-residence;
monks who possess only three robes and stay apart from their robes in an unbounded area incur a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* offense;
likewise in a seven-fathom boundary, or in a place sufficient for a shared bed, staying together with women who are not ordained.
It should be understood that these rules were prescribed for the sake of monks who are modest and virtuous so that they may truly know when dawn has broken,

because otherwise numerous disadvantages would arise: such as the offense of *pācittiya* for those sleeping [past dawn], likewise for monks eating food that is only permissible until the same day (*yāvakālika*), and for those on probation (*pārivāsika*) and others who would be breaking their observances and causing the interruption of the night.
However, some monks, because the water-jars were empty at the time of midnight, let the midnight hour pass until it became another day;
thinking that the dawn had risen at that time, they ate hard and soft foods after midnight.
Not knowing the Buddha’s system, they merely kept the Vedic system in mind.
They act in this way precisely because they do so; therefore, their doing so is not an authoritative standard.
However, many bhikkhus—failing to recognize the actual presence of dawn, unable to reflect through inference, and merely placing their trust in the hearsay of others—say:
"Our teachers rose at the time of sunrise and departed, [arriving] at the time of the sun's rising."
They say, "They reach a place the size of two thousand *daṇḍas*," or "They reach a place the size of three thousand *daṇḍas*.
They also say things such as, "From this monastery, they reach a monastery named so-and-so, a shrine named so-and-so, or a village named so-and-so.
Such are their words based on hearsay; that too is not authoritative. Why?
A journey is short for one who is strong and swift, but long for one who is weak and weary.
For it was said by the Blessed One:
"Long is the night to the wakeful; long is the league to the weary."
"Long is the saṃsāra of fools who do not understand the true Dhamma.
Therefore, it is not the case that the duration [of life] is the same for everyone; thus, it is impossible for [the dawn] to serve as the defining characteristic [of the limit].
Furthermore, those venerable ones do not cite any statement from the Tipiṭaka that serves as proof [for their position].
They speak according to their own inclinations, like those who bring a lawsuit without witnesses; thus, they are not authoritative.
Others, however, say:
"The watch of the past night..."
Or the uppermost part of the back;
the blow of the *bhāvini* and so forth;
or half of that is said to be the measure here.
Having recited the verse found in the *Kaccāyanasārapakaraṇa*, they say: "The final watch of last night has now entered into today;
therefore, from the beginning of the final watch until the rising of the sun [the day is counted]. This doctrine is stronger than the previous ones because it indicates a supporting reason;
nevertheless, it is indeed incorrect. Why? Because this verse belongs to the external science of grammar (*bāhirasaddasattha*).
The term *ajjatani* is stated in order to show the time for the occurrence of the conventional usage "today" (*ajja*) as expressed in the passage in the *Jaṅgadāsa-pakaraṇa*,
namely "today is the present," and not to show the time of sunrise as described in the Three Piṭakas; therefore,
because that which is to be proven by one thing has been proven by something else, it is indeed untenable.
Others, however, [hold that it is now] because the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* states, "The watch is called *pahāra*," and thus the terms *pahāra* and *yāma* have the same meaning;
and because it is stated in that very same work, "The night consists of three watches (*tiyāmā saṃvarī*"), and since the night has three watches; and because it is recorded in the Canon:
"Venerable sir, the night has passed; the last watch has emerged; the dawn has risen. Therefore, now...
At the end of the third watch of the night, the dawn has risen;
therefore, they might say that the remaining time, consisting of only one watch, belongs to the portion of the day. This position is even stronger than the third position. Why?

Because of the correspondence between the indicator (*ñāpaka*) and the indicated (*ñāpya*). For instance, the indicator "a watch is designated as a *yāma*" [applies] to both the watches and the *yāmas*.
The phrase "three watches of the night" (*tiyāmā saṃvarībhave*) is appropriate for the state of having three watches of the night;
likewise, the phrase "and in the Pāḷi," etc., refers to the dawn at the end of the third watch. Nevertheless, this remains inconsistent.

Why? Because it contradicts the statement: "The remaining time, consisting of only one watch, constitutes a portion of the day. For in the Middle Country, [the duration of a watch] is measured by ten *ghaṭikās*.
Because time consists of a single watch (pahāra), the entire night consists of only three watches (tiyāma) and not four;
however, at present, in the border regions, because a period of only seven or eight *ghaṭikās* constitutes a single watch, it becomes four watches.

Therefore, adopting the conventional usage of the Middle Country, it is stated in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*: "The night (*saṃvarī*) shall consist of three watches," and in the Pāḷi: "He has departed..."
"The last watch [of the night], the dawn has risen. Therefore, it should be understood that the dawn has indeed risen at the very end of the night.
For it is said in the *Vimativinodanī*: "Likewise, for those such as those on probation who lay down their duties without waiting for the dawn, a break in the night is mentioned;
for it is stated that [the duties] should be laid down once the dawn has risen."
In the *Sahaseyya-sikkhāpada* as well, it is stated: "Having gone out before dawn for the purpose of avoiding the state of dwelling together with those not fully ordained," and so forth.

Thus, in all instances such as the *cīvara-vippavāsa* (separation from one's robe), the rising of the sun is indicated by way of its arrival at the end of the night, and not by way of having already passed.
In the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā* also, [it says]: "At the end of the night..."
“...the meaning. It is not only during the night in the Middle Country that there is a state of three strikes; rather, it occurs even during the day.

For thus it is said in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*: “The conclusion of the Perfectly Enlightened One’s teaching of the Abhidhamma and those bhikkhus’ mastery of the seven treatises occurred simultaneously,” and in the *Mūlaṭīkā* it says: “Simultaneously...”
"In this context, 'pahāra' refers to one-third of a day"; therefore, it is understood that one night-and-day consists of six *pahāras*.

Thus, according to the terminology of the Middle Country (*majjhima-desavohāra*), at the end of the three *pahāras* designated as the three watches (*tiyāma*)—that is, at the conclusion of the entire night—one takes the dawn that has arisen to mean "at the end of the three *pahāras*" according to the terminology of the Bordering Countries (*paccanta-desavohāra*), and [this occurs] at a time when only one *pahāra* remains.
Since it is stated that "the dawn has arisen," this view also must be regarded as incorrect.
However, many wise ones [cite] what is said in the *Khuddasikkhā-nissaya*:
"The first is the 'White Dawn' (*setaruṇa*), the second is the 'Joyful Turn' (*nandiyāvaṭṭa*);..."
"Third, the color of copper; fourth, the face of a donkey.
Based on this verse, during a single night the dawn rises four times:
there, the first is white in color, the second is the color of the *nandiyāvatta* flower, the third is the color of copper, and the fourth—

Having said, "The color becomes like that of a donkey's mouth," they perform duties such as laying down the bowl before the glow of the night has even faded, while it is still the time of the past night.
That action of theirs constitutes acting without due reflection. For this verse is found neither in the Canon (Pāḷi), nor in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), nor in the Sub-commentaries (Ṭīkā);
it appears only in the *Nissayas*, and among the *Nissayas*, only in the *Khuddasikkhā-nissaya*.

It is not seen [in that context], nor in other commentaries; even there, neither a connection between what precedes and what follows is seen, nor a relationship of cause and effect, nor a restriction of grammatical gender. Therefore, it could not have been established by the master Nissayakāra;
rather, it must have been written later by other scribes according to their own wishes. Consequently, from where was this verse brought—was it from the Canon (Pāḷi)?
Or, having failed to investigate the source— whether from the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), the sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*), the Vinaya, the Suttantas, or the Abhidhamma—

and instead grasping at the mere appearance of what was seen in the supporting texts as being essential, one falls into the fault of acting without reflection because of failing to consider the words spoken in the Canon,
the commentaries, and the sub-commentaries.

In this regard, the canonical text says: "Now at that time, during the cold winter nights in the middle of the eight-day fortnights, at a season when snow was falling, the Buddha, the Blessed One, sat in the open air at night wearing only a single robe; yet the Blessed One did not feel cold.
When the first watch had passed, the Blessed One felt cold, so he put on a second robe; yet the Blessed One..."
It became cold. When the middle watch had passed, it was cold for the Blessed One; the Blessed One put on a third robe, and it was no longer cold for the Blessed One.
When the last watch had passed, at the rising of the dawn, during the "face of joy" of the night, it was cold for the Blessed One;
the Blessed One put on a fourth robe, and it was no longer cold for the Blessed One.
“It became cold. This is the Vinaya text found in the Cīvarakkhandhaka of the Mahāvagga.
In the text, *nandimukhiyā* means “with a face of joy,” that is, “with a face [turned] toward confidence. This is the reading from the *Vimativinodanī*, which is a commentary on that [text].
“Now at that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.”
Now at that time, on the Uposatha day, the Blessed One was seated surrounded by the community of monks.

Then, when the night had advanced and the first watch had passed, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One: "The night has passed..."
"Venerable sir, it is night; the first watch has passed; the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been sitting for a long time.
Venerable sir, let the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the bhikkhus. When this was said, the Blessed One remained silent.
And a second time, when the night had advanced and the middle watch had passed, the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder...
Having done so, he extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One and said this to the Blessed One:
"The night has passed, venerable sir; the middle watch has ended. The community of monks has been sitting for a long time.
May the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the monks. A second time, the Blessed One remained silent. And a third time, the Venerable Ānanda...

When the night had advanced, during the last watch, at the rising of the dawn, at the beginning of the night’s joy, he rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One:
“The night has advanced, venerable sir; the last watch has passed; the dawn has risen.”

“It is the night of the ‘Joyful Face’; the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been seated for a long time. Let the Blessed One, venerable sir, recite the Pātimokkha for the bhikkhus. “The assembly, Ānanda, is not pure.
This is another passage from the Vinaya Piṭaka found in the Cūḷavagga, in the Khandhaka on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha.
Regarding the phrase “the night of the Joyful Face”: at the time when dawn breaks, the night appears as if its face were filled with joy. Therefore, he said, “of the Joyful Face.”
This is the reading from the *Samantapāsādikā* commentary: “*Abhikkantā* means completely exhausted.
*Uddhaste aruṇe* means when the head of the dawn has risen. *Nandimukhiyā* means with a face of joy. This is the reading from the *Sāratthadīpanī* commentary.

In the *Pāḷi*, “*Nandimukhiyā*” refers to one whose face is joyful because it is turned toward the bright quarters of the sky. This is the reading from the *Vimativinodanī* commentary on that same passage.

A third time, when the night had advanced, during the last watch, at the rising of the dawn, at the beginning of the night’s joy, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One:
“The night has advanced, Bhante; the last watch has passed.”

"The dawn has risen; it is the night of the 'Joyful Face' (Nandimukhī); the visiting bhikkhus have been seated for a long time. May the Blessed One, venerable sir, exchange greetings with the visiting bhikkhus.
This is the Sutta-pāḷi as it appears in the Udāna. "The dawn has risen" means when the dawn has emerged.
"Dawn" (aruṇa) refers to the light that arises in the eastern direction even prior to the rising of the sun. Of the "Joyful Face" (nandimukhī)...
"At night" means: because the dawn has already risen, when the night—whose face is the joy of beings who live by the light of the sun—has become radiant with the glow of the dawn;
the meaning is "when it is becoming bright. This is the Udāna-aṭṭhakathā, which serves as a commentary on that [passage].
Thus, in all these commentaries and sub-commentaries on the Pāḷi of the Vinaya and Sutta Piṭakas, in not even a single instance does the dawn appear four times.
The term "exalted" (*uggata*) does not occur; it is mentioned only once. The phrase "endowed with four kinds of color" (*catubbidhavaṇṇasamannāgata*) also does not occur;
only a single color is mentioned. In the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā* as well, only the red color (*rattavaṇṇa*) is mentioned, not white or other colors.
Furthermore, the term "Nandimukhī" refers to the night itself, which brings joy to sentient beings, and not to the dawn possessing a color like that of the *nandivārṭa* flower.
Therefore he said: “beings at the end of the night of delight.

Since this [position] contradicts the statement in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* manual, does not harmonize with the Canon (*Pāḷi*) and its commentaries (*Aṭṭhakathā*), and lacks a weak proof, it should be understood that this doctrine is likewise untenable.
Therefore, if anyone—by a modest bhikkhu who has not transgressed the command of the Perfectly Enlightened One—...
In an uncovered, open space, from the moment when the glow of twilight becomes visible— just as it would for one with fish-eyes or for an unskilled person—
the duties such as setting out the water for washing must be performed.
However, if there is a place concealed by a mountain or the like, [the time is determined] by how long it takes for the glow of twilight to appear in that open area.

It is discerned as follows: having observed for a period of about one or two *ghaṭikās* from the time the solar disc becomes visible, one should make the calculation, "At this time, the dawn will have arisen.
One who does not desire doubt should wait for some further time beyond that and perform it at the time when there is no uncertainty. This is [the method].

In this regard, there is consistency (*sāmīci*). This discourse, moreover, perfectly accords with the statements in the aforementioned treatises, just as the waters of the Yamunā accord with the waters of the Gaṅgā;
therefore, it should be kept in mind by the wise, repeatedly reflecting upon what precedes and follows.
Having thus kept it in mind, one should sever doubt regarding those points connected with the dawn, and [sever] doubt...
Having severed [these ties], one should perform each respective task with confidence.
This compassionate discourse was composed for the sake of the purity of the virtue of monks who are dear for their virtue;
it was not made for the sake of contentiousness or other such motives.
"Therefore, having reflected thoroughly, let the virtuous accept what is appropriate;
if anything is inappropriate, let them discard it, and let them not be dejected or the like.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
The First Chapter: The Ornament of the Discussion on the Determination of Day-Sleeping.
2. The Discussion on the Determination of Requisites.

6. Having thus explained the determination regarding the daytime rest (*divāseyya*), he now speaks the words beginning with “Requisites (*parikkhāra*) means the requisites of a recluse (*samaṇa-parikkhāro*)” in order to explain the determination regarding the requisites.

In that context, having brought forward the word “therein” (*tattha*) which was stated at the beginning of the discourse on the determination of the daytime rest, [he explains] the word “requisites” (*parikkhāro*)—which is firmly established among those items of the summary table (*mātikā*)—as “the requisites of a recluse.”
The construction is: "the meaning is to be seen. This same method applies to what follows as well.

The intention is that the requisites of a recluse (*samaṇa-parikkhāra*) are being discussed, not the requisites of a householder. It is called *parikkhāra* because it is used all around (*parisamantato kariyati*); examples include the umbrella and so forth. In this context, "therein" refers to the requisites of a recluse.

That which is allowable is *kappiya*; that which is not allowable is *akappiya*; that which is both allowable and unallowable is *kappiyākappiya*. This also applies to a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvanda*).
The wise maintain that this is masculine. "Both allowable and unallowable requisites" means likewise;
the determination of these is the "determination of allowable and unallowable requisites.
Some say that "a palm-leaf umbrella" is merely an illustration; for indeed, every kind of umbrella, when made in that manner, [is included].

It is not permitted. For this very reason, it should be understood that in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā* it was stated, "It is not permitted," by way of illustrating that "for one who effects a change in the color or glossiness of any requisites, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

By the phrase "not for the sake of color or glossiness," [it is implied that] if, while binding with a single-colored thread for the purpose of making it firm, there occurs a change in color or glossiness, then in that case—
He shows that there is no fault. "With the tip" means with the point of the socket. If it is not suitable, one might ask: "Having obtained such a parasol handle, what should be done?
To this he says: "Or a ring," and so forth. Or the handle should be wrapped with thread so that the lines are not visible;
it should be wrapped in such a way that the markings do not appear. "At the base of the handle" means at the root of the handle, that is, at the lower end of the parasol handle.
The meaning is as follows: *Chattamaṇḍalikaṃ* refers to a small circle inside the umbrella, or the ring of handle-ends bound in a circular shape within the frame of the umbrella.
*Ukkiritvā* means having leveled it by making what was low high and what was high low. *Sā vaṭṭatīti*:
whether that line is bound with cords or not, it is permissible because it is a place suitable for binding. Therefore it was said:
The great elder teacher Buddhadatta stated:
“Any leaf-made umbrella, whether entirely on the outside or inside,
may not be sewn with thread of five colors.”
“It is not permissible to draw lines on a staff depicting a half-moon, a leaf,
a makara-tooth design, a water-pot, or a beast of prey.
It is permissible to sew a parasol with thread of a single color.”
One may decorate a five-colored lattice or a frame with a protective charm.
Alternatively, it is permissible to wear a small amulet, a beast-shaped figure,
or even a mere line-drawing, provided they have been cut out or engraved.
“The shape of an ahicchattaka (snake’s hood) is suitable for the handle-end;
a line drawn by sprinkling [powder] is suitable for the purpose of binding.
Regarding its description as well: “A leaf-parasol is something made of leaves,” meaning any covering made of leaves such as palm leaves and so forth.
A sunshade (*chatta*). "Outside" means above; "inside" means below. "To sew" means to perform needlework after displaying the form.
"Leaves" refers to roofing leaves. "Half-moon" means having the shape of a half-moon. "Makaradantaka" means having the shape of a makara’s tooth, which is called a "mountain peak.
"It is not permitted to cut"—this is the connection [of the sentence]. Having bent it toward the rim of the opening...
They make mountain peaks and the like out of either bound leaves or the tips of a top-knot;
this is prohibited by that [rule]. "Staff" (*daṇḍa*) refers to a parasol-staff. "Jar" (*ghaṭaka*) means having the shape of a jar.
"Or a beast-form" (*vāḷarūpaṃ vā*) means an image of beasts such as tigers and so forth. "Lines" (*lekhā*) refers to lines made by engraving, carving, or by means of painting. Of five colors...
The construction is as follows: it is permissible to sew a parasol inside and out with thread of a single color, such as blue, among the various colors of thread, for the sake of firmness;
or to bind together the handle of the parasol, the grasping-staff, and the lattice-work for the sake of firmness.
By the phrase "with one color from among five colors for the sake of firmness," it is implied that one may sew and bind with threads of multiple colors for the sake of a glossy finish.
This indicates that it is not permitted. However, in the manuscripts the reading "with five-colored [thread]" (pañcavaṇṇena) is seen;
for that, the construction should be made thus: "it is permitted to sew or braid for the sake of strength with either single-colored or five-colored thread.
And here, by means of the reading stated below, "it is not permitted to sew with five-colored thread," [the same point is clarified].
"Some sew palm-leaf umbrellas, either on the inside or the outside, with thread of five colors and make them smooth and glossy;

that is not permitted. However, it is permissible to sew them on the inside or the outside with thread of a single color—whether blue, yellow, or whatever—or to bind the umbrella-staff holder or the lattice-work frame."
This contradicts the reading of the Aṭṭhakathā, which states, "And that [polishing] is for the sake of making it firm, not for the sake of its glossiness";
therefore, that [interpretation] should not be accepted.
Or else, "the entire design" means the whole design of the kind already described. "Having cut" means having carved it.
"Having cut. "Having rubbed" means having rubbed [the surface] by means of painting and so forth.

"In the handle-bundle" (*daṇḍabunda*) means in the split bundle intended for gripping the lattice-work of the umbrella-handle; the meaning is "at the base. This is the method stated here without doubt.
However, in the *Khuddasikkhā-gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "At the base of the umbrella-fiber. "Shaped like an *ahicchattaka* mushroom."
