[It should be] in the shape of a blooming *acchattaka* flower. Having had it grasped by ropes, they bind it to a staff;
at that place of binding, "having carved out like a ring" means having made it appear like a ring.
"For the purpose of binding" means for the purpose of binding the cage to the staff with ropes so that it does not move due to the wind. It is appropriate to draw lines [there] after carving.

The application [of the rule] is as follows: Just as, for the sake of preventing movement caused by the force of the wind, they have a circular parasol tied to its handle with cords and, at that point of binding, carve out a ring-like shape and make a mark; that is permissible.
Even if it does not actually bind [the cloth], because it is the place where it ought to be bound, it is permissible to carve out a ring-like shape; thus it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*.
The phrase "they proceed" has been handed down; therefore, one should deal with the parasols according to the very method handed down for the fans.
Regarding the robe, however, "with various-colored threads" means with threads of different colors. This is stated with reference to those who act in that manner;
it is not even permissible [to use] a thread of a single color. For it is said: "Only ordinary needlework is permitted."
"Paṭṭamukha" refers to the place where two strips of cloth are joined together. "Pariyanta" means at the edge of the robe;
this is said with reference to the wind. "Veṇī" is sewing in the shape of a braid.
"Saṅkhalikā" is sewing in the shape of a double-linked chain, or sewing in the shape of a cat's chain. "Making a veṇī or a saṅkhalikā" refers to the act of making them.
The connection [is as follows]: "Agghiya" means the shape of a shrine (*cetiya*), which they call an "agghiya pillar.
"Gayā" refers to a seam made in the shape of a *gada* (club), being narrow at the base and wide at the top.
"Muggara" refers to a seam made in the shape of a club, being uniform at both the base and the top. "They carve out crab-eyes" refers to the decorative bands at the joints and the bands at the loops.
Having first fixed the border, they set up the eye-shaped parts of the crabs; the meaning is that they fashion them.
“The ‘thread-knots at the corners’ (koṇasuttapiḷakā) are the ends of the threads drawn out from the corners of the knotted loops,” so it is stated in all three commentaries on the knots.
But how are those knots to be made when their form is difficult to discern? [They are made] from the threads drawn out from the corners.
Previously, by making a knot once or by sewing it back again, one should make the nature of the thread-ends difficult to discern, and then cut them short. However, the Elder Dhammasiri said:
"The corner-threads and the protrusions are indeed difficult to discern even when clipped," and likewise the Elder Ācariya Buddhadatta said: "The threads..."
And it is said: “The corner-cords and the knots therein are explained as being difficult to discern.
Therefore, according to their opinion, the meaning here should be understood as *koṇasuttapiḷakā*—that is, the corner-cords and the knots.
In the *Vimativinodanī* as well, *koṇasuttapiḷakā* refers to the cords that have come out from the corners of the loops and the cloth-straps.
Some say that the ends [of the threads] are placed in the form of a pimple (*piḷaka*); their intention is that after cutting the pimples, they should be made so as to be difficult to discern.
However, some say, "There are only two: the corner-threads (*koṇasutta*) and the pimples.
According to their opinion, the "corner-threads" are the threads drawn from corner to corner of the loops, toggles, and strips on all sides; furthermore, by means of a boundary all around...

The "four-cornered threads" (caturassasuttā) are what are called "pustules" (piḷakā). Regarding both of these, some people make them into decorative features distinct from the robe for the sake of identification;
to prohibit this, it is said that "a form difficult to discern is permissible.

However, this is not because they must entirely remain outside the range of sight, for it would be impossible to sew them in such a way for the purpose of sewing, as is the case with the original robe.
The meaning is that no alteration is perceived, such that it should be sewn in this manner.
Although a distinction was perceptible prior to the dyeing process, once the robe is dyed, it is not perceived because of its uniform color; thus he says, "when the robe is dyed.

8. "With a gem" means with a stone such as a blue sapphire (*nīlamaṇi*); shoulder-straps, waist-bands, and so forth, are excluded because they are not robes, [as are items] made of conch shells and the like.

They say it is proper to cut [the threads]. "Ear-thread" (*kaṇṇasuttaka*) is the name for the ends of the threads that emerge from the four corners—the ears—and from the lengthwise and crosswise seams of the robe; one must put on the robe only after cutting those.
Therefore he said, "It should be cut at the time of dyeing. There is also a single ear-thread permitted by the Blessed One.
In order to show that although it is similar in name, it is nonetheless something different from this [other type], the passage beginning with “yaṃ pana” was stated.
“For the purpose of fastening” means for the purpose of binding the robe to the robe-string. Only this much is stated in the *Vimativinodanī*.
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it says: “Having made a loop, it should be bound; it should be bound at the time of dyeing, but at other times...”
"It should be set aside after being loosened," so it was said. This very point is also stated in the ancient commentary (*porāṇaṭīkā*) on the *Vinayasaṅgahappakaraṇa*.
Furthermore, regarding that [passage] in the *Cīvarakkhandhaka*: "They hung [the robes] by the middle, and they slipped from both sides;
they reported this matter to the Blessed One. 'Monks, I allow you to tie a loop at the corners. The corner wore out. To the Blessed One..."

They reported this matter. "I allow, monks, an ear-string," he said. This should be understood as referring to a hanging cord for a robe that has been spread out after being dyed, in accordance with the rope for dyeing robes thus permitted. Regarding "a toggle" (*gaṇṭhika*):

it refers to a toggle made of ivory or other materials, fashioned for the purpose of fastening [the robe] to the loops at the time of wearing it. Regarding "pustules" (*piḷaka*): these are pustules that should be raised by making small dots here and there. For this has been stated in the *Vinayavinicchaya-pakaraṇa*:
“It is not permitted to sew a robe for the sake of ornamentation using threads of various colors,
even if it is the same as those of the hundred-petaled lotus and so forth.
Nor [is it permitted] at the edge of the bowl, nor likewise at the mouth of the bowl.”
For one who makes a braid or even a chain, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
They also make ribbons, knotted stones, octagonal shapes and other such designs;
and there they fashion the forms of swords, clubs, mallets, and so forth.
“In that regard, it is not permissible to pick out the eyes of a crab;
there, both threads and pustules are described as being difficult to discern.
Only those that are four-cornered are permitted—namely, knots, loops, and patches.”
Threads at the corners and those dyed for robes should be cut out.
Whether it be needlework, alterations, or anything else whatsoever,
it is not permitted for a bhikkhu to do or cause to be done on a robe.
“And whatever monk puts a robe into things such as sour gruel,
flour paste, or oil-cakes, desiring a superior glossy color— ”
For him, however, there is no release from an offense of wrong-doing.
“In the making of needle-cases, hand-bags, and so forth, as well as robes,
and likewise when they are soiled, it is permissible for the purpose of washing.”
“Furthermore, it is not permitted for a bhikkhu to put anything into it— whether perfume, oil, or even lac.
Nor [should he use] a conch shell, a gem, or any other such thing.”
One should not strike the robe, nor should it be struck against the edge of the bowl.
Having placed the robe on the edge of the bowl, one should not strike it too forcefully with the fist;
it is permissible to strike at something stained with dye using only the hands.
“However, at the knot [of the robe], neither lines nor pustules are permitted;
nor any modification of the ‘auspicious dot’ (kappabindu), due to the distinction between the border and the ear-flap.

In the *Vinayasāratthasaṃdīpanī* as well, “similar to the hundred-padded [robe] and so forth” means similar to those with a hundred pads and the like. This is used in the sense of equality (*tulyatthe*).
In the context of the instrumental case, this is the genitive case. "On the edge of the cloth" means on both edges of the lengthwise seam.
"Or at the mouth of the cloth" means at the place where two lengths of cloth, in terms of their width, are joined together;

or "on the border," meaning even at the place where a single piece of cloth is joined for the purpose of filling a deficiency. "Veṇī" (braid) refers to the shape of the head of a *kudrūsa* grass stalk.
*Sibbaṇaṃ*: some say it is "in the shape of a *varaka* seed. *Saṅkhalikaṃ*: a sewing [pattern] resembling a cat's collar;
some say it is "like a hundred-petalled [flower].
*Paṭṭampi*: even a strip of cloth. *Aṭṭhakoṇādikavidhiṃ*: that which has a method or manner such as eight corners and so forth.
The elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) occurs by way of the metrical composition of the verse, as in the phrase "beginning with the eight-pointed [lotus]" (*aṭṭhakoṇādikaṃ*).

This term "the procedure beginning with the eight-pointed" (*aṭṭhakoṇādikaṃ vidhiṃ*) is either a coordinate qualifier (*samānādhikaraṇa-viśeṣaṇa*) or an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) for the word "cloth" (*paṭṭaṃ*), and it is connected with the verb "making" (*karonti*).
Alternatively, in the word "on the cloth" (*paṭṭe*), the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative; thus, the meaning is "on the cloth. In this...

"Eight-cornered and so forth on the wings" is the locative case. "Design" (*vidhi*) is its qualifier. Here, "eight-cornered and so forth" refers to shapes other than the four-cornered shape that will be described hereafter.
"Therein" means in those two cloths. "The form of a trident and a mace" refers to stitching in the shape of a trident (*agghiya*) and the shape of a mace (*gadā*).
"A club" refers to stitching in the shape of a staff (*laguḷa*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of shapes such as a *cetiya* (stupa) and others is intended.
*Tattha* means in that place, on the two strips of cloth. *Kakkaṭakakkhīni* refers to sewing-eyes resembling the eyes of a crab.
*Uṭṭhāpentī* means they make them. *Tattha* means on that knotted cord-strip.
*Suttā* refers both to the threads sewn from corner to corner and the threads sewn in a square pattern. *Piḷakā* refers to those same threads having been turned back.
And the ends of the stitches. "Difficult to discern" means that at the time of dyeing, those which are not coarse and whose form is difficult to discern are permitted;
as it is said: "Threads at the corners and knots on a dyed robe are permitted as forms difficult to discern.
The construction is: "the loop-bands and the cord-bands. "Threads at the corners" refers to both the threads and [the knots] at the edges of the robe.
And one cuts away the threads at the corners of the border-strip.

Herein, when the robe has been sewn according to its length and breadth, the threads that protrude outward from the seam toward the wind are called "windward binding-threads" (*anuvāta-bandhasuttāni*) and "corner-threads" (*kaṇṇasuttāni*), because they are used for tying and hanging the robe on a rope or a clothesline after it has been dyed and is drying in the wind. As it is said:
“A thread for the corner of the robe is not permitted; it should be cut off at the time of dyeing.
However, that which was authorized by the statement, ‘Monks, I allow a corner-thread,’ should be tied as a loop facing the wind at the time of dyeing for the purpose of securing it.”
"Various needlework" means sewing with various threads in a manner resembling a *satapadi* (centipede) for the purpose of decorating robes, such as attaching a border-strip (*āgantukapaṭṭa*);

this refers to such varieties of needlework. "Or any other" means any other kind of embroidery work, such as floral designs, animal figures, or footprints. "To do" means to do it oneself. "To cause to be done" means...
Or one may have it made by another.

The construction is as follows: for that monk who, desiring for another a supreme, beautiful, and glossy appearance, puts the robe into sour gruel, flour-dough, oil-cakes, and so forth, there exists no release from the *dukkaṭa* offense. Regarding "sour gruel" (*kañjika*):
*Vāyanatantamakkhanaṃ* is *sulākañjika*, which resembles sour gruel (*kañjika*). *Piṭṭhaṃ* refers to rice flour. *Khali* is that which is cooked with rice flour.
*Allikā* is a decoction (*niyyāsa*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), lac and other such substances are included.

For the purpose of washing the needle, hands, and so forth that have become soiled during the time of making a robe, or for washing [the robe] itself when it has arisen [from dirt] while being made, [one may use] sour gruel, rice flour, *khali*, *allikā*, and so on.
The construction is: "He puts it in; it is allowable.

*Tattha* means: in that dye with which one dyes the robe—whether it be perfume for the sake of making the robe fragrant, oil for the sake of making it bright, or lac for the sake of color. *Kiñci* means: whatever of such a kind...

"Something" (*kiñci*). "With a stone" (*maṇinā*) means with a rock. "And with anything else whatsoever" (*aññenapi ca kenaci*) means with any other object such as a mallet or the like by which it becomes bright.
"In a trough" (*doṇiyā*): it should not be rubbed against a dye-vessel, nor should it be taken up by grasping it with the hand.
The construction is: "It is permissible to strike the dyed robe slightly with the hands. Where...
They throw in dyed cloth; that is the dye-vat. Regarding this, it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* that it is permissible to strike against shoulder-straps, waist-bands, and so forth.
"In a knot" means in a knot made of bamboo, ivory, horn, or similar materials. "Or lines" refers to lines distinguished as circular and so on. "Pustules" [refers to...]
"Small bubbles are like mustard seeds. "By way of breaking the rim of the bowl" means by way of breaking the rim in the form of a jeweled necklace or a flower garland.
It is said that "the modification of a fortune-mark (kappa-bindu) is not permissible," and therefore one should act accordingly with regard to the robe.
Regarding the phrases "in a bowl or in a dish" and so forth: "dish" refers to any of the three kinds of personal allowable dishes made of copper or other materials.
"It is not permitted" means that the practice of coloring [the bowl] like a gem is not permitted, whereas the practice of coloring it with oil is permitted.
"Oil-colored" is said with reference to a color suitable for a recluse; however, they say that if one obtains a gem-colored bowl made by another, it is permitted to use it.
"In a bowl-stand" refers to a stand for placing the bowl, made of tin, lead, or other such materials.
Because it was said, “Monks, you should not carry variegated alms-bowl rims that are covered with figures or made as wall-paintings,” it is stated that “wall-painting is not permitted.
Because it was said, “Monks, I allow you to cut shark-teeth [patterns],” it is stated that “the shark-tooth pattern, however, is permitted. Thus say the ancients:
“Whether on the rim or the bowl, whether on the outside or the inside,
no line whatsoever made with a needle is permitted. If,
having mounted the rim and polished the bowl, they cook it;”
It is not permissible to do it with the thought, "We shall make it the color of a jewel.
"Nothing at all on the bowl-rim; no wall-painting is permitted."
"There is no fault whatsoever therein;
one may fashion a *makaradantaka* (a shark-toothed ornament).
Also, in the *Vinayasāratthasaṇḍīpanī*, it says "with an awl" means with the point of an awl-thorn or with the tip of a needle. "Any writing at all."
Any streak whatsoever, shaped like a quail’s droppings, cow’s urine, or the like. "Having applied it to the rim" means having caused it to adhere to the rim.

"On the bowl-rim" (*pattamaṇḍalake*) means on the bowl-rim—which is made of tin, lead, or the like for the purpose of protecting the surface of the bowl—located below the bowl and above the stand or support.
"Wall-painting" (*bhittikamma*) refers to work variegated by figures in various forms. As it was said: "Monks, you must not... [and so forth].
“Various circular patterns, filled with figures and executed as wall-paintings, should be worn.
“Therein” means in that bowl-pattern. “His” refers to the bhikkhu. “Makaradantaka” is said to mean a mountain peak;
therefore, one should act in this same manner regarding the bowl, the stand, and so forth.
“Dhamakaraṇa…pe… a line does not count”: a line made with a metal stylus does not count, but a line made with colors such as red lead (jātihiṅgulika) and so forth does count.

“On the rim of the umbrella-handle” means on the rim of the handle shaped like an umbrella, which is made for the purpose of holding the water-strainer (dhamakaraṇa) by the hand. Some say: “At the place where the strainer is bound. Also in the *Vinayavinicchaya*: [text follows].
“It is not permissible to draw even a single line on the Dhamma-making umbrella;
however, having placed that line upon the belly, one may draw it on the rim of the mouth.
Thus it was said. But in the commentary (*ṭīkā*), it says: “The line on the rim of the mouth which was permitted for the purpose of binding the water-strainer...”
The construction is: “Having set aside that [specific] mark, no other mark whatsoever is permitted on the water-strainer (*dhamakaraṇa*) or on the bowl (*kucchi*);
therefore, one should proceed regarding the water-strainer according to the method stated therein.
10. Regarding the waist-band (*kāyabandhana*), “crab-eyes” (*kakkaṭakkhīni*) means those resembling the eyes of a crab. “Crocodile-mouth” (*makaramukha*)...
“Shaped like a crocodile’s mouth” means it has a shape resembling the head of a water-snake (*deḍḍubha*). “Eyes” means they have the shape of an elephant’s eye.
“Only one is allowed” means that here, it is not permitted to bind [the waistband] by folding a single cord twice or thrice;
however, it is permitted to bind it even if a single cord encircles the body a hundred times. “Having joined many cords together... [and so forth].
Since it has been stated, "One should not say that it is 'many-stringed' merely because it was made by wrapping [the frame] continuously with a single string;

that is permissible," it should be understood that this does not fall under the category of a *muraja* drum. For they make a *muraja* by wrapping threads of various colors around the frame of the drum in the shape of a *muraja*.
However, this [object] is a soft lute (*maddavīṇā*) known as a *pāmaṅga*, which has the shape of a *pāmaṅga* and [is attached] to its fringes...
It is permissible because it is said: "The fringes of the waistband are worn out. Monks, I allow a *muraja* and a *maddavīṇā*.
A "fringe" (*vidha*) refers to the decorative work made of ivory, horn, thread, and so forth, at the end of the fringe, for the sake of its durability.
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it says: "At the edge of the waistband, at the base of the fringe, [work] made of ivory, horn, etc., should be made for the sake of its durability..."

"Arrange it," he said. The eight auspicious signs (*aṭṭha-maṅgalāni*) are: the conch, the wheel, the full water-pot, the elephant, the *sirīvaccha* (prosperity tree), the hook, the banner, and the *sovatthika* (swastika).
Some also mention them by way of the pair of fish, the parasol, the *nandiyāvatta*, and so forth.
"Merely a line of demarcation" means merely a boundary line to be made at both ends of the pattern fashioned from ivory and other materials.
Also in the *Vinayavinicchayapakaraṇa*:
“Or having doubled the cloth, they cut it here and there for the sake of the beauty of the waistband;
that is not permitted for a bhikkhu.”
“At the ten-faced [image], it is permitted for the sake of firmness at both ends;
however, even making garlands, creeper-work, or painting is not permitted.
Having depicted eyes there—”
But what need is there to mention ground [grains]?
It is not permitted to put crab-eyes into it either.
“A jar, or the head of a turtle, or even the mouth of a sea-monster—
whatever has a distorted shape is not permitted at the opening of the fringe.
It should be straight, like a fish-bone, or smooth, or even like a strip of cloth.”
Having made it in the shape of a date-palm leaf, it is proper that it be pounded smooth.
There are two kinds of waist-bands: the strip and the pig-tail;
ropes, cloth strips, and so forth—all these are suitable for that purpose.
“The *muraja*, the *madda-vīṇā*, the *deḍḍubha*, and the *kalābu-ka*;
and strings—these are not permitted. There should be twelve [fingers] at the front.
The fringes of the waist-band are specified as being shaped like a *pāmaṅga*.”
One, two, or four [strings] are permitted, but not more than that.
The waistband made of a single cord was taught by the Sage;
even a single one in the shape of a *pāmaṅga* (a jeweled girdle) is not permitted.
“Having joined many ropes together into one,
and having wound them tightly around each other, it is permissible to tie [the belt].
It may be made from tooth-sticks, horn, bone, iron, reed, or bamboo.”
“Beads made of lac, conch-shell, thread, or fruit are considered [permissible] for the *vidhaka* (necklace).
Even in the case of the method for the waist-band (*kāyabandhana*), a modification is not permitted; however, a mere line marking the boundaries here and there is allowed.”
It has been stated.

In the *Vinayasāratthasaṇḍīpanī* as well, it says "here and there" in various places on the relevant sections. "That" refers to the binding of the body with a double-folded thread that has been cut in that manner.
The construction is: "They cut it by making a double fold at the ends of the fringe for the sake of strength; this is permissible. Also, "cittakampi" (even a thought).
A waistband may also be fashioned with garland-work, creeper-work, or patterns. "Eyes" refers to elephant eyes. Regarding that:
since it is not permitted even on a waistband, what need is there to mention other cases?
"To raise up" means to carve out. "Jar-shaped" means having the shape of a jar. "Or like the head of a *deḍḍubha*" means the mouth-shape of a water-snake (*udakasappa*). Whatever...
The construction is: "No form of alteration is appropriate at the front of the fringe.
And here, that which is woven on both sides with fish-bones, like the backbone of a fish, upon a strip of cloth—this waistband is called the *macchakaṇṭaka* (fish-bone).
That which is woven in the shape of a date-palm leaf is called the *khajjūripattakākāra* (date-leaf-shaped).
The strip of natural material with a pig’s-tail end is called *sūkaranta*; it is shaped like a key-case. Regarding these two types of waistbands:
there, the cord conforms to the pig’s-tail end, while the cloth strip conforms to the *paṭṭikā* (the flat strip).
By the word "etcetera," the *muddika*-waistband is included, and that also conforms to the pig’s-tail end. As it is said: "But the single-corded *muddika*-waistband..."
"...it conforms to the end of a boar's tail. In this context, "rope" (*rajjukā*) refers to one that is twisted; the author will later explain that a rope with many strands is not allowable.
Regarding the "grape-shaped waist-band" (*muddikakāyabandhana*), it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* that it is prepared without being made square.
A "muraja" is made by wrapping [the cloth] around it in the shape of a muraja drum. "Wrapping" means wrapping it with various types of thread.
In the *Sikkhābhājanavinicchaya*, however, it is stated: "Having joined many cords together, [the instrument] is wound with one cord.
A *maddavīṇā* is shaped like a *pāmaṅga*. A *deḍḍubhaka* resembles a water-snake. A *kalābuka* has many cords. Regarding "cords" (*rajjuyo*):
they are many cords that are not tied together at both ends; those that are so tied are likewise [referred to as such].
It is called a *kalābu*. "They are not permitted" means that all these waist-bands, such as the *muraja* and so forth, are not permitted.

"The first two" refers to the *muraja* and the one called the *maddavīṇā*. Where it should have been said, "there may be ten fringes" (*dasāsu siyuṃ*), it is stated as "there may be ten" (*dasā siyuṃ*) due to the elision of a syllable for the sake of the metrical composition of the verse.
As it has been said: "The *muraja* and the *maddavīṇā*—this is permitted only for the ten fringes."
"Shaped like a waist-band" means it is square-shaped, like a waist-band string. Regarding "made of a single cord":

it is permissible to call a waist-belt made of cord "made of a single cord" when various cords have been twisted together into one; thus, in the phrase "cords, cloth strips, etc.," a single-twisted cord was intended.
However, here [in this specific case], it refers to a single cord that has been made by twisting various cords together into one.
"Taken. "And that" means even that method of binding the body with a single cord, knotted in the shape of a *pāmaṅga* (a type of leg-binder).
"Even one is not permitted" means that even a single one is not allowed.
"Having joined many cords together" is the construction. "It is permitted to bind" means provided it is not a *muraja* (drum-shaped) or a *kalābu* (gourd-shaped) [cord].
The intention is that it is simply a body-binding made of ropes. However, this analysis—stated here from the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"When many ropes are joined together and wrapped continuously with one [rope], it should not be called 'made of many ropes';
that is permissible"—is found in the analysis of the *Sikkhābhājaniya*. [In the passage: "When many ropes are joined together, with one..."
Regarding what was said, “the one called the *veṭhita-muraja*,” that should not be accepted because it contradicts this [text].
By the word *danta*, elephant tusks are meant. *Jatu* means lac. *Saṅkhamayaṃ* means made from the shell of a conch.
Regarding *vidhakā matā*, here there is also the reading *vedhikā*; it is a synonym for *vidha*. In the phrase *kāyabandhanavidha*, it refers to a type of waistband.
The modification (*vikāra*) refers to things such as the eight auspicious signs (*aṭṭhamangala*) made from wood, ivory, and so forth, for the purpose of providing stability to a cloth.
"In this or that place" means in each respective location. By the word "but" (*tu*), it is indicated that the shape of a jar is also appropriate; thus the meaning is clarified.
Therefore, by that method, an investigation into the waist-band (*kāyabandhana*) should be carried out.

11. Regarding the *añjani* (eye-salve container): because it is stated that it must be "straight," one that is curved or shaped like a square and so forth is not permitted. Regarding the *sipāṭikā* (box):
this refers to a container for tools such as axes and the like. Furthermore, in the *Vinayavinicchaya-pakaraṇa*:
"Adorned with various forms of floral and creeper designs, An eye-salve box that delights the people is not permitted for monks."
“However, having rubbed such [an ointment-stick] and wrapped it with thread,
there is no fault whatsoever for a bhikkhu who uses it.
Whether it be round, square, or even eight-sided, [it is permitted as] an ointment-stick.”
It is explained that it is permissible for it to be rounded,
but it is not permissible for it to be polished. Likewise,
it is not permissible for the eye-salve applicator or the eye-salve box to have decorative work done with threads of various colors.
“It is permitted for one who uses a needle-case made with thread of a single color,
or with whatever [thread] is available, after having sewn anything [into it]. — Thus it is handed down.

In the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) as well: "Variegated" (*cittita*) means variegated by means of floral designs (*mālākamma*), vine-work (*latākamma*), and various forms such as those of animals and birds.
"Delighting the people" (*janarañjanī*) means that which entices foolish people. Regarding "an eight-cornered pond," the word "also" (*api*) here includes sixteen-cornered ponds and so forth.
"Smooth with color" (*vaṇṇamaṭṭhā*) means smooth with the colors of floral designs and the like. The same applies to the collyrium and the applicator stick.

The construction is: "It is not permitted for the sake of beauty. Regarding the reading, "embroidery with threads of various colors on a case for a cosmetic box (añjanī-thavikā) is not permitted," this reading is appropriate;
however, the reading "or even a case" (*thavikāpi vā*) is found [in some texts], but that should not be accepted.
[This refers to] one who uses a small bag made of cloth or similar material, having sewn it together with any single-colored thread such as yellow and so forth.
The connection [of the text] is: “it is allowable. 12.
Regarding *ārakaṇṭaka* and so forth: *ārakaṇṭaka* refers to a long-pointed knife made for the purpose of preparing books and such;
some say it is a knife for woodworkers used for carving wood and the like. *Vaṭṭamaṇika* refers to a bubble that must be raised by making it circular.
By the word "other" (*añña*), one includes pustules and the like. "Pipphalika" refers to any small cutting tool.
"Maṇika" is a single-round gem. "Piḷaka" refers to many circular lines resembling mustard seeds or *muttarājī* (a type of medicinal plant).
Since this is not mentioned in the present context, they say that anything smooth and colored is suitable for a stylus. [This is stated] in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*.
However, it is stated: "Because a key is an accessory for lodgings, even one made of gold or silver is permitted; thus its reflection is seen.

But because of the statement, 'Polishing with a key is not permitted,' other keys made of allowable metals and so forth are allowed, as they are accessories to be carried. An *ārakaṇṭaka* is a type of tool for making books and such.
They say that the *āmaṇḍasāraka* is made from the fruit of the *āmalaka*.
Regarding the term "valitaka": at the time of cutting with the fingernails, they make it provided with folds for the sake of a firm grip; therefore, it is appropriate.
By this [statement], they perform other modifications for the purpose of strengthening and so forth, not for the sake of beauty or polish.

"It is fitting" is what is illustrated; and by that, it is implied—even though not explicitly stated—that there should be rings and so forth made at the ends of the walking stick for the purpose of producing sound through their mutual clashing.
Here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "strengthening and so forth," one includes the warding off of dangers and the like;
thus, by the mutual clashing of the rings made at the ends of the walking staff—
The utterance of the word *sadda* is for the purpose of warding off dangers such as snakes and the like; therefore, he indicates that it is appropriate.
Thus the excellent teacher said:
“Whether it be a jewel, a boil, or even a thorn in a plum,” etc.
However, it is not permissible for a bhikkhu to place anything [on his nails] at all.
But it is permissible to have even a mere line as a demarcation on the nail-stalks;
for it is said that it is permissible to have them filed down and trimmed with the fingernails.
In its description: *maṇika* refers to a large bubble; *pīḷaka* refers to a small bubble. *Pipphala* refers to a cloth-cutting knife.
*Ārakaṇṭaka* refers to the prongs that pierce the rings holding the bowl. *Ṭhapetuṃ* means to raise up.
*Yaṃ kiñci* includes whatever else has a smooth, variegated appearance. *Daṇḍaka* refers to the handle of the *pipphala*. As it has been said:
“Even on a *pipphalika* (a small wooden block), it is not permitted to place a jewel or a blister-like protrusion; however, a demarcation line on a handle is permitted.
Regarding “merely a demarcation line”: once the handle has reached the point where it is bound to the ring, only a single line is permitted for the purpose of defining its limits.
“Having curled [the nail]” means having formed both ends into a loop and having made folds in the middle, [one cuts] the nail.
The connection is made as follows: "Because they do it, therefore it is permissible.
Regarding "a circle for the upper fire-drill" (*uttarāraṇiyaṃ maṇḍalaṃ*): there is a circular pit for the purpose of inserting the upper fire-drill.
The connection is that [the handle] should be tied straight onto the tooth-stick-cutter. And here, by the phrase "straight indeed," it is implied that one should not tie it after making it crooked.
This shows that it is not permitted; for that very reason, the collyrium box is also shown in the same way.

The phrase "on both sides or on one side" is an elliptical expression (*vacana-sesa*); the meaning is that they should be bound on both sides of the handle-staff so that the ends of the staff do not move.
The construction is: "It is permissible to make [the box] square or eight-sided out of allowable metal."
13. *Āmaṇḍasāraka*: This refers to a vessel for oil made from the paste produced by grinding *āmalaka* fruits. It is said that the oil placed therein becomes cool. Thus it was stated by the Teacher:
"Whether on the upper fire-drill, or on a bow, or on a pressing-stick, or on anything such as a floral design—any glossy coloration is not permitted."
“Regarding tooth-sticks, it is permissible to tie them with metal at both ends using a pair of pliers;
likewise for a knife-handle, decorative work is not permitted.”
"Like circular lines, they may be round— one or even two—
at the bottom. Likewise, on the prongs, the tube, the rim of the bowl,
and on the oil-container, everything that is smooth and polished is permitted."
In the *Ṭīkā* as well: "The stick used for the lower fire-drill (*araṇi*) is called the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇī*). The word ‘and’ (*vāpi*) includes the lower fire-drill (*adharāraṇi*).
This is a designation for the pestle-stick of a mortar. A bow for drawing [a string] is called a *dhanuka*.
A pressing stick at the head of a mallet is called a *pelladaṇḍaka*. ‘Sandāsa’ refers to tongs for fire. Tooth-sticks..."
The connection is that for a woodcutter’s axe (*vāsī*), any kind of polished surface is not permitted.
"On both sides" means on both faces of the axe. "With iron" means with allowable iron (*kappiya-loha*).
"It is permissible to bind it" means it is permissible to bind it straight, or square, or octagonal. "A sandāsa" refers to a fire-tongs; this is stated without doubt. [This is] in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Here, the needle-tongs are shown. "Below" means below the iron ring-base. "Above, the size of a mushroom (ahicchattaka) bud" is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā.
"On horns" refers to the horns of cattle, gayals, buffalo, and so forth, used for pouring oil. "In a tube" means in a tube such as a bamboo stalk;
by the word *api*, the gourd is included. "In a jar with an āmaṇḍa-stand" refers to an oil-jar made from the powder of *āmalaka* fruit.

"In an oil vessel" means in an oil vessel of the kind already described. "All polychrome work is permitted" means that all polychrome work—such as floral designs and the like—is permitted, provided it is devoid of male or female figures; thus it is stated.
"Floor-covering" refers to a carpet to be spread upon a prepared floor made of straw mats and so forth. "Water-jar" refers to...
By this, he includes all vessels. Regarding the statement "all... is permissible," they say that even images of men and women are permissible among the aforementioned items such as beds and so forth;

for while images of men and women are prohibited specifically in the case of oil-vessels, beds and the like are mentioned separately from oil-vessels. Although they say this, regarding these beds and so forth—
It should be understood that because it is an object to be touched with the hand, a female form is not permitted here.
However, in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, it is stated: "Polishing with color and lacquer on palm-leaf fans, whisks, and so forth, is permitted.

Although these items are to be carried about like keys, they were stated [in the commentary] because there is no prohibition against possessing them, provided they are not of various high or low (luxurious) types.
For those [items] were indeed mentioned only in such passages as: “I allow you, monks, the fan and the palm-leaf fan.
However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: “Polishing with color-gloss on oil containers is permitted, because they are requisites for lodgings.
This has been stated by the teacher, the Elder Buddhadatta, as well.
“In a water-pot, or even in a wooden trough;
in a dye-vat, or even on a jar, a wooden seat, or such things as bracelets and stands.
Likewise, on a bowl-cover, a palm-leaf fan, or a whisk.”
“Whether it be a foot-wiping cloth or even a broom;
on a bed, a floor-covering, a chair, or on cushions and bolsters;
mental work such as weaving garlands and so forth—all of this is permitted.”

14. Having thus explained what is allowable and what is not allowable regarding the requisites of a recluse, he now speaks the passage beginning with "But as regards lodgings" (*senāsane pana*) in order to explain [the rules] concerning lodgings. Here, the word *pana* indicates a distinction.
By it, he illuminates the meaning that even decoration made of all kinds of gems is permitted, let alone decoration made of other materials. If this is so, then in some cases...
Thinking that even though there might be something to be prohibited, it should still be stated accordingly, he said: "In the lodging, there is nothing whatsoever to be prohibited.
And this was also said by the teacher, the Venerable Buddhadatta Thera:
"With pillars, door-panels, doors, and walls made of various gems;"
“Even the lodgings have been approved— what need to mention the polished stone slabs?
With golden door-panels, walls and floors adorned with various gold and gems.”
“Not even a single thing is to be prohibited;
every kind of lodging is permissible.
Also, in the *Samantapāsādikā*, in the commentary on the first *saṅghādisesa* rule, it says: “But the use of lodgings is allowable in all cases.”
"Therefore, all the requisites for lodgings, even those made of gold and silver, are permitted.
In the place where the monks recite the Dhamma and Vinaya, they construct a jeweled pavilion with pillars of crystal adorned with jeweled garlands.
There, it is stated that it is permissible for the monks to look after all the necessary utensils. In the *Vimativinodanī* commentary on that passage, however:

“‘All is allowable’ (sabbakappiya) means that the use—by way of touching, guarding, and so forth—of the requisites for lodgings made of gold and other materials as previously described is allowable in every respect; this is the intended meaning. Therefore, he says ‘Therefore,’ and so on.

Because it was stated, ‘In the context of describing the Dhamma and Vinaya for bhikkhus,’ only gold-made lodgings and lodgings-requisites belonging to the Saṅgha are permitted, not those belonging to an individual (puggalika).”
"It should be understood" is how it is praised.

Also, in the *Samantapāsādikā* commentary on the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*, it says: "'The enjoyment of all palaces' refers to doors, beds, chairs, and palm-leaf fans adorned with gold, silver, and other materials;
as well as water-jars and water-bowls made of gold and silver—whatever [is used]."

Whatever is made of ivory is all permissible. If they say, "We give slaves, male and female, fields, land, cows, and buffaloes for the palace," there is no need for separate acceptance; once the palace is accepted, these are already included.
Blankets such as *gonaka* and others may be used by spreading them over beds and chairs in either a communal monastery (*saṅghika-vihāra*) or a private dwelling (*puggalika-vihāra*).

"It is not permitted [to lie down]; however, on a Dhamma-seat (dhammāsana), it may be obtained under the designation of 'householder's property,' yet even there, it is not permitted to lie down"—so it is stated.
In the *Vimativinodanī* commentary on that passage, it says:

"The phrase 'variegated with gold, silver, and so forth' refers to monastic lodgings belonging to the Saṅgha; however, as for private property variegated with gold and so forth, a bhikkhu may indeed accept it."
"It is not permissible [to say that this applies only to monasteries], because it was stated: 'But in no way whatsoever, monks, should gold or silver be accepted.
For that very reason, it is not stated in the commentary here as 'in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha or in one belonging to an individual';
rather, it is explained thus with reference specifically to unallowable articles such as woolen blankets and the like, since there is no fault in a single monk's taking possession of them."

In the commentary on that same Khandhaka, it is stated: "Even if kings, royal ministers, and others should give a hundred or a thousand beds all at once, all these allowable beds (kappiyamañca) may be accepted.
Having accepted them, they should be given out for the communal use of the Saṅgha according to seniority; they must not be given out on an individual basis."

In the *Vimativinodanī* commentary on that very passage, it is explained: "By the statement 'proper beds (kappiyamañca) are to be accepted,' it is shown that an improper bed (akappiyamañca) decorated with gold and so forth is not permitted to be accepted even when said to be 'for the Saṅgha.
When it is said, 'We give this to the monastery,' it is permissible for the Saṅgha alone, and should be understood as not being for an individual, unlike the case of fields and such."
Therefore, this matter must be carefully attended to by those monks who accept the command of the Blessed One—those who are modest, refined, learned, and desirous of training.
Now, is it not the case that in regard to lodgings, there is indeed a "disputed lodging" that must be prohibited? Then why [is it mentioned] regarding lodgings...
Regarding the objection that it was stated, "there is nothing whatsoever to be prohibited," he says, "except for incompatible lodgings.

The meaning of this is as follows: setting aside incompatible lodgings—that is, excluding incompatible lodgings—with reference to other matters such as painting or plastering, it was stated that there is nothing whatsoever to be prohibited regarding the lodging; it does not mean that those [other matters] are non-existent. If this is so...
Regarding that "conflicting dwelling," when asked by the teacher, "What is called a conflicting dwelling?", he says:
"Conflicting... is so called. In this context, "others" refers to the owners of the boundary (*sīmā*).

"By those favored by the king" refers to shameless monks who possess broken views and who cause obstacles to the Uposatha and other ceremonies for those who are modest and virtuous; for it is improper to perform the Uposatha and such rites together with them.
And by that, it is said, "of the boundary. "A modest assembly for them" means a modest assembly capable of providing support to those who are the owners of the boundary.
"Done by bhikkhus" refers to whatever—such as the breaking up of lodgings and so forth—is done toward shameless individuals by modest bhikkhus;
all that is indeed well-done, because it must be carried out for the purpose of restraining the shameless.
And here it might be asked: "The *Aṭṭhakathā* states, 'the boundary of others,' yet there are many kinds of boundaries; with reference to which kind of boundary is this said?
It should be understood that this refers to a formally established (*baddha*) boundary.
How is this known? Because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* itself: "'Do not cause an obstruction to our Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies,'" and likewise in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.

Because it is stated [in the *Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā* 2.85]: “Those who cause obstacles to the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies, being shameless and attached to royal families, are called ‘those who frequent the courts’”;
and because it is precisely the boundary (*sīmā*) that constitutes the field for formal acts of the Vinaya, such as the Uposatha and so forth, that is intended here.

If this is so, then the village boundary, the seven-intermediate-space boundary, and the water-splashing boundary are also fields for those same acts; therefore, they too are included by way of reference.
Is it to be said [that they are the owners]? It should not be said that they are the owners because their boundary has not been fixed;
nor are they the owners because the formal act of monks is established only within a fixed boundary. Therefore it was said: "But by the monks who are the owners of the boundary.
As for what some say—that even the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*) constitutes that field—that should not be accepted.
We shall explain its status as a non-field later in the discussion on the determination of boundaries (*sīmāvinicchaya*) and other such texts. Furthermore,

it should be understood that the *baddhasīmā* (formally established boundary) alone is intended here, because it is improper to prohibit others from constructing dwellings within a village boundary (*gāmasīmā*),
and because the seven-cubit (*sattabbhantara*) and water-sprinkling (*udakukkhepa*) boundaries do not persist at all times.
The statement, "One may have it cut down or have it broken; there is no offense," was said with reference to things that are entirely unfit for use, such as a hut made of clay.
However, regarding items such as a parasol bound with five-colored threads, only the unallowable portion (*akappiya-bhāga*) therein may be cut;
the remainder is allowable (*kappiya*). Therefore, one who cuts it [in this manner] is indeed at fault.
Therefore it is said: "One may even carry [the bowl] after cutting away the handle or the animal-shaped ornament," and so forth.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Ornament of the Discussion on Requisites" within the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
The Second Chapter.
3. Discourse on the Determination of the Making of Medicines, etc. 15.
Having thus explained the determination of requisites, [the author now treats] the making of medicines, protective charms (*paritta*), and hospitality.
In order to explain the detailed analysis (*vinicchaya*), he said, "medicines" (*bhesajja*), and so forth. In this context, that which belongs to a physician is "medicine" (*bhesajja*).
What is it? It is healing. That which is performed is an "action" (*karaṇa*); the performance of medicine is "the act of administering medicine," meaning the performance of medical treatment.
That which protects and guards on all sides is "protection" (*paritta*); the meaning is "guarding. "Hospitality" (*paṭisantharaṇa*)...
*Paṭisanthāro* means making a connection with others by means of oneself.

Regarding that, when the determination (*vinicchaya*) stated by me in the *Mātikā*—namely, "the preparation of medicine and the protective charm (*paritta*), as well as hospitality" (*paṭisanthāro*)—has been thoroughly mastered, specifically regarding that determination on the preparation of medicine:
those who have the same Dhamma as these are *sahadhammikā*; of them, [of one] teacher...
The meaning is: "those training in the Dhamma together within the Dispensation. Alternatively, *sahadhammika* means those connected with the Dhamma;

the meaning is "those connected by way of training in the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) which are designated as the Dhamma. By virtue of being endowed with virtue and so forth that are directed toward liberation, they are "equal" (*samatta*) in their virtue, faith, and wisdom.
By this, he shows that it is not even permitted to do so for those who are immoral or who hold divergent views.
"From a place where relatives have invited [him]" means from a place where either his own relatives or theirs have invited him. "Was not done" means it was unmade;

a request that has never been made before in an improper manner is an "unmade request" (*akataviññatti*). However, in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, it says: "'Unmade request' means not by way of a formal request.
For that [request], although it has been made, because it was not authorized, it is as if it were unmade; thus it is an 'unmade request. [One] should speak..."
It is stated [in the *Sāratthadīpanī*]: "In the case where it has not been done, such as 'Venerable sir, whatever is needed,' this is called an 'unmade request' (*akataviññatti*).
Because a request from a place where permission has not been granted is permitted for the sake of one who is ill, even though it has been made, it is like what has not been made;
thus it is an 'unmade request. And in a place where an invitation has not been made, such as 'Speak, venerable sir, regarding requisites'..."
“Intimation is unmade intimation. 16.
“He prepares” means he accomplishes. Regarding the phrase “it is not permitted not to do it,” they say there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) here;
however, it should be understood that the prohibition against non-performance is stated here on account of its impropriety, and not on account of an actual offense. All the preliminary work...
"By not touching" means it is stated because the body of a woman and so forth are not to be touched. "As long as his relatives do not see" means as long as his relatives do not see [it].
It is stated in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*: "It is not permissible to give with one's own hand to parents who have become members of a non-Buddhist sect."

17. *Pitucchā* means a paternal aunt; *mātula* means a maternal uncle. Regarding the phrase "they are not sufficient," it is stated in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*) that this means they are unable to provide [the medicine].
However, after stating, "Having taken medicine belonging to those very persons, one should simply compound it and give it," it is further said:
"But if they are insufficient and they request, saying, 'Venerable sir, please give us some; we shall repay you. Therefore...
The intention of the Aṭṭhakathā appears to be that they ask for medicine itself because their existing medicine is insufficient;
this should be investigated. "They do not ask" means they do not ask out of modesty or out of respect.

Because it is stated, "having made an effort (ābhogaṃ katvā)," there is indeed an offense for one who gives otherwise. However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it says: "'Having made an effort'—this is said by way of showing what ought to be done."
It is stated [in the *Gaṇṭhipada*] that "it is written in the three *Gaṇṭhipadas* that it is permissible to give [the robe] even without making a formal mental application (*ābhoga*).
This very same point was also recorded in the *Porāṇaṭīkā*. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, that statement is rejected.
For it is said there: "But some say that it is permissible to give [the robe] even without making a formal mental application; that is not correct."

Regarding the preparation of medicine, because it is prohibited in general terms in the Canon by way of showing an intermediate offense— stating, "There is no offense for the bhikkhu regarding a *pārājika*, but there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)"—
it should be understood that for one who prepares it in a manner not explicitly mentioned in the Commentary,
the offense is established by the Sutta itself. For this very reason, even in the Commentary, [it says] "of those very..."
The phrase "belonging to [them]" and so forth has been stated.
Regarding the expression "setting aside these ten relatives": since their sons, grandsons, and others are also relatives by virtue of being connected to them, they too are included herein.
Therefore, it should be understood that by the words "others," non-relatives are being referred to. For this very reason, he said:
“Of their succession of sons,” and so forth. *Kulaparivaṭṭā* means the sequence of families; it is what is meant by “the lineage of families.
Regarding “one who prepares medicine”: this refers to one who prepares it according to the aforementioned method.

However, even for one who gives it without forming the intention, “I shall give it for a limited time,” there is an intermediate offense of *dukkaṭa*, provided it is not done through wrong livelihood or with the defilement of a family.
Or rather, it simply does not exist. Therefore he said: “There is neither medical practice nor an offense involving the defilement of a family.

For it is permissible to take even what belongs to relatives after having requested it; therefore, in that case, there can be no defilement of the family or similar faults. In the *Sāratthadīpanī* as well, it is stated:
“Even for one who acts out of the expectation that ‘they will give to me’ or ‘they will do [it] for me,’ since it is a place from which one may take after requesting...”
It is stated: "They say that there is neither the offense of performing medical treatment among kinsmen nor the offense of corrupting a family.

However, in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, it is stated only as follows: "Because of the statement that 'there is neither the offense of performing medical treatment nor the offense of corrupting a family,' they say that it is permissible to provide medicine for up to the seventh generation of the family circle. This is the analysis regarding all locations.

"It should be understood" means that in all such phrases as "of the junior mother," the explanation should be understood according to the method stated below, by connecting them with "the husband of the junior mother," and so forth.
"We are bringing for the preceptor" refers to those who have been commanded by the preceptor, saying, "Bring medicine for my relatives."

This was stated for the purpose of showing the procedure to be followed. By this, he demonstrates that it is not permissible for a novice or others to prepare medicine for another person even when there is no expectation of anything in return.

By the phrase "having sought in the manner already described," he refers back to the matters previously explained in the passages beginning with "by the conduct of going for alms" and "by novices who are relatives. [The term] "without expecting anything in return" means...
Even when one performs [services] for guests, thieves, and the like, people are indeed benefactors;
thus, the intention is that there is no fault for one who acts without desiring gain for oneself from them, provided one does not act out of expectation.
For when such assistance is rendered, they become confident after recognizing the excellence of the Teaching (sāsana), or they become benefactors of the Saṅgha—this is the meaning of "in doing so."

However, there is no fault [in this]. Some, however, say: "It is permissible for one who does not expect anything in return to give even to persons such as guests or those whose admission has been refused";
that is not correct, because it would follow that the distinction between what ought and ought not to be done would be rendered purposeless;
for one who does not expect anything in return should simply say: "It is permissible to give and to act for the benefit of everyone."
And it should be understood that the "not expecting anything in return" was stated solely for the purpose of preventing faults such as wrong livelihood and the defiling of families;
it is not for the purpose of being released from this intermediate offense known as "making medicine," since one is released from that offense simply by giving what has been permitted,
such as to guests or thieves.
18. To show that even one who does not expect anything in return must not perform certain actions, it is said: “A faithful family,” and so forth.
Even when it is said, “Prescribe the medicine,” the phrase “but they may converse with one another” is permissible because it is a secondary allowance (*pariyāya*).
Thus, for one who speaks according to this method—even while saying, “Having taken this and that in the manner described above, they prepare [the medicine]”—it is likewise acceptable.
"There is no fault," say the teachers. By the word "they ask," he shows that it is improper to wander about even by alternating between those who have seen and those who have not seen [the patient].
However, they say that even for one who has been asked, if he expects something in return, even a figurative discourse (*pariyāyakathā*) is not permitted.
"They conversed" means that, without expecting anything at all, they initiated conversation with one another.

Regarding the term *ācariyabhāga* (the teacher’s share), it is stated in the *Vimativinodanī* that its meaning is: "attaining the status of a physician-teacher by prescribing medicine without violating the conduct prescribed by the Vinaya.
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is said:
"Because for one who does not know the characteristics of the Vinaya and is thus not a teacher, such appropriate terminology cannot possibly exist..."
"It is said: 'There is no arising of such a gain; therefore it is called "the teacher’s portion.
This means that it is the portion to be received by a teacher who is proficient in the Vinaya. It is further stated:
"'By way of what is allowable' is said because, even when given for the purpose of flower-offering, the procedure is improper if expressed through an unallowable term; [therefore] 'flower...'"
"In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: 'The meaning is "by way of allowable speech," as in [the phrase] "bring it," and so forth.

However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: 'Even silver that is accepted for the purpose of flower-offering becomes subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*) by virtue of being treated as one's own property;
therefore, it says "having had it taken by way of what is allowable. [It continues: "'Silver is not permitted for us; for the purpose of flower-offering...'"
It is said: "Having rejected [the act] by means of such statements as 'a flower is not permitted,' one should have it accepted through a formal act (*kamma*) that is allowable (*kappiya*).
However, in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, only this much is stated: "'By way of what is allowable' means [saying], 'Bring us flowers,' and so forth.

Because it is said, 'He made an offering,' they say that it is not permitted for him to take [them] himself. This is the ornament of the discussion on the determination of the preparation of medicine (*bhesajja*).

19. Having thus explained the determination regarding the preparation of medicine, he now says, “But as for the protective chant (*paritta*),” etc., in order to explain the determination regarding the performance of a protective chant.

Therein, if they perform it when told, “Recite the protective chant,” it becomes like the preparation of medicine or like a layperson’s work; therefore, it is said, “It should not be performed. However, if told, “Recite the protective chant,” [it is permissible].
However, because it is a search for the Dhamma, the Dhamma may be spoken even by one who has not been requested, let alone by one who has been requested;
thus it is said, "it should be performed. By the phrase "having moved the thread and smoothed it," he shows the procedure to be followed when performing a protective recitation (*paritta*).
Or, "having moved the thread and smoothed it" refers to the protection (*parittāṇa*) performed with the thought, "I shall cause this protection to enter here."

It is said that "she has entered therein" refers to this. Regarding the statement, "From the monastery... [etc. ...an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," they say this was spoken with reference to an unrelated householder.
"Having sprinkled water on the feet"—this was stated because it was the custom in that region.
For there, water was poured on the feet of the monks seated according to the *pāḷi* (textual order) for the purpose of allaying disease and so forth.
Having sprinkled [water] and performed the protective rite (*paritta*), and having set up the thread while saying, "Recite the *paritta*," they depart.
For if they were to do so and remove the foot [of the image], people would consider it an ill omen and think, "The illness will not be pacified.
Therefore he said, "The feet must not be removed."
"Just as when seeing a single corpse, so too when seeing a whole charnel ground, the perception of death arises: ‘This is the place where beings born [into this world] reach their end.
Thus he said: ‘It is fitting to go with the thought, “I shall obtain mindfulness of death at the sight of a charnel ground.
Without making a formal appointment (*lesa-kappa*), with a mind that has arisen in purity, one says: ‘Let them come for the sake of an escort.’"
It is stated in the *Vimativinodanī* that even when this has been said, it is permissible to go.

By this, he shows that it is not permissible to go with an impure mind, thinking: "By making a mere pretext out of the words 'seeing the foul,' the relatives of the deceased will have confidence; they will give alms, we shall obtain gain, and we shall obtain an attendant. This is under the heading of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
However, this indicates that it is permissible to go even if [the bowl] has been set aside with a pure mind by thinking,

"We shall obtain the recollection of death," and so forth, whether it has been set aside or not. Because the palm leaf is the place for writing protective charms (*paritta*) and because the protective thread serves as the sign for performing the protective rite,
he said, "The palm leaf and the protective thread," meaning that non-human beings depart upon seeing them, perceiving them as protective charms.
"or it should be tied to the hand or the foot.

And here, from the beginning up to the words "or the Āṭānāṭiya-paritta should be recited," this alone constitutes the section on the procedure for performing protective recitations (paritta) outside of the canonical text, as derived from the Vinaya-ṭīkā;
nothing further than that is stated there. Therefore, [the passage] beginning with "But here... and so forth...
The method of exposition (*kathāmagga*) is not found in the *Samantapāsādikā*, nor is that method of commentary present in the three sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*);

nevertheless, since it does appear in the Sutta Commentary (*Sutta-aṭṭhakathā*), he said, "In this context, however, the preparatory rite (*parikamma*) for the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta should be understood," and so forth, in order to demonstrate that.
Therein, "in this context" (*idha*) refers to the statement, "Or the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta should be recited."

*Panā* is a particle used in the sense of specification (*visesatthe*). The construction is to be understood as follows: "The preparatory rite (*parikamma*) for the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta, which appears in the Pāṭhika-vagga of the Dīgha Nikāya, should be known thus.
If it should not be recited right from the beginning, then what should be done? To this he says: "The Metta Sutta," and so forth.
For in this way, having become familiar through repeated practice, it becomes exceedingly powerful.
In the phrase "either dough or meat," the word *vā* has the sense of non-restriction; by it, [the text] includes fish, cakes, snacks, and so forth.
"They find an opportunity" means they gain entry by obtaining a place to sit that is connected to foodstuffs dear to themselves.
"Smeared with green matter" means smeared with fresh cow dung; for this is an ancient custom for the purpose of purifying the ground.

By the phrase "It should be sat upon, completely pure," etc., it is shown that the purification of the mind through loving-kindness (*mettā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) is also required for the monk performing the protective rite (*paritta*). For if this were so, it would accord with the provision of protection on both sides which will be explained below.
However, in the *Ṭīkā* it is stated: "It is shown that the purification of the body is also required. This point must be investigated.
For it is not said that "one becomes dear to non-human beings merely by bodily purity";

rather, it is said specifically by way of loving-kindness (*mettā*). Indeed, this was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, from the liberation of mind through loving-kindness... eleven benefits are to be expected. What are the eleven?
One sleeps happily; one wakes happily; one sees no evil dreams; among humans..."
“He becomes dear to humans; he becomes dear to non-humans,” and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with “one who performs a *paritta*... surrounded by a retinue”: this refers to the provision of protection from the outside by performing the *paritta*;
the instruction to “recite the *mettā* [sutta], etc. refers to the provision of protection from within. Thus, there is the provision of protection on both sides.
Thus it is. For in this way, non-human beings (amanussa) are unable to create obstacles for one who recites the protective chant (paritta).

"The discourse on auspiciousness (maṅgalakathā) should be spoken" means that, having prepared a gift (paṇṇākāra) to satisfy the non-human beings, the Great Discourse on Auspiciousness (Mahāmaṅgalakathā) should be recited.
This is according to the statement to be made later: "The Great Discourse on Auspiciousness has been spoken for the sake of your gift."
It is settled. In the *Ṭīkā*, however, it is stated: "It should be announced by way of prior custom.

"The assembly of all" means that an announcement must be made for the assembly of all monks in that monastery and within that village district, saying: "Everyone must assemble at the cetiya courtyard.
"Not to come is not permitted" means that even a non-human being [is not exempt] due to the fear of the Buddha’s command and the fear of the king’s command.

One does not obtain [the opportunity] to go away, because of being subject to the command of the Four Great Kings. By the expression "seized," it is a non-human being who is questioned; thus it is said:
"The one seized by a non-human being should be asked, 'Who are you by name? Regarding "in garlands, perfumes, and so forth," this refers to offerings such as garlands and perfumes.
Regarding "in the worship of the seat," this refers to the worship of the Buddha’s seat at a cetiya. Regarding "alms-food," this refers to [the offering] for the Saṅgha of monks.
Regarding the giving of alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*): thus, volition (*cetanā*) has been explained by way of the object and the location; therefore, the transfer of merit (*pattidāna*) is possible.
"To the deities" (*devatānaṃ*) refers to the generals of the *yakkhas*. For it is said in the *Āṭānāṭiya Sutta*:
"One should cause these *yakkhas*, great *yakkhas*, generals, and great generals to be informed," and so forth. *Āṭā* are the *dabbimukha* birds; they cry out "āṭā."
"Herein" means in Āṭānāṭa, the city of the devas; "Āṭānāṭiya" refers to the discourse (sutta) composed in Āṭānāṭa.

In the commentary (*ṭīkā*), regarding the instruction "the protective chant (*paritta*) should be recited," all the preliminary practices (*parikamma*) mentioned for laypeople's recitation of the *paritta*—such as "having preceded it with a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*)," "the discourse on blessings (*maṅgalakathā*) should be delivered," and "in the grove of the monastery"—are also applicable here.

It is stated, "it must indeed be done. This being so, when the *Aṭṭhakathā* first says, "This, for its part, is the preliminary service for householders," and then speaks of it as "this is the preliminary service for monks" together with the word *pana* (but/however)—which indicates a distinction—such a statement would seem to be purposeless.
For if there were no distinction [between the two], then a differentiation [of the cases] ought to have been made.

It would not be so. For monks, external protection as previously described is difficult to maintain; therefore, it is our opinion that even if the preparatory rites prescribed for householders' protective charms (*paritta*) are not performed, it is permissible to perform them according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
However, having heard this preparatory rite for the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta included here, [one thinks]: "This sutta is unpleasant to non-human beings..."
Thinking, "Non-human beings might create obstacles for one who recites [the scriptures] or performs a protective chant (*paritta*)," they have set aside the *Āṭānāṭiya-sutta*—
which was announced by the four Great Kings, taught by the Omniscient Buddha, serves as the root text, and is included in the *Dīgha Nikāya*—
and instead have taken only the six verses from that root text, omitting all the rest of the sutta.
Having set aside other verses and inserted others, they established it as the "Āṭānāṭiya Paritta.
Because that paritta lacked a fixed root text, being unable to preserve it in a single form, some memorized it in brief, some in detail, some added certain verses, and some omitted them;
furthermore, some monks [used] even this mixed paritta on occasions such as when performing auspicious rites.
Unable to explain it, they set that aside and recite other suttas; all of this appears inappropriate.

Why? Because the Four Great Kings, when establishing this Āṭānāṭiya protection, did so solely for the purpose of inspiring faith in non-human beings toward the Buddha’s teaching and for the sake of not harassing the four assemblies, and not for any other reason.
For it is said there: "In that place there dwell powerful yakkhas who have no faith in this word of the Blessed One;

for their inspiration, may the Blessed One, venerable sir, learn the Āṭānāṭiya protection for the guarding, protection, non-harming, and comfortable dwelling of the bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās."
In the conclusion of this sutta, the Fully Enlightened One also said: "Monks, learn the Āṭānāṭiya protection;
monks, master the Āṭānāṭiya protection; monks, retain the Āṭānāṭiya protection.
For it is beneficial, monks, the Āṭānāṭiya protection for monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen."
“for the protection, preservation, non-harming, and comfortable dwelling [of the Saṅgha],” thus was the memorization by the bhikkhus enjoined and the benefit made manifest.
And the masters of the commentaries have stated: “In that which was spoken by the Buddha, there is not even a single syllable or a single word to be removed.
Therefore, this was arranged by the Four Great Kings and spoken directly by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
It is appropriate to memorize and recite only the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta as it was included in the three councils,
and not a "mixed" sutta that was not spoken by the Blessed One and was not included in the three councils.

However, this preparatory rite for the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta mentioned in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* was [prescribed] by the masters of the commentaries with reference to ordinary recitation, study, and so forth.

It was not stated [as a general rule], but rather it was stated with reference to the recitation of mantras by worldly people for the purpose of releasing one who has been seized by non-human beings (amanussa), whether they be householders or those gone forth. For it is said there:
"One seized by a non-human being should be asked, 'Who are you? and so forth."

The *Āṭānāṭiya* protection is not the entire sutta; rather, it is only a portion of the sutta spoken beginning with the words “May there be safety for Vipassī” and occurring four times in relation to the four Great Kings, ending with the words “We pay homage to the Victor Gotama. How is this known? “Then Vessavaṇa... [and so forth].
Having understood the Blessed One’s consent, the Great King spoke this Āṭānāṭiya protection;
for at the conclusion of the aforementioned portion of the sutta, it is handed over with the words: "This, dear sirs, is the Āṭānāṭiya protection.
Therefore, just as tigers and other wild beasts become possessed of powerful, malevolent thoughts when they are plundering their own prey, [so too does this protection guard against such].
Thus, non-human beings become malevolent toward those who seek to release a person captured by them.

Therefore, it should be understood that this preparatory ritual for the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta was taught by the masters of the commentaries for the purpose of dispelling dangers for monks at the time they begin such efforts to secure release.
This is the ornament of the discourse on the analysis of the performance of the Paritta.

20. *Anāmaṭṭha-piṇḍapāta*: Here, "touched" (*āmaṭṭha*) means that which has been touched; "untouched" (*anāmaṭṭha*) is that which is not touched. It is called "alms-food" (*piṇḍapāta*) because it falls down in morsels (*piṇḍa*).
Thus, "untouched alms-food" means alms-food that has not been grasped by the tip [of the tongue] and has not been consumed.
By the phrase "even if it is worth a kahāpaṇa," [the text indicates] that the donors [provided it] with many flavors.
This demonstrates that what has been given with due care is indeed a gift of faith (*saddhādeyya*). Therefore it is said: "There is no misappropriation of a gift of faith.
The intention is this: even if one gives very costly food to one's mother and father after having prepared it with great care and faith, it does not constitute a misappropriation of a gift of faith;
how much less so in the case of food of little value. Having mentioned only the pentad beginning with the mother, [the text proceeds] regarding the preparation of medicine...
Since it was not stated that "it is proper to give [the gift] to another ten [people] as well," it is established that it is not proper to send it to other relatives;

however, because it will be stated later, "But for any guest who has arrived at the monastery," etc., it is proper to give it even to one's own relatives who have arrived at the monastery, by virtue of their common status as guests. "In a bowl" means in a bowl belonging to the Saṅgha.
"In a bowl made of bronze (*kaṃsa*) and so forth" includes a plate (*patta*) here as well. By the phrase "it is not proper," he indicates that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"Of a murderous thief" refers to a notorious thief who seeks to seize a kingdom. The connection is: "even when [the food] is not being given, they become angry, thinking, 'They are not giving it.
Through the failure to obtain both material goods and the Dhamma, a rift arises between oneself and another.
The "reception" (*paṭisanthāra*) is the covering or closing up of a gap. That, moreover, is twofold: by way of material goods (*āmisa*) and by way of the Dhamma (*dhamma*).
With reference to the reception of material goods, it was asked: "To whom should it be done? To whom should it not be done?

In order to clarify the meaning already stated—that it "should indeed be done for a guest"—he said, beginning with "First, for a guest," and so forth. [Regarding the phrase] "whose provisions are exhausted":
By this, he shows that [the recipient] is in a state of misfortune and is an object of compassion.
And by that, it is established that it is not proper to give even to those who are prosperous but are strangers, as they are the opposite of such [objects of compassion].

Having said, "by one who expects nothing in return," the phrase beginning with "human beings indeed" was spoken to show the manner of such expectation. However, it is not proper to give even to those who expect nothing in return if they have not been invited.
Because of the squandering of what has been given in faith, and because there is still expectation [of more], there is also the defiling of families.

"Having cleared away" means having driven off the people who were plundering all around for three *yojanas*. "A variegated carpet of choice cloth" refers to a rug of many kinds, variegated with the excellent forms of women, men, and so forth.
This is the ornament of the discourse on the determination of hospitality (*paṭisanthāra*).
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Ornament of the Discourse on the Determination of Medicines and Other Matters," in the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
4. Discussion on the Determination of Intimation (Viññattivinicchayakathā) 21.
Having thus explained the determination regarding medicines and so forth, he now speaks to explain the determination regarding intimation, beginning with:

“Intimation (viññatti) is requesting (yācanā),” and so on. In this context, *viññatti* is the act of making known (*viññāpanā*); it is the making known that “we have need of this,” which is requesting.
This has been stated. Therefore he said: "‘Request’ means begging. Here, the construction is: “In this regard, this explanation which I shall state must be understood concerning the request.
Regarding the phrase “by cutting off the root”: it means by releasing [the object] from the state of being another’s property and making it one’s own.
For one who requests in this manner, there is both the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for requesting from an unrelated person and the offense of wrong-doing for accepting a slave.
This is because it is rejected in the *Aṭṭhakathā* based on the statement: “He abstains from accepting male and female slaves.

However, for one who asks for a slave from a relative or a place where he has been invited, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) precisely by way of consenting to the severance of the slave’s livelihood.
“One’s own work” refers to the act of killing living beings. And this is stated for the purpose of avoiding the fault of taking life, not for the purpose of avoiding the formal request itself.
The statement "it should not be requested even without making it indefinite" was said for the purpose of showing respect;
however, there is no offense for one who requests manual labor with a pure mind. It is permissible to have it done as one wishes;

thus, even without saying "I request manual labor, please give it," it is allowed, for there is no formal intimation (*viññatti*) when one has someone perform such work while they are already engaged in their own duties.
Thus it is; however, it was spoken by way of analysis for the purpose of showing the *sāmīci* (proper conduct).
"For the purpose of illustrating that everything is allowable" means for the purpose of demonstrating that all things are entirely allowable.

"It is permissible to say, 'Give the root'" is because it was first stated, "We shall give the root," which constitutes a formal request (*viññatti*), and because the word "root" is a general term applicable to both allowable and unallowable objects.
It is stated [in this way] because there is no acceptance of an unallowable thing, since one causes those who have completed their building-work to give what is unallowable speech.
"For the cutting off of the root" is said here because pillars and so forth lack the status of female or male slaves and the like.
"Uninhabited" means unclaimed; the meaning is that it has no owner.

22. And not only...
