[as in the full text] ...but also in such cases as "one desiring to have robes and so forth made," it should be understood that although there is no offense of *dukkaṭa* for requesting manual labor from unrelated weavers who have not been invited to do so when one wishes to have robes made, there are nevertheless *pācittiya* and *dukkaṭa* offenses as appropriate under the training rule concerning having robes woven. Unsuitable coins and the like must not be given.
Even if something is obtained through a permissible means (*kappiyamukha*), it is stated that "it is allowable to give" provided one says, "Give this coin for the purpose of performing work here.
Although no fault is seen in making someone perform work that was previously done [for them], they nevertheless say that it is simply inappropriate.
However, there is no fault in making someone give wages by means of a figurative expression using permissible terminology (*kappiyavohāra*) even for the sake of work already performed.

In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, however, it is stated: “Regarding the rule that ‘unallowable coins and so forth should not be given,’ although it is permissible for one who does not accept unallowable coins and so forth to give them by means of allowable terminology, nevertheless, it is not appropriate;
furthermore, people would think, ‘He has something belonging to him,’ and thus might harass him. Therefore, the giving of unallowable coins and so forth is prohibited.”
It has been stated. "Having cooked it in that very same way" means having cooked it by means of manual labor alone. Even when asked, "What is it, venerable sir?
one is permitted to explain the purpose for which one entered [the village], because it is a question that has been asked.
23. "Conduct" (*vatta*) refers to proper behavior; the intention is that there is no offense. "Having had it made allowable, they should be accepted."

This was stated for the purpose of protecting against the offense of destroying leaves and so forth by using the "seed of a fly" (a tiny insect) on a branch, and also to protect against the offense of not having accepted dust that adheres there when one has disturbed a seed-village;
however, if there is no suspicion of either of these two cases, there is no fault in not acting in that manner.
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, however, it says: "Having had them made allowable, they should be accepted—even if a leaf with dust adhering to a branch falls into the bowl..."
It is stated that even when there is a desire to eat after cutting a branch, it is said [to be permissible] for the sake of pleasant enjoyment.
Regarding rivers and so forth, because the water is not privately owned, it is stated that "it is allowable to say, 'Bring [some]. Regarding [water from] a house... pe ...

"it is not allowable" means that since the water is privately owned, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) due to the formal request; this is the intended meaning. "One should not enjoy what has not been brought."
Even after confessing the *dukkaṭa* incurred through speech or intimation (*viññatti*), for one who continues to use that object, there is a *dukkaṭa* for every act of use;
it is not permitted even for the five types of fellow practitioners (*sahadhammika*).
Furthermore, it is stated as a general rule: "One must not have manual labor performed by shameless monks or novices."
Because it has been so stated, it is not permissible to have any manual labor performed for one's own benefit.
However, as for fanning and such acts that a shameless person performs even when being restrained, there is no fault in that;

furthermore, it is stated in the *Vimativinodanī* that it is permissible to have stūpa-work and the like performed by them. But in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it says: "By shameless persons... [they] must not be employed."
"This was stated with reference to food that is to be swallowed, because it concerns the section on solid food (uttaribhaṅga);
however, regarding external requisites, it is permissible even for those who are shameless (alajjī) to have manual labor performed," so it is said.

And here, since it is stated "by shameless novices (sāmaṇera)," the characteristic of being shameless—namely, "one who intentionally commits an offense"—is applied to one who is fully ordained (upasampanna) by way of the strictest standard (ukkaṭṭhavasena).
Since it is stated [as such] by way of defining [the term] based on its dependence [on the preceding], it should be understood that the characteristic of shamelessness—

even for those who merely claim to be monks, such as novices and others who lack that specific characteristic, including those of immoral conduct— is common to all, and consists simply in not abiding in the practice as it has been established.
24. Furthermore, for one who causes a bull to be brought [to him]... it is a *dukkaṭa* offense. At the moment of the request, it is a *dukkaṭa* due to the act of requesting;

at the moment of acquisition, it is a *dukkaṭa* due to the acceptance of the bulls. For even if a bull is obtained without being requested for one's own sake, it is not permitted to accept it, because it is stated:
"He abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares. Therefore, he said:
“Even from a place where one has been invited by relatives, it is not permissible to ask for [something] so as to cut off the root.

And here, although there is no offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) regarding the act of requesting, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing both in the case of requesting an unsuitable object and in the case of accepting it. “Having protected” means having protected [the cattle] from dangers such as thieves.
“Having tended” means having nourished them with grass, fodder, and so forth. “It should not be accepted” refers to accepting cows and the like for one’s own use.
It was stated because [such a thing] is prohibited.

25. However, it is permissible in a place where one has been invited by a relative; this means that since a cart may be accepted, it is permissible to ask for it on the grounds of cutting off the root [of future need].
"It is permissible as a temporary loan" means that it is permissible in both cases; such is the meaning according to the *Vimativinodanī*.
This has been stated. However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is said:
“‘Give me a cart…’ … ‘It is not permitted’ means that it is not permitted to say, ‘Give me a cart,’ by way of cutting off the very root [of the request].

‘It is permitted for a temporary period’ means that it is permitted to ask for anything after making it a temporary loan. He says, “The same principle applies to axes and so forth,” because even personal items such as axes are permitted.

And in the case of creepers (*valli*) and so forth that are owned by others, this same method should be applied. The phrase "only when it is sufficient for a heavy article" is said with reference to formal solicitation (*viññatti*);

however, regarding taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), if one takes even a blade of grass belonging to another with a thieving mind, it is indeed theft (*avahāra*), and one must be dealt with according to the value of the article. In the expression "creepers and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) [includes other such items].
The inclusion of the items mentioned in the Pāli—namely, bamboo, muñja grass, reeds, and clay—should be understood here.

Furthermore, in a place where substances such as yellow orpiment or vermilion are of high value even in small quantities, they are considered "heavy goods" (garubhaṇḍa) even if they are less than the size of a palm fruit;
it is not permitted to ask for them.
26. *Sāti-viññatti* (Direct Intimation). Among these, *parikathā* (indirect intimation) is speech by way of a circuitous expression, such as saying, "The lodging is crowded," and so forth.
*Obhāsa* (hinting) is speech that makes one's intention clear without speaking directly, such as saying, "Is it not fitting for the monks to have a mansion?
and so forth. [It also includes] performing ground preparation and so on for the sake of obtaining lodgings and the like.

Making a sign for the arising of a requisite is called *nimittakamma*. Since the modes of intimation (*viññatti*) and so forth have been shown in relation to three requisites, he asks, "But how is it in the case of the requisite for the sick?

and says, "But as for the requisite for the sick," and so on. Furthermore, regarding medicine that has arisen in such a way, is it permissible to consume it once the illness has subsided, or is it not?
In this regard, the Vinaya-dharas [say]: "By the Blessed One, under the heading of 'sickness'..."
Some say, "The door for its consumption has been opened; therefore, it is permissible to eat even when one is not ill, and no offense occurs.
However, those learned in the Suttas say, "Even though there is no offense, it nevertheless disturbs one's livelihood;
therefore, for one established in the practice of austerity (sallekha), it is not permissible, as it disturbs that austerity."
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Ornament of the Discourse on the Determination of Intimation," in the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
5. Discourse on the Determination of the Gathering of Families (Kulasaṅgahavinicchayakathā) 27.

Having thus explained the determination of formal gestures (viññatti), he now speaks of the determination of the gathering of families (kulasaṅgaha) with the words beginning, “The gathering of families.
In this context, *saṅgaha* means gathering; the gathering of families is *kulasaṅgaha*. It refers to laypeople, such as those who provide the requisites (paccaya-dāyaka).
It is an act of assistance. Here, the word *saṅgaha* has the sense of assistance, as in the expression "support for one’s wife and children.
28. In that context, *koṭṭana* means cutting it oneself; *koṭṭāpana* means having others cut it by saying, "Cut this.
*Āḷiyā bandhana* means binding it all around so that water remains at the base of the tree.

"Of water" means of unallowable water; since "sprinkling with allowable water" will be explained separately, and since it will be explained that for the purpose of planting in an arama or similar place, sprinkling with allowable water and so forth is permissible even when using unallowable terminology as well as allowable terminology, a distinction is made here too and sprinkling with allowable water and so forth is shown separately. And herein, what is unallowable water?
What, then, is allowable water (*kappiya-udaka*)? Water containing living beings is unallowable water; water free of living beings is allowable water.

How is this known? Because of the statement: "Whosoever, a monk knowingly sprinkles or causes grass or clay to be sprinkled with water containing living beings, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Just as physical actions such as pounding or digging [are defined by their nature].

Since [the term] is included within unallowable speech (*akappiyavohāra*), it is likewise so in the case of allowable speech (*kappiyavohāra*) such as straightening a dry bedstead; thus he says, "straightening a dry bedstead.
By the phrase "washing hands, feet, and face, bathing, and sprinkling water," he also demonstrates by this other way of speaking that it refers specifically to the sprinkling of allowable water.
Regarding unallowable speech, there is also the act of doing it oneself by means of pounding, digging, and so forth.

How is it included? It should be understood that "unfit transaction" (*akappiyavohāra*) refers to everything—including both performing and causing others to perform what is unfit—rather than merely the verbal expression of the unfit.
The same principle applies to "fit transaction" (*kappiyavohāra*). By the phrase "straightening the dry stalk," the removal of old leaves and so forth is also included.

It should be seen. Having placed the spades and other tools on the ground, one takes them by hand from that spot; because the spot itself becomes more clearly manifest, it is called "illumination" (*obhāsa*).
29. Desiring to establish the *Mahāpaccarivāda*, he speaks later. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of a grove" (*vanatthāya*), some read it as "for the sake of a fence" (*vatatthāya*);
for them, the meaning is "for the sake of an enclosure" (*vatiatthāya*). This is stated likewise in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*: "Those who plant orchards... (*ārāmaropā*).
However, that [matter] must be investigated based on the statement: "Those men who plant trees are makers of bridges.
To show that even in the case of unallowable terminology (*akappiya-vohāra*), certain things are permissible, he said: "And not only the rest," and so forth.
"Any kind of bedrock" means either dry bedrock or non-dry bedrock. By the phrase "to sprinkle allowable water," it is shown that one may also say, "Sprinkle allowable water."
He shows that it is permissible. By the phrase "it is also permissible for one to plant it oneself," it is established that it is also permissible to say, "Plant it.
30. "Both a *pācittiya* and a *dukkaṭa*": there is a *pācittiya* offense due to the digging of the earth, and a *dukkaṭa* offense due to the purpose of winning over a family.
"By means of improper speech" means by such improper speech as, "Dig this; plant this. "Only a *dukkaṭa*" [refers to the offense incurred].
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the purpose of supporting a family. "In both cases" means on ground that is either allowable or unallowable.
"In all instances" means in the case of trees planted for the purpose of supporting a family, for personal enjoyment, or for the sake of a monastery and so forth.

"Also an offense of wrong-doing" means that it is not only an offense of expiation (pācittiya). "By what is allowable" means by allowable water. "Of those two only" refers to supporting a family and personal enjoyment. "An offense of wrong-doing."

In the case of sprinkling oneself for the purpose of supporting one's family, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) whether one sprinkles it oneself or causes it to be sprinkled by means of either a permissible expression or an impermissible expression.

In the case of sprinkling oneself for the purpose of personal consumption, there is an offense of wrong-doing for both sprinkling it oneself and causing it to be sprinkled by means of an impermissible expression.

"Due to the multiplicity of applications" means that in the act of doing it oneself, there is a multiplicity of verbal application (*vacīpayoga*) alongside the physical application (*kāyapayoga*) in having it done.
"Abundance of offenses should be understood": here, when one sprinkles oneself, the number of offenses should be understood according to the count of the stream's interruptions.

However, when causing another to sprinkle, for one who repeatedly commands, there is an offense for every word; but for one who has commanded only once, there is only a single offense even if many sprinklings occur.
Regarding "plucking [leaves] entails a dukkaṭa and a pācittiya": there is a dukkaṭa for the sake of supporting a family, and a pācittiya for the destruction of living plants.

"For another purpose" means for the sake of worshipping a shrine (*vatthupūjā*) and so forth when plucking [the flowers]. "Once commanded" means commanded by means of an improper expression (*akappiyavohāra*).

"It is indeed a *pācittiya*" means that because he was commanded by means of an improper expression, it is a *pācittiya* offense under the training rule concerning living plants (*bhūtagāma-sikkhāpada*).
However, for one who causes [flowers] to be plucked for the sake of worshipping a shrine and so forth using a proper expression (*kappiyavacana*), there is no offense at all.
31. A "knot-made" (ganthima) garland is one produced by knotting. This same method applies to the others as well.

"It is not allowable" means that for one who makes or causes to be made [a gift] according to the stated method for the purpose of supporting families or for the purpose of honoring the site (*vatthupūjā*) and so forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "It is allowable" means it is allowable for the purpose of honoring the site and so forth;
however, even for one who causes it to be made using appropriate terminology (*kappiyavohāra*) for the purpose of supporting families, it is allowable.
It is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "In the same manner as before" refers to the method stated by the words "of a bhikkhu," and so forth.
The connection is: "she places flowers by piercing them through the thorns tied to the canopy of the Dhamma-seat.

It is said to be "like an umbrella over an umbrella" because it is hung after being pierced layer upon layer to form a shape resembling an umbrella. [This is explained] by the passage beginning with "in the trunk of a plantain tree," and so forth.
Referring to all that has been stated, it is said, "That is indeed too coarse";
the meaning is that in every case, both when one acts oneself or causes another to act through improper speech, it is merely an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Because this [prohibition] is illustrative, some maintain that even tying a rope for the purpose of hanging flower garlands or ornaments and so forth is not permitted, as it includes even tying a thorn for the purpose of piercing flowers.
So they say. Others, however, say: "Because it is specified as 'a thorn' for the purpose of piercing flowers, it is not permissible to tie a thorn for that purpose;
and this is according to the authority of the Aṭṭhakathā. This should be investigated and then accepted.
What is called a "flower-receptacle" (pupphapaṭicchaka) is a support for flowers made from ivory and so forth. This too, as well as a peg (nāgadantaka), must have holes.
It should be understood thus: *asokapiṇḍiyā* means a cluster of *asoka* branches or flowers.
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: "*asokapiṇḍiyā* means a cluster of *asoka* blossoms. Regarding the *dhammarajju*:

it is a cord used for tying [a structure] after having been threaded through a cetiya or a Bodhi tree for the purpose of attaching flowers. In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, regarding the *dhammarajju*...
It is said: “Having surrounded the Nāma Cetiya and other such monuments, there is a binding cord between them and the [main] rope for the purpose of inserting flowers;
or rather, it is said that one binds them in this way for the purpose of inserting flowers inside a loosely wound coil.
*Matthakadāma* means a garland hanging from the top of the Dhamma-seat and so forth. *Tesaṃ yeva* means of those very same [flowers], such as blue lotuses and the like.
The flower stalk is blown by the wind; having split it open, the flower remains attached to the stalk, which is itself still attached to the *vāka* grass.
Because of this, the flower does not fall under the category of "seed-plant" (*bījagāma*), as it has not entered into the five types of seeds, just like a leaf.
Therefore, there is no fault in damaging it even without having it prepared as allowable (*kappiya*). And as for the blooming of the bud even after it has been cut—

Even that [opening] does not possess the characteristic of growth because it lacks extreme youth; rather, for a mature bud, when the moisture of the leaves has been exhausted, the very state of separation is its blossoming.
For this reason, the blossoming of a severed bud is seen to be inferior to the blossoming of an unsevered bud, or it appears as if withered.
And as for the non-withering that occurs when a withered [bud] comes into contact with water—
Even that [betel leaf] does not possess the characteristic of growth found in betel leaves and the like.

Furthermore, nowhere in the Pāḷi or its commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) is there mention of flowers being rendered "allowable" (*kappiya*). Therefore, it is understood that a flower is entirely seedless; this should be accepted after careful investigation.
Because it is stated, "as if in a pouch," the flower may be placed in a pouch, or bound in something similar to a pouch, wherever appropriate.
It is established that it is permissible to place [the flowers] inside the robe (*cīvara*). However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated:
"Regarding 'a saffron robe placed on the shoulder,' this refers to the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭī*) placed upon the shoulder; for that could indeed be tied in such a manner.
And by this, it is also permitted to tie another similar saffron robe or cloth in the manner described and place the flowers therein."
"It is established that it is permissible. Because it is similar to being placed in a shoulder-bag or a side-pouch, what is called 'wrapped' does not arise;
therefore, they say that it is also permissible to insert [the flowers] here and there within a loose binding.
This was said with reference to binding with ropes and the like; however, binding below the stalk [of the flower] is not permitted. Only for the flower itself...
However, it is indeed permissible to bind them with undamaged cords.

Regarding the phrase "it should be seen on a cloth of flowers," this is said with reference to the filling out of a long floral pattern for one making a cloth of flowers by means of taking away and bringing back [the threads];
whereas taking away [the threads] across [the width] is called "weaving" (*vāyima*), not the former. "The place of the former... [etc.]

Because it is stated generally as “he exceeds [the limit],” there is indeed an offense for one who exceeds by way of encircling, whether he causes the previous tip of the flowers to be touched or not.
“It is permissible to bind” means it is permissible to bind with a tip of thread or bark-cord that is devoid of flowers.
“Having carried it once and encircled” refers to the previously mentioned encircling of the cetiya and so forth.

This was said with reference to making a flower-canopy; therefore, when one who is encircling a shrine or a Bodhi tree has finished encircling it once and reaches the starting point, he should hand it over to another, and that person, having likewise encircled it once, should do the same.
Furthermore, when one making a flower-canopy has carried it [to the destination], he should hand it over to another, and that person should likewise do the same.
It must be done. They say that even if only two monks stand on both sides and carry it by turns, it is indeed permissible.
"Filled by others" means stretched out lengthwise. "To be carried" means to be carried crosswise; however, that is not permitted even once.
"By those placing flowers" refers to natural, unstrung flowers, even if they are made to touch one another.

Regarding one who places [it]: they say that when placing a flower garland on the ground for the purpose of worship, it is not permissible to place it by doubling it over—whether touching the ground or not touching it.
32. *Ghaṭikadāmaolambaka*: a hanging ornament at the lower part, shaped like a water-pot (*ghaṭikā*), or having the form of a wooden water-pot.
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, however, it is stated: "A 'pendant of a chain of bells' means a pair of twin chains of bells fitted with bell-shaped ornaments at their ends.
In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, however, it is stated: "'A pendant of a chain of bells' is written as 'a pendant of twin chains.
Yet, each individual chain ought to be hung by tying it precisely at the tip of the cord that emerges from it; thus, there are two flower garlands.
Even for one who wishes to join [the threads], it is permissible to join one end of the thread to the other end once the previous end has been brought out.
"Encircling with a string of garlands in the shape of a half-moon" means encircling by filling [the space] through repeatedly drawing back and forth a string of garlands in the shape of a half-moon;
thus, because that [subsequent part] enters into the previous [part], this too is in the shape of a half-moon.
It is not permissible to complete [the arrangement] by repeatedly taking it away and bringing it back.
However, they say that it is permissible to take up the garland-string once when forming the shape of a half-moon.

Regarding "making a flower wreath," they say that here too, it is not permissible to make it all at once even after grasping the ends of the thread. This refers to a ball made of thread; [it is forbidden for] balls, rough leaves, and wreaths.
Because it has been rejected, they say that even a garland made of cloth and other such materials is not permitted, as it conforms to what is unallowable (*akappiya*).

"He gives what belongs to another" means it is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); this is said with reference to one who takes what belongs to another through trust and then gives it away. "A grave offense" (*thullaccaya*)—in this case, there is also the forfeiture of the object (*bhaṇḍadeyya*).

33. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "for the purpose of honoring the physical remains": this shows that even when giving flowers to one's parents, they must be given solely for the purpose of honoring the remains.

However, because it was stated only as "for the purpose of adornment" or "for the purpose of worshipping the *śivaliṅga* and so forth," it is permissible to sell these [flowers] to one's parents for their livelihood; but for other relatives, they may only be used temporarily.
It is permissible to give it. To whom? To anyone—whether a relative or a non-relative.

"By the novice monks themselves" is said for the purpose of releasing them from their domestic duties. "The others" refers to those who are non-relatives. Even by those novice monks, it should be brought [to the donors] under the heading of service to their teachers and preceptors.
It is permissible to give half a share to the novice monks who have arrived; this refers to what belongs to the Saṅgha.
It is stated thus because, since novices residing within the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*) also have a share in the acquisition, they too receive half a portion;
"small" (*cūḷaka*) means half of that half—a designation for a fourth part. The statement, "the novices...
set it aside," is said with reference to what is unguarded and unprotected. (From the *Sāratthadīpanī*).

However, it is stated that this was said "with reference to what is not to be shared according to the year of seniority. Regarding the phrase "here and there," it means either on the path or at the shrine courtyard (cetiyangaṇa).
The statement "they are not permitted to have novices give [the offering]" is said because it would be as if the novices were being made to perform lay-work;
it is not, however, because giving flowers is not permitted even for novices. And so it is said: "by oneself," and so forth.

For that would not indeed be called a gift of flowers. If giving to those who have arrived in such a manner were to be called a gift of flowers, then it would not be permitted even for novices to give.

"By themselves" means by the novices themselves. Regarding the phrase "taking rice porridge, food, and so forth," because this was said with reference to the preparation of rice porridge, food, and so on for the sake of the monks, it is stated that "it is not allowed."
It was stated without distinction. By saying "stated without distinction," he shows that it is not permissible for anyone at all [to do so]. 35. "In the manner already stated" means:
first, in the case of one's mother and father, it is permissible to give [the requisites] even by taking them oneself, or by having them taken, or by inviting them, or by having them invited;
however, for other relatives, one must have them invited. And when having them taken for one's mother and father, it must be by means of relatives who are novices (*sāmaṇera*).
"It should be caused to be brought. But as for the others, if they themselves desire it, it is permissible.

This method stated regarding the giving of flowers is extended by analogy to the giving of fruit; therefore, it is also permissible to give fruit to one's mother and father by having it brought or by causing it to be brought, but for other relatives only after having them summoned.
Now, [regarding] "he who, having brought it or caused it to be brought... [gives it] out of a sense of lordship..."

Having condensed the method stated for the giving of flowers under the heading of a *thullaccaya* offense, he says "but for the sake of gathering [support from] families," etc., while demonstrating it in the context of the giving of fruit.
"Those whose provisions are exhausted" is said with reference to newcomers (*āgantuka*).
"By a limit of fruit" means either by a limit of fruit such as, "this many fruits are to be given," or by a limit of trees.
“[The fruit] should be given from these trees”—this refers to the delimitation by trees. However, even when the trees have been delimited, if one says, “The fruits here are excellent;
take them from here,” it is called forming a connection with a family (*kulasaṅgaha*);
therefore, he said, “but one should not speak thus. “Tree bark” (*rukkhacchallī*) means the tree’s skin; that is considered “an article for distribution” (*bhājanīyabhaṇḍa*).
It has been stated. By "in the manner stated" he shows that the maintenance of families occurs in the same way as described regarding flowers, fruits, and so forth.
36. Carrying messages and counter-messages for various householders between villages, districts, and so on, is "running on foot" (*jaṅghapesaniya*).
Therefore he said: "The errand of householders is the work of carrying messages. The work of a messenger is *dūteyya*. First...
"Even if one does not convey the message... [omission] ...a *dukkaṭa* offense for every step"—this was said with reference to going with the intention, "I shall deliver his message.
However, if one refuses that message and, standing out of compassion, goes and delivers a suitable message oneself, there is no offense. And this applies to laypeople regarding a permissible message.
"It is right to remove him" is the connection [of the sentence]. "By these eight acts of defiling a family" refers to the following as previously stated:
giving flowers, giving fruits, giving powder, giving clay, giving tooth-sticks, giving bamboo, giving leaves, and sending messages on foot.
"One who has had the act of banishment performed against him" means one against whom the act of banishment has been carried out on account of defiling a family.
37. By the phrase "or on the plane of training" (sekkhabhūmiyaṃ vā), he includes the planes of meditative absorption (jhānabhūmi) as well.

"Of the three kinds of seclusion" refers to the three types of seclusion consisting of seclusion of body, mind, and material requisites. Because walking for alms ends with the meal, it is said: "until the conclusion of the meal.
Even for one who returns after eating, if they again perform such acts as adjusting their robes while making a formal aspiration according to the method already described, [it is included].
"It should be understood as a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) alone.
Thus ends the "Ornament of the Determination of the Grouping of Families," which is the "Ornament of the Vinaya" serving as a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
The Fifth Chapter.
6. Discourse on the Determination of Fish and Meat. 38.
Having thus explained the determination regarding the inclusion of families, [the author] now explains the determination regarding fish and meat: "Regarding fish and meat..."
The passage beginning with “panā” has been stated. Therein, it is called *maccho* because it dies as soon as it is placed on dry land, or because it is killed by fishermen (*kevaṭṭa*) and others.

That which belongs to a fish is *macchaṃ*; that which is rubbed (*masiyate*) or touched (*āmasiyate*) is *maṃsaṃ*. *Macchamaṃsāni* refers to both fish and meat; the construction is that the detailed analysis regarding these fish and meats should be understood in this way.
Regarding the phrase “by the inclusion of ‘fish’”: [The text continues: ...here... (Note: The provided source text ends mid-sentence. The translation above reflects the portion available.)
No selection (*niddhāraṇa*) should be made here. The word *pana* has the sense of an alternative position;

the meaning is that after the determination regarding daytime rest and so forth, another determination regarding fish and meat is to be understood. "Grasping" (*gahaṇa*) means that by which something is grasped. What is it? It is sound.
"Fish-grasping" (*macchaggahaṇa*) means the grasping [indicated] by the word "fish"; the meaning is "by that fish-grasping," i.e., by the word "fish. Regarding meats...
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "they are not allowable" (*akappiyāni*): here, human flesh is prohibited because it belongs to the same species as humans.

The flesh of elephants and horses is prohibited because they are royal mounts; that of dogs and snakes because they are loathsome; and the rest because they are wild beasts—this should be understood as being prohibited for the purpose of freeing the monks from obstacles.
"Pure in three respects" means pure in three ways, by three aspects, through three reasons, consisting of what is seen, heard, and suspected;

the meaning is that it is liberated. In this context, what is not seen and not heard should be understood as such because they are not objects for eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness respectively.
But how is what is not suspected to be known? To this he says: "What is not suspected..."
Regarding the passage beginning with "panā," the meaning is that having recognized the three things to be suspected,

one should understand the non-suspected state by way of their opposites. Now, in order to show in detail those three things to be suspected, as well as the procedure to be performed by the bhikkhus when such suspicion exists,
and the necessity of performing that procedure when there is no such suspicion, he says "kathaṃ" and so forth.
In that context, what is suspected after having seen it is called "suspected by sight. What is suspected after having heard it is called "suspected by hearing.
What is suspected through conjecture and inference without having seen or heard it is called "suspected apart from both.
These three types, by virtue of their commonality as suspicion, constitute one category; that which is free from these is "not suspected."
Thus, fish meat that has not been seen, heard of, or suspected is "pure in three respects.
A "net" is a device for catching fish; a "snare" is a device for catching deer. It is "allowable" (*kappati*) if, by their word, suspicion is removed—it is permissible [to eat it];
however, it is not permissible to treat that word as a mere pretext (*lesakappa*). For this very reason, he will say: "And where one is free from doubt..."
“Whatever exists, all that is allowable. Regarding “meat that has come into circulation”: this refers to dead meat that has been brought into circulation for sale in marketplaces and the like.
Regarding “for auspicious occasions and so forth,” the word “and so forth” (ādi) includes offerings to guests, hospitality, and similar events.

In the phrase “not prepared specifically for the monks,” the particle *eva* is used in the sense of exclusion; it should be connected as “not prepared specifically for the monks alone” (*bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya akatameva*).
Therefore, it should be understood that even if [the formula] is composed by mixing [the terms] "of the monks" and "of auspicious things" and so forth, it is not permissible.
Some, however, say, "It is permissible if one takes the restriction according to how it stands [in the text]," but that is not sound.
And regarding the phrase "where one is free from doubt," this expresses the total absence of suspicion even when [the formula] is made for the sake of the monks.
39. To clarify this very point, the passage beginning with "But if" was spoken. "It is permissible for others" means it is permissible for those who do not know;
however, in this case, there is an offense even for one who knows. "Those very ones" refers to those specifically intended when the meat was prepared.

In order to show the distinction between the consumption of meat prepared specifically for oneself and the consumption of unallowable meat, the passage beginning with "But unallowable meat" was spoken. Regarding the former...

There is an offense when one is conscious of the nature of the object, and no offense in the other case when one is unconscious of it. Therefore he said: "Even for one who eats unallowable meat without knowing it to be so, there is indeed an offense.

Because of the statement, "At the time of consumption, having asked [the donor], or having taken it with the intention 'I shall consume it after asking,' one must consume it only after having asked," there is an offense at the very moment of receiving for one who receives unallowable meat without knowing it to be so.
The non-offense is established. For it is stated that an offense occurs only for one who consumes [the food] without knowing [it is forbidden].
By saying "they say it is allowable," he shows that there is no offense.
Thus ends the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
The Sixth Chapter: The Ornament of the Discourse on the Determination of Fish Meat.
7. The Discourse on the Determination of What Is Untouchable.
40. Having thus explained the determination regarding fish and meat, he now speaks the words beginning with “anāmāsa” in order to explain the determination regarding what is not to be touched.
In this context, *āmāsa* means that which is to be touched; *anāmāsa* means that which is not to be touched, the meaning being that it is not to be grasped.

*Pāripanthikā* means those that cause agitation, which is to say, those that constitute obstacles. The phrase “a mother being carried away by the current of a river” is stated for the purpose of showing the upper limit of the offense.
It has been stated. However, they say that for one who acts toward other women with the intention of compassion, following the same method as prescribed for a mother, there is no fault at all.
Yet, there are also those who say that because it is specified "toward a mother," it is not permitted toward others.
In this context, one should not say, "Take [this]," for touching with a body-part connected to the body out of domestic affection constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.

This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). However, in the case of one who is unable to grasp her clothing or other belongings due to distress, even if one says "grasp them," because she has fallen into a state of helplessness and is sinking in the water, there is no offense even for one who—out of compassion and without considering it improper to touch her—grabs her by the hair or elsewhere and pulls her out with the intention of saving her.
For it is not right to remain indifferent toward a mother who is dying.
It is permissible. The same principle applies even to a woman who is not a relative.

The word "mother" is used to demonstrate that even for one's own senior mother, eating together is not permitted; however, as for what must be done for her, there is no offense even when doing so for other women as well, because there is no distinction in their status as being unsuitable for such a meal.
*Tiṇaṇḍupaka* refers to a head-covering made from the roots of *hirivera* and other plants for the purpose of hair ornamentation.

*Tālapaṇṇamuddikā* refers to a finger-ring made from palm leaves. By this, it is established that everything made of palm leaves and the like—such as waist-bands, earrings, and so forth—is not permitted.
*Parivattetvā* means having removed [the item] from its status as one's own lower garment (*nivāsana*) or upper robe (*pārupana*).
"Having dedicated it for the purpose of robes" is what is meant. "He places it at the foot [of the monk] for the purpose of robes" is merely an illustration;
it is likewise permissible for the purpose of a rug, a canopy, and so forth. It is also permissible to touch it temporarily for the purpose of worship and the like.

"A head-ornament made of *sīsa* wood and ivory needles"—this refers both to a head-ornament made of strips of cloth (*paṭapilotika*) fashioned from *sīsa* wood for the purpose of decorating the head, and...
"Two or three such as the ivory needle, etc. This indicates the respective purposes:
the *sīsapasādhana* is to be taken for the purpose of the *sipāṭika* equipment, and the ivory needle for the purpose of the needle equipment.
Having tied up a mass of hair, the needle made for the purpose of inserting [the hair] crosswise therein is the "ivory needle for hair-ornamentation"; thus, it is treated as a single item.

The term *sipāṭikasūciupakaraṇaṃ* should be construed as follows: it is the needle-case (*sipāṭika*) itself, which must be carried, together with the needles to be inserted therein, serving as the requisite tool for various tasks;
or alternatively, the construction may be made thus:

[the phrase refers to] the needle-case and the tools consisting of the needles. A "cloth-image" (*potthakarūpaṃ*) is one made of plaster and the like, having the form of female animals belonging to the animal realm, which constitute grounds for an offense of defeat (*pārājika*).

Even that which is "not to be touched" (anāmāsa) is the same. Having displayed the forms of women, it is permissible to use a building, a wall, or the like—even without touching the form of a woman—for such things are "not to be touched";
provided there is no lust for physical contact, there is no fault in touching them with something connected to the body. Regarding the phrase "having broken":
here, one should break it with some instrument such as a staff, without grasping it with the hand.
And herein, since it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā that even touching [a snake] with a staff, stones, or the like constitutes breaking [the rule],
and since it is stated in the Pāḷi that there is no offense for one whose intention is liberation in times of distress even when touching [it],

one may take hold of various things such as snakes by warding them off with a staff and the like, in order to release creatures seized by predatory animals such as female snakes, or [to save] a mother and so forth.

The meaning to be understood here is that when [a woman] is being weighed in water, it is permissible to take hold of her with a cloth or similar object if she cannot be held, and to lift her up out of compassion by grasping her hair or other parts of her body. Regarding this, the *Vimativinodanī* states:
"In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, the statement 'she must not be touched' was spoken with reference to an object that is not being weighed; this is our own position."
41. "Having resolved upon the path" means having generated the perception of it as "this is the path.

"Having prepared [a seat] and giving [it]" is said by way of formal courtesy; however, when they say, "Please sit after having prepared a seat," it is permissible to sit after one has prepared it oneself.
In that context, "birth stories" (jātakāni) refers to those told without omitting anything, in their very state as actual events.
[The fruits] remain [unripe]. Because it is stated, "by one playing," there is no offense for one who touches [them] when a requisite condition exists;

and this is said with reference to what belongs to a layperson. However, as for what belongs to a monk, it is not permitted to touch it at all even if it is fit for use, because it constitutes a bad practice (*durupaciṇṇa*).
And here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "tāla, panasa, etc.," there is the inclusion of coconut, cucumber, *tipusa*, bottle-gourd, pumpkin, *pussaphala*, and *eḷāluka* fruits.

The inclusion [of these items] is to be understood. Since it has been stated, "In this context, touching even those very things mentioned as fruits with the intention of playing is not permitted," it is permissible to touch stones, gravel, and so forth, even with the intention of playing.

The phrase "I will give them to those who are not fully ordained" is said with reference to taking them without having formally accepted them. However, in the case of taking them after having formally accepted them for one's own benefit...
There is no fault because of the absence of the state of being untouchable.
42. *Muttā* (pearls) refers to the eight kinds of pearls originating from the frontal globes of elephants. For thus there are eight sources of pearls:
the elephant’s frontal globe, the boar’s tusk, the serpent’s head, the cloud (*valāhaka*), the bamboo, the fish’s head, the conch, and the oyster shell. Among these—
Those born from elephant frontal globes are yellow in color and radiant. Those born from boar tusks are like the color of boar tusks.
Those born from serpent heads are blue and other colors, very pure and rounded. Those born from clouds are brilliant and difficult to distinguish;
they remain dispelling the darkness during the night and serve as objects of enjoyment for the gods. Those born from bamboo have a color similar to that of *karakā* fruit. They are not...
The *bhāsurā* [gems] grow only in places frequented by non-human beings (*amanussa*), and those bamboos are likewise. The *macchasirajā* [gems] have a color like the back of a *pāṭhīna* fish;
they are round, light, and radiant, yet devoid of power, and those fish grow only in the midst of the ocean.
The *saṅkhajā* [gems] have a skin-color like the interior of a conch shell; though they may be the size of a *kola* fruit, they too are indeed devoid of power.

Shell-born pearls are endowed with specific lusters and exist in various shapes. Thus, among the eight kinds of pearls according to their origin, those born from fish, conchs, and shells are oceanic. Some snake-born pearls are also oceanic, while others are not.
Since, for the most part, only oceanic pearls are seen in the world—and even among those, only shell-born ones, while other types appear only rarely—[the former are considered preeminent].
Therefore, in the *Sammohavinodanī*, it is stated: "Pearls are ocean pearls.
"Gems" refers to all gems other than beryl (*veḷuriya*), such as the various kinds of *jotirasa* and so forth. "Beryl" is a gem with the color of fresh *veluva* wood;
some also say it has the color of a cat's eye (*majjārakkhi-maṇḍala*). "Conch" refers to the ocean conch. "Crystal" is the color of a mung bean.
An exceedingly smooth black stone. They say that even stones of red, white, or other colors, though well-polished, are untouchable if they have not attained the designation of "jewel" (*maṇi*).
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: "'Conch' refers to the ocean conch; 'stone' refers to all stones, including the distinctions of black stone, pale stone, white stone, and so forth.
"Coral" is a naturally red gem produced from the ocean. "Silver" refers to the various types such as the *kahāpaṇa* coin, the *māsa* coin, and others.
Everything remaining that has been mentioned, beginning with lac and resin, is included under "gold" (*jātarūpa*). "Gold" means gold. "Ruby" (*lohitanka*) means a red gem.
"Masāragalla" means a mottled-colored gem; some also call it "emerald" (*marakata*).
"For the sake of the price of goods" means for the sake of the price of bowls, robes, and so forth. "Of leprosy" is merely an illustration. By that...
It is indeed permissible for the purpose of curing any disease whatsoever that needs to be pacified.
Regarding the statement, “Pearls are permissible even when not perforated for the purpose of medicine,” this is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.

Because pearls ground and compounded for the purpose of medicine lose their status as a treasure (*ratana*), there is no regard for them as having the form of a treasure even at the moment of taking them; thus, “for the purpose of medicine... [is said].
It is said, “It is allowable. However, as long as those pearls remain in the form of gems, they are not allowed to be touched.
Likewise, it is indeed allowable to grind other precious stones and take them for the purpose of compounding medicine.
But gold and silver, even for the purpose of compounding medicine, are not allowed to be accepted [directly]; however, they are allowable if prepared by householders.
Even if medicine has been given, if it remains in the form of gold or the like, and can be separated [from its medicinal state], such medicine is not permitted.
It is permitted only if it has reached a state where it is no longer designated as such (abbohārikatta).

Because it is stated, "taking into account natural crystals," it should be understood that sun-crystals, moon-crystals, and so forth—natural stones—are included within the category of gems (maṇi) alone. "Mined" (ākaramutta) means merely extracted from a mine.
By the phrase "it is permissible to accept for the sake of merchandise," it is shown that it is likewise permissible to touch it.
"Made by boiling" means made by glass-makers through boiling.
It should be construed as: "a conch shell for blowing, one that has been cleaned and perforated, and one mixed with gems. "Perforated" and so forth refers to one in which holes have been made.
"Variegated with gems" (*ratanamissa*) means variegated with gold creepers and the like, and inlaid with gems such as pearls.
By this, he shows that another object, though not made of bone, which is mixed with gems, is also "untouchable" (*anāmāsa*). The same principle applies to stone as well.
By the term "counted as water-vessels" (*pānīyasaṅkha*), it is established that vessels made of shell, fashioned in the shape of bowls and so forth, are permitted for monks to accept.
They know [the rule] by setting aside those mixed with gems. They make it green like a mung bean (*muggavaṇṇa*) only when mixed with gems, and not otherwise;
thus he said, "green like a mung bean. This means that what is green like a mung bean is permissible only when mixed with gems; otherwise, it is not allowed.
"The rest" refers to the remaining stones, setting aside those mixed with gems.
"From the seed onwards" means from the relic-stone onwards. "The golden cetiya" refers to the relic casket.
"He refused" means that he refused because it was sent with the instruction, "Take this for yourselves," rather than saying, "Take this for the purpose of enshrining the relics.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: "'He refused' [refers to] the golden relic casket, the image of the Buddha and so forth..."
And it is said: "Because making it one's own constitutes an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya). "A golden bubble" means a gold star.
Because it is stated, "in the place where money is discarded," it is said that it is permissible for the discarder of money to touch and discard gold and silver.
"To play with" means to touch and move it here and there. This is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
It has been stated: "It is permissible to remove only refuse. Whether they be cowherds or others, it is permissible to clear away refuse even by wiping it with the hand;
"it is likewise permissible to wipe away dirt," as stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: "It is permissible to remove only refuse, whether they be cowherds or others..."
It is said: "Some say that it is permissible to remove rubbish by wiping with the hand, and even permissible to wash away dirt;
however, this does not accord with the Aṭṭhakathā because it is similar to mere playfulness. How does it not accord?
In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is stated that the guardians of the shrine-hall were standing at the place where money was discarded; thus, it refers specifically to their playfulness.
It was permitted [only] for them, not for others; therefore, the statement in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* that "whether they be cowherds or others" does not accord with it.
In the *Kurundi*, however, even that is rejected; only this much is permitted: that it is allowable to remove only refuse from a golden cetiya.
Therefore, because it is stated with such a restriction, [the phrase] "even having wiped it with the hand" [is used].
Furthermore, the statement that "it is even permissible to wipe away the dirt" does not accord with the Kurundi-Ṭīkā; therefore, this matter should be investigated.
*Ārakūṭaloha* is a specific type of base metal (kittimaloha) with the color of gold. For there are three kinds of base metal:
bell-metal (*kaṃsaloha*), brass (*vaṭṭaloha*), and *ārakūṭaloha*. Among these, bell-metal is made by mixing [copper] with three parts of tin.
*Ārakūṭaloha* is the name for round metal made by mixing copper with lead; it is copper colored with mercury and tin, known as *ārakūṭa*.
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: "The *ārakūṭa* is made by mixing natural mercury with copper.

However, because it is said to belong to the category of gold (*jātarūpagatika*), some maintain that it constitutes an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*) for one who acquires it among precious metals.

However, because it was not counted [in the formal calculation], there is no offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*); rather, it should be understood that there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for both the touching and the acceptance.
"All is allowable" means the intention is that the use of the aforementioned requisites for lodgings made of gold and so forth—by way of touching, guarding, and so on—is in every respect allowable.
Therefore he said, "Therefore," and so forth. "In the context of the exposition of the Dhamma and Vinaya for bhikkhus."
Because it has been stated [that way], it should be understood that only those lodgings made of gold and so forth belonging to the Saṅgha, as well as the requisites for lodgings, are permitted;
those belonging to an individual (puggalika) are not. "It is permissible to look after them" is said because they are connected with the lodging.
43. "A message should be sent to the owners": a message should be sent to the owners. "Having broken [it]" means from the very beginning.

Without touching it, one may make some slight break with a stone or similar object; afterwards, having determined it for the purpose of a permissible article (kappiyabhaṇḍa), it is allowable to take it up with the hand.
Therefore he said: "It is allowable to accept [the gift] with the thought, 'I shall make it a permissible article.

Here too, that [object] must be separated [from its original state] before being touched. Regarding "boards, lattices, and so forth," here [one may touch] with the hand for the purpose of protecting oneself from arrows.

It should be accepted. A *kiṭikāphalaka* (screen-board) is called a *jālika* (meshed screen); it is made of iron, copper, or other materials in a lattice pattern for the purpose of protecting the eyes, and is to be fastened to the head and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), armor and similar items are included. The phrase "not to be touched" (*anāmāsāni*) is said with reference to fish-nets and such things that obstruct others, not to protection against arrows, because the latter lacks the status of being a weapon or a tool for harming.
Therefore, he will say: "For [it is] for the purpose of preventing the obstruction of others," and so on.
“Of the seat” means of the cetiya together with its surrounding platform (*paribhaṇḍa*). “I shall bind” means I shall bind it for the purpose of preventing crows and other birds from defiling it.
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: “A *bherisaṅghāṭa* is a drum with leather stretched over it; a *vīṇāsaṅghāṭa* is a lute with leather stretched over it.
However, because the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* states, “Lutes, drums, and so forth, covered with leather,” there is no distinction [between the two terms].

Because the *Kurundi* commentary begins its explanation of the specific distinctions with the words “But in the *Kurundi*...,” it should be understood that the collection of binding accessories for the drums (*bheri*) and so forth is called the “drum-and-lute assembly” (*bherivīṇā-saṅghāṭa*), based on the derivation:

“that which is to be assembled (*saṅghaṭitabbo*) is an assembly (*saṅghāṭo*). A “hollow drumhead” (*tuccha-pokkhara*) refers to the drumhead of drums or lutes that have not yet had leather bound upon them.
“Leather already applied” (*āropita-camma*) refers to that which was applied previously and subsequently [remains so].
Having removed [the skin] from that, only the face-skin itself is set aside separately, not together with the other accessories; this is the distinction, namely that it is a "saṅghāṭa.
"Onahituṃ" means to cover by stretching skin over [instruments such as] drums or lutes, and to bind them with all the accessories such as leather straps.
"Onahāpetuṃ" means to have them bound in the same manner by others.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Ornament of the Discussion on the Determination of the 'Anāmāsa' [Non-Touching Rule]," in the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
8. Discussion on the Determination of Resolution and Designation (Adhiṭṭhānavikappanavinicchayakathā) 44.

Having thus explained the discussion on what is not to be touched (anāmāsa), he now speaks the words beginning with “But regarding resolutions and designations” in order to explain the determination of resolution and designation.
In this context, that which is resolved upon is a *adhiṭṭhāna* (resolution); it means grasping or discerning.

*Attha*: it means purpose. *Vikappanā* is that which is designated; its meaning is fixing, intending, or reflecting. In this context, "having stated the name 'I resolve upon the three robes,' one should resolve;
having stated the name 'one does not designate,' one should not designate. This method applies everywhere.
Therefore, by one who resolves upon the three robes, it should be resolved after stating the name, such as: "I resolve upon this outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*)," and so forth.

However, when assigning it, one should not assign it by taking the specific name of each robe, such as "this outer cloak" (saṅghāṭi) and so forth, but rather assign it by saying, "I assign this robe to you.
Whether it be the triple-robe (ticīvara) or another, if one assigns it by taking its specific name, it is not properly assigned; it remains in the category of an extra robe (atirekacīvara).”
This is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: "To resolve upon the three robes (*ticīvara*) means to resolve upon them by their specific names, such as the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*) and so forth.

'One should not assign them' means one should not assign them under this [general] name; one who has assigned his three robes in this manner does not become a possessor of the three robes (*tecīvariko*)."

It is stated: "This shows that for that [robe], the procedure such as 'not being separated from it' (avippavāsa) and so forth—which is to be performed as with a robe formally determined (adhiṭṭhita-ticīvara)—need not be performed;
however, there is no fault in the act of assigning (vikappana). But in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, it says:

"'One should determine the three robes'—here, 'the three robes' refers to what is suitable to be determined by means of the determination of the three robes, or that which [is determined] by means of the determination of the three robes..."

I allow one to determine [the robe] but not to assign it; because there is no fixed limit to the time of its determination, I allow one who desires it at all times to simply determine it. I do not allow one to assign it after having made a time-limit for that determination.
However, when a requisite is available, it is permissible to assign it after relinquishing it at any time. Thus: "There is no offense within ten days..."
"It is established by the statement: 'He resolves; he designates. Thus it was said.

Now, among these three interpretations in the *Ṭīkā*, the third interpretation appears to be the more reasonable. Why? Because of its consistency with both the Canon (*Pāḷi*) and the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).

How so? For in the Canon, [the allowance] applies only to the two specific items—the rains-bathing cloth (*vassikasāṭikā*) and the itch-covering cloth (*kaṇḍupaṭicchādī*)—for which a definite limit has been set.
Regarding the statement, "after that, one may assign [it]," this means that one must not assign it to others beyond that point;
therefore, when those [other monks] are absent, even if there is a need, it must always be determined (adhiṭṭhātabba) and not assigned—this is seen to be the intended meaning of the text.
However, in the other two cases, it should be determined only at the time it is permitted, according to the phrase, "after that, one may assign."

This accords with the Pāḷi. In the Commentary, regarding one who maintains the three robes by way of the "three-robes summary," it is permitted only to determine (*adhiṭṭhātuṃ*) them, not to assign them for use (*vikappetuṃ*).
However, as for the rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*), after the four months [of the rains], it may only be assigned for use, not determined.
This being so, for one who wishes to dwell apart from even one of the three robes, there is the determination of that robe.
Having relinquished [the robe], the opportunity for assignment is granted for the sake of the comfort of being apart from it.
In the first statement, having stated the name "one should not assign," the meaning "one should not assign" was expressed;
this being so, in the phrase "thereafter one may assign," having stated the name "thereafter," the meaning would be "one may assign."

And that meaning is stated by way of the section on designating; for if the qualification "having uttered the name" were required, there would be no need for the distinct statements "one should not designate" and "one may designate after that," since one must designate all robes even without uttering their names.
Furthermore, in the second interpretation, by the phrase "one should not designate," it means one should not designate by means of that specific name.

The phrase "I do not allow" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Regarding the first [case], it says: "Whether it be the three robes or something else, if one designates it by taking its specific name, it remains undesignated and stays in the category of an extra robe. Regarding the second, it says: "But there is no fault in the act of designation.
These two appear as if they contradict each other; therefore, this matter must be investigated.
"Beyond that, one may assign it" means "having assigned it beyond four months, one may use it"—this is stated in three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.
However, some say: "Beyond that, having assigned it, it is permitted to set it aside for as long as the four months of the rains in the coming year.
"I authorize you to assign it beyond that"—up to this point...

One should not understand the meaning to be that it is permitted to assign (*vikappeti*) the rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭika*) and the itch-covering cloth (*kaṇḍupaṭicchādi*) by mentioning each of their respective names.

For beyond that, since the very names "rain-cloak" and so forth no longer exist, why should one who assigns them beyond that point not assign them by mentioning the name? Because for both of these, usage after that point has been permitted.

"It should be used after having determined it as something else by means of a different name; thus it is stated in the three *gaṇṭhipada*s," so it is said in the *Sāratthadīpanī*. In the *Vimativinodanī* as well:

"Regarding the phrase 'beyond that,' some say it is permitted to use [the robe] after having determined it for more than four months. Others, however, [say] 'having determined it, until the coming rains...'"
"It is appropriate to set it aside for that long," they say. Others, however, say: "There is no fault in designating [the robe];
having thus designated it, one should use it after determining it by means of its name as a requisite (parikkhāra) and so forth.
However, in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, it is stated: "The rain-cloak (vassikasāṭikā) may only be designated beyond that period; it must not be determined [as a formal possession]."
"For I allow that a robe which has been finished may be determined as one's own within ten days, starting from the day of the commencement of the rains within the four-month period;
beyond the four months, for one who wishes to keep it as his own property, I allow him to assign it [to another].
Thus it is said. Here too, the latter view appears to be more commendable; why? Because it is easier to understand.
However, the intention of the earlier teachers is difficult to discern, as they have spoken of various different doctrines.
"The fist-fifth" (*muṭṭhipañcaka*) means a group of five characterized by the fist;
the intention is that one should measure by making the fifth [measurement] a closed fist after having measured four cubits. Some, however, say: "A group of five of fists and cubits..."
"The five-fist measure. They say that even the five cubits must be measured by making them into fists.

The same principle applies here to the "three-fist measure" as well. He said, "and with the upper robe," etc., because it is possible to cover the three circles (the body) with an inner robe of two cubits.
"Excessive" means exceeding the Sugata’s robe. "Deficient" means less than the five-fist measure, etc.
"Deficient. This shows that by means of that [deficiency], the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of the three robes among them is not valid.
"I relinquish this outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*)" means: "I set aside this determination of the outer robe;
I renounce it"—this is the meaning. However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: "'I relinquish' means 'I set aside,' or 'I renounce'—this is the meaning."
It has been stated: "By one making a bodily movement" means by touching or shifting the robe with the hand.

Regarding the phrase "it must be determined by speech," it should be understood that here the determination by both body and speech is also included—by first moving with the body and then breaking into speech—because it must be said, "without having touched it with the body," [this being] by way of not being within hand-reach or arm's reach.
There are two kinds of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*). Regarding this, it is stated in the *Vimativinodanī*:
“The term ‘hand’s reach’ (*hatthapāsa*) refers to two and a half cubits (*aḍḍhateyyahattha*). Some say it is twelve cubits, but that does not apply here.

However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, in order to show the two kinds of formal determination—distinguished as being in the presence of or out of the presence of the person—it says: “If [the object is] within hand’s reach,” and so forth.
“Within hand’s reach” (hatthapāse) is said with reference to a distance of twelve cubits;
therefore, some say that what stands within twelve cubits must be designated by saying “this,” while beyond that it must be designated by saying “that.
However, nothing is stated on this point in the *Gaṇṭhipadas*, nor anywhere in the Canon or the Commentary.
"‘Hand’s reach’ (hatthapāsa) refers to two and a half cubits; therefore, one must seek the reason for this specific qualification," it is said.
Thus, in both the Canon and the commentaries, "hand’s reach" is stated to be exactly two and a half cubits, and that very definition has been accepted by the authors of the sub-commentaries (ṭīkā).
Therefore, a robe situated within two and a half cubits [of oneself] is [referred to as] "this."
Having said, "This is outside," it should be determined.
The phrase "in a neighboring monastery" is stated with reference to what stands within range of observing the designated place;
even if it stands at a distance from there, it must still be determined by one who observes the designated place. And therein, regarding the robe—
The mere observation of the state of having been placed [in storage] is the criterion. For it is not possible to observe the persistence of something permanent;
it is not permissible to resolve that what was placed in one dwelling has been placed in another.
However, some say, “Even so, there is no fault once it has been resolved,” but this does not accord with the Aṭṭhakathā; it should be investigated—thus it is stated in the *Vimativinodanī*.
Thus it was said. However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: "A 'neighboring monastery' (*sāmantavihāra*) is one where it is possible to go and return on the very same day.
The term 'neighboring monastery' is merely a heading for the teaching; therefore, they say that once the designated place has been observed, it may be determined even if it is situated at a distance.
And as for the phrase 'having observed the designated place,' this refers to the observation of the designated place."
It is stated that this was said because it is appropriate, and it is further stated that "the mere inspection of the robe is the measure here. And in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*:
"The names *saṅghāṭī*, *uttarāsaṅga*, and *antaravāsaka* are the same for both those that have been formally resolved (*adhiṭṭhita*) and those that have not.
In such cases as 'this is the *saṅghāṭī*,' those that have not been resolved are mentioned. In the phrase 'one should be separated from the three robes,' those that have been resolved are meant."
It has been stated [thus]. Regarding "the neighboring monastery" (*sāmantavihāra*), the Elder Dhammasiri says it refers to the monastery within the village of one's alms-round.

The teachers (*ācariya*) maintain that it can indeed be obtained even from a much greater distance. In the *Anugaṇṭhipada* it is also said: "'The neighboring monastery' is merely a heading for the teaching;
therefore, having observed the designated location, it may be resolved upon even if situated far away. A "neighboring monastery" is one where [one can go] on that very same day.

It is possible to go and return. For one observing the rule against staying overnight apart from one's robes, it is not permitted to resolve upon [the robe] as being located far away; for thus it is said in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. Some say:
"If another person replaces a robe that has been placed on a robe-stand and sets it on a peg, the resolution succeeds even for one who resolves upon it without knowing this, provided it is a robe."
"Because it has been clearly observed," they say; therefore, one should adopt [a position] after reconciling the differing opinions of the teachers.
"By means of robes set aside after being resolved upon" means by means of robes set aside under the designation of "requisites-robes.
For that very reason, he shows the relinquishment of the requisites-robes with the words, "I relinquish this"; and by this, the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) of the three-robed one is [fulfilled].

This shows that one who, while maintaining [the practice], is unable to finish making, dyeing, and wearing a robe obtained as rag-robe material (*paṃsukūla*) and so forth within ten days, must resolve upon it as a requisite cloth (*parikkhāracola*) and then allow the ten-day period to pass;
otherwise, it becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).
For this very reason, it is said: "From the time it has been dyed, however, it is not permitted to store it; [to do so] is a thief of the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*)."

"...is the name [it receives]," as stated in the *Visuddhimagga*. "They must be resolved upon again" is said with reference to one who wishes to use them after resolving upon them by means of their specific names, such as "outer robe" (*saṅghāṭi*) and so forth;
however, it should be understood that for another person, the previous resolution alone is sufficient.
By the phrase "they must be resolved upon again," he shows that even a "permissible dot" (*kappabindu*) must be applied. [This concludes] the function of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-kicca*).

By the word "there is not," it is shown that even the duty of giving a small fragment (*kappabindu*) does not exist; "it is indeed much greater," etc., is the characteristic common to all formal determinations (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

In this regard, "it must be determined again" means that because it is a part of an undetermined robe, if it is undetermined, then by virtue of its smallness, that part which belongs to what was determined goes into the category of being determined; likewise, if it is determined...
The characteristic is that a portion of what has not been formally resolved (anadhiṭṭhita) comes to be reckoned as "not resolved.
And herein, it is not only the second cloth, but also the third cloth and so forth. As it is said: "I allow you, monks...
a fourfold outer robe made of cloths gathered during the season... [and] as much as needed from rags (paṃsukūla)."
The passage beginning with “But the three robes,” and so forth, is stated with reference to the measurement of the three robes starting from the five-fist measure.
“To determine the requisites cloth” means to determine it after having made it into requisites cloth.
“The remaining bhikkhus” refers to the bhikkhus seated at the time when [the allowance] will be spoken of. Therefore, it is permitted, as in: “I allow you, bhikkhus, to determine the three robes.”
It is stated, “one must not exchange them,” and thus it is also stated regarding the requisites-cloth (*parikkhāracola*). Neither a superior limit nor a numerical limit has been specified for it;
therefore, the meaning is that after relinquishing even the three robes, it is permissible to use these robes after determining them as requisites-cloth. This is the opening to the storehouse.
This is the formal act of designating requisites and robes; it is the means of depositing and the means of setting aside.
The meaning is that it is the cause for setting aside extra robes. If one asks how this is known, [it is said]:
"Now at that time, the monks had a complete set of the three robes, yet they were in need of water-strainers and bags. Regarding this matter, [the Blessed One said]: 'I allow you, monks...'"
Since the "requisite cloth" (*parikkhāracoḷaka*) has been permitted for monks, and because there is no prohibition against having only one water-strainer (*parissāvana*) or a bag (*thavikā*),

it is established that requisites such as water-strainers— whether they are of the maximum allowable size suitable for formal assignment (*vikappanūpaga*) or even exceeding that size— are permissible. First, by means of the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of the three robes (*ticīvara*).
It must be formally determined; furthermore, by one who is unable to maintain [the robe], it should be relinquished and the requisite cloth (parikkhāracola) re-determined.

This was not stated from the very beginning. Because the formal authorization for non-separation (avippavāsa-sīmā-sammuti) is possible within a fixed boundary (baddhasīmā), there is no fault in being separated from the robe;
thus, it is not difficult to maintain there. Therefore, he said: "In an unfixed boundary (abaddhasīmā), it is difficult to maintain."
45. Regarding the statement, "The offense of expiation involving cutting [the robe] when it exceeds the proper measure," he says, "not exceeding the proper measure.

Beyond that, it should be relinquished and then formally assigned (*vikappetabba*); that is, after relinquishing the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) beyond the four months of the rainy season, it should be formally assigned.
By this, it is understood that the formal determination remains in force for more than four months of the rainy season, since relinquishment is not applicable to what does not exist.

As for what is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*—that “the *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-cloth) loses its formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) even by the passing of a month of the rains, and the *kaṇḍupaṭicchādi* (itch-covering cloth) loses it even by the subsiding of the affliction”—this is not found in the *Samantapāsādikā*.

Furthermore, in the *Parivāra-aṭṭhakathā*, regarding the passage “there is an offense one incurs in winter, not in summer,” that [statement] is not mentioned there; rather, [it refers to] the full moon day of Kattika.
If one wears the *vassikasāṭikā* (the rainy-season robe) that was set aside after being formally assigned on the last day of the first fortnight (*pāṭipada*), one incurs an offense in the winter.
However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated: "If one does not formally relinquish it on the full-moon day of the month of Kattika, one incurs an offense in the winter.
This too is well-said; for it is stated: "One may determine [its use] for four months, and beyond that, one must assign it [to another]. In this regard:

In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) is stated on account of the wearing [of the robe]; however, in the *Kuruṇḍi-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated on account of not relinquishing it.

Therefore, according to the method explained in the *Kuruṇḍi*, it is understood that even when the rains-retreat period has passed, the rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*) does not lose its formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
Regarding the loss of the formal determination, the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* also states that it is lost upon the passing of the months of the rains or the disappearance of the illness.

It has not been removed; therefore, according to the method found in the *Samantapāsādikā*, it should be understood that the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) remains until its relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*).
Because it was permitted for the purpose of bathing, it is stated: "Even if it is dyed merely by a change in color, this is allowable.

However, by the statement "but two [colors] are not allowable," it follows that a second formal determination does not take effect even for the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) and the other robes; such [a robe] is considered an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*).

This shows that [it] exists. In the *Mahāpaccarī*, with reference to the absence of the function of use (*paribhogakicca*) by way of a robe (*cīvara*), it is stated "there is no offense" (*anāpatti*), as in the case of a spread given for the purpose of using it as a lodging (*senāsana*).

However, as for what was stated—"even a spread (*paccattharaṇa*) must be formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*)"—that is not restricted to being for the purpose of a lodging alone, among the nine types of robes.
Because it has been taken, one should understand that after having determined it by means of one’s own name and set it aside like a requisite-cloth, it may be used in whatever way is appropriate.

As for *pāvāra* and *okoja*, although these are also designated as "bedspreads" and so forth in common worldly usage, they are mentioned separately from the bedspreads given for the purpose of furniture for lodgings. If...

They say that at the end [of the year], when a new *aparāvaṣṭika-sāṭikā* robe-cloth has arisen, one should relinquish the previous *purimavaṣṭika-sāṭikā*, make a formal assignment (*vikappana*) of it, and then determine its use (*adhiṭṭhātabba*).
Regarding the sitting mat (*nisīdana*), "measured according to the standard" means: two *vidatthis* in length by one and a half *vidatthis* in width, using the Sugata-span.

It is appropriate by this measure of "ten spans" (*vidatthi*); however, by the "carpenter’s hand"—which is reckoned as the hand of a medium-sized man—it is three cubits (*hasta*) in length, two cubits and six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in width, and one cubit and ten spans in [the length of] the fringe.
