Now, by the ordinary hand of men today, it is four cubits and one span in length, and in width—
The saṅghāṭi is one *hattha* and nine *aṅgulas* in length; the *udakasāṭikā* is two *hatthas* and six *aṅgulas* in length.
It is permissible for it to be less than that, but not more, because it is stated: "For one who exceeds that [measure], there is an offense of expiation involving cutting.
Regarding the itch-covering cloth (*kaṇḍupaticchādi*), it has a fixed measure, as it is stated: "In length, four spans of the Sugata-span; in width, two spans."
Thus, it is endowed with the aforementioned measurements; however, by the carpenter’s hand (vaḍḍhakīhattha), it is six cubits in length and three cubits in width.
Now, by the standard hand (pakatihattha), it should be understood as nine cubits in length and four cubits and two spans (vidatthi) across.

Regarding the phrase "the requisite cloth (parikkhāracoḷa) which is the minimum measurement for a robe fit for assignment (vikappanūpaga)," here, the "minimum measurement for a robe fit for assignment" refers to...
In terms of the Sugata’s finger-breadth, it is eight finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in width;
in the carpenter’s hand, it is one cubit in length and one span in width;
but now, in the ordinary hand, it is one cubit and one span in length, and one span and six finger-breadths in width. Therefore, he said: “Its measurement,” and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of medicine" and so forth, it is stated that "there is no offense even if it has not been formally resolved (*anadhiṭṭhita*)," with reference to what was set aside after being released from the state of being one's own property.
The intended meaning is that for one who sets it aside after having distinguished it—saying, "This is for the purpose of medicine;

this is for my mother"—and thus released it from the state of being their own property, there is no necessity for a formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*). [One might think: "With this, I shall have medicine purchased..."
However, they say that when one is setting it aside with the thought, "I will give this to my mother," it must indeed be formally resolved (adhiṭṭhātabba).
Regarding the phrase "a bedspread given for the purpose of bedding and requisites":
they say that even if it belongs to oneself, it is permissible not to resolve it, provided it is used merely as a spread upon beds and benches, without being worn as an undergarment or an upper robe.

However, since it was stated without qualification that even the under-sheet (*paccattharaṇa*) must be determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*), our view is that only what belongs to oneself should be determined;

this should be investigated and accepted. Regarding the statement "it should be determined as it stands there," once the place where it was spread has been determined, it remains determined; there is no need for a further act of determination. If...
However, they say that after showing the limit, it must be woven again from time to time, and then resolved upon once more.
"The same method applies" means that when the thread has been woven up to the measure required for the intended purpose, one must resolve upon it while it remains exactly as it is. 46.
Regarding "returning to the inferior state," the *Gaṇṭhipada* on all three [texts] states: "By returning to the state of a householder without having formally renounced the training."
What was stated is logical, because the robe has been relinquished with a state of non-attachment, just as in the case of giving something else.

However, some—taking the phrase "by returning to the lower state" to mean "only by a bhikkhunī’s assuming the status of a householder"—hold that even for a bhikkhu who disrobes, he remains a bhikkhu as long as he has not formally renounced the training (*sikkhā*). [They argue] that there is no [intentional] determination...
They say, "she abandons [the training]," but that should not be accepted, because it was not stated with the qualification, "by a bhikkhunī’s falling back to the lower state.

For in the case of a bhikkhunī, there is no need to separately mention the abandonment of the formal undertaking through her returning to lay status, since by that very act of departing from the religious life (*vibbhamana*), she ceases to be a non-monastic. However, as for the phrase "by renouncing the training," if—

In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: "It is said for the purpose of showing that even if one who remains in the outward marks of a bhikkhu renounces the training, the resolve regarding the robe still clinging to his body is lost. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says:
"'By returning to the lower state' refers to one who, having committed the ultimate offense, remains under the designation of a bhikkhu..."

It is said with reference to the assumption of the layperson’s mark or the sectarian mark by one who has gone over to the faction of the *titthiyas* and by a nun, due to their lack of regard for the state of being a monk or a nun.
Some say it is said with reference to the entering into the state of a householder without having formally renounced the training;
however, that is not correct, because even then he remains fully ordained (*upasampanna*), and the robe remains his property.
Regarding the statement "from abandoning," these two expressions appear to be mutually contradictory.

However, because it is stated separately in the *Aṭṭhakathā* as "by returning to the lower state and by renouncing the training," when one returns to the lower state, even if one has not renounced the training, the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of the robe is abandoned; whereas when one renounces the training...
The intention appears to be that [the vow is lost] even when one returns to the inferior state; therefore,

although the status of a monk still exists for one who merely enters the state of a householder without having formally renounced the training, and although there is a relinquishing of the robe because it belongs to him,
nevertheless, because it is stated "by returning to the inferior state," the relinquishing of the formal determination occurs precisely through the act of entering the state of a householder.
It may be so through the transformation of gender. And for one who, without returning to the state of a householder, merely renounces the training—
although the marks of a bhikkhu still exist and the robes remain his property because they have not been relinquished—
nevertheless, because it is stated "by the renunciation of the training," the relinquishment of the formal resolve occurs solely through that renunciation of the training.

It may be as it is in the case of relinquishing [the robes]; therefore, whether it be a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī, by taking up the marks of a householder with the thought, "I shall return to the lower state," one loses the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) regarding the robe. However, our own view is this:

through the renunciation of the training (*sikkhāpaccakkhāna*), the robe is lost for a bhikkhu alone, whereas there is no such thing as the renunciation of the training for a bhikkhunī. This applies also to those who have committed an offense involving defeat (*antimavatthu*), those who have gone over to the faction of the *titthiyas*, and those who have deserted.

However, since the relinquishment of the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) regarding a robe is not mentioned in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), and because there is no conventional usage for those [monks] who have returned to the lower life, this matter must be investigated.
By "in accordance with the nail of the little finger," he shows the lower limit. Regarding the phrase "on this side" (*orato*) and "beyond" (*parato*), it is stated here:
"A hole on this side destroys the formal determination; one beyond that does not destroy it. How is the distinction between 'this side' and 'beyond' to be understood?
Just as, when a place is delimited by a river, the bank on the side where people dwell is called the "near shore" (orima),
while the bank on the other side is called the "far shore" (pārima); so too, the central portion of a robe that serves as the location for monks' undergarments and upper robes—
relative to the area measured by the aforementioned span of a vidatthi and so forth— is called "this side" (ora), whereas the edge of the robe is "the other side" (para).

As for the term "nāma": according to worldly convention, when it is said that a robe must be placed "having made this side the limit and that side the end," the position facing the monk is called "this side" (oraṃ) and the other position is called "that side" (paraṃ); likewise, the place where monks wear their lower and upper robes is called "this side," and the other is called "that side.
Thus, the distinction between "this side" and "the other side" may also be understood according to the Dispensation (sāsana).

It should be understood. For this very reason, if one first places a bolt in a weak spot and subsequently removes it after cutting through that weak spot, the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is not broken. This same method applies even when turning over the circular patches;
thus, the state of whether the formal determination is broken or not is demonstrated for the entire robe. Therefore, it is said in the *Vimativinodanī*: "This..."
By the word “nayati” (he leads), there is included the sense that the determination [of the robe] is abandoned at any opening whatsoever among those parts joined by measurement, and so forth.
“A small robe” means a small robe that is not deficient even by the measure of five handfuls and so on. Regarding the phrase “or he makes a large one small”:
here, it refers to whichever part among the four sides of the three robes has a hole.
The intention is that the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is not relinquished; even when one cuts it all around that spot and makes it small, the determination is not relinquished.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated regarding the phrase "whether making it large or small":
"In this context, having made a robe that is excessively large—measuring five hand-fists or more at the minimum limit—and [cutting] all around..."
Even at the time of cutting or tearing, the place being cut does not become a "hole" (chidda) and does not lose its status as a determined object (adhiṭṭhāna);
thus it is established. This is also consistent with the statement: "Having joined [the pieces], one cuts, yet it is not broken.

However, regarding the robe-requisite (parikkhāracoḷa), if it is made smaller than the minimum allowable measurement for formal assignment (vikappanūpaga), it becomes a hole and loses its status as a determined object.

They are relinquished because the formal resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*) lacks a fixed basis; however, it should be understood that once those [pieces] have been sewn together and joined again, they must indeed be resolved upon once more.

Some, however, maintain: "In the case of a rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*) that has been cut into two parts, even if each individual fragment meets the required measurement, the formal resolve remains valid for only one fragment and not for the other; thus, two [separate fragments] are not permissible."
"Because it has been so stated, the same method applies to the sitting mat and the itch-covering cloth as well," they say. 47.
*Sammukhe* (in the presence) is the nominative singular; it is an adverbial modifier.
Therefore, they explain the meaning by treating *sammukhe* as an ablative used in the sense of a locative, meaning "facing towards" (*abhimukhe*).

Alternatively, *sammukhā-vikappanā* (assignment in the presence) means assignment by one’s own speech in the very presence [of the recipient]. *Parammukhā-vikappanā* (assignment in the absence) means assignment in the absence [of the recipient];
this meaning should also be understood in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). This alone accords with the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
"The state of being near or far" refers to proximity and distance. "At this point it is permissible to store" is said because the function of assignment is completed by this much alone.
"It is not an extra robe" means the intention is that it does not generate an offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) upon the lapse of ten days. "It is not permitted to use...

and so forth, is said with reference to the *pācittiya* for using it oneself without having formally relinquished it (*apaccuddhāraṇa*), and the *dukkaṭa* for either formally designating it (*adhiṭṭhahana*) or giving it away to others.
"Using and so forth are also permitted" refers to the acts of using, giving away, and formal designation.
It is permissible. By the word "api" (also), the meaning is that it is also permissible to store it.

By this, it is shown that even when the act of relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*) has been performed, if one wishes to determine (*adhiṭṭhātuṃ*) the robe, it remains a robe that has been formally assigned (*vikappita-cīvara*), not an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*).

Furthermore, it should be determined by one who wishes to determine it by way of its specific name, such as "the three robes" (*ticīvara*); otherwise, having merely made it an assigned robe, it may be used.
However, some say: "That robe which has been assigned should be stored away until the time of use, without having it formally relinquished;
but when the time for use arrives, it should be used after first having it relinquished and then formally determined.
For if one were to relinquish it even before that, then because the assignment would have ceased through the act of relinquishment, it would become an extra robe."
It is so called; once ten days have passed, it becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). Therefore, whatever is to be set aside without being used must be assigned (*vikappetabba*).
And when the relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*) has been performed, it must be formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*) within those very ten days.
As for what is stated in the Commentary—that "after that time, using it and so forth is permitted"—they say that this contradicts the Canon (*pāḷi*). This...
That is merely their opinion. For in the *Pāḷi*, it is stated in general terms: “He resolves or designates [it] within ten days”;
“Having designated a robe for himself, if he should use it without relinquishing it, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);
and “There is no offense if he gives it away, or if he uses it with the trust that it belongs to another. Furthermore, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it says: “This robe...”

Because it is stated that relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*) occurs by way of using, giving away, or doing as one pleases with the item— without demonstrating relinquishment through such phrases as "I relinquish" or "I assign"—
and without releasing its status as one's own property by saying, "Use this which belongs to me, or give it away,
or do with it as you see fit," it follows that from that point onward, even using and so forth are permissible, even without a formal act of determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
Since both use and storage have been mentioned separately, it appears that this is a distinct formal act of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*):

after performing the assignment (*vikappanā*) immediately thereafter, one must relinquish the robe and, without formally determining (*anadhiṭṭhahitvā*) it, use or store the robe fit for assignment while being devoid of the three robes (*ticīvara*).
Furthermore, because it is stated that many bowls may be assigned and relinquished [in this manner], [the procedure for robes is distinct].

It is established that the state of being an "extra bowl" (*atirekapatta*) is shown in reference to their relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*), because only one among them may be formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*).
Therefore, it should be understood according to the method transmitted in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

"A friend" (*mitta*) means a close friend. "One seen" (*saṇḍiṭṭha*) means merely someone who has been seen, not a close friend. "He is not skilled in what has been prescribed" (*paññattikovido na hoti*)...

When it has been thus assigned, he does not know that the formal act of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*) must be performed immediately thereafter by means of this renunciation (*paccuddhāra*). Therefore, it is said:
"He does not know how to renounce. By this also, it should be understood that "the renunciation must be made immediately after the assignment.
The intention is that this so-called "assignment of what has been assigned" (*vikappitavikappanā*) is permissible, just like the "re-affirmation of what has been affirmed" (*adhiṭṭhitādhiṭṭhāna*).

48. Having thus shown the method for the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and the assignment (*vikappanā*) of robes, he now says, beginning with “But as for the bowl,” in order to show the method for the formal determination and assignment of the bowl.
Therein, it is called a *patto* because alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*) falls (*patati*) into it;

it is a specific type of alms-bowl belonging to the nature of the Victor’s dispensation (*jinasāsana*). For it is said: “*Patta* means a wing or a leaf; it means a vessel when it has gone [into usage].”
Regarding that bowl: *pana* is a particle used in the sense of introducing an alternative position. *Naya* refers to the method of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and assignment (*vikappanā*).

The construction is as follows: this method of formal determination and assignment for the bowl, which is about to be explained, should be understood as being distinct from the method of formal determination and assignment stated for the robe.
When one formally determines the bowl, it must be determined only when it is of the proper measure, not when it is of an improper measure.
This refers to the connection. Therefore, if a bowl is deficient or excessive in measure, the formal act of determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) does not succeed;
thus, it shows that such a bowl may be used by way of being treated as a vessel (*bhājanaparibhoga*). For he will say: "These are to be used by way of being treated as a vessel;
they do not come under the category of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*), nor do they come under the category of assignment (*vikappa*)."
Regarding the phrase "two Magadha-measures" (*dve magadhanāḷiyo*): here, a "Magadha-measure" is that which holds water weighing thirteen and a half *pala*s according to the Magadha scale.
In the island of Sri Lanka, it is smaller than the standard local measure, but larger than the Tamil measure.
For this is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "A 'Magadha-measure' consists of thirteen and a half *pala*s," as recorded in the Andhaka commentary.
It has been stated: "In the island of Siṃhala, the standard *nāḷi* is large; the Tamil *nāḷi* is small.
It corresponds to the measure of the Magadhan *nāḷi*. According to that Magadhan *nāḷi*, one and a half *nāḷis* make one Siṃhala *nāḷi*; thus it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
Alternatively, what is called a Magadhan *nāḷi* consists of five *kuḍuvas* and one fist (*muṭṭhi*), and with one fist, it is a third part [of a *nāḷi*].
It takes [it]. For this has been stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: "Some say that what is called a Magadha-measure (*nāḷi*) is six *paṭa* measures;
others say it is eight *paṭa* measures. Therein, according to the opinion of the former, two *nāḷis* of three *paṭas* each make one Magadha-measure.
According to the latter, two *nāḷis* of four *paṭas* each make one Magadha-measure. By the Elder Master Dhammapāla..."
However, it is stated that by nature, four *muṭṭhikas* make a *kuḍuva*, four *kuḍuvas* make a *nāḷika*, and sixteen *nāḷikas* of that measure make a *doṇa*;
furthermore, that [Magadhan *doṇa*] amounts to twelve *nāḷikas* of the Magadhan *nāḷika*.
Therefore, according to that method, it should be understood that what is called a Magadhan *nāḷika* takes five *kuḍuvas*, one *muṭṭhi*, and one-third of a *muṭṭhi*.
In this context, *kuḍuva* means one *pasata*. For it is said in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*:
"One *kuḍuva* is one *pasata*;
four of those would be a *pattha*."
"Four *pattha* make one *āḷhaka*;
four *āḷhaka* make one *doṇa*.
Alternatively, what is called a Magadhan *nāḷi* is that which holds four *nāḷi* of the four-*kuḍuva* *nāḷi*. For this has been said:
In the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated: "The term 'Damila-nāḷī' refers to an ancient *nāḷī*.
That [ancient *nāḷī*] consists of eight *kuḍuva*s of four-fist-measures; two such *nāḷī*s make one Magadha *nāḷī*.
However, they say that the ancient Sinhalese *nāḷī* takes three [Magadha] *nāḷī*s; according to their opinion, the Magadha *nāḷī* is now equal to four *kuḍuva*s."
Four *nāḷikas* make one *damilanaḷi*; half of that, according to the Magadha measure, is what is called a *pattha*, which is the former *damilanaḷi*.
This accords with the canonical statement: "A bowl called 'small' takes a *pattha* of boiled rice. Even among worldly people it is said:
"The worldly and the Magadhan—these two *patthas* are proclaimed."
"It is said that a worldly [measure] is sixteen *palas*, while the Māgadha [measure] is considered double that.
Thus, it is shown that in the world, the Magadha *nāḷi* is double the size of a *nāḷi*.

And when understood in this way, both the small bowl and the taking of a portion of alms-food sufficient for maintenance are established. For it is not possible with a bowl that takes less than eight *kuḍuvas* of boiled rice.
Thus, one may sustain oneself by seeking almsfood that has been gathered up. Therefore it is said in the *Verañjakanda-aṭṭhakathā*:
“A *pattha* is the measure of a *nāḷi*; it is sufficient for the sustenance of one man. And this is also said in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*:
“A *pattha* of rice is not enough for two,” and “What is given to one [is enough] for two or three.”

And because it is said [in the suttas], "it is obtained," therefore it should be understood here according to the method stated. "Proportionate to each morsel of food" means the measure of one-fourth of a portion of rice.
For this has been stated in the commentary on the Brahmāyu Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya: "The measure of sauce is indeed one-fourth of a portion of rice.
"Those which follow the course of the rice" means those whose course (gati) is the same as the course of the rice; thus they are "those which follow the course of the rice."

"Course" (*gati*) means the space; because it has the nature of allowing rice to enter within it, that very space of the rice becomes the space for those [grains], meaning they do not seek any other space for themselves.
"By the use of the vessel" means by the use of the vessel for carrying water and so forth.

Having thus shown the bowl according to its measure—whether it is suitable for a formal resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*), for receiving food, or for storing food—one should now [consider it] from the perspective of its cooking and its source.
To demonstrate this, he said, “Even those that are of the proper measure,” and so forth. In that context, an iron bowl is called a “bowl” after five firings;
it must be fired repeatedly with various ingredients—not by the smith’s firing alone—but for the purpose of producing a dark-blue color suitable for a recluse.
Because of the extreme hardness of iron, the dark-blue color suitable for a recluse is achieved only after five firings, including the smith’s firing.
...it exists. The same principle applies here regarding the clay bowl that has been fired twice:
because of its softness, even though it has been fired two times along with the firing for a potter’s vessel, it possesses a blue color suitable for a recluse.

Only when it has been made in this way does the bowl become fit for formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and for assignment (*vikappana*), not if it has not been so made. Therefore, he will say: "In the firing and at the root..."
And as soon as it has been finished, it becomes subject to formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*). That which is subject to formal determination is also subject to assignment (*vikappana*).
By this, he shows that even if [the object] has not yet come into one's hand, it may be formally determined or assigned;
thus, even if it stands at a distance, one is permitted to determine or assign it, for the only criterion is the recognition of the place where it was set down. Now, regarding that very point:

He says “If indeed,” etc., in order to explain this in detail. The word *hi* indicates an elaboration. Therein, the phrase “I shall cook and set it aside” is said with reference to cooking it until it turns black.

Now, in order to show the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) regarding the bowl, he says: “In that regard, there are two ways of determining the bowl,” and so forth. Therein, “the neighboring monastery” refers to—
This is stated by way of illustration; even that which stands far away must likewise be resolved upon.
"Having observed the place where it was set down" is also merely a conventional expression; here, the actual observation of the bowl itself is the criterion.

Now, in order to show the loss of the resolution, he says: "For one who is thus heedful," and so forth. In this context, "there is a crack in the bowl" means that there is a crack anywhere from a space of two finger-breadths below the rim downwards.
Regarding "of the seven grains":
"Rice, paddy, millet;
wheat, beans, and barley."
“Kaṅgu and so forth are the seven grains;
nīvāra and the rest are their varieties”—
thus are the seven kinds of grain that have been mentioned.

49. Having thus shown the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of the bowl, he now says, “But regarding the assignment (*vikappana*),” etc., in order to show the assignment of the bowl. This should be understood according to the same method explained in the section on the assignment of robes (*cīvara-vikappana*). 50.
Having thus shown the method of assignment, he now says, “Having determined it in this way,” etc., in order to show the procedure to be followed when the bowl is broken.
Therein, by the term “without a bowl,” he indicates the relinquishment of the formal determination as well. Even in the case of [a bowl] with five repairs...
In a bowl whose baking is incomplete, the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) does not take effect, just as in the case of a raw bowl.
Because it is stated, "or with a triple patch," it is permissible to cover a hole in an iron bowl with allowable metals such as copper or bronze.

For this very reason, it is said, "with a metal saucer. As for the statement, "it is not permissible with pure [metals]," etc., this is said because [the pure metal] would melt when placed into hot food.
Thinking, "It is proper to bind [the plaster] after the molasses has been heated with stone powder," one should cook the molasses together with stone powder;
it is proper to bind it with that stone powder while still raw. "By improper use" means by an unsuitable use.
Because it was said, "I allow you, monks, a support," one may place a support anywhere on beds, chairs, and so forth.
They say that it is permissible to place the bowl there [on the ground] without using a stand, because the location for placing a support has not been specifically restricted.
Thus ends the "Ornament of the Determination of Formal Acts and Designations" within the *Vinayālaṅkāra*,
which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
The Eighth Chapter.
9. Discussion on the Determination of Separation from Robes. 51.
Having thus shown the discussion on the determination and assignment [of robes], there now follows the determination regarding living apart from one's robe.

To demonstrate this, he said, "Living without robes" (*cīvarena vinā vāso*), and so forth. In that context, it is called *cīvara* because it is accumulated (*cīyati*); the meaning is that it is made into a collection or a hoard.

It is a specific kind of cloth that serves as the banner of the Noble Ones (*ariya*). However, here it refers specifically to the three robes (*ticīvara*) which have been formally resolved upon (*adhiṭṭhita*) and worn according to the resolution.
*Vinā* is a particle used in the sense of exclusion or absence. *Vāsa* means dwelling; thus, *vināvāsa* means dwelling without [robes], that is, living without robes.
“Living apart from [one’s robes]” (*vināvāso*) means living apart from one’s robe-cloths (*cīvaravināvāso*).

It should be understood that although it ought to be said “living separated from one’s robe-cloths” (*cīvaravippavāso*), it is stated thus either by way of a desire for brevity or by forming a compound without elision (*aluttasamāsa*) for the purpose of completing the verse line. And so he will say:

“By means of the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of the three robes... [separated] from them,” and: “I determine this outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*), I determine this upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), I determine this inner robe (*antaravāsaka*).”
The meaning is: "for each one of the three robes determined [as one's own] by name with the words 'I determine'";

it is not permitted to dwell even without one of them. For a monk who dwells [without it], as soon as the dawn breaks, the robe becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) and he incurs an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);
such is the connection. Regarding the phrase "one must dwell," here the act of dwelling is common to all four postures.
Therefore, whether it is attached to the body or not, as long as one remains within the space of two and a half ratanas—
whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down— one is said to be "dwelling within arm's reach.
Having thus shown the characteristic of non-separation in general, [the text now] shows it specifically by way of the fifteen locations such as villages and so forth.
To demonstrate this, he said: “villages,” and so forth. Among these, villages and settlements are well known. An *udosita* is a hall for goods such as vehicles and the like.
An *aṭṭa* is a specific type of dwelling with thick walls made of bricks, four or five stories high, built for the purpose of repelling rival kings and others.
A *māḷa* is a square palace comprised of a single roof-peak. A *pāsāda*...
A *nāma* is a long palace. A *hammiya* is a flat-roofed palace; a flat-roofed palace is said to be a palace provided with a courtyard (*candikaṅgaṇa*).
A caravan (*sattha*) is either a foot-caravan or a cart-caravan. A field (*khetta*) is a place where the primary and secondary crops grow.
A threshing floor (*dhaññakaraṇa*) is a circular threshing area. A grove (*ārāma*) is a flower-grove or a fruit-grove.
Monasteries (*vihāra*) and so forth are indeed well known. In this context, it should be understood that dwellings (*nivesana*) and the like situated outside the village are included.
For those located within the village are already included by the mention of "village," and thus they are excluded from the category of "village.
Furthermore, by the mention of "village," market towns (*nigama*) and cities (*nagara*) are also included.
By the phrase "or surrounded by a moat," it is shown that even if it is surrounded on all sides by water such as rivers or ponds, it is indeed considered "surrounded.
"Exceeding that measure" means exceeding the measure of two and a half ratanas in the space above the house.
By the phrase "or one should dwell in a *sabhāya*," it is indicated that the word *sabhāya* is a synonym for the word *sabhā*, and is neuter in gender.
It shows that [the word] *atthi* exists. For the word *sabhā* is feminine in gender, while the word *sabhāya* is neuter in gender.
"At the gate of the city" (*dvāramūle vā*) means at the city gate. "Of those" (*tesaṃ*) refers to the assembly hall (*sabhāya*) and the city gates (*nagaradvāramūlānaṃ*).

By the very mention of the assembly hall and the gates of that street, all the houses there as well as that inner lane (*antaravīthi*) are indeed included. And here, among the gates, streets, and houses—
In the spring season, having avoided faults such as entering a village or sharing a bed, one must remain properly covered and so forth.

However, it should be understood that if a hall has been built like a mountain cave for the residence of everyone, it is permissible to stay there at one's ease, just as in an inner monastery (*antarārāma*).
"Having brought it and placed it in the house" means having set it down after leaving the street.
He deposits it in another house. Therefore he said: “The hand’s reach of the street does not protect.
By saying “in front or behind the hand’s reach,” he refers to the hand’s reach of the house.
Having thus shown separation and non-separation by way of the village, he now shows it by way of the dwelling: “If... [he says]”...
He said, beginning with, "The dwelling belongs to a single family. Therein, they say that an *ovaraka* is another chamber within a chamber;
or rather, it is a synonym for a chamber. Now, showing it by way of a warehouse (*udositādi*) and so forth, he said, "A warehouse," and so on.
Therein, "in the manner already stated" means: "The warehouse belonging to a single family is enclosed..."

This is according to the method stated in the section on "dwelling" (*nivesana*), beginning with the words “and so forth. The word *eva* has the sense of excluding other qualifications (*visesanivatti*). By this, he shows that there is no distinction [in that case].
Now, showing those cases where a distinction does exist, he says: “If the boat belongs to a single family,” and so forth.
Therein, “having exhausted” (*pariyādiyitvā*) means having pierced through, or having overwhelmed. He clarifies this very meaning with the words “by that which has entered inside,” and so forth.
In this context, "having entered within" means having entered within a village or a river. The words "by a road" (*satthena*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

Regarding the phrase "the exemption for a river is obtained," it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "Since no separate exemption for a river has been mentioned here, the exemption for a river is simply the reach of the hand holding the robe, just as it is elsewhere in the case of villages and so forth. Others, however, [say] by this...
They say that because the exclusion of a river is established separately by the words of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, the "hand-span of the river" must not be abandoned.
However, just as the exclusion of a forest is obtained in the open air by way of seven *abbhantara*s, so too the exclusion of a river is obtained in a river by way of the throwing of water;
having taken this into account, the exclusion of the river [is stated] in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
It may be mentioned separately because it is obtained by way of the unbound boundary (*abaddhasīmā*) in forests and rivers—namely, the seven-intermediate-space and water-throw boundaries.
This being the case, the exemption [from the hand-span rule] is established even for oceans and lakes, as they share the same characteristics as rivers;
however, when the meaning is "the river-hand-span must not be left," this is due to the extreme breadth of the river.

Furthermore, because it is common to many, if one were to place the robe inside the river, it would not be possible for someone standing on the riverbank within arm’s reach to know the whereabouts of the robe.
This same principle applies to the ocean and mountain lakes as well.
However, our own opinion is that it would be possible for someone standing either within the splash of the water or within arm’s reach of it; this should be considered after due reflection.
This was said with reference to the monastery boundary (*vihārasīma*) and the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsasīma*).

Here, even though the monastery may belong to various families, because it is possible to remain without being separated from one’s robe (*cīvara*) everywhere within the limits of the non-separation boundary, and because that [boundary] is the primary factor, the exemption from the caravan [rule] does not apply there;
thus it is said, "one must go to the monastery and dwell. "In the vicinity of a caravan" (*satthasamīpe*)...
This has been stated by way of the aforementioned internal boundary. Since it is said,
"Having deposited the robe-cloth in a field belonging to various families that is enclosed,
one must dwell at the foot of the field-gate or within arm's reach of it," therefore, even when living elsewhere in the field than at the foot of the gate, [one remains in contact].
Having set aside one’s robe, one must remain within arm’s reach of it.
Regarding the term "vihāra," they say it refers to the entire dwelling place (āvāsa), whether it be enclosed by a boundary wall or unenclosed.
However, in the phrase "in which vihāra," only a single building is intended. In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it states: "A 'vihāra' is the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*). In which..."

It is said that "he dwells" refers to the interior of his own courtyard and so forth. Furthermore, the fact that it belongs to a single family and so on should be understood from the perspective of those who have it built.
As for the phrase "when the shade covers it all around at midday," this refers to when [the sun] is moving directly across the main street.
When the solar disk reaches midday, it is with reference to the area that the shadow covers at that time that this was said.

However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated: "Regarding 'the place touched by the shadow,' he speaks with reference to the space within which a clod of earth thrown straight ahead and without deviation would land.
Regarding "a path not traveled," this refers to a place where one is unable to go and return on that very same day.
The construction is: "those which are islands in the midst of the ocean. "In the other" refers to the robe [left] in the eastern direction.
"He descends into the river" means he descends having released the reach of his hand. "He does not incur" means he does not incur a *dukkaṭa* offense on account of using it.
Therefore he said, "For he," and so forth. By the phrase "unfit for use," [it is shown that] without having relinquished the forfeitable robe (*nissaggiyacīvara*),...
It is established that for one who consumes [the food], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) which is unintentional.

Regarding the rule "one should go having covered oneself with one [robe] and placed the other on the shoulder," this was stated because going in such a manner is not appropriate for a place where many people frequent;

it was not stated because it constitutes a factor of an offense. It was also stated that even when staying outside the village, one must not leave [the robe] uncovered, because "this is a formal act of the Vinaya."

"should be performed. Alternatively, if one does not see a fellow monk in the monastery, then having gone to the assembly hall (āsanasālā), the legal act (vinayakamma) should be performed—this is the construction.
To the question, "When going to the assembly hall, should one go with all three robes?", he says:
"with the inner robe and upper robe (santaruttarena)," because for one whose robes have been lost, only the inner robe and upper robe are permitted. But what about the outer cloak (saṅghāṭi)?

He said, "It should be done," by adding, "having placed the *saṅghāṭi* outside the village. After first performing the formal legal act (*vinayakamma*) regarding both the *uttarāsaṅga* and the *saṅghāṭi* that was placed outside the village, one should subsequently put on the *uttarāsaṅga* and perform it with respect to the *antaravāsaka*.
And here, because there is a statement regarding the formal legal act even for that which is placed outside the village, one may relinquish [the robe] even when it is standing out of sight.
It should be understood that it is permissible to give [the formal support] once it has been relinquished.
Because there is an intention to go when young monks travel, it is said: "But the formal support (nissaya) is not suspended.
Regarding the phrase "for a moment... it is suspended," this is said because the intention to go has been interrupted; however, for them, until dawn... [the support remains].
For those who set out with enthusiasm and travel until dawn has risen in the interval, the offense does not cease, because it is stated: "lying down until the rising of the dawn.
For this very reason, it is said: "having entered a village... [etc. ...it does not cease.
In the passage beginning with "without heeding one another's words," there is cessation at the moment of departure due to the presence of enthusiasm.

It is not stated [that they are prohibited]. "Out of fear of the cow" means out of fear of young calves and cows rushing toward one and striking with their horns. Regarding the phrase "the support (nissaya) is suspended":
this is said because those who remain due to fear of the cow and so forth must stay until that fear has subsided;
since it is impossible for them to resolve, "I will depart before dawn," [the suspension occurs]. However, where it is possible to resolve thus...
It is possible that, even if dawn breaks there in the interval, the formal support (nissaya) does not cease, as in the case of young monks who have entered a village for the sake of medicine.
By "a village within the boundary," he refers to a village established after the designation of the non-separation boundary (avippavāsa-sīmā).
Because it must be authorized by excluding both the village and its precincts. Regarding "those who have entered":
for teachers and pupils who have gone separately, their robes do not become subject to forfeiture because they remain within the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*);
furthermore, because they have made a formal commitment, the dependence (*nissaya*) does not lapse. Regarding "on the road": this refers to those returning after hearing the Dhamma on the way back.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Ornament of the Discussion on the Determination of Separation from Robes," in the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
10. Discussion on the Determination of the Return of Goods (Bhaṇḍapaṭisāmanavinicchayakathā) 53.

Having thus explained the determination regarding being separated from one's robes, he now spoke the words beginning with "the returning of goods" (*bhaṇḍassa paṭisāmana*) in order to explain the determination regarding the return of goods.
In that context, it is called *bhaṇḍa* because it is to be dealt with (*bhaḍitabba*) or divided (*bhājetabba*). It is to be dealt with...
Alternatively, *bhaṇḍa* means that which is desirable; or, it is called *bhaṇḍa* because beings "deal with" (*bhaṇḍanti*) or "attend to" (*paribhaṇḍanti*) it;
thus it refers to capital wealth or equipment. For it is said in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*:
"In the case of equipment such as vessels, and also in the sense of capital wealth, it is *bhaṇḍa*."
The "replacing" (*paṭisāmana*) of that property means its restoration, guarding, or protecting; thus he said, "the guarding of others' property.
Regarding the phrase "even a palm leaf [or] an earring worn by one's mother," the word *pi* (even) has the sense of inclusion;

by this, he shows that it applies even more so to the belongings of those who are unrelated. By the term "belonging to householders" (*gihisantaka*), [he excludes] the five types of fellow practitioners (*sahadhammika*).

This indicates that it is permissible to store away what belongs to another. By the phrase "by means of the treasurer," he shows that there is no offense for one who takes [an item] through trust or similar means and then stores it away.
Therefore, he will say: "Having taken it for one's own use, it should be stored away.
"By desire or by fear" refers to [taking from] carpenters and the like out of desire, or [from] royal favorites and the like out of fear.
It should be connected thus: "And when they have departed after having been made to fall [from their position] by fear or force, it is proper to restore [the goods].

Regarding an article placed in one's own hand for the purpose of protection, if at a time such as a royal upheaval, one has not performed another act—such as saying "I will not take it"—without the application of restoring it to its secure place, then [it is not theft]. "Now, for that... [and so on].
"I will give it; he will not give it to me now"—even though both have sat down in their respective places and abandoned their efforts, there is no offense of theft.
However, some here say, "It is indeed a *pārājika* because the preliminary effort of taking back has been performed";
that is merely their own opinion and should not be accepted as authoritative. For at the time of taking it back, his mind was one of theft.

There is no bodily or vocal effort on the part of the owner that serves as the cause for the arising of the thought of relinquishing responsibility at the very moment the thought of theft arises—by means of which [the thief] would incur an offense.
For this offense does not originate from non-action (*akiriyasamuṭṭhānā*).
As for the statement, "If he is intent on giving, he protects it for the time being," this was not said with reference to theft (*avahāra*); therefore, [I say] "I am not..."

It should be understood that in the case of making a false statement with words such as "I take [it]," there is only a *pācittiya* offense, not a *dukkaṭa*, because in the absence of the intention to steal (*theyyacitta*), there is also an absence of the concurrent application (*sahapayoga*).
Even if one says, "I will give it by mouth," ... [and so on] ... regarding the phrase "it is a *pārājika*," by which application does the offense arise? Not yet...

Is it because at the time of the first application of returning the goods there was no intention to steal, or because at the time of the application of saying "I will give," even though an intention to steal existed, that application was permissible? It is said in reply: although he was requested many times by the owner, "Give [it back]," he did not give;
rather, by whichever application he made known to the owner his own unwillingness to give, and by whichever... [he indicated] that [owner].
If, knowing "this person does not wish to give and is merely evading me," one lays down the burden [of the debt], there is an offense for that very act.

For in this case, there is no exemption by way of a pretext regarding the goods deposited. Indeed, even if the owner is made to lay down the burden through pretexts such as "When was it given to you? or "Where was it given to you?"—if done out of a desire not to give—it is still an offense.
For this very reason it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “What are you saying? ... [omission] ... by the relinquishing of responsibility for both, there is a *pārājika* offense for the monk.
It should be understood that indirect acquisition (*pariyāyato*)—that is, causing another to take what belongs to another—is indeed a form of theft, but not in all circumstances.
Regarding the phrase “because it was placed in his own hand,” this refers to the state of being a storekeeper (*bhaṇḍāgārika*), since the owner has placed it in his hand.

It should be understood that because it remains in its place, there is no taking away even when it is moved from its position; however, one is not exempt from an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for grasping it with a thieving mind.
"The same method applies" means that while there is no taking away (*avahāra*), there is still the obligation to pay the value of the goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*).
54. "Of the five who share the same Dhamma" refers to monks, nuns, female trainees (*sikkhamānā*), male novices (*sāmaṇera*), and female novices (*sāmaṇerī*). By this...
This shows that it is not only for householders, but also for ascetics, wanderers, and others, that it is not permissible to store away property belonging to them.

Even if it is lost, there is no liability for compensation; why? The meaning is: because it was not accepted [as a deposit]. In the second case, the same principle applies, so there is no liability for compensation;
why? Because it was not recognized. And in the third case, the same principle applies, so there is no liability for compensation.
Why? Because it has been refused. And in this context, even if something is refused by body, speech, or mind, it is indeed called "refused.
The liability for that belongs to him alone, not to the other bhikkhus. Why? Because he alone possesses the authority over the storehouse of the storekeeper.
It does not become the liability of the storekeeper himself if [the goods] were taken through the negligence of one who is lazy by nature. Regarding the second [case], [it concerns] the storekeeper.
There is no liability for him because he did not report it. When it is lost, there is liability for him because he deposited it.
It is his liability alone, and not that of others, because it was accepted and deposited by that storekeeper. There is no liability when it is not lost because it was rejected by him.
When it is lost, it is indeed lost [to the owner] because the storekeeper did not accept it; yet when it is lost, there is liability for him because he deposited it.
"All of it" refers to everything taken through the negligence of that storekeeper.
"While it was still within the precincts" means while it was still in the vicinity of the storekeeper, specifically in the place where excrement and urine were disposed of. 55.
"When I am dead and the Saṅgha’s lodging has been destroyed"—here, it refers exclusively to the lodging belonging to the Saṅgha.
They say that it is indeed permissible to open [the door] with the intention, "May he not perish.

Even when only this much is said, "I shall kill him," it is permissible to open it, because it has been stated that [killing] is not within one's scope due to being situated on the side of those who are ill.

For there is no state of illness greater than death, nor is there anything beyond it that is outside one's scope. This is also the case when only this much is said: "Having broken down the door, I shall carry him away."

It is indeed proper to open [the storehouse]. "One should have companions" means that they too, having sought out alms-food and so forth, should give whatever little they possess; this is what is meant. For this is the proper conduct (*sāmīcī*):
this is the duty for those residing in the storehouse. "The Elder Lolamahāthera" refers to an elder who is dull-witted, deluded, living in a cluttered manner, and always addicted to play.
56. "By the others" means by the monks dwelling in that very same monastery cell. A *vihāravāriko* is one appointed to the duty of guarding the monastery;
he is the one who guards the cell during his own turn according to the seniority order. "Wages" (*nivāpa*) refers to food and salary.

"When the thieves had gone out on their path" means that, having learned of the thieves' approach, [the monks] thought, "We shall go ahead of them and raise an alarm," and thus [regarding] the thieves...
"When they have come face to face. The same principle applies even when they follow after them, thinking, "We shall recover the goods stolen by thieves.
"Having made it fixed" means having established a restriction such as, "In such-and-such a family, the rice gruel and meal are for the monastery attendants alone.
"Receiving two or three tickets for rice gruel, and four or five tickets for meals" refers to this.
This is merely an illustration; whether it be less or more than that, one should understand that the measure is simply obtaining enough for the maintenance of oneself and one’s attendant.

"They have their dependents look after [the monastery]" means that while supporting their respective dependents through alms-gathering, they have those dependents maintain the monastery. "Of one without a companion" means of one who is without a companion.
The reading “of one who is without companion, of one who is alone” (asahāyassa adutiyassa) is appropriate. The latter is a synonym for the former.

However, regarding the reading “of one without companion or with oneself as the second” (asahāyassa vā attadutiyassa vā), they say that because food brought by one person is not sufficient for two, the turn for even one who has oneself as a second is prohibited;
this refers to [the case] where “there is no fellow monk who, having brought almsfood, would give it.”
"This does not agree with that; it should be investigated. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated: "'With oneself as the second' means for one who has few desires.
For 'with oneself as the second' means that one's own body alone is the companion, and no other;
this explains the meaning of both [terms] in the passage beginning with 'for whom. By all of this, it is shown that the turn of each individual should not be reached."
"For the sake of the cooked-food custom" means for the sake of the regular custom consisting of rice gruel and cooked rice that must be prepared daily.
"They set it aside" means the donors set it aside. "Having taken that" means having taken that portion being given by the monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) and others.

"One who lives by it should remain" means that even one who dwells in the open air or at the foot of a tree, if they live depending on the cooked-food custom, should remain there for the purpose of protecting their own bowl and robes.
When the turn for the monastery arrives, one must remain there. Regarding the phrase "he should not be made to take [the requisites]":

here, even if one is an open-air dweller (*abbhokāsika*), if he has extra personal requisites set aside, or if he has an attachment even to the share belonging to the Saṅgha such as robes and so forth, he too should be made to take them.
"They inquire" means answering questions that have been asked, or [reciting] the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). "Twofold" means compared to what is obtained by others.
"Twofold. "By the fortnight" means by the half-month period.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Ornament of the Discussion on the Decision Concerning the Return of Goods," within the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
The Tenth Chapter.
11. Discussion on the Determination of Buying and Selling. 57.
Having thus explained the determination regarding the returning of goods, he now explains the determination regarding buying and selling:
He says, “The attainment of buying and selling,” and so forth. Therein, *kaya* is buying, which is the taking of another’s goods;
*vikkaya* is selling, which is the giving away of one’s own goods. *Kayavikkayaṃ* is both buying and selling.
*Samāpatti* is the act of entering upon [that state], namely, the performance of those two types of activity. He shows its specific form with the words, “By this,” and so forth.

Because it is possible for the gifts of faith given by other relatives to fall into ruin, the passage beginning with “or his mother or his father” was stated in order to show that even in their absence this [fault] does not occur.
By this, he shows that while there is no causing the gift of faith to fall into ruin when one says,
“Give this to him,” one nevertheless incurs the offense of buying and selling when one says, “Give this for that.”
This shows that there is no formal intimation (*viññatti*) when one says "give this" to a non-relative regarding what remains after [the initial portion],

but rather there is the misappropriation of a gift of faith (*saddhādeyya*) when one gives it saying "take this," and there is an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*) for one who enters into buying and selling by saying "give this for that.
This meaning is also demonstrated by the analogy of the "marking of the deer's tracks."

Therefore, even in the case of the passage beginning with "Tasmā iccādi," it should be understood that although one could have stated—"with mother and father, there is buying and selling; with other relatives, two offenses;
with non-relatives, three offenses"—it was not so stated because it can be understood by that same principle.
Otherwise, there would be the fault of non-comprehensiveness (*abyāpitadosa*).

When it is said, “Having eaten this food, do this,” because it expresses an action connected with what precedes and follows, it is similar to saying, “Give this by means of that. Or [it may be said]: “Eat this food; do such-and-such,” or “You have eaten this food; do such-and-such,” or “You will eat this food; do such-and-such.”

However, since it was stated that the action was unrelated [to the gift], there is no buying or selling. Furthermore, because there was no expectation regarding the giving of food to those who eat leftovers, there is no misappropriation of what was given in faith;
and because the act of having it made was merely manual labor performed by others, there is no solicitation.

Therefore, it is permissible. With the words "And here," etc., it is shown that even though the object for which one would be liable to relinquish (nissaggiya) is absent, there is nevertheless an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
He shows that it should be pointed out.
It is permissible to ask the price; the meaning is that up to this point there is no buying or selling.

It is permissible to take [the goods] because there has been no statement such as "give me this for this," and thus there is no buying or selling; furthermore, because the price exists, there is no solicitation either.
[The bowl] exists. A bowl must not be accepted because of the high value of another’s goods. If this is so, how should it be handled? He said:
"One must declare, 'My goods are of little value. Once the goods have been appraised, one incurs the offense of being made to pay for them due to the possibility of a fraudulent transaction;
if they are worth less than a māsaka, it is a dukkaṭa. From a māsaka upwards, up to less than five māsakas...
If it is worth [that amount], it is a *thullaccaya* offense. If it is worth five *māsakas*, it is stated that it is a *pārājika* offense.

If he gives it, it is permissible because it was given for the sake of merit; however, for the sake of what is in excess. But for the *kappiyakāraka* (the one who makes things allowable) … it is permissible because the articles are allowable for both parties.
If the article is unallowable for either one or for both, it is not permissible. “Do not take it!”
It should be said: why? Because the attendant (kappiyakāraka) is not skilled.

Why is there need for [oil] that has not been formally accepted (appaṭiggahita)? Because oil is permitted only for seven days (sattāhakālika). Oil that has been formally accepted may be kept for a maximum of seven days;
therefore, for one who wishes to keep it beyond that period, there is need for oil that has not been formally accepted.

One might spoil what has not been accepted; one might cause unaccepted oil, for which no time limit has been set, to last until one’s own [intended] time by means of a remaining *nāḷika* of accepted oil. 58.
"This is to be understood as the fourfold bowl" refers to the fourfold set of unbefitting bowls that have been mentioned; however, the fifth is the fitting one.
Therefore, one will say: "This bowl is suitable for all ages and worthy of being used even by the Buddhas.
This bowl is called *mahā-akappiya* (extremely unsuitable). Why? Because silver was taken, iron ore was extracted, and the bowl was made from that metal;
thus, it has been defiled starting from its very seed-source. And just as in the case of the third *pārājika* offense regarding permanent objects such as snares, stakes, and so forth...
In the case of things made from the very beginning, one is not released as long as even a mere measure of wood or a mere measure of bark remains;

one is released only when everything has been destroyed. Likewise here, because it was made starting from the seed, even if some portion of that bowl remains, it cannot become allowable. And so he will say: "Even if, having destroyed that..."
“He has a bowl made; that too is unallowable,” and so forth. Even though this is the case, one might wonder:

“If it were given to the owners of the original bowl at its base, and to the owner of the second bowl for the second bowl itself, would it then be possible to make it allowable? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
“It cannot be made allowable by any means whatsoever. The meaning of this is: having accepted the second bowl [purchased] with silver...
One buys [the bowl] already finished by householders and does not spoil it starting from the seed;

therefore, a second bowl can be made allowable. However, in this case, because it has been spoiled starting from the seed, that monk is unable to make it into a seed of iron and stone again, and because the accepted money has been used up, he is unable to give it back to the owners again.
"It is not possible by any means to make it allowable.
Now, in order to elaborate upon that impossibility in another way, he says "Even if... and so forth.
By this, he shows that as long as even a tiny portion of what is not a substance remains, it is indeed unallowable. Therefore, it is stated in the *Vimativinodanī*:
“Having acquired silver”: this is stated by way of the maximum limit;
even having acquired articles such as pearls that constitute an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), it is likewise not permitted for the five [monks] to have them made.

“He causes to be produced”: he causes it to be produced either by going himself or by commanding another, saying, “Give this coin and so forth to the laborers and cause the seed to be produced. “A great unallowable thing” (mahā-akappiya).
This is stated because it has been defiled by oneself from the very seed onwards, and because there is no other owner of the root.
For even if it were recovered after being stolen by thieves, it is not permissible for anyone who knows [the circumstances].
If it were indeed permissible, the teachers would have said, as they do regarding ponds and the like, "what was stolen is permissible. It cannot be made permissible by any means whatsoever.
It is not possible to make something allowable by means of giving it away to the Saṅgha or by having thieves and others steal it;
and this was said with reference to that which exists in its own form and that which exists in the form of cloth, pearls, and so forth, derived from that [unallowable object].
For neither an article of wrongdoing nor an allowable article derived from it can be made allowable by anyone through that very form. However, if...
"It should be understood that if that bhikkhu were to exchange that money again for allowable goods or for goods that are an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),
it would be possible to have that money forfeited and then have other allowable goods made [for him]. However, as for what has been elaborated upon in the *Sāratthadīpanī*,
and what has been elaborated upon in the ancient commentary (*porāṇaṭīkā*) by adopting that very same [position], that will now be stated in detail.
It would have been too extensive and difficult for listeners to comprehend; therefore, we have spoken only this much.
However, those who desire further detail should consult and study various other treatises.
Regarding the second bowl, it is not permissible even for those five who share the same Dhamma, because of the acceptance of money and because of buying and selling.

And because it has been prepared. However, it can indeed be made allowable (*kappiya*) because the bowl has already been purchased by laypeople, because it has not been damaged from the time of its seed onwards, and because both the original owners of the materials and the current owners of the bowls are present.
To show how this is possible, he said, "In the roots," and so forth.
Regarding the third bowl, the phrase "it is exactly the same" indicates this principle: "It is not permissible even for those who are in accordance with the Dhamma, but it can be made allowable.
Anticipating the objection, "But surely the third bowl was taken up using allowable terminology;
then why is it unallowable? he says: "Even though it was taken up using allowable terminology, it is exactly like the second bowl, because of its root..."
“Because it has been accepted, it is not allowable. As for the second objection, however, he states it himself.

And here, because it is said, “It is exactly like the second bowl,” it should be understood that if the root is given to the owners of the root and the bowl is given to the owners of the bowl, it becomes allowable;
having received it after giving something allowable in exchange, it is permissible to use it. Regarding the phrase “because the root has not been relinquished”: by whatever root was taken up...

The bowl has been purchased; because its price was not relinquished in the midst of the Saṅgha, this shows that only the money itself must be relinquished, not the non-monetary item resulting from it.

For if the price agreed upon by him had been relinquished in the midst of the Saṅgha, then the bowl—having been acquired through that permissible transaction by monastery attendants and others and handed over—would be allowable for the rest [of the monks], with the exception of the receiver of the money.

"Because it was improperly deliberated upon in the fourth bowl": the meaning is that because the coins belonging to a householder were taken [with the thought], "Having given these kahāpaṇas, give me this," they were wrongly deliberated upon;
therefore, it is not permissible for this very monk who performed the deliberation.
"Because the price was not accepted": by this, he shows that the price belongs to the householder; for that very reason, [the bowl]...

This shows that [the offense] has not arisen through trading with silver; by this, it indicates that there is no need for the bowl to be forfeited (*nissaggiya*) and that there is no *pācittiya* offense for the monk.
Furthermore, it clarifies that by mere misconduct alone, there is only a *dukkaṭa* offense.
The term "forfeited" (*nissajjī*) is stated here in the sense of giving, not in the sense of a formal disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*). For that very reason, [it says] "of the ghee... [and so forth].
It is said, "having filled [it].

Regarding the fifth case, "suitable for all" (sabbakappiya) means it is suitable for oneself, for one's five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, and for Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas. Therefore, he said, "it is worthy of being used even by Buddhas.
Thus ends the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
The Eleventh Chapter: The Ornament of Discourse on the Determination of Buying, Selling, and Bartering.
12. The Discourse on the Determination of Receiving Precious Metals and Other Valuables.
59. Having thus explained the determination regarding buying and selling, he now speaks on the determination regarding the acceptance of money and so forth, saying:

“The acceptance of money and so forth,” etc. In this context, that which has money (*rūpiya*)—meaning any wealth consisting of commercial goods—made for the purpose of identification is called *rūpiya*. Thus it is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*: “But here...”
"Whatever is fit for common transaction, such as kahāpaṇas and so forth, is intended. "First it is taken," etc.; what is that? It is *rūpiya* (money/precious metal).
Those things of which *rūpiya* is the first are "those beginning with *rūpiya*" (*rūpiyādayo*), namely female and male slaves, fields, land, and so forth.

Receiving is "acceptance" (*paṭiggaho*), meaning the act of receiving. The acceptance of those things beginning with *rūpiya* is "the acceptance of *rūpiya*-beginners" (*rūpiyādipaṭiggaho*). At the moment of its arising...
That which, once arisen, remains as form itself and does not undergo transformation is *jātarūpa*, meaning gold.
Because it is pleasing (*rañjiyati*) to beings due to its white nature, it is *rajata*, meaning silver. A *māsaka* coin made of *jātarūpa* is a *jātarūpa-māsaka*;
a *māsaka* coin made of *rajata* is a *rajata-māsaka*. These four types alone constitute the object subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya-vatthu*), and not copper coins and the like.

He said: "It is comprised of copper, iron, and so forth... pe ... it is included. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "copper, iron, and so forth," he shows that even a copper coin made from bell-metal (*kaṃsa*), brass (*vaṭṭaloha*), tin (*tipu*), lead (*sīsa*), and the like, is indeed a "copper coin" (*lohamāsaka*). Is this alone the object for which there is forfeiture (*nissaggiya-vatthu*), or are pearls and other items also [objects of forfeiture]?
He said: "Pearls... pe ... they are objects of an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa-vatthu*). To the question, "What is the distinction between these two types of objects? he said: "In that regard..."

“...the object of forfeiture... [and so on] ...is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Herein, the construction is as follows: regarding the object of forfeiture, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya) when for one’s own sake, and an offense of wrong-doing when for the sake of others; regarding the object of wrong-doing, it is an offense of wrong-doing for all [cases].
Now, in order to show in detail the determination of what is allowable and what is unallowable among those objects, he said: “In this regard, the determination is as follows.”
In that case, it is not permissible to accept it. Why? Because it has been given using an improper expression, namely, "I give this to the Saṅgha.
It is permissible if one departs after having given it; why? Because it was not placed in the hands of the Saṅgha, but rather in the hands of carpenters and others.
It is likewise permissible because it was placed in the hands of laypeople. However, it is not permissible to refuse it.
Because it does not refer to the Saṅgha, the group, or the individual. It must be rejected as "not allowable" because of the statement, "Having taken [it], set it aside.

Regarding both the acceptance and the consumption, there is an offense: because of the statement "I give it to the Saṅgha," there is a *pācittiya* for the acceptance and a *dukkaṭa* for the consumption.
"He is one who has committed an offense" refers to the *dukkaṭa* offense.
He speaks. It is permissible for him to say, “Enjoy these requisites,” because this is spoken using allowable terminology (*kappiya-vohāra*).
That which is given for the sake of robes must be applied specifically to robes; why? Because one must act in accordance with what the donors have stated.
To show the distinction of the lodging-requisite from the other three requisites, he said, “for the sake of lodging,” and so forth.
By this, he shows that [the object] is neither to be given away nor to be divided. Even so, showing the procedure to be followed in cases of distress, he says, "If, however," and so forth. 60.

Having thus shown the procedure to be followed regarding the objects involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*), he now [shows] the procedure to be followed regarding the objects involving an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Showing this, he said, “If anyone [should give] to me,” and so forth. Here, however, it is stated with reference specifically to a *dukkaṭa* offense, meaning that there is an offense both in the act of receiving and in the act of using. Since even a pond is included within the category of “fields,” an offense is stated for its reception as well.
Regarding the phrase, “He gives [thinking], ‘Use these four requisites,’” here [the intention is]: “For the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, the four requisites...”
In the *Sāratthadīpanī* it is stated: "If one says, 'I give this pond for the purpose of using [it],' or 'I give this pond for the purpose of enjoying the four requisites,' it is indeed permissible.
However, if one says, 'I give the requisites arising from this pond,' there is nothing at all that can be said [against it].
The *Vimativinodanī* also states the same, adding: "And this [gift] belongs to the Saṅgha..."

This was stated with reference specifically to that which is being given; however, even if it has been given in this manner, it is not permissible for an individual to [use] ponds, fields, and so forth.
But for one of pure mind, wells, lotus ponds, and the like are permitted for the purpose of utilizing water.
For it is said: "In all such cases, it is stated by way of the Saṅgha alone, as in: 'The Saṅgha possesses a pond; what shall be done with it? etc.
“It will be in his hand” means it will be under his control.
The phrase “appoint a kappiyakāraka” is stated by way of formal propriety; even if not so stated, there is no fault for one who appoints one.
Therefore he said, “it is permissible to withhold the water. Because [one might] destroy what belongs to others belonging to the monks...
It is not permissible; therefore, it is said, "not at the time of the harvest. Even at the time of the harvest, it is permissible to release [the person] after having threatened him;

however, if one does not release him, there is an obligation to pay the value of the goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*). By the phrase "the owner of the district," they say that even if it is given by one who governs that district, provided it was given after taking it away [from the thief], it is indeed permissible.
"Gives back again" means he gives it back again after having taken it away.

The connection is: "In this way, it is also permissible. By this, he shows that whatever has been given by any lord, having been taken by oneself under the perception that "this has been relinquished by the monks and is ownerless," is permissible. "Water-channel" (*udakavāha*) means a watercourse.
The ellipsis is: "I shall also explain the determination regarding allowable terminology (*kappiyavohāra*). "By way of water" means for the purpose of using the water.
"Of those with pure minds" means solely for the purpose of using water. This was said with reference to one who acts both with their own hand and through improper speech.
However, even for those with impure minds, it is indeed permissible to command another to act by means of proper speech, provided they do not do it themselves "for the sake of preparing crops.
As for the statement "it is not permissible to appoint a steward," this refers to acting by one's own hand and so forth.

It is said that [the construction] is suitable if it is a well-made pond. However, no offense is recognized for the Saṅgha either when it establishes that requisite or when it makes use of it; rather, the offense here should be understood according to the authority of the Aṭṭhakathā.

He says "by a conscientious bhikkhu" because there is nothing at all to be said regarding what is caused to be done by one who is shameless; the intention is that this refers to cases where [the work] is caused to be done, such as the removal of clay and so forth.

61. "In a field where nothing has been done before" means in a field that has not been previously cultivated. By the term "kahāpaṇa," it is shown that the harvesting of grain is itself what is improper.

"In a field where the portions have not been demarcated" means in a field where the portions have not been defined such that one might say, "On this much area of land, this much portion should be given.

He plows for the purpose of harvesting grain; even in the preliminary effort (*payoga*), there is indeed a *dukkaṭa* offense, but not as in the case of harvesting for the sake of a *kahāpaṇa*. [The Buddha said: "Plow and sow!"
He said "without saying" because, by the mere act of speaking, it would become improper for everyone.
Regarding the phrase "such an amount of a portion," he says this with reference to "such an amount of kahāpaṇas.

For even if it were stated in that way, since kahāpaṇas were not available at that time, it would still be permissible for others in the future. Therefore he said, "That is improper for him alone. For him...
However, in all instances of the preliminary effort (*payoga*) and in the actual consumption (*paribhoga*), there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Some, however, claim that the offense occurs only at the time of the consumption of grain and not during the prior stage; this is not correct, because it would be illogical for there to be no offense when one performs the very effort—such as measuring or guarding—that subsequently results in an offense upon the consumption of the grain.
According to the method of figurative explanation (*pariyāyakathā*), however, [the offense applies] everywhere.
There is no offense. For that very reason, it was stated that what is spoken in a restrictive command such as, "Bring this and that with so many grains of rice," is unallowable.

The same principle applies to the handling of kahāpaṇa coins. Furthermore, the statement beginning with, "In this case, such a thing exists, yet there is no attendant to make it allowable," serves as proof here.
Regarding the phrase "with a rope or with a staff," [it continues] "even with one's feet..."
"It is not permissible even for a moment," they say. Regarding the phrase "or standing in a threshing floor he guards":
here, if he sees people taking things by stealth and stops them, saying, "Do not take it," this is called guarding.
However, if he stands silently watching for the purpose of guarding without investigating [the situation], it is permissible. "Even if, while he is silent, they carry it off by theft..."
They say, "It is also permissible to say, 'We shall inform the Saṅgha of monks.
Regarding the phrases "has it removed" and "has it put away," they also say, "If one speaks by way of a figurative expression, it is permissible.
Because it has not been produced previously, it is permissible for others; therefore he said, "This is not allowable for him alone."
"It is improper for everyone; why? Because of the handling of kahāpaṇas. Regarding this, the following analysis is given in the *Sāratthadīpanī*:
"Is it not the case that by the mere act of handling, it is improper for that person alone, and not for everyone, just as in the fourth offense regarding the exchange of money?
For it is said there: 'But he who, without accepting money, [says] "The Elder's bowl...'"

“Having bought it, give it to me”—having gone with the attendant who was sent to the smith’s workshop, he saw the bowl and, having caused the coins to be given by saying, “Take these kahāpaṇas and give this [bowl] to me,” he took it.
This bowl is not permissible for that very bhikkhu because of his improper conduct; however, it is permissible for others because the price was not accepted. Therefore—
Whatever they bring for you, it is unallowable for all. Why? Because of the exchange of kahāpaṇas.
Why was this said? On this point some say: "This was said with reference to what was exchanged after having accepted the kahāpaṇas.
Furthermore, because it belongs to the Saṅgha, it cannot be relinquished; therefore, their intention is that it is not allowable for anyone at all.
However, some say: "Even though he did not personally accept them, because he handled the coins, a transaction involving money has been committed;
and since they belong to the Saṅgha, they cannot be relinquished. Therefore, it is not allowable for anyone.
But in all three *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, this is stated: "The fourth bowl was handled only by coins belonging to householders, and not by those of others..."
