"It is allowable [in that case], but here, because it has been assigned to the Saṅgha, it is not allowable for anyone. Thus, the position of everyone is indeed consistent with their respective arguments.
62. "At the door of the four-hall" refers to the dining hall.

63. Regarding the statement, "If one says, 'I give a grove,' or 'I give a forest,' it is permissible," this means that because it is a place of residence, it is permissible for an individual to accept it with a pure mind.
As for the statement, "It is permissible" [in the case of] "We give a boundary," this is said because it is expressed by a general term such as "the monastery boundary" (*vihārasīmā*) and so forth.
It is because it was spoken by way of a synonym; that is, instead of saying "Take it," it was said by way of a synonym, "The boundary has been reached."
Because it has already been mentioned. The words "the sand taken below," and so forth, were spoken for the purpose of making it the natural ground.
Regarding the phrase "I give a slave," they say that it is permissible if one says "I give a human being.

When it is stated as "a servant" (*veyyāvaccakara*) and so on, it is also permissible to accept a person as a slave, because it was specifically authorized by the rule: "I allow you, monks, a monastery attendant" (*ārāmika*). And that...
This refers to the sequence of use established by Pilindavaccha, not to the sequence of servile use for householders.
Furthermore, it should be understood that all things such as fields and so forth are permissible only for the Saṅgha, because taking them for an individual is not authorized in the Canon.
Regarding the phrase "chickens, pigs... it is permissible": when chickens or pigs are being given, [one should say], "These [animals] are for us..."
"It is appropriate to say: 'There is no need; let them live happily; release them into the forest.
The statement "We give it to the monastery" refers to a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha.

The Blessed One’s intention was that the prohibition found in the Suttantas—such as "He abstains from accepting fields and land"—was established by him because such acts serve as a cause for an offense.

It should be understood that this entire exposition on the meaning outside the canonical text (*pāḷimutta-vinicchaya*), concerning the acceptance of land for a field and so forth, was spoken by the Great Elders who compiled the Council while they were fully aware [of the circumstances].
64. *Cīvaracetāpannaṃ*: the price for a robe. *Pahiṇeyya*: should send. *Cetāpetvā*: having exchanged. *Acchādehi*:
this is a conventional expression; however, the meaning here is "give it to the monk named so-and-so. *Ābhataṃ*: brought.
Regarding this point, the following analysis is made in the *Sāratthadīpanī*:

"And here, that which was stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*—namely, 'Having purchased a robe with these robe-funds, clothe the monk named so-and-so with a robe'—was said in order to demonstrate purity of source (*āgamanasuddhi*).
For if [one were to say], 'Give this to the monk named so-and-so'..."

"If one were to send [a messenger], because the arrival would be impure, even a 'maker of what is allowable' (kappiyakāraka) could not be designated by the monk with regard to an unallowable thing"— in this case,
no specific purpose for the purity or impurity of the arrival is seen; for even though the arrival is impure, through the messenger's own skillfulness, by means of allowable terminology...
As for the statement that "the kappiyakāraka need not be pointed out," this is not the case;
nor is it found that when something is spoken by a messenger using a formula of what is allowable (kappiya-vohāra), the donor engages in such deliberation as, "How was this sent?
For one cannot know [the source] without such deliberation. However, if the arrival [of the gift] is impure, then the kappiyakāraka must indeed be pointed out.

If it were not so, then when an improper object is sent into the hand of a messenger for the sake of robes, the maker of the allowable [gift] would have to be pointed out by the donor after asking, "How was this sent? everywhere;
therefore, even though there is no purity regarding the arrival [of the gift], if that messenger speaks by way of allowable terminology through his own skill, [it is valid].
The word of the messenger alone must be accepted as authority.

For if, in this case, the purity of the messenger's arrival were the sole criterion, then even if a messenger sent by the owner of the root goods speaks using improper terminology instead of permissible terminology, one who prepares what is permissible would still have to be pointed out [as the transgressor].
Therefore, in all instances, it must be understood that the word of the messenger alone is the authority. By this—
By the passage beginning with "with robe-fund" (cīvaracetāpannena), however, he shows this meaning:
"Even if the price for robes has been brought in a permissible manner, it becomes impermissible through such a message from a messenger; therefore, it must be refused. For this very reason, he said:
"That bhikkhu should speak to that messenger thus," and so forth.

In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it is stated thus: "That which was said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*—namely, 'Having purchased a robe with this robe-fund, clothe the bhikkhu named so-and-so with a robe'—was said in order to demonstrate the purity of the source.
For if one were to send [the gift] saying, 'Give this to the bhikkhu named so-and-so,' because the source would be impure..."
If one were to say, "A monk should not even designate a 'maker of what is allowable' (kappiyakāraka) with regard to an unallowable object," then, since that unallowable cloth-money—

which constitutes both an article for forfeiture (nissaggiya-vatthu) and an article of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa-vatthu)— is an unallowable means of procuring cloth, and thus lacks purity of source when one says,
"Give this to such-and-such a monk," and the wording of the messenger is also impure according to the method set forth in the training rule (sikkhāpada):
It is permissible only to make a total refusal; one must not say, "We do accept the robe," nor point to an attendant on that basis, because both the messenger's arrival and his words are impure.

However, according to the method found in the Pāḷi, when there is purity regarding the arrival—even if the messenger's words are impure—according to the method set forth in the training rule (sikkhāpada):
This was stated for the purpose of showing that it is permissible to perform everything. By this, the following meaning is established by implication:

just as it is permissible to designate someone as a service-provider when the messenger’s speech is pure even if his arrival is impure, so too is it permissible when the messenger’s speech is pure even if his arrival is impure;
thus, there is nothing further to be said regarding the purity of both.

It should be understood that it was stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* with reference specifically to the side of impurity in both cases: "The one who makes [the food] allowable (*kappiyakāraka*) would also not need to be pointed out.
However, regarding what is here in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: "Whether there is purity or impurity of the arrival [of the food], there is no specific purpose..."

The statement beginning with “is not seen” was spoken without having observed the intended meaning of the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary on the Schedule), because [the latter] possesses a specific purpose according to the method already stated, such as the purity of the source and so forth.

As for the undesirable consequence raised here: “Even if the owner of the root [of the goods] speaks by way of an allowable expression (*kappiya-vohāra*), while the messenger sent [by him] speaks by way of an unallowable expression (*akappiya-vohāra*), the one who makes it allowable (*kappiyakāraka*) should still be identified. [This is incorrect.]

That which was stated does not entail the undesirable consequence, because it is intended [in that way]. For indeed, in the very training rule (*sikkhāpada*), regarding a messenger who speaks using an improper expression (*akappiya-vohāra*) such as, "May the venerable one accept the robe-fund," it is stated that the attendant must point out the allowable action (*kappiya-kamma*), because of the purity of the messenger's arrival;
however, if the arrival itself were impure, even by means of an allowable action—
"There is indeed a purpose for investigating whether the arrival [of the robe-cloth] is pure or impure, on the grounds that 'one who performs a service through work should not be pointed out.
But how is the purity of the arrival known by means of the messenger's words? This is no burden.

For the purity of the arrival must be sought only when the messenger speaks using an improper expression (*akappiya-vohāra*), and not otherwise. And in that case, according to the sequence of his speech—"
And it is possible to understand [the meaning] by means of inquiry, logical reasoning (*yutti*), and so forth.
For here too, in the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), the fact that one has been sent to purchase and give a robe is understood from the messenger’s statement alone: “A robe-fund has been brought.
For if the purity of the acquisition were not understood in every respect, a prohibition would indeed have to be made.
Gold, silver, a kahāpaṇa coin, and a māsaka coin—these four are indeed the objects for which there is forfeiture (nissaggiya-vatthu).
Pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells, crystal, coral, red pearls, and cat’s-eye; the seven kinds of grain; male and female slaves;

fields, land, flower gardens, fruit gardens, and so forth—these are the objects for which there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa-vatthu), whether they belong to oneself or to a cetiya, the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
Since it is not permissible to accept [the funds] for that purpose, it was said, "Friends, we do not accept cloth-money," in order to show that it is therefore not permissible to consent to it.

The passage beginning with "But we do accept robes" is intended to show the method of proceeding for the sake of purity regarding the messenger's arrival, even though the messenger's words themselves are unallowable.
It has been said. "At the proper time, what is allowable" means that at the appropriate and fitting time, when one has need, one accepts an allowable robe;
this is the meaning. "A service-provider" (veyyāvaccakara) means one who performs a task; the meaning is "an attendant.
The statement, "The service-provider must be pointed out," is because it was spoken using the allowable phrase: "But does the venerable one have anyone as a service-provider?"
It is permitted. However, if the messenger says, "Who will take this? To whom shall I give it?", the recipient must not be pointed out.
The mention of "an attendant (ārāmika) or a lay follower (upāsaka)" is stated because they are suitable;

however, anyone who is a provider of what is allowable (kappiyakāraka), with the exception of the five types of fellow practitioners (sahadhammika), is permissible. "This, friend, is the attendant for the monks"—this was said by the messenger.

This was stated in order to show that a monk may use permissible speech (*kappiya-vacana*) corresponding to the nature of the question asked when one asks, "Does the Venerable One have anyone who can perform services for you?
For it is precisely thus that a monk should speak; he must not say, "Give this to him," and so forth.
For this very reason, the Pāḷi says, "He must not be told, 'Give this to him,'" and so on. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*...
It is stated: “This... [etc.]... was said for the purpose of releasing one from the taking of unallowable things, such as saying ‘give it to him’ and so forth.
Regarding the phrase “I have been instructed by him,” the meaning is that he has been told, “In the event that you have need of a robe, he will give you a robe.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is said: “When he has been thus addressed again by means of a messenger—‘I have been conciliated,’ and so forth—it is permissible to press him for the robe.”
It is stated that this was said for the purpose of showing that it is not otherwise. Here, however, it is expressed thus because it appears in the Pāḷi as "He has been informed by me.

But in the preceding sentence in the Vinaya-saṅgaha-pakaraṇa, it is expressed in that way because it was established by substituting the synonymous term "commanded" (*āṇatta*) for "informed" (*saññatta*).
And by that, [it is shown] that when the one who makes things allowable (*kappiyakāraka*) has been informed by means of a messenger...
This shows that a monk must first inform the *kappiyakāraka* (the one who makes things allowable) before he can urge him; it cannot be done without such notification.

The phrase "I have need of a robe, friend" is an illustration of the characteristic of the urging. For either this specific statement must be used, or its meaning may be expressed in any language whatsoever.
However, phrases such as "Give me a robe" and so forth are shown here for the purpose of demonstrating forms of speech that should not be used.

These have been stated. For these words, or their meaning, cannot be expressed in any language whatsoever. "And one who speaks thus incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense for violating the rule because it has been prohibited;
however, there is still a formal accusation (*codanā*)," so it is said in the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada* and the *Majjhimagaṇṭhipada*.
But in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: "'Give me my robe... [and so forth] should not be spoken.
Regarding the statement, “Exchange [this] for a robe for me,” because one has designated oneself as the “maker of what is allowable” (kappiyakāraka) for accepting silver brought by a messenger,
one who says, “Give me a robe... exchange it for a robe for me,” is indeed engaging in a monetary transaction with that silver—
since silver is a primary object of trade— and thus incurs that fault.
It was stated [in the previous case] that one should avoid [the offense] from afar, just as in the case of a monk who accepts silver and relinquishes it in the midst of the Saṅgha.

For it was said there: "One should not say, 'Bring this or that,'" and therefore it should be understood that this [present rule] was not stated in order to avoid the fault of requesting; otherwise, it would follow that even saying, "Friend, I have need of a robe," would be improper.

It is stated that because there is no suspicion of trading in money among those indicated by the messenger for that very reason, one may have the robe brought even after appointing another person as the "maker of what is allowable" (kappiyakāraka).

Furthermore, it is stated that the intended meaning should be understood as follows: one should have the robe brought not by saying, "Having exchanged [the value] with the money deposited by the messenger, bring back the robe," but simply by saying, "Bring back the robe."

"If this is successful"—meaning, if after being urged thus up to three times, he is able to procure that robe for himself by means of his own acquisition—"this is successful," meaning it is good, well-done, and excellent.
"He should stand silently in dedication [for the donor] at most four, five, or six times" is an indication of the characteristic of standing. "At most six times" means...
And this is a neuter singular form used as a locative. By the phrase "at most six times," the characteristic of standing is defined:
one should simply stand in silence with reference to the robe, and nothing else should be done. For this very reason, it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā:
"not on a seat," and so forth. However, in the science of grammar (saddasattha):
"According to the statement: 'In grammar, it is called an adverb of action;

in the [Buddhist] teaching, it is proclaimed as a neuter abstract noun (bhāvanapuṃsaka) which is specifically an adverb of action,' it follows that according to the terminology of the Teaching, only an adverb of action becomes what is known as a neuter abstract noun."
"‘He cooks softly’—here, ‘cooking’ is [the action];
and ‘he sleeps happily’—here, ‘sleeping’ is [the action].
According to this statement, even an intransitive verb may stand in grammatical apposition with a qualifying word that expresses the action.
Since even a transitive verb must be connected with the *bhū-dhātu* (the root "to be") and the *kar-dhātu* (the root "to do"), by this principle it should be understood as:
"the state of being limited to six times" (*chakkhattuparamaṃ ṭhānaṃ*) is to be [attained], meaning "the state of being limited to six times is to be performed.
By this, it is shown that the state of being limited to six times is to be thus attained, not more than that; the state of being limited to six times is precisely what is to be performed.
This shows that one does not rise from there. "One should not sit on a seat" means that even when told, "Venerable sir, please sit here," one should not sit.

"One should not accept food" means that even when requested, "Venerable sir, please take some food such as rice-gruel or solid food," one should not accept it. "One should not speak the Dhamma" [means] "a blessing..."
"Even when being requested, 'Speak something in praise or in approval,' one should not say anything at all;
rather, when asked, 'For what reason have you come? one should simply say, 'Know for yourself, friend.
'He breaks the ground' means he ruins or provokes the reason for his coming. 'Ground' (*ṭhāna*) refers to both a standing place and a cause."
This refers to the name; therefore, by sitting on a seat, the occasion (*ṭhāna*) is spoiled as well as the reason for coming.
However, in cases such as receiving material gifts, it is only the reason for coming that is destroyed, not the occasion. Thus he said, "he destroys the reason for coming.
Some, however, say, "By receiving material gifts and so forth, the occasion is also destroyed"; that does not accord with the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

In the *Ṭīkā* as well, after demonstrating various doctrines, the "shattering of the position" (*ṭhānabhañjana*) was stated; however, because it does not correspond with the words of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, we did not mention it for fear of making the text too cumbersome.

Now, regarding the three challenges and six positions that were stated, he says, beginning with "If he challenges four times," in order to show the increase and decrease therein. And because of the increase in a single challenge...
The loss of two positions has been stated; therefore, the characteristic is shown that the charge is double the number of positions.
Thus, by this characteristic, after charging three times, one must stand six times;
after charging twice, one must stand eight times; and after charging once, one must stand ten times.

“Standing in this or that place” means that this was said by the challenger with reference specifically to standing in various designated locations after having moved away from his own original position.
“What need is there to mention different days?”—the intention is that for one who acts in this way on different days, what further need is there to say anything;
it requires no further explanation. “Either one must go oneself, or a messenger must be sent.”
They say: "This must certainly be done even by one who does not wish to be reproved on account of its inherent nature.
"It serves no purpose for that bhikkhu" means that this robe-fund accomplishes not even the slightest task for that bhikkhu.
"Venerable sirs, apply yourselves to your own" means: "Venerable sirs, may you obtain the wealth belonging to yourselves."

In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it is stated: “The passage beginning ‘whatever robe-fund for him’ and so forth is an indication of what must be done by one who has been designated as the agent, provided that the robe itself has not yet been produced.
Thus, when the monk has spoken to the owners of the property and they give after being urged, it is permissible;
for it is stated in the section on non-offenses that ‘there is no offense because the owners gave after having been urged. For this very reason...”

Thus, if he himself does not urge [the donor] but, having spoken to lay followers (upāsaka) and others by way of indirect means, causes them to urge [the donor], and they, after urging him even a hundred times, cause the robe to be given, there is no offense for him;
this is established because the training rule (sikkhāpada) was not specifically prescribed [for such a case].
65. One who has been designated by no one else, but has reached the status of a personal attendant (veyyāvaccakara) through his own mouth, is called a "mouth-attendant" (mukhavevaṭika).

By the phrase "because of the desire not to investigate," he shows that even Noble Ones (ariya), though possessing [the goods], may say from conventional usage that "it does not exist" when they do not wish to give it away, even without an intention to deceive. In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, however, it says:
"Regarding 'because of the desire not to investigate,' in this position, one who acts as a *kappiyakāraka* [purifier] thinking, 'We have no *kappiyakāraka*,' acts as a *kappiyakāraka*..."
It is said that this was spoken with the intention of [showing that] "it does not exist. In the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka*, within the account of the merchant Meṇḍaka, it is stated:
"The very words beginning with 'There are, monks... constitute what is called the Meṇḍaka training rule (*sikkhāpada*). For therein, the merchant named Meṇḍaka said:
"Venerable sir, there are indeed wilderness paths that have little water and little food, which are not easy to traverse without provisions."
“...to go, it would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would allow provisions for the journey for the bhikkhus. When this was requested, the Blessed One said:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, to seek out provisions for the journey:

rice for one who needs rice, mung beans for one who needs mung beans, kidney beans for one who needs kidney beans, salt for one who needs salt, sugar for one who needs sugar, oil for one who needs oil, and ghee.”
Having said, "with that which contains ghee," this was stated: "Bhikkhus, there are people who have faith and confidence;
they place gold in the hands of the kappiyakārakas (officials of allowable goods), saying, 'With this, give whatever is allowable for the noble one.
I allow you, bhikkhus, to accept from that what is allowable, but I certainly do not, bhikkhus..."
“I say that gold and silver may be accepted and sought after by some means.

Regarding the statement, “They place money in the hands of a kappiyakāraka (one who makes things allowable),” there is indeed still the requirement for informing the bhikkhu; otherwise, he would not be subject to censure for falling into the category of one who uses an unspecified kappiyakāraka.
However, this was said with reference to a kappiyakāraka who has been specifically designated by means of a messenger.
But a monk must not [do so] whether [the offense] has been specified or not. For this very reason it was said: "In this matter there is no limit to the accusation," and so forth.
If one accuses with reference to the root [offense], that would amount to an admission; therefore it was said: "by one who does not admit the root.
One should proceed as if toward strangers or those who have not invited one; this means that one should not create a position for oneself as an accuser.
It is stated for the purpose of showing [this]. By the phrase "for the sake of alms-food and so forth," it is demonstrated that this does not apply solely for the sake of robes.

By the phrase "in the same manner," it is shown that when the steward of the property has designated the stewards of allowable goods (*kappiyakāraka*) as well, and these have been given for the sake of alms-food and so forth, then all matters such as the formal act of assigning the place (*ṭhānacodanā*) and so on must be performed according to the method explained below.
66. Regarding the phrase "In the case of accepting what has been set down," and so forth:
whether in the presence [of the giver] by saying, "May this be for the noble one," or in his absence by saying, "I have gold and silver in such-and-such a place;
may that be yours"—if, having merely said "yours" through speech or by means of a hand-gesture, [the object] has been relinquished and not refused by body or speech, [it constitutes an offense].
“Accepting with the mind” means accepting what has been set down. The word “accepts” clarifies the meaning already stated, namely, “he wishes to take it.
“This is a guarded place” should be pointed out; this should be pointed out specifically with reference to the use of requisites.
When it is said, "Place it here," it becomes an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*) by the characteristic already stated regarding "having it picked up.
Therefore, he says: "One should not say, 'Place it here. Alternatively, when pointing out, "This is a secure place," one demonstrates only the security of the location;
one does not touch upon the object itself. Therefore, it may be pointed out [as a location]. "Place it here."
However, when one says, "Set aside the object that must be set aside," one is indeed referring to the object; therefore, it should not be said [that there is no basis].
In the subsequent phrase, "one takes this," the same principle applies. It stands depending upon both what is allowable (*kappiya*) and what is unallowable (*akappiya*);
because the enjoyment of requisites arising from that is permissible, it thus depends upon what is allowable.

It is "established" (ṭhitaṃ); however, because it is not permissible to consume requisites arising from that [wealth] through improper conduct, it should be understood as being established in dependence upon what is impermissible (akappiya).
Alternatively, this wealth is established in dependence upon what is permissible (kappiya) because it has been prohibited with the thought, "This is not permissible";
yet, because it has not been relinquished in any way whatsoever, it is established in dependence upon what is impermissible.

It stands. Alternatively, since that wealth will become allowable (*kappiya*) through mindfulness accompanied by thorough investigation later on, and will become unallowable (*akappiya*) through mindfulness accompanied by poor investigation, it therefore stands in dependence upon both the allowable and the unallowable.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, regarding the passage beginning with "one hundred or one thousand," [it refers to] the minimum limit in terms of silver (*rūpiya*).
It was said "to show the mode of occurrence," and "to show that one should not act in this way,
he said 'it is not to be said, "put it here," because if one says "put it here," there is the taking of it,'" and "'And it is allowable...'"—
because the requisites arising from that [gift] are permissible since they have not been personally received, therefore it is allowable.

It is said: "Because it stands supported [by something], and because what arises from that is not allowable when there is improper conduct, it should be understood as 'standing supported by what is unallowable' (akappiya-nissita). 67.
"It should be forfeited in the midst of the Saṅgha" means that since what is called "money" (rūpiya) is unallowable, therefore it belongs to the Saṅgha... or...
It is not stated that it should be relinquished to either the Saṅgha or an individual.

However, because it has merely been accepted and no allowable article has been purchased with it, it is said that "it should be relinquished in the midst of the Saṅgha" in order to show a means for its use. [The reason] is that nothing allowable has been purchased with it.
If it has been bartered for by means of this [forbidden item], there is no way to use it, because it was bartered for using unrenounced money after having been received.
This shows that such an object must be forfeited in the midst of the Saṅgha, discarded, and then one must confess the *pācittiya* offense.
However, some say: "Because even after receiving an article subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*), if it has been bartered for into allowable goods (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*) within the Saṅgha..."
Some say, "What has been relinquished by the makers of allowable goods is like allowable goods brought back after being exchanged for money that was relinquished;
therefore, it is permissible to divide and consume it even without [the usual] means. However, this does not accord with the discussion regarding the set of four bowls and so forth.
For in that context, it is shown that a bowl exchanged for money is simply not to be used at all, rather than being a consideration regarding its relinquishment.
"Kappiyaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ" means it should be declared thus: "For those who have gone forth, ghee or oil is permitted, O lay follower.
"Ārāmikānaṃ vā pattabhāgaṃ" is said because, even when it has come into the hands of householders, it is considered to be that very same portion belonging to the monastery attendants (ārāmikas).
However, if they give it after having exchanged it for something else, it is permissible to consume it; this is stated in the *Majjhimagaṇṭhipada*.
And this is stated in the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada*. "Having taken it from there" means having taken it from the portion of another’s bowl.
"The preliminary work for the kasiṇa" refers to the preliminary work for the light-kasiṇa (*ālokakasiṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "or beds, chairs, and so forth," they say that if one exchanges the beds, chairs, and so forth taken from there and takes something else, it is permissible. "Even the shade" refers even to the shade of dining halls and the like. "Exceeding the boundary" means...
The intention is that once one has passed beyond the boundary of the house, the place where the shadow has moved on is no longer considered "the house.
Regarding the phrase "even by way of the path": they say that if there is no other path available, it is permissible to go after having resolved upon the path.
Regarding "bought with it": bought with that specific object. If a lay follower [says], "The Saṅgha uses the requisites after setting aside a deposit..."
Having said, "This gold is too much; this, Venerable Sir, must not be lost this very day," he himself deposits it as a pledge or has another deposit it.

If the Saṅgha, having thus deposited it as a pledge, makes use of the requisites arising from that, they are making use of requisites [that are improper], because the object was taken by means of that property; therefore it is called "unallowable" (*akappiya*) in the *Vimativinodanī*.
However, it is said: "The phrase 'having set aside as a deposit' is stated with reference to the purpose of interest through the use of a kappiyakāraka (one who makes things allowable).
It is called 'unallowable' because it has been accepted by means of that object.
If he discards it, he throws it anywhere; even if he does not discard it, he takes it himself and goes away.
He should not be prevented. "If he does not discard it" means: if he neither takes it away nor discards it, but thinking, "What business have I with this?
departs wherever he wishes, then one who possesses the aforementioned characteristics must be appointed as the discarder of the money.
One who, in cases such as "not out of favoritism," etc., makes that object his own or exalts himself through greed—

One goes by way of bias through desire (*chandāgati*). Through hatred, one goes by way of bias through hatred (*dosāgati*) when, out of malice, one disparages another, saying, "This person does not know the *mātikā*, nor does he know the Vinaya.
Through delusion, one goes by way of bias through delusion (*mohāgati*) when, being forgetful, one falls into a state of confused mindfulness.
One goes by way of bias through fear (*bhayāgati*) when, being unable to bear discarding [the object] for fear of one who accepts money.

He does not fall into a state of partiality. One should understand that by acting in this way, he does not fall into a state of partiality through desire, nor does he fall into a state of partiality through hatred, nor does he fall into a state of partiality through delusion, nor does he fall into a state of partiality through fear.
68. "The area where [the robe] has fallen should be discarded by one who is not competent" means this is for the purpose of demonstrating a state of detachment.
It should be understood that therefore, even when the place where one has fallen is known, the criterion here is simply the state of being indifferent, like one who discards excrement.
"By claiming what is not true" is said with reference to announcing superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) that do not exist within oneself.
"Enjoyment by theft" means the enjoyment of what one is not entitled to. For by the Blessed One, in his own teaching—
The requisites are permitted for one who is virtuous, not for one who is immoral.
Even among donors, the relinquishment is for the sake of one who is virtuous, not for one who is immoral, because the latter expects his own acts to yield great fruit.
Thus, because it is not permitted by the Teacher and not relinquished by the donors, the use of requisites by an immoral person is "use by theft" (theyyaparibhoga). It is a use by way of debt.
“Enjoyment of debt” means that it is like enjoying something after having taken on a debt, because there is no purification of the offering (*dakṣiṇā*) on the part of the recipient.
Therefore, with the words “of one who is virtuous,” etc., he refers back to the very point already stated by way of its causal nature.
“In every enjoyment of robes” means in each and every instance of enjoying them after having removed them from the body. “Before the meal... [omission] ...in the last watch of the night.”

The connection is with the word "should be reviewed. One who is unable to do so should review it four times, three times, twice, or even just once a day, according to the specific time periods mentioned above.
If dawn should rise while he has not yet reviewed it, he stands in the position of one who has consumed what was borrowed; for here, [the rule applies] from yesterday...
"If I have used this robe, it is only for the purpose of warding off cold... [and so on] ...for the sake of covering the private parts.

If one does not reflect upon past usage in such a way—as "The alms-food I consumed yesterday was neither for sport," and so forth—it is said that one stands in the position of consuming what is like a debt;
this should be investigated. The same applies to the lodging-place.

"At each enjoyment" means at each act of consuming; "at each entry" means at each occasion of entering. However, for one who is unable to do so [in this way], it should be reviewed before the meal and so forth.
Since that can be understood by the method already explained below, it is not stated separately here.

"The state of mindfulness being a condition" (satipaccayatā) means the quality of mindfulness acting as a condition. It is appropriate that mindfulness of reviewing both the receiving and the consumption serves as a condition.
The meaning is that one should accept and consume [the medicine] only after reflecting. For this very reason, he said, "having established mindfulness," and so forth.
"Even though this is so" means: even though reflection is appropriate in both instances, even so. Others, however, say:
"The condition of mindfulness" (*satipaccayatā*) means mindfulness in its state of being a condition for the consumption of medicine; the sense is "as a condition. "Even though this is so" means...

The claim that "there is mindfulness regarding requisites" is merely their own opinion; for it is through reflection that virtue dependent on requisites is purified, not by the mere presence of the requisites.
But does this not refer to the Pātimokkha-restraint virtue by saying, "there is no offense for one who uses [them]"; therefore—
What is the distinction between virtue dependent on requisites (*paccaya-sannissita-sīla*) and the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (*pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla*)? It is said:

first, the distinction among the former three requisites is indeed evident. Regarding the requisite of medicine, however, just as when a fence is built around the root of a tree, its fruits are likewise protected; even so, through reflection (*paccavekkhaṇā*), in virtue dependent on requisites...
When these are guarded, the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha, which is bound up with them, is also said to be accomplished.
For one who consumes the requisites of life without reflecting upon them, it is precisely the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha that breaks;
however, the virtue dependent on the requisites does not break for one who fails to reflect until the dawn has risen, even during the periods after the meal and in the first watch of the night.
It is divided. For there is no offense for one who consumes the requisite of medicine before the meal even without having reflected upon it;
this is the distinction between these two cases, as stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: "Consumption by theft [is so called] because it has not been permitted by the Blessed One, the owner of the requisites."
It has been said. "Enjoyment on credit" is said because one enjoys things without having performed what was authorized by the Blessed One;
and by this, he shows that the virtue dependent on the requisites fails. "In each act of enjoyment" means in each act of enjoyment after having repeatedly removed [the object] from the body.
The construction is: "it should be reflected upon in the latter watches. In the place of "enjoyment on credit,"...
Regarding the phrase "it remains": here they say that retrospective reflection on the past is also appropriate, such as by thinking, "The robe which was used by me yesterday," and so forth.
"With every act of use" refers to each time it is brought inside from the place where water falls, as well as during sitting and lying down.
"It is appropriate for mindfulness to be a condition" means it is appropriate to obtain the status of being a condition through the mindfulness of reflective observation. Regarding "in receiving":
This shows that mindfulness of reflection regarding both the requisites and their enjoyment is inevitably to be obtained. Therefore he said, “having established mindfulness,” and so forth.
Some, however, explain the meaning as follows: “the state of being conditioned by mindfulness means that when the requisite exists—that is, when the cause for the consumption of medicine exists.
Even for them, the phrase “when the requisite exists” has the meaning of “when there is the discernment of the presence of the requisite.”

It must be accepted that virtue is not purified by the mere presence of the requisite conditions. By the statement, "An offense occurs even for one who does not actually consume [the requisites]," the breach of the *pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla* (vow of restraint according to the Pātimokkha) is shown;
it is not the breach of the virtue dependent on requisites (*paccaya-sannissita-sīla*), because that is purified through retrospective reflection on what has passed.
However, regarding these and the remaining requisites, by the expression "using them like a debt" and so forth, it is specifically the virtue dependent on requisites that is addressed.
"Thus the distinction between these two should be understood"—so it has been handed down.
Regarding these two treatises, in the passage "it stands in the place of the enjoyment of a debt," it is stated: "Yesterday, I used such-and-such a robe...
and so forth, until "...they say. Now, relying on this method, some wise ones [say]:
They say: “One who reviews what was used from dawn until evening should perform the review by way of the past, thinking: ‘Whatever robe was used by me today,’ and so forth.
Some, however, say: “The review by way of the past should be performed only for what was used yesterday, not for what was used today; that [latter] is simply a review by way of the present.”
They say this. Regarding that, the investigation should be conducted in this way within the root statement itself. How so?

Is this statement beginning with "Yesterday" (*hiyyo*) a Sutta, or is it in conformity with a Sutta (*suttānuloma*), or is it the opinion of a teacher (*ācariyavāda*), or is it one's own thought (*attanomati*)?
In this regard, it is certainly not a Sutta, because it has been stated that "a Sutta is the Pāḷi throughout the entire Vinaya Piṭaka," and because this statement is not part of the Pāḷi.

Nor is it in accordance with the Suttas, because it has been stated that "what is called 'in accordance with the Suttas' refers to the four great authorities (mahāpadesa)," and this [work] lacks the status of being one of those great authorities.

Nor is it the "Teacher's Word" (ācariyavāda), because it has been said that "the Teacher's Word refers to the lineage of commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) established by the five hundred Arahants who compiled the Dhamma,
which exists apart from the canonical text (pāḷi) and functions as a descending determination," and this [work] lacks the status of being a commentary text.
Furthermore, *attano-mati* (one’s own opinion) is defined as "the statement of a mental aspect established by means of inference through one's own intellect,
by grasping a method while setting aside the Suttas, the Suttas’ conformity, and the teachers’ doctrines"; moreover,

because it has been stated that "all the Theravāda found in the commentaries on the Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya is called *attano-mati*," and because this [work] lacks the status of being the Theravāda found in those commentaries.
Thus:
"The great elders of great psychic power, the compilers of the Dhamma in former times,
having extracted it, proclaimed the Vinaya in its fourfold division."
Since this statement is not included within the fourfold Vinaya already mentioned, it must be investigated. Therefore, the commentator in the *Sāratthadīpanī* stated:

"That should be examined. Alternatively, by the definition "the statement of a mode of presentation established through the grasping of a method" (*nayaggāha*), the statement made according to the respective modes of presentation of various teachers might be one's own opinion (*attano mati*).
It must likewise be investigated in this way: “One’s own opinion should be compared with the teacher’s doctrine.
If it fits and accords with it there, it should be accepted; if it neither fits nor accords, it should not be accepted.
For this so-called ‘one’s own opinion’ is the weakest of all,” according to the statement that this particular teaching does not fit and does not enter into the words of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).
For it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “If dawn breaks upon him while he has not yet reflected [on his actions], he stands in the position of one who consumes what is borrowed.
Another method of inquiry: Is this statement a word of the *Pāḷi*, or a word of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, or a word of a *Ṭīkā*, or a word from another treatise?
In that regard, it is certainly not a word of the *Pāḷi*, nor a word of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, nor a word from another treatise.

"Now, it is the word of a commentary (ṭīkā). Let it be the word of a commentary; whether it be one's own statement or another's statement, an intended statement or an unintended statement—it is not one's own statement here, but rather another's statement.
Therefore he said, "they say. It is not a statement intended by the commentator of the commentary, but rather an unintended statement.

Therefore he said, "That should be investigated. However, regarding the phrase "reviewing past enjoyment" (*atītaparibhogapaccavekkhaṇā*), it may have been formulated by those teachers by first conceptualizing it as "reviewing by way of past enjoyment" (*atītaparibhogavasena paccavekkhaṇā*), and then joining it with a word expressing the past.
[In this analysis: enjoyment in the past is "past enjoyment" (*atītaparibhogo*); of that past enjoyment...
"Reflection on past enjoyment" means reflection on what was enjoyed in the past.
When this is done, because the past enjoyment has come near to the present, it is expressed by a word denoting the present;
just as when a man who has come from a city and is sitting down is asked, "Where are you coming from?", he replies, "I am coming from the city," expressing it with a word denoting the present.

Furthermore, in the *Vinaya*, the *Suttanta*, the *Visuddhimagga*, and other texts, the reading is found as a present-tense statement: “He uses the robe with wise reflection,” and not in the past tense.

Moreover, "past use" in this context must be understood as use during the morning mealtime and so forth, starting from the period after the midday meal on that very same day; it does not mean use on the previous day. How is this known?
Why? By the authority of the *Aṭṭhakathā*. For it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Almsfood, with every morsel;

likewise for one unable [to do so], during the morning meal, the afternoon meal, the first watch, and the last watch. If dawn rises while he has not yet reflected upon it, it stands in the place of consuming a debt.
By this, one who reflects upon almsfood with every morsel [is described] regarding the act of eating.
Because it has not yet been concluded, there is primarily a reviewing of the present;
he shows that when one reviews during the four periods such as before the meal, because the act of eating has been concluded, it is a reviewing of the past.
However, because that [reviewing] is close to the present, it is expressed by a term denoting the present. For if [the food] were consumed yesterday...

They might be subject to review by means of reviewing the past; they might even be subject to review as things consumed on the second day, the third day, and so forth, up to months and years in the past.
And if that were the case, the statement in the aforementioned Commentary would be purposeless.
Therefore, the word of the Commentary alone must be taken as the authority. As it says:
“The Dhamma and the Vinaya were spoken by the Buddha;
they are known exactly as such by his sons.
Those who abandon the wisdom of those [sons]—”
Since they composed the commentaries in the past,
therefore, having excluded whatever was stated in those commentaries that contains errors of negligence;
"And because, for the wise here, reverence for all the trainings is the standard. And because,

at the time when the Blessed One taught the *Sabbāsavasutta* and other discourses, the monks were the agents and the subject was directed toward them, it is expressed according to the present active voice (*paṭhamapurisa*).

“Reflecting wisely, he uses the robe”—this was taught; by way of following that example, at the time of reflection, because monks are the agents of their own actions and are under our own control, it should be reflected upon as “I reflect wisely, I use the robe,” according to the mode of a supreme person currently existing.
The phrases beginning with “for the warding off of cold” are words intended to fulfill that purpose.
And these [words] must be connected specifically with the act of consuming mentioned as "he consumes" and "I consume"; furthermore,
those verbal forms are either in the present tense or in the present indicative mood (vattamānavibhatti) by way of being proximate to the present,
and therefore, at the time of reviewing conditions that have been consumed either in the present or in the past—
It should be understood that the statement “I am using it” is indeed appropriate because it follows the word of the Blessed One.

This same investigation should also be applied to the recitation: “By one reflecting this evening on what was used this morning, reflection should be made by way of the past, thinking ‘Whatever robe was used by me today,’ and so forth. Those who...
Those who say this should be asked as follows: "Do you maintain that the Blessed One taught reflection by way of the past with respect to things used in the past?
"He did not teach it. "How then was it taught? "It was taught thus: 'He reflects,' by way of the present alone.
"Is there then no reflection upon things used in the past during the time of the Blessed One? "There is."
Now, why was the review taught by the Blessed One solely by way of the present?

It was taught either by way of proximity to the present or by way of generality. This being so, one might think that, following the example of the Blessed One, even now a review of requisites used in the past should be performed by way of the present. However, as for those who say: "Yesterday... [and so forth].
“Only for those things already consumed should there be reflection on the past, not for those consumed today; rather, for those [latter], there should be only reflection on the present.
To them, one should say: “Is it the case, sirs, that what you say exists in the Pāḷi?
“No. “Does it exist in the Aṭṭhakathā? “No. This being so, [it does not exist] in the Buddha-words of the Tipiṭaka together with the Aṭṭhakathā.
"How is your statement, which is not being perceived, to be understood? "By way of the succession of teachers. "Let it be that you speak by way of the teachers' tradition;
however, time is threefold: past, future, and present. Among these, completed action is called 'past';
action directed toward the future is called 'future'; and action that has begun but is not yet finished—"
This is what is called "the present. Regarding this, the ancients said:
"A state that has begun but is not yet finished is the present; it is well-established.
Past and future states are, respectively, activity that has already arisen and activity that has not yet reached the present."
In this context, whether it occurred today, yesterday, or even before that, the condition of having consumed [food] is called "past" because the act of eating has been fully completed.
Regarding that, if the condition of having consumed [food] occurred yesterday or before that, it is not fit for review because the dawn has already passed;
even if it were reviewed, it would be as if not reviewed at all, standing in the place of a debt-consumption.
It remains. For it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “If dawn breaks for him while he is still not reflecting, it stands in the place of the consumption of a debt.

However, for one who reflects upon the robe and the lodging at every instance of use, and upon the alms-food at every mouthful, and upon the medicine both at the time of receiving and at the time of consuming, because the act of eating is not yet finished, [the offense] remains.

There is what is called the reflection on what has been consumed in the present. When one reflects upon what was consumed previously within the four portions [of the meal] afterwards, it is called the reflection on what was consumed in the past, because the act of eating has been fully completed.
This much is the field for reflection, neither before nor after that. As it is said in the Commentary:
“For one who is virtuous, using things without reflection is called ‘using on credit.
Therefore, with regard to robes, in each instance of use… [and so on] …even in the case of accepting and using medicinal requisites, mindfulness as a requisite condition is required.

Consequently, because what was used yesterday constitutes using on credit, one should not touch upon that; rather, regarding what was used today—both past and present—the word of the Blessed One applies.
It should be understood that reflection is well-established by means of the verb "I partake," which is used in the present tense as an imitation [of the original vow].

It is with reference to this very kind of reflection that it is stated in the *Vimativinodanī* and other works: "Because the virtue dependent on requisites is purified through reflection on the past."

Having thus shown the purification of virtue dependent on its conditions, he now says, "For purification is fourfold," and so forth, in order to show all types of purification within that same context.
In this regard, it is called *suddhi* (purification) because one is purified by means of it.
Purification as the teaching in accordance with the Dhamma is *desanā-suddhi*. Herein, the act of emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*) should also be understood as included within the teaching itself.
For those whose offenses have been severed at the root, however, confession is performed simply by acknowledging them as non-recurring.

Purity consisting in restraint (*saṃvara-suddhi*) is restraint itself distinguished by its resolution. Purity consisting in seeking (*pariyeṭṭhi-suddhi*) is the very seeking of requisites in accordance with the Dhamma and with justice.
Purity consisting in reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa-suddhi*) is the very reflection upon the four requisites according to the method prescribed. This, first of all, is...
This is the method for the purifications. Regarding the virtues (*sīla*) that possess purification, "purification of the teaching" (*desanāsuddhi*) means that which has teaching as its purification.
The same method applies to the others as well. In the phrase "I shall not do it again," the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) is said with reference to the breach of restraint.
"Having abandoned" (*pahāya*) means having avoided; the sense is "having not done. In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it says: "It is purified by means of the teaching and so forth; it is cleansed."
Or purity is the fourfold virtue (*sīla*). Therefore, it was said: “Because of purification through confession,” and so forth.

Here, by the inclusion of the term “confession” (*desanā*), both formal rehabilitation (*vuṭṭhāna*) and the admission of being a non-monk (*abhikkhu*) for those whose roots [of the offense] have been severed are also included.

For even in the case of offenses whose roots have been severed, the monk’s virtue (*bhikkhusīla*) that was protected below [the point of severance] is indeed called purified by means of rehabilitation from a defeat offense (*pārājika*). By that...
It is said: "For them, even the attainment of the path succeeds. In that context:

it is taught (*desīyati*) and uttered (*uccārīyati*), thus it is a "teaching" (*desanā*). The verbal root (*dhātu*) is *dis* meaning "to utter. Alternatively, it is a "teaching" (*desanā*) because by means of it one is taught (*desīyati*) or made known (*ñāpīyati*);
here the verbal root is *dis* meaning "to see. In both cases, [the teaching] is originated from a wholesome state of mind characterized primarily by abstinence (*virati*).
The sound of the words of the teaching (*desanāvacībhedasaddo*). Restraint (*saṃvara*) is *saṃvaraṇa*; it is derived from the verbal root *vara* preceded by the prefix *saṃ*, meaning "to restrain.

It is a mental state (*cittuppāda*) dominated by mindfulness (*sati*). Seeking (*pariyeṭṭhi*) is *pariyesanā*; it is derived from the verbal root *isa* preceded by the prefix *pari*, meaning "to seek. It is a mental state dominated by energy (*vīriya*).

Reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇā*) is the act of looking back again and again after having repeatedly entered [into an object]; it is derived from the verbal root *ava* preceded by the prefixes *paṭi* and *ava*.
“Ikkha” and “dassana” are verbal roots meaning "seeing. These consist of a mental state (cittuppāda) dominated by wisdom (*paññā*).
Among these, the first two do not succeed for one who is unable to produce vocal expression or who does not obtain a companion, because they exist as vocal sounds through speech in the teaching.
However, the remaining ones do succeed even for one unable to produce vocal expression and even for one not obtaining a companion, because they consist merely of a mental state.
Thus, for that reason, even one who is unable to recite the formula for reflection during times such as when ill should perform the reflection by means of the mind alone, keeping the meaning in mind.
It is called "inheritance" (*dāya*) in the sense of being something to be given;
they are "heirs" (*dāyādā*) because they take up that inheritance, since there is no enjoyment whatsoever of things not permitted.
Furthermore, because the use [of requisites] exists only when they have been permitted, the requisitions to be used by the bhikkhus are the property of the Blessed One.
In this regard, the *Dhammadāyāda Sutta* (The Discourse on the Heirs of the Dhamma) is the proof:
"Bhikkhus, be my heirs in the Dhamma, not my heirs in material things; I have compassion for you, thinking, 'How may my disciples become heirs of the Dhamma?'"
The *Dhammadāyāda Sutta* (Discourse on the Heirs of the Dhamma), which proceeds thus: "There are no heirs to material things," is the proof for this point here.
For those who are not free from lust, there is no state of ownership regarding the enjoyment of conditions because they are enslaved by craving;

whereas for those free from lust, there is ownership therein due to the presence of enjoyment according to their own preference. For it is thus that they perceive even what is repulsive as non-repulsive.
They consume the requisites by way of equanimity, avoiding both the unrepulsive and the repulsive by regarding them as such;
thus they fulfill the wishes of the donors. Therefore it was said: "For they, having transcended the slavery of craving, consume [the requisites] as masters.
As for this consumption by a virtuous worldling through reflection:
Because it is the opposite of indebted enjoyment, it is called "debtless enjoyment.
Just as a debtor is not permitted to go to whatever place he desires by his own will, so too one who is engaged in indebted enjoyment is not permitted to escape from the world;
therefore, because it is the antithesis of that, the reflective enjoyment of the virtuous person is called "debtless enjoyment."
Therefore, it should be understood that, in an absolute sense, this enjoyment is distinct and separate from the four kinds of enjoyment;

it is not mentioned separately here, as it is included within the enjoyment of inheritance. For even one who possesses virtue is called a "learner" (sekha) precisely because he is endowed with this training.
"Of all" refers to both noble ones (*ariya*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*). How do these enjoyments arise for worldlings? By way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

For when even a worldling, established in the practice of effacement (*sallekha*), abandons greed for requisites and enjoys them with a mind unstained by them, that enjoyment is like the enjoyment of a master. This is the case for one who is virtuous.
However, enjoyment after due reflection is like the enjoyment of an inheritance, because it does not frustrate the wishes of the donors.
Therefore it is said: "Or rather, it is included within the enjoyment of an inheritance.

There is no need to speak of the enjoyment by a noble worldling (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*), since he is already included among those in training (*sekkha*). This is established by the meaning of the *Sekkhāsutta*.
In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it is said: “It is a ‘heritage’ (*dāya*) in the sense of being something to be given; they ‘take up’ that, thus they are ‘heirs’ (*dāyādā*).

Regarding the phrase ‘of the seven trainees’ (*sattannaṃ sekkhānaṃ*), it should be understood that even noble worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) are included here, because their enjoyment [of requisites] free from debt is subsumed under the enjoyment of an inheritance.
The *Dhammadāyāda Sutta* [is cited] by way of the passage beginning: ‘Monks, be my heirs to the Dhamma, not my heirs to material things.’”
This is the commentary on the sutta. Regarding that, it is said: "The meaning should be understood by bringing in the word 'me' [in the phrase] ‘mā me āmisadāyādā’;
for in this way, it establishes the meaning as previously stated. Therein, "my heirs to material things" (*me āmisadāyādā*) refers to those who consume the four requisites;
thus, the requisites—which are related to the Blessed One who stands as the possessor—are spoken of as being related to him. Therefore, even though they are given by donors...
It is said that the *Dhammadāyāda Sutta* serves as the proof for this meaning: that because requisites were authorized by the Blessed One, they belong to the Blessed One alone.
"Using [requisites] together with one who is conscientious" means using them after taking what belongs to a conscientious person. "Together with one who is unconscientious" means...

The same principle applies here as well. By the statement, "From the very beginning, there is no such thing as one who is shameless," it is shown that one should not entertain suspicion only toward those whose misconduct has been personally witnessed. "One's own burden" refers to the students (*saddhivihārika*) and others.
They too must be restrained; thus, the reading is: "Whoever sees [them] should restrain them. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it says: "Even he who, by means of his own burden..."
Although the reading "he who shares in the use [of requisites] with one who is shameless must also be restrained" is seen, it nevertheless fits both ways in terms of meaning.
One's own students (*saddhivihārika*) and others must also be restrained from being shameless.
Furthermore, others who share in common enjoyment (*ekasambhoga*) with shameless students and others must certainly be restrained as well. If he does not desist, this person too—

Regarding the phrase "he becomes just as shameless": here, when that person has been thus restrained, it is wholesome if he desists and refrains from using things in common with one who is shameless. If he does not desist, then he too becomes just as shameless;
the meaning is that by engaging in communal use with him, he too becomes just as shameless. Therefore it was said: "In this way, one shameless person [leads even a hundred shameless ones...]"
"...he makes [it]. "Non-dhammic" means obtained through improper search (*an-esanā*) and so forth. "Dhammic" means obtained through alms-round (*bhikkhācariyā*) and so forth.
"He gives it to the Saṅgha alone" means that without taking the meal [intended for himself], he gives only the voting-ticket (*salāka*) he himself received.
In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it says: "'Consumption together with one who is conscientious' refers to a state of being mixed by way of both the Dhamma and material gifts."

"Along with one who is shameless": here too, the same principle applies. By the statement "from the very beginning there is no such thing as a shameless person," he shows that one should not entertain suspicion regarding every single instance seen;
rather, it should be applied only when there is a basis such as what has been seen or heard. "Those who have become his own burden" refers to the students (saddhivihārikas) and others.
"If he does not desist" means [desisting] from the consumption of the Dhamma and material gifts by way of following an evil course.

"He does not desist. The statement "there is no offense" was said with reference to those who are shameless (*alajjī*) and to *dhammakamma* (legal acts) performed on the basis of requisites that have arisen in accordance with the Dhamma.

For even for them, there is indeed an offense when they consume requisites that have arisen through such things as corrupting families, or when they perform factional acts (*vaggakamma*) and so forth.
"The use of requisites, whether according to the Dhamma or contrary to the Dhamma, is to be understood solely by way of the requisites themselves."

It should be understood that because it was stated [in this way], the preceding sections on the use by the modest (*lajji*) and the use by the immodest (*alajji*) were already explained by way of the requisites (*paccaya*) and by way of a single act (*ekakamma*), etc.

For this very reason, in the commentary on the *Dutthadosa-sikkhāpada*, regarding two immodest persons who stand in the position of accuser and accused, it is said with reference even to the use of the Dhamma: "Live together, sharing a single enjoyment."

"Because there is no conflict between them in the shared enjoyment of both the Dhamma and material gifts. For it is said that for those possessed of shame (*lajjī*), the shared enjoyment of both with one devoid of shame (*alajjī*) is not permissible.

However, as for the passage: "If a person possessed of shame encourages one devoid of shame... [and so on]... he causes [the latter's faults] to disappear," here it refers solely to the desire to encourage [them].
It should be understood that while it is not permissible to act in this way [for one's own sake], it is permissible for the purpose of supporting the Dhamma, the Teaching, and those who listen to it.
Because it was stated in the previous method, "He is to be dealt with according to the offense," they say that this is indeed an offense.

The "utilization of the Dhamma" (*dhammaparibhoga*) refers to the enjoyment of the Dhamma through such means as receiving recitations and so forth. For one who receives [the teaching] through support for the Dhamma...
Even though there was no actual offense, the Elder spoke those words beginning with "He is indeed a wicked man," referring specifically to his lack of shame.
"In his presence" means in the presence of the Elder Mahārakkhita.
Furthermore, this has been explained in detail at this point in the *Vimativinodanī*. How so? [It is said: "The enjoyment of the Dhamma..."

One should understand that the communal living described by the passage beginning with “a single act, a single recitation,” as well as the taking of formal dependence (nissaya) and so forth, and all non-material sharing, are included.

Because it is stated, “He is not to be dealt with for an offense,” it should be understood that there is an offense for one who is conscientious (lajjin) when supporting one who is unconscientious (alajjin).
“The other too” means the conscientious one as well; [this refers to] the unconscientious one who supports himself, and by this...
This shows that by supporting an immoral person— whether out of a craving for material gain such as receiving praise and so forth from those who are modest,
or out of worldly affection— the one who is modest causes the Dispensation to disappear. Thus, an immoral person, being bolstered among householders and others,
gains strength, overcomes the virtuous, and before long causes the Dispensation to become contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya.
By the statement, "The enjoyment of the Dhamma is also appropriate there," he shows that the enjoyment of the Dhamma is weightier than the enjoyment of material things;
therefore, it must be performed with an extreme degree of shame and seclusion.

Because it is said, "It is appropriate to take [the precepts] by means of support through the Dhamma," when the teaching is declining due to the prevalence of the shameless, and when those who possess shame are insufficient, even a shameless person who is a regular member of the community [may be admitted].
It is indeed appropriate to uphold the Dispensation by admitting those who complete the quorum for ordination and so forth,
by winning over certain shameless individuals through the enjoyment of the Dhamma and material gifts, and by restraining the rest of the shameless group.
However, some maintain that "the enjoyment of the Dhamma consists solely in the mastery of the texts," because it is said that "the text is what stands at the beginning."

They say, "It is not [restricted to] a single formal act (*ekakamma*) and so forth; therefore, it is permissible to perform formal acts such as the Uposatha together with those who are shameless (*alajjī*), and there is no offense.

This is not correct, for this [passage] is merely a textual illustration intended here to show that among the many communal enjoyments of the Dhamma (*dhammaparibhoga*)—such as the single formal act and others—even when performed together with one who is shameless, the communal enjoyment of the Dhamma remains dependent upon the specific situation.
Because it has been extracted. For it cannot be said that a procedure such as a single act of merit (*ekakamma*) and so forth is not the enjoyment of the Dhamma;

this is because it is free from worldly motives (*anāmisattā*), and because there exists nothing whatsoever that is not included within the gifts of the Dhamma. For this very reason, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, in the discussion on the hospitable reception of the Dhamma, it is said:

"The meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) should be taught, the Dhamma should be recited... [and so on]... the acts of rehabilitation (*abbhāna*), emergence from probation (*vuṭṭhāna*), penance (*mānatta*), and the period of probation (*parivāsa*) should be granted."
"One worthy of going forth should be given the going forth; one worthy of full ordination should be fully ordained... [and so on]... this is called a 'welcome based on the Dhamma'.
Thus, even formal acts of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma) and other such categories of the Dhamma are shown.

Among those categories of the Dhamma, there are matters such as the Uposatha and the like which depend upon shameless persons acting as "completers of the quorum," or the receiving of the Dhamma and the receiving of formal dependence (nissaya) from them.
Or whatever is performed, that which is both the Dhamma and the enjoyment is called "enjoyment of the Dhamma" (*dhammaparibhoga*).
It is not permissible to perform this without such appropriate conditions; for one who does so, it becomes an enjoyment of the shameless and constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

However, that which is done without regard for the assembly of the shameless—whether it be an act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*) and other disciplinary acts, or an act of assistance such as probation (*parivāsa*) and so forth, or the granting of formal instruction and inquiry—is [permissible].
Or if it is performed, that is merely the formal act (*dhamma*) itself, not the actual enjoyment;

this is permissible for those who are suitable, and there is no offense, as in the case of giving material gifts (*āmisa*). However, granting dependence (*nissaya*), granting the thirteen permissions (*sammuti*), and so forth, are not permissible because they are causes for the enjoyment of the undertaking of duties and observances.

But as for one who is greatly shameless and acts contrary to the Dhamma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Teacher’s instruction, [the granting of these] to his resident pupils (*saddhivihārika*) and others—
It is not permitted to perform supportive acts such as granting full ordination (*upasampadā*) or providing instruction and answering questions;
this constitutes an offense, and only a disciplinary act (*niggaha-kamma*) should be carried out. For that very reason, even the conferring of honors upon those who are shameless is prohibited.

Indeed, the intended purpose of the discipline is the restraint of difficult individuals by depriving them of the enjoyment of the Dhamma and material requisites; and this is for the sake of the comfortable dwelling, the stability of the true Dhamma, and the support of the Vinaya for those who are well-behaved.
Because the formulation of the training rules has this purpose, therefore, whatever serves as a support for the wicked, causes discomfort for the well-behaved,
or leads to the decline of the true Dhamma and so forth— all that is forbidden to do, whether it be an object of use or not an object of use.
Those who act in such a way cause the Dispensation to disappear and incur an offense regarding the use of the Dhamma and the material requisites.

And herein, it is precisely the shared enjoyment of the Dhamma—such as communal formal acts (*ekakamma*) and so forth—by those who are shameless that leads to the lack of comfort for the well-behaved, to the decline of the true Dhamma, and other such evils;
the shared enjoyment of material requisites does not do so to the same extent.

For the mere use of the four requisites by the shameless does not cause the lack of comfort and so forth for the well-behaved in the way that the aforementioned shared enjoyment of the Dhamma does. By avoiding that [latter], however, there is comfort and so forth.
For indeed, when shameless persons who have transgressed the training rules enter the Uposatha and other ceremonies,
they must be addressed by the bhikkhus with words such as, "You are committing transgressions through both the door of the body and the door of speech.

Without failing to properly restrain them— by means of exclusion from the Saṅgha and other disciplinary measures for those who do not abide by the Vinaya— one should [deal with them] together with them.
Even while living together, they become like those who are shameless, according to such statements as: “Even a single shameless person makes a hundred shameless people.
For if they were not thus restrained, they would increase quarrels and the like within the Saṅgha;
by obstructing communal acts such as the Uposatha, they would cause discomfort for the well-behaved, and gradually, like Devadatta or the Vajjiputtakas, they would increase their following.
By illustrating their own misconduct according to the Dhamma and the Vinaya, they might even cause a schism in the Saṅgha and, before long, cause the Dispensation to disappear.
However, when such individuals have been restrained by means of exclusion from the Saṅgha and other disciplinary measures, this entire calamity does not occur.
For it is said: "Relying on persons of immoral conduct, the Uposatha does not stand; the Pavāraṇā..."
"It does not stand; the formal acts of the Saṅgha do not proceed; there is no concord...
[and so on]... But when those who are immoral are restrained, all this calamity ceases, and consequently, the well-behaved bhikkhus dwell in comfort.

Therefore, it should be understood that the enjoyment of the Dhamma—such as the performance of formal acts and so forth—is even more important than the enjoyment of material things, because it must be carried out with extreme freedom from shamelessness, and because its violation causes the decline of the true Dhamma.

Furthermore, this is established because it is declared in the Commentary that when one performs sangha-kamma together with those who are shameless (alajjī), "the Uposatha does not stand, the Pavāraṇā does not stand,
and sangha-kamma does not proceed. Likewise, there is the discourse on the proper conduct for a monk whose gender has changed as he goes to the nuns' residence.
“If they are devoted, supportive, and modest, one should not go elsewhere after having offended them.
If one goes, one is not released from the offenses for going to another village, crossing a river, staying overnight apart, or leaving the group... [etc.
...If they are shameless but provide support, one may leave them and go elsewhere. Thus it is regarding those who are shameless.
In the case of taking a companion and so forth, because the Buddha permitted heavy offenses such as crossing a river when there is a danger of falling into communion (saṃvāsāpatti),
it is understood that even more than that, the offense of communion with those who lack shame is a heavier offense that serves as a cause for the decline of the True Dhamma.
For one cannot avoid transgressing a heavy offense simply to avoid a light offense or a non-offense.
The teachers permit it. Likewise, regarding the term *asaṃvāsa* (non-residence), the Commentary states:
"Because they are to be trained together with all modest persons (*lajjipuggala*), they are called 'of equal training' (*samasikkhātā*).
Here, since all modest persons dwell together in these formal acts (*kamma*) and so forth, and not even one of them is seen outside of them, therefore, taking all of those [acts] together, this..."
By the phrase “co-residence indeed,” it is thus shown that only for those who possess a sense of shame (*lajjī*) is co-residence through common formal acts (*ekakamma*) and so forth permissible.
If this is so, why were those lacking a sense of shame (*alajjī*) not included among those who are not in communion (*asaṃvāsika*)? There is no contradiction here;

for those who, when serving as the quorum for a group, cause a formal act to be invalidated, they are included as being "not in communion" precisely because they have committed a defeat (*pārājika*) or other such offenses that render them unordained (*apakatatta*).
However, there are also those who are shameless (alajjino) even though they are regular members (pakatattabhūto);

if they act as the quorum-filler and complete the formal act (kamma), they become liable for an offense merely by performing it through a wrong course of action, just like those who have fallen into a common offense (sabhāgāpatti).
This is because both shamelessness and shamefulness among worldlings (puthujjanā) are dependent upon moments of consciousness (cittakkhaṇa-paṭibaddha) and are not constant at all times.
For when a mind intent on intentional transgression has arisen, those who were previously shameless become possessed of a sense of shame through the thought, "I shall not do such a thing again.
Among them, only those who do not desist even when exhorted by the virtuous and who commit the act repeatedly are unfit for communal living;

the others are not so, because they have entered into the nature of shame. Therefore, one should not count the shameless among those with whom one must not live, but rather avoid them for that very reason.

Performing the Uposatha and other rites only after having purified [the assembly] is not unknown. For it has been declared that performing the Uposatha for an impure assembly is improper, as in the passage beginning: "Venerable sirs, announce your purity; I shall recite the Pātimokkha.
Likewise, even one who is shameless is expected to possess the quality of shame when it is said: "Whoever has an offense, let him reveal it... [and thus] there will be comfort."

Having established [the assembly], the manner of performing the Uposatha was explained; and in the case of the *pārisuddhi-uposatha*, the purity of those performing the Uposatha was declared by the formula:
“Are you pure here? … Are the Venerable Ones pure here? and by the formula: “I am pure, Bhante; may you remember me as pure.
Furthermore, the procedure for suspending the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā for those who do not remain silent after being addressed was set forth.

Furthermore, it has been stated that because it is improper to live in association with those who do not adhere to the quality of shame (*lajjidhamma*) in every respect, the granting and receiving of formal dependence (*nissaya*) is prohibited;

and it has also been stated that by means of disciplinary acts such as censure (*tajjanīya-kamma*) and acts of suspension (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*), the method for rendering one who is shameless (*alajjī*) unfit for communal living along with his following is established.
Therefore, according to the methods of the Suttas and the words of the Commentaries as they have been stated:

It must be concluded here that communal residence—such as performing formal acts (*ekakamma*) and so forth—with all shameless persons, whether they be regular members (*pakatatta*) or not, is not permitted;
