for all the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) were laid down solely for the purpose of restraining individuals who are difficult to manage, and thus those who perform such acts incur an offense.
For this very reason, at the Second Council, the Vajjiputtakas, though they were regular members, were [excluded] because they were shameless.
They were separated from the Saṅgha with great effort by Yasatthera and others. For there was no offense of non-co-residency such as a *pārājika* among them;
it is stated that the ten grounds cited by them fall within the scope of light offenses (*lahukāpatti*).
"In his presence" means in the presence of Mahārakkhita Thera.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Ornament of the Discourse on the Determination of Accepting Money and Other Valuables," in the *Vinayālaṅkāra*,
which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
13. Discussion on the Determination of the Characteristics of Giving, etc. 69.

Having thus explained the determination regarding the acceptance of silver and so forth, he now speaks the words beginning with "By means of giving, trust, and taking" (*dānavissāsaggāhehi*) in order to explain the determination regarding the acquisition and dedication of gains.
In this context, that which is given is "giving" (*dāna*); it refers to the object or basis, such as robes and other requisites.
It is a mental state arising from wholesome or functional consciousness of the sense-sphere, dominated by non-greed (*alobha*).

"Sāsana" means instruction; it is derived from the verbal root *sas*, meaning "to injure," thus signifying "injury. "Vissāsa" refers to that which is free from such injury (*vigata-sāsa*) regarding grasping.
"Gāha" means grasping. "Vissāsaggāha" is grasping by way of confidence. Here, the instrumental case is used for emphasis: grasping by means of confidence, and not [grasping] otherwise.
The meaning is: "by way of a thieving mind. "Lacchati" means acquisition; it refers to the object of acquisition, such as robes and so forth. "Pariṇamiyate" means dedication (*pariṇāmana*);
it is the dedicating of what has been acquired for oneself or another for the sake of others; the meaning is "causing [it] to be given.
Regarding the phrase "the dedication of the acquisition by means of giving, trust, or seizure," this refers to that which is fixed upon in the summary list.
The construction should be understood as follows: first of all, the analytical determination of the meaning of the term "giving" (*dāna*) is to be known in this way.
The connection is: "the giving of one's own belongings, such as robes and other requisites. The phrase "to anyone whatsoever" is a designation of the recipient;
the meaning is "to any recipient whatsoever."
Regarding what was stated as "giving" (*dāna*), [the question] is asked: "What is its characteristic? To this, it is said:
"In this regard, this is the characteristic of giving. The construction is as follows: "I give this to you"—this is the characteristic of giving endowed with three factors.
Therein, "this" (*idaṃ*) indicates the object to be given; "to you" (*tuyhaṃ*) indicates the recipient; and "I give" (*demī*) indicates the giver.
Expressions such as "I give" are merely figurative synonyms. For it has been said:
"As with the gift, the giver, and the recipient," and "Wholesomeness arises from the coming together of these three.

As for the statement, "Because giving has the characteristic of relinquishing the object," this is merely a description of one partial characteristic; for how could that which is being given in this manner be considered "given" only when in the presence [of the recipient]?
Or is it even when face-to-face? To this he said: "Whether face-to-face or behind one's back, it is indeed given.
Regarding such phrases as "Take from you," the meaning is this: when "take" is said, it is equivalent to saying "I give";
therefore, because it is given in the primary sense, it is well-given (*sudinna*). And when "I take" is said, there is a primary act of taking; therefore, it is well-taken (*suggahita*).
However, the phrases “yours” and “mine” are expressions used for establishing a connection with the recipient.
Phrases such as “make it yours” and so forth, on the other hand, are figurative ways of giving and receiving; therefore, what is given in this manner becomes poorly given and poorly received.
For in the world, even those who do not wish to relinquish or who wish to take back later hand over their property saying, “let it be yours,” just as [in the case of a loan].
This was the offering of the kingdom by Kusarāja’s mother. Therefore he said: “Neither does the giver know how to give, nor does the other know how to receive.

But in the passage beginning with “If, however,” etc., even when a figurative expression is used due to the giver’s lack of skill regarding the designation, the recipient takes it in its primary sense because of his own skill regarding the designation; therefore it is called “well-received.”

However, in the case of "if [there is] one," and so forth, if the donor gives with a formal declaration (*mukhyavacana*) and the recipient also accepts with a formal declaration, then even a robe previously determined by the donor loses its status as a determination because it was given;
since it has been relinquished and is no longer his own property, it does not constitute an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*). Therefore, even if ten days have elapsed, [no offense occurs].
There is no offense. Since it was not refused by the recipient, it does not become his own property;
therefore, as it is not "extra robe-cloth," there is no offense even if the ten-day limit is exceeded. Regarding the phrase "to whomever it pleases":
because this robe-cloth has no owner and stands in the place of a rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*), it is [given] as a rag-robe to whomever it pleases.

Having taken it, it should be consumed. However, when consuming it, one should understand that even if the donor had previously made a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhita*), because the act of giving has now occurred, the previous determination has been relinquished;
therefore, it must be determined anew before consumption. For others, however, since there was no prior determination, this does not apply.
Furthermore, in cases such as "Give it to so-and-so," because the fifth case ending is used in the sense of an injunction (*āṇatti*), [the recipient] by virtue of being commanded...
At the very moment it is given to the recipient, it becomes the property of the recipient, not before; prior to that, however, it belongs only to the sender.

Therefore, it is said: "It belongs to him who sends. But because the phrase "I give to such-and-such a person" is spoken using the present tense (*vattamāna-vibhatti*) which functions in the sense of the present, from that point onward it belongs only to the recipient.
It belongs to him; therefore it is said, "it belongs to the one by whom it is relinquished.

By the word "therefore," he shows that among the determinations (adhiṭṭhāna) taught here by the Blessed One in the case of the venerable Sāriputta’s sending of a robe-cloth by the venerable Revata Thera, this should be understood through non-confusion regarding the characteristic stated here.
In that context, the terms "doubly determined" (*dvādhiṭṭhita*) and "well-determined" (*svādhiṭṭhita*) are not said with reference to the determination of the three robes (*ticīvara*);
rather, they are said with reference to taking [the robe] as a robe held in trust while the owner is alive, and as a robe belonging to the deceased when the owner has died.
Furthermore, within ten days of its acquisition, there is either the determination of the three robes or the determination of requisites-cloth (*parikkhāracola*).
Or a formal assignment (*vikappana*) must be made. "He who sends" refers to the donor; "to whom it is sent" refers to the recipient.
Having relinquished [the object]... [he] does not obtain [it]; the meaning is that one who causes it to be brought back should be dealt with according to the value of the goods.
By the phrase "by oneself... [is] an offense entailing relinquishment" (*nissaggiya*), it means that one who, knowing it belongs to another, seizes it by means of theft or force.

This shows that one becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense. However, in the ancient commentary (*porāṇaṭīkā*), it is stated: "One who takes [an object] without the perception that it belongs to oneself must be dealt with according to the offense after having the value of the goods assessed.

Even without the perception that it belongs to oneself, one who takes [it] under the perception that it is a temporary loan or a rag-pile (*paṃsukūla*) and so forth need not be dealt with according to an offense.
But in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is said with reference to the manner of taking by force (*pasayhākāra*).
Therefore he said, "For one who takes it back, there is an offense of expiation (nissaggiya). However, when he says, "If... it is allowable," he refers to a gift given out of satisfaction;

whereas by the words "But then... and so forth, he refers to a gift given in anger. In both cases, because it was given by oneself, it is allowable; the meaning is that there is no offense in taking it. Regarding the passage, "In my presence...
but it is not allowable to give in this way," this is because the characteristic of giving consists in the relinquishment of the object.
Thus, it is not permissible to say that "giving does not constitute a gift because one has not relinquished it while giving," for precisely because of that, it becomes an *dukkaṭa* offense.

However, it is permissible to have [the goods] brought back; this was stated on the grounds that since it was previously said, "I will not give to one who does not perform [the duties]," the property belongs to the teacher alone if the aforementioned acts such as receiving the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) are not performed. But when they are performed, it belongs to the resident pupil (*antevāsika*).

It would be [an offense] because it was given without having been entirely relinquished. Since the perception of ownership still exists, it might be said that "it is permissible to have it brought back.
However, in the *Ṭīkā*, it is stated: "Even though it has been given in this way, because it is similar to wages (*bhata*), it is permissible to have it brought back.
Even when work is performed that is similar to wages, the wages must be received; therefore, it would not be permissible to have it loaded [onto a vehicle]. [This is stated] in the *Vimativinodanī*.
However, it is stated that "it is permissible to have [the robe] brought" because, when the formal act has not been performed, it is similar to a hire;
by this, it is established that once the formal act has been performed, it is not permissible to have it brought. "He will take up a preceptor" indicates the giving [of the robe] to a novice;

and by this, it is indicated that there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) even for one who, having given it during the time he was a novice, takes it back at the time of full ordination. This, first of all, is...
By the phrase "the exposition on giving" (*dāne vinicchayo*), he illuminates the fact that the three expositions—beginning with the exposition on giving—are treated as a single section.
70. The Exposition on the Characteristic of Trusting Acceptance:
Regarding "lying down without rising," it refers to that bed upon which one lies until the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) reaches its cessation.
Thus it is said. Regarding the giving of the deceased’s wealth, it should be given to those—whether householders or renunciants—who have authority over that wealth.
In this regard, who are the householders, who are the renunciants, and for what reason do they have authority over his wealth?
First, as for the householders, they are the attendants of the sick; for that reason, they have authority over that wealth which constitutes their share as attendants of the sick.
The masters are those from whose hands the requisites, such as bowls, were caused to be taken by the attendant;
they are the masters of whatever price must be paid for them and of that wealth.
Also, those parents for whose sake robes were set aside after being apportioned are likewise the masters of that wealth. By such reasons as these, whatever [is the case]—
Whatever requisites and wealth are to be obtained by whichever householders, those householders are the masters of that respective wealth for that specific reason.
However, when it comes to external renunciants, they are likewise masters provided that the same conditions apply. But among the five fellow practitioners, the bhikkhus—
Novices (sāmaṇera) receive the property of deceased monks and novices by virtue of being heirs, even without a specific cause, whereas others do not.
Likewise, nuns, probationary nuns (sikkhamānā), and female novices (sāmaṇerī) receive the property of those same classes of persons, while others do not.

Furthermore, that distribution of the property of the deceased will be explained in the section on the determination of the distribution of the four requisites; for many Elder Vinaya-holders [have said this].

Relying on the reading, “Those who are masters of that wealth, whether householders or those gone forth,” some conclude that “relatives who have become householders receive the wealth of a deceased bhikkhu.
We shall address both that legal decision and its validity or invalidity right there [in the relevant context].
"Belonging to one who is displeased" means the property of one who has fallen into a state of dejection either through verbal expression—
such as saying, "You have done wrong, you who took what was not given, my own property"— or merely through a mental impulse. However, that which belongs to one who, even at the very outset,
[expresses approval] through verbal expression or a mental impulse such as, "Well done by you, you who took my property."
Having expressed appreciation, if he later becomes angry for some reason, he is not permitted to demand that it be withdrawn.
As for one who is unwilling to give but nevertheless assents in his mind and says nothing at all—regarding this, the Ancient Commentary states:
"The phrase 'he assents in his mind' was said, and in order to clarify that very meaning, it was further stated 'he says nothing at all. This being the case, [the word] "by mind" (*cittena*)...
This is the instrument for the act of acquiescence (*adhivāsanakiriyā*). In the phrase "one who does not wish to give," this same [body] might also be the instrument;
however, in that case, the statement "with the mind he does not wish to give, with the mind he acquiesces" would not be consistent with propriety.
Excluding that [mind], in the phrase "one who does not wish to give," no other instrument—such as "by body" or "by speech"—is possible.
Since that [instrumental case] is impossible, even the word *pana*, which expresses a specific meaning, would be meaningless.
In the phrase "he says nothing," the word "by speech" (*vācāya*) must be understood as the instrument of the act of speaking;
and if that were so, there would be one instrument for the act of enduring and another for the act of speaking, and the act of enduring would be one thing while the act of speaking would be another.
Therefore, it is not appropriate to say, "in order to clarify the very meaning already stated.
Consequently, even if one is unwilling to give with the mind, yet nevertheless assents by means of speech, one should apply the construction as follows:
"it is said 'he does not say anything' in order to explain the very meaning already stated as 'he assents. In this context, however, the word *pana*...

The purpose [of the phrase] is to indicate the characteristic of lack of interest (*aruci*). “By mind” (*cittena*) is the instrument for the action of not wishing to give; “by speech” (*vācāya*) is the instrument for the action of assent (*adhivāsana*) and the action of not speaking. And the action of assent is indeed the very same as the action of not speaking.
When it is said “he assents,” because the action of not speaking is not manifest, it is stated “he says nothing” in order to clarify that; thus...

When it is being accepted, the meaning of the preceding and following statements should be such as to enhance its propriety; therefore, it should be accepted after investigating it within this much scope.
71. Discussion on the Determination of the Dedication of Gains:
Regarding the determination of the dedication of gains, the statement "ghee and so forth have been brought for you" means they were brought for your benefit.

Regarding clarified butter and the other items: even if one knows they have been digested, if one requests them according to the prescribed method, it is considered as if one has requested what belongs to those very persons themselves;
thus he said, "If one says, 'Give me some too,' it is permissible.
As for the statement, "It is not even permissible to offer flowers," this was said with reference to that which has been digested; however, if [it is fresh], in a single case...
"In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: 'Having taken a flower worshipped at one cetiya, if one worships it at another cetiya, it is permissible.

However, since the *Aṭṭhakathā* specifies, 'from a sapling planted for the sake of another cetiya,' it is not only the state of having been transformed [into an offering] that is mentioned, but rather the state of having been planted specifically for that purpose."
By the word *pi* in the phrase *pupphampi*, it is shown [by implication] from where the garland was obtained. In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it is stated:
"‘A planted garland’ is said with reference to one planted by someone specifically; a garland that has not been plucked, even if it is wilting, may be plucked and offered anywhere.
"Having seen it standing" means having seen it remaining after the remainder had been taken. Of this dog...
"Do not give it; give this instead"—this [refers to what] has already been dedicated.

However, if one gives after having relinquished it to an animal, it is permissible to drive that [animal] away and have someone else eat [the food]. Therefore, by means of the phrase "Where shall we give? and so forth, an offense-free state is shown in one way.
But even if one has not asked in this manner, if one knows "This has not yet been dedicated," then according to one's own preference, wherever—
"It is permissible to have it given there where he wishes," so it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.
Regarding the phrase "give it where you wish," since it is said "according to your own preference," one is permitted to have it given wherever he desires.
However, in the *Parivāra*, nine types of gifts are declared unrighteous (*adhammika*), such as that which has been dedicated to the Saṅgha [but diverted] to another Saṅgha or to a *cetiya*.
It is said thus: "one dedicates [an offering] intended for a cetiya to another cetiya, or to the Saṅgha, or to an individual;
or one dedicates what was intended for an individual to another individual, or to the Saṅgha, or to a cetiya.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "nine recipients and nine modes of enjoyment," these refer to the recipients and the modes of enjoyment of those very same gifts.

Regarding "three gifts that are in accordance with the Dhamma": these three are giving what is intended for the Saṅgha to the Saṅgha alone, giving what is intended for a shrine (cetiya) to the shrine alone, and giving what is intended for an individual to the individual alone.
It is stated that their "acceptance and enjoyment" refer to both their acceptance and their use.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Ornament of the Discourse Determining the Characteristics of Giving and Other Topics," in the *Vinayālaṅkāra*,
which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
14. Discussion on the Determination of Digging the Earth 72.

Having thus explained the determination regarding gifts, placing trust, seizing, and the dedication of merit, he now spoke the passage beginning with “the earth” (*pathavī*) in order to explain the determination regarding the earth.
In that context, it is called *pathavī* because it spreads out (*pattharati*); the root *pa-thara* means to spread or to cover.
*dhātu*: the letter *ra* becomes *va*, [referring to] earth together with its constituent parts (*sasambhārapathavī*).
He states its classification as: “Two kinds of earth: born earth and unborn earth. To show the distinction between them, he says:
“Therein, that which is called ‘born earth’,” and so forth. Therein, pure dust... [omitted] ...for the most part, clay-earth is what is called “born earth. Not only... [omitted] ...
That very same [earth], even when unburnt, is called "arisen earth. The construction is as follows: not only these two, but even a heap of dust... pe...
that has been rained upon for four months, is also called "arisen earth. The same method applies elsewhere as well.
In that context, there is only pure dust here on this earth, and no stones or other such things; thus it is "pure dust. Likewise...
*Suḍḍhamattikā*: pure clay. *Appapāsāṇā*: having few stones; the same method applies to the other terms as well. *Yebhuyyenapaṃsukā*: mostly dust;
this is a compound without elision (*aluttasamāsa*), and likewise for *yebhuyyenamattikā*. Therein, stones larger than the size of a fist are [called] stones; pebbles the size of a fist are gravel;
"potsherds" (*kathalā*) refers to fragments of broken vessels and the like; "sand" (*marumpā*) refers to coarse gravel.
"Sand is just sand. Regarding the phrase "mostly dust": here, out of three portions, two portions are dust, while one portion consists of something else, such as stone.
"Even when not burnt" means not burnt in various ways by means of hearths, cooking pans, kilns, heat, and so forth;
however, that [burnt portion] does not exist separately, but should be understood as being included within one of the categories such as pure dust.

“Abounding with gravel” means having more gravel than anything else. It is said that after having one basketful brought from the elephant’s belly and washed it in a trough, he realized on the ground that it was abounding in gravel; then the monks themselves dug the lotus pond.
As for the two phrases in the middle, “little dust, little clay,” these refer specifically to the five [substances] beginning with stone.
They enter. For this is a statement classifying those same two types, namely: "pure stone" and so forth.

And here, although for the most part the earth with much dust and the earth with little dust have been mentioned, while the earth with half-dust has not been explicitly stated, nevertheless, because it is possible to have a rule with a remainder even within the training rules that are offenses by formal prescription (*paṇṇattivajja*), [the case of] half-dust [earth] is also included.
It should be understood that regarding earth, it is indeed a *pācittiya*. However, some say:
"Since a *dukkaṭa* is stated for half-covered [earth] among the categories such as 'all-covered,' a *dukkaṭa* is also appropriate here. That is not correct;
for apart from the two kinds of earth—those whose basis is a *pācittiya* and those whose basis is non-offense—there is no third kind whose basis is a *dukkaṭa*.
Because of the non-existence of earth [in that sense]. For only two kinds of earth have been mentioned: "earth that has arisen" and "earth that has not arisen.
Therefore, it must be one or the other of these two kinds of earth.

And when a decision regarding the Vinaya is reached, since one must stand by what is grave among the grave and light offenses, it is not possible here to be without an offense. However, in the case of those [roofs] entirely covered and so forth—
A *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) is appropriate for half [of the measure], because in that case there is the possibility of such a *dukkaṭa*-offense. In the *Vimativinodanī* as well, it is stated:

"Since it is declared that there is no offense when the ground consists of merely a little dust or clay, it should be understood that even with half-dust or half-clay there is still a *pācittiya* (expiation).
For it cannot be said that this is a matter of *dukkaṭa*, as it is distinct from both what has arisen and what has not arisen."
It is said: “Because of the absence of a third earth.
Regarding “whether digging or having it dug”: this refers to either digging oneself—even with one’s big toe—or having another dig it, even with a broom or a small shovel.
When one says, “Dig a lotus pond,” it is permissible; thus, in this [case]...
Because it was stated without specifying "in a place," it is permissible [to dig].

Even when it is said, "Dig this creeper," since the conventional expression is used with reference to digging the earth, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) under this very training rule (sikkhāpada), not under the training rule concerning living plants (bhūtagāma-sikkhāpada).
However, if it is stated with reference to both, then there are two offenses of expiation.
73. *Kuṭehīti* means with jars. *Tanukakaddamo* means mud mixed with water; because it flows with the water, it is permissible.

*Udakapappaṭako* means that when water has entered into the ground, a thin layer of dust or clay rises up, floating as a film covering its surface; even when that water has dried up, that film remains.
"That which remains while being moved by the wind" refers to what is called a "water-film. "Less than four months" means fewer than four months.
"Covered over" means covered by rain. The phrase "on an unprepared slope" is stated for the purpose of showing a place where there is no access;
for such a place exists on an anthill. "A mouse-hill" refers to a mound of dust made outside by mice after they have dug.
"The same method" means that even a minor four-month *ovaṭṭha* (boundary) is permissible.
"Not even for a single day" means that it is not permitted to violate it even after a single day has passed beyond the four-month *ovaṭṭha*.
Furthermore, even regarding a connection to a lower ground, because the *gokaṇṭaka* (a thorny plant) has risen by being cut repeatedly from the ground, one must cut it down from its very summit.
They say it is permissible to take [the earth]. It is also permissible to take even muddy earth that has been trampled and churned up by feet after being made to leave its original place.

Because it is stated by the words "covered" and so forth, one should understand that the ground becomes wet only by rainwater falling directly from the sky, and not by water flowing from it after having fallen upon a roof or similar structure. "From there" means from the old dwelling-place.
The statement beginning with "I take the brick" was spoken with reference to a pure mind. Regarding "by water," they say it means by water falling directly from the sky;
however, if it becomes moistened by water that has fallen after striking elsewhere, it is permissible.
"A pillar of the bower" refers to a pillar of a leafy bower.
74. "Having lifted up" means having thrown up. "By that pretext" means by that excuse. Regarding "there is no offense because it is not within one's domain":
even if it were possible to extinguish it, if one remains there having first given it with a pure mind and observing, "Let it burn," there is no offense. "Great clay" refers to plaster for walls.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Ornament of the Discussion on the Determination of Digging the Earth," in the Vinayālaṅkāra,
which is a commentary on the Vinaya-saṅgaha.
15. Discussion on the Determination of the Community of Beings (Bhūtagāmavinicchayakathā) 75.
Having thus explained the determination of earth, he now spoke the passage beginning with “the community of beings” (bhūtagāma) in order to explain the determination of the community of beings.

In this context, they “are” (bhavanti) and “have been” (ahuvuṃ), thus they are called “beings” (bhūtā); the meaning is that they are born, grow, have been born, and have grown. “Community” (gāma) means—
“Rāsi” means a collection; thus, “bhūtagāma” is a collection of beings (*bhūtānaṃ gāmo*). Or, the beings themselves are the collection, hence “bhūtagāma.

This is a designation for established green grass, trees, and so forth. In this context, the explanation of “bhavanti” (they come into being) is “they are born and they grow,” and the explanation of “ahuvuṃ” (they were) is “born and grown.
Thus, the word *bhūta* has both a present and a past referent. Therefore, it was said in the *Vimativinodanī*:
“*Bhavanti* means they grow; *ahuvunti* means they were. Now, in order to show that category of beings (*bhūtagāma*), he said:

“‘Category of beings’ is a designation for trees, creepers, and so forth, which are born from the five kinds of seeds. By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) in the phrase “creepers and so forth,” medicinal herbs, shrubs, and the like are to be understood.

Now, showing those seeds according to their specific forms, he says: “In this regard, there are these five kinds of seeds,” and so forth. Therein, that which is a root itself as a seed is a “root-seed” (*mūlabīja*).

The same applies to the remaining types. Alternatively, it is a “root-seed” because its seed is the root; or, it is a “root-seed” because it is produced from a root-seed. The same applies to the remaining types.
Therein, by the first grammatical analysis (*viggaha*), only the category of seeds (*bījagāma*) is obtained.
The category of living beings [is explained] by the second and third [factors]. Now, showing that category of living beings according to their specific forms, he said:

"In this regard, what is called 'root-propagated seed' (*mūlabīja*)," and so forth. Therein, among those five types beginning with root-propagated seeds, turmeric... [and so on] ... up to *bhaddamuttaka* is called "root-propagated seed. These alone are not the only root-propagated seeds;
rather, there are others besides these, namely whatever species belong to the category of living beings.
The construction is as follows: "There are plants that are born from roots, they are produced from roots; this is what is called 'a plant-life born from a root-seed'.
The same method applies to the remaining cases as well. For it is said in the Commentary: "Now, showing that plant-life by dividing it up, he says:
'Plant-life consists of five kinds of seed-origins,' and so forth. In that context, "plant-life" (bhūtagāma) means...
In order to show that which, when present, constitutes a "group of living beings" (bhūtagāma), it is stated in the commentaries: "He said, 'the five kinds of seeds.
Even so, such statements as "or whatever others there are that grow from roots" do not harmonize [with the definition].
For root-seeds and the like do not grow *in* roots and the like; rather, those things that grow *from* roots and the like are what constitute the "kinds of seeds. Therefore...
The commentary on the meaning should be understood as follows: “A grove of living beings” (*bhūtagāma*) is the term to be analyzed. “Five” is the delimitation of its divisions.

“Born from seeds” (*bījajātāni*) is the indication of the phenomena so delimited; for they are called “born from seeds” because they are produced from seeds, and this is a designation for trees and the like.
It is just as in such expressions as “if one eats rice-gruel of *sāli*,” where it refers to *sāli* grains.
Just as boiled rice is called "rice from paddy," so too it should be understood that a group of living beings produced from a seed is called a "seed.

"Creeper-seed" means a seed from a climbing plant. Because it is the specific cause for the production of a similar fruit when other conditions come together, the word *bīja* (seed), which is conventionally established for a hard fruit capable of sprouting, is used by extension for certain roots and other parts as well, since they fulfill that same purpose.

It is stated as "seed" (*bīja*)—distinguished by the word "seed" from among others—in order to exclude [the meaning of] "arising from a root," just as [in the cases of] "material form" (*rūpa-rūpa*) and "suffering-as-suffering" (*dukkha-dukkha*). In the *Niddesa*, in the passage:

"Or whatever other [things] there are that are born from a root, produced from a root," it is the seed itself that is shown by means of that which is produced from a seed; therefore, this is the meaning here.

It should be understood as follows: furthermore, there are other things such as varieties of roots—including those of the *āluva*, *kaseruka*, *malanīluppala*, *puṇḍarīka*, *kuvalaya*, *kunda*, *pāṭali*, and so forth—from which stems, creepers, trees, and the like are produced and generated;

and both that root from which they are produced and generated, as well as the turmeric and other items mentioned in the Canon—all this is called "root-seed" (*mūlabīja*) by way of metaphorical designation based on its function.
He shows that the cause has been demonstrated. This same method applies to the seed-types of the aggregates (*khandha-bīja*) and so forth.

Among the miscellaneous aggregate-seeds mentioned here, the *ambaṭaka*, *indasāla*, *nuhi*, *pālibhaddaka*, *kaṇikāra*, and others are seeds propagated from stems (*khandha-bīja*). The *ambilā* creeper, the four-cornered creeper (*caturassa-vallika*), *kaṇavera*, and others are seeds propagated from joints (*phalu-bīja*).

The *makaci*, *mallikā*, *sumana*, *jayasumana*, and others are seeds propagated from the tip (*agga-bīja*). Mangoes (*amba*), rose-apples (*jambu*), breadfruit (*panasa*), *ṭṭhi*, and others [are seeds propagated from roots].

"Seeds and things containing seeds" should be understood as follows: "In a grove of living plants, perceiving it to be a grove of living plants, he cuts it or has it cut" means that having taken up knives or the like, he cuts it himself or has another cut it.
"He breaks it or has it broken" means that having taken up stones or the like, he breaks it himself or has another break it. "He cooks it or has it cooked" means that having applied fire...
The connection is: "If one cooks it oneself or causes another to cook it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
In that context, showing the classification of the offenses, he says: "In the case of a living plant," and so forth. Therein, "freed from the living plant" means separated from the living plant.

Regarding the statement, "It is not permitted to intentionally shake it off," because the word "intentionally" (*sañcicca*) is used here, [the offense applies] even to the state of [the grain] adhering to the body.
Even if one knows [the plant is there], it is permissible to pick it up because there is no perception that "I shall pull this out.

By the mention of "endless" (ananta), even a speck of mustard-seed mold is included; for that is the name of that species of moss. Because it lacks roots and leaves, it is called "an incomplete habitat of living beings" (*asampunnabhūtagāmo*).
Regarding the term *abhūtagāmamūlattā*: here, "habitat of living beings" (*bhūtagāmo*) is the root or cause of this, thus it is "rooted in a habitat of living beings" (*bhūtagāmamūlo*).

The phrase *bhūtagāmamūlaṃ* means that the root is the cause of the community of beings (*bhūtagāma*). For indeed, what is called a "community of seeds" arises from a community of beings and serves as the cause for that community of beings.
However, this [tree stump] is not like that; therefore, it is said: "because it has its root in a non-community of beings (*abhūtagāmamūlattā*).
For although the stump of a palmyra palm, a coconut tree, or the like is not the cause of a community of beings because it does not grow upward, [it is still called such].
Nevertheless, because it arises from seeds consisting of leaves, roots, and bulbs that have grown from a cluster of living beings (*bhūtagāma*),

it is said to be "produced from a cluster of living beings" and thus is included within the category of "seeds. It is stated [in the text] that "it is included within the category of seeds" because it has its root in a cluster of living beings, even though it does not increase [further].
Having said, “When the sprout is green,” he clarifies that same point by saying, “when it has grown blue-colored”;
the meaning is that a leaf resembling the color of a blue leaf has grown—or rather, the reading “nīlavaṇṇe jāte” (grown blue-colored) should be accepted.

“It is included within the rootless category of living beings” (amūlakabhūtagāme saṅgahaṃ gacchati): this is stated specifically regarding the coconut. “The algae on the outside of water-jars, etc.”...
They say that because it does not remain in water and because it conforms to the category of seed-plants, it is a basis for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Even a *kaṇṇaka* [flower] is indeed not subject to formal designation;

even one of blue color is likewise not subject to formal designation. 77. *Seyyaka* is a certain kind of fragrant substance produced from stone. "From the time of its flowering" means from the time of its blossoming.
"Starting from... "Taking an *ahicchattaka* mushroom" means taking it when it has opened. However, it is not permitted to take a bud even without damaging the bark of the tree.

Some say: "Because it is stated that 'one damages the bark of the tree,' it is permitted to take any *ahicchattaka* growing on a tree by cutting it from the top without damaging the bark"; but that is incorrect.
Because it is stated: “As long as the *ahicchattaka* (mushroom) remains unopened, it is a matter of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*). Regarding the phrase “having detached from the tree,” they say:
“Even if it remains clinging to the tree in some small measure, if it is taken from the tree without damaging the bark of the tree, it is permissible.
Regarding the statement “it is not permissible [to take] from a fresh tree,” here too, provided that the bark of the tree is not damaged—
It should be understood that it is permissible to take [the water] after cutting it off from the surface. "With hand-twitching" means with the twitching of the hand.
"Water should not be stored" is said with reference to what has been drawn for one's own use;

however, there is no prohibition against storing it after having received it later from one who drew it solely for the sake of a person not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*). (From the *Vimativinodanī*)
However, the statement “water should not be stored” was said with reference to water for one’s own drinking;
for others, it is permissible because it is not being kept for personal use. Therefore it was said: “by one who wishes to drink it oneself.
Because it is stated, “of those trees whose branches grow,” there is no need to perform the ritual of making them *kappiya* (lawful) in the case of those whose branches do not grow.

They say this. In the *Vimativinodanī* as well, it is stated: "Regarding those trees whose branches grow even without their roots being watered, and which increase by the mere emergence of leaves—even if one does not perform what is allowable (*kappiya*) there, it is permissible to disturb cut coconut palms, bamboo poles, and so forth.
Because it was said, "I shall show the place for walking," [it refers to] either solely with the intention of walking (*caṅkamana*) or with the intention of going along a path.
There is no fault for one who steps on them, nor for one who sits upon them with the intention of sitting on the grass.
78. "By means of allowable expressions for recluses" means by means of the conventional terminology used by recluses.

Although seeds and the like do not become subject to non-growth merely by being touched by fire or merely by being scratched with fingernails and so forth, nevertheless, it is only when this has been done that [they are considered allowable] for recluses.

"It is allowable" (*kappati*) means that terms such as "refined by fire" (*aggiparijita*) and so forth have become what are known as "monastic designations" (*samaṇavohāra*). Therefore, the intended meaning is:
"I authorize you to consume the fruit by means of those monastic designations acting as instruments. Even seeds produced without seeds (*abīja-nibbaṭṭa-bīja*) are considered "allowable for monks";

because they have been established by formal proclamation (*paññatta-pannatti*), they have come to be designated simply as "monastic designations. Alternatively, [the term applies] to things such as those refined by fire.

The intended meaning here should be understood as follows: "I allow you to consume fruit for five reasons known as the 'five monastic permissions' (samaṇakappiya), precisely because these five are permissible. Regarding the phrases "won by fire" and so forth, some also read "cultivated" (*paricita*).
"Seedless" refers to young mango fruits and the like. "From which the seed has been removed" refers to mangoes, jackfruits, and so on, from which the seed— [...is] the seed—has been extracted.
Once it has been extracted and separated, it can be consumed. That fruit, such as a jackfruit (*panasa*), in which the seed is to be extracted or separated, is called "having an extractable seed.
Regarding the statement "it must be made *kappiya* (lawful)," one should not conclude that it is permissible for a monk to do so even if he has not been told to do so;
for this is because only the specific manner in which one who makes it *kappiya* must act has been prescribed.
Furthermore, since it was stated at the very beginning that "the making allowable must be caused to be done," it should be understood that when a monk says,
"Make it allowable," the person who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna) must say, "It is allowable," and then perform the acts such as purifying by fire.
They say, moreover, that the statement "it is allowable" may be uttered in any language whatsoever.

Because of the statement, “It must be made allowable after having said ‘allowable’,” it should be understood that one must first say “allowable” and afterwards perform the touching and so forth with fire and other means. Some also say,
“After first placing it in the fire or piercing it with a fingernail and the like,
it is permissible to say ‘allowable’ even without removing it.”

In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it says: "Even though it is stated by way of a prior action that 'having said, "It is allowable" (*kappiya*),' because of the statement that 'the wound must be made upon the seed-plant at the very moment of speaking by means of fire, a knife, or the like,' it is not permitted to do so beforehand.
Furthermore, that [allowance] should be shown as consisting solely of cutting and breaking, without dividing it into two parts. And the monk who performs it should say, 'Make it allowable.'"

"It must be done in whatever language is spoken. Regarding the statement, 'For the sake of releasing the seed-planting ground, one must again have it made allowable (kappiya),' because the act of having it made was already performed at the very beginning.
It is said that in cases such as "in one seed," etc., even though there is a single connection [of the seeds], if the intention is "I am making only one," then everything is indeed considered made.
They say, "It happens. Regarding the phrase "he pierces the wood," they say here: "Even if he pierces it or causes it to be pierced after having known [the rule], it is indeed permissible.
Regarding the phrase "he pierces the rice-crust," the same principle applies here as well. They say: "He pierces that;

it is not permissible because ropes and such things fall under the category of vessels (*bhājana*). And regarding the phrase "mixed with pepper, pākka, and so forth," here [the prohibition applies] by virtue of its connection with the rice-crust.
It should be understood as being tied together as one, not merely by way of the mutual connection between the fruits themselves.
Because it is stated, “It is permissible to do so even in a bowl,” it is indeed permissible to pierce the kernel or the seed wherever it has been removed from the bowl.
It is said, “Having had it split, one should have it made allowable,” because a bowl that is devoid of seeds falls under the category of a vessel.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Ornament of the Discussion on the Determination of Living Things," in the *Vinayālaṅkāra*,
which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
16. Discussion on the Determination of Sleeping Together (Sahaseyyavinicchayakathā) 79.

Having thus explained the determination regarding living beings (bhūtagāma), he now speaks the words beginning with "sleeping together is of two kinds" in order to explain the determination regarding sleeping together.
Therein, that sleeping together which has two kinds or modes is "of two kinds" (duvidha).
“Sahaseyyā” means lying down together, or that in which one lies down together; “sahaseyyaka” is simply “sahaseyyā,” by means of the suffix *ka* used in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*).

That [offense] is twofold: by way of lying down with one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) and by way of lying down with a woman. Therefore he said, “The offense of lying down together is twofold.
Regarding the phrase “for two nights or three nights,” this is merely for the sake of the euphony of the expression.

It should be understood that the inclusion of "two nights" (*diratta*) is for this purpose. For if staying together for three nights were already permitted, there would be no need at all to mention two nights;

thus, the inclusion of "two nights" is not employed separately. Therefore it was said: "The Blessed One granted the exemption of 'three nights' for the sake of gathering the novices under himself, [referring to] 'more than two nights and three nights.
This is for the purpose of establishing the inclusion of three nights as being continuous.

Or rather, the inclusion of the term "two nights" (diratta) has been made. For if only "three nights" (tiratta) were stated, one might include even a three-night period that was interrupted by staying elsewhere.
However, when "three nights" qualified by "two nights" is spoken of, it indicates a three-night period that is indeed uninterrupted. In the *Vimativinodanī* as well, it says:
"The inclusion of 'two nights' is for the sake of poetic ornamentation [of the expression]. It is continuous..."
It is stated: "The offense applies to one who sleeps for three nights and then continues sleeping on the fourth day and so forth;

it should be understood that this is also for the purpose of showing that it does not apply to one who sleeps by skipping days (alternating days) and the like. "Sleeping together" (*sahaseyya*) means sleeping in the same place.
Here, "sleeping" (*seyya*) refers both to the act of lying down characterized by stretching out the body, as well as the lodging where they sleep.

"Regarding the phrase 'he should make a bed': the meaning is that having entered the bed known as a lodging (*senāsana*), he should make—that is, prepare—the bed known as the stretching out of the body. "By one and a half cubits high":
here, the "one and a half cubits" should be understood according to the carpenter’s cubit (*vaḍḍhakihattha*). "By five coverings": these consist of brick, stone, plaster, grass, and leaves.
By five coverings. "By way of what has come forth from speech" means by way of mastery.
"A single access" (*ekūpacāra*) is said with reference to the unity of the door of utilization. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated:
"A single access is that which, having entered by one path and without stepping out into the open air, is suitable for traversing everywhere."

Even if there are many doors, it is still a single precinct (*ekūpacāra*). However, where they construct separate doors by enclosing [the space] with walls and the like, it becomes multiple precincts (*nānūpacāra*).
But if they do indeed enclose it yet do not construct separate doors, this too should be understood as a single precinct, like a chamber whose door has been sealed with clay and so forth.
Otherwise, if one enters a chamber and [sees] those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) lying in the vestibule and other such areas...

It is said: "Even for one who causes the entrance to the womb-chamber to be opened at dawn after having it closed with clay and so forth for the sake of escaping from sleeping together, there would be no offense.

The connection is: "A four-sided hall constitutes a single common area. Regarding the statement, "For each of their actions, there is an offense for the monk," some say: "By means of non-performance, an offense originating from non-action is stated."
Because at that moment, for one who is sleeping, there is an absence of activity. For this training rule may originate from activity, and it may also originate from non-activity.
And its origination from activity is stated by way of its predominance,” they say.
“And as this is so, so too is the daytime practice. For through non-performance and through lack of restraint of the sense-doors, this also originates from non-activity.”
They say, “It happens,” and this appears reasonable; it should be accepted after investigation.

80. Regarding the phrase “of one whose wall is not connected with the upper floor,” this is stated for the purpose of showing that there is nothing at all to be said regarding a wall that *is* connected.
Since there is no suspicion whatsoever for one lying on the upper floor, [the text says] “in the lower palace,” and so forth.
It has been stated. Regarding "in various approaches": this was said with reference to such places where people ascend to the upper floor by constructing a ladder on the outside;
thus it says, "even on the upper floor. Because there is no offense for one lying down in an open courtyard, it says, "inside the roof-covering.
"In the form of a hall" means by way of a hall-structure. Regarding "in a dwelling with a half-wall": here, "half-wall" [refers to...]

"Regarding the term *nāma*: it refers to a dwelling where walls are built on three sides leaving half [open], or where, having erected a wall on one side, they erect walls on both sides making them each half-[height].
This is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries; however, in the *gaṇṭhipada*, it says: "In the case of 'half-walled' (*aḍḍhakuṭṭaka*)..."
It is said, "A roof that has not reached the half-wall," but even that is not incorrect.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: "By the phrase 'half-wall' [which follows] what was stated as 'by way of a brief classification,' it demonstrates the shape.
Where walls are built on three or two sides, or where the roof has not reached the wall by half, this is a 'half-wall' (*aḍḍhakuṭṭaka*)."
Thus it is said. A "hair-fringe" (*vāḷasaṅghāṭa*) refers to a fringe made of hair-figures placed upon pillars and so forth inside the enclosure.

Regarding the phrase "gone outside the enclosure," it should be understood that even where there is no enclosure on a particular side, there is likewise no offense if one has gone outside the area that would otherwise require an enclosure.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: "Regarding 'gone outside the enclosure'..."

In this context, regarding the side where there is no enclosure: if the site is high above the ground, then even within the space of a *nibbakosa* (the area directly below) beneath both high sites, there is indeed no offense, because the designation "lodging" (*senāsana*) does not apply there.
However, if the site is low, standing at the same level as the ground so that it rests on the lower floor of the lodging, then in the direction free from enclosure...

It is stated: "An offense occurs everywhere within the interior of the enclosure; because there is no demarcation for the enclosure, it should be understood that there is no offense only outside of it. Regarding the phrase "in an unenclosed vicinity of a dwelling":

in this context, in the case of great four-winged halls (mahācatusālā) which have open courtyards in their centers, one may enter all the rooms by proceeding through the main entrance without descending into the open courtyard.

It is not possible; thus, that which is made by removing a wall from two sides of each individual cell is called a "delimited precinct of a cell," but since this [monastery] is not like that, it is said to be "in a monastery with undelimited precincts.
Because the precincts of the cells are undelimited, they enter all the cells even without descending into the courtyard, but rather through the entrance itself.
Having gone, they enter this or that cell. Now, as for the statement, "How then is its enclosure alone [considered] its complete enclosure?", he says:
"For its enclosure is indeed the enclosure of the cell. And this was said with reference to the walls surrounding the cells on all sides.
For in a dwelling arranged according to a four-winged layout (catusāla), even if the entrance to the cell is not separately enclosed, [the entire structure constitutes the enclosure].
That which stands on all sides and is enclosed by the walls of the inner chambers is called "enclosed. 81.
A palace constructed by being made long and straight in only one direction is a structure with a single hall (*ekasāla*).

Structures with two halls (*dvisāla*) and so forth should be understood as those built in two, three, or four directions in the shape of a crossroads (*siṅghāṭaka*) and the like. This is merely an illustration of the different types of halls.
And here, there is a distinction from what precedes. Regarding "eight *pācittiya* offenses":

since the *pāli* presents [the cases] beginning with a lodging that is half-covered and half-fenced—which is the basis for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)—everything exceeding that, such as one that is fully covered or half-fenced, even if not explicitly mentioned in the *pāli*, is shown to be the basis for a *pācittiya* offense because the training rule is a prohibition by formal injunction (*paṇṇattivajja*).

It should be understood that [the offense] must be treated with gravity. Regarding the phrase "seven pācittiyas," this is stated by taking the two types of pācittiya mentioned in the Canon collectively as a single unit.
In the Canon, the statement, "having gone out before dawn on the third night and lying down again," is said according to the strictest (ukkaṭṭha) standard;
it refers to rising before dawn without having gone out, yet remaining within the roof-covering.
Even for one who has sat down, there is no offense on the following day if they share the same sleeping place.

Here, one-fourth is "a small portion" (*cūḷaka*), two portions are "a half," and when two out of three portions constitute the majority—by this characteristic, "partially covered," "completely covered," and so forth, are to be understood.
Now, extending the aforementioned method to the second training rule as well: "With a woman... pe..."

“This is the very decision,” he said. They say: “Even though a dead woman has become the basis for a *pārājika* offense, because she stands on the side of what is not clung-to (*anupādinnapakkhe*), she does not give rise to the offense of sleeping together.

From the statement, “If one lies down while a woman is lying down after the sun has set, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)”, it should be understood that for one who sleeps during the day with her, there is no offense of sleeping together.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Ornament of the Discussion on the Decision Regarding Sleeping Together," in the *Vinayālaṅkāra*,
which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
17. Discussion on the Decision Regarding the Proper Conduct Toward Beds, Chairs, and Other Seating Belonging to the Saṅgha. 82.
Having thus explained the decision regarding sleeping together, he now speaks the passage beginning with “In a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, a bed...

in order to explain the decision regarding what should be done with beds in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha. In this context, it is said that “the act proceeds when there is a concordant assembly.”
The meaning of the word *saṅgha* is common to all [types of] Saṅghas. That which is given to the Saṅgha is *saṅghika*. A *vihāra* is so called because one dwells (*viharati*) therein;
in that [place]. One lies down (*sayanti*) upon it, thus it is a *seyyā* (bed); that [bed]. *Asanthari* means having spread out.
*Pakkama* is departure; the meaning is "going. Regarding the phrase: "Having spread out a bed in a *saṅghika* monastery (*vihāra*), he departed."
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "In a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha... pe ... when departing" is how the meaning is to be understood.
Regarding that departure, the meaning is that this decision (vinicchaya) which is being stated by me should be known.

To the question "What is that decision?", he says: "In a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha... pe ... an offense of expiation (pācittiya). The "proximity" (upacāra) of an unenclosed [monastery] is from the lodging...
There are two throws of a clod. Regarding "an offense of expiation" (*pācittiya*): for one who steps over the first throw, it is an act of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
upon stepping over the second, it is an offense of expiation. How is this known? It is said: "Because of the words, 'Whosoever monk...
In that context, the monastery belonging to the Saṅgha is well-known, while the bedding is not; as to how many kinds that bedding is, he says: "Bedding, by name... and so forth.
"Of ten kinds. Regarding that, as to what a *bhisī* is and what a *cimilika* and so forth are, he said:

"In this context, *bhisī*... [and so on]... this is the method for the leaf-mats (*paṇṇasanthāra*). In that regard, those to be spread upon a bed are "bed-mats" (*mañcakabhisī*); likewise for the others.
Those made for the purpose of protecting the color are "sewn together with pieces of cloth and so forth. Those to be spread upon the ground are—
If a coverlet exists, it should be spread over it; if not, it should be spread on the bare ground.

By the phrase "only the avoidance of lion-postures and so forth is prohibited," it is meant that for one's own use, it is not permitted to spread it on beds, chairs, and the like, and then fold it up and store it away;
however, its use as a ground-covering and so forth for oneself is allowed.
This shows that there is no "keeping" [of such items]. For in the Khandhaka, it says: "There are mats spread both inside the bed and outside the bed.
Having thus prepared beds and so forth for one's own use, regarding the matter of keeping them, [it says]:
"Monks, great skins are not to be worn: the lion skin, the tiger skin, the leopard skin; whoever..."
“...one would incur an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” thus a prohibition was made;
therefore, the intended meaning here should be understood according to the method already stated. However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, having raised the objection:
“If this is so, why was it said that ‘the prohibition applies only to wearing [it]’?”—[the author replies]: “Because of the statement: ‘Monks, I allow the use of all palaces.’”
Even in the case of a lodging belonging to an individual, although it is permissible to use items such as golden vases that have been designated for the use of that lodging,
it is not permissible to use them by making them one's own private property. Likewise,
although this [floor-covering] is permissible to use as a floor-covering, it is not permissible to use it by making it one's own property and taking it from one monastery to another.
It is said: "The prohibition should be understood as being for the purpose of excluding [the use of] only those items that are to be worn, in order to show that it is not permitted.
*Pāvāra* and *kojava* are specific types of rugs with raised hair, kept specifically for the purpose of bedspreads.
It is stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that "only this much was spoken. This was stated for the purpose of showing that it was indeed spoken in that manner in the commentaries.
"In addition, there is also another such covering that should be spread over beds and chairs," so it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.
However, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated with a specific definition: "A *paccattharaṇa* is a woolen rug (*pāvāra*) or a blanket (*kojava*).
Therefore, what is stated in the *gaṇṭhipadas* does not agree with this; [it has been said] in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: "It should be accepted after investigation."
This has been stated. However, when investigated, the following intention is discerned: the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* is indeed an *aṭṭhakathā*;
therefore, it was stated according to the method found in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* and other texts, defining [the term] as "a cloak (*pāvāra*) is a rug (*kojava*).
Even though such a definition is given, it is just as when one says, "Prince Ātapatta," where the name is used by defining the state of being Ātapatta as something he has acquired.
By way of illustration, even items such as yak-tail fans and the like are included under the category of "royal insignia" because they share the common characteristic of being royal regalia;

likewise, although "woolen blankets" and "felt rugs" are mentioned specifically, by way of illustration other coverings are also included because they share the common characteristic of being spread over beds and chairs. Therefore, in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries...
It should be understood that what has been stated here does not contradict the words of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, but is indeed in accordance with them.

However, in this context, relying on the reading, "He by whom a monastery was caused to be built is the owner of the monastery," certain holders of the Vinaya maintain that "whether it be a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha or one belonging to an individual, the donor alone is the owner."
They make the determination: "The owner alone is the master; one may dwell there only by his consent, not by the consent of the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
This must be examined: what does this reading establish—is it the sense of ownership or the sense of having to ask for permission?
When thus examined, because of such statements as, "When a monk is present, a monk must be asked for permission," and so forth...
It is understood that he accomplishes only the purpose of asking for permission, not the purpose of lordship.
Now, it might be argued: "When the purpose of asking for permission is accomplished, the purpose of lordship is necessarily accomplished as well;
for it is precisely because of his state of lordship that he must be asked for permission. To this, one should say: "And when the one asking for permission exists, there must also be a monk..."
Based on such statements as, "He should be asked for permission; in his absence, a novice (sāmaṇera);

in his absence, a monastery attendant (ārāmika)," according to the opinion of the Venerable Ones, even a monk, a novice, a monastery attendant, a builder of the dwelling, or any person whatsoever belonging to that family might be considered the master.
Even when such a person is known to exist—whether it be a monk, a novice, or a monastery attendant—[the following applies].
They alone are the owners, not the builder of the monastery. Even if one among them is absent, the builder would still be the owner.
However, in this context, it is stated that one must indeed ask permission for the sake of protecting the lodging belonging to the Saṅgha;
it is not asked for because of [the builder’s] ownership. For it is said in the Commentary: "Or he may go without asking permission..."
"In this case, when a bhikkhu is present, that bhikkhu must be asked for permission," and so forth.
Furthermore, one might say: "We did not speak with reference to the intended meaning of the entire passage;
rather, we spoke specifically with reference to the word-meaning of the phrase 'the owner of the vihāra. How so? *Saṃ* refers to him..."
“Owner” (*sāmika*) means one who possesses; “owner of the monastery” (*vihārassāmika*) means the owner of the monastery. When it is asked, “Who is called the owner of the monastery?

one should say, “He by whom the monastery was caused to be built is called the owner of the monastery. Therefore, it is understood that the donor who builds the monastery is the owner of the monastery.
This being understood, an “owner” is one who is the master (*issara*) over his own property. Of him...

"Others obtain [permission] solely by the donor's own wish; therefore, it was said with reference to this meaning that monks may dwell there solely by the wish of the donor who is the owner of the monastery, and not by the wish of the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
They should be told: "Venerable sirs, do not speak thus; it is just as if one were to say, 'Ghaṭīkāra is Brahmā.'"
That Brahmā does not make pots now, but he did so in a previous existence; therefore, by virtue of the meaning of the expression "he makes a pot," he receives the name "Ghaṭikāra.
Thus, because of the name he received previously, even though he has become a Brahmā, he is still called "Ghaṭikāra" according to his former designation.
In this way, from the time he gave it over to the monks as a dwelling-place...

From the moment [the gift] is established, one is no longer the owner of the monastery, because giving is characterized by the relinquishment of the object. However, previously, at the time when it had not yet been relinquished, one was indeed the "owner" of the monastery due to being its builder;

thus, because he had previously acquired that name, he is called the "owner of the monastery" by way of that former designation, and not because of any lordship over the monastery once it has been relinquished. For this very reason, the Perfectly Enlightened One—
It should be understood that the assigner of lodgings was authorized without saying, "Let the monks dwell according to the wish of the donors of the monastery.

For it is stated thus in the *Vimativinodanī*: "Regarding the phrase 'their houses,' even if they have been built for the purpose of monks staying there, it should be understood that they remain the property of those [donors] until they give them away. Therefore, from the time they are given...
This shows that from that point on, those items do not belong to them. However, this discussion is presented at this point because the text is directly present here.
The determination regarding monasteries (*vihāra*), however, will be clarified in the section on the determination of the distribution of the four requisites (*catupaccaya*).
"Whoever" means anyone, whether a relative or a stranger. "That by which they weave a bed or a chair" refers to the weaving of beds and chairs.
83. *Siluccayaleṇaṃ*: a cave in a rock formation; the meaning is a mountain cave.

Regarding the matter that "the lodging was gnawed by termites," since this was formulated as a rule based on that specific incident, the Commentary states there is no offense when, in accordance with the circumstances, there is no suspicion of termites.
In the *Vattakkhandhaka*, while prescribing the duties for those traveling, it says: "The lodging must be asked permission [to leave]."
Because it was so stated, the phrase "but asking for permission is a duty (*vatta*)" was said solely for the purpose of showing that this is merely something that ought to be done;
it was not said for the purpose of showing that a transgression of the duty (*dukkaṭa*) occurs if the duty is breached.
For this very reason, in the Andhaka-ṭīkā, regarding the statement "the lodging must be asked for permission," [it explains] "that lodging which is made upon a stone surface or on stone pillars..."
It is said: "Where termites do not infest, there is no offense even for one who does not ask permission.
Therefore, that which is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*—"In such a lodging, there is no *pācittiya* for one going without asking permission;
however, if one goes without asking permission regarding the lodging while on the duty of a traveler, there is a breach of the rule, and thus one incurs a *dukkaṭa*"—is not to be accepted.
"There is no release by means of the last one's attention" is said because there is no other person following behind him. "Or, having sent one [person], he should take leave":
here, for one who goes without taking leave from the place where the intention to go arose, there is a *pācittiya* offense upon lifting the second foot.
"In a pavilion" means either in a leaf-pavilion or in a wooden-plank pavilion.
"At the foot of a tree" (*rukkhamūle*) means beneath any kind of tree whatsoever. "It decays" (*palujjati*) means it perishes.
84. "Tied having made a narrow middle with the shape of a drum" means:
having made a braid from *eraka* grass leaves and so forth, one wraps it many times around the wide parts on both sides of that braid; starting from there, up to the middle part—
Having wound it by drawing it inward from both ends, having gathered it together in the middle, and having tied it here and there—it is thus made.
"Where crows or hawks do not scatter [the bedding]" means: where these crows and hawks, or other birds dwelling in nests through long-term residence, do not scatter that lodging;
it is in such a place, at the foot of a tree, that I allow you to deposit it—this is the meaning.
85. *Navavāyima*: a bed recently covered with a woven cloth and free from frayed edges. *Onaddha*: covered with a permissible hide;
that very thing is called *onaddhaka* by means of the suffix *-ka* used in its own sense (*sakatthe*). Indeed, because of that, it does not quickly perish during the rainy season.
*Ukkaṭṭha-abbhokāsika*: this is merely a demonstration of his pleasant practice; however, even for one who is austere (*ukkaṭṭha*)...
A robe-shed is indeed permissible. "Following the body" indicates that the monk remains sitting right there;
by this, it shows that an offense occurs for one who goes elsewhere himself due to fear of the rains.

Even if a robe-shed has been specifically designated and given by donors for the purpose of keeping those living in the open air from getting wet, it must still be protected by one who seeks to protect himself. "Because... [text continues].
However, if at the very time of giving, donors give even a blanket worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] with the instruction,
"Use this as a foot-wiping cloth," it is permissible to use it exactly in that way. Therefore,
if these lodgings such as beds and chairs are given by donors with the instruction, "Use them as you please even in the open air," they may be placed in the open air at all times.
"It is permissible," it is said in the *Sāratthadīpanī*. Regarding "having sent, one should go":
here, one should send [the messenger] after saying, "Give this to whichever bhikkhu comes to this place and stays.
"Having observed that the clouds have not arisen" means that even in the summer, when clouds have arisen, [one may stay] in the open air.

It indicates that it is not permissible to set [the refuse] down there. "In this or that place" means it is placed after specifying particular open spaces such as the courtyard of a cetiya and so forth.

"Starting from the middle and directed toward the footprints" refers to a place where, having swept all around, sand has been accumulated in the middle of the courtyard by constantly gathering the refuse together; therein—
This was said for the purpose of showing the procedure to be performed: the meaning is that the sand should be carried away toward the base of a high structure or toward the base of a wall.

Some, however, explain the meaning as follows: "Or rather, wherever the sand has accumulated in the corners, from there it should be carried away toward another direction. Others, however, [say] regarding the well-swept place...
They say: "It is stated that one should stand in a place not swept by oneself and remove the sand toward one's own feet for the purpose of not disturbing the footprints.
However, the purpose of the expression "starting from the middle" is not seen there. In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, however, it says:
"'Toward the place where they sit with their feet' means toward the place where those sitting have their feet."

Some say [the dust should be swept] toward the place where one stands; others say toward the outside; some say it is stated that it should be carried toward the place where one stands so as not to go beyond the sand.
By the statement, "The refuse should be taken up with the hands and thrown outside," it is indicated that the sand should not be thrown away with the thought, "I will throw away the refuse."

86. "Having obtained permission" means having obtained permission by being told, "Go. For there is no offense for one who goes by the command of an elder. "In the same manner as before" refers to the method previously stated, beginning with "going himself after sitting down," and so forth.
"He goes elsewhere" means he goes to another place after passing beyond that path.

Because he stands outside the vicinity of a stone's throw (*leḍḍupāta*), it is said, "he is to be dealt with according to the lifting of the foot"; that is, for one going elsewhere, at the lifting of the first foot.

The meaning is: an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), and for the second time lifting up the feet, an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). "Without having made it as it was before" means without having settled it.
"In an intermediate gathering" means in a gathering from time to time.
87. "An obstacle for the residents alone": here, even if guests have arrived and, having said nothing, are sitting there...
Even when those who have departed think, "The residents themselves will remove it," once they have sat down, it remains an impediment for the residents alone.
However, according to the *Mahāpaccarī*, the intention is that it is an impediment for those who have sat down, whether they say, "This is ours," or not.

According to the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that this is indeed a *pācittiya* offense. But in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is held that there must be a *pācittiya* offense regarding the act of having [the bedding] spread out.
Because it was prescribed as not being a formal command (*anāṇatti*), a *dukkaṭa* offense was stated. "Reciter" (*ussāraka*) means one who recites aloud.
For he is called a "reciter" because he causes the text of the scriptures to be repeated and set in motion from top to bottom.

With the intention that—since it was prescribed separately as "this for the reciter, this for the Dharma-preacher"—there must be a *pācittiya* even though it was prescribed as not being a formal command—it says: "In that..."
It is said: "When he has arrived and is seated, there is an obstruction for him. However, some say:
"Even though it was prescribed without a formal injunction, since the preacher is not to be made to rise, there must be an offense of expiation (pācittiya);
but since the newcomer is to be made to rise by those who arrive later and are senior, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated."
88. A "foot-wiping cloth" (pādapuñchanī) is something made with ropes or rags for the purpose of wiping the feet. A "wooden bench" (phalakapīṭha) is a bench made of wooden planks;
or alternatively, it refers to both the planks themselves and the wooden bench.
Furthermore, a "wooden bench" should be understood as being made specifically of wooden planks. A "footstone" (pādakaṭhalikā) is a support for placing unwashed feet. [In] the open air...
“Having boiled the dye … it should be put away”: here, when there is no more dye remaining and the work of dyeing is finished, it should be put away.
They say that because it is stated, “a bhikkhu, a sāmaṇera, or an ārāmika who is conscientious,” it is not permissible to go without asking permission from one who is unconscientious.
“While drying it … he goes”: here, although [one might think], “I must go only this far,” … [the text continues].
"There is no fixed limit; nevertheless, one should not go too far beyond the range of a thrown clod," they say.
Thus ends the section on how to behave regarding communal lodgings such as beds and chairs, within the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
The Seventeenth Chapter, titled "An Ornament of Discourse on Legal Decisions. 18.
Discourse on the Decision Regarding Timely Matters.

89. Having thus explained the decision regarding what should be done with the lodgings belonging to the Saṅgha, he now says, “There are also four times,” etc., in order to explain the decision regarding the four times.
In this context, *kāra* means making (*karaṇa*), that is, an action (*kiriyā*). *Kāla* is simply *kāra*, with the substitution of the letter *l* for the letter *r*, as in the word “mahāsāla.

Furthermore, in this case, “time” (*kāla*) refers to present and other actions. For it has been said: “... [the verse] ... (Note: The source text appears to be truncated here; the provided excerpt ends mid-sentence.)
“An undertaking is uncompleted; the present is well completed;
the arising of the past and future is an action that has not yet reached its objective.
Herein, the divisions of time—termed "action"—consist of such periods as "before the meal," "one day and night," "seven days," and "the limit of one's life."
A specific time is intended. They are called "time-bound" (*kālika*) because they are to be consumed at various specific times.
The word *pi* has the sense of conjunction; by it, one conjoins "the four kinds of allowable things. "Four" is a numerical designation;
by this, it shows that there are exactly four things called "time-bound," neither three nor five. This refers to the heading of the matrix (*mātikā*).
The Explanation of the Meaning (*Atthavivaraṇa*). Therein, regarding the summary (*uddesa*):

as it was stated in the matrix (*mātikā*) that “there are also four [kinds of] timely [medicines],” the construction here is that these four timely [medicines] are to be understood in this matrix phrase. To the question “Which are they?”, he says:

“that which is for as long as life lasts,” and so forth. The meaning is that these substances—“that which is for as long as life lasts” … pe … “that which is for as long as one lives”—are called the four timely [medicines].
Now, showing their basis, their specific characteristics, and the cause for obtaining their names, he says: "In that regard, before the meal," and so forth.

Therein, among those four types of [medicines] taken at the proper time (*yāvakālika*), whatever is edible or consumable is [taken] at the proper time; the eight kinds of drink are [taken] during the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*);
the five kinds of medicine, such as ghee, are [taken] for seven days (*sattāhakālika*); and all that is received is [taken] for as long as life lasts (*yāvajīvika*).

The connection is: "it is thus called. To avoid the fault of over-extension regarding the phrase "whatever kind of solid or soft food," he provides the qualification beginning with "before the meal" (*purebhatta*).
The meaning is that only what is to be consumed after being received before the meal is "temporary" (*yāvakālika*);
it does not refer to other kinds of solid or soft food. The phrase "as long as... [pe] ...to be consumed" is the reason for obtaining that name.
By this, he shows the meaning of the term *yāvakālika* as "that which lasts as long as time (*yāva kālo assa*).
