Regarding the phrase "eight kinds of drinks," he says "together with the conforming drinks" (*saddhiṃ anulomapānehi*) in order to exclude what is not included therein. By the phrase "as long as... [pe] ...that is its duration" (*yāva...pe... tabbatoti*), he shows the etymological derivation of the name;
by this, he shows the meaning of the term *yāmakālika* as "that whose time is the watch of the night (*yāmo kālo assa*). "To be stored for seven days" (*sattāhaṃ nidhetabbaṭo*).
The phrase "the cause for obtaining the name" indicates the meaning of the term *sattāhakālika* (seven-day medicine), namely that its duration is seven days.

Regarding the statement "all that has been accepted," he says "excepting water" in order to avoid over-extension (*atibyāpita*). The phrase "as long as... [pe] ...should be used" indicates the cause for obtaining the name;
by this, he shows the meaning of the term *yāvajīvika* (lifetime medicine), namely that its duration lasts for as long as one lives.

Here it is asked: "Since there is the statement, 'Whatever monk should take food into his mouth that has not been given, except for water and tooth-wood, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya),' surely water should not be received by formal acceptance (paṭiggahaṇa).
Then why is it said, 'With the exception of water, everything else must be accepted'? True; pure water should not be received by formal acceptance.
However, that which contains mud and so forth must be formally accepted; therefore, because it is included within those things already accepted, it is stated as "except for water.
Even so, one might ask: is not the inclusion of water that is to be accepted already established by the phrase "all [food] is accepted"?
True; nevertheless, it is stated as "all is accepted" in its general sense as water.
When this much has been said, it might be understood that water is also called "for life" because some water is to be accepted;
however, pure water is not "for life" because it is not to be accepted. Therefore, this is what is meant:
even though some water is to be accepted, pure water is not to be accepted.
Setting aside that water, everything else that has been accepted is called "for as long as life lasts" (*yāvajīvika*).
90. The radish roots and so forth are to be understood from the instruction itself; even if they were stated by way of synonyms, they could not be discerned.
For if they were stated by means of another synonym, there would be only confusion for those who do not know those respective names.
Therefore, we shall say nothing further on that point. Regarding the phrase "in the case of solid food, the purpose of solid food":

they neither fulfill nor accomplish the function of solid food—the purpose or utility consisting in the removal of hunger—which exists in solid foods such as cakes and the like, and which ought to be performed by solid foods.
Whether in one place it accomplishes the function of nourishment or does not accomplish it, in another...
It might be possible that even if it does not fulfill its function of removing hunger and providing nourishment due to differences such as the soil or climate of the region where it grows;

therefore, he said, "In various countries," and so forth. Some, however, say that this was stated to show that even if it fulfills its function of providing nourishment in one country, it is still not permitted at the wrong time in other countries as well. "By way of ordinary food" means:
It is not joined with other temporary [nutriments], but functions as nutriment by its own nature alone.
"There is only confusion" means that because there is the possibility of names having multiple meanings and being uncommonly established, there might indeed be confusion.

For this very reason, we too have not taken care to show alternative synonyms for the "root-roots" and so forth here, since they are to be understood from the traditional instruction (*upadesa*) itself.
They go to the root-stock of the *vaṭa* tree.
"The rhizome" (*muḷāla*) refers specifically to the thick, young root.
"Of trees, creepers, and so forth" is stated by summarizing what was already mentioned above.
"Found on the earth" is said with reference to the trunk of the *sāla-kalyāṇika* tree.
"All allowable" means they are entirely allowable by way of their roots, bark, leaves, and so forth; the connection is that it is impossible to show a limit even for those [trees] by name.
It is stated as "unripe" in order to show that the fruits of the *acchi* and other such trees are lifetime-medicine only when they are unripe.
Regarding the phrase "the bones of the *harītakī* and so forth," the teachers (ācariyā) maintain that the shells situated covering the marrow (*miñja*) are "for as long as life lasts" (*yāvajīvika*).
Some, however, say that even the marrow itself is "for as long as life lasts. But in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated:

"Regarding the 'bones of the *harītakī* and so forth,' some here say that 'the marrow is [only] for the time being' (*yāvakālika*); that is not correct, because it was not so stated in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*)."
*Hiṅgūti* is the resin that has flowed from the *hiṅgu* tree. *Hiṅgujatu* and the others are likewise products of the *hiṅgu* tree.
Among these, *hiṅgujatu* is the resin made by boiling the stalks and leaves of the *hiṅgu* tree. *Hiṅgusipāṭikaṃ* is the resin made by boiling the leaves of the *hiṅgu* tree;
some also say it is made by mixing [the leaves] with something else. *Takam* is [the resin] from the tip of the [stalk].

“Nikkhanta-sileso”: a preparation made from the outer husk of the *taka* fruit. “Takapatti”: a preparation made from the inner pulp of the *taka* fruit. “Takapaṇṇī”: a preparation made by roasting the leaves of the *palāsa* tree.
Some also say it refers to a preparation made from the stalk of the *daṇḍa* plant. 91.

Regarding the phrase “but among those [medicines] that last for a watch of the night,” although in the Canon only those things that last until the end of the day are mentioned by the terms “hard food” (*khādanīya*) and “soft food” (*bhojanīya*), [it is understood here to include these as well].
Although it is included [among the medicines], it is not *yāmakālika* (suitable for use during the watch of the night);

nevertheless, because it is stated here that "there is no offense if one stores a *yāmakālika* medicine during the watch and consumes it," and because it is stated elsewhere—"Monks, by means of a *yāmakālika* medicine, a *sattāhakālika*...

up to a *yāvajīvika* medicine, if received on that same day, it is allowable during the watch, but when the watch has passed, it is not allowable"—the term "yāmakālika" is used here by virtue of its functional significance.

And it should be understood that the commentators (aṭṭhakathācariya), who knew the Blessed One’s intention, stated that [the offense] is indeed a *pācittiya* for storing what is permitted only during the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*).
Regarding the phrase "except for the juice of grain and fruit," they say here: "Even water used for washing rice is indeed the juice of grain and fruit."
92. Regarding the "five medicines for seven days": whether they perform the function of medicine or not, these five are designated by that conventional term.

Having shown what is well-known in the world through the phrase "cow's ghee" and so forth, he indicates by the phrase "the ghee of those whose meat is allowable" that the ghee of other animals as well—such as the red deer—is included. For wherever there is milk, there is necessarily ghee as well.
Whether that [ghee] is easy or difficult to obtain was stated for the purpose of avoiding confusion. The same applies to butter.
Furthermore, the statement "the meat of which is allowable" is intended to show the substance from which a *nissaggiya* offense arises;
it is not intended to show that for those for whom meat is not allowable, ghee and so forth are also not allowable. For even human milk and the like are not allowable.
93. Regarding the statement, "It is permissible to consume [food] as long as the time has not elapsed," here "time" refers to the mealtime for monks;
and that, at the very latest limit, is the established midday. For even the established midday is included within the category of "time";
however, from that point onward, it is no longer possible to chew or consume food, except in cases of sudden emergency.
It may be possible to drink it, yet one who is scrupulous should not do so.
Furthermore, a time-marker pillar should be set up for the purpose of knowing the time limit, or the meal-duty should be performed at another time.

Regarding "receiving," this was said with reference to the act of taking [the food] itself; for although it has already been received, since storing it is not permitted, the duty of receiving must be performed again.
It does not exist; for that very reason, it is said: "in the receiving by one who takes [the food] with the desire to swallow it.
However, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated simply as: "in the taking by one who takes [it] thinking, 'I shall swallow it.
"Yaṃ" means which bowl. "Sandissati" means it appears on top of the gruel. Even though there is an absence of oiliness (*nisnehabhāva*) in a bowl that has the color of oil...

When one rubs with a finger, a line appears by way of color alone; therefore, it is said that "this is not subject to formal designation" (*abbhohārikā*) in order to show that there is no offense in that case.
For what has been personally accepted and not yet relinquished is not permitted on the second day;
here, the acceptance is relinquished either by giving it away without regard for it, or by giving it to one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) without regard for it.
The phrase "it is indeed relinquished" (*pariccattameva*)—by means of this term "not relinquished" (*apariccatta*)—expresses that the act of receiving has not been abandoned in either way.

Therefore, it should be understood that even if something has not been given by another after being relinquished, if there is a relinquishment of the act of receiving through an indifferent dismissal [of the object], that is also permissible on the second day. If this is so, [regarding] the bowl...
In passages such as “he becomes difficult to clean,” why is an offense mentioned? Regarding this, it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries:

“If one has not relinquished the bowl’s acceptance [of ownership], and even after making it empty—whether by oneself or by another—has not properly washed it, then even if something remains stuck in the finished bowl, it is still considered that the acceptance has not been relinquished;
therefore, an offense occurs therein. However, some say: “They relinquish it to the novices.”

"Based on this section, because it is stated that 'it must not be relinquished at all,' it follows that for one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna), only what has been relinquished is permissible, while what has not been relinquished is not permissible;

therefore, they say that even if the relinquishment occurs through acceptance with a sense of detachment (nirālaya-bhāva), what has not been relinquished by one who is not fully ordained is not permissible. This does not appear to be correct.

For at the very moment that the act of receiving is relinquished, at that same moment one does not create storage (*sannidhi*), because what has been relinquished is equivalent to what has not been received.
Furthermore, it is stated that an offense due to storage occurs only when something has been received and then set aside. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is said:
"‘Only as long as it has not been relinquished’ means [it remains] not given by one who is not fully ordained, due to a lack of indifference."
And he speaks with reference only to the object, such as that which is to be used for a limited time (*yāvakālika*), and not to the acceptance [of the food] that has gone there.
For it is not possible to relinquish the acceptance that has gone there without first relinquishing the object;

nor is there any such statement [in the Vinaya]. If there were, it would have been: “If the bowl is not well-washed... [and so on] ...for one who eats, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).”
[This] would contradict the statement. For one who strives to remove the food by washing it, there can be no expectation regarding its acceptance.
That expectation which would give rise to a *pācittiya* offense for one eating on the following day exists indeed with respect to the food contained in that bowl;
thus, here "lack of expectation regarding food" is not applicable. Therefore, regarding food...
It has been stated that "accepting [food] without having relinquished it on the following day gives rise to a *pācittiya* offense. Now,
if it is thought that "to the same extent that lack of regard for the food (*āmisa*) is not found here,

to that same extent lack of regard for the acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*) is also not found," then it follows that wherever there is regard for the food, there also cannot be an absence of regard for the acceptance.
And in this way, giving without expectation regarding acceptance would not need to be mentioned separately;

furthermore, even in the Aṭṭhakathā, this too might be intended as a cause for the relinquishing of acceptance. Having made this point more clearly, it should be stated separately, just as the relinquishing of the formal determination occurs through renunciation (*paccuddhāra*) even while there is still expectation for a robe. And in this method...
It has already been stated that there can be no "fixing" (avaṭṭanā) regarding alms-bowls struck by a knot; therefore, what was said in the *Sāratthadīpanī*— namely,
“If something has been relinquished by another and, even though not given,
has been abandoned through a disposal made without regard for receiving it, that is permissible on the second day,” and so forth— that should not be accepted as authoritative.
In the Pāḷi, it is stated: “If one accepts seven-day medicines or lifetime medicines for the purpose of food, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Since wrong-doing is thus declared even when consuming seven-day or lifetime medicines before the midday meal for the purpose of food, there must likewise be a separate offense of wrong-doing for consuming a watch-of-the-night medicine;
therefore, he says: “for one who consumes it for the purpose of food...”
“Together with a *dukkaṭa*, there is a *pācittiya*. Regarding “natural foodstuffs”: this refers to permissible foodstuffs such as cooked rice and so forth. “Two” means:
for one who eats with the mouth what was received before midday and is to be used within the watch of the night, there is one *pācittiya* due to the condition of storage (*sannidhi*);

and for eating what is mixed with what is to be used until the end of the day, using a vessel for what is to be used until the end of the day, there is one *pācittiya* due to the condition of not having had it formally offered (*anatiritta*). Thus, there are two *pācittiya* offenses.

"In the two alternatives" means in the two sides of the worldly (sāmisa) and the unworldly (nirāmisa). "A grave offense (thullaccaya) and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) increase" means that regarding human flesh there is a grave offense, while for the remaining types of unfit meat, an offense of wrong-doing increases.
"First of all, on account of receiving [the meat], there is an offense of wrong-doing"—here, because it is present, even before the meal there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing.

However, when there is a requisite condition, there is no offense at all for one who takes and consumes even seven-day medicine or lifetime medicine that is already present, provided it is for the purpose of medicine. 94.
"Set aside after having been received" means that which was not formally received [by a monk], but was taken by oneself and set aside. (From the *Vimativinodanī*)
“Taken up” means “taken by oneself for the purpose of consumption,” as it is said. “He makes it himself” means he makes it after having cooked it.
“Before the meal” means that only what was received before the meal on that very day is permitted, because it has been accepted with its physical basis intact.
“Made by oneself” refers to butter made by cooking [milk]. “Only without meat” is said with reference to what was received before the meal on that very day.
95. To the question, "Why is it not considered 'self-cooked' (sāmaṃpāka) for one who eats only what has been prepared by oneself and is entirely free from meat?
he replied, "For one who is heating butter," and so forth. The phrase "by means of those received after the meal" refers to milk and curds. The construction is:
"that which is prepared by those who have received [the milk and curds] should be applied as an ointment and so on. The phrase "for both of them" refers to the milk and curds received after the meal.
And [this applies] to those things prepared from what was received before the meal. "This is the method" means that it does not constitute an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).

"In the case of unallowable meat-ghee" refers to the ghee of elephants and so forth. "Having stated a semblance of a reason" means having stated a semblance of a reason such as, "because it is of the same nature as ghee.
"It should be understood according to the principle of ghee" means that even if it is not meat, it is permissible for seven days. "In this case" refers to fresh butter (*navanīta*).
Regarding the statement "it is permissible if washed": if it is unwashed, it is considered "received with its base" (*savatthuka-paṭiggahita*);
therefore, the intention of the elders is that it is permissible to receive what has been washed and store it for seven days.

However, according to the Venerable Mahāsīva, because the substance [of the milk] has been separated, it is considered "received with its base" merely by being mixed with curds, sugar lumps, and so forth.

The intended meaning is that it does not constitute [the offense of] "having received"; therefore, having accepted only what has been extracted from the curd, and having washed it or cooked it so as to make it entirely non-fatty, they ate it.
It does not mean, however, that they ate it at an improper time together with lumps of curd and the like.
Hence he said: "Therefore, for one consuming fresh butter... [etc. ...there is no such thing as 'acceptance with a base'. In this regard:
The meaning is that even after accepting it unwashed, one who wishes to consume that butter should do so after removing the curd and other such substances.
However, some, not understanding the intended meaning of the statement,

"They ate only what had just been extracted from the buttermilk," claim that "it is permissible to consume at an improper time even unwashed butter that has just been extracted from buttermilk, provided it is accompanied by curd balls and the like."
What they say should not be accepted. For it cannot be argued that it is permissible to consume butter whose flavor has been mixed with the bait of curd-balls and the like.
"By one consuming butter" means by one consuming butter that was received without having washed [the hands].
"Curd itself" is *dadhigata*, just as there are expressions such as "feces-soiled" (*gūthagata*) or "urine-soiled" (*muttagata*). "It will go to destruction" means...
It should be understood that even prepared ghee and the like, after milk has been added to them by verbal instruction, are permissible outside of the proper time.
"It will go to destruction" means it becomes non-material; therefore, the meaning is that it is allowed even at the improper time.

"To this extent" means by a mere amount clinging to the butter, which has not yet acquired a separate designation such as curd and so forth, [but is still] a small quantity of curd and the like; by this, [it is distinguished] from curd and the like that have been received separately.
This shows that it goes together with what is cooked, being indeed accepted along with its base.
"In that too" means even when it has become non-material (nirāmisa). However, for those who are scrupulous, this is the intention:

first, regarding the acceptance, because its flavor is not mixed with curds and so forth, it is called "accepted along with its base," like a lump of sugar and the like taken together with rice. But that [rice], by the one cooking it—

It should be cooked only after being washed. Otherwise, at the moment of cooking, because its flavor becomes mixed with the curd-rice balls (*guḷikā*) and other ingredients that are being cooked, it becomes "self-cooked" (*sāmaṃpakka*);
even when those [ingredients] are exhausted, it remains "self-cooked. Therefore, it should be cooked while entirely free from meat.
For this very reason, the cause is stated as: "because it has been cooked together with meat."

And here is the investigation: in the absence of being accepted with a physical basis (*savatthuka*), one might suspect either the fault of "cooking by oneself" (*sayaṃpākadosa*) or the state of being "only for the time being" (*yāvakālika*) regarding food cooked by a monk together with raw provisions.

In this regard, the fault of cooking by oneself cannot possibly apply here, because it is "to be kept for seven days" (*sattāhakālika*). For whatever among those items, such as curd and so forth, constitutes raw provision (*āmisa*), that has already been exhausted.

If it is suspected that [the food] might be as if cooked with its own basis (savatthuka-pakka)—as if it were cooked together with the lumps of curd and so forth received [by the monk]—then the reason should be stated as "because it was received together with material food" (*āmisa*), and not "because it is cooked.
In that case, the opinion of the Upaḍḍhattheras alone would have to be accepted. And in that context, even that which has been cooked by novices and others [is considered cooked].

It might be argued that [the milk] should be considered as "only for the time being" (yāvakālika) once it has been boiled after being accepted, like the ghee and so forth prepared by those who are not fully ordained (anupasampanna).

However, this is not tenable, because it would follow that one could not consume butter and other such items obtained through alms-round (bhikkhācāra) due to the possibility of their being mixed with non-nutriment (āmisa) such as buttermilk;
for there is no fixed rule that householders must pour [their offerings] into the bowl only after washing or cleaning it.
And this is contradicted by the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “Just as rice grains and such that have fallen there do not cook, so...
[omitted] ...he cooks it again and gives it; it is permissible for seven days in the same manner as before.
Therefore, here no cause whatsoever for the arising of scruples is seen for those who are conscientious. And just as it is here, so too [regarding] “the modest one” (*lajjī*)...
Nor is there any indication for the statement: “The novice, having caused it to melt in the fire so that the rice-grains and such do not cook therein, gives it [to the monk]”;
for if this were said for the purpose of avoiding contact with *yāvakālika* (food to be consumed during the day), then one would have to act accordingly oneself.
Furthermore, there would be a suspicion of contact with solid food (*āmisa*) regarding the ghee and other items given by householders.
It would not disappear. For householders do not cook again after having dissolved [the mixture], strained it, and removed the husks, broken rice, and so forth.

Moreover, if one were to add milk and such things along with the medicinal ingredients, then just as the milk and so forth would perish, the cooked medicinal oil and other substances prepared by others would likewise become *yāvakālika* (only for the duration of the day), and that too would not be appropriate.
Because it is stated that one may "cook it again and give it" for the purpose of making curd and so forth, therefore—
according to the opinion of the Elder Mahāsīva— one should not feel remorse; even butter that has not been washed may be cooked on that very day or on subsequent days,
and it is also permissible to cook ghee and the like mixed with rice and other ingredients by melting it oneself over a fire for the purpose of making buttermilk and so forth.

In this regard, it should be concluded that even when something exists, at the moment it is being cooked, because it has become of mixed flavor, it is no longer subject to the designation of "yāvakālika" (food to be consumed within the same day);
thus, even for those things received with a physical basis (*savatthuka*) or received beforehand (*purepaṭiggahita*), they are no longer subject to that designation.
For this very reason, it is said: "To this extent, it is not what is called 'received with a physical basis'. [This applies] to that which was received separately.
However, when a monk or others mix milk and other such foodstuffs with butter and so forth to prepare medicinal oils and the like, it is indeed reckoned as having been accepted along with its base;
for there is no absence of designation [as "accepted"] regarding the non-time-allowed (yāvakālika) substance that has entered therein.
But as for the medicinal oil and the like prepared by adding unaccepted milk and so forth to medicines already previously accepted—
Even when cooked by those who are not fully ordained (anupasampanna), it is neither "cooked" nor "received with a physical basis," nor is there "storage.

In that case, even if mixed with milk and so forth that were placed [into the vessel] at that moment, because the flavors have merged at that very instant and because it was received previously, it falls under the offense [of storage].

However, if it is by those who have not yet received [the food], or if the flavor of the "raw meat" (āmisarasa) is still discernible in other cooked oils and such, it should be understood as being "only for the time being" (yāvakālika).
This method of exposition appears in the *Vimativinodanī*. However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it states only this much:

“By the phrase ‘they are prone to remorse’ (*kukkuccāyantīti kukkuccakā*), he also demonstrates that remorse exists even within himself regarding that matter. For this very reason, it is said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*:
‘It is permissible to cook clarified butter or fresh butter that has been extracted.’”

"Having taken up" means having taken it oneself. "Having received those" means having received that milk and curd. "Taken" means having cooked it again for the purpose of removing the husks of the rice and so forth;
this is the meaning. "And with medicines kept after being received" refers to medicines kept for more than seven days or medicines kept for life;
by this, even ghee and other such items combined with those [medicines] are considered "received for more than seven days."
He shows that [the food] does not exist [in the usual sense]. "At the time of the hail" means at the time of the rainy season; the meaning is "at a time when there is no heat.
By the method already stated, just as rice and so forth do not cook [naturally], he gives it only after having it prepared by one who possesses a sense of shame (*lajjī*);

thus, the mention of "the modest novice" (*lajjisāmaṇera*) is made. Furthermore, it is not permitted for one who lacks a sense of shame to have anything whatsoever prepared for consumption; therefore, he speaks in this way.
96. "Having received oil that has been prepared" means oil that has been prepared by oneself without having performed the roasting and so forth.
For this very reason, it is said: "Even that which contains meat is permissible. "Because it has been extracted" means because it has been separated from the time-limited (yāvakālika) category;

by this, he shows both the absence of the status of being time-limited due to the lack of cardamom (elā), and the attainment of the status of being time-limited through the monk’s acceptance of it as having a physical basis (savatthuka). "Both kinds" refers to that which was prepared by oneself and that which was prepared by others.
"Until sunrise": if oil prepared on the seventh day remains until sunrise, it is an offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).

Regarding "animal fat" (*acchavasa*): since animal fat is permitted for an object that constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), the fat of those animals whose flesh is likewise unallowable is what is permitted;
it is not the fat of humans, who are the subject of an offense of grave transgression (*thullaccaya*). Thus he said, "excluding..."
"Human food. "Mixed" means strained. "Three offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" is said with reference to the three dukkaṭas incurred for every swallow.

Although no offense is mentioned in the Canon or the Commentary regarding the preliminary acts—such as receiving, cooking, or straining [food] at an improper time—for the purpose of consumption, nevertheless, in this case, there is indeed an offense.

It must be understood as such because it involves doing what has been prohibited, just like accepting food at an improper time (vikāla) or during the watch of the night (yāmakālika) for the sake of nutriment.

They say: "For one who consumes what was accepted at the proper time (kāla), even if it has been cooked or mixed by one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna), there are indeed two offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."

Because it is not permissible for a monk to either accept or cook oil together with the dregs of cooked medicinal oil—which, having had milk and other ingredients added, have become "flesh-bound" (āmisagatika)—therefore it is said: "He is scrupulous regarding the dregs of cooked oil.
Those who ask, "If it is not permissible because it has been cooked together with fat (vasā), why is this [other case] permissible? [should be answered as follows:]...
“Venerable sir... [it] is permissible,” they said. Out of excessive scrupulousness, the Elder said, “Friends, even this is not permissible.
However, having observed that fat had been permitted specifically for the purpose of curing disease, he later accepted it, saying, “Very well.
97. Regarding the phrase “by honey-bees (*madhukarī*)," this is a qualification of only two types of small bees.
Some say this. Others, however, say: "Among the *daṇḍaka* plants there are those called *madhukārikā*, which are honey-bees;
together with them, there are three species of honey-bees. The *bhamara-makkhikā* (bumblebee) is the large *paṭala-kārikā*.
"Resembling resin" means it has become thick due to being dried or cooked. "The other" refers to thin honey. "Honey-comb" means that which is devoid of sweetness.

It is merely the honeycomb. They say: "If they receive and store a comb together with the honey, because the comb serves as the container, there is an offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) upon the lapse of seven days due to the honey.
This is consistent with the statement: "But that which is smeared with honey belongs to the same category as the honey itself."
98. Since it is stated without qualification in the *Pāḷi* that "molasses (*phāṇita*) is produced from sugarcane," and since the *Aṭṭhakathā* states, "Taking sugarcane juice as the basis...

[omission] ...a sugarcane product that has not yet reached the stage of solidification should be understood as 'molasses,'" it should be understood that even pure sugarcane juice is permissible for seven days. However, some say: "In the case of honey, there are four periods..."
"Should be applied according to what is possible, and also in the case of sugarcane," he said. "Sugarcane with its stalks and joints is *yāvakālika* (to be consumed within the same day);
pure sugarcane juice mixed with water is *yāmakālika* (to be consumed within a watch of the night); unmixed [juice] is *sattāhakālika* (to be consumed within seven days);

pure honey-wax is *yāvajīvika* (to be kept for life). Likewise, sugarcane juice with its sediment is *yāvakālika*; juice from which the sediment has been removed and which is mixed with water is *yāmakālika*."
Having stated, "That which is unmixed is for seven days; pure *kasaṭa* is for life," much further elaboration was provided.
In that regard, the statement, "Honey or sugarcane juice mixed with water is *sakasaṭa* (with sediment) and is for the time of the day (*yāvakālika*);

[the same] when free from sediment and mixed with water is for the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*)," is found neither in the Canon (*pāḷi*) nor in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). Regarding "that which is for the time of the day":
"Water, though lighter, brings the grape-juice—which is equal in weight but heavier—into contact with itself and renders it light, making it permissible for a watch of the night;

whereas water, though lighter, brings the seven-day permissible substance—which is equal in weight but heavier—into contact with itself and renders it heavy, making it permissible for a watch of the night.
Regarding this, that very reason must be asked. In all instances, [the rule applies] by means of water-mixed [substances], as stated in both the Canon and the Commentary.
Even for that which is very heavy, only the attainment of lightness is demonstrated. For even in the Pāḷi, by saying, “Monks,

I allow sugar for the sick, and sugar-water for the healthy,” it is authorized that although raw sugar is unfit for consumption by the healthy, when mixed with water, it is permissible even for the healthy.

Furthermore, having shown the commentary’s statement: “If it is sugarcane, it is ‘to be taken at the proper time’ (yāvakālika); if it is sugarcane juice, it is ‘to be taken during the watch of the night’ (yāmakālika); if it is molasses, it is ‘to be taken for seven days’ (sattāhakālika);

if it is the bark, it is ‘to be taken for as long as life lasts’ (yāvajīvika),” even that which was stated by someone else—namely, “sugarcane juice mixed with water is ‘to be taken during the watch of the night’”—is [contradicted] by such a commentary statement in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the Vinaya commentary.
It should not be understood as having substantial value because of its lack of essence;
for that very reason, some teachers say, "Sugarcane juice, whether mixed with water or unmixed, is only for seven days.

And in the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka*, regarding the passage "I allow you, monks, sugarcane juice," it is stated without distinction in all three commentaries (*gaṇṭhipada*) that "sugarcane juice is for seven days."

Regarding the statement, "Only that which is self-made and non-material is permissible," it should be understood here that even if [the juice] was received unstrained, it must be strained at the time of preparation and the dregs removed before it can be considered "self-made. This is the reading in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated that by the phrase "starting from sugarcane juice," even juice that is free of dregs is subject to the seven-day limit.
It is shown [to be] "produced from sugarcane" because it is stated in the Pāḷi in general terms. However, as for what is stated in the Suttanta-aṭṭhakathā—"If it is sugarcane, it is *yāvakālika*;
if it is sugarcane juice, it is *yāmakālika*; if it is molasses, it is *sattāhakālika*;
if it is the skin, it is *yāvajīvika*," that was said with reference to its status as *yāmakālika* due to being mixed with the juice of mango fruit and so forth.

It should be accepted; however, because it is not a statement of the Vinaya, that [other source] is not authoritative. For this very reason, it was said: "with unsqueezed sugarcane juice received before the meal," and so forth.

Only that which is non-material (nirāmisa) is permitted there, because what is for life-long use (yāvakālika) once it has entered [the mixture] is no longer subject to the designation [of its original status].
Thus it is said that when sugar is made, even the dregs present therein, by virtue of the cooking and their state of dryness, partake of the status of being for life-long use.
Because it is a "time-limited" (yāvakālika) food, even if cooked by oneself before midday, it may not be consumed.
Regarding the phrase "because it was accepted with its physical basis," this was said with reference to the thick scum remaining after the sugarcane juice has become broken down into fine particles;
and by that, it is shown that "what is made by those who are not fully ordained is permissible for seven days, provided it has not been strained and has not been formally accepted."
“Jhāma-iccuphāṇita” (boiled sugarcane juice) is that made by heating sugarcane over a fire.

“Koṭṭita-iccuphāṇita” (crushed sugarcane juice) is that which has been cut into small pieces, crushed, pressed, and cooked. Although the dregs (kasaṭa) remain therein, at the time of cooking they lose their status as “yāvakālika” (to be consumed within the same day);
thus he said, “that is appropriate. “Made with cold water” means that madhuka flowers have been ground with cold water.
[It is] made by straining and cooking. Some say, "It is made without straining," but no reason for that is seen there.
Regarding the statement, "Honey-syrup (*madhukaphāṇita*) made by adding milk is *yāvakālika* (to be consumed within the same day)":

if one asks why clarified butter (*pakkatela*) cooked by adding milk is permitted outside the proper time (*vikāla*), [the answer is: the milk added to the clarified butter becomes simply clarified butter; it is not [ordinary] milk.
The reason for this is that once it has been placed [in the milk], it takes on the state of milk.
If that is so, why is it permissible to make candied sugar by adding milk? To this he says, “But as for candied sugar,” and so forth.
In that context, *khīrajallikā* means the froth of milk.

99. The passage beginning with “But the madhuka flower,” etc., is commenced to show that even that which exists as a substance for the time-being (yāvakālika) is a basis for intoxicants (meraya-bīja-vatthu), by way of its transformation.

In order to resolve the objection—“Why should these things, while performing the function of food, be consumed in such a manner?”—the author shows the specific exceptions regarding medicine (bhesajja-uddissa).
In connection with that, he presents all the specific exceptions together in the passage beginning with “For it is sevenfold,” etc.
This is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*. However, it is not stated in the *Vinayasaṅgahappakaraṇa*, which says:
"Because it is stated that 'from after the meal onwards, provided there is a requisite,' medicines received [as medicine] may be consumed even before the meal starting from the second day;
for they were received for the purpose of medicine, not for the purpose of food."
They say: "On the doors, windows, and door-panels" means on the panels of the large doors and the windows.
Regarding the statement, "Those [substances] placed in the glue relinquish their own nature;
they should be smeared," the meaning is that they should be smeared for the purpose of warding off wood-boring insects and the like. "He resolves" means: "Now this is my food to be swallowed."
The meaning is that one arouses the thought: "It will not be [consumed]; it will be for the purpose of external use. For this very reason, he said:
"Ghee, oil, fat, whether as an ointment or an unguent on the head," and so forth.

The intention is that by thus having no regard for personal enjoyment, one relinquishes the acceptance [of the gift]. In the same way, regarding other things that are to be used at a specific time (*kālika*), there is the desire not to consume them.
Even when there is a restriction for the sake of external enjoyment with a pure mind, the relinquishing of acceptance occurs;
this too should be understood as one separate instance of the relinquishing of acceptance.
Regarding the phrase "he should be told by another bhikkhu," because it was given with a pure mind, he may himself also cause [it] to be brought and consume it.

It is indeed permissible. "There is no offense for either" means that just as when something belonging to another is accepted by one person, it does not become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) even after seven days have passed—because it remains the property of another—so too, because this [gift] has not been divided and is common to both, there is no forfeiture due to the absence of a formal separation;
such is the intended meaning. However, it is not permissible to consume it.

Because it has been received by a bhikkhu, it is not permissible for any bhikkhu to consume it after seven days have passed, since the consumption of ghee and other such items that have been received is restricted to exactly seven days.
For it is said: "Having received them, they may be consumed from storage for a maximum of seven days."
By the statement, “Friend, it is permissible to use this oil for only seven days,” he shows that by the very person who received it, it was relinquished to another within those same seven days.
Regarding the question, “Whose offense is there?”—first, no offense was stated because it was common to both; however, now [an offense arises] because one has relinquished it to the other.
Since there is no commonality between the two [cases], it stands as if they were distinct;
therefore, thinking that "in this case, upon the lapse of seven days for what has been accepted, there must be an offense for one [of the two]," he asks:
"Is the offense for the recipient on account of the acceptance, or rather for the one to whom the property belongs? And because of the very state of having been relinquished (*nissaṭṭha*), here...
Without stating the reason as "because its state is undivided," it is said: "because it has been relinquished by him who accepted it.

And this, because of its being relinquished, having abandoned common ownership between both, even though it remains the property of one person, becomes the property of another different from the one who accepted it;
therefore, just as in the case of accepting the property of another, there is for the recipient the condition of acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇapaccaya*).

This was stated for the purpose of showing that there is no offense; however, it was not stated for the purpose of showing that an offense occurs upon the passing of seven days even when [the goods] have not been distributed, provided they have not been relinquished—since the absence of an offense is already established by the very fact that they have not been relinquished and have not been distributed, based on the statement:
"Because it has been relinquished by him who received it. But if the other person [to whom it was given] is the very one by whom it was received...

Within seven days, one may even give away one's own share; however, after the lapse of seven days, there may be an offense for the one by whom it was received, because it has come to be the property of that very person.

By the phrase "because the other did not receive it," he indicates that even though it is his property, since it was not received by him—just as in the case of another's property received by someone else—there is no offense for him. This...
However, not understanding the intended meaning, the commentators on the *Gaṇṭhipada* and others have elaborated [on this] in a manner different from this;
that should not be accepted as the core essence. This is the statement from the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
But in the *Vimativinodanī*, the reading "if for two... and so forth, ending with "...it is not permissible," has been omitted; however, here it is as follows:
The reading should be understood as follows: if the property belonging to two people has been accepted by one and not yet divided, there is no offense for either of them upon the lapse of seven days;
however, it is not permitted to consume it. Otherwise, even the application of the word [in that way] would not be included [in the tradition];
for this very reading is also shown in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, according to the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
It was stated: “There is no offense for either of the two. This was stated because [the rule] was not specifically distinguished.
“But it is not permitted to consume it,” this was stated because of the statement: “It may be consumed after being stored for at most seven days.
“Because it was relinquished by the one who received it”—by this, referring even to the giving to one who is fully ordained, it is said that “he relinquishes it.”

[The text] shows this. Even though the acceptance of an article given without expectation by one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*) has not ceased, the state of being one's own property (*sakasantakatā*) has indeed ceased;
therefore, it does not become an offense requiring relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).

It becomes an offense requiring relinquishment only through these two causes—namely, "having been accepted by oneself" and "being one's own property"—and not by either one alone. In the case of giving without expectation to one who is not fully ordained...
However, it abandons both of these; here, mere utilization is sufficient, because the characteristic of giving is absent in a gift given with expectation.

Furthermore, regarding the scriptural term "he relinquishes" (*vissajjati*), it should be understood that even discarding without giving anything to anyone—provided there is no expectation—is included.
And the phrase "having given without expectation" is stated solely for the purpose of demonstrating the method of relinquishing after having received [the gift].
For when the act of receiving has ceased, one may again receive and consume [the object], which will then be permissible by itself;
and that cessation of receiving occurs through the relinquishing of the sense of ownership over the object.

By this it is established that as long as there is an expectation of swallowing the object, there can be no such thing as a separate "relinquishment of the receiving. Otherwise, regarding the phrase "in the receiving... [the following would apply].
One might say: "Having relinquished the acceptance without expectation, he accepts it again and eats.
By the phrase "because it was not accepted," it is shown that even if something belonging to one person has been accepted by another, it becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).
The word "thus" (*evaṃ*) refers to the state of having completely renounced with a pure mind, without forming the expectation, "I will take it again."

The phrase "for the purpose of showing there is no offense for one who uses [it]" means the intention is to show that there is no offense regarding the *pācittiya* and other offenses rooted in the *nissaggiya*.

Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of showing there is no offense in the act of using," the intention here is to show that there is no offense concerning the *dukkaṭa* offense mentioned in relation to physical use and so forth of what has been relinquished and then reacquired.
100. Having thus shown the requisites for the four periods of time, he now says, “But among these...,” etc., in order to show their specific characteristics.

Therein, in a house capable of accommodating two people on an improper ground, even for a single night, [the use of] anything belonging to the Saṅgha or to an individual, whether it be the property of a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī, that is *yāvakālika* (to be used during the day) or *yāmakālika* (to be used during the watch of the night), [is not permitted].
That which has been set aside is called "stored overnight" (*antovuttha*); therein, that which has been cooked [overnight] is called "cooked overnight" (*antopakka*).

However, that which is for seven days and that which is for life-long use are permissible. But regarding anything—whether it be for the time of the day (*yāvakālika*) or for the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*)—if one takes it with the intention of consuming it after it has been received and has passed one night, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the very moment of receiving it; and for one who consumes it...
The meaning is that for each individual swallow, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) due to the condition of storing (sannidhi). Now, showing another specific characteristic, he says:
"But as for what is to be used within the proper time (yāvakālika)," and so forth. In this context, "mixed flavors" (sambhinnarasa) means combined flavors.
He says "what is to be used within the proper time" because long-lasting substances, when mixed with short-term substances, follow the duration of those short-term substances alone.
“...but [the three beginning with] ‘time-for-a-watch’ (yāmakālika) and so forth. The same method applies to the others as well. Regarding the phrase “therefore,” etc., the meaning is:
only that which was received on the very day before the meal is permitted; not that which was received after the meal on that same day, nor during the night, nor on the second day and so forth.
Why is this? Because it has been mixed with what was received on that same day and is time-limited (yāvakālika). And here, regarding “with what is time-limited”:

By not saying merely "because of being mixed" (*saṃsaṭṭhattā*), but by stating the qualification "received on that very day" (*tadahupaṭiggahitena*), it is understood that if something is mixed with what was received previously and is still within the permissible time (*yāvakālika*), even if it was received earlier that same day, it is not allowed; it becomes inedible (*anajjhoharaṇīya*).
By the term "of mixed flavor" (*sambhinnarasa*), it is indicated that even if it is mixed, if the other three types of permissible food (*sesakālika*) have not lost their own flavor...

This shows that it is permissible at its own [specific] time. Regarding the phrase "by what is for the watch of the night" (*yāmakālikena*), the third-case qualifying word "received on that very day" (*tadahupaṭiggahitena*) must be supplied here, or it should be carried over from the preceding sentence.
Its fruit is exactly as stated by the method already mentioned.
However, in the manuscripts, it is seen as: "But the other two mixed with what is for the watch of the night are 'received on that very day'."
That is not correct. That which is absent [in the rule] is precisely what is correct; why?

Because the word ending in the second case (the accusative) qualifies the other two. Therefore, when seven-day medicines and lifetime medicines received on that very day are mixed with time-of-the-watch medicines, they are permissible until sunrise;
the meaning would be that those received previously are not [permissible].

That is not correct. Why? Because seven-day medicines and lifetime medicines do not produce the condition of non-storing, and because they contradict the characteristic [of the rule] that "long-term medicines follow the short-term ones.

Therefore, whether it was received on that very day or received previously, a seven-day medicine and a lifetime medicine must be used together with what was received on that day and is of the "watch-period" (yāmakālika) type.
The meaning "it is permissible until sunrise because of being mixed" is appropriate; and in this way, it would be consistent with the statement to be explained below:

"But when mixed with what was received on that same day from among the seven-day [medicines], then what was received on that same day, or what was received earlier, or what is for life-long use, is allowable for seven days."

Furthermore, there must have been an earlier reading: "But the other two [types of food], when mixed with that which is allowable until the watch of the night, are permissible until the rising of the sun on that very day.

Seeing this phrase "received on that very day" (*tadahupaṭiggahita*) existing in other readings, the scribes—assuming that the word "received" (*paṭiggahita*) had been omitted from the word "on that very day" (*tadahū*) here—inserted it and wrote it down.
It might be so; however, the word "tadahū" (on that very day) qualifies the phrase "until the rising of the dawn.
This shows the meaning to be: it is permissible until the rising of the dawn on that very day, and not until the rising of the dawn on the second day or subsequent days.

For this very reason, in the subsequent text as well, the qualifying phrase "received on that very day" (*tadahupaṭiggahitena*) stands in grammatical apposition with the short-term category term "seven-day [medicines]" (*sattāhakālikena*).
It qualifies [the seven-day medicine], not the term "for as long as life lasts" (yāvajīvika) for the purpose of its long duration; therefore it is said:
"If mixed with seven-day medicine received on that same day, then the seven-day medicine—whether received on that same day or received previously—is allowable for seven days.

The same applies to the cases beginning with "mixed with two-day medicine received," etc., where it means: "if mixed with seven-day medicine received two days prior, then the [seven-day medicine] received on that same day..."
Or, that which was received previously or is life-long (yāvajīvika) is permissible for six days.
That which was received on the third day and mixed with what is permissible for seven days, whether received on that same day, received previously, or life-long, is permissible for five days.
That which was received on the fourth day and mixed with what is permissible for seven days, whether received on that same day or received previously...

Or, for as long as life lasts, it is permissible for four days; if mixed with seven-day food received on the fifth day, or received on that same day, or previously received, then the lifetime medicine is permissible for three days.
If mixed with seven-day food received on the sixth day, or received on that same day, or previously received, then the lifetime medicine [is permissible for two days].
"Two days are permissible: that which was received on the same day, or that which was received earlier, when mixed with seven-day medicine received within the seven-day period;

likewise, lifetime medicine is permissible on that very day. In this way, for seven-day medicine alone, one should apply the rule by subtracting the past day and considering the remaining days, but not for lifetime medicine.
For indeed, there is no subtraction to be made for lifetime medicine.
The so-called "day past" exists because, provided there is a suitable condition, [the substance] may be consumed for as long as life lasts. Therefore he said:
"Even that which is kept for seven days, when mixed with what is for life-long use, brings its own inherent nature along with it.
Based on the reading written in some manuscripts—"But the other two, when mixed with what is for a watch of the night, are received on that very day"—it is understood that...
In this reading as well, those who think, "Only this [reading]—'received on that day'—should be accepted," reject the reading "previously received.
In some places, they write "received before the meal";
all of this should be understood as being done by those whose minds have wandered, failing to attend to the method already explained.

Regarding these four types of [medicines] taken at specific times, it is stated that for one who consumes what is "to be taken as long as life lasts" (*yāvakālika*) after the midday time has passed, what is "to be taken during the watch of the night" (*yāmakālika*) after the final watch has passed, or what is "to be taken for seven days" (*sattāhakālika*) after the seven-day period has passed, there is an offense.

To the question, "By which training rule (*sikkhāpada*) does the offense arise?", he says: "At the time, during the watch," and so forth. Its meaning is: when the "to be taken as long as life lasts" is consumed after the time has passed...
For one consuming [it], there is an offense under the training rule on eating at the improper time:

“Whosoever, as a bhikkhu, should chew or eat solid or soft food at an improper time, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya). For one consuming what is to be used within a watch of the night after the watch has passed, there is an offense under [the rule]:
“Whosoever, as a bhikkhu, should consume stored-up solid or soft food...”
"Or if one should chew or eat [it], it is an offense of expiation"—by this training rule concerning hoarding (*sannidhi*), an offense occurs.
For one who consumes for more than seven days those medicines that are to be taken by sick monks, namely:
ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses—these are [the substances].
"Having accepted them, they may be used after being stored for a maximum of seven days; for one who exceeds that limit, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
Thus, by this training rule regarding medicinal requisites (*bhesajja-sikkhāpada*), an offense occurs.
These four types of [medicines] taken at different times, when combined together and blended in flavor, are designated according to the time of their respective original categories.
It was stated that they "should be consumed. To address the question of how they should be consumed if their flavors are not blended, he said, "But if," and so forth.
The meaning of this is indeed easy to understand.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
The eighteenth chapter, titled "The Ornament of Discourse on the Determination of the Four Times. 19.
The Discourse on the Determination of the Proper Ground (Kappiyabhūmi).

101. Having thus explained the determination regarding the four periods of time, he now spoke the words beginning with "The four allowable grounds" (*kappiyā catubhūmiyo*) in order to explain the determination regarding the allowable hut (*kappiyakuṭi*).
In this context, they are called "allowable" (*kappiya*) because they are permitted; the root is *kappa*, meaning capability.
They are called "grounds" (*bhūmi*) because food stored within or cooked within them comes into being; "four grounds" means four types of allowable huts.
The meaning [of the term]. To the question "Which are they?", he says: "They are to be understood as those ending with the proclamation (ussāvanantikā)...

etc. To the question "How is this known?", he says: "From the statement: 'I allow... etc. This was said with reference to the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka* of the Vinaya Piṭaka. Therein, "ussāvanā" means a proclamation;
a "kappiyabhūmi" (a place where what is allowable is kept) that has such a proclamation within its boundaries is called "ussāvanantikā. A place where cattle sit down is "gonisādikā."
The root *ni* preceded by *vi* and having *go-saddu* as its prefix means "to scatter," "to go," or "to destroy. "Given by householders" (*gahapatīhi dinnā*) refers to a *gahapati*;

this is a *tappurisa* compound consisting of a third-case term with the elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*). "Those who are to be authorized by the formal proclamation" (*kammavācāya sammannitabbā*) are called *sammuti*;

thus, the analysis (*viggaha*) of these [terms] should be made in this way. "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to the determination regarding the kitchen (*kappiyakuṭi*). However, even without stating that [analysis], it is said in the *Andhakaṭṭhakathā*.
Even without stating the method already explained, the word "also" (*pi*) permits that same way of speaking. "Stated according to the method stated in the commentaries" means:
when it is said, "Let us build a *kappiya-kuṭi*," or "A *kappiya-kuṭī*," according to the method stated in the remaining commentaries.
"The common characteristic" refers to the characteristic of building a hut by means of formal proclamation (*ussāvanantika*), which is common to all the commentaries.
They establish the determination upon a high place. "From which point" means from whichever brick, stone, or lump of clay one begins.

It is not permitted below the first brick and so forth; that is to say, bricks and other materials being placed on the ground beneath the first brick and so forth are considered to belong to the earth-plane (*bhūmigatika*), and thus one may not have them established while saying, "We are building a *kappiyakuṭi* (a kitchen)."
They are not permitted. If that is so, why does he say that pillars which are set up by being buried in the ground are permitted to be established after having spoken thus?
[The text says: “But as for pillars... they are permitted.

He says “only belonging to the Saṅgha” with reference to a communal dwelling (senāsana) made for the purpose of residence. “Belonging to a monk” refers to an individual dwelling (puggalika-senāsana) made for the purpose of residence for a single monk.
102. By the phrase "in the presence of the face," this indicates precisely the offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) incurred for staying overnight [within the monastery].
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated thus: "By the word 'even' (*pi*) in the expression 'even without saying that,' he also permits speaking in such a manner.
"In the commentaries" (*aṭṭhakathāsu*) refers to the remaining commentaries excluding the Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā. "The common characteristic" (*sādhāraṇalakkhaṇaṃ*).
This is common to all the *Aṭṭhakathās*, including the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā*. "Cayanti" means a foundation or a high place.
"Yato paṭṭhāya" means starting from where—starting from the bricks and so forth; the meaning is that they wish to erect the wall beginning with the layer (*caya*).
By the statement, "But the pillars rise upwards, therefore they are permissible," it is implied that the bricks and stones are below.
It is established that even when being laid down, if they remain raised even by a single finger’s breadth from the ground or the floor, it is permissible.

"Garden" (*ārāma*) refers to the entire monastery as delimited by the precinct boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*). "Dwellings" (*senāsana*) refers to the residences of the Saṅgha within the monastery, such as grass huts and so forth.
"Those called the 'boundary-markers for dwellings'" (*vihāra-gonisādikā*) means those called the "boundary-markers for dwellings" (*senāsana-gonisādikā*). [The term] "dwellings" (*senāsana*).
For even though these [monasteries] are themselves enclosed, they are called "cow-pen-like" (*gonisādikā*) due to the absence of a formal enclosure for the garden.

By the phrase "even if half-enclosed," it is shown that what is enclosed by less than that—or for the most part unenclosed—is reckoned as "unenclosed"; therefore, it falls under the category of the unenclosed.
"In this case" refers to that which is half-enclosed or otherwise. It is permissible to obtain a kitchen (*kappiyakuṭi*) in a cow-pen-like monastery.
The meaning is that, by way of non-existence [of a formal act], any one of the three remaining allowable huts (kappiyakuṭī) may be constructed.

Regarding the phrase "their houses," it should be understood that even if a house has been built for the purpose of monks' residence, it remains the property of those [laypeople] until they hand it over.
"Excluding the monastery" refers to a house built for the purpose of residence for those who are fully ordained (upasampanna).
"Excluding" is the meaning. "House" refers to a dwelling-house. However, anything other than that—such as an Uposatha hall and so forth—is a non-dwelling house;
it is the fifth type of *kappiya-bhūmi* (permissible ground), excluding the four [other] types of permissible grounds.

For even in such a house belonging to the Saṅgha, even if it is well-enclosed and situated within a monastery, there is no fault regarding food stored inside, just as there is none in the open air (*abbhokāsa*). [This applies] wherever it is covered by anything whatsoever.
In a dwelling that is enclosed and sufficient for sleeping together, there is the fault of "dwelling within" (*antovutthādi-dosa*) for a monk or for the Saṅgha’s residence, but not elsewhere.

Therefore he said, "But as for which... and so forth. Therein, although the phrase "whether belonging to the Saṅgha or to an individual" is stated generally for both monks and nuns, [the distinction is that] what belongs to the Saṅgha or to an individual for monks [is different from] that for nuns.
It should be understood that among those [types of property], both what belongs to the Saṅgha and what belongs to an individual remains in the place intended for householders’ belongings.
Regarding "storing in the mouth": for the fault of internal storage indeed incurs an offense by way of entering the mouth, and not otherwise; therefore, it is called "storing in the mouth.
In that context, "they become broken here and there" means they are broken into pieces larger than half. "When the entire roof has collapsed" means...

When the roof-covering that protects against rain—consisting of grass, leaves, and so forth—is destroyed; even though the poles remain bound above the rafters by creepers, they have indeed lost their structural foundation.
"The circle of wing-supports" refers to the covering of grass, leaves, and so forth situated above three rafters on one side.

103. By the phrase “Having given to one who is not fully ordained, [it becomes allowable] for that person,” etc., it is shown that even if something has been kept in an unallowable storehouse (*akappiyakuṭi*), it becomes allowable once it has been given to one who is not fully ordained;
furthermore, in this case, giving with expectation is permitted, as it does not constitute an act of receiving.

However, regarding what has been stored inside, what has been cooked inside, and what has been cooked by oneself, [the Buddha said]: “Monks, you must not consume what has been stored inside, what has been cooked inside, or what has been cooked by yourselves.”

Whoever should consume it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If, monks, it was stored indoors, cooked indoors, and cooked by oneself, and one should consume it, there is an offense of three wrong-doings.
If, monks, it was stored indoors, cooked indoors, and cooked by others, and one should consume it, there is an offense of two wrong-doings. If, monks, indoors...
If one should consume what has been stored outside, cooked outside, and cooked by oneself, there is an offense of two *dukkaṭas*.
Monks, if one should consume what has been stored outside, cooked inside, and cooked by oneself, there is an offense of two *dukkaṭas*.
Monks, if one should consume what has been stored inside, cooked outside, and cooked by others, [there is an offense of two *dukkaṭas*].
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Monks, if food has been stored outside, cooked inside, and cooked by others, and one should consume it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Monks, if food has been stored outside, cooked outside, and cooked by oneself, and one should consume it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Monks, if food has been stored outside, cooked outside, and cooked by others, and one should consume it, [there is an offense of wrong-doing].

Because of the statement, “there is no offense,” there are eight cases: one that is easy to commit, three that are difficult to commit, three that are easy to commit, and one where there is no offense.
In this context, “dwelling within” means dwelling in an improper hut. The same principle applies to “within the vicinity.
“Cooking by oneself” refers to any kind of food; it is not permitted for a bhikkhu to cook anything himself. In this regard:
Whatever needs to be said has already been stated in the Aṭṭhakathā.
Thus ends the "Ornament for the Determination of the Proper Ground" (Kappiyabhūmivinicchayakathālaṅkāra) within the Vinayālaṅkāra, which is a commentary on the Vinaya Piṭaka.
The Nineteenth Chapter.
20. Discussion on the Determination of Acceptance. 104.
Having thus explained the determination of the proper place (*kappiyabhūmi*), he now explains the determination of acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*).

He said, “Receiving solid food, etc. Therein, it is called *khādanīya* (solid food) because it is chewed; this is a designation for everything that is to be swallowed, with the exception of the five kinds of soft food (*bhojana*).
By the word “etc.,” he includes soft food (*bhojanīya*). Receiving, accepting, or taking up is *paṭiggāho*.
The receiving of solid food, etc., is *khādanīyādipaṭiggāho*. Therefore he said: “Of what is to be swallowed...”
“Of whatever kind of food, whether hard or soft, there is the receiving. Regarding the five factors, “mere lifting up” means merely picking it up;
by this, he shows the measure of the burden that may be received.
By that very fact, he demonstrates that receiving does not count as valid in the case of an object that cannot be lifted by such a person. “Within arm’s reach” indicates proximity.
This demonstrates that receiving from one who brings [the gift] while standing at a distance is not valid. "Bringing" (*abhihāra*) means the state of having been dedicated;

this demonstrates that it is not valid in cases such as those involving one who is staying right there (*tatraṭṭhaka*). With the words "Whether a deity," etc., he shows the three modes of application regarding the donor.
With the words "If that," etc., he shows the two modes of application regarding the recipient.
Now, because the extent of the hand’s reach (*hatthapāsa*) among those five factors is difficult to discern, he says “In that case,” etc., in order to demonstrate it.
Therein, the construction is: “Two and a half cubits is called the hand’s reach.

By the phrase “by its near side,” even for one who stands upright in the air and takes [something] lifted by another, the hand’s reach begins from the sole of the foot, which is the nearest part of the body.
It should be delimited; it shows that this is not to be done starting from the head. In this context, for the phrase "by the near side," the meaning should be understood as "by the lower side.

Furthermore, here in the commentary on the *Pavāraṇā-sikkhāpada*, it is stated: "But if a monk is sitting, [the delimitation] starts from the rear edge of the one who is nearby," and so forth; thus, the delimitation begins from the far side of the limb closest to the recipients.

Because it has been demonstrated [in the previous case], here too it should be understood that the range of the hand (hatthapāsa) is to be delimited starting from the lower surface of the recipient—who stands in the air—from the limit of the far side, which is the edge of the sole of the foot nearest to him;
and for the donor, starting from the lower limit of the toes, which constitute the near side. By this same method...

Even when one is lying on the ground and receives [the gift] from the hand of someone sitting at the head, the reach of the hand must be measured starting from the neck—the far limit—rather than from the soles of the feet.
This should be understood accordingly even when giving while lying down; for it is said: "That limb which is closer."
One who is not well (*akallaka*), being ill and unable to eat with his own hands, receives [the medicine] with his mouth.
In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it is stated only as: “‘Akallaka’ means one who is ill, or ‘one who is unable to take [it].

By this, the meaning is shown to be: either one who is ill (*gilāna*), or else one who is not well (*akallaka*)—that is, incapable of taking [it]. Therefore he said: “Even if there is no nasal medication...”
“He receives it through the nostril, or if he has no nasal obstruction, through the mouth.
105. “Even by a single part”: by the mere touch of a finger.
If he receives it [in that way], it is considered entirely received because it was placed there after being tied to the end of a bamboo cane. If...
If a donor stands within arm’s reach of a pot already placed on the ground and gives it with the intention,
“I will give you the pot,” and the recipient accepts it by grasping the tip of a bamboo pole, then everything connected to both ends of that pole is considered accepted.
This is called an *abhihāra* (an offering) because the donor said, “Take this,” referring to sugarcane juice that is naturally flowing without having been pressed into the hand of the monk.
It is said, “it is not discernible”; however, it is permissible to take the juice dripping from sugarcane being pressed for the sake of a monk standing within arm’s reach.
It is also permissible to take sugarcane juice flowing from a trough even if one has blocked its middle and diverted it.
Regarding the perception of receiving: “I shall receive it with a bed or other such items.”
By the phrase "with the perception already produced," it is shown that there is no need to utter the words "I accept.
In certain portions of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), it says: "On a plank that cannot be carried away" means one that cannot be carried by a person of medium strength.
Regarding the statement "on leaves such as those of the *tintiṇika* tree," it should be understood that accepting [alms] on branches is permissible, according to the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
This has been stated. It is likewise stated in the *Porāṇaṭīkā*; therefore, this must be investigated. For in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is said:
"Receiving [food] on very fine leaves such as *tintiṇika* and so forth, when spread out on the ground, is not permissible (*na ruhati*).

This is because, due to the extreme thinness of the *tintiṇika* and other such leaves, the food placed upon them does not remain stable, and thus it is "not permissible" because it is equivalent to having placed it directly on the ground.
It has been stated that even if [the bowl] is placed on branches such as those of the *tintiṇika* tree, it would be exactly the same;
therefore, the statement that "receiving [food] on branches is permissible" appears inappropriate.

In the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), when the reason for the verb "is not permissible" is sought with the word "why," nothing else need be sought, for the qualifying phrase "on delicate [branches]" itself [provides the answer].
It becomes a qualified [statement] possessing a reason; therefore, receiving [alms] in things such as *tintinika* leaves does not apply.
Why? Because of their subtlety (*sukhumattā*). However, it does apply in other cases such as lotus leaves, why? Because of their grossness (*oḷārikattā*).
Thus, it is seen that a connection between cause and fruit must be intended; therefore, it was said: "This must be investigated. Likewise—
For it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “Indeed, those [leaves] are not capable of supporting them; however, it grows on large lotus leaves and the like. (106) “Having wiped and having received”:
this is stated for the purpose of receiving even when [the bowl] has been wiped, provided there is a suspicion of dye-powder; it is not so when there is no such suspicion. “That, moreover”:
the alms-food already held in the hand above, without having received the dust that had fallen [into the bowl]. “There is no offense.”

There is no fault such as improper conduct (*durūpaciṇṇa*). It was stated, “Having given to one who is not fully ordained... it is permissible,” according to the suitability of one’s prior intention (*pubbābhoga*).

However, since that [gift] does not become the property of another merely by the arising of the thought, “I will give it to someone else,” therefore it is permissible to accept and consume it even without having given it to him. “To one who is not fully ordained...”
The phrase “I shall give,” and so forth, is stated for the purpose of avoiding an offense of wrong conduct (*vinayadukkaṭa*);
likewise, even if one has not performed [the formal act], there is no offense for one who accepts and consumes it after having already accepted it. “Gives to a monk” means gives to another monk.

“Gruel” (*kañjika*) is said with reference to any liquid substance, such as the essence of milk and so on. Having released it from the hand, he takes it again; this constitutes an “accepted item” (*uggahitaka*).
He said, "Without releasing it from the hand," because [the food] is still being held. "Āluḷentānaṃ" means "of those stirring [it]," or this is indeed the reading.
Because it has been brought and placed on the ground, there is no "bringing forward" (abhihāra); therefore he said, "The bowl must be received. 107.
Regarding the phrase "a little falls first from the ladle into the bowl": here, as in the case of a small amount that has fallen first...
They say: "There is no fault; likewise, for those who remove [the ash] after having scattered it, there is no fault at all because it was brought [to them] even though it fell later.
*Carukena* means by a small vessel. "Because it was brought" is said with reference to the moment it is being given.
However, at the time of removing it after it has been given, if ashes or drops fall, it must be received again.
They say, "Because the offering has ceased," but that is appropriate only when one is warding it off so that it does not fall;
if one removes it with a natural perception [of ownership], the offering is not severed, and it is considered well-fallen.
For it is indeed accepted. It is also permissible to take it from the rim of the bowl (*mukhavaṭṭi*) of the bowl from which it is being offered.
It is permissible to stretch out one’s hand from above and touch it. "Having struck with the foot" means having stepped on it with the foot with the intention, "I shall receive it.

"Some" refers to the residents of Abhayagiri. "Merely a matter of words" means that there is only a difference in terminology—such as *paṭibaddha* (bound) and *paṭibaddhapaṭibaddha* (bound-to-the-bound)—but it remains merely bound to the body; therefore, their statement should not be accepted.

This is the underlying intention (*adhippāya*). "This is the method" means that this is the principle according to which even that which is attached to what is attached [to the body] is indeed considered "attached to the body.
And so, in that regard, only a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) is stated for both that which is attached to the body and that which is attached to what is attached to it.
"To have it brought by him" means having commanded the monk to whom it was brought, saying, "Bring it here."

The meaning is that it is permissible for another person to have it brought by him. "Therefore" means: because the use [of the medicine] is permitted only for the one who was the original owner (mūlaṭṭha), therefore.
For one who takes it with the hand on that day and consumes it after having formally accepted it on the second day, it becomes "accepted after being taken up" (uggahitaka-paṭiggahita);
thus he said, "without touching. Because it has not been formally accepted, it is stated: "there is no offense due to storage" (sannidhi-paccayā).
It is said, "Having accepted, one should consume," because for one who consumes without having accepted, there is an offense of taking what is not given through the door of the mouth.
Regarding the phrase "not beyond that," they say it refers to what was not personally accepted on that very day;
however, what was accepted on that very day may be consumed even without being re-accepted on subsequent days and so forth.
108. "They perish" means they go to destruction; the intention is that through their powderings, there are no offenses of a grave nature (thullaccaya) or of non-acceptance (appaṭiggahaṇāpatti).
"With a knife" means with a knife that has already been accepted. "Freshly arisen":
