by this very term, he shows that because it has just recently adhered to sugarcane and so forth, it is not subject to the formal designation (abbohārika). "The same method applies" [to] the fault of storage (sannidhi-dosa) and so on.
He speaks with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). Therefore he says, “Indeed not,” and so forth.

But why, in this case, would there be no fault regarding the condition of having received it (*uggahita-paccaya*) or the condition of storage (*sannidhi-paccaya*)? To this he says: “For they do not keep it for the purpose of personal use.

By this, he illuminates that it is permissible to keep [the bowl] either by taking it oneself for the sake of external use, or as given by one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*); therefore, [it may be kept] for the purpose of wiping the bowl and so forth.
If one has personally taken oil and such items that have been kept aside and wishes to consume them, there is no offense for one who consumes them after having formally received them.
However, for one who consumes what was personally taken for internal use without having formally received it,
there is an offense of consuming what has not been given through the door of the mouth (*adinnamukhadvāra*).

There is an offense. For one who, having accepted what was given by a person not fully ordained for the purpose of internal use, keeps it, there is an offense due to storage (*sannidhi-paccaya*), similar to the case of refined salt (*siṅgīloṇa-kappa*).

However, some say that because the acceptance is valid through the fulfillment of the five factors—as stated in the passage beginning "it is merely enough for the excretion of a man of medium strength"—it may also be for the purpose of external use.

If they say, "If one takes what is given by those who are not fully ordained, it is indeed accepted," then in this case, for one who takes and carries [an item] given by a non-ordained person for the purpose of external use, an offense due to storage (*sannidhi*) would have to be stated.
Furthermore, it could not be said, "For they do not carry it for the purpose of use"; therefore, for the purpose of external use...
It should be understood that what has been taken is not called "received.
If this is so, should the qualification "for the purpose of use" be stated regarding the five factors of receiving?
It need not be stated; for since receiving is always for the purpose of use, it is not mentioned separately as "for the purpose of use."
“‘If a bhikkhu receives it with his own body or with something connected to his body’—this much alone is stated.

However, others say: “Even though there is receiving, because it says ‘he does not carry it for the purpose of use,’ here it is stated that there is no offense when one carries it for a purpose other than use.
And by that [statement], when the five factors of receiving are fulfilled...
This shows that what is taken with the desire to swallow it is indeed called "received" (*paṭiggahita*), because receiving is permitted only for things intended to be swallowed.
Likewise, it shows that oil and so forth, which were taken and set aside for external use, may be received and consumed once there is a desire to swallow them.
[The phrase] "the mortar, pestle, and so forth wear out" means:
In this context, regarding medicines that have been ground and pounded in mortars and pestles, if a foreign color is perceived, it is not permitted.
"It is pure water" refers to water that has fallen after dripping from tree branches and so forth.
"Or his bowl should be accepted" means that even here, when one gives by touching what is in the bowl, [if] there is anything clinging to the hand...

The holding of the bowl for the purpose of receiving food, in order to avoid faults regarding material things, should be understood as the holding of the bowl solely for the purpose of internal consumption.
Regarding the passage, "Whatever falls into the novice's bowl... [etc.

...the act of receiving is not relinquished," here it means that because one who receives repeatedly forms the definite resolve that what has been placed in his own bowl is his own property, it is considered to have come into his possession.

One does not relinquish the act of receiving. However, for one who accepts what has been given after it has been set aside, because the determination that "this is my own" is made at the very moment of taking hold of it, the act of receiving is relinquished once it has come into the hand.
Regarding the phrase "he puts rice into [the bowl] for the sake of some [persons]," even if he puts it there for the sake of one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna), [if that person] comes...
Regarding the phrase "he will take it": because one places it there oneself after having picked it up, the act of receiving (*paṭiggahaṇa*) is not relinquished.

However, when it is placed in the hand of one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), it is said to be "placed by one who is not fully ordained"; thus, the act of receiving is relinquished because of the state of having been abandoned.
Therefore it is said: "A novice... [etc. ...because of having abandoned it. Regarding the phrases beginning with "of some," [it refers to] those who are not fully ordained.
Even when something is being placed somewhere for a specific purpose, the act of receiving (*paṭiggahaṇa*) does not cease merely upon its release from the hand;

rather, the receiving ceases only when it has fallen into the vessel. And since the vessel is expected by the monk for the sake of the following day, the food contained therein also ceases to be received, just like food in a bowl that has not been washed.
It should be understood that it was stated [in the Vinaya] that "it must be placed in the hand of a novice. For in such cases, one need not seek logical justification;
one should simply proceed according to the manner in which it has been stated.
110. Regarding the phrase "rice-gruel contained in a bowl": by this, it is meant that even if the rice-gruel touches only the rim of the bowl, it is considered accepted and received.
This shows that it does not become an offense for a monk when he is touched against his will. "He causes [it] to be placed" means he causes the hand to touch it.
A "load suitable for receiving" is one that can be lifted by a man of medium strength.
Although there is no fault for one who covers it with the other hand without having relinquished it, nevertheless, it should not be covered; this is according to the authority of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
It should be taken up. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated: "‘It should not be covered’ refers to what has been released from the hand;

but there is no fault for one who covers with the other hand what is already in the hand, or for one who lets a covering fall over it without touching it, even though it has been released from the hand."

111. "He receives" means: if a large branch held above for the sake of shade should break off by any means, and the dust clinging to it should fall into the mouth, he receives it after having had it made allowable (*kappiya*). Regarding "for the purpose of warding off flies":
here, even if dust clinging to the branch falls into the bowl, one is able to consume [the food] with ease;
because it was received by the branch, this receiving is for the purpose of internal consumption. Thus, it is indeed the original receiving (*mūla-paṭiggahaṇa*) itself.
"It is allowable," it is said. Others, however, say that having taken the mere words "for the purpose of preventing [the fish] from escaping," it was intended for external use.
*Kuṇḍaka* means a large jar. *Tasmiṃ pi* means even in a small jar. *Gāhāpetvā anupasampannan* means having had that very same edible article taken by one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).
Regarding the phrase "the elder’s bowl to the second elder": having caused the elder to relinquish it by saying, "Give me the elder’s bowl," he gives it to the second elder.
Regarding the phrase "give me your rice-gruel": having said this, he takes the novice’s bowl and gives his own bowl to him.
As for the phrase "but here": this refers to the discussion on the exchange of bowls, beginning with "The novice is wise."

"The reason must be examined" means that one should investigate the underlying cause as follows: "Just as one who takes oil and other items from his mother or others is permitted to use them for such purposes without having to exchange them with another person who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), why then is one not permitted to use [the bowl] here without having exchanged it?
This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the rice taken by the novices (*sāmaṇera*)...
They state the reason as follows: "When [the property] has been completely exhausted, the thought may arise that 'the novices will surely take care of us';

therefore, it must be used only after exchanging it [for something else]. However, when taking it for the sake of one's mother and father or for the sake of shade, there is no expectation of personal use;
therefore, that is permissible. For this very reason, the Venerable Ācariya Buddhadatta Thera also said:
“Even for one who carries oil and such for the sake of his parents,
or cuts a branch for the sake of its shade and so forth, there is no distinction from this [ordinary person].
Therefore, one must consider the cause that constitutes his distinction.”
"But we consider his state of attachment to be the distinguishing factor.
This alone is more reasonable here, because such a type of thought necessarily arises [in that case]. For it is not possible to purify one's thoughts in this instance.
However, when taking [something] for the sake of one's mother and so forth, such a type of thought does not necessarily arise.
It is possible to purify one’s thoughts. For where it is possible to purify one’s thoughts, there is no fault at all. Therefore he will say:
"But if one is able to purify one's thoughts, then it is permissible to eat what has been obtained. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, [it says]:
"In this context, 'here' refers to the exchange of bowls. The reason is that here, just as with novices..."
It is said: "The thought arises, 'She is giving this to us,' and not so elsewhere; they state this as the reason, and that is appropriate.
However, for one who does not have such a thought, it is permissible to eat even without turning [the food] over.
112. "To remove" means to shake and thereby remove stones, gravel, and so forth. "It should be placed on the hearth" means...

This was said with reference to a fireless hearth (*anaggika-uddhana*). Regarding the churning of what is being cooked on the hearth, he said, "and it is cooked by oneself," because the uncooked rice above sinks down and cooks below.
113. "The bowl is placed on a stand" means that the bowl containing food not yet formally accepted is set aside for the purpose of being accepted again.
"Causes to move" means he causes it to move without a reason; even when there is a reason, it is not permitted to cause [the food] that is fit for the monks' consumption to be moved.

Although the acceptance of raw meat for one's own sake was permitted in such an affliction by the rule, "Monks, I allow raw meat and raw blood in the case of a non-human affliction," [it is forbidden] from the acceptance of raw meat...

Although it is generally prohibited by the statement, "he is abstinent," nevertheless, because it was not taken for his own sake or for the sake of another bhikkhu, it is said: "The lion's leftovers, etc., are permissible.
He is able to purify his thoughts means he is able to observe the non-arising of the thought, "He is giving it to me," [and instead thinks], "I shall give it to the novice."
Or he is able to perceive, "I have accepted it with a pure mind. However, regarding the phrase "if it has also been accepted at the root," they say:
"If it has been accepted with the intention, 'Having taken it, let them give it to me as well.
114. "He makes portions" means: "Let the bhikkhus and sāmaṇeras each take a portion according to their own preference."
He makes equal portions for everyone. "The remainder of what was taken" means the remainder from the portion taken by the novices.
"Having taken" means having taken [thinking], "I will take this for myself. Here, "the remainder of what was taken" refers to that which was placed back after he had taken it.
"Having received" means having received on that very day. For this very reason, there is a fault in the mixing of what is for the time being with what is for life-long use.
Thus it is said. However, if it was received and kept on the previous day, it is not permitted to inhale the smoke from that stick with a mouth containing food.
"By ocean water" means by ocean water that has not been formally received.
"Himakarakas" (frost-motes) are a specific kind of water that occasionally falls along with rainwater, becoming solidified like stone-etchings.
In those cases, there is no requirement for formal acceptance; therefore, he said, "they are simply like water.
Because the *kataka* nut, having clarified the water, remains separate from it, it is called "not subject to legal proceedings" (*abbōhārika*).

By this, he shows that it is not subject to legal proceedings regarding offenses involving non-acceptance, nor is it subject to legal proceedings regarding offenses of eating at the improper time. It "adheres" [to the mouth] when the mouth is dry.
It adheres even when showing the color of clay on the hand. Even if it is thick enough not to adhere to the hands or mouth, it must still be formally received (*paṭiggahetabba*).
"Merely a residue" indicates the absence of dust or milk. "Having taken water" means having taken it for one's own use.
However, if one takes it thinking, "I shall pour what remains after drinking right back here," there is no further need for formal reception.
"It scatters" and "it should be accepted" are stated because the flower-juice is being manifested. "Having suppressed" means having dispersed; the meaning is "having removed. 115.
"In the great elements" refers to the great elements such as earth and so forth, which are dependent upon the bodies of living beings.

"Everything is allowable" means that everything dependent upon one's own body or the bodies of others is allowable, because it conforms to what is not unallowable meat; [otherwise] there would be a grave offense (thullaccaya) and so forth.
The intended meaning is "does not produce [new growth]. "Falls" means it falls after being severed from its own body.

Since it is stated, "having cut it from a tree," it should be understood that for the sake of clay, it is permissible to dig the earth and to cut any other medicinal root, leaf, or the like—even if one does not make ash and even if it has not been formally received.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Ornament of the Discourse on the Determination of Acceptance," in the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
21. Discussion on the Determination of the Invitation (Pavāraṇā-vinicchaya-kathā) 116.

Having thus explained the determination regarding the acceptance [of the invitation], he now spoke the words beginning with “the prohibited invitation” (*paṭikkhepa-pavāraṇā*) in order to explain the determination regarding the invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
In this context, *paṭikkhepa* means the act of prohibiting; the sense is non-acceptance. *Pavāriyate* means “it is invited”; the sense is the act of forbidding.
An invitation consisting of a refusal is a "refusal-invitation" (*paṭikkhepapavāraṇā*). Alternatively, an invitation by way of a refusal is a "refusal-invitation.
The connection is: for one who is eating any one of the five kinds of cooked food, when another kind of food is brought to him, there is an invitation consisting of a refusal.
117. "Whatever he eats" means whatever he consumes. In the phrase "sour rice-porridge and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes milk-rice-porridge and other such items.
Therein, by the mention of sour rice-porridge, thick gruel mixed with sour substances such as buttermilk is indicated;

by the mention of milk-rice-porridge, gruel mixed with milk is included. "It produces an invitation" refers to the basis for the offense regarding eating food that has not been made *atiritta* (leftover).
He establishes a refusal. Even if a refusal is made, it does not become the basis for an offense regarding eating what is not left over; it remains in its very place where it was not made.
Therefore, he said: "it does not generate an invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
Because the word *yāgu* (gruel) is common to both gruel that generates an invitation and [ordinary] gruel, even when it is said, "Take the gruel," there is an invitation.
"It is said that 'it occurs' means it simply generates the invitation (pavāraṇā)"; this is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipadas*.
However, that does not agree with the reason given later in that very same work, under the passage: "having brought rice-gruel mixed with food.

For it is stated there—referring to an invitation where no rice-gruel was served—that it refers specifically to boiled rice (*bhatta*) that has been kneaded together with water, sour gruel, milk, and so forth.

Because it was said, “Take rice gruel,” there is an invitation (*pavāraṇā*). However, in the case of the statement, “Having brought rice gruel mixed with cooked food,” there is no invitation because the rice gruel exists separately [from the food].

Therefore, in that instance, following the same method as stated there, since it was said “Take rice gruel” referring specifically to the cooked food itself that had been kneaded together with milk and so forth, it is by means of the rice gruel alone that [the invitation occurs] there.
"The invitation (pavāraṇā) takes place because of non-existence"—this is how the reason should be stated here. For if this is so, it accords with the reason stated later in the Aṭṭhakathā:

"Because of the existence of him to whom one has asked permission. Otherwise, a contradiction between what precedes and what follows would arise within the Gaṇṭhipada itself, and it would not harmonize with the Aṭṭhakathā. By the words "If... [is] discerned," etc., [the meaning is established].
It indicates the mere presence of a piece of fish or meat, or of sinew, of the dimensions already mentioned. "By those" means by various kinds.
"Flour made from rice, paddy, and barley" is stated according to the general rule; however, flour is indeed flour even when made from seven types of grain after they have been roasted.
For this very reason he said: "Kaṅgu, varaka... [etc. ...all fall under the category of flour. "Flour-cakes" (sattumodaka).
Uncooked barley-sugar (*sattuguḷa*) is that which is made by kneading together parched barley flour (*sattu*). However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated:

"Barley-cake (*sattumodaka*) is that which is made by moistening parched barley flour; but having ground the parched barley into flour, moistened it, and made it into a cake (*pūva*), they cook it—that [latter] one does not count as an invitation."
Because the state of having left a meal unfinished has been interrupted by means of one of the five kinds of food, it is said: “Not even a mustard-seed’s worth [of food] remains in his mouth...
he does not invite others to eat. From the statement, “He rejects unallowable meat;
he does not invite others to eat,” it follows that if he rejects a gift belonging to the Saṅgha—whether knowing or not knowing that it will not reach him—[he incurs an offense].
One does not perform the *pavāraṇā* because that which ought to be refused has already been refused; even one who refuses what belongs to an unashamed person does not perform the *pavāraṇā*.
"Because it lacks a basis" means because the *pavāraṇā*, which establishes the offense of eating non-leftovers (*anatiritta*), lacks a basis.
By this, he illustrates the state of having already refused that which ought to be refused. For whatever is to be refused...
The refusal of an offense is not a factor; therefore, it is said that this is not a basis for the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*).
118. Regarding "the nearer factor": for one who stands outside the reach of the hand and gives by leaning over, the head is the nearer part;
it must be delimited by its lower limit. "Brings near" indicates the extension of the body. "Having brought away" means having moved toward oneself. This is the meal.

"He takes" and "he says" means he speaks while diverting the matter slightly. Or rather, because the verbal offer itself was not intended, [the phrase] "take it" refers to one who has begun to take it.

Even for one standing outside the reach of hand-contact, although there is an offer made with the desire to give, because the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) is absent due to the distance for one who refuses, the absence of the invitation is understood by taking the mere fact of the elder's distance as well.
He said, “Because the elder was far away,” and so forth; it was not because the act of bringing [the food] to him was possible.
Even if one had taken it and returned to stand within arm’s reach, since he remained in his place of support without saying anything, there would be no such thing as “bringing”;
thus it is said, “because the messenger did not bring it. [The Buddha said: “By the one who came having taken it, [saying] ‘Take the meal’...”

"In the three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries it is stated: 'When this has been said, there is what is called an "invitation" (abhihāra); for it is said: "If, however, a monk comes having taken [the food]... pe... there is an invitation. However, some say: "'It should be understood that it is said:
"Offer even a little from the bowl and say, 'Take this meal. This appears to be the more reasonable view, as it constitutes a verbal invitation (*vācābhihāra*).
Because it is not intended here [as such].
"In the refectory" means in the dining hall. "It has already been brought" means it has been brought by the server himself.

Regarding the statement, "There is an invitation (*pavāraṇā*) for one who refuses someone wishing to give from that," there is also an invitation for one who refuses even when [the food] is not being taken.
It certainly is so. Why? Because it has been brought forward out of a desire to give; for it is said: "Therefore, that [gift] is indeed one that has been brought forward.

For this very reason, in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries it is stated: "When there is a bringing forward out of a desire to give, the mere act of taking [the object] with the thought 'I will give' does not constitute a bringing forward.
Whether one takes it with the thought 'I will give' or does not take it, it is only the bringing forward consisting in the desire to give that constitutes a bringing forward. Therefore..."
It is said: "Whether at the time of taking or at the time of not taking, for one who refuses it, there is an invitation (pavāraṇā).
Now, in order to show that even if one refuses it at the time of taking—provided there was no prior expression of a desire to give—it is not an invitation, the passage beginning with "But if...
is stated. Even if [the food] has not been lifted up by a ladle, because it was brought previously, it is an invitation.
"It has been brought" means "it has indeed been brought. "As soon as it has been removed" means as soon as it has been separated from the vessel.
"Even when the weight of two [portions] is equal" means even when the weight of the food-bowl is shared between the distributor and another person.
Regarding "Take the broth": here, because only the meat broth—which causes the suspension of the meal—is mentioned by name.

If one rejects [the offering], the invitation (pavāraṇā) does not take place. In cases such as "fish and sauce," because the meaning "fish and flavor" is possible, and because the substance is of that nature, the invitation does indeed take place.
Even if one rejects what has been brought by someone remaining silent without saying, "Take this," it still constitutes an invitation.
“Karambaka” is a term for a mixture. For whatever they prepare by mixing together many ingredients is called “karambaka.

Even if it is made by mixing meat, because it is spoken of under the name of something that is permissible to accept—namely, “Take the *karambaka*”—there is no offense for one who refuses it. However, if it is said, “Take the meat-*karambaka*,” [it is otherwise].
However, since it was said, "Take it mixed with meat," it is indeed an invitation (*pavāraṇā*). Regarding the phrase "one who thinks it is prepared specifically for him":

here they say that because the substance is allowable, even though there is a prohibition based on the perception of it being unallowable, this training rule constitutes an invitation because it is unintentional.
[This refers to] the previous instance of an invitation involving non-gruel.

They say that because the statement "Take rice gruel" was made with reference specifically to rice that has been kneaded together with water, sour gruel, milk, and so forth, there is an invitation (*pavāraṇā*);
however, in the case of the phrase "having brought rice gruel mixed with rice," since the rice gruel exists separately, there is no invitation.
This is the intended meaning here; thus, the point expressed by the passage beginning with "by whom [he] was asked" is precisely this.
He speaks with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*). But the reason for this is difficult to see; regarding this, some first say:

"Since what is called 'rice-mixed-gruel' (*yāgumissaka*) is not merely rice, but includes milk and so forth as well, therefore—as in the case of *karambaka*—there should be no invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
And this being the case, [the rule] states: 'If the gruel is more abundant or equal in amount, one does not invite; if the gruel is weak...'"
"The reason why it is difficult to see whether there is an invitation (*pavāraṇā*) or not when one refuses food that contains rice gruel is hard to discern. However, some say:
"Food mixed with rice gruel is called *bhatta* (food); therefore, for one who refuses it, there must necessarily be an invitation.
And this being the case, the reason why it is difficult to discern whether there is an invitation here or not is hard to see."
Just as the reason here is difficult to see, so too should it be understood that the reason for the statement "take them mixed" from the subsequent passage is likewise difficult to see.
For the quantity—whether few or many—of those sufficient for an invitation (*pavāraṇā*) is not the cause for the presence or absence of the invitation;
rather, in this case, the sole criterion is the taking of the name of one who generates the invitation. Therefore: "And this, with the *karambaka*..."
As for the reason stated in the passage beginning with “it should not be brought,” that too does not accord when compared with what was stated previously.
For if the term “mixed” were established only in the sense of being mixed with food, then, just as when it is said,
“Take the food-mixture,” one would still perform the *pavāraṇā* (invitation to stop eating) regardless of whether the food is more, equal, or less [than the solid food].

Likewise, even when it is said, "Take mixed [food]," there must be an invitation (*pavāraṇā*) even if the food is less than that amount, because the term "mixed" is conventionally established only for food that is mixed.

For it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "Since 'mixed' is a conventional expression used only for food that is mixed, this, moreover, refers specifically to food that is mixed. Now, as for "mixed":
The term "mixed" (*missaka*) does not apply to what has become hardened; rather, it was said, "Take the mixed," with reference to mixed rice.

Thus, just as when an invitation consists of non-gruel, and one says, "Take the gruel," referring specifically to rice that has been moistened with milk and so forth, the formal invitation (*pavāraṇā*) is valid—even so here, it is with reference to mixed rice alone that "the mixed" was said.
When it is said, “Take [it],” whether the food be little or much, there must indeed be an invitation (*pavāraṇā*).

Therefore, whether the term “mixed” (*missaka*) is a conventional usage for food mixed with other things, or is spoken with reference to something else that is mixed—in either case, the earlier and the later do not agree;
so what is the point of investigating the reason here? In such instances, one must proceed solely by the authority of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
This is our position regarding patience (*khanti*).

However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated: "Regarding the phrase 'one who thinks it was prepared specifically for him,' because the substance is allowable (*kappiya*), it is said that 'he has indeed been invited.
If it is indeed prepared specifically for him, there is no prohibition. This is the intended meaning here."
He speaks with reference to the very point already stated by the words “by whom [he] was asked,” and so forth. However, the reason here is difficult to see;

that is to say, when there is a large quantity of food, the reason for the *pavāraṇā* (invitation to eat more) is difficult to perceive. Otherwise, even in the case of a *karambaka* (rice-and-vegetable mash), if there were a large quantity of fish and other such items, there would have to be a *pavāraṇā*. And just as the reason here is difficult to see, so too...
It should be understood that even here, the reason for [the rule] "Take it mixed from others" is difficult to discern.
Furthermore, as for the reason stated, namely, "But this is indeed mixed with food," and so forth, that too does not accord with the statement, "One does not invite [others] when there is less.
This much alone has been said.
"‘He gives after separating’ means he gives having taken out the sauce and so forth that is on top of the meal," so it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.
However, some have stated: "He presses it firmly with his hand and strains it so that no rice grain falls.
Even in that case, no reason is seen; for [the rule applies] just as when it is mixed with the meal.
When one has brought rice gruel and, having said, "Take the rice gruel," refuses it even while being offered rice mixed with the gruel,
there is no formal invitation (pavāraṇā). Likewise here, when rice mixed with much milk, curd, and so forth is offered—
whether one is given the milk and such alone after saying "Take the milk," or rice mixed with milk and such— in either case, there is no formal invitation.
It should not be so; therefore, the statement "he gives having separated [it]" refers to one giving in that specific manner.
It should be understood that this is said for the purpose of showing that there is no *pavāraṇā* (invitation to eat) for one who refuses food when it is being given mixed with other food.
However, if the intention were that there is a *pavāraṇā* when food is being given mixed with other food, then [the following] would apply in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Regarding the statement, “he gives having separated [the items],” since this is the case, one must accept that the commentary alone is the authority here, and no other reason should be sought.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is explained:
“‘He gives having separated’ means the sense should be understood as giving by means of speech, saying ‘Take the juice,’ and so forth; it does not mean separating the juice and such with the body.”

"‘Having separated’: even though it has not been separated in that way, because the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) is impossible for one who refuses, and because it is stated by name as something that precludes the invitation—just as in cases such as when rice-mixed gruel is brought and one says, ‘Take the gruel’;
otherwise, the intended meaning here must be understood in such a way that there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows. Thus it was said.

In cases such as a boat or a bridge, even though one stands for a moment at the time of boarding and so forth, there is no "standing" in the technical sense because one is intent on the act of going, despite the necessity of performing the boarding and other actions.
However, it is not permitted to stand [there] due to the lack of space caused by the crowding of people.
"Without moving" means without pushing [the object] to another seat or upwards from its stated location.
However, one is permitted to turn it over in that very place. Therefore, he said, "In whichever direction," and so forth.
If one sitting in the squatting posture (ukkuṭika) sits on the ground without releasing the feet, one is indeed disturbing the posture; thus, it is said, "But beneath it...
a seat-cloth should be given," so that one may sit comfortably without disturbing the squatting posture.
“‘Without moving from one’s seat’ means without rising, without releasing the flesh of the buttocks from the spot where they touched the bench;
it should not be understood as ‘moving from one’s place,’ as in the case of taking what is not given. Thus it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.
121. Regarding the phrase “made unallowable”: since that which has been made unallowable itself lacks the status of being *atiritta* (leftover), [one must] have it made allowable [again].
Only the roots, fruits, and so forth placed in that bowl are not considered "leftover" (atiritta), as are unallowable foods (akappiyabhojana) or those obtained through such acts as defiling a family.
However, everything else contained within the bowl is indeed "leftover" and is permitted to be consumed.
Yet, for one wishing to consume those roots, fruits, and so forth, they must be removed from the bowl, made allowable (kappiya), and [placed] in another [vessel].
Having placed it in a vessel and had it declared as leftover, it may be consumed.
122. "He is not allowed to do it again" means that when it is being done in that very same vessel, it becomes "done together" with what was done first;
therefore, he himself is not allowed to do it again, though another may. However, in another vessel, by him—
Or it is permissible for someone else to do it. Therefore he said: "That by which it was not done, by that it must be done;
and that which was not done, that must be done. In the phrase "by that too," the word *pi* (too/also) indicates the meaning:
"not only by another [person]. "Done in this way" means done in another vessel.

"Having sent" means having sent it into the hand of one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*). Because this constitutes a formal act of discipline (*vinayakamma*), it is stated: "That which is held in the hand of one who is not fully ordained must not be [accepted].

However, regarding the phrase "if they are mixed with food," it should be understood that if they are mixed even with food that has been taken into the mouth and is not leftover (*anatiritta*), there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) alone;
therefore, one who has already finished eating should have the food made into leftovers before [accepting it].
Even while eating, one should eat having made the mouth and hands clean so that it is not mixed with what has not been formally offered;

for although there is no offense for one who has been invited to eat before midday when consuming items such as those permitted for the watch of the night for the purpose of food, for one who has already been invited, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) rooted in that invitation. Thus: "the watch-of-the-night [medicines]... [down to] ...in swallowing."
“[If] he swallows it, there is an offense of wrong-doing”— thus it is stated in the Pāḷi.
Thus ends the chapter titled “The Ornament of the Exposition on the Refusal and Invitation,” within the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
The Twenty-First Chapter.
22. Discussion on the Determination of Going Forth (Pabbajjā). 123.
Having thus explained the determination regarding prohibitions and invitations, I shall now explain the determination regarding going forth.
He says, “Regarding ‘going forth’ (*pabbajjā*), however,” and so on. Therein, it is called *pabbajjā* because one must first go away (*vajitabbā*);
the meaning is that it is to be approached before full ordination (*upasampadā*). The verbal root is *vaja* preceded by *pa-*, meaning “to go.

He speaks of a “son of good family” (*kulaputta*) with reference to one who is of a family characterized by right conduct. The connection is: “having avoided those persons who have been excluded. “Free from the faults of going forth” means:
He is free from the five defects, such as diseases, which act as obstacles to the going-forth.
Regarding the phrase "the size of the back of a fingernail," it is the back of the nail of the little finger that is intended here.

By the statement, "If even that which is the size of the back of a fingernail is on the side of growth, he should not be admitted to the going-forth," the general characteristic [of the defect] is shown; therefore, in whichever part of the body it may be—
It is established that if [the mark] is the size of a fingernail’s back and is situated during the waxing phase of the moon, it is not permitted.
This being the case, it follows that if it is even the size of a fingernail’s back but is situated during the waning phase, it is permitted in all instances;
however, since that is not intended as a general rule, he says “But if,” etc., demonstrating the restriction specifically to certain locations.

For if it were permissible without distinction for [the amount] the size of a fingernail’s back to remain in the category of “not increasing” anywhere, then the restriction of location as “in places naturally covered by the lower and upper robes” would not have been made.

Therefore, it is established that elsewhere than in places naturally covered by the lower and upper robes, even if it remains in the category of “not increasing,” the size of a fingernail’s back is not permissible. From the size of a fingernail’s back...
"However, whether it is smaller or situated on the non-growing side or the growing side, it is permissible provided it is smaller than the surface of a fingernail;
for that which is smaller than a fingernail is prohibited only in the case of the mouth and so forth,
regardless of whether it is on the growing side or the non-growing side," as stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.

In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it is stated: "Since it is said that in a concealed place, [a mark] the size of a fingernail’s back, if it remains in its natural state and does not increase, is permissible, it follows as a matter of course that even such a mark is not permissible in an unconcealed place;
and furthermore, even in a concealed place, one that remains in a state of increasing is not permissible. Moreover, even in a manifest place, beyond the size of a fingernail’s back..."

It is said: "The statement beginning with 'But in the mouth' was spoken in order to prohibit those who might take [the medicine] thinking that it is permissible if it is less than the full measure or if it is an addition.
By the phrase "Godhā... it is not permissible," he shows that even such a disease as this is included within leprosy (*kuṭṭha*) itself.
The determination regarding swellings (*gaṇḍa*) should also be understood by this same method. However, in that context, regarding the mouth and so forth...
A boil even smaller than the size of a jujube fruit (*kolaṭṭhi*) is not permitted; therefore, it is not mentioned separately.
For in that context, it is simply stated: "Even if it is in an uncovered place and remains on the side of not increasing, it is not permitted.

Nevertheless, according to the method explained regarding leprosy (*kuṭṭha*), it is understood that a boil even smaller than the measure of a jujube fruit is not permitted on the face and other such areas.
Regarding the phrase "therefore, even when standing on the side of non-increase," the word *pi* (even/also) here has the sense of including what is not explicitly stated;
by this, the meaning that even something smaller than a jujube fruit is not permitted is indeed shown—this is our conviction.
The expression "born in its natural color" is said with reference to the absence of any disfigured color caused by disease.
“Kolaṭṭhimatta” means the size of a jujube stone. The reading is “sañjātachaviṃ kāretvā,” which means having caused the skin to grow back.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: “‘Sacchaviṃ kāretvā’ means having caused the existing skin to remain;
or the reading is ‘sañchaviṃ,’ which means having caused the skin to be produced. Even when the abscesses and so forth have subsided, that spot...”
It is said: "Even if it is discolored, that is permissible.

"Having the color of a lotus or white lily petal" means having the color of the petals of a red lotus or a white lotus flower. "In the same manner as stated for leprosy" refers to the method already explained:
"It is permissible [to use] what does not grow in a concealed place; otherwise, nothing is permissible."

[He] shows [this]. Sosabyādhi is a wasting disease. Yakkhummāda is a disease that is indeed a *yakkha* which, having occasionally arrived, throws one down on the ground and rubs parts such as the hands and face against the earth. 124.
*Mahāmatta* means one endowed with great authority and power. “I am no longer a servant of the King,” [he says].
"He asks for permission" is said with reference specifically to a position granted by the king.
However, one who has been appointed by royal officials such as ministers, or who is a servant of those very ministers, may also ask for permission from those respective ministers and others.

(125) Because it is stated "one who bears the banner," it is understood that even a thief who is not publicly known may be ordained. Therefore, he will say: "But those who are thieves of mangoes, wood-apples, and so forth," and so on. "Knowing thus" means they know him as "one born virtuous."
126. "Having broken" means having broken the bond of leather thongs. "Having cut" means having cut the bond of chains.
"Having released" means having released the bond of ropes. "Having opened" means having opened the village gates and so forth among the various village enclosures.
"Or he escapes while they do not see him" means he escapes while the men guarding the guard-post—the protectors—do not see him.
129. *Purimanayeneva* means by the very same method stated here [in the rule]: "one who has been struck with a whip and undergone punishment. 130. *Palātopi*:

even one who has fled out of fear upon learning that the creditors have arrived is a debtor (*iṇāyika*). He is considered to be "under obligation" (*gīvā*) because, having been identified as a debtor, he was admitted into the state of a monk while being negligent regarding his debt.
*Upaḍḍhupaḍḍhaṃ* means little by little. *Dātabbameva*: the debtor must pay the money, whether it succeeds for him or not.
Or rather, it shows that one must be diligent in giving, and that other monks should act as companions, saying, "Do not abandon your burden.
For by abandoning the burden, he might be made to pay compensation for the value of the goods.
By the phrase "bought after being subjected to the status of a slave," it excludes one who was bought for the purpose of liberating him from slavery.
For even one who has been purchased with wealth is indeed not a slave. In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, however, it is stated:

"Local custom means such various local customs as the filing of a legal plaint, the presentation of a document, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by way of local custom in this or that place," it refers to the procedure for making someone no longer a slave through the burning of a slave-document and other such means in various regions.
In royal consecrations and similar ceremonies, they cause all bonds to be released.
With reference to this, it is said: "by one common to all.

If they were to enter their own names on the document themselves, it would not be permissible; therefore, those free-born women, thinking "we too shall become colored slaves," have their own names written by themselves on the royal slave-documents for the sake of their own protection.
Their sons also become royal slaves; therefore, it is not permissible to ordain them.

"They should not be ordained unless given by them" means that however many owners there may be, they must not be ordained if they have not been given by even one of those owners. However, it is permissible to ordain them after making them free men (*bhujissa*);
that is, having informed the Saṅgha in the monastery to which those monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) were assigned, [one may ordain them] through manual labor (*phātikamma*).
It is permissible to ordain someone after first making them a slave by means of wealth or other such means. However, in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, it is written:

"In the case of the sons of a temple-servant woman (*devadāsī*), it is permissible. It is stated: "If one wishes to ordain a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*), one should ordain him after giving another person [in his place].
This is the intended meaning here according to the *Mahāpaccarivāda*: because [the parents] gave him away with the words, "We give this to the Saṅgha of monks as a monastery attendant."
They are not slaves; since it is stated that "a monastery attendant (ārāmika) is neither a slave nor a free man," he is recorded as not being a slave.
The practice of pouring oil [on the head] is customary in the island of Sri Lanka, and they are to be ordained because they serve as monastery attendants for the Saṅgha.
It is said: "One is permitted to make even a masterless slave one's own free man."
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, however, it says: “They are just like those whose heads have been sprinkled with buttermilk;

the intention is that, just as those making mirrors wash their heads with buttermilk before making them, so too, because they were given [the going forth] by the words of a monastery attendant, they are indeed like mirrors.
They say, moreover, that ‘the sprinkling of buttermilk is a custom in the island of Ceylon. He should not be ordained.”

Regarding the word "said": even though it was given with a permissible statement (*kappiya-vacana*), it is said to be "stated thus" because [the recipient] is merely a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*) or a slave of the Saṅgha.

In the *Vimativinodanī* as well, it says: "In certain regions, when making mirrors, they pour buttermilk on the head—just like pouring [it] on a head—as if it were similar; by that, it is said, they become mirror-makers. In the same way, this too [is stated] by means of the term 'monastery attendant' (*ārāmika*)."
The intention is that even if he has been given [to the Saṅgha]. Likewise, even if he has been given, because he is merely a monastery attendant (ārāmika) or a slave of the Saṅgha, it is stated:

“He must not be ordained. Because it is said, “What is called ‘temporary’,” everything given—whether by setting a time limit or with the desire to take him back later—must be understood as being only temporary.
As for one called a “slave without an owner,” it refers to one whose family of owners...

"One who is unrelated and whose life has ended without any heir must first be made free—either by those of his own kin, or by the inhabitants of his village, or by his masters—and only then may he be ordained. As for temple slaves (*devadāsa*), they are indeed slaves;
for in some places they are royal slaves, while in others they are monastery slaves. Therefore, it is not permissible to ordain them. Thus it was said.
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, however, it is said: "A masterless slave is one whose owners, including their children and wives, have died, and no one remains to claim him as property;
such a person may not be ordained, yet it is permissible for [the monk] himself to make him a free man.
Or, if there are owners in that kingdom, it is also permissible to have [his freedom] granted by them, [saying]: 'The son of a divine slave...'"
"It is permissible to grant him the going-forth," so it is stated in the three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.
Furthermore, it is said: "There is no offense for a slave who, having gone forth, flees upon seeing his own master. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated:

"Even if one has granted a slave the going-forth, if he is led away for the purpose of concealment upon seeing his master, he should be dealt with according to the offense of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) for every step taken."
"However, there is no offense for one who runs away while being a slave," it is said.
132. Regarding the cases of those whose hands have been cut off and so forth: "at the base of the ear" refers to the cutting off of the entire ear.
"The ear-socket" means the lobe of the ear. "For whom the ear is pierced" refers to the hole below for inserting earrings and the like.
This was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*). For that [bone] is capable of bearing contact. "At the *ajapada*" means at the tip of the nasal bone shaped like a goat's hoof;
for beyond that point, it is not possible to cut it off. "To join together" (*sandhetuṃ*) was said with reference to a symmetrical shape;
however, an asymmetrical one brings about what is offensive to the assembly.
"Khujjasarīro" means one with a crooked body. "Brahmujugatto" refers to the Blessed One, whose limbs and body are as straight as those of Brahmā.

"The rest are beings" refers to those beings devoid of these characteristics. By this, he shows that, setting aside the Great Man (Mahāpurisa) and the Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti), all other beings belong to the class of the hunchbacked.
For, generally speaking, [the bodies of] beings are [crooked] at the shoulders and the waist...
They bend at three places: when they bend at the waist, they bend backward; when they bend at two places, they bend forward.
Furthermore, some have long bodies that are crooked on one side; some walk with their mouths upturned as if counting the constellations;
some have little flesh and blood and are like spikes; and some [bend] forward.
They become protruding and move while quivering. "Parivaṭuma" means a body that is rounded all over;
by this, he shows that such types of dwarfs are not permitted.
133. "A body consisting only of bones, sinews, and skin" means a body that is merely bones, sinews, and skin. "Kūṭakūṭasīsa" refers to one who has many protuberances in various places.
The repetition (*āmeḍita*) is used to show the state of the flesh being compacted. Therefore he said, “resembling a cluster of palm fruits.
A cluster of palm fruits is called a *piṇḍi*. “With a head that gradually tapers” means with a head that becomes progressively thinner, like a stupa-shrine (*cetiyathūpikā*).
He was endowed with a head that was even in thickness from beginning to end, like a large bamboo joint.
“Nāḷisīso” means one whose head is like a bamboo tube. “Kappasīso” means one whose head is split in two like the top of an elephant’s head.

The phrase “or *kaṇṇikakeso*” is explained by the passage beginning with “by insects,” and so forth. The expression “with hair on the head” (*sīsalomehi*) refers to the fact that, as in a monkey, hair grows even upon the forehead.
“Monkey-faced” (*makkaṭabhamuko*) means one whose eyebrows are undifferentiated due to the hair on the forehead. “With eye-circles” (*akkhicakkehi*) means with the sockets of the eyes.
*Kekaroti tiriyaṃ passanako*: one who looks askance. *Udakatarakā* refers to the reflected images in water for those looking down.
Some say it means "water bubbles. *Akkhitārakā* refers to the reflection of those standing directly in front; they also call them "eye-ornaments" (*akkhibhaṇḍaka*).
*Atipiṅgalakkhi* means having very tawny eyes, like those of a cat. *Madhupiṅgalaṃ* means tawny with the color of honey. Regarding *nippakhumakkhī*, here the word *pakhuma* [means eyelashes].
"Having eyelashes" (*nippakhuma*) means that [the term] is established as referring to the eyelids; due to the absence of those [eyelashes], it is "eyelashless.

"By inflammation of the eyes" (*akkhipākena*) means by a disease arising from putrefaction at the margins of the eyelids. "Flat-nosed" (*cipiṭanāsika*) means one whose nose is not prominent. A "cricket-frog" (*paṭaṅgamaṇḍūka*) is a large-mouthed frog. "Split-mouthed" (*bhinnamukha*) means...
"Having his mouth covered at the beginning and end" means that his mouth is always kept closed. "Crooked-mouthed" refers to one whose lower jaw bone is positioned off to one side.
"One with severed lips" is one who possesses lips from which the flesh has been removed by a weapon or other means, whether by birth or subsequently.
"Slobbering-mouthed" is one whose mouth constantly drips with saliva.

“Split-necked” (*bhinnagaloti*) means one whose neck is bent down. “Split-chested” (*bhinnoroti*) means one whose middle of the chest is deeply sunken. “Likewise, split-backed” (*evaṃ bhinnapiṭṭhīti*) is explained in the same way.

The phrase “all this” (*sabbañcetaṃ*) is said with reference to [the description] beginning with “itchy body” (*kacchugatto*). And here, since the detailed analysis (*vinicchayo*) has already been stated regarding leprosy (*kuṭṭha*) and other diseases, he says “the analysis,” and so forth.

“One with testicular swelling” (*vātaṇḍiko*) means one who possesses a disease characterized by the enlargement of the testicles; due to the wind-disease of the testicles, the seed-filled scrotum becomes swollen.
Or one who possesses [such a deformity]. He whose high protuberance is revealed even when covered by his lower robe must not be ordained.
"Vikaṭa" means one who has feet that move sideways; when he walks, his kneecaps protrude outward.
"Saṅghaṭṭa" means one who moves with feet that turn inward; when he walks, his kneecaps enter within.
"Mahājaṅgho" means having thick calves. "Mahāpādo" means endowed with large soles of the feet. "Pādavemajjhe" refers to the middle of the insteps;
by this, he shows that the forepart of the foot and the heel are similar [in size].
(134) "Because the feet are contracted in the middle" indicates the cause for having stunted feet; "because the feet are contracted at the tips" [indicates the cause for having long feet].
Regarding "having stunted feet": the manifestation of the walking of one with stunted feet is described as "walking with the back of the foot.
And the expressions "with the outer edge of the foot" and "with the inner edge" are stated with reference to walking with both edges of the sole of the foot.
“Mammana” is a term for faltering speech; it is a designation for one who utters a single syllable four or five times.

Due to the absence of purity in the points of articulation (*ṭhāna*) and the modes of formation (*karaṇa*), his speech fails to touch the phonemes clearly. Indeed, he is called “mammana” because of his imitation of speech.
Furthermore, one who, though possessing the proper modes of articulation, repeatedly utters a single syllable with a hiccup-like sound, is also included here.

Alternatively, one who is capable of speaking with relaxed yet coherent speech—even if it requires restraining [the urge to speak quickly]—and who uses syllables that are not mumbled, may be ordained.
Those who act while knowing that they will not be freed from an offense do not indeed become free from it.
There is no offense for one who, out of aversion, grants formal communal agreement (*kāyasāmaggi*) during emergencies such as threats to life.

135. Regarding the discourses on persons incapable [of spiritual attainment], some say: "One who is a woman during the dark fortnight and a man during the bright fortnight is a *pakkhapaṇḍaka* (a fortnight-impotent).

However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, because it is stated that "during the dark fortnight he is a *paṇḍaka*, but during the bright fortnight his feverish passion (*pariḷāha*) is pacified"—referring specifically to the pacification of passion during the non-*paṇḍaka* fortnight—it follows that there is an intensification of passion during the *paṇḍaka* fortnight.
One should investigate and adopt the more appropriate interpretation, namely that it is understood as "falling into the state of a *paṇḍaka*.

An *abhāvaka* is one who lacks either the female state or the male state. Regarding the statement, "In that very same category, his admission to the order is forbidden," it is said in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries:
"Having admitted him when he is in the non-*paṇḍaka* category, he is to be expelled when he falls into the *paṇḍaka* category. However, some [hold that] "in the non-*paṇḍaka* category..."
If they say, “Once he has gone forth, if he reaches the destruction of the defilements (*kilesakkhaya*), he should not be expelled,” that is merely their own opinion.
For it is impossible for a paṇḍaka to reach the destruction of the defilements, and one whose defilements are destroyed cannot incur the state of being a paṇḍaka.

Indeed, in the discussion on rebirth-linking without roots (*ahetuka-paṭisandhi*), it is stated without distinction that a paṇḍaka possesses rebirth-linking without roots; and as for the *āsitta*, *ussūya*, and *pakkha* types of paṇḍakas, [this applies] from the moment of rebirth-linking.
They say that the state of being a *paṇḍaka* exists from the very moment of conception, and not only during the course of existence (*pavatti*).

For this very reason, in the description of rootless rebirth-linking (*ahetuka-paṭisandhi*), the *paṇḍaka* is not specified by the term "birth" (*jāti*) as are those who are blind from birth, deaf from birth, and so forth.

Furthermore, in the commentary on the fourth *pārājika*, while pointing out individuals incapable [of spiritual progress], it states that there are three types of those whose basis is defective: the *paṇḍaka*, the animal, and the hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*).
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated without qualification that for those who possess a rootless rebirth-linking (*ahetukapaṭisandhika*), heaven is not barred, but the Path is barred. However,
in the *Vimativinodanī*, regarding the case of the eunuch (*paṇḍaka*),
it is said that the three types— the eunuch by birth, the eunuch by injury, and the eunuch by envy— are all endowed with the male nature, gender marks, and so forth.

Those who have a rootless rebirth-linking (ahetukapaṭisandhika) are called "paṇḍakas" because, due to the strength of their obsession by defilements (kilesapariyuṭṭhāna), they resemble eunuchs and impotent men.
Among them, it is possible to restrain the obsession by defilements of the two types—the *āsitta* and *ussūya* paṇḍakas—by means of proper attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and so forth;
therefore, it is said that these two may be ordained. However, as for the *pakkha-paṇḍaka*...
The fever of the defilements (*kilesapariḷāha*) comes surging forward like madness during the dark fortnight (*kāḷapakkha*), and it only subsides after reaching transgression;
therefore, it is said that one in such a state should not be ordained during that fortnight. To demonstrate this distinction, it is said:
"for whom others... In this context, "of one who has been poured in" means of one into whose mouth [impurity] has been poured by his own emission of filth.
The fever subsides. Regarding "when envy has arisen": when, by way of envy, a lust for one's own desire to indulge [another] has arisen, the fever of impure emission subsides.
Because it is said, "the seeds have been removed," a paṇḍaka does not cease to be one merely when the signs are removed while the seeds remain.
For a bhikkhunī as well, if she removes it for reasons other than illness, there is likewise a thullaccaya offense, but not the status of a *paṇḍaka*.

However, when the seeds have been removed, even the sexual organ is no longer capable of action through lust; the male state disappears, the male characteristics such as facial hair and so forth vanish, and even the full admission (*upasampadā*) is lost;
furthermore, the fever of the defilements in a *napuṃsaka-paṇḍaka* becomes difficult to restrain and leads to transgression.
Therefore, they say that even one who has been fully ordained in such a manner should be expelled.

If this is so, why was an offense of defeat (*pārājika*) not prescribed for the uprooting of a seed? Regarding this, some say: "This was indeed already prescribed by the Blessed One, because it was stated:
'Monks, a paṇḍaka who is unordained should not be ordained; one who is ordained should be expelled.'"
However, some say: "Because one who is a *paṇḍaka* is not such at the moment of extracting the seed, the offense of defeat (*pārājika*) was not prescribed for that moment.

But because that monk, whose seed has been extracted, later becomes a *paṇḍaka* in the manner described, becomes incapable [of the religious life], and thus ceases to be a fit subject for full ordination (*upasampadā*), his ordination consequently lapses."

Therefore, from the time he undergoes the state of being a *paṇḍaka* (impotent person), having been classified together with one who is a *napuṃsaka-paṇḍaka* by birth, it is said that he is "incapable" (*abhabba*)—meaning he should be expelled even though he has received full ordination (*upasampanna*)—but not prior to that.

And although this [latter type] possesses a cause, because his [sexual] faculty is destroyed, it is similar to the acausal [type], and thus even the Path does not arise for him; so they say. Others, however, [say...]
The statement, “It was said that one who has become a paṇḍaka through self-inflicted means prior to going forth must be expelled once ordained,
but for one already ordained, even if they later become so through self-inflicted means, the ordination does not cease,” is not correct.
For by the very same principle by which one is incapable [of the training] due to self-inflicted means prior to going forth, one remains so afterward as well.
It should be accepted after investigating whether it is so.

"Abhāvaka" means one for whom there is no state (bhāva) such as femininity and so forth. Regarding the phrase "renunciation is not prohibited," by the mention of "renunciation" alone, "full ordination" (upasampadā) is also included.
Therefore he said, "And for whom renunciation is prohibited here," and so forth. In that very same faction of his...

Regarding the phrase "ordination is forbidden": here it should be understood that even in the case of one who is not a *paṇḍaka*, he receives only the mere going-forth (*pabbajjā*), but even then full admission (*upasampadā*) is not permitted;
however, in the case of one who has come under the category of a *paṇḍaka*, he is to be expelled by the removal of his marks.
136. "He who has both sexual organs" means *ubhatobyañjanaka*; this refers to a domain of non-co-referential [terms].

This is a *bahubbīhi* compound with the elision of the case-ending (*vibhattialopa*) in the first member; this is what is being shown. Here, "sex organ" (*byañjana*) is intended to mean both the male characteristic (*purisanimitta*) and the female characteristic (*itthinimitta*).
Now, does a hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*) have only one faculty (*indriya*), or two?
It has only one, not two. If it is asked how this is known: "In whomsoever the female faculty (*itthindriya*) arises... [and so forth].
"Does femininity-faculty arise for one in whom masculinity-faculty arises? "No. Or, "Does masculinity-faculty arise for one in whom femininity-faculty arises?
"No. This is because, in the Abhidhamma, the simultaneous arising of two faculties within a single continuum is prohibited;
and this refers specifically to the femininity-faculty of a hermaphrodite female and the masculinity-faculty of a hermaphrodite male.

Regarding the "male faculty" (*purisindriya*): If this is so, does it not follow that there is an absence of the second sexual characteristic (*byañjana*), since the faculty has been stated to be the cause of the characteristic, and yet that [characteristic] is absent for him?
It is replied: His faculty is not the cause of the second sexual characteristic.
Why? Because of its constant absence. For when a thought of lust arises in a woman who is a hermaphrodite (*itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka*), [the male faculty is not present].
At that time, the male characteristic becomes manifest, while the female characteristic remains concealed and hidden;
likewise for the other in the case of the second person. If their faculty were the cause of the secondary characteristic, both characteristics would persist at all times;
yet they do not persist. Therefore, it should be understood that the faculty is not the cause of those characteristics.
"However, the cause here is precisely the lustful mind that acts as an assistant to the kamma.

And because he possesses only one sexual faculty (*indriya*), therefore, according to what is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, a hermaphrodite female (*itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka*) both conceives a fetus herself and causes another to conceive;
whereas a hermaphrodite male (*purisa-ubhatobyañjanaka*) causes another to conceive, but does not conceive himself.

In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it is stated: "The female hermaphrodite (*itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka*) is associated with the female faculty (*itthindriya*); the other [the male hermaphrodite] is associated with the male faculty (*purisindriya*).
For two natures do not arise simultaneously in a single individual, because this is rejected in the *Yamaka*.

The second sexual characteristic, moreover, arises devoid of its essential nature through an unwholesome consciousness accompanied by karma. In the case of ordinary females and males as well, it is karma alone [that determines the faculties]."

The cause of the physical marks (*byañjana*) and gender characteristics (*liṅga*) is [the faculty], not the existence itself, because the status of that existence as a condition for anything has not been stated in the *Paṭṭhāna*.
It is merely for the purpose of showing the occurrence of the physical marks and gender characteristics together with the existence that the commentaries state,
"dependent on the female faculty, the female marks, etc.," thus describing the faculty as the cause of the physical marks.

Furthermore, it should be understood that here, due to the power of unwholesomeness, a sexual organ arises even without [the other] organ. This applies to both types of hermaphrodites (*ubhatobyañjanaka*).
When passion arises in the female, then the male organ becomes manifest while the other remains concealed; when passion arises in the male, then the female organ becomes manifest.
The former is stated as "unconcealed," while the latter is stated as "concealed.
137. One who lives in communion through theft is a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*. And here, he is not intended merely as one who steals the communal life;
rather, he is one who steals the emblem, both of those, or both. Thus he said, "There are three kinds of *theyyasaṃvāsakas*," and so forth.
"He does not accept veneration according to seniority" means that he does not accept veneration from monks or novices according to their actual seniority.

"He accepts veneration according to seniority" means that, having himself committed a falsehood regarding his years, he accepts veneration according to seniority in accordance with the number of years he has falsely claimed.
By the phrase "the counting of a monk's years and so forth," it is indicated that this refers not only to formal acts (*ekakamma*) and the like.
This shows what is meant here by "living together.
Regarding the phrase "by fear of kings... etc.," the word "fear" (*bhaya*) should be applied to each [term] individually, such as "by fear of kings, by fear of famine," and so forth.

He does not consent to living together; that is, until he is one whose mind is pure, because he has abandoned the outward signs assumed out of fear of kings and other such causes, he remains one whose mind is pure.

The meaning is: "as long as he does not consent to living together. For if one, without fear of the king or other such motives, but solely out of a desire to live together with monks by deceiving them, takes the outward signs (liṅga), he becomes known as a "one who lives in communion through theft" (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*) precisely because of taking the signs with an impure mind.
However, this [person] does so with such an impure mind, out of a desire to deceive the monks...
As long as one does not consent to living together [with the Saṅgha] because of the absence [of such intent], so long one is not called a "thievish co-resident" (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*).

For this very reason, it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "In the case of those who have taken the outward signs out of fear of kings and the like, even though there is a deceptive thought—'Let them know me as a recluse rather than a householder'—no fault arises because of the absence of a desire to deceive the monks. However, some say that here [the condition] is "the subsiding of fear."

They say, “It is purity of mind. And this being so, it is understood that as long as one whose fear has been stilled does not consent to co-residence, he is not a thief-in-co-residence (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*).
And when this meaning is understood, it would follow that even if one consents to co-residence while his fear is not yet stilled, he would not be a thief-in-co-residence;
yet in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), for one whose fear is not yet stilled...
Even by accepting co-residence, it is shown that one must not accept co-residence with those who do not share the same views.
By the phrase "eating the food of all heretics," it is indicated that even when the danger has not yet subsided, one must certainly not accept co-residence;
for this very reason, it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "Because for one who, having come to the monastery, takes what belongs to the Saṅgha..."
"It is difficult to avoid [such food]; therefore, it was said: 'eating the alms-food of all sectarians.
Consequently, in this context, purity of mind should be understood as being restricted solely to those who have assumed the outward signs out of fear of kings and the like.
"The alms-food of all sectarians" means having set aside [food] at crossroads and the like, making it common to all members of all religious orders.
"Portions of food should be given. "To be carried by the body" means they must be borne by the body.
"They go forth toward" means they go directly forward. "By not performing their work" means by not doing such tasks as plowing or tending cattle.
"Taking that very same bowl and robe, he goes to the monastery" means taking the robes for the purpose of wearing them as an undergarment and an upper garment, and the bowl upon the shoulder.
Having fastened it on, he goes to the monastery.

Nor does he know for himself [the consequences], meaning he does not know: "One who goes forth in this way is called a thief-living monk," or "It is not permitted to do it in this way," or "One who has gone forth in this way is not truly a recluse. One who [does] thus...
"He goes forth; he is called one who dwells in communion by theft"—this, however, is merely an illustration.

By the phrase "even while still unordained," it is shown that even if one hears [the accusation] at the time of ordination and does not report it, one does not become one who dwells in communion by theft.
"Without having renounced the training... one does not become one who dwells in communion by theft"—this refers to one who has received the outward signs from the monks.

It is said that because he has not abandoned [the robes], he does not become one who lacks the characteristic mark (liṅga), and because he has consented to a communal life (saṃvāsa) corresponding to that mark, he does not become one who lacks communal life.
In the passage, "A certain bhikkhu, still intent on the yellow robe, put on white clothes," this same reason should be understood.

Furthermore, regarding the rules stated for a novice (sāmaṇera) later on, such as "the novice remains established in his own characteristic mark," it should be understood that he stands on the side of non-robbery and communal life.

This is the same method. The statement, "The same method applies to a bhikkhunī as well," clarifies the aforementioned point by means of the passage beginning with, "She too, desiring the state of a householder...
If someone says, "one who went forth late in life," this refers to a *sāmaṇera*. By the phrase "in the *mahāpeḷā* and so forth," that which belongs to a householder is indicated.

Regarding the passage, "...by way of the sequence of the *sāmaṇeras*... he does not become one living in communion through theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*)," although he may indeed be a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* here—
It does not exist [as such], yet one certainly incurs a *pārājika* offense. "The rest here is self-evident," it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: "Even the mere assumption of the outward marks for the purpose of theft constitutes 'co-residence' (*saṃvāsa*) here;
thus, it says 'three types of those who co-reside through theft. 'Not according to seniority' refers to the salutation of monks by novices."
"He does not consent" means that he consents to the monks’ paying him homage according to his seniority by means of a false declaration of his years of seniority (*vassa*).

However, even if a young novice consents to being paid homage by older novices, or young bhikkhus consent to being paid homage by elders, they do not become "living in communion through theft" (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*). In this context, the meaning is "in the sense of living together."

"Bhikkhu-years" is stated here according to the reading given for one who lives in communion; however, even one who has gone forth on his own and counts the years as a novice is likewise one who lives in communion.

And not only a man, but a woman also who behaves in this way toward the bhikkhunīs is indeed one who lives in communion by theft. Furthermore, even a first offender here is not exempt [from the offense]. Regarding those who are fully ordained...
Thus, the first offender (*ādikammika*) is mentioned with reference to an offense that has been formally defined; for that very reason, even the first offender is not exempt here.
Regarding the phrase "by the king... by fear," the word "fear" (*bhaya*) should be construed with each [term].

As far as the expression "he whose mind is pure" (*suddhamānasa*), it means one whose mind is pure due to the absence of impure intent, such as thinking, "I will deceive these monks by this outward sign and live together with them. By that—
For if one has taken up the outward marks with an impure mind, then whether he lives together with other monks afterwards or not, he is a "mark-thief" (liṅgatthenaka).
Even if he later lives together with them, he lives having become incapable [of the training];

therefore, it should be understood that even one who is a "both-thief" (ubhayatthenaka) is included within the category of "mark-thieves. However, one who, out of fear of kings and the like, takes up the marks while his mind is indeed pure and wanders about...

Later, if he generates an impure thought, thinking, "I shall live by counting my years as a monk," he does not become one who dwells in communion through theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*) merely by that arising of thought, because the outward sign has been received with a pure mind. However,

if he goes into the presence of the monks and performs the counting of novice-years and so forth, then he becomes one who dwells in communion by means of both [the sign and the count], or one who dwells in communion by means of both.

This must be understood. As for what is stated later—"With the laying down of the burden, he too is one who dwells in communion through theft"—that refers to the laying down of the burden by way of the monks coming together and consenting to live in communion with him. Therefore it is said:
"As long as he does not consent to communion," meaning that for that long he is not called one who dwells in communion through theft.
The connection should be understood. And here, it should be understood that even one who— without fear of thieves or the like— takes the marks with the intention of playing,
shows the dwelling place of those gone forth in the presence of monks, and does not consent to acts such as prostration, yet takes them with a pure mind, thinking,
"Does this mark of one gone forth look good on me?", is not a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one living in communion by theft).
“Meals for all sectarians” refers to meals prepared by making them common to all members of all religious communities.
This is stated because, if one were to take meals designated exclusively for monks, even co-residency (*saṃvāsa*) might occur; therefore, it is called “meals common to all.
However, even if one eats meals provided to monasteries in forest hermitages or similar places where no monks reside, provided that one does not consent to co-residency, [there is no offense].
He is indeed not one who dwells in communion through theft. "By not performing work" means by not engaging in such tasks as plowing and so forth.
"Taking up bowl and robe" means wearing them on the body by way of the outward signs of a bhikkhu.
That one who goes forth in this manner is called a "thievish dweller in communion"—this is merely an illustration. "Thievish dweller in communion."
However, even if one does not know the name [of the rule], if one knows that "it is not permissible to act in this way," or "one who acts thus is not a recluse," or "if I confess it,
they will cast me out," or "by any means my going-forth has failed," he is a thief-living-in-the-community (theyyasaṃvāsaka).
But he who initially perceives, "I have received the going-forth in this manner"—
If he does not speak merely because he is ashamed to reveal his own disfigurement, such as the wearing of white garments and so forth, during the interval,

he is not a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*. Regarding the phrase "even at the time when he was not yet ordained," the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) here indicates that even if he knows the characteristics of a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* at the time of his ordination and does not disclose them out of deception, he is still not a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*.
For one who has taken the outward signs with a pure mind is not a "sign-thief" (*liṅgatthenaka*);

and because he has received full ordination (*upasampadā*) and has consented to a communal life consistent with that, he is also not a "communal-life-thief" (*saṃvāsatthenaka*). However, one who is not fully ordained is a sign-thief;
and one becomes a communal-life-thief merely by consenting to communal life while having taken the signs of one who is eligible for such communion.
“Abiding in the outward mark” means abiding in the state of possessing the outward mark.

“He is not one who dwells in communion by theft” means that because he has not relinquished the outward mark bestowed by the monks, he is not one who steals the mark; and because he has not relinquished his claim to being a monk, he is not one who steals communion.
As for what is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: “Nor is he one who steals communion, because he has consented to a communion corresponding to the mark.”
The reason that was stated was also stated with reference to this very reason.
