Otherwise, since even for a novice (sāmaṇera) living in communion according to his outward mark (liṅga) is admitted in matters such as counting the number of years since ordination as a monk, there would be no sense in specifying "living in communion" because the mark given by the monks is common to both.
And just as it is here for a monk, so too for a novice who has fallen into a defeat (pārājika).

It should be understood that because he has not renounced [the training] by means of a novice’s formal declaration (*sāmaṇerapaṭiññā*), he does not lose his status as one who lives in communion (*saṃvāsatthenaka*).
"He shines" means having accepted; that is, having set aside the burden of wearing the saffron robes and having accepted the state of a householder.
If it says "somebody who went forth when old," this is said with reference to a novice (*sāmaṇera*). "In the great baskets, etc. refers to those made of bamboo and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "when various food vessels have been placed at the doors of houses," it is stated that this indicates the non-performance of the calculation of the rainy season retreat (*vassa*) and other such duties with the monks in the monastery. 139.

In the discussion on those who have gone over to other sects (*titthiya-pakkantaka*), it is said: "As soon as they have taken up their [heretical] marks, they become one who has gone over to another sect."

It is stated [in this way] because, for one who has gone forth with the thought, “I shall become a sectarian,” by the very act of assuming their outward signs (*liṅga*), their tenets (*laddhi*) are also necessarily included.
However, some have said, “As soon as their signs are taken up, whether their tenets are grasped or not, one becomes a sectarian renegade (*titthiyapakkantaka*);
that should not be accepted. For [the rule applies] to one who thinks, “I shall become a sectarian...”

There is no other way of adopting a tenet (*laddhi*) than by accepting the outward signs (*liṅgasampaṭicchanato*). Indeed, it is precisely through the acceptance of the signs that one becomes a holder of that tenet.
For this very reason it is said: "For the sake of testing, [if he wears] grass-cloths and so forth... as long as he does not accept them, that tenet remains intact;
the moment they are accepted, he has gone over to the faction of the heretics (*titthiyapakkantaka*). He is [then] naked indeed.
Regarding the statement, "For every step taken toward the dwelling place of the Ājīvakas,

it is a dukkaṭa offense," this refers to a dukkaṭa committed on account of going with an impure mind, thinking, "I shall become an Ājīvaka. It is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī* that even for the offense of going naked,
one is not exempt from a dukkaṭa for every step taken.
In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, regarding the discussion on those who have gone over to other sects (*titthiya-pakkantaka*) and so forth:

"Merely having taken up their marks" means that, without the intention for investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) and so on, but by way of the resolve, "I shall become a member of another sect," one has merely physically assumed the marks.

"By oneself" means that, without going into the presence of the members of other sects, one personally puts on the grass-cloth (*kusacīra*) and so forth even within a monastic park (*saṅghārāma*). [This refers to] an Ājīvaka.
“He will become... [etc. ...he goes”: thinking “I shall become an Ājīvaka,” he goes into the presence of the Ājīvakas according to their procedure for going forth.

For although his resolve regarding the act of entering the state of a sectarian (titthiya) exists, because he has merely conceived the thought “having gone, I shall become one,” only a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) is stated for each step taken.
Regarding the *dukkaṭa*, even though it was not explicitly mentioned in the Canon in the case of sexual intercourse and so forth—
This was stated because it conforms to the previous mention of the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

By this, it should be understood that when the sign is accepted through formal determination, there is a *pārājika* offense; and prior to that, in the preliminary effort, a *thullaccaya* must indeed be mentioned. Even one who turns back at the moment of the *thullaccaya* is freed only after being made to confess the offense.
And as it is here, so it is also in the case of schism in the Saṅgha and in the shedding of blood.
The boundary for monks' exemption from *dukkaṭa*, *thullaccaya*, and *pārājika* offenses regarding prior applications and so forth should be understood.
Because it contradicts the Dispensation (*sāsana*), even for first-time offenders (*ādikammika*), non-offense is not stated here.

However, in order to demonstrate their incapacity even for the going-forth (*pabbajjā*), these and others are included here among the "incapable" (*abhabba*)—without showing the *pārājika* and other offenses as separate training rules (*sikkhāpada*) in the *Pārājika-khaṇḍa*.
It should be understood that it was said thus.
"That doctrine" (taṃ laddhi) is said with reference specifically to the grasping of the state of being superior while in the guise of a sectarian (titthiya).

For even if one adopts the graspings of those sectarians, such as eternalism and so forth, one does not become one who has gone over to the sectarians (titthiyapakkantaka) unless the sectarian insignia (liṅga) is accepted; [it refers to] that doctrine.

Even if one has not actually taken them up, one becomes a renegade who has gone over to another sect (titthiyapakkantaka) simply by accepting their outward signs, thinking, "How beautiful indeed is the conduct of these [ascetics].
"By the absence of such a conviction" means by the absence of the conviction to adopt the state of a non-Buddhist ascetic due to a lingering attachment to the status of a monk.
By this, he shows that even when one wears a garment of kusa grass or similar materials during times of distress, there is no offense, as if one were naked.

Regarding the phrase "spoken by an ordained bhikkhu": here, even one who causes a schism in the Saṅgha is spoken of as an "ordained bhikkhu," whereas it should be understood that those such as matricides are spoken of as "not ordained. 140.
Regarding "animal talk" (tiracchānakathā): "anyone belonging to the class of non-humans is, for the purpose of this context, considered an 'animal' (tiracchānagata)."
By the phrase "is to be known," it is shown that only those belonging to the human race are permitted to go forth or receive full ordination in the Blessed One’s teaching, and no others.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "You, O Nāgas, are of a nature not to grow in this Dhamma and Vinaya."

141. In the discussion on the immediate offenses (*ānantariya*), it is said that for those born as humans, even such qualities as loving-kindness toward the children of human parents become sharp and intense, just like supramundane virtues; thus he says, “the mother who has become a human woman is the progenitor.
Just as the occurrence of wholesome states is sharp and intense only for humans, so too is the occurrence of unwholesome states; thus he says, “he himself being of human birth,” and so forth.
Alternatively, since an action is weightier when it involves the violation of one of the same species rather than one of a different species, he said, "having become a human woman.

The designation "mother" and "father" is established through the connection of having a child; however, the term "child" is also seen in common usage in the world by way of being given away, being adopted, and so forth.
To show that this is merely figurative (pariyāya), he said, "the mother who gave birth," thereby demonstrating its establishment in the non-figurative sense (nippariyāya).

It has been said: just as for one remaining in a human existence there is the attainment of a sharp, clear, and courageous state regarding wholesome states—as occurred during the arising of the threefold enlightenment of the three Bodhisattas—so too for one remaining in a human existence there is the attainment of a sharp, clear, and courageous state regarding unwholesome states; thus he said, "he himself, being of human birth."
Regarding the term *ānantariya*: here, "immediate" (*anantara*) refers to the result of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in hell immediately after death;
that which is connected to this immediate [result] by way of being its producer is called *ānantariya*. Alternatively, "immediate" refers to the result immediately following death;
that which is connected to this immediate [result], having the nature of producing it and having it as its purpose, is *ānantariya*.
Or [it refers to] an immediate offense (*ānantariya*); by that immediate offense of matricide. Regarding patricide as well, everything should be understood in the same way, starting with:
"When one who is human intentionally deprives his own father, who is also human, of life, this person is a patricide by virtue of the immediate offense of patricide.
Thus he said: "The same method applies to patricide as well."
Even for one who deprives of life a mother or a father whose gender has been changed, there is indeed an immediate kamma (*ānantariya-kamma*).

For even though the gender has changed, that very same continuum of existence (*bhavaṅga-pabandha*) and continuum of life (*jīvita-pabandha*), produced by that single kamma, remains the same and is not something else.
Furthermore, if a person who is himself human kills a father or a mother who has become an animal, or if he himself—
If one who has become an animal deprives a human being of life, or if an animal itself deprives another animal of life, that action does not constitute an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense;
however, it is grave, and it remains as having reached the level of an *ānantariya*.
Herein, the "fourfold set on sheep," the "fourfold set on battle," and the "fourfold set on thieves" should be explained. Even with the intention, "I shall kill a sheep," [the act is grave].
For indeed, when a human being kills his mother or father— who are standing in the position of a sheep— while intending their death,

he incurs an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense because the basis for such an offense has been destroyed by the very intention to kill. However, one who kills a sheep with the intention of killing a sheep,
or with the intention of killing his mother or father, does not incur an *ānantariya* offense, because the basis for an *ānantariya* offense has not been destroyed.
Because of the absence [of the object]. One who kills his mother or father with the intention directed toward them certainly incurs [the full offense].
This same method applies to the other two tetrads as well. And just as it is with respect to mother and father, so too should these tetrads be understood regarding Arahants.
For in all cases, the preliminary volition is immeasurable; however, the murderous intent and the life-faculty that serves as its object [are the decisive factors].
This is the measure. And one who has committed an act of immediate retribution—

even if they were to fill the entire world-system with golden stupas the size of the Great Cetiya, even if they were to give a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of monks seated filling the entire world-system,
and even if they were to wander about never letting go of the corner of the Blessed Buddha’s outer robe— [would still not escape].
Upon the breakup of the body, he is reborn in hell and does not obtain the going-forth. The phrase "the son of a courtesan who killed his father" is merely illustrative;

even the son of a woman of good family who commits adultery becomes a patricide if he kills his own father without knowing him to be his father. Regarding the act of killing an arahant, the term "the remainder" refers to those such as non-returners (anāgāmin) and so forth.
This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be taken from the commentary on the third *pārājika*.
“With a corrupt mind” (*duṭṭhacittena*) clarifies the very same meaning as “with a murderous mind” (*vadhakacittena*).
For here, a mind defiled by the volition of killing is what is called a “corrupt mind. Regarding the phrase “he draws blood”:
because the Tathāgata possesses an indestructible body, there is no shedding of blood through external assault that results in the cutting of the skin; rather, it occurs only within the body itself.
In one place, blood collects; agitated by resentment, it becomes accumulated.
Even the splinter that had split off from the stone hurled by Devadatta struck the edge of the Tathāgata’s foot, so that the foot became filled with internal blood as if struck by an axe.
However, at the Tathāgata’s own wish, Jīvaka [removed it] with a lancet.
Having cut away the skin and removed the foul blood from that place, he made it healthy; thus, for him, there was only meritorious karma.
Therefore, it says, "like Jīvaka," and so forth.
Now, as for those who, after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, destroy a shrine, cut down a Bodhi tree, or take action against the relics—
What happens to them? It is a grave offense, similar to an *ānantariya* (immediate) deed.
However, it is permissible to cut down a branch of a Bodhi tree that is damaging a stupa or an image containing relics.

Even if birds perched there void their excrement upon the shrine (*cetiya*), it is still permissible to cut it down; for the relic-shrine (*sarīracetiya*) is more venerable than a shrine used for enjoyment (*paribhogacetiya*).
It is even more so. When one goes after breaking up the site of a cetiya, it is permissible to cut down [trees] even at the foot of the Bodhi tree and carry them away.
However, if a branch of the Bodhi tree obstructs the Bodhi hall, one is not permitted to cut it down for the sake of protecting the building.
For the house exists for the sake of the Bodhi tree, not the Bodhi tree for the sake of the house. The same principle applies to the seat-hall (*āsana-ghara*). But in whichever...
If a relic is enshrined in the seat-house (āsana-ghara), it is permissible to cut that branch for the purpose of protecting it.
It is likewise permissible to cut a branch that withers the vitality [of the tree] or a rotten spot for the sake of tending to the Bodhi tree;
merit is gained just as if one were tending to the physical body of the Teacher.
Regarding "of the four formal acts in the case of schism in the Saṅgha": this refers to the four formal acts beginning with the *apalokana* (motion).
The statement "this is a schismatic" is said with reference to a regular (*pakatatta*) bhikkhu.

Even one who splits the Saṅgha while already having fallen into a *pārājika* offense, or whose higher ordination has been invalidated due to defects in the subject matter (*vatthu*) and so forth, does not incur an immediate retribution (*ānantariya*); however, the Saṅgha itself remains split.
It should be understood that he exists and his going forth has not been prohibited.
Regarding the phrase "desiring to defile a bhikkhunī," it means desiring one who is dressed in white robes. For this very reason, it says: "as soon as [the state] of being a householder is accepted.
The construction is: "neither is there going forth" (for him). And as for one who, having recognized a person who is rejected or incapable, nevertheless grants him the going forth—
Or if one ordains [her], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). It should be understood that for one who does not know, there is no offense in all cases.
142. "Twenty years together with the months of pregnancy" means *gabbhavīsa*.
It should be understood that "subtracting or adding" refers to subtracting when there are extra months of pregnancy, and adding when they are deficient. "Nineteen years" means twelve...
Having dwelt in the mother’s womb for one month, [he spent] nineteen years from the time of his birth until the Great Pavāraṇā.
“On the first day of the month” means on the day of entering the rains retreat at the later term (*pacchimikā*).
Because of the statement, “A month consists of thirty nights and days,” it is said that “four months are omitted. “They postpone the rains” means they draw the rains retreat upward.

The meaning is that because there is an extra month in the third year, they extend the rains-retreat (*vassa*) by means of relinquishing that month; therefore, the third year consists of thirteen months.
However, since a year consists of twelve months, it is stated—taking the extra months separately over the course of eighteen years—that "six months increase. From that...
"By the month": having become free from doubt means having become certain because she has reached twenty full years of age, including the extra months.

As for what is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "Because the calculation was made by taking the extra months of eighteen years only, there are also extra days for the remaining two years; it is with reference to those extra days [that this was said]."
As for the statement, “having become free from doubt,” that should not be accepted. For extra days do not exist separately during two years;
rather, it is only when an extra month is set aside by means of the postponement of the rains in the third year that an excess of one month occurs.
Therefore, extra days do not occur separately during two years.
Why was it said, “Having taken those two months, twenty years become complete”?
It is because when one who is nineteen years old adds another year, twenty years become complete; thus he said, “In this case, however...
[etc. ...it is said. Since particles have multiple meanings, the word *pana* has the sense of *hi*; that is, it is as if he had said, “in this case, for (*hi*)...”
This is stated by way of supporting the very point already mentioned. And by this he illustrates the following:

regarding what was said—that "one ordains a novice who is nineteen years old on the first day of the month, having passed the full-moon day of the departure-month"—therein, the term "nineteen years old" refers to one who is less than twenty years of age by two months, including even the months spent in the womb.
It has been stated; therefore, when two extra months (*adhikamāsa*) have been included, the twenty years are indeed considered complete.
"Therefore" means because even the months spent in the womb (*gabbhamāsa*) are subject to calculation, therefore [he is so called].

"He becomes one who is twenty-one years old" means that while he is twenty years old starting from the day of birth, he becomes twenty-one years old together with the months of the womb. "He ordains another."
"It ordains [the candidate] by acting as either a preceptor (upajjhāya) or a master of the formal ritual (kammavācācariya)"—this is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.

"One who has completed twenty years including the time spent in the womb" means one who has fulfilled the twentieth year counting from the period of lying in the womb; thus, he is "twenty-with-womb" (*gabbhavīso*).

"The full-moon day of the departure" refers to the full moon of the month of Sāvaṇa, which is the full moon immediately following the full moon of Āsāḷhī. "On the first day of the waxing moon" refers to the later [fortnight].

The meaning is that they confer full ordination on one born during the Great Pavāraṇā, after having dwelt in the mother’s womb for twelve months following the commencement of the rains-residence (*vassūpanāyikā*).
Because of the statement, “A month consists of thirty nights and days; a year consists of twelve months,” it is said that “four months are lost.
They “postpone the rains” means they draw the rains period upward; [this refers to] the fact that “one month is an intercalary month.”
The meaning is "entering the rains-retreat after having discarded [the previous one]"; therefore, every third year consists of thirteen months.

"Taking those two months" means: taking the two months obtained from the intercalary month for the sake of those two months that have not yet arrived, from the full moon of the departure until the Great Invitation (Mahāpavāraṇā) which is the day of birth. Thus he said.
“‘He who, having performed the *pavāraṇā*, will become twenty years of age,’ and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “having become free from doubt,” this is said with reference to the state of being fully twenty years of age in every respect; that is, by taking the extra months of eighteen years and then subtracting four months for the sake of the fourteenth-day observances even within those twenty years.

"Having performed the *pavāraṇā*, he will become twenty years [of seniority]" means that when the day of the Great *Pavāraṇā* has passed, he will become twenty years [of seniority] including the months spent in the womb.
"Therefore" means because even the months in the womb are included in the calculation;
therefore, "twenty-one years" is said with reference to being twenty years [of seniority] by birth. "He ordains another" refers to the preceptor (*upajjhāya*).
"Or, having become a teacher, he confers full ordination. "He too" refers to one who confers full ordination; this is stated in the *Vimativinodanī* as "one who is not fully ordained.

Here it may be asked: In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*), it is said that "within eighteen years, six months are added," but now they say "within nineteen years, seven months are additional. How is this to be understood?

It is said: in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*), following the terminology of the Dispensation (*sāsana-vohāra*) and not conforming to worldly reckoning, they adopt the practice of omitting a month every three years;
thus it is stated that "in eighteen years, six months are added.
However, now, calculating by adopting the lunar day (*tithi*)—which is defined as the movement of the moon and sun according to the terminology of the Vedas—it is said: "In nineteen years..."
"...and seven months additional," they say; this will become clear in the discussion on entering the rains residence (*vassūpanāyika*).
143. "Or the mother has died"—this is the connection. "He himself" refers to the one seeking admission to the order (*pabbajjāpekkha*).

144. "And there are other monks within the same boundary"—by this [it is shown that] when no monk is present within the same boundary, there is the duty of announcing the shaving of the head (*bhaṇḍukamma*).

He shows that [the rule] does not apply. By saying "standing within a broken boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) or having gone to a river, the ocean, and so forth, he may be ordained," he indicates that all monks residing within the boundary must be informed; it is not permitted to ordain him without informing them. 145.
"Almsfood not yet touched" means almsfood for which the portion for the foremost has not been taken. "A share of material goods equal to the novice's portion" means...
In this regard, although there is no separate portion for the novices (*sāmaṇera*) because they are given an equal share of the material goods,
the intention is that since the alms-food going downward might sometimes be insufficient, it should not be taken from above,
but rather given by taking it specifically from the novices' row. Furthermore, this portion is given only to one who is certain to go forth.
For this very reason, it was said: “The bowl is uncooked,” and so forth. The connection is: “or other bhikkhus may wish to give. 146.
“He himself should ordain” means he should ordain while performing the acts himself, such as cutting the hair and so on.
For one who performs these three—cutting the hair, donning the saffron robes, and granting the refuge—is said to “ordain”; among those [three], even one...
Even when performing both [acts], one is described in exactly that way; therefore, the statement "ordain him" refers specifically to the cutting of the hair and the donning of the saffron robes.

The same principle applies here to the phrase "he ordains with reference to a preceptor. "Having led him to the broken boundary" is stated for the purpose of avoiding the announcement of the shaving of the head.
By this, in a monastery containing monks, another [person] also... [of him].
It is not permissible to say, "Cut the hair. The word "having ordained" (*pabbājetvā*) is said with reference to the cutting of the hair.
The statement that no one other than a bhikkhu is allowed to ordain refers to the granting of the refuges (*saraṇadāna*).
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī* (Mahāvagga 3.34): "But as for the novice... and so forth. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*—

Regarding the phrase "he himself should be ordained": here, because of the statement beginning with "having shaved off hair and beard," what is called "ordination" consists of the cutting of the hair, the donning of the saffron robes, and the granting of refuge.
Among these, the latter two must be performed by the monks themselves, or caused to be performed by them.

The command "ordain him" is spoken with reference to all three of these. "Having led him to a delimited boundary (khaṇḍasīma)" is for the purpose of avoiding the need to announce the shaving of the head.
Indeed, without having informed the monks, it is not even permissible to command another within the same boundary, saying, "Shave this person's hair.

The phrase "having given the going-forth" (*pabbājetvā*) is stated specifically with reference to the shaving of the hair and so forth, because the phrase "having clothed him in the saffron robes" (*kāsāyāni acchādetvā*) is mentioned separately.

The statement "he is not permitted to give the going-forth" refers to the granting of the three refuges (*saraṇadāna*). [This applies] when one who is not fully ordained acts on the command of a monk.
It is stated that even if [the refuge] is given, it does not take root.
In the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā* (Vajira-ṭī. Mahāvagga 34) as well, it says: "Having led him to the broken boundary" is stated for the purpose of avoiding the announcement of the shaving of hair;
therefore, in a monastery where monks are present, it is not permissible to say to anyone else, "Shave this man's hair."
The phrase "having ordained" (*pabbājetvā*) is stated as "clothe him in the saffron robes and come" (*ehī*) for the purpose of clarifying its intended meaning.
If the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) grants the refuges for the sake of ordination without having first shaved the hair and beard and so forth, the ordination (*pabbajjā*) is not valid.

If he confers full admission (*upasampadā*) after announcing it through the formal ritual procedure (*kammavācā*), the full admission is valid; this is because it is shown that full admission is accomplished even for those who do not possess the robes and bowl.
Some say that this is indeed appropriate because there is no failure of the kamma. On this point there is a verse:
"Ordination is for one who possesses the [proper] marks; the other is also for one who lacks them.
For one who has discarded his former dress, it is both—so say others."

For it has been handed down that the intention of those [teachers] was this: "Only a yellow robe (kāsāva) that has been given by a monk either personally or by his command is permissible; one that is not given is not permissible. However, this applies only when yellow robes are available, for it is impossible when they are not.

"Of a capable nature" means having a nature that is competent. He clarifies that same meaning through a synonym: "having a cause. "Well-known" means famous. "Renowned" means endowed with a perfection of retinue.
By making manifest the state of being impure, loathsome, and repulsive through its color, shape, smell, location, and source...
The connection. In this regard, these head-hairs are repulsive by way of color, by way of shape, by way of odor, by way of their habitat, and by way of their location.
For even when one sees something with the color of head-hair in a bowl of pleasant rice gruel or a bowl of cooked rice, people feel disgust and say, "This is mixed with hair;
take it away! Thus, head-hairs are repulsive by way of color. At night...
Even while eating, people feel such loathing upon touching hair—whether it be the shape of a cock's comb or a piece of coarse cloth—that they are thus repulsive by way of their shape as well.

Furthermore, the smell of hair when devoid of any refinement such as oil-anointing, flowers, or incense is extremely foul; it becomes even more loathsome when thrown into a fire. For hair is [repulsive] by way of its color and shape...
They may not be repulsive by way of color, but they are indeed repulsive by way of odor.
For instance, the excrement of a young child is yellow in color like turmeric and in shape like a lump of turmeric;
whereas a black dog’s corpse, swollen and discarded in a rubbish heap, is the color of a ripe palmyra fruit and in shape like a discarded, round *mudiṅga* gourd.
His fangs are like jasmine buds; both of these might be non-repulsive in terms of color and shape, yet they are indeed repulsive by their odor.
In the same way, even hair might be non-repulsive in terms of color and shape, yet it is indeed repulsive by its odor.
Just as potherbs grown from village runoff in a place of filth are loathsome to city-dwellers, [so too are these things repulsive].
They are not to be used; likewise, because the hair is produced from the discharge of pus, blood, urine, feces, bile, phlegm, and so forth, it is supremely loathsome.
Thus, it is repulsive even by way of its source. Furthermore, these things called "hair" are born upon a heap of thirty-one bodily parts like sprouts growing on a mound of dung;
they are like vegetables grown in charnel grounds, rubbish heaps, and the like, or in moats and such places.

The meaning is: by demonstrating the repulsiveness of the five-skin group (*tacapañcaka*) through its color and other qualities, according to the method beginning with "repulsive from the standpoint of location" (*okāsato paṭikūla*), just as a flower such as a *jātaka*, lotus, or water-lily is utterly loathsome because it grows in a place of impurity;
or, by making manifest its state of being devoid of life and soul (*nijjīvanissattabhāva*): "These things called 'hair' are on the skin that envelops the skull."
Just as, when short grass grows on the top of an anthill, the top of the anthill does not know,
"Short grass has grown upon me," nor do the short grasses know, "We have grown on the top of an anthill"— even so,
the skin enveloping the skull does not know, "Hair has grown upon me," nor do the hairs know [the same].
“‘We are born on the skin that envelops the skull’—these phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.

Thus, by demonstrating their state of being soulless and insentient in this manner: “What are called ‘head-hairs’ are a distinct component in this body, unconscious, indeterminate, empty, insubstantial, rigid, and the earth element,” and so forth. “In the past” means among the previous Buddhas.

"In the presence. "One who has rubbed away formations" (*madditasaṅkhāra*) is one whose formations have been thoroughly rubbed away by knowledge through the discernment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-vavatthāna*) and the investigation of conditions (*paccaya-pariggaha*).

"One who has developed development" (*bhāvitabhāvana*) is one who has developed development by completely fulfilling all wholesome development through the comprehension of groups (*kalāpasammasana*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "what is not given is not permissible," it is said here: "They say that the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) does not take root [in such a person]."
This is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: "Yasassī" means endowed with a retinue. "The state of being devoid of a living soul and a sentient being" refers to the method [of analysis] beginning with:
"Hair is a distinct constituent part in this body; it is insentient, indeterminate, empty, devoid of a sentient being, rigid, and the earth element."
He should collect [the requisites]; everything should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Visuddhimagga*.

"In former times" means during the appearances of previous Buddhas. "One who has crushed the formations" is said by way of insight (*vipassanā*). "One who has developed meditation" is also said by way of serenity (*samatha*).
Regarding the phrase "the saffron robes should be accepted three times...": here, [one should say], "For the sake of escaping all suffering, this..."

Having said, "Take the saffron robe," or "Give that saffron robe [to me]," he causes the robe to be accepted after first making the request: "Venerable sir, please grant me the going-forth out of compassion.
Now, the phrase "Then again" (*athāpi*) and so forth shows the procedure to be performed after the robe has been caused to be accepted three times;
"then again" means "even beyond that. However, some [commentators] say: "Without having caused the robe to be accepted..."
The phrase “then also” (*athāpi*) is stated for the purpose of showing the different modes of banishment. They say: “*Athāpi* means *atha vā* (or else).
By the statement “what is not given is not permitted,” it is shown that the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) does not succeed.
147. “Having had him make obeisance at his feet” means having made him bow down facing the feet; for even one who bows from a distance is said to be “bowing at the feet.”
It is said: "By the preceptor" (*upajjhāyena vā*). Herein, he in whose presence one receives the formal support (*upajjha*) is the preceptor (*upajjhāya*).
He whom they hand over as a teacher (*ācariya*) for the purpose of training in the *Ābhisamācārika* duties is the teacher (*ācariya*).
However, if the preceptor himself teaches everything and does not hand him over to another, then the preceptor is also his teacher.

It exists. Just as it was stated that at the time of full ordination (*upasampadā*), the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) himself, while reciting the formal ritual procedure (*kammavācā*), is also the teacher of the ritual procedure;

thus he is both. "Ordination by permission" means ordination permitted through a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*). Regarding "perfection of place and effort" (*ṭhānakaraṇasampadā*):

here, the chest and so forth should be understood as the places (*ṭhāna*), and the closed [lips] and so forth as the efforts (*karaṇa*). At the time of giving [the gift], having made [the word] end with a nasalization (*anunāsika*).
It is said "connected as one" (*ekasambandhāni*) in order to show that they should be given without making an interruption in between.
"Having interrupted" (*vicchinditvā*) means having made an interruption at the time of giving, using the form ending in the letter *m*.

148. "Everything, both allowable and unallowable, should be explained to him" refers to [matters] distinct from the ten training rules (*sikkhāpada*), such as the various classifications of misappropriation (*parāmāsa*) and non-misappropriation.
What is allowable and what is unallowable must be explained. Regarding the phrase "he should be trained in the matters of proper conduct (*ābhisamācārika*)," the *Sāratthadīpanī* states:
"By this [precept], he must fulfill the training rules (*sekhiya*), the duties toward the preceptor (*upajjhāyavatta*), and other such matters of proper conduct.

It indicates that if one fails to do what ought to be done therein, or does what ought not to be done, one becomes subject to disciplinary action. Having made the final syllable nasalized, there is an interruption at the time of giving.

"It should not be done," he said, [referring to] "those connected as one. In the *Ābhisamācārika*, by the phrase "he should be trained," it is shown in the *Vimativinodanī* that novices must conduct themselves according to the rules of training (*sekhiya*), the duties of the *Vatta-khandhaka*, and other world-transgressing precepts such as those concerning seminal emissions;
furthermore, it shows that one who fails to act accordingly therein is shameless and subject to disciplinary measures (*daṇḍakamma*).
The places beginning with *ur* are called "locations" (*ṭhāna*), while those beginning with *saṃvuta* are called "actions" (*karaṇa*).

Having made the end [of the word] nasalized and forming a single connection, one should speak without pausing in the middle at the time of giving [the recitation]. Even when dividing [the recitation] at the time of giving, the division must occur only at the aforementioned locations;
it is written that it is not permitted elsewhere. When the nasalized end is being given, if one stumbles and says "Buddhaṃ... [the rule applies].
Regarding the statement, "I go for refuge," the Elder Upatissa maintains that it is permissible because one has entered the field [of the Saṅgha] which is mixed with the letter *ma*.
The Elder Dhammasiri maintains that while it is permissible to speak by mixing [the letters], at the time of speaking, one must not make a pause at the position of the nasal (*anunāsika*).
It is stated, "The same applies to the formal ritual utterance (*kammavācā*). Regarding the phrase, "It is permissible only through purity on both sides": here—
The Mahāthera speaks while omitting [the name] because of reasons such as the loss of teeth;

however, it is not permissible for a learned novice standing nearby to cause the candidate for ordination—who is himself learned—to speak [on his behalf], nor for him to cause someone else to speak what was not spoken by the Mahāthera.
If the other monk (the novice) speaks during the formal ritual (*kammavācā*), it is permissible, for it is the Saṅgha that performs the ritual, not the individual person.
No, because it must be rejected according to the general method [of the Vinaya] regarding formal acts (*kammavācā*) performed within different boundaries.

Now, if a novice speaks for himself and causes one who cannot speak—who was described by the Elder as being "four-cornered" (*caturassa*)—to speak the words for seeking admission, there is purity on both sides, since what was spoken by the Elder has indeed been spoken.
"When going for refuge to the Buddha, [one recollects] the unique qualities of the Buddha..."

The construction should be made by way of including what has not yet been included: "One going for refuge to the Dhamma goes for refuge to Nibbāna; one going for refuge to the Saṅgha goes for refuge to both the qualities of those in training (sekha-dhamma) and the qualities of those beyond training (asekha-dhamma). Otherwise, there would be the fault of confusing the three refuges.

"All that is allowable and unallowable for him" refers to everything other than the ten precepts, including the various categories such as adherence to wrong graspings (parāmāsa) and non-adherence. [In] the *Ābhisamācārika*...

Because of the statement, “He is to be disciplined,” it is shown in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā* that he must fulfill the morality of higher conduct (*ābhisamācārika-sīla*), such as the training rules (*sekhiya*) and the duties toward the preceptor (*upajjhāya-vatta*).
In this regard, it is explained: “If one fails to do what is prescribed (*cāritta*) and does what is forbidden (*vāritta*), one becomes liable to disciplinary action.
Regarding passages such as, “I allow you, monks, ten training rules (*sikkhāpada*) for novices (*sāmaṇera*),” the term *sikkhāpada* refers to those points (*pada*) which are to be trained in.

The meaning is "sections of training" (*sikkhā-koṭṭhāsā*). Alternatively, they are "training-rules" (*sikkhā-padāni*), meaning they are the means for attaining the trainings in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom.

In terms of their actual nature, however, they are the abstentions associated with wholesome sense-sphere consciousness; the factors associated with them should be understood as being included by the mention of those [abstentions] themselves.
As for "living being" (*pāṇo*), in the ultimate sense it is the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*); its "taking away" (*atipātana*)—

Taking life (pāṇātipāta)—the meaning of which is the killing of a living being—is the act of causing a creature to fall by means of weapons and so forth, overcoming and surpassing it, not allowing it to continue its existence according to its natural course.
In terms of its essential nature, it is simply the murderous volition that originates the effort to sever the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) in a living being while perceiving it as such.
Therefore, "abstention from taking life" refers to the avoidance of unwholesome states such as taking life, which are designated as "enmity" because they are the cause of enmity.

Because it expels or removes [unwholesome states], it is called *virati*; it is termed *veramaṇī*. Alternatively, because one abstains by means of this, what should be called *viramati* is, according to the rules of etymology (*nirutti*), stated as *veramaṇī*;
thus, *samādāna-virati* (abstinence through formal undertaking) is expressed. This same method applies to the remaining [precepts] as well. The taking of what is not given is *adinnādāna*;
it is the volition of theft. *Abrahmacariya* means non-noble conduct; it is that which originates from practicing a path that is not the [true] path.

Sexual misconduct is the volition of sexual intercourse. False speech is a non-existent matter; false speech is the volition of making known as real what one knows to be unreal after having understood it as such.
Surā-meraya refers both to the fermented liquor produced from flour-cakes and the like (*surā*), and to the distilled spirits of various kinds such as *pupphāsava* and so forth (*meraya*).

That very same thing is intoxicant in the sense of causing intoxication (*majja*) and a basis for negligence in the sense of being a cause of heedlessness (*pamādaṭṭhāna*); that [abstinence] is by means of which volition...
"Drinks" is a designation for that very [act].
From the rising of the dawn until midday is called the time for food for the Noble Ones;
any other time is "the wrong time. In the sense of being something to be eaten, "food" here refers to everything that is "timely" (*yāvakālika*); its swallowing is—
Here, by the elision of the latter member of the compound, "food" (bhojana) is intended. "Unseasonable eating" (vikālabhojana) means the swallowing of food at an improper time;
or rather, the meaning should be understood as the swallowing of non-timely food at an improper time.
In terms of its actual meaning, it is simply the volition (cetanā) of swallowing non-timely food at an improper time.

Because it is not in conformity with the Dispensation (*sāsana*), watching spectacles is an obstacle; thus, "watching spectacles" (*visūkadassana*) is a term for both the seeing and hearing of dancing, singing, and so forth, as well as all games such as cockfights, dice games, and the like.

Furthermore, in this context, "seeing" (*dassana*) includes hearing as well, since all five types of consciousness (*viññāṇa*) are to be subsumed under the term "seeing" due to their common nature of perceiving their respective objects.
It is included. Herein, it should be understood that by the sounds of dancing, singing, and instrumental music, one's own dancing, singing, and so forth are also included.
"Garland" (*mālā*) refers to flowers, whether strung or unstrung; even that made of thread and the like, when worn for the sake of ornament, is called a garland.
"Fragrance" (*gandha*) refers to any kind of fragrant substance other than scented powders and ointments. "Ointment" (*vilepana*)...
Having ground it, one takes both the substances that color the skin and various perfumes. "Wearing" (dhāraṇa) means adorning oneself with them.
"Adorning" (maṇḍana) means filling out deficient parts of the body. "Decoration" (vibhūsana) means taking pleasure in them by way of their fragrance or by way of their coloring of the skin;
or else, wearing and so forth in relation to garlands and other such items should be applied respectively. The basis for these acts of wearing and so forth is the volition of transgression.
*Uccā* is a particle with the same meaning as the word *ucca*. "High bed" (*uccāsayana*) refers to items such as thrones that exceed the prescribed dimensions.
"Large bed" (*mahāsayana*) refers to one spread with improper coverings and having a canopy with red trim.

For in these cases, both the seat and the bed are included by the terms "high bed" and "large bed" through the elision of the final member of the compound. "Accepting gold and silver" (*jātarūparajatapaṭiggahaṇa*).
Here, by the term “silver” (rajata), all forms of money such as wooden māsakas and so forth are included.

It should be understood that pearls, gems, and the like, as well as grain, fields, land, and so forth, are also included here. Furthermore, by the term “acceptance” (paṭiggahaṇa), both causing another to accept and requesting [an item] are included.
149. By the phrase “the taking of lodgings is suspended,” he indicates the suspension of the rains-residence (vassaccheda). This applies even to those who are fully ordained (upasampanna).

Because the state of a novice—including the going for refuge and so forth—is destroyed by the attainment of a *pārājika* offense, it should be understood that his assignment of lodgings ceases and he no longer receives a share from the Saṅgha.

"The refuges were taken again during the first [rainy season]" indicates that, together with the taking of the refuges, he entered the rains retreat on that very same day. During the second [rainy season]...
"Rainy-season residence" (*vassāvāsika*) is merely a way of showing the taking of the share belonging to the rainy-season residence;

even before or after that, a novice who has not lapsed in virtue obtains the *vassāvāsika* robe-cloth, as well as the timely robe-cloth arising for the Saṅgha, by entering the rains-retreat during the earlier period.
"If they were taken during the later period" refers to the entering of the rains-retreat during the later period.
It also indicates one whose rains-residence has been cut short. For such a person does not receive the gain of a timely robe;

therefore it is said, "Having informed [the Sangha], the gain should be given. However, as for the *vassāvāsika* (rains-residence) gain, if the donors who are the owners of the lodging have entered during the later period (*pacchimikā*) for the purpose of guarding the lodging and have performed the duties, the *vassāvāsika* must be given even to one staying in his own lodging.
They say that it must indeed be given even without seeking permission. As for what is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*:

“One receives the *vassāvāsika* during the later period because one has entered the rains residence again during the later period”—if that was said based on this intention of the donors regarding the *vassāvāsika*, then it is excellent;
however, it was also said with reference to the *kālacīvara* belonging to the Saṅgha.
If it were stated [otherwise], it would not be tenable; thus it should be understood.
"Not unknowingly" means that one who drinks without knowing it is *surā* does not incur a breach of any of the precepts, such as the abstention from taking life, nor a breach of the refuges.
However, there is unwholesomeness (*akusala*) and a breach of the precept of abstaining from drinking *surā*, just as there is in the case of wearing garlands and so forth.
It should be seen thus. "The others" refers to the abstention from eating at improper times and so forth.
For even these are indeed broken for one who intentionally transgresses them; however, because they are not broken by mutual transgression, they do not constitute factors of destruction.
For this very reason, the expression "when these are broken" is used in reference to their breaking.

"He must be made to confess his transgression" means that after he has been made to confess in the midst of the Saṅgha by saying, "Venerable sir, a transgression has overcome me," and so forth, the refuge-precepts should be given to him;
this is the intention, because they have committed a *pārājika* offense. Therefore it is said: "He is to be expelled by the removal of his signs.
For it is this very expulsion that is intended here; thus, [the text] refers to the disparagement and so forth resulting from the causes for expulsion, such as the taking of life and the like.
It was stated [thus] because they fell together. But surely the novice Kaṇṭaka was also one of wrong view, and for him, below, only suspension by means of a formal act (daṇḍakamma) was mentioned;
here, however, the removal of the signs (liṅganāsanā) is stated for one of wrong view.
Keeping this objection in mind, he said: "For he held either the eternalist or the annihilationist view. And herein, this—

The underlying intention (*adhippāya*) is as follows: if one speaks while firmly grasping any eternalist or annihilationist view (*sassatuccheda-diṭṭhi*) imagined by the heretics—whether it be "the self is the Lord," or "it is permanent and stable," and so forth, or "the self will be cut off and destroyed," and so forth—that constitutes a ground for defeat (*pārājika-ṭṭhāna*), and he must be expelled by the removal of his religious marks (*liṅga-nāsanā*). Whoever...

However, if one does not hold such a view but remains a follower of the Teaching (sāsana), yet speaks while failing to relinquish [the wrong grasp] even when being exhorted by the monks—doing so because they have misunderstood the intent of the Buddha’s word alone—that view of theirs does not constitute a *pārājika* offense;
rather, he is to be expelled solely for the removal of a thorn (from the community). This is stated in the *Vimativinodanī*. At this point...
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, a detailed commentary beginning from the tenth training rule (*sikkhāpada*) has been included;
since that [commentary] was entirely incorporated into the manuscript of the ancient sub-commentary (*porāṇaṭīkā*), we have not elaborated upon it here.
Regarding the phrase "one's own cell," it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* that this was said with reference to private property.
Now, this is the intention of the authors of the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries here:
by the phrase "a dwelling obtained by him through the [rainy] season," a communal dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha is meant; and by the phrase "his own cell," his own private dwelling is meant.
However, this is our own preference: by the phrase "wherever he dwells," it may be either communal or...
Or it is individual property; that is said to be his permanent dwelling-place.

But by the phrase "or where he goes back," that place where he regularly enters the residence of his teacher or preceptor for the purpose of attending upon them and so forth is said to be the place of entry for the teacher and preceptor.
Therefore, to show both of these, [it says] "by either of the two..."
He said, "One's own cell and the lodging obtained by lot according to the *vassa* period.

Therein, by the phrase "one's own cell," the dwelling place of the preceptor (*ācariya*) and the teacher (*upajjhāya*) is indicated; by the phrase "lodging obtained by lot according to the *vassa* period," however, his own residence is indicated.
Therefore, whether both of these belong to the Sangha or to an individual, they constitute an obstruction.
"It must indeed be done. "By way of the mouth-door" means it should be eaten through the mouth-door. "Having performed the disciplinary act" means having applied the disciplinary act.
It is called *daṇḍa* because by means of it they punish (*daṇḍenti*) or discipline (*vinenti*). That very thing, because it is to be performed, is called *kamma*;
thus it is *daṇḍakamma*, such as the act of exclusion (*āvaraṇa*) and so forth. "Perform the disciplinary act for him" means apply the disciplinary act to him; command it. *Daṇḍakamma*.
Or [it refers to] an act of censure; therefore, it is meant that "you must carry out a censure against him. This same method applies in all such instances.
By the phrase "and the taking of lodgings is suspended," it indicates that his *vassa* (rainy-season residence) is broken.
If he remains full of faults and does not abide in future restraint, he should be expelled; here, if he is being told up to three times...
If he does not desist, he should be expelled after having informed the Saṅgha; they say that even if he requests ordination again, he should be ordained only after having informed [the Saṅgha].
"He shall receive the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe) during the later period" means that he shall receive it because he has entered the rains residence once again during the later period.
"The gain should be given after having informed [the Saṅgha]" refers to one whose rains residence has been interrupted. "The other five training rules... [is as follows].

The five [offenses] beginning with eating at the improper time. Regarding the phrase "one should cause him to confess his transgression," it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī* that he should be made to confess in the manner beginning with, "Venerable sir, a transgression has overcome me.
Thus ends the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
The Twenty-second Chapter: The Ornament of the Discourse on the Determination of Going-forth.
The Discourse on the Determination of Ordination.
Having thus explained the determination of going forth (*pabbajjā-vinicchaya*), the determination of full ordination (*upasampadā-vinicchaya*) should be explained immediately thereafter.

Even so, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), the discussion on the determination of full ordination is presented only by way of an exposition of the Canon (*Pāḷivaṇṇanā*), and not by way of a determination independent of the Canon (*Pāḷimuttaka-vinicchaya*).

Since this treatise consists of a discussion of determinations independent of the Canon, [the author] does not explain that [section from the Commentary], but rather the determination of dependence (*nissaya-vinicchaya*).
Although this has been stated by the Teacher, we— because the determination of full ordination (*upasampadā-vinicchaya*) is exceedingly subtle,
exceedingly profound, and very difficult to obtain— will, for the sake of favoring the Dispensation, extract it even though not explicitly stated by the Teacher from the *Samantapāsādikā*,
adorn it with the determinations found in works such as the *Vimativinodanī*, and then explain that determination.
Now at that time: it was at the time when the Blessed One had not yet laid down the training rule beginning with, "Monks, [one should not be ordained] without a preceptor.
"Without a preceptor" means one who has not been made to take a preceptor and is entirely devoid of a preceptor;
those who have been ordained in such a manner receive neither support in the Dhamma nor support in material things.

They indeed decline; they do not increase. "Monks, one who has no preceptor" means that one should not be ordained without having been made to take a preceptor—that is, one who is without a preceptor.
From the time the training rule was established, for one who ordains in this manner, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
however, the formal act (*kamma*) itself is not invalidated. Some say, "It is invalidated."
What they say should not be accepted. The same principle applies to the cases beginning with "by the Saṅgha as preceptor" and ending with "one who has both sexual organs as preceptor.
"They wander for alms with food in their hands" means they wander for the sake of whatever alms-food can be obtained in the hands.
"Just like the heretics" means just like the heretics known as Ājīvakas. [Mixing it] with soups and condiments in the hands...
For they eat only alms-food that has been set aside. "There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means that the offense belongs to the one who confers the full ordination (*upasampadā*) itself;
however, the formal act (*kamma*) is not invalidated. This same principle applies to the grounds concerning robes and so forth.
"By way of a loan" means by what is taken after requesting, saying, "Please give this until we have performed the full ordination. "For the time being" means...

The meaning is as follows: for one who confers full ordination with such a bowl, or robe, or bowl-and-robe, there is indeed an offense, but the formal act (*kamma*) itself is not invalidated; therefore, one should confer full ordination only upon one who possesses a complete bowl and robe.
If he does not have them, but his preceptor (*ācariya*) or teacher (*upajjhāya*), or other monks, are willing to give them, [he may be ordained] provided they are not indifferent [to the matter].
Having relinquished them, one should give away the bowl and robes that have reached the stage of being formally resolved upon.
“One may also announce the clan”: the meaning is that I allow one to announce the clan by saying, “He is seeking full ordination for Mahākassapa.
“Two [may perform] the single announcement”: this refers to two people announcing together; that is, one person [announces] for one, and another...
"Of the other": the meaning is that I authorize ordination to be conferred in this way by two teachers, or by one, simultaneously reciting the *kammavācā*.
"To perform two or three [recitations] with a single *anussāvana*":
I authorize two or three persons to perform the *anussāvana* together in the same manner as before, provided they have a single *upajjhāya*; and furthermore, regarding the act of recitation...
The meaning is: "I authorize [it] with one preceptor. Therefore, two or three [candidates] should be announced by one teacher;
or, by two or three teachers, each for one individual—thus, the formal act (*kammavācā*) should be performed simultaneously for two or three persons.
However, if they have different teachers and different preceptors, as in the case of Elder Tissatthera [acting for] Elder Sumanatthera...

If the Elder Sumana makes his own *saddhivihārika* announce [the invitation] to the Elder Tissa’s *saddhivihārika*, and they both act as mutual complements to the group (*gaṇapūrakā*), it is permissible.

If they do not have different preceptors (*nānupajjhāyā*), but rather share a single teacher (*ācariya*), it is not permissible because of the prohibition: “But not with one who does not have a different preceptor.
For this prohibition was made with reference to this very case.
"First, one must have [the candidate] take a preceptor": here, one who contemplates (upanijjhāyati) what is blameworthy and what is blameless is a *upajjhā* (preceptor);
having had him say, "Venerable sir, please be my preceptor (*upajjhāyo*)," he should be made to take one.

"Becoming bloated" means their limbs become swollen. "Whatever has been born" means whatever has been produced, arisen, and exists within your body—when they ask you about that in the midst of the Saṅgha...
"One should say, 'It exists,' when it is peaceful," and so forth. "Ullumpatu maṃ" means "may he lift me up.
"Tāvadeva" means immediately upon full ordination (*upasampadā*). "The shadow must be measured" means the shadow must be measured as being one person's height or two persons' heights.
"The measure of the season must be announced" means the measure of the season as "the rainy season, the winter, or the summer."
It must be announced. And here, "the measure of the season" refers to the season itself.
If the rains and other seasons are incomplete, one should observe for how many days each particular season is incomplete and announce that portion of the days.
Alternatively, the measure of the season should be announced in this way: "This is the season; moreover, it is complete or incomplete."
“Either forenoon or afternoon”—in this way, the portion of the day should be specified. As for the summary:
having brought all of this together into one, when asked, “What do you receive? What is your shadow? What is the measure of the season? What portion of the day?
one should reply, “I receive such-and-such—either the rainy season, or the winter, or the summer; this is my shadow; this is the measure of the season.”
"You should say, 'This is part of the day,'" thus it should be explained.
"Having left behind" means having discarded. "To give a companion" means I allow giving a companion to one who is going from the ordination hall to the courtyard;
the meaning is that he should be told the four things not to be done. "Pale-leaf" means yellow-colored.
"Fallen": fallen from the stalk, that is, fallen from its stem. "Unable to become green again": unable to become green once more. "Large stone": a great rock.
This determination regarding full ordination (*upasampadā*) has been extracted and brought forth from the *Samantapāsādikā*.

Regarding the cases of those without a preceptor (*anupajjhāyaka*) and so forth, the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) has not yet been laid down; thus it says: "One who is without a preceptor should not be ordained."
This was said with reference to a training rule being announced right here [in the presence of the Sangha].

However, as for the statement "the formal act (kamma) does not become invalid," this refers to cases where—even in the absence of an actual preceptor—one uses the name of a deceased person, one who has left the order, an old preceptor, or anyone else whose name is available, saying: "The candidate for full ordination named so-and-so [seeks ordination] with such-and-such a person as preceptor."

This is stated because the naming of the preceptor has been performed in all instances. For if one were not to name the preceptor, it would constitute a failure of the ritual procedure (kammavipatti), as it was said:
"he does not misrepresent the person. For this very reason, it is stated in the Pāḷi as "one without a preceptor" (anupajjhāyaka);
and in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) as well, instead of saying "without naming a preceptor," it says "without having caused a preceptor to be accepted."

The meaning stated is simply "entirely devoid of a preceptor. In the Pāḷi, the phrase "with the Saṅgha as preceptor" means that one has designated the Saṅgha itself as the preceptor by means of the formal ritual (kammavācā), as follows:
"This person named so-and-so desires ordination from the Saṅgha; this person named so-and-so requests ordination from the Saṅgha with the Saṅgha as preceptor. Thus is the meaning.

In the same way, regarding the phrase "by a group" (*gaṇena*) or "by a preceptor" (*upajjhāyena*), the construction should be understood as: "This person named so-and-so desires full ordination by the group," and so forth.
Even when stated in this way, the formal act (*kamma*) is certainly not invalidated, because only a *dukkaṭa* offense has been mentioned;
otherwise, it would have said, "And that person is unordained. Therefore, he said "by the Saṅgha," and so on. In that context, [regarding] preceptors who are eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*), etc.:
It should be understood that when formal acts (*kamma*) are being performed, if the assembly of five or more members is complete even without those such as a *paṇḍaka*, the act is not invalidated;
otherwise, it is invalidated.
Even in the case of the grounds for the bowl and robe, although the bowl and robe may be absent, the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) states, "The bowl and robe are complete."
Because the proclamation was made, it is stated that there is only an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing), without mentioning a disturbance of the formal act (*kammakopa*).

Otherwise, by omitting the proclamation, there would indeed be a disturbance of the formal act. However, some say: "Just as one who was ordained by the previously authorized formal procedure, even now, although ordained by the formal procedure without saying 'the bowl and robes are complete,' one is nonetheless fully ordained"; this [they maintain].

That is not appropriate. For from the time it was permitted, the failure to mention [the candidate's name] constitutes a deficiency in the proclamation (*sāvanā*), just like the deficiency of omitting the words, "So-and-so requests ordination from the Saṅgha. That too was permitted later;
thus, even when one ordains someone without having them make the request with the formula, "Venerable Sir, I request ordination from the Saṅgha," and so forth—[thinking], "This..."
Having said, “The one named so-and-so requests full ordination from the Saṅgha,” if he then performs the formal act (kammavācā), the act is indeed well-performed.
If not, it is defective. For after the formal act has been authorized, it is not permissible to omit anything whatsoever;
there is only the omission of the proclamation (sāvanā). Or, the connection is that other monks may wish to grant [the ordination]; this is the meaning here.
The analysis has been extracted from the *Vimativinodanī*. Furthermore, the analysis from the *Sāratthadīpanī* is included right here [in this work], as it is both brief and non-distinctive.
As for what was stated in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, namely, "Some say 'it is agitated' (kuppati), but that should not be accepted,"...

Because it has been stated in such a manner as, "Monks, if a formal act (kamma) that requires a quorum of five is performed with a nun as the fifth member, it is not a valid act and is not to be done," and so forth, one should conclude that an act is invalidated only when a paṇḍaka serves to complete the quorum, and not in all cases;
otherwise, [the text would have said], "If one were to perform a formal act with a paṇḍaka acting as preceptor (upajjhāya), it would be an invalid act... and so on.
There should have been a textual passage beginning with "and what is to be done," and so forth.

Just as at the time of ordination for one whose bowl and robes are incomplete, the ordination is valid even though that person lacks them, because the formal act (*kammavācā*) mentions the non-existent fact—"his bowl and robes are complete"—once the ordination has been performed;
in the same way, [regarding the statement] "This Buddharakkhita [is the pupil] of the Venerable Dhammarakkhita..."

Regarding the phrase "one desiring full ordination": even if one has declared a non-existent basis—such as a foolish preceptor (*paṇḍaka*) or the like—or if the basis is not actually present, the full ordination is indeed valid provided that those who complete the quorum are present. This is because there is no such statement as:
"Monks, one should not be ordained with a foolish preceptor; whoever should ordain him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), and that person is unordained. And so forth.
This meaning is established as a matter of fact; for Buddhas do not fail to speak what is appropriate to be said. Therefore it was stated:
“But whichever bhikkhu, knowing [a person] to be less than twenty years of age... that person is unordained,” and so forth.

Likewise, from the statement, “The Saṅgha should be informed by a learned and competent bhikkhu,” [it follows that] by teachers such as those who live in communion through theft (theyyasaṃvāsaka), etc.
When the proclamation (*anussāvanā*) has been performed, the full ordination (*upasampadā*) does not take effect; furthermore, the statement that "they are not monks" must not be accepted.
Moreover, when the success or failure of formal acts (*kamma*) is being explained according to the method beginning with, "These four formal acts fail in five ways," it is said:
"Formal acts fail in seven ways: either by way of the subject matter (*vatthu*), or by way of the motion (*ñatti*)."

It should not be accepted [as a separate ground for invalidation] because it was not mentioned [in the text]: "either from the proclamation, or from the boundary, or from the assembly, or from the preceptor, or from the teacher.
If it is argued that the phrase "or from the assembly" includes both the teacher and the preceptor, this is not so;
for in the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the statement, "In twelve ways the formal acts fail due to the assembly," those two are not included under that name.

Since this meaning can be understood through the very wording of the Canon as it is stated here and there in its own form, it was said: "Having shown the method, [the matter] is abbreviated"; this constitutes the investigation of its reasoning. Herein, this must be considered:
those monks who were conferring full ordination without a preceptor [acted] according to the method already described.
They proclaimed a non-existent matter; or was it that, out of fear of lying, they did not recite those very words? What is the point here?
If, first of all, they did not recite them because of the absence of a preceptor (upajjhāya), there follows the contingency of a failure (vipatti) stated as: "he does not misrepresent a person.
But if they did recite them, would they be guilty of lying? It is said in reply: they certainly did recite them, for fear of the aforementioned contingency of failure.
Furthermore, because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that "the formal act (*kamma*) does not fail," [this objection is] not [valid].

This is because lying is impossible [in such a context], and because even through lying, the formal act can still take place; for it is not possible to cause the failure or success of a formal act by means of lying.
Therefore, the meaning of the statement, "They ordain one who has no preceptor," must be sought as being free from both faults.

This is the reasoning here: just as previously, although preceptors for going-forth and full ordination existed, it was stated, "At that time, monks were without a preceptor," because they had not been taken [as preceptors] according to the sequence of taking a preceptor;
so too here, although a preceptor existed, it was stated, "They grant full ordination to one without a preceptor," because he had not been taken [as a preceptor].
However, the *kammavācā*-teacher, perceiving that "the preceptor has been accepted," should recite the *kammavācā* after having named the preceptor.
Or, if for some reason the preceptor does not provide physical presence, one may recite the *kammavācā* after obtaining the consent (*chanda*) of the preceptor;
or if the preceptor, having given the sponsorship (*upajjha*) to the candidate seeking ordination, subsequently [departs] after the person has already been ordained.

In such a case, whether he is being interrogated or not, if the novice admits before the formal act of giving him away to the preceptor that he has renounced the training or that he has committed an ultimate offense,
or if the preceptor is located within another boundary— just like those who bring the consent (*chandahāraka*) and so forth— the formal act (*kammavācā*) is valid.
This is because it was stated: "I allow you, monks, in border regions, ordination by a group consisting of five members, including one who is an expert in the Vinaya.
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada* that some say, "The preceptor who is the fifth member of the group must be present as an expert in the Vinaya.
However, that reading is not authoritative, because that specific statement does not exist for the central regions.
If it is argued that the formal act (*kammavācā*) is valid even when the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) is not present, and thus the offense is incurred—no. Why?

Because in the context of the successful performance of a formal act, the very text stating "he designates a person" (*puggalaṃ parāmasati*) is our authority. For in that case, a person designated as a "preceptor" who is not present cannot be the object of designation;
therefore, just as there is designation of the Sangha in that instance, so too is there designation of a person.

It should be understood as follows. The ancient teachers say that when the Saṅgha, a group, or a preceptor ordains someone who is actually a paṇḍaka (eunuch) and so forth, it is because, in terms of their actual status, they are individuals [of that class], and because at the time of the ordination, they were not recognized as such.

Regarding the phrase "they ordain one who lacks a bowl and robes," this refers to the master of the ritual formula who, under the impression that "the bowl and robes are complete," [proceeds with the rite].
Or, disregarding the actual fulfillment of the requirements, he proclaims the formal act (*kammavācā*) with the words, "The bowl and robes are complete," by way of making a peaceful declaration.
Just as nowadays even one whose parents have passed away, when asked, "Have you been permitted by your parents?
says, "Yes, Venerable Sir,"—what need for more? But this is the essential point here: "At that time, the four..."

"Karmas fail in five ways. Because the characteristics [of a valid candidate] have not yet been defined, they grant full ordination (*upasampadā*) even to those who lack a preceptor (*anupajjhāyaka*), and so forth. Because the persons to be avoided have not been mentioned, they grant full ordination even to those with a foolish preceptor (*paṇḍupajjhāya*), and so forth. Because the inquiry regarding the thirteen obstacles has not been performed, they grant full ordination to one who has not obtained the robes (*apattacīvaraka*). [The Buddha said: "Monks, I allow you to perform a formal act consisting of a motion followed by a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*)."... [text continues] ...because the characteristics have not yet been defined, they grant full ordination even to one who lacks a preceptor, and so forth. Because the persons to be avoided have not been stated, they grant full ordination even to one with a foolish preceptor, and so forth. Because the inquiry regarding the thirteen obstacles has not been made, they grant full ordination to one who has not obtained the robes. "I allow you, monks, to perform a formal act consisting of a motion followed by a fourth proclamation... [text continues] ...Because the characteristics have not yet been defined, they grant full ordination even to one who lacks a preceptor, and so forth. Because the persons to be avoided have not been stated, they grant full ordination even to one with a foolish preceptor, and so forth. Because the inquiry regarding the thirteen obstacles has not been made, they grant full ordination to one who has not obtained the robes. It should be understood that in this context, the non-mention of the phrase "his bowl and robes are complete" serves as the proof for the formal act (*kammavācā*) being authorized for the very first time with the words "let him confer full ordination. For that statement was authorized in successive order.
Let that much stand for now; however, how could it be possible [to say] that "they ordain one who is mute" or "they ordain one who is deaf"?
Is it because [ordination] was authorized from the very beginning by such statements as, "Monks, I allow you the going forth by means of these three goings for refuge"?
It is replied: No; for in the passage, "And thus, monks, he should be given the going forth; he should be told: 'Speak thus...
up to "...for the third time I go to the Saṅgha for refuge," the statement "he should be told: 'Speak thus'" is incorrect [if applied to the three refuges].

Having understood the meaning, they ordained the mute man. Having instructed the one seeking ordination, saying, "Speak thus," the preceptor himself was to say, "For the third time, I go for refuge to the Saṅgha.
Whether that person seeking ordination, having been thus instructed by the preceptor, repeats the words of the preceptor or not, in each instance the Blessed One [said]: "By means of the body..."
If he makes it known, makes it known by speech, or makes it known by both body and speech, the preceptor is considered accepted.
It is said: "The *chanda* has been given; the *pārisuddhi* has been given; the *pavāraṇā* has been given.
Or, by inference from that, the going for refuge is made known by the body by that person seeking ordination; for even in the world, one makes things known by means of the body.
It is said that he speaks thus; taking this as a figurative expression, it should be understood that they ordain a mute person.

In the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, having raised the question, "How do they ordain a mute?", it is stated: "Because bodily intimation (*kāyapasāda*) can arise in him, they give him a blow with their hand and ordain him by making his meaning known through hand gestures. What more need be said?
This, however, is the essential point here: just as previously, while the section on going forth (*pabbajjā*) was being discussed,

the expression for "going forth" was set aside and the discussion was conducted by way of "full admission" (*upasampadā*) alone— according to the method beginning with, "Monks, one who is a paṇḍaka, if not yet fully admitted, is not to be fully admitted"—

even though that [expression] was not used in the section on those living in communion through theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*) because it was impossible there, nevertheless, "going forth" itself is what is intended therein.

[The term] "done" refers everywhere to full admission (*upasampadā*), intended by way of its influence; for when going-forth (*pabbajjā*) has been prohibited, full admission is thereby prohibited as well.

Thus, while this section concerns full admission, one should understand that the expression "going-forth" is employed here by setting aside the term "full admission" and intending full admission itself. Granted, that...

It should not be performed, because it is impossible for one who is mute; however, by way of that very term "mute," it appears as if the expression for full ordination (*upasampadā*) should be used from the beginning.
Nevertheless, by way of that same term "mute," the expression for going forth (*pabbajjā*) is used from the beginning in order to prevent a wrong assumption.
How so? "Monks, a mute person has not reached the stage of being admitted [to the Sangha]; if he..."
From the statement, "The Saṅgha reinstates him; he is reinstated," it is established that a mute person may be fully ordained (*upasampanna*).
It is a misconception to think that such a person is merely fully ordained but not one who has gone forth (*pabbajita*), because his going forth is impossible;
rather, having avoided that [misconception], one who is fully ordained is indeed one who has gone forth. However, there is someone who is [merely] one who has gone forth...
It should be understood that the Blessed One produces this correct understanding: "One who is fully ordained exists; one who is not fully ordained also exists.

Furthermore, the mention of "going forth" (pabbajjā) is used here both to demonstrate that those with severed hands and so forth who have gone forth have indeed gone forth well, and to prevent any suspicion regarding their status as having gone forth.
How so? By such statements as: "Monks, one with severed hands should not be given the going forth," and so on.
Due to the prohibition and because there is no mention of the phrase "those who have gone forth have gone forth well," there might be a suspicion regarding their status as renunciants;
just as such a suspicion would arise, he establishes that suspicion. In the Khandhaka, with reference to full ordination (*upasampadā*), it is stated:
"Monks, one whose hand has been cut off is not eligible for reinstatement (*osāraṇā*); if the Saṅgha reinstates him, he is not reinstated," and so forth.
