The Blessed One prohibits it by that same principle. By that very principle, he demonstrates that all these who have gone forth are indeed well-gone-forth (*supabbajita*).
Otherwise, the undesirable consequence would follow that all these are merely fully ordained (*upasampanna*) but not gone-forth (*pabbajita*). How so? [Because of the rule:
"Monks, one with a severed hand should not be admitted to the going-forth; if he has already gone forth, he should be expelled."
Or, when the rule has been established in the Campeyyakkhandhaka—“Monks, one with severed hands should not be ordained;

whoever should ordain him incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), and he is not ordained”—and because it is stated there that such a person is “one who has been reinstated” (sosārito), it follows that these individuals, such as those with severed hands, are indeed fully ordained (upasampanna) but not ordained (pabbajita). Or, even though they are fully ordained...
The intended meaning is that one falls into an undesirable position by saying, "This person has gone forth;

he must be expelled. However, this point must be examined here: since there is no statement to the effect that "he has not gone forth," and because it would follow that the going forth of a mute person is established, how is it that one does not fall into this undesirable position—that going forth occurs through partial purity? [It is not so] because of the expression "going forth" (*pabbajjā*).

If one does not fall into [this error] by correctly grasping that "ordination" (*upasampadā*) is intended here, otherwise—were the meaning taken according to the literal phrasing—one would incur another undesirable consequence, namely the absence of the *dukkaṭa* offense as it was prescribed. How so?

Because the *dukkaṭa* mentioned in the statement, "Monks, a mute person should not be given the going-forth; whoever should give it, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*," applies at the conclusion of the going-forth (*pabbajjā*).
It does not exist because of its incompleteness. For he first incurs only the *dukkaṭa* of preliminary effort;
therefore, since there is an absolute absence of the conclusion of the going-forth for one who is mute, the occasion for this *dukkaṭa* could not arise at all times.
However, if the meaning is understood by way of full ordination (*upasampadā*), it can arise once the formal act (*kamma*) has been performed. For that very reason, it is said in the Pāḷi: "No..."

“Monks, a paṇḍaka should not be ordained; whoever should ordain one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Thus, the offense of wrong-doing was not prescribed [for the act of ordination itself].
Because it was not so prescribed, only the dukkaṭa pertaining to the preliminary effort (pubbapayoga) is possible here, and not the other.

By this much, it is established that what is intended there by the expression “going forth” (pabbajjā) is actually the full admission (upasampadā) itself, and not merely going forth. Here, one might say:

How is it known that the going forth as a novice (sāmaṇera-pabbajjā) does not depend on physical action? It is said: because it is established by the observation of the rule beginning with "one makes it known by means of the body.
Furthermore, from the statement, "He may also announce his clan," it is proven that whatever conventional term one uses is permissible;
therefore, it is proven that when asked, "What is your preceptor's name?", one may speak by treating the clan name itself as the name.
Therefore, they say that among the four kinds of names, the proclamation (*anussāvana*) may be made using any one of them.
A single person may have many names; in such a case, it is not permissible to use one name for the motion (*ñatti*) and another for the proclamation.
The proclamations must be identical both in meaning and in phrasing. Even though [the name] "so-and-so" ...
In the canonical text (pāḷi), the word "of the venerable one" (*āyasmato*) is mentioned later as "of the venerable so-and-so";
however, in the formal ritual text (kammavācā-pāḷi), they write first, "This Buddharakkhita [is the property] of the venerable Dhammarakkhita.
One should not consider this to be stated out of sequence; for in the canonical text, only the general sense is shown as "so-and-so [is the property] of so-and-so."
Therefore, although not explicitly stated in the Pāli text, the formula "this Buddharakkhita [is the pupil] of the Venerable Dhammarakkhita" is shown in the Kammavācā Pāli.

They say this is because the usage of the word "Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is first seen in such instances as "The Venerable Sāriputta said: 'I have never seen him before,'" and "The Venerable Sāriputta is skilled in the meaning. In some places, "of the Venerable... [is used].
Having said, "Of Buddharakkhita," if in some places he announces simply, "Buddharakkhita's," it is not said that he omits the announcement because the name has not been omitted;

so say some. If, having said in one place, "Of the venerable Buddharakkhita," he announces in another place, "Buddharakkhita's venerable one," they say that because it conforms to the wording, it has indeed entered the field [of the proclamation].
Some say that because it would entail a difference in the phrasing, it is not permissible for there to be a single proclamation (*anussāvanā*).
However, if one speaks in the same manner at every point, it is permissible.
Regarding the term *ekānussāvana*: here, "those whose proclamations are together" is *ekānussāvanā*; this refers to a non-co-referential (*asamānādhikaraṇa*) relationship.
It should be understood as a compound with the external object [as its first member]. For this very reason, he said: "The two together in the proclamation.
In that context, "together" (ekatō) means "at one moment"; this expression is formed by the elision of a case ending.

Regarding the phrase "the two together in the proclamation," it should be performed according to the method previously stated—namely, "by one for one, and by another for the other," and so forth—using either two or three [monks].
The teachers may perform the proclamation (*anussāvana*) either individually or together.

In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is explained that the word *upajjhā*—meaning "one who contemplates what is blameworthy and what is blameless" (*vajjāvajjam upanijjhātīti upajjhā*)—is shown to have the same meaning as the word *upajjhāya*.
Regarding the phrase "even by clan name" (*gottenāpi*), this means that instead of stating the name as "the venerable Pippali’s candidate for full ordination," one may use the clan name.
This is the meaning; therefore, it is established that when asked, "What is the name of your preceptor? one should say, "The Venerable Kassapa," using the name of his clan (*gotta*).

Consequently, whether it be any other well-known name of his, or a name assigned at that moment for the sake of easy identification, the formal proclamation (*anussāvana*) may be performed by including all such names. Just as in the case of the preceptor, so too—
It is permissible to perform the formal proclamation (*anussāvana*) for one seeking full ordination (*upasampadāpekkha*) by means of their clan name and so forth, as well as their temporary name;
at that very moment, the name—such as "Tissa" or "Nāga"—should be assigned by those [acting] from the very beginning through the authorization of the instructor (*anusāsaka-sammuti*).
Even if this has not been done, at the times of instructing on the obstructing factors (*antarāyika-dhamma*) and asking questions, [one should say]: "What is your name? I am, Venerable Sir..."

One should make the announcement such that the perception arises in the minds of both [the preceptor and the candidate], "This is my name," by announcing, for example: "Nāga is my name; what is the name of your preceptor? My preceptor, venerable sir, is named Tissa.
However, if at that moment one speaks using the natural name and afterwards makes the proclamation using a new name, saying "named Tissa," it is not permissible.
In this regard, although the name of the preceptor himself has not been mentioned, if a person is designated by whatever name— such as "Tissa’s candidate for full ordination"—
the ritual act is indeed well-performed. This is because, even in the absence of a preceptor or in cases where [the candidate] is incapable,
the ritual succeeds provided the person is designated within the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), just like the ordination ritual for those who are without a preceptor and so forth.
However, if for one who seeks full ordination (*upasampadāpekkha*), the proclamation (*anussāvana*) is performed using a name other than his own proper name, the ritual act (*kamma*) is invalid;

he remains unordained. One standing there [in that situation] is like any other unordained person, because the individual who is the subject (*vatthupuggala*)—who has taken that name—is absent from that location, and because that specific name was not uttered during the proclamation. Therefore, for one seeking full ordination...
Having changed the natural name, if one wishes to recite [the candidate] by a new name such as "Nāga" and so forth, one must first inform him, saying, "You are Nāga," and so on.
Then, even at the moments of asking about the obstructing factors (*antarāyika-dhamma*) and during the instruction, one must announce it clearly so that it is evident both to him and to the Saṅgha;
only then should he be recited by the name "Nāga" and so forth. [This applies] when one person has many [names].
There are [several] names, and it is permissible to take one among them.

However, the name that was taken for the candidate for full ordination and the preceptor in one instance must be the very same name used in the motion (*ñatti*) and in all the proclamations (*anussāvana*).
For if another name is taken than the one already taken, the phrasing is said to be "divergent" (*byañjana-bhinna*).
The formal act (kamma) fails. For in meaning as well as in phrasing, the motion (ñatti) and the proclamation (anussāvana) must be identical; they are not permitted to differ.
However, regarding the preceptor’s name, one may proclaim it by prefixing the word "Venerable" (āyasmato) to every instance, such as saying "of the Venerable Tissa," and so forth.
Even if it is not thus prefixed, there is no fault.
In the Pāḷi, although the word "of the venerable one" (*āyasmato*) is stated after the phrase "of the venerable so-and-so," nevertheless,

because the application of the term "venerable one" (*āyasmanta-pada*) is seen before the name in such passages as "the venerable Sāriputta was skilled in the meaning" (*āyasmā Sāriputto atthakusalo*),
the usage before [the name] is more appropriate; and that [usage] applies even when it is joined in one place but not joined in another.
Even if one applies [the name] elsewhere after having joined it at the beginning, there is no "dropping" of the proclamation, because the name has not been dropped.

For this very reason, they say that although in the Pāḷi it is stated, "of the venerable so-and-so," having joined it once, the word "of the venerable" is not repeated in such phrases as "with the preceptor so-and-so. And although that is so, nevertheless, in every instance, by means of the same...
It should be understood that the proclamation (*anussāvana*) is more highly praised whether it is joined with [the formal act] in this manner or not so joined.

Those for whom the proclamation is made at one time, simultaneously, are "those subject to a single proclamation" (*ekānussāvanā*); these are the candidates for full ordination (*upasampadāpekkhā*) who are to be subjected to the single proclamation.
Therefore he said, "in the simultaneous proclamation. And this is a single word formed by the elision of a case-ending.
It should be understood as follows: "By one" means by a single preceptor (*ācariya*) during the proclamation (*anussāvana*) of a single formal act (*kammavācā*) at one moment for both [candidates].

The method of proclamation for two [candidates] at one moment by a single preceptor is according to the following pattern: "This Buddharakkhita and this Dhammarakkhita are desirous of receiving full ordination from the venerable Saṅgharakkhita," and so forth.
It should be looked upon in this same manner; thus, by this very method, it should be understood that the proclamation for all three may be performed at one moment by a single teacher.

Regarding the performance of the proclamation together according to the previous method, it was stated previously—by the method beginning with "one [teacher] for one [candidate], another for the other"—that it may be done either by two teachers for two [candidates] or by three teachers for three, or by a single teacher for all three.
The meaning is that it is to be performed by means of a single proclamation (*ekato-anussāvane*).

The phrase, “And that indeed [must be] by one preceptor (*upajjhāya*), and not by those who do not have a preceptor,” is a prohibitive statement indicating that it is not permissible for two or three persons seeking full ordination (*upasampadāpekkha*) to be ordained simultaneously by a single teacher (*ācariya*) or by two or three preceptors through a single proclamation—that is, by means of one and the same proclamation. It is not...
However, it was stated that "it is not permissible for three persons with different teachers and different preceptors to perform the single proclamation (ekānussāvana)," and thus he said:

"But if there are different teachers and different preceptors... [it] is permissible. Regarding this, as in the case where "Thera Tissa is the co-resident pupil (saddhivihārika) of Thera Sumana, and Thera Sumana is the co-resident pupil of Thera Tissa," such is the mutual relationship of the co-resident pupils through their respective preceptors.
The performance of the proclamation (*anussāvana*) has been stated; that is merely illustrative.

Therefore, if the Elder Tissa proclaims [the name] of the Elder Sumana’s resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*), and the Elder Sumana proclaims [the name] of the Elder Nanda’s resident pupil, and they mutually serve as the complements of the quorum (*gaṇapūrakā*), it is indeed permissible.
However, if the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) himself [proclaims] his own resident pupil...
Regarding the proclamation (*anussāveti*): there is simply nothing more to be said here; the formal act (*kamma*) is indeed well-performed.

Full ordination (*upasampadā*) takes place even for one who does not have a preceptor (*anupajjhāyaka*) when the proclamation is made by anyone at all; how much more so, then, in the case of one who has a preceptor (*saupajjhāyaka*), where it must be understood that the proclamation is made by the preceptor himself.
It is for this very reason that he says, "But if... and so forth, in order to demonstrate the position of the nine-fold assembly (*navaṭṭhanapakkha*).
The term *upajjhāti* indicates that the word *upajjhā*—ending in the vowel *ā*—has the same meaning as the word *upajjhāya*.
Alternatively, it should be understood that the word *upajjhāya* itself is called *upajjhā* by eliding the letter *y* in the accusative and nominative cases;
this is because the word *upajjhā* is not employed in the instrumental case and other such forms. In the Pāḷi, it is stated: "One should appoint oneself by oneself."
By means of oneself acting as the agent and the instrument, one must perform the act of authorization toward oneself acting as the object;
or, "oneself" is the accusative case used in the sense of identity (*paccatte*), meaning that by oneself alone, oneself is to be authorized.
And this applies not only here, but elsewhere as well—in the thirteen types of authorization and so forth—by this same characteristic, it is by oneself that oneself [is authorized].

He must indeed be appointed. Furthermore, because he himself is qualified for the formal act (*kamma*), a group consisting of at least four members is required in all cases, setting aside the one who is performing the act himself.
"The time of truth" (*saccakāla*) means the time when, having abandoned the deception of thinking "I will conceal [the fault]," one must necessarily seek only the truth.

"The time of reality" (*bhūtakāla*) means the time when, even in the absence of deception, one must necessarily acknowledge the actual state of the basis (*vatthu*)—such as being a human being—and so forth; otherwise, [the confession would be invalid].

The intention is that there is an obstruction due to the corruption of the action. "Maṅku" means with face cast down. "Uddharatu" means let him establish [the candidate] in full ordination (upasampadā) from the state of being unordained; this is the meaning.
However, for the sake of proficiency in the meaning of all formal proclamations (kammavācā), the meaning of the full-ordination proclamation should be understood here as follows:

"—*Suṇātu*" is the third person singular form used in an injunction for listening. Although that which is enjoined to the act of listening—the Saṅgha—is present before one, and thus it ought to be addressed with the second person singular "Listen!

(*suṇāhi*), nevertheless, in the presence of the word *saṅgha*, grammarians have established the usage of the third person alone, as they do in the presence of words such as *bhavanta*, *bhagavant*, and *āyasmant*.
It is as in such passages as: “May the venerable Gotama consent for me; O Sugata, this is the time for the Blessed One to lay down a training rule for his disciples;
let the venerable ones listen to me,” and so forth. Therefore, the use of the first person is employed here.
Alternatively, it is stated thus out of respect; for even when the second person is used toward those worthy of respect, it arises out of a sense of reverence.
It should be understood that they employ the first-person construction as in such instances as "May the Sugata teach the Dhamma.
However, some say that the first-person construction is used here because it depends upon the words "Venerable Sir" (bhante) and "Friend" (āvuso);
but that is not correct, as seen in such passages as "Be my teacher, Venerable Sir," and "Come, friend Upāli, instruct this one who has gone forth."
Because even in the application of that [formula], only the use of the second person singular is seen.
*Me* is the genitive case used for self-reference by one who announces [the news]. *Bhante* is a term of respect used toward elders in the sense of address;
however, the word *āvuso* is used toward juniors. Both of these are indeclinables (*nipāta*), as in the expressions *tumhe bhante* and *tumhe āvuso*, which are used even when addressing many.
Because they share a common form. "The Saṅgha" refers, without distinction, to a collection of regular (pakatatta) individuals consisting of at least a quorum of four;
however, in this context, it should be understood as meaning a group of five or more in border regions, and a group of ten or more in central regions.
Herein, the summarized meaning is: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear my words."
And this is the speech that should be spoken by one who is junior. However, if the proclaimer (anussāvaka) is senior to all the bhikkhus, he should say, "Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me.

Even if he should address them as "Venerable Sir" (bhante), or if one who is junior addresses them as "Friend" (āvuso), there is no invalidation of the formal act (kamma). Some, however, say that having said "Friend" in one instance, one may say "Venerable Sir" in another.
They say: "Even if [the name] has not been stated, there is no fault, because the addressing of both parties is accomplished.
Now, desiring to make known the matter for which he says "Let him listen," he enjoins the Saṅgha to listen; in making that known, he says, "This one named so-and-so," and so forth.
Therein, "this" indicates the presence of the candidate for full ordination within arm's reach.
And it is established that ordination succeeds only for one who stands within arm’s reach (*hatthapāsa*);

for it cannot be said of one standing outside of arm’s reach, "This [person]. For this very reason, in the formal authorization of the instructor, he is not referred to as "this" because he stands outside of arm’s reach;
therefore, the candidate for ordination, being unordained, must be placed within arm’s reach. This—
The word *itthannāmo* must necessarily be employed; and it should be understood that this occurs only in this first application of the name.
"Itthannāmo" is an indefinite indication of his name; by both [terms], one shows a name such as "Buddharakkhita.
"Upasampadāpekkho" is a *bahubbīhi* compound in the sense of a different grammatical relation (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*).
The meaning is: "the Saṅgha is looking toward my full ordination. To show that he possesses the status of being a preceptor (*upajjhāya*), it is said, "of the Venerable [so-and-so].

By this, the meaning is expressed through the application of names in such a manner as: "This Buddharakkhita, being the co-resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*) of the Venerable Dhammarakkhita, is looking toward full ordination."
It has been shown. And here, even without stating the word "of the venerable one" (*āyasmato*), it is permissible to say, "This Buddharakkhita is seeking full ordination from Dhammarakkhita.
For that very reason, the word "of the venerable one" is not mentioned in the Pāḷi at the point where it says, "with such-and-such a person as preceptor.
And whatever needs to be said regarding this has already been stated above.
But surely, in this case, the preceptor (upajjhāya) must also be desired to stand within arm’s reach, just like the candidate for full ordination;

so why, when the preceptor’s name is mentioned thus, "This person named so-and-so is seeking full ordination from this person named so-and-so," is the use of the word *idaṃ* (this) not employed? This is not a contradiction, even in the absence of a preceptor.

Because there is no invalidation of the formal act (*kamma*). For even in cases such as the full ordination (*upasampadā*) of one who lacks a preceptor (*anupajjhāya*), the naming of a preceptor—who does not actually exist—is performed solely by way of a peaceful state produced by the formal act;
therefore, since the act is accomplished merely by that reference even when the preceptor is absent, it is not permissible to designate [the candidate] with the words "of this one" (*imassā*).

"Pure with respect to obstructive states" means he is liberated from those things that by their very nature are obstructions—namely, those such as incapacity and so forth which render one unfit for full ordination (*upasampadā*), as well as those such as the five diseases, mutilation of the hands, and so forth, which cause an offense.
When this is said, full ordination is valid even for one who is not yet liberated from mere offenses such as the five diseases and the like; it is not otherwise.
"His bowl and robes are complete" means that the bowl and robes of this person seeking full ordination (*upasampadā*) are complete.
When this has been stated, the full ordination is valid even for one who does not possess a bowl and robes; it is not otherwise.

"He requests full ordination" is said with reference to the fact that he has made the request by saying, "Venerable Sirs, I request full ordination from the Saṅgha," and so forth. Thus, by him [the request] was made before the Saṅgha...
Even when there is no formal request, the act is not invalid provided it is stated: "The one named so-and-so requests full ordination from the Saṅgha";
it is not otherwise. "By the preceptor" means by the preceptor acting as the instrument;

the meaning is that he requests the Saṅgha—acting as the agent—to grant and accomplish the full ordination, having made such-and-such a person his preceptor. As for the verbal root *yāc* (to request):
Because it has two objects (dvikammaka), two action-phrases are stated: “the Saṅgha” and “ordination.
Regarding the phrase *yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ*: here, “the time has arrived for this action” is *pattakālaṃ*.

The fourfold formal act (*gaṇakamma*) of the Saṅgha, beginning with the motion (*apalokana*), is itself called *pattakallaṃ* by means of the suffix *-ya* in its own sense (*sakatthe*). However, in this context—
The formal act of ordination consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-upasampadā-kamma*) is intended; the Saṅgha has become fit to perform it.
By the word "if" (*yadi*), he makes known the fitness of the act through the taking of consent. For whoever should think that it is unfit for that purpose will speak out.
It is with reference to this very meaning that, in the formal announcements (*anussāvanā*), it is said: "To whichever venerable one it is pleasing... [etc.]"

"He should speak thus," it is said. This [act] is comprised of five factors: the perfection of the subject matter (*vatthusampadā*), his purity from obstructive states (*antarāyika-dhamma*), the perfection of the boundary (*sīmāsampadā*), the perfection of the assembly (*parisāsampadā*), and the completion of the preliminary duties (*pubbakicca-niṭṭhāna*).

Among these, "perfection of the subject matter" refers to [the candidate being free] from the eleven types of persons incapable [of ordination] as previously stated, and those who have committed the ultimate offenses (*antimavatthu*).
And there must be another human male, twenty years of age, who has not yet been ordained.
For it is only when such a person exists that this formal act of ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*) of the Saṅgha is said to be "fit" (*pattakalla*); it is not fit when he is absent.

Furthermore, even if performed in his absence, the act is indeed invalid. And his purity from obstructing factors (*antarāyika-dhamma*) refers to the very same basis for ordination as previously described.

Regarding the person: those defective conditions—such as being afflicted by the five diseases prohibited by the Blessed One, not being permitted by one’s mother and father, and having hands severed and so forth—which were designated by the Blessed One as "obstructive" because they cause obstacles such as legal offenses for the Saṅgha that performs the act;
freedom from these obstructive defective conditions, and only when this [freedom] exists, is this formal act [valid].
It is called "fit" (pattakalla) when it does not fail; however, once a formal act (*kamma*) has been performed, it is indeed well-performed, with the exception of a person under twenty years of age.

As for the perfection of the boundary (*sīmāsampadā*), it should be understood according to the two types of boundaries—both those formally established and those not so established—as will be explained in the *Uposathakkhandhaka*, provided they are free from all defects. For it is only when such a boundary exists that this formal act is fit.
There is no name [for him], he does not exist, and the performed action fails.
As for the perfection of the assembly (*parisāsampadā*), however, it refers to those monks who, at the very least required for the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadākamma*),
number no fewer than ten or five, who have not fallen into a defeat (*pārājika*), who have not been suspended (*anukkhitto*), and who belong to the same communion (*samānasamvāsaka*).
Their standing within hand’s reach without leaving the common boundary; the bringing of the consent (*chanda*) by those entitled to give it;

the absence of protest from those present; and the exclusion of persons who are ineligible for ordination, those prohibited in the Uposatha-khandhaka, laypeople and others not ordained, those suspended for a *pārājika* offense, and nuns belonging to a different community (*nānāsaṃvāsaka*).
And the absence from the reach of the Saṅgha’s hand—these four factors comprise it.
It is only when such an excellence of the assembly exists that this is called "the proper time" (pattakalla), not when it does not exist.
Among these, if there is an absence of even one of the first three factors, the formal act (kamma) fails; but not if there is an absence of the last one.
The completion of the preliminary duties (*pubbakicca*) refers to those matters stated in the Canon beginning with, "First, he should be made to take a preceptor (*upajjhāya*)," namely:
the making of him take a preceptor; the pointing out of his bowl and robes; then, having sent him beyond arm's reach, the performance of the formal act of appointment of an instructor;
the going and instructing by the one so appointed; and by him [the candidate], being the first to...
Having arrived, he makes known the motion to the Saṅgha; then, while still within arm’s reach, he says to the candidate for ordination, “Come hither”;
then he has him pay homage at the feet of the monks and make the request for ordination;

then there is the formal act of appointment to inquire about the obstructing conditions, and the inquiry by the one so appointed—these are the eight preliminary duties. By performing all of these exactly as they are:

[This refers to] the completion. And it is only when these preliminary duties have been brought to completion that this formal act of ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*) of the Saṅgha is said to be "timely" (*pattakalla*); it is not so when they have not been completed.

However, even if these preliminary tasks have not been performed, the act remains unshakeable provided that the requirements such as the perfection of the subject matter (*vatthusampatti*) and so forth exist. Thus, in this context, "timeliness" consists of these five [factors].

It should be understood that [the action] is comprised by the constituent parts (*aṅga*). By this very method, the fitness for all actions—both those already mentioned below and those yet to be mentioned—should be known by applying it appropriately as the case may require.
"One should ordain such-and-such a person" means: in the sense of a resolution, "by bringing about ordination, one should make him a possessor of it; let him do so."

Or this should be understood according to the grammatical rule (*vidhi*). For just as when it is said, "One should cause Devadatta to sleep happily," the meaning is that one should bring about happiness for him and make him a possessor of that happiness;

so too here, the meaning is that one should bring about his full admission (*upasampadā*) and make him a possessor of that full admission. And this refers to the activity of the instigator (*payojaka-vyāpāra*). Just as...

Just as one who brings about happiness is called "one who makes happy" because they cause happiness to arise through the agency of a cause, so too here, the Saṅgha—acting as the causal agent—causes the person who is the pure agent of the act to attain full ordination by producing the cause of ordination;
this is what is meant. And by this, [the Saṅgha] is like the giver of happiness toward the one who experiences happiness.

It is established that when the Saṅgha grants full ordination (*upasampadā*) to an individual, there exists a conventional truth (*sammutisacca*), because it is designated by the Noble Ones based on the ultimate phenomena (*paramatthadhamma*) as they actually occur.

And here, because it is stated, "The person named so-and-so requests full ordination from the Saṅgha," the [ordination] conforms to the request, as in the case of probation (*parivāsa*) and other such procedures; thus, "[the ordination] of the person named so-and-so..."

Since it was stated, "one should ordain so-and-so," rather than "one should give [ordination]," this formal act of ordination (*upasampadākamma*) should be understood as not being included under "giving" (*dāna*), but rather as being included specifically within the characteristics of a formal act (*kammalakkhaṇa*). By this same method, the meaning should also be understood in the passage:
"He ordains so-and-so; he has been ordained by the Saṅgha. For in that case, the distinction is made solely on the basis of the present tense versus the past tense.
In this case, however, the only difference is by way of the time when it is not yet formally proposed (*anāmaṭṭha*).

"This is the motion" (*ñatti*) refers to the act of making known (*ñāpanā*) stated as "the Saṅgha is to be informed. And this is said for the purpose of indicating the presence of the formal proclamations (*anussāvanā*) as well.
This must certainly be stated; it need not be stated only in the case of a formal act consisting solely of a motion (*ñattikamma*). However, in that case...
It should be understood that as soon as the syllable *yya* is uttered, the formal act (*ñattikamma*) is completed. "It is pleasing" (*khamati*) means it is approved.
"Ordination" (*upasampadā*) refers to the ordination being granted and brought to fulfillment by the Saṅgha. The construction is: "He for whom it is pleasing should remain silent.
*Tuṇhī* is a particle used in the sense of not speaking; the meaning is "he should be one who does not speak. It is pleasing.

The connection with the standard formula is: "the full ordination of such-and-such a person for the Saṅgha. Regarding that, he states the reason: "therefore, [the Saṅgha is] silent. Here, the word "was" (*āsī*) is to be supplied.

Since the Saṅgha remained silent and voiceless even though it was asked three times, "He to whom it is not pleasing should speak," therefore the meaning is: "it is pleasing to the Saṅgha. By this word "thus" (*evaṃ*),...
"By this manner. "I maintain, I perceive, I know that this very state of silence is the approval of the Saṅgha"—this is the meaning.
The word *iti* is used here in the sense of completion; however, it is not a constituent part of the formal act (*kammavācā*).
Therefore, the one who makes the proclamation (*anusāvaka*) should conclude by saying only "I maintain" (*dhārayāmi*), ending with the syllable *-mi*, and the word *iti* should not be employed.
It should be observed. In this manner, the meaning of all formal ritual utterances (*kammavācā*) is to be understood.

The passage beginning with "of one man’s height" (*ekaporisā va*) is a demonstration of the method for knowing the shadow of beings by measuring it with the feet. For a shadow measured at six or seven steps is called "one man’s height" (*porisā*);
and this, as well as the explanation of the measure of the season and so forth, should be examined together with visiting guests.

This was stated for the purpose of performing acts such as paying homage and causing others to pay homage, having understood the state of seniority and juniority. It comes and goes, thus it is "season" (*utu*);
that by which the year is measured is "measure" (*pamāṇa*). Therefore he said: "The measure of the season is simply the season itself.
"Incomplete" means incomplete by way of full ordination (*upasampadā*) and so forth. If one has been fully ordained in the middle of the season, then at that time—
This shows that "indicating the remaining days of the season" means indicating the portion of the days [remaining]. Therefore he said:
"those days by which whichever season of a person is incomplete. Therein, the construction is:
"those days by which whichever season belonging to that person who has received full ordination at that moment is incomplete."
Because everything beginning with the shadow must be gathered together and sung—that is, recited—it is called a *saṅgīti*;
thus he said, "This very... and so forth. In that context, it should be explained by bringing [the items] together.

"What do you receive? means: at the time of your full ordination (*upasampadā*), which rainy season (*vassa*) and which month (*utu*) do you receive, and in which [season] was your full ordination obtained? "Rainy season" (*vassa*) refers to the months of the rains.
And since this mention of the year would not be understood even if stated without [specifying] the season, it should be seen that by this very mention of the season, it is shown:
"In the years of the Dispensation, or in the years of the Kali Age, etc., or in the thousandth, or in the hundredth, I obtain such-and-such a season.

The term "shadow" (*chāyā*) is stated with reference to the sequence found in the Pāḷi; however, according to the calculation of the elapsed time, in the years of the Kali Age, etc., [the shadow is determined].

"You should declare: 'In all places where it is established, in such-and-such a year, in such-and-such a season, in such-and-such a month, in such-and-such a dark or bright fortnight, on such-and-such a lunar day joined with such-and-such a weekday, during such-and-such a portion of the day beginning with the forenoon, at such-and-such a measure of shadow or such-and-such a measure of *nāḍikā*, I received the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Having learned this well in this manner," so it should be explained.

It should be said: "Having recognized the order of seniority among those who have arrived as guests, you should proceed accordingly. Thus far, this much of the method of exposition has been included in the *Vimativinodanī*.

However, according to the system of the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, some [explanations] are included right here, while others—because they involve a decision without final certainty—are based on doubt; therefore, they are not taken up here.
Thus concludes the Ornament of the Determination of Ordination, within the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*. 23.
The Discourse on the Determination of Dependence (*Nissaya*).

151. Having thus explained the determination regarding full ordination (*upasampadā*), he now speaks the determination regarding dependence (*nissaya*) with the words, “But here, ‘dependence’ (*nissaya*)...
and so forth. In this context, *nissaya* means the act of depending (*nissayana*); its meaning is service (*sevana*) or attending upon (*bhajana*).

The verbal root *si*, preceded by the prefix *ni*, is used to denote an abstract state (*bhāva-sādhana*); it is not, as in the expression “he dwells depending on that, therefore it is dependence,” a word denoting an unspecified object (*avutta-kamma-sādhana*).
For there, a person to be associated with is found; here, however, it is the act of associating.
Now, in order to establish that dependence (nissaya) in detail by means of an answer preceded by a question, he says: "By whom should it be given? and so forth.
Therein, "by whom should it be given? By whom should it not be given? asks about the agent who is the giver of dependence; "to whom should it be given? [asks about the recipient].

"To whom it should not be given" refers to the recipient who accepts dependence (*nissaya*). "How is it received? and "How is it extinguished? refer to the cause. "By whom should one dwell in dependence?
and "By whom should one not dwell in dependence? refer to the one practicing dependence.

Then, in order to answer according to the sequence of the questions, he said, "In that regard," and so forth. This is not only in this context; rather, the term "by one who is competent" (*byattena*) also occurs in the section on being released from dependence.

Regarding the question, "What is the distinction here?", he said: "And here, by the word 'competent' (*byatto*), one who is learned (*bahussuto*) and capable of presiding over the assembly (*parisupaṭṭhāpako*) is to be understood.
Now, in order to show the characteristics of one who presides over the assembly, he said: "By one who presides over the assembly," and so forth.
Therein, "in the Abhivinaya" means in the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. "To discipline" (*vinetuṃ*) means to train. "The two Vibhaṅgas" refers to those [texts] which are well-mastered.
They say that the instruction "it should be made to emerge in speech" was stated with reference to learning by means of questioning.
He said, "It should be made capable of being recited back and forth with three people," so that what one person has forgotten might become familiar to the others.
"In the Abhidhamma" refers to the *Nāmarūpapariccheda*. Or else, "the lower three sections" refers to [the sections] from the *Mahāvagga* onwards.
These three sections— the Sagāthāvagga, the Nidānavagga, and the Khandhavagga— are the lower [sections].
Since it is stated in the Mahāpaccarī that “it is appropriate to learn even the Dhammapada together with its *vatthu* stories,” a reciter of the Jātakas,
even after learning the Jātaka together with its commentary (*saṭṭhakatha*), must certainly learn the Dhammapada together with its *vatthu* stories as well.

Regarding the passage beginning with “Endowed with five factors, monks,” [the phrase] “a novice should not be attended” means that one should not, acting as a preceptor (*upajjhāya*), have a novice attend upon oneself.
“With the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training” (*asekkha*) refers to the aggregate of virtue belonging to one beyond training;
it is called the “aggregate of virtue of one beyond training” because it is the aggregate of virtue of one who is beyond training (*asekkha*). This applies in all instances.
And having done so, this discussion has arisen by taking into account even the knowledge of review (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa), which is termed the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Furthermore, by "the virtue of one beyond training" (asekkhasīla), not only the virtue of the highest fruit is intended;
rather, it refers to whatever virtue occurs within the continuum of one beyond training, because here virtue—both mundane and supramundane—is what is intended.
This same method applies to the sections on the aggregate of concentration and so forth, ending with the aggregate of liberation;

therefore, just as the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom were explained as being mixed with the mundane, so too is the aggregate of liberation. Thus, it should be understood that this includes liberation by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgavimutti*) and the others, not merely liberation by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhivimutti*).
However, the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuttiñāṇadassana*) is exclusively mundane. For this very reason, in the commentary to the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*:
It is said: “By the first four terms, mundane and supramundane virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation are explained;
the knowledge and vision of liberation is reflective knowledge, and that is purely mundane.
Regarding the three bases beginning with “one who lacks faith”: one who has no faith is “one who lacks faith” (*assaddho*). One who has no sense of shame is... [one who lacks shame] (*ahiriko*).
"Shameless" (ahirika) is a designation for one who does not feel disgust toward unwholesome attainments.
"Not feeling shame" (anottappī) means one who does not fear unwholesome attainments. "Lax" (kusīta) means one who sinks into what is contemptible;

this is a designation for one of inferior energy. "One whose energy is aroused" (āraddhavīriyo) means one whose energy has been set in motion; this is a designation for one who is engaged in the right exertions (sammappadhāna).
"One whose mindfulness is muddled" (*muṭṭhassati*) means one whose mindfulness is lost; that is what is meant.
"One whose mindfulness is established" (*upaṭṭhitassati*) refers to one whose mindfulness constantly proceeds directed toward the object; this is a designation for such a person.

One who has failed in virtue regarding higher virtue (*adhisīla*) and has failed in conduct regarding higher conduct (*adhi-ācāra*), having committed an offense and not having emerged from it, is intended here.
It is called "holding to extremes" (*antaggāhikā*) because it grasps, or causes one to grasp, an extreme defined as either eternalism or annihilationism; this refers to wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*).
"The first two phrases" refers to these two phrases: "He is not capable of attending to a pupil or a co-resident who is ill, or of having them attended to;
nor is he capable of comforting one who is dissatisfied, or of having them comforted."
"Abhisamācāra" means excellent and supreme conduct; "ābhisamācārika" refers to that very conduct, and it is called "training" (*sikkhā*) because it is to be trained in.
Thus, "ābhisamācārika-sikkhā" is the training pertaining to excellent conduct. Alternatively, the training prescribed with reference to excellent conduct is "ābhisamācārika-sikkhā";
this is a designation for the training included within the Khandhaka rules of conduct. It is the beginning of the holy life of the Path (*magga-brahmacariya*).
“Pertaining to the fundamental spiritual life” (*ādibrahmacariyaka*) is a designation for the training included within the two Vibhaṅgas. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*:

“That which is included in the two Vibhaṅgas is ‘pertaining to the fundamental spiritual life,’ while that which is included in the Khandhakas and the Vatta is ‘relating to higher conduct’ (*ābhisamācārika*).

Therefore, regarding the phrase “in the description of those in training” (*sekkhapaṇṇattiyaṃ*): they are called “those in training” (*sekkhā*) because they must train, and [the rules] are so called because they were prescribed by the Blessed One.

It should be understood that "formal proclamation" (*paṇṇatti*)—referring to every formal proclamation of training rules included within the two Vibhaṅgas—is called a "proclamation for those in training" (*sekkhapaṇṇatti*).
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*: "In the 'proclamation for those in training' means:
in the proclamation of the training rules to be practiced, beginning with the *pārājika* [offenses]. The rest here is of plain meaning, according to the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
In the discussion regarding preceptors and teachers, "a novice should not be attended upon" means that one should not be ordained by acting as a preceptor.

"Of one who is beyond training" (*asekkha*) means belonging to one who is beyond training; it refers to the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*), both mundane and supramundane. "By one who grasps at extremes" means by one who grasps at the positions of eternalism or annihilationism.
"The last two" refers to these two factors: "he is of little learning" and "he is lacking in wisdom. "The last three" refers to...
There are these three: being unable to dispel arisen remorse according to the Dhamma, not knowing the offense, and not knowing the emergence from the offense.
For the inability to dispel remorse according to the Dhamma—consisting of the texts, the commentaries, and the methods—is due solely to lack of proficiency;
thus, that too is stated as a factor of the offense itself.
"Abhisamācāra" means excellent or supreme conduct; it refers to the virtue of performing one's duties (*vatta-paṭipatti-sīla*).

The training prescribed with reference to that, known as the rules of training in the *Khandhaka*, is called "ābhisamācārika. Indeed, even a rule of training (*sikkhāpada*) is called "training" (*sikkhā*) because it must be practiced through learning and so forth by those who desire the fulfillment of its purpose.
It is the beginning and the cause of the holy life of the Path (*magga-brahmacariya*).
The training rules included in the two Vibhaṅgas are those pertaining to the beginning of the holy life (*ādibrahmacariyaka*). For this very reason, it is stated here in the *Visuddhimagga*:
"The training rules included in the two Vibhaṅgas pertain to the beginning of the holy life; those included in the Khandhakas and the Vatta pertain to higher conduct (*ābhisamācārika*).
Therefore, regarding the phrase "in the description of the trainee" (*sekkhapaṇṇattiyaṃ*), they are called "trainees" (*sekkhā*) because they must train.

It is called a "proclamation" (*paññatti*) because it was proclaimed by the Blessed One himself. It should be understood that all the proclamations regarding the training rules (*sikkhāpada-paññatti*) included in both the *Vibhaṅgas* are referred to as "proclamations for those in training" (*sekkha-paññatti*).

Regarding the "delimitation of name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa-pariccheda*), here [is explained] the fourfold aggregate of feeling and so forth, as described in the "Triads of the Wholesome" (*kusalattika*) and other texts, through their various classifications such as genus, plane, person, association, basis, object, kamma, door, characteristic, function, and so on.
"Name" (nāma) refers to nibbāna; "form" (rūpa) refers to the classification of the primary elements and derived matter.

The wisdom that knows these by way of such analysis is called *Nāmarūpapariccheda*, and the treatise that elucidates this is also named *Nāmarūpapariccheda*. By this, he shows that one must become skilled in the meaning of the Abhidhamma.
Regarding the phrase "to cause to train," the *Vimativinodanī* states it means "to cause to learn."
153. Regarding the phrase “I shall dwell depending on the Venerable One” (*āyasmato nissāya vacchāmi*): here, *āyasmato* is a genitive used in the sense of the accusative;
the meaning is “I shall dwell depending on the Venerable One. As for what was stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*—“one who is competent...

[and] possesses the aforementioned characteristics”—that refers to one who is learned and capable of attending to the assembly. [This applies] to those who have gone forth, those who have received full ordination, and to dharma-disciples (*dhamma-antevāsika*).

Furthermore... [as before] ... "the duties must be performed until then" means that the aforementioned duties must be performed for the teacher of going-forth (*pabbajjācariya*), the teacher of full ordination (*upasampadācariya*), and the teacher of the Dhamma (*dhammācariya*). In this context, he by whom the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) were given is the teacher of going-forth;
he by whom the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadakammavācā*) was recited is the teacher of full ordination; and he who [gives] the recitation or the interrogation...
Or he gives [it]; this one should be understood as a teacher of the Dhamma (*dhammācariya*). The rest here is of plain meaning. 154.

In the discussion on the cessation of dependence (*nissayapaṭippassaddhi*), "gone to a direction" means having gone to some region for the sake of staying, whether intending to return again or not intending to return.
"Having observed the fellow-student's state" means having observed his state of being well-behaved (*pesala*). "Having looked" means...
Having investigated. Regarding "if he departs... [etc. ...he should go there":
here they say that if, being unable to go on that very day due to some business, he is intent on going with the thought, "I will go in a few days," he maintains [the status of a resident].
"Do not retreat here" means do not enter here. "He should dwell right there" means having received formal dependence (*nissaya*) right there.

One may dwell [there]. Regarding the statement, "It is permissible to dwell in that very same monastery...": because it has been relinquished by the preceptor (upajjhāya), there is no exemption from the rule concerning co-residence with a preceptor;
therefore, even for one who has gone into co-residence with a preceptor, the formal support (nissaya) received in the presence of a teacher (ācariya) does not cease.

Regarding the cessation of dependence (*nissaya*) due to the teacher (*ācariya*), as for the phrase "the teacher has departed," the determination stated there concerning the departure of the preceptor (*upajjhāya*)— beginning with "departed means gone to a distant region"— can be understood here in the same manner as explained in that context;
therefore, rather than repeating that, [the text] states something different, beginning with "a certain teacher departs after having taken leave."

This method has been undertaken. And this same method should be understood to apply even when the preceptor departs. For in such instances, the characteristic of being used in one sense should be seen as applying elsewhere as well.
If he returns after having gone beyond two *leḍḍupāta*s (the distance of a stone’s throw), it is said that "he has ceased [his departure]";
in this context, he is called one who has departed to another region (*disāpakkanta*), even if the resident pupil (*antevāsika*) has not yet relinquished his duty.

The dependence (nissaya) is suspended. When the teacher and preceptor reside in another monastery beyond two clods' throw from [the student], they are residing in a lodging outside the boundary of the precincts (*upacārasīmā*) beyond two clods' throw from the dwelling place of the resident pupil (*antevāsika*) and the co-resident (*saddhivihārika*).
However, even if they are beyond two clods' throw within the boundary of the precincts (*antoupacārasīmā*), [the dependence remains].
While one is living [under dependence], the dependence is not suspended.

It is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī* that everything beginning with, "Even if the teacher, desiring to release him, dismisses him by means of a dismissal from dependence," should be understood as applying even to the command of a preceptor (*upajjhāya*).
153. *Sāhu*: good, excellent. *Lahu*: not heavy; the meaning is "easy to support. *Opāyika*: connected with a skillful means (*upāya*).
The meaning is that practicing in this way is the means for crossing over. "Appropriate" (patirūpa) means proper conduct (sāmīcikamma).
"With what is pleasing" (pāsādika) means with a bodily or verbal application that inspires confidence; the meaning is: "Accomplish it.

"By body" (kāyena) means he makes his request by means of the body, such as by showing hand gestures (hatthamuddā) that communicate this purpose. "Regarding 'Sādhū' as acceptance" refers to when the preceptor says "Sāhū" and so forth.

The intention behind the statement beginning with "he makes it known by body" is that it refers to the words of acceptance, "Very well," spoken by the co-resident (saddhivihārika) when these [instructions] have been spoken.
"By the mere act of requesting and giving" means: first, by the mere act of the co-resident's request, and then, by the mere act of the preceptor’s (upajjhāya) words such as "Very well" and so forth.
Regarding the taking of formal dependence (nissaya) in the presence of the teacher (ācariya):
"Relying upon the Venerable One, I shall go" means "relying upon the Venerable One, I shall dwell.

In the discussion on the cessation of formal dependence (*nissayapaṭippassaddhi*), the statement "formal dependence must be taken in the presence of one who shares both communal enjoyment and common use of requisites" enjoins the taking of dependence only toward those who possess a sense of shame (*lajjī*), because it is prohibited in the case of those lacking shame (*alajjī*). Here...
And by the term "use" (*paribhoga*), co-residence (*saṃvāsa*)—such as sharing the same meal—is included, because the use of requisites is already covered by the term "enjoyment" (*sambhoga*).
By this, he shows that one should not engage in enjoyment or co-residence with those who are shameless (*alajjī*).

"There is no exemption" means there is no exemption from the offense. "Such a person" refers to one where support (*nissaya*) was previously received, and one who shares in the same enjoyment and use.
"Such is the case. "So it was said" means that it was said, "He will return quickly. "Four or five days" is merely an illustration;
if his kinship is recognized within one or two days, he should be accepted on the very day he is known.
Even if it is not recognized after four or five days, one must wait as many days as it takes for him to be recognized.

However, one must not entertain even the slightest thought, "I shall look for someone of similar status. Regarding the phrase "while the young women are listening," even if they have not actually heard [the message], the exemption still applies provided there is the perception that "she will come" or "she is delaying due to some obstacle. Therefore it was said:
"If she sends word, 'I will stay right here,' there is no exemption"; this means there is no exemption even for a single day, indicating a lack of enthusiasm for going.

This was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*). However, there is no fault even if several days have passed, provided that the pupil remains willing (*saussāha*) through acts such as returning the lodging (*senāsana-paṭisāmana*).
"He must dwell right there" means he must dwell having taken formal dependence (*nissaya*) in that very same common dwelling place (*sabhāga-ṭṭhāna*).

By the statement, "It is permissible to dwell in that very monastery...," the formal dependence (*nissaya*) ceases when he is in the company of his preceptor (*upajjhāya*), provided that he is indeed supporting him.
However, it is stated that when [the teacher] does not provide support due to anger or indifference toward the group, the dependence already established with others is not extinguished;

this is shown by the method beginning with "a certain teacher" mentioned in the section on the extinction of dependence from a teacher, which applies likewise to the departure of a preceptor and so forth.
Having been explained there, it should also be applied here as appropriate after being brought forward.

"Living in another monastery beyond two clods' throw" means that they live beyond two clods' throw from the place where the resident pupils and others dwell, outside the boundary of the precinct (*upacāra-sīma*).
Therefore, even if it is outside the precinct, [the distance is measured] from the place where the resident pupils and others dwell.
This shows that if one lives in a place near the distance of two clods' throws, the formal support (nissaya) is not suspended.
However, it is stated in the *Vimativinodanī* that for one living beyond two clods' throws within the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā), the formal support is indeed not suspended.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Ornament of the Discourse on the Determination of Dependence," in the *Vinayālaṅkāra*,
which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
24. Discussion on the Delimitation of the Boundary (Sīmāvinicchayakathā) 156.
Having thus explained the delimitation of dependence (*nissaya*), he now speaks of the delimitation of the boundary (*sīmā*) with the words, “*Sīmā* means here,” and so forth.
In this context, *sīmā* refers to that which is delimited—that is, it is bound by a formal act (*kammavācā*) performed by a harmonious Saṅgha. [The root] *si* means to bind.

The term *dhātu*, the suffix *ma*, and this class of verbs beginning with *kiyati* [apply here]. Since the manifestation of the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of things possessing distinctions cannot occur without analysis, he said:
"This is called a boundary... it exists. Therein, in order to first demonstrate the established boundary (*baddhasīma*), he said: "Therein, eleven... and so forth.

Because the formal act of the Saṅgha (*saṅghakamma*) has twenty as its minimum requirement for its performance, [the boundary] must, at the very least, be where—along with those eligible for the formal act—...
Twenty-one monks are able to sit; it is permissible to bind the boundary (sīmā) over that much space, but not less than that.
He said: "Too small" means where twenty-one monks cannot sit.
"In the eastern direction" is merely an illustration; however, if there is no landmark (nimitta) in that direction, wherever—
There is; from that point on, after first designating the signs in all directions where they exist— beginning with "in the intermediate eastern direction," "in the southern direction," and so forth—

it is permissible to designate them again by repeating the first one mentioned, "in the intermediate eastern direction," because a boundary may be formally established even for one shaped like a crossroads (siṅghāṭaka) by means of three signs.

"Binding the boundary-circle three times by means of connecting [the markers]" means that the holder of the Vinaya, standing himself in one place alone, binds the boundary-circle all around by means of one marker after another through the mere act of announcing the characteristics (*nimitta*).
For it is permissible to announce them even without going to each respective location of the markers. This applies even to a boundary that extends for up to three *yojanas*.

Because it is difficult to circumambulate [the boundary] three times in every direction in a single day, even if the boundary marker has not been personally seen by the *vinayadhara*, he may still perform the formal proclamation (*kittana*)—
saying, for example, "This stone is the marker," and so forth— by observing the marker as it was previously defined by other monks according to what someone had stated,
such as "Venerable sir, this is a stone. This is indeed permissible.
By the phrase "with interlocking branches," it indicates their mutual proximity. "It is bound" is said with reference to the boundary in the western direction.
It is stated, "a space of one *ratana* is easier to discern," and for this reason it is said, "a boundary interval of the measure of a hand should be established at the western limit.
An interval even of the measure of a single finger is indeed permissible; by that much alone—
For the boundary remains unconfused. It is said that "it becomes a marker for two boundaries" because, since the marker is outside of the boundary, there is no confusion of boundaries.

It is said that "it causes a mixing of boundaries" because when [the marker] has been enlarged and has entered the area of the boundary, the place where the two boundaries meet is difficult to discern;
however, it does not mean that one may perform formal acts (*kamma*) there.
This is for the purpose of showing that [the original boundary] is no longer valid. For a boundary does not cease to be a boundary merely by that much;

rather, two boundaries become joined as one because they are subsequently encompassed by the tree that has grown. Therefore, those performing an act while standing in one place must do so after clearing the other [boundary].
"In a portion of it" means at a place where monks are able to perform the act while standing.

However, when those who are binding [the boundary] include within it a place where it is impossible for those standing therein to perform an act (*kamma*), they are said to "break the boundary with the boundary" (*sīmāya sīmaṃ saṃbhindanti*). "They do not make the *kammavācā* incomplete" means they do not break the *kammavācā*;
the intended meaning is that they do not invalidate the act.
158. "A mountain of pure sand" means it was not made by anyone, but is said to have arisen spontaneously; the same applies to the others as well.

"The other too" refers even to mountains such as the mountain of pure sand. Regarding the phrase "the size of an elephant," here the measurement of an elephant should be understood in terms of its height above the ground.
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī* and the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, it is stated: "A mountain the size of an elephant..."
"It is said that at its lowest limit, it is seven and a half ratanas in height. Regarding "by four or by three":

this means by those standing in four or three directions within the boundary area; however, it is not permitted to elect [the Saṅgha] even by many more than that if they are standing in only one direction.
Nor is it permitted by two people standing in two directions. Therefore, because it cannot be done by one...

It is permissible; therefore. "Having placed that outside" means that because the marked boundary (kittita-nimitta) lacks the quality of a formal boundary (sīma), performing [the rite] within the formal boundary is improper;
thus he said, "If," and so forth.
The measure of thirty-two *palas* of sugar-lump should be understood by way of its shape, not by way of weighing or counting, as it would be too heavy [otherwise].
The measure in *palas* should be taken according to the Magadhan scale, and they say that this is double the size of the worldly scale.

However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: "The measure of thirty-two *palas* of a lump of sugar should be understood in terms of weight (*tulatā*), not in terms of the counting of scales (*tulagaṇanā*).
"Even though it is very large" means that even if it extends from the ground for the height of an elephant and descends into the subterranean depths for many *yojanas*.
For if a peak the size of an elephant were to rise from there, it would simply be considered a mountain. In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*,

regarding the statement "if it is a single continuous mass, it need not be made," this refers to the fact that although the four mountain peaks in the four directions are connected as one because they rest upon rocks similar to the back-slab, their connection extends upward from the earth.
When there is no connection with the earth below, it is permissible to designate it as "not a stone" (abbohārika) and to describe it as such.

For this very reason, it is said: "Even a back-slab, though very large, is reckoned simply as a stone. However, if its great size is considered in relation to the earth below it, it becomes a mountain;
thus it is stated in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*. [This applies] to a heap of sand made by piling it up.
If grass, shrubs, and trees grow [there], it is a mountain—thus says the Elder Dhammasiri;

"not so" says the Elder Upatissa. Regarding "stone," they say that even a stone made of plaster (sudhā) is permissible; this should be investigated, as such a thing is excluded by the mention of bricks.

"That too" refers even to a stone that has risen up like a stump. Regarding the phrase "even a mere sign of four or five trees," it is stated that in some [recensions] the word *nimitta* (sign) is absent.
"Containing pith" (*antosa-rānaṃ*) is said with reference to the fact that although pith is not present at that moment due to their youth, it will exist through their subsequent development.
For even a grove of as many as four or five such trees, each having a circumference of about the size of a needle-shaft, is permissible.
"Mixed with those containing pith" means mixed with trees that possess internal pith; by this, it is also implied that they may be mixed with trees that have pith only in their bark.
This shows that a forest is required. The phrase "even as much as four or five trees" is said with reference to trees of heartwood (*sāra*).
However, in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, it is stated: "In this context, if there are three heartwood trees and two non-heartwood trees, a plurality of heartwood trees should be desired.
Even a cemetery is reckoned here as a 'forest' because it is self-grown. Some, however, [say] regarding the four...
It is said: "If there are two [trees] with solid heartwood inside, it is permissible; if there are more than two, or if they are equal [in number], it is permissible;
therefore, even if there are many, if there are two with solid heartwood inside, it is permissible. Regarding the phrase "building a monastery in the middle of a forest":
having defined the boundary of the monastery by means of fences and so forth, without cutting down the trees within the clusters of trees, one builds it precisely among the trees inside.
The meaning is that they build the monastery in such a way—by constructing surrounding cloisters, leaf-huts, and so forth—that even the interior of the monastery becomes as if it were forest itself.

For if they were to cut down all the trees and build the monastery, then because the monastery would no longer be surrounded by forest, the forest standing around it would have to be designated as a single unit; however, since there is forest even inside here, [it is called] "forest."
"It should not be praised," it is said. For if they were to praise it, the fault stated immediately below—namely, "the dwelling is above the sign," and so forth—would ensue.
"A portion" means a portion of the forest; the meaning is a portion of the forest situated on one side of a dwelling built in a place devoid of trees.
"Of the measure of a needle-shaft" means of the measure of a bamboo shaft. Some say it is "of the measure of a writing-reed.

However, since it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary on the Schedule), in the section on the determination of what is indivisible: "Any bamboo even as small as a needle-shaft of eight finger-breadths...
[is] heavy property," it should be understood that the bamboo shaft is thinner than [the former], and it is called a "needle-shaft. "In bamboo tubes, bowls, and so forth..."
The meaning is: "in bamboo joints, in reed joints, or in earthenware vessels such as potsherds.
The phrase "even at that very moment" is said with reference to young seedlings of a kind that grows without wilting.

However, those which are mature and, even when uprooted and replanted, wither like severed branches and only survive after a long time through the emergence of new roots and sprouts—or else perish entirely—[are not included].
It is not appropriate to praise such [a person]. "This" refers to the emergence of nine new roots and branches. However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated:
"Regarding 'the size of a needle-shaft,' they say it is the size of a writing-stick in the island of Sri Lanka; that should be understood as the measure of the little finger."
"Midway" means within the four great directions of the boundary. "Corner" refers to the points where two roads meet at each of the four corners of the boundary.
Regarding the statement that it is appropriate to designate [the boundaries] on the opposite side:

this means that having gone outside those four corners, one designates one road among the eight roads situated in one direction and another in the opposite direction; thus, all four [corners] are designated.
The intention is that it is appropriate to praise the paths in the four directions.

However, it is not understood how the state of being a single continuous whole disappears by merely praising them in this way. Furthermore, even in the subsequent passage, these same four paths are mentioned:
"Four paths go out in the four directions. Since this has been stated, the underlying reason for this must be investigated here.
This is stated in the *Vimativinodanī*. However, when investigating, the reason becomes clear as follows:

both in the preceding statement, "having surrounded the monastery with four paths," and in the subsequent statement, "the path that goes out through the middle of the monastery," it is spoken specifically with reference to the monastery;
therefore, here too, in the commentary, the phrase "having gone out through a corner" [is used].
Because it was stated thus, these paths reached only the corner of the dwelling; they did not intersect with one another.
Therefore, since there is no state of being joined together, it is appropriate to designate the four paths at four separate locations.
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it says: "It is appropriate to designate them on the opposite side" means that when eight paths stand outside after having exited, [one should designate] from one...
Only this much was stated: "It is appropriate to recite it thus for the four locations: 'one [direction] from this direction, one [direction] from that direction.
However, in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, it is said: "'In the subsequent part'—here, it is appropriate because [the person] has gone from the place bound by these [directions];
likewise, even on a long road, it is because the place reached is different from the place previously occupied. That too...
It should be examined because of the state of being connected as one.
Regarding the phrase "for a nun who is crossing over": this was stated because the definition of a river is given in the Pāḷi in the context of nuns crossing to the other side of a river;
for monks, even merely wetting their inner robes (antaravāsaka) is permitted. This is also stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
“Only a *bhikkhunī* is mentioned here because the definition of a river in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga* was set forth according to the category of a *bhikkhunī*;
it is stated thus for the sake of showing it by that same method.
For those binding a boundary, this river possessing the stated characteristics serves as the landmark, whether it flows into the ocean or a lake; starting from its source, it is the landmark.”

It is said, “it becomes [wet]”. However, in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, it is stated: “Some say that because it is said ‘the inner robe becomes wet’, it is permissible to do so only in water of such a measure.
By the word ‘becomes wet’, the definition of a river is stated as its lower limit;
in such a river, at whatever place the water flows for four months, whether little or much, having overflowed [the banks].”
It is said: "In that place, it is permissible to perform [the ritual] even while standing in shallow water," according to some.

By the phrase "The same method applies to the four rivers," he shows that once one has designated [the boundary] in one place, it is not permissible to designate it again in another place further away.
For this very reason, it is said: "However, it is permissible to designate all four unmixed rivers."

The term "unmixed" (*asammissa*) has been employed. Because the obstruction flows forth after having completely overwhelmed [the water], it is said that the obstruction flows forth after having overwhelmed it. "Not flowing" (*apavattamānā*) means not moving;

for wherever in a river the water remains standing without flowing after reaching an obstruction, it is not permitted to establish the boundary-mark (*nadīnimitta*) there, but only in the place where it flows above.

It is permissible. However, it is permissible to establish a water-mark (udakanimitta) in a place where the water does not flow. For only water that is stationary is permissible as a water-mark, not water that is flowing.
Therefore he said: "In a place where there is a flow, a river-mark (nadīnimitta) may be established; in a place where there is no flow, a water-mark may be established.
Because it was stated, "In a place where there is a flow, a river-mark," [it follows that] beyond the bridge...
"If that much water flows [constantly], they say it is indeed a river.

Water standing in natural ponds (*jātassara*) and the like may be used as a boundary marker even for the intervening space by means of the term 'natural pond' and so forth, just like a marker for the river-bank boundary.
If that place, over time, reaches the status of a village field, it is permissible to establish another boundary there," according to the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*.

It has been said: "At the root" means at the beginning. "Having broken the river" means just as it is impossible for farmers who do not wish [the water to flow] to turn back a great flood, so too having broken the bank.
Alternatively, "having broken the river" means having broken the river bank by means of the opening of the channel-mouth.

*Ukkhepimaṃ* means that which is to be drawn up by means of a long rope and pulleys. Or, *ukkhepimaṃ* means that which is to be taken after being lifted up like [water] from a well. Or, *ukkhepimaṃ* means that which is to be taken after having been extracted.
*Asammissehi* means by those standing on mountains in all directions, or by any of the stones and so forth not separated by other landmarks (*nimitta*).
*Sammissehi* means by those eight standing such that there is a mountain in one place and a stone in another. [This refers to] the landmarks (*nimittānaṃ*).
By the phrase "even with a hundred," it is shown that it is permissible to describe many signs in a single direction, such as: "What is the sign in the eastern direction?
A mountain, Bhante. Again, what is the sign in the eastern direction? A rock, Bhante. "Shaped like a crossroads" means triangular.
Alternatively, "shaped like a crossroads" means shaped like a street junction where three roads meet.
"Square" means perfectly square. However, "shaped like a mudiṅga drum" refers to a long quadrangle that is contracted at one end and broad at the other;
or alternatively, "shaped like a mudiṅga drum" means it is broad in the middle and contracted at both ends, like a mudiṅga kettle-drum.

159. Having thus shown the perfection of the boundary-mark for the established boundary, he now says, "Those endowed with the perfection of the assembly," etc., in order to show the perfection of the assembly.
Therein, "at the very least limit" means at the lowest numerical limit; the intention is that if the group is smaller than that. However, of this...
Because the formal act for the authorization of a boundary (*sīmāsammuti-kamma*) is to be performed by a quorum of four, it is said, "by four monks.
"Assembled" means having gathered together in concord, without leaving one another's reach of hand. By this, the first characteristic of sufficiency is stated:
"In a formal act to be performed by a quorum of four, there must be four regular monks who are eligible for the act, and they must have arrived."

He shows this. "As far as that village precinct" means: the connection is that the monks standing within the village precinct—which is the source of revenue for a single village headman and the specific area where they wish to establish the boundary—[should perform the act].

By the phrase "without crossing over a bound boundary, or a river, the ocean, or a natural lake," it is shown that these [latter] boundaries, such as the bound boundary, constitute intervals between the village boundaries.

Those standing within those [boundaries] do not constitute a *vagga* (an incomplete assembly) for those performing an act on the village boundary; therefore, it is shown that their consent (*chanda*) need not be brought.

"Having placed them all within arm's reach" means: having placed all the monks situated within the village field—who are capable of assembling to avoid a *vagga*-act—within the arm’s reach of the Saṅgha. [Regarding] the consent...
"Or having brought [the consent]" means having brought the consent of those who are unable to assemble.
Even if there are a thousand bhikkhus within that village precinct, only four among them are eligible for the formal act (*kamma*); the remainder are entitled to give their consent.

Therefore, the meaning is that the consent of those not present must be brought; by this, he states the second characteristic of perfection, namely: "the consent of those entitled to give consent has been brought."
The third characteristic of perfection, namely that "those who are present do not protest," is stated here by implication.

Having thus shown the perfection of the assembly regarding the established boundary (*baddhasīmā*), he now says, "They are endowed with the perfection of the formal act" (*kammavācāsampattiyuttā*), and so forth, in order to show the perfection of the formal act (*kammavācā*).
Therein, the meaning of the words beginning with "Let my [words] be heard" (*suṇātu me*) is as follows:
This has already been stated below in the commentary on the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kammavācā*).

"Thus spoken" means thus spoken by the Blessed One in the Uposatha Khandhaka according to this sequence. "Pure" means completely pure with respect to defects in the motion (*ñatti-dosa*) and defects in the proclamation (*anusāvana-dosa*).
"By means of a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation" is because it is performed with one motion and one proclamation.
"Motion as the second" means a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation; [it is performed] by that.
