Within the boundary markers there is the boundary, while the boundary markers are outside the boundary; this is because the boundary has been established by placing the markers outside and taking the water supporting the earth below as the limit.

161. Having thus shown the success of the formal act (*kammavācā*) for the agreement on the boundary for common residence (*samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmāsammuti*), he now says, "And when it has been bound in this way," etc., showing the success of the formal act for the agreement on the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmāsammuti*) which was prescribed by the Blessed One for the sake of the comfortable use of robes by monks who have resolved upon the three robes (*adhiṭṭhitatecīvarika*).
Therein, "one should agree upon non-separation from the three robes" means:
Just as a monk who has resolved to live with only three robes (*ticīvarika*) remains as one not separated from his three robes even when staying apart from them within the boundary (*sīmā*),

and thus incurs no offense under the second *kathina* training rule, so too he should resolve that there shall be no separation from the three robes within that common-ordination boundary (*samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā*).
"Except for the village and the vicinity of the village" means, if within that common-ordination boundary...

The meaning is: "There is a village; having set aside that village and its precincts, one should designate as the 'non-separation from the three robes' boundary that which is distinct from them, yet belongs to the same communal residence.
It "becomes reckoned as a boundary" means it becomes reckoned specifically as a non-separation boundary. Even when a single family has entered [that area]...
"Vāti" means that in newly built houses, there is not even a single family that has entered first.
"Agataṃ vā" means that in an old village, even though people have abandoned their homes and departed for other families, there is not even a single family that has not arrived. 162.
Having thus shown the authorization of the boundary in brief, he shows it again in detail: "This is the summary here..."

"But this is the detailed explanation," he said, beginning with those words. "Having established a precinct around the boundary" means: having established a precinct sufficient to serve as a buffer zone outside the limits of those monasteries for the sake of the boundary that is to be bound in the future.
"In which monasteries the boundary has been bound" refers to those [monasteries] where the boundary has been fixed;
they are "bound-boundaries. "Separately" means individually. "Resembling bound boundaries" means as follows:
It shows that those standing within established boundaries (*sīmā*) are permitted to perform formal acts (*kamma*) individually, without regard for one another’s consent (*chanda*) and so forth;

it is the same for those standing within village boundaries (*gāmasīmā*). As for the phrase "by those who have gone inside the markers," this is said because if there is a desire to designate half of a single village as being inside [the boundary], there would be no purpose for everyone to come together. "One must come" means...
And this was stated by way of courtesy; it is not a fixed rule that "one must certainly come. For this very reason he said, "Both coming and not coming are permissible.

Because in the case of an unbonded boundary (*abaddhasīmā*), the various village-fields have the nature of distinct boundaries, there is no *vagga-kamma* (a quorum-deficient act) even when they do not come;
therefore, not coming is permissible. However, in the case of a bonded boundary (*baddhasīmā*), because it constitutes a single boundary, [the situation is different].
Furthermore, when another formal act (*kamma*) is being performed, those within the boundary must indeed come; thus it is said:

"The non-separation boundary... [etc]... they must come. At the time of proclaiming the boundary marks, there is no fault even if the boundary has not been purified, because the proclamation of the marks lacks any one of the requirements such as the formal motion (*apalokana*).
Regarding the phrase "or by the sign of a drum," it is recorded that one says, "We shall conclude the formal authorization.
By this, it is established that at such a time, that [action] is permissible.

Furthermore, regarding "by the sign of a drum or the sign of a conch," this refers to the purpose of preventing visiting monks from entering the village precinct once they have heard those sounds and realized, "The Saṅgha is now binding the boundary."
Furthermore, for the sake of preventing those such as the monastery attendants (*ārāmika*), the signal is made at the very moment the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) begins;

when this is so, that performance becomes purposeful. For this very reason, instead of saying "having made the sound of a drum or a conch," the inclusion of the term "signal" (*saññā*) is made by saying "having made the signal of a drum or a conch.
And having stated the prior action with the phrase "having made the signal," [the text continues] with "by means of the formal proclamation..."
When it is said, “The boundary (sīmā) should be bound,” this refers to the performance at a later time;
however, it should be understood that at the conclusion, after sounding all musical instruments and cymbals, a thanksgiving (anumodana) must be made for the gods and humans.
163. Taking up the going-forth (pabbajjā) with reference to the inquiry regarding the shaving of the head (bhaṇḍukamma). “For the sake of making happy” means for the sake of all.
Having abandoned the exhaustion of a formal assembly, it is for the sake of bringing about happiness with fewer [monks].
"He takes twenty-one monks" means that since a formal act of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma) requires a quorum of twenty, he takes twenty-one monks including the one entitled to perform the act.
And this is stated by way of those who are seated; for at the very least, where there are twenty-one monks...
If they are able to sit down, it is permissible to bind the boundary (sīmā) over that extent of space.

This statement is made so as to provide sufficient room for both those who are eligible for the formal act (kammāraha) and those who perform the rehabilitation (abbhāna). Regarding the instruction that "stones serving as markers (nimittupaga) must be placed," this is because trees and other such markers are difficult to find in a location chosen according to one's preference;
furthermore, it is to prevent the confusion of two boundaries being bound together as they expand.
And it is stated [in the text] because, since that [boundary] is absent in the case of a stone-marker, it is easy to bring and place it anywhere;
likewise in the case of the statement, "The boundary-stones at the dividing line (sīmantarika) should be placed. Regarding the phrase "even if they are only four finger-breadths in measure":
this means that from outside the delimitation of the broken boundary (khaṇḍasīma), the space occupied by the marker-stone extends for only four finger-breadths all around.

The remaining space belongs exclusively to the internal boundary of the district; thus, it should be understood that when those [stones] are placed, there is a boundary-interval (*sīmantarikā*) measuring only four finger-breadths.
"Boundary-interval stones" (*sīmantarikapāsāṇā*) are the stones established as markers for the boundary-interval. Furthermore, when describing them, one should [begin] from the south.
They should be recited while walking around [the meditation hall]. How so?
Standing in the western part of the boundary facing east, one should recite all the signs there in succession, asking, "What is the sign in the eastern direction?
Likewise, standing in the northern direction facing south, one should ask, "What is the sign in the southern direction?"
Having recited them in succession, and likewise having stood in the eastern direction facing west and recited in succession,
"What is the sign in the western direction?", and likewise having stood in the southern direction facing north and recited there in succession,
"What is the sign in the northern direction?", [he recites] all the signs therein in succession.
Again, standing in the western direction facing east, one should recite once more the previously mentioned [boundary marks] in the manner already described.
In this way, the boundary-stone markers for the intermediate boundaries (*sīmantarika*) of even many fragmented boundaries (*khaṇḍasīmā*) must be recited individually.
"Thereafter" means subsequently. "The remaining markers" refers to the remaining markers on the outer perimeters of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*). "They will not be able" means...

If, failing to recognize the state of having established the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*), they strive with the thought, "We shall abolish the very boundary of common affiliation (*samāna-saṃvāsa-sīmā*"), they will not succeed.

For even if a formal act (*kammavācā*) is performed with the intention, "Having abolished that [non-separation] boundary, we shall abolish the boundary of common affiliation," the boundary remains unabandoned so long as the non-separation boundary has been established. First, the non-separation...
Having first abolished [the boundary markers], the boundary itself must subsequently be abolished.

Since it is customary to bind [the territory] starting from a partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*), and because confusion does not arise through following established custom, it is said: "It should be bound starting precisely from a partial boundary.

"They do not invalidate both" means they do not invalidate the legal act (*kamma*) of both. However, when [the boundaries] have been bound in this manner... [the boundary] is indeed a village field (*gāmakkhetta*).
The statement "he frequents" is said not to define the boundary by way of residence, but rather to show that it is defined solely by way of the *sīmā* (boundary).
"In a hut or house" means in a grass hut built on the ground. "A mortar" refers to a small trench similar to the pit for a mortar.
"A sign should not be made" means that neither a line nor a mortar should be made as a sign. And this [applies] to those [cases] already mentioned.

It was stated that because it is not present among the eight signs, it is not permissible—even though it is established as such—to form a sign through the perception "this is a non-perishing mark," lest someone out of delusion should do so; this was said for the purpose of avoiding misfortune from afar.

Regarding the phrase "having placed [it] on a stone fixed to the sign," this was said because a mobile sign would be subject to shaking. The same applies to the subsequent phrases, such as "without scratching a wall," and so forth.

The reason for stating this established matter again and again should be understood as follows: since the failure of the *sīmā* (boundary) is the root of all failures of formal acts (*kamma*), such as ordination (*upasampadā*) and so forth, it must be discussed here by way of closing that door in every respect.
It should be seen that the teachers have provided their detailed exposition (*vinicchaya*) here only after having explained everything.
"A wall" means one made of bricks, wood, or clay. However, for a wall made of stone, it is appropriate to designate a single stone that serves as the sign (*nimitta*) in its respective direction.
It is not appropriate to designate an entire wall constructed from many stones; this is because it must be referred to using the singular form:
"This stone is the sign. Regarding the phrase "only within the inner wall," here, even within the inner wall—
The boundary should be understood as being right within the space occupied by the markers.

Having placed stones as markers at the front means that stones should be placed in a location facing the interior of the cell and measuring the same width as the cell’s front, and then the site should be formally designated.
For in this way, even including the wall standing between the interior and exterior of the cell, the area both inside and outside takes on a square shape.
There is a boundary. "Outside" means outside all around the entire cave-dwelling (*kuṭileṇa*).
"There is a boundary both inside and outside" means that, together with the wall standing in the middle, there is a square boundary (*caturassasīmā*).
By the statement, "It exists only on the upper story of the palace," because the wall standing between the inner chamber (*gabbha*) and the vestibule (*pamukha*) is one, there [are] twenty-one...
Because there is no space for the monks [to move], it does not descend below; however, it shows that the upper wall remains within the boundary.
"It does not descend below" means that because signs have been established and marked on the inside of the wall, it does not descend into the space below;
the meaning is "in a building constructed above. "On the lower floor" (heṭṭhimatale) refers to the four directions on the lower floor.
"Standing on the wall. For if the wall were to stand in only two or three directions, it would not descend below.
"It also descends below" means that if there is space for twenty-one bhikkhus within the wall below, it descends.
And as it descends, it does not descend by the measure of the upper boundary, but descends by the measure of the wall all around. Of the four...
However, it descends by making the water’s limit at the lower ground-level, defined by the outer edge of the walls;
it does not go even a hair’s breadth beyond the walls. "From the wall of the palace" means from the wall on the upper floor.
Whether there is descent or non-descent should be understood according to the method already stated: if, below, there is space for twenty-one bhikkhus...
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated that the intended meaning is: "it exists" and "it enters," whereas "if not, it does not enter.

However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated: "This was said with reference to the fact that the walls on the four sides at the lower level are connected as one unit with the lintel-beams within the measurement of the upper boundary, and to the fact that the interior [of that space] constitutes the measurement of the western boundary, and so forth. Whatever may be the case here—
At the moment when the spouts and other such features are being bound [as markers], they do not constitute a boundary because they are merely locations where the signs are situated;
however, once the boundary has been bound, they should be understood as being situated within the boundary (*sīmaṭṭha*).
The phrase "of the boundary pillars" (*pariyantathambhānaṃ*) is said with reference to stone pillars located at the signs. It is connected by way of its upper surface.

The phrase "it is so" is stated because there are no boundary-posts (sīmaṭṭha-thambha) within the wall. For if such posts were present, even if the upper surface of the wall were not connected [to the posts], a palace standing upon those boundary-posts would still be considered to be within the boundary. The boundary is established by placing boundary-stones within the row of pillars; how is this to be understood?
Here too, regarding the upper surface of the beams supported by the boundary-located pillars, all of that is indeed "within the boundary," and there is no dispute on this point.
However, as for [the space] between the row of boundary-located pillars and the outer row of pillars which are not located within the boundary...
Some say that "half of it" is the boundary there on the upper surface of the balance-beams held at equal weight. Others say, "The entire village boundary.
Still others say, "It is only the formally established boundary (*baddhasīmā*).

Therefore, when performing the formal act (*kamma*), the elders, standing in a place free from doubt, must clear away all such doubtful areas before performing the act; this is the reason for reaching a definitive conclusion.
Or, having investigated [the terrain], one should act accordingly. Regarding "Tālamūlaka mountain":
it is like the base of a palmyra trunk; being thick at the bottom and gradually becoming slender as it rises up, it is said to resemble the base of a *hintāla* tree.
"In the shape of a canopy" means in the shape of an *ahicchattaka* (a mushroom). "In the shape of a drum" means...
It is thin in the middle and broad at the bottom and top. "At the bottom" refers to one shaped like a *mudiṅga* drum;
"in the middle" refers to one shaped like a *paṇava* drum. A mountain resembling a snake's hood means it is humpbacked like a snake's hood, with its peak bent over elsewhere from its base location.
An "overhanging cliff" (*ākāsapabbhāra*) is a cliff that is not enclosed by a wall.
"Of the measure of the boundary" means [the area] including the interior space up to the limit of the western boundary.

And that stone is "situated within the boundary" (*sīmaṭṭha*)—by this it is shown that the boundary is established only on a portion of ground delimited by such things as hollow stones, caves, or walls, and not on what is undelimited.
Furthermore, those things are boundaries because they are situated within the boundary, not because they are boundaries in their own nature, like a bed or other furniture situated within a boundary.
[The text] shows this. However, if that hollow rock does not touch the ground but hangs suspended in the air, the boundary does not extend into it.

Since the hollow rock itself is a boundary because it is connected to the boundary, how is it to be believed that the boundary does not extend into these hollow rocks and the like when they lack the required dimensions for the western limit?
[This is to be understood] from the authority of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Furthermore, in this case, there is no need for the boundary to descend to the lower surface— as occurs, for example, with mice following the course of a hollow stone wall;
rather, when the space below, even to the extent of the measurement of the western boundary,
is entirely or mostly delimited by stone walls and the like standing as thick as two finger-breadths and touching the upper surface, then [the boundary] being bound above...
The boundary established for the ground below, which is separated and delimited by those stones and other such objects, becomes fixed at one and the same moment together with the upper surface;

just as in the case of a river-bank boundary, even when the caves and other structures on both banks separated by the river are removed, the boundary that has descended below does not disappear until the disappearance of the Dispensation. However, first, regarding the upper boundary...
Even when a cave or similar structure is built after the boundary has been fixed, the boundary still descends into the ground below;

some do not accept this, but it should be understood that such a boundary established in both places is indeed one, just as a lineage or birth remains the same despite differences in individual manifestations.
For all boundaries—whether formally fixed (*baddha-sīmā*) or unfixed (*abaddha-sīmā*)—are based upon their respective natural supports.
In fields such as villages or forests, [concepts] pervade everywhere according to their respective boundaries in a single moment;

although they do not exist in an ultimate sense, they possess a single form together with their respective bases because they are designated as a unity—either based on those various ultimate phenomena that serve as their supports, or based on specific functions—as appropriate by both worldly people and those within the Dispensation. Likewise...

For indeed, in the world, a single designation is seen for a village, a forest, a river, a lake, and the ocean; and likewise in the Teaching, a single expression is used in such passages as: "That boundary has been agreed upon by the Saṅgha;
and if it be in a forest where there is no village, monks, within seven *abbhantara*s on all sides, this is therein a common residence with a single *uposatha*," and so forth.
This is not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*). There is a pervading of a single [term] across multiple phenomena.
It is our opinion that the loss of unity occurs because of the lack of uniformity in the conceptualization of a single part of the *kasiṇa* and so forth.
"Below this" means below the mountain-peak of the cobra's hood, in the expanse of space. "Of the cave": if a cave has been made, it means "of that cave.
Having again conceptualized that very cave in five ways, there is the determination of whether one enters or does not enter.
To demonstrate this, he said, "But if below," and so forth. Therein, "below" is connected with the phrase "there is a shelter.
Regarding "below there is a shelter in one place," he said "inside"; that is, inside the mountain, meaning at the foot of the mountain.
To specify that very word "inside" by way of a boundary limit, [he says] "of the upper boundary limit..."

It is said, "on the far side" (*pārato*). Although it should have been said "on this side" (*orato*) with reference to the foot of the mountain, it should be understood that "on the far side" was said with reference to the mountain peak, which is the basis for the boundary.

For this very reason, in the phrase "outside the cave," he specified the word "outside" by saying, "on this side of the upper limit of the boundary. Thus, [the boundary] does not extend beyond the boundary.
Here, "outside" refers to the cave located at the foot of the mountain.

The meaning is that the boundary does not descend into the lower part of the area above the boundary-limit that lies outside the cave. "Inside the boundary" means that it does not descend into the place within the cave and the foot of the mountain that is suitable for its own descent.
"The boundary does not descend outside; the boundary does not [descend] inside..."

And here, it should be understood that by the statement "it descends," the complete non-descending into the boundary is shown due to the absence of a shelter (leṇa) at the place where one's own descent would be appropriate.
For in this regard, the decision found in the *Vimativinodanī* is: "Not descending there, it remains above.
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it says only: "'It has a shelter within' means it has a shelter within the mountain."
It has been stated [in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*]: "‘Inside the cave’ means the interior of the mountain cave;
however, with reference to the door, it is said ‘from the far side to the near side,’ the intention being that in every respect one descends by way of the outer cave from the boundary.
But the teachers say: "This determination regarding the inner cave and the outer cave is profound, difficult to see, and difficult to understand."
Nevertheless, the wise should thoroughly determine this by relying on the method presented in the *Vimativinodanī*.

It should be understood that by the statement "fallen outside the boundary" (*bahi patitaṃ asīmā*), it is shown that even a boundary established upon unstable foundations such as upper palaces and the like perishes with their destruction.

Regarding the phrase "they dig a lotus pond, [thinking] it is indeed within the boundary": here, if a subterranean river below flows from the very beginning without being less than the measure of the boundary, and the boundary is subsequently demarcated only above the river, then it should be understood that the boundary will be destroyed when the lotus pond is dug down to touch the river.
Regarding "below the surface of the earth," this refers to the immediately adjacent cavity in the ground.

"Sīmamāḷaka" means in the courtyard of a broken boundary. "Vaṭarukkha" (banyan tree) is said here because it possesses branches capable of reaching even very far due to the support of its aerial roots.
A connection with any other kind of tree, creeper, and so forth, is likewise not permitted;
for that very reason, even a connection by means of a boat-rope bridge is prohibited. "Tato" means from that branch. "Mahāsīmāya pathavītalaṃ" means the ground-level of the great boundary.

In this context, since the village boundary has not been taken as something more proximate, but rather because the established boundary (*baddhasīmā*) itself has been taken, there is no fault of confusion (*sambhedadosa*) even when the village boundary and the established boundary are connected by means of trees and so forth;
it should be understood that they function through a mutual relationship of support and supported.
For if there were a fault of connection even between those two, how [could it be said] regarding the village boundary?

Should a boundary be authorized? For if there would be a fault in a boundary being connected with another boundary, it is not permitted to bind it there—just as a formally established boundary (*baddhasīma*) cannot be bound within a water-throwing boundary (*udakukkhepasīma*), nor as a water-throwing boundary cannot be bound within one’s own non-dependent grove-boundary (*gāmasīma*) and so forth. Therefore, [the text says]: "But if..."

By such statements as, "the branch of a tree or a shoot emerging from it has fallen onto the bank of a river, or is situated within the boundary of a monastery, or within the boundary of a village," the fault of connection with the boundaries of a village and so forth—which do not constitute one's own support—is shown for the water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*), but not for the river boundary;
it should be understood that the same applies here. And this meaning will become clear further on. *Āhacca* means having touched.

"Or, having cleared the great boundary (*mahāsīma*)" means: having cleared the entire great boundary by means of bringing [the monks] within arm's reach (*hatthapāsa*) and obtaining their consent (*chandāharaṇa*), etc., for all the monks residing within that great boundary.

By this, it is shown that even for two previously well-bound boundaries, a textual flaw (*pāḷimuttaka sambandhadosa*) may arise later through connection with trees and so forth, because they have not been released from all defects.

He shows that [the boundary] exists; and having rejected the mutual overlapping and encroachment of established boundaries by means of such statements as, "Monks, a boundary should not be joined with a boundary," he then permits it by saying, "Monks, I allow you, when establishing a boundary, to establish the boundary after setting aside an interval between the two boundaries.
Thus, there is an interval between the two established boundaries.
Since it is established that even for those [trees] already bound, standing by touching one another is not permitted—
just as in the case of "overflowing through division" (sambhedajjhottharaṇa) due to the permission to bind them while excluding [the rule against touching]— so too, for those already bound,
standing after later touching one another with a single tree or similar object is not permitted; thus [it was stated] by the compilers who knew the Blessed One’s intention.

This has been determined because, at the time of the binding, the fault of connection (*sambandha-dosa*) which was rejected is, by way of its conformity, a conformity to what is unallowable (*akappiya-anuloma*).
However, this fault of connection—because it arises after things have already been well-bound—is unable to act as a boundary-marker at the very moment they are being bound;
therefore, as soon as the connection with trees and so forth is removed, those boundaries (*sīmā*) return to their original state.

...they are. And just as it is not permissible [to do so] later, so too at the moment of binding, it should be understood that if there is a connection with trees or the like, it is not permissible to bind them.
However, some [interpret] "or having cleared a large boundary" (*mahāsīmaṃ vā sodhetvā*) here as: "The bhikkhus who have gone to the large boundary, just as that branch..."
Some say: "Just as sprouts do not touch the body or what is connected to the body, so here only the cleansing [of the boundary] itself is intended, not the cleansing of the entire perimeter.
This is not correct, because it contradicts the Aṭṭhakathā. For [the Aṭṭhakathā] states:
"It stands touching either the surface of the earth of the Great Boundary (mahāsīmā) or the trees and such growing thereon"—thus [describing how] branches and sprouts touch the Great Boundary.
It is the very act of standing [there] that is stated to be the cause for the fault of connection,
and not the touching of branches and so forth by monks standing there. For if the mere act of standing were the cause after monks have touched a branch or the like,
then it would follow that even if "some monk standing there touches a branch of that tree or a sprout growing from it which has entered the great boundary," [the fault would still apply].

Only the "touching by a bhikkhu" should be stated. For whatever is the reason for clearing the great boundary (mahāsīmā) in that case, that alone should be shown as the primary factor in that sentence.
Indeed, a bhikkhu standing while touching branches or the like that are fixed directly [to the ground] need not be cleared;
for even a bhikkhu standing while touching branches or the like situated in the air must be cleared. What is the use of a meaningless [qualification]?
By the expression "having struck," it is stated that the reason is simply the monk’s touching of branches situated in the air;
and the purification is stated as the purification of that very monk by means of bringing him within hand-reach and so forth.

Here, however, by the phrase "having purified the great boundary" (*mahāsīmaṃ sodhetvā*), purification is stated through an expression common to the entire boundary; furthermore, regarding the branches and so forth—

If it were intended that only those monks standing while touching [a branch] are to be cleared, then the specific inclusion of the "ground surface" within the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) would be purposeless;
for one could be cleared even if standing anywhere—even in the air—provided they touch a branch or the like.

Furthermore, because of the statement that those standing outside must be "cut off," this refers to the separation from the state of being established within those dissimilar boundaries (*visabhāgasīmā*).
It should be understood that there exists this one fault of connection established by the *Aṭṭhakathā*—namely, that the very act of touching is the cause for purifying the entire boundary.
For this very reason, even in the discussion on the water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*), it says:
"Whether established within the monastery boundary or the village boundary," and "But it is not permitted [for a boat] tied to a stake driven into the riverbank," and "If..."
However, it has been stated that if a bridge or the legs of a bridge are established on the outer bank, it is not permissible to perform the ritual action;

thus, in the case of village boundaries consisting of dissimilar things, only the touching of branches and so forth is mentioned as the cause for the fault of confusion (*saṅkara*), and not the touching of monks.
For likewise, regarding the binding of a boat in a river, it is said: "The ritual action should be performed after tying [the boat] to a tree grown within the river."
It is permitted because a river boundary is similar [to a natural boundary] by virtue of its being a support for the throwing of water.

For if the fault of "connection" were stated to apply everywhere merely on account of the monks' physical contact, then even in the case of a river, the establishment of a boundary would have to be rejected;
for there too, the monks' contact is a cause for the invalidation of the formal act (*kamma*). Therefore, among similar boundaries...
Having entered [the boundary], whether touching the ground or not, a monk standing on a branch or similar object must be cleared while still touching that branch or object.
However, in the case of heterogeneous boundaries (*visabhāgasīmā*), all monks—even those not touching the branch or object—must be cleared if they are standing while touching it;
but if they are standing without touching it, only those monks who are touching the branch or object need be cleared.
The conclusion here must be reached as follows:
As for the point that some [scholars] claim that, just as between two formally established boundaries (*baddhasīmā*), so too between the village boundary and the formally established boundary,
or indeed between all other boundaries of common affiliation (*samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā*), when there is a connection by means of trees and so forth, both of them—

They say that after purifying them as if they were a single boundary, the legal act (kamma) must be performed in one place alone; otherwise, the act performed fails, and there is no distinction here between "similar" and "dissimilar" boundaries.

However, that is merely their own opinion, for according to the methods of the Vinaya—such as the Sutta and its conformity—the absence of the fault of mutual connection exists among similar boundaries, while its presence exists only among dissimilar boundaries.

Because it is established by the Sutta. For it is established by the Sutta itself that these [boundaries] share a common nature through their relationship as the supported and the support, and that they are free from the faults of division and overlapping; this is because the Buddha, in saying, "Monks, I allow you to establish a boundary," authorized the establishment of a boundary only within the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*) at the time of its binding.
Furthermore, subsequently, in accordance with the connection authorized at the time of binding...
Even the connection with trees and so forth that have grown there is indeed permissible for them.

Because it was said: "Monks, whatever conforms to what is allowable (*kappiya*), excludes what is unallowable (*akappiya*), that is permitted for you," thus first of all the mutual commonality of village-bound boundaries and the absence of faults such as their intermingling are established by means of the Sutta and its conformity;
by this same method, [the same applies to] forest boundaries and seven-abhantara boundaries.

It should be understood that the mutual similarity between boundaries such as rivers and water-throw boundaries (*udakukkhepasīmā*)— based on the principle of following the thread (*suttasuttānuloma*)— and the absence of faults such as their intermixture (*sambheda*), are established.
Furthermore, it is established by prohibition that one cannot establish another bound boundary (*baddhasīmā*) within an existing bound boundary or within river and other such boundaries.
Furthermore, by the force of the restrictive rule that the *udakukkhepa-sattabbhantara-sīmā* (the boundary defined by the distance of a water-splash) can only be established in rivers and the like,

the prohibition against establishing it within the boundaries of villages enclosed by fixed boundaries (*baddha-sīmā*) is established; likewise, the mutual similarity of these [two types of] boundaries,

as well as the possibility of defects such as their intermingling with trees and so forth at the moment of their origin and subsequently, are proven through the aforementioned method of following the rules and the consistency of the suttas.
For this very reason, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, after demonstrating the fault of connection (*sambandha-dosa*) regarding dissimilar boundaries (*visabhāga-sīmā*) through examples such as the *vaṭa* tree,

the fault of connection for similar boundaries (*sabhāga*), such as the boundaries of consecrated monasteries (*baddha-sīmā*) or village boundaries, was not shown. Not only was it not shown, but moreover,
the absence of any fault even when those similar boundaries are connected to trees and so forth is made known in the Canon (*Pāḷi*) and the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
It is indeed so. For in the Pāli, enlarging signs such as "the sign of a mountain, the sign of a rock, the sign of a forest, the sign of a tree," and so forth, are permitted;
by this, it is made known that there is no fault of confusion regarding the boundaries of bound villages when those signs of trees and so on are enlarged.
However, such a connection between two bound boundaries is not allowable.
For it is said: "Even a single tree can serve as a boundary marker for two boundaries; however, as it grows, it causes a confusion of boundaries, therefore it should not be used.
This is also made known by the statement: "I allow you, monks, to bind a boundary up to three *yojanas* in extent.
For when a boundary is limited to three *yojanas*, there may be trees, creepers, thickets, and so forth on its surrounding periphery.
Since a mutual connection necessarily arises between villages that have established boundaries,
it is not stated even in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that "the boundary must be formally designated only after destroying such a connection.
Furthermore, if there were a failure of the ritual (*kammavipatti*) due to a connection by means of trees and so forth, it certainly would have had to be mentioned here.
For indeed, in order to prevent failure, the teachers have repeatedly stated—even in places free from danger—the established meaning by saying, "without marking out a wall," and so forth;

however, here, by saying, "they build a monastery in the middle of a forest, but the forest must not be marked out," and so forth, they have taught the binding of the boundary even in the middle of a forest that is dense with trees, creepers, and the like. Likewise, above the pillars...
In the case of palaces and similar structures that are joined as one unit from below by pillars and so forth, the binding of the boundary on the upper floors and such has been described in many ways;
therefore, the connection of trees and other features with the boundaries of villages that have a fixed boundary was established by those [authorities] themselves.
Furthermore, because village boundaries also possess an individuality similar to fixed boundaries, when performing an act within a single village boundary, even by means of mere grass or straw...

The connections—successive lineages from one village to another, as well as those through the forest, rivers, and oceans—must be cleared; thus, it may be necessary to clear the entire island before proceeding.

However, if this is not cleared in such a manner, because the acts of ordination and so forth, as well as the formal delimitations of boundaries (*sīmā-sammuti*), performed since the time of the First Great Council would be invalidated, the suspicion that all monks might be considered unordained (*anupasampanna*) would be difficult to avoid.

This is not tenable; therefore, it should be understood that, according to the method already stated, the defect of connection with trees and so forth applies only to dissimilar boundaries (*visabhāga-sīmā*), and not to similar boundaries such as those of a bound boundary or a village boundary.
Because it is difficult to purify a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), he said that the performance of Saṅgha formal acts (*saṅghakamma*) is generally carried out within a partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*).

“‘At the boundary-mark’ and so forth. However, in the case of great assemblies of the Saṅgha, even when a formal act is being performed within the great boundary because the small boundary is insufficient, this same method must be adopted.
By the phrase ‘having caused [him] to throw up,’ it is shown that even one who touches the boundary with something connected to his body is still considered to be within the boundary.
‘In the former method as well’ means even in the case of the method of the branch that has entered from the small boundary into the great boundary.”
Sitting on a branch of a tree that stands within the boundary, one is indeed considered to be within the boundary; thus it is said, "he must be brought within arm's reach.

And here, regarding these [branches] which are mutually connected by means of tree branches and so forth, [the rule is]: in the case of a *khaṇḍasīma* (partial boundary), three monks [are required], and in the case of a *mahāsīma* (great boundary), two;
thus, without touching the interval between the two boundaries and without relinquishing arm's reach, those standing [therein...]
Some say that it is permissible for a formal act (kamma) such as ordination to be performed by five monks; however, this is not correct, because of such statements as:
"If one who is the fourth [member] stands within a different boundary (sīmā), the act is invalid and should not be performed.

For this very reason, even here, after clearing out the great boundary (mahāsīmā), the performance of the act is prescribed specifically within the precinct boundary (māḷakasīmā). Otherwise, due to being situated within a divided boundary, [the act would be invalid].
In that case, because one who is standing there cannot serve as a mere filler for the quorum, there is indeed a disturbance of the formal act (*kamma*).

If this is so, how can there be a purification of the Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*) by means of bringing forth the consent and purity (*chandapārisuddhi*)? Those learned in the Vinaya do not accept even that;
rather, they accept purification here through the bringing within arm’s reach (*hatthapāsānayanā*) and the making of the outer boundary (*bahisīmā*). Even if [consent] has been given...

"By the non-arrival of consent, one who stands within the great boundary (*mahāsīma*) invalidates the formal act (*kamma*). If his consent and so forth do not arrive, how could he invalidate the formal act?
This is because of the fault of connection between two dissimilar boundaries, and that fault of connection is established by the authority of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
For it is not possible to know the underlying logic in every instance of the Vinaya, as it is the domain of the Buddha.

This should be understood. However, some say: "If two boundary zones (*sīmā*) are filled and monks standing continuously within them perform a formal act (*kamma*), and if the group, the candidate for full ordination (*upasampadāpekkha*), and the proclaimer (*anussāvaka*) all stand together within one single boundary zone, the act is indeed well-performed.
But if either the person eligible for the act or the proclaimer stands in another boundary zone..."
When they say, “The ritual action (kamma) fails,” this applies only to cases of contiguous boundaries (sabhāga-sīmā), such as those of villages with fixed boundaries.

In those [contiguous boundaries] where there is no fault even when trees and so forth connect one another, but where there is a fault, it is not in those [other] non-contiguous boundaries (visabhāga-sīmā);

for in the case of non-contiguous boundaries, when there is a connection by means of trees and so forth, one standing in one place necessarily invalidates the ritual action in the other place—so says the Aṭṭhakathā.
It is our own preference that this has been stated as a general purification; it should be accepted after investigation. In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is said:

“It is not permissible to perform [the act] by having [the tree] lifted up; because the tree stands within the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*), one standing there must bring it within the reach of the hand;
therefore, it is not permissible to perform [the act] by having it lifted up. In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*...

However, it is not permissible to perform [the ritual] after having caused [the tree] to be uprooted. Why? Because it remains within [the boundary]. For the root of the tree that has entered the earth below is indeed part of the *khaṇḍasīmā* (fragmentary boundary).
Others say it is "indeterminate" (*abbohārika*). But when [the tree] is cut in the middle, the root situated within the *mahāsīmā* (great boundary) belongs to the *mahāsīmā* itself;
the root situated within the *khaṇḍasīmā* belongs to the *khaṇḍasīmā* itself, because of the earth and other factors dependent upon it.

And it is said: “Because they have been supported. Having stated, “It is permissible to perform the formal act (kamma) while sitting on trees that grew up after the boundary was established, just as in the case of a house built later within the boundary,” they give the reason:

“It is not permissible to perform it while sitting on trees that were already standing at the time of the binding [of the boundary], because they did not extend beyond the upper limit of the boundary. This being so, at the time of the binding... again.
There is no such thing as "climbing"; rather, it follows that one climbs at the very time of binding.

However, a tree that has grown later is nonetheless included within the boundary because it is connected to that [original tree]. This should be understood to apply equally to a tree that grew previously.
Because of the expression "whatever [there may be]," even grass and the like are included; for it is said that even the Great Elders perform the rite only after clearing away the grass.
"It does not descend" means that it does not descend into a space below the mountains shaped like drums and so forth that lacks a fixed measure.

Although at the moment of being bound, one might also ascend upward onto mountains and such that lack a fixed measure, nevertheless, because they are situated within the boundary later on, they constitute the boundary.
However, the space below the drum-shaped formations and so forth does not count as part of the boundary, even for a boundary that is bound above.
It does not go; by virtue of that very fact, it is said "it does not descend.
Otherwise, since "it does not descend" and so forth could have been stated on the basis of the commonality of both descending and ascending. "Whatever has arisen" means:
whatever exists above the established boundary—whether previously situated or subsequently produced, whether entered or not, and whether animate or inanimate—all of it whatsoever.
The meaning is as follows: For even a bhikkhu sitting on the back of an elephant or other conscious beings within the boundary remains one who stands within the boundary (*sīmaṭṭho*).
The phrase "in a bound boundary" is stated by way of illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*) according to the context of this treatise;

for in all unbound boundaries as well, one standing therein is likewise reckoned as being within that boundary. The expression "gone by way of a single connection" refers specifically to things such as trees and creepers growing there.
It has been stated. For such a thing deserves to be called "gone from here.

But what should be done regarding those things—such as ropes, poles, and so forth—that cannot be said to have "gone from here" or "come from there," and which fall across both the village boundaries and the water-boundaries (udakukkhepa) of rivers and the like? In this regard:

However, the portion established within a formally demarcated boundary (*baddhasīmā*) is part of that formally demarcated boundary, and the portion established within a village boundary (*gāmasīmā*) is part of that village boundary—just like a mountain or other terrain situated within both types of boundaries.

The same principle applies to the shoots of a *vaṭa* tree growing out from a formally demarcated boundary, as well as to the shoots of a *vaṭa* tree growing out from a village boundary; even though they are established within the [respective] boundaries, the rule remains the same. [This applies] to the roots.
For from the moment it is established, since it is impossible to say that "it has gone from here" or "it has come from there," that portion belongs only to the extent of the boundary already entered.

However, some say that in the space between those tree-sprouts, the branches standing in the air and the ground constitute a dual boundary according to the measure of the boundary's delimitation. But because of this... [text continues]

A shoot that has entered the boundary of a branch, even though it is established in the earth by its roots, does not lose its status as being within the root-boundary for as long as it is unable to stand independently of the branch.
However, when it is able to stand on its own, even then it merely attains the status of being within the boundary of the shoot;
therefore, every portion of the branch situated in space—

It is our view that [the robe] does not lose its status as being within the previous boundary because the portion from which it came has not been abandoned. This same principle applies to cases involving the throwing of water, rivers, and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding those instances, the purification of the entire boundary when one has entered a dissimilar boundary (*visabhāga-sīmā*), and the purification of only those monks who remain after contact when one has entered a similar boundary (*sabhāga-sīmā*), are all exactly according to the method previously stated.
164. And here, in the discussion regarding the river-bank boundary, "it reaches across" means it overflows.
A boundary established on both banks of a river is called a "river-overflowing" boundary; thus he says, "overflowing the river. For a boundary does not enter into the interior of a river.
However, when the characteristics of a river are absent, it does enter. And at that time, it is no longer a river-bank boundary.
He said: "The characteristics of a river are exactly as described in the section on river-signs. *Assa* means "it would be. The connection is:
"But it must necessarily be a permanent boat (*dhuvanāvā*). By the phrase "not [by] a boat," he shows that even without a boat, a boundary that has been tied is indeed well-tied;
the boat is mentioned for the purpose of avoiding an offense.
"Made of a collection of trees" means a bridge constructed by joining many trees together. "Made by cutting down trees" is the remainder of the reading.
"Having placed the monks standing within all the landmarks within arm's reach" is said with reference to the fact that both banks belong to the same village field.
"Shaped like a mountain" is because one side rises up like a mountain peak.
It is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
"In the discussion on the removal of boundaries (*sīmāsamūhanakathā*), 'he' refers to the community of nuns (*bhikkhunīsaṅgha*). 'Both of them' refers to two types of boundaries:

the boundary for common residence (*samānasaṃvāsa*) and the boundary for non-separation (*avippavāsa*). By 'boundary for non-separation,' he means the great boundary (*mahāsīma*). 'For the most part, there is non-separation right there'—this refers to non-separation."
"Even if they do not know" refers to those who are unaware of whether the Great Boundary (mahāsīmā) exists or does not exist, and of its external delimitations;

it is stated with reference to such persons. Thus, even for those who do not know, if the formal proclamation (kammavācā) is performed while standing within the boundary, that boundary is indeed abolished;
therefore he said, "they will be able both to abolish and to bind it. "In a place free from apprehension" means in a location devoid of a fragmented boundary (khaṇḍasīmā).
And it is said that even though this [small] boundary exists within the great boundary, a "broken boundary" (khaṇḍasīmā) is desired for the sake of the ease of performing formal acts;
therefore, it is not established in places of great assembly such as the courtyard of a cetiya. Even there, if it is bound, it is indeed well-bound, just like the great boundary.
However, they will certainly not be able to perform the binding [of another] because the broken boundary has not been abolished and its non-existence is not recognized.
And this was said with reference to the binding of a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*). However, a partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*) can indeed be bound in a place free from apprehension.
"Having created a breach of the boundary" means: in the case where a partial boundary already exists, having created a breach by overstepping one boundary with another;
and in the case where it does not exist, having created the apprehension of a breach because the apprehension of a breach has not been averted. "Not a monastery" (*avihāraṃ*).

"Should perform" means they should perform formal acts (*saṅghakamma*) that are not appropriate [for such a place]. For previously it was possible to perform formal acts in places free from danger, such as the courtyard of a shrine (*cetiyaṅgaṇa*);

the intention here is that even those [places] have now been destroyed. "They should not abolish" means they should not abolish [the boundary] by those who do not know the broken-off boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*).
"Neither knows" refers either to the restriction of the locations of both [communities], or to both of them [not knowing].
Or, they do not know whether a certain person exists or does not exist; in every case, there is only doubt.

This was said with reference to the meaning: "Even those who are able to abolish [the boundary] while standing in a place free from doubt will not be able to establish a great boundary (*mahāsīma*). They will be unable either to abolish it or to bind it.
"And it is not possible... [etc]... to perform the *kammavācā*"—this was said with reference to the *kammavācā* for binding the boundary.
Therefore, because it is impossible to bind [the boundary], the meaning is that it should not be removed.
Some, however, say: "Even in such monasteries, having taken five or six bhikkhus and starting from the edge of the monastery..."
When, having stood continuously throughout the entire area within and outside the monastery enclosure, extending for the distance of a clod-throw on all sides,
the first non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) and then the common-residence boundary (*samāna-saṃvāsa-sīmā*) have been abolished by means of their formal dismantling,
and while that monastery still exists with either a fragmented boundary (*khaṇḍa-sīmā*) or a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) established therein—
If there were necessarily one bed in that place, those monks situated in the midst of them would have to remove those [other] monks;
consequently, only the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*) itself would remain. For here, neither the knowledge of the boundary nor the knowledge of its delimitation is a requisite factor.

Rather, the requisite factors here are standing within the boundary and performing the formal act (*kammavācā*) with the intention, "We shall abolish [the boundary]. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, regarding a "fragmentary boundary" (*khaṇḍasīma*)...

"However, since it has been stated that even those who do not know the delimitation of the great boundary (mahāsīmā) will be able both to abolish and to bind [the boundary], and since only the village boundary (gāmasīmā) remains,
it is permissible there to bind either of the two kinds of boundaries as one desires, and to perform formal acts such as ordination."
They say that this appears reasonable; it should be accepted after investigation—such is the decision recorded in the *Vimativinodanī*.
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: "The statement that 'the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) should not be dismantled' refers to the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).
The phrase 'standing in places free from apprehension' is said because there is no room for a partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*) within the courtyard of a shrine (*cetiyaṅgaṇa*) and similar locations."
When they are establishing a *khaṇḍasīma* (fragmentary boundary), they establish it in another secluded place, avoiding such a location [as the one in question].
Thinking, "Perhaps they will be able to abolish it," they mean they will be able to abolish only the *avippavāsa-sīma* (non-separation boundary), not the *khaṇḍasīma*.
However, they will certainly not be able to re-establish it; because it is unknown within the *khaṇḍasīma*, they will not be able to do so.
"It should not be rescinded" means that it should not be rescinded by those who are unaware of the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*).

Having thus explained the determination of the established boundary (*baddhasīmā*), he now said, "But the unestablished boundary (*abaddhasīmā*)," in order to show the determination of the unestablished boundary.

To the question "Of how many kinds is it?", he replied: "It is of three kinds: the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*), the seven-abhantara boundary (*sattabbhantarasīmā*), and the water-splash boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*)."

In the Pāli, by the passage beginning “Bhikkhus, for an unbounded boundary,” it is shown that the village boundary alone is the field for a bounded boundary—just as a forest, a river, and so forth are [the fields] for the seven-abhyantara, the water-sprinkling, and other [distances];
and that village boundary is itself of common affiliation in a place devoid of a bounded boundary. “Whatever is the village boundary of that village.”

Here, the term "of the village" (*gāmassa*) is stated with reference to the entire village-field—including fields, dwellings, forests, mountains, and so forth—both inside and outside the village boundary, and not merely the interior of the houses; therefore, the meaning should be understood as follows:
the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*) is that which pertains to that entire village-field. For, among the many [locations] such as the fields within the interior of the houses...
The conventional designation "village" is established by worldly people as a unity upon certain portions of ground;
it is precisely that which is intended here by the term "village boundary" (*gāmasīmā*). For the village itself is the village boundary.

By this same method, [the terms] "forest," "river," "ocean," and "lake" are likewise understood as those very things—forest and so forth—which are designated as unities by worldly people upon their respective locations on the earth.

The nature of forest boundaries and so forth should be understood; however, in common worldly usage, the conventional designation "village boundary" and so on is appropriate only for the actual limits of villages and the like, not for their fields and all other surrounding areas.
In the Teaching (Sāsana), however, those villages and so forth are themselves considered their own boundaries in the sense of excluding everything else:
thus, the village itself is the village boundary, the forest itself is the forest boundary, and the ocean...
Thus, it should be understood that they are spoken of by way of a metaphorical designation (*vohāra*) as having the ocean as their boundary.
In the text, the phrase "or of a town" is stated to indicate, by way of illustration, the various types of village boundaries. Therefore, he said: "The city is also included.
The expression "they receive tribute" is stated in a general sense. [This is shown] by such statements as, "this village consists of this much area of *karīsa*," and so forth.

Furthermore, when land has been demarcated by royal edicts, any area such as a pond, a source of water, a cemetery, or a mountain where taxes are not collected is also indeed part of the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*).

For it should be understood that all land demarcated by kings and others constitutes the village boundary, with the exception of rivers, salt-flats, and natural lakes. Therefore he said: "Having demarcated [the land], the king [bestows it] upon someone..."
...gives it. However, if the king there assigns some area between villages, it belongs to the boundary of the village already entered.
The same principle applies even when rivers and natural ponds are destroyed and converted into the state of reservoirs or fields and the like.
Furthermore, there are villages that have been abandoned by people oppressed by fear of kings, thieves, and so forth, and which remain uninhabited for a long time;
yet, if there are other villages nearby, those [abandoned ones] are also distinct village boundaries (*gāmasīmā*).

For in such cases, kings collect taxes either by having the inhabitants of the surrounding villages cultivate them, or by recording the area cultivated by anyone at all, or by means of another village.

They bring about unification; however, those villages which have been abandoned even by kings, and whose village-fields and boundaries have become one with a great wilderness, reach the status of non-village wilderness boundaries (*agāmakāraññasīma*). The previous village boundary perishes.
But when kings, having established a large village in a certain region of the wilderness and settled many thousands of families there...

When they give [land] to those residing there as "villages for enjoyment," they demarcate the surrounding area of the *bhūtagāma* (the inhabited territory), yet they do not destroy the former name nor the previous boundaries;
these too are each indeed village boundaries (*gāmasīmā*), and to this extent they do not abandon their status as the boundary of the preceding village.
The phrase "both that and the other," etc., is an explanation of the intended meaning of the canonical passage: "belonging to the same communion, sharing a single *uposatha*."
For in that case, the former [boundary] has arisen anew by being transformed according to the king’s wish, while the other remains untransformed as the natural village boundary (*pakatigāmasīmā*).

Just as all *saṅgha*-kamma is permitted to be performed within a formally established boundary (*baddhasīmā*), so too these two are similar to a formally established boundary in their fitness for all *kamma*;
they constitute a single community (*samānasamvāsa*) and a single *uposatha*. This is the intended meaning. In general terms, they are said to be "similar to a formally established boundary."
Since it was stated that they consider the boundary for not being separated from the three robes to be the very same as the established boundary,
the phrase beginning with "only" was spoken here to show the method of demonstrating that a similar quality also exists in the upper seven-intermediate boundaries by way of excluding that similarity.

"In a forest like the Vindhya jungle" means in a wilderness where there is no common designation of a village such as "this is the field of such-and-such a village," and where neither plowing nor sowing takes place; such is the kind of forest intended.

Isolated islands in the middle of the ocean that are not accessible to fishermen and are devoid of human habitation are also included herein. For whatever place is not a village-field—that is, a region lacking rivers, oceans, and natural lakes—is meant.

All of that should be understood as the forest boundary (*araññasīmā*). And this [boundary], even without a seven-abhyantara boundary (*sattabbhantarasīma*), is itself a common affiliation (*samānasaṃvāsā*);

it is similar to a formally established boundary (*baddhasīmā*), and it is permissible to perform all Sangha transactions (*saṅghakamma*) therein, just as in the case of river and other types of boundaries.

As for rivers, oceans, and natural lakes, their status as boundaries is established by the fact that they are stated in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) to be "similar to formally established boundaries by their very nature," and so forth.
But how is the boundary of the forest defined? It is from the authority of such suttas as the one authorizing the seven-abhantara boundary.

For just as many established boundaries were authorized to prevent a *vaggakamma* (an illegal act performed by an incomplete assembly) within the village boundary, and as the *sīmantarikā* (intermediate space) was authorized between those two to prevent them from merging with one another, so too here in the forest is there the seven-abhantara boundary.

Furthermore, it should be understood that even between those two [villages], the status of the boundary (*sīmā*) for the forest is established by its very nature—just as it is for rivers and the like—due to the efficacy of the procedure prescribed in the *Pāḷi* and the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

This is because a seven-fathom intermediate boundary (*sattabbhantara-sīmā*) was specifically authorized there solely for the purpose of avoiding a *vagga-kamma* (a formal act performed by an incomplete assembly) within that area.
For it is only when one stands within that very boundary that one is considered to be "standing at the boundary" (*sīmaṭṭha*) for the sake of a *vagga-kamma*.
They do not act like those standing in the air within a non-boundary (asīmā), [which] is merely a location in space. In the same way, having understood this capacity,
one should grasp from the Aṭṭhakathā that even for rivers, oceans, and natural lakes whose boundaries have been formally prohibited by such statements as, "Bhikkhus,
all rivers are non-boundaries," their status as a boundary exists by their very own nature.
"From its standing place" means from the standing place of that bhikkhu.

For even if a thousand bhikkhus are standing, starting from the outer limit of that standing place, the seven-fathom boundary—which arises by itself when the expectation of a boundary arises for the purpose of avoiding a *vagga-kamma* (a formal act performed by an incomplete assembly) among the bhikkhus—arises together with that expectation; such is the intended meaning: they are of the same communion.

However, where in a small forest there is no need for a seven-abhyantara boundary because it is filled with many monks and thus there is no suspicion of a *vaggakamma* (an illegal act by an incomplete assembly), the seven-abhyantara boundary does not arise there. Only the forest boundary (*araññasīmā*) exists;
in that case, the legal act (*kamma*) must be performed by the Saṅgha. This same principle applies to rivers and so forth as well. For it will be said: "If the river is not very long..."
"From its source up to the mouth-opening, the Saṅgha sits everywhere; there is no formal act (kamma) within a water-throw boundary (udakukkhepasīmā)," and so forth.

By this very statement, it should be understood that when there is a dependence on a [formal] boundary for the purpose of avoiding a quorum-deficient act (vaggakamma), the water-throw boundaries of one hundred and twenty cubits arise, but not otherwise.
However, some say: "The boundary is produced only by measuring out the interior on all sides and thereby establishing its delimitation, not by itself.

This should not be accepted. For if the boundary were to arise merely through the manner of establishing an internal delimitation, it would not be a "bound" boundary (*baddhasīmā*), because the monks' performance of formal acts (*kiriya-pakāra*) would not be accomplished.
Furthermore, [this would apply] to both the cubits of carpenters and the natural cubits.

Because there is such variety in the world and because it is not stated in the Vinaya that "the hand-measure must be of this specific kind," there might be a suspicion regarding the failure of the boundary (*sīmā*), thinking:
"Was it measured with whatever hand was permitted by the Blessed One, or was it not?
Furthermore, since it would be impossible for those measuring to do so without making even the slightest deficiency or excess, there would indeed be a failure.
And this [boundary], increasing by way of inclusion, increases or decreases according to their measurement.
When the Saṅgha has performed the formal act (*kamma*) and departed, does this boundary—which arose through the effort of the monks—cease to exist through their departure, or does it not?
How could it be that, like a formally established boundary (*baddhasīmā*), it would not persist until the disappearance of the Dispensation (*sāsana*), for the sake of its stability?
And just as in the case of ancient monasteries, there would be no fear of the boundary being breached even when a separate boundary is established in the entire forest;

therefore, it should be understood that [the fear] arises only in relation to the boundary and ceases with its removal. And just as it is here, so it is also regarding the water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) in rivers and other such places.
For even there, a middle-sized person is not discerned; likewise, throwing with all one's might [is not possible].
Furthermore, in both cases, how could there be measuring or throwing in a direction where there is no space for seven *abbhantara*s or for the splash of water?
Since it enters into village fields and the like, how indeed could a boundary enter what is not a field?

The boundary (*sīmā*) would not fail. However, regarding the arising of a boundary through dependence (*apekkhā*), wherever it extends, there a seven-fathom water-throw boundary (*sattabbhantara-udakukkhepa-sīmā*) arises spontaneously and in its entirety.
But wherever it does not extend, there it arises only according to the measure of its own field and not beyond it.
As for the act of throwing sand or other materials here within that non-measure, [it is as follows]:
And that demonstration is for the purpose of defining the location where the self-arisen boundary stands;
it is like the demonstration of the method for throwing a clod of earth or a stone for the purpose of knowing the village precinct and the house precinct.

For this very reason, it is said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "Either one demarcates a boundary, or one defines the water-throw. Even when such a definition has been made, [regarding] its reality as it truly is...
Having recognized the breadth by its impossibility of being known [otherwise], those standing inside must remain in a place free from apprehension;
those sending others outside must send them to a place free from apprehension that is very far away.
Others, however, say: "There is no need for consideration of the boundary; even if there is but one bhikkhu for purposes such as traveling on the road or bathing..."
When one has entered a forest or by rivers and so forth, a boundary consisting of a water-spray of seven *abbhantara*s arises spontaneously around that person, like the radiance of a lamp.
In village fields and the like, it vanishes as soon as one has stepped into them.
For this very reason, when two Saṅghas perform separate formal acts (*kamma*) here, there is a "boundary-interval" (*sīmantarika*) between the two boundaries.
It is permitted to leave a space between beings and to leave a gap of water.

For if a boundary were established by some act within the vicinity of an existing boundary, and the newly arisen boundary of one monk were to touch the boundary of others, it would cause a confusion of boundaries (*sīmāsambheda*).
To prevent this, or otherwise because a gap of at least four finger-breadths must be allowed here as a separation between boundaries, [this is ordained].
Furthermore, this is established by the statement regarding the disturbance of the ritual act (*kammakopa*) for one standing at the boundary-line (*sīmantarikā*).
This is because, when a boundary has arisen of its own accord by encompassing that [area], there is a confusion of both boundaries—or rather, of a single boundary.
Otherwise, the statement regarding the disturbance of the ritual act would not be logical. For it is said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "Within the limits..."
"Even if one stands outside the boundary, having left the reach of the hand, yet without overstepping another boundary of exactly that same extent,
one still commits an offense. Furthermore, for a monk staying in a forest uninhabited by villages who lacks the desire to perform formal acts,
the Blessed One has permitted the separation from his robes within an open space defined by a distance of seven *abbhantara*s.

"And that delimitation is the boundary (sīmā), which thus arises independently [of mutual expectation]. For this very reason, it is said here: 'This boundary also obtains exemption from being separated from one's robes.
Therefore, one should understand its arising according to the stated method even without the desire to perform formal acts (kamma)," so they say.
That is not correct, because—like the light of a lamp—a boundary can exist for each individual person separately.

When a formal act (*kamma*) is being performed by a Saṅgha or a group, there is the danger of the fault of mutual confusion among the many boundaries that have arisen individually around the monks standing therein.
Furthermore, through the process of overflow (*parisava*), both expansion and contraction would occur;
for those who arrive later, there would be the arising of a new boundary within, while for those who have already departed, there would be the destruction of the boundaries situated all around them.
In the Pāḷi, however, it is stated: “Seven *abbhantara*s all around—this is the common boundary therein,” and so forth;

thus, only a single *sattabbhantara* and the throwing of water (*udakukkhepa*) were permitted. Furthermore, this boundary does not arise by its own nature or through the efficacy of some cause, like the radiance of a lamp;
rather, it arises solely through the permission of the Blessed One. And when the Blessed One granted these permissions for the monks—
It was permitted solely for the sake of making the performance of formal acts (kamma) easy by avoiding the fault of acting with a fragmented assembly.
How then could there be the simultaneous arising of boundaries all around those who have entered for the purpose of bathing and other such duties?

Since there is no purpose [for multiple boundaries], and since there is only one single purpose, how could there be the arising of many boundaries according to the individual count of monks? [The rule is: "Without departing from hand-reach within a single boundary..."
For it is said, "They are established. As for the statement regarding the establishment of a boundary-line (*sīmantarikā*) with a specific delimitation between two boundaries,
and the statement regarding the invalidation of an act (*kammakopa*) for those standing therein—

that too was spoken in order to avoid from afar the suspicion of a confusion of boundaries and the suspicion of the invalidation of an act, due to the difficulty of discerning the delimitations of these boundaries.
Furthermore, the seven-abhyantara (sattabbhantara) boundary shown by the Blessed One for the purpose of being away from one's robe is not itself a *sīmā*;
rather, it is merely a single type of boundary here, like the boundaries of fields, ponds, and so forth.
And in that case, when many monks are standing together, [the distance] starts from each individual monk’s own position.
The robe must be placed within the boundary of seven *abbhantara*s all around, not beyond the edge of the assembly.

For if it were taken from within starting from the edge of the assembly, then at the end of the seven *abbhantara*s, the robe placed there would be outside the seven *abbhantara*s for one standing in the middle;
thus, at the rising of the dawn, it would become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). This is the boundary (*sīmā*).
However, it must be understood as being limited only by the boundary of the assembly (*parisā*).

Here, the exemption from the offense of being separated from one’s robe (*cīvaravippavāsa*) is mentioned because the delimitation of the open air (*ajjhokāsa*) exists; it is not, however, because the delimitation of the formal boundary (*sīmā*) is applicable, as is the case with the designation "non-separation" (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) in relation to the Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*).

For even within the Great Boundary, a robe becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) if it is left in the vicinity of a village (*gāma*) or its outskirts (*gāmūpacāra*); here too, for one standing in the middle [of the assembly], [the same applies].

It becomes subject to forfeiture at the boundary limit; therefore, our view is that the arising and the destruction of those seven-abbhantara and water-throw boundaries should be understood precisely through their dependence on the aforementioned boundary, and this should be investigated and accepted.
Or else, another method more logical than this should be sought.

Furthermore, because this [boundary] is established within a seven-abhyantara limit even in a forest where trees and other growth are continuous— both in the Pāḷi text, which says "in the forest, seven abhyantaras all around," and in the Aṭṭhakathā, which says "in a forest like the Viñjhāṭavi wilderness, seven abhyantaras all around"—
there is no fault in its connection with trees and so forth, as it shares the same forest boundary that serves as its own basis.

It should be understood that it is established that even in a place dependent on a tree in a non-village area, the allowance for being in the open air is permitted without the exception made for trees regarding separation from one's robe.
"For the purpose of the precinct" means for the sake of the boundary line (*sīmantarikā*). It is permissible to exceed seven *abbhantara*s; however, less than that—
It is not permissible [to stand] within the seven-cubit boundary because it is difficult to discern.
Therefore, even when standing outside with only one monk, he must stand at a distance, having crossed beyond another seven-cubit limit;

otherwise, there is the risk of the ritual act being corrupted or confused. The same principle applies to the "throwing of water" (*udakukkhepa*). For this very reason, he will say: "But if it is less..."

"It is not permissible. Herein, this rule for the boundary-interval (*sīmantarika*) should be understood as established in accordance with the sutta permitting a boundary-interval between two established boundaries (*baddhasīmā*).

For although the Blessed One, by way of the introductory narrative, prescribed a boundary-interval only for two established boundaries situated in the same village and belonging to the same community, in order to avoid the faults of mutual overlap and encroachment; [the principle applies more broadly].

Although this was permitted, nevertheless, because it conforms to that [prohibition], the commentators (Aṭṭhakathācariyas) understood that the Blessed One did not approve of the mutual overlapping and encroachment of two forest boundaries,
river-boundaries, and so forth, nor of two adjacent seven-fathom boundaries for those residing together,
nor of water-sprinkled boundaries, nor of standing in a place without an intervening boundary-space.
Here too, they established the procedure for the boundary-interval (*sīmantarikā*).

For it should be understood that even in the case of dissimilar boundaries (*visabhāgasīmā*), a place becomes subject to division only when two conditions are present—namely, being situated within a single boundary and having a common nature (*ekasabhāgatta*)—and not when these are absent.
And by the very power of establishing this boundary-interval, even the connection between these [trees] and so forth constitutes a bound boundary (*baddhasīmā*).
It should be understood that this principle—that they do not fit together with one another—is also shown by way of this method.
By the phrase "by its very nature," it shows that this is an unbound boundary (*abaddhasīmā*), like a village boundary (*gāmasīmā*).

By the statement "all sangha-acts (*saṅghakamma*) are permitted to be performed here," it shows that they belong to the same community (*samānasaṃvāsā*) and share the same observance day (*ekūposatha*). By the phrase "by anyone whatsoever," it includes even such animals as pigs and the like.
