By way of its essence: however, when a great flood falls from a high place into a low place, a pool that is struck—whether small or large and possessing the defining characteristics—is called a "natural lake" (*jātassara*).
Here too, there is no requirement for splashing water in the case of a small one.
But in the case of the ocean, the formal act (*kamma*) must be performed within the very boundary of the splash of water everywhere, because it is difficult to purify [the site otherwise].

"Furthermore, regarding 'therein' (*tattha*): the intention is to show the delimitation of the unbound boundary established by the terminology of the Teaching (*sāsana-vohāra*)—for the purpose of avoiding a *vagga-kamma* (an illegal act performed by an incomplete assembly)—within those three [types of] unbound boundaries, such as rivers and so forth, which are established by worldly terminology (*loka-vohāra*).

In the Canon, in passages such as ‘that which a man of medium height... and so on, *udakukkhepa* means that water is thrown (*khipīyati*) after being lifted up (*ukkhipitvā*) therein; thus it is water-throwing."
The falling point: from that splash of water. This is the meaning here according to the connection of the words:

starting from the edge of the assembly and extending all around as far as the falling point of the water for a man of medium height—that delimited area is what is meant here by "the boundary of the water-splash," which constitutes another common residence within rivers and so forth.
“Within it” means within that place delimited by the throwing of water. And not only within that [specific area], but even beyond it;

for the statement, “It is not permitted to stand within the range of a single throw of water,” is made because the delimitation by the throw of water is difficult to discern, lest there be suspicion of a violation of the rule (kamma-kopa).
For this very reason, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* it says: “Within the delimitation...”
"Even if one stands outside the boundary, having left the reach of the hand, provided one does not exceed another boundary of exactly that same extent, the action is still sublated;
this is the conclusion in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*)," so it is said. As for what is stated here in the *Sāratthadīpanī*:
"One standing inside its reach of the hand, having left [the original location], sublates the action"—by this, from the perspective of the boundary...
Having stated, "Standing anywhere outside, one does not invalidate the *kamma*," he rejects even the words of the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*,
elaborating extensively with such claims as, "It is found neither in the *Pāḷi* nor in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. This is not sound,
because here the word of the *Aṭṭhakathā* [of the *Mātikā*] is consistent with, analogous to, and connected with the word of the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*.
For indeed, if one does not leave even a space of four finger-breadths or a span as a boundary (sīmantarika) between two water-sprinkling limits, [the text] says:
"Another water-sprinkling limit must be established at the boundary; more than that is certainly permissible, but less is not.
Thus, by this statement from the Aṭṭhakathā spoken right here, regarding the vicinity of the boundary:

It has already been stated that when [the boundary] is established less than the distance of a water-splashing, there is a disturbance of the formal act (*kammakopa*) due to the overlapping of boundaries (*sīmāsambheda*).

And to the extent that it is stated thus, to that same extent, even if a single bhikkhu enters therein, because he exists within the boundary, a disturbance of the formal act is indeed stated to have occurred.
Furthermore, this statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*—"but what is deficient is not permitted"—is as follows:
This was stated for the purpose of avoiding the suspicion of boundary-conflict even by one who finds it difficult to discern the limits of the water-sprinkling boundary.
Furthermore, because the rule for the intermediate space between the seven *abbhantara* boundaries is stated as being of that same extent, these [boundaries] are difficult to discern;
and for those standing therein, the suspicion of the disruption of formal acts (*kamma*) arises. Indeed, this is a place where the suspicion of the disruption of formal acts occurs.
It should be understood that the teachers, for the sake of avoiding complications, established [the rule] by stating "the establishment of an act" (*kamma-upaṭṭhāna*).
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: "Unbounded" means not having a boundary defined by means of a formal boundary-marking (*baddha-sīmā*).
"Not made by anyone digging" means not made even by digging as little as with a mere animal's hoof. Within its reach of a hand’s span...
By the phrase "having left [the boundary], he stands and violates the act," it is shown that he does not violate the act if he stands anywhere outside the boundary.

However, as stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "Even if one stands having left the hand’s reach within the boundary, provided one does not cross beyond another boundary of exactly the same size outside the original boundary..."
"Even when standing [within the boundary], one may invalidate a formal act (kamma); this is the conclusion in all the commentaries.
Regarding that, the statement "even when standing without exceeding that very same extent of the boundary, one invalidates the formal act" is found neither in the Canon (pāḷi) nor in the commentary;
for if this were so, it would have been stated in the section concerning the performance of formal acts such as the Uposatha separately for two distinct Saṅghas.

It might be said with this intention: "The Saṅgha, standing for the purpose of performing the Uposatha and other rites without crossing beyond another water-sprinkling boundary (*udakukkhepa*) from the original one, subverts the formal act (*kamma*) because of the resulting confusion of boundaries (*sīmāsambheda*). Even so, it would be appropriate.
For that very reason, it is stated in the *Līnatthappakāsanī*, the commentary on the *Mātikā*: "Another [boundary] of exactly that same extent..."
"Even one who has not transgressed the second *udakukkhepa* boundary causes a disturbance. Why?
Because when one's own *udakukkhepa* boundary completely covers the *udakukkhepa* boundary of others, there is a merging of boundaries (*sīmāsambheda*); therefore, he causes a disturbance.
This should be understood as having been stated with this very intention, for it is the definitive conclusion found in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
This is because the breaking of boundaries is not intended. For this very reason it is said:

"Another splashing of water must be placed between the splashing of water that marks one's own boundary and those of others, for the purpose of a boundary-line. However, others here elaborate differently;
that should not be accepted.
"The Saṅgha sits everywhere" means that they sit without relinquishing the range of hand-contact (*hatthapāsa*).

"There is no formal act (*kamma*) within a water-splashing boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*)" means that because the entire river area is encompassed by the monks, there is no need for the purpose of splashing water, as there is no river on all sides.
A boundary interval (*sīmantarikā*) measured by the distance of a water-splash is much easier to discern.
And so that there may be no apprehension of the confusion of boundaries, it is stated: "Another water-sprinkling should be established for the purpose of marking the boundary.
However, it is indeed permissible to establish as much as is necessary to prevent the confusion of boundaries. Therefore the ancients said:
"It is permissible to establish even as much as is required so that there is no confusion of boundaries."

Regarding the statement, "But a deficiency is not permitted," it is said that this was stated precisely to prevent the suspicion of a boundary overlap (*sīmāsambheda*), since even this [boundary] can expand by means of the water-splashing limit (*udakukkhepasīmā*) overflowing.
In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā* as well, concerning the phrase "the water-splash all around for a medium-sized man," it is stated: ...of this [boundary], however—

The teachers maintain that when the Saṅgha consisting of four or more groups performs formal acts such as those requiring a quorum of four separately on a river, the description of the river's boundaries is stated for the purpose of demonstrating the delimitation of non-separation from the three robes;
it is also like the demonstration of the boundary of the "seven-abhyantara" (sattabbhantara) zone for the purpose of showing the delimitation of separation and non-separation from the three robes.
Therefore, even in the absence of a delimitation by the throwing of water, within the river—
It is established that it is permissible to perform the formal act (*kamma*). However, there is this distinction: in that case, if he is on a boat, it is according to the method stated for a boat;

if he is on a caravan, it is according to the method stated for a caravan. If he has resided [there] for more than four months, the non-separation from the three robes (*ticīvara-avippavāsa*) should be understood according to the method stated for a village.
Even in that case, there is this further distinction: if the caravan is within the range of a water-splash (*udakukkhepa*),...
Some say that the boundary established by the throwing of water is the measure; the teachers (ācariyas) say that the range of the voice is the measure.

Furthermore, in the passage beginning "If there are many bhikkhus here," the word "bhikkhus" was used instead of saying "many Saṅghas" because some intended to speak of the *adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha*, some of the *gaṇa-uposatha*, and some of the *saṅgha-uposatha*. However, a deficient number is not permitted.
Regarding this, the Elder Upatissa says: "Because of the possibility of a confusion of boundaries. For when they are being established, one should not establish it deficiently;
thus it is said, "It is even permissible to not establish it.
"That" refers to the boundary. By the phrase "it passes over very quickly," [it is implied that] while it has not yet passed over that [boundary], it is still revolving within.
This shows that it is proper to do so. For it is for this very purpose that the boundary is demarcated by means of sand and other materials;
otherwise, there might be a suspicion of the invalidation of the formal act (*kamma*) as to whether [the person] has moved outside or not.

"The proclamation of another" refers to the proclamation regarding the entire river-boundary. "Regarding trees growing within the river" refers to those situated outside the limit defined by the splashing of water.
"Or when trees are standing. Indeed, only the bank outside the river is a place where [the boundary] should not be bound, because it is of a different class (*visabhāga*) due to being the limit;

the interior of the river is not, because it is of the same class (*sabhāga*) by virtue of being the support. For this very reason, in the passage beginning with "or on the bank outside the river within the monastery boundary," the bank alone is shown as the place where [the boundary] should not be bound, but not the river itself.
As for the phrase "even when trees have grown," this refers to the state of being submerged within the water.
It has been stated. For it is not permissible for monks to stand outside the range of the water-splash.
"Of the tree" means of that very tree standing within the range of the water-splash.

"Or having cleared the boundary" means by way of bringing the monks standing there within hand's reach, thereby establishing a boundary outside [the area] of the monastery-boundary and the village-boundary as previously described.

Having cleared [the area]. And just as by those performing an act within a water-splashing boundary (*udakukkhepa-sīmā*), so too by those performing an act within a fixed boundary (*baddha-sīmā*) or a village boundary (*gāma-sīmā*), it must be done only after clearing the area occupied by the water-splashing boundary.

By this same method, the fault of connection with trees and so forth regarding these boundaries—namely, the water-splashing boundary together with the seven-fathom forest boundary (*sattabbhantara-arañña-sīmā*) and this [fixed] boundary—is also to be understood through inference.

It is indeed shown [in this way]. By this same method, the fault of connection should be understood to exist between the boundary of a village enclosed by a seven-abbhantara boundary and those [other] boundaries, as well as between these [village boundaries] and the seven-abbhantara boundary itself.
However, since all of this can be understood from the method already stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), only their mutual proximity is shown here.
In this regard, here is the method for grasping the guiding principles according to the Sutta:

Just as a formally established boundary (*baddhasīmā*) within a delimited area becomes a "defective boundary" (*vipattisīmā*) if it is connected to those other boundaries by means of trees and so forth, so too a formally established boundary, even if established over rivers and the like, becomes a defective boundary; therefore, its connection with them by means of trees and so forth is likewise not permitted.

"It is not permissible" is established. By this method, one should understand that the non-permissibility of establishing a connection between trees and so forth with villages, rivers, etc., in the case of the seven-abhyantara boundary (*sattabbhantara-sīmā*), and with forests, etc., in the case of the water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepa-sīmā*), is likewise understood.

Thus, these boundaries authorized by the Blessed One—the seven-abhyantara boundary and the water-throw boundary—when bound together, and when devoid of their own respective supports, [are not permissible].

It should be understood that the method of conforming to the Sutta is as follows: when there is a connection between trees and so forth through mutual dependence or boundaries, it incurs the fault of "confusion" (sambheda).

However, at the time of establishing the three types of boundaries—such as the *baddhasīmā*—together with the respective natural villages (*gāma*) and other supports upon which they depend, even a connection between trees and so forth is permitted, because it conforms to the "overflowing of confusion" (*sambhedajjhottharaṇa*) authorized by the Blessed One.
It should be understood that [the boundary] exists. If this is so, why is a *sīmantarikā* (an intermediate space) not established between boundaries such as those defined by the throwing of water?
Because it is itself divided by differences in support (*nissaya*) and differences in nature (*sabhāva*).

For it has already been stated that only when [two areas] share a single support and a single nature does the *sīmantarikā* cause their destruction. By this very principle, [it follows that] for a boundary established using a river as its mark...
It is established that when the Saṅgha is performing an act within a boundary, even if a river stands touching the village territory,

it is permissible for others to perform an act within the water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*). Furthermore, regarding these five boundaries established by worldly convention— village, forest, river, ocean, and lake— even if they are connected to one another by trees and so forth,
they do not incur the fault of "confusion" (*sambhedadosa*), because such [technical] worldly convention does not exist between them.
For people in the world do not say that villages and the like are "intermingled" merely by their connection with other villages, rivers, trees, and so forth.
And regarding things established by worldly convention, their intermingling or non-intermingling must be understood solely through worldly convention, not otherwise.
For this very reason, no method for the mutual intermingling of those [elements] is shown anywhere in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).
It is shown as established by the conventional usage of the Teaching (*sāsana-vohāra*).

Herein, regarding the *baddha-sīmā* (formally bound boundary) first, the delimitation of the lower portion is shown in every respect in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) by such statements as, "The boundary has reached its limit at the water that supports the earth below," and so forth; [this applies likewise] to village boundaries (*gāma-sīmā*) and the rest.

However, it has not been shown. How is this to be understood? On this point, some say that even village boundaries and the like stand touching the water that supports the earth, just as a formally established boundary does.
Others, however, reject that view and maintain that the boundaries of rivers, oceans, and natural lakes extend only as far as the splash of the water dependent upon them.
They remain only on the surface of the earth and in those places submerged by water below; they do not go further down because there is no submersion by water beyond that point.
However, if there is a low-lying area measuring even a *yojana* due to a flood of water and so forth, it constitutes the river boundary and such, but not what lies beneath it.
Therefore, in the case of rivers and the like, [the boundary extends] from the lower bank outward.
A bhikkhu who has entered [the water] by means of a limb or through psychic power does not disturb the kamma of those standing in the river;

however, he disturbs the kamma of the bhikkhus in the nearby village. But if he is sitting in the middle between both villages on either bank, he disturbs the kamma of those residing in both villages.
And if the bank is not the domain of a village, it is simply a non-village wilderness.
In that regard, however, on both shores, the formal act (kamma) is invalidated solely by a minor boundary of strangers (*khuddakāraññasīmā*),
even in the absence of a seven-cubit internal boundary (*sattabbhantarasīma*). If they perform it within a seven-cubit internal boundary,
then if the limit of their seven-cubit internal boundary stands beyond this seated area by more than one seven-cubit interval, [the act is not invalidated].

There is a disturbance of the formal act (*kammakopa*). If there is no disturbance of the formal act, however, within the village boundary—whether by digging in a hollow or a hole where one can enter, or wherever they dig for gold, gems, and so forth, or where there is the conviction that it can be taken—the area as far as that below is also the village boundary;
therein, even one sitting inside by means of supernormal power (*iddhi*) [is subject to] the formal act.

It provokes anger. However, wherever there is not even the possibility of ordinary humans entering, all that—down to the water that supports the earth—is the forest boundary (*araññasīmā*) alone, not the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*).
The same principle applies to the forest boundary as well;
for even within it, only that much area where there is the possibility of entry constitutes the forest boundary on the surface. Below that, however, it does not.

The forest boundary (*araññasīmā*) does not include the upper surface because there is no conventional designation of "forest" for that area. For people do not say of one who has entered what is merely the entrance to a forest that he has "entered the forest";

therefore, one standing there does not invalidate the formal act (*kamma*) performed in the forest area above, just as one standing on the bank of a lower stream does not invalidate the act of those standing on the upper stream.
This is because within a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), there may be villages, rivers, oceans, and lakes.
Excluding that remaining non-human habitation, everything from the world of the gods and the Brahmā-world downwards is indeed forest (*arañña*).
For since it is stated, "either from a village or from a forest," even rivers, oceans, and natural lakes are considered forest.
However, because rivers and so forth are here taken separately as distinct boundaries, only what remains [after excluding them] should be understood as forest. And therein, to whatever extent...

In certain locations, people refer to "a single forest"; this is one forest boundary (*araññasīmā*). Indeed, the entire city of Indra is one forest boundary, as are the cities of the asuras, yakṣas, and so forth.

Furthermore, the celestial palaces (*vimāna*) of the devas and brahmas situated in space are each separate forest boundaries, delimited by the surrounding space, like mountains and islands in the middle of the ocean.
In all such cases, within the seven-league (*sattabbhantara*) boundary, [the rule applies].
Or rather, the formal act (kamma) should be performed within the forest boundary itself;

therefore, even here, because there is no single designation as "forest" for both the upper forest canopy and the lower earth, it should be understood that there is a separate forest boundary. For this very reason, regarding the discussion of boundaries such as villages and rivers in the Commentary, it is stated:
"A monk possessing psychic power, standing on the surface of the lower earth, performs the formal act," in reference to a bound boundary (*baddhasīmā*).
They say, "The method for showing [the boundary] has not been shown.
This presentation of the lower limit for these village boundaries and so forth appears reasonable, as there is no contradiction with the Suttas and other texts;

it should be accepted after careful investigation. And when it is accepted in this way, a formally established boundary (baddhasīmā) within a village boundary does not extend beyond the upper limit of that village boundary.
Because it extends down to the water’s edge and includes the forest boundary (*araññasīma*), that forest boundary also becomes established as a "field" (*khettam*).

Furthermore, by such statements as, "Bhikkhus, all rivers are not boundaries," the Blessed One has declared that rivers, oceans, and natural lakes are not fields in relation to a formally established boundary (*baddhasīma*);
however, he did not say this of the forest. Therefore, the forest too is indeed a field within a formally established boundary.
It should be accepted. If this is so, why is it not bound there? Because of the absence of a purpose.

For immediately after depending on a boundary, since a seven-abhyantara boundary can occur, and because that would lead to a conflict or an overflow with a previously established boundary approved for the area above it, it would simply be a defective boundary (*vipatti-sīmā*).
However, when one stands within a village precinct (*gāmakkhetta*) and approves [a boundary] including even a portion of a non-village forest (*agāma-arañña*), [it is valid].

Furthermore, although the Blessed One has prescribed a boundary of seven *satta-bbhantara*s in uninhabited forest areas that is well-recognized as such, because it does not preclude [the performance of an act], those who have entered there to perform a formal act (*kamma*) must still leave three *satta-bbhantara*s between themselves and the edge of that area, even if they are performing it in the open forest beyond.
Otherwise, there would be a failure of the act; thus, [to disregard this] is entirely useless in every respect.
It should be understood that this refers to the establishment of a boundary in a forest where there is no village.
"A branch that has entered into a river" means even a branch standing touching the surface of the earth within a river, let alone one not touching it;
the same principle applies to a shoot (*pāroha*). By this, [the boundary] is established by touching a common river-boundary through a branch or the like connected to a dissimilar boundary.
This shows that a connection with a water-sprinkling boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) is not permitted.

By this very [statement], it should be understood that a connection with a hut boundary (*māḷakasīmā*) by means of a branch or similar object standing while touching both a great boundary (*mahāsīma*) and a village boundary (*gāmasīma*) is also not permitted.

The inclusion of the word "within" (*anta-*) in the phrase "only within the river" (*antonaḍiyaṃ yeva*) excludes the state of being situated on the bank. Therefore, even if it is established outside the limit of the water-sprinkling boundary, [the connection is not valid] if it is situated in the river.
This demonstrates the absence of any breach [of the boundary]. Therefore, he said: “Established on the further bank,” and so forth.

For if there were a breach simply because one is established even within a river beyond the splash of water, then that too would have to be rejected, since it is identical in being a violation of the ritual action (*kamma*);
yet it is not rejected. Therefore, in all cases, it is within the boundary of one's own support...
It should be understood that there is no fault of division.
"By means of an obstruction" means by digging [a trench] for wood and so forth to block the water.
"Or by means of a dam-binding" means by building a bridge-dam filled with clay and so forth; both expressions indicate nothing other than an obstruction. "Having destroyed the river."

It clarifies the meaning already stated by the phrase "the embankment was built below," which means the embankment was constructed after blocking the river below. "Discarded water" refers to surplus water.
By the phrase "from the place where it flows after descending into the river," it shows that it is not permissible in a location situated between a pond and a river.
"Leaping up" means [the water] spreading widely by breaking through the banks and so forth.
"Having offered. "Within the monastery boundary" means within a boundary that has been formally demarcated.
"On a pathless track" refers to a place where it is impossible to go and return on the very same day.

He speaks with reference to a forest boundary established by worldly convention—that is, a forest boundary devoid of villages—which is reckoned as such among the forest boundaries. "Therein" refers to [the places] of fishermen by nature.
"On paths for travel" means on lamps [placed there].

"That place" means precisely the place where those pits and so forth were made, not one that was not made; this is the meaning. "A salt-water channel" (*loṇī*) is a watercourse that flows in the manner of a conduit, sloping toward the force of the ocean's rising tide.
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, regarding the statement "it is not permitted to do so on a moving boat," it says: "without exceeding the splash of the water..."
It should be understood that it is permissible to do so when [the boundary] is being shifted. Regarding the phrase "or having cleared the boundary" (*sīmaṃ vā sodhetvā*):

here, "clearing the boundary" refers to bringing [the boundary markers] within hand's reach of those situated in the village boundaries and so forth. The statement "building a dam by destroying the river" clarifies this very point;
"a dam was built below" means that the dam was constructed after blocking the river at its lower course.
Meaning: "Discarded water" (*chaḍḍitodaka*) refers to water discarded to one side for the purpose of protecting a pond.
"When the rain does not fall" (*deve avassante*) means even when it rains during a time of drought, the rain does not fall. "Having surged up" (*uppatitvā*) means having overflowed.

"It flows, covering the boundaries of villages and market towns" (*gāmanigamasīmaṃ ottharitvā pavattati*) means that during the aforementioned rainy season, it flows continuously for four months. "The monastery boundary" (*vihārasīmaṃ*).
He speaks with reference to a boundary that has been established.
"A place not within the range of travel" means a location where one, having gone on that very day, is unable to return; it refers to such a region.
"It comes to be reckoned as a forest boundary" means he speaks with reference to a boundary of seven *abbhantara*s. "Of them" refers to the fishermen. "Of the limit of travel..."
"Orato" (on this side) is said with reference to a lamp-post or a mountain on the near shore at the limit of the journey, not to a specific location within the ocean.

"They encroach" means that where it is impossible for four monks to sit, they encroach from that point onward by establishing their own boundary even by as much as the breadth of a hair; [this is so] because it would suffice for all four monks.
It should be understood that they "envelop" (ajjhottharanti) by starting from the base and covering the entire interior.
"Intertwined branches" (saṃsaṭṭhaviṭapa) refers to the great roots of the branches standing as if sewn together; by this, he illustrates their extreme proximity to one another.
For even branches that touch branch to branch might still be far apart; therefore, the characteristic of complete intermingling would not have been demonstrated [otherwise].

The mention of "taking hold of a branch" was made to show that it *might* be so. For thus it is shown that when monks, while building a new vihāra within their own boundary by making a place insufficient for the monks to sit in fall inside the boundary, they are said to "confound one boundary with another," but not beyond that.
"It is bound" refers to the boundary of the old vihāra.

It was said: "That mango tree" refers to a mango tree that served as a boundary marker for the old monastery's precincts when, at a later time, those precincts and other features had fallen into ruin and were no longer known.

Having established it as being within one's own boundary and having designated a rose-apple tree (*jambu*) as being within the boundary of the old monastery, the area situated between the mango and the rose-apple trees is brought into one's own boundary and thus demarcated.
This is the meaning. And here it should be understood that it is stated explicitly that, although the mango tree standing within the old boundary— which served as a boundary marker—
had its branches intermingled with the rose-apple tree standing inside the [new] boundary, there was neither a failure in the binding of the boundary at the time of its establishment,
nor a subsequent merging with the village boundary, nor a failure of the formal act (*kamma*).
"Padesa" refers to a portion of space sufficient for the Saṅgha to sit upon.

By the phrase "having set aside the boundary-line (sīmantarika)," etc., it is shown that even a *baddhasīmā* (formally established boundary) that has been flooded over by a breach, or one where two boundaries have been made to touch each other without an interval, is no longer a valid boundary (*asīmā*).
Therefore, a boundary-line of even a single or two finger-breadths is indeed permissible. However, in the Aṭṭhakathās, it is stated that this [boundary-line] is difficult to discern.
It should be understood that [the boundary] is stated to be four finger-breadths and so forth. "Of two boundaries" means of two established boundaries (*baddhasīmā*).

"It becomes a marker" (*nimitta*) means that because the marker is outside the boundary, there is no fault of confusion (*sambhedadosa*) at the time of its establishment; this is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, it does not cause confusion merely by being a marker, but rather, anything else situated within the intermediate space between the boundaries (*sīmantarikā*) also [does so].
The tree itself acts [as the agent]; therefore, trees that grow within a small boundary line (*sīmantarikā*) are certainly not permitted.

Furthermore, since the fault of confusion (*saṅkara-dosa*) has been shown in all cases regarding the entry of visible trunks, branches, and so forth, it is established that there is no fault even when invisible roots enter, because they belong to the earth-element (*bhūmi-gatika*).
But if even the roots, though visible, do not enter [the territory], it is indeed a confusion; however, mountains and rocks, even if visible, are simply of the nature of the ground.
If, at the very time of binding, a single large tree stands touching both boundaries, it should be understood that the boundary subsequently bound is invalid.
“Confusion of boundaries” (*sīmasaṅkara*) means the overlapping of boundaries. As for what is stated here in the *Sāratthadīpanī*:

“It is said ‘he creates confusion of boundaries’ because, when [a new boundary] has been extended and entered the area of the existing boundary, it is difficult to discern the location where the two boundaries meet,” that is not correct;
for even in the case of a village boundary, one must say that he creates confusion together with it. There too—
For when the boundary markers have increased, it becomes difficult to discern the location where the village boundary and the formal boundary overlap.

However, since the confusion between two formal boundaries has been stated there without further elaboration, it should be understood that the fault of the aforementioned connection is what is expressed by the word "confusion" (*saṅkara*).
In the Pāḷi, however, by way of the introduction: "Bhikkhus, for those whose boundary..."
Although it is stated that "if they are appointed afterwards, that act of theirs is contrary to the Dhamma," and so forth— referring to the absence of a boundary for one appointed later—
even if two Saṅghas, standing within the boundaries of two villages, effect a schism or an encroachment, or fail to establish a *sīmantarika* (intermediate space),
or fail to separate the connection of tree-sprouts and the like, by means of completing the formal ritual (*kammavācā*) at a single moment; [this remains invalid].
It should be understood that the absence of a boundary (*asīmatā*) for even two boundaries formally authorized on one side has been declared.
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is said: "By the phrase 'interlacing branches,' the proximity of each other is illustrated.
'It is bound' refers to the boundary in the western direction. 'In its location' means where, standing [there], the monks..."

It is possible to perform the ritual action (*kamma*) in such a location. However, when those standing within a certain area are unable to perform the ritual action, they define that area as the limit and bind it;
this is called "overlapping one boundary with another" (*sīmāya sīmaṃ sambhindanti*).
It is said that there is no overlapping of boundaries because the two boundaries share a common landmark (*nimitta*), since the landmark lies outside of both boundaries.

"He creates a confusion of boundaries" is said because, when one has expanded [the boundary] and entered the area of another boundary, it is difficult to discern the location where the two boundaries meet;
however, this is not intended to show that it is improper to perform formal acts (*kamma*) there.
For a boundary does not cease to be a boundary by that much alone; rather, the two boundaries are subsequently encompassed by the expanded tree.
"They are joined as one; therefore, those performing the formal act while standing in one place must do so after having cleared the other [area].
Thus ends the "Ornament for the Determination of Boundaries" within the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
The Twenty-fourth Chapter. Discourse on the Determination of the Definition of Boundaries.
Having thus explained the determination of boundaries, since the discourse on boundaries in the Canon is included within the Uposatha Khandhaka, [the following is stated].

Since the Pavāraṇakkhandhaka follows immediately after the Uposathakkhandhaka, and since the exposition on the determination of the Uposatha and Pavāraṇa follows in that sequence from the determination of the *sīmā*,

one might begin by explaining the determination of the Uposatha and Pavāraṇa. Nevertheless, for the sake of promoting the growth of the Dispensation, and in order to generate wisdom, mindfulness, and energy in those modest, virtuous, learned, and desirous monks who wish to establish a *sīmā*—
which serves as the locus for performing the formal acts (*kamma*) of the Vinaya such as full ordination (*upasampadā*)— [the following is set forth].
The discourse on the binding of boundaries (sīmābandhana) is now commenced by us.

In this context, the boundary (*sīmā*)—which serves as the locus for performing the four types of formal acts beginning with the *apalokana* (request)—is twofold: bound (*baddha*) and unbound (*abaddha*). Furthermore, the bound boundary is threefold:

the partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*), the boundary for common residence (*samānasaṃvāsakasīmā*), and the boundary for non-separation (*avippavāsasīmā*). Likewise, the unbound boundary is also threefold: the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*), the water-splash boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*), and the seven-fathom boundary (*sattabbhantarasīmā*).
For this was said by the teacher, the Elder Buddhadatta, in the *Vinayavinicchaya*:

“‘Those who share a common residence though in a broken communion,’ and ‘those who are separated’—thus they are declared to be threefold when bound; and they are likewise considered to be threefold when unbound.”
“From the water-splash outside the village, and even within seven *abbhantara*s;
therein the delimitation of the village is called the ‘village boundary.
In that regard, for one wishing to bind a fixed boundary (*baddhasīma*), [one must avoid] one that is too small, too large, one with broken markers, or one with shadow-markers.
The signless (animittā), those approved as being outside the boundary, those approved as being in a river, those approved as being in the ocean, those approved as being in a lake,
those approved by one who merges one boundary into another, and those approved by one who completely covers one boundary with another—
having transcended these eleven defective boundaries (vipattisīmāyo), there is the perfection of the signs, the perfection of the assembly, and the perfection of the formal act (kammavācā).
Having joined it with the threefold perfection already stated, one should bind it by connecting the first-mentioned sign with the last-mentioned sign.
For this was said by the Master of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathācariya*) in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*:
"In that regard, having transcended the eleven boundaries of failure and being endowed with the threefold perfection, one should connect sign with sign by means of a sign."
"A boundary that has been formally approved is what is called a 'bound boundary. By this, it is shown that among these eleven defects, if even one is present;

among the three kinds of success, if even one is absent; and if the markers have been made unconnected with the markers, then even if the boundary has been formally approved, it is not a [valid] boundary.
Thus, a bhikkhu who wishes to bind a boundary must exert great effort to ensure that all the required characteristics are fulfilled.
Therefore, at the time of binding a boundary, among the three requirements, first the village boundary must be examined for the sake of establishing the perfection of the assembly (*parisasampatti*).
Here it may be asked: "Should not an already-bound boundary be bound, or why [examine] the village boundary?"
“Should it be investigated? Because one must bind the formal boundary (sīmā) while standing within the village boundary (gāmasīmā). For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Monks, when a boundary has not been authorized and a zone has not been established, whatever village or town one dwells in dependence upon, the village boundary of that village or the town boundary of that town constitutes the common community (samānasaṃvāsā) therein.”

"...one Uposatha. Although this is not mentioned explicitly in the text (*pāḷi*) here, because it is stated in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) that "by the mention of 'village,' the city is also included therein," the city boundary (*nagarasīmā*) is also included.
Therefore, in a monastery where no formal boundary has been established, the extent of the village upon which the monks reside is called the "village boundary" (*gāmasīmā*). That which...
When they dwell in dependence upon a market town (*nigama*), the boundary of that market town is called the "market-town boundary" (*nigama-sīmā*).
When they dwell in dependence upon a city (*nagara*), the boundary of that city is called the "city boundary" (*nagara-sīmā*). All of these are termed "village boundaries" (*gāma-sīmā*).

For those monks, it constitutes a common community (*samāna-saṃvāsa*)—like a boundary established for a single *uposatha*—and they are entitled to perform communal acts of the Saṅgha, such as the *uposatha*, together.
It is said that the boundary may be established only in such a location as this, and not in a location unfit for communal sangha transactions (saṅghakamma) such as the Uposatha;
therein, "the extent of the area from which the village headmen of each respective village receive tax [is the area]."
"Whether it be small or large, it is reckoned as being within the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*)," according to the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Thus, the village boundary is the place where those who rule over villages and so forth receive their tax-tribute (*bali*). And this is stated by way of the majority.
Even for a place not receiving tribute, if it is a location inscribed on a royal edict, it is indeed the village boundary of that village. For it is said in the *Vimativinodanī*:
The statement "they receive the tax" is said by way of the majority.

However, regarding those portions of land recorded on royal edicts such as "this village consists of this much in karīsa-measures," even those specific locations—such as ponds, irrigation channels, charnel grounds, or mountains—where they do not collect the tax are still part of the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*).
For all land demarcated by kings and others [is included].
“Excluding rivers, salt-pans, and lakes, it should be understood as the village boundary. This is what is called the natural village boundary (*pakatigāmasīmā*).

Furthermore, according to the statement in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): “Even when, within the area of a single village, a king demarcates a certain portion and gives it to someone, saying, ‘Let this be a separate village,’ that too becomes a separate village boundary,” it follows that the king [may do so] within the very area of the natural village.
The area that one grants with the thought, "Let there be a village separate from the natural village, unmixed with the natural village," is called a separate-village boundary (*visuṅgāmasīmā*).

Thus, both the natural village boundary and the separate-village boundary—which functions according to the will of kings—are eligible for all formal acts (*kamma*), just like a formally established boundary (*baddhasīmā*);
therefore, those who wish to establish a newly established boundary [must first consider] the natural village boundary.
Or, having purified either a separate village boundary (*visuṃgāmasīma*) or a city boundary (*nigamasīma*), it must be performed. For thus it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
“Therefore, both that [new] and the other [original] boundaries of the natural village, town, or market town are just like boundaries that have been formally established (*baddhasīmā*).
And in the *Vimativinodanī*: “For therein, that [old] one has changed by way of the king’s desire and is newly arisen, while the other remains unchanged.”
It is said: "The natural village boundary (pakatigāmasīmā) is similar to a formally established boundary (baddhasīmā) in that it is fit for all formal acts of the Saṅgha;
the intention is that it shares the same communal affiliation and the same Uposatha as the established boundary.
However, some teachers say: "We wish to establish a boundary; therefore, this much extent of land is a separate field..."

Having requested permission from the king with the words, "Let it be so," and once that space has been prepared by him, they attend to the thought, "This place shall be a separate village territory (*visuṅgāma-khetta*).
Right there, having cleared the area by bringing monks within arm's reach and so forth, they perform the lifting of the boundary (*sīmā-samūhana*) and the binding of the boundary (*sīmā-bandhana*).
This performance is supported by the commentary’s statement: "The king, having demarcated it [thinking], 'Let this be a separate village,' gives it to someone."
Furthermore, this does not appear to be consistent with the statement from the *Vimativinodanī-Ṭīkā*:
“And that [village] has arisen as something new, having been transformed according to the king’s desire. How so? First, regarding the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) passage:
by the words “let this be a separate village,” it is not only the previous village that becomes a village; rather, even this newly demarcated area is now indeed a separate [village].
The phrase “let it be a village” shows that one makes two villages out of a single village-field.

By the words “the king gives to someone,” he indicates that [the land] has been given to a village headman; however, in this case, he neither makes two villages nor gives it to a village headman, but merely creates an opportunity for the sake of the monks as a temporary provision (*yāvakālika*) by their consent.
Thus, even according to the words of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it does not appear as if they coincide.

Furthermore, by the words of the *Vimativinodanī-Ṭīkā*, “having been turned around by the desire of the king,” it shows that a field which was not a village becomes a village after being turned around by the desire of the king.
And by the phrase “and new,” it indicates both the boundary of an old village and the boundary of a new village.
In the previous village, it was shown that the field possessed the characteristic of being a distinct village, unmixed with others.
Here, however, because it has been transformed by the king’s desire, both its state of being a distinct village and its characteristic of being a distinct village due to its newness are not seen;
likewise, it does not appear to accord even with the words of the *Ṭīkā*.
And in the *Vinayavinicchayaṭīkā*, it is stated that delimitation by means of income (*āyavasena*) is as follows:

"The village boundary is a portion of the village delimited by the amount of produce (*karena*), having been properly demarcated in all directions, such that it is determined: 'This area has this much produce. This refers to delimitation by means of income alone, not merely by the act of granting permission.
Therefore, because it does not meet the specific characteristic of a separate village, it is [treated] as a natural village (*pakatigāma*).
There is a confusion; in such a case, it is not fit to perform sangha-kamma, such as the Uposatha, etc.

Only in a place fit for performing sangha-kamma, such as the Uposatha, etc., is it also fit to perform the kamma of abolishing a boundary (*sīmā-samūhanana*) or establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandhana*), because those kammā consist of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñatti-dutiya-kamma*).
Therefore, other teachers do not approve of that performance by those teachers. However, other teachers [say]: "That..."

They say: "When a king gives a delimited area to someone, saying, 'Let this be a separate village (visuṅgāma),' and the village headman (gāmabhojaka) receives the tax (bali) from it, then it becomes a separate village; it was not so before that.

Their statement, as well as the passage from the *Vinicchaya-ṭīkā* stating, "The area thus determined by the act of [granting] is [the village]," refers to villages and the like being delimited by the collection of taxes (*karaggāha*).
This may have been stated with reference to the statement in the *Sīmālaṅkāra-ṭīkā* that "the area on all sides is the village boundary.
However, in those [texts], the delimitation of the tax is expressed as "this much is the tax for this area," not the seizing of force by the village headman (*gāmabhojaka*).
And in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it speaks only of the king's giving, saying "the king gives to someone," and not of the village headman.
And because he accepts the tax (*bali*), that constitutes acceptance; therefore, other wise men do not accept that statement either.

Consequently, the king, the lord of the earth, having demarcated it by saying, "In this village district, let a portion measuring so much *karīsa* become a separate village apart from the previous village," he gives it away.
Up to this point, that region may indeed be considered as having accepted the tax.
Or, it should be understood that what is not formally accepted constitutes a separate village (*visuṅgāma*).

Having thus understood, in accordance with reality, both the characteristic of a natural village (*pakatigāma*) and the characteristic of a separate village, one who wishes to establish a fixed boundary (*baddhasīma*) should,
if the natural village boundary is not too extensive and is easily protected, [delimit] that very natural village boundary well.
Having had it well guarded and thoroughly cleaned, the formal acts for the abolishing of the boundary (*sīmāsamūhanana*) and the authorization of the boundary (*sīmāsammuti*) should be performed.

However, if the original village boundary is too extensive—whether it be a town boundary or a city boundary—and because it is a place where many monks sit and move about, they are unable to clean it or guard it; and this being the case:

Having thoroughly cleansed and well-secured a village boundary that has been demarcated by kings who are lords of the earth, the formal act for the abolishing of the boundary (*sīmāsamūhanana*) and the authorization of a new boundary (*sīmāsammuti*) should be performed.
How, then, should the thorough cleansing and the thorough securing be carried out?
For one desiring to bind a boundary, monks in the neighboring monasteries [should be informed] of the delimitation of the boundary of each respective monastery.

Having asked [for permission], and having set aside the intermediate space between the boundaries for those monasteries with established boundaries, and the precincts for those monasteries without established boundaries, if those wishing to establish a boundary within a single village district during a time when monks traveling in all directions are not in transit, they should inform the monks in those monasteries that have established boundaries: "Today we shall establish a boundary; you..."
The following should be sent: "Do not depart from the delimitation of each respective boundary.
In those monasteries where boundaries have not been formally established, the monks should be assembled together; the consent (*chanda*) of those entitled to give it must be obtained.

When the monks have thus assembled and the consent of those entitled to give it has been brought, [the announcement should be made] at various places such as on the roads, at river crossings, at village gates, and so forth.

And for the sake of quickly bringing visiting bhikkhus within hand’s reach and for the sake of establishing the outer boundary, one should—setting aside the monastery attendants and the novice monks—give the signal with a drum or a conch, and then the boundary should be abolished.
But is it not the case that this purification and protection were stated in the Aṭṭhakathā only at the time of the formal authorization of the boundary? Now...
Why is this stated here in the context of the formal act of abolishing a boundary (*sīmāsamūhanana*)?

It should be understood that this too is stated for the purpose of ensuring the completeness of the assembly (*parisā*), since this formal act of abolishing a boundary is also a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*).

Even so, this formal act called the abolishing of a boundary must be performed—if there is an ancient established boundary—when other monks have come within arm’s reach (*hatthapāsa*) of the Saṅgha gathered for that purpose.
Even when [monks] have entered the village boundary (*gāmasīma*), there is no breach of the formal act (*kammabhedo*).

If there is no ancient established boundary (*baddhasīmā*), even in that case, because it is merely the village boundary, there is no fault even if the formal act of abolishing the boundary (*sīmāsamūhanana*) does not succeed;
so why was "purification" (*sodhanā*) mentioned? True, nevertheless, it must be abolished because the delimitation of the ancient boundary is difficult to discern.

For if, when the Saṅgha has assembled with the thought, "We shall abolish the boundary in one place within a large, ancient, established boundary," a monk enters another part of that very same boundary—even if he is unaware of it—the formal act fails;
therefore, it should be understood that the area must be cleared with great effort. Thus, the clearing of the village boundary [is accomplished] by the perfection of the assembly.
"Appointed" means that at the very least, having assembled with four bhikkhus, all those bhikkhus who are situated within that village boundary—
whether it be a fixed boundary, or one established by a river, the ocean, or a lake— without having crossed over them,
having either come within arm's reach of one another or brought their consent (chanda), they are thus appointed; for this is stated in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*.
It is understood that this is a cause for the perfection of the assembly. Therefore,
in order to be freed from the two faults of failure mentioned— namely, "by one who joins one boundary with another boundary" and "by one who covers one boundary over with another boundary"—
the formal act of abolishing the boundary (sīmasamūhanana-kamma) must be performed.
If the boundary has not been abolished, how could one incur the two failures? This is the case even with a village boundary that has been cleared in such a manner.
If an ancient established boundary were still existing, those unaware of its existence might establish a new boundary.
For [the new boundary] would have to include within it a landmark of the ancient boundary and be established near it, inside the ancient boundary.
Having made another sign, they may bind a new boundary. When one boundary is joined with another boundary, it is called "authorized" (*sammatā*).

Therefore, it is said in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*: "When one boundary is joined with another boundary, it is called 'authorized' when one's own boundary is joined with the boundary of others. For if, in the case of an ancient monastery..."
In the eastern direction, there are two trees, a mango tree and a rose-apple tree, whose branches are intertwined with one another;
among them, the rose-apple tree is situated on the western side of the mango tree. The monastery boundary was established by including the rose-apple tree within it and excluding the mango tree.
Later, when a monastery was built to the east of that [original] monastery, those establishing the boundary—
“Monks, having made the mango tree inside and the rose-apple tree outside, they bind [the boundary]; this is called a boundary that is ‘intermingled’ with a previous boundary.

If they were to bind a new boundary, making either a portion of the old boundary or the entire old boundary inside, it is called a boundary that is “encompassed” by another boundary. For this is said in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*: “Regarding a boundary...”
"By one who overflows the boundary, it is called 'authorized' when one's own boundary is authorized while overflowing the boundary of others.
For if they authorize their own boundary by including either the entire bound boundary of others or a portion of it within it,
it is called 'overflowing boundary with boundary.'"
In whatever place four bhikkhus cannot sit down and perform a formal act (*kamma*), from that point onward,
if one includes even as much as a hair’s breadth of another person’s previously established boundary within one’s own boundary,
this is called "merging one boundary with another" (*sīmāya sīmaṃ sambhindati*). This applies starting from a location sufficient for four bhikkhus to sit down.
Even when one brings the entire extent of another’s ancient established boundary within one’s own boundary, this is called "overlapping one boundary with a boundary.
For it is said in the *Līnatthappakāsanī* commentary on the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*: "Its location means a portion of it;
that place where, standing there, four bhikkhus are able to perform a formal act (*kamma*)."

"Such a place is what is meant by 'one part' (ekadesa). However, it should be understood that when those standing where it is impossible to perform the ritual action delimit such a location and thereby cause one boundary to merge with another, this is called 'merging' (sambhindanti), not 'overlapping' (ajjhottharanti).
This is also stated in the *Vimativinodanī*: "Where four monks cannot sit down, from that extent..."
It is said: "From the foundation up to even a mere hair’s breadth of one's own boundary, they are 'intermingled' (sambhindanti);
from the point where it is sufficient for four bhikkhus up to the entire interior, they are 'overspread' (ajjhottharanti)—thus it should be understood.
Let it be so; within that village boundary-limit, while the ancient boundary still exists, [this is done] for the sake of liberation from the two-fold failure.
The act of abolishing a boundary is purposeful; how could it be purposeless when [the boundary] is no longer present? To dispel doubt:
if the act of abolishing the boundary were not performed, doubt might arise regarding the binding of a new boundary.
From the time of the Blessed One’s own lifetime until the present day, monks who have exceeded the path of calculation [in number] have performed formal acts such as ordination.
They establish a boundary in various locations. It is impossible to know whether that boundary exists here or does not exist there;
therefore, a doubt might arise as to whether "the ancient boundary might exist in the place where we are establishing our new boundary.
When this is the case, the newly established boundary becomes subject to suspicion, and thus even formal acts such as ordination (*upasampadā*) performed within that boundary [are likewise suspect].

It becomes a matter of suspicion; therefore, for the purpose of removing such suspicion, those foremost among the self-controlled who wish to bind a new boundary must certainly perform the formal act of abolishing the previous boundary. And for those abolishing it, [the Blessed One has said]:
"Monks, when one abolishes a boundary, first the non-separation from the three robes must be abolished, and afterwards the boundary itself must be abolished."

According to the sequence of the words, first the non-separation boundary (avippavāsa-sīmā) must be abolished, and thereafter the common affiliation boundary (samāna-saṃvāsaka-sīmā) must be abolished.
At the time of that abolition, one standing within a partial boundary (khaṇḍa-sīmā) must not abolish the non-separation boundary;
likewise, one standing within a non-separation boundary must not abolish the partial boundary. However, by one standing within a partial boundary, only the partial boundary itself must be abolished.

According to the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Likewise, by one standing within the other," a *khaṇḍasīmā* (fragmentary boundary) must be abolished while standing within that very *khaṇḍasīmā*, and a *mahāsīmā* (great boundary) must be abolished while standing within that very *mahāsīmā*; a boundary must not be abolished while standing within a different boundary.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, the term "non-separation boundary" (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) refers specifically to the *mahāsīmā*. Only there...
Because they are generally separated from their robes.
In that case, if they know both the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*) and the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsasīma*), they will be able both to abolish and to bind it.
However, even if they know the broken boundary but do not know the non-separation [boundary], they will still be able both to abolish and to bind it.

They will be able [to do so]. However, those who do not know of the *khaṇḍasīma* (fragmentary boundary), but only know of non-separation (*avippavāsa*), might perhaps be able to abolish it by standing in places free from apprehension—such as the courtyard of a shrine (*cetiyaṅgaṇa*), the courtyard of the Bodhi tree (*bodhiyaṅgaṇa*), or the Uposatha hall—but they certainly will not be able to establish it.
If they were to establish it, they would create a breach of boundaries and turn the monastery into a non-monastery.
Therefore, it should not be abolished. Furthermore, those who do not know both [the boundary and the procedure] will neither be able to abolish it nor to bind it.
For this so-called *sīmā* ceases to be a *sīmā* either through the formal act (*kammavācā*) or through the disappearance of the Teaching;
yet it is impossible for those who do not know the *sīmā* to perform a formal act. Therefore, it should not be abolished, but rather [it should be maintained] with great care.
Because it is stated in the Commentary: "Having understood [them],

they must be abolished and bound," those monks who do not know whether the *khaṇḍasīmā* and *mahāsīmā* exist or not within the village boundary that has been delimited [by the thought] "Now we shall abolish the boundary," nor know the delimitation of those boundaries— such monks [are as described].
They would not be able to abolish the ancient boundaries; and being unable to abolish the ancient boundaries, how could they possibly establish new boundaries?

Therefore, relying on the method of conformity correctly determined by successive teachers, and putting forth great effort, one should proceed according to the correct method without omitting any essential factor.
They will be able to abolish the ancient boundary. How so?
At the time of abolishing that boundary, if it was begun within the boundary of a natural village, they must mark out the limits of that natural village;
if it was begun within the boundary of a separate village, they must mark out the limits of that separate village, so that other monks do not enter.
Having caused a well-arranged protection to be established on all sides, together with a Vinaya-expert who is capable of proclaiming the formal act (*kammavācā*) and endowed with wisdom and strength,
[one should perform it] with four monks who are of the same communion, modest, and virtuous; for since this act is to be performed by a quorum of four,
and because the status of being a regular monk (*pakatatta*) among the monks is difficult to discern, [it should be done] with a number greater than that.
Having taken the bhikkhus, they should now, within the boundaries to be demarcated— including both inside and outside the monastery enclosure—
in every place within the range of a stone’s throw, stand or sit without being separated by more than a hand’s breadth at intervals of one bed’s length throughout;
and having done so, they should first perform the formal act (*kammavācā*) for abolishing the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*).
Then, having announced the formal act for the removal of the boundary of common residence,
once the boundary has been abolished— even though the old boundaries still exist— since twenty-one monks must be capable of sitting within the western limit,
the monks standing in each space the size of a bed within that boundary would necessarily be standing within those [old] boundaries; therefore...
Having become established within the boundary and having uttered the formal motion (*kammavācā*) for the abolition of the boundary, they may abolish those boundaries.
Then, because the previously established boundaries have been abolished, only the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*) would remain. For this has been stated in the *Vimativinodanī*:
"In such monasteries, some [teachers] say that five or six monks, taking them from the edge of the monastery, [should proceed] along the enclosure of the monastery..."
Having stood continuously inside and outside, all around within the range of a clod-throw, in every place measuring the extent of a bed,
first the boundary of non-separation and then the boundary of common affiliation are abolished by means of their formal removal;

when this destruction of the boundary has been performed, even though both the fragmentary boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*) and the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) still exist in that monastery, [the following must necessarily occur].
“In one place where there is a single bed, those monks standing in their midst should remove them; then only the village boundary (gāmasīmā) would remain.
Since the Commentary states, “But having understood it thoroughly, they must both remove and bind [the boundary],” only those who know the boundary will be able to remove it;
how then could those who do not know do so? Regarding this section on the removal of the boundary:
The state of not knowing the boundary or the delimitation of the boundary is not a constituent factor (*aṅga*).
Rather, these two alone are the constituent factors: the state of standing within the boundary and the performance of the formal act (*kammavācā*) with the intention, "We shall abolish the boundary.
Therefore, when these two constituent factors are fulfilled, they are able to abolish it even if they are unaware of this [fact]. When these two constituent factors are fulfilled...
How is it to be understood that those who do not know the boundary have the capacity to abolish it? Because in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is stated:
"But those who know the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*), even if they do not know [the rule of] non-separation (*avippavāsa*), will be able both to abolish and to bind it";
thus, since the abolition is mentioned even in a place where the delimitation of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) is unknown, so too in the *Vimativinodanī*.

“In this case, knowledge of the boundary or its delimitation is not a requisite factor; rather, standing within the boundary and performing the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) with the intention, ‘We shall abolish it,’ are the requisite factors.

In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: ‘But those who know of a broken-off boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*), even if they do not know of the non-separation [from robes], will be able both to abolish and to bind it.
Thus, even when the delimitation of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) is unknown,”
It is said: “Because of the statement regarding the eradication [of the boundary].
Therefore, since the ancient established boundaries have been eradicated, only the village boundary would remain. When that remains, what should be done next?
Since the village boundary remains, one should perform the purification and protection of that village boundary according to the method previously stated, and within that village boundary—
One may bind either a partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*) or a great boundary (*mahāsīma*) according to one’s preference;
furthermore, even without binding a formal boundary, one may perform sangha-acts such as ordination (*upasampadā*) within the mere village boundary (*gāmasīmā*).
For it is said in the *Vimativinodanī*: "And regarding the remaining village boundary itself, there [one may perform] both types [of acts] according to one’s preference."
They say that it is permissible both to bind the boundary and to perform formal acts such as full ordination (*upasampadā*);
this appears reasonable, and should be accepted after investigation.

Therefore, if they wish to establish only a "broken boundary" (*khaṇḍasīmā*) measuring sixty cubits in length and forty cubits in width, it is appropriate in measure if it occupies a space sufficient for the placement of beds over such an area.
"Bed" (mañca) refers to a bed of the maximum permissible size. For that is nine or eight spans (vidatthi) long, based on a standard span.
A bed smaller than that is not sufficient for lying down with one's head resting on a pillow and one's legs stretched out;
thus, according to the *Samantapāsādikā*, it must be at least as long as the maximum permissible length of a bed. Furthermore, it may even be longer than that.
It is indeed so. However, the width of a bed is half its length;

therefore, taking the space occupied by a bed as five cubits in length and five spans (vidatthi) in width, one who measures by that standard finds that a boundary area sixty cubits in length contains twenty-four beds, and forty spans in width contains eight beds.

When grasped in this way, the bed is oriented from south to north; with a boundary area sixty cubits long, it constitutes twelve beds, and with a width of forty cubits, it constitutes sixteen beds. When grasped in this way, the bed is oriented from east to west.
Multiplying the length by the width in both cases, the entire interior boundary area constitutes one hundred and twenty-two beds.
One must take even a place outside the boundary that has a single bed or two beds on all sides;
the count must be increased by including it with that. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated:
"within the distance of a clod-throw," which may have been said with reference to the precincts outside the enclosure of the monastery at the time of establishing the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).

Even in the case of a *khaṇḍasīmā* (fragmentary boundary), there is no fault in removing [the boundary markers] from afar; however, because it is difficult to perform, the measure for those who carry them out must be known.
In the case of the boundary called *Kalyāṇī*, they remove it by making a single portion of a place measuring five cubits in both length and breadth.
That too was done considering it to be merely more than the size of a rear bed.
Now, however, the phrase "at this place" (*idāni amhe*) should be understood as more appropriate because it correlates with the method of the treatise.
The manner of abolishing [the boundary] should be understood as follows:

at this time, the area within and outside the signs of the boundary to be bound—the location where the boundary is to be abolished according to the aforementioned method—should be made level, clean, and stainless, like the surface of a mirror.
Having determined the size of the bed as previously described, one should have a line marked with a cord or a staff like an eight-square checkerboard;
then, following that line, one should have the various colors applied using either copper-colored clay powder or white clay powder,
arranging them row by row and section by section according to the method explained before.
Having had the protection and purification performed, and thinking, "Now we shall abolish the boundary," he should take four or more bhikkhus belonging to the same communion;

standing on the first tier at the first section in the place of the bed, he should first recite the formal act for abolishing the non-separation boundary, and then the formal act for abolishing the boundary of common communion.
Having announced it, he should repeatedly exchange his standing position with that of the other person within that very same section,
and after uprooting [the defilements] three or seven times, he should exit from there and stand in the second section of the first row; having done exactly the same there,
he should then proceed in the first row itself in direct order (anulomanaya) as far as the final section, in each one—
Having done so with that section, when the first row is exhausted, he stands at the final section of the second row and does the same;
starting from there, he proceeds through the second row itself in reverse order back to its first section, doing the same.
In this way, having proceeded through the third row and the others, sometimes in direct order and sometimes in reverse order, he completes all the rows.
When every single portion has been completely exhausted, this formal act of abolishing the boundary (*sīmāsamūhanana-kamma*) is said to be finished.
As for the phrase "four or more than that," this is stated because this formal act must be performed by a quorum of four.

However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is noted that because the status of monks as being of "normal standing" (*pakatatta*) is difficult to discern, and because conscientious and virtuous monks are rare...
It is stated: “five or six.
However, at the Kalyāṇī boundary, it was established by fourteen bhikkhus who had been sought out and selected by King Dhammaceti;
these bhikkhus had returned from the island of Sri Lanka after receiving the new ordination and had not encountered even a trace of censure or dispute. This is recorded in the stone inscription.

It has arrived. Furthermore, during the time of the younger king named Sirīsudhammarājādhipati in the city of Ratanapūra, the eminent Great Elder (Mahātheravara) named Sirīsaddhammakitti—renowned as the "Great Sīhaḷappatta"—was binding the boundary on a mountain peak not far from his own residence;
instead of taking those who were dependent upon him, he took those whom he himself favored.
They say that he takes other great elders who are modest, learned, and desirous of training, and performs the formal act (kamma) with himself as the fourth member.
This would have been done because this formal act requires a quorum of four, and because those elders were free from suspicion regarding his status as a regular monk (pakatatta).
Even so, because the status of monks as regulars is difficult to discern, [the rule was established].
Since there is no fault in performing an act that requires a quorum of four with more than four members, the fact that it was performed by a greater number of monks is more praiseworthy.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Vinaya-ṭīkā* named *Vimativinodanī*:
"having taken five or six monks," and in the *Kalyāṇī-sīmā*, it is said that it was performed by fourteen monks.

It should be observed. Even when the formal act of abolishing the boundary (*sīmāsamūhanana-kamma*) has been thus concluded, for the sake of pleasing the minds of monks who hold various views, follow various teachers, belong to various sects, and reside in various regions, and for the sake of releasing them from censure and dispute, that same procedure must be performed again and again by those monks as well.
For it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "But it should be done again and again."
"For that [merit] remains as the actual deed for a deed that has been performed; it serves to make a deed that was unstable become stable.

And for this very reason, at the time when the boundaries were abolished in the four directions from the Mahācetiya—which had become a source of merit for the Great Dhammarāja Anekapaṇḍarahaṃsi Sāmi—in the city of Haṃsāvatī, by the Mahātheras residing in the Rāmañña country and those residing in the Maramma country...
It should be understood that he had [the boundaries] established separately by each of the Mahātheras.
However, if he wishes to establish a great boundary (mahāsīma), then, having selected a site measuring one usabha, two usabhas, or more,
and having had a perimeter wall constructed with the thought, "We shall build a monastery in this much space,"...
Within the enclosure of that monastery, both inside and outside, throughout the entire area within the range of a stone’s throw,
one should designate secluded portions measuring the size of a bed in each location according to the method described above. Then,

standing continuously together with the monks who have attained the status of having performed the formal act (*kammappatta*), the first non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) and the common-residence boundary (*samānasamvāsaka-sīmā*) must be abolished.
Thus, when the boundary has been abolished, provided that both a broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*) and a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) exist within that monastery,
those monks would necessarily have to abolish them by meeting in the middle at the place of a single bed;
thereafter, only the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*) would remain, and within that village boundary, there would be a twofold boundary by way of the broken boundary and the great boundary.
It may be bound according to one’s preference; however, we shall explain the manner of binding later on.
But why was the abolition of the old boundary performed even outside the marks? Is it not the case that a new boundary should be desired only within the marks?
It is for the purpose of resolving the confusion and clearing away the overlap [of boundaries] right there that the abolition of the old boundary is performed.
"Should it be done? Yes, it is true; however, because it is difficult to discern, it should be understood as having been done in this way.
For the existence or non-existence of the ancient boundary is difficult to discern;
therefore, if one were to abolish the boundary only within the marks, the ancient boundary would remain outside of them, and thus a small area would enter within [the new boundary]. That area...
If the Saṅgha acting to abolish the boundary were not sufficient in number to stand together with the reciter of the formal proclamation (kammavācā),
then that ancient boundary would remain unabandoned. If, perceiving it as abolished, they were to designate the interior boundary-mark at the time of establishing the new boundary,
[that new boundary] would be a "boundary within a boundary" because it has entered the limits of the ancient boundary which was not actually abolished.
There is the fault of division; however, if that place were sufficient for four people to sit, there would be the fault of one boundary overlapping another.
Even if it does not enter within, if it merely touches [the boundary] continuously, there is likewise the fault of confusion of boundaries.
To avoid these three faults, the removal of the boundary markers even outside [the area] is performed.
Thus it was said. Therefore, it should be understood that in the *Vimativinodanī* it is stated:
“Outside and all around, within the range of a clod-throw,” and so forth. However, some teachers hold that one should perform the drawing of the cord all around the boundary marks;
then, standing inside, having placed the feet below the cord, and having crossed even a small distance outside the cord, one effects the abolition of the boundary.
This must be investigated: the ancient boundary is not dissolved merely by the placing of the feet;

rather, dissolution occurs through the establishment of the Saṅgha within the voting circle (*kammavāca-patta*) together with the reciter of the formal act (*kammavācā*), and by the recitation of that formal act itself.
For it is said in the *Vimativinodanī*: "Regarding the standing within the boundary [with the thought], 'We shall abolish it'..."

"And here, the performance of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) is a constituent factor. Therefore, if the ancient established boundary (*porāṇaka-baddha-sīmā*) has entered within [the new markers] even in part and remains connected [to them], one would not be freed from the three faults mentioned by way of the aforementioned method unless its abolition (*samugghāta*) is performed.
Consequently, it is more praiseworthy to perform the act of abolishing [the boundary] while standing even outside the markers. Others, however...

The teachers establish a connection between the path and the movement of the laboring bhikkhus and then abolish [the boundary]; there is no fault in this if it is understood as being done for the sake of showing respect.
