However, some elders hold the view that "the boundary is abolished only at the place actually traversed by the performing Saṅgha, not at places not traversed," and thus they first construct a hall and afterwards [abolish] the boundary.
They say that because it cannot be stepped upon at the site of a pillar once it has been uprooted,
therefore the boundary is not uprooted. Furthermore, in the past, in the city of Sirīkhetta during the time of the Great Being Dhammarāja,
after the first Jetavana hall had been built in front of the Nandana Monastery established by that king, the queen-consort of that king established a boundary there.

Later, they established the boundary. At that time, there was a leading elder of the community named Mahārukkhamūlika who said, "If I am able to place my foot upon a pillar after piercing it, only then will I come," and so he did not come.
All the elders [said], "The ancient boundary does not stand by a mere pillar; of the pillar—"
"Having stood all around and performed the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), the boundary (*sīmā*) is abolished," yet they did not accept his words;

they both abolished and then re-established [the boundaries]. Also, at the time of King Dhammacetiya’s establishment of the Kalyāṇī boundary in the city of Haṃsāvatī, they first constructed the hall and only afterwards abolished it;
nor is there any mention in the Canon, the Commentaries, the Sub-commentaries, and so forth, of "the connection of the sequence of words..."
There is a reading stating, "having made a connection [between the steps], the boundary should be abolished," and there is also the reading, "in places measuring the size of a bed, the size of a bed.
When the formal act (*kammavācā*) for abolishing the boundary is performed in one place while standing within the ancient boundary, the entire boundary is indeed abolished;
therefore, the statement "having made a connection between the steps, it should be abolished" is [included].
The wise do not accept [such a view]. However, if it is understood that such a statement was spoken for the sake of showing respect, there is indeed no fault;
nevertheless, it becomes a cause for disciples and their followers to fall into conformity with that view.
For they will grasp it as a matter of firm conviction, thinking, "Our teachers speak thus and act thus," and will proceed accordingly.

They think that when the boundary has not been formally established, it is not abolished; therefore, it should be understood that performing the act according to the method found in the formal procedures (*pakaraṇa*) is superior and praised.
Furthermore, those who uphold the Vinaya and respect the Dhamma should reflect upon this profound matter concerning the abolition of boundaries.
There is a state that is difficult to see; if one asks what that is:

because of the statement, "Monks, I allow you to establish a boundary (sīmā) of up to three yojanas," there are great boundaries (mahāsīmā) of three yojanas and so forth, established by the Blessed One, which extend across the fields of various villages.
Then, having cleared out a single village field and provided protection, once the boundary has been dismantled—
If there are monks in other village districts than that one, the village boundary is not able to delimit the established boundary;
therefore, those monks would constitute an incomplete assembly (*vagga*) for that formal act. This being the case, the boundary would not be abolished;
and since it has not been abolished, the new boundary cannot be formally authorized. Thus, this...

This point is difficult to understand and difficult to see; therefore, those who are experts in the Vinaya—being modest, refined, learned, and desirous of training—should reflect upon it thoroughly, honoring the Blessed One’s injunction as they would a stone parasol.
While reflecting, searching, and investigating this matter, the following reason is seen: the great boundaries (sīmās) measuring three yojanas and so forth.

They would have been permitted by the Blessed One with reference to that [Mahā-Sīmā] because it was possible for monks possessing psychic powers to assemble or to purify it while they were still living.
However, at all times and in all places, it is not possible for all monks to purify such a great boundary or to assemble there; nor did the Blessed One permit what is impossible.

One might state an untenable reason. For it is seen in the treatises that during the lifetime of the Blessed One, the eighteen great monasteries in the city of Rājagaha were authorized as a single boundary (ekasīmā) by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma;
and that in the island of Siṃhala, the boundary of the Mahāvihāra was authorized by the Elder Mahinda and established so as to include Anurādhapura within it. Such is not the case here.
It is seen that in certain places a boundary (*sīmā*) of two or three *yojanas* was established by such-and-such a monk.
Furthermore, it must be understood through investigation that in this land of Burma (*Maramma*), there are no such boundaries.
For instance, the established boundaries (*baddhasīmā*) that arose many hundreds or thousands of years ago, together with their stone pillar markers—

It is seen in various locations. And in the city of Ariñjaya (Arimaddanapura), the Great Boundary—authorized by King Anuruddha, measuring one hundred and sixty-two cubits in length and one hundred and forty-seven cubits in width—is seen together with its boundary markers.
And in the city of Ratanapūra, during the time of the Great King Narapati Jeyyasūra, in the Kali age [reckoned] as four hundred and seventy-eight years...
The boundary that has been formally authorized is seen together with stone markings.
If there were great boundaries limited by three *yojanas* and so forth, the ancient teachers would not have bound new and new boundaries;
yet they do bind them, and within those new boundaries they perform sangha-acts such as ordination (*upasampadā*), and for this very reason, [the number of such acts] exceeds the path of calculation.
The monks, increasing [the community] by succession, establish the Dispensation (sāsana) as long as the world endures.
For this reason, it is understood that in this region there are no boundaries (sīmā) extending for three leagues (tiyojana).

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "inside and outside the enclosure of the monastery (vihāraparikkhepa), within the range of a clod-throw" (*leḍḍupāta*), [it refers to] the enclosure of the monastery...

Furthermore, because the *Vimativinodanī* states that the lifting of the boundary (*sīmāsamūhanana*) occurs precisely within the vicinity of the monastery and outside the range of a stone’s throw, it is understood that such great boundaries do not exist.
If they did exist, the masters of the treatises would not have mentioned the lifting of the boundary;
even if they were to mention it, they would have performed the lifting of the boundary after clearing an area extending three *yojanas* all around.
However, since it was not stated in that way, but rather because the removal of the boundary (*sīmāsamūhanana*) was taught only in relation to the monastery and its precincts,
it is understood that there are no great boundaries (*mahāsīmā*) measuring three *yojana* or more.
Alternatively, those who know of a "broken boundary" (*khaṇḍasīma*), even if they do not know of [the rule on] non-separation (*avippavāsa*), may both remove and establish it.

From the statement in the Aṭṭhakathā, “They will be able [to do so],” it is understood that in those various districts there were no great boundaries (mahāsīmā) measuring three leagues (tiyojana) or more.
How so? If such boundaries existed, the Aṭṭhakathā teachers would not have spoken of the abolishing of a boundary without first purifying the entire extent of that boundary;
rather, they spoke of non-separation (avippavāsa) for those who knew of a fragmented boundary (khaṇḍasīma).
Even those who do not know [the extent of] the boundary speak of the capacity to abolish and to bind it;

that speech, having become merely separated by the intermediate boundary (sīmantarika) from the aggregate boundary (khandhasīmā), would constitute a non-separation boundary (avippavāsa-sīmā) within that village precinct.
Therefore, the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā state that one has the capacity to abolish it while standing in that place, but not across the precincts of various different villages.

Because it is capable of abolishing the boundaries— such as those measuring three *yojanas* and so forth— which have been formally established by means of demarcation even when other village districts exist and other monks are present,
it is understood from this that "it is not the case that large boundaries measuring three *yojanas* and so forth do not exist in all places.
Such reasons [should be accepted] by those learned in the Vinaya who hold the Blessed One’s injunction in high esteem.
The holders of the Vinaya must reflect upon and investigate this matter again and again; other reasons for this should also be sought.

Furthermore, because of such statements as, "If they wish to include other village territories within [the boundary], those monks who reside in those villages must also come," they do not establish a boundary (*sīmā*) within only a single village territory. Now, if...

They also bind [the boundary] by including other village fields within it; therefore, one should not take it to mind that the natural village field—which serves as the basis for the boundary now to be authorized—has been cleared out.
For the purpose of cutting through doubt, when reciting the formal act (*kammavācā*) for the removal of the boundary, they connected it with that village field.
Even monks living in other village districts should be requested and then made to dwell far outside that village district.
For by doing so, even while including other village districts within [the boundary], they are unable to form a faction (*vagga*) as long as the ancient boundary still exists.
Consequently, the formal act (*kammavācā*) for abolishing the boundary succeeds; therefore, such a subtle [method]—

The precise meaning must be considered by those who uphold the Vinaya. Thus, by means of this procedure for abolishing a boundary, when it is said that one boundary is being joined with another or one boundary is being overlapped by another, [the boundary] becomes free from the two faults of failure mentioned therein.
Thereafter, for the sake of liberation from the faults of failure mentioned as "too small" or "too large," the measurement of the boundary—
It must be understood. How so? Regarding what is called a *sīmā* (boundary): if it is too small to accommodate twenty-one monks sitting down, even if formally authorized, it is not a valid *sīmā*.
If one includes even a space the size of a hair-tip beyond three *yojanas*, it is called "too large," and even if authorized, it is not a valid *sīmā*.
Therefore, [it must be] from the point of being sufficient for twenty-one monks to sit down...

"Starting from [the boundary], without exceeding three *yojanas*, wherever the Saṅgha desires whatever measurement, there that measurement should be established and the boundary (*sīmā*) formally designated. How is this understood? [It is said:
'In this regard, what is called "too small" is where twenty-one monks cannot sit down. What is called "too large" is even by so much as the breadth of a hair..."
It is understood from the statement in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*, “Having exceeded three yojanas, it is [thereby] authorized.
Thus, by determining the measurement of the boundary (*sīmā*), it becomes free from the two faults mentioned as being "too small" and "too large.
Thereafter, for the sake of being released from the three faults of deficiency mentioned as "having broken marks," "having shadow-marks," and "having no marks":

The description of the boundary markers (nimitta) must be performed. In that regard, by describing them without connection [to one another], the markers are called "fragmentary boundary markers" (khaṇḍanimitta).

How so? Having described the marker at the eastern direction among the markers placed at the four directions of the boundary, and having subsequently described the markers in the southern, western, and northern directions, one then [returns to] the eastern direction.
The sign (nimitta) must be defined; when this is done, it is called a "complete sign" (*akhaṇḍanimitta*).

However, if one defines the sign in the eastern direction and then proceeds in order to define signs in the southern, western, and northern directions, but does not again define a sign in the eastern direction, it is called a "fragmentary sign" (*khaṇḍanimitta*). There is another [type] as well:

A "broken-sign" (*khaṇḍanimitta*) is that which is designated by making a single sign out of something like a stone that has lost its original form, a hollow tree trunk, a stump, or a heap of dust located between [the boundary markers].
A "shadow-sign" (*chāyānimitta*) is that which is designated by making any kind of shadow—such as the shadow of a mountain—a sign.
An "unmarked" (*animitta*) is that which is designated without indicating any sign at all.
The proclamation of the boundary markers (*nimitta*) should be made for the purpose of liberation from these three faults.

How so? Having performed the removal of the ancient boundary (*porāṇasīmā*) through the formal act (*kammavācā*), the Saṅgha, within a village boundary that is entirely pure, should establish the boundary circle (*sīmamaṇḍala*) of the desired extent at its four or eight cardinal points.

Alternatively, having placed stones in the various directions—using the lower limit of a mass of thirty-two *palas* of *guḷa* (molasses) and the upper limit of a size smaller than an elephant—the Vinaya-holder who recites the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) while standing within the boundaries of the markers should ask:
"What is the marker in the eastern direction? Another [person] should reply: "A stone."
“Venerable sir,” he should say. Then the Vinaya-master, having said, “This rock is the sign (nimitta),” should proclaim it.
Following this method, while circumambulating the boundary circle clockwise, [he should proclaim:

“In the southeastern intermediate direction, in the southern direction, in the southwestern intermediate direction, in the western direction, in the northwestern intermediate direction, in the northern direction...”
"What is the sign for the northern intermediate direction? "A rock, venerable sir.
Having designated it thus, "This rock is the sign," he should then designate again: "What is the sign for the eastern direction? "A rock, venerable sir.
"This rock is the sign," having thus designated it, he should finish. For it is said in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*: "A 'broken sign' is called an unjoined sign," and so forth.
Thus, by the description of the marks, she is freed from the three faults of failure mentioned as "the mark of a broken [boundary]," "the mark of a shadow," and "the markless [boundary].

Thereafter, for the purpose of being freed from the fault of failure mentioned as "consented while standing outside the boundary," the place where the Saṅgha stands must be known at the time of reciting the formal motion (*kammavācā*) for the authorization of the boundary (*sīmā-sammuti*). How so? If, after the marks have been described, the Saṅgha...
If one designates a boundary by means of a formal act (*kammavācā*) while standing outside [the intended area], it is called "designated while standing outside the boundary";
it is not a [valid] boundary. Therefore, after the signs have been proclaimed, the Saṅgha, standing within those signs, must designate the boundary by means of a formal act.

For this has been stated in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*: "That which is called 'designated while standing outside the boundary' refers to [the case where one stands] outside the signs after the signs have been proclaimed..."

"Consent is valid for one standing outside. Thus, by defining the location for the delimitation of the boundary, it is freed from the fault of failure mentioned as "consent given by one standing outside the boundary.
Beyond that, it is freed from the three faults of failure mentioned as "consent given in a river," "consent given in the ocean," and "consent given in a lake."
And for the sake of liberation, one should attend to the mind in this way:

because of the Blessed One’s statement, “Monks, every river is without boundary, every ocean is without boundary, every natural lake is without boundary,” a formally established boundary does not exist within rivers, oceans, or natural lakes;
rather, only that which is formally established within a pure village boundary—devoid of any ancient boundaries—is truly a boundary. Therefore...
The boundary should be designated as precisely the village boundary itself, and not [the boundaries] of rivers and so forth. For it is said in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*:
“‘Designated in a river, in the ocean, in a lake’—this means they are designated within these [features] such as rivers,” and so on.
Up to this point, [it has been shown that] this boundary is too small, too large, has broken marks, has shadows as its marks, has no marks, or is designated while standing outside the boundary.

Being free from the eleven defects mentioned as "consented by a river," "consented by the ocean," "consented by a lake," "consented by one boundary while intersecting another boundary," and "consented by one boundary while covering over another boundary," it is like the lunar disk freed from the five minor stains mentioned as "clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu."
It becomes as perfectly pure as the moon’s disk or the sun’s orb.

What is called the threefold perfection consists of the perfection of the sign (*nimitta-sampatti*), the perfection of the assembly (*parisa-sampatti*), and the perfection of the formal act (*kammavācā-sampatti*). Among these, [the signs are]:
the sign of a mountain, the sign of a rock, the sign of a forest, the sign of a tree, the sign of a path, the sign of an anthill, the sign of a river...
Regarding the eight signs mentioned as "the water sign" (*udakanimitta*), one should designate them by reciting the specific signs obtained in each respective direction.
For it is said in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*: "What is the sign in the eastern direction?
A rock, venerable sir. 'This rock is the sign'—in such a manner they were designated. And among those eight...
Because signs such as trees and the like are difficult to find in the places intended by those who desire them, and because they can cause a confusion between two established boundaries,
whereas a stone sign cannot so confuse them and is easy to bring and place wherever desired, monks who are binding a boundary [should use a stone].
Stones that serve as boundary markers should be placed all around the perimeter of the boundary circle (*sīmamaṇḍala*). Therefore, it is stated in the *Mahāvagga-ṭīkā*:
“Those who are binding [the boundary] should place stones that serve as boundary markers all around. And in the *Vimativinodanī*:
“‘Stones that serve as boundary markers should be placed’—this is said because trees and other such markers may be difficult to find at a location chosen according to one’s preference,” and so forth.
To this extent, the first factor, known as the perfection of the signs (*nimitta*), is well-established.
Then, for the purpose of performing the formal authorization of the boundary (*sīmā-sammuti*), at least four monks must assemble;

and as far as possible within that village, all those monks who have not entered a fixed boundary (*baddha-sīmā*) or who do not stand within the limits of a river, the ocean, or a lake [must be present].

If all those who are present are brought within arm’s reach or summoned by means of their consent (*chanda*), then that boundary which has been formally established is said to be "endowed with the perfection of the assembly.
Therefore, it is stated in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*: "Endowed with the perfection of the assembly means having gathered with at least four monks as the minimum limit," and so forth.
Now, when the monks are binding that boundary, [they should consider] the neighboring monasteries...
In the spring, after the monks have inquired about the boundary limits of each respective monastery—

having established a buffer zone within the boundary of those monasteries where a formal boundary has been fixed, and having established a precinct within the boundary of those where no formal boundary has been fixed—
if they wish to fix a boundary within the area of a single village field at a time when wandering monks are not moving about, then [they may do so].
To those bhikkhus who reside in monasteries where a boundary has been formally established, a message should be sent: "Today we shall establish a boundary;

you must not go outside the limits of your respective boundaries. Those who reside in monasteries where no boundary has been established should all be assembled together in one place, and the consent of those entitled to give it should be brought forward.

If they wish to include even another village-field within the boundary, the monks residing there may either come or not come at the time of delimiting the *sīmā* for common affiliation (*samānasamvāsaka*).
However, at the time of delimiting the *sīmā* for non-separation (*avippavāsa*), the monks must come from within the marked boundaries;
those who do not come must have their consent (*chanda*) brought to them. For this has been stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
“‘Let the monks in the neighboring monasteries be summoned by those desiring to bind him,’ and so forth.

When the monks had thus assembled and the consent (*chanda*) of those entitled to give it had been brought, he stationed monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) and novices (*sāmaṇera*) at various points along the roads, at river fords, village gates, and other locations, for the purpose of quickly bringing the visiting monks within arm’s reach and for the purpose of establishing the outer boundary (*bahi-sīmā*). He then gave the signal with the gong (*bheri*).

Or, having had a conch-shell signal made, the boundary should be bound by means of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) beginning with "Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs," as stated immediately after the description of the sign.
For it is said in the Commentary: "When the bhikkhus have thus assembled," and so forth.
At this point, the second factor, consisting of the perfection of the assembly, is properly established.

Thereafter, at the time of reciting the formal act (*kammavācā*), because of the statement: "Monks, by one who is establishing a boundary (*sīma*), first a boundary for common affiliation (*samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā*) must be established;

afterwards, the non-separation from the three robes (*ticīvara-avippavāsa*) must be established," first the boundary for common affiliation must be established, and afterwards the boundary for non-separation must be established—at the very conclusion of the formal act for common affiliation.

Having set aside the boundary markers, by the very measure of those markers, the common residence boundary (samānasamvāsakasīmā) passes through the great earth—extending two hundred and forty thousand yojanas in width—and reaches as far as the water that supports the earth, making it its limit. Therefore, it is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
“At the very conclusion of the formal act (kammavācā)… it has gone. [This applies] at the conclusion of the formal act concerning non-separation (avippavāsa).

Regarding the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*): if there is a village within the [formal] boundary, then—excluding both the village and its precincts—it extends only as far as the delimitation of the common-residence boundary (*samāna-saṃvāsa-sīmā*) that has been traversed.
Thus, the non-separation boundary does not encompass the village or its precincts;
it encompasses only the common-residence boundary, and the common-residence boundary proceeds according to its own inherent nature.
The non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*), however, extends only as far as the common-residence boundary (*samāna-saṃvāsa-sīmā*) goes. Therefore, it is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
“Thus, the monks’ non-separation boundary...

[etc] ...extends. Consequently: “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. As far as the marks have been proclaimed all around—if it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should designate a boundary by these marks as a common residence with a single Uposatha. This is the motion. [This is the formal proposal.]”
“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs: as far as the marks have been proclaimed all around, the Saṅgha designates this boundary by these marks as a common residence with a single Uposatha.
Whoever among the venerable ones approves of the designation of this boundary by these marks as a common residence with a single Uposatha, let him be silent. Whoever does not approve, let him speak.”
"That boundary has been approved by the Saṅgha through these markers as one of common affiliation and a single Uposatha;
it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
This is the formal proclamation regarding common affiliation.

“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. That boundary which has been authorized by the Saṅgha as a common residence for a single Uposatha—if it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha authorize that boundary as ‘not being apart from the three robes,’ except for the village and the vicinity of the village. This is the motion.

“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. That boundary which has been authorized by the Saṅgha as a common residence with a single Uposatha—let the Saṅgha authorize that boundary as one where one is not separated from one’s three robes, excluding the village and its precincts.
Whichever venerable one approves of this authorization of non-separation from the three robes within this boundary, excluding the village and its precincts...”

And the village and its precincts [are excluded]. He who does not consent should speak. This boundary has been authorized by the Saṅgha as one where one is not separated from the three robes, with the exception of the village and its precincts. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent.
Thus do I understand this.

This *avippavāsa-kammavācā* (the formal act of non-separation) should be recited properly, ensuring that no faults regarding the motion (*ñatti*) or the proclamation (*anussāvana*) remain. To this extent, the third factor, known as the perfection of the formal act (*kammavācā-sampatti*), is well-established.

Thus, this boundary—like the lunar disk, which is endowed with three factors: within it is a jeweled palace, outside it is encircled by silver, and there is a divine son who is the owner of the palace;
or like a golden palace within, encircled by crystal on the outside—is likewise perfected by these three factors.

It should be understood that, like the solar disc which is endowed with these three factors—the celestial mansion, its owner, and the son of a god—it shines and radiates exceedingly when it is endowed with the three factors known as the perfection of the site (*nimitta*), the perfection of the assembly (*parisā*), and the perfection of the formal ritual act (*kammavācā*).
Thus, having become the cause for the long endurance of the Conqueror’s Dispensation, it remains. For this has been said in the Uposatha-kkhandhaka of the Pāḷi: "Bhikkhus, regarding the boundary..."
"When appointing [the boundary], the boundary for common affiliation must first be appointed," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "having connected landmark with landmark," one should proceed by first starting from the eastern direction and moving clockwise, announcing all the landmarks;
then, having reached the north-eastern direction, one should establish it right there.

The meaning is that, having again proclaimed the sign in the eastern direction as it was previously proclaimed, this boundary is thus established. Being thus established, this boundary is free from the eleven defects,
endowed with the three perfections, complete in all respects, and serves as the locus for the fourfold performance of formal acts—
beginning with the *apalokana*— for bhikkhus for a period of five thousand years or indefinitely.
It should be understood that this refers to a boundary that has been fixed.

However, if they wish to establish a large boundary (mahāsīma) that includes smaller sub-boundaries (sakhaṇḍasīma), they must first thoroughly clear the area according to the method previously described;
then it should be established either upon the original village boundary alone after the ancient boundaries have been removed, or upon a distinct village boundary.

And within those two boundaries, for the sake of making it easy to perform the formal acts of the Saṅgha—such as ordination (*pabbajjā*) and full admission (*upasampadā*)—the boundary must first be established.
Those establishing it, however, should know the proper procedure (*vatta*).

For if they establish it after having already settled all the sites, such as the Bodhi tree, the shrine (*cetiya*), and the refectory (*bhattasālā*), in a monastery that has already been built, [they should do so] in the middle of the monastery, at a place where many people gather.
Having fastened them, they should be tied in a secluded spot at the edge of the monastery.
When tying them in an unconstructed monastery, those who do so should first observe the location where all sites for the Bodhi-tree, the cetiya, and other structures are established;
they should then tie them in such a way that there is a secluded spot at the edge of the monastery within those established sites. For it is said in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "But this..."
“By those who are designating a boundary for a common residence,” and so forth.
But how large a fragmentary boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) should be bound? At the minimum limit, it is permissible if it includes twenty-one bhikkhus;
less than that is not permissible. Even if it includes as many as a thousand bhikkhus, it is permissible.
It is permissible. For it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “She [is included] as the lower limit,” and so forth.

And the phrase “twenty-one bhikkhus” is stated with reference to those who are seated; this is mentioned for the purpose of ensuring that the Saṅgha, consisting of a group of twenty, is sufficient to sit together with the bhikkhu eligible for the formal act (*kamma*) at the time of performing the rehabilitation (*abbhāna*). For it is said in the *Vimativinodanī*: “Twenty-one bhikkhus,” and so forth.
The monks binding that fragmentary boundary (khaṇḍasīma) must place stones designated as boundary-marks all around the precinct of the boundary.

Standing within that very fragmentary boundary, the fragmentary boundary is to be bound. Having thus proclaimed the marks, saying, "This stone is a mark," the boundary is to be bound by means of the formal ritual (kammavācā); this is for the purpose of strengthening that very boundary.
The formal act of non-separation (*avippavāsakamma*) must be performed. For it is said in the Commentary: "By those binding that [boundary]," and so forth.

Having thus designated the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*), stones for the intermediate boundary (*sīmantarikā*) must be placed outside. An intermediate boundary of one *ratana* at its furthest limit is permissible;
a measure of one *vidatthi* or even a measure of four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) is also permissible. However, if...
If the monastery is large, two, three, or even more fragmentary boundaries (khaṇḍasīmā) should be established. For it is said in the Commentary:

“Having demarcated the boundary,” and so forth. Thus, having demarcated the fragmentary boundary, at the time of the formal authorization for the great boundary (mahāsīmā), one should emerge from the fragmentary boundary and [enter] the great boundary.
Standing there and walking around on all sides, the boundary-stones at the junctions (*sīmantarika*) should be designated;

then, having designated the remaining signs, they should—without leaving the reach of hand (*hatthapāsa*)—formally designate the common-residence boundary (*samānasamvāsaka-sīmā*) by means of the ritual proclamation (*kammavācā*).

Furthermore, for the purpose of strengthening that [boundary], the ritual proclamation regarding non-separation (*avippavāsa-kammavācā*) should also be performed. For it is said thus in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "In this way..."
“Having demarcated a partial boundary,” and so forth.
It is said: “The boundary-stone markers at the junctions must be designated by those walking all around. How should they be designated?
They should be designated by one walking specifically from the south. For it is thus that [the boundary] is established from the western direction of the partial boundary.
Standing facing the east, one should enumerate all the signs there in succession, asking, "What is the sign in the eastern direction?
Likewise, standing facing the south in the northern direction, one should enumerate them in succession, asking, "What is the sign in the southern direction?
And likewise, standing facing the west in the eastern direction...
Having stood [in the west] and sequentially recited, "What is the sign in the western direction?",
and likewise having stood in the southern direction facing north and sequentially recited all the signs there, "What is the sign in the northern direction?",
he then stands again in the western direction facing east and recites what was previously recited.

It should be proclaimed again in the same manner as previously stated. In this way, for many fragmentary boundaries (*khaṇḍasīmā*), the boundary-stone markers (*sīmantarikapāsāṇa*) must each be proclaimed individually;
after that, the remaining markers are to be proclaimed. These are the markers for the external boundaries of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).
Thus, the boundary-stone markers serve as internal markers within the great boundary for the purpose of removing the fault of the overlapping of two boundaries.
Because boundary-stone markers must be established. Thus, while walking around the perimeter, one should designate the boundary-stone markers.
For it is said in the *Vimativinodanī*: "Boundary-stone markers are stone markers placed at the boundary;
they should be designated by one who walks around them keeping them to the right," and so forth.
"Is the boundary to be established by this very sequence, or may it also be established by another sequence? If, however,
after having designated the marks for the *khaṇḍasīmā* (fragmentary boundary), and then having designated the marks for the *sīmantarikā* (intermediate boundary),
they designate the marks for the *mahāsīmā* (great boundary)— having thus designated the marks in these three places— then whichever boundary they desire, that [is established]."
It is proper to bind [the boundaries] first. Even so, they should be bound starting from the *khaṇḍasīma* (fragmentary boundary) according to the method already described.
For it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "But if there are signs within the *khaṇḍasīma*," and so forth.
If one asks, "What is the benefit for the monks by binding the boundaries in this way, both as *khaṇḍasīmas* and *mahāsīmas*?"—it is because when the boundaries have been bound in this manner...

Monks standing within a *khaṇḍasīmā* (a partial boundary) do not invalidate the formal act (*kamma*) of monks performing it within a *mahāsīmā* (a great boundary), nor do those standing within a *mahāsīmā* invalidate the act of those performing it within a *khaṇḍasīmā*.
However, those standing in the *sīmantarikā* (the intermediate space between boundaries) invalidate the acts of both.
Furthermore, those standing in the village precinct (*gāmakkhetta*) invalidate the acts of those performing them within the *sīmantarikā*.
For the intermediate space (sīmantarikā) belongs to the village precinct. Thus it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā: “But when boundaries have been thus fixed,” and so forth;

monks dwelling in monasteries where boundaries have been fixed in this manner are permitted to live according to their preference without being separated from the three robes that have been formally determined (adhiṭṭhita).
However, if there is a village, [the boundary] extends to the village and its surrounding vicinity (gāmūpacāra).
"It should be understood as 'he does not obtain [it]'.
Thus ends the Ornament of the Determination of Boundaries, within the *Vinayālaṅkāra*,
which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*."
25. Discussion on the Determination of the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā 168.

Having thus explained the determination of the boundary (*sīmā*), he now speaks the words beginning with "In this regard, 'Uposatha and Pavāraṇā'" in order to explain the determination of the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā. Therein, first, as for the word *uposatha*:
"In the recitation of the Pātimokkha, in the formal announcement, [it is] Uposatha;..."

Because of the statement, "And on the Uposatha day, there should be the eight-factored fast," it applies to the recitation of the Pātimokkha, to the formal rule regarding the eight-factored virtue of the fast,
and to the Uposatha day itself. For instance, this term appears in reference to the recitation of the Pātimokkha in such passages as, "Come, friend Kappina, let us go to the Uposatha."

In such passages as “The *nāga* king named Uposatha,” it refers to a designation (*paṇṇatti*). In such passages as “For the pure one, indeed, there is always softwood; for the pure one, there is always the *uposatha*,” it refers to the observance (*upavāsa*).
In such passages as “Thus, Visākhā, the *uposatha* endowed with eight factors is observed,” it refers to the eightfold precept (*aṭṭhaṅgasīla*).
And in such passages as “Monks, on the *uposatha* day, one should not go from a monastery with monks to a monastery without monks,” it refers to the [observance] day.
It applies on the Uposatha day. It also applies to the purity (pārisuddhi) and the formal resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) in such expressions as “the Uposatha of purity” and “the Uposatha of resolution.
However, because those two are included within the recitation of the Pātimokkha, they are not mentioned separately here.

In this context, it applies both to the recitation of the Pātimokkha and to the Uposatha day. Therein, in the case of the recitation of the Pātimokkha, the Uposatha is the act of fasting (upavasana); [those] endowed with virtue...

The meaning is: "dwelling after having offered. It is called *uposatha* because they dwell (*vasanti*) there while observing the fast (*upavasanti*); the meaning is that on this day they dwell endowed with virtue (*sīla*).
Furthermore, regarding the word *pavāraṇā*, it is stated in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*: "Pavāraṇā [is used] in the sense of dismissal, and in the sense of requesting what has been told."

It applies to both prohibition and invitation. In this regard, it applies to prohibition in such passages as, “Whosoever, however, a monk who has finished his meal and been invited should eat or consume solid or soft food that is not left over, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)”;
to invitation in such passages as, “The Saṅgha should invite”; and to [the announcement of] the invitation day in such passages as, “Today is the invitation day on the fourteenth.”
On the day of the *pavāraṇā*. However, since that very day is the day of the formal invitation (*ajjhesanā*), it is not mentioned separately here.

But in this context, it applies to the invitation; therefore, *pavāraṇā* means "that by which one invites" (*pavārīyate*). The meaning is: "it is desired in a specific manner" (*pakārena icchīyati*). The verbal root *var* preceded by *pa-* belongs to the *curādigaṇa*.
And here, although in the Canon the *Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka* follows immediately after the *Uposathakkhandhaka*, and after that—

The Pavāraṇa-khandhaka has been recited; nevertheless, because the Uposatha and Pavāraṇa formal acts (kamma) are for the most part identical and exist as a pair of twins, the Teacher, considering that explaining them together makes them easy to understand and results in a concise text, presents the material contained in these two Khandhakas in a single chapter. Therein, [the section on] the fourteenth day...
The connection is that there are three types of *uposatha* according to the day: the fifteenth-day (*pannarasika*), the fourteenth-day (*cātuddasika*), and the *sāmaggī-uposatha*.

That which is connected with the fourteenth day is the fourteenth-day; likewise for the fifteenth-day. The *sāmaggī-uposatha* is the *uposatha* to be performed on a day when there is concord within the Saṅgha.
Regarding the phrase "of the three seasons—winter, summer, and the rains"—here, the winter season (*hemanta-utu*) refers to the dark fortnight of the month of *Aparakattika*.
The four months beginning from the first day of the waxing moon of Phagguna and ending with the full moon of Phagguna constitute the winter season (*gimha-utu*).
The four months beginning from the first day of the waning moon of Phagguna and ending with the full moon of Āsāḷha constitute what is called the summer season (*gimha-utu*).
The four months beginning from the first day of the waning moon of Āsāḷha and ending with the full moon of Kattika constitute what is called the rainy season (*vassāna-utu*).
In the third and seventh fortnights, making two each, there are six fourteenth-day observances (*cātuddasika*);
that is to say, two fourteenth-day observances in the dark fortnight of the month of Māgasira and two in the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha during the winter season.
Likewise, in the third and seventh fortnights of the summer season, [there are two] in the dark fortnight of the month of Citta and [two] in the month of Jeṭṭha.

And in the dark fortnight of the rainy season, that is to say, in the third month of the rains, the month of Sāvaṇa, in its dark fortnight; and in the seventh month, the month of Assayuja, in its dark fortnight—this is the meaning.
"The remaining [days] are the fifteenth" means that the remaining eighteen days are the fifteenth. And there is this [verse] on the matter:
“From the dark fortnight of Kattika until the full moon of Phagguna;
this should be known as the winter season.”
There are eight Uposatha days:
from the dark fortnight of Phagguna until the full moon of Āsāḷha.
It should be understood as the summer season;
there are eight Uposatha days.
From the dark fortnight of Āsāḷha...
Up until the full moon of Kattika,
it should be understood as the rainy season;
there are eight Uposatha days.
“On the three seasons, on the third and seventh fortnights, and on the fourteenth—thus those who know the method recite the Pātimokkha.
In this way, there are twenty-four Uposatha days in one year; thus, by the method stated here, [the Uposatha occurs] during the three [seasons] beginning with Hemanta.

The meaning is that because there are eight Uposatha days for each season, there are twenty-four Uposathas in one year, which consists of the convergence of three seasons. This, first of all, is the "natural observance" (*pakaticāritta*);
this refers to the performance of six Uposathas on the fourteenth day and eighteen on the fifteenth day in one year, which is the primary natural rule.
The meaning is that the formal act (kamma) must be performed according to its own intrinsic nature (sabhabhāva), and not on account of reasons such as there being more residents;
for when such conditions exist, it is permissible to perform the Uposatha even on another fourteenth day, based on the statement:

"Once every half-month, on the fourteenth or the fifteenth, the Pātimokkha is to be recited. Furthermore, regarding the passage: "But whichever [resident] by the newcomers... [the sense is as follows].
From such statements as "one must follow [the residents]," the meaning is that when the necessary conditions are present, it is permissible to perform the Uposatha on another fourteenth-day as well.

In this context, "once" (sakim) means one time. "One must follow the residents" means that when the residents are performing the preliminary duties, thinking, "Today is the fourteenth-day Uposatha," one must follow them and not oppose them.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the statement, "The residents should comply with the newcomers," and the statement, "Monks, I allow those monks to perform two or three Uposathas on the fourteenth day [thinking], 'How might we perform the Invitation (*pavāraṇā*) before them?
are included. And here, regarding the first sutta, for each season, during the third and seventh fortnights...

It should be understood that the suttas beginning with "by those who have arrived" are shown because there is a possibility for such a situation to arise even according to the normal course of events— namely, that on the fourteenth day, or on the fifteenth day for the remainder [of the community], the Pātimokkha should be recited once.
"When such a condition exists" refers to cases such as when, although it is the fourteenth day for the Uposatha, the resident monks are more numerous [than the newly arrived ones].
"When the requisite condition exists": on another fourteenth day—that is, on a fourteenth day other than the third and seventh fortnight-fourteens of the three seasons.
Here is the canonical text:
"But here, monks, it is the fourteenth for the resident monks, while it is the fifteenth for the incoming monks."
If the resident monks are more numerous, the visiting monks must comply with the residents.
If they are equal in number, the visiting monks must comply with the residents. If the visiting monks are more numerous, the residents must comply with the visitors.
“Furthermore, monks, it may happen that for the resident monks it is the fifteenth day, while for the incoming monks it is the fourteenth.
If the residents are more numerous, the incoming monks must follow the residents. If they are equal in number, the incoming monks must follow the residents.
If the incoming monks are more numerous, the residents [must follow the incoming monks].”
One should comply with the visiting monks.
"In this case, monks, it may happen that for the resident monks it is the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipada), while for the visiting monks it is the fifteenth day.
If the residents are more numerous, the residents must, even if they do not wish to, grant their formal unity (sāmaggī) to the visitors; by the visitors—"
Having gone outside the boundary, the Uposatha should be performed. If they are equal in number, the resident monks must not unwillingly grant their consent to the visiting monks;
rather, the visiting monks should go outside the boundary and perform the Uposatha.
If the visiting monks are more numerous, the resident monks must either grant their consent to the visiting monks or go outside the boundary.
“Furthermore, monks, it may happen that for the resident monks it is the fifteenth day, while for the visiting monks it is the first day of the fortnight.
If the residents are more numerous, the visitors must either grant their consent to the residents’ formal assembly or go outside the boundary.
If they are equal in number, the visitors must either grant their consent to the residents’ formal assembly or go outside the boundary.”
Or [the boundary] should be entered. If the incoming monks are more numerous, the incoming monks must, against their will, grant their consent to the resident monks;
the residents, having gone outside the boundary, should perform the Uposatha.
Regarding this, here is the commentary:
Regarding the statement, "For the resident monks it is the fourteenth day; for the incoming monks it is the fifteenth":
here, those for whom it is the fifteenth should be understood as having either come from another kingdom or as having observed the previous Uposatha on the fourteenth day.

"The resident monks should be followed" means that when the preliminary duties are being performed by the residents—such as [the announcement], "Today is the Uposatha, the fourteenth"—they [the incoming monks] should follow them.
It should not be rejected. "It should not be given unwillingly" means it should not be given against one's wish.
Regarding the passage beginning with "I allow you, monks," this is the text found in the Pavāraṇā Khandhaka:
"But here, monks, a number of monks who are friends and companions enter the rains residence together in a certain monastery; of them..."
If other monks who are quarrelsome, contentious, disputatious, argumentative,
and creators of legal issues in the Saṅgha enter the rains residence, thinking, "Having spent the rains with those monks,
we will cancel their invitation at the invitation ceremony," I allow, monks, that those monks [who are canceling the invitation] should attend two or three Uposatha days on the fourteenth.
"How can we perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) before those monks?
Regarding this, the commentary says: "To perform two or three Uposatha days on the fourteenth"—here, the fourth and fifth [days] are the two;
however, the third day is already the fourteenth by its very nature. Therefore, it refers either to the third and fourth, or to the third, fourth, and fifth.
Or two or three *cātuddasika* (fourteenth-day) observances should be performed. Then, if they hear [the announcement] when the fourth has been performed, a fifth *cātuddasika* should be performed;

thus there are two *cātuddasika* observances. Those performing it in this way [think]: "These quarrelsome ones will perform the *pavāraṇā* on the fifteenth day, even though it is the thirteenth or fourteenth."
In this regard, the reading in the *Sāratthadīpanī* is as follows:

"When the fourth [day] has been made, they hear" means that when the fourteenth-day uposatha has been performed, they hear, "They will cancel our invitation (*pavāraṇā*). Thus, there are two fourteenth-day [uposathas];
together with the third, there are two fourteenth-day [uposathas].

In this regard, here is the reading from the *Vimativinodanī*: "There are two fourteenth-day [Uposatha] days" means that in the third fortnight, there are two fourteenth-day days together with the [usual] fourteenth day.

"For those who cause quarrels, on the thirteenth or the fourteenth, these will perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) on the fifteenth"—by this, the designation "fourteenth" or "fifteenth" for the monks is used starting from their respective day for performing the Uposatha.
This shows that it is not by way of the lunar day established by the movement of the moon. Nevertheless,
although there is the statement, "Monks, I allow you to follow the kings," even when following the worldly lunar calendar,
one must follow them only by performing the Uposatha according to one's own sequence— either making the fourteenth the fifteenth or the fifteenth the fourteenth.
However, they should not observe the Uposatha on the sixteenth day or the thirteenth day. For this very reason, it is stated in the Pāḷi:
"Two or three Uposathas should be observed on the fourteenth day. Otherwise, it would have had to be said: "The Uposatha should be observed on the twelfth or the thirteenth day.
This is also evident from such statements as: "Once a fortnight, on the fourteenth or the fifteenth," and so forth.
It should be understood that this is stated according to the sequence of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) themselves, and not according to the sequence of the lunar days (*tithi*).

Not only are there three [observance days] on the Uposatha days alone, but there are also those on the Pavāraṇā days and so forth; thus he said, "But for those who have completed the preceding rains-retreat," and so on.
*Mā* refers to the moon, because the day is measured by its movement; here, it [the moon] is [referred to] due to the completion of all its phases.
*Puṇṇā* means the full moon. *Pubbakattikapuṇṇamā* is the full moon of the former Kattika month; it is the full moon of Assayuja.
It is so called because it serves to turn back the latter Kattika month. *Tesaṃ yeva* means of those very same [monks] who have spent the preceding rains retreat.
*Bhaṇḍanakārakehi* means by those who cause quarrels. *Paccukkaḍḍhanti* means they draw back; [it refers to] the quarrelsome ones.
By way of restatement, the meaning is that those who relinquish the full moon of the Assayuja month and so forth, "draw it upward," thinking:
"The dark fortnight is the bright fortnight. [They say: "Venerable sirs, let the residents listen to me.

If it is the proper time for the venerable ones, let us now perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha; we shall perform the Pavāraṇā later when the dark fortnight arrives. "Let them listen... [and so on].
"Venerable sirs, residents of this dwelling, if it is now the proper time for you, let us perform the Uposatha now, let us recite the Pātimokkha;
we shall perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony during the bright fortnight"—this is what is meant by "postponing the Pavāraṇā by means of a formal motion (*ñatti*).
The word *atha* is a particle used in the sense of immediate succession. *Cātuddasa* refers to the fourteenth day, which completes the number fourteen. With reference to that—

They established a formal motion (ñatti), saying: "We shall perform the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) when the dark fortnight has arrived. "The full moon of the latter Kattika" means the day of the full moon of the Komudi Cātumāsinī;
it is with reference to this that they established the motion, saying: "We shall perform the invitation ceremony when the bright fortnight has arrived.
When that bright fortnight of the Komudi Cātumāsinī has arrived, the invitation ceremony must certainly be performed. For one must not perform it by passing that time over.

It is possible. For this has been said: "If, monks, those monks who are makers of quarrels, makers of strife, makers of disputes, makers of contention, and makers of legal issues in the Saṅgha should dwell through that bright fortnight, then, monks, all those monks must, even against their will, perform the invitation ceremony on the following bright fortnight, on the Komudī Cātumāsī day.
Therefore he said: "And for those who have spent the last rains..."
“Or indeed on the full moon day of the later Kattika. For if they were to perform the *pavāraṇā* after that [date] has passed, they would incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
For this has been said: “Monks, one should not perform *pavāraṇā* when there is no invitation, except for the sake of harmony in the Saṅgha.

Because it is associated with the *pavāraṇā* for the sake of purification, it is called the “day of *pavāraṇā*. By the word “and” (*pi*), it is indicated that it is not only the day of *pavāraṇā*, but furthermore—

This shows that there were other Uposatha days as well. "This too" refers to the three Pavāraṇā ceremonies. "On such an occasion" refers to occasions such as when more than half the community resides [in one place].
"Of the two Kattika full-moons" refers to the two full-moons of Āśvina and Kārttika, known as the prior Kattika and the posterior Kattika.
Now, in order to show that day of the *sāmaggi-uposatha* which was mentioned, as well as, by way of connection, the day of the *sāmaggi-pavāraṇā*, he said, "But when," and so forth.
Therein, "when that monk has been reinstated" means when the suspended (*ukkhitaka*) monk has been reinstated;

having taken him [with the rest of the community] to the boundary (*sīma*), having had him confess his offense, and by means of the formal act (*kammavācā*) through the cessation of the legal procedure (*kamma*).
"Has been entered" is what is meant. "Of that matter" means of that legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*). The connection is:
"At that time, setting aside the fourteenth and fifteenth, any other day whatsoever is called an Uposatha day. He asks, "Why? and says: "Because the Uposatha must be performed at that very moment;
for it is said, 'The Pātimokkha should be recited. In this context, "at that very moment" means on that very day.
Regarding the phrase "because it is stated [in the scriptures]": this is because it is stated in the *Kosambaka-kkhandhaka*.

However, in cases where those quarreling over a minor matter for the sake of alms-bowls, robes, and so forth, suspend the *Uposatha* or the *Pavāraṇā*, they are not permitted to perform an intermediate *Sāmaggi-uposatha* (reconciliation *Uposatha*) once that legal dispute has been settled, thinking, "We have become united. If they were to do so on a day other than the *Uposatha*, [it would be invalid].
The Uposatha is said to have been performed.

Regarding the phrase "within the month of Kattika": here, the month of Kattika refers to the twenty-nine days and nights from the first day of the dark fortnight of the former Kattika month until the full moon of the latter Kattika month; it is within that period. From there...
It is permissible either before or after [the invitation ceremony]. "This very day" means any day whatsoever.
Here too, the term *sāmaggī* (concord) should be understood as being identical to that used in the *Kosambaka-kkhandhaka*.

However, those who become concordant by setting aside the *pavāraṇā* (invitation ceremony) for some trivial matter should perform the *pavāraṇā* at that very time; it must not be performed immediately [at the scheduled time].
When the *pavāraṇā* is performed by those who should be performing the *apavāraṇā*, it is said that the *pavāraṇā* has indeed been performed;

however, this indicates that if one performs it under the restriction that "it simply must not be done," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). For in that case, there is an offense of wrong-doing for performing the *uposatha*. Indeed, this has been stated:
"Monks, the *uposatha* must not be performed on a day other than the *uposatha*, except for the sake of the harmony of the Saṅgha."

169. The Uposatha of the Saṅgha is the Uposatha to be performed by a Saṅgha consisting of at least four members assembled within a single boundary; and that is precisely the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
The Uposatha of the group (gaṇa) is the Uposatha to be performed by two or three bhikkhus assembled within a single boundary;
and that is precisely the Uposatha of purity (pārisuddhi-uposatha). The Uposatha of the individual (puggala) is...
The Uposatha must be performed by a single bhikkhu seated within a single boundary (ekasīmā); moreover, that is specifically the Uposatha by formal determination (adhiṭṭhānuposatha).

Therefore it is said: "There are three other types of Uposatha according to the agent. Among the three types of Uposatha described according to the manner in which they are to be performed, the one called the recitation of the Sutta is the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
That is twofold: the recitation of the Pātimokkha as exhortation (ovāda-pātimokkhuddesa) and the recitation of the Pātimokkha as an injunction (āṇā-pātimokkhuddesa).
And herein, the *ovāda* (exhortation) itself is the *pātimokkha*; the recitation of that, its explanation in its own form, is the "recitation of the exhortation-pātimokkha" (*ovādapātimokkhuddeso*).
The "injunction" (*āṇā*) is the commanding and making known [of the rules] by way of offenses, such as: "In the case of this transgression, this is the specific offense.
The remainder is exactly the same as the preceding [section].
In this context, the recitation of the *Ovāda-pātimokkha* is as follows:
“Patience is the supreme austerity;
nibbāna is supreme, so say the Buddhas.”
For one who harms others is not a renunciant;
one who oppresses others is not a śramaṇa.
"To refrain from all evil, to cultivate the wholesome;”
“The purification of one’s own mind— this is the teaching of the Buddhas.
Non-provocation, non-injury, restraint according to the Pātimokkha,
moderation in food, and a secluded dwelling;”
“And application to higher consciousness—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.
These are the three verses.
Therein, “patience is the supreme austerity”: patience as endurance is indeed the supreme austerity. “Forbearance” refers to patience.
This is a synonym: the meaning is that patience characterized as endurance (*titikkhā*)—that is, forbearance through acceptance (*adhivāsanakhanti*)—is the supreme austerity (*tapas*).
"They say Nibbāna is supreme" means that the Buddhas declare Nibbāna to be supreme in every respect.
"For one who goes forth does not harm others" means that he who, being devoid of forbearance through acceptance, harms, oppresses, or injures another, is not truly called one who has gone forth.
It does not exist. The fourth quarter, however, is a synonym for that very same thing. For "not a renunciant" (*na pabbajito*) has "not a recluse" (*na samaṇo*) as its synonym.
"One who harms others" (*parūpaghātī*) has "one who harasses another" (*paraṃ viheṭhayanto*) as its synonym.
Alternatively, "one who harms others" means one who harms virtue (*sīla*); for virtue is called "the other" (*para*) in the sense of being supreme. And the recluse who [harms] another...
The meaning is that anyone who harms any living being and becomes a destroyer of others is a destroyer of his own virtue; he is not called one who has gone forth (*pabbajita*).

Alternatively, he who, due to the absence of patience through endurance, becomes a destroyer of others—even intentionally depriving another of life, down to a mere gadfly or mosquito—is not a *pabbajita*. For what reason?
Because of not having cast off the stain. For this is the characteristic of one who has gone forth: “Having cast off the stain from oneself, therefore one is called ‘one who has gone forth.
Even one who does not indeed strike or kill, but rather harasses another with sticks and so forth—even such a person, while harassing another, is not a recluse.
Why? Because of not being stilled (*asamita*) regarding harassment. “Because of being stilled... [the Blessed One is called a recluse].”
“Indeed, one who has abandoned evil is called a *samaṇa*. This, indeed, is the characteristic of a *samaṇa*.

In the second verse, “of all evil” means of all that is unwholesome (*akusala*). “Non-doing” means non-arising. “Of the wholesome” refers to the wholesome states belonging to the four planes of existence.
“Accomplishment” means the bringing about of attainment or acquisition. “The purification of one’s own mind” means—
The purification of one’s own mind means making it luminous and cleansing it completely; that, moreover, occurs through Arahantship.

Thus, having abandoned all evil by means of the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara), and having accomplished the wholesome through mundane and supramundane serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), the mind must be thoroughly purified by the fruit of Arahantship—this is the teaching, the exhortation, and the instruction of the Buddhas.
In the third verse: *anupavāda* means not reviling anyone by way of speech. *Anupaghāta* means not causing harm to anyone by way of body.
Regarding *pātimokkha*: it is that which is *pātimokkha*, *paatimokkha*, *atipamokkha*, the supreme virtue (*uttama-sīla*).

Or, it is called *pātimokkha* because it protects (*pāti*) one from specific misfortunes and liberates (*mokkheti*) one from the fears of miserable rebirths; or, it is *pātimokkha* because it protects (*pāti*) that which is liberated (*mokkheti*).
...is said, and in that *pātimokkha*. "Restraint" (*saṃvara*) is the restraint characterized by the non-transgression of the seven classes of offenses.
"Knowing the proper measure" (*mattaññutā*) is the knowledge of the right amount with respect to receiving and using [alms].
"A secluded lodging" (*pantañ ca sayanāsanaṃ*) is a dwelling place devoid of the bustle of crowds, free from the congestion of people, and solitary. And here, by means of these two alone—
It should be understood that contentment with the four requisites is illustrated by these conditions;

for, by virtue of the commonality of "contentment with requisites," the other two [types of contentment] are also manifested through the method of characteristic-assignment (*lakkhaṇahāra*). And regarding "exertion in higher consciousness" (*adhicitte ca āyogo*):

"higher consciousness" (*adhicitta*) refers to the mind of the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) which serves as the basis for insight (*vipassanā*), and even more so, it refers specifically to the minds of the paths and fruits; "exertion" (*āyoga*) is the application toward that aforementioned higher consciousness.
And "practice" (anuyoga) is the meaning. "This is the teaching of the Buddhas":

this non-reproaching of others, non-harming, restraint according to the Pātimokkha, moderation in receiving and using [alms], and resorting to secluded lodgings for mastery of the eight meditative attainments—this is the teaching, the exhortation, and the instruction of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, these three verses are the verses for reciting the Pātimokkha for all Buddhas.

It should be understood that these [rules] exist; the Buddhas themselves recite them, not the disciples. That which is spoken in the manner beginning with "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs," is called the *Āṇā-pātimokkha* (the Pātimokkha of Command); this the disciples alone recite, not the Buddhas.
And it is precisely this that is intended by the term "Pātimokkha" in this context.
“Not having arrived” means either having been ordained right there, or not having arrived because of the absence of the first [invitation] period.
“In the four-monthly” means during the four months. For that is the completion of the four months, thus it is the “four-monthly” (*cātumāsī*);
that very thing is called the “four-monthly” (*cātumāsinī*). In that four-monthly, meaning on the full moon day of the last month of Kattika. “Physical concord” means—
"Being in harmony with the body" means coming within arm's reach;

this is the detailed explanation here: if five monks have entered the rains residence during the earlier period and another five enter during the later period, then when the former have performed the formal motion (*ñatti*) and the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), the latter may perform the Uposatha of purification (*pārisuddhi-uposatha*) in their presence.

It should be done; two motions (*ñatti*) must not be established at a single Uposatha site. If there are four, three, two, or one who have arrived for the later period (*pacchimikā*), the same procedure applies.
If there are four for the earlier period (*purimikā*), and likewise four, three, two, or one for the later period, the same procedure applies.
If there are three for the earlier period, and likewise three, two... [for the later period], the same procedure applies.
Or there may be only one; the same method applies. Herein is the characteristic:

if those who have entered for the later invitation are fewer than, or equal in number to, those who entered for the earlier invitation, and they complete the quorum for a formal act of the Saṅgha, then a motion (ñatti) should be put by way of a Saṅgha-invitation.
But if there is only one person for the later invitation, then together with him they become four.

It is not permissible to perform the *pavāraṇā* by setting aside the motion (*ñatti*) for the fourfold assembly. However, in the case of a group motion (*gaṇañatti*), he serves as the one who completes the quorum;
therefore, having set aside the motion according to the number of the group, the preceding monks should perform the *pavāraṇā*.
The other [monk] should perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* in their presence. If there are two in the earlier period, or two or even one in the later period, here too—

The same method applies here. If there is one person from the earlier group and one from the later group, one should perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) in the presence of the other, and the other should perform the Uposatha of purity.
If those who entered the rains-residence later are even by one more numerous than those who entered it first, then after first reciting the Pātimokkha, [the procedure] for the fewer number of them...
The invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) should be performed in the presence [of the Saṅgha].

However, regarding the invitation at the end of the four-month period in the month of Kattika, if those who have entered the rains retreat for the first time are more numerous than, or equal in number to, those who have already performed the Great Invitation (*mahāpavāraṇā*), then the invitation should be performed after setting aside a formal motion (*ñatti*) for the invitation;
once they have invited, the others should subsequently perform the Uposatha of purity (*pārisuddhi-uposatha*). Then...

If many have performed the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) for the Great Invitation (*mahāpavāraṇā*), while those who have entered the rains retreat (*vassa*) afterwards are few or even only one, then after the *Pātimokkha* has been recited, he should perform the invitation ceremony in their presence.
However, on any other day than the day of the invitation ceremony—that is, on another *Uposatha* day—[the procedure is as follows]: as soon as [the *Pātimokkha*] has been recited...

Regarding the term *pātimokkha*: "when it has been recited in its entirety" means that if [the assembly] arrives before the recitation is finished, it is not permissible to perform the Uposatha of confession (*pārisuddhi-uposatha*), because the remainder of the *pātimokkha* must still be heard.
The phrases beginning with "if they have not risen," etc., also specify the time of the conclusion of the *pātimokkha* for the sake of qualifying the assembly.
"Equal in number" (*samasamā*) means having an identical measure compared to those previously mentioned.
"Fewer" means having a smaller number than those previously mentioned. By this, it is shown that when more [monks] have arrived, the Pātimokkha must be recited again;
the Uposatha of confession of purity (pārisuddhi-uposatha) should not be performed.
"Having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder" means having properly placed the upper robe over one shoulder.
In the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it says: “Regarding ‘having arranged the robe over one shoulder’:
this is stated because of readjusting it once more. ‘Over one shoulder’ is a designation for one who stands having draped [the robe] over the left shoulder.
Therefore, its meaning should be understood as: ‘having arranged the robe in such a way that it remains draped over the left shoulder.’”
It has been said. "Having raised the hands in añjali" means having lifted up the añjali, radiant with the joining of the ten fingernails.

However, if there is also one who is on probation (pārivāsika) present there, he should sit in the place of the youngest member of the Saṅgha and, while sitting right there, perform the Uposatha of purity for himself according to the text.
But when the Pātimokkha is being recited, one should not remain seated without the text.
One should sit down without releasing the hand’s reach from the Pāḷi. This same method applies to the Pavāraṇā ceremony as well.
"The entire preliminary duty" refers to the ninefold preliminary task beginning with sweeping.

By this it is meant that on the Uposatha day, the preliminary duty need not be performed only at the dwelling place of many; rather, it must indeed be performed even at the dwelling place of a single person.
...he shows. And just as the entire Saṅgha, having incurred a common offense, is permitted to perform the Uposatha after proposing a motion thus: "Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me...
[as before] ...it shall be made amends," so too here, by means of three [monks], [the motion is made]:
"Let the venerable ones hear me; these bhikkhus have incurred a common offense. When another bhikkhu who is pure and free from offense..."

Having established a formal motion (*gaṇañatti*) stating, "When we see another who is pure, we shall then confess that offense in his presence," it is permissible for two [monks] to perform the Uposatha after saying, "We shall confess it upon seeing another who is pure.
It is also permissible for even one [monk] to perform it after forming the intention (*ābhoga*), "I shall confess it once I have found someone pure."
"At that time" means on that very day. "By those of different affiliations" means by those who differ in their tenets.
"A non-residence" refers to any location such as a construction site or the like. "Except for the Saṅgha" means without monks who are sufficient to constitute a Saṅgha.
"Except for obstacles" means excluding the ten kinds of obstacles previously mentioned. At the very least...
However, it is permissible to go if there is a boundary or an obstacle such that one is accompanied by oneself as the fourth person.

Just as one should not go to other residences and so forth, likewise, if they perform the Uposatha in a monastery, one should not go even to a boundary or a river for the purpose of determining the Uposatha;
yet, if there is any monk present there, it is permissible to go into his presence, even if the Uposatha has been relinquished.
It is proper to go to one’s own residence. Having gone there, one may also make a formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna).

Even a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, having wandered for alms in the village on the Uposatha day, should return to his own monastery. If he enters another monastery, he must return only after performing the Uposatha there;
it is not permissible to return without having performed it, provided he knows: "I shall [return] this very day."
"However, one may go to such a residence [thinking], 'I am able to go. For by performing the Uposatha there together with the monks, he will not have created an obstacle to the Uposatha. 170.
"Having performed the Uposatha outside and then returned": this refers to having performed the Uposatha anywhere—whether at a river, within a boundary, or elsewhere—and then returning.
The intention is that one who has come after having performed [the Uposatha] must give his consent; he is not permitted to remain [there] thinking, "I have already performed the Uposatha.

"Or intent on business" means intent on duties such as attending to the sick. "The Saṅgha is not sufficient" means it is not sufficient for them to stand in a continuous line without relinquishing the reach of the hand between each pair of persons.

Regarding the phrase "by means of what is contrary to the Dhamma and in an incomplete assembly": here, when four monks are present within a single boundary (sīmā), only the recitation of the Pātimokkha is permitted;

when three or two are present, only the Uposatha of confession of purity (pārisuddhi-uposatha) is permitted. However, because it was not done in that manner here, it is said to be "by means of what is contrary to the Dhamma.
Furthermore, since the transmission of consent and purity occurs only in the Saṅgha, and not in a group (gaṇa) nor in an individual (puggala), therefore—

It is said, “a faction. But if two Saṅghas within a single boundary bring their respective consent (*chanda*) to one another and perform separate Saṅgha-acts at the same moment, how is this to be regarded?
Some say, “That is permissible,” but that should not be accepted because it constitutes a factional act (*vaggakamma*).
For those performing a factional act, the bringing of consent and the declaration of purity (*pārisuddhi*) elsewhere [is required].

It should be understood that [the formal act] does not proceed because there is no such statement [of unity], and because the boundary was authorized specifically for the purpose of performing separate legal acts.
However, in the case of a monastery boundary (*vihāra-sīmā*), even while the Saṅgha exists within it,

if for some reason three or two [groups] perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* within a fragmented boundary (*khaṇḍa-sīmā*), the legal act is to be regarded as both legitimate (*dhamma*) and unanimous (*samagga*), because they are situated within distinct boundaries.
Because it was said by the Blessed One, “I allow you, monks, when giving the declaration of purity on that very Uposatha day, to give the consent as well,
since there is business for the Saṅgha,” one who carries out the Blessed One’s injunction says, “I give my consent. Furthermore, because of such statements as, “Monks,
if the one who brings the consent departs from that very place after the consent has been given, the consent must be given to another,” and so forth.
Furthermore, for the purpose of dispelling the fatigue caused by the exertion of giving his consent (*chanda*), he said, "Bring my consent. Because it is stated, "Monks,
if one who brings consent does not intentionally announce it once the consent has been given and he has reached the Saṅgha, the consent is considered brought,
and there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the bringer of consent," he said, "Announce my consent" in order to free himself from that *dukkaṭa* offense.

"By body, or by speech, or by both, it must be made known" means that one who has not even thought [it] in the mind, but performs a bodily exertion with any limb or member whatsoever, or—being able to utter speech—likewise by speech, or being able to do both ways, by both body and speech;
the meaning is "it must be made understood. This is because of the statement: "This is the meaning."
However, it is permissible to make the declaration in any language whatsoever.
Regarding the giving of *pārisuddhi* (purification), the analysis is similar to what was stated for the giving of consent (*chanda*).
But when giving it, one must first confess any existing offense. For one who is still possessed of an offense cannot say, "I give *pārisuddhi*; take my *pārisuddhi*."
One ought to say, "Declare my purity. When it should have been said, "There are duties for the Saṅgha," it was stated as "there are duties for the Saṅgha" due to a grammatical inversion.
Regarding the phrase "he gives his consent and purity": here, "consent and purity" (chandapārisuddhi) is a compound of consent (chanda) and purity (pārisuddhi); he gives that.
The meaning should be understood by means of the grammatical rule of *sarūpa-ekasesa* (the retention of one from among similar forms).

"The other" refers to the *chandapārisuddhi* (purification through consent) of others. Regarding the expression "the *chandapārisuddhi* like a cat’s chain": here, a "cat’s chain" (*biḷālasaṅkhalikā*) is a cat’s tether.
For in that case, the first link of the chain reaches only the second link, not the third; in the same way, this *chandapārisuddhi* [is so called].
Once given by a donor, it does not go elsewhere; therefore, because it is like a cat’s chain, it is called a “cat’s chain.
Furthermore, the mention of the “cat’s chain” here should be understood as merely an illustration for any kind of chain whatsoever.
173. The same method applies to the giving of the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) as well. However, this is the distinction:

there, one says, "Proclaim my consent (*chanda*)," whereas here, one says, "Invite on my behalf. There, it is accomplished as soon as the conveyor of consent has merely come into the hands of the Saṅgha;
but here, when the invitation has been given in this manner, the conveyor of the invitation approaches the Saṅgha.
