The invitation should be performed in this way: "Venerable sirs, three [categories of offenses] for a bhikkhu... [as above] ...I shall make amends.
In the *Vimativinodanī*, regarding the passage "Thus do I remember this; but have you heard it, venerable sirs?", it says: "Having said 'Thus do I remember this,' one should say:
'Venerable sirs, the introductory narrative has been recited; but have you heard, venerable sirs, the four rules entailing defeat (pārājika-dhamma)? and so forth.
It should be stated thus, for it is explained exactly like this in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*. By the word "heard" (*suta*), it means by the term of hearing. 174.
Since the Pātimokkha is not yet fully expounded when the introduction (*nidāna-uddesa*) has not been completed, he says: "In the second and subsequent introductions," and so forth. 175.
"By all three methods" refers to exposition (*osāraṇa*), recitation (*kathana*), and declamation (*sarabhañña*). And here, it is because of the desire to speak the meaning...
Or, the causing of another to recite with the desire for them to speak is called "introducing" (*otāraṇa*) or "concluding" (*osāraṇa*) a sutta.
The explaining or speaking of its meaning is called "exposition" (*kathana*). The mere reciting of the text with the proper tone is called "chanting" (*sarabhañña*).
"Having resolved upon the recitation" means having generated the thought, "I am performing recitation. "But by one who concludes and then speaks" means [speaking] the text oneself.
Having spoken thus, one should later explain the meaning. "Ninefold" means ninefold by way of the Saṅgha, the group, and the individual;
three by way of the recitation of the Sutta, the declaration of purity, and the formal resolution (adhiṭṭhāna); and three by way of the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the general assembly (sāmaggī).
"Fourfold" means fourfold as the unlawful and incomplete (adhammena-avagga) and so forth. "Twofold" means twofold as the Pātimokkha for monks and the Pātimokkha for nuns.
"Ninefold" refers to the ninefold recitation of the Pātimokkha: five for the bhikkhus and four for the bhikkhunīs. "How many?
(katimī) should be understood as a feminine gender form dependent on the word *kati*.

"Only during the season" (*utuvasse yeva*) means only during the winter and summer seasons. "Indicates" (*viññāpeti*): here, it refers specifically to making a physical gesture after having reflected with the mind.

It should be understood as "making known. In the Canon, the phrase "the *pārisuddhi* (declaration of purity) to be given to another" means that it must be given again by the giver of the *pārisuddhi* in the presence of another bhikkhu.

Because it is stated, "one declares one's actual status as a *sāmaṇera*," this applies to those who were ordained when they were less than twenty years of age, as well as to those who have violated the ultimate offenses (*antimavatthu*), those who have renounced the training (*sikkhāpaccakkhātaka*), and so forth.

It should be understood that this is shown to mean: as long as one maintains the recognition of being a bhikkhu, even if the *chandapārisuddhi* (consent and purity) is brought by those [novices], it remains valid;
however, from the moment they themselves acknowledge their status as novices (*sāmaṇera*) and so forth, it no longer comes. For in the Pāḷi itself it says:
"If, after the *pārisuddhi* has been given, he disrobes before reaching the Saṅgha... [or] if he is a *paṇḍaka*..."
Because it is stated: "He claims [to be a monk], he claims to be an animal, he claims to be a hermaphrodite;

the purity has been brought forth," it is established that when eunuchs and others are currently living under the designation of monks, their arrival [of the formal act] occurs solely through the conveyance of consent and purity (*chandapārisuddhi*).
Therefore, he said: "This method applies everywhere. [This also includes] those who are insane, deranged, or overwhelmed by pain.
However, it shows that even if regular members (pakatattā) on the way declare themselves to be insane or otherwise incapacitated,
consent (*chanda*) and so forth still arrive for them by the mere fact of their reaching the Saṅgha.
By the phrase "within the reach of the hands of the bhikkhus," it indicates that consent and purification (*pārisuddhi*) do not fail to arrive among groups or individuals [if they are within range].

For it is said in the Pāḷi: “When [the assembly] has reached the Saṅgha. The preliminary task (*pubbakaraṇa*) to be performed prior to the gathering of the Saṅgha should be understood as the preliminary duty (*pubbakicca*) to be performed once the Saṅgha has assembled.

Regarding the passage in the Pāḷi, “If he does not determine it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*),” here there is no offense if it was unintentional or due to forgetfulness. And as it is in this case, so it is in the subsequent cases as well.
However, where there is an offense involving a state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), we shall explain that later.

By the phrase "it has been laid down" (*paññattaṃ hoti*), it is shown that even though there is no explicit separate prohibition stating "the Uposatha should not be performed by one who has committed an offense," it is nonetheless "laid down" by the force of the aforementioned Sutta.
By this same method, [it is understood that] "Bhikkhus, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that a Tathāgata... [should do so with an impure assembly].

It should be understood that even performing the Uposatha together with shameless individuals is strictly prohibited by the method of the Suttas— such as "one should perform the Uposatha with the assembly" and "one should recite the Pātimokkha"—
because all training rules (sikkhāpada) are intended for the purpose of restraining the shameless.
By the phrase "by the proclamation of the giving of purity," it is indicated that even a formal declaration of purity (pārisuddhi) must not be given by one who is guilty of an offense.

176. Regarding the phrase "both incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," they say that for one who confesses by the name of the offense alone, without recognizing the nature of the shared offense (*sabhāgāpatti*), and for the one who accepts it, there is only an unintentional (*acittaka*) offense of wrong-doing.

Just as the Saṅgha is permitted to perform the Uposatha after having put forward a motion (*ñatti*) stating, "The Saṅgha has fallen into a shared offense," so too [should] you three [say]: "Venerable sirs, let my words be heard."

Following the method stated in the passage beginning, "These bhikkhus have fallen into a common offense," it is permissible for them to perform the Uposatha after establishing a formal motion (*gaṇañatti*) and announcing [the matter] to one another by pairs.
However, even if a single bhikkhu who has an offense must go a long distance, he should indeed make amends;
if he cannot reach [a place where he can do so], he may perform the Uposatha with the thought, "Having found other bhikkhus, I will make amends."
It should be performed; and having made amends, the Uposatha should be performed again.
"Having gone away for some business" means having gone outside the boundary (sīmā) to either a village or a wilderness.

By this very [statement], it is established that they indeed laid down the motion (*ñatti*) as a complete assembly at the time of laying down the Uposatha motion. For that very reason, it is said in the Canon: "It has been recited, well-recited."
This is also stated in all fifteen cases.
"But if he is senior" means that the monk who gives the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) is senior. For it is in this way that he has invited on his behalf;
thus, even if he has not invited in this manner, by the mere fact that it has reached the Saṅgha, it belongs to the Saṅgha.
It should be understood that the *pavāraṇā* procedure is indeed a formal act performed by a complete assembly (*samagga-kamma*).

"By that bhikkhu" refers to the bhikkhu who is offering the *pavāraṇā*. "Even many who have the same number of rains may perform the *pavāraṇā* together" means that all those who have received full ordination within the same year—that is, those whose years since ordination (*vassa*) are identical—may perform the *pavāraṇā* together.
In this regard, however, there is a reason that should be reflected upon and investigated by the wise. What is it? At the present time, when the Pātimokkha is being recited:
“The broom, the lamp, water, and the seat—these are called the preliminary duties for the Uposatha.”
“Zeal, purification, the announcement of the season, the counting of the monks, and the exhortation—
these are called the preliminary duties of the Uposatha.
The Uposatha [should be performed] by as many monks as are entitled to participate in the formal act.”
“Shared offenses do not exist,
and persons who are to be avoided are not present therein;
therefore it is called ‘the right time.’”
The reciter of the Pātimokkha explains the meaning of these verses after having the requester recite them as the text itself.
Then, having properly completed the preliminary tasks and duties, he has the requester recite this sentence:
"Let us perform the formal act of invitation (*ārādhana*) so that the Pātimokkha may be recited with the consent of the harmonious Saṅgha of bhikkhus who have confessed their offenses."
Having caused [the monks] to recite [the verses], but without explaining the meaning, he says "Very well" and then recites the Pātimokkha.
This same method applies to the Pavāraṇā as well. The only difference lies in these two phrases: "these [verses] for the Pavāraṇā" and "to perform the Pavāraṇā.
Are these the words of the Dhamma-reciter (Dhammajjhesaka), or rather those of the Pātimokkha-reciter (Pātimokkhuddesaka)? What is the point here—if...

Regarding the words of the Pātimokkha-reciter: since this is the case, after having spoken these three verses and explained their meaning, he himself should say, "These preliminary acts and these preliminary duties have been performed by the Saṅgha; this which is appropriate for the Saṅgha has been brought forward.
Therefore, Venerable Sir, let the Pātimokkha be recited. Then, for the Pātimokkha-reciter—

And this being so, after the one who requests the Dhamma has requested it up to three times with the words, “Venerable sir, the Saṅgha requests the Elder to recite the Pātimokkha; let the Elder, venerable sir, recite the Pātimokkha,” and having spoken the verse beginning, “The broom...
is addressed,” [it is understood that] these preliminary duties were performed as stated by the teachers of the commentaries.
Having asked the one who kindles the Dhamma, when he replied, “Yes, venerable sir,” [the author] spoke the verse beginning with “The purity of intention (chandapārisuddhi)…”;
then, having asked, “Are these preliminary duties (pubbakicca) stated by the masters of the Commentaries (aṭṭhakathācariya) performed?

and when he replied, “Yes, venerable sir,” [the author] spoke the verse beginning with “The Uposatha (uposatha)…”; then, having [asked], “By the masters of the Commentaries... [and received the same reply].
Having asked, "Has this been brought forward at the proper time? and being told, "Yes, Venerable Sir," the reciter of the Pātimokkha should say:

"Now that the preliminary duties and preliminary tasks have been properly completed and the proper time has been brought forward, with the consent of the harmonious Saṅgha of bhikkhus, we shall perform the act of reciting the Pātimokkha. This being so:
The words of the exhorter and the exhorted should be understood without confusion.

Furthermore, the fact that these three verses were spoken by the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā is recorded in the Aṭṭhakathā itself. However, the final sentence is found neither in the Pāḷi, nor in the Aṭṭhakathā, nor in the Ṭīkās and other such works. Also, in the *Khuddasikkhā-pakaraṇa*:
"And in the performance of preliminary duties..."
"When the reciters have been brought together,
the Saṅgha recites the Sutta;
it is analyzed in five ways."
“When the preliminary duties have been performed, when the proper time has arrived and the assembly has gathered,
the Saṅgha, having made a formal motion...”

And as for the statement, "The invitation (pavāraṇā) should be performed thus," it has not been stated in that way. It was stated in that way only in the *Mūlasikkhāpakaraṇa*; therefore, it may represent the personal opinion of the teachers.
In this regard, by the phrase "having properly completed the preliminary duties and the preliminary tasks," the meaning of the preceding two verses is precisely [conveyed].

Having spoken thus, the meaning of the third verse has not been explained. By the phrase “of one who has confessed an offense,” only the state of having confessed the offense is expressed, not the entirety of what constitutes *pattakalla* (fitness).
Furthermore, regarding the state of having confessed an offense, only the confession of a similar offense (*sabhāgāpatti*) is included within *pattakalla*, and not the other.
For it is said in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*: “For among these [offenses], regarding similar offenses...”
“Even when there are no offenses, or even when there are offenses of a different category, it is indeed the proper time. When only this much has been said— namely,

“Having properly completed the preliminary duties and preliminary tasks, let us perform the act of propitiation to recite the Pātimokkha with the consent of the harmonious Saṅgha of monks for one who has confessed their offense”— the remaining three factors of the proper time are as follows:
—The Uposatha [is valid] provided that as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the formal act (kamma) are present, and no persons who ought to be excluded are there.
Even if those [excluded persons] are not present, it follows that the Uposatha should be performed; yet it should not be performed. Therefore it was said:
"Bhikkhus, the Uposatha should not be performed on a non-Uposatha day; whoever should perform it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," and also: "I allow you, bhikkhus..."
Because of such statements as, "the Pātimokkha is to be recited for the four [assemblies]," and, "Monks, the Pātimokkha is not to be recited in an assembly that includes laypeople," and so forth;
therefore, on the Uposatha days, when the Saṅgha has assembled, if there is already an appointed Dhamma-reciter (dhammajjhesaka), this is good.
If not, the Saṅgha [should appoint] one monk who is experienced and capable.

Having had him appointed, that one who has requested the Dhamma should approach the reciter of the Pātimokkha, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, sit in the kneeling position with his hands joined in reverential salutation, and address him thus:
"Venerable sir, the Saṅgha requests the Elder to recite the Pātimokkha; may the Elder recite the Pātimokkha. A second time, venerable sir...
The Saṅgha... [as before] ...For the third time, venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha... [as before] ...let the Elder recite the Pātimokkha.
Having thus made the request three times, the reciter of the Pātimokkha should then say:
"Sweeping broom, lamp, water, and a seat; ... [as before] ..."
"These are called the preliminary duties for the Uposatha.
When asked, "Are these four preliminary duties mentioned by the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā performed? Dhammajjheshaka replied, "Yes, venerable sir. Then the Pātimokkha-reciter said:
"Consent, purity, the announcement of the season, the counting of the monks, and the exhortation;"
"These are called the preliminary duties of the Uposatha.

When asked by the Dhammajjhesaka, "The five preliminary duties spoken of by the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā—have those been performed?", the Pātimokkhuddesaka replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir. [Then the Pātimokkhuddesaka said:
"The Uposatha and as many bhikkhus as are competent for the formal act..."
There are no shared offenses,
nor are there persons to be avoided therein;
it is called "the right time."
When asked, "Are the four *pattakalla* factors spoken of by the masters of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*) now brought together?

Dhammajjheshaka replied, "Yes, venerable sir. Then the reciter of the Pātimokkha said, "Having properly completed the preliminary duties and the prior tasks, and having brought together the *pattakalla* factors, I shall recite the Pātimokkha with the consent of the Saṅgha."
Having said this, when it was accepted by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with cries of “Excellent! Excellent!
the reciter of the Pātimokkha recites the Pātimokkha beginning with the words, “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This is our tradition.
And here, regarding what is stated, “By the one who has requested the Dhamma... he should be addressed thus,” that state of being addressed by the one who has requested the Dhamma—
How is this to be understood? It is because of the statement: “Monks, the Pātimokkha must not be recited in the midst of the Saṅgha by one who has not been requested;
whoever should recite it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). It was said, “having had him appointed by the Saṅgha”;
how is that so? Here, the request is dependent either on the Dhamma-requester appointed by the Saṅgha, or on the Elder of the Saṅgha.

Because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “‘Or’ [is used] because of what has been said in the commentary. [Question: “From where is this manner of requesting obtained—namely, ‘Venerable sir, the Saṅgha requests the Elder to recite the Pātimokkha;
may the Elder, venerable sir, recite the Pātimokkha’? [Answer: From the *Pāḷi*.
For in the *Pāḷi* it appears thus: “They request the Elder: ‘May the Elder, venerable sir, recite the Pātimokkha.’”

But if the one who requests the recitation of the Dhamma is senior and the reciter of the Pātimokkha is junior, it should be said: "Friends, the Saṅgha requests the venerable one to recite the Pātimokkha; may the venerable one recite the Pātimokkha. Where is this found? From the Canon itself.
For in the Canon, by this very method, it continues until they request the most junior member of the Saṅgha, saying: "May the venerable one..."
The phrase “the Pātimokkha” has been introduced. From where, then, is this [detailed account] obtained—namely, that “the Pātimokkha-utterer [prepared] the broom...
[and so on]... and when asked by the Dhamma-inquirer, he replied, ‘Yes, Venerable Sir’”? It is from both the Canon (Pāḷi) and the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). For in the Canonical Nidāna, it is stated:
“What is the preliminary duty of the Saṅgha? And in the Commentary as well: “What is the preliminary duty of the Saṅgha?”
“The Saṅgha should perform the Uposatha... [and so on]. Thus, the ninefold preliminary duty (*pubbakicca*) has been shown by means of two names;
he asks, “What is that which has been done? This is what has come down in the *Antonidāna*.
But surely this has already come down in the *Antonidāna* itself; why, then, must it be stated beforehand by the reciter of the Pātimokkha?
True; nevertheless, it should be stated because they are to be understood as being in conformity with that [monastic practice].

For in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, these verses were spoken solely to indicate their status as preliminary acts (*pubbakaraṇa*) such as sweeping and so forth, not because they are to be recited at the time of commencing the *Pātimokkha*.
Nevertheless, they are recited now; thus, when considering for what purpose they are recited, the internal cause (*antonidāna*) is as follows:

It should be understood that they speak for the purpose of asking whether the preliminary duties (*pubbakicca*) and so forth have been completed, in accordance with the question asked: “What is the Sangha’s preliminary duty?
For it has been stated: “Having performed the fourfold preliminary duty as thus described, the Uposatha should be performed.
Therefore, when [the ceremony] is conducted in this sequence in accordance with the Canon and its commentaries, the one who kindles the Dhamma...
The request is discerned; the manner of that request is discerned; the reciter of the Pātimokkha is discerned;
the inquiry as to whether the preliminary duties and so forth have been completed is discerned; the response of the one who requested the Dhamma is discerned;
and having brought those matters to a conclusion, the promise of the reciter of the Pātimokkha to recite the Pātimokkha is discerned—thus, of these verses and sentences...
Considering that a purpose for speaking is evident, this method of discourse—which has been concealed for a long time—should be adopted by the wise who are conversant with the Vinaya.
This same principle applies to the *pavāraṇā* as well;
for this method is appropriate for the Pāḷi, the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), and so forth.
"Let the wise, who are knowers of the Vinaya, reflect upon this again and again.
Having reflected again and again, let them retain it if it is appropriate;
if it is not appropriate, let them discard it, for they are disciples of the Perfectly Enlightened One."
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Ornament of the Exposition on the Determination of the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā," in the Vinayālaṅkāra,
which is a commentary on the Vinayasaṅgaha.
26. Discussion on the Determination of the Entrance into the Rains Retreat (Vassūpanāyikavinicchayakathā) 179.

Having thus explained the determination regarding the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies, he now speaks the words beginning with "Regarding the 'entrance into the rains retreat' (*vassūpanāyikā*)," in order to explain the determination of the entrance into the rains retreat. In that context, *vassa* means dwelling. What is it? It is the act of dwelling, used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).
By means of the suffix -ṇya. *Upanayana* is *upanaya*. What is it? It is the act of approaching (*upagamana*). The approach to the rains is *vassūpanaya*;
that which possesses this designation, or in which it exists, is *vassūpanāyikā*. What is that? It is the designation *vassūpanāyikā*.
Alternatively, it is called *upanāyikā* because one approaches by means of it, with the vowel lengthened in the middle. The approach to the rains is *vassūpanāyikā*.

That very same [rainy season] occurring in the city is called *purimā* (the first) by means of the suffix *-ima*; that very same [season] is called *purimikā* (the first) by means of the suffix *-ka* in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*).

When that [suffix] follows, there is a substitution of the vowel *i* for the letter *a* in the feminine gender. That which occurs later is *pacchimā* (the latter); that very same [season] is *pacchimikā*.
However, if one does not enter the rains retreat, one should make a vocal declaration: "I enter the rains retreat for these three months in this monastery."
"Having made [this], one does not enter [the rains residence]. "Monks, one should not enter the rains residence without a dwelling-place;

whoever should enter it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). They say that this prohibition refers to entering for the rains residence after having made a verbal declaration, and not to entering by way of making a mental attachment (*ālaya*).
However, because it is stated without distinction in the Canon (*Pāḷi*), and because of the commentary on the second *pārājika* in the *Aṭṭhakathā*...
“Indeed, one entering for the rains—even if practicing the Nālaka practice—should enter a lodging provided with a door-bolt and covered by one of the five types of roofing.
Therefore, during the rainy season, if one obtains a lodging, that is well;
if not, one should build it even by seeking manual labor. Manual labor...”

Since it was stated emphatically, "One who does not obtain [a dwelling] should make one for himself, but one who lacks a lodging (asenāsanika) must certainly not enter the rains residence," it is our view that it is not permissible for one without a lodging to enter [the rains residence] elsewhere except by way of a boat or similar means, even if it is merely for the purpose of taking up residence.
For it is only in the cases of boats and carts that it is said: "Monks, I allow you to enter the rains residence on a boat," and so forth.

Since the going into residence for the rains has been separately authorized whether or not there is a dwelling place, the prohibition—"Bhikkhus, one should not go into residence for the rains without a dwelling place"—is intended to exclude that.
In this context, "does not obtain" means that in the absence of a dwelling place, even by way of taking possession, entering upon boats and the like is mentioned.
For among the four types of dwellings, it is the *vihāra* (monastery) dwelling that is intended here, not the other three.
"A hut" (*kuṭī*) refers here to various types such as the *ṭaṅkitamañca* (suspended bed) and so forth.
In this context, a *ṭaṅkitamañca* is a bed made by boring holes in the middle of long bed-legs and inserting cross-pieces (*aṭanī*); there is no "this is above" or "this is below" for it.
Even when turned over, it remains the same; they place it in cemeteries or shrines for deities upon four stones.
Even a house built by spreading out stones is called a "stilted bed.
Because it is not a monastery (*vihāra*), one should not say, "In this monastery," but rather only, "I enter the rains residence here," as it must be recited three times.
However, one should not enter the rains residence in a caravan (*sattha*).

"It is not permissible" means that it is not permissible to enter [the rains residence] by making a verbal declaration such as "I enter the rains residence here," due to the absence of a hut or similar structures;
the intention is that it is permissible merely by establishing one's dwelling. "It disperses" means it goes separately.
"In the three cases there is no offense for breaking the rains residence" means that there is no offense for one who goes along with them.
But if one departs after being separated from them, it is indeed an offense, and one is not permitted to perform the *pavāraṇā* ceremony.
"Having fixed the entrance door" means having fixed it so that it is secured with its own door-panels. "In the first [rainy season]...
one must not depart"—by this, it is meant that having entered the first rains-retreat on the first day (*pāṭipada*) immediately following the full moon of Āsāḷhī, during the rainy season...
During the four months, one should reside for the first three months, excluding the very last month.
Having entered the later rains residence on the first day following the full moon of the month of Sāvaṇa, one should reside for the final three months, excluding the very first month.
If a monk who has entered the earlier rains residence does not reside in this manner, then at the Great Invitation (mahāpavāraṇā),...

This shows that for one who has entered upon the later *cātumāsinī* (four-month) invitation (*pavāraṇā*) without rising before dawn, and then sets out on a journey in the interim without rising before dawn, a *dukkaṭa* offense occurs for that monk precisely upon crossing the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīmā*).
To support this meaning with the Canon, it is said: "It was stated [in the Pāḷi]: 'Monks, [you should not... and so forth."
Addressing the objection that if this were so, there would be an offense in every case for one who has entered the rains residence and then departs when there is business to be attended to, he says:

"But having entered the rains residence... and so forth. This being the case, it might follow that there would be no offense only for one who departs on the very same day for a seven-day purpose, but not for one who departs after staying for two or three days; therefore, he says: "What need is there to mention... and so forth.
180. Now, in order to show in detail the characteristics of the "seven-day business" (*sattāhakaraṇīya*), he said, "I allow you, monks," and so forth.
Therein, it says: "I allow you, monks, to go when sent for by seven [classes of persons] on account of a seven-day business, but not if not sent for:
namely, by a monk, a nun, a female trainee, a male novice, a female novice, a lay follower, or a female lay follower."
One [text] says: "I allow you, monks, to go for seven days on business even if not invited, much less if invited:
for a monk, a nun, a female trainee, a male novice, a female novice, a mother, and a father.
Another says: "But if a monk’s brother or another relative is ill... Another says: "In one case..."
One [case] is: "A supporter of monks living with the monks in a monastery"; one is: "If in a monk...
[as above] ...there has arisen dissatisfaction, or remorse, or a wrong view"; one is: "A certain monk has committed a heavy offense and is subject to probation";
one is: "Also for a nun who is subject to the trial period (mānatta)"; and one is: "A novice desiring full ordination... [as above]..."

There are eleven points: one [case] beginning with "a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*)... or a novice nun (*sāmaṇerī*"); one [case] beginning with "the Saṅgha intends to perform a formal act (*kamma*) against a monk or a nun, such as a censure (*tajjanīya*)";

one [case] stating "even if the formal act has already been performed"; and one [case] stating "I allow you, monks, to go on account of business for the Saṅgha. Among these, by way of the first, third, and fourth [points]:
One must go only when sent for in three instances, not when not sent for. In the remaining eight cases, one must go even when not sent for, let alone when sent for.
For it is said in the *Vimativinodanī*: "Regarding 'one must go,' one must go even when not sent for by the Saṅgha on account of a duty of the Saṅgha.
And here, even when sent for by non-upāsakas who wish to know the nature of the Dispensation, even though they have attained an increase in faith—
It should be understood that it is permissible to go on account of a seven-day business (*sattāhakaraṇīya*).
"One who takes meals with the monks" (*bhikkhubhattika*) means one who depends upon the monks. Since he lives together with the monks, it is therefore said, "living together with the monks.
181. *Apicettha* is a compound meaning "moreover, in this [case]"; that is, moreover, in this determination regarding the seven-day business.
The construction is as follows: "This other such method, which is a method extracted from the Pāḷi, should be understood as a method extracted from the Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka-pāḷi.

In the *Samantapāsādikā*, however, it appears as "the determination of the cutting off of the nights extracted from the Pāḷi" (*pāḷimuttakaratticchedavinicchayo*). For thus it is said in the *Vimativinodanī*:
"'Determination of the cutting off of the nights' refers to [the offense incurred] by one who, having gone on business for seven days, causes the dawn to rise outside [the monastery]."

“...the definition of the breaking of the night. In the *Sāratthadīpanī* it is also stated: “The breaking of the night consists in causing the dawn to rise outside [the monastery] after having gone on a seven-day mission.
Regarding the statement that it is not permissible to go without being invited:

here it should be understood that for one who goes while designating a seven-day task because they have not been invited, there is both a breach of the rains-residence (*vassaccheda*) and an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

For they say that there is a breach of the rains-residence for one who departs with the thought, "I will stay in another monastery and return," without the aforementioned reason for interrupting the night. It is permissible to go:

having remained within the boundary of the precincts (*upacārasīmā*), one may observe a purpose to be accomplished within seven days, and having set out with the intention, "I will return within the interval of seven days," it is permissible to go.
If one has formed the intention at the time of departure but forgets it at the moment of going, there is no fault even if he goes;

for it is said, "He departs having something to do. However, they say that for one who goes without forming the intention in any way whatsoever, there is a breach of the rains-residence (vassaccheda).
But as for one who, even in the absence of a seven-day necessity, goes after forming the intention, "I will return within seven days,"...

If he returns within seven days, there is indeed an offense for him; they say that because the seven-day period has been completed, there is no interruption of the rains-retreat, but this must be examined before being accepted.
"Bhaṇḍaka" means robe-material. "They send" means they send it by way of such tasks as washing the robes. To reach [the destination]...

Regarding the statement "it is not possible; it is permissible": they say that if one goes to a neighboring monastery thinking, "I will return this very day," and the dawn breaks while on the way back, there is neither a breach of the rains residence nor an offense for breaking the night.
This is because, since there was the intention to return on that very day, there is no breach of the rains residence or any offense.
This is the underlying intention. However, one is permitted to go with the thought, "I shall see my teacher," as it is said:
"Even if not ill, one is permitted to go for a seven-day business on the grounds of thinking, 'I shall see my teacher' or 'my preceptor'";

this applies to the formal support teacher (*nissayācariya*) and the Dhamma teacher (*dhammācariya*), let alone the ordination teacher (*upasampadācariya*) and the preceptor (*upajjhāya*). If the teacher says to him, "Do not go today," it is permissible.
Thus, for those who have come on business lasting seven days, if they return again within those very seven days and the teacher or preceptor says, "Do not go today," it is permissible;
the intention is that there is no offense even if the seven days are exceeded.
However, it should be understood that the interruption of the rains residence (vassaccheda) still occurs, because the seven-day period has been spent outside [the monastery].
"If one who has gone far away should cause dawn to rise after seven days," by this it is shown that when there is a reason for interrupting the rains retreat,
it is permissible to go on a journey for seven-day business. In this case, having spent six days outside,
on the seventh day one should enter within the boundary of the precincts before dawn, cause dawn to rise, and then resolve upon the seven-day period for the following day.
The intention is that one must go. However, some say, "Having arrived on the seventh day, it is permissible to go even during the daytime of that very day without waiting for the dawn to rise";
this should not be accepted, because it is stated that "the dawn must be made to rise.
For it is with reference specifically to making the dawn rise there on the seventh day that the text says, "the seven-day stay."

It is said, "it should be done. One who departs without having caused the dawn to rise, and one who spends seven days entirely outside without re-entering within, will indeed have their rains-retreat interrupted, because the dawn has risen only outside.
Otherwise, the statement "the dawn must be caused to rise" would be meaningless. [One may enter] within the monastery during the course of the seven-day period...

Because it must be said that one should depart without waiting for the dawn to rise, and because in other instances only the rising of the dawn is mentioned—for instance, in the *Cīvarakkhandhaka* it will be stated:
"While dwelling in one monastery, he causes the dawn to rise on the seventh day in the other [monastery]. Furthermore, they might say:
"On the seventh day, whenever one has entered [the boundary], the dawn of that very day has already passed."
Regarding the statement, "It is said in the Commentary with reference to this meaning that 'it is called raised,'" that does not even accord with the course of linguistic usage.
For one who enters [the monastery] after the dawn has already risen cannot properly be considered the raiser of that dawn.
If he were, then [the rule would apply to] one who, having entered for the rains residence, fails to raise the dawn and departs on the very same day for some seven-day business.
Regarding the phrase "even for one departing," the statement "without having caused the dawn to rise" would be contradicted.

For that reason as well, since the dawn of that very day has already been caused to rise, it would follow that even for a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who goes to a suitable forest area in the evening and returns at that very time, the dawn would have been caused to rise and the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) would have been purified; yet this is not tenable.

This is because it is stated that the dawn must be made to rise at the very time of sunrise. For it is said: "Having set out early, one should make the dawn rise at the place where the limbs are afflicted.
If their affliction increases at the time of the dawn's rising, one should perform what is necessary for them;
one should not be intent on the purification of the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga). The same applies to those on probation (pārivāsika) and others.

For those who lay down the formal act (*vatta*) without having caused the dawn to rise, a break in the night (*ratticcheda*) is stated. For it is said: "It should be laid down when the dawn has risen.
Also, in the training rule regarding sleeping together (*sahaseyyasikkhāpada*), for the purpose of escaping the state of having slept together with those not fully ordained, it is said:
"Having gone out before the dawn," and so forth. Thus, in all cases such as being separated from one's robe (*cīvaravippavāsa*), at the conclusion of the night—
The rising of the dawn is shown by way of the *aruṇa* that is yet to come, not by way of the *aruṇa* that has already passed;
therefore, the rising of the dawn here should be understood according to the method already stated, for otherwise there would be a breach of the rains residence (*vassaccheda*).
As for the statement regarding one who has entered the rains residence departing on some business that very day without having caused the dawn to rise: [End of excerpt]
From the time one has entered that rainy-season residence, it is appropriate to go whenever there is a reason, as going is permitted;
however, for one who has gone on a seven-day visit, it is not proper to depart on the very same day without letting the dawn rise, because it is stated that "the dawn must be let rise.
Or, as it is said: "If, before the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) has arrived after seven days, one departs having business to attend to..."
"Monks, that monk might come to that residence, or he might not come"— by such words, although it was permitted for him not to return during the final seven-day period,
it is not allowed for him to do so during other seven-day periods. Likewise, although it was permitted to depart without waiting for the dawn during the first seven-day period,
departing without waiting for the dawn after having returned during the subsequent seven-day periods is not allowed.
Thus, one must reach this conclusion here.
If it is understood that even the *vassāvāsika* robe— by such statements as "if they give the *vassāvāsika* at the time of the invitation (*pavāraṇā*)"— is, like the *kathina* robe,
dependent upon the monastery where one has spent the rains, then [the rule applies] even if they cause the dawn to rise every seven days.
However, because it is stated that "it should be accepted," those who have gone on a seven-day errand and return within the seven-day period do receive [the robe].
Yet, they do not receive the robe that is the benefit of the kaṭhina without having asked the Saṅgha. For it will be said:
"Even for those who have gone on a seven-day errand, such an unrighteous practice should not be performed as 'let them receive the goods to be distributed. Here...
"Bringing in" means brought to a place outside the monastery.
"They are harassed by wild beasts; they seize them and they overwhelm them": here, "seize" means having seized them, they eat them;
"overwhelm" means they drive them away, the sense being that they pursue them. Regarding these [passages], such as "they are harassed by wild beasts," and so forth...

It should be understood that while there is no offense at all regarding the matters ending with schism in the Saṅgha, one is nevertheless not permitted to perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony. However, in the case of "if, however," and so forth,
because for one who enters the rains residence in two dwellings within different boundaries,
the first taking of lodgings ceases as soon as he steps out from the precincts with the thought, "I will stay in the second [dwelling]."
Therefore, in the Pāḷi, when it says, "Bhikkhus, for that bhikkhu the earlier period is not recognized," this is said with reference to the first taking of a dwelling-place (*senāsanaggāha*).

However, in the case of the second taking of a dwelling-place, the earlier period is indeed recognized; staying there for those three months, he is considered one who has already spent the previous rains-residence (*purimavassa-vuttha*). Or, from the second day onwards, in the first dwelling-place...
It should be understood that when one exceeds the boundary of the vicinity [of the residence], even the first period (purimikā) is no longer recognized as valid.
Although a dukkaṭa offense may arise due to the breach of a promise, it occurs only while the promise itself still stands; therefore, he said:
"In the breach of each respective promise, there is a dukkaṭa. For this very reason, he said: "And that indeed... [up to] ...due to the breach of the promise."
Since it is stated in the Pāḷi, “He departs with business on hand seven days before the Pavāraṇā,” it should be understood that even on the day of the Pavāraṇā itself,
it is not permissible to go without a seven-day purpose. Regarding the statement in the Aṭṭhakathā for this passage,
“It is permissible to go from the ninth day onwards,” one must consider whether the ninth day is intended in relation to the Uposatha day.
Or do they suspect it is according to the worldly lunar date? In this regard, it should be determined as follows:
it must be reckoned in relation to the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhaddapada, not by way of the worldly lunar date.
For, taking the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhaddapada as the limit, when counting from the following first day (pāṭipada) onwards, whichever day is the ninth—
"From that time on," is what is meant. However, by way of observing the lunar days (*tithi*), the feminine gender is used;
thus, from the ninth day thereafter, the *pavāraṇā* occurs seven days before [the full moon].
"Seven days not yet arrived" means: she (it) has seven days remaining. Which one? The *pavāraṇā*. On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Assayuja.

A bhikkhu who has set out on a journey having resolved upon a seven-day business, having resided for only seven days of the rainy season, is considered to have completed the rains residence at the mere rising of the seventh dawn; on the tenth day, he has resided for only six days;
on the eleventh day, for only five days; on the twelfth day, for only four days; on the thirteenth day, for only three days; on the fourteenth day, for only two days; and on the fifteenth day...
Only one day remains; therefore, when the dawn has risen at the conclusion of the day of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he is considered to have completed the rains residence.
Thus, for the purpose of dispelling the anxiety of those bhikkhus, the Blessed One, the Lord of Dhamma, said:
"If he departs with business to attend to seven days before the Pavāraṇā, he should come back, O bhikkhus."
“Monks, if that monk does not come to that residence, for that monk the earlier period is recognized and there is no offense regarding the promise,” he said.
The same method applies here as well for the phrase “seven days before the Komudī Cātumāsinī.
In that context, “Komudī Cātumāsinī” refers to the full moon of the later Kattika month; for it is so called because of the presence of water-lilies (*kumuda*) [at that time].
*Komudī* is called *cātumāsinī* because it marks the conclusion of the four months of the rainy season. For at that time, water-lilies (*kumuda*) are in full bloom;
thus, it is called *komudī* in the sense that "water-lilies bloom here," which is to say it is "possessing water-lilies" (*kumudavatī*).

182. Regarding the discussion on the duties during the rains, the phrase "having established the fixed duties" refers to those tasks that must be performed continuously, such as recitation (*sajjhāya*) and mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Having made an agreement regarding the duties to be performed. "Bordering with kaṣāya" means preparing the ground with astringent substances.

"Duty" refers to the agreed-upon rule. Such an unrighteous rule should not be established; for monks from various kingdoms assemble there, and among them, some who are weak and lacking in strength are unable to observe such a rule. Therefore, [the rule] concerning those who have come here...
In the commentary on the fourth *pārājika*, it is stated: having delimited any place whatsoever— whether a dwelling, a pavilion, or a boundary—
and having made an agreement, saying, "Whosoever departs first from this dwelling, we shall know him to be an *arahant*," if one who thinks,
"May they know me to be an *arahant*," departs first from that place, he commits a *pārājika* offense.
There is no offense, however, for one who, on account of some duty to his teachers or preceptors, or some business for his parents, or for the sake of the alms-round practice,
or for the purpose of recitation, questioning, and so forth, or for some other similar business,
passes beyond that boundary and goes; even if, having gone thus, he subsequently behaves according to his own will.
If the thought arises, "I will not go there now; they will respect me in this way," there is no offense.

Also, if one has reached that place for some business and is distracted by recitation, mental attention, and so forth, or is pursued by thieves and the like, or seeing a cloud rising wishes to enter a place sheltered from rain—there is no offense.
He passes beyond that point; there is no offense. Even one traveling by vehicle or by psychic power (*iddhi*) does not incur a defeat (*pārājika*);
it is incurred only by traveling on foot. Furthermore, if he travels neither before nor after those with whom he made the agreement, he incurs no offense.
For all who travel in this manner protect one another. Even if [they stop] at a pavilion, at the foot of a tree, or elsewhere—
If they delimit a certain place, thinking, "Whoever sits or walks here, we shall know him as an Arahant," or having placed flowers,

they make an agreement in such a manner as, "Whoever takes these and performs an offering, we shall know him as an Arahant," then for one who acts accordingly by way of intentional conduct, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense— even if...
If a lay follower has built a monastery along the way, or has set aside robes and other requisites with the thought, "May those who are Arahants dwell in this monastery,
or may they take these robes and so forth," even in that case, for one who dwells there or takes those items out of a desire for personal gain,
it is indeed a *pārājika* offense; however, this is an unrighteous formal agreement (*adhammikakatikavatta*), and therefore it should not be made.

Or something else of this kind, such as: "Within these three months, may everyone become forest-dwellers, or may they all become bearers of the remaining ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas) such as the alms-food practice (piṇḍapātika), or else may they all become those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). For monks from various kingdoms assemble there;
among them, some who are weak and lacking in strength are unable to maintain such a routine. Therefore, even such [a proposal]...

No formal duties (vatta) should be performed. Furthermore, one must not do such things as saying: “During these three months, no one at all shall give a teaching, no one shall ask questions, no one shall grant the going-forth, and the vow of silence should be observed;
even to one standing outside the boundary, the community’s alms-food (saṅghalābha) must be given.
This and similar acts are likewise not to be done.
"Threefold" means threefold by way of the study (*pariyatti*), the practice (*paṭipatti*), and the realization (*paṭivedha*).

"Having purified them, let them go forth" means: having examined those sons of good family who are capable, let them go forth. "Knowing the measure in speech" means: knowing the proper limit in words.

The ten topics of discourse (*dasakathāvatthu*) are: the discourse on fewness of desires (*appiccha*), the discourse on contentment (*santuṭṭhi*), the discourse on seclusion (*paviveka*), and the discourse on non-association (*asaṃsagga*).
[These are] discourse on the arousal of energy, discourse on virtue, discourse on concentration, discourse on wisdom, discourse on liberation, and discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation.
"Controversial speech" means speech that leads to dispute. "Not letting go of the four protections" means not letting go of these four protections:
recollection of the Buddha, loving-kindness, foulness, and recollection of death. "The rule regarding the use of tooth-sticks should be explained."
In this regard, the rule concerning the use of tooth-sticks is as follows:

he who enters the midst of the Saṅgha daily should take only one tooth-stick each day from among those placed in the tooth-stick shed for the monks to use as they please, after having been brought there by novices and others.
However, he who does not enter daily at the meditation hall...
Having stayed [there], one may be seen at a Dhamma discourse or at the Uposatha hall;
having observed the measure [of the brushwood] by that, one should place four or five tooth-sticks in one's own dwelling place and chew them.
When those are finished, if there are still many in the tooth-stick storeroom, they should be brought back again and chewed. But if...
If one takes [the food] without observing the measure, it may be exhausted in the storeroom even while those portions have not yet been consumed;
then some elders might say, "Let those who took [their shares] give them back," while others might say, "Let them eat them; the novices will bring more.
Therefore, for the sake of avoiding dispute, the measure must be observed; however, there is no fault in the act of taking itself. [Regarding] the path:
Even when going [on alms-round], one should go having placed either one or two [robes] in the bag.
The conduct regarding the alms-round will be made clear in the section on the conduct of the alms-collector (*piṇḍapātika*).
Regarding the passage "within the village... [etc. ...no conversation should be held," here, among the four requisites, there is also the soliciting of robes and alms-food.
Even talk about signs or appearances is not permitted. Regarding lodgings, only requesting them is not permitted; the other three are permitted.
Regarding the requisite of medicine, everything is permitted. Even so, these must be well guarded by monks who purify their livelihood.
By this, the virtue of purity of livelihood is shown. One must be one whose sense faculties are guarded.
The virtue of restraint of the sense faculties; and the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha, which consists in fulfilling the duties of the Khandhakas and the duties of the Sekhiyas.
Furthermore, the virtue dependent on the requisites is shown by way of its threefold efficacy.
Thus, the intention is that many such expositions leading to liberation, connected with the fourfold purification of virtue, should be spoken.
Regarding this matter of the commencement of the rains retreat (*vassūpanāyika*), there has been endless debate in various cities throughout different royal eras.

How so? In the *Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka*: "Now at that time, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Māgadha, desiring to postpone the rains retreat, sent a messenger to the presence of the bhikkhus, saying: 'If, venerable sirs..."
Thinking, "In the bright fortnight of the month Āsāḷha, they should enter the rains retreat," they reported this matter to the Blessed One.

Relying on the words, "Bhikkhus, I authorize you to follow the kings," and assuming that the Blessed One had prescribed an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), they reconcile [the Buddhist calendar] with the Vedic system and, while doing so, engage in various kinds of disputes. For it is said that in the Vedic system...
There are two types of intercalary months (*adhimāsa*): the intercalary month by request (*yācādhimāsa*) and the intercalary month by attainment (*pattādhimāsa*).

In that regard, when divided by a count of nineteen in the calculation of the *kaliyuga*, there are seven remainders—namely, five, eight, ten, thirteen, sixteen, eighteen, and twenty—and according to these, there are the leather intercalary month, the five-fold intercalary month, the animal intercalary month, the ten-fold intercalary month, the thirteen-fold intercalary month, the sixteen-fold intercalary month, and the eighteen-fold intercalary month.
They are so designated. However, they also designate the final intercalary month as the "eighteenth intercalary month.

Among these, because in the Kaliyuga when sixteen intercalary months have already fallen before even reaching [the end of] the *pasu* period, one must request the addition of a month due to the danger of the inequality of the year, months, and so forth, it is designated as the "requested intercalary month" (*yācādhimāsa*).
As for the remaining ones, there are only about five [such months] in the Kaliyuga when intercalary months fall.
"Because a month must be drawn forward, it is called a 'requested intercalary month' (*yācādhimāsa*). In this regard, this is the definition of a requested intercalary month:

because those who did not know [the truth] about it, having compared it with the Canon, requested an intercalary month from the Blessed One on behalf of King Bimbisāra, it is called a "requested intercalary month.
Therefore, they say that the month must be drawn forward together with the day only in the case of these two requested intercalary months, and not in other cases.
Others, however, say that the month should be drawn forward together with the extra day only during the five *pattādhimāsa* (added months), but not during the *yācādhimāsa* (requested added months).
Still others, however, [cite]: "Monks, there are these two rains-retreats: the earlier and the later.
The earlier retreat should be entered on the day after the full moon of Āsāḷhī; the later retreat should be entered when one month has passed from the full moon of Āsāḷhī. In that very [context]...
Having incorrectly grasped the meaning of the text as it appears in the *Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka*, [some claim]:
"The Blessed One has permitted entering the rains-retreat (*vassūpagamana*) only when there is a conjunction of lunar days (*tithi*) and constellations (*nakkhatta*);

therefore, the first day (*pāṭipadadivasa*) immediately following the full moon of Āsāḷhi must coincide with the full-moon lunar day (*puṇṇātithi*), and it must occur under one of the two constellations known as Pubbāsāḷha or Uttarāsāḷha."
And if such a time is reached without the drawing of a month by day, then only the drawing of a full month should be made;
if it is not reached, then the drawing of a month together with the day.
This, they say, is the decision that is in accordance with the Piṭaka and the Vinaya.

Regarding this, some say: "The moon (*canda*) is so called because it measures the day by its movement; when it is full here through the completion of all its phases, it is called 'Puṇṇamā' (Full Moon)," and so forth.

Since this is found in sources such as the *Vinayatthamañjūsā*, the conjunction with the lunar day (*tithi*) of the full moon must be intended for the *puṇṇamī* itself, not for the first day of the waxing moon (*pāṭipada*). Likewise, the conjunction with the lunar mansion (*nakkhatta*) [is intended] for the bright fortnight of Āsāḷha.
Regarding the statement in the *Mahāvaṃsa*, "On the fifteenth day of the Uposatha, under the constellation Uttarāsāḷha, thus was the relic established," those who come before [the commentators] say:

"If that were so, there would have to be an eclipse of the moon and an eclipse of the sun on the very day of the Uposatha; however, at present, eclipses of the moon occur only on the first day of the dark fortnight (*kāḷapakkha*) and so forth, and eclipses of the sun occur only on the first day of the bright fortnight (*sukkapakkha*) and so forth."
A solar eclipse is observed; therefore, the conjunction with the lunar day (*tithi*) and the lunar mansion (*nakkhatta*) must be sought on the very first day of the fortnight (*pāṭipada*).

Those who hold the latter view say: "By the words of proponents such as yourselves, because the days that were previously to be drawn forward have not been drawn forward, it happens thus by way of the accumulation of days; but in truth, the lunar eclipse and the solar eclipse occur on the Uposatha day itself."
"And it should be accepted. "Let it be; say as you wish.
Is there such a previous account existing in the word of the Buddha, together with the commentary on the Tipiṭaka? "There is.
For in the *Gandhāra Jātaka*, a lunar eclipse occurred twice on the Uposatha day. That Jātaka is included among the Suttas within the three Piṭakas and among the five Nikāyas."
"It is included within the *Khuddakanikāya*, and among the nine branches of the Dispensation (*sāsanaṅga*), it is included within the *Jātaka*.
When this was said, the former [opponents] would not have been able to give a reply.
Then some [said]: "In the three Piṭakas there are only extra months (*adhikamāsa*), not extra days (*adhikadivasa*). In the *Sāratthadīpanī*: 'That which..."
However, what is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries— that because the calculation was made by taking the extra months of only eighteen years,
there are likewise extra days for the remaining two years as well, and that the phrase "having become free from doubt" refers to those extra days—
should not be accepted. For there are no such things as "extra days" belonging separately to two years.
They say: "They are found in the third year because an extra month occurs only when an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) has been set aside by means of the postponement of the rains;
therefore, in two years, so-called 'extra days' do not exist separately," according to this statement. Then others say: "Extra days are indeed mentioned in the Three Piṭakas;
in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā* it says: 'Of the remaining... [The text continues with a citation from the Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā regarding the calculation of days].
"Because there are indeed extra days in two years, one should confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) having become free from doubt"—this is the statement.
Beyond this, they speak in various ways. Those who maintain the pure enclosure (*suddhavedikā*) speak thus;
the *vinaya*-holding monks speak according to the principles of the *vinaya*. However, in our own Vedic tradition, it is by way of counting the number of hands [held] that...

"It should be known"—enough with excessive prolixity. It should be understood by consulting the *Adhimāsa-pakaraṇa* (Treatise on the Interpolated Month), which was composed because it was requested by the Dhammarāja during the Kali Age more than thirteen hundred years ago.
Here, however, we shall explain only the intended determination. Regarding the first and second positions, King Bimbisāra [is not the subject].
He requested the Blessed One to establish an intercalary month, but the Blessed One did not establish it;

nor is there any mention in the Canon, the Commentaries, or the Sub-commentaries of saying, "In this year, such-and-such is the intercalary month," or that "it should be drawn forward by a full month, or by a month together with a day.
However, when the time for the rains-retreat was approaching, during the season of the Vedas, the King...

Because of the occurrence of the delay in entering the rains residence, he sent a messenger to the bhikkhus with the words, "If, venerable sirs, you would enter the rains residence in the coming bright fortnight," so that they might enter in the second month of Āsāḷha instead of entering in the first month of Āsāḷha.
The phrase "it would be well" (*sādhu vata*) should be connected [to this]. However, the bhikkhus [received] the message sent by the king...
They reported this to the Blessed One. However, because there would be no loss of virtue for the monks in deferring the commencement of the rains-retreat, the Blessed One said:
"I allow you, monks, to comply with kings. Therefore, it is stated in the Commentary:
"Regarding the passage 'I allow you, monks, to comply with kings,' there is indeed no loss whatsoever for the monks who defer the commencement of the rains-retreat."
It is permitted to follow [the lunar month] because there is no decline. And in the *Vimativinodanī* it is stated: "Decline means the decline of virtuous qualities (*guṇa*).

Therefore, whether it be an intercalary month by request (*yācādhimāsa*) or an intercalary month by bowl (*pattādhimāsa*), one should follow whichever time ensures that there is no decline in the monks' virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*).

But how should one follow [the observance], and how should one not follow it? If, while following, the day on which the fast is to be observed now—whether the fourteenth or the fifteenth—is later than the day previously observed, then one should follow it.
But if it is the thirteenth or the sixteenth, one should not follow it; for by following it on a non-fast day, one would commit an offense.
If one performs the Uposatha on a day other than the Uposatha day, one incurs the dukkaṭa offense stated in the rule: "Monks, the Uposatha is not to be performed on a non-Uposatha day;
whoever should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Therefore, because it is possible for the quality of virtue to decline, one should not follow [such a person].
For it is said in the *Vimativinodanī*: "I allow you, monks, to follow kings."
"However, according to the word [of the Buddha], even those who follow the worldly calendar should follow it by observing the Uposatha according to their own sequence—
whether on the fourteenth or the fifteenth, or whether they observe the fifteenth as the fourteenth—
but they must not observe the Uposatha day on the sixteenth or the thirteenth."
In the third and fourth sections as well, for the purpose of dispelling the doubt of those who were questioning, "How many are the rainy-season retreats (*vassūpanāyikā*)?", the Blessed One said:

"Bhikkhus, there are these two rainy-season retreats: the earlier and the later. Thereafter, in order to show the time for entering upon those two rainy-season retreats, he said: "The earlier one should be entered upon when the month of Āsāḷha has passed by one day..."
"It should be entered upon for the latter [period] of the month of Āsāḷha," so it is said. Herein, this is the summarized meaning:

on the first day (pāṭipada) immediately following the full moon of Āsāḷha, the former [period] should be entered upon; on the first day immediately following the full moon of Sāvaṇa, the latter [period] should be entered upon.
Therefore, it is stated in the Commentary: "Therefore, immediately after the full moon of Āsāḷha..."
On the first day of the lunar fortnight following the full moon of Āsāḷha, or on the first day of the subsequent full moon,
one should attend to the monastery, prepare drinking water and water for washing, complete all acts of reverence such as the worship of the cetiya,
and then, once or two or three times, declare: "I enter the rains residence for this three-month period in this monastery."
In the *Sāratthadīpanī* it is said: "On the following day means a day after Āsāḷhī; the meaning is 'the first day of the fortnight' (*pāṭipada*)";
and in the *Vimativinodanī*: "On another day means on the second day, the first day of the fortnight.

Thus, in the commentaries and sub-commentaries on the Canon, the entering of the rains residence (*vassūpagamana*) is stated to take place on the very day of the first of the fortnight (*pāṭipadadivasa*).
It is not stated that it must be "on such-and-such a lunar day" or "in conjunction with such-and-such a constellation.

Therefore, it should be understood that on the first day of the month (pāṭipada), from dawn onwards, one may enter the rains retreat at any time during the entire day or the entire night until the next dawn, according to one's preference.
For this very reason, at the time of entering the rains retreat, there is no requirement for the conjunction with a full-moon lunar day.
The statement of those who say, "Let there be a conjunction with the Uttarāsāḷha constellation," is contrary to the Vinaya.
Even if one were to enter the rains retreat after waiting for the conjunction of the full moon day and the conjunction of the Uttarāsāḷha constellation by accepting that statement,
it should be understood that they are prescribing what has not been prescribed by the Tathāgata.

Thus, in the Pāḷi, the Aṭṭhakathā, and the Ṭīkās, it is stated that the rains-retreat (vassa) must be entered only during the conjunction with the full-moon day (puṇṇātithi), and not when joined with any other lunar day;
or that it must be entered only during the conjunction with the Uttarāsāḷha constellation, and not during the conjunction with the Sāvaṇa constellation.
This has been written in books by some who have established it based on what was laid down by the Tathāgata after taking into account only future shadows [of the sun]. Therefore, the entire...

Not seeing the Vinaya Piṭaka, those belonging to the Vedic tradition, having placed their trust in that statement, seek only for the conjunction of the full moon with the Uttarāsāḷha constellation at the time of entering the rains retreat;

thus, even when the time to be drawn forward is together with a month and a day, they draw it forward by only a month, and even when only a month is to be drawn forward, they draw it forward together with a day.
Therefore, monks who speak in such a manner [are said to] "not have it laid down."
They fall into the position of having to say, "It was prescribed by the Tathāgata; it was taught by the Tathāgata.
Therefore, those who are wise, possessed of shame, and endowed with reverence for the Blessed One do not accept such a view.

Furthermore, the conjunction of lunar dates and constellations has appeared in many places within the Three Piṭakas specifically on the Uposatha day, and it is praised in the ancient Vedic texts; however, at times it is also a matter of conventional usage.

If the lunar day (*tithi*) and the constellation (*nakkhatta*) do not coincide, then in order to bring them into harmony at the time of the occurrence of an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), they draw forward both a month and a day;
therefore, even when it is out of alignment at another time, it must be brought into harmony at the time of such drawing forward.
When this is so, it should be understood that there is an equality of months, seasons, and years.
In the fifth and sixth expositions, the term *adhimāsa* (intercalary month) is stated by taking a month in excess of eighteen years;

therefore, it is expressed in the masculine gender because it is a *kammadhāraya* compound, namely, "an additional month (*adhiko māso*) is an intercalary month (*adhimāso*). However, previously it was stated by taking the additional *ghaṭīs* from a mass of months;
therefore, it is [expressed] as an *abyayībhāva* compound, namely, "that which is additional to a month (*māsato adhikaṃ*) is an intercalary month (*adhimāsan*)."
This was stated using the neuter gender. Here, however, it is said:

"The ancient elders ordain a novice who is nineteen years old on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipada), having passed the full-moon day of the month of departure (nikkhamanīya). Why is that? It is replied:
in one year there are six Uposatha days on the fourteenth; thus, in twenty years there are four..."
The months decrease; kings advance the rainy season retreat every third year. Thus, over eighteen years, six months are added.
Then, having subtracted the four months lost due to the observance of the Uposatha, two months remain.
By taking those two months, twenty years become complete—of this one may be free from doubt.
Regarding the commentary statement, "Having offered [the sacrifice] and having passed the full-moon day of the departure,

she ordains on the first day of the waxing moon," the *Sāratthadīpanī* explains that the meaning of "having become free from doubt" is "having become free from uncertainty because she has completed twenty years of age, including the extra months."

Regarding this, although it was stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, “In all three *Gaṇṭhipadas*, [it is] said that for the eighteen...,” and with reference to such an objection, it was further stated, “But as for what was said...
that should not be accepted,” nevertheless, the meaning is that the statement found in the *Gaṇṭhipadas* should not be accepted. To the question “Why should it not be accepted? he says: “Not...”
“*Hi*” and so forth. The construction is: because they are not apprehended (*na upalabbhanti*), therefore they should not be grasped.
How is this known? He says: “In the third [case],” and so forth. Because they are possible only when delimited (*pariccatte*) and impossible when not delimited, they are not apprehended;
thus, the connection between cause and fruit is established by way of negative concomitance (*byatireka*). “Therefore,” and so forth, refers to the quality that has been attained.
In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, however, he speaks by taking only what was stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.

These statements serve only to establish that novice monks have reached twenty years of age; they do not establish the drawing forward of full days and months during the occurrences of an intercalary month.
Therefore, by citing these [statements], they are unable to decide that legal case. As for the bhikkhus, many...
Considering that one who is capable of bringing forward and explaining some passage when in a formal assembly shines forth, they bring forward such a passage.
However, those wise ones who have accumulated what they have heard do not bring forward such things, because it does not establish the intended meaning.
Even for those who are pure in their conduct, when speaking, the holders of the Vinaya know only the Vinaya, not the external systems. But this discussion concerns the external system.
Because it is thus transmitted, some think that it is not within the domain of those who hold the Vinaya and say so.
However, among those who hold the Vinaya, some know only the Vinaya, some know the entire Tipiṭaka, and some know the Tipiṭaka along with the non-Buddhist systems;
therefore, the capacity to explain it is itself the authoritative criterion.
The words of the Vedikas are authoritative only insofar as they have entered into the Vedic treatises themselves, not merely whatever happens to be in their hands.
Therefore, when King Pathavissara, desiring to draw [the moon] for an entire month, shall request,
"Let them perform the Uposatha on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jeṭṭha," then [the reply shall be], "Once every fortnight, either on the fourteenth or the fifteenth."
According to the word [of the Buddha], there is no fault in performing the Uposatha on the fifteenth day;

however, when one wishes to draw out the month itself and requests, "Let them perform it on the fourteenth," then—since even the natural Uposatha of the dark fortnight of the month of Jeṭṭha is indeed on the fourteenth—there is no fault. In either case, the Uposatha is well-performed; therefore, it should be followed.

After that, having observed the fifteenth-day Uposatha on both the bright and dark fortnights of the first Āsāḷha month, and likewise on both the bright and dark fortnights of the second Āsāḷha month,
on the first day of the waxing moon (pāṭipada), without regard for the conjunction of lunar days or constellations,
from the moment after dawn until the next dawn— throughout the entire day and night— one should act according to one's inclination.

One who enters the rains residence should be regarded as having entered it properly; there is no fault whatsoever. Let it be so; but is there anyone who enters the rains residence early in the morning?
There is. For this is said in the commentary on the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*:
"If, when a lodging has already been taken early in the morning, another monk who is wandering about with thoughts comes and asks for the lodging, [one should say]: 'It has been taken...'"
"Venerable sir, there is lodging; the Saṅgha has entered the rains retreat; the monastery is delightful;
dwell wherever you wish among the foot of trees and so forth.
Thus ends the Vinayālaṅkāra, which is a commentary on the Vinaya-saṅgaha.
The Twenty-sixth Chapter, titled "The Ornament of the Discussion on the Determination of the Entrance into the Rains Retreat.
The first part is completed.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Vinayālaṅkāra-Ṭīkā (Second Part) 27.
Discussion on the Determination of Duties Toward the Preceptor and Others.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Duties Toward the Preceptor (Upajjhāyavattakathāvaṇṇanā) 183.

Having thus explained the determination regarding the entry into the rains-retreat, he now speaks the discussion on the duties toward the preceptor and so forth, beginning with the words, "They are performed here" (*vattanti ettha*).
In that context, *vatta* means that which is to be performed or put into practice by the co-resident disciples (*saddhivihārika*) and others.

The morality of proper conduct (*ābhisamācārika-sīla*) is that which should be practiced toward the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) and others. To the question of how many kinds this is, it is said: "This duty (*vatta*)... is of many kinds.

Regarding the phrase "the duty concerning the privy" (*vaccakuṭi-vatta*), the word *iti* here has the sense of "and so forth" (*ādi*). By this, the duties toward the co-resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*), the resident pupil (*antevāsika*), and the duty of thanksgiving (*anumodana-vatta*) are included.
For it is stated in various places in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that there are "the fourteen duties of the Khandhaka. [This refers to] the Khandhaka on Duties (*Vattakkhandhaka*).

And this is indeed included in the Pāḷi; however, it is included there starting from the duties toward guests (*āgantuka-vatta*), whereas here it begins from the duties toward the preceptor (*upajjhāya-vatta*).
Other than these, the seventy-five training rules (*sekhiya-vatta*) and the eighty-two major rules (*mahā-vatta*) are also simply duties (*vatta*).
Among them, the training rules are found in the Mahāvibhaṅga, and the major rules are found in the Kammakkhandhaka and the Pārivāsikakkhandhaka.
Therefore, only the fourteen duties of the Khandhakas are shown here. Among them, demonstrating first the duty toward the preceptor (*upajjhāya*), he said:
"In this regard, the duty toward the preceptor should be understood as follows," and so forth.
Therein, who is the preceptor? In what sense is he a preceptor? How is the preceptor to be accepted? By whom should the duty be performed?
The duties toward the preceptor: what is that duty? In this context, who is the preceptor?

According to the statement, "Monks, I allow a learned and competent monk who has ten years or more than ten years since his full ordination to grant full ordination," it refers to a monk endowed with learning and competence who has ten or more than ten years since his full ordination.
The Preceptor (*upajjhāya*). In what sense is he called a "preceptor"? He is called a preceptor because he reflects upon what is blameworthy and what is blameless;
the meaning is that he considers thoroughly the minor or major faults of his co-residents (*saddhivihārika*). How is he "accepted" as a preceptor?
By the co-resident, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, sitting in a squatting position, and joining his palms...
Having taken hold [of him] and said three times, "Venerable sir, be my preceptor," if the preceptor—

by means of any one of these five phrases: "Very well," or "Be quick," or "It is appropriate," or "It is fitting," or "Accomplish it with a pleasing manner"— accepts him by body, or by speech, or by both body and speech, he is accepted.
By saying "I request a preceptor," one makes the request for a preceptor; thus, a preceptor is accepted. In this context, *sāhu* means "well.
*Lahu* means "not heavy"; the meaning is "easy to support. *Opāyika* means "connected with a skillful means";
the meaning is that proceeding in such a manner is the means of crossing over. *Patirūpa* means "this is proper conduct. *Pāsādika* means "inspiring confidence."
The meaning is: "Accomplish it through the employment of body and speech.
By whom should the duties toward the preceptor be performed? They should be performed by the co-resident disciple who has taken a preceptor.
What are those duties? These have already been introduced: "Having risen early and removed his sandals... and so forth.

If his sandals have been put on for the purpose of walking in the early morning or for the purpose of tending to his washed feet, he should remove them as soon as he rises at the proper time. Water for washing the face should be given in exactly the same manner;
that is, it should be given in the same way when the water and the condition of the body are of the same nature and of the same appearance.
“Having made it with a border” means having joined together two robes—the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) and the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭī*)—both of these *saṅghāṭīs* should be given.
For indeed, every robe is called a *saṅghāṭī* because it is stitched together (*saṅghaṭita*). Therefore it is said: “*Saṅghāṭīs* should be given.
Regarding the phrase “by strides”: here, that wherein one strides forth is a “stride” (*padavītihāra*), which is to say, the place of striding.
Without making a hurried gait (*dutavilambita*), one should walk with even steps, keeping the distance between two footsteps at the measure of a fist.
Or, "stepping" (*padavītihāra*) means moving forward and then placing the foot; this is how the meaning should be understood here.
One should not interrupt the conversation by interjecting remarks while the preceptor is speaking, whether in an inhabited area or elsewhere.

Or, while he is speaking, another topic must not be introduced before his speech is finished. "From here on" means from the negative particle (*na*) in the phrase "not [while] the preceptor is speaking.
By this, he shows that there is no offense regarding the prohibitions expressed by the negative particle in such cases as "not too far," etc.
In all instances, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), except in cases of emergency, insanity, mental derangement, being afflicted by pain, and so forth.
