For one who speaks even without knowing the formal designation (paṇṇatti), and for one who is ill, there is likewise only an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Indeed, in times of emergency (āpadāsu), it is permissible to speak intermittently; such is the case with other prohibitions involving the negative particle (*na*). However, in other instances, even one who is ill is not exempt.
An offense of wrong-doing is to be understood in all such cases. Thus, [the text] says "even one who is ill is not exempt in such cases" in order to demonstrate this.

It has been stated. For in all other cases as well, for one who, being not ill, neglects the aforementioned duties toward the preceptor (*upajjhāya*), there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the breach of duty; therefore, he will say:

"Indeed, even by a co-resident (*saddhivihārika*) sixty years old, all the duties toward the preceptor must be performed; for one who, out of disrespect, does not perform them, there is a breach of duty."

It is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, in cases connected with the word "not" (*na*), even for one who is ill, performing an action that is prohibited constitutes an offense of wrong-doing as well.
"Speaking words bordering on an offense" means speaking words that are close to an offense by way of the *padasodhamma* or *duṭṭhulla* offenses and so forth.
And "words close to an offense" refers specifically to speech that gives rise to an offense.
He speaks thus: for whatever speech one commits an offense by means of, that speech is said to be "proximate to the offense.
Regarding the phrase "having wrapped the bowl with the robe," it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "having wrapped it with one corner of the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).
Regarding the phrase "or having touched the lower surface [of the seat]," this is for the purpose of avoiding contact with the bowl or other items previously placed there.
It has been said. Even after looking with the eye and knowing that there are no others, it is indeed permissible to set it aside.
"Having turned up the edge by four finger-breadths" means having made the edge of the robe four finger-breadths wide; in this way the robe should be folded.
"The waistband should be placed in the fold" means having folded the waistband and inserted it within the fold of the robe.
It should be set aside. Regarding the phrase "if there is almsfood": here, for one who has already eaten in the village, or in a house within the village, or on the way back, and then returns;
or for one who receives no alms at all—such a person does not have almsfood. However, it belongs to one who has not eaten in the village or to one who has received alms.
Therefore, it is said, "if there is almsfood," and so forth. In that context, "in the village" means...
In some such place not included within the village. "In the interior of a house" means inside a dwelling. "At the place of returning" means in the assembly hall.
Even if he has nothing [to offer], if he wishes to eat, one should give water and bring over the alms-food that one has received oneself.
"He should be asked three times for drinking water" is the connection; thus, at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end.
The meaning is that he should be questioned three times. "Upakaṭṭha" means near. "Dhotavālikāya" means on sand that has been washed by water, free from dust and completely pure.
"Niddhūme" means in a sauna (jantāghara) that is devoid of the smoke of a burning fire; for a place called a "sauna" is [used] when there is much falling of snow...
The place for sweating the body is for the purpose of warding off afflictions such as diseases caused by those conditions.

It is said that there, because it was concealed by darkness, many people would enter together, lay down their robes, smear their faces with clay to avoid the heat of the fire, sweat their bodies as much as they desired, rub them with powders and the like, and bathe. For this very reason, it is said in the Pāḷi: "Powder..."
“Should be examined,” and so forth, was said. “If he is able” means if he has the capacity.
He clarifies this very meaning by saying, “he is not overcome by any illness. “Without knocking” means without knocking against the ground.
“The door-sill and the frame” means without touching both the door-sill and the wooden frame. “A cobweb” refers to any kind of insect nest or spider’s web.
"First the ceiling should be removed" means that, starting from the ceiling—that is, beginning with the ceiling—it should be taken away.
"Ceiling" (*ulloka*) refers to the place where one looks upward; the meaning is the upper portion.
"The light-entrances and the corners" refers to the portions of the light-entrances and the corners, as well as the inner and outer window-frames and shutters of the chamber.
And the meaning is that the four corners must be swept.

"He should be led elsewhere" means that from wherever dissatisfaction with the Teaching has arisen within the monastery, he should be led elsewhere to a place endowed with the attainment of spiritual friends and so forth.
And one should not depart while even a small amount of moisture remains from the dyed robe.

The dye is still dripping; one must not depart yet. "One should not give a bowl to anyone without asking the preceptor," and so forth—all this was said with reference to persons who are dissimilar to the preceptor.
And here, "persons dissimilar to the preceptor" refers to those, whether modest or shameless, who do not desire the preceptor's welfare. But if the preceptor...
One who is shameless does not accept advice, and those who possess a sense of shame are of a different character from him;
in such a case, setting aside the preceptor, one should share the enjoyment of food and other requisites only with those who possess a sense of shame.

It should be understood that here the status of being a preceptor and so forth is not the determining factor. "Having gone to the courtyard" means having gone to the preceptor’s courtyard. "The cemetery" is an illustration (upalakkhaṇa).
It is not permissible for one who wishes to go outside the boundary of the monastery precincts to do so without having asked permission.
"One must wait for his recovery" means that one must wait for his recovery from illness.
The commentary on the discussion of the duties toward the preceptor is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of Duties Toward a Teacher (Ācariyavattakathāvaṇṇanā) 184.
In this discussion of duties toward a teacher: who is a teacher; in what sense is one a teacher; how many kinds of teachers are there; how is a teacher to be accepted;
by whom should the duty toward a teacher be performed; and what is that duty? Regarding these questions, "Who is a teacher? [is explained as follows:]
“Monks, I allow you to rely upon one who has ten years [of seniority], and for one who has ten years [of seniority] to give reliance.
From such statements as these, a monk who has ten years or more of seniority and is endowed with proficiency and strength is an *ācariya*. In what sense is he an *ācariya*?

He is an *ācariya* because he must be thoroughly (*ābhūso*) practiced (*caritabbo*) by the resident pupil (*antevāsika*); the meaning is that he must be attended upon. How many kinds of *ācariyas* are there?

It is fourfold by way of the teacher of dependence (*nissayācariya*), the teacher of going-forth (*pabbajjācariya*), the teacher of full ordination (*upasampadācariya*), and the teacher of the Dhamma (*dhammācariya*). Among these:

the teacher of dependence is one from whom one has taken dependence and who must be relied upon for that dependence; the teacher of going-forth is the instructor of the training rules at the time of going-forth;
the teacher of full ordination is the proclaimer of the formal ritual (*kammavācā*) at the time of full ordination; and the teacher of the Dhamma is the instructor of the Buddha’s word.

Regarding the "Teacher of Dhamma" (dhammācariya): How is one accepted as a teacher? When the resident pupil has arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, sat down on his heels, and raised his joined palms, he says three times: "Venerable sir, be my teacher;
I shall live in dependence upon the Venerable One. To this, the teacher says: "Very well," or "Be it so," or "It is appropriate."
Or if he indicates by body, or by speech, or by both body and speech, saying “it is suitable,” or “fulfill it with pleasing conduct,” then the teacher is considered accepted.
How should one conduct oneself? One should conduct oneself according to the duties toward a teacher. By one who is competent...
A bhikkhu must live in dependence for five years; one who is incompetent must do so for as long as he lives.

In this regard, if this bhikkhu does not find an elder teacher, even if he has been ordained for sixty or seventy years, he should sit in the *ukkhuṭika* posture before a more junior but competent person, raise his joined palms, and say: “Teacher...”
"Friend, be my support; I will go in dependence upon you"—having spoken thus three times, one should receive formal support (nissaya).
When requesting permission to enter a village, one must also sit in the kneeling posture (ukkuṭika), raise the joined palms (añjali), and say:
"I request permission from the teacher to enter the village. This same method applies to all requests for permission. Regarding the phrase, "What is that duty?"—here:
He said, "There is nothing other than the duty toward the preceptor (upajjhāya)," [expressing] "And this very thing... is called the duty toward the teacher (ācariya-vatta). [Objection:
But are not the preceptor and the teacher distinct entities? Then why is this very thing called "the duty toward the teacher"? [Response: He said, "Because it is to be performed for the teacher.
Just as even a single monk, because he has been a mother or a brother, is called a "maternal uncle" (mātula) with respect to the Dhamma...

Because he trains [others], he is called an "ācariya" (teacher); likewise, although it is the same single duty, it is called "upajjhāyavatta" (the duty of a preceptor) because it must be performed by a preceptor, and "ācariyavatta" (the duty of a teacher) because it must be performed by a teacher—this is the intended meaning.
Even though the names are thus different, the actual duty would not be different; therefore, he says: "In this case, there is only a difference in name."
Just as in expressions such as “Indo Sakko,” only the names differ while the meaning remains the same, so it should be understood here as well.
Now, pointing out a certain distinction that applies to that procedure in relation to the co-residents (*saddhivihārikas*) and pupils (*antevāsikas*), he says:
“In that regard, until the dyeing of the robes,” and so forth. Thereafter, in order to show the distinction in relation to the preceptors (*upajjhāyas*) and teachers (*ācariyas*), [he says...]
He says, “Regarding the preceptor,” and so forth. The offense occurs when they consent to the service;
there is no offense when they do not consent, or when they are unaware of it, or even when the burden is placed upon only one of them—this is the summary of the meaning here.
Now, in order to show the distinctions that arise according to the specific qualities of the resident pupil (antevāsika), he says, “And in this case,” and so forth.
The commentary on the discourse concerning the duties toward the teacher is finished.
Commentary on the discourse concerning the duties toward the co-resident pupil:
Regarding the duties toward the co-resident pupil—who is the co-resident pupil, in what sense is he a co-resident pupil, and by whom must the duties be performed?
The duties of a *saddhivihārika* (resident pupil). What are those duties? In this context, who is a *saddhivihārika*?

Whether he be one who has received full ordination (*upasampanna*) or a novice (*sāmaṇera*), whoever takes a preceptor (*upajjhāya*) is called a *saddhivihārika*. In what sense is he a *saddhivihārika*?
He is a *saddhivihārika* in the sense that "he has a dwelling together with a preceptor. By whom should these duties be performed?
The duty toward a co-resident student (*saddhivihārika-vatta*) is that which must be observed by the preceptor (*upajjhāya*). Therefore, it was stated in the *Vattakkhandhaka*:

"In that case, monks, I shall prescribe the duty for preceptors toward their co-resident students, as to how preceptors must conduct themselves toward their co-resident students. What is that duty? It is now presented in this section. In this regard:
However, because those who prefer brevity in this treatise, and because the duties toward teachers, co-residents, and pupils are identical, both have been mentioned together.
Nevertheless, since they appear separately in the *Vattakkhandhaka*, we shall explain them separately.
"He should be supported and assisted" means that his support and assistance should be rendered through recitation and other such means. In that regard:
"Recitation" (uddesa) refers to the wording of the text. "Interrogation" (paripucchā) refers to the commentary on the meaning of the text.

"Exhortation" (ovāda) is the instruction, when a matter has not yet been undertaken, saying: "Do this; do not do that. "Instruction" (anusāsanī) is [the instruction] when a matter has already been undertaken.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the initial statement, whether regarding a matter already undertaken or not yet undertaken, is exhortation, while the repeated statement is instruction.
"If the preceptor has a bowl" means if he has an extra bowl. This same method applies everywhere.
"Requisites" refers to other requisites for a recluse as well. Here, "exertion" means the seeking of a means that arises according to the proper Dhamma method.
From this point forward, the duty begins with the giving of tooth-sticks and ends with the sprinkling of water from the rinsing-pitcher.

It must be performed for the *saddhivihārika* who is indeed ill. However, the removal of dissatisfaction (*anabhirati-vūpakāsanā*) and so forth must certainly be performed even for one who is not ill.
"While dyeing the robe" means while dyeing after having heard the method from the preceptor, [who said], "You should dye it in this way.

The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated. Regarding the phrases "should be supported" (*saṅgahetabbo*), "should be assisted" (*anuggahetabbo*), and so forth, [these refer to] out of disrespect (*anādariya*).

For teachers and preceptors who do not support [their students] with the gift of the Dhamma, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is incurred because of the breach of the proper conduct. For that very reason, it is stated in the Parivāra:
"One does not incur an offense by not giving. The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the discussion of the duties toward a co-resident student is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Duties of a Resident Disciple (*Antevāsika-vatta-kathā-vaṇṇanā*).

Regarding the duties of a resident disciple: who is a resident disciple? In what sense is one a resident disciple? How many kinds of resident disciples are there? By whom should the duties of a resident disciple be performed?
And what are those duties? In this context, "who is a resident disciple? refers to one who has received full ordination (*upasampanna*).
Whether he be a novice (sāmaṇera) or anyone else who receives formal dependence (nissaya) from the teacher, or one who goes forth after receiving the teacher’s instruction,
or one who receives full ordination (upasampadā) having been sponsored by him, or one who masters the Dhamma in his presence—
all such persons are to be understood as a resident pupil (antevāsika). Among these, the first is called a resident pupil by way of dependence (nissayantevāsika).

The second is called the *pabbajjā-antevāsika* (resident pupil at the time of going forth); the third is called the *upasampadā-antevāsika* (resident pupil at the time of full ordination); the fourth is called the *dhamma-antevāsika* (resident pupil in the Dhamma).
Elsewhere, however, the *sippa-antevāsika* (resident pupil in a craft) is also mentioned, but that is not intended here. In what sense is one an *antevāsika*?

One is an *antevāsika* because one dwells near (*ante vasati*), according to the rule of a non-elided compound (*aluttasamāsa*). How many kinds of *antevāsikas* are there? According to the method already stated...
There are four kinds of pupils.
Regarding the question "By whom should the duty toward a pupil be observed?"—it is by the four kinds of teachers that the duty toward pupils must be observed.
As it is said in the Vatta-khandhaka: "Therefore, monks, I shall prescribe for teachers the duty toward their pupils."

"Regarding how teachers should behave toward their pupils. What is that conduct? It is that which was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Vattakkhandhaka* (the Chapter on Conduct) and is here shown in brief;
that is the conduct. Here, however, the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated in the *Saddhivihārikavatta* (the Conduct toward Pupils).
This, however, is the distinction: among these, there is the pupil under one for going forth (*pabbajjā*) and the pupil under one for full ordination (*upasampadā*).

The burden rests upon the teacher for as long as he lives; however, it lasts only so long as the one who lives under dependence (*nissayantevāsika*) and the one who lives as a student of the Dhamma (*dhammantevāsika*) remain in his presence.

Therefore, the teachers must also conduct themselves properly toward them. Indeed, among both teachers and students, whichever individual conducts himself improperly, that person’s offense (*āpatti*) must be recognized.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Duties of a Resident Pupil is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Duties of a Visitor (Āgantuka-vatta-kathā-vaṇṇanā) 185.
One who comes is a visitor (*āgantuka*); that which is to be performed by him is the duty of a visitor (*āgantuka-vatta*). "Now... [the text continues].
By the phrase "I shall enter the monastery," he indicates the vicinity of the boundary (upacārasīmā);

therefore, having reached the vicinity of the boundary, all actions such as removing the sandals must be performed. Regarding the word "having taken": it means having taken them by means of the sandal-strap.
After asking for the cloth used for wiping the sandals, the sandals should be wiped; thus [he asks the residents]: "In which place is the cloth for wiping the sandals?"
"Having asked the bhikkhus. "It should be spread out" means it should be spread out in the sun for the purpose of drying.
"If he is junior, he should be made to pay homage" means that when his seniority is inquired about, if he is younger, he will pay homage of his own accord;
in that case, he has been made to pay homage by this [senior bhikkhu]. "He should be looked at" means he should be observed. "By one standing outside" refers to one who is departing.
One must look out [for dangers] by standing on the path while a snake or a non-human being is stationed there. The remainder should be understood according to the method already explained above.
The commentary on the discussion of the duties for incoming monks is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of the duties for resident monks.
186. Regarding the *āvāsika-vatta* (duties of a resident): one who dwells [there] is a resident (*āvāsika*); that which is to be performed by him is the *āvāsika-vatta*.

In this regard, the duties of a resident monk—such as "upon seeing an incoming monk who is senior, he should prepare a seat," and so forth—should be understood as they appear in the Canon (*pāḷi*) and as they appear in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Since these have been taken from those sources, they are well known; [the first of these is] the wiping of the sandals.
However, it may be done according to one's own preference. For that very reason, it is said here: "If one is able.
Therefore, there is no offense even for one who does not wipe the sandals. Regarding the instruction "the lodging must be assigned":
when asked, "Where will my lodging fall? the lodging must be assigned, saying, "This lodging falls to you."
The meaning is that it should be explained in this way. However, it is indeed permissible to shake out and spread [the bedding].
By this, he shows that even giving a bedspread after shaking out and spreading a bed, chair, or the like, and placing a coverlet on top, constitutes the very act of preparing the lodging.
Furthermore, even in a large monastery, it is not permitted for one who has arrived to neglect the duties toward a guest who has come into their presence.
The remainder is exactly as before.
The commentary on the discussion of the duties for residents is finished.
Commentary on the discussion of the duties for those going away.

187. Regarding "the duty of one who is about to go" (*gamikavatta*): one who is capable of going is "one who is about to go" (*gamika*); that which is to be performed by him is "the duty of one who is about to go.
Herein, this is the commentary on the words not [yet] explained: "Wooden articles" refers to beds, chairs, and so forth, as mentioned in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*.
"Earthenware articles" also includes dye-vessels and all other varieties mentioned therein. All of these [should be placed] in a fire-hall or some other [suitable place].
Or one may go after putting it away in a protected place; it is also permissible to leave it on a sheltered slope that is not subject to rain.

Regarding the rule "one should depart after informing the monastery": if the lodging is constructed on a stone surface or upon stone pillars, such that termites do not infest it, there is no offense even for one who does not inform [the resident].
The phrase "on four stones," etc., refers to [a situation involving] termites.
This was said for the purpose of showing the manner in which the dwelling place, such as a leaf-hut, should be constructed at the site of its erection.
"Perhaps even the parts [of the furniture] might remain" refers to the advantage of placing [the bed] in the open air;
however, in a house subject to rain, when grass and lumps of clay fall from above, even the parts of the bedsteads are destroyed.
The commentary on the discourse concerning the duties of one going on a journey is finished.
Commentary on the discourse concerning the duties regarding the meal-hall:
In this section of the Chapter on Duties (Vattakkhandhaka), the duty of giving thanks (anumodanavatta) is presented here, followed by the duty regarding the meal-hall (bhattaggavatta).

In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, the sequence is stated thus: "The duties of guests, residents, those about to depart, the expression of thanks, the meal-hall, alms-rounders, forest-dwellers, lodgings, the sauna, the privy, preceptors, teachers, co-residents, and pupils—these fourteen duties mentioned in this Chapter on Duties (*Vattakkhandhaka*) are called the 'Fourteen Major Duties' (*cuddasa mahāvattāni*). However, in this work, the *Vinayasaṅgahappakaraṇa*, the duty of the meal-hall follows the duty of those about to depart;
furthermore, the duty of the expression of thanks is not mentioned separately, as it is included within the duty of the meal-hall itself.

The Master’s intention is that these [duties] are included within the duties regarding the dining hall (*bhattagga-vatta*) because they are performed after going to the dining hall and offering the words of thanksgiving (*anumodanā*) once the meal has been eaten;
furthermore, since they do not appear in the Canon as a separate category of duty— unlike other duties where it says, "Therefore, monks,
I shall lay down the duty of thanksgiving for the monk"— they are subsumed under the duties of the dining hall itself.
It may be so. Since this work, the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, is a commentary upon that [text], we shall explain the commentary according to the sequence of what is to be commented upon.

"That which is to be eaten" is food (*bhatta*). It is called "the tip" (*agga*) because it is born there, goes there, and proceeds there. "In the beginning, the first portion, and the tips... [and so forth].

Although the word *bhattagga* appears in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* in the sense of "the best of food" (*puratoggaṃ vare tīsū*), it is also used in other senses, such as in the phrases "rājagga" (meaning "fit for a king") and "salākagga" (meaning "the place where voting sticks are taken").
Therefore, the analysis of the compound is as follows: *bhattassa aggaṃ* is *bhattaggaṃ*, meaning the place where food is served;
and *bhattagge vattitabbaṃ vattaṃ* is *bhattaggavattaṃ*, meaning the duty to be performed at the place where food is served.
In that regard, "the time has been announced in the monastery" means it has been announced: "Venerable sir, it is time; the meal is ready.
"Covering the three circles" means covering the two knee-circles and the navel-circle.
"Having put on the lower robe all around in a circular fashion" means having put it on so as to form a circle all around, [extending] above the navel-circle and below the knee-circles.
When covering oneself, one should put on the lower garment after letting it hang down eight finger-breadths from the point where the shins begin below the kneecaps;
it is stated that for one who lets it hang further than that, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
It is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that for one sitting in the usual manner, the area below the kneecaps is covered by a space of four finger-breadths.
"Having fastened the waistband" means having fastened the waistband over that lower robe (*nivāsana*), because it was stated:
"Monks, one should not enter a village without a waistband; whoever should enter, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"Having made it with a loop" refers to what has already been stated regarding the duties toward a preceptor (*upajjhāya*). "Having tied the toggle" means having tied the toggle to the cord.
"Whether it be inside a village or a monastery, when one goes to a place where people are being served food,
it is proper to go wearing the robe and having fastened the waistband," so it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
And here, "a place where people are being served food" refers to wherever, even within a monastery, people dwell together with their wives and children.
They take the monks and feed them.
"Well-covered" means not with the head wrapped, but rather by fastening the neck-tie,
covering the neck so that it does not flap in the wind, bringing both ears level and tucked in, and covering down to the wrists.
"Properly restrained" means not playing with the hands or feet; "well-disciplined" is the meaning. "With downcast eyes" means with eyes cast downwards.

If one, out of disrespect, walks looking here and there, looking toward this or that direction, toward a palace, a gabled chamber, or a street, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, in one place...
It is appropriate to stand and look for the absence of dangers such as elephants and horses.

Regarding the phrase "with little noise": to what extent is one considered to have little noise? Suppose in a house twelve cubits long, the senior of the Saṅgha is seated at the beginning, the second senior in the middle, and the third senior at the end;
if the senior of the Saṅgha converses with the second, and the second senior [converses] with him... [and so on].
He hears; and how does he discern? However, the third elder hears only the sound and does not discern;
to this extent, there is little noise. But if the third elder were to discern, it would be called a great noise. "Not with the body raised" means not by lifting up;
the instrumental case is used here as a characteristic of the state of being (itthambhūtalakkhaṇe), or [it refers to] from one side or both sides.
"Or having lifted up his robe" means this. One should not walk in this manner starting from the inner threshold (*indakhīla*).
However, when sitting, even while taking out the water vessel (*dhammakaraṇa*), one must take it out without lifting the robe.
"Not laughing loudly" means not laughing with a loud laugh; here, the instrumental case is used according to the method already stated. "Not shaking the body" [means] the body...
Without moving the body, having exerted it and made it motionless, with an upright body and an even posture.

"Not swinging the arms" means without swinging the arms, having exerted them and made them motionless. "Not shaking the head" means without shaking the head, having exerted it and made it motionless, keeping it upright.
"Not with hands on hips": one who stands with hands on hips is called *khambhakata*. At the waist...
"Having placed the hand," this refers to making a supporting pillar. "Not squatting":

here, "squatting" means walking while lifting the heels and touching the ground with the tips of the feet, or lifting the tips of the feet and touching the ground with the heels. The word expressing the agent here has the very characteristic already mentioned.
"Not with a covered head" means with the head wrapped. "Not with the arms folded across the chest."
Not with the robe folded over [the knees]. Here, "folding the waist-band" is also included under "folding the robe.
One should not sit encroaching upon elder bhikkhus—that is, one should not sit by excessively leaning against elder bhikkhus.
"Not having spread out the outer robe" means one should not sit after having spread out the outer robe [over the seat].
"Carefully" means having established mindfulness. "Perceiving the bowl" means having formed the recognition that it is a bowl.
"Equal curry" means where the curry is one-fourth the measure of the rice. "Level with the rim" means filled to the brim, completely full.
Regarding the statement, "If he receives almsfood piled up like a stupa, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," here "piled up like a stupa" refers to [the food] in the bowl...
The meaning is that it has been made by exceeding the circular rim inside the mouth [of the bowl], and it is placed in the bowl, filled, and full.

Not taking what is made in this way, one should take what is equal in measure to the circular rim inside the mouth. Whatever liquid rice-gruel, boiled rice, or fruit—anything of the nature of food—it must be taken only level with the rim;
and furthermore, it must be done with a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
With one bowl, however, it is also permissible to pile [the food] up like a stupa.

Furthermore, for those things that are to be used at the proper time (*yāmakālika*), for seven days (*sattāhakālika*), or for as long as life lasts (*yāvajīvika*), even when piled up like a stupa, they are permissible provided they have been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhānupaga*) for the bowl.
As for taking food from two bowls and sending one filled with it to the monastery, that is also permissible; so it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*. Regarding what is being placed into the bowl...
If one descends with cakes, sugar-cane pieces, fruits, or other such items, it is not called "heaped up" (*thūpīkata*).
However, if they give almsfood after placing a cake on top, it is indeed "heaped up.
But if it is given after placing flowers, *takkolaka* berries, bitter fruits, or the like on top, it is not "heaped up. [Likewise,] if one places a platter or a bowl on top of the rice...
If one takes it after filling [the vessel], it is not called "heaped up" (*thūpīkata*). It is also stated in the *Kurundi*:

"Having placed it in a bowl or a dish and setting that on top of the alms-bowl, they give it; a separate vessel is permitted. Here, the sick person has not been mentioned in the context of what is not an offense (*anāpatti*);
therefore, even for the sick, what is heaped up is not permitted. However, in all cases, it is only for the purpose of receiving."
"It is not permissible [to accept it], but once accepted, it is permissible to eat it.
Both "carefully" (*sakkacca*) and "perceiving the bowl" (*pattasaññī*) are explained according to the method already stated.

"In regular order" (*sapadāna*) means without skipping here and there, but following the sequence. What is to be said regarding "equal curry" (*samasūpaka*) has already been stated. "From the top" (*thūpakato*) means from the summit.
The meaning is "in the middle. "Neither soup nor condiment," and so forth, is self-evident. There is nothing further to be said regarding the formal communication (*viññatti*).
Even in the training rule concerning those who find fault (*ujjhānasaññī*), one who is ill is not exempt.

"A mouthful that is not too large" means that a peacock's egg is too large and a chicken's egg is too small; it refers to a measure that is intermediate between these two. "A rounded mouthful" means...
The morsel must not be too long. "Not brought" (*anāhaṭe*) means not carried [to the mouth], that is to say, not yet delivered to the gateway of the mouth.

Regarding the phrase "the whole hand," here the word *hasta* (hand) should be understood as referring to its parts, namely the fingers—just as in expressions such as "hand-gesture" (*hatthamuddā*), where a designation applied to a whole is used for a part.
It is not permitted to place even a single finger into the mouth. Not...
"With a mouthful" (*sakabaḷena*): here, while preaching the Dhamma, one may place a myrobalan fruit (*harītaka*) or licorice root (*laṭṭhimadhuka*) in the mouth and speak;
it is permissible to speak as long as the mouth remains full enough for the speech to be complete.
"Throwing up morsels" (*piṇḍukkhepakaṃ*): having repeatedly thrown up morsels of food. "Breaking off morsels" (*kabaḷāvacchedakaṃ*): having broken off morsels of food.
"Having bitten off. "Making cheek-bags" means making them like a monkey's cheeks.
"Shaking the hands" means shaking the hands repeatedly. "Scattering rice-grains" means scattering grains of rice repeatedly.
"Protruding the tongue" means protruding the tongue repeatedly. "Making the 'capu-capu' sound" means [making the sound] "capu-capu."
"Making such sounds repeatedly" means making the sound "surusuru" over and over again.
"Licking the hands" means licking the hands repeatedly. For one who is eating, it is not even permitted to lick so much as a finger;
however, in the case of thick gruel, molasses, milk-rice, and the like, one may take them with the fingers and insert the fingers into the mouth.
It is permissible to eat. The same principle applies to licking the bowl or licking the lips;
therefore, the bowl must not be licked with the fingers, nor should even one lip be licked with the tongue.
However, it is permissible to take [food] with the flesh of the lips and place it inside [the mouth].
"A water-pot with a hand soiled by food" is prohibited on account of its repulsiveness;
therefore, one must not take even a vessel belonging to the Saṅgha, an individual, a householder, or oneself, if it is smeared with food—even if it be a small jar or a shallow bowl.
For one who takes it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, if only a portion of the hand is smeared with food...
If there is no [food], it is permissible to take [the bowl-washing water] by that portion. Regarding the rule "bowl-washing water with rice grains should not be discarded within an inhabited area":

here, "having removed" means either having removed the rice grains together and discarding the water after making them into a heap in one place, or having broken them up and made them flow away with the water before discarding it; one who receives it with a receptacle [is not at fault].
If he discards it in a receptacle or discards it after carrying it outside, there is no offense for one who discards it in this manner.
The statement "the Elder has not yet washed [his hands]" refers to the water for washing the hands;
however, if one is thirsty in the interim, or if there is food stuck in the throat, one may drink water and need not wash.
The commentary on the section concerning the duties of the alms-food receiver is finished.
Commentary on the section concerning the duty of thanksgiving:

Regarding the duty of thanksgiving (*anumodana-vatta*), it is called "thanksgiving" (*anumodanā*) because one rejoices and exults again and again (*anu punappunaṃ modiyate pamodiyati*). What is that? It is a discourse on the Dhamma.
The duty to be performed for the sake of appreciation is the "duty of appreciation" (*anumodanavatta*). "Seated in the fifth place" means seated for the purpose of appreciation.
"A conversation among those seated nearby" refers to the delivery of a formal discourse when many have assembled. The remainder is easily understood.
The commentary on the section concerning the duty of appreciation is concluded.
Commentary on the Duties of the Alms-Seeker (Piṇḍacārikavattakathāvaṇṇanā) 189.
Regarding the duties of the alms-seeker (*piṇḍacārika*): that which is to be gathered or collected is called *piṇḍa*, meaning alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*).

One whose habit (*sīla*) is wandering for alms is an alms-seeker (*piṇḍacārī*); the same person is called an alms-seeker (*piṇḍacārika*) by means of the suffix *-ika* added in its own sense (*sakatthe*). By the alms-seeker...
The duty to be performed is the duty regarding alms-gathering. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not [yet] explained:
a "dwelling" (*nivesana*) is a place where women, girls, and so forth reside.
Because one who enters hastily without having observed the door for entering and exiting might see an unsuitable object or encounter danger, therefore: "A dwelling... [etc.]"
It is said, "One should enter. Standing too far away, one might not see [what is happening] or might think, "He is standing in another's house.
Standing too close, one might see what should not be seen or hear what should not be heard;
thereby, people might feel disrespect or lack confidence [in the monk]. Therefore, it is said, "One should stand neither too far nor too close."
It has been said: "If one stands for too long, there may arise mental resentment in those who do not wish to give, and elsewhere alms-food may be exhausted;
if one turns back too quickly, there may be a loss of merit for those who wish to give, and the monk’s alms-round may fail.
Therefore, one should not stand for too long, nor should one turn back too quickly."
"It should be observed by one who is standing," it is said. He shows the manner of observation with the words, "If she puts down her work," and so forth.

Therein, "puts down her work" means that she sets aside whatever she was using to do her work—whether it be cotton, a winnowing fan, or a pestle—and whether she was standing or sitting. "Touches" means she takes hold of it. "Sets it down."
“Vāti” means that she sets it down while saying, “Wait, venerable sir.
“A bowl for leftovers” (avakkārapāti) refers to a single casket-like bowl used for setting aside extra almsfood. Here, a “casket-like bowl” (samuggapāti) is a bowl resembling the lid of a casket.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the discourse concerning the duties of one who goes for alms is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse Concerning the Duties of a Forest-Dweller (Āraññika-vatta-kathā-vaṇṇanā) 190.
It is called *arañña* because people do not delight in it as their dwelling place. For it is said:
“Delightful are the forest retreats, where people do not find pleasure;
those free from passion will delight there, not those who seek sensual desires.
One who dwells in the forest is a *āraññika*; the duty to be performed by him is the *āraññika-vatta*. Herein, this is the meaning of the specific terms:
"Having risen early" is said because the forest dwelling is far from the village;
for that very reason it is said, "As one goes along taking the bowl and putting on the robe, there is fatigue.

Having placed the bowl in its bag and slung it over the shoulder, and having placed the robe on the back, the forest path is not difficult to clear; therefore, for the sake of being freed from dangers such as thorns and reptiles—

Having put on his sandals. As for "the forest" (*arañña*): because it is a place where thieves and others roam, it is therefore said, "Having put away wooden and earthenware vessels and having closed the doors and windows, one should depart from one's dwelling place.
The sections following this are identical to what has been stated regarding the rules for the meal hall and the rules for the alms-round. Having departed from the village...
If there is no water outside the village, one should perform the meal duties within the village itself; however, if there is water outside the village,
then after performing the meal duties, washing the bowl, rinsing it with water, placing it in its bag, folding the robe,
slinging it over the shoulder, and putting on the sandals, one may go.
The phrase beginning with "not obtaining a vessel" and so forth is stated because the necessary materials for a forest dwelling are difficult to procure;

the instruction that "a fire must be maintained" and so forth is because it is required both during times of external dangers such as wild beasts and reptiles, and during times of internal dangers such as wind and bile disorders.
However, in a place where many people reside, such things are easily obtained; thus he says: "for those living in a group..."

"But it is also permissible even without that. A "staff" (kattaradaṇḍa) is for warding off dangers; therefore, it must certainly be desired by one dwelling in the forest—thus it is said, "a staff should be kept ready. "Nakkhattāni" means lunar mansions (nakkhattapadāni).
When thieves and others arrive, they might ask: "Venerable sir, under which lunar mansion is the moon joined today?"
When those questioned reply, “We do not know,” they become angry; therefore it is said, “The lunar mansions (nakkhattapada) should be mastered, either in their entirety or in part.
Likewise, when those who have lost their way ask, “In which direction is this, venerable sir? they become angry;
therefore it is said, “One must be skilled in the directions.”
The commentary on the discourse concerning the duties of forest-dwellers is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse Concerning the Duties Regarding Lodgings (Senāsanavatta):

191. Regarding the term *senāsana*: that wherein one lies down (*sayanti*) is a *sena*; thus, it means "lying down. That wherein one dwells (*āvasanti*) is an *āsana*. Thus, the compound means "lodging" (*senāsana*).

“Senā” means bedding; “āsana” means seating; thus, “senāsana” means bedding and seating. “Senāsanavatta” refers to the duties to be performed regarding those beddings and seats. Furthermore, whatever needs to be said here has already been stated in the discussion on the duties toward a preceptor (*upajjhāya*). However, there is this distinction: in that context, the dwelling occupied by the preceptor was mentioned, whereas here it is the dwelling occupied by oneself. They say that one must ask permission regarding his private cell and its precincts. The phrase "one should act in the same way in the dining hall and so forth" means that in the dining hall and other such places, one must perform the assignment of duties and so on only after having asked for permission.
The commentary on the discussion of the rules for lodgings is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Duties Regarding the Sauna (Jantāgharavatta):
It is called *jaṃ* because it is born (*jāyati*). What is that? It is the body. It is called *jantā* because it protects (*tāyati*) or guards (*rakkhati*) that *jaṃ*.

What is that? It is medical treatment (*tikicchā*). It is called *gharaṃ* because it is taken up (*gahyate*). What is that? It is a dwelling (*nivesana*). Thus, it is a sauna (*jantāghara*) constructed for the sake of medical treatment for the body.

"House" (*ghara*) means a sauna (*jantāghara*). "Sauna-duty" (*jantāgharavatta*) refers to the duty to be performed in the sauna. Therein, "the surrounding area" (*paribhaṇḍa*) means the outer courtyard.
The rest is easily understood because it follows the method already stated in the section on the duties toward a preceptor (*upajjhāyavatta*).
The commentary on the discussion of the sauna-duty is finished.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Duties Regarding the Latrine (Vaccakuṭivattakathāvaṇṇanā) 193.
Regarding the duties regarding the latrine (*vaccakuṭivatta*): that which is evacuated or voided is *vacca*, meaning excrement.

That by which heat is warded off or cut off is a *kuṭi*, meaning a hut. A hut made for the purpose of evacuation is a *vaccakuṭi*. The duty (*vatta*) to be performed in relation to the latrine-hut is the *vaccakuṭivatta*.
In the *Vattakkhandhaka*, the rule regarding rinsing (*ācamana-vatta*) was presented first, and the rule regarding the toilet (*vacca-kuṭi-vatta*) followed later.
However, in this treatise, the rule regarding the toilet is presented first with the intention that one first defecates and afterwards rinses;
therefore, we shall explain it according to that sequence. Regarding the phrase "while chewing a tooth-stick" (*dantakaṭṭhaṃ khādantena*): this...
The prohibition applies in every respect even to a restroom (vaccakuṭi). "For the purpose of regular visits" means for one's own regular visits.
"A private place" is said with reference to one's own monastery (vihāra). The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the discussion of the restroom duties is finished.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Ornament of the Exposition on the Duties such as those Toward a Preceptor," in the *Vinayālaṅkāra*,
which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
28. Discussion on the Analysis of the Distribution of the Four Requisites; Explanation of the Discussion on the Distribution of Robes. 194.
Having thus explained the fourteen Khandhaka observances comprised within the duties toward preceptors and others, [the author] now [addresses] the four...
While explaining the vessel for the requisites, he said, "The vessel for the four requisites," and so forth. Therein, *cattāro* is a numeral and a pronoun.

That which one relies upon (*paṭicca eti*) for the sake of results such as warding off cold is a *paccaya* (requisite), namely the robe and so on. *Paccayo ca paccayo ca paccayā* (a requisite and a requisite are requisites);
four requisites are *catupaccayaṃ*. It is called a *bhājana* because it is apportioned (*bhājīyate*) or distributed. Of the four requisites...
“Vessel” means a vessel for the four requisites. Therefore he said: “the vessel for the four requisites, beginning with robes.
Therein, regarding that vessel for the four requisites, first, in the case of the robe-vessel, the recipient of the robe must be understood... Why?
Because it is difficult to distribute the robe belonging to the Sangha—this is the connection. Therein, as each one arrives...
One who receives a robe is a "robe-receiver," for whom the mere act of receiving it is the burden.
One who stores a robe received by the robe-receiver is a "robe-storer," for whom the mere act of storing it is the burden.
A "storekeeper" (bhaṇḍāgāriko) is one appointed to the storehouse (bhaṇḍāgāre). A "storehouse" is a building that serves as the place for depositing goods such as robes.
One who distributes robes (*cīvara*) by dividing them into portions is called a *cīvarabhājaka*. The distribution of robes—the act of dividing them—is *cīvarabhājana*;
it is the action of apportioning.
Regarding this, it was stated that "one who receives the robes (*cīvarapaṭiggāhaka*) should be known"; as to where such a person is obtained, he says: "By five factors... and so forth.
“He should be appointed. How is this understood? He says: “Because of the statement: ‘I allow... etc. *Chandanaṃ* means desire;
the sense is wishing or longing. *Gati* means going, doing, or action. *Gāreyhā gati* is a bad course of action; thus, *chandāgati* is a course of action driven by desire.
The same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. How does one go by way of a course of action driven by desire? To this he says: “In that regard...”

"...and even for those who arrive later," and so forth. The same applies to the other [factors] as well. However, the fifth factor shows the state of being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*).
In the case of the "white side" (the virtuous path), this should also be understood by way of the opposites of these [faults]. Therefore he said, "Therefore," and so forth.
The phrase "by means of this formal act (*kammavācā*) or by means of a motion (*apalokana*)" is stated because this formal act of convention (*sammutikamma*) is a light procedure (*lahukakamma*).

Thus it was said. For it is stated in the *Parivāra-aṭṭhakathā*: “The remaining thirteen formal acts (*sammuti*), such as the formal act for the taking of lodgings, the giving of robes to the deceased, and so forth—these light formal acts may be performed even without seeking permission (*apaloketvā*).

Regarding the statement, “It is permissible to appoint [an official] within the monastery, in the midst of the entire Saṅgha, or even within a broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*)”: here, “within the monastery” refers to a monastery where a formal boundary (*baddhasīma*) has been established.

It has been stated. Indeed, it is not permissible to perform the fourfold formal act—such as the *apalokana* (request for permission) and so forth—in a monastery where the boundary (*sīmā*) has not been formally established, because such an act would be difficult to purify.
"In the place of the main monastery" means in the area directly facing the gate of the monastery. 197. Regarding the authorization of a storehouse:
"in the very middle of the monastery" refers to the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), which is designated as the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) of the monastery.

It must be authorized right there in the middle [of the monastery]. However, in this case, it is not permissible to go to this storehouse—which constitutes a *khaṇḍasīma*—and authorize it while sitting within that *khaṇḍasīma*.
Rather, it must be done right in the middle of the monastery by means of a motion such as: "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha authorize such-and-such a monastery as a storehouse," and so forth.

Relying on the statement, “It should be authorized by means of a formal motion (*kammavācā*) or by means of a mere announcement (*apalokana*),” and taking it to mean that a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) may be performed within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*),
some perform even the formal act of offering the *kaṭhina* robe within the precinct boundary of a monastery that lacks a formally established boundary (*abaddhasīmā*).
Others likewise take this to apply to formal acts consisting of a motion alone (*ñattikamma*) and perform them only within the precinct boundary of such an unestablished monastery.
They perform the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā; that is improper. The reason for this, however, will become clear in the discussion on the determination of the *kathina* robe.
198. "Like a scale" (*tulābhūto*) means similar to a scale. "This" refers to the giving of half a share to the novices (*sāmaṇera*).
It is said that those who do not pay attention to this reading now give even the *kālacīvara* (timely robe-material) to the novices as a half-share. "Phātikamma" means...
"Appropriate work" means having done as much manual labor as is required by the Vinaya—such as binding brooms and so forth—to ensure there is no deficiency in the monastery; this is the meaning.
"Of all" refers to all the monks and novices who receive the *tatruppāda* and *vassāvāsika* distributions. "In the storehouse robes" is said with reference to out-of-season robes (*akālacīvara*).
"They make a loud clamor" means they raise a great noise. "This" refers to the equal distribution made when the clamor has been raised.
"They act by skipping over [the proper time]" means they do not act at the times when it ought to be done, but act at whatever moment they please.
"An equal share must be given" means that even by the mere fact of their requesting with the words "We shall give," an equal portion must be allotted.
"By way of an excess portion": there are ten monks and there are ten cloths; among them, one cloth is worth twelve [units], while the rest are worth ten each.

When the *kuśa* grass has been cast down for all of them by way of their value being ten [units] each, that monk for whom the *kuśa* grass worth twelve [units] has been cast down thinks, "This much will suffice for my robe," and thus he desires to go away with that excess portion.

And here, the meaning is that one who desires to take everything—thinking, "With this much my robe will suffice," or "My robe is complete with twelve [pieces] worth of value, not less than that"—is addressed by the monks: "Friend, this is an excess; it belongs to the Saṅgha.
Having heard that, the Blessed One said: "In what belongs to the Saṅgha and in what belongs to a group, there is nothing such as 'a little'."
To show that "restraint must be exercised in all cases, and one who receives [something] should feel remorse," he said: "I allow you, monks, when a non-excess has been given.

In this context, "non-excess" (anukkhepa) refers to any allowable article (kappiya-bhaṇḍa) that may be set aside or provided, which is worth as much as, or more than, the value of its specific counterpart.
The meaning of "whatever allowable article has been given" is stated as "if there are ten bhikkhus," and so forth, in order to show this matter in brief.
Regarding the phrase "having satisfied those who are deficient": here, there are two types of deficiency—deficiency of robes and deficiency of persons. Among these:
"Deficient in robes" means that while all [monks] have five robes each, there are some remaining robes, yet they do not reach every individual;
these must be cut up and distributed. When cutting them, they should be made into pieces sufficient for half-mandalas and so forth, or for sandals, bags, and so forth;
at the very least, even a piece four finger-breadths wide may be given.
It is permissible to give it after cutting it into pieces sufficient for a single robe; however, it must not be made unusable.
In this way, the insufficiency of the robe constitutes a deficiency of robes (*cīvaravikalaka*). But once it has been cut and given, this deficiency is satisfied.
Then, the drawing of lots (*kusapāta*) should be performed, even if there are one or two robes in the portion of a single monk.
If they are not sufficient, one should set aside another minor requisite there;

having given that portion to whoever is satisfied with it, the drawing of lots (kusapāta) should be performed afterwards. This is also called "deficiency of robes" (*cīvaravikalaka*), as stated in the *Andhagaṭṭhakathā*.
"Deficiency of persons" (*puggalavikalaka*) refers to when those counting ten monks each time to form a quorum find that one group does not reach the full number.
If there are eight or nine [robes], those eight or nine portions should be given with the instruction: "Having taken these, divide them among yourselves.
This deficiency in the number of persons is called *puggalavikalaka*. When they are given separately, however, it satisfies them;
having satisfied them in this way, the drawing of lots (*kusapāta*) should be performed. Alternatively, "having satisfied the deficiency" means:

The passage beginning with “If all [monks] have five robes each” demonstrates this point: that whatever portion of the robe-distribution is deficient, it should be made equal by adding other requisites, and then the drawing of lots (kusapāta) should be performed.

From here on, regarding the various items mentioned in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) according to how they appear in those respective texts, the following are the specific determinations (*vinicchaya*).

Although those determinations exist, because they are not included within the determination of the eight matrices (*mātikā*), he said, "Now, monks, these eight," and so forth, in order to show them by including them specifically within the determination of the eight matrices. The construction is as follows:
"The determination according to those eight matrices which were spoken by the Blessed One is now to be understood. By way of the location suitable for the enclosure...

By the word "delimited" (*paricchinnā*), it is shown that for an unenclosed monastery, the "proximate boundary" (*upacārasīmā*) is within the range of the first stone-throw from a place where there is a regular assembly (*dhuvasannipātaṭṭhāna*).
Now, in order to show that even the range of the second stone-throw is likewise the proximate boundary, the passage beginning with "Furthermore" (*apicā*) is commenced.
Even the place of the regular assembly must be understood as being situated within those very limits. "Thus..."

By the statement, “Those standing within three *yojanas* shall receive the gains,” etc., it is shown that these matters such as the receiving of gains occur only by way of the *upacāra-sīmā* (the precinct boundary),
and not by way of the *avippavāsa-sīmā* (the non-separation boundary). Furthermore, it indicates that these very matters,

such as the receiving of gains, are to be performed within the *upacāra-sīmā*, whereas the four formal acts (*kamma*), beginning with the act of seeking permission (*āpattikamma*), are to be performed only within the *avippavāsa-sīmā* and the other [boundaries].
He declares that these things are to be performed. For it is said in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: "The entry into the nuns' arama, the inquiry regarding lodgings, and so forth;

the announcement of the probationary period (*parivāsa*) and the penance (*mānatta*), the cutting off of the rains-residence (*vassaccheda*), the granting of support (*nissaya*), the taking of lodgings, and so forth—all this is to be understood as being by way of this very 'boundary of approach' (*upacārasīmā*)."

A boundary established for the sake of gains is a "boundary of gains" (*lābhasīmā*). There is no such thing as a "boundary of gains" well-known as a distinct category in the world, like village boundaries and so forth;
therefore, he asks, "By whom was this authorized? and replies with the words "Neither by the Perfectly Enlightened One," etc.

By this, he shows that this [boundary] is not established by the terminology of the Dispensation (*sāsana*), but is established solely by worldly terminology (*loka-vohāra*). The phrase "the delimitation of the country" is stated according to the meaning of the term *sīmā* as it is well-known in the world.

It has been stated that everything within the boundaries [of a territory] should be understood as the "boundary of the country" (*janapadasīmā*). The country itself is the boundary of the country; the same applies to the boundaries of kingdoms and so forth.
Therefore, he said: "the place where the royal command prevails," and so on. Regarding the phrase "situated in the middle of the earth":

this was said because, up to the edge of the water, it constitutes a "broken boundary" (*khaṇḍasīmā*). However, in the case of unbound boundaries such as the "proximate boundary" (*upacārasīmā*) and others, [it refers to] the lower earth.
It does not reach those situated everywhere; rather, it reaches only those situated in places suitable for entering a well or similar locations.
Thus, the status of being within a particular boundary should be understood according to the method explained below in the discussion on boundaries (*sīmakathā*).

As for the world-system boundary (*cakkavāḷasīmā*), what is given there reaches even those situated in the place where the water that supports the earth stands, because the term "world-system" applies everywhere.
Regarding what is given within the boundaries of common residence and non-separation, this is the distinction:

that which is given with the words, “I give it within the boundary of non-separation,” does not reach those staying in a village. Why? Because it has been stated, “except for the village and the vicinity of the village.
However, that which is given with the words, “I give it within the boundary of common residence,” reaches even those staying in the village.
200–1. *Buddhādhivuttho* means authorized by the Blessed One, the Buddha. *Ekasmiṃ* means in one monastery.
*Pākavattaṃ* means a fixed, regular gift. *Vattati* means it proceeds.
*Tehi vattabbaṃ* means it should be spoken by those monks in whose presence he gives it.

Regarding the second portion: the meaning is that when the Elder’s seat has been ascended [by the distribution], after one round of portions has been given to everyone down to the most junior member of the Saṅgha, if the robes are not yet exhausted, they are to be given to everyone once more; thus, it is given to the Elder in the second portion.
"In the manner previously stated" means in the manner stated by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhu, those robes are yours alone. This applies even to the paṃsukūlikas.

Regarding the phrase "it is allowable": it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī* that because [the donor] did not say, "We give this to you," but rather said, "We give it to the bhikkhus" or "We give it to the elders," it is allowable even for *paṃsukūlika* (rag-robe wearers).

However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, they state the reason for the allowance for *paṃsukūlikas* as being that [the donor] did not say, "We give this to you. If that is so, then even when it is said, "We give it to the Saṅgha," [it would likewise be allowable].
Since no distinction is seen from the statements, "We give to the bhikkhus," "We give to the elders," or "We give to the Saṅgha," the reason for this must be investigated here.
"It is allowable to wear it" means it is allowable for those who follow the paṃsukūla practice.
"It has already been allocated by the owners" means it has already been set aside for the purpose of sandals, bags, and so forth.
203. "Half is to be given" means that of what has been given to both Saṅghas, half must be given to the monks and half to the nuns.
Even if there is only one monk or only one nun, or even if it is for one who is not fully ordained, half must still be given.
However, when it is said, "I give this to the community of monks and to the nuns," [it is not so].
Regarding the instruction "it should be given after dividing [the portion] in the middle":
here, because the Saṅgha on the side of the nuns is not treated as a single unit, it is established that the donor’s intention is that the share should be given according to the number of nuns;
likewise, the distribution of the gift is appropriate only if the monks are also counted. Otherwise, [one would have to ask]: "How much should be given to the monks, and how much..."

It is not understood [from the text] whether it refers to "the bhikkhunīs"; therefore, he said, "Having counted both the bhikkhus and the bhikkhunīs, it should be given," because even the expression "of the bhikkhu-saṅgha" is identical in meaning to the expression "of the bhikkhus. For this reason he said:
"An individual... because it is included by the mention of the bhikkhu-saṅgha. [And for the bhikkhu-saṅgha and the bhikkhunīs...]"
However, when it is said, "and to you," the person is not obtained separately; this must be accepted solely on the authority of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, for no specific reason is found here.
For instance, just as when it is said, "I give to both the Saṅgha and to you," the person is obtained separately because they are included by both general and specific terms, so too is it here.
Because there exists both a general and a specific expression in the phrase “for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and for you,” it is understood that there must indeed be a separate individual portion;
therefore, the word of the Aṭṭhakathā alone is the authority here.
“He receives only one from the place where it reaches” means he receives only one portion from the place reached according to his own seniority (*vassa*). In that regard:
He states the reason: “Why? Because [the individual] is included by the mention of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated that the intention is that the individual is indeed included by the very mention of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is said that because the word “Saṅgha of bhikkhus” refers only to the bhikkhus, [the individual is not included].

However, it should be understood that because "and for you" (*tuyhañca*) is mentioned separately and because he was not included therein, the intended meaning is that it is similar to the passage where it is said, "for the monks, for the nuns, and for you.

For here, the word *saṅgha* (community) should be understood as referring primarily to the individual. Some, however, write the reading: "because he is already included by the mention of the community of monks."
That is not correct, because it provides a reason for the separate mention of the gain.
For indeed, the reason for the individual’s separate receipt of a share has been stated as being "because he is included by the separate mention of the Saṅgha.

And just as there is no separate mention of the individual here, so too in the subsequent passages such as "to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and to you," [the individuals are not separately mentioned] by means of terms like *saṅgha*.

The non-inclusion of the individual (puggala) is to be understood. For if there were inclusion, it would follow that two parts—both as part of the Saṅgha and separately—would be obtained, since [the individual] is included in both cases;
thus it was said. The statement beginning with "to be honored" is spoken for the purpose of showing that this is not the business of a householder.
"Carries to the community of monks" is said with reference to the carrying of almsfood. Therefore he said: "in order to eat..."

"It is permissible. Even when it is said, "Bring it to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus," it must be brought; this is stated because such service for a layperson does not exist [in that context]. 204. Regarding the phrase "during the winter":
by this, [it is meant] that what was given in the last month of the rains, when the Kathina has not been spread, belongs only to those who have spent the previous rains residence.

It reaches [the recipient] from that point; furthermore, what is given during the winter reaches even those who have completed their rains-residence in the subsequent year, because they too have completed the rains-residence.

However, what is given after the winter, during the dry season, specifically designated as "for the Saṅgha that has completed the rains-residence," belongs to those who have completed the rains-residence in the immediately following year, or in any subsequent year, throughout that state of being a monk.
It reaches all of them. However, it shows that it does not reach those who have not yet spent the rains retreat in every respect.
"Those who know the characteristics say" means the teachers who know the characteristics of the Vinaya say. "Those who know the characteristics say" is a statement of certainty;
however, it is stated thus because it has not been included in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). "Outside the precinct boundary... [etc] ...it reaches all of them."
The intention is that it reaches all those who have completed the rains residence wherever they may be. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*:

"But if one standing outside the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*) says, 'I give [this] to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains residence,' it reaches all those who have completed the rains residence wherever they may be, provided they are present. However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada* [commentaries],...

It has been stated that "because it was spoken while standing in a place unsuitable for the rainy-season residence, it applies to all—both those who have completed the rains-residence and those who have not";
this should not be accepted. For when it is said, "I give to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains-residence," it does not apply to those who have not completed the rains-residence.
The phrase "to all" means to all those who have completed the rains-residence within that state of being a bhikkhu.
The meaning should be understood from the statement, "of the Saṅgha that has completed the rains residence.

The same method applies here as well regarding the phrase, "to all who are present. "He speaks thus" means he says, "I give it to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains residence. "The past rains residence" refers to the most recently concluded rains residence. 205.
Now, analyzing the phrase "he gives by specifying," he says, "In this regard, 'he gives by specifying'... and so forth. Therein:
The construction is as follows: a donor who gives after having specified and delimited [the gift] by saying, "Yāgu (rice gruel)... or "...medicine," etc., is said to "give specifying.
The remainder is self-evident. 206.
Now, explaining the phrase "he gives to a person," he says: "He gives to a person here," and so forth.
When one gives to a person who is one's own family member or associate, being free from both the Saṅgha and a group, that donor is said to "give to an individual.
Furthermore, that gift to an individual may be given either in the person's absence or in their presence. In that regard, when giving in the person's absence, one gives by reciting the name, saying:
"I give this robe to [so-and-so]. When giving in their presence, one gives...
Having placed the robe at the foot of a bhikkhu and saying, "Venerable sir, I give this to you," he gives it;
the meaning is that in both these ways, one is said to give to an individual (*puggala*).

Not only is one said to give to an individual when giving to a single person, but rather, it is shown that even when giving together with a pupil (*antevāsika*) and others, one is still said to give to an individual.

He said, “But if...,” and so forth. In that context, “came to receive instruction” means that from the moment he arrived with the intention, “I will receive instruction from him”—even if he had not previously received instruction from him—until he entered into the status of a resident pupil (*antevāsika*).
“Going after having received it” means going once the instruction has been completed. “Having performed the duties, [such as] instruction, interrogation, and so forth...”
"Of those wandering about having taken [it]" is a qualification of "those who are students for recitation.
By this, it excludes those who, having come at the time of recitation and taken the recitation, go elsewhere and dwell there as itinerants without a fixed residence.
Thus, having shown the distribution of robes according to the eight headings (mātikā) found in the Cīvarakkhandhaka, now, in that very same [section]...
Having set aside the method presented in the middle of the *Cīvarakkhandhaka* among the topics that have been introduced, he says, "If any monk...
and so forth, in order to demonstrate it. Therein, in response to the question "What should be done?", the answer is "those very robes of his";
the remaining [terms] are stated by way of illustration and so on. In the phrase "for five months," the accusative case is used in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). *Vaḍḍhiṃ*.
"From what has been invested as a deposit" means from a deposit placed by attendants after they have invested it for the purpose of the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe).
"From what is produced there" means from what is produced there, such as coconut groves and so forth. However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it says:
"That which is given after saying, 'We give this to the Saṅgha who has spent the rains retreat here,' or 'We give the *vassāvāsika* [robe-fund]'"—that is [what is meant].
It is said, “Even for one whose *kaṭhina* has not been spread, [the robe] accrues for five months”;

this was stated in order to show the specific distinction that arises regarding acquisitions pertaining to the rainy-season residence (*vassāvāsika*). In that context, the word “here” (*idha*) is merely a conventional expression;
even if one says, “We give to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains,” the same principle applies, even without the word “here. Even for one whose *kaṭhina* has not been spread, for five...

"It reaches [the recipient] within five months" means that because it arises by way of the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) gift, even one for whom the *kathina* has not been spread receives it within five months after the rains have been completed.
However, beyond that period, one must inquire regarding the *vassāvāsika* that has arisen:
"Does this *vassāvāsika* belong to the past year, or to the future year? In this context, "beyond that" means beyond the five months.
The meaning is: "starting from the first day of the summer season. Regarding the phrase "but the period of suspension does not persist":

here, if while the period of suspension has not yet expired another robe arises, and a monk arrives, both [the original owner and the new claimant] may take it after dividing it in the middle. However, if the period of suspension has already expired...
Furthermore, when another robe has arisen [for distribution], if one who is junior arrives, the standing place moves downward;
if one who is senior arrives, the standing place ascends upward. If there is no other [junior person], it should be taken again after making it one's own.
"Duggahitāni" means they were not taken; the meaning is that they remain the property of the Saṅgha alone. "Pātite... [is explained as follows:]... [text continues].
"Kusa grass" means that as soon as even a single bundle of kusa stalks is laid down, if there are even a thousand monks,
the robe-cloth is indeed considered "taken. Regarding the commentarial statement,

"A portion must not be given against one's will," the phrase "it is indeed considered taken" implies that although it may not be known specifically which portion belongs to whom, those portions are in fact their own by right.

The statement "he causes dawn to rise every seven days" is said for the purpose of showing that even in a single monastery, one has resided in two separate dwellings according to the method prescribed for monasteries with distinct boundaries;

by the very rising of dawn, one is considered to have completed the residence there, but it is not for the sake of avoiding a break in the rains residence. For within the precinct boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*), wherever one may be—
If one causes the dawn to rise while still at the lodging one has taken up, even if one has not yet entered [the rains residence], one is indeed considered to have completed the rains.

However, one is not said to have "dwelt" in the lodging one took up; rather, such dwelling occurs only when the dawn rises there. Therefore he said: "In the former case, one is said to dwell for a longer time.
By this, it is shown that in the other case, even if the dawn rises during the seventh day-period, one dwells for only a shorter time.

"It exists" means it is present; "it does not exist" is what is being illustrated. "This" refers to a gift with a single intention. Regarding the phrase "by various gains" (*nānālābhehi*) and so forth:

those in which there is a gain that is "various" (*nānā*), meaning separate or distinct, are "those with various gains"; these are two monasteries (*vihāra*). By "those with various gains" is meant by those [monasteries] possessing such gains.

Those in which the precincts (*upacāra*) are "various," meaning separate or distinct, being delimited by walls and so forth, are "those with various precincts. By "those with various precincts" is meant by those [monasteries] possessing such precincts. "By monasteries within a single boundary" (*ekasīmavihārehi*)...

"In two monasteries within a single boundary" is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*. "With separate acquisitions" means with the acquisitions for the rainy-season residence (*vassāvāsika*) assigned individually.

"With separate precincts" means with different enclosures and different gates. "In two monasteries within a single boundary" means that because the two monasteries are enclosed by a single wall, they are situated within one precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*); this is according to the *Vimativinodanī*.
“The taking of lodgings is suspended” means that what was previously taken is suspended.
“Therein” means where the taking of lodgings is suspended, there.
Regarding the phrase “when a bhikkhu has died,” the word *kālakata* here functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*); thus he says, “by the act of dying (*kālakiriyāya*).”

In the Pāḷi, regarding the giving of robes to those who attend to the sick, because novices lack the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for the three robes, the phrase "a robe and a bowl" and so forth is stated in all instances. 208.
Even if it is worth a thousand [pieces], it should be given only to those who attend to the sick; this is the connection. "Another" means...
Other than the three robes and the bowl. "Inferior" means diminished by being excessively worn out and so forth. "Than that" means than the remaining requisites.

"All" refers to both the bowl and the robe. Because the word "there" (*tattha*) is used instead of "here" (*idha*) with reference to the place where a monk has passed away, it is a distributive expression meaning "in each respective [monastery] of the Saṅgha alone."
And it is understood that the place where the requisites are deposited is thus prescribed. In the Pāḷi, the phrase "not to be given away, not to be divided" means:
"I authorize [this] to remain the property of the Saṅgha of the four quarters—both present and future—and to be neither given away nor divided by anyone.
Because it is stated, "provided there are suitable recipients," if no such recipients exist, one should not give it away.
Even when it has been distributed, it should be understood as being well-distributed. Regarding the phrase "the water of dedication (*dakkhiṇodaka*) is the measure," the *Sāratthadīpanī* states:
"But where 'the water of dedication is the measure,' the intention is that in whatever kingdom the mere acceptance of the water of dedication makes the recipients the owners of the gift.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, regarding "the water of dedication... [it says:]...
"Measure" means that after first pouring water with the thought, "I will give this many robes," they subsequently give them;

the intention is that those by whom [the water] was poured are indeed the ones entitled to the share. It is said, "in the other ocean" refers to Jambudīpa, for it is spoken thus with reference to the island of Tambapaṇṇi.

Regarding the phrase “he determines a robe for one who has died”: if, while traveling on a road, he hears of that person’s death and, knowing that there are no other monks within twelve cubits of his current location, he determines it, thinking, “This robe falls to me,” it is properly determined.
Now at that time, a certain monk had many goods and many requisites.
He has passed away. They reported this matter to the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has passed away, the Saṅgha is the owner of his bowl and robes.
