However, those who attended to the sick have been of great help; therefore, I allow you, bhikkhus, to give the three robes and the bowl to those who attended to the sick.
Whatever light goods or light requisites there are in that place, those should be given by the assembly present."
"Let it be distributed by the Saṅgha. Whatever therein is heavy property or heavy requisites, that is not to be alienated or divided from the Saṅgha of the four quarters, both present and future"—
with this passage, the Blessed One, the All-Knowing One, ordained the distribution of material inheritance for the monks.
In that regard, the inheritance of material goods (*āmisa-dāyajja*) is threefold, according to the categories of the three robes, the bowl, and the remaining light and heavy articles.
Among these, the three robes and the bowl belong to the attendant of the sick; the remaining light articles belong to the *saṅgha* present there;
and the twenty-five kinds of heavy articles belong to the *saṅgha* of the four quarters. By this [rule], anything other than these three types of articles—
There is no such thing as "monk's property"; this shows that there is no heir other than these three types of persons.
Now, however, the Vinaya-holders say, "Relatives who have become householders receive the monks' unallowable goods.
If one asks why that is, it is because [the rule states]: "It should be given to those who are masters over his wealth, whether they be householders or renunciants."

"Because it is stated in the commentary. It is true that it is stated there; however, that reading occurs in the context of taking what is given out of trust, not in the context of receiving an inheritance.
It is stated simply as "whether householders or those gone forth," not as "whether kinsmen or strangers";
therefore, whether they be kinsmen or strangers, those who attend upon that sick person [are entitled to] the portion belonging to the attendant of the sick.
Both householders and those who have gone forth are masters of wealth, even including women.
It was with reference to them that it was said, "It should be given to them," and not with reference to those who do not attend to the sick. For it is stated in the Commentary:
"One who attends to the sick may be a householder or one who has gone forth, even including a woman; all of them receive a share."
Alternatively, it refers to a monk who, while still alive, relinquished all his own requisites and gave them to someone—
whether a relative or a stranger, a householder or one gone forth—
and to whom some relative, stranger, householder, or one gone forth placed trust. It is with reference to such a person that [the rule was established].
It is said: “It should be given to those who were masters of that wealth, whether they be householders or renunciants,” but not to relatives other than those [specifically mentioned].

For it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “But if, while still living, he had relinquished all his own belongings and given them to someone, or if someone had taken them on trust—[then they belong] to the one to whom they were given, by whom [they were received]...”
"And what has been accepted belongs to him alone; the attendants of the sick receive it only by his consent. "Let that be so, but how is it with regard to allowable goods (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*)?
Regarding that as well, there is nothing stated in the Canon (*pāḷi*), the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), or the Sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*) saying, "It should be given to lay relatives";
therefore, this matter must be investigated.
The commentary on the discussion of the bowl for robes is finished.
Now, in order to explain the determination regarding the bowl for alms-food, he said: “But as for the bowl for alms-food,” and so forth. (209)

In this regard, although the distribution of lodgings (*senāsana-bhājana*) occurs first in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*, because of the determination regarding the distribution of the four requisites (*cattāro paccayā*), he shows the distribution of almsfood (*piṇḍapāta-bhājana*) first according to the sequence of the requisites.
As for the distribution of almsfood, the connection is that "this is the determination regarding the communal meal (*saṅghabhatta*) and so forth.
How were these communal meals and so forth authorized by the Blessed One?
He said: “I allow... [as above] ...in regard to those things already permitted. Food brought for the sake of the Saṅgha is *saṅghabhatta*;
just as food brought for a guest is called *āgantukabhatta*. Food that is to be given after being specifically designated for the Saṅgha is *uddesabhatta*.
Food that is to be given after having invited [the monks] is *nimantanabhatta*. A voting-ticket (*salāka*)...
The meal that is to be distributed by casting lots is *salākabhatta*. The meal to be given on the fortnightly day is *pakkhabhatta*.

The meal to be given on the observance day (*uposatha*) is *uposathabhatta*. The analysis of the compound for *pāṭipadabhatta* is: "the meal to be given on the first of the fortnight, which is the second day after the observance day.
There is no fixed order [of distribution]; [it begins] from the senior monk of the Saṅgha.
"Taking [the dwelling] by lot according to the year of seniority" (*vassaggena gāhaṇaṃ*) is what is meant by "establishment" (*ṭhitikā*).
"At the door of one's own monastery" refers to the vicinity of the gatehouse of the monastery.
"In the dining hall" means in the dining hall that serves as the place for the distribution of meals. "By lot" means by means of a portion of the year. "But when it has been given... [and so forth].
Having spoken thus, in order to demonstrate the procedure as the donor describes it, he said, "From the Saṅgha, venerable sirs," and so forth.

"In the interior of a house" (*antaraghare*) means within the household. Regarding "those who have gone into the vicinity" (*antoupacāragatānaṃ*): here, the "vicinity" (*upacāra*) refers to the space within twelve cubits of the village gates, streets, and crossroads.
To show the specific distinctions found in the vicinity of a house, he said, "And herein, the vicinity of a house is... and so forth.
“Ekavaḷañjaṃ” means that which is to be used through a single door. “Nānānivesanesu” means in dwellings belonging to various families and situated in various locations.
Because one who is modest (*lajjī*), amiable (*pesala*), and wise (*medhāvī*) teaches after avoiding wrong courses and having investigated [the matter], it is said:
“One who is amiable, modest, and wise is to be desired. In the phrase “even for one who is sitting or even for one who is sleeping,” the genitive case is used in a sense of disregard.

The meaning is that when the more senior [monks] are sleeping, what has been received by the junior monk is well-received. Regarding the phrase "or accompanied by the three robes," it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries:

"Just as one who obtains only water, if he receives many kinds of things such as cloth and so forth without having received a meal for recitation (*uddesabhatta*), it belongs to him alone. Having said whatever one wishes according to one's own preference...
Because he was dispatched to fetch [the food], he is called "one who has sent a messenger" (*vissaṭṭhadūta*).

"Whatever he desires" means whatever he wishes for when saying things such as, "Give us meal-by-assignment" (*uddesabhatta*) and so forth. "In accordance with the nature of the question" means similar to the question.
Having stated, "There is one called 'standing on a peak' (*kūṭaṭṭhitikā*)," he spoke the passage beginning with "Or for a king" in order to clarify that very standing.
Because it must be taken separately, without being mixed with other designated meals (*uddesabhatta*) and so forth, it is called "meals for those wandering alone" (*ekacārikabhatta*).
"They take by theft" means they take as bowl-carriers (*pattahāraka*). "There is a penalty" means there is a penalty for the one who ordered it.
"Everything belongs to the owner of the bowl" means that even everything such as robes and so forth belongs solely to the owner of the bowl; [thinking] "by me..."
Having said, "This was stated with reference specifically to alms-food (bhatta), not to robes and so forth," the meaning is that it is permissible to accept [it].
Regarding the phrase "they go having been told by the monk that it is permissible to comply with the request of people":

they go because they have been told by that monk, "It is permissible to comply with the request of people. "The portion called 'unassigned' (akatabhāga)" means the portion for newcomers (āgantukabhāga); it is a portion that has never before been given.
"Meaning. Regarding the statement "Let the entire Saṅgha consume it," it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* (Commentary on Difficult Points):
"Even if one has first said, 'Give the food belonging to the entire Saṅgha,' if one does not subsequently say, 'Let the entire Saṅgha consume it,' it may still be divided and consumed.
"Without saying, 'Which meal is being brought? means [not asking] the donor, "Which specific meal is being brought by you?"
"Without having asked. "In the state of natural stability" means: in the state of receiving a meal by formal invitation (*uddesabhatta*).
The commentary on the discussion regarding the vessel for alms-food is finished.
The commentary on the discussion regarding meals by invitation (*nimantanabhatta*) follows.

210. Without saying, “Give [food] having designated so many bhikkhus from the Saṅgha,” etc., but rather saying, “Give food for so many bhikkhus,” that which is given is called an invitation belonging to the Saṅgha.
It is permissible even for alms-collectors because it is stated as a turn for alms-food (*bhikkhāpariyāya*). “In order” means according to the order received. “Having interrupted” means...
This was said without saying the words, "Take the meal. For this very reason, it says, "by one who does not say, 'It is the meal. "By way of mouthfuls" means by way of each individual lump.

And this method applies only to an invitation (*nimantana*), not to a meal designated for a specific group (*uddesabhatta*). For in the case of the latter, only a quantity sufficient for one person should be distributed;
therefore, there is no such thing as a "standing of mouthfuls" in a designated meal.
"Having ascended the list itself": regarding the phrase "eight bhikkhus from the Saṅgha," it should be construed as "those who have ascended the list are the eight bhikkhus.

Among the lists of food belonging to the Saṅgha—such as food designated by a formal announcement (*uddesabhatta*), invited food (*nimantanabhatta*), and so forth—one should go after having either had the meal-designator assign it from the Saṅgha's portion, or having assigned it oneself, and then taking it, according to the standing rule for the list of invited food.
The intended meaning is: "not having taken it for oneself according to one's own preference. "Having entered it into the schedule" means:
having informed the donor of the various types of schedules stated as "I take from the Saṅgha," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "at one time," it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries:
"As long as there are bhikkhus residing in that monastery, they all receive [it]. However, the intended meaning here is as follows: "at one time" means...
This was not said with reference to a single day; rather, it refers to all those bhikkhus who reside in that monastery.

If one knows—either by oneself or through others who know—that on a particular day all the bhikkhus have been fed, then one should go taking along those [bhikkhus] who were included at the time of the commitment (*paṭibaddha-kāla*). "Starting from the time of the commitment" means...
From the time of fixing the period for residence right there.
The commentary on the discussion regarding meals by invitation is finished.
The commentary on the discussion regarding meals by tickets.
211. *Upanibandhitvā* means having written down. *Gāmavasenapi* means even by way of a village that is mostly [made up of] those who receive equal gains.
*Bahūni salākabhattāni* means thirty or forty meals. *Sace honti* should be construed by supplying the word "if.
*Sallakkhetvā* means having observed those meals by way of their quantity. *Niggahena datvā* means having given [the punishment] with censure.
Having made him accept [the meal] by means of restraint, even though he did not wish to go far. Regarding the phrase "having returned again to the monastery":
it is also permissible there to take the meal without returning to the monastery, and afterwards bring it into the monastery for oneself to eat.
"By way of a single house" means even on a street, by way of a row of houses on one side. "Even after having designated" means: "In such-and-such a family..."
Having said, "The *salākabhatta* (tickets for meals) are reaching you," [he continued]:
212. "In the village of Vāra" means a village to which one must go by turn because it is too far away.

"From sixty or fifty [leagues]" is said with reference to a water-jar for the purpose of carrying out punitive labor (*daṇḍakamma*). "The turn of the monastery" refers to the turn for guarding the monastery when all the monks have gone out for alms.
"They come" refers to those appointed as *vihāravārika* (monastery stewards). "Only as a token of gratitude" means merely providing what is sufficient for the duty of protecting the monastery.
Because it is distant, a village that must be taken by rotation even after being restrained is called a *vāragāma* (rotational village). Those appointed to the monastery rotation are *vihāravārikā*;
they are those who protect the monastery by rotation. "A change [of state]" means a change in one's faith (*pasāda*). "They become only a token of gratitude" means...
"Extra gains are to be given by the Saṅgha for the purpose of protecting the monastery.
"They fall to one person alone" means that they are assigned to each individual day by day. "At the time when the junior member of the Saṅgha receives them" means:
when, in the same manner as two or three *ekacārika*-meals are assigned to each person day by day, they fall to one's own share at the time the junior member of the Saṅgha receives them.

Regarding the phrase "having brought it before anyone who is present": here, it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* that "if the majority of the monks have gone outside the boundary, it should be brought before anyone who is present; because they are of like status, what is obtained by one belongs to all.
Even if such a person is not available, it should be given after having brought it before oneself. "A sample of the flavor" (*rasasalāka*)—
"Ucchu-rasa-salākaṃ": because it is taken by means of a tally-stick (*salāka*), it should not be accepted;

this was stated on account of its unsuitability, not because it constitutes a breach of the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*). For it is said in the *Visuddhimagga*: "A non-material tally-stick from the Saṅgha...
is indeed permissible. And in the *Sāratthadīpanī* it is also said: "Even a non-material tally-stick from the Saṅgha, or cooked rice prepared within a monastery, is indeed permissible."
Since this is common [to all] and because it is stated in the *Visuddhimagga* that "when things are thus accepted, they may be consumed;
when they are not thus accepted, they may not be consumed," without making such a distinction, the underlying intention here must be investigated as follows:

"Although medicinal sticks (*salākā*) and the like are permissible even for those who subsist on alms-food (*piṇḍapātika*), because they are accepted by way of counting sticks (*salākā*), they should not be consumed. For if...
Voting sticks for medicine and the like, once they have been taken by way of a vote, must not be accepted;
one should not say, "A non-material voting stick from the Saṅgha is permissible," because of such statements as, "An extra gain consists of a meal for the Saṅgha, a designated meal," and so forth.
Furthermore, when saying, "I refuse an extra gain," it is specifically the meal that is refused by way of the voting stick.
It is not medicine. For it is stated that the fourteen types of meals, such as *saṅghabhatta* (meals for the Saṅgha), are precisely those which he must not accept.

Or, according to the opinion of the reciters of the *Khandhaka*, it should be understood that this is stated here [in this specific context]. "Almsfood to be given from the best" (*aggabhikkhā*) means almsfood to be given from the very top.
"The measure of the best almsfood" (*aggabhikkhāmatta*) means the measure of a single ladle of almsfood. Whether he has received it or not.
The phrase "you might take it tomorrow" was said even when [food] has been obtained, in order to encourage heedfulness. Therefore he said: "He receives as much as needed... [etc.
...if he does not receive it, he should be told: 'You may take it tomorrow. For here, the word *matta* (measure/only) excludes the idea of abundance (*bahubhāva*).

"Salākabhatta" (ticket-food) is designated specifically for the monastery; because it is given with reference to the monastery alone, he says, "but that which has not been assigned to the monastery," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in the assembly hall there": it means in the assembly hall in that village. "Having brought it to the monastery, it should be distributed":
having said this, the food given on that day must be brought to the monastery and distributed according to the established order (*ṭhitikā*).
*Therein* means in that direction or region. *Having taken that* means having taken that voting-ticket (*salāka*) of the ward-village (*vāragāma*) for oneself.
*By him* refers to the one who gave the ticket in the ward-village assigned to himself to the person traveling to the district.

"The ticket must be given to him while he has not yet passed beyond" means that since the ticket reaches only one who is still within the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*), therefore, in that [case]...
The voting tickets (*pattasalākā*) should be distributed to that traveler once he has reached the boundary of the vicinity (*upacārasīma*) but before he has actually crossed it.
"They should be distributed daily" means they should be distributed by lot (*vassaggena*) to anyone standing within the boundary of the vicinity.
Thus, if these [tickets] have not arrived, it is permissible for the monks in the nearby monastery to eat; otherwise, it is [the property] of the Saṅgha.
[It] exists. If it is asked: "How is the state of having arrived or not yet arrived understood regarding those monks in the phrase 'on the day yet to come'?
It is because the monks who have arrived from here and there assemble in that village at the assembly hall; therefore, their state of having arrived or not yet arrived can be known.
"In our alms-village" means in the village of those who give the *salākabhatta* (ticket-food).
“They are coming to eat,” they think, imagining: “The Great Elder must have stayed behind alone in the monastery, and he will surely have received all the voting-slips for himself.
The commentary on the discussion of the *salākabhatta* (ticket-food) is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of Fortnightly Meals, etc. (213).
A meal to be given on four specifically marked days of the fortnight is called *pakkhika* (fortnightly). Regarding the word "specifically marked" (*abhilakkhitesu*):

here, *abhi-* is merely an intensifier; the meaning is simply "in those that are marked. This refers to [days] for the purpose of undertaking the Uposatha, listening to the Dhamma, performing offerings, showing respect, and so forth.
"Among those things to be characterized" means they are to be observed, noted, and distinguished. "Tomorrow's portion" means that which belongs to today must not be taken;
it should be eaten on the eighth day, and it must not be taken for the purpose of eating on the seventh.
The meaning is that it should be taken only on the day specifically determined by the donors. Therefore he said, "But if," and so forth. "Rough tomorrow" refers to today.
Because of performing auspicious rites such as the welcoming ceremony (*āvāha*), very refined food is prepared; the intention is: "It will not be like that tomorrow;
we shall feed the monks this very day. However, it is stated differently in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
In order to show the distinction between the fortnightly meal (*pakkhika-bhatta*) and the Uposatha-day meal, he said: "Having undertaken the factors of the Uposatha," and so forth. On the Uposatha...
The meal for the Uposatha day should be given.
The commentary on the discussion concerning the fortnightly meal and so forth is finished.
Commentary on the discussion concerning the meal for guests and so forth.
214. "Nibandhāpitaṃ" means it has been designated, as in: "Let guests eat at such-and-such monastery.
"A traveler [may receive] even guest-food" is said with reference to one who, having come from another village and stayed with the intention of traveling not yet extinguished, then goes elsewhere;
however, for a resident monk who wishes to go, only traveler's food is obtained. "Having cast a hint" means...

It should be understood that because it was stated [in the rule], it is made known that it is permissible to eat as long as the obstruction to going away has not disappeared due to the absence of *lesā*.

215. Regarding the commentary on the discussion of "regular meals" (*dhurabhatta*) and so forth: "They send rice and other provisions... it is permissible. It is permissible because these are gifts brought specifically for the monk (*abhihaṭabhikkhā*).

216. "Because it was accepted in that manner" means because it was accepted under the name of alms-food. "Given after filling and setting aside the bowl" means given with the words, "We give you a lump of rice. The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the vessel for alms-food is finished.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the vessel for medicinal requisites.

217. Hereafter, although a discussion on the distribution of lodgings and vessels should be spoken of according to the sequence of the requisites, because that subject is vast, and because the discussion on the distribution of the requisite of medicine is limited in scope, and because it follows the sequence of the distribution of alms-food, the author says, "Now, as for the distribution of the requisite of medicine," etc., in order to present that next.
In this context, "kings, royal ministers, and great officials" refers to...
This is merely by way of illustration; Brahmin mahāsālas, householder mahāsālas, and others do exactly the same.
"Having struck the bell," and so forth, is easily understood because it follows the method explained below and is self-evident. "The boundary of the precincts...
should be divided"—this is stated because [the property] was given for the sake of the Saṅgha. "But having turned toward the water-jar" means the water-jar.
Having turned it toward the direction [of the wind]. "If there is ghee that is 'thina' (stiff)" means if the ghee is hard.
"It is permissible to give even a little bit" means that if it is prepared in this way, it will remain stable.

"Medicine such as ginger, black pepper, and so forth, as well as the remaining requisites of a monk such as bowls, pots, and so on"—by this it is shown that not only medicine is a requisite for the sick, but rather, the remaining requisites are also included within the requisite for the sick.
He shows that [the bowl] is indeed included within [the requisites].
The commentary on the discussion regarding the vessel for medicinal requisites is finished.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the assignment of lodgings begins.

218. Regarding the discussion on the distribution of lodgings (*senāsanabhājana*), the "determination regarding the taking of lodgings" (*senāsanaggāhe vinicchayo*) refers specifically to the distribution of lodgings itself. Therein, the construction is as follows:
the taking of lodgings is twofold by way of time—namely, the taking of lodgings during the [ordinary] seasons (*utukāla*) and the taking of lodgings during the rainy-season residence (*vassāvāsa*).
Among these, "during the seasons" means during the winter and summer seasons; "during the rainy-season residence" means during the period of the rains.

Having roused a bhikkhu, the lodging should be given to him; for there is no such thing as an "inopportune time" regarding lodgings belonging to the Saṅgha that have been given by donors with the words, "I give this to the Saṅgha of the four quarters, both present and future.
"One cell each" means one cell for each individual bhikkhu. "Therein" means in that cell which has been obtained. "Long hall" means a walking-hall.
“Maṇḍalamāḷa” means a hall for attendance. “Anudahati” means to oppress.

“He does not get to take it” indicates that for one who intentionally prevents entry by not giving [the space], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). “In Jambudīpa, however,” is said with reference to monks in the Noble Land;
it is said that they indeed designate it in such a manner.
219. "The village within one's range should not be disturbed" explains the meaning already stated by the words "no people there should be addressed," and so forth.
"Having cut off thought" means not giving rise to such a thought as, "Seeing me going in this manner, they will stop me and give me requisites.
"If one among them" means if one wise person among those people. "Concealment of goods" [is explained as follows].

"Concealing goods" means a robe for concealing the body; this is the meaning. The statement "it is blameless precisely because of a pure mind" is said with reference to the explanation of the reason at the moment of being questioned;
it does not mean that there is no fault even for one with an impure mind when answering a question that has been asked.
Rather, it should be understood as being said with reference to the refusal to go [to the city] out of the thought, "They will question me once things have come to such a pass."
"Should be looked after" means they should be maintained by repairing broken or dilapidated parts, sweeping, and so forth.
"On the circular railing" refers to the square railing on top of the hemispherical (ghaṭākāra) railing of the shrine (*cetiya*).
"Where should it be asked?"—the answer is that it should be asked where the answer is naturally obtained. "Why should it be asked? and so forth.
Since it is obtained by way of its nature, this was stated there as well for the purpose of showing the reason for the inquiry.
"Having stepped back" means having moved away from the monastery. Showing that meaning, he said: "It is at a distance of one or two *yojanas*.

"Depositing" means having handed over a field, or a grove of coconut trees and so forth, or coins such as *kahāpaṇa*s, to the monastery attendants [with the instruction]: "From this, [let the produce] arise..."

“May there be an increase for the sake of the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season residence) provisions”—thus it was given. “Having performed the duties” means having performed the duties that must be done in that dwelling place.
“In this gift of faith” means, in the sense of what is to be given out of faith regarding the object of the *vassāvāsika* gain, according to the manner explained above.
“But as for the property” refers to the money (*rūpiya*) arising from that source; and that [is meant by] “you should enjoy it as the four requisites from that.”

Because it arises from a field or other property given [to the Saṅgha], it is similar to the items given by donors to the *kappiyakārakas* (those who prepare what is allowable) with the words, "Enjoy these allowable goods"; thus he said, "For the *kappiyakārakas*," and so forth.

"For the welfare of the Saṅgha" means for the benefit of the Saṅgha. "It should be done by way of an individual alone" refers to the method that will be explained later, whereby the monks [are provided] with robes.

[The transaction] should be performed by way of referring to individuals (*puggalaparāmāsa*), such as saying, "The monks find it wearisome [to receive] this much portion of rice for making robes," and so forth;
however, it should not be performed by way of referring to the Saṅgha (*saṅghaparāmāsa*), such as saying, "The Saṅgha finds it wearisome regarding the robe.
To clarify the meaning already stated generally by the term "suitable goods" (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*), [the text says]: "By way of robes, rice, and so forth..."
And so it is said. Here, the letter *ca* should be understood as having the sense of the particle *pana* (moreover/furthermore), and not the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
To show the manner of seeking permission (*apalokana*) both with respect to the person and with respect to the allowable object (*kappiya-bhaṇḍa*), it was said:
"But that should be done thus," and so forth.

"Having observed the requisite of robes" means having delimited the requisite known as the robe obtainable during that *vassāvāsa*—by way of what is given out of faith or what arises by chance—as being "only this much.
"Of the lodging" refers to the person who assigns lodgings. "It is said" means it is said in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
To the question "Why is it said thus?", he says "For in this way," etc., [referring] to the one who assigns lodgings.
It is improper for one to take [the lodging] oneself; therefore, the intention is that both should take it from each other.
It should be understood that even if another has already taken it by the command of the one who has been appointed to assign lodgings, the taking is nonetheless valid.
It is permissible to appoint eight or sixteen people; this means it is permissible to appoint them individually. Or rather—
"Is it permissible to do so together? It is indeed permissible to do so together. It is permissible for all to be appointed together by a single formal act of motion (*kammavācā*).
For the Saṅgha does not carry out a disciplinary action (*niggaha-kamma*) against itself;

however, it is permissible to grant an appointment (*sammuti-dāna*) to many people together. For this very reason, in the Sattasatika-kkhandhaka, eight persons were appointed together in the appointment of a committee of officials (*ubbāhika-sammuti*). "The house of seats" (*āsana-ghara*)...
"A shrine room" (*paṭimāghara*): "A grove" (*magga*) refers to a hall built on a path leading toward a village that is within the boundary of the vicinity (*upacārasīma*);
the same applies to lotus ponds, the foot of a tree, and so forth. The foot of a tree and other such places are dwellings only when they are covered and secured with doors.
The passages following this are easy to understand.
220. In the discourse on the Mahālābha courtyard, "they receive" means that the monks residing there receive [the gifts].
"Having separated" means having divided [the goods] into portions sufficient for each individual. "In the residences" means in the lodgings (senāsana).
"Having placed therein" refers here to the placing of the *vassāvāsika* gift arising from this [courtyard] for those living in them. "It should be entered" means by other monks.
The intention is that, having stayed in that large dwelling (*pariveṇa*) and performed the duties toward the shrine (*cetiya*), one should receive the alms-offering (*lābha*). 221.
"He rejects the requisite" means he does not accept the robe-requisite (*cīvara-paccaya*). "This too" refers even to the requisite rejected by him.
"Placing it at the base of his feet and giving a cloth" means the donors of the requisite give it; by this, [it is shown] that from householders, at the base of the feet—
This shows that even what is given [to them] after being set aside is permissible for *paṃsukūlika* monks.
Regarding the phrase "if they say, 'We give it as a *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season gift),'": here, one must supply and connect the words "it is not permissible for *paṃsukūlika* monks.
"To the monks who have completed the rains residence" refers to monks other than the *paṃsukūlikas*. "Having bound it, it should be distributed" means: "In this tree... or...
"Having stayed in the pavilion or performed the duty at the shrine, receive [the rains-residence],"—having thus bound [the invitation], it should be given.

The phrase "from the dawn of the first day of the month," etc., is said with reference to the day of entering the rains-residence (*vassūpanāyika*). However, it is permissible to give the invitation even after passing the first day of the month, in the case of one who has entered the rains-residence in between.
"Where indeed shall I dwell? Where, dwelling, will there be comfort?"...
One who "wanders with thoughts" (*vitakkacāriko*) is so called because they act upon a thought that has arisen such as, "Will there be [something]? or "Where will I obtain the requisite conditions?

Now, in order to show the procedure for dealing with the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe) that donors give to those who have spent the final rains-retreat, the passage beginning with "But on the day of the later invitation (*pacchimavassūpanāyikā*)" was commenced.
"If he is a visiting monk... (*āgantuko ce bhikkhū*)... [and so forth].

After the robes have been taken, a visiting monk arrives later. "In the place where the alms-bowl is kept" means in the place where the visiting monk’s bowl is kept according to the seniority of the rains-residence.

"Those who entered the rains-residence earlier" means those who had already entered for the later rains-retreat even before the visitor arrived. "Whatever has been obtained" means whatever cloth has been received repeatedly from donors as they arrive.
For it is said that even those who have accepted [the invitation] are considered to have broken their rains-residence because they are the owners of the *vassāvāsika* (rains-residence gift).
It is stated that "they do not get to withhold" because the agreement was made at the very outset; the intention is that there is liability for those who prevent the gift from being given.
"It must be given to them alone" means that it must be given only to certain individuals among those who have entered the rains-residence but have not yet received the *vassāvāsika*.
"Bhatiniviṭṭhaṃ" means obtained as if by performing labor (*bhati*); or alternatively, "bhatiniviṭṭhaṃ" means obtained by performing labor such as serving with water and so forth.
"But that which belongs to the Saṅgha," etc., is a presentation of the arguments of certain [teachers].

Therein, "but that which belongs to the Saṅgha was taken after performing an act of formal announcement (*apalokanakamma*)" is said with reference to what arises from that source. In that context, "taken after performing an act of formal announcement" means...

Having performed the formal announcement (*apalokana*) according to the method stated immediately before— “It is pleasing to give this to both those whose rainy-season residence has been cut off and those for whom the rainy-season residence is about to arise”—
what was taken by the Saṅgha is indeed obtained even by one who has left the order (*vibbhanta*), let alone one whose rainy-season residence has been cut off. However,
regarding what was taken on account of requisites (*paccaya*), after having resided for three months, it may be taken by oneself and by the donors.

Some teachers say that even one who has been assigned as a laborer (*bhati-niviṭṭha*), or one whose rains-residence (*vassa*) has been interrupted, or one who has gone away (*vibbhanta*), does not receive [the robe-cloth].
This statement, however, is authoritative because it was stated later;

for that very reason, on the day of entering the rains-residence, it was established below that only the actual dwelling by a monk who has accepted the *vassāvāsika* cloth given by donors—provided he does not break his rains-residence—is intended, and not merely the performance of labor such as providing water and so forth.

For if it were already fixed as a share of the alms-food (*bhakti*), then only the act of making the offering would need to be performed; therefore, it should be understood that those who have taken the *vassa* but then break it, such as those whose *vassa* has been interrupted, do not receive [the share]. This is because of the statement:
“In this case, monks, if a monk who has completed the *vassa* disrobes, it belongs to the Saṅgha alone. From the words: “In the place of retreat... [and so forth]...”

"It becomes the property of the Saṅgha," it is said. By the phrase "it becomes the property of the Saṅgha," it is shown that even for those who have completed their rains-residence, their share of the *vassāvāsika* (rains-bathing robe) has not been released from the status of being the Saṅgha’s property; thus, through their departure (*vibbhama*), it becomes the property of the Saṅgha. "Among men" refers to the donor-men.
"He receives" means that by having the donor accept [the robe] with the words, "Give this to him as his rightful portion," it is [received] from the status of being the Saṅgha’s property.

It is said, "it becomes separated. Regarding the phrase "the superior portion for the novice": this is stated because he is the first to take a seat, because the Elder had previously taken the first portion, and because what is being taken now constitutes the second portion. 222.
Now, in order to show the taking of a lodging that has been vacated in the interim, he says, "This is another," and so forth. Therein, "another" means...
The meaning is that there is another [method] besides the two ways of taking lodgings mentioned previously.
One might object: "Has it not been stated that 'this taking of lodgings is twofold: for the [dry] season and for the rainy residence'? So why is it said, 'This is another,' and so forth?
Anticipating this challenge, he says, "By way of the day," and so on. "On the Āsāḷhī full moon of the following day" refers to the day of the first entry into the rains residence.

This was said with reference to the first day of the month following the full moon of Āsāḷha; "the Āsāḷha month having elapsed" refers to the first day of the month following the full moon of Sāvaṇa, which is the day of the second *vassa*-ordination (*vassūpanāyikā*).
"The invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) having taken place on the following day" refers to the first day of the month following the full moon of Assayuja.
223. "One may not refuse [entrance] during the proper season" means that one may not refuse other monks who have arrived during the winter or summer seasons.
“He does not obtain it. “New construction” (*navakamma*) means formal authorization for new construction (*navakammasammuti*). “Unbuilt” means not yet fashioned. “Incomplete” means unfinished.
“Having given one place for a bed” means having given one place for a bed as private property (*puggalika*).
“A third part” means a one-third share. Thus, even such a relinquishment falls within the very scope of the exchange of durable goods for durable goods.
Not otherwise, because all lodgings must be relinquished. "If he wishes to give [the bedding] to his co-resident and others" means:

if he does not wish to give it to the Sangha’s storehouse or to the dwelling place of other bhikkhus, but wishes to give it only to his own co-residents and others—[the Buddha said] to such a person: "It is yours alone as private property."

The intention is that not everything must be given [to him] by saying, "Having prepared it, he took charge. In that context, showing the procedure to be followed for him, he said, "The work," and so forth.

For in this way—referring to the phrase beginning with "Evañhi"—the meaning is that when a third part or a half-part has been taken according to the accumulation, he is entitled to receive that portion.
"By whom" means by whichever one among those two or three monks; "he is the owner" means...
The intention is that he alone is the master in the construction of a dwelling on that ground; having excluded him, it must not be done by anyone else.
224. "In a place where no structure has been built" means in a place outside the monastery where a heap or the like has not been made.
"A heap or a front porch" refers to either a single dwelling constructed outside and adjacent to the property of the Saṅgha. "Outside the wall" means outside the wall.
"Outside" means in one's own assigned place. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the taking of lodgings is finished.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the commonality of the four requisites.

225. Regarding the discussion on the commonality of the four requisites: "by one appointed as a distributor of trifles" means by one who has been formally authorized through either a formal act consisting of a motion followed by a second (ñattidutiyakamma) or a formal act of intimation (apalokanakamma).
"Undivided property belonging to the Saṅgha"—the phrase "there is no need to ask" regarding "undivided property belonging to the Saṅgha" is an illustration of the manner in which remorse arises.
Thus, having raised this doubt, the intention is that there is no need for a formal inquiry, and it should simply be given without asking. Why is that?
Because the formal act of authorization (*sammutikamma*) was performed with the consent of a unanimous Saṅgha specifically for the purpose of distributing such property belonging to the Saṅgha.
Regarding the phrase "a lump of sugar... should be given," here a "lump of sugar" is the size of a palm fruit.
This should be understood. "Even for one who has entered for alms" is merely an illustration;

the same principle applies even to one who has gone outside the boundary for some other reason. "A share of rice" refers to a share of rice belonging to the Saṅgha, such as that from a communal meal (*saṅghabhatta*).

"Standing within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*)" uses the genitive case in a sense of disregard; it is permissible to take [the portion] only for one standing within the precinct boundary, not otherwise.
The meaning is: "having reached the outer boundary (upacārasīma). For this is said in the Commentary: "They say, 'Let them take [the robe] from those standing outside the outer boundary';
it should not be taken [from there]. Regarding the phrase "even for one standing inside the village," the word *pi* (even/also) here has the sense of including what was not explicitly mentioned;
thus the meaning is that it is permissible to take [the robe] from one standing either inside the village or outside the village. Or, it has the sense of esteem (*sambhāvana*); by that—
It is permissible to take possession even of a place within the village, let alone a place outside the village.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the commonality of the four requisites is concluded.
Thus ends the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
The Twenty-eighth Chapter, titled "The Ornament of the Discourse on the Analysis of the Distribution of the Four Requisites.
Explanation of the Discourse on the Analysis of Monasteries.

Now, because the monastery is included among the four requisites, the exposition analyzing the monastery is commenced immediately after the exposition on the distribution of the four requisites. Regarding this, it is said:
“What is a monastery? In what sense is it a ‘monastery’?
Of how many kinds is that monastery?”
By whom was it seized, and to whom should it be given?
How, and who, is its master? By whom was it taken, and for whom?
How many are those not to be sent away?
With how many factors is one endowed [to receive it]?
To whom who dwells permanently is it given?
In this context, what is a "dwelling" (*vihāra*)? Among the four requisites, it is that which is reckoned as a lodging;

among the four types of lodgings, it is the specific residence serving as the abode for monks, known as a monastery-lodging (*vihāra-senāsana*). In what sense is it a "dwelling"? It is a dwelling because "they dwell here" (*viharanti ettha*);
the meaning is that the Noble Ones dwell here by means of the four dwellings known as the postures, the divine, the sublime, and the noble.
Thus, as to how many kinds there are: it is threefold by way of a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, a monastery belonging to a group, and a monastery belonging to an individual.

For this has been stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "In the case of one who makes a claim against a monastery, a courtyard, or a dwelling given to the monks for the sake of the Saṅgha of the four quarters—whether large or small—the claim does not hold; nor can he take it back by force."
He is not able. Why? Because there is no laying down of the burden by all [the monks]. For it is not the case that all the monks from the four quarters lay down their burden here.

However, one who seizes and takes possession of what belongs to a group—such as those distinguished as Dīghabhāṇakas and so forth—or to a single individual, is able to make them lay down their burden;
therefore, in that case, according to the method stated for the monastery:
“The detailed exposition should be understood. By this, it is shown that there is no such thing as a monastery belonging to a donor.
By whom should it be given? It should be given by a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, or whoever else.
To whom should it be given? It should be given to the Saṅgha, to a group (gaṇa), or to an individual (puggala). How should it be given? If to the Saṅgha...

If he gives it to the Saṅgha, saying, “I give this monastery to the Saṅgha of the four quarters, both present and future,” if to a group, saying, “I give this monastery to the Venerable Ones,” or if to an individual, saying, “I give this monastery to the Venerable One”—it should be given in this manner.
As for who is its master: if he gives it to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha is the master of that monastery. If...
If he gives it to a group, the group is its master; if he gives it to an individual, the individual is its master.
For thus it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "It belongs to a group, such as the Dīghabhāṇakas, or to a single individual.
By whom was it taken? It was taken by the assigner of lodgings (*senāsanaggāhāpaka*). For this was said by the Blessed One: "I authorize..."
“Monks, one endowed with five qualities should be appointed as the assigner of lodgings:
he should not fall into a wrong course through favoritism, nor through hatred, nor through delusion. And thus, monks, should he be appointed:
first, the monk should be requested; having requested him, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:”
“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha appoint the monk named so-and-so as the assigner of lodgings.
This is the motion. “Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. The Saṅgha appoints the monk named so-and-so as the assigner of lodgings.
Whichever venerable one approves of the appointment of the monk named so-and-so as the assigner of lodgings, let him be silent. [End of motion]”
"Whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The Saṅgha has appointed the monk named so-and-so as the assigner of lodgings; this is approved by the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this. To whom was it assigned?
That monastery was assigned to the monks. For this was said by the Blessed One: "I allow..."
“Monks, first the monks should be counted; having counted the monks, the beds should be counted; having counted the beds, they should be assigned by way of the beds.

How many are those who are not to be made to rise? There are four who are not to be made to rise: one who is senior, one who is sick, the storekeeper, and one who has received his lodging from the Saṅgha.
For this has been said in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*: “Indeed, one who is old...”
One who is exempt from service due to his own advanced age, or one who is ill due to his illness;

however, the Saṅgha—having observed the great assistance and distinguished virtues of a storekeeper, or of Dhamma-preachers, Vinaya-holders, or masters of the recitation of the texts—and having designated a monastery for permanent residence, formally appoints and grants it to him.
Therefore, as for whomsoever it has been granted by the Saṅgha...
"He too must not be made to perform [the duties].
To how many qualities must one be endowed to be granted permanent residence?
At the highest limit, a monastery is granted for permanent residence to one endowed with two qualities. Which two? Being of great assistance and being distinguished by special virtues.
If it is asked, "How is this known?"—it is because of the statement in the *Vinayathamañjūsā*:

"The phrase 'of great service' refers to the state of being of great service through various roles such as a storekeeper and so forth; he says 'and distinguished by qualities' to show that it is not merely this [one role].

By this, he demonstrates that it is appropriate to give [the robe] even when there is great service but an absence of distinction in qualities, and also when there is distinction in qualities but an absence of great service. This is stated with reference to the minimum requirement.
"Even for one endowed with only a single factor. With which single factor? Either with "great helpfulness" (*bahūpakāratā*) or with "excellence of qualities" (*guṇavisiṭṭhatā*).
If it is asked how this is known, it is because of the statement in the *Sāratthadīpanī*:
"Observing great helpfulness and excellence of qualities" means observing the great helpfulness of the storekeeper and the excellence of qualities of those such as the Dhamma-preachers.

The taking of lodgings (*senāsanaggāha*), moreover, is twofold according to time: during the season (*utu-kāla*) and during the rains residence (*vassa-āvāsa*). Alternatively, there are three ways of taking lodgings: the earlier, the later, and that which is released in the interim.
Their distinction has already been stated below. "The taking of lodgings during the season is twofold:
that which is released in the interim and that which is seclusion for that moment (*taṅkhaṇa-paṭisallāna*). The taking of lodgings during the rains residence is the earlier..."

The teachers say, "There are four ways of taking lodgings: the first, the last, and the 'released in between'—thus there are two types," but that statement appears neither in the Canon nor in the Commentary.
In the Canon, however, it is stated thus: "Monks, there are these three ways of taking lodgings:
the first, the last, and the 'released in between. And in the Commentary as well, regarding the three ways of taking lodgings...
"The two acquisitions—the 'prior' and the 'subsequent'—are fixed; this is the analysis regarding those acquired in between," so it has been handed down.
Now, however, some teachers say: "At this time, all monasteries belong exclusively to the Saṅgha; there is no such thing as a private monastery. Why?

Because at the time when the donors of the monasteries were giving them away, they [the donors] designated [them] for their own families, saying: 'This monastery is for those who have come and those yet to come...'"
They cause a verbal declaration to be made, saying, "We give this to the Saṅgha of the four quarters"; therefore, even the new monasteries belong to the Saṅgha.
Regarding certain monasteries where they give without making such a statement, it is said: "While he lives, it belongs to the individual; when he is dead, it belongs to the Saṅgha alone.
Because of this being stated, they say that even the ancient monasteries belong to the Saṅgha. In this regard, it should be investigated as follows:
Even regarding monasteries built by donors after they have had verbal instructions given, those who build them specifically for the Saṅgha are few;
rather, having thought, "I will have such-and-such a bhikkhu or such-and-such an elder dwell here," they establish them after consulting with their children, wives, friends, ministers, and so forth.
Although they may not speak at the time of the formal establishment, for the most part they do speak at the time of the donation.

However, when personal attendants (*kulūpaka*) instruct donors at the time of giving and cause them to speak thus, even though they do so, those donors give only a small portion dedicated to the Saṅgha;
the greater portion they give dedicated specifically to their own personal attendant.
This being the case, the words of the personal attendants are included among the nine "unrighteous gifts" described as: "what was dedicated to an individual, one dedicates to the Saṅgha."
One incurs an unrighteous gift (*adhammikadāna*). Regarding the reading, "While he lives it belongs to the individual;

when he is dead, it belongs to the Saṅgha," this has not been handed down in reference to a fundamentally individual monastery (*mūlapuggalikavihāra*); rather, it is handed down in the context of having an individual monastery built where there was previously none, in order to maintain a fundamentally communal monastery (*mūlasaṅghikavihāra*).
Therefore, even new monasteries exist that were indeed given for the sake of an individual. As for ancient monasteries, they too [originated] at their foundation...

Even if [a dwelling] given as private property is later given as private property to a student (*saddhivihārika*) or others, or even if it is taken on trust while the donor is still alive, it remains private property.
Therefore, the claim that there is an absolute absence of private monasteries (*puggalika-vihāra*) must be examined.
However, other teachers maintain: "At this time, so-called 'monasteries belonging to the Saṅgha' do not exist; all are indeed private."

"Why? Because even the nine new monasteries were built specifically for a particular monk (*puggalika*)—both at the time of their foundation and at the time of their donation—and because even the ancient monasteries were already occupied by disciples, grand-disciples, or other individuals;
since they were never occupied by the Saṅgha, they remain *puggalika* and not *saṅghika*," so they say. Regarding that as well, it is thus:
It should be investigated: even when establishing a new monastery, or at the time of making a gift, some build for the sake of the Saṅgha, while others build for an individual (puggala).

Even in the case of those who have previously built for an individual, upon hearing the words of wise people who desire their welfare, they may come to believe that a gift to the Saṅgha is far more fruitful than a gift to an individual, and thus they may build for the Saṅgha.
There are donors; even in ancient monasteries that were accepted as private property, some monks, at the time of death, hand them over to the Saṅgha.
Some die without having given anything to anyone, and then that monastery becomes the property of the Saṅgha.
However, when kings, royal ministers, and others are constructing a great monastery with a specific foundation, they [specify] "for a measure of five thousand years..."
Having made the aspiration, "As long as the Dispensation endures, may the Saṅgha dwell in my monastery and enjoy the four requisites," they give villages,
fields, and so forth— which produce requisites for the Saṅgha over a long period— saying, "We give these to our monastery.
And by saying "to the monastery," they give them specifically for the Saṅgha dwelling in that monastery, not for one who has become a family-dependent (kulūpaka).
[The dwellings] belong to a single individual; therefore, they are mostly seen as belonging to the Saṅgha, and they even record this by inscribing characters upon stones.
Consequently, the claim that there were no monasteries belonging to the Saṅgha at all must also be investigated.
However, other teachers maintain: "At this time, [the dwellings] belonged only to the donors of the monasteries; therefore, it is the donors themselves who should be consulted."
The owners are the [donor's] family, not the Saṅgha, nor an individual.

Even when the donor of the monastery is no longer present, his sons, daughters, grandsons, great-grandsons, and so forth, remain the owners of that monastery for as long as the lineage continues. Why is this? Because it is stated:
"He by whom the monastery was caused to be built is the master of the monastery," and because of the statement: "Or anyone from his family may be consulted."
The owner of the monastery, the donor, or one born in his lineage is the master with authority to manage it.

According to the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "When the family lineage has been cut off, whoever is the lord of that district may take it back and give it again—just as the chief queen of King Aḷanāga took back and gave again the water-conduit brought by a monk at Cittalapabbata—this is also permissible," [the authority belongs] to the donor of the monastery.

Some say: "Even when the family lineage has been cut off, it is appropriate for whoever is the lord of that district—whether a king, a royal minister, or any other authority—to manage the monastery and grant [benefits] according to their inclination. Other wise men do not approve of this. How so?
The statement, "He by whom the monastery was built is the owner of the monastery," was spoken according to ancient usage.
This is not now by way of ownership, as in the case of Jetavana, where [one says] "the owner of the bowl," and so forth.

For just as when the analysis "Jetavana" is formed as "the grove (vana), the pleasure garden (uyyāna) of Prince (jetta) Jeta," even though from the time Anāthapiṇḍika purchased it and established the monastery,
the prince was no longer the owner of that garden, nevertheless, from the time it was purchased by Anāthapiṇḍika...
Because it was formerly the property of a lord (*issara*), it is always designated as "Jetavana" by way of that former designation.
And just as when the term "owner of the bowl" (*pattassāmika*) is formed from the compound *pattassa sāmiko*,
even though the smith ceases to be the master of the bowl from the moment it is purchased and given to the monk by the donors, nevertheless, from the time it was purchased by the donor—
Because he was previously a master, he is designated by way of that former usage as "the owner of the monastery"; likewise,
although from the time the gift is made the donor is no longer the master of the monastery— since the characteristic of giving is the relinquishment of the object—
nevertheless, because he was previously a master before the time of the gift, he is designated by way of that former usage as "the owner of the monastery."
It is understood that [the Sangha] is designated as such by way of conventional usage (*vohāra*), and not primarily because of its status as an owner (*issara*).
Therefore, from the moment a gift is given to the Sangha, a group, or an individual, it is the recipients—the Sangha and so forth—who have authority over it, not the donor.
If one asks how this is known: even though there were donors of monasteries such as Anāthapiṇḍika, [the Buddha said]: "I allow you, monks... [and so on].

Having authorized a monk endowed with five qualities as the assigner of lodgings after he had been formally appointed by the Saṅgha through such statements as, “...to appoint a monk as the assigner of lodgings,” and having further stated regarding the authority of that very assigner of lodgings, “I authorize you, monks...
to assign [lodgings] down to a single bed,” [the text continues]: “Two monks [may take] what belongs to the Saṅgha...”
"Having taken and cleared the ground, they make it a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha; he by whom that ground was first taken is the owner.
And: "If both of them make it their own private property, he alone is the owner. Furthermore:

"But if someone, without taking even as much as a creeper’s worth of land belonging to the Saṅgha, causes a private vihāra to be built on Saṅgha land using imported materials, [the Saṅgha owns] half."

It is understood from the fact that the *Aṭṭhakathā* states, "Half belongs to the Saṅgha and half is personal," thereby indicating that ownership belongs specifically to the Saṅgha and the individual;
and even the *Aṭṭhakathā* statement, "Or anyone from his family may be asked for permission," demonstrates their lordship over the monastery.

It is not that [the offense does not exist]; rather, it indicates that when a monk intending to travel departs while the monks, novices, or monastery attendants who should have been informed in the monastery are absent, he must depart only after having informed them. For this is said in the Commentary:
"But having spread out, or having caused to be spread out, this tenfold bedding in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, one who is departing..."
"One must depart after having taken leave. And when taking leave, if a monk is present, a monk should be asked for leave...
if he is not there, a monastery attendant; if he too is not there, the one by whom the monastery was built, that is, the owner of the monastery;

or anyone belonging to his family should be asked for leave. Thus, since one must also take leave of a monastery attendant, [the rule] is for the purpose of observation, being governed by the standard of proper conduct.
It should be understood that [the donor] must ask for permission; it is not because they possess ownership over the Sangha’s lodgings.

Furthermore, regarding the statement beginning with "when the family lineage has been cut off," this refers to fields, lands, reservoirs, and so forth—which were acquired through improper means or accepted by means of improper speech—and which have been relinquished by monks because they are unallowable (*akappiya*);
these are [given back] by kings and others for the purpose of making them allowable (*kappiyakaraṇa*).
Having received it, he explains that it is a gift for those very monks alone; it is not a gift for those kings and others, nor for other Saṅghas, groups, individuals, or shrines by those monks.
If they were to give it away, there would be unrighteous giving, unrighteous receiving, and unrighteous enjoyment.
For this has been stated in the Parivāra: "There are nine kinds of unrighteous gifts: [giving] what is dedicated to one Saṅgha to another Saṅgha..."
“Or he dedicates it to a shrine, or to an individual; what was dedicated to a shrine he dedicates to another shrine, to the Saṅgha, or to an individual;
what was dedicated to an individual he dedicates to another individual, to the Saṅgha, or to a shrine.
And in the Commentary it is said: “There are nine unrighteous gifts... [and so on]... thus they are spoken of.”
"Nine kinds of acceptance and enjoyment" means "the acceptances and the enjoyments of these very same gifts," as it has been said.
Therefore, if kings and others, considering themselves masters, were to give to another, that gift would be an unrighteous gift;
that gift and its acceptance would be unrighteous acceptances, and those who enjoy that gift would be unrighteous enjoyers—this is how it should be understood.

Furthermore, they might say: "In such passages as 'The gift of a monastery to the Saṅgha is the foremost, praised by the Buddha,' the word 'to the Saṅgha' (saṅghassa) does not have a connection with ownership (*sāmibhāva*) here in relation to the word 'gift';
rather, it is simply the recipient (*sampadāna*). However, a connection with ownership must be supplied for the word 'of the donor' (*dāyakassa*);
therefore, the donor alone, being the owner, is the master, and not the one who is the recipient."

‘The Saṅgha. They should be told as follows: “‘A gift of a dwelling to the Saṅgha’—this was said with reference to the state of affairs at the time of giving, not with reference to the state of affairs at the time it has been given.

For at the time of giving, the donor gives after having relinquished to the Saṅgha the dwelling which is his own property; therefore, at that time, the donor is the owner and the Saṅgha is the recipient.”
At the time of giving, however, the Saṅgha alone is the owner because the monastery has been accepted; the donor is not, because it has been relinquished.
Therefore, the Saṅgha is the master to decide [its use]. Thus the Blessed One said: "That, bhikkhus, has been relinquished by the donors.
This was stated so that those who value the characteristics of grammar might have faith; but in terms of meaning, regarding the four requisites such as robes and so forth—
It is evident to everyone that at the very moment of giving, the requisites become the property of the donor, and from the time they are given, they become the property of the recipient;
therefore, this statement also should be understood as not proving that they remain the property of the donor.
Let it be so; nevertheless, [the opponent might argue]: "If, having learned that the items have been relinquished by the monks, the owner or his sons and daughters..."

Since it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Or if anyone else born in the lineage gives again by means of a permissible transaction (*kappiya-vohāra*), it is allowable," it follows that the authority to give belongs either to the donor who is the owner of the monastery or to those born in the lineage of his sons, daughters, and so forth.
[Objection: This is not established. Why? Is it not said: "The state of having been relinquished by the bhikkhus..."?

"Having understood [this]"— therefore, because it is unallowable, if the donors and others give again using allowable terminology for the sake of making it allowable that which has already been relinquished by the monks, it is permissible. Just as, because it has not been accepted and thus not consumed by the monks,
the donors and others may have it formally accepted for the sake of releasing one from an offense, even though the food— both hard and soft— is still the property of the monks.

It has not been used. And just as those who prepare what is allowable (kappiyakāraka) and others make allowable what belongs to a monk that is included within the category of seeds, for the purpose of releasing it from the state of being seed-life or vegetation-life, but not what is not so included;

even so, donors and others give back a pond or similar thing that was previously relinquished by monks because it was unallowable, for the purpose of making it allowable, but not [what was not relinquished].
Since it has not been relinquished, this statement is understood to establish only the state of being made allowable (*kappiyakaraṇa*), and not lordship (*issaratta*).

Nevertheless, they might say: "From the statement that 'the lay followers (*upāsaka*) of the native land expelled the Venerable Dhammatthera from seven monasteries of the native land,' it is understood that the donor is the lord of the monastery."
"For only those who possess authority can ordain an elder, not those who lack it"—this, however, should not be viewed in such a way.
Why? Because it was said, "lay followers of that birthplace," and not "donors of the monastery.
Therefore, many lay followers living in that region [expelled] the Venerable Dhammika Thera from his entire dwelling because of his improper conduct.
They expelled him not because of his ownership by virtue of being the donor of his own monastery, and therefore this example also should be understood as not illustrating ownership,
but rather as illustrating the principle of taking action in accordance with an offense.
Thus, when a donor establishes and gives a monastery, from the moment it is given— having reached the intention of relinquishment—
It should be understood that neither those born in his lineage, nor the kings who are lords of the country and so forth,
have the authority to act as masters or to exercise control; rather, it is the recipient— the Saṅgha, the Gaṇa, or the individual—
who alone has the authority to act as master or to exercise control.
If it is asked how it is known that the donor and others lack mastery over the object, the *Vimativinodanī* states:
"Because giving has the characteristic of relinquishing the object, and because it is improper to take back what has been relinquished as an object such as earth.
Furthermore, [the Buddha said]: "Monks, I allow you to take for yourselves and consume whatever falls while being given."
This is understood both because it was said by the Blessed One, "Monks, that has been relinquished by the donors," and because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"By the statement, 'Monks, that has been relinquished by the donors,' the absence of ownership by others is indicated here.
If one asks, "How is it to be known that [the Sangha] has the status of being the owner and the right to use [the property]?"—it is because it belongs to the Sangha (*saṅghika*).

Because it is stated in the Pācittiya-vinaya text: "If a monastery has been given and dedicated to the Saṅgha, for one who perceives as 'personal' that which belongs to another person, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);

but there is no offense regarding that which belongs to oneself," and because even something as small as a four-finger-high footstool made by village children playing in sand-houses becomes [an object of offense] once it has been given to the Saṅgha.
And because of the statement in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "From the time [the gift] is established, it becomes 'heavy property' (*garubhaṇḍa*). Furthermore:

"In this regard, even if there is a legal challenge (*abhiyoga*), for one who challenges—whether the dwelling, courtyard, or residence given to the monks was intended for the Saṅgha of the four quarters, and whether it is large or small—the challenge does not succeed;
he cannot take it back by seizing it. Why? Because it belongs to all."
This is because there is no laying down of the burden (*dhuranikkhepa*). For it is not the case that all monks from the four directions lay down their burden here.

Furthermore, this is understood from the commentary on the second *pārājika* offense, which states: "But one who seizes property belonging to a group—such as a group of long-reciters (*dīghabhāṇaka*) and so forth—or to a single individual, is able to make them lay down their burden."

If it is asked how the impossibility of investigating the donors and so forth is understood: It is because, even though there were donors such as those who gave the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Buddha did not authorize their investigation;

rather, he authorized the monks themselves to appoint a monk endowed with five qualities as the distributor of lodgings, saying: "Monks, I authorize you to appoint a monk endowed with five factors as the distributor of lodgings."
And when the quarrelsome monks of Kosambī had arrived at Sāvatthī, and Anāthapiṇḍika and the great female lay disciple Visākhā reported—
having been the donors of the Jetavana Monastery and the Eastern Park Monastery respectively— "Venerable sir, how should I deal with those monks?"—
even though they were thus informed, the Venerable Elder Sāriputta, without assigning them lodgings, said: "How indeed..."
“Venerable sir, how should one proceed regarding those bhikkhus’ lodgings? When this was reported, [the Blessed One] said, “In that case, Sāriputta, secluded lodgings should be assigned.
When it was asked, “But if, venerable sir, they are not secluded, how should one proceed?
he replied, “In that case, Sāriputta, they should be assigned even after making them secluded; however, I do not say, Sāriputta—”
"I say that by some means or other, the lodging of a more senior bhikkhu should be yielded;
whoever should yield it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). From this, it is understood because the allocation of lodgings for the Elder alone was authorized.
But how is it understood that the Saṅgha and others are entitled to have their lodgings allocated? [It is understood] from the passage: "And thus, bhikkhus..."
He should be appointed as follows: first, a monk should be requested; having requested him, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:

"Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me... [the rest of the formula] ...the Saṅgha has appointed the monk named so-and-so as the assigner of lodgings. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
Having thus had the assigner of lodgings appointed by the Saṅgha, that assigner of lodgings, authorized by the Saṅgha, should again...
From the statement, "I allow you, monks, to authorize the procedure for the distribution of lodgings; first, monks, count the monks;

having counted the monks, count the beds; having counted the beds, distribute them by way of the beds," it is understood that the communal lodging belonging to the Saṅgha may be managed and allocated by the Saṅgha itself.
"Furthermore, according to the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is a *pārājika* offense for one who seizes a monastery or other property given to a group—
such as the Dīghabhāṇakas— or to a single individual, because the act of relinquishing responsibility (*dhuranikkhepa*) occurs; and according to the canonical text (*pāḷi*),
'there is no offense regarding what belongs to oneself,' and [the phrase] 'but that which belongs to him in whom trust is placed, his own...'"

From the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary), "It is said in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other [texts] that it is as if it were private property (*puggalika*)," it is understood that a monastery belonging to a community (*gaṇa*) given to a community is managed by the community itself, and not by the donors and so forth.
Likewise, a private monastery (*puggalika-vihāra*) given to an individual is managed by the individual who received it, and not by the donors and so forth. Thus, in the Vinaya Piṭaka...
Furthermore, because the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*) state that a monastery is of three kinds—
belonging to the Saṅgha, belonging to a group (*gaṇa*), or belonging to an individual (*puggala*)— and because wandering in a monastery is permitted only for those very same [categories of] Saṅgha,

group, and individual, and because no separate mention is made of a monastery belonging to a donor, nor is wandering in a monastery permitted for donors, [it follows that] the Saṅgha and the others...
It should be understood that they alone are the masters of the monastery and they alone are entitled to manage it.
Let it be so; among those—the Saṅgha, the group, or the individual—who have become the recipients, to whom does that monastery belong, and by whom must it be managed?
It is said: first, regarding a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, [it belongs] to the four quarters of the Saṅgha, both present and future...
Because it was given with the words, “I give this to the Saṅgha,” even when the recipients have passed away, the Saṅgha of the four quarters and the future Saṅgha remain its masters;

it belongs to them and must be administered by them. However, regarding property belonging to a group (gaṇa), as long as even a single member of that group remains, it continues to belong to that group; it must be administered by whichever monk remains from that group.
If, among all those who have passed away, the entire community (*gaṇa*) or the remaining individuals belonging to that community gave [the property] to anyone while still living,
and it was accepted by that person on the basis of trust, he is the owner.
Even if the entire community gives it to another community, to the Saṅgha, or to an individual while still living, those other communities, the Saṅgha, or the individuals [are the owners].

They are the masters. However, in the case of a private dwelling, while that owner of the dwelling is still alive, he may give it to the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual; they then become the masters.
Or rather, it should be understood that whoever takes possession of it during his lifetime by way of a trust becomes the master.
If it is asked, "How is this known?"—because a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha is considered a heavy object (*garubhaṇḍa*), it is not to be disposed of nor divided, and must not be given to anyone.

However, in the case of property belonging to a group (*gaṇa*) or an individual (*puggalika*), because those [groups or individuals] are the owners, giving, entrusting, or taking on trust are permissible.
Therefore, while he was still alive, he relinquished all his own requisites and gave them to someone.
It is understood from what is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: "No one took it on trust.
That which was given belongs only to him by whom it was received," and "The property of two remains undivided; when one has died, the other becomes the owner;
the same principle applies even in the case of many."

However, having made a relinquishment in this manner, a gift given with the thought, "After my passing, let it belong to so-and-so," does not take effect because it is a gift for after one's passing (*accaya-dāna*).

For this has been stated in the Commentary: "If, among the five types of fellow-practitioners, anyone who is dying should say, 'After my passing, let my requisites belong to my preceptor, let them belong to my teacher, let them belong to my co-resident disciple...'"

‘Let it be for him; let it be for his pupil; let it be for his mother; let it be for his father; or let it be for anyone else whatsoever,’ yet it does not belong to them—it belongs only to the Saṅgha.
For the transfer of merit to five who are within the Dhamma does not take effect, but it does take effect for laypeople.
And here, some holders of the Vinaya [interpret] the word “laypeople” as the recipient.
They say: "If one takes what belongs to the monks and gives it to householders as a gift of atonement (*accaya-dāna*), it is permissible;

however, if one gives it to five types of fellow practitioners (*sahadhammika*), it is not permissible. If that were so, then even giving to one's mother and father would be permissible, because they have become householders.
And yet, [the Buddha said]: "'Let it be for the mother; let it be for the father; or let it be for anyone else.'"
From the statement, "It does not exist for them," it is understood that [the offense] does not arise;
therefore, this phrase "but for householders" (*gihīnaṃ pana*) should be regarded not as a dative of purpose, but rather as a genitive of possession.
Consequently, the connection should be made thus: "But for householders, a gift given after the lapse of time (*accayadāna*) is valid."
Furthermore: because it begins with, "If any one among my five fellow-practitioners should pass away after me,
[let him have] my requisites," and concludes by stating, "For a gift to those who have passed away does not succeed for five fellow-practitioners,
but it does succeed for laypeople," the genitive plural is established here in the sense of equality.
If that is so, when the word "to householders" (*gihīnam*) lacks the status of a recipient (*sampadāna*), what then constitutes the recipient?
It is the phrase "to whomever" (*yassa kassaci*). For it is said in the Commentary: "Let it be for the mother, let it be for the father, or let it be for anyone else.
This meaning should be illustrated by the story of Ajjuka. Thus, having given while still alive, the legal determination applies to those who have died.
"We know this; but when no one has been given [the property], how is the legal decision regarding those who have died to be known? Regarding that as well:
