first, in the case of what belongs to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha alone is the master according to the method stated below. However, in the case of what belongs to a group (gaṇa), among some [deceased members], the remaining [members] are the masters;
but when all [of them] have died, the Saṅgha alone is the master. For it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā: "When all have died, [it remains] belonging to the Saṅgha..."

...it belongs [to the Sangha]. However, because a dwelling belonging to an individual (*puggalika*) is considered a heavy article (*garubhaṇḍa*), it is not to be distributed and is not subject to sharing;
it belongs exclusively to the Sangha. If one asks how this is known: “Monks, when a monk has passed away, the Sangha is the owner of his bowl and robes;
however, those who attended to the sick have been of great service. Therefore, monks, I authorize that the Sangha [retain] the three robes and the bowl.”
"To be given to those who have attended to the sick. Whatever light goods or light requisites there are therein, these shall be distributed by the Saṅgha present before them.

Whatever heavy goods or heavy requisites there are therein, these are not to be sold nor divided, belonging to the Saṅgha of the four quarters, both those who have come and those yet to come"—thus it was said by the Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
It is understood because it has been so stated. Even thus, the Blessed One spoke of "heavy goods" and "heavy requisites," but not of a "monastery";

therefore, how is it understood that a monastery constitutes heavy goods? [The answer is found] in the Pāḷi: "A monastery and the site of a monastery—this is the second item that is not to be divided."
“The second consists of two groups; the third, four groups;
the fourth, nine sections; and the fifth, eight divisions.
Thus, with these five aggregates, he whose five eyes are stainless—”
It is understood from the fact that it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “The Lord has declared twenty-five kinds of heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*).

Thus, when a donor, having built a monastery, gives it to a monk who visits families, [the offense arises] at the time prior to the arising of the volition of relinquishment (*muñcacetanā*) for that [monk].
The donor is the owner of the monastery; he is the master with the power to give or to dispose of it.
From the moment the intention to relinquish arises, the recipient monk becomes the owner; he is the master with the power to use it or to give it to others.
If that person gives it away to his students (*saddhivihārika*) and others while still alive, then those students and others—
They are the owners; they have the authority to use it or to give it to another.
However, if he dies without having given anything to anyone, then the Saṅgha alone becomes the owner of that monastery, neither the donor nor any individual.
It should be understood that only with the consent of the Saṅgha may an individual use it, not by virtue of his own ownership.

Thus, because it was given to the Saṅgha from the very beginning, a monastery that has become the property of the Saṅgha—or one that, though originally belonging to a group or an individual, was given to them at its foundation—must be adjudicated by the Saṅgha.

This applies whether the monastery later attained the status of being Saṅgha property because those groups or individuals passed away without having handed it over to another. By the Saṅgha as well...
Having obtained the Blessed One’s permission, one should appoint a distributor of lodgings and have him distribute them. For this was said in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*:
“Then it occurred to the monks: ‘By whom, indeed, should the lodgings be distributed? They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
‘I allow you, monks, to appoint a monk endowed with five qualities as the distributor of lodgings,’ and so forth.”

In this context, "taking possession of a dwelling" (senāsanaggāha) is threefold: taking possession of a dwelling by way of the rainy season, taking possession of a dwelling by way of the [other] seasons, and taking possession of a dwelling by way of permanent residence. Among these, taking possession of a dwelling by way of the rainy season is twofold:
taking possession of a dwelling by way of the first rains and taking possession of a dwelling by way of the later rains. By way of the [other] seasons...

Regarding the taking of lodgings (*senāsanaggāha*), the teachers say it is twofold: the taking of lodgings by way of intermediate release (*antarāmuttaka*) and the taking of lodgings by way of momentary seclusion (*taṅkhaṇapaṭisallāna*).
However, this appears not to accord with either the Canon (*pāḷi*) or the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
For in the Canon it says: "Then it occurred to the bhikkhus: 'How many kinds of taking of lodgings are there? To the Blessed One... [and so forth].
They reported this matter: “Monks, there are these three ways of taking up lodgings: the early, the late, and the intermediate-release.
When the Āsāḷha full moon has passed, the early [lodgings] should be taken up; when one month after the Āsāḷha full moon has passed, the late [lodgings] should be taken up;
when the Pavāraṇā ceremony has passed, the intermediate-release [lodgings] should be taken up for the purpose of the upcoming rainy-season residence. These, monks...”
“Monks, there are three ways of taking up lodgings,” thus it is handed down. In the *Aṭṭhakathā* as well, it says:
“Of the three ways of taking up lodgings, these two—the first and the last—are fixed. This is the detailed analysis regarding the intermediate case...
[omission] ...This, then, is the discussion on the taking up of lodgings as it appears in the Canon (*pāḷi*) by way of the entry into the rains retreat and so forth; but this—”

The "taking of lodgings" (senāsanaggāha) is said to be of two kinds: that for the [dry] season and that for the rainy-season residence (vassāvāsa). Thus it has been handed down; therefore, it should be investigated by the one appointed by the Saṅgha as the distributor of lodgings.
The "taking of lodgings" is twofold: the taking of lodgings during the [dry] season and the taking of lodgings during the rainy-season residence. In this regard:
"Season" (*utukāla*) refers to the eight months according to the winter and summer seasons; during that time, monks have no fixed residence.
Therefore, whenever anyone arrives, the monks must vacate their lodgings and give them to those visitors; there is no such thing as an "inappropriate time.
This is called the taking of lodgings during the season. As for the taking of lodgings during the rains retreat (*vassāvāsa*), however...
It is threefold according to the method set forth in the Pāḷi: “the first,” “the last,” and “the one released in between.

For even the one released in between, because he has taken it for the purpose of the future rains-residence (*vassāvāsa*), enters only the taking of lodgings during the rains-residence, not the taking of lodgings during the [other] seasons.
Indeed, it was said by the Blessed One: “On the day after the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) has passed, for the sake of the future rains-residence...”
“The one who has died in the interval should be assigned a dwelling. Regarding the assignment of a dwelling by way of immediate seclusion (*taṅkhaṇapaṭisallāna*):
this does not appear separately in either the Canon or the Commentary.

They say that the assignment of a dwelling during the [proper] season is itself the “assignment of a dwelling for that purpose,” and it is also called the “assignment of a dwelling by way of immediate seclusion. Therefore, the assignment of a dwelling by way of the season—
It should not be said that "the taking of lodgings by way of temporary release and the taking of lodgings by way of momentary seclusion are two types.

Furthermore, they say: "Among the five ways of taking lodgings as previously stated, four ways of taking lodgings [are fulfilled] by a monk who, having obtained the formal authorization (*sammuti*) for assigning lodgings endowed with the five factors, while standing within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*), [assigns them] to those standing within the boundary..."

"It is said: 'Matters concerning the monks must be settled according to the Vinaya; however, those matters of settlement do not remain fixed as permanent until the time of the Uposatha (yāvajjakāla), whereas only the settlement by way of permanent residence (dhuvavāsa) remains fixed as permanent until the time of the Uposatha.
This also cannot be stated in that way. Why? Because in the section on the distribution of lodgings, it says: 'The taking of lodgings by way of permanent residence.'"

This is not found in the Pāḷi or the Aṭṭhakathā. Furthermore, the deliberation regarding permanent residence (*dhuvavāsa*) is not to be carried out by a lodging-assigner who has obtained his authority through formal consent (*sammuti*);

rather, it is simply the granting [of the status] after the Saṅgha, being unanimous, has performed an act of intimation (*apalokanakamma*) and designated a monk endowed with the two factors as one whose proposal cannot be set aside. Therefore, the unanimous Saṅgha—on account of qualities such as great helpfulness and distinction of virtue—
Having formally appointed a monk endowed with two qualities by means of an act of intimation (*apalokanakamma*),
and having designated a comfortable dwelling for him as his permanent residence, one gives it to him; that [dwelling] should be said to remain stable for as long as the time lasts.
If it is asked, "How is this matter to be understood— that it is the Saṅgha as a whole that gives [the dwelling] by way of permanent residence,
and not the assigner of lodgings?"— [the answer is: "The Saṅgha, however, perceiving the great service and distinguished virtue of the storekeeper,
or of those such as the Dhamma-preacher and Vinaya-holders, or of the teacher who recites for the group, designates a monastery for permanent residence."

[He asks: "Does the Saṅgha give [it]? [The reply is: "The Saṅgha gives it after having made a comfortable residence exempt from labor for one who is learned, who is of great benefit through recitation, interrogation, and so forth, and who carries out the burdens;

and the Saṅgha gives it after having observed the great usefulness and distinguished virtues of a storekeeper, or of a preacher of the Dhamma, a master of the Vinaya, or a teacher who recites the collections, and having designated a monastery for his permanent residence."
In the commentaries, it is stated: "Having appointed [him], he gives [the robe]"; "even a lodging that does not require maintenance for a learned monk who carries out the burdens of the Saṅgha";

and "an act of formal announcement (apalokanakamma) is a legal act to be performed by announcing three times with the consent of a harmonious Saṅgha, after having cleared the Saṅgha residing within the boundary and having brought the consent of those entitled to give their consent."
It must be understood from the words themselves with certainty and without doubt.
But how is it known that the state of being granted [the robe] occurs through a formal act of intimation (*apalokana-kamma*)?

It is because even for a monk who is highly learned and capable of carrying the burden of the Saṅgha, his unoccupied lodging is [granted], as well as the food and wages for the kitchen attendants and others who perform the duties of the Saṅgha.
It is understood from the *Kammavagga* of the *Parivāra-aṭṭhakathā*, where it states: "It is appropriate to give [the robe] by means of a formal act of seeking permission (*apalokanakamma*).

But how is it understood that it is to be given specifically to a monk endowed with the two factors? [The text says: "'Of great service' means the state of being very helpful through such roles as storekeeper and so forth.
He says 'and excellence of qualities,' etc., to show that this is not the only [reason]."

This is understood because it is stated in the *Vinayathamañjūsā*: "It is shown that it is not permissible to give [the robe] if there is great helpfulness but an absence of distinguished virtue, or if there is distinguished virtue but an absence of great helpfulness.
But why must the assignment of lodgings be investigated by the assigner of lodgings, given that the assignment of lodgings does not persist until the end of the rainy season?

It does not remain [in the Saṅgha] for two reasons: because a bhikkhu who is endowed with five factors as an assigner of lodgings is rare, and because it is difficult for bhikkhus dwelling in various regions and born of various lineages of teachers to share in the same enjoyment and use of requisites.
For this was said by the Blessed One: "I allow you, bhikkhus, [to appoint an assigner of lodgings] who possesses five factors..."

“A monk endowed with these qualities should be appointed as the assigner of lodgings—one who would not follow a wrong course through favoritism, nor follow a wrong course through ill will, nor follow a wrong course through delusion, nor follow a wrong course through fear, and who would know what has been assigned and what has not.
In the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) it is also said: “By such a person of similar character, [whether] in a single dwelling or a single courtyard...”

It has been said: "Or there is no need for the *vasanta* [invitation]. But why does the deliberation regarding the gift for the purpose of permanent residence (*dhuvavāsa*) persist until this very day?
Because it must be performed with the consent of the harmonious Saṅgha residing within the boundary (*sīma*), even in the absence of the five constituent factors.
For it is said: "A formal act of notification (*apalokanakamma*) means that, having cleared the Saṅgha residing within the boundary, [one seeks] the consent of those entitled to give..."
“Having brought forth the formal motion (*chanda*) and, with the consent of the harmonious Saṅgha, having announced it three times, the legal act (*kamma*) should be performed.
A monk staying in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha during the season must not be turned away, except in the case of one who is not to be admitted.
For it was said by the Blessed One: “Monks, I allow you to turn away [a visitor] for the three months of the rains, but during the [other] season...”
"But it cannot be prevented. It was said, "Except for those who are not to be displaced. Who are those who are not to be displaced?
There are four who are not to be displaced: one who is senior, the storekeeper, one who is ill, and one who has obtained a dwelling from the Saṅgha.
In this regard, a senior monk [is not to be displaced] among the monks within the boundary of that monastery by anyone senior to himself.
Because there is no one else [to take his place], he is not to be made to rise by anyone according to seniority.

Since the storekeeper has been appointed by the Saṅgha and resides guarding and protecting the Saṅgha’s goods because the storehouse was given to him, that storekeeper is not to be made to rise by anyone.
One who is ill, being overcome by sickness, residing in his own allotted lodging, [is not to be made to rise] by anyone...
It is not to be vacated. Because he has received his lodging from the Saṅgha—that is, because it was assigned to him by a complete Saṅgha—it cannot be vacated by anyone.
For it is said in the Commentary: "There are four who should not be made to vacate:

one who is senior, the storekeeper, the sick person, and one who has received his lodging from the Saṅgha. Among these, the senior [is exempt] by virtue of his own seniority... [regarding one junior].
He should not be dismissed: because the storekeeper has been appointed by the Saṅgha and the storehouse has been handed over to him; because the sick man is ill;

and because the Saṅgha, having made a comfortable dwelling place exempt from service for one who is learned, helpful through instruction and interrogation, and capable of bearing the burden, grants it to him—therefore, he is exempt due to his helpfulness and because it was obtained from the Saṅgha.
"And he must not be ordained. With these four exceptions, all remaining cases are indeed subject to ordination.
When another monk arrives, having ordained him, one should provide him with a dwelling place. For it is said in the Commentary:
"At the time of the seasons, some incoming monks arrive before the meal, while others arrive after the meal or during the first watch of the night..."
“Whether it be during the middle watch or the last watch, whenever they arrive, the monks must rise at that very moment and give them lodging;

there is no such thing as ‘the wrong time. But nowadays, faithful and confident people, having built monasteries and having heard the words of some wise men, knowing that “what is given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit,” [dedicate them] to the four quarters.
Some give by referring to the Saṅgha, saying, "We give this monastery to the Saṅgha of the four quarters, both present and future.
Others, having built a monastery with a particular bhikkhu in mind who inspires their faith, are later urged by that bhikkhu to give it at the time of the offering;
they then give it according to the aforementioned method, referring to the Saṅgha of the four quarters. Still others do so both at the time of construction and at the time of giving.
They make offerings specifically for their own personal attendant bhikkhu; nevertheless, at the time of pouring the water of dedication,
they utter the aforementioned formula as instructed by him, yet in their hearts they give only to their personal attendant and do not intend it for the common property of the entire Saṅgha.
Among these three types of gifts, the first belongs entirely to the Saṅgha because it was set aside for the Saṅgha both at the time of its initial dedication and at the time of the actual offering.
The second, although initially dedicated to a specific individual, belongs to the Saṅgha alone because it was set aside for the Saṅgha at the time of the offering.
The third, however, belongs to the individual who is a family associate (*kulūpaka*) both at the time of the initial dedication and at the time of the offering.
It proceeds for the sake of [an individual], not for the Saṅgha; they merely utter vocal expressions following what has been spoken by a monk.
This being so, regarding the reflection, "Is this dwelling private due to the influence of the mind, or communal due to the vocal expression?
some might say as follows:
“Phenomena are preceded by the mind, led by the mind, and made of the mind.
If one speaks or acts with a pure mind,
happiness follows one, like a shadow that never departs.”

“Because of the words, it belongs to an individual by virtue of the intention of the mind. Others say: “Because of the words ‘one should act according to what the donors say,’ it belongs to the Saṅgha by virtue of the verbal expression.
Regarding this, the investigation is as follows: this gift was previously dedicated to an individual and subsequently dedicated to the Saṅgha;

therefore, when it is said to “belong to the Saṅgha,” among the nine types of gifts that are contrary to the Dhamma, it is the one described as “dedicating to the Saṅgha what was dedicated to an individual.”
The eighth type of gift mentioned is an unrighteous gift (*adhammika-dāna*); both its acceptance and its enjoyment constitute unrighteous acceptance and unrighteous enjoyment.

When it is said, "given to an individual" (*puggalika*), among the three righteous gifts (*dhammika-dāna*), this refers to the third righteous gift—namely, "what is given to an individual is given to that very individual";
both its acceptance and its enjoyment [are likewise righteous].
These are legitimate acquisitions and legitimate enjoyments; therefore, it falls on the side of personal property.
Some, having gained confidence in a group such as a community of Suttantikas and having built a monastery, give it to the group, saying, "I give this monastery to the Venerable Ones.
Others, having gained confidence in an individual and having built a monastery, give it to that individual, saying, "I give this monastery..."
“I give it to the Venerable One. However, these monasteries—whether belonging to a community or to an individual—become the property of the recipient from the very moment of the gift;
they do not remain the property of the donor. Among them, first, regarding those belonging to a community: if some have died, they belong to the remainder;
while they are still living, if they give it to someone, it belongs to that person. If they do not give it to anyone and all have died, [it belongs to the community].
It belongs to the Saṅgha. For it is said in the Commentary: "The property belonging to two [monks] remains undivided; when one has passed away, the other becomes the owner.
This same principle applies even to property belonging to many. When all have died, it belongs to the Saṅgha alone.
As for a private dwelling (puggalika-vihāra), if that individual who received it, during his own lifetime, [gives it] to his students and so forth...
Either he gives it away, or someone takes that monastery on trust from him, and thus it becomes his property.
If he dies without having given anything to anyone, it belongs to the Saṅgha. For it is said in the Commentary:
"While he was still alive, he relinquished all his own requisites and gave them to someone, or someone took them on trust. To whom they were given, and by whom they were taken..."
“It belongs to him alone. And in the Canon it says: “Monks, when a monk has passed away, the Saṅgha is the owner of his bowl and robes;
however, those who attended to the sick have been of great service. Monks, I allow that the Saṅgha give the three robes and the bowl to those who attended to the sick;
whatever light goods or light requisites there may be, those should be given by the Saṅgha in their presence.”

"It is to be distributed by the Saṅgha; whatever among it is heavy property or heavy equipment, that is not to be relinquished and is not to be divided for the Saṅgha of the four quarters, both those who have come and those yet to come.
Since this has been stated, the legal determination should be made according to this method.
Regarding items belonging to the Saṅgha, there are those mentioned in the Canon as "the first," "the last," and "that which is released in between."
Because of the non-observance of the three types of lodgings (senāsana-ggāha) mentioned in the Commentary,

and because of the non-observance of the two types of lodgings mentioned as being for the "season" and the "rainy-season residence," and because of the non-observance of that which is mentioned in the Canon as not to be observed— namely,
that which is not to be observed by its own nature— and because it was granted by the Saṅgha for the purpose of permanent residence, it is [treated] solely by way of that which is not to be observed.
There is a formal decision [on this matter]. For those who are senior or sick cannot be made to rise by their very nature. Indeed, it is said in the Commentary:
"One who is senior should not be made to rise by one who is junior because of his seniority; one who is sick [should not be made to rise] because of his sickness.
Since the storekeeper, the Dhamma-preacher, and others have been assigned by the Saṅgha for the purpose of permanent residence...
They are not to be set aside. For it is said: "But the Saṅgha may assign a dwelling to a storekeeper, or to a preacher of the Dhamma, a master of the Vinaya, and so forth...
having authorized it for permanent residence; therefore, even he to whom it has been given by the Saṅgha is not to be set aside.
This should be understood as follows: nowadays, in monasteries belonging to the Saṅgha, when the senior monks have departed according to their business.
In that monastery, the senior monk there also says, "This monastery must be inhabited by me.
The one who is experienced and capable there likewise speaks in the same way. The one by whom that monastery was built also says, "The person in whom I have placed my confidence must be appointed.
And the Saṅgha also says, "We alone are the masters; therefore, the person desired by us..."
[He] says, "It should be offered. When [the Saṅgha] is split in this way into two, three, or four factions, there arises a great legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*).
Among them, the elder [monk], referring to the textual passage: "Monks, I say that by no means whatsoever should the seat of one who is senior be preempted;
whoever should preempt it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," and considering his own seniority...
Having taken up the words of the commentary, "One who is junior should not ordain [a senior]," he perceives: "I alone am the most senior here;
there is no one else more senior than I; therefore, I alone am fit to dwell in this monastery.
Even one who is experienced [perceives]: "Even a lodging that should not be assigned to a learned monk who carries the burden of the Saṅgha..."

Taking both the words from the *Parivāra-aṭṭhakathā*, “Monks, I allow a learned and competent monk—whether ten years or more than ten years ordained—to confer full ordination and to grant formal dependence,” and the canonical passage beginning with those same words, [he thought]:
“I alone am learned and competent in this matter; there is no one else more learned than I; therefore, I alone...”

The resident [monk] perceives: "This is suitable for this monastery. The builder of the monastery also perceives: "There is a Vinaya text stating that he by whom a monastery is caused to be built is the owner of that monastery;
since I have caused this monastery to be built by relinquishing much wealth, therefore a person who has confidence should be appointed by me, and no one else.
And the Sangha perceives: "A monastery belonging to the Sangha is one that has been given to the Sangha."

Having taken both the canonical statement beginning with “pariccatto” and the commentary’s statement beginning with “even if it is made by village children playing in sand-houses with legs only four finger-breadths high, from the moment it is given to the Saṅgha, it becomes ‘heavy property’ (garubhaṇḍa),” one should hold the conviction:
“This monastery belongs to the Saṅgha and is the property of the Saṅgha; therefore, only a person approved by us may be appointed, and no other.”

In that regard, even though the words of one who is senior are [normally authoritative], the statement beginning with “But not so, monks,” was spoken by the Blessed One with reference to the fact that the most senior person is entitled to the foremost seat in various dining halls and such places;

it refers to a monk who, having sat down after eating his meal, must rise and offer his seat when a more senior monk arrives, and not with reference to permanent residence (*dhuvavāsa*). “The more senior...”

Regarding the statement beginning with "Because of one's own seniority," when bedding and seats are being distributed according to seniority, if a more senior person arrives, the junior person must vacate;
having vacated, he should give his bedding and seat to the more senior person. However, the more senior person should not be made to vacate by the junior.
Why? Because of the rule "Because of one's own greater seniority" during the [appropriate] season. When bedding and seats are being distributed according to seniority...
This was said with reference to the gift of lodgings, not with reference to the gift for the purpose of permanent residence;
therefore, even this statement must be examined and should not be accepted hastily.

Regarding the words concerning the "competent person" (*byatta*), the phrase "one who is learned and capable of carrying out the burden of the Saṅgha," and so forth, does not apply merely by virtue of being learned.

This was said with reference to the ownership of a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha; however, having recognized that a particular monk is of great service and distinguished in virtue, if the Saṅgha has designated a comfortable residence as one from which he is not to be removed, then that monk may not be removed from that monastery by anyone—it is with this meaning that it was said: “I allow...”

The statement beginning with "O monks," etc., was spoken by the Blessed One to clarify the characteristics of the supporting preceptors (*nissayācariya*), not to grant ownership over a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha;
therefore, this statement too must be examined and should not be accepted hastily. However, the words of the donor should neither be accepted nor rejected.
Why? Because of the passage beginning with: "By whom the monastery was caused to be built," etc.

Because it is not a primary designation. For just as an Arahant might still be called a "being" (satta) due to having previously existed during the stage of an ordinary person (puthujjana) with respect to form and so forth—referring to his past state—likewise, because that monastery was previously owned by him prior to the time of the gift, the donor is called the "owner of the monastery," but not because of current sovereignty.
Indeed, [this is] not found anywhere in the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, nor in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) or sub-commentaries (ṭīkā).

Furthermore, there is no reading stating that "the donor is the master of a monastery given after having relinquished it," nor that "it may be disposed of by the donor," nor that "the monastery is the property of the donor";
rather, it exists only as "belonging to the Saṅgha," "belonging to a group," or "belonging to an individual.
Therefore, his statement should not be accepted.

Even in the statement of the Saṅgha, such words as “the monastery belongs to the Saṅgha” and so forth, illuminate the fact that it is the property of the Saṅgha and that it must be administered by the Saṅgha.

When the Saṅgha administers it, however, having appointed a monk endowed with five factors as the assigner of lodgings, it is to be administered by him according to seniority; or, [alternatively], by a unanimous Saṅgha for one endowed with two factors.
Or, it may be given for the purpose of a permanent residence by means of a formal act of intimation (*apalokana-kamma*).
Since a monk endowed with five factors is rare, if there is no one authorized as a distributor of lodgings (*senāsanaggāhāpaka*), a monk endowed with two factors should be sought.

However, if one does not seek such a person, [one should instead appoint] someone who is suitable due to being very helpful—such as a storekeeper—and who, though lacking distinguished qualities like great learning, is otherwise fit.

Because a dwelling cannot be granted by the Saṅgha to a bhikkhu on account of his being preoccupied with material gain and the like, the Saṅgha’s words must also be scrutinized; it should not be granted immediately.
Then, all three statements must be compared. In that regard, because the Saṅgha is the authority, the Saṅgha should be questioned.
Having asked, "Which person is pleasing to you? and being told, "This one," he asked again, "Why is this person pleasing?
and [the reply was: "Because this person has assisted us with the requisites such as robes;
he is our kinsman or blood relative, our preceptor, teacher, co-resident student, resident pupil, fellow preceptor, fellow teacher, or dear companion."
When it is said, “He is gainful and famous; therefore he is approved by us,” one should refuse by saying, “A dwelling should not be given for permanent residence on that account alone.
Then, [if it is argued], “This person is senior to all of us and deserves the best seat, the best water, and the best alms-food;
therefore a dwelling should be given to him for permanent residence”—thus say the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā.

Having said, "He is not mentioned," it should be refused. But if he says, "He is a preacher of the Dhamma, an expert in the Vinaya, a teacher who recites for the community," one should express approval, saying, "He is suitable for a monastery given for permanent residence; it should be given to him. If it is asked, "How is this known? [the answer is:
"But the Saṅgha [should give it] to the storekeeper, or to the preacher of the Dhamma, the expert in the Vinaya, and so forth..."

This is understood from the statement: "Or, perceiving the great helpfulness and distinguished virtues of the teacher who instructs the community (gaṇavācaka-ācariya), he designates and gives a monastery for the purpose of permanent residence.
However, since the word "or the storekeeper" (bhaṇḍāgārikassa vā) exists here in the text of the means (sādhakapāṭha), why is the storekeeper not mentioned in the text of the goal (sādhyavacana)?
Is it not said [that he should live in a comfortable residence]? Because at present there is no storehouse (bhaṇḍāgāra).
If he were to appoint a storehouse in certain monasteries, he—sitting in that storehouse-monastery—would provide service to the Saṅgha, such as guarding the bowls and robes;
perceiving his great helpfulness, the Saṅgha [should grant] even now a comfortable residence for the storekeeper.

If one should give [a dwelling] for the purpose of a permanent residence, that becomes a separate permanent residence for him. Here, in the explanatory text (*sādhakapāṭha*), by the phrase "or for those such as Dhamma-preachers and Vinaya-holders," it includes those possessing the aforementioned qualities:

one who is learned, one who has mastered the scriptures, a Dhamma-holder, a Vinaya-holder, a Mātikā-holder, one who is wise, competent, intelligent, modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training. Furthermore, "this person..."
If someone says, "This learned man (bahussuta) is of great benefit to the bhikkhus through his recitations and inquiries;

he is one who carries the burden of the Saṅgha," and [another] says, "Excellent! This one too is worthy of a comfortable dwelling. Having made it exempt from service, a monastery should be given to him for permanent residence," then he should be thanked.
If you ask how this is known, [it is because of the passage]: "But the Saṅgha [should give a dwelling] to the learned man... through his recitations and inquiries... and so forth.
This is understood from the statement: "He gives a comfortable residence that does not require [the recipient] to perform labor, to one who is of great benefit and who relieves them of their burdens.

Furthermore, if one says, "This person is a preacher of the Dhamma, an upholder of the Vinaya, a teacher who recites for the community, of great benefit to the Saṅgha, and endowed with distinguished virtues," then it is appropriate to designate a monastery for this person as well for the purpose of permanent residence.
Having said, "It should be given only after formal authorization," he should then be offered words of appreciation.

If one asks how this is known, it is known from the statement: "But the Saṅgha, having observed the great service and distinguished virtues of a storekeeper, or of those such as Dhamma-preachers and Vinaya-holders, or of a teacher who instructs groups, authorizes and gives a monastery for the purpose of permanent residence."
Furthermore, if one says, "This person is learned and capable of relieving the burden of the Saṅgha," and [the donor] says, "It is well;
it should be granted even to him by making it non-enforceable," then he should offer the blessing of appreciation (anumodana). How is this known?
It is known because it is stated in the *Parivāra-aṭṭhakathā*: "Even for a learned monk who relieves the burden of the Saṅgha, there may be a dwelling that is non-enforceable. From that...
Having asked, “Is a person endowed with these six factors standing within the boundary or outside the boundary?
if it is said, “He is standing within the boundary,” one should accept it by saying, “Very well, it should be given to him thoroughly.

If it is said, “He is standing outside the boundary,” it should be rejected by saying, “It should not be given. Why? Because: “Monks, the lodging of one who is standing outside the boundary [is not to be assigned].”
"One must cause it to be received; whoever should receive it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Thus says the text. Then, having asked, "If there is no one within the boundary (*sīma*) endowed with two factors, is there someone within the boundary endowed with even one factor?
and being told, "There is," one should accept it, saying, "Very well, it should certainly be given to him. How?
If it is asked, "How is this understood?"—it is understood because it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī* according to each individual factor:

"Observing the great assistance [provided] and the excellence of qualities" means observing the great assistance provided by the storekeeper and the excellence of qualities in those who preach the Dhamma and so forth.
Furthermore, it is said: "There is no one within the boundary (sīmā) who possesses even a single factor; there is only one who stands outside the boundary."
When this has been said, it should be stated: "It should be given to one who has come and is standing within the boundary. Why?

Because it is understood from the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) that: "Even if they have not yet arrived, it must indeed be given when the pupils and others take [the requisites] from those who have entered the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*).
However, if two or three monks—whether by virtue of being joined in a single factor or joined in two factors—are within the boundary...
If [the robes] were to exist [in sufficient quantity], to whom should they be given? To the senior-most. How is this known?
Because of the statement: “Monks, one must not withhold what belongs to the Saṅgha according to seniority; whoever withholds it incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
However, if within the boundary (sīmā) there is no monk associated with even a single or two factors [of the Saṅgha], [then...]
If all the residents are foolish and incompetent, then to whom should it be given?
If a visiting monk comes to that monastery who is modest, amiable, learned, and desirous of training,
those resident monks should provide him with support so that he does not go elsewhere, and then that residence should be given to him.
If it is asked, "How is this matter to be understood? [the answer is: "In this case, monks, in a certain residence there dwell many monks who are foolish and incompetent;
they do not know the Uposatha, nor the Uposatha ritual, nor the Pātimokkha, nor the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
Then another monk arrives there, one who is learned, of traditional knowledge, and a bearer of the Dhamma."
“Monks, those monks who are holders of the Vinaya, holders of the Mātikā, learned, competent, wise, modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training—
by them that monk should be gathered, assisted, consoled, and attended to with powder,
clay, tooth-sticks, and water for rinsing the mouth. If they do not gather him, assist him, or console him...”

“Because it has been prescribed by the Perfectly Enlightened One: ‘If they should attend upon him with powder, clay, tooth-sticks, or water for rinsing the mouth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),’ and because in the Commentary it says:
‘He should be welcomed means he should be welcomed with affectionate words such as: “It is good, venerable sir, that you have come;
here almsfood is easily obtained, there is soup and condiments; dwell here without weariness.”’”
He should be assisted by doing so again and again; he should be won over by making him give the reply, “Yes, I will stay.
Alternatively, he should be gathered and assisted with the four requisites;

he should be flattered with pleasant words—the meaning is that he should be addressed in a way that is pleasing to the ear—and served with powders and such. There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If even the entire Saṅgha does not perform it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for all. In this case, neither the elders nor the juniors are exempt;
it must be attended upon by everyone in turn. For one who does not attend upon him during his own turn, there is an offense.
Furthermore, he must not accept from the great elders such things as the sweeping of their cells or the offering of tooth-sticks. Even so, in the evening and morning, the great elders—
One must go to attend upon them. However, having learned of their arrival, one should go first to attend upon the senior elders (*mahātheras*).
If there are fellow monks who are his attendants, he should say: "I have attendants; you may remain free from anxiety. Even if he has no companions, in that very [situation]...
However, because it has been stated: “If one or two [monks] who are perfected in their duties say in a monastery, ‘We shall do what must be done for our elder;

let the rest dwell in comfort,’ there is no offense for anyone,” thus, when such a monk—one who is modest, amiable, learned, and desirous of training—has come from outside the boundary into the interior boundary, [one may invite him] for the purpose of permanent residence within that boundary.
It is understood that a comfortable residence should be given after making it non-obligatory for the recipient to maintain.
But has it not been stated by the Blessed One: "Monks, a lodging should not be assigned to one standing outside the boundary; whoever should assign it, there is an offense of wrong-doing"?
Then why is a vihāra [assigned] to one who has come from outside the boundary for the purpose of permanent residence?
"Should it be given? It is said: "To one standing outside the boundary"—this is a genitive used in a sense of disregard;
therefore, the meaning should be understood as: "the lodging itself must not be assigned [if it is] standing outside the boundary.
It does not mean that the lodging must not be assigned to that bhikkhu even when he has entered within the boundary while standing outside; therefore, previously, while outside the boundary...
Even when [a robe] is already present, from the moment it enters within the boundary (*sīma*), a share of the four requisites is obtained.
For it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Having heard that much robe-cloth has arisen in such-and-such a monastery, monks even from monasteries a league away come;
it must be given starting from the place where each person arrives. This applies to those situated within the boundary.
When they are unable to recite the Pātimokkha, they must go to that residence where there is a reciter of the Pātimokkha.

Even during the rainy season, it is not permitted to dwell for the rains retreat without a reciter of the Pātimokkha. One must go where there is a reciter of the Pātimokkha and dwell for the rains retreat there;
therefore, even if he has come from outside the boundary, a bhikkhu who is modest, amiable, learned, and desirous of training [must go].
He is one who should be included. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"In this case, monks, in a certain residence on the Uposatha day, there dwell many monks who are foolish and incompetent;
they do not know the Uposatha, nor the Uposatha ritual, nor the Pātimokkha, nor the recitation of the Pātimokkha."
Or alternatively, monks, one monk should be sent by those monks straightway to a neighboring residence with the words:
"Go, friend, and having mastered the Pātimokkha either in brief or in detail, come back.
If they should succeed in this way, that is well. If they should not succeed, then all those monks should go where they know [the Pātimokkha].
Whether it be the Uposatha, the Uposatha ritual, the Pātimokkha, or the recitation of the Pātimokkha—that residence must be gone to.
If they do not go, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
But here, monks, in a certain residence many foolish and incompetent bhikkhus spend the rains retreat; they do not know the Uposatha or the Uposatha ritual.
Either the Pātimokkha or the recitation of the Pātimokkha. In that case, monks, one monk should be sent immediately from that residence to a neighboring residence with the instruction:
"Go, friend, and having mastered the Pātimokkha either in brief or in detail, return.
If they can manage it in this way, that is good. If they cannot manage it, one monk should [go] for a period of seven days.
He should be sent away [with these words]: "Go, friend; having mastered the Pātimokkha either in brief or in detail, come back.

If this can be managed, it is well. If it cannot be managed, monks, those monks must not spend the rains residence in that monastery; if they should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).”

Thus, it is understood that even for one who has come from outside the boundary, if they are capable of assisting the Saṅgha and are endowed with distinguished qualities, they are worthy of receiving [the robe];

therefore, one should not refuse them by saying, "We do not belong to a group," "We do not belong to a lineage or tradition," or "We have no long-standing friendship," and so forth. This refers to the state of belonging to a group and so on.
Indeed, it is immeasurable; rather, the very state of being of great assistance as previously described is its measure.
For from the moment of creating harmony (*sāmaggī*), one becomes a member of the same community (*samānagaṇa*).

Thus, even for those who follow the suspended monks (*ukkhitānuvattaka*)—who are of a different communion due to their views (*laddhi*)—and for those who are of a different communion due to the formal act (*kamma*) of the three kinds of suspension, once reintegration (*osāraṇā*) has been effected by creating harmony, [they become members of the same community].
Living together with [such a person] has been permitted by the Blessed One. However, it is not appropriate to include even one who is shameless (*alajjī*), even if he is learned (*bahussuta*).

For such a person increases the assembly of the shameless and diminishes the assembly of the modest (*lajjī*). Furthermore, one who creates strife (*bhaṇḍanakāraka*) must be expelled even from the monastery.
Indeed, it is said: "One who creates strife and quarrels should be expelled from the entire monastic community (*saṅghārāma*)."
"He obtains [support]. For having obtained a faction, he might even split the Saṅgha. However, those who are shameless and so forth should be expelled from their own residence only;
it is not permitted to expel them from the entire Saṅghārāma," so it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā.
One may not include even a person of a different character (visabhāga-puggala) in one's support if they lack the qualities of concord such as honoring the elders and so forth.
For it has been said: “There is no purpose for one to dwell in the same monastery or the same pariveṇa with such a person of a different character;
therefore, his residence in all places is prohibited.
Consequently, whether he be a resident or a visitor, whether he belongs to one’s own group or another group, a monk who is learned and virtuous should be welcomed. For it was said by the Blessed One:
“Who could possibly find delight in one who is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, wise, and a disciple of the Buddha—like a gem from the Jambū River?
Even the gods praise him; he is praised even by Brahmā.”

This is the exposition regarding the giving of a comfortable residence to a bhikkhu who, by virtue of being within the boundary (*sīma*), is endowed with qualities such as great helpfulness and distinction of virtue, and who carries out the burdens of the Saṅgha— after the Saṅgha has designated that residence as one not to be occupied by others.
However, when the Elder of the Saṅgha, due to weakness from old age, affliction by illness,
or a disposition for seclusion, does not wish to maintain a group, but desires to give it to another, or wishes that there be no quarrels or disputes after his passing;
When he wishes to hand over [the dwelling] to his co-resident students and others, it should not be given away by virtue of his own authority;

rather, thinking "this monastery belongs to the Saṅgha," he should convene the Saṅgha, explain the reason, and have them seek out a person who is distinguished by the quality of being very helpful and worthy.
Then the Saṅgha, without falling into the four wrong courses, in accordance with the Blessed One’s intention...
Having sought out a person who is modest, amiable, learned, and desirous of training, he announces: "This bhikkhu is suitable for this monastery.
If it is pleasing to the senior elder as well, that is good.
If it is not pleasing, and he wishes to give a person who has become a burden to him—one lacking the aforementioned qualities—then, such being the case, the Saṅgha...
One does not go by way of desire and so forth; rather, it is the person who goes. Therefore, a dwelling should be given only with the consent of the Saṅgha.

However, if the Saṅgha, having obtained some material gift, wishes to give it to a monk devoid of the aforementioned qualities, whereas the individual [donor]—in accordance with the Blessed One’s intention—wishes to give it only to a monk endowed with the aforementioned factors...

If one wishes to give [a monastery], then since even an individual is included within the Saṅgha at that time, the monastery should be given with the consent of the individual who performs the *dhammakamma* (legal act), not with the consent of the Saṅgha. For this is stated in the Commentary:
"If the Saṅgha, having received something, does not prevent [the gift] due to being weighed down by material gain, but a single bhikkhu prevents it, that very bhikkhu is the master."
"For in matters pertaining to the Saṅgha, he alone who performs a legal act (dhammakamma) is the master. For it has been said:
"He who transgresses the Dhamma out of favoritism, hatred, fear, or delusion..."
His glory diminishes,
like the moon in the dark fortnight.
[One who acts] out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion—
He who does not transgress the Dhamma,
his fame increases like the moon in the bright fortnight.
But when the Elder also remained silent and departed according to his kamma,
and the Saṅgha likewise did not investigate anyone, while the monastery belonging to the Saṅgha remained thus empty and devoid of monks,
then any teacher in that region who desires the growth of the Dispensation should thus encourage the monks residing within the boundary: "Venerable sirs, do not act in this way."
"Search among the monks residing within the boundary for a person who is suitable for being of great assistance;
having searched and found such a person, you should have the Saṅgha, being in concord, designate a dwelling for him as a permanent residence and grant it to him.
If you do not find one among the monks residing within the boundary, then [search] among the monks residing outside the boundary."
Search. Having searched among the monks residing outside the boundary, and provided that a person endowed with the aforementioned requisites is found, bring that person inside the boundary.
With the consent of the Saṅgha residing within the boundary, designate a dwelling for permanent residence and, having made it non-removable, grant it.
For by acting thus, you, venerable sirs, [will fulfill your duty].

By relying on a person who is endowed with the ten topics of discourse— namely, the discourse on fewness of desires, the discourse on contentment, the discourse on effacement, the discourse on seclusion, the discourse on the arousal of energy, the discourse on virtue, the discourse on concentration, the discourse on wisdom, the discourse on liberation,
and the discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation— you shall hear the Dhamma not heard before, you shall clarify the Dhamma already heard,
you shall dispel doubt, you shall straighten your view, and you shall gladden your heart. For one who is modest...

“By training in accordance with a bhikkhu who is well-behaved, learned, and desirous of training, they will grow in faith, they will grow in virtue, they will grow in learning, they will grow in generosity, and they will grow in wisdom.
For this has been said in the *Visuddhimagga*: “What is the object of dependence (*upanissaya-gocara*) endowed with the qualities of the ten bases of discourse?”
A virtuous friend is one who, by depending upon whom, one hears what has not been heard, clarifies what has been heard, overcomes doubt, straightens one’s view,
and gladdens the mind; or, by training in accordance with whom, one grows in faith, grows in virtue, grows in learning,
grows in generosity, and grows in wisdom— this is called the resort of the decisive support.
Having thus encouraged them and delivered a discourse on the Dhamma, the monastery should be assigned as a permanent residence by the Saṅgha itself, consisting of those within the boundary.
Thus did that wise and excellent monk, desiring the growth of the Conqueror’s dispensation,
properly carry out the formal determination of the residence.
Thus ends the "Adornment of the Discussion on the Determination of Monasteries," the twenty-ninth chapter in the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*. 29.
The Discussion on the Determination of the Spreading of the Kathina.

226. Having thus explained the determination regarding the four requisites, he now says, "Regarding 'the Kathina,' however... and so forth, in order to explain the determination regarding the Kathina.
Therein, as for "the Kathina": what is the Kathina? It is a collective designation (*samūhapaññatti*).

For in the ultimate sense, there is no single phenomenon called "Kathina"; rather, it refers to the monks who have completed the preceding rains-retreat and the Saṅgha consisting of a quorum of not fewer than five.

In such cases as "the robe-month" or "a robe acquired in accordance with the Dhamma and justice," when those name-and-form phenomena arise, the *kaṭhina* is merely a collective designation (*samūha-paññatti*) for that mass and combination of those name-and-form phenomena.
How is this meaning to be known? [It is known from the statement: "The collection and combination of those very phenomena is called 'name' and 'naming'."
And because it is stated in the Parivāra-pāḷi: "It is a name, a designation, a syllable, an expression—namely, 'kaṭhina'";
and [because of the statement]: "'Of those very phenomena' means that when certain phenomena such as form (rūpa) exist, there is what is called 'kaṭhina'; their combination is their mixture.
Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "Name, naming-act," etc., this term "kaṭhina" is merely a name for many phenomena.

And because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "It shows that from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), there is no single phenomenon (*dhamma*) that exists [independently]. Furthermore:

"In those phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth" refers to those phenomena, both material and immaterial, in such contexts as "the monks who have spent the preceding rains-retreat," "the Saṅgha not deficient by five [members]," "the month for robes," and "robes lawfully and equitably acquired.
"While existing" (*satī*) means while they are present. "State of being mixed" (*missībhāva*) means the state of association (*saṃsagga*).

It is merely a designation for a collection. Therefore, it should be understood from its appearance in the *Vimativinodanī*, which states: "He shows that there is no single dhamma existing in the ultimate sense.

In what sense is it called *kathina*? In the sense of being firm (*thira*). Why is it firm? Because [it is free from] the five conditions known as: wandering without having been invited, wandering without having undertaken [the practice], eating in a group, wearing robes as much as one desires, and the arising of robes while staying in a monastery.

Because it is capable of encompassing the five benefits (*pañcānisaṃsa*). For it is said in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: "The meaning is that it is 'firm' (*thira*) because of its capacity to encompass the five benefits";
likewise in the *Vimativinodanī* and the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*. Alternatively, in what sense is it called *kathina*?
In the sense of gathering together (*saṅgaṇhana*). How does it gather them together? By not allowing [the monks] to go elsewhere, [thereby securing] the five benefits.

"Saṅgaṇhāti" means he takes [them] by collecting [them]. For it is said in the *Vinayatthamañjūsā*: "The *kaṭhina* is so called in the sense of 'gathering' (saṅgaṇhana), because it does not allow one to go elsewhere while there are five benefits [to be realized].

By what grammatical suffix (*paccaya*) is the word *kaṭhina* derived from the verbal root *kaṭh*? The commentators on the grammatical treatises (*ṭīkācariyā*), without considering the verbal roots and suffixes, [state as follows...]
They explain it solely by way of the unformed *pāṭipadika*; therefore, this term—which is both conventional (*ruḷhī*) and a pure name—is called the "unformed *pāṭipadika* term.
If one asks how this is known, it is because in all three Vinaya commentaries it is explained simply as "the meaning is 'firm' (*thira*).
Furthermore, the capacity for encompassing the five benefits is the very causal phrase for its firmness. Alternatively, the word *kathina*—
It is established by means of the *ina* suffix from the verbal root *katha*.

How so? From the word *kathin*, which has received the designation "verbal root" (*dhātu*) for the expression *saṅgahaṇeti* ("it gathers"), the *ina* suffix is applied—either by the rule-splitting (*yogavibhāga*) "the *ina* suffix occurs in all cases" or by the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule "from *sup* and [others]"—after changing the final consonant, and thus it is derived from the word *kathina*.

The form *kaṭhinam* is established when the [suffix] *-i* is added at the beginning of the word. If one asks how this is known, it is understood by relying on the reading in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-ṭīkā*, which states:
"In the sense of 'collecting' (*saṅgaṇhana*). Alternatively, it is established by adding the suffix *-ina* to the verbal root *kaṭh* in the sense of "living with difficulty" (*kicchajīvane*).

This meaning is understood because it is stated in the commentary to the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*: "The root *kaṭh* is in the sense of living with difficulty; it is a root ending in *muddha* and *jadu*, and the suffix is *-ina*."

However, many scholars, having taken this very reading, both say and write that "the word *kaṭhina* refers only to what is produced from the gums (*muddhaja*) and not from the teeth (*dantaja*). But it should not be stated categorically in this way. Why?

Because in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā-ṭīkā*, it was stated with reference to the word *kaṭhina* as a quality-term (*guṇasadda*) in the sense of hardness (*kakkhaḷa*), and not according to the conventional usage of the Dispensation (*sāsanavohāra*).

It is the word *nāma*. For this very reason, it says: "The pentad [is used] for the hard. However, in many manuscripts of the Pāḷi and its commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), according to the conventional usage of the Jina’s Dispensation, the word *kathina*—which is synonymous with *nāma*—is generally found as *danta-joya* (tooth-stick) alone;
and for that same reason, even in the commentary on the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*, it is stated that in the case of a change of vowel, it is also called *kathina*.

Alternatively, where do they praise? By adding the suffix *ina* from the verbal root (*dhātu*), and by changing the letter *k*—which has the sense of conjunction—into one that lacks conjunction, [the form] is established.

This meaning is understood from the statement in the commentary on the *Silāghādi-sutta*, "Silāgha means to praise," and because it is described in the *Saddanīti* as "praising is eulogizing. And this statement [is confirmed by the fact that] "for this..."
This accords with the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "The *kathina-vatta* is praised by the Buddha.
However, the teachers (*ācariya*), having analyzed it as "the root *kaṭh-* with the suffix *-ina-," state the meaning as "to endure" (*kaṭha samatthane*).

That [explanation] disregards the statement in the *Ṭīkās*, "the meaning is 'firm' (*thira*)," and instead treats the cause—namely, "the capacity for internalizing the five benefits"—as the actual meaning.
It might be said that [the word] has been mentioned after being taken up, yet that is merely for the sake of establishing its stability.
How should the analysis (*viggaha*) be performed? This word *kathina* is a noun-word (*nāmapada*) in four contexts; among the five types of nouns, it is a pure noun (*suddhanāma*);

among the four types of pure nouns, it is a conventional pure noun (*ruḷhīsuddhanāma*); and among the two types of derivative words (*pāṭipadika*), it is a non-derived derivative word (*anipphannapāṭipadika*).
Therefore, no grammatical analysis (viggaha) should be performed.
For it has been said: “Conventional terms, verbs, particles, prefixes, vocatives, and pronouns—among these six, no analysis is performed.”
This meaning is understood from the commentaries’ statement: “*Kathina* means... [etc. ...it is firm (*thira*), this is the meaning.

Alternatively, it is called *kathina* because it “binds” (*kathati*)—that is, it holds together—by not permitting one to go elsewhere while there are five benefits; this etymological derivation is understood according to the reading in the aforementioned *Vinayathaṃmañjūsā*.
Or else, it is called *kathina* because it “suffers” (*kaṭhati*), meaning it lives with difficulty, like a tree; that which belongs to such a tree is *kathina*.
It is *thira-bhāva* (the state of being firm); that which possesses this is called *kathina*. By changing the letter *ṭha* to *tha* in the word *paññattijāta*, it is stated as *kathina*.
This method should be understood as being consistent with the definition of the root-meaning in the phrase "kaṭha in the sense of living with difficulty," and with the commentary’s statement:
"The meaning is 'firm' because of its capacity to encompass the five benefits within. Now...
It is called *kathina* because it is spoken of (*kathīyate*), praised (*silāghate*), and extolled (*pasaṃsīyate*) by the Buddha and others;

this method should be understood as being consistent with the commentary on the meaning of the verbal root in the phrase "praising in what" (*kattha silāghāya*), and also with the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "For this so-called *kathina-vatta* is praised by the Buddha."

In this context, however, because the Teacher was inclined toward brevity, he did not investigate the characteristics of grammar (*saddalakkhaṇa*) but instead posed and answered the question regarding the meaning alone, saying: "Who is entitled to spread the *kaṭhina*, and who is not entitled? and so forth.
In that regard, "who are entitled" means "who accomplish it. "Five persons are entitled" means five persons accomplish it. [Regarding] the *kaṭhina*-cloth...
For there are four donors at the very minimum and one recipient. In this regard, monks, because it is stated in the Campeyya-khandhaka:

"As for that Saṅgha of monks consisting of a group of four—excluding the three formal acts of ordination, invitation (*pavāraṇā*), and rehabilitation"—it should not be understood as requiring a group of five.
Regarding the phrase "invited by the first invitation": this...

This was stated for the purpose of demonstrating that the status of having completed the rains residence is established even for those who were prevented from entering by an obstacle, because the spreading of the *kaṭhina* cloth is possible for them as well. For this very reason, instead of saying "or those who were not invited," it was said only:

"or those whose rains residence was interrupted, or those who entered during the later period, do not receive [the robe]. This applies even to those who have completed the rains residence in another monastery.
"They do not obtain" means that those who have completed the rains-residence in another monastery within a different boundary do not obtain the spreading of the *kathina* in this monastery.

"All" refers to those whose rains-residence has been interrupted and so forth; even those who have not entered the rains-residence are included therein. "Benefit" refers to the robe resulting from the benefit of the *kathina*.
For indeed, only one robe for which the *kathina* has been spread is called a *kathina*-robe; the remainder—
Whether they be robes (*cīvara*) or garments (*sāṭaka*), they are indeed called the benefits of the *kathina* ceremony. For it will be said:
"The remaining benefits of the *kathina*, such as strong cloths, should be given to those who have stayed for the rains-retreat. "To the others" means to those who entered during the first period.
"If he receives full ordination during the second period, he both completes the quorum and obtains the benefits"—by this [it is meant].
The entry into the rains retreat for novices was permitted. For by entering the earlier [rains], he gains the benefit;
but by being ordained during the later [rains], he becomes one who completes the quorum.

If those who entered during the earlier [rains] are not skilled in the spreading of the kaṭhina, etc., then it is said: "A monk who is proficient in eight things is worthy of the spreading of the kaṭhina."
Because it is included in the *Vinayavinicchaya*, if one is oneself skilled in the eight matters (*aṭṭhadhamma*), one should spread the *kaṭhina* oneself.
If not, one should seek out others who are skilled in the eight matters and have them bring [the requisites]; it is shown that it is not permissible to spread the *kaṭhina* without doing so.
"Having had the *kaṭhina* spread" means by way of a causative expression, by those elders who have come from outside.

This shows that one should not spread the *kathina* oneself; rather, after arranging all the preliminary duties and so forth, those very monks who entered the rains residence within the boundary during the earlier period (*purimikā*) should have it spread.
Otherwise, it would follow that one person spreads the *kathina* while another receives the benefit (*ānisansa*), which is not tenable. For he will say: "The benefit..."
"But it belongs only to the others. "Having enjoyed the gift" means having enjoyed the gift of food and drink consisting of hard and soft edibles.
For they do not receive gifts of robes.
Regarding the phrase "it is permissible to say, 'We give a kaṭhina robe,'" here one should say, "We give a kaṭhina robe to the Saṅgha."
For if this were so, it would accord with the formal ritual statement (*kammavācā*): "This cloth for the *kaṭhina* has arisen for the Saṅgha.
Nevertheless, because of previous familiarity with the practice, even though "for the Saṅgha" is not explicitly stated, the recipient (the dative case) is understood as being evident;
thus, it may have been left unstated. Regarding this, some teachers say: "Even if 'for the Saṅgha' is not stated, what is given at that time belongs to the Saṅgha."
In this regard, it should be stated: "Not everything given at the proper time becomes the property of the Saṅgha. If one asks how this is known:

because it is stated in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* that even that which belongs to an individual—given by way such as, "This is an out-of-season robe for the Saṅgha," or "I give this to you, sir"—is called an "out-of-season robe. Thus, even what belongs to an individual [is included].

It is understood as "it belongs to [a person]. Therefore, whether one gives by mentioning the name in the person's absence, or places it at their feet in their presence, it belongs to that individual alone and not to the Saṅgha. For this is said in the Commentary: "One gives to an individual" means:
"I give this robe to so-and-so"—thus either in the person's absence, or having placed it at their feet, saying: "Venerable sir, this..."
‘I give it to you’—thus he gives it in person. When it is thus personal property, should that robe-cloth be distributed to the Saṅgha or not?

If that person wishes to distribute it to the Saṅgha consisting of his own pupils and students, or to another legitimate Saṅgha, he may distribute it; if he does not wish to distribute it, [he need not].

"One should not say to anyone, 'Let him share it. If one asks how this is known: it is known from the commentaries (*ṭīkā*) which state, "For that which is given specifically for an individual is not to be shared by anyone. Now, some teachers say:

"Because it is stated that the Saṅgha is the sole basis for the kaṭhina, even when something is given for the sake of an individual, it remains under the control of the Saṅgha and belongs to the Saṅgha."
It is so. For example, even when it is said, "I give this to the boundary" or "I give this to the lodging," that gift belongs to the Saṅgha;
and likewise, when it is said, "I give this Kathina-cloth," it belongs to the Saṅgha. In this regard, it should be investigated thus:
"The Saṅgha is the sole root of the Kathina"—this statement [concerns] the root of the Kathina.

This demonstrates the cause for the *kathina*. For just as a tree stands when its root exists and does not stand when it does not exist, therefore the root is the cause and the foundation of the tree;
in the same way, the *kathina* exists when the Saṅgha exists and not when it does not exist. Therefore, the Saṅgha is called the root and the cause of the *kathina*.

It exists. How does the kaṭhina exist when the Saṅgha exists? At the very least, when the kaṭhina-cīvara has been given by a Saṅgha consisting of a quorum of four monks through a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (ñattidutiyakamma) to a monk who is worthy of the spreading [of the kaṭhina], then by that robe it is called "the kaṭhina spread";
it is not so when it has not been given. Therefore, when a Saṅgha of four members cannot be obtained...
Even if one says "I give the *kaṭhina*" a thousand times,
it does not constitute a *kaṭhina*. Therefore, when one, two, three, or four monks reside in a monastery delimited by an *upacāra-sīmā*,
if a *kaṭhina-cīvara* arises there, one monk from among five— having sought it elsewhere— is the single recipient for the Saṅgha consisting of a quorum of four.
When there is a full assembly, one is permitted to spread the *kaṭhina*; it is not permitted when there is not.
Thus, the name *kaṭhina* exists only when the Saṅgha is present, not when it is absent. Therefore, with reference to the Saṅgha being the root and the cause of the *kaṭhina*, it is said:
"The Saṅgha is one root of the *kaṭhina*. When the term "*kaṭhina*" is mentioned, it refers specifically to that which belongs to the Saṅgha.
In this passage, the intended meaning—that [the legal act] exists for the Saṅgha and not for an individual—is not obtained.

For example, as in the statement, "The Saṅgha is the single root of a legal matter concerning duties (*kiccādhikaraṇa*)," here the legal matter concerning duties—consisting of the *apalokana-kamma*, *ñatti-kamma*, *ñattidutiyakamma*, and *ñatticatutthakamma*—exists only when a Saṅgha of four or more members is present, and not when one is absent; therefore, it belongs to the Saṅgha.
With reference to its being the root and the cause of a legal issue arising from business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*), it is said: "The Saṅgha is the one root of a legal issue arising from business.
This should be understood in the same way.
Even though it was stated: "Just as in cases such as 'I give to the boundary' or 'I give to the lodging,' that gift belongs exclusively to the Saṅgha..."
Likewise, when it is said, "I give the kaṭhina," even though it is given with reference to a specific individual, it belongs only to the Saṅgha, it is indeed the property of the Saṅgha.
Nevertheless, one should investigate in this way: in cases such as "I give to the boundary" or "I give to the lodging," the boundary and the lodging are not the recipients of the gift;
therefore, [the benefit accrues] to those residing within the boundary and those residing in the lodging.
Furthermore, [the robe] belongs to the Saṅgha, whereas an individual is merely a recipient of a gift;

therefore, how could that which is given—whether by saying "I give this Kathina robe to the monk named so-and-so" in the absence of that monk, or by placing it at the feet of that monk, or in his presence—become the property of the Saṅgha, belonging to the Saṅgha? In this way, it would not be transferred to the Saṅgha.
If one should divert a robe belonging to an individual to the Saṅgha, it would be one of the nine unlawful gifts;
the acceptance of that robe would be one of the nine unlawful acceptances; and the use of that robe would be one of the nine unlawful uses.
How is this known? Because there are nine unlawful [acts].
Regarding "gifts": if one dedicates what was intended for the Saṅgha to another Saṅgha, or to a shrine (cetiya), or to an individual;
or if one dedicates what was intended for a shrine to another shrine, or to the Saṅgha, or to an individual;
or if one dedicates what was intended for an individual to another individual, or to the Saṅgha, or to a shrine—these nine are unrighteous (adhammika).

This is understood by consulting the *Parivāra-pāḷi*, where it is stated: "There are nine kinds of acceptance and enjoyment," as well as the *Aṭṭhakathā*, where it is stated: "These are the acceptances and enjoyments of those very same gifts.
Furthermore, they say this: when a donor [offers] to the Elder of the Saṅgha, or to one renowned for his mastery of the scriptures and the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*),...

Or if one sends a message to the distributor of meals, saying, "Come taking eight bhikkhus for the purpose of receiving our meal," even if it has been sent by relatives or attendants, these three types of people are not permitted to go.
Only when the heading has been entered—having had eight bhikkhus assigned from the Saṅgha—one may go with oneself as the ninth. Why?
For it is by depending on these monks that gain arises for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
However, a resident bhikkhu who is not well-known for his mastery of the texts or his ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas) may be asked;
therefore, he should set forth the terms of the inquiry, saying: "Shall I receive from the Saṅgha, or shall I come together with those whom I know? and then act according to what the donors say.

Regarding the phrase "it should be practiced": in such instances, by reference to the statement, "The gain of the Saṅgha arises depending upon an individual," it is understood that "the gain of the Saṅgha arises depending upon an individual;
when one gives the bowl-gain of an individual while touching the Saṅgha, it becomes dependent upon the Saṅgha."
Regarding this statement as well, one should reflect in this way: "In that invitation, he does not invite a person alone;
rather, he invites a person together with the Saṅgha. However, since it is stated there as "eight bhikkhus" instead of saying "the Saṅgha," one who is not well-known [to the host] might wonder:
"Do I take [the meal] from the Saṅgha, or shall I come together with those whom I know?"

An individual may be asked [about his status]. However, because the senior monk of the Saṅgha lives having presided over the Saṅgha, when it is said "eight bhikkhus," there is no reason to include anyone other than the Saṅgha;

even an individual renowned for his mastery of the texts and the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) is included within the Saṅgha alone when it is said "eight bhikkhus," because the merit of the Saṅgha is dependent upon the Saṅgha itself.

[The text] takes [the eight]; because the meal-designator (*bhattuddesaka*) also arranges the daily meal for the Saṅgha alone, when it is said "eight bhikkhus," there is no reason to take anyone other than the Saṅgha.
Thus, because they were invited together with the Saṅgha by the instruction, "Come having taken eight bhikkhus," these three persons do not obtain permission to ask.
It is stated [thus], not that when there is an invitation specifically for an individual—such as "Come, you"—one must nevertheless come taking the Saṅgha along.
Thus, because the individual was invited together with the Saṅgha by saying, "Come taking eight bhikkhus," the Saṅgha must be included;
it is not because the individuals alone were invited by saying, "You [plural] come. Therefore, regarding the individual...

It cannot be said that "the gain belongs to the Saṅgha. In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and other treatises (*pakaraṇa*), it is stated only as "gain arises for the Saṅgha depending upon an individual," not as "the individual's gain belongs to the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, in the eight matrices (*mātikā*) concerning the fields for the acquisition of robes, it appears separately as "he gives to the Saṅgha" and separately as "he gives to an individual."
"He gives to a person" means that he gives either in the absence [of the recipient], saying, "I give this robe to such-and-such a person," or in the presence [of the recipient],
having placed it at the feet [of the monk], saying, "Venerable sir, I give this to you. Now, however,
laymen or laywomen desiring to give a robe do not come themselves, but rather [send] their sons, slaves, and so forth.
Even when having [others] send it, they say, "Give this robe to the elder named so-and-so," and thus cause it to be given to an individual;
even when giving it themselves, they give by placing it at the feet, or placing it in the hands,
or making it touched by the hand, saying, "Venerable sir, this robe was made after we renounced such an amount of wealth for your sake."

When they say, "It was acquired by performing manual labor in such and such a manner; therefore, you may wear it, put it on, and enjoy its use," they intend for that person alone to have the right of use, not for the Sangha to receive the gift.
Some even speak of a "non-contented" discourse (*atuṭṭhakathā*). Such is the reason why a robe given specifically for an individual is placed under the control of the Sangha.
There is none. However, if one says, "I give this to you and to your students," it reaches both the Elder and his students.
Having spoken thus according to the traditional source, when one gives in this manner, it reaches both teacher and student;
but it does not reach one who has no students. [Regarding the case of] one who has come to receive a recitation and is departing after having received it...
And it is said: "It also reaches him. Thus, it reaches even a Dhamma-pupil who is outside the boundary from where [the robe] was brought.

When it is said, "I give it to the bhikkhus who travel in regular company with you," it reaches all those who, having performed the duties for their recitation-pupils, travel about receiving recitations, cross-examinations, and so forth; thus, by way of its arrival, it is so.
Having spoken thus, it reaches those who give, as well as the Dhamma-pupils and the pupils who perform the duties of service.
Thus, because the giving proceeds exactly in accordance with the words of the donors, the masters of the Aṭṭhakathās say: "One should act in the very manner that the donors speak."
Thus, at present, donors mostly give to individuals alone; among hundreds or thousands, only one wise and learned donor might give to the Saṅgha.

Furthermore, a robe intended for an individual, if it is not being made for the purpose of a communal dwelling, is not subject to formal authorization (*ñatti*) or the ritual proclamation (*kammavācā*).
