How is this known? Because it would contradict the formal act of authorization and proclamation.

If it is asked, "How is there a contradiction?"—In the motion (*ñatti*) and the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), it is stated that "this cloth for the kaṭhina has arisen for the Saṅgha," thus expressing the cloth's status as belonging to the Saṅgha;
yet now, that same robe becomes personal (*puggalika*) according to the meaning of the words, "it is given to an individual.
In this way, too, there is a contradiction. [The text continues: "The Saṅgha [bestows] this cloth for the kaṭhina upon [the person named] so-and-so..."

Regarding the phrase, "One should give the kaṭhina to a bhikkhu so that he may spread it": here, the Sangha is the agent (*kattā*) by virtue of its constituent elements (*dhātu*), while "to a bhikkhu" is the recipient (*sampadāna*).
However, in this case, because the Sangha lacks ownership over that kaṭhina robe-material, the Sangha is not the agent;
and because the bhikkhu lacks the characteristic of being a recipient (*paṭiggāhalakkhaṇa*), he is not the recipient. Thus, there is a contradiction. By the donor...
However, because it has been relinquished to the Saṅgha, the kaṭhina-cīvara becomes the property of the Saṅgha.
At the time when the Saṅgha bestows that [robe] upon a bhikkhu endowed with the eight qualities for the purpose of spreading the kaṭhina,

at that time people nowadays refer to the formal motion (*ñatti*) as "the motion" (*ñatti*), and they call that robe "the robe obtained by motion" (*ñattiladdhacīvara*), as well as [the one who gives] that robe-giver.

Regarding the phrase “one who gives what has been obtained through a formal motion (*ñattiladdhadāyaka*”), it is therefore only a robe belonging to the Saṅgha that is “obtained through a formal motion,” not a robe belonging to an individual (*puggalika*).

However, from the moment it is obtained through a formal motion, that robe becomes the property of an individual. Why? Because it has become the robe of the individual who performed the formal resolution (*atthāraka*).
Furthermore, they also cite the readings “it is given,” “they accomplish,” and “they obtain the benefit.”
"By comparison, this meaning is understood. In this regard, the intention of the teachers is as follows:
regarding the phrase "this has been given by the Saṅgha," here the root *dā* (to give) has "by the Saṅgha" as its agent and "this" as its object.

Because this kaṭhina-cīvara belongs to the Saṅgha, it is "given by the Saṅgha"; thus, it is understood that when the word "kaṭhina" is mentioned, it refers to something belonging to the Saṅgha. "The spreading of the kaṭhina..."
Regarding the phrase "who obtain," here "who obtain" means "who accomplish. In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, it is stated: "Five persons accomplish it.
In that context, "five persons" refers to the Saṅgha; by this also it is understood that "when 'kaṭhina' is mentioned, it belongs to the Saṅgha.
Regarding the phrase "they obtain the benefit," because it belongs to the Saṅgha, all the bhikkhus within the boundary (*sīmā*) obtain the benefit.
They obtain [it]; by this it is also understood that "when 'kaṭhina' is mentioned, it refers to what belongs to the Saṅgha.

In that regard, one should investigate as follows: since the four former donors give the four requisites almost exclusively to the Saṅgha, the discussion regarding the Saṅgha’s distribution of the four requisites is very extensive; however, [the case] of an individual is minor.
Therefore, it was said with reference to the *kathina* robe-cloth given to the Saṅgha being assigned by the Saṅgha to a specific individual who performs the spreading (*atthāraka*).
"They accomplish" means that five persons—the four donors of the *kathina* cloth and the one recipient—accomplish the formal act of giving the *kathina*.
"They obtain the benefit" refers to this [benefit] for the one who performs the spreading.
It should be understood that in these passages, only the benefit obtained by the monks through their rejoicing (*anumodanā*) is stated;
the meaning should not be understood as that when "kaṭhina" is mentioned by these texts, it becomes the property of the Sangha.

How is it known that the robe-cloth arisen for the Sangha was given to the one who performs the *atthāra* (spreading) of the kaṭhina? [It is known from the statement: "This is the kaṭhina-cloth for the Sangha."

This is understood by observing both the canonical text which states, "The Saṅgha gives this *kathina*-cloth to the monk named so-and-so in order to spread the *kathina*," and the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) which states,
"If the Saṅgha, having received the *kathina*-cloth today, gives it on the following day,
this constitutes 'accumulated storage' (*nicayasannidhi*). Thus, it is the robe itself, belonging to the Saṅgha, that is the object of the act of giving.

The action, the Saṅgha as the agent, the individual as the recipient, and the state of being worthy [of the gift] are all understood by referring precisely to the aforementioned scriptural passage. This being so,
how should one proceed regarding what must be done to convert a personal robe given to an individual into one belonging to the Saṅgha?
If that recipient person says this to the donors:
"Lay follower, a gift given to the Saṅgha is more fruitful than a gift given to an individual; therefore, give it to the Saṅgha.

Having given it to the Saṅgha, let it then be given by the Saṅgha through formal proclamation (kammavācā) to a monk worthy of the distribution, and let it be distributed by that person according to the Vinaya."
"It is called *kathina*; it is not for an individual to give to another person and have that person spread it themselves; therefore, give it to the Saṅgha.
Even if, having been thus urged, the robe is given to the Saṅgha, that robe belongs to the Saṅgha and is eligible for the *kathina* ceremony.
However, if the donor, due to lack of learning, says, "Venerable sir, I know nothing; this robe is for you alone," [it is not so].
If he says, "I give," then even though that robe was given to the Saṅgha by that individual after having been accepted as a personal gift,
it becomes the property of the Saṅgha. If this is so,
how could a robe given by one ascetic to another ascetic be eligible for the Kathina-privilege?
It would not be so. For this is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: "By whom may the kaṭhina-cloth be given such that it is valid?
It is valid if given by any deity whatsoever, or by any human being, or by any one of the five who share the same Dhamma.
Now, why [is it that] from the robe obtained through a formal motion (ñatti) by the lineage of teachers, the remaining robes belong to the Saṅgha?
"Should they be used only after having been divided? It is said: some monks act solely according to the tradition handed down through the lineage of teachers;
some act out of conformity with what they have seen by observing the practices of many others;
some learned elders, even though they do not approve, act out of fear of breaking the tradition; and others act according to their own preference and for the sake of the meaning.

They accept [the robe] after transforming its intended purpose. However, monks who follow the manual (*pakaraṇa*) accept the meaning exactly as it appears in the manual, taking both what belongs to the Saṅgha and what belongs to an individual without mixing them, and taking both seasonal robes (*kālacīvara*) and non-seasonal robes (*akālacīvara*) without mixing them.
In the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga*, it says: “The nun Thūlanandā [accepted] a non-seasonal robe, thinking, ‘It is a seasonal robe.’”

It is stated that [the donor] will cause [the robe] to be distributed after having made a formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhahitvā*); therefore, the Blessed One prescribed an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiyapācittiya*).

Consequently, a monk who is modest, amiable, learned, and desirous of training should consult and reconcile various treatises such as the Canon and its commentaries (*pāḷiaṭṭhakathā*), and follow the treatises themselves;
he should not place his trust in the actions of others, nor...
And this must be understood. For during the Blessed One’s lifetime or thereafter, donors for the most part gave the four requisites to the Saṅgha alone;
therefore, because communal lodgings and communal robes were so abundant, the ancient teachers divided them among the Saṅgha and then used them.
Nowadays, however, donors mostly give the four requisites to individuals;

therefore, even lodgings that are newly built are for the most part the private property of an individual, and robes likewise are mostly the private property of an individual. Even poor people, from the time they begin spinning thread, think:
"I will give this robe at the time of the Kathina ceremony to such-and-such a monk."
Having thought thus and spoken accordingly, they perform all their duties; those of great wealth,
from the moment they have purchased a robe, likewise think and speak in that manner, and at the time of giving, they either send their sons, servants,
and others with the instruction, "Give this robe to such-and-such a person," or they go themselves and place the robe at the feet of that bhikkhu.
Or, having placed it in their hand and said, "I give this robe to you," or having thought [thus], they give it;

or among hundreds or thousands [of people], a single wise person, knowing that "what is given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit compared to what is given to an individual," says, "I give this Kathina robe to the Saṅgha," or gives it after thinking [thus]; for him, that...
The offering becomes dedicated to the Saṅgha. However, if the donor wishes to give to an individual, but that individual— desiring for the gift to be of great fruit—
makes known through a Dhamma teaching such as the *Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga-sutta* that an offering to the Saṅgha is of greater fruit than an offering to an individual,
and then urges [the donor], saying, "Give this robe of yours to the Saṅgha," [the offering becomes dedicated to the Saṅgha].
The donor, having accepted his words, gives either by saying, "I give this *kaṭhina*-robe to the Saṅgha," or by thinking [the same];
in this way, too, that offering goes to the Saṅgha.
However, if the donor—though urged by the monk—is of poor wisdom and, disregarding his words, gives it to an individual...

If he gives it, that offering belongs to the individual person. However, if that person, having accepted it himself, subsequently relinquishes it to the Saṅgha, then that robe-cloth also becomes the property of the Saṅgha and must be distributed according to the rules for the Saṅgha.
But if the donor gives it to the individual person, and the person, having accepted it, does not relinquish it, [then it remains his].
This being so, that robe belongs to an individual; it does not become the property of the Saṅgha merely by the time of the kaṭhina or merely by the word "kaṭhina.
Now, however, according to this method, there is mostly only private (puggalika) robe-cloth.
Even so, wishing not to break the lineage of the succession of teachers, they treated it as if it were the property of the Saṅgha, divided it, and used it.
If it were primarily the property of the Saṅgha, then no individual would be permitted to take even so much as a single needle beyond what has been given by the Saṅgha.
Yet some elders say that although it belongs to the Saṅgha, they exercise ownership at the time of distribution and dispose of it according to their own pleasure.

Some monks, thinking [the property] belonged to the Saṅgha as a whole, would cause it to be divided even against the will of an individual who did not wish for a division, saying: "Give it to our son; give it to our relative who is a monk;
give it to our family's dependent. Others, being faithful and confident, [would likewise urge the division].

Donors, having deliberated, "We give this to such-and-such a person," may give the robe-cloth either behind the person's back by saying, "I give this robe-cloth to such-and-such a person," or they may give it in the person's presence by placing it at their feet or into their hands.
Such a robe-cloth belongs to that individual; because the Sangha was not mentioned, it does not belong to the Sangha. [Thinking], "I shall give the kaṭhina..."

Furthermore, expressions such as "gone to give the kathina" or "the kathina robe" used at earlier or later times are merely figurative designations based on metaphorical application, because [the robe] was given at the time of the actual *saṅghika* robe which constitutes the primary *kathina*. How so?
Just as the food described as "for the Uposatha" is included among the fourteen types of *saṅghika* food and is thus primarily *saṅghika*.
There are donors who, having observed the Uposatha, give to the Saṅgha a portion of food that ought to be eaten in the evening;
the Saṅgha, treating it like a ticket-food (*salākabhatta*), consumes it by establishing a fixed schedule. Thus, because it was given to the Saṅgha, it belongs to the Saṅgha.
Now, however, on Uposatha days, donors [give] to their own family’s dependents or to kinsmen monks...
They give almsfood, but because it has not been given to the Saṅgha, it does not belong to the Saṅgha.
Even so, because it was given on the Uposatha day, it is conventionally designated as "Uposatha almsfood" by way of its proximity—just like the Uposatha almsfood that occurs primarily on that day;
this case should be understood in the same way.

Thus, at this time, because it is for the most part given to an individual, a robe that has become the property of an individual (*puggalika*) is not subject to the formal act of motion and announcement (*ñattikammavācā*);
rather, only that which belongs to the Saṅgha (*saṅghika*) is subject to the formal act of motion and announcement, and that alone is the cause for the five benefits.
Therefore, a wise person [should say]: "Lay followers, give to the Saṅgha; what is given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit," and so forth.
Having directed her, she should have it given; or, having accepted it herself, she should dedicate it to the Saṅgha.

Because it has been thus dedicated, the robe becomes the property of the Saṅgha and is fit for a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñattikammavācā*), and it produces five benefits. Such direction is as follows:
"Give it to the Saṅgha, Gotamī; when it is given to the Saṅgha, I shall be honored, and the Saṅgha..."
It should be understood that this conforms to the words spoken by the Blessed One: “and so forth.
It was stated that it is permissible to give rice gruel and food to monks who are performing the preparatory work (*parikamma*), because there is no fault in doing so when they have been asked;
however, it is not permissible to speak in this manner if they have not been asked. “A cloth stained with groats” (*khalimakkhitasāṭaka*)—
This was said with reference to new cloth. By the phrase "having washed well," etc., he shows the spreading out (atthāra) together with its preliminary actions.
For by the washing, sewing, dyeing, and making fit, the examining, cutting, and stitching are also shown;
and by showing the spreading out, he also shows the relinquishing (paccuddhāra) and the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna). The needle and so forth are the requisites for the work on the robe.

"Having prepared [it] together with many bhikkhus"—this is an indication of the requisites for sewing. "On that very day"—this is stated for the purpose of releasing the storage of what has been made.
On the very day the robe-cloth is received from the hand of the donor, it must be given to the bhikkhu who is performing the *atthāra* (the formal spreading of the *kaṭhina*).
If one does not give it in this manner, there is the offense of storing for accumulation (*nicaya-sannidhi*). By the one performing the *atthāra* as well...
The *kaṭhina* should be spread on the very day it is obtained from the Saṅgha; if one does not do so, there is the offense of "storing what has been prepared.

By stating that it gives many other benefits (*ānisansa-vatthu*), he shows that only the cloth intended for spreading is called the *kaṭhina-cloth*, whereas other cloths, even if many, are merely called the "benefits of the *kaṭhina*. And by this [statement], "the benefit of the *kaṭhina*"...

This indicates that only the robes themselves were mentioned, not the value. If the value had been mentioned, then in that case it should have been said, "He gives robes for the kaṭhina which have many benefits";
however, instead of saying that, it was said, "He gives many robes that are the benefits of the kaṭhina.
By this it is known that the value was not mentioned; therefore, the state of having many benefits is [determined] by way of value.

It should not be accepted; rather, it should be accepted only by way of the material object (*vatthu*). "The other" refers to another donor. Having exhorted and persuaded him in such and such a manner, [one should say]:
"Lay follower (*upāsaka*), a gift indeed becomes of great fruit and great benefit from the very moment it is given to the Saṅgha.
However, the distribution (*atthāra*) was permitted by the Blessed One for the purpose of assisting the monks. Therefore..."
“Whether it is obtained through request or not obtained at all, it is indeed of great fruit,” or:
“Upāsaka, this donor gives to the Saṅgha alone, and you too give to the Saṅgha alone; and by the Blessed One it was said:
‘He who, being virtuous, gives a gift to those who are virtuous;’”
‘What is obtained righteously with a well-clarified mind,
having full conviction in the sublime fruit of action—
that indeed I call a gift of abundant fruit.’”
Having said such things as, "It has been stated; therefore, from the time it is given to the Saṅgha onwards, it is indeed of great fruit," he should be persuaded.
The construction is: "The Kathina robe-cloth which the Saṅgha gives, that Kathina must be spread by that monk. The connection is: "It should be given to whichever monk has worn-out robes.
At this point, the monks [should recite]: "Acceptance and suitability, the motion and the proclamation;"
Having recited this verse: “The determination of the period, the relinquishment, the formal resolution,

the spreading, the assignment, and the appreciation— this is the procedure for the Kathina,” one first performs the acceptance of the Kathina robe-cloth according to the ritual formula for the offering of the Kathina.
And they ask whether it is suitable; this appears as if improper. Why is that? Because [the text states]:
"A person endowed with eight factors is capable of spreading the *kaṭhina*...
[as above] ...he knows the preliminary act, he knows the relinquishment, he knows the determination, he knows the spreading, he knows the summary, he knows the obstacles, he knows the suspension."
“He knows [the robe-material] and he knows the benefit,” as stated in the Parivāra-pāḷi:
“A bhikkhu who knows these eight things is worthy of the kaṭhina-spreading:
the prior relinquishment, the determination, the spreading, and the matrix.”
“There are obstacles and removals, but these are the benefits.
Furthermore, because it is not included among the eight factors mentioned in the *Vinayavinicchaya-ppakaraṇa*, [it is said]:
“The preliminary action (*pubbakaraṇa*) is comprised of seven things: washing, examining, cutting, binding, sewing, and dyeing.”
And in the Parivāra-pāḷi: "Washing, stretching, cutting, and also binding;
sewing, dyeing, and making allowable (kappa)—this is called the preliminary task."
Furthermore, it is because [the act of eating] is not included among the seven preliminary actions (*pubbakaraṇa*) mentioned in the *Vinayavinicchaya-pakaraṇa*.
Not only is it absent from the treatises, but no logical justification (*yutti*) for it is seen either. How so? For "acceptance" (*paṭiggahaṇa*) is defined as:
"Whosoever, monks, should eat food that has not been given, by way of the mouth, except for water and tooth-wood... [and so forth].

Regarding the phrase "an offense of expiation" (*pācittiya*), this was stated by the Blessed One concerning the four types of allowable things—such as those for immediate consumption—that are to be swallowed, but not regarding robes.
For even if a robe is given while placed at one's feet or given in one's absence, it is indeed obtainable. For it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*):
"Saying, 'I give this robe to such-and-such a person,' [one gives it] either in their absence or by placing it at their feet..."
‘This is for you,’ thus he gives it in the presence [of the Saṅgha]. Therefore, there is no need for the act of formal acceptance;
when the robe has been given by the donor, the mere mental acceptance on behalf of the Saṅgha is sufficient.
And they perform the inquiry as to suitability in this way: one monk says, “Venerable sirs, the Saṅgha’s Kathina...”
When it was asked, "To which person is this appropriate and worthy? one bhikkhu, having stated a name, said, "It is appropriate and worthy for the elder named so-and-so.
They say "appropriate" (*sappāya*) with reference to what is to be used for wearing as an undergarment (*nivāsana*) and as an upper robe (*pārupana*).
In this statement, the consistency must be sought both from the perspective of the word (*saddato*), its meaning (*atthato*), and its underlying intention (*adhippāyato*).

How so? From the perspective of the word (*saddato*), the plural number must be used only when there is a division into groups, not when there is no division; thus it is from the perspective of the word.

Furthermore, the expression "suitable" (*sappāya*) must be used only in the sense of being appropriate, not in the sense of wearing as an undergarment or upper robe; thus it is from the perspective of the meaning (*atthato*).
And this robe-cloth, which the Saṅgha gives to an individual for the purpose of spreading the *kaṭhina*, is not for the purpose of wearing as an undergarment or upper robe.
For it is stated in the Pāḷi: “The Saṅgha gives this *kathina*-cloth to the monk named so-and-so for the purpose of spreading the *kathina*.

Therefore, the logical consistency must be sought. Furthermore, the verse beginning with “Acceptance is appropriate” is not found in any part of the Pāḷi, nor in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*), and so forth; therefore, one should proceed here according to the method already explained.
"If there are many worn-out robes, they should be given to the senior [monk]"—this was stated according to the method of the Pāḷi:
"And, monks, that which belongs to the Saṅgha must not be withheld according to seniority; whoever should withhold it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
By this same method, even when all the strong robes are present, [they belong] to the senior alone.

"It should be given" is established. Regarding the phrase "among those who are senior"... [etc. "...it should be given," this is stated for the purpose of releasing the formal act of storage (*karaṇa-sannidhi*). For that very reason, he said, "If one is senior," and so forth.

Indeed, even by a junior person, having released the formal act of storage, there is the attainment of the five benefits for the Saṅgha when it performs the expression of appreciation (*anumodanā*) once the Kathina has been spread.
Furthermore, by the words "Moreover," etc., [he indicates] the duty to be performed by the Saṅgha.

[The text] shows this. However, the sequence of the words should be arranged as follows: having obtained the *kathina* cloth, when the Saṅgha has assembled within the boundary, if one monk says, "Venerable sirs, this *kathina* cloth has arisen for the Saṅgha;
to which monk of such-and-such a name should the Saṅgha give this *kathina* cloth so that he may spread the *kathina*?", another [monk] says, "He whose robes are worn out..."

The words “to him” should be spoken. Then, when the former says either “many worn-out robes” or “there are no worn-out robes here,” the latter should say “in that case, to the senior. Again, when the former asks “who is the senior here?
the other should say “the monk named so-and-so. Then, when the former says “that monk, on that very day...”
When it is said, "Having made the robe-cloth, he is able to spread it," the other should say, "He is able," or "The Saṅgha will show favor to the Great Elder.
Again, when the former says, "That Great Elder is endowed with the eight qualities," the other should say, "Yes, he is endowed.
Then [the former should say], "It is well; it should certainly be given to him."
When this has been said, the Saṅgha should be informed by a learned and competent monk.
And here, the words “Venerable sirs, for the Saṅgha,” etc., mean: “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me;
this cloth for the kaṭhina has arisen for the Saṅgha. If it is timely for the Saṅgha, may the Saṅgha [resolve] upon this cloth for the kaṭhina for the one named so-and-so...”
This accords with the formal motion (ñatti-pāḷi): “One should give the kaṭhina-cloth to a bhikkhu so that he may spread it.

The passage beginning with “To him whose robes are worn out” accords with the commentary (aṭṭhakathā) which says: “By whom [should it be given] by the Saṅgha? and “To whom should it be given by the Saṅgha? To him whose robes are worn out,” and so forth.
The passage beginning with “That great elder is endowed with eight qualities” accords with [the commentary on] the eight qualities...
It should be understood that this accords with the Parivāra-pāḷi, beginning with: "A person endowed with these qualities is capable of spreading the kaṭhina.
Furthermore, the connection is that it must be given to the one to whom it is being given by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one announcement (*ñattidutiyakamma*).
By this, because this formal act of giving the kaṭhina is weighty, it should not be given by mere consultation (*apalokana*); such is the meaning.
He explains. The distinction between what is grave and what is light will be made clear in the discussion on the determination of what constitutes an act and what does not.
However, when the kaṭhina has been thus bestowed, there is the connection that it must be relinquished, determined, or the speech [of its distribution] broken.
By the phrase "if that kaṭhina-cloth has already had its preparation completed," it is shown that what is called "kaṭhina-cloth" is not merely...
This indicates that it is not merely a natural robe (*pakatisāṭaka*), but rather a robe for which the seven preliminary duties have been completed;

therefore, once the robe has been finished and given, there is no need to perform the seven preliminary duties, and one need only carry out the acts of relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*) and so forth. However, if anything remains unfinished, even if only...
Even if it is only the size of a drop on a fingernail, one must perform the acts of relinquishing and so forth only after that [sewing] is finished.

As for the loops, the strips, and the shoulder-straps, these are included within the sewing; they too must be made only after [the sewing] is finished. One who does not finish it has simply failed to complete the task of sewing.
For it is said in the Commentary: "In this context, 'made' means made by the completion of the needlework; the completion of the needlework..."
"Whatever is to be done with a needle—having finished the loops, the cloth-straps, the knots, and the ends of the cloth—it should be sewn together with a needle.
For this so-called *kathina* duty is praised by the Buddha; it is praised by such statements as, "Monks, for you who have spread the *kathina*, five things will be permissible," and so forth.
"But having taken up the kaṭhina that has reached its conclusion" means:
"Washing and stretching, cutting and sewing,
as well as dyeing and making it allowable— this is called the preliminary task."
Having performed the seven kinds of preliminary acts as prescribed, and having taken the *kathina* robe that has been completed, the connection [of the sentence] is:
"The robe must be relinquished by the monk who is spreading the *kathina*, or it must be formally resolved upon, or the speech must be broken.
A monk desiring to spread the *kathina* with an outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*) must first relinquish his old outer robe which was previously resolved upon as part of the triple-robe set.

Having said, "I relinquish this outer robe (saṅghāṭi)," it must be relinquished; thereafter, a new outer robe that has not yet been determined (anadhiṭṭhita) must be determined by saying, "I determine this outer robe.

Then, at the time of spreading the kaṭhina, one must make the formal declaration with words regarding that very determined outer robe, saying, "By means of this outer robe, I spread the kaṭhina"—this is the meaning.

The same principle applies to the others. By this, it is shown that what is called the "spreading of the Kathina" consists solely of an utterance of speech and does not involve any physical movement of the body. For it is said in the *Vinayatthamañjūsā*:
"It is to be spread means it is to be performed as a spreading; and that should be understood as being accomplished solely through such an utterance of speech."
In this context, relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*) is threefold: the relinquishment of the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) with the words, "I relinquish this outer robe";

the relinquishment of the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) with the words, "I relinquish this upper robe"; and the relinquishment of the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) with the words, "I relinquish this inner robe.
For this has been stated in the *Parivāra*: "Relinquishment..."
"It is comprised of three things: the outer robe (saṅghāṭī), the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), and the inner robe (antaravāsaka). The formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) is threefold:
the determination of the outer robe, "I determine this outer robe"; the determination of the upper robe, "I determine this upper robe";
and the determination of the inner robe, "I determine this inner robe."
For this has been stated in the *Parivāra*: "The formal act of determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is comprised of three things: by means of the outer robe, the upper robe, and the inner robe.
Alternatively, determination is twofold: determination by body and determination by speech.
In that regard, having relinquished the old outer robe with the words, "I relinquish this outer robe," one [takes up] a new outer robe with the hand...

Having taken it up, one should resolve upon it by means of the mind, making an application of thought such as, "I resolve upon this outer robe (saṅghāṭi)," either through bodily movement or by resolving with the body, or by making a vocal utterance, one should resolve it with speech. For it is said in the Commentary:
"In that regard, there are two ways of resolving a robe: one resolves it with the body, or one resolves it with speech."

It has been said; therefore... [etc. "...it must be determined. Alternatively, determination is twofold, by way of presence-determination (*sammukhādhiṭṭhāna*) and absence-determination (*parammukhādhiṭṭhāna*).
In that regard, if the robe-cloth is within arm's reach, it should be determined by making a vocal utterance: "I determine this outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*).
But if it is inside a chamber or in a neighboring monastery, one should observe the place where it is kept.
One should perform the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) by making a vocal utterance, saying: “I determine this outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*). For it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
“In that regard, the determination is twofold: if [the robe] is within arm’s reach,” and so forth; and in the *Vinayatthamañjūsā*:
“‘Twofold’ means twofold by way of the distinction between being in the presence of others and being out of their sight.”
How many kinds of spreading (atthāra) are there? Spreading is of one kind.

For spreading is accomplished only by means of a verbal expression, not by means of a physical gesture. This meaning is confirmed by the aforementioned Parivāra-pāḷi and by the statement in the Vinaya-ṭṭhamañjūsā:
“‘It should be spread’ means it should be performed as a spreading; and that should be understood as being precisely such a verbal expression.”
And it is understood thus. Alternatively, the spreading (*atthāra*) is threefold according to the distinction of the material.

In that regard, if one wishes to spread the *kaṭhina* with an outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*), the old outer robe must be relinquished, the new outer robe must be formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*), and the speech must be uttered:
"With this outer robe, I spread the *kaṭhina*. Then, [if one wishes to do so] with an upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*)...
If one wishes to spread the kaṭhina with an upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), the old upper robe must be relinquished;
the new upper robe must be determined upon, and the formal declaration must be made: "With this upper robe, I shall spread the kaṭhina.
Then, if one wishes to spread the kaṭhina with an inner robe (antaravāsaka), the old inner robe must be relinquished; the new inner robe...
It must be resolved: "With this inner robe, I shall spread the *kaṭhina*"; thus the speech must be uttered.
For this has been stated in the *Parivāra*:
"If [he spreads it] with the outer robe," and so forth. Here it might be asked: "But must it not be relinquished only after making a specific distinction, such as 'I relinquish this outer robe'?"
Or rather, should it be relinquished in a general way by saying, “I relinquish this”?
A robe that has been determined by means of determining it as a requisite-cloth must be relinquished in a general way by saying, “I relinquish this”;
it should not be relinquished specifically by saying, “I relinquish this outer robe (saṅghāṭi)”. Why? Because previously it had not received a specific name.
However, a robe that has been determined by means of the determination for the three robes (*ticīvarādhiṭṭhāna*) must be relinquished specifically [by its particular name], not generally.

Why? Because it possesses a specific name once obtained. In this context, however, regarding the section on the Kathina, since it was previously determined by means of the determination for the three robes, it should be understood that it must be relinquished specifically. For this has been stated in the *Parivāra*, in the section on the Kathina:
“Renunciation is comprised of three things: the outer robe (saṅghāṭī), the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), and the inner robe (antaravāsaka).
Now, is it only one who is a wearer of the three robes (tecīvarika) who is permitted to spread the kaṭhina, or is it also one who is not currently wearing the three robes?

There are two kinds of wearers of the three robes: by way of the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) of wearing the three robes and by way of the discipline (vinaya) of wearing the three robes. Among these, the wearer of the three robes by way of the ascetic practice...
Having resolved, "I renounce extra robes; I undertake the practice of the three-robed one," he wears [only those robes] at all times.

However, one who follows the discipline regarding the three robes (vinayatecīvariko) wears them by resolving upon them as the three robes only when he wishes to wear them after having so resolved; but when he resolves upon them as requisites-cloths...

If he wishes to maintain [the robes] after having performed the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna), then he maintains them by determining them accordingly; therefore, because the determination of the three robes (ticīvara) is difficult to maintain,
even one who is unable to maintain them at all times and maintains them instead as requisites-cloth (parikkhāracola),
having relinquished that [determination], may— by performing the determination of the three robes when the time is near— spread the kaṭhina.
It should be understood that he indeed obtains it.
"Venerable sir, should the kaṭhina be spread only within the boundary where the formal act (kammavācā) of giving the kaṭhina is recited, or rather within another boundary?

If the boundary fixed by the recitation of the formal act of giving the kaṭhina is the same as the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā) which constitutes the field for the entry into the rains retreat (vassūpanāyika), [then...]
If they are standing inside, then the spreading [of the robe] must be performed within that very boundary circle (*sīmamaṇḍala*). If it is asked how this is known:
“If the donor gives to the Saṅgha when the preliminary formal act (*pubbakaraṇa*) has already been completed, it should be given by means of a formal motion (*kammavācā*) after it has been accepted.
And by him, having determined [the robe] within that very boundary circle and having spread it, the Saṅgha should be made to express its appreciation (*anumodāpetabbo*).”
"It is understood because it is found in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*. If that is so, since the commentary states only 'in that very boundary-circle (*sīmamaṇḍala*)', one should say:
'Having recited the formal act (*kammavācā*) in whichever boundary-circle, it must be spread out in that very same boundary-circle';

and not [that it must be done] in the secondary boundary (*upacārasīmā*) which constitutes the field for entering the rains residence (*vassūpanāyika*), as bound by the recitation of the formal act for the offering of the *kaṭhina*."
Should it be stated with the qualification, “standing within”? It should not be so stated.

For the boundary established by the recitation of the *kammavācā* constitutes a formally bound boundary (*baddhasīmā*), whereas the boundary for the distribution of the *kaṭhina* robe constitutes a proximate boundary (*upacārasīmā*). And what is called a proximate boundary extends even beyond the formally bound boundary;
therefore, that very boundary is both a formally bound boundary and a proximate boundary. Thus, in that very case—
Having recited the formal act (*kammavācā*) for the bestowing of the *kaṭhina* within the boundary circle (*sīmamaṇḍala*), the spreading [of the *kaṭhina*] must be performed right there;
it should not be understood that after reciting the formal act in just any boundary circle, the spreading must be performed right there.

Even so, it should be stated simply as "within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*)," and not as "within the precinct boundary that constitutes the field for the entry into the rains retreat (*vassūpanāyika-khettabhūta-upacārasīmā*)."

That too must certainly be said. Those monks are permitted to perform the *kaṭhina*-spreading only within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*) that constitutes their specific residence for the rains-retreat, and not within any other precinct boundary. For it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"Even those who have spent the rains in another monastery do not [perform it]; so it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*."

"As you wish, so let it be; however, as for what was said by you—that 'the boundary established by the recitation of the *kammavācā* becomes a formal (*baddha*) boundary, while the boundary for the spreading of the *kathina* becomes a functional (*upacāra*) boundary'—how is that state to be known? It is replied:
First, regarding the fact that the boundary for the spreading of the *kathina* becomes a functional boundary, [it is stated]: "If, however, there are many monasteries within a single boundary..."

It is understood from the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, which comments on the meaning of this commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*)—“Having assembled all the bhikkhus, the *kathina* should be spread in one place”—that the phrase “in one boundary” means “in one functional boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*).

However, regarding the state of being a formally established boundary (*baddha-sīmā*) within the boundary where the formal act (*kammavācā*) is recited, it says: “And those [bhikkhus] within arm’s reach...”

"Without having left the single boundary, they remain standing within it. And this so-called 'boundary' (sīmā) is of two kinds: the established boundary (baddhasīmā) and the unestablished boundary (abaddhasīmā)," because this is stated in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*.

Furthermore, with reference to the inquiry, "And what is this so-called 'boundary'? It is that place where those who remain without leaving the reach of hand (hatthapāsa) are said to have attained the status for performing the formal act (kamma)," [the author], in demonstrating the boundary while showing the distinction between those possessing divisions, clarifies their essential nature.
This is understood from the *Vinayathamañjūsā*, which states: "And it occurs precisely by way of showing the classification; therefore, [the author] said, 'Now, as for this boundary... etc.

In that regard, how many kinds of established boundaries (*baddhasīmā*) are there, and how many kinds of unestablished boundaries (*abaddhasīmā*)? There are three kinds of established boundaries: by way of the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*), the common-residence boundary (*samānasaṃvāsasīmā*), and the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsasīmā*).
The unbound boundary (*abaddhasīmā*) should be understood as being threefold:
by way of the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*), the water-splash boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*), and the seven-abhantara boundary (*sattabbhantarasīmā*). How is this known? It is known thus:

"Having transcended these eleven faulty boundaries (*vipattisīmā*), a boundary that is established by connecting one marker with another and is endowed with the three kinds of perfection should be understood as a 'bound boundary' (*baddhasīmā*). [It consists of] the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*) and the common-observance boundary (*samānasaṃvāsasīmā*)."

It is understood from the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* that "the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) is a sub-division of that very [boundary]; however, the unbonded boundary (*abaddha-sīmā*) is threefold:

the village boundary (*gāma-sīmā*), the seven-abhantara boundary (*sattabbhantara-sīmā*), and the water-splash boundary (*udakukkhepa-sīmā*). Thus, because it is stated that the Saṅgha entitled to perform formal acts (*kamma*) must carry out such acts as those requiring a quorum of four (*catuvagga-karaṇīya*) within these six boundaries—namely, the three bonded boundaries and the three unbonded boundaries—it is clear.
It is understood that for a pure precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*), the state of being one where a formal act (*kammavācā*) is not to be recited [is required].

When there is a fixed boundary (*baddhasīmā*) within a precinct boundary, it should be understood that even if it does not extend over that fixed boundary, because one can go to the precinct boundary,
that fixed boundary must be subject to the recitation of a formal act and is fit for the spreading of the kaṭhina cloth.
But surely, fifteen kinds of boundaries are mentioned in the commentaries; so why are only six stated here? It is true;

however, among those fifteen boundaries, the *upacāra-sīmā* (proximity boundary) serves only as the place for distributing the Saṅgha’s gains and so forth, and the *lābha-sīmā* (gain boundary) serves only as the place for receiving the specific offerings arising there.
Thus, these two boundaries are not places for performing formal acts (*saṅghakamma*) of the Saṅgha.

It should be understood that these boundaries—the boundary of a market town (*nigama*), the boundary of a city (*nagara*), the boundary of a district (*janapada*), the boundary of a kingdom (*raṭṭha*), the boundary of a realm (*rajja*), the boundary of an island (*dīpa*), and the boundary of a world-system (*cakkavāḷa*)—belong to the same category as the village boundary;
they are included within the village boundary itself and are therefore not mentioned separately.
Furthermore, in this context, how is it to be known that the state of having passed beyond a formally established boundary (*baddhasīma*) by overstepping its precincts (*upacārasīma*) has occurred?

Because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “The precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*) is delimited by the enclosure of a monastery that has an enclosure, and by the place suitable for an enclosure in the case of one that does not have an enclosure,” the precinct boundary extends over and covers that [formal] boundary already established within the enclosure and the places suitable for an enclosure.
For thus it is said: “Within this precinct boundary, for the Saṅgha...”
It is said: "But what is given with the words 'I give' reaches even those standing within the intermediate space between the broken boundaries.
By this it is known: "The formal boundary (baddhasīmā) situated inside the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā) is also called a precinct boundary. Let it be so;
since that is the case, when there is a formal boundary within the precinct boundary, one should have the ritual formula for the giving of the *kaṭhina* recited right there.
The kaṭhina should be spread right there. If no formal boundary has been established within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*), how will they proceed?

If no formal boundary has been established within the precinct boundary, one should go either to a place where a formal boundary exists outside the precinct boundary or to a place where water-sprinkling is possible, and have the ritual formula (*kammavācā*) recited.

Furthermore, it should be understood that after returning to the monastery, one must spread the *kaṭhina* while standing within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*) which constitutes the field for the commencement of the rains residence (*vassūpanāyika*).
But, sir, if this is so, would there not be a formal motion (*ñatti*) in one boundary and the spreading of the *kaṭhina* in another? If this were the case, [the rule states]:

"If the donor gives to the Saṅgha only after the preliminary formal act (*pubbakaraṇa*) has been concluded, it should be accepted and then given with the ritual proclamation (*kammavācā*). And by him, in that very [boundary]..."

Does this not contradict the statement in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*: “Having established and spread [the cloth] within the boundary circle (*sīmamaṇḍala*), the Saṅgha should be asked for its formal approval (*anumodāpetabbo*)”?

Have we not already said: “The boundary formed by the recitation of the *kammavācā* is a ‘bound boundary’ (*baddhasīmā*), whereas the boundary for the spreading of the *kaṭhina* is an ‘adjacent boundary’ (*upacārasīmā*)”?
Therefore, it does not contradict the statement in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*. In that regard, previously, for the most part...

This was said with reference to the spreading [of the robe] in that very monastery which has become both a monastery with a fixed boundary (*baddhasīma*) and one possessing a precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*), after having convened a united Saṅgha and had the formal act (*kammavācā*) recited. Even if there is no monastery with a fixed boundary,
provided that a fixed boundary exists within the precinct boundary, the state of being spread must take place right there within that same boundary circle after the formal act has been recited.

We too have already said this. However, if it is neither a monastery with a formally established boundary (*baddhasīma*) nor is there a formally established boundary within its precincts (*upacārasīmā*), one is not permitted to recite the formal act (*kammavācā*) in such a monastery.

Instead, having gone to another monastery that has either a formally established boundary or a water-sprinkling boundary (*udakukkhepa*), and having had the formal act recited there, one may then return to one's own monastery when it has become the field for the commencement of the rains retreat (*vassūpanāyika*).

Standing within the boundary of the precincts (*upacārasīmā*), the *kaṭhina* robe should be spread out. In this very way, it should be understood that many excellent teachers, acting in succession, perform [this act].

However, other teachers maintain that when there is a pure precincts-boundary (*suddha-upacārasīmā*) devoid of a fixed boundary (*baddhasīmā*), [the spreading] must take place within that very precincts-boundary.

They say that the motion and the formal proclamation (*ñattikammavācā*) must be recited, and the kaṭhina cloth must be spread; however, a motion cannot be made in one boundary, nor can the spreading be performed in another. But this is their intended meaning:

"In the boundary where the kaṭhina has been spread" refers to the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*), according to the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, which states that it refers to the boundary that constitutes the site for the spreading of the kaṭhina.

The absence of a formal boundary (upacāra-sīmā) has been stated; and in that very commentary (*ṭīkā*), in the previously cited passage—“Having determined [the area] within that very circle of the boundary and having spread [the robe], the Saṅgha should be requested for its approval”—the state of being spread is stated specifically in relation to the boundary where the formal act (*kammavācā*) is recited.
Therefore, a motion (*ñatti*) should not be made in one boundary, nor should the spreading be performed in another; it must be done in that very same one.
Having announced the formal act (kammavācā) within the boundary of the precincts (upacārasīmā), the spreading [of the Kathina cloth] must be performed right there;
there is no requirement to go outside the precincts to the established boundary (baddhasīmā) to perform the act of spreading.
Regarding this, the following investigation should be made: this act of giving the Kathina, which is called "the motion" (ñatti) in other languages, is as follows—

Among the four types of formal acts of the Saṅgha, there is the act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*). Of the nine matters for which the *ñattidutiyakamma* is prescribed, the giving of the *kaṭhina* robe-material is one;

likewise, among heavy and light offenses, the heavy offense is one. If it had been stated in the legal texts that "the four formal acts of the Saṅgha are to be performed within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*)," then, in accordance with the words of those teachers, the formal act of the motion for the giving of the *kaṭhina* would [be performed] within the precinct boundary.

It would have had to be recited; however, it is not stated in the treatises (*pakaraṇa*) that "the four sangha-legal acts are to be performed within the functional boundary (*upacārasīmā*)," but rather [it is stated] regarding "the distribution of the community’s gains,
entering the monastery after performing the duties for guests, asking permission from a departing bhikkhu for his lodging,
the suspension of formal dependence (*nissaya*), and [the procedures for] bhikkhus undergoing the period of probation (*pārivāsika*) and penance (*mānatta*)."

It is stated: "The rite of causing the dawn to rise, the requesting of permission for bhikkhunīs to enter the monastery, and so forth—these alone are to be performed within the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā).
Therefore, it is established that the formal motion and the second proclamation for the offering of the *kathina* cloth are not to be recited within this precinct boundary alone.
If one asks how this is known: "The boundary for non-separation (*avippavāsasīmā*) may even extend for three *yojanas*."
This being the case, those staying within three *yojanas* will receive their alms;

staying within three *yojanas*, one must fulfill the duties toward visitors (*āgantuka-vatta*) before entering the monastery; a departing monk must ask permission for his lodging after traveling three *yojanas*;
for a monk under formal dependence (*nissaya*), the dependence shall be suspended upon exceeding three *yojanas*; and for one on probation (*pārivāsika*), having exceeded three *yojanas*...

"It will be necessary to rise at dawn; it will be necessary for a bhikkhunī standing three *yojanas* away to request permission to enter the monastery—all of this is permissible only by way of delimiting the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*); therefore, it should be apportioned within the precinct boundary itself.
This is understood from such passages in the Aṭṭhakathā.

Or if they should say: "It has been stated by you that the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīmā*) is not a valid location for a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*); nevertheless, such acts have indeed been performed previously.

For instance, the formal acts for the appointment of the receiver of robes (*cīvarapaṭiggāhakasammuti*), the appointer of the storer of robes (*cīvaranidahakasammuti*), and the distributor of robes (*cīvarabhājakasammuti*)—whether by means of this formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation, beginning with ‘Let the Sangha hear me... and ending with ‘I so declare,’ or by means of a simple announcement (*apalokana*)—were carried out even within the monastery in the midst of the entire Sangha."

"It is indeed permissible to appoint [the boundary] even for a *khaṇḍasīmā* (a partial or broken boundary). Thus, the fact that it must be accomplished by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*) is recorded in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
Regarding the storehouse, however, [it says]: "But this storehouse must not be appointed while sitting within a *khaṇḍasīmā* after having gone to that *khaṇḍasīmā*;
rather, it must be done right in the middle of the monastery [with the words]: 'Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me...'"
"The Saṅgha, if it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, should appoint such-and-such a dwelling as a storehouse," and so forth;
according to this method, it should be appointed either by a formal act (*kammavācā*) consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation, or by a simple announcement (*apalokana*).

Thus, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), the fact that it is to be appointed within the functional boundary (*upacārasīma*) by a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation is recorded.

They should be addressed as follows: "Even if you venerable ones spoke thus, thinking that the readings 'within the monastery' (*antovihāre*) and 'in the middle of the monastery' (*vihāramajjhe*) found in the Commentary refer to the *upacāra-sīma* (the precinct boundary), those readings were not stated by the teachers of the Commentary with reference to the *upacāra-sīma*;
rather, they refer to what is known as the *avippavāsa-sīma* (the non-separation boundary)."
This was said with reference to the great boundary (*mahāsīma*). How is this known? Because the fragmentary boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*) is what will be discussed [next].
For the great boundary is indeed the counterpart to the fragmentary boundary. If it is asked how this meaning of "proximate boundary" (*upacārasīmā*) is to be understood:

[it is because] "those who designate this common-residence boundary (*samānasaṃvāsakasīma*) do so for the sake of making the formal acts of the Saṅgha—such as ordination (*pabbajjā*) and full admission (*upasampadā*)—easy to perform."
"First, the fragmentary boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) should be authorized... [etc.]...

But when the boundaries have been thus established, monks standing within the fragmentary boundary do not invalidate an act performed by those within the great boundary (mahāsīmā), nor do those standing within the great boundary invalidate an act performed by those within the fragmentary boundary.
However, those standing in the intermediate space between the boundaries (sīmantarikā) do not invalidate either. This is according to the reading of the Aṭṭhakathā.
"It should be known. Alternatively, this meaning is also understood from the wording of the authorization for the storehouse brought forward by those venerable ones.

How so? While the authorizations for individuals such as the receiver of robes and so forth may be authorized within the monastery, in the midst of the entire Saṅgha, or even within a partial boundary (khaṇḍasīmā), the authorization for the monastery designated as a "storehouse" (bhaṇḍāgāra) must be authorized only in the middle of the monastery itself.
It is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*; therein, the specific reason [for this distinction] must be sought.

In this regard, the specific reason is understood as follows: it was stated for the purpose of avoiding the fault of saying, "The site for one boundary is different from the formal act (*kammavācā*) for another.

For, since the formal appointments of individuals have the individual as their basis, if one wishes to perform [the ceremony] within a monastery that constitutes a great boundary (*mahāsīma*), [this distinction is necessary].
They should perform it while keeping that person who is the subject of the matter within arm’s reach in the midst of the entire Saṅgha.

If they wish to perform it within a *khaṇḍasīmā* (an incomplete boundary), they should bring that person who is the subject of the matter into the *khaṇḍasīmā*, and perform it while keeping him within arm’s reach of the Saṅgha assembled there who has attained the legal capacity for the act. In either case, the aforementioned fault does not exist; however, regarding the authorization of a storehouse (*bhaṇḍāgārasammuti*)...
Because a storehouse is not a monastery (*vihāra*), it is impossible to bring it within the partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*).

Therefore, if they were to perform that formal act (*sammuti*) while standing within the partial boundary, the site would be in the great boundary (*mahāsīma*) while the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) would be in the partial boundary;

thus, the aforementioned fault arises. And when that fault exists, because the site is defective, the formal act fails. Therefore, [the formal act] must be performed right in the middle of the monastery that constitutes the great boundary.

The opinion of the commentators (*aṭṭhakathācariya*) is that this agreement (*sammuti*) must be made; it does not mean that a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (*ñattidutiyakamma*) should be performed for the access zone (*upacārasīmā*).

Furthermore, if they should say, "By the word 'monastery' (*vihāra*), it is the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) that constitutes the non-separation zone (*avippavāsasīma*) which is meant, not the access zone," how is this statement to be understood?
It is by this very commentarial statement. For if it were the access zone...
It would be as follows: what is called a "proximity boundary" (upacārasīmā) occurs even by extending over a fixed boundary; when monasteries or monks increase, it expands without restriction.
Therefore, because it functions by extending over a fragmented boundary (khaṇḍasīmā), the fragmented boundary is indeed one and the same boundary as the monastery.
This being so, a storehouse situated within the monastery [is included] in the fragmented boundary.

It would be possible to designate [the boundary] after standing [there], but it is not permissible to designate it while sitting within a *khaṇḍasīmā* (fragmentary boundary), because this is prohibited in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

By this, it is understood that in this context, by the term "monastery" (*vihāra*), the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) which constitutes the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsasīmā*) is meant, and not the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*). This is because [designation] within the precinct boundary occurs without a fixed location.

How is the state of expansion to be understood? It is delimited by the enclosure of a monastery that has an enclosure for the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*), or, in the case of one without an enclosure, by the place suitable for an enclosure.

Furthermore, it extends from the place where monks regularly assemble, or from a dining hall situated at the edge, or from a residence where they dwell permanently, [to a distance of] a medium-sized man’s [throw].
The boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīmā*) should be understood as being within the distance of two stone-throwings;
furthermore, it expands when monasteries expand and contracts when they contract. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated that "it also expands when the monks increase";
therefore, if [the monastery] remains connected as one unit with the monks assembled in the vihāra, even if it extends for a hundred leagues—
"Having filled [the space], they sit down; even a hundred yojanas becomes the boundary of the precinct (upacārasīmā), and the gain accrues to all"—such is the statement in the Commentary.
If this is so, why is it stated that the formal spreading of the kaṭhina occurs within the precinct boundary?

The spreading of the kaṭhina is not an act of the Saṅgha; it is merely an act of an individual. Therefore, regarding the precinct boundary which serves as the field for entering the rains residence...

It must be performed. However, since the formal proclamation (*ñattikammavācā*) constitutes a formal act of the Saṅgha (*saṅghakamma*), it is not permitted to perform it within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*);
rather, it should be understood that it is only permitted within a boundary—whether formally established or not—that has been well-cleared of the assembly. But surely, sir, regarding the question:
"Who is entitled to spread the Kathina, and who is not? First, by way of enumeration, at the very least..."
It is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “Five persons receive [the robe], even if it is worth more than a hundred thousand; below five, they do not receive it. Yet, why is it said:
“The act of spreading the *kaṭhina* is not a formal act of the Saṅgha (*saṅghakamma*); it is indeed an act of an individual (*puggalakamma*)”?
[For] “it is not the Saṅgha that spreads the *kaṭhina*, nor is it a group (*gaṇa*) that spreads the *kaṭhina*; an individual spreads the *kaṭhina*...”

This is because it is stated in the *Parivāra* that "it is spread" (*attharati*), and because it is not included among the four types of formal acts of the Saṅgha, such as the act of seeking permission (*apalokanakamma*).

However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, this was said with reference to the time of reciting the formal procedure for the gift of the *kaṭhina*, which constitutes the preliminary stage (*upacāra*) for the spreading of the *kaṭhina*.
For at that time, there are four givers of the *kaṭhina* and one receiver; thus, even by the minimum limit (*pacchimakoṭi*), [the quorum is met].

There are five [kinds of formal acts], and below that, none are obtained. How is it to be known that the *ñatti* (motion) and the *kammavācā* (proclamation) constitute a formal act of the Saṅgha? It is because it is stated:

"Of the four kinds of Saṅgha formal acts, the *ñattidutiyakamma* (formal act with a motion followed by one proclamation) applies to nine matters, namely, the offering of the Kathina cloth," and because it is said:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me; this Kathina-cloth has arisen for the Saṅgha," and so forth.
However, other teachers say: "The formal act of giving the *kathina* cloth, which is called a 'motion' (*ñatti*) in other languages, enters into the act of spreading [the cloth];

and since the act of spreading must be performed within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*), therefore the formal act of giving the *kathina* cloth must also be performed within the precinct boundary.
Their intention is as follows: in the *Mahāvagga-pāḷi*, it says: "And thus, monks..."

Beginning with the words, "The *kaṭhina* should be spread," and continuing from the formal act (*ñatti-kamma*) consisting of the motion for the gift of the *kaṭhina*—from "A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha...
[etc. ...In this way, monks, the *kaṭhina* is considered spread" up until the expression of thanks (*anumodanā*), the text has been handed down;
and in the *Parivāra-pāḷi*, there is the summary statement: "The spreading of the *kaṭhina* is to be understood."
In the *Niddesa*, having raised the question: "If a cloth for the *kaṭhina* has arisen for the Saṅgha, how should the Saṅgha proceed?
How should the one who spreads the *kaṭhina* proceed? How should the one who expresses appreciation proceed?"—it is stated:
"The Saṅgha should give [the cloth] to the monk who is to spread the *kaṭhina* by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second [announcement]... [and so forth]."
The text has come down from the motion (*ñatti*) up to the expression of appreciation (*anumodanā*).
Therefore, the entire procedure from the motion up to the appreciation pertains to the act of spreading the Kathina cloth;

consequently, since the act of spreading the Kathina must be performed within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*), the formal act of giving the Kathina, which consists of the motion, must also be performed within that precinct boundary.

In this regard, the following investigation should be made: If the act of spreading (the kaṭhina) were not mentioned separately, one might have to say that "the entire procedure is included within the act of spreading.

However, since the act of spreading is indeed mentioned separately both in the Mahāvagga-pāḷi and in the Parivāra-pāḷi, therefore the formal ritual utterance (kammavācā) for the giving of the kaṭhina, known as the motion (ñatti), [is distinct] from the act of spreading.
It does not enter [the formal act]; however, because it serves as the preliminary stage for the performance of the *atthāra* (spreading out), it is stated from that point onward in due sequence.

Just as, after granting permission for the delimitation of a boundary with the words, "Bhikkhus, I allow you to establish a boundary," and then showing the procedure for establishing the boundary by saying, "And thus, bhikkhus, it should be established," [the text begins]: "First, the signs..."

"The boundaries are to be proclaimed... [etc. ...thus do I remember this. Along with the proclamation of the boundary marks (*nimitta*), the formal act of authorization for the boundary (*sīmāsammutikamma*) was taught through the ritual formulas (*kammavācā*).

In that context, the proclamation of the boundary marks is not itself the formal act of authorization for the boundary; rather, it is the ritual formula alone that constitutes the formal act of authorization for the boundary.

Nevertheless, because the ritual formula for authorizing the boundary exists within the vicinity of the proclamation of the boundary marks, it is referred to as "the ritual formula for authorizing the boundary along with the proclamation of the boundary marks."

It has been taught. And just as, when teaching the procedure for the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma-vidhi*), the full ordination act was taught together with the taking of a preceptor (*upajjhāya*) and so forth—beginning with "First, one should have [the candidate] take a preceptor... [and so on]...

thus do I remember it"—in that context, the taking of a preceptor and so forth is not itself the formal act of full ordination; rather, only the motion followed by the third proclamation (*ñatticatuttha-kammavācā*) is the formal act of full ordination.

Nevertheless, because it occurred in proximity to the formal act of ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*), the procedure consisting of the motion followed by the fourth proclamation (*ñatticatuttha-kammavācā*) was taught together with the taking of a preceptor (*upajjhāya*) and so forth; likewise,

although the act of spreading the *kaṭhina* cloth is not present here within the formal act of giving the *kaṭhina*, nevertheless, because it constitutes the preliminary stage for the act of spreading,
the act of spreading the *kaṭhina* is taught together with the formal act consisting of the motion followed by the second proclamation (*ñattidutiya-kammavācā*) for the giving of the *kaṭhina*.
Therefore, it should be understood that the formal act of the *kathina* offering (*kathinadāna-kammavācā*) does not enter into the act of spreading the *kathina* cloth (*atthāra-kiriyā*).

Alternatively, these two things—the formal act consisting of a motion followed by a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakammavācā*) and the spreading (*atthāra*)—are of unequal functions, have unequal agents, are unequal acts, and occur at unequal times;
by this it is known that what is called "the motion" (*ñatti*) in other languages refers to the formal act consisting of a motion followed by a second proclamation.
"...it does not enter into the act of spreading. In that regard, how are the acts unequal? The formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) is the act of giving;
the spreading is the act of spreading which serves as the cause for fifteen factors. Thus, the acts are unequal. How are the agents unequal?
The agent of the formal proclamation is the Saṅgha; the agent of the spreading is an individual (*puggala*). Thus, the agents are unequal.
They are so. How are their actions unequal? The action of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) concerns the cloth for the *kaṭhina*;
the action of the spreading concerns the collective designation known as the *kaṭhina*. Thus, their actions are unequal. How are their times unequal?
The formal proclamation for the giving of the *kaṭhina* occurs prior to the preliminary acts, the relinquishment, and the determination; [whereas] the spreading...

After them, they are thus of unequal duration. Alternatively, the act of spreading [the kaṭhina] is comprised by a single factor consisting of vocal expression, such as the words "I spread the kaṭhina with this outer robe," and is not comprised by multiple factors such as the motion (*ñatti*) and the proclamation (*anussāvana*).
For this has been stated in the Parivāra: "The act of spreading is comprised by a single factor."
"By means of a verbal distinction. For this reason also, it should be understood that "the motion (*ñatti*) has not entered into the spreading of the kathina.
However, other teachers say as follows: "Who obtains the spreading of the kathina, and who does not?
First, by way of number, at the minimum five persons obtain it; above that, even up to a hundred thousand, but below five," [they do not].

Because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) that "they do not obtain [it]," it is understood that "at the very least, five monks obtain the spreading of the *kaṭhina*; fewer than that do not obtain it.
Regarding the statement "it is suitable for five people," this refers to a minimum of four givers of the *kaṭhina* cloth and one recipient, making five people.
Since it is stated in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-Ṭīkā* that "it is permissible," in that sentence the agent of the action "it is permissible" is called "that person who performs the *kaṭhina*-spreading.
Therefore, by the term "spreading" (*atthāra*), the act of spreading expressed in the words "I spread the *kaṭhina* with this outer robe" is not intended;
rather, it refers to the formal motion (*ñatti*) made by the four monks for the monk who is performing the spreading.
It is understood that "giving" (dāna) is intended here. Regarding the statement, “Who receives the spreading of the Kathina...
up to one hundred thousand [pieces]?”—this was said with reference to the act of giving Kathina-cloth to the Saṅgha by the monk who performs the spreading, as stated in the *Vinayavinicchaya-ṭīkā*.
Even in that reading, it is with reference specifically to what is given through a formal motion (ñatti) that it says, “five persons receive the spreading.”

This statement was uttered by the commentators of the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "The intention of the commentator of the *Ṭīkā* is that such phrases as 'I spread the *kaṭhina* with this outer robe' were not spoken with reference to the spreading [of the *kaṭhina*] by an individual.

Thus, because the masters who composed the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-Ṭīkā* and the *Vinayavinicchaya-Ṭīkā* have determined that "the formal act consisting of a motion and a second resolution (*ñattidutiyakamma*) is what is called the spreading," the formal act of the proclamation of the motion for the gift of the *kaṭhina* must take place within the functional boundary (*upacārasīmā*).
"It is understood that it is appropriate," they say.

Regarding this, the following investigation should be made: "The teachers of the *Ṭīkā* would not have said that 'only a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*)' is what is called an 'announcement' (*atthāra*).
If they had so stated, it would contradict the *Aṭṭhakathā*. How would it be contradictory? [As it says: "One whose rains-residence has been interrupted..."

Because it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā (the Commentary) that “it is said in the Mahāpaccarī that those who have entered [the rains residence] during the later period do not obtain [the kaṭhina], nor do those who have completed the rains residence in another monastery,” it is understood that “those whose rains residence was interrupted and so forth do not obtain the spreading of the kaṭhina.
If the formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) were called “spreading,” then in that case, they...
The monks might not have entered into the formal act consisting of a motion and a second (*ñattidutiyakamma*) by way of being members who complete the quorum.

Nevertheless, because it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) that "all those who have arrived during the first *pāṭipadā* are indeed quorum-completers," they have indeed entered into the formal act consisting of a motion and a second;
therefore, the commentator [states] that which serves as the cause for the five benefits: "By means of this outer robe..."

He says that only the verbal expression beginning with "I am spreading the kaṭhina" constitutes the "spreading," and not the formal act consisting of a motion followed by a second proclamation (ñattidutiyakamma).
Therefore, it is understood that those five types of persons, such as those whose rains-residence is broken, do not obtain the spreading of the kaṭhina which is the cause for the five benefits;

however, in the case of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by a second proclamation, they do obtain the status of completing the quorum of a fourfold Saṅgha. Furthermore, it is stated in the Commentary:
“If there are four, three, two, or even one person who has entered during the first period, the kaṭhina should be spread by making the others fulfill the quorum.
Thus, when the spreading of the kaṭhina cannot be obtained [otherwise], those whose rains-residence is broken and so forth should be made to fulfill the quorum;

having caused the cloth for the kaṭhina to be given through a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakammavācā*) by those who have entered during the first period, [the kaṭhina is spread].

We said, "The commentators would not say that 'the formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (ñattidutiyakamma) alone is called the spreading (atthāra),' because the Kathina is something that must be spread.
But, sir, does this statement from the Aṭṭhakathā— "having made the others fulfill the quorum, the Kathina should be spread"— not [support your view]?
Is it the case that only a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) to be performed by a Saṅgha of four members is called "the spreading" (*atthāra*)?

No, because of the contradiction between what precedes and what follows. For previously, it was stated that the spreading of the kaṭhina is not permitted for those whose rains-residence has been interrupted and so forth;
whereas here, if it were said that "the formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation is the spreading," it would imply that it is permitted even for them.
The commentators of the *Aṭṭhakathā* would not speak anything that contradicts what precedes or follows;
therefore, the word "having made" (*katvā*) should be connected with the word "to be spread out" (*attharitabbaṃ*) not as a simultaneous qualification, but specifically as a prior-time qualification.
This being so, the subsequent statement accords with the preceding statement, just as the waters of the Yamunā accord with the waters of the Gaṅgā. Furthermore...
And because it is stated that they will depart after having announced the formal act (*kammavācā*), having had the kaṭhina spread, and having partaken of the gift,
the separate announcement of the formal act and the separate spreading of the kaṭhina are mentioned according to their sequential order; therefore,
the motion with one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) is not itself called "the spreading," but should be understood as merely the cause for the spreading, or its preliminary procedure.
Furthermore—“The Saṅgha does not spread the *kaṭhina*; a group (*gaṇa*) does not spread the *kaṭhina*;
an individual (*puggala*) spreads the *kaṭhina*”—this meaning should be understood from the statement in the *Parivāra*.
If this is so, how is the intended meaning of the passages found in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-ṭīkā* and the *Vinayavinicchaya-ṭīkā* to be explained?

It ought to be stated thus: In the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-Ṭīkā*, is it not the case that for the verb "is permissible" (*vaṭṭati*), the agent is said to be "that person who performs the spreading of the Kathina" (*so kathinatthāro*)?

And in the *Vinayavinicchaya-Ṭīkā*, the phrase "the act of giving the cloth for the Kathina" (*kathinadussadānakamma*) is the object of the verb "with reference to" (*sandhāya*); and [the phrase] "the spreading of the Kathina... this was said" (*vutta*) is the object of the verb "was said."

It is so. Thus, when there are readings found in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*) as being of explicit meaning (*nītattha*), should it not be said that "the teachers of the commentaries would not have stated that the motion with a second resolution (*ñattidutiyakamma*) alone is what is called 'proclamation' (*atthāra*)"?

The intention of the commentary readings is to be understood in such a way that the words of the commentary do not contradict the words of the [older] commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*)—both preceding and succeeding.
It should be accepted. How so? In the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "At the very minimum, it is permissible for five persons.
Since that commentary passage implies the existence of someone to be censured by the accuser, in order to avoid that [implication], [the text] says:
"It is permissible for five persons" refers to the four [persons] at the lower limit regarding the *kathina* cloth.
The commentator (Ṭīkācariya) stated: "The reading is 'givers' and 'one recipient,' which is permissible for five persons.

How then can it be challenged? [One might say: "O Master of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathācariya), you have said that 'at the very least, it is permissible for five persons'; if that is so, then this spreading of the kaṭhina belongs only to those five who perform the kaṭhina-spreading ceremony."

[If one were to say] "it is permissible for five people, but not for one, two, three, or four persons"—such being the case, it would entail a contradiction with the tradition (*āgama*), because it would conflict with the canonical text (*pāḷi*) which states: "The Saṅgha does not spread the *kaṭhina*; a group (*gaṇa*) does not spread the *kaṭhina*;
an individual (*puggala*) spreads the *kaṭhina*. Avoiding that objection, [the author] says: "It is permissible for five persons..."
The commentator (Ṭīkācariya) stated: "At the very limit, it is permissible for five people—four donors of the *kathina* cloth and one recipient.
