Regarding this, the intended meaning is as follows: "O teacher who challenges [the commentary], according to the teacher of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathācariya*), at the time of the *kathina* spreading, with reference to five monks who perform the spreading, [he said]: 'At the very minimum limit...'"
The reading "it is permissible for five persons" was not stated; rather, when the Saṅgha gives the cloth for the kaṭhina to the one who performs the spreading,
it is permissible for that subsequent spreading to be performed because of the existence of five individuals— four givers of the kaṭhina-cloth and one recipient—
since the perfection of the result follows from the perfection of the cause.
Therefore, no contradiction with the scriptures arises regarding that statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
In the *Vinayavinicchaya-ṭīkā* as well, it is said: "Who receives the *kathinatthāra*, and who does not?
First, by way of number, at the minimum five persons receive it; above that, even up to a hundred thousand, but below five [they do not]."
In response to the existence of a question that ought to be asked by others regarding the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*—"they do not obtain [it]"—the commentator (*Ṭīkācariya*) stated:
"This was said with reference to the act of a monk who spreads the *kaṭhina* cloth making a gift of the *kaṭhina* material to the Saṅgha.
If one asks, "How is it to be questioned? [the answer is: "O Master of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, according to the lower limit..."

Regarding the statement, "It is appropriate for five persons," does this refer to the act of spreading (*atthārakiriyā*)—such as "I shall spread the *kaṭhina* with this outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*)"—which serves as the cause for the five benefits, or rather to the act of giving the *kaṭhina*-cloth (*kathinadussadānakamma*), which serves as the cause for the spreading itself?
How is this to be resolved? O gentle sir, [starting] from the lower limit...

The statement, “It is suitable for five persons,” was not spoken by the commentator with reference to the act of spreading the kaṭhina—such as “I spread the kaṭhina with this outer robe”—which serves as the cause for the five benefits;
rather, it was spoken with reference to the act of giving the kaṭhina material, which is the cause for that act of spreading. This is the intended meaning therein.
The spreading of the *kaṭhina* occurs only with cloth given by the Saṅgha to the one who spreads it;
it does not occur with robe-cloth obtained through a formal assignment (*ṭhitikā*) or with private robe-cloth (*puggalika-cīvara*).

Furthermore, that act of giving the *kaṭhina*-cloth succeeds only when five monks are present—namely, four givers of the *kaṭhina*-cloth and one receiver—and not with fewer than that; such is the minimum limit.

It is permissible for five [monks]. Since the establishment of the fruit follows from the establishment of the cause, it is for that very reason—not stating it in its primary sense as "the act of giving the cloth for the kaṭhina has been described"—but rather using a figurative sense, he says "it was said with reference to [that].

When this is stated, there is no contradiction between the preceding and following passages of the Aṭṭhakathā; however, the statement in the Ṭīkā is in contradiction with the statement in the Aṭṭhakathā.

It should be understood that [the robe] does not exist; furthermore, this accords with the characteristic of the Vinaya in the statement: “The Blessed One authorized a bound boundary for the purpose of performing formal acts of the Saṅgha, such as seeking permission.
However, the act of spreading [the Kathina], such as saying, “With this outer robe, I shall spread the Kathina,” pertains to the four [procedures] beginning with seeking permission.

Since it is merely an act of an individual— like a formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and so forth— that serves as the cause for obtaining the five benefits, but does not enter into formal *saṅgha* procedures,

it must be performed within the *upacārasīmā* (the precinct boundary) which constitutes the field for the commencement of the rains retreat. Therefore, where no formally established boundary exists within the *upacārasīmā*,
one may perform it either within the *upacārasīmā* outside [the monastery], or in a place that can accommodate the seven-fathom distance required for the throwing of water (*udakukkhepa*).

Or, having gone [to the donor] and caused him to give the cloth for the kaṭhina by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiyakamma), one should return to the monastery and understand that the spreading of the kaṭhina within the boundary of the precinct (upacārasīmā) itself was performed by the former teachers; thus it is indeed well-performed.

If, however, it were understood that the formal act consisting of a motion and a second should be carried out only within the pure precinct boundary (suddhaupacārasīmā) without taking [the donor] in this way, then for those venerable ones...

Following the example of their teacher, the students and their own students— whether for the purpose of permanent residence, performing the formal act of requesting permission for the donation of a monastery and so forth, or the formal acts consisting of a motion such as the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā,
or the formal acts consisting of a motion and a second proclamation such as the demarcation of a boundary, or the formal acts consisting of a motion and a fourth proclamation such as ordination—
should perform these very within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*). By acting in this way, they will cause great entanglement and great confusion in the Blessed One’s Dispensation.
They might bring great disorder to the Saṅgha; therefore, for the sake of preventing that, we have spoken by adducing numerous reasons from both logic and scripture.
Having shown reverence for the Dispensation and in accordance with the True Dhamma—
"May the virtuous consider the judgment made by me with right reflection.
Having reflected upon it again and again, if it is logical, let them accept it;
if it is not logical, let them not accept it, for they are disciples of the Perfectly Enlightened One."
The teachers bring forward other reasons as well to establish this point, but a refutation of them would result in excessive prolixity;
for it has already been stated previously that the status of the functional boundary (upacārasīmā) as the locus where the four sanghakammas are performed is established.
Therefore, having taken that statement to heart and without harboring doubt, it should be retained.
Regarding the statement, “I spread the kaṭhina with this outer robe (saṅghāṭī),” the question arises:
is the kaṭhina considered spread by this much verbal expression alone, or must some other physical gesture be performed? It need not be performed;
for by this verbal expression alone, the kaṭhina is indeed spread. For it is said in the Parivāra: “The spreading [of the kaṭhina] is by means of one factor...”
“It is included by way of a verbal expression.
Having thus shown the spreading of the *kathina*, he said, “By that monk who spreads the *kathina*,” and so forth, in order to demonstrate the requesting of thanksgiving and the thanksgiving itself.
In that context, it refers to the monk who [expresses] the *kathina* through a verbal expression such as, “With this outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*), I spread the *kathina*,” and so on.
Because it is stated in the *Parivāra* that "fifteen qualities arise from the spreading of the *kaṭhina*," the five benefits are presented together with the act of spreading the *kaṭhina*.

Now, why is the Saṅgha asked for its approval? Although the five benefits are stated for the monk who performs the spreading, they are not stated for the Saṅgha; therefore, [it is for the sake of the Saṅgha...]
If one causes the Saṅgha to give thanks for the purpose of the robe-making ceremony, and the Saṅgha performs the thanksgiving, then when this has been done, the benefits accrue to both.
For it is said in the Parivāra: "The Kathina is considered spread for two persons:
for the one who spreads it and for the one who gives thanks. And here, [the one giving thanks] is one senior to the monk who spread the Kathina.

There is a monk present in that Saṅgha; here, according to the method stated, he should be addressed as "Venerable Sir" by the one performing the formal act (*atthāraka*), and as "Friend" by the one offering the thanksgiving (*anumodaka*).
However, if the monk performing the Kathina-spreading ceremony is the most senior of all, he should address them as "Friends," while the others should address him as "Venerable Sir";
this same principle applies to the other two methods as well. In this way, the formal act is performed for everyone.

Regarding the term *kathina*: among these members of the Saṅgha and individuals, only those who entered the rains residence in that monastery during the earlier period (*purimikā*) and performed the first invitation ceremony (*paṭhamapavāraṇā*) are permitted to offer the expression of appreciation (*anumodana*). Those whose rains residence was interrupted, those who entered during the later period (*pacchimikā*), or those who completed their rains residence in another monastery do not receive permission;
nor do they obtain the benefit (*ānisaṃsa*) if they do not offer the expression of appreciation.
Having thus shown the spreading of the *kathina*, he now said, "But when the *kathina* has been spread in this way," etc., in order to show the distribution of the robes (*cīvaravibhāga*).

Therein, by the phrase "if there is a benefit brought along with the *kathina*-robe," it is indicated that the robe which is actually spread as the *kathina* itself is called the *kathina-robe*; all other robes brought along with it are *kathina-benefit-robes*.
He indicates by the word "name" (nāma). For he will say: "The remaining benefits of the *kathina* are established as being powerful," and so forth.
By this it is known that "here, 'benefit' (ānisansa) refers only to the cloth itself, not to its value;

it should be spread out according to the abundance of other cloths brought along with the *kathina* robe-cloth, and not according to the high value of the *kathina* robe-cloth. [The] Saṅgha of bhikkhus...
It is not the owner; the monk alone is the master of the spread kaṭhina. Why? Because it has been assigned by the donors. The Saṅgha of monks is the master; why?
Because it has not been assigned by the donors, and because the original kaṭhina was given to the Saṅgha. Regarding the remaining benefits of the kaṭhina:
these are the robes that constitute the remaining benefits of the kaṭhina from the cloth given for it. "Strongly determined" refers specifically to the kaṭhina robe-cloth that is to be spread.

It is permissible to give either new cloth or that which is nearly new; however, as for the *ānisaṃsa-cīvara* (robe of merit), it is permissible to give it according to one's means and power, whether old or new, weak or strong.

Therefore, if a robe made of weak cloth is given for the sake of its durability, it does not provide benefit to the monk who receives it; thus, [one should give] strong cloths that are suitable for providing such benefit.

The intention is that they are to be given. "They are to be given according to the order of the rainy-season residence" means that setting aside those monks who received the rainy-season robe-cloth, they are to be given in successive order starting from those below them.
"Starting from the senior seat" means starting from the most senior monk among those present within the boundary where the *kathina* has been spread.

[These benefits] should be given starting from [the day of] the Kathina ceremony. However, the rule regarding the taking of seats was made with reference to those who have already sat down according to seniority.
By this, it is indicated that the benefits of the rainy-season residence (vassāvāsika) and the Kathina robe are of the same category.

"Heavy goods (garubhaṇḍa) are not to be divided" means that among the items brought along with the Kathina cloth, such as beds and benches, which are classified as heavy goods, they are not to be divided; rather, they remain the property of the Saṅgha.
The meaning is that it should be used. In this regard, the determination concerning heavy goods will be clarified in the subsequent discussion.

However, there is something that must be said at this point. How so? It may appear as though it is not appropriate for monks now to distribute the robe obtained through the benefits of the *kathina* ceremony by casting lots with blades of *kusa* grass. Why is that? [Because] regarding the remaining benefits of the *kathina*:
"Strong cloths should be given by means of a rain-season lottery; in the absence of a lottery, they should be given starting from the seat of the senior elder"—so says the text.
This being the case, where should the "falling of the blade of kusa grass" (the method of distribution) be performed? It should be performed upon the robes kept in the storehouse.
How is this known? Because it is said: "'It is abundant' means it has been made into a large heap; it does not fit within the storehouse."
"By being present" means by standing within the precinct boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*). "To divide" means to call out the time [for distribution] and then divide it in order...

[as follows]... because it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) that "once the special robe-cloths have been thus set aside, a blade of *kusa* grass should be cast [to determine the lot]," therefore it is our view that they should be divided according to the method stated in this very Commentary.
However, some monks, not being able to provide each person with one robe, exchanged robes and took unallowable items to distribute;
that was indeed too gross. Others also, because some robes were expensive and others were cheap, were unable to equalize their value, so they did exactly that; that too was gross. In this regard:
For indeed, even in the case of exchanging it for an improper object, or in its distribution, or in the taking of shares, there is an offense.
Some, saying "the kaṭhina is difficult to distribute," do not perform the spreading;
they distribute it according to their own inclination as if it were private property. However, if that has been given by the donors to an individual, and by that individual...
If it has not been relinquished to the Saṅgha, then because it remains one's own property, it appears as though it is appropriate [to use].

However, if it has been given to the Saṅgha or a group (gaṇa), or even if it was given to an individual but subsequently relinquished to the Saṅgha or a group—this being the case, because it is the property of the Saṅgha or the group, it would be inappropriate.
Others, however, [hold that] when it is accepted by virtue of the kaṭhina...
Thinking it difficult to deliberate upon [the matter], they say, "We do not accept this by way of the *kaṭhina*;

we accept it solely as a *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe)," and then they deliberate as they please. That too is improper. For even that which is given to the Saṅgha as a *vassāvāsika* remains the property of the Saṅgha;
that which is given to an individual remains the property of that individual. If you ask how this is known: "If..."
However, if a *paṃsukūlika* (rag-robe wearer) is staying in their lodging, and seeing him arrive they say,
"We shall give you the *vassāvāsika* (rain-retreat gift)," he should inform the Saṅgha. If those families do not wish to give it to the Saṅgha and say,
"We shall give it to you alone," a bhikkhu who is a member of that community [should say], "Accept it after performing the proper service (*vatta*)."
For it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "It may be spoken [of as permissible], but this is not allowed for one who wears rag-robes (*paṃsukūlika*).

There are two kinds of *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe-cloth): by way of what is given out of faith (*saddhādeyya*) and by way of what arises locally (*tatruppāda*). For it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Thus, in the case of what is given out of faith, the donor people should be asked;
but in the case of what arises locally, the stewards (*kappiyakāraka*) should be asked. This applies even to *vassāvāsika* given out of faith.
It is twofold, according to whether one dwells [there] or does not dwell [there]. For this is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
“But the Elder Mahāpaduma said: ‘It should not be done in this way. For people give requisites for the purpose of maintaining their own residence;
therefore, other bhikkhus may enter there. However, as for those who have no lodging and give only requisites...”
“...and it is permissible to have them procure the requisite for those [robes] at a lodging where one resides during the rains.

What is called "arising there during the rains" refers to that which is produced from the cloth given into the hands of the kappiyakārakas (monastic stewards) for the purpose of using as a permissible article.
This is also stated in the Commentary: “For into the hands of the kappiyakārakas [it is said]: ‘Use this permissible article.’”

“Whatever is allowable from among the gifts of cloth that have been given, all of that is permitted to be used. Thus, even in the case of the rainy-season robe-cloth (*vassāvāsika-cīvara*), they previously gave it almost entirely to the Saṅgha;
therefore, when it is said, “We give this as Kathina-cloth,” it should be accepted in its capacity as Kathina-cloth;
when it is said, “We give this as rainy-season robe-cloth,” it should be accepted precisely in its capacity as rainy-season robe-cloth.
Why? Because of the statement: "One should act in accordance with what the donors say.
If they have departed without saying anything, having merely placed the gift in one's hand or at one's feet, what should be done?
In that case, if one should know: "This property has been dedicated for the sake of a shrine (cetīya), the Saṅgha, or a specific individual," [one should act accordingly].
It may be accepted for their sake. If, however, one should know that it has been dedicated "for my sake," it may be accepted for one's own sake.
For this has been stated in the Parivāra: "There are nine unrighteous gifts," and so forth.
If one knows nothing of the matter, and it has been placed in one's hand or at one's feet without saying anything, it becomes the private property of that person alone.
For one does not place anything dedicated for the sake of a shrine or the like in the hand or at the feet of a monk without saying anything;

for this has been stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "One gives to an individual" means either by saying in the person's absence, "I give this robe to so-and-so," or by placing it at their feet and saying, "Venerable sir, I give this to you."
“Or he gives it in person,” and so forth.
It is stated, “It should be distributed according to the method explained in this commentary. How should it be distributed?
Because it is stated: “The remaining benefits of the kaṭhina cloth, being of great value, should be given to those who have spent the rains residence.”
To those bhikkhus who did not receive the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe) during this year, one robe or one *sāṭaka* (garment) each should be given, starting from the lowest [in seniority].
Then, if there are robes or *sāṭakas* remaining, a second portion should be given again, starting from the seats of the elders (*therāsana*). After that, when the robes or *sāṭakas* are exhausted—
Among those who receive [the robes], the latter part of the year and so forth must be noted.
Not only are the cloths given on the very day the Kathina is spread called "benefits of the Kathina," but furthermore, robes given for the sake of the Saṅgha until the dismantling of the Kathina,
as well as robes brought by monastery attendants through funds belonging to the Saṅgha, are indeed benefits of the Kathina.
Therefore, when such robes arise, they should be distributed repeatedly starting from the monk who has been designated as having completed the rains retreat as previously described.

Because of the statement, "In the absence of a fixed order, they should be given starting from the seat of the senior elder," or because no *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) robes have arisen during that particular year, even if they were arising, [the distribution would proceed] by way of the fixed order (*ṭhitikā*).

Alternatively, if there is no *vassāvāsika-ṭhitikā* (distribution of robes at the end of the rains) because it has not been made available, then when the benefits of the *kaṭhina* robe have been obtained, all the monks should be seated in order within that precinct boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*).

Starting from the seat of the senior elder (*therāsana*), a distribution should be made by assigning one robe or one *sāṭaka* (lower garment) to each monk. Even at the time of giving to the most junior member of the Sangha (*saṅgha-navaka*), the great elders...
When they arrive, one should not say, "Venerable sirs, the [alms] for those of twenty years' seniority are being given; your turn has passed.
Rather, having set aside the turn for them, one should give it to them afterwards according to their seniority.

However, regarding the second portion, once the seats for the elders have been ascended, the first portion does not reach those who arrive later; from the second portion, it should be given according to seniority.
This discussion on the determination [of value] should be understood from the discourse on the distribution of the four requisites.

Now, sir, since some robes that are the benefits of the *kaṭhina* period are expensive while others are inexpensive, how can there be an equal value when one robe is given to each person? It is said: in the distribution of robes from the storehouse—
The value should be determined according to its worth. For it has been stated in the Cīvarakkhandhaka:
"Now at that time, robes were abundant in the Saṅgha’s storehouse. They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
'I allow you, monks, to distribute [the robes] by means of a Saṅgha present in assembly... Then, regarding the monks who were robe-distributors:
The thought occurred to them: “How now should the robe-cloth be distributed? They reported this matter to the Blessed One:

“I allow you, monks, having first gathered it up, weighed it, sorted it by quality and lack of quality, counted the monks, and formed groups, to set aside the portion for each monk’s share. And in the commentary: “Having gathered it up means: ‘This...’”
Having sorted through the robes thus: "This is coarse, this is fine, this is thick, this is thin, this has been used, this has not been used, this is this much in length, this is this much in width";
having weighed them thus: "This is worth this much, this is worth that much," having determined their value; and having praised or disparaged them...
If each person receives exactly ten coins worth ten [units], that is well;
if not, then whatever is worth nine or eight [units] should be bound together with another worth one and another worth two, and by this means they are placed as equal shares—this is the meaning.
"Having counted the monks and formed a group" means...

"If a single day is not sufficient when [the robes] are being given one by one, I authorize you to set aside the robe-quotas by counting ten monks at a time, binding ten individual robe-portions together into a single bundle, and making them into one parcel.

This is the meaning. It is said: "When the robe-quotas have been set aside in this manner, a blade of kusa grass must be cast [to determine the distribution]. By this, it is known that [this applies] to the distribution of robes from the storehouse.
"In that case, the value should be determined and the *kusapāta* (lot-casting) should be performed.
However, in this distribution of robes for the benefits of the *kathina*, the value need not be determined, nor should the *kusapāta* be performed.
For it is said in the *Kathinakkhandhaka-ṭīkā*: "But when the *kathina* has been spread in this manner..."
If the donors, together with the *kathina* robe, offer the resulting benefit saying, "We give this only to him who accepted our *kathina*," the Saṅgha of monks has no claim to it.
But if they depart after giving it without making such a distinction, the Saṅgha of monks has the right to it;
therefore, even if the remaining robes of the one who spread the *kathina* are also worn out, [the Saṅgha may take them].
After the Saṅgha has obtained permission, robes should be given for their sake as well; however, only a single formal act (kammavācā) is required.
As for the remaining benefits of the kaṭhina, the valuable robes should be given according to the order of seniority (vassāvāsika-ṭhitikā).
It is stated that "in the absence of such an order, they should be given starting from the seat of the Elder," but it is not stated that "one should determine their value."

Or: "a throw of kusa grass should be made. By this it is understood: "The robes that are the benefits of the kaṭhina should be given starting from the one who has been in residence for the rains or from the senior;
neither should their value be estimated, nor should a throw of kusa grass be made.

But now, because they have not been given as a rain-season gift (vassāvāsika) and because the rain-season residence has not been established, [the distribution] is from the robe for which the kaṭhina was spread...

Furthermore, from the cloth given for the purpose of providing the remaining robes for the one who has performed the *kathina* ceremony, and from the remaining *kathina* benefits, starting from the most valuable cloth, one cloth must be given to each monk;
among those, however, the best of the best should be given to the senior monk. If it is asked how this is known: on the day of the final entry into the rains retreat...

But if, after the time has been announced and the Saṅgha has assembled, someone brings a cloth ten cubits long and offers it as a *vassāvāsika* gift, it should be given to him if the newly arrived monk is the senior of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.
If he is junior, the appointed monk should say to the senior of the Saṅgha: "Venerable sir, if you wish, setting aside the first portion, this..."
"Take the cloth! It should not be given to one who does not let go [of what he already has]. However, if he lets go of what was previously taken and then takes it, it should be given.
By this same method, starting from the second elder and passing it along, it should be given to the newcomer at the place where the bowls are kept.
If those who entered the rains retreat for the first time received two, three, four, or five cloths, that which was obtained—
Having caused [the robe] to be distributed by this very means, it should be given until it becomes equal to that of the newcomer.
When it has become equal with him, the remaining portion should be given to the senior seat (therāsana).
This is because of the statement in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka-ṭīkā*, and also in the *Vimativinodanī* which is its commentary: "If the newcomer is a bhikkhu regarding the robe..."
After [the robes] had been distributed, a visiting monk arrived. "In the place where he has reached" means in the place he has reached according to his seniority (*vassaga*).
"Those who have entered the rains retreat first" means those who had already entered the rains retreat during the later period (*pacchimikā*) even before the visiting monk arrived.
"Whatever was obtained" refers to the fact that it is stated in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*: "from the donors, as each saṭaka arrived... and "the first portion..."
"Having released [the robe]"—this is understood from the statement: "And this was written because it is more valuable than the first cloth that was taken.

Thus, according to the *Aṭṭhakathā* and the *Ṭīkās*, regarding the gift of the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) robe, if a more valuable cloth is brought later, one should exchange it starting with the Great Elder (*Mahāthera*);
even if they do not desire it, [it belongs] to the one who has received it at the end of the *vassa*.

Since it is stated that [the robe] must be given to the monk who has arrived, it is understood that "the best [robe] should be given to the most senior. Because it is stated specifically in terms of the *number* of robes— namely,
"if those who have entered the rains-retreat for the first time received two, three, four, or five robes"— and because it is not stated in terms of the *value*,
and because the cloth that constitutes the benefit of the Kathina is of the same category as the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) robe, [it follows that the number of robes is the relevant criterion].

It should be understood that, according to the textual tradition, the requisites for the *kaṭhina* privileges are to be distributed solely by counting the number of items, and not by their equal monetary value;

for this very reason it is said: "If one person gives many requisites for the *kaṭhina* privileges, the *kaṭhina* should be spread using only what belongs to him. For indeed, when many requisites for the *kaṭhina* privileges are being divided...

"May those who are discerning consider the robe for the kaṭhina ceremony, having determined the legal decision by means of the scriptures, commentaries, and so forth, [concluding] that these things are beneficial to the Saṅgha."
“Having reflected again and again, let them retain that which is appropriate;
if it is inappropriate, let them seek another reason for it.
And as for the robe-offering in that case, it shall belong to those monks who have performed the *kaṭhina* ceremony.

Because the Blessed One has stated that [these items] belong to the Saṅgha, alms-food and other requisites given for the sake of the Saṅgha—other than robes—belong to whichever members of the Saṅgha arrive one after another once they have entered the functional boundary (upacārasīma).
For it is said in the Commentary: "Having had the kaṭhina spread and having partaken of the gift, they will depart; this is the benefit..."

"But for others, it belongs only to those [monks]. Based on the reading, "I allow you, monks, to give half a share to the novices," some give even the *kathina*-benefit robe as only half a share to the novices; however, this should not be done.
For it is only the out-of-season robe (*akālacīvara*) kept in the storehouse that is given as half a share to the novices.

It should be given after making [the calculation]. However, the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) robe, the *kathina* benefits, and so forth, as well as robes for the appropriate time, should be distributed equally.
For this is stated in the *Cīvarakkhandhaka-ṭīkā*: "Regarding the phrase 'for novices, half a share':
here, those novices who are independent and do not perform the duties that ought to be performed for the Saṅgha of monks—whether in recitation or in interrogation..."
Those who perform their duties and services toward their own preceptors and teachers alone, and not toward others, should be given half a share.
However, those who perform the necessary tasks for the Saṅgha of monks both before and after the meal, to them an equal share should be given.
And this [gift] is to be given from what has arisen during the afternoon and has been placed in the storehouse.
"It was said specifically regarding out-of-season robes; however, a robe for the proper season must be given equally.
"Have the novices entered the rains residence, such that they might receive the benefit? "Yes, they have entered.
"How is this known? "Then four monks had entered, and one novice who had completed his full year of training."

"Because of the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: 'One who receives full ordination during the later period (*pacchimikā*) both completes the quorum and obtains the benefits,' and because of the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*:

'One ordained during the later period is permitted to perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) even at the first invitation, and being one who has entered the rains retreat (*vassiko*), he obtains the benefits'—the entering of the rains retreat by novices (*sāmaṇera*) is thus authorized."
“...it exists. They say that novice monks receive the benefits of the kaṭhina.

Regarding the benefits of the kaṭhina arising from those sources, if monastery attendants exchange robes for rice and so forth, or exchange rice and so forth for robes, how should one proceed in that case?
At the time of distribution, it should be done according to the goods actually present.
It should be done accordingly. For it is said in the Vajirabuddhi-Ṭīkā:
"When robes are exchanged for rice and such items by means of what arises there [at that place], those robes reach only those who have performed the *kathina* ceremony.
But when rice and such items are exchanged for robes, it is said that they reach all [monks]. Furthermore: "If, however, there are many monasteries within a single boundary..."

Regarding the phrase "they exist," which boundary is intended here? It is the *upacāra-sīmā* (proximate boundary). For it is only within the *upacāra-sīmā* that the distribution of communal gains (*saṅghalābha*) and so forth is accomplished.
Indeed, this is stated in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*: "The phrase 'within the boundary where the *kaṭhina* has been spread' refers to the *upacāra-sīmā*;

for one who stands within the *upacāra-sīmā* is entitled to share in robes left by the deceased and other such items, whereas there is no arising [of such entitlement] within a formally bound (*baddha*) boundary."
"This should be understood as meaning that only the 'proximity boundary' (*upacārasīmā*) is intended.

Having thus shown the spreading of the *kathina*, and without showing the removal of the obstacles (*palibodha*) regarding the consent of the Saṅgha in the summary list (*mātikā*), he spoke the passage beginning with "For you, monks, who have spread the *kathina*," etc., in order to show the benefits at the end. Therein, the summary list (*mātikā*) is eightfold.
[The ten offenses involving the robe-making season are: departure, completion, determination, destruction, hearing, frustration of hope, crossing the boundary, and simultaneous removal.

In this context, a monk who has performed the *atthata-kathina* takes a finished robe and departs with the thought, "I will not return to this monastery"; for that monk, [the offense occurs] simply by crossing the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīmā*).
The suspension of the *kathina* occurs, and one becomes incapable of obtaining the five benefits.
This suspension of the *kathina* is called "terminating upon departure" because departure itself constitutes its end.
A monk for whom the *kathina* has been spread, having taken up his own portion of robe-cloth even before it is finished, goes to another monastery...
He has gone; while he is still outside the boundary of the precincts, the thought occurs to him: "I shall have this robe made in this very monastery; I will not return to the old monastery.
He has that robe made while still outside the boundary. When that robe is finished, there is the suspension of the *kaṭhina* for that bhikkhu.
This suspension of the *kaṭhina* occurs precisely upon the completion of the robe.
"End" means "ending with the conclusion.
A bhikkhu who has participated in the Kathina ceremony takes an unfinished robe and departs; while he is outside the vicinity of the boundary, the thought occurs to him:
"I will neither have this robe made up, nor will I return to my former monastery. For that bhikkhu...
By that formal determination, there is the suspension of the *kaṭhina*. This suspension of the *kaṭhina* is called "ending with the determination" because the determination itself is its limit.
A monk who has spread the *kaṭhina* departs taking an unmade robe; for him who has gone outside the boundary, it is thus...
If one thinks, "I shall have this robe made right here, and I will not return to my former monastery," and while the robe is being made,
it is lost by thieves and the like, or destroyed by fire and the like, there is a suspension of the *kaṭhina*.
This suspension of the *kaṭhina* is called "ending with loss" (*nāsanantika*), because loss itself is its limit.
A monk for whom the *kaṭhina* has been spread takes an unmade robe and, thinking, "I will return to that monastery," departs.
While he is outside the boundary, the thought occurs to him, "I shall have this robe made right here. Once the robe is made, he hears:
"It seems the *saṅgha* has suspended the *kaṭhina* in the monastery. By the mere hearing of that, his *kaṭhina* is suspended.
This is called "ending with hearing" (*savanantika*), because for this burden of the *kathina*, merely hearing [the announcement] constitutes its end.
A monk who has spread the *kathina* departs elsewhere for the sake of obtaining robe-material; while he is outside the boundary, it occurs to him:
"I shall attend here, right outside the boundary, to my expectation of robe-material; I will not return to the monastery."

He waits right there for that expectation of robe-cloth; failing to obtain that expectation of robe-cloth, his hope for the robe is cut off, and by that very fact, the *kaṭhina* suspension occurs for that bhikkhu.
This suspension of the *kaṭhina* is called "cutting off of hope" because it is accompanied by the cutting off of hope.
A bhikkhu who has spread the *kaṭhina*, taking an unmade robe and thinking, "I will return to this monastery," departs.

He goes outside the boundary and has that robe made. Having had the robe made, while thinking, "I shall return to the monastery," he spends the time for the suspension of the *kaṭhina* right within the outer precinct boundary; for him, there is the suspension of the *kaṭhina*.
This suspension of the *kaṭhina* is called "transgressing the boundary" because it occurs due to the passing of the boundary defined as the last day of the robe season.
A monk for whom the *kathina* has been spread takes his robe and, thinking, "I shall return to this monastery," departs.
Having finished making the robe, while thinking, "I shall return to the monastery," he returns and encounters the suspension of the *kathina* in that monastery;
for that monk, the suspension of the *kathina* occurs in the monastery together with the other monks. This is the suspension of the *kathina* in the monastery.
Because it is performed together with the bhikkhus, it is called "shared suspension" (sahubbhāra). These eight kinds of kathina-suspension are known as the eight matrices (mātikā).
For this has been stated in the Kathina-kkhandhaka of the Pāḷi: "Bhikkhus, there are these eight matrices for the suspension of the kathina:

that which ends with departure (pakkamanantika), that which ends with completion (niṭṭhānantika), that which ends with determination (sanniṭṭhānantika), that which ends with loss (nāsanantika), that which ends with hearing (savanantika), and that which ends with the cutting off of expectation (āsāvacchedika)."

"Exceeding the boundary together with the suspension. This refers to the passage beginning: "A bhikkhu, having taken up a robe that has been made when the kaṭhina has been spread, departs with the thought, 'I will not return';
for that bhikkhu, the suspension of the kaṭhina occurs at the moment of departure," and so forth.
And in the *Vinayavinicchaya-pakaraṇa*: "Departure, completion, determination, and loss."
“Savanamāsa, sīmā, and sahubbhāra—these are the eight.
Obstacles are of two kinds: the obstacle of residence (*āvāsa-palibodha*) and the obstacle of robes (*cīvara-palibodha*).
In this regard, even one who goes elsewhere thinking, “I will dwell in that monastery where the kaṭhina has been spread,” [does so] with the thought, “I will return to that monastery again.”

He remains dependent [on others]. This is called the impediment of the residence (*āvāsa-palibodha*). For that bhikkhu, his robe has either not been made or is not yet finished, or his hope—thinking, "I shall obtain a robe from elsewhere"—has not ceased. This is called the impediment of the robe (*cīvara-palibodha*).
For it is said in the Kathina-kkhandhaka: "And what, bhikkhus, are the two impediments to the Kathina? The impediment of the residence..."
And there is the impediment of robes. And how, monks, is there the impediment of a dwelling?
Here, monks, a monk either dwells in that dwelling or departs from it with longing, thinking, "I shall return.
In this way, monks, there is the impediment of a dwelling. And how, monks, is there the impediment of robes? Here, monks—
“Monks, when a monk’s robe is not yet made or is only half-made, or his expectation for a robe has not ceased—in this way, monks, there is the impediment of the robe.

The lifting (ubbhāra) is twofold, by way of the eightfold formal lifting (aṭṭhamātikā-ubbhāra) and the internal lifting (antarubbhāra). Therein, for those who have gone outside the precincts of the boundary...

The seven ways of the suspension of the *kathina* robe prescribed for monks, and the one way of suspension known as "simultaneous suspension" (sahubbhāra)— which occurs when, after going outside the boundary of the precinct (*bahi-upacāra-sīma*) and returning,
one reaches the internal suspension (*antarubbhāra*) in the monastery where the *kathina* was spread and it is performed together with the other monks—
these eight ways of suspending the *kathina* constitute the "suspension of the eighth rule," as they are included within the eighth section of the *mātikā*.

[The term] "name" [is used]. Without going outside the boundary, while sitting in that very monastery, the suspension of the Kathina by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakammavācā*)—being not included in the eighth heading [of the *Mātikā*], and being performed prematurely before the time limit has arrived—is called "suspension in the interim" (*antarubbhāra*).

Since both the suspension in the interim and the simultaneous suspension (*sahubbhāra*) are performed by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation, what is the distinction between them?
The "internal suspension" (*antarubbhāra*) is performed by monks remaining within the boundary itself, without having gone outside the boundary.

The "joint suspension" (*sahubbhāra*) is performed by a monk who has gone outside the boundary returning and joining with those monks staying within the boundary once he has reached that internal suspension;
this is the distinction between them. The seven types of suspension of the *kaṭhina*, such as that by departure (*pakkamanantikā*), do not...

When performed by means of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), they are called "the lifting of the *kaṭhina*" simply because the two obstacles have been removed and one has become free from the five disadvantages.
For this was said by the Elder Ācariya Buddhadatta in the *Vinayavinicchaya*:
"Whether by means of the eight headings (*mātikā*) or even by an intermediate lifting..."
"Two types of *ubbhāra* (lifting) were also taught by the Great Seer regarding the *kaṭhina*.
Regarding this, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "The eight headings (*mātikā*) are taught with reference to those who have gone outside the boundary (*bahisīma*).

The seven headings beginning with *pakkamanantikā* are taught with reference to one who, having gone outside the boundary, has reached the *antarubbhāra* (internal lifting); the *sahubbhāra* (simultaneous lifting)..."

And by way of these eight headings (*mātikā*): "Internal suspension" (*antarubbhāra*) is so called because it is obtained through the formal act of suspending the *kaṭhina* while remaining right there, without having gone outside the boundary;
thus, the Great Sage has stated that there are two ways of suspending the *kaṭhina*. "With suspension" (*sabbhāra*) refers to one who has gone outside the boundary and then returns.

It is said: “The ‘internal robe-offering’ (antarubbhāra) is so called by way of [the robe] not having gone outside the boundary; thus, there is only one single robe-offering that is spoken of in two ways.
But why is the kaṭhina robe offered out through the formal act (kammavācā) by way of the internal robe-offering?

Because it was requested by lay followers who, desiring to give a great gift, wished to give non-seasonal robes (akālacīvara) to the Saṅgha that had arrived. For it is stated in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga-pāḷi:
Now at that time, a certain lay follower had had a monastery built for the Saṅgha;
he wished to give out-of-season robes to both Saṅghas on the occasion of the dedication ceremony for that monastery.
At that time, however, the kaṭhina period had been spread for both Saṅghas. Then that lay follower approached the Saṅgha...
“...request the suspension of the *kathina*,” and so forth. But how should the formal act (*kammavācā*) be performed? “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha suspend the *kathina*. This is the motion (*ñatti*). Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
The Saṅgha suspends the *kathina*. Whosoever among the venerable ones approves of the suspension of the *kathina*, let him be silent.”
"Whoever does not approve should speak. The kaṭhina has been removed by the Saṅgha; it is approved by the Saṅgha, therefore there is silence;
thus do I understand this. It should be done in this way. For it is said in the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga: "I allow you, monks, to remove the kaṭhina.
And furthermore, monks, the kaṭhina should be removed in this way: by one who is competent..."
A competent monk should inform the Saṅgha: "Let the Saṅgha hear me...

[as before] ...I so declare. By this removal of the kaṭhina, they say that the formal act consisting of the motion and second proclamation for the gift of the kaṭhina-cloth previously performed is considered removed;

however, it is not the formal act consisting of the motion and second proclamation for the gift of the kaṭhina-cloth itself that is removed, but rather only the formal act of the spreading (atthāra-kamma).

This must be understood. For if the formal act (kamma) consisting of a motion and a second proclamation for the gift of the Kathina-cloth had been performed, then because the gift of the Kathina-cloth would have been accomplished by that formal declaration, that cloth previously given would have to be brought back again by this formal declaration for the suspension of the Kathina;
there would not be a loss of the five benefits. However, since it is by this formal declaration for the suspension of the Kathina...
There is only the removal of the five benefits, not the bringing back of the cloth for the kaṭhina that was previously given.
By this it is understood: "It is the act of spreading [the kaṭhina] itself—the cause for obtaining the five benefits—that is lifted by this formal act (kammavācā) for the suspension of the kaṭhina;

it is not the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation (ñattidutiyakamma) for the gift of the kaṭhina-cloth. Therefore, from the performance of the formal act for the suspension of the kaṭhina..."
It should be understood that if a robe-cloth arises for the Saṅgha after [the Kathina has been spread], it becomes an out-of-season robe (akālacīvara);
the Saṅgha does not obtain the five benefits, and the robe, having become the property of the entire Saṅgha, is to be distributed to whichever members of the Saṅgha arrive.
This meaning applies both to the formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation for the gift of the Kathina cloth and to the formal act for the suspension of the Kathina.
Having thoroughly determined the underlying intention and having reconciled what precedes and what follows, it should be understood.
Here, it might be asked: "Should the lifting of the kaṭhina robe be granted to all who request it, or only to some? What is the point here?
If it were to be granted to all, then because the five benefits would cease upon the formal act of lifting the kaṭhina...
"Would there be an obstruction to the Saṅgha’s gain? Or would it be like looking at the faces of some [individuals]?

If the gain resulting from the suspension of the Kathina is greater than the gain resulting from the spreading of the Kathina, then the suspension of the Kathina should be granted to those who ask for it. If it is small, it should not be granted.
If it is equal, it should be granted for the sake of inspiring confidence in the family. For thus it has been said:
In the *Aṭṭhakathā* it says: "What kind of robe-offering ceremony (*kathinuddhāra*) should be granted, and what kind should not be granted?
For one whose benefit rooted in the spreading [of the robe] is great, while the benefit rooted in the lifting [of the robe] is small—such a case should not be granted.

However, for one whose benefit rooted in the spreading is small, while the benefit rooted in the lifting is great—such a case should be granted. Even if the benefits are equal, it should be granted for the sake of protecting the faith."

By this it is understood that "only the formal act of spreading (atthārakamma), which is the cause of the five benefits, is being lifted up, and not the formal act consisting of two announcements (ñattidutiyakamma) that constitutes the gift of the Kathina cloth.
In the discourse on the benefits, "five" refers to the five actions now to be mentioned, beginning with going without having asked for permission (anāmantacāra). "They shall be allowable" means...

"Kappā bhavissanti" means they will become allowable; "anāpattikāraṇā bhavissantī" means they will become grounds for non-offense. "Anāmantacāro" means wandering without having informed [the resident monks].

For if one who has been invited by donors for a meal, being already fully satiated, enters among families without informing a monk present in the monastery, that monk incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya) under the training rule concerning wandering.
The meaning is that this offense does not apply to one for whom the *kathina* has been spread. In that regard, the training rule concerning visiting families (*cāritta-sikkhāpada*) is as follows:

"Whosoever, being a monk who has been invited to a communal meal, should visit families before or after the meal without having informed a monk present—except on an appropriate occasion—it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). In this context..."

"The proper occasion is the occasion for giving a robe, the occasion for making a robe; this is the proper occasion therein"—this is the fifth training rule in the section on the naked ascetics (*acelaka*).
"Separation from the robes" means the passing of dawn without being within arm's reach of any one of the three robes or all of them together;
the intention is that even if one acts in this way, there is no offense under the second *kathina* training rule.
In that context, the second training rule concerning the kaṭhina is the second rule among those involving forfeiture, which is stated as follows:
"When a robe has been finished and the kaṭhina has been removed, if a bhikkhu should be separated from his three robes for even one night,
except by the consent of the bhikkhus, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture."
"Group meal": the connection is that by this training rule concerning group meals, it is stated that there is no offense. In that context, a "group meal" means:
either through the solicitation of monks saying, "Give us food," or through the invitation of donors saying, "Take our food," when four or more monks accept together using an improper expression.

Eating on one side. The training rule concerning eating in a group is stated in the Chapter on Eating as follows: "In eating in a group, except at the proper time, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

Herein, this is the proper time: the time of illness, the time of giving robes, the time of making robes, the time of traveling on a journey, the time of boarding a boat, the time of a great assembly, and the time of a meal for ascetics; this is the proper time therein."

The second training rule. The intention is that there is no offense according to the first *kaṭhina* training rule because [the robe] is not formally determined (*anadhiṭṭhita*) nor assigned (*avikappita*). In this context, the "first *kaṭhina* training rule" refers to:
"When a robe has been finished and the *kaṭhina* has been removed, a monk may keep an extra robe for a maximum of ten days. That...

The first training rule among the *nissaggiya* offenses, which states, “For one who exceeds [the limit], it is a *nissaggiya pācittiya*,” has been cited. Regarding the phrase “within the boundary where the *kathina* has been spread”:
this is said with reference to the precinct boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*). “Clothing for the deceased” means clothing belonging to one who has died.

“From that source” refers to property belonging to the Saṅgha, such as monastery grounds, gardens, fields, or building sites. The sense is: “Whatever monastic robe-material arises shall belong to them.”
This shows that the robe itself belongs to the monks who performed the *kathina* ceremony,
whereas other requisites such as alms-food and medicine belong to the Saṅgha of whoever arrives.
Thus, a modest monk endowed with these eight factors is truly dear.
"One should properly perform the spreading of the *kathina* and also its removal.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Ornament of the Exposition on the Spreading of the *Kathina*" within the *Vinayālaṅkāra*,
which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
The Twenty-ninth Chapter. 30.
Discussion on the Determination of Valuable Goods (Garubhaṇḍa). 227.

Having thus explained the determination regarding the Kathina, he now spoke the words beginning with "In this context, 'valuable goods' (garubhaṇḍāni)" in order to show the determination concerning valuable goods and so forth. Therein, "valuable" (garu) means—
“*Garu* [is used] for a teacher and so forth, for parents who are venerable, for the three great ones, and for that which is difficult to carry and light.
Among these various meanings stated, it denotes the sense of being “light. The word *bhaṇḍa* [is used] for requisites such as vessels, and also for capital wealth.

And here, [the word] *cā* has the sense of requisites such as vessels. As for the meaning of the words: they are called *garūni* because they rise up (*uggacchanti*) and become manifest (*uggatā pākaṭā*).
They are called *bhaṇḍāni* because they are things to be cherished (*bhaḍitabbāni*) and desired (*icchitabbāni*). Being both *garūni* and *bhaṇḍāni*, they are *garubhaṇḍāni*:
sites such as monasteries (*ārāma*) and so forth. Thus, by this method, [the matter was dealt with] by the Blessed One in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*.
It should be understood that these five items shown here are called "heavy goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*).
Regarding beds: a *masāraka* is one made by boring holes in the bed-legs and inserting tenons (*aṭani*) therein.

A *bundikābaddha* is one made by fixing the bed-legs with tenons and shaping them into the form of a couch (*pallaṅka*). A *kuḷīrapādaka* is one [made from] the legs of donkeys, goats, and so forth...
It is made with feet resembling those of a crab; or whoever has crooked feet is called "crab-footed. Regarding the term "stake-footed" (āhacca-pādaka), it is stated later in the text itself:
"A stake-footed bed is one made by piercing holes in the frame [and fixing the legs there].
Therefore, having pierced the side-rails (aṭanī) and inserted the foot-tips therein, above—
Having inserted a pin, it should be understood as a bed with fixed legs. The same method applies to a chair as well.

"One of the five, such as a woolen mattress" means one of these five types of mattresses: a woolen mattress (*uṇṇabhisi*), a cotton mattress (*coḷabhisi*), a bark-fiber mattress (*vākabhisi*), a grass mattress (*tiṇabhisi*), or a leaf mattress (*paṇṇabhisi*).
"Five mattresses" refers to mattresses filled with the five materials beginning with wool.
For their enumeration is by way of counting the types of wool. In this context, by the mention of "wool" (*uṇṇā*), not only sheep’s wool is included;
rather, with the exception of human hair, all the feathers or fur of birds and quadrupeds—whether of the class of allowable or unallowable meat—is included here by the very term "wool.
Therefore, [this applies] to the six kinds of robes and the six kinds of secondary robes.
It is permissible to make a mattress by using some kind of inner stuffing and placing all of that inside.
However, even if one does not include wool fibers but instead places a blanket folded four or five times inside, it is still considered a "wool mattress" (*uṇṇabhisi*).
Regarding cotton mattresses and the like, whatever new or old cotton cloth has been gathered together—whether rolled up or placed inside—[is acceptable].
A cotton mattress (coḷabhisi) should be understood as one made by stuffing it with cotton; a flax mattress (vākabhisi) as one made by stuffing it with any kind of flax;
a grass mattress (tiṇabhisi) as one made by stuffing it with any kind of grass; and a leaf mattress (paṇṇabhisi) as one made by stuffing it with any kind of leaf except for pure *tāla* leaves.
However, a *tāla* leaf is permitted only when mixed with other materials, not when it is pure.

It is not permitted. There is no fixed measurement for a mattress; having observed what is appropriate for these—namely, a bed-mattress, a chair-mattress, a floor-covering mattress, a walking-path mattress, and a foot-wiping mattress—one should determine the size according to one’s own preference.
Furthermore, whatever five kinds of stuffing, such as wool and so forth, are permitted for a mattress, they are also permitted for a bolster.
"It is permissible" is stated in the *Kurundi*. Therein, "on a cushion" (*masūraka*) means on a mattress made of leather.
By this, it is established that it is permissible to use a cushion.

Regarding the three types of stuffing for a bolster: cotton from trees, cotton from creepers, and cotton from silkworms. Therein, "cotton from trees" refers to [the fibers] of the *simbali* tree and so forth.
The cotton of any kind of tree; "creeper-cotton" is the cotton of any kind of creeper, such as the milk-vine (*khīravallī*) and so forth;
"silkworm-cotton" is the cotton of any kind of grass species, such as the *poṭakī* grass and so forth, including even sugarcane and reeds.
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated that "silkworm-cotton" refers to the cotton of the *eraka* grass. By these three...
All classes of living beings are included. For there is no other class of living beings apart from trees, creepers, grasses, and shrubs;

therefore, if the cotton of any such class of being is suitable for stuffing a bolster (*bimbohana*), yet having reached the state of a mattress (*bhisi*), all of it is called "unallowable cotton" (*akappiyatūla*). And this is not only the case with cotton used for bolsters.
The feathers of all birds, such as swans and peacocks, and even the fur of all four-footed animals, such as lions, are permitted.

However, any kind of flower, including the *piyaṅgu* flower, the *bakuḷa* flower, and so forth, is not permitted. A *tamāla* leaf is not permitted when used alone, but it is permitted when mixed with other materials.
The five kinds of stuffing permitted for mattresses, such as wool and the like, are also permitted. As for those that cover half the body...

Cushions are not permitted. "Half-body [cushions]" refers to those measuring half the size of the body, which one places so that they support from the waist up to the head. However, a cushion the size of the head is permitted;
"the size of the head" means that when measured across the three ears, the distance between two ears is one cubit and four finger-breadths.
The middle part is one *ratana* in width; however, according to the *Kurundi*, it is one and a half *ratanas* or two *ratanas* in length.
This is the maximum limit for the size of the head; more than this is not permitted, but less is permitted, as stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Regarding that, [the phrase] "of the two ears among the three ears" refers to...
Some people, following the text, make the cloth to be placed at both ends of the pillow triangular;
they say, "This is the place for the knot. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says:
"The measure of the head is that where the entire head, together with the neck, can be placed."
It is possible; and in order to show that the measure of its fist-jewel is the same as its width, he said, "in width," and so forth.
This is a demonstration of the measure of the cloth to be placed at both ends of the bolster; by means of that, the width of the bolster is delimited.
It should be sewn together, having been made either circular or square, as follows:
From corner to corner, the width at its broadest part is the size of a fist;
it should be sewn in this manner, and anything more than this is not permitted.

Furthermore, when the cloth placed at the corners is doubled by joining corner to corner, it becomes three-cornered (*tikaṇṇa*); among those three corners, the distance between two corners is one span and four finger-breadths (*vidatthicaturaṅgula*).
Because it is stated that "the middle part, from end to end, is a fist-sized jewel," the cloth to be placed at both ends of the pillow is not naturally three-cornered;
rather, it is only when doubled up so that end meets end that it becomes so. Therefore, that cloth may be round or...
Whether it be square or doubled over, when measured, it remains triangular;
the distance between its two corners is exactly one span (vidatthi) plus four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula), and the middle portion of that cloth is one fist-span (muṭṭhiratana);
by the measurement of that very cloth, it is understood that the middle portion of the pillow is also one fist-span.
“Since it is stated in general terms that ‘only a blanket...

and so forth, ending with ‘it becomes what is called a woolen pad (uṇṇabhisi),’ it should be understood that even an unallowable woolen spread such as a *gonaka* is permissible to lie upon once it has been placed inside a pad (*bhisi*).
Furthermore, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated: ‘A *masūraka* is a leather pad; however, a leather bolster, even if filled with cotton, is not allowed.’”
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, however, it says: "Regarding 'the measure of the head': that is the measure of the head where they place the entire head starting from the nape of the neck;
and to show that this, by way of the maximum limit, is one fist-cubit (*muṭṭhiratana*) across, it says:
'where, in width, at the three corners,' and so forth. 'The middle part is one fist-cubit' refers to the pillow."
"It is said that its middle part is one fist-span in width horizontally. *Arañjara* means a large bowl that holds much water.

It is called *arañjara* because it cannot hold [too much] water; it is described in the *Gaṇṭhipada* as being like a round bowl, somewhat long-mouthed, and fashioned with a constriction in the middle.
"For this is stated in the Commentary" (*vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ*)—this is the connection through ellipsis (*ajjhāhāra*).
“Two have two groupings” means there are two [items] that cannot be relinquished which consist of two groupings of objects as stated:
namely, “a monastery and a site for a monastery,” and “a dwelling and a site for a dwelling. The third item that cannot be relinquished consists of a grouping of four objects as stated:
“a bed, a bench, a mattress, and a pillow. The fourth item that cannot be relinquished...
It consists of nine sections as stated: "an iron pot, an iron vessel, an iron bowl, an iron cauldron, a hatchet, a small axe, a large axe, a spade, and a pickaxe.

The fifth [category] is not to be given away; it consists of eight types as stated: "creepers, bamboo, muñja grass, pabbaja grass, grass, clay, wooden articles, and earthenware," thus possessing eight divisions.

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "Pañcanimmalalocano" means one who possesses five stainless eyes by way of the flesh-eye (*maṃsacakkhu*), the divine-eye (*dibbacakkhu*), the Dhamma-eye (*dhammacakkhu*), the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakkhu*), and the universal-eye (*samantacakkhu*).
Regarding the phrase "in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*, at the Kīṭāgiri episode, it is 'not to be relinquished' and 'not to be shared out,'" here, in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*...
Regarding the case of the village residence (*gāmakāvāsa-vatthu*), it should be stated as "not to be relinquished" (*avissajjiya*);

regarding the case of Kiṭāgiri (*kīṭāgiri-vatthu*), it should be stated as "not to be divided" (*avebhaṅgiya*). Why? Because both cases are recorded in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*. "In the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*" is the general heading (*sāmaññādhāra*);
"in the case of the village residence" and "in the case of Kiṭāgiri" are the specific headings (*visesādhāra*). This meaning is to be understood by consulting the Pāḷi text.
For this very reason, in the *Samantapāsādikā*, instead of saying "in the Senāsanakkhandhaka," it is simply stated as "here" (*idha*).
By this term "here," he indicates the site of the village monastery; however, the site of Kīṭāgiri has already been shown in its own form.

As for the general heading (*sāmaññādhāra*), although it is not explicitly mentioned because there is no commentary on that [specific section], it is understood to be established by implication; thus, it was not stated.

228. Regarding the phrases "permanent for permanent" and "valuable property for valuable property," it should be understood that among these five categories, the first two are permanent and the latter three are valuable property. As for the phrase "he gives an equal amount":
even if he gives less, he may take land from the vicinity of the monastery site and assign it further away where it is difficult to guard.
"It is allowable" (vaṭṭati) is how it should be understood. For he will say: "If [the robe] is more valuable for the monks...
it is allowable to accept it. "Having made known" means having made known to the Saṅgha of monks; the sense is "having informed them.
As for the phrase "Should you not rather say, 'The trees are yours in greater measure'?"—this was said because the owners were unaware that their own property was of great value.
It is stated that once one has identified [the property] among the teeth and takes it with a thieving mind, there is an act of theft (*avahāra*). Regarding the exchange of one monastery for another:
a monastery together with its site (*savatthuka*) may be exchanged for the site of another, such as a palace (*pāsāda*) built on the ground, or for one without a site (*avatthuka*);
or a [monastery] without a site may be exchanged for one without a site, because the palace itself is merely a structure standing upon the ground.
In the same way, even regarding immovable things, one must exchange them only after understanding the classification of immovable things.
By the statement, "Acceptable beds may be accepted," it is shown that an unacceptable bed decorated with gold and so forth is not permitted to be accepted, even if it is said, "For the Saṅgha.
If it is said, "We give this to the monastery," it is acceptable for the Saṅgha.
"It should be understood that [the gift] does not belong to an individual, like a field or similar property," so it is stated in the *Vimativinodanī*.
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it says: "‘Acceptable beds may be accepted’—this was said with reference to what has been given saying, ‘We give this to the Saṅgha.
But if they say, ‘We give this to the monastery,’ then even beds made of gold, silver, or other such unallowable materials may be accepted."

"It is allowable," it is said. By the statement "not only... but it is allowable to exchange [them]," he shows that it is allowable to exchange a durable good for both a durable and a non-durable good. Indeed, it is not allowable to exchange a durable good for a non-durable good alone.
Regarding the phrase "whether it is unallowable or valuable, or whether it is allowable": here, "unallowable" refers to things such as beds made of gold.

"Unallowable [items] include chairs and pillows. 'Allowable but expensive' refers to beds made of ivory and the like, as well as allowable coverings such as woolen rugs," so it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated: "'Unallowable' means a high-backed chair (*āsandi*) and the like, or a pillow that exceeds the prescribed dimensions.
'Allowable but expensive' means something adorned with gold and the like, which has been given under the designation of being allowable."

229. Because it is stated, “Black iron... [etc. ...should be distributed,” they say that even a vessel made of tin or brass, though belonging to an individual (puggalika), is permitted to be accepted and carried;
for it is to be distributed precisely because it is something to be carried by individuals.
Regarding this, it is said further on: “A vessel or its derivative made of brass or tin, whether used by the Saṅgha or discarded by a householder...”
This contradicts the statement from the *Mahāpaccarī*: "It is not permitted," and so forth.

For that statement from the *Mahāpaccarī* was presented later as a refutation of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* passage which says: "A bowl made of any kind of round iron or bronze, if it is worth a foot-measure in the island of Sri Lanka, should be distributed. Therefore, [it refers to] that which is made of round iron or bronze...
Starting from even the smallest measure of a handful taken by the hand, it is entirely unfit for use; it is not permissible for an individual to accept even what is being given by householders.

"It is not permissible to take it as one's own property" means that, unlike requisites such as a bowl, it is not permissible to store it away oneself and then consume it. If the monastery attendants and others were to guard it themselves, as if it belonged to a householder—
When the time for distribution arrives, if they bring it back and present it, it is permissible to use it; it is also permissible to say, "Having stored it away, give it to the monks.

They say that *paṇṇasūci* means a stylus. By the phrase "even those obtained by oneself," etc., he shows that there is no fault in the act of receiving, but that using it after having carried it about constitutes an offense.
And as it is here, so it is with regard to vessels, axes, and other items belonging to oneself mentioned further on.
“Anāmāsappīti” means even gold and other such things; it is permissible to touch and use all of them. “Upakkhare” means utensils.

“Sikharaṃ” is that by which those who wander about cut [wood]. “Pattabandhaka” is one who makes the knots and so forth for the bowl. Some also say, “Paṭimānaṃ” is one who makes bowls of gold and other materials.
Regarding “aḍḍhabāhu,” it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* (Commentary on Difficult Points) as “from the elbow up to the shoulder. “Aḍḍhabāhu... [The text continues:]... [is] half an arm’s length.
"It is also called 'four *vidatthi*s' or 'four fingers,'" as stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā* it is also said: "'Half-arms' is written [to mean] from the elbow up to the shoulder-joint.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī* it is said: "'The measure of half-arms' means just half an arm; some also say it is the measure of half a *vyāma*."
“Yottāni” means leather thongs. “Tatthajātakā” means those produced on land belonging to the Saṅgha.
Regarding the phrase “the size of an eight-finger-breadth needle-shaft,” the *Sāratthadīpanī* states it is “eight finger-breadths in length and the size of a leaf-needle shaft in circumference.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: “The size of an eight-finger-breadth needle-shaft means even the size of a slender shaft having the shape of a needle, such as a reed-shaft and so forth.”
It has been said. "Measuring eight finger-breadths" means measuring eight finger-breadths in length. "Even an empty book" means even one that is not written upon;
this is mentioned here by way of the discussion on leaves.
"Āsandika" refers to a square stool, according to the statement, "An *āsandika* is also high. On one side...
It should be understood that only a long bench with feet eight finger-breadths high is permitted; however, a square chair (āsandi) is permitted even if it exceeds those dimensions.
A "seven-limbed" bed (sattaṅga) is a couch made by providing supports on three sides; this too is permitted even if it exceeds the standard measurements.
A "Bhadra-chair" (bhaddapīṭha) refers to a chair made of rattan. A "small stool" (pīṭhikā) is one bound with strips of cloth.
It is simply a seat. A "sheep’s-footed seat" (eḷakapādapīṭha) is said to be a seat made by placing a wooden plank on top of a footrest, like a food-tray.
An "āmaṇḍaka-stem seat" (āmaṇḍakavaṇṭakapīṭha) is a multi-legged seat constructed in the shape of an *āmalaka* fruit.
These, first of all, are the seats mentioned in the Canon. However, every seat made of wood is permissible.
"In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: 'A rubbing-board (*ghaṭṭanaphalaka*) is that upon which one places dyed cloth and rubs it with the hand.
A rubbing-mallet (*ghaṭṭanamuggara*) is said to be made for the purpose of rubbing [the cloth] in the direction of the wind and so forth. In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it says:
'Regarding the rubbing-board and the rubbing-mallet: this refers to a smooth staff-mallet upon which the dyed cloth is placed.'"
Having wrapped it [with cloth], placed it upon a smooth wooden plank, and turned it over with another smooth wooden plank on top, one person stands treading upon it;
two people grasp the upper plank at both ends and pull it back and forth.
It is with reference to this that it was said: "making them place it in their hands and striking it with the hand."
However, it is said: "This [rubbing] should be done while the dyed robe is still wet;

this striking with wooden mallets, moreover, should be understood as being for the purpose of releasing stiffness when it has dried. "Ambaṇa" refers to a water vessel made of wooden planks resembling a lotus pond.
"Dye-vat" (rajanadoṇī) is that in which they place the boiled dye after having poured it in.

In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, however, it is stated: "An *ambaṇa* is a vessel resembling a lotus pond made from the planks of a single-droṇa boat; some also call it a water-vessel. A dye-tub (*rajanadoṇī*) is a dye-vessel made from a single wooden plank.

A water-tub (*udakadoṇī*) is a water-vessel made from a single wooden plank. In the *Vimativinodanī*, on the other hand, it says: "'Ambaṇa' refers to a vessel like a lotus pond constructed from the planks of a single-droṇa boat.
Some also say it is a drinking vessel. A 'dye-tub' is a dye-container made from a single piece of wood. A 'water-tub' is a water-container made from a single piece of wood."
"It is said that 'it is permissible to make a floor-covering' refers to non-permissible skins.

By the phrase 'it falls under the category of bedspreads,' it is indicated that it is also permissible to spread it over beds and chairs. Some say that even bedspreads such as curtains (*pāvāra*) are 'heavy goods' (*garubhaṇḍa*);
others say they are not; this should be determined after investigation," so it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*. In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*:
However, because it is stated that "the staff-mallet (daṇḍamuggara)— by which they beat dyed robes—

is indeed a heavy article," and because it is stated that [it] "belongs to the category of bedspreads (paccattharaṇagatika)," they say that by means of the word "also" (api), all bedspreads such as woolen blankets (pāvāra) and so forth are indeed heavy articles.
By this very Sutta, having explained the meaning otherwise, [some claim] that bedspreads such as woolen blankets are not heavy articles.
They say that only what is suitable for use, specifically a rug given for the purpose of bedding, is "heavy goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*).
It is stated that "this must be examined. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: "It is permissible to use it as a floor-covering; this was said with reference to an unallowable skin.
In that case, it is even permissible to lie down upon it by way of its being a floor-covering. It falls under the category of a rug (*paccattharaṇa*)."
By this, it is shown that the large hide to be spread upon beds and such is called "sheepskin" (*eḷakacamma*).
"Umbrella-leaf" refers to the palm leaf. "Bowl-vessel" is the vessel for cooking the bowl. "Knots" refers to the knots for robes.
"Lacing" refers to the lacing for the waistband.
Now, the method found in the *Vinayatha-mañjūsā* is stated: "Garden" (*ārāma*) means either a flower garden or a fruit garden.
"Garden site" (*ārāmavatthu*) means a space set aside and demarcated for the purpose of those very gardens;
or, when those gardens have fallen into ruin, it refers to their former ground area. "Monastery" (*vihāra*) means any kind of lodging, such as a palace and so forth.

“Monastery site” (vihāravatthu) means the place where it is established. “Bed” (mañca) means any one of the four types of beds previously mentioned: the stuffed-cotton bed, the bound-felt bed, the bed with crocodile legs, or the bed with detachable legs.
“Chair” (pīṭha) means any one of the four types of chairs beginning with the stuffed-cotton chair.
“Cushion” (bhisi) means any one of the five types of cushions beginning with the woolen cushion.
A "cushion" (*bimbohana*) is one filled with any one of the following: tree-cotton, creeper-cotton, or silk-cotton.
A "metal pot" (*lohakumbhī*) is a pot made of any metal whatsoever, whether black iron or copper. The same principle applies to "metal vessels" (*lohakaṭāha*) and so forth;
here, however, *bhāṇaka* refers to a basin, while *vāraka* refers to a water-jar. *Kaṭāha* is simply a large pan. Regarding the "axe" (*vāsī*) and other such items...
And among creepers and so forth, there is nothing that is difficult to understand...
[etc. ...In this context, "by a permanent thing" means by a dwelling or a dwelling-site; "a dwelling-site" refers to a monastery or a monastery-site. "By another" means by what is not permanent;
it is said to be by the latter three heaps. "By what is unallowable" means by things such as beds made of gold and so forth.
And by means of unallowable beds and seats. "By means of a costly allowable [article]" refers to a bed made of ivory and so forth, as well as a woolen rug and so forth.
"The other" means the latter. "To exchange by means of an allowable exchange" means to exchange in such a way that it does not become unallowable...
[as above] ...In this manner, first, the exchange of a durable good for a durable good is to be understood. By means of the other...

But regarding other exchanges: whether a bed or chair be large or small—even one with legs only four finger-breadths high, or even one made by village children playing in sand-pits—it becomes "heavy property" (*garubhaṇḍa*) from the moment it is given to the Saṅgha...
[and so on] ...or if one obtains another hundred beds in exchange for a bed worth a hundred or a thousand [coins].

It should be taken after being exchanged. Not only may a bed be exchanged for a bed, but it is also permissible to exchange a monastery (*ārāma*), a monastery site (*ārāmavatthu*), a dwelling (*vihāra*), a dwelling site (*vihāravatthu*), a bench (*pīṭha*), a mattress (*abhisī*), or a pillow (*bimbohana*).
