This same principle applies to benches, mattresses, and pillows as well.
Regarding the phrase "black iron, copper, bronze, brass, and tin": here, bronze (*kaṃsaloha*) and tin (*vaṭṭaloha*) are alloys.
For there are three kinds of base metals: bronze (*kaṃsaloha*), brass (*vaṭṭaloha*), and *hārakūṭa*.
Among these, bronze is made by mixing copper and tin; brass is made by mixing lead and tin; and *hārakūṭa* is made by mixing mercury and tin.
Therefore it is said: "Bronze, brass, and base metals. One who takes more than that is "one who takes more than that."
One vessel should be made by showing a bud at the center of the rim, widening the circumference of the mouth, and bending it back toward the rear;
they also call this a *sarāvanta*. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), household utensils such as golden vessels and the like are included.
For even those that are small are indeed "heavy goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*) because they are household utensils. By the word "also" (*pi*), it is implied that this applies even more so to large ones.
This shows that these items, moreover, are "to be used" (*bhājanīya*), meaning they belong to the requisites of a monk.

And just as these [other items], so too is the water flask (*kuṇḍikā*) to be used. For he will say: "And just as with earthenware vessels, so too with metal vessels, the water flask belongs to the category of those things to be used.
Regarding the phrase "for the use of the Saṅgha," this refers to visiting monks who are senior.
"By means of use after having given. "Made unseemly by householders" means made unseemly by being fashioned by householders, or made unsightly by making it one's own property.

"It is not permissible by way of private use" means it is not permissible to take it as if it were one's own and use it without giving it to guests. "A pair of scissors" (pipphalika) is a knife. "An awl" (ārakaṇṭaka) is a needle-piercer.
A moving cymbal. A probe for a lancet is a ring for a lancet.
Iron made solid—whether it be a bar of iron, a lump of iron, a mass of iron, or an iron ball—such is iron made solid.
"Made of milk-stone" means made of stone that has the soft color of milk.

Even items belonging to householders are not permitted because they are untouchable (*anāmāsa*). By the word "even" (*pi*), he shows that this is all the more true for items belonging to the Saṅgha or for personal use.
However, the use of lodgings (*senāsana*) is allowable in every respect; therefore, all requisites for lodgings, even those made of gold and so forth, are touchable (*āmāsa*).
Thus he said: "But regarding the use of lodgings," and so on.
"Sesā" means those [tools] are even larger than that. "Yā pana" means as for the axe. A pickaxe—even if it is only four finger-breadths in size—is indeed a heavy article.

Whether a chisel has four faces, or a scoop-shaped face, or whether it is curved or straight—even down to a probe for a broom-handle—if it has a handle-fastening, it is indeed a heavy article. Therefore he said: "A pickaxe..."
“There is no such thing as an agaru-tool for binding the handle or for sharpening. A *sipāṭikā* is a sheath for razors;
however, since the *sikhara* (the tip) conforms to the function of binding the handle and sharpening, he said, “The *sikhara* is also included under sharpening.
But if it is a handleless adze consisting merely of the blade, it is subject to distribution (*bhājanīya*). Regarding *upakkhara*: this refers to tools such as adzes and the like.
The *pattabandhaka* is one who makes the loop and other parts of the bowl. Some also say it is "one who makes images, such as bowls out of gold and so forth.

Regarding the three types of small knives—the knife for cutting wood, the knife for cutting gold, and the small knife for cutting leather after preparation—it is said that these three are suitable for a *pipphalika* (a small box or case), hence the words "but this is the distinction," and so on.
"The others" refers to the large knife (*mahākattari*) and the rest.
"Measuring half an arm" means from the elbow up to the level of the shoulder-blade;
that is to say, measuring four finger-breadths (vidatthi) [in width]. "Born there" means produced on land belonging to the Saṅgha.

And it is "protected" because it is guarded by the provision of protection; it is "guarded" because it is kept safe, like something placed inside a casket or similar container, so that it does not go astray.
"And so" means protected and guarded. However, even items produced there [within the monastery] that are unprotected do not constitute "heavy goods.

By the phrase "used for the business of the Saṅgha or the business of a Cetiya," it is indicated that it is permissible to protect or exchange what belongs to the Saṅgha with what belongs to a Cetiya.
"Thread, moreover" refers to both wound and unwound thread.
“A mere eight-finger-breadth needle-handle” means that it should be at least eight finger-breadths in length and as thick as a Sinhalese palm-leaf needle-handle.
“Therein” refers to the bamboo container. “Those whose houses have been burnt” means those for whom the house has been consumed by fire.

“They should not be prevented” means they should not be stopped with the words, “Do not take these and go. When one has arrived from another region, they should be deposited in the Saṅgha’s residence within the monastery where he has reached.
"And the remaining thatching grass" refers to whatever remaining thatching grass there may be other than *muñja* and *pabbaja*.
"Even if it measures eight finger-breadths" means even if it is eight finger-breadths in width. Furthermore, a written manuscript is not considered a heavy article.
"Permissible hides" refers to the hides of deer and so forth. "Every wheeled vehicle" refers to every vehicle equipped with wheels, such as chariots, carts, and the like.
The unconditioned wheel, however, is a vehicle that may be used. "Permitted to be kept" means that which is stated to be capable of being carried about by placing it in a box.
"Fist-leaf" refers to a palm leaf; for it is called a "fist-leaf" because one carries it about holding it in the fist.
Some say, "A 'fist-leaf' is simply a leaf used as a sunshade. "Together with a fire-drill" means...
"A pair of fire-drills" means the two fire-drills, namely the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇī*) and the lower fire-drill (*adharāraṇī*).

"Having performed a formal act of enhancement" means having performed an act of stabilization by means of even as much sand as that [fire-drill] is worth. "A water-pot" refers both to an iron water-pot and a copper water-pot.
"He resorts only to the portion that is to be shared" means he uses only those items belonging to the category of shared property, and not heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*).
The meaning is as follows: however, the intention is that gold is indeed a "heavy article" (*garubhaṇḍa*).
Thus ends the "Ornament of the Determination of Heavy Articles," titled the "Ornament of the Vinayālaṅkāra," which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
The Thirtieth Chapter. 31.
Discussion on the Determination of Accusations, etc. 230.
Having thus explained the determination regarding heavy goods, he now explains the determination regarding accusations, etc., [beginning with]: "The determination regarding accusations, etc."
Regarding this, he said, "But here... and so forth. In that context, *codanā* (reproach) means that which is reproached; the meaning is the attribution of a fault. By the word "etc.

(*ādi*), he includes reminders (*sāraṇā*) and so on. For this has been stated in the Kammakkhandhaka: "It is done after having reproached; it is done after having reminded; it is done after having attributed an offense.
As for the question, "Who is permitted to reproach, and who is not?"—this refers to one whose intention is to expose [a fault].

This was stated in order to show that [the offense] exists even without the characteristic of formal admonition (*codanālakkhaṇa*). The statement "one endowed with virtue" (*sīlasampanno*) was said with the intention that the word of one who is immoral (*dussīla*) is not authoritative.
Furthermore, because nuns lack authority to admonish a monk, it was specified as "only a nun.
Even though nuns lack authority over monks, an admonition made by them is nonetheless subject to the requirements of a valid admonition (*codanārahattā*).
With the intention that it is indeed the formal accusation (*codanā*) itself [that is authoritative], it is stated: "The five who are in accordance with the Dhamma also receive [the verdict].

In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is said: "The Elder cited the Sutta," in order to show that since the accuser accepts the statement of those from whom he hears and then accuses, their testimony is likewise authoritative, and thus their accusation is indeed valid.

In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it is stated: “In connection with the discussion on groundless accusations (*amūlakacodanā*), the following was begun in order to show the characteristics of accusations based on grounds (*samūlakacodanā*) and so forth: ‘Who is permitted to accuse, and who is not?

This is because the Sutta beginning with ‘Having heard from a bhikkhu, he accuses’ refers even to those who point out the failure of others regarding the accuser; at that very moment, they too stand in the position of the accuser.”
It is said: "They explain [this], and because one may accept their words, even the other person—
since he is able to cause the first accusers (from the end of the list of sectarian disciples) who did not initially accept the charge to accept it—
these [disciples] are to be understood as being cited here by way of proof."
"Of the two grave offenses" refers to the *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa* rules. "The remaining" refers to the five types of offenses beginning with the *thullaccaya*.
Wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*) is the ten-based view proceeding in the manner of "there is no giving," and so forth.
The view that grasps at extremes, such as "the world is finite" or "the world is infinite," is called the view of grasping at extremes (*antaggāhikā diṭṭhi*). For the sake of livelihood...

Regarding "of the six proclaimed [offenses]": for the sake of livelihood, one may incur a *pārājika* offense for claiming superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), a *saṅghādisesa* for acting as a go-between,
a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) by the indirect method of saying, "He who dwells in your monastery is an *arahant*," a *pācittiya* for requesting exquisite food from a monk,
and a *paṭidesanīya* for requesting exquisite food from a nun.
"An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for requesting soup and boiled rice"—these six [offenses] are mentioned in the Parivāra.
These offenses were not prescribed solely on account of livelihood (ājīva), because they can be committed in other ways as well, such as through acting as a go-between (sañcaritta).

However, this was stated with reference to the commission of these very offenses on account of livelihood; the meaning is that they are "prescribed even on account of livelihood. [This is said] in contrast to failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti) and failure in livelihood (ājīvavipatti).
Even when reproving, one reproves only for an offense rooted in that very matter.
When asked, "Why do you not pay homage to me?", because the reason for not paying homage has been stated—namely, "You are not a samaṇa;
you are not a son of the Sakyan"—they say that one who has committed a final (antima) offense is not to be paid homage. It is precisely out of a desire to reprove that one does not pay homage.

In the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada* and the *Majjhimagaṇṭhipada*, it is stated that apart from the matter already mentioned regarding what one may say to oneself, there is no other reason for the state of being unworthy of salutation (*avandiya*).
This is because one who has committed an offense involving the ultimate ground (*antimavatthu*) is not mentioned among those who are unworthy of salutation;
consequently, there is no offense of sleeping together (*sahaseyyāpatti*) with such a person, and because that very acceptance [of the requisites] takes root.

It is understood that this is more appropriate. Although he is to be saluted as long as he continues to claim the status of a bhikkhu, when he claims, "I am no longer a samaṇa," then he is not to be saluted; this is the distinction to be understood here.
For one who has committed the ultimate offense, his status as a bhikkhu exists only as long as he still claims the status of a bhikkhu, and not beyond that.
"Furthermore. For one who does not claim the status of a bhikkhu belongs to the side of those who are not fully ordained.

Since one giving material gifts gives them only to the place of one's own choosing, it is said, "it is not yet an accusation," meaning that when one distributes rice porridge, meals, and so forth to those seated in order, even if one does not give to someone because of a desire to accuse them, it is still not called an accusation.
231. "One who should be reproved" (*codetabbo*) means one who has been reproved; "one who has been reproved" (*cuditako*) refers to a person who possesses an offense.
"One who reproves" (*codako*) is one who makes an offense known. Both the one reproved and the one reproving are "the reproved and the reprover. "By a committee" (*ubbāhikāya*):

by that which extracts (*ubbahanti*) or separates—either a formal act of censure (*tajjanīya*) or a quarrel—from those who are shameless; it is a resolution of the Saṅgha, and by that [resolution] there is a decision (*vinicchana*).

The term "consent" (*sammata*) refers precisely to the decision made by the monks. For in an assembly crowded with those lacking a sense of shame, two or three monks endowed with the ten factors mentioned in the *Samathakkhandhaka* should be appointed right there by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second announcement (*ñattidutiyakammavācā*).
Indeed, this is stated in the *Samathakkhandhaka*: [text follows]
“Monks, if while that legal issue is being decided by those monks,
endless speeches arise and the meaning of even a single statement is not understood, I allow you, monks, to settle such a legal issue through a committee.
A monk endowed with ten qualities should be appointed to a committee.”

He is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.

He is learned, a retainer of what he has heard, and a storehouse of learning—those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which are entirely complete and pure.
They proclaim the holy life to be completely pure; such teachings as these are well-learned by him, retained, mastered verbally, examined by the mind, and well-penetrated by view.
Furthermore, both Pātimokkhas have been properly received by him in detail, well-analyzed, well-expounded, and well-determined, both as to the rules and their specific characteristics.

Furthermore, he is skilled in the Vinaya and unshakable; he is capable of comforting, persuading, convincing, instructing, enlightening, and inspiring both those who support his cause and those who oppose it;
he is adept in the arising and the subsiding of legal disputes (*adhikaraṇa*);
he knows the legal dispute, he knows the origin of the legal dispute, and he knows the cessation of the legal dispute.
He knows the practice leading to the cessation of legal issues. Monks, I allow you to appoint a monk endowed with these ten qualities as a committee member (*ubbāhikā*).
And thus, monks, he should be appointed: first, a monk should be requested; having been requested, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: while this legal issue is being decided by us, endless discussions arise and the meaning of no single statement is understood.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint the monk named so-and-so and the monk named so-and-so as a committee to resolve this legal issue.”
This is the motion for the purpose of bringing about pacification:

"Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me. While this legal issue of ours is being decided, endless disputes arise and the meaning of what has been said by any single person is not understood. The Sangha [should appoint] so-and-so and so-and-so..."
He appoints two monks by means of a formal resolution to settle this legal dispute.
Whichever venerable one approves of the appointment of monk so-and-so and monk so-and-so by means of a formal resolution to settle this legal dispute, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
“The Saṅgha has appointed the bhikkhus so-and-so and so-and-so as a committee to settle this legal issue; it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.

Those who have been so appointed, having sat down either separately or within that very assembly, should announce: “Nothing must be said by others,” and then they should adjudicate that legal issue. The phrase “by you” is said with reference to the one who is being accused and the one who accuses.
“*Kimhi* means *kismiṃ vatthusmiṃ* (in what matter). *Kimhi nampi na jānāsī* means you do not even know the expression *kimhi nan*.
‘*Nāssa anuyogo dātabbo*’ means no questioning or cross-examination should be given to him. Thus it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: “*Kimhi* means *kismiṃ vatthusmiṃ*; the meaning is ‘in which failure?’. *Kimhi*...
“By which name?”— this question is asked by the accuser, who, despite it being stated in whatever intelligible language possible, “By which failure do you charge me?”,
is unable to understand due to his lack of knowledge regarding the Vinaya, thinking, “He asks me ‘by which’ among the failures of virtue, conduct, view, or livelihood?
It does not refer merely to the literal meaning of the word “in what” (*kimhi*) and so forth.
It is for one who does not know. For indeed, an investigator does not ask a foolish accuser, who is unfamiliar with the language, "In what [matter]?

It is not said with reference merely to the words "Do you not know in what? When it is asked, "By which failure?", even the statement "You do not know" is made with reference specifically to the intended meaning of saying, "By such-and-such a failure."
"It should be accepted as stated. For that very reason, he will say: "No further questioning (anuyoga) should be given to him.

"'The method (naya) should be given to him'—to whom? To that foolish person who possesses a sense of shame. Having said, "The method should be given to him," the subsequent passage beginning with "In what [matter] do you charge him?
In a failure of virtue (sīlavipatti)" is stated precisely as the disclosure of the intended meaning (adhippāya), which constitutes the giving of the method.
However, this is not merely a demonstration of the synonyms for the words *kim* and *naṃ*.

For even if the meaning of the statement "In which failure do you accuse me? were understood, a fool would still be unable to discern the specific categories of failure or the actual nature of the failure with which he himself is being charged;
therefore, because of that very ignorance, the shameless one must be censured. Furthermore, the phrase *kimhi naṃ* is merely illustrative.
Or, having manifested ignorance in some other way whatsoever, he must indeed be made to answer. Because of the statement, “For the restraint of persons who are difficult to correct,” it is said:
“It was laid down for the purpose of restraining those who are shameless... [and so forth]. *Ehiti* means “he comes”;

the letter *hi* should be understood here as an augment (*āgama*), meaning “he will come. *Diṭṭhasantānena* means “by the continuity of what has been seen,” that is, by the established method of what has been observed.

The meaning is that even though the fault has been made manifest through the sequence of question and answer, it must be dealt with as an offense solely on the basis of the admission of the shameless person, who acknowledges the fault by saying, "I am impure. However, some say:
"Since this [admission] does not exist for a shameless person, it must be dealt with as a non-offense solely on the basis of the admission of purity; this is the meaning here."
They say, "He is included," but that is not correct, because it would result in the adjudicator being rendered useless, and because the accuser alone must stand by his admission of shamelessness.
For here, what is intended by "admission" (paṭiññā) is specifically the admission of having committed an offense;
for this very reason, he will later say: "He does not give an admission, saying 'This is not so, that is not so,'" and so forth.

"‘For the purpose of illustrating that meaning’ means for the purpose of illustrating that even when the fault of one who is shameless has been made manifest, the verdict must be passed based solely on his own admission of that fault.
‘Those who are adversaries regarding the matter known as the subject of dispute’ means those who oppose the matter.

‘Having given notice’ means having made a sound for the purpose of interrupting their speech and for the purpose of bringing them face-to-face. ‘Unfit to adjudicate’ means [unfit] because of the perception that he is impure."

This was said with reference to the impossibility of investigating, because [the accuser] has entered the side of the accuser (*codaka-pakkha*) and is thus excluded from the state of being an investigator (*anuvijjaka*). For it is only when there is doubt that investigation is possible;
however, when one holds the view that [the accused] is impure, everything said by the accuser appears untrue, so how could there be any investigation in such a case?
By the phrase "he will thus become one who has been expelled," it is shown that even without passing a formal verdict, this act of separating him from the Saṅgha—
just like the *liṅga-nāsanā* (expulsion by change of robes)— is itself one mode of expulsion (*nāsanā*).
The expression "sharing of food and requisites" is stated for the purpose of releasing them from his own presence, and not for the purpose of joining them together in mutual sharing.
“*Viraddhaṃ hotī*” means that one has intentionally committed an offense.

The statement, “From the very beginning there is no such thing as one who is shameless (*alajjī*),” is a statement made for the purpose of establishing the possibility of the characteristic of being shameless in the context of “not giving a formal promise (*paṭiñña*) for the sake of protecting the factions.
From the time the offense is concealed onward, one is indeed called shameless; the previous state of being conscientious (*lajjibhāva*) does not [persist].
The meaning is that he guards [himself]. "He does not give a formal admission" means:

thinking, "If I speak of the fault committed by me, those who follow me will break away," he does not give a formal admission. "He does not stand firm in his position" means: he does not stand in the position of one possessed of shame;
the intention is that there is transgression in body and speech. Therefore it was said: "No judgment should be given," [referring to] those previously belonging to the faction.
The intention is that even for a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) settled by admission, because it has not been properly settled, this too will be as good as lost.

232. Regarding the statement, "By one who is deciding upon the matter of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), twenty-five types of theft must be carefully observed," here "twenty-five types of theft" refers to five sets of five;
therein, the "five sets of five" are as follows: the pentad of various goods (*nānābhaṇḍa-pañcaka*).
The fivefold group of single articles, the fivefold group of [taking] with one's own hand, the fivefold group of prior preparation, and the fivefold group of taking by theft.
For it is said in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*: "Those acts of taking, having combined them into five groups of five, should be carefully examined," and so forth.
Among these, the fivefold group of various articles and the fivefold group of single articles are those mentioned in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*).
They are obtained by way of these phrases: “should take up,” “should carry away,” “should steal,” “should disturb the postures,” and “should move from one place. For it has been said by the ancients:
“Taking up and indeed carrying away;”
"By destroying his deportment,
by displacing him from that position,
and even by causing him to move away, he is defeated."

In this context, the group of five consisting of various articles should be understood in terms of both animate and inanimate objects, while the other [group] is to be understood only in terms of animate objects.
How so? "Should take up" means he makes an assault upon the monastery; there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). He causes doubt to arise in the owner;
there is an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*). When the owner relinquishes his responsibility, thinking, "It shall not be mine," there is an offense of... [expiation].

Regarding an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*): "Should carry away"—if, while carrying another’s goods, one touches a load on the head with a thieving intention, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If he makes it move, it is a serious offense (*thullaccaya*). If he lowers it from his shoulder, it is an offense entailing expulsion.
"Should misappropriate"—if, when asked regarding goods deposited with him, "Give me my goods," he says, "I will not take them," it is an offense of wrong-doing for the owner.
If she gives rise to doubt, it is a thullaccaya offense. If the owner, thinking, "It will not be mine," relinquishes his responsibility, it is a pārājika offense.
"Should disturb her posture" means: if, thinking, "I shall take the goods along with the carrier," she steps across the threshold with the first foot, it is a thullaccaya offense;
if she steps across with the second foot, it is a pārājika offense. "Should move it from its place" means: goods situated on dry land...

If one touches it with a thieving mind, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If one makes it move, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya). If one moves it from its place, there is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
In this way, first, the pentad of various articles is to be understood.

Furthermore, regarding the taking, seizing, stealing, disturbing of posture, and moving from its place—by means of the aforementioned method of application and so forth—of a slave belonging to an owner, or of an animal, [the same offenses apply].
The fivefold group of single articles should be understood. Regarding this, the ancients said:
“In that regard, it is not by virtue of multiple articles or fivefold groups;
rather, the fivefold groups beginning with ‘taking up’ (ādāna) are declared to be of two kinds.”

What is the pentad of personal action (sāhatthika-pañcaka)? It consists of: that which is done by one's own hand, that which is done by command, that which is relinquished, that which accomplishes a purpose, and the laying down of the burden. For it has been said:

“That which is done by one’s own hand, That which is done by command, That which is relinquished, that which accomplishes a purpose, And the laying down of the burden— This is the pentad of personal action.”
In this context, "by one's own hand" means that one steals another's property with one's own hand.
"By command" means that one commands another, saying, "Steal such-and-such a person's property.

"By relinquishment" means causing [the goods] to fall outside while standing inside a place designated as a customs house or a place where duties are collected. "Accomplishing the purpose" means saying, "When you are able, steal such-and-such a person's property."
He gives an order. In that case, if another person, being free from obstacles, takes it away, the one who gave the order incurs a *pārājika* offense at the very moment the order is given.

Or, if he places a quantity of oil worth a *pāda* into another’s oil-jar—such as sandals or other items that must necessarily be used with oil—he incurs a *pārājika* offense the moment it is released from his hand.
However, the relinquishing of responsibility (*dhuranikkhepa*) occurs by way of abandoning the task or depositing goods entrusted to a monastery.
It should be understood that the same method applies even to one who does not give back goods borrowed for a limited time. This is the pentad of direct manual action (*sāhatthika-pañcaka*).
What is the pentad of preliminary effort (*pubbapayoga-pañcaka*)? It consists of: preliminary effort, simultaneous effort, making an agreement, giving a signal, and making a sign. Thus it is said:
“Preliminary and simultaneous effort, And likewise the making of an agreement;”
“Symbolic action is the sign; this is the fivefold [category] of acting by one’s own hand.

Therein, the preliminary effort is to be understood by way of giving an order. The simultaneous effort is to be understood by way of causing displacement from its place, and by way of taking fields and so forth after transferring barren lands and the like.
What is called “conveying by agreement” is: “Such-and-such a commodity...”
"Let us steal," having thus made an agreement and deliberated together, there is the act of stealing.

For when they have gone after making such an agreement, even if only one person moves that article from its place, the theft belongs to all of them. "Making a signal" means the act of establishing a recognition.
For if, having delimited some time such as before the meal and so forth, [one says], "At such a time, [let us meet] at such-and-such a place..."
When told, "Steal the goods," if he steals them later than the agreed time, the theft belongs to the one who made the agreement at the very moment the agreement was made.
"Giving a sign" (*nimittakamma*) means making a sign, such as winking an eye, for the purpose of producing recognition.
For if, after such a sign has been made, he is told, "Steal that which [is indicated]," and he steals it, [the theft belongs] to the one who made the sign.
"The taking [of the object] at the very moment of the sign" refers to this fivefold preliminary effort.
What is the fivefold taking by theft? Taking by theft, taking by force, taking by contrivance, taking by concealment, and taking by deception. Therefore it was said:
"By theft, by force, by contrivance, By concealment, and likewise by deception."
"These are the five types of taking away; this is the pentad of theft.

In this context, when one takes by means of breaking into walls and so forth while remaining invisible, or by deceiving through false scales, false measures, or counterfeit coins and the like, the taking of one who takes in such a manner should be understood as "taking by theft" (*theyyāvahāra*). However, when one [takes] by force...
When one takes what belongs to others by force, like village raiders and the like,

or when one takes more than one’s own allotted share according to the aforementioned method, like royal officials and the like— such taking on his part should be understood as *pasayhāvahāra* (forcible appropriation).
However, taking after having made a plan is called *parikappāvahāra* (appropriation by design).
Thus, it is twofold according to the nature of the object (*bhaṇḍa*). Herein, this is the illustration regarding the object:
one who desires a cloth enters an inner chamber and, having made the mental reservation, "If it is a cloth, I will take it;

if it is thread, I will not take it," he takes a bundle in the darkness. If it is a cloth there, there is an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*) at the very moment of lifting it. If it is thread...
It exists; he guards it. Having carried it outside and released it, and having recognized it as "stolen," he brings it back and places it [in its original spot];
he indeed guards it. Even if he recognizes it as "stolen," thinking "whatever has been found must be taken," he goes [to take it]; he must be dealt with according to the value of the object.

If he takes it after placing it on the ground, there is a *pārājika* offense upon the act of lifting it. If one who was pursued crying out, "Thief! Thief! abandons [the goods] and flees, [he is not guilty].
He guards it. When the owners see it, they take it; he simply continues to guard it. If someone else takes it, there is an obligation to pay for the goods.

Even if the owners have turned back and he himself, seeing it, takes it with the perception that it is a rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*), thinking, "I took this long ago; it is now my own property," there is still an obligation to pay for the goods.
In this regard, as for the one who thinks, "If it is a robe-cloth (*sāṭaka*), I will take it," and so forth...
A conceptualization that proceeds by way of a method is called a "conceptualization of goods. However, the "conceptualization of space" should be understood as follows:

someone who has entered another’s monastery grounds or similar places, seeing some object capable of arousing greed, defines a boundary by means of the door to a room, the main entrance, the base of a palace, a gatehouse, the foot of a tree, or the like, thinking: "If they see me within this interval..."

"If I take it with the desire to see it and wander about as if showing it, and they do not see it, I shall steal it"—if he conceives this, then as soon as he takes it and exceeds the limit thus conceived, there is theft.
Thus, this kind of mental construction that proceeds in the manner described is called "construction by occasion" (*okāsa-parikappa*). In this way, by means of these two types of construction—
The theft committed by one who takes after having made a mental reservation should be understood as "theft by reservation.
However, taking by way of concealment is "concealed theft. This is to be understood as follows:

when a monk sees a finger-ring or similar item belonging to others that has been taken off and left behind in a garden or such place, and thinking, "I will take it later," he covers it over with dust or...
If he conceals it with leaves, there is no theft so long as there is no removal; thus, for that duration, it does not constitute an act of taking what is not given.

However, when the owners, searching for it and not seeing it, depart still longing for it, thinking, "We shall find out tomorrow," then for one who removes it, there is theft at the moment of removal.
This is because, at the very time of concealment, he perceives it as his own, thinking, "This is my property."
Or, if one takes it with the perception that it is a rag-robe (*pāṃsukūla*), thinking, “These have been taken by you; this is discarded property,” it is *bhaṇḍadeyya*.
Even if those [owners] come on the second or third day, search for it, do not see it, and depart having abandoned their claim, what was taken remains *bhaṇḍadeyya* alone.
If, after learning of it later, one who is being exhorted does not give it back, there is theft (*avahāra*) once the owners have abandoned their claim.

It is so. Why? Because they did not see it through his effort. However, if one with a thieving mind, without covering it, steps on a piece of property that remains exactly where it was and pushes it into mud or sand, the theft is complete at the very moment it has been pushed in.
But stealing by means of shifting the *kusa* grass is called "stealing by means of *kusa*. That too should be understood as follows:

when a robe is being distributed, whichever monk, having laid down some *kusa* grass—whether made of reeds or made of palm leaves—that has been used as a marker, stands near his own portion, [taking] one that is either of lesser value, greater value, or equal in value to it; [this constitutes the offense].
One who wishes to take a portion from another pulls up a blade of *kusa* grass that has fallen into his own portion with the intention of throwing it into the other’s portion;
at that time, he is still protected. As long as it remains in the other’s portion, he is indeed protected.
But when, after it has fallen there, he pulls up a blade of *kusa* from the other’s portion, at the very moment it is pulled up, there is theft (*avahāra*). If [he does so] earlier...
When one pulls up *kusa* grass from another’s portion, one guards against its being pulled out with the desire to drop it into one’s own portion, and one guards against its falling as well.
But for one who pulls up their own *kusa* grass from their own portion, one guards only against its being pulled out;
once it has been pulled out and is dropped into another’s portion, theft occurs the very moment it leaves the hand. This is theft by means of *kusa* grass.
This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be taken from the *Samantapāsādikā*.
"Having weighed" means having investigated.
"Proper conduct" (*sāmīcī*) refers to the routine duties (*vatta*); the intended meaning is that there is no offense.
“*Mahājanasammaddo*” means a great commotion among the people. “*Bhaṭṭhe janakāye*” means when the crowd of people has departed.
For what reason did he say, “Having made this saffron robe your own possession, give it to this very bhikkhu”? Because the owner of the robe had relinquished his responsibility;
therefore, it is not permissible to take what was not given. Even for a thief, there is remorse...
From the moment it arose, he wandered about seeking the owner of the robe, thinking, "I will give it back.
When the owner of the robe said, "This is mine," even this thief abandoned his attachment; therefore, he spoke thus.
If that were so, why did the owner of the robe himself not say, "Take what belongs to you"? It was for the purpose of dispelling the remorse of both.
How so? In the case of the one who took the goods, remorse might arise, thinking, "I did not give this with my own hand; this is merely a debt for the goods.
In the case of the other, remorse might arise, thinking, "Having first laid down the burden [of responsibility], I later took what was not given.
*Samaggha* means of little value.

"It serves the purpose of wood" means it accomplishes the task that must be done with wood. The entire passage beginning with "While I am present" was spoken out of the king's favor; however, one should not think that the Elder acted inappropriately.

As for this decrease in value mentioned regarding the cutting of tooth-sticks and so forth on a single day, that was said with reference specifically to what the owner of the goods had already purchased and taken.
All of this, moreover, should be accepted according to the authority of the *Aṭṭhakathā* masters. And the stone...

“Gravel and pebbles. The phrase “A discerning person would grasp the meaning” is the explanation for this very point, beginning with “Whether it be an offense or a non-offense,” and so forth. The line “The training rule is equal to that” refers to a verse that precedes this:
“The second [teaching] by the Peerless One, which was proclaimed by the Victor;”
"By one who has conquered the defilements, here is the Pārājika section.

Having combined this with that [previous verse], the second Pārājika section—which was proclaimed by the Victor, who is without a second and has conquered the defilements—is here presented together with it, interspersed with numerous methods, as a determination of its profound meaning. Furthermore, there is nothing else...

The construction is: "the training rule does not exist. In that context, "by one who has conquered the defilements" means by one in whose continuum all defilements have been eradicated along with their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) by means of the four path-knowledges, thereby establishing the state of non-arising again in the future. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated:
"'By one who has conquered the defilements' means by one who has won over the defilements; the meaning is 'one free from defilements' (*nikilesa*'). "Here" means in this teaching (*sāsana*).

"By that" means by that second *pārājika* training rule (*sikkhāpada*). "Meaning" (*attha*) refers to the meaning of the canonical text (*pāḷi*). "Analysis" (*vinicchaya*) refers to the analysis independent of the canonical text.
"Meaning and analysis" are *atthavinicchaya*; it is called "having deep meaning and analysis" because its meaning and analysis are profound.
"Having entered into the subject matter" (*vatthumhi otiṇṇe*) means either by way of an accusation or by way of one's own confession of a transgression in the midst of the Saṅgha.

"Regarding the matter of taking what is not given": "In this" means when one has fallen into such a matter. "Decision" (*vinicchaya*) means the determination of whether there is an offense or no offense.
"Without even saying": without even saying, "You have committed a *pārājika* offense. "Even regarding a permissible matter" (*kappiye pi vatthusmiṃ*):

even regarding a matter belonging to one's mother, father, or others that is permissible for oneself to take. "Lightly shifting" (*lahuvattino*): those whose minds shift quickly due to the arising of a thieving thought.
"Āsīvisa" means poison capable of pervading the entire body very quickly.
(233) "Uttarimanussadhamma" refers to the qualities attained by supreme persons such as Buddhas, who are superior to ordinary people;
the proclamation of that to others is "uttarimanussadhammārocana. When determining this matter, there are six points.

The construction is: "they are to be purified. In that context, "What have you attained? is a question regarding attainment (*adhigama*). "How have you attained it? is a question regarding the means (*upāya*).
"When did you attain it? is a question regarding time (*kāla*). "Where did you attain it? is a question regarding place (*okāsa*).
"Which defilements (*kilesa*) have you abandoned? is a question regarding the abandoned defilements. "Of which states (*dhamma*) are you a possessor? is a question regarding the states acquired.
Now, in order to elaborate upon that very purification of the six points, he said, "If indeed," and so forth.
Therein, "by this much" means that one should not show honor based on mere words of prediction; for a prediction may even occur regarding someone who is not as they appear.
For the purpose of purifying these six points, he should be addressed in this way, just as one would address even a counterfeit piece of gold.

It is called *jātarūpa* because it appears like gold; just as gold must be purified by rubbing, heating, and cutting, so too should he be subjected to the six points just mentioned for the sake of purification. By the word "etc.

(*ādi*) in the phrase "liberations, etc.," one includes attainments, knowledge, vision, development of the path, realization of the fruit, and so forth. He becomes manifest to one who has attained distinction.
Because there is no forgetfulness of mindfulness. This same method applies to the word "is manifest" (*pākaṭo hoti*) in the remaining questions as well.
For it is said, by way of general rule, that the defilements abandoned by all [arahants] through the path they themselves have attained become manifest;
for in some cases, doubt indeed arises regarding those defilements to be abandoned by the path attained by oneself, as in the case of Mahānāma.
It was like that of Sakka. For although he was a once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*), he said: "Venerable sir, this thought occurs to me:
'What dhamma of mine has not yet been abandoned within myself, because of which at times states of greed still persist, taking possession of my mind;
states of hatred still persist, taking possession of my mind; and states of delusion still persist, taking possession of my mind?'"

"Are they still remaining? he asked the Blessed One. It is said that this king had the perception that greed, hatred, and delusion were being abandoned without remainder by means of the path of a once-returner (*sakadāgāmi-magga*).
That practice by which the noble path (*ariya-magga*) of a particular person is reached is the preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipatti*), the practice of arrival (*āgamana-paṭipadā*).

“*Sodhetabbā* means they are to be cleared; that is, they are to be cleared by way of investigating whether they are pure or not pure. ‘It is not purified’ is because of the possibility of practicing negligence here and there.
‘He should be removed’ means he should be removed by his own admission,” so it is said in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, regarding the question “Is it not purified? [it says] the sequence of practice...
"He spoke by transgressing [the sequence]. "'He should be removed' means he should be removed from his conceit of attainment, thinking:

'This Dhamma cannot be realized by you according to the method you have described. Having said "he is purified," the words beginning with "for a long time" were spoken to show the manner of purification.
Regarding the phrase "it is manifest," one should also supply the word "if" here; thus: "If that bhikkhu, by that practice..."

The connection is with the word "is manifested. Because of being unattached to the four conditions, it is said: "with a mind like a hand in space. The construction is: "the explanation is similar to what was stated.
In that context, "similar to what was stated" means that the explanation of that bhikkhu is similar to what was stated in this sutta;
the sense is "equal. It is a practice similar to the practice of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
"It does not happen" means that because the defilements have been well-subsided for a long time; this is stated with reference to one who claims the state of an Arahant.
Therefore he said, "of one whose taints are destroyed," and so forth. "Of one whose taints are destroyed...

it does not happen" means it does not happen because the perversions have been abandoned and because there is an absence of attachment to life. However, for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), it does occur because the perversions have not been abandoned and because attachment to life still exists.
And even with a slight [defilement], so it is for one whose defilements have been well suppressed;
this profession of being a trainee (sekha) in conduct cannot be tested by the arising of fear through the sight of sour things and the like, nor by the production of saliva and so forth.
Therefore, that must be believed on his word alone.
"This bhikkhu is accomplished in his exposition"— this should be understood as stated not only with reference to fearlessness alone,
because even some ordinary persons (puthujjana) of a brave nature are fearless; rather, it is stated with reference to one who is entirely well-purified,
being devoid of the arising of craving such as the production of saliva even when using sour, pungent, or stimulating objects like jujube fruits, *sālava* leaves, and so forth.

234. Regarding the phrase “having extracted,” it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī* that this means “having extracted from the teaching (*sāsana*); however, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated that “‘having extracted’ means having drawn out from the Canon (*pāḷi*).
For instance, [this is seen] in such Canonical passages as: “O Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors should not be questioned.
Which five? He does not know the Sutta; he does not know what is in accordance with the Sutta,” and so forth.

They extracted the Sutta and that which conforms to the Sutta, saying, "There is no offense; such is the learning and inquiry of our teachers," thus extracting the Teachers' Statement (*ācariyavāda*).
They also extracted their own opinion (*attanomati*), saying, "The Venerable Upāli said: 'Friend, there is no offense even in a dream,'" and so forth.
And because that personal opinion of the Elder was included within the Sutta, it is [considered] the Sutta.
It should be understood that other [texts] as well, such as the Suttas, must be taken as included in this way, and not otherwise. Alternatively, "having extracted" means having analyzed;

the intention is that they proclaimed the Vinaya by dividing it into four parts—having placed the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, together with its commentary (Sāṭṭhakathā), within the four categories beginning with the Sutta—since there is nothing existing apart from it. This is also stated in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*.
“‘Having removed’—here the meaning is ‘having removed from the Teaching. … [etc] … For by means of that personal opinion, the Elder receives the designation of being ‘foremost.

Moreover, this was said by the Blessed One: ‘If one, when being spoken to by one who is not fully ordained, whether regarding what is laid down or what is not laid down, shows disrespect, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). In that context, ‘what is laid down’ refers to the Sutta.”
"The three knowledges (*sesattaya*) are called 'not laid down' (*apaññatta*). Therefore, this verse—'The Vinaya is fourfold, O Great Elders'—is well-spoken," so it was said.
"It was said" means it was spoken by the Elder Nāgasena in the *Milindapañha*. That by which a meaning is traversed is a "word" (*pada*);
a word uttered by the Blessed One, having been articulated by striking the throat and other places of vocal production, is an "articulated word" (*āhaccapada*), [belonging] to the Blessed One alone.
“Speech. Therefore, it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: “The sūtra intended here is ‘the struck word’ (*āhaccapada*). However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated:

“A ‘struck word’ is speech uttered by means of one’s own vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*), having been brought forth from the places of articulation (*karaṇa*) and so forth, which are the locations for the production of the phonemes (*vaṇṇa*) such as the throat.
In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, however, it says: “Having struck the eight places of phoneme-production...”
The meaning is "by the collection of words spoken," the intention being "by the group of words uttered and committed to memory.

[It is said: "Without making such distinctions as 'this is allowable' or 'this is not allowable,' O monks, whatever has not been prohibited by me saying 'this is not allowable,' if it conforms to what is unallowable and excludes what is allowable, that..."

He says, "‘Rasa’ means ‘in accordance with the Sutta,’" because here the general characteristic (sāmaññalakkhaṇa) stated in the passage beginning with "It is not allowable for you," etc., is intended by the term *rasa*.

*Rasa* means "essence" (*sāra*), as in expressions such as "the essence of leaves" (*pattarasa*); the meaning is that it is the essence of the Suttas regarding what is prohibited and what is permitted.
Alternatively, *rasa* means "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*), because it is stated in conformity with the characteristics without omitting the underlying basis (*paṭivatthuka*).
"By its essence" (*rasena*) means by the essence of that which was spoken directly [by the Buddha], that is, by the analytical determination (*vinicchaya*) extracted from it;

for "in accordance with the Sutta" (*suttānuloma*) is like the shadow of the Sutta. Here, the "tradition of the teachers" (*ācariyavaṃsa*) intended is the lineage of commentaries (*aṭṭhakathātanti*) brought down from the succession of teachers beginning with the compilers of the Dhamma;
thus he says, "The tradition of the teachers means the teaching of the teachers. It is the teaching of the teachers.
The phrase "the lineage of teachers" (*ācariyavaṃsa*) is stated for the purpose of showing that the succession of teachers mentioned in the Canon is indeed the authoritative source.
"Intention" (*adhippāya*) refers to that which is established through logical reasoning and the application of methods of inquiry, resembling a means of valid cognition such as direct perception.
Regarding the term "intention," some explain its meaning as "one's own opinion."

"Vinayapiṭake pāḷīti" (The text in the Vinaya Piṭaka) is stated here by way of primary reference; however, the four methods, beginning with the Sutta, are likewise found accordingly in the remaining Piṭakas as well.
"Mahāpadesā" means great opportunities. They are the great bases for the establishment of the Vinaya, wherein the Vinaya, once established, is decided upon without doubt.
Alternatively, "mahāpadesā" means great grounds; they are the great grounds for the adjudication of the Vinaya.
This has been stated. However, they say that the very text beginning with “Whatever, monks,” which expresses the intended meaning, is itself a Great Authority (mahāpadesa).
For this reason, he says: “Those which were thus spoken by the Blessed One,” and so forth. Furthermore, these Great Authorities are recorded in the Khandhaka;
therefore, since the detailed exposition of them will be revealed right there, it is not discussed here—thus it is said in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
It has been stated [thus]. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is said: "The 'great authorities' (*mahāpadesā*) are great opportunities and great spheres of application.

In their actual meaning, they are simply methods of interpretation (*atthanayā*), being grasped by individuals in various ways according to the scriptural passages beginning with 'O monks,' through both what conforms to the permissible and what conforms to the impermissible.
For even though the Blessed One did not state them explicitly as specific forms, they are established regarding those conformities and prohibitions."
And because they are the cause for the cessation or occurrence of the remaining permitted and conformable duties, they are called "great authorities" (*mahāpadesā*);

however, it is not the actual textual passage itself—such as "Monks, that which has been declared by me as 'this is not allowable' (*na kappati*)"—that is so called, since that [passage] is already included within the Sutta. For it is said:
"That which conforms to the Sutta must also be brought down into the Sutta... [and so on]... the Sutta alone is more authoritative."
For it has been said: "This passage, which possesses its own underlying intention (*adhippāya*), should not be inserted into the Sutta, nor should it be taken as part of the Sutta itself.

Since it is through this that [the commentary] becomes in conformity with the Sutta (*suttānuloma*), therefore, based on this underlying intention of the Pāḷi, the meanings as they have been stated—which are grasped by individuals—are in conformity with the Sutta;
and because this Pāḷi elucidates them, it too should be understood as being 'in conformity with the Sutta'. Thus he said: "Those..."

“Thus it was said by the Blessed One,” and so forth. For the meaning is as stated: “Those matters such as the *akappiyānuloma* (permissible adaptations) which were spoken according to the method of the Pāḷi beginning with ‘Bhikkhave’ (O monks), and which are to be accepted by individuals, are the Great Authorities (*mahāpadesā*). In the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā* as well, it says:
“In the *Parivāra-aṭṭhakathā* and here [in this work], although it is said that ‘the *suttānuloma* (conformity to the Suttas) consists of four...’”

"Great authorities" (*mahāpadesā*) has been stated; however, in actual meaning, this refers to what is established by the method of great authorities—namely, what is rejected or not rejected, what is permitted or not permitted, and what is allowable or unallowable.

In that context, since "place," "occasion," and "authority" (*padese*) are synonyms for "reason"—as seen in the Teaching such as, "Ānanda, it is impossible, it is out of the question," and so forth—and because they are also referred to as "the ground for censure" and "the ground for lack of right view," [it follows that...]
And because it is said, "it is not a matter of mere opinion, but a specific point," they are called *mahāpadesā* (great authorities) from the perspective of the world;

thus, the meaning is that they are great reasons (*mahākāraṇāni*). Here, what is intended by "reason" (*kāraṇa*) is an indicative cause (*ñāpaka-hetu*). Their greatness, however, is due to their vast scope, just like the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
They are twofold: the great authorities of the Vinaya and the great authorities of the Suttanta. Among these, the great authorities of the Vinaya...
They apply themselves to the Vinaya; the others [apply themselves] to both. For that very reason, in the *Parivāra* and the *Anuyogavatta*, it is said:
“He does not know the Dhamma, he does not know what is in accordance with the Dhamma. Therein, “the Dhamma” refers to the remaining two Piṭakas, excluding the Vinaya Piṭaka;
“what is in accordance with the Dhamma” refers to the four Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*) and so forth for the Suttantika.
If that commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) is indeed the miscellaneous teaching (*pakiṇṇakadesanā*) delivered by the Blessed One here and there,

it is nevertheless called the "Teacher's Statement" (*ācariyavāda*) because the compilers of the Dhamma first recited the Three Pitakas and then established the path of recitation for it in accordance with its explanation of meaning; thus, "the teachers speak"— that is, they comment upon— the Pāḷi.
"By this [it is meant]"—having said this, he stated: "The so-called 'Teacher's Word'... [etc. ...the lineage of the commentaries.

For indeed, the method of exposition consisting of the commentary on the meaning of the Buddha's word, which had already been established by the three councils, was brought to the Island of Tambapaṇṇi by the Elder Mahāmahinda;
subsequently, it was set down in the Sinhalese language by the Great Elders of Tambapaṇṇi for the purpose of avoiding the confusion of the tenets of other schools.

Since the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*)—which consists of both the miscellaneous teachings of the Blessed One and those that accord with the Suttas—was compiled and set forth by the Elders of the Dhamma-council in accordance with the sequence of the Pāḷi commentaries, it is therefore called the "Teacher’s Word" (*ācariyavāda*).

By this, it should be understood that the commentary is included within the Suttas and the Suttānulomas in terms of its meaning. And just as this [commentary] is so, so too is one's own opinion (*attanomaṭi*).

It is the authoritative standard. For even the Chief Disciples and others are not able, without relying on the word of the Blessed One and that which is in conformity with his word, to explain by their own power of knowledge any meaning—whether conventional or ultimate—contained within the Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya.
Therefore, all such [authoritative] speech is included within the Sutta and that which conforms to the Sutta. However, the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and so forth are treated separately.
Because it has been included therein, the remainder of the Vinaya is demonstrated in four ways by taking it from the Suttas and that which conforms to the Suttas (Suttānuloma).
Although one’s own opinion (*attanomati*) is formulated only after being cross-referenced with the Suttas and so forth, nevertheless, it is not specifically demonstrated within the Suttas and such;
therefore, he says, "setting aside the Suttas, the Suttānulomas, and the Teachers' Traditions (*ācariyavāda*). Regarding the phrase "by means of subsequent understanding" (*anubuddhiyā*):

"By means of a following understanding" refers specifically to the discourses (*sutta*) and so forth. "By grasping the method" means by grasping the method obtainable from the discourses and other sources.
Having first shown his own opinion in general, he now says "Moreover... and so forth, showing that very same view in its specific detail.
In this context, because of the statement "in the commentaries on the Suttanta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya," it follows that this discussion is common to all three Pitakas.
[The term] *theravāda* (the doctrine of the elders) refers to the tradition of the great Elder Mahāsumma and others.
Now, showing the manner in which one should proceed therein, he says, "But that... and so forth. Therein, *by the meaning* means by the meaning taken from his own method.

*The text* (*pāḷi*) means the canonical text together with its commentary (*sāṭṭhakathā*), which serves as the basis for his own tradition. *By the text* [is used] in the sense of refuting that [tradition], referring to what has been brought forward by another.
"Along with the commentary on the canonical text (pāḷi)" means: having compared the canonical text with the meaning he himself has grasped.
"In the teachers' doctrines" refers to the commentaries extracted by himself and by others. "Should be brought down" means they should be introduced by means of knowledge.
"It both descends and accords" means: it descends by way of comparison with what was extracted by himself, and [it accords] with what was extracted by another.

"It agrees. "Extremely weak" is said because, for a person who is not omniscient, there is an absence of the correct realization of the meaning due to the latent tendencies of defilement (*doṣavāsanā*).
He says, "The other should not be accepted," because it may happen that even a teacher's statement, due to a careless reading, does not accord with the Suttas.
"Only that which agrees should be accepted" means that those meanings which accord with the Suttas are to be accepted from the Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*).

He shows that [the Vinaya] "should be extracted" because the meaning extracted in such and such a way conforms to the Sutta. Therefore he said: "For, by way of conformity to the Sutta, the Sutta itself is more authoritative.

Alternatively, although conformity to the Sutta is but a portion of the Sutta, there is nothing spoken as a direct utterance—delimited as "this is allowable" or "this is not allowable"—in the same manner as the Sutta; thus he said: "By way of conformity to the Sutta... and so forth.

"More powerful" means more forceful. "Irresistible" means unopposable. "Similar to the Saṅgha of the compilers" means similar to the Saṅgha of those who compiled [the teachings] because of their authoritative nature.
By the phrase "similar to the time when the Buddhas were present," he shows that this is the very Dhamma spoken by the Buddhas themselves;
it is said to be like a Buddha who is currently living. For if the Sutta is opposed, it is as if the Buddha himself were opposed. "The proponent of our own position, having taken up the Sutta..."
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: "‘He speaks’ means that the proponent of his own school (*sakavādī*) speaks by taking up his own sutta;

‘one who speaks in accordance with the sutta’ means that the proponent of another school (*paravādī*), belonging to a different Nikāya, speaks by taking up what is in accordance with the sutta within his own Nikāya.

However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, regarding the passage beginning with “the proponent of his own school speaks by taking up the sutta,” it is explained that whoever [speaks] the meaning as it actually is...
One who speaks after having grasped [a position] is the proponent (*sakavādī*). "Sutta" refers to the words of the Canon (*pāḷi*) as recorded in the three councils.
One who speaks after having grasped a meaning erroneously—whether he be a resident of the Mahāvihāra or a resident of another school—is here called the opponent (*paravādī*).
"In accordance with the Sutta" refers to that which has been recorded in the three councils or that which has not been so recorded.
Some [texts] are in conformity with the Suttas, being presented either through some misconception or as a deception, claiming: “This has come down from the three councils.

Some say that these belong to “another Nikāya,” but that is not correct, because both our own school and opposing schools must accept only those suttas and so forth that have been recorded in the three councils. For it will be said: “That which has ascended into the three councils...”
"It is found in the Pāli; it should be accepted," and so forth. For the proponent of his own position does not accept the suttas and other texts of another school as authoritative.
If he did, he would have to stand by those suttas and other texts when they are presented [by the opponent]; yet he will say:
"The opponent shows many reasons and detailed explanations from the suttas establishing its improper nature... 'It is well.'"
"Having accepted [the teaching], one must remain within what is not allowable (akappiya). Therefore, even that which was not included in the three councils is shown by the opponent as "not included";

the distinction lies solely in the falsity of those respective suttas and other texts that were not included in the three councils, and in the misinterpretation of the intended meaning through the mere shadow of the phrasing of those that were included. And therein...
That which is a fabrication is removed. That which has been interpreted otherwise is compared with other suttas and so forth in order to demonstrate its erroneous nature.
Furthermore, whatever intention was grasped by the opponent that accords with the suttas and so forth must be accepted even by one's own proponent, having relinquished their own position;
thus, for both parties, [the interpretation] remains exactly as it came down in the three councils.

It should be understood that "the Sutta is the authority. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Kathāvatthu-pakaraṇa*: "In our own school there are five hundred suttas, and in the opposing schools there are five [hundred];
even a thousand suttas are taken as they appear in the three councils due to the diversity in grasping the underlying intention, and not from other Nikāyas."
In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, however, it is stated: “‘An opponent’ (paravādī) means one belonging to another school who understands our own tenets.
How is it that ‘the opponent’s [position] conforms to the Sutta’? The Sutta passage, ‘Except for water and tooth-wood,’ belongs to our own school;
because it conforms to that, even the water inside a coconut fruit is indeed water, and thus it is the opponent’s [position].”
“When the water of a coconut is old, it increases bile;
that very same water, when young, subdues bile and increases strength.
When the opponent had spoken thus, the proponent, because he understands the nature of grain-fruits and because he pervades the purpose of nutriment, [replied:]

‘He rejects it by saying, “That is only for the time being. Without casting it aside or censuring it means: without casting it aside with the thought, “What is the use of this? or rejecting it, discarding it;
or without censuring, reviling, or disparaging it with the thought, “What does this fool say? What does this fool know?
*Suttānuloma* (conformity with the Suttas) means a passage in conformity with the Suttas that was not spoken by oneself but found in another Nikāya.
"In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: ‘It should be brought down into the Sutta means that it should be brought down into the Sutta by the proponent himself.

However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: ‘It should be brought down into the Sutta means that, because this conforms to a certain Sutta, one should verify—by way of reconciling the meaning—the conformity to the Sutta accepted by oneself within that Sutta, or within some other Sutta similar to it.”’
"It must be brought down [into the text]. The meaning is that, having shown how it 'harmonizes' by means of this and that reason, it should be demonstrated as being consistent within this sutta.
"One must remain within the sutta itself" means one must remain within one's own sutta. "This one" refers to the proponent (sakavādī).
"The other" refers to the opponent (paravādī). "The teacher’s doctrine must be brought down into the sutta" refers to the commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanā*) upon whichever sutta [is being explained].
This teacher’s doctrine has been handed down; it should be integrated by way of reconciling the preceding and following meanings within that [text] and in other similar suttas.
The phrase "the teacher’s doctrine is censurable" is a scribal error or was inserted by those of a different school; this same method applies everywhere.
However, in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*—regarding the statement "another teacher’s doctrine" concerning the passage "he avoids the toll"—it says: "In this context, 'approach' (*upacāra*)..."

Based on the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*—"Even if one avoids [the tax] after having entered [the territory], it is indeed theft"—when the opponent asserts, "One who acts in that way incurs a *pārājika* offense," the proponent refutes this by citing the Sutta, "He avoids the toll;
there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*"), together with the corresponding passage from the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. Thus, for one who acts in that manner, there is only an offense of wrong-doing.

Regarding the phrase "one steals for oneself," when the opponent says: "In this case, if one who intends 'I will steal another's property before the meal' exerts effort thinking 'I will take it before the meal,' but it becomes after the meal, that is still the preliminary effort of the 'before-meal' [intention];

therefore, the person in the fundamental position (*mūlaṭṭha*) is not exempted. Thus, according to your Theravāda school, the person in the fundamental position incurs a *pārājika* offense," the proponent replies: "That..."
Having shown the Sutta: "If one steals that goods either before or after making a sign, there is no offense for the original owner," he rejects [the opponent's position].
Regarding "another Sutta": "A phenomenon with an undetermined cause is a condition, by way of object-condition, for a phenomenon with a cause determined as rightness."

Having shown that the *Sutta* has been written in the *Paṭṭhāna*, when the opponent asserts that "Nibbāna alone is not the object of the Noble Path," the proponent rejects it by descending [into the argument] in accordance with such *Sutta* passages as those concerning the triad of objects (*ārammaṇattika*). For only that which descends in accordance with the *Sutta* is truly a *Sutta*, and nothing else.
Therefore it is said: "It is evident that it comes down in the Canon. Even though this much suffices, [the author says] "Tisso... [and so on].
"It is recognized as having been included in the compilations and entered into the Canon," and so forth.
For the Teacher [Thera] says that such a passage is a "careless scribal insertion. Because of the statement, "Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless;

heedlessness is the path of death," one who dwells having eaten what was given, having avoided dangers, and having established mindfulness, becomes eternal. A sutta that has ascended to such a meaning—

It should not be accepted. Therefore it was said: "If it is not thus discerned. Even though this is established, because it was stated, "If it is not thus discerned, it does not descend, it does not coincide;
or else it is a non-Buddhist sutta," even one's own sutta should not be accepted if it does not coincide with the meaning.
In the two methods beginning with "another [teacher] says" and "the teacher’s doctrine," [these errors occur] here and there due to scribal negligence.
The statement from the *Aṭṭhakathā* should be understood by correlating it with the Theravāda tradition.
Now, if one speaks while adopting the teacher’s (ācariya) opinion, another [teacher] says, "It is a Sutta": "What is called 'root-seed' is turmeric, ginger, *vacā*, and so forth...
one who, perceiving it as seed, cuts it, has it cut, or breaks it... [omission] ...an offense."

Because you have recited, "For a *pācittiya* offense," when it is said, "There is a *pācittiya* for one who cuts a turmeric root," the proponent of the opposing view (sakavādī) demonstrates the passage beginning with, "Or whatever other [plants] there are that grow from roots, are produced from roots," and so forth;
he then rejects that by means of the teacher’s opinion (ācariyavāda), which is equivalent to the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), stating: "For a node does not grow upon a node."
"Paro suttānulomaṃ" means that because it conforms to the statement of the opponent, "In this way, there is no offense; such was the training of our teachers," [the author says]:
"Our ancient bhikkhus, having closed off a cell in a single-story building, came back after sleeping with one who was not fully ordained, saying, 'It is permissible for us.
Therefore, while you yourselves alone are saying, 'It is permissible for us'—" [he addresses] you.
When it was said, "Nothing can be said," the proponent refutes it by showing a passage from the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) beginning with:
"The authority belongs only to those teachers who have mastered the Suttas and that which is in conformity with the Suttas. The opponent states his own opinion:
"But in the case of [the rule] 'Who are released when they lie down without asking for permission after opening the door,' both persons are released."
— He refutes [the opponent’s view] by stating that, according to your Theravāda doctrine, not only those possessed by a *yakkha* and those who have been bound and laid down,
but all others as well— even those lying in any manner whatsoever— are released. Furthermore, if he speaks while adopting his own personal opinion,
the proponent of the opposing view [argues] that they "incur an offense" because it is [presented as] a Sutta of another.

When this was said, the proponent of his own view (sakavādī) refutes [the opponent's position] by showing that the commentarial statement— “one who is weary from the day, sitting on a couch, falls asleep without having lifted his feet from the ground,
there is no offense for him,” and so forth— implies that those who lie down in a single legged posture (*ekabhaṅga*) and others are also exempted.
Now, if this person speaks by relying on their own opinion, the opponent says:
"It conforms to the Suttas," because it can be reconciled with such statements as, "O Lord of the Devas, I declare that mental distress is twofold: to be cultivated and not to be cultivated.
When the opponent has thus stated, "There is no fault in you for maintaining a wife; therefore it is said, 'the supporting of children and wife,'" [the respondent replies]: "Even though..."
The proponent [of the opposing view] rejects [the argument], saying: "He is not one who has heard much; rather, it must be unwholesome [action] accompanied by lust.
In the remaining cases as well, this same method should be applied accordingly.

All of this was stated by the Elder Upatissa and others. However, the Elder Dhammasiri says: "In this context, 'another' refers to one belonging to another school (nikāya); he, moreover, [quotes] his own suttas and so forth..."
“He brings them forward; the proponent of his own position, having compared them with his own suttas and so forth, accepts them if they agree. If not, he rejects them”—this is what is stated.
But has it not been said above that “the sutta itself is more authoritative than what conforms to the sutta”?

Why, then, is it said here that “the sutta must be compared with what conforms to the sutta,” and so forth? There is no contradiction here; for [it was said] that “the sutta itself is more authoritative than what conforms to the sutta... [and so on].
"Stronger" refers specifically to this very sutta; for therein, with reference only to those things included within one's own opinion, it is said:
"One's own opinion is the weakest of all; the teacher’s doctrine is stronger than one's own opinion;
that which accords with the sutta is stronger than the teacher’s doctrine; and the sutta itself is stronger than that which accords with the sutta."

This has been stated. However, here, with reference to a sutta brought forward by an opponent from another Nikāya, it is said: "A sutta should be compared with a sutta that accords with it," and so forth.

Therefore, this method is explained here: a sutta or similar text brought forward by an opponent must be accepted only if, when compared with one's own suttas, the teachings of the masters, and one's own reasoning, it is found to be consistent; otherwise, it should not be accepted.
“There is no contradiction whatsoever between what precedes and what follows”—this is the method found in the *Sāratthadīpanī*. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated:

“In order to show that any so-called ‘fraudulent sutta’ (*kūṭasutta*) or the like, such as the words of non-Buddhist texts, must not be accepted, it was said: ‘A sutta should be brought down into conformity with the sutta (*suttānuloma*), and so forth.’”
The *Bāhirakasutta* refers to suttas such as the *Guḷhavessantara*, which were not included in the three councils, belonging to those who dwell in the Mahāsaṅghika school.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "Vedalla, etc.," it should be understood that the *Guḷha*, *Ummagga*, and others are included. The other type of sutta, the censurable (*gārayha*), should not be accepted.
By the statement, "One should stand by one's own judgment alone," it is shown that even from a sutta brought from another school, within one's own school—

This shows that one's own opinion alone is more powerful. A sequence [of arguments] based on similar types—such as "the proponent speaks by taking up a sutta, while the opponent speaks by means of a sutta itself"—has not been stated.
For the application of one sutta to another sutta does not appear as something divided; rather, it can be connected precisely according to the method already explained.
Now, with reference to the nature of what is allowable (*kappiya*) and what is unallowable (*akappiya*) for one's own school and opposing schools when a dispute has arisen,
the author speaks the words beginning with "But if he takes this as allowable and speaks," in order to show the procedure to be followed therein. Alternatively,

having thus shown the dispute in general terms by way of the Suttas and what is in conformity with the Suttas (*suttānuloma*), etc., he now [shows] the specific subject matter of the dispute and the Suttas, etc., by way of their determination.
To demonstrate this, it was said: "But furthermore, this is allowable" (*atha panāyaṃ kappiyaṃ*), and so forth.

Therein, "it should be brought down into both the Sutta and that which conforms to the Sutta" means that the proponent himself must bring it down into his own Sutta and that which conforms to the Sutta.
"The other finds no reason" means that the opponent does not obtain a reason. "He demonstrates much reason and determination from the Sutta" refers to the opponent.
Having brought forward many reasons and determinations from his own sutta, he shows [this].

By the statement, "Having accepted it as 'well,' one must remain precisely on what is improper," he says that the proponent of our own side (sakavādin), who does not find sutta and so forth in his own school (nikāya), must remain precisely on the words of the opponent.

In the phrase "in the sutta and in what is in conformity with the sutta," the word *ca* has the sense of an alternative; by this, [it includes] the teacher’s doctrine (*ācariyavāda*) and so forth as well.
This is the summary. Therefore he said: "He shows both the reason and the determination.

In this context, "reason" refers to the cause extracted by one's own judgment based on the method of the discourses and so forth. "Determination" refers to the determination found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
