Since the shadow of the reason is seen in both, it establishes the status of what is allowable and what is unallowable for both the proponent and the opponent.
The shadow of the semblance of a cause (*kāraṇapatirūpakacchāyā*) is seen.

In this context, "shadow of a cause" refers to a cause that is not manifest and must be established with difficulty by means of signs such as the thread [in the *Sutta*], which serves as the basis for the apprehension of what is "allowable" (*kappiya*) and the apprehension of what is "unallowable" (*akappiya*).
This is the meaning of "the semblance of a cause. If the shadow of the cause is seen in both cases, why [is it said] only in the case of the unallowable?
"One should stand firm" is what he said with the words "Having reached the Vinaya," and so forth.

To make the meaning already stated—namely, "having reached the Vinaya"—even clearer, he said, "by resorting to the investigation of what is allowable and what is unallowable. Regarding the phrases "should be obstructed" and so on:

when there is a difficult-to-understand determination concerning the state of being allowable or unallowable, the apprehension that it is "allowable" should be obstructed, and the apprehension that it is "unallowable" [should likewise be obstructed].
It must be made firm; the stream of taking what is allowable (kappiya) that occurs repeatedly must be cut off;

the meaning is that one must stand only upon what is unallowable (akappiya), which is characterized by its heavy nature. Alternatively, "it must be restrained" means that the cause for transgression through the perception of what is allowable must be restrained;
the mind that prevents it must be made stronger. "The stream must be cut off" refers to that [stream] therein.
The occurrence of transgression must be cut off. "In its gravity" means in its state of being unallowable (*akappiya*).
"By many reasons for the determination of the Suttas" means by many Suttas themselves and by the reasons for determination derived from them;
or alternatively, by the reasons obtained through the Sutta and the determination of the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). "One's own grasp is not to be relinquished."
The meaning is that the proponent’s own apprehension of it as "unallowable" (akappiya) must not be relinquished.
Now, concluding the very point just stated, he says "evaṃ" and so forth. Therein, "yo" refers to anyone among the proponents or opponents.
However, some say, "In this context, anyone among the proponents themselves is intended"; if that were the case, [the text would have said] "atha... [and so on].

In all such instances as "having taken it as allowable (kappiya), he speaks," both [the preceding and following terms] would be proponents of their own position (sakavādin) alone, because they are stated by way of a conclusion for what was already explained below with words such as "thus" (evaṃ). Therefore, that [interpretation] should not be accepted.

Regarding the phrase "it obtains an additional reason" (atirekakāraṇaṃ labhati): here, among the Suttas and so forth, each preceding one is called an "additional reason" (atirekakāraṇa). That which...
Or, when one obtains a greater number of reasons among the four—such as the discourses (sutta) and so forth—one is said to "obtain an additional reason.

It is called *suppavatti* because it proceeds well (*suṭṭhu pavatti*), or because it has the nature of proceeding well (*suṭṭhu pavattati sīlena*). Therefore he said: "*Suppavattī* means 'well-proceeding' (*suṭṭhu pavatta*).
*Vācuggata* means "emerged through speech" (*vācāya uggataṃ*); what is meant is that it is well-grasped by means of speech (*vacasā suggahitaṃ*). Then...
Or "vocal" (vācuggataṃ) means that which has emerged through speech; the meaning is that it stands there without interruption.
The phrase "from the Sutta" is an explanation of this [term], namely "from the Pāḷi.

And here, since it is stated that "Sutta means the entire Vinaya Piṭaka," the term "Sutta" used again refers to the words of the Sutta and Abhidhamma Pāḷi which convey that meaning. "From the letter" (anubyañjanaso):

The explanation of this is: “From the interrogation (*paripucchā*) and from the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). For the interrogation and the commentary are called *anubyañjana* because they clarify the meaning through the phrasing (*byañjana*) by following the canonical text (*pāḷi*).

And here, since the commentary is mentioned separately, “interrogation” refers to the tradition of the Elders (*theravāda*). Alternatively, “interrogation” [refers to] [asking questions] in the presence of a teacher.

Hearing the meaning of the Pāḷi; the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) is the investigation apart from the Pāḷi. Both of these, having followed the Pāḷi, are called "the secondary characteristic" (*anubyañjana*) because they [clarify] the meaning through the phrasing.
Regarding "in the Vinaya": this refers to the conduct of the Vinaya. For this very reason, he will later say, "without abandoning the Vinaya, without overstepping it," and so forth. In that context:

"Establishment" (paṭṭhāna) occurs through such things as not intentionally committing an offense; thus he said, "established by way of conscientiousness" (lajjibhāvena paṭṭhito), which means that one is "conscientious" (lajjī).
When the characteristics of a Vinaya-holder were to be stated, [the question] was asked: "What is the use of this conscientiousness?

To which he replied, "But one who is unconscientious," and so forth. In that context, by the phrase "even though he is well-versed in the scriptures" (bahussuto pi), he demonstrates the possession of the first characteristic.
"By 'being intent on gain' (lābhagarukatā)"—this shows that in the absence of being established in the Vinaya, one who possesses the first characteristic does not perform what ought to be done;
rather, he performs what ought not to be done and brings about harm. "Schism in the Saṅgha" (saṅgharājī) is a designation for the quarreling that occurs prior to a formal schism in the Saṅgha.
"Anxious" (kukkuccako) means having a sense of anxiety (kukkucca) by way of seeing danger even in the slightest faults.
"Causing to arise. "Without contradicting that" means without altering the text (pāḷi).
"Not overstepping" means not transgressing. "Snorting" means snorting because one does not see the meaning, or it means gasping. "Quivering" means shaking.
"Unable to settle" means unable to remain established in a single meaning. Therefore he said: "Whatever is spoken by another..."

"He approves of this and that. To abandon one's own position and adopt the opponent's position means: when the opponent says, "In sugarcane, the dregs (*kasaṭa*) may be kept for as long as life lasts, the juice (*rasa*) may be kept for seven days, and apart from these two, there is no such thing as sugarcane itself;
therefore, even sugarcane is permitted at the wrong time," he accepts that as well. "A single hair" (*ekaloma*) is said with reference to grey hair (*palita*).
"In whom" means in which person. "Complete exhaustion" and "termination" are one in meaning.
"The lineage of teachers" refers to the succession of the teachers' interpretations. For this very reason, he will say:
"Having abandoned one's own opinion... it is appropriate to know it just as the teacher and the teacher's teacher state the text and its detailed inquiry."
For there is no purpose in knowing the mere succession of the names of the teachers.

"By way of connection between what precedes and what follows" means by way of knowing the connection of meaning between a preceding statement and a subsequent statement. "By way of meaning" means by way of the literal meaning, the collective meaning, the intended meaning, and so forth. "By way of reason" means by way of the logical justification for that meaning.
"The lineage of teachers" is a synonym for this very term, "the constituent of the Elder's tradition."
The meaning is "the sequence of the elders. "Two or three rounds" means two or three successions.
Regarding the phrase "by these three characteristics," the first characteristic describes the state of having properly mastered the Vinaya;
the second, through the sense of shame and steadfastness therein, describes its well-established nature; and the third, regarding the Pāḷi and the commentaries...
The capacity to determine even future cases by means of their form, through conformity with them, and by following the methods provided by the teachers.
"When the matter has been brought forward" means when the matter of transgression has been brought forward in the midst of the Saṅgha by way of an accusation.
"What should be said when the accuser and the accused have spoken" means that, based on the matter thus brought forward, the accuser says "I have seen," "I have heard," and so forth.
The meaning is that when that which is to be stated by means of the "cuditaka" formula beginning with "it exists," etc., has been stated;
"the basis (vatthu) should be examined" means that the basis for each respective training rule (sikkhāpada) should be examined. "With grass or with leaves...

whoever should come [to fetch it], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)"—this refers to the training rule concerning the solicitation of what belongs to another (aññātakaviññatti) within the section on forfeiture (nissaggiya).
It is prescribed regarding the basis [of the offense].

Because the offenses of a grave transgression (*thullaccaya*) and a minor fault (*dubbhāsita*) do not appear in the matrix (*mātikā*), it is stated as "any one of the five offenses. Regarding the threefold *dukkaṭa*:
"If one perceives someone who is not fully ordained as being fully ordained, and one reviles or censures them, there is an offense..."

The "triple *dukkaṭa*" mentioned in such passages as "of a *dukkaṭa* offense" refers to that. Or, "any other offense" is said with reference to the "double *dukkaṭa*" found in such passages as: "If it is the right time, but one perceives it as the wrong time, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*; if it is the right time, but one is doubtful, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*," and so forth. Regarding "an intermediate offense":
here, this refers to something other than the transgression of the specific subject matter (*vatthu*) mentioned in each respective training rule (*sikkhāpada*).

Regarding the transgression of the object (*vatthuvītikkama*), the offense described here—starting from the origin (*nidāna*) up to the conclusion of the case of discipline (*vinītavatthupariyosāna*)—is one that occurs intermittently.
However, because the phrase "he looks at the object" is mentioned separately here, the remaining offenses occurring in the interval are what is intended.

The expression "he tosses up a burning brand" (*paṭilātaṃ ukkhipati*) is also found in the training rule concerning fanning (*visibbana-sikkhāpada*); there, it refers to a burning brand (*alāta*) from a firebrand or similar source.
If he throws back exactly what fell outside and was not yet pierced, the meaning is that he places it again in its original position.
However, for one who rejects what has already been pierced, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Regarding "there is no offense" (anāpatti): here there is also an occasion of no offense mentioned intermittently, such as: "Monks, there is no offense for one possessing psychic power (iddhimā)."

It is also included [in the category] such as "in the domain of psychic power" (*iddhivisaya*). "In the intervals between the training rules" (*sikkhāpadantaresu*) means in each interval between the training rules, having included the specific case of the offense (*vinītavatthu*) within it.

Regarding the statement "it should not be called an offense entailing defeat" (*pārājikāpatti*): this refers to the person who has committed the offense abiding in a sense of shame (*lajjidhamma*) and seeing things as they truly are.
This was said with reference to acts such as taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), which are difficult to determine even when being disclosed.

However, that which is the conscious awareness regarding sexual intercourse (*methuna*) and so forth must certainly be stated; therefore he said, "The transgression of the practice of sexual intercourse," and so on.

But as for one who, out of shamelessness, does not give a formal admission and instead creates evasion—for him, it is impossible to determine the offense even as a gross one, until he [speaks] according to reality.
As long as he does not resolve [the matter] and the Saṅgha’s doubt regarding the offense does not disappear, he shall remain as one who has been expelled.
"Subtle" is said because of the rapid transformation of the mind, which is difficult even for oneself to discern and is subject to quick change.
Alternatively, it is "subtle" due to the subtlety of the mind's transformation. Therefore, he said, "light as the mind."
The meaning is "light as the mind. Alternatively, they are called *cittalahukā* because their minds (*citta*) are light and quick to change.

"Those" (*te*) refers to those transgressions. "Based on that" (*taṃvatthukaṃ*) means that those transgressions—such as taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech—are its basis (*vatthu*), foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*), and cause (*kāraṇa*). Thus, it is "based on that."
Everything beginning with "Do what the teacher says" was spoken with reference specifically to one who is modest, amiable, and conscientious.

It was also said by one who explains things as they truly are and seeks only purity: "One should not say, 'You are one who has committed a pārājika offense,'" because even at the extreme limit of non-offense, it is still regarded as such.
For that very reason, it is called "the shadow of a pārājika. Regarding the precepts...
Regarding the phrase "having purified," it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī* that one should not attend to whatever basis for remorse has arisen, but rather purify the remaining precepts.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: "Having purified the precepts means:

having adopted the position that there is no offense of defeat (*pārājika*) in a case where a suspicion of defeat might arise, [one purifies] those [precepts] which lead to emergence from the confession."
"Having purified his virtues by means of purifying his offenses. Because it is well-known and easy to handle, it is said:
"First, attend to the thirty-two aspects," or [this is said] as an illustration. One who has already practiced another meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) should attend to that very one.
Or rather, it is entirely permissible to attend to whichever one pleases. The meditation subject...
"He joins together" means that without showing gaps in between, he joins [the object] with the mind as its objective support for a long period of time.
"The formations appear manifest" means that if one is a practitioner of the meditation subject of insight (vipassanā-kammaṭṭhānika),
the formations appear manifest to him.
If one has committed an offense involving defeat (pārājika), then even though one may wish to remember [the meditation subject], it keeps recurring due to being a ground for remorse;
thus, one does not find one-pointedness of mind. Therefore it is said: “The meditation subject does not cohere,” and so forth.
“The meditation subject does not cohere” means that even for one of pure virtue, because of the abundance of mental agitation and the like...
The mind does not become concentrated; this should not be taken here as the root of a *pārājika* offense.

It is with reference to the non-concentration of the mind due solely to remorse (*vippaṭisāra*) rooted in committed evil that it was said, "the meditation subject does not coalesce," and so forth. Therefore he said, "by the fire of remorse," and so on.
By "oneself" (*attanā*), the person—the agent—knows by means of the mind acting as the instrument; or else, the instrumental case is used in the sense of identity (*paccatte*), [meaning] "self."

The meaning is that she knows by herself. "And other deities know" means that deities other than the protective deities (*ārakkhadevatā*), namely those deities who possess the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittavidū*), know [this].
There is a point here that should be investigated by the wise. How so?

Now, some holders of the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*) maintain that when a case has arisen concerning the subject matter of the first *pārājika* offense, whether by a woman, a man, a householder, or one gone forth...
Or, when being urged, after questioning the monk who has been charged and his admission not being given, they have that monk lie down all alone in a charnel ground. If, while lying there,
that monk is able to remain for the entire night in that charnel ground— whether lying down or sitting— free from fear and agitation, they decide, "This one is pure."
If, however, one who has fallen into fear and terror is unable to lie down or sit for the entire night, they determine that person to be "impure";
this appears to be improper. Why? Because it contradicts the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā);
for in the Commentary, such an investigation is stated only regarding the second and third Pārājikas, not regarding the first and fourth Pārājikas.
For it is said there: "The transgression of sexual intercourse and the transgression of claiming superhuman states are gross;
however, the taking of what is not given and the transgression involving a human being are subtle and light in mind.
One commits them subtly and guards against them subtly; therefore, when questioned specifically regarding remorse based on those grounds... And in the *Ṭīkā*:

It is said: “*Tatvatthukan* means that those instances of taking what is not given and transgressing against human beings are its basis (*vatthu*), its foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*), and its cause (*kāraṇa*);
thus it is *tatvatthuka*. This too is one reason.
Furthermore, even after having other wise men adjudicate the matter there, their decision likewise appears as nothing but the shadow of a *pārājika*.
It should be done; it is not [to be done] when seeing a state of pure innocence. For it is said in the Commentary:

“Without saying ‘an offense,’ if his teacher maintains [the precepts]… even if, for a junior [monk], the shadow of a *pārājika* offense appears, he should still not be told, ‘You are one who has committed a *pārājika*.
For the arising of a Buddha is rare, and the going forth and full ordination are rarer than that.”
"But it should be stated thus," this is one point. Even when being requested to sit, he should be made to sit only in a secluded place, not in a charnel ground.
For it is said there: "Having swept a secluded spot and sat down for the day's abiding," and so forth; this is one point.
Even when being requested to sit in a secluded place, he should be made to sit only during the day, not at night. For likewise—
It is said: "He does not even know that the day has passed; when he comes for attendance after the day has elapsed, he should be addressed thus"—this is one case.
Such a procedure should be carried out only when [the offense] has been confessed by oneself, not when being exhorted by others. For it is said:
"The procedure should be undertaken when a monk who has committed such a transgression has come and confessed it himself. Now...
"Why do they act in this way now? [One might ask. They act thus because they consider it to be like making someone dive into water during a legal dispute that has not been witnessed by householders.
Even in that regard, people skilled in deception produce falsehoods through various means;
therefore, it may be true, and it may also be untrue. For that very reason, Bodhisattvas such as the wise Mahosadha and others—

Even in a case where there are no witnesses, they do not decide the legal dispute by means such as making the parties dive into water; rather, having caused both parties to enter the assembly, and having examined their words and their actions, they decide only after knowing what is true and what is false.
In the Dispensation, however, there are monks who are of a courageous nature and those who are of a timid nature. And as for the cemetery, it belongs even to ordinary people...
It causes fear and terror; moreover, at the time of night, it appears exceedingly terrifying.
When such is the case in a charnel ground, how could a monk of fearful nature—not even one who is pure in virtue—not be afraid when lying down alone and without a companion?
How could he possibly manage to lie down or sit through the entire night in such a place? Thus it is.
How can one who says of a bhikkhu, "He is impure," be considered one who acts according to his duty?
However, an unashamed person of bold nature, desiring to conceal his own fault, might—though actually afraid—act as if he were not afraid;
thinking, "If I show any sign of agitation, they will bring me harm," he may endure it out of fear of such harm and lie down.
Or even sit down; how could one who speaks of such a person as "pure" be considered well-investigated?
This too is one reason. Furthermore, they might say:
"Just as when people who speak untruthfully are submerged in water, by the power of the deities..."
Crocodiles and other such creatures appear as if they have come to seize them; therefore, those who speak untruths float away quickly.
However, these creatures do not appear before those who speak truth, and thus they are able to sit down in comfort.
In the same way, for those monks whose virtue is impure, lions, tigers, and other beasts appear as if they have arrived through the power of the deities.
Therefore, they are unable to lie down or sit throughout the entire night. However, for those of pure virtue, such things do not appear;

thus, being protected by deities throughout the entire night, they are able to lie down or sit in the charnel ground free from fear and terror. This is because the case was adjudicated with the deities acting as witnesses.

As for the statement that "it is indeed well-determined," that too cannot be asserted as such. Why? Because it is not stated so in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, the *Ṭīkā*, and other such works. For in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it says:
"Having swept a secluded place, having sat down for the midday rest, and having purified his moral discipline, he should be told:
'First, attend to the thirty-two aspects. If his moral discipline is pure, [then] the meditation subject..."
It joins together; the mental formations (*saṅkhārā*) appear clearly, and the mind becomes one-pointed as if it had reached access or absorption concentration (*upacāra-ppanā*).
Even though a whole day has passed, one does not realize it... However, for one whose virtue (*sīla*) is broken, the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) does not join together;
the mind trembles like a horse struck by a goad, and it is consumed by the fire of remorse, like [a drop of water on] a red-hot stone.
It is stated only thus: "Even while sitting, he emerges at that very moment. In the *Ṭīkā* as well, it says:
"'He joins the meditation subject' means that without showing any gaps in between, he joins it for a long time with the mind as its object.
'Formations appear clearly' refers to one whose meditation subject is insight (*vipassanā-kammaṭṭhānika*)."
"His mental formations appear clearly to him.
If he has committed an offense involving defeat (pārājika), then even though he wishes not to remember it, because it is a basis for remorse, it keeps appearing to him again and again;
thus, he does not find one-pointedness of mind. This much alone was said.

In the *Vimativinodanī* as well, it is said: "He joins the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) means that he connects it with the mind by way of continuity, without showing gaps here and there due to distraction rooted in remorse. 'Formations' (*saṅkhārā*) is stated by way of the meditation subject for insight (*vipassanā*).
For indeed, even a meditation subject that is well-mastered does not appear clearly to one who has committed an offense, let alone one who has committed a *pārājika*."
For his mind does not become one-pointed because it is inclined toward remorse.

However, the mind of even one who possesses pure virtue does not attain concentration if he is full of mental distraction through discursive thought and the like; that [distraction] should not be taken here as the root of a *pārājika* offense.
It is with reference specifically to the non-concentration of the mind due to remorse rooted in committed evil that [the text] says, “the meditation subject does not succeed,” and so forth.
Only this much was stated; it was not said, "By the power of a deity," and so forth.

Therefore, if a bhikkhu who has reverence for the Buddha’s teaching and desires to train in it, having seen some transgression of his own regarding the second or third pārājika offense, falls into doubt, wondering, "Have I incurred a pārājika, or have I not?", and approaches a master of the Vinaya—
Having explained that transgression as it truly is, he should ask; then the master of the Vinaya should say only this much, according to the method stated in the Aṭṭhakathā:

"Having performed all the preliminary arrangements, having swept a secluded place, having sat down for the day's rest, and having purified your moral discipline, attend first to the thirty-two aspects."
One should not say, "Make your bed in the charnel ground," and so forth.

It should be understood that even when he has arrived, one must question him according to the method set forth in the Aṭṭhakathā, and his state of purity or impurity must be declared according to the method set forth in the Aṭṭhakathā.
This being so, how should the decision be made for those who now raise an objection regarding the first *pārājika* offense?
When the matter has been announced by means of a formal accusation (*codaka*), the one being accused (*cuditaka*) should be asked, "Is this true, or not?

Having thus examined the matter and having accused and reminded him by means of the actual facts, that legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) should be settled through the perfection of the motion (*ñatti*) and the perfection of the proclamation (*anussāvana*). Even so, one who is shameless says, "This does not exist, that does not exist."
If he should speak [of his offense] but not grant a formal admission (*paṭiñña*), then what should be done?

In this case as well, even for one who is shameless, he should be dealt with according to the offense based on his admission alone, just as was done by the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷābhaya. For it is said in the Commentary:
"When a shameless person, being thus exhorted by one who is conscientious, does not grant an admission even though many grounds for offense have arisen..."
“It should not be called ‘pure,’ nor should it be called ‘impure’; this is what is known as a ‘living corpse’ (jīvamataka) and what is known as a ‘raw corpse’ (āmaka-pūtiko).
But if another similar substance arises for him, it need not be adjudicated; in that case, it will simply be discarded.
Thus, having understood the characteristics of one who holds the Vinaya and the examination of the six points, now... [the] adjudication.

"It should be understood" is the construction. To the question "For what purpose?", he says: "That which... for the purpose of knowing. The meaning is: the detailed analysis (vinicchaya) of that very same charge (codanā) previously mentioned in its various divisions—by way of its beginning, middle, end, and so forth—should be understood for the purpose of knowing its success (sampatti) and failure (vipatti);
it is not for the purpose of knowing the divisions of charges not previously mentioned. "Seyyathidaṃ" is used in the sense of a question.
This is a grammatical particle; the meaning is: "What is this analysis?
Regarding the questions, "How many roots of accusation are there? How many bases? How many grounds?", one should also say here, "In how many ways?
For this has been stated in the *Parivāra*, in the section on accusations (*codanākaṇḍa*): "How many roots of accusation are there? How many bases? How many grounds?"
“In how many ways does one admonish?”—to this, [the text] will say, “With a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner hatred.
Following that, it should also be stated: “There are these five grounds for admonition. In which two ways does one admonish? One admonishes either by body or by speech;
in these two ways one admonishes. Why? Because it is found thus in the Section on Admonition (*Codanākaṇḍa*). Among the fifteen...
"One should be established in the teachings" means: purity of bodily conduct, purity of verbal conduct, being established in a mind of loving-kindness,
great learning, proficiency in both Pātimokkhas, speaking at the proper time, speaking what is true, speaking gently,
speaking what is beneficial, speaking with a mind of loving-kindness, and compassion.
It consists of: being intent on welfare, compassion, the restoration from offenses, and having the Vinaya as one’s primary concern. For this has been said in the *Upālipañcaka*:
“When a monk, Upāli, wishing to reprove another, he should reflect thus:
‘Am I pure in bodily conduct? … Am I pure in verbal conduct? … Is my mind established in loving-kindness?’”
Among my fellow celibates... [as before] ...am I indeed one who has heard much, who retains what he has heard, and who stores up what he has heard?
... Both Pātimokkhas have been properly received by me in detail... I shall speak at the right time, not at the wrong time;
I shall speak truthfully, not falsely; I shall speak gently, not harshly; I shall speak in a way that is beneficial, not in a way that is unbeneficial.

“I shall speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner hatred... [and so on] ...with compassion, with a desire for welfare, with sympathy, with the intention of emerging from offenses, and with the Vinaya as my primary concern.

In this context, “compassion” (*kāruññatā*) means the state of being compassionate. By this, both compassion (*karuṇā*) and the preliminary stage to compassion are shown. “Desire for welfare” (*hitesitā*)...

Seeking welfare means being intent on providing that welfare. Compassion means connecting [others] with that welfare. Restoration from an offense means establishing them in the state of purity after having raised them out of the offense.

Having charged the matter, reminded [the offender], and obtained their admission, then performing the formal act according to that admission is what is called "having the discipline as the primary concern. They say that even when there is no basis, or when there is a basis, it is taken as "having a basis" and spoken of as such.
He said: "There are two roots. Regarding such statements as "I will speak at the proper time," one who reproves after having requested a specific opportunity is said to speak at the proper time.

One who reproves in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, or in places such as the hall for voting sticks, the top of a rice-offering post, the meditation hut, the path to alms-gathering, or the dining hall, or at a moment when surrounded by attendants, is said to speak at the improper time. One who reproves with a matter that is factual...
One speaks by means of what is factual. One who urges by means of what is empty speaks by means of what is non-factual.
To say, "O elder, you who frequent assemblies, you rag-robe wearer, you preacher of the Dhamma—this is fitting for you," is to speak harshly.
To say, "Venerable sir, you who are elders, who frequent assemblies, who are rag-robe wearers, who are preachers of the Dhamma—this is fitting for you," is [to speak kindly].
"He speaks gently" means he speaks with gentleness. "He speaks for the benefit" means he speaks by taking recourse to a valid reason.
"I will speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with a mind of hatred"—this means he will speak having established a mind of loving-kindness, not being possessed of a corrupt mind.
"In truth and in steadfastness" refers to verbal truthfulness and to being unshakable. For the one who is reproached must indeed speak the truth.
The meaning is: one should not be angry, one should not reproach oneself, and one should not provoke another.
In this context, it is said: "The Saṅgha must determine whether a case has been brought to a conclusion or not;
the investigator must resolve that legal dispute in such a way that it is settled according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Teacher’s instruction."
It should be stated. For this has been said in the *Codanākaṇḍa*: “How should the accuser proceed?
How should the accused proceed? How should the Saṅgha proceed? How should the investigator proceed?
‘How should the accuser proceed? The accuser, having established himself in five qualities, should accuse the other.”
"I shall speak at the proper time, not at an improper time; I shall speak what is true, not what is untrue; I shall speak gently, not harshly;
I shall speak in a way that is beneficial, not in a way that is unbeneficial; I shall speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner hatred.
This is how the accuser should proceed. How should the accused proceed? By the accused, [two things should be considered] in two ways...
One should be established in the Dhamma, in truth, and in imperturbability. This is how the one who has been accused should act.
How should the Saṅgha act? The Saṅgha must determine whether the matter has been entered upon or not.
This is how the Saṅgha should act. How should the investigator act? The investigator should [act] according to that Dhamma, according to that Vinaya, according to that...
"That legal issue is settled by the Teacher’s instruction; thus should that legal issue be settled.
This is how the investigator should proceed.
Regarding this, in the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), in the response to the questions beginning with "Who is the accuser? and so forth, it says: "In truth, and without anger... and so on.
One should be established in truth and remain unshaken. Whether something has been done or not done, that alone should be stated;

anger should not be aroused toward the accuser, the investigator, or the Saṅgha. "One must know what has been entered upon and what has not been entered upon" means that one must discern the speech of what has been entered upon and what has not been entered upon.
In this regard, the method of discernment is as follows: "So many were the preliminary statements of the accuser..."
It should be understood that there is this much subsequent talk, this much prior talk regarding the one who has been accused, and this much subsequent talk.
The measure of the accuser must be taken; the measure of the accused must be taken; the measure of the investigator must be taken.
Without letting even a trifling matter go to waste, the investigator should say: "Friend, attend closely and act with integrity."
"Bring it forth," he should be told; thus should the Saṅgha proceed.
"By whatever Dhamma, by whatever Vinaya, by whatever Teacher’s instruction that legal issue (adhikaraṇa) is settled"—here, "Dhamma" means the factual basis (bhūta-vatthu).

"Vinaya" means both the formal charge (codanā) and the reminder (sāraṇā). "Teacher’s instruction" means both the perfection of the motion (ñatti-sampadā) and the perfection of the proclamation (anussāvana-sampadā). By this...
For it is said: "An legal dispute is settled by means of the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction;

therefore, the investigator, having charged [the accused] with the actual matter and reminded them of the offense, should settle that legal dispute through the formal motion (ñatti) and the formal proclamation (anussāvana). Thus must the investigator proceed. Therefore:
"Only so much should be said; thus there are two.

Having thus shown the method of challenging by way of a partial [charge], he now says, "The investigator should question the accuser," etc., showing the method of the Great Council (Mahāsaṅgāma) by way of a partial [explanation]. Therein, "Friend, as for this bhikkhu whom you..."
"You charge him"—this is stated according to the general sense of "charging" (codanā);
however, in the Pāḷi, with reference specifically to the act of suspending the invitation (pavāraṇaṭṭhapanavasena), it says: "Friend, you have suspended the invitation of this bhikkhu.
The rest is easy to understand.

Having thus shown the method for the Great Council (mahāsaṅgāma) by way of one part, he now says, "by a monk who dwells in the midst of a conflict" (*saṅgāmāvacarena bhikkhunā*), etc., in order to show the method for the Small Council (*cūḷasaṅgāma*) by way of one part as well.

Therein, "a monk who dwells in the midst of a conflict": a conflict (*saṅgāma*) is said to be the assembly of the Saṅgha for the purpose of deciding a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*). For therein, both those who are adversaries to oneself...
And enemies of the Dispensation, proclaiming a teaching contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya,
gather together, just like the Vajjiputtakas of Vesālī. Any bhikkhu who, having crushed the views of those adversaries,
frequents that place for the purpose of proclaiming his own doctrine, and having plunged in, carries out a formal adjudication— he is called a "warrior of the battle," such as the Elder Yasa.
Just as that, so too, when approaching the Saṅgha, that monk who dwells in the battle must approach the Saṅgha with a humble mind.
"With a humble mind" means having cast down the banner of pride, with a mind in which pride is subdued. "Equal to a dust-sweeper" means equal to a foot-wiper;
just as when a foot—whether soiled or unsoiled—is wiped by a dust-sweeper, there is neither lust nor...
"Free from hatred": the meaning is that one should not be attached to or hostile toward things pleasant or unpleasant. "In a suitable seat":
having recognized a suitable seat, one should sit in the place that falls to one's lot, without turning one's back on the elder monks.
"Without engaging in various kinds of talk": without speaking various sorts of useless talk. "Without engaging in excessive talk": [as above].
One should not speak of "frivolous talk," such as talk about kings and so forth, nor of what has been seen, heard, or thought. Alternatively, the Dhamma should be spoken by oneself:

in the place where the Saṅgha has assembled, the Dhamma refers to discourse concerning what is allowable and what is unallowable, or discourse concerning the analysis of form and the formless, or the conduct of calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), or the standing, sitting, and duties (vatta).
Such Dhamma should either be spoken by oneself or requested from another. Whoever...
If a bhikkhu is capable of delivering such a discourse, he should be told: "Friend, when a question arises in the midst of the Saṅgha, you should speak.

Or, the noble silence should not be despised; for when noble ones sit in silence, they do not sit like foolish worldlings, but rather sit having taken up a particular meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Thus...
The state of silence resulting from attention to a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is called "noble silence.

It should not be despised, nor should it be disregarded with the thought, "What is the use of devotion to a meditation subject? The meaning is that one should sit down only after taking up a meditation subject suitable for oneself.
"One should not ask about the preceptor" means one should not ask, "What is your preceptor's name?
This same principle applies everywhere. "One should not ask about birth" means one should not ask about birth in such a way as, "Are you of kṣatriya birth? Are you of brahmin birth?
"One should not ask about the lineage" means one should not ask about the lineage in such a way as, "Are you a Dīghabhāṇaka? Are you a Majjhimabhāṇaka? Nor should one ask about family status.

It should be understood by way of the noble warrior class and so forth. "Affection or aversion toward him" means that toward that person there may arise either affection or aversion due to one or another of these reasons.

"Not as a partisan of the assembly" means that one should not be a partisan of the assembly or one who conforms to the assembly; [whatever the assembly thinks]— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
The meaning is that once one has reflected upon and determined what is pleasing, one should not speak of it.
"One should not display hand gestures" means that one should not make movements with the hands for the purpose of giving a sign regarding what may or may not be spoken.
"Adapting oneself to the meaning" means observing precisely the penetration of the analysis [of the text], thinking: "This sutta is found..."
The meaning is that one should sit while reflecting thus: "In this decision, I shall say this.
And "one should not rise from the seat" means that having risen from the seat, one should not wander about in the assembly circle.
For when the holder of the Vinaya (vinayadhara) has risen, the entire assembly rises; therefore, one should not rise. "One should not step across" means...
The legal decision (*vinicchaya*) must be set aside. "One should not follow a wrong path" means that no offense should be pointed out [for such a person].

"One should be non-violent" means one should not act impulsively; the meaning is that one should not speak harsh words impulsively. "Patient in speech" means having a disposition to endure harsh words.
"Seeking welfare" means desiring welfare, seeking welfare, and possessing both compassion (*karuṇā*) and the preliminary stage of compassion (*karuṇā-pubbabhāga*).
"And he should be attended to"—this is the intended meaning in both instances of the phrase.
"Without discourteous speech" means not with discourteous speech; "discourteous speech" refers to unpleasant words characterized by contentious talk, the sense being that such should not be spoken.
"One should examine oneself" means one should examine oneself thus: "Will I be able to judge and to settle [the dispute]?"
The meaning is that one’s own measure must be known. "The other person must be examined" means: one must examine the other person thus, "Is this assembly modest?
Is it possible to convince them, or not? "The accuser must be examined" means: he must be examined thus, "Is he an accuser according to the Dhamma, or not?
"The accused must be examined" means: "Is he an accused according to the Dhamma, or not?"... [and so forth].
"It is not"—thus it should be discerned. "The one who reproaches unlawfully should be discerned" means that his measure must be known.
The same method applies to the others as well.
It is said, "without letting [the matter] drop": without letting the words spoken by the accuser and the accused fall away. "Without making known what was not spoken."
By one who does not reveal the matter that has not been brought forward: "The dull-witted should be made to laugh" means the dull and deluded person should be encouraged;
having inspired him with the thought, "Are you not indeed a son of good family?", and having had him speak on the proper conduct of interrogation, his interrogation should be undertaken.
"The timid should be comforted" refers to one in whom timidity arises because he has never before entered the midst of the Saṅgha or the midst of a group.
To such a person, one should say, "Do not fear; speak with confidence;
we shall be your support," and then have him undergo the formal questioning. One who is fierce should be restrained, meaning he should be removed and threatened.

One who is impure should be exposed, meaning the shameless one should be made to confess his offense. "With straightforwardness and gentleness" refers to a monk who is upright, virtuous, and free from crookedness of body and so forth.

He should be approached with gentleness alone. Regarding the phrase "toward both teachings and persons," it should be understood that one who values the teaching (*dhamma*) and does not value the person (*puggala*) is precisely the one who maintains equanimity toward both teachings and persons. The rest is easily understood.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
The Thirty-First Chapter, titled "The Ornament of Discourse on the Determination of Exhortations and the Like. 32.
The Discourse on the Determination of Emergence from Grave Offenses.
The Discussion on the Concealed Probation (Paṭicchannaparivāsakathā). 236.

Having thus explained the determination regarding the formal charge (*codanā*) and so forth, he now spoke the words beginning with "the emergence from a grave offense" (*garukāpattivuṭṭhāna*) in order to explain the determination regarding the emergence from a grave offense.
In this context, it is called a "grave offense" because its atonement (*paṭikaraṇa*) is not light.

"Serious" (*garuka*) means it is an offense that must be committed; it is both serious and an offense, thus a "serious offense" (*garukāpatti*). "Emerging" (*vuṭṭhāna*) means emerging from; the emergence from a serious offense is the "emergence from a serious offense. What is that?

It is the state of being purified from an offense involving formal meeting of the Sangha (*saṅghādisesa*). Therefore he said: "Emergence from a serious offense by means of disciplinary acts such as probation (*parivāsa*) and penance (*mānatta*). Although [the offenses] are fourfold...
However, since *appaṭicchannaparivāsa* (probation for unconcealed offenses) is not intended here, he says, "probation is threefold.
For it is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "In that regard, probation is fourfold:
*appaṭicchannaparivāsa*, *paṭicchannaparivāsa*, *suddhantaparivāsa*, and *samodhānaparivāsa*. Among these, 'O monks, whoever..."

"Furthermore, if anyone who was formerly a member of another sect desires the going-forth and desires the full ordination in this Dhamma and Vinaya, a probation of four months must be granted to him"—this is what is called the "probation for former members of other sects" (tīthiyaparivāsa) mentioned in the Mahākhandhaka, which is known as the probation for those who have not concealed their past.
Whatever needs to be said regarding that has already been stated; however, this [specific case] is not intended here.
From this point onward, since the matter is easily understood according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, we shall explain only those points that are difficult to understand.
237. Thus, having taken the name of each individual who has committed an offense, the formal act (*kammavācā*) should be performed;
by this means, as a common formula for all cases in the *Pāḷi*, it says: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this monk named so-and-so..."
And [the text] shows that even when the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) is being recited upon the arrival of the words, "If it is timely for the Saṅgha,

let the Saṅgha [act] for the monk named so-and-so," one should not speak in that manner; rather, the formal proclamation must be performed by explicitly uttering each individual's name, such as, "This monk is Buddharakkhita," and "Of this monk Buddharakkhita."

The observance (vatta) must be undertaken within the boundary of the hall (*māḷakasīmā*) itself, and not outside of it. Why? Because there would be the fault of having the formal act (*kammavācā*) in one place and the undertaking (*samādāna*) in another; because it is impossible for one who has not undertaken the observance to announce it;

and because if even a single monk among those assembled within the boundary of the hall does not announce it, the interruption of the night (*ratticcheda*) would occur. [Regarding] the probation (*parivāsa*):
Regarding the two phrases, "I undertake" and "I undertake the duty," it should be undertaken either by each one individually or by both together.
If it is asked how this is known: because it will be stated later, "In this matter, the probation is established even by a single phrase, but it is well-established by both;
the same method applies to the undertaking as well. Having undertaken it, one must announce it to the Saṅgha right there.
One must not go elsewhere without having announced it there. Why? Because once the assembly has risen, it is difficult to reconvene it;
and because if dawn breaks without having announced it to even a single bhikkhu, it constitutes a breach of the night-period.
The connection is that the one announcing it should announce it in this way: “Venerable sirs... [as before] ...may the Saṅgha bear it in mind. This much alone [is required].

Since it was not stated as in a formal request—“a second time and a third time”—it should be understood that when there is an urgent matter to be done, it is appropriate even if it is announced only once.
Regarding the phrase, “Venerable sir, I feel [pleasure]; let the Saṅgha remember me as one who feels,” here the meaning is:
“I accept this with my mind, saying ‘I feel,’ and thus I experience pleasure; I am not pained on account of that.”

"The intended meaning [is as follows]," it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*. And here, as in the expressions "I experience a pleasant feeling" (*sukhaṃ vedemi vedanaṃ*) and so forth, the particle *pi* has the sense of experiencing. However, in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, it is written:
"'I experience' means 'I know'; having received it with the mind, I experience pleasure; the intended meaning is not that 'I am pained by reason of that.'"
It has been stated. Here, however, as in the case of “Dīpaṅkaro lokavidū” and so forth, the meaning is that of knowledge and experiencing.
In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it says: “‘We cause to be known’ means ‘we make known,’ which is to say, ‘we announce’; they also state that its meaning is ‘we experience.
Yet they prefer the former [meaning], because it is a word of announcement. But here—
In passages such as, “O Brahmin, crows are eating the ripe rice-field;
I inform you, O Brahmā, I am unable to prevent it,” it should be understood as having the sense of making an announcement.
"Having informed... it should be set aside" is stated for the purpose of escaping an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Some, however, say it is also for the purpose of avoiding the interruption of the night for one who wishes to resume the observance on that very day and bring forth the dawn.
For one to whom it was not announced in the storeroom, it should be set aside after informing him; for one to whom it was announced, [it should be set aside] again...

There is no duty to announce [the time]; it need only be set down. Since it is stated, "Bhikkhus who are like-minded are dwelling [there]," it should be understood that it is permissible to perform the duties even outside [the monastery], without undertaking the duties in a place where dissimilar persons dwell.

Regarding the phrase "having passed two claps of a stone": this is for the purpose of leaving the vicinity within which the sound of the bhikkhus' recitation and so forth can be heard in the monastery.
It was said, “having descended from the main road,” for the purpose of exceeding the range of hearing of those monks who have set out on the road;
and “by a thicket,” etc., for the purpose of abandoning the range of sight.

By the statement, “he too goes before dawn for some business,” it is shown that even when all the monks have gone outside the monastery after the announcement has been made, there is no fault in traveling with a small group.
This shows that there is no fault of being away from one’s residence because of the purpose of announcing [one’s absence] while living together. Therefore he said, “And this,” and so forth.
It should be announced to all those who have entered within the boundary (upacāra) by one who has not laid down the duties (anikkhittavatta).
Regarding the statement, “This is the exemption for one who has laid down the duties,” therein “one who has laid down the duties” means one who lives apart after having laid down the duties.

The meaning is as follows. Herein, this is the Elder’s intention: for one who has laid aside the duties (*vatta*) and is living in retreat, there is no obligation to announce [everything] to all those who have come within the vicinity;
rather, what has been seen or heard should be announced. Even regarding things not seen or heard, they should be announced if they are within twelve handspans (*dvādasahattha*).
This is the characteristic of one who lives in retreat having laid aside the duties.
“Of the Elder” means of the Elder Mahāpaduma. 238.

“For the purpose of dispelling remorse”: [he reflects] whether among these days spent in probation according to the measure of the days of concealment, there might have been any days associated with the three causes for the interruption of the night; if that were so, then because the days of probation would not be complete...
"Otherwise, one would not be eligible for the *mānatta* penance;

and if there were no eligibility for *mānatta*, even if the *mānatta* were granted, it would be as if it had not been granted at all, and in that case, there would be no purification from the offense committed.
For the purpose of dispelling such anxiety regarding the Vinaya, [the monk] should live on probation for more days by adding one, two, or three days.
Now, one might object: "Since this monk has already completed his probation (*parivāsa*), he ought to request only the trial period (*mānatta*);
why then is it said that he must first undertake the duties (*vatta*) before requesting the *mānatta*? Addressing this objection, it is stated:

"For when this [monk] has undertaken the duties," and so forth. For it is because this monk becomes worthy of the *mānatta* only when the duties have been undertaken, and not when they have not been undertaken.
Thus, the connection is that after having undertaken the duties (*vatta*) for him, the *mānatta* penance is to be requested. Now, one might object:
"In the formal ritual statement (*kammavācā*), it is said only, 'He, having completed his probation, requests the *mānatta* from the Saṅgha';

it is not said, 'having undertaken the duties. So why is it stated that 'only when the duties have been undertaken does he become worthy of the *mānatta*? Addressing this objection, he says: "By one who has laid aside the duties..."

"Because he has completed the probation. Since this bhikkhu has completed the probation while having laid down his duties (*nikkhittavatta*), and not while not having laid them down, the construction is as follows:

because he has completed it while having laid down his duties, this bhikkhu becomes eligible for the *mānatta* penance only when the duties have been formally undertaken (*samādinna*), and not when they have not been undertaken.
For it has been said: "But for one who has not laid down his duties, there is the necessity of undertaking them again..."
There is none. For he becomes eligible for the *mānatta* penance only upon the passing of the day [of his offense] while it was concealed; therefore, the *mānatta* must indeed be granted to him.
“Together with four or five bhikkhus” is said for the purpose of being freed from the fault of wandering with a group smaller than the required number.

Although the phrase “from the enclosure of an enclosed monastery,” and so forth, does not appear in the Canon (*pāḷi*), nevertheless, according to the teachers of the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*)...
It is said that one should act exactly according to the instruction. It is further stated:

"Having observed their presence" means having observed them within the twelve-cubit vicinity (*upacāra*), and having observed that those who have not laid down their formal duties (*vatta*) have arrived within the boundary of the vicinity (*upacārasīmā*), one should ascertain their co-residency and so forth.
It is also stated: "By one laying [the robe] down, it should be laid down after announcing it, provided there is a purpose."
And it is said [in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*]: "But that purpose was not shown. It should be understood that the purpose is to be freed from the dukkaṭa offense for breaking the observance (*vatta*).
"It is not permissible to perform the rehabilitation (*abbhāna*)" means that even if it is performed, it is as if it were not done at all. "By him also, having undertaken the observance..."

Since it is stated, "Having announced [the offense], one should request rehabilitation (*abbhāna*)," it follows that even at the time of undertaking the trial period (*mānatta*) for the purpose of requesting rehabilitation, one must indeed announce it.
Because it was already announced previously during the time of practicing the trial period, it is understood that one should not request rehabilitation without having announced it.
In the same way, it should be understood that at the time of requesting the trial period as well, one must announce it after having undertaken the probation (*parivāsa*).

240. "A monk who has performed the *mānatta* penance is to be rehabilitated (*abbhetabbo*)"—this is stated because there is no distinction between one who has performed the *mānatta* and one who is worthy of rehabilitation.
Otherwise, it would have been said, "one who is worthy of rehabilitation is to be rehabilitated.

Even for one who has undergone a formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), if there is a fellow monk with whom he shares the same status, he is not permitted to fail to inform him by virtue of his own acceptance of the [disciplinary] matter.

The reading is: “But for one who perceives what is not an obstacle as an obstacle while concealing it, it is unconcealed. “Averisabhāga” means sharing the same nature through the state of being free from enmity.
“It is not permitted to disclose [an offense] in the presence of one who has committed a *saṅghādisesa* that is of the same category” is explained right here by way of a relevant digression.
There is no prohibition regarding minor offenses (*lahuka*). In that regard, having disclosed it after a formal motion (*ñatti*),...
It is said that because it is permitted to perform the *uposatha*, it is allowable to disclose a minor offense of the same class (*sabhāga*);

however, it is not allowable to announce a *saṅghādisesa* offense of the same class by means of a formal motion (*ñatti*). Since it is stated, "He shall confess that offense in his presence," this permission applies only to a minor offense;
for it is not possible to confess a *saṅghādisesa* offense in the presence of a single pure person.
It is written: "to perform the act of making amends. Even in minor matters, it is not permissible to disclose what is similar [to the offense].
For that very reason, disclosure by means of a formal motion (*ñatti*) was permitted; otherwise, it would be purposeless.

Disclosure by means of a formal motion was permitted solely for the purpose of demonstrating that mutual confession is permissible, whereas from that point onward it is not. Therefore, in this context...
The phrase beginning with “one who has committed a saṅghādisesa offense of the same class,” and so forth, has been stated;

this meaning is also clarified in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* by the statement: “Up to this point, those two are free from offenses; in their presence, the remaining offenses of the same class should be confessed.
However, it is permissible to perform the Uposatha after announcing the saṅghādisesa offense through a formal motion (*ñatti*). Regarding that motion:
This is the meaning: when he sees a pure bhikkhu, he shall confess it in that person's presence by means of mutual announcement;
once it has been confessed in this way, there is liberation from the offense stated thus: "Bhikkhus, one who is possessed of an offense must not listen to the Pātimokkha;
whoever should listen, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Therefore, whether it be grave...
It is said: "Whether it is light, it is appropriate to disclose it through a formal motion (*ñatti*). One should adopt whichever of these two methods is more suitable. It is written:
"'Name and offense'—the offense incurred through various transgressions is the 'offense'; 'name' refers to the name of that offense.

Regarding the instruction "having announced it, it should be set aside," it should be understood here that the purpose of the announcement is to avoid the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) arising from the breach of the rule of conduct.
“If one who perceives an obstacle as an obstacle conceals it while it actually is an obstacle, it remains unconcealed.

Furthermore, for one who conceals an obstacle—whether perceiving it as an obstacle or not perceiving it as an obstacle—it remains unconcealed. This is another reading. “Free from enmity” means desiring welfare.
“When the dawn has risen” means when the dawn has appeared. “In the presence of one who is pure” means in the presence of one who has not committed a similar *saṅghādisesa* offense.
"Vatthu" (the basis) refers to the transgression consisting of the emission of impurity and so forth. "Sukkavissaṭṭhi" (emission of semen) is both the basis and the class (gotta).

This term "sukkavissaṭṭhi" is the basis because it clarifies the transgression characterized by the emission of impurity; and it is the class because it clarifies the emission of semen itself, which possesses a nature that excludes what is of the same genus and what is of a different genus.

For "gotta" means that which protects (gaṃ tāyati). "Saṅghādisesa" [is explained as follows:]... The translation above reflects the available portion of the text.)*
"Name and offense" refers to the *saṅghādisesa* [offense]: it is called "name" because it reveals the name of the class of offenses incurred through various transgressions;
it is called "offense" because it possesses the essential nature of an offense.

"Of one who is pure" means of one who has not committed a similar *saṅghādisesa* offense, or of one who has emerged from such an offense. "In another" refers to by way of a probationary period (*parivāsa*) following purification.
"Other than the emergence from that offense" means other than the emergence from a particular offense. "Was concealed" (*paṭicchannā*) means it was hidden.
What was it? An offense. "Living while delimited by days and so forth" is *parivāsa*. What is it? The performance of a disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*).
*Parivāsa* for a concealed offense is "concealed *parivāsa*" (*paṭicchannaparivāsa*).
The Discussion on the Concealed Probation is finished.

The Discussion on the Probation for One Who is Pure (Suddhanta-parivāsa). 242. "Pure" (*sujjhana*) means one who is pure (*suddha*). Who is that? It is the disappearance of the offense. It is called "end" (*anto*) because it reaches the state of completion; [thus] he is "pure" (*suddho*).
The end of which probation is the "pure end" (*suddhanta*); that which is both a pure end and a probation is "probation with a pure end" (*suddhantaparivāsa*).
This refers to a probation performed by taking the period of purity as its limit and defining it by the measure of the period of impurity.
The discussion on probation with a pure end is finished.
The Discussion on Probation by Combination (Odhānasamodhānaparivāsakathā) 243.
*Samodhīyate* means "is combined. *Samodhāna* refers to the combining or unifying—by way of value and so forth—of offenses belonging to different times and different bases.

Probation performed after having thus combined them is called "probation by combination" (*samodhānaparivāsa*); this is the grammatical analysis (*viggaha*). In the formal ritual statement (*kammavācā*):
In the passage: “The Saṅgha has sent back the monk so-and-so to the beginning for several unconfessed offenses; it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent;

thus do I understand this,” there is a transformation of case endings (vibhattipariṇāma) from the object of a verbal root meaning "to go" and from the object and recipient of a verbal root meaning "to lead."

Because the prefix *ā-* has been stated in these four instances, and because the root *kassati* preceded by *pati-* has the sense of "leading back," the word "from the root" (*mūlāya*) is the object (*kamma*) here in the phrase "reinstated" (*paṭikassito*).
Therefore, it should be only "reinstated... from the root" (*paṭikassito…pe… mūlāya*), and not "reinstatement from the root" (*mūlāyapaṭikassanā*).
Thinking thus, those skilled in grammar [should understand] "reinstatement" (*paṭikassanā*).
They might say, "This is superior," or they might defame it; however, this should not be said.

One should consider whether this reading is consistent with the rules of grammar (*saddalakkhaṇa*) only among the new readings, but not among the ancient readings handed down from the Canon (*pāḷi*) and the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
For how can this reading be joined to those [ancient readings] in a way that is consistent both with grammatical correctness and with the sense?
The construction to be considered is simply: "and he would be endowed with [these qualities]. This reading is indeed the ancient Pāli text;

therefore, having transformed the term *mūlāyapaṭikassanā* into the instrumental case as an instrument, it should be construed as: "he has been sent back by means of a sending-back to the beginning" (*mūlāyapaṭikassanāya paṭikassito*).
How, then, is it to be known that this is an ancient reading? Because it has come down in the treatise (*pakaraṇa*). For it is said in the *Vimativinodanī*:
“In the Pāḷi, ‘The monk Udāyī was sent back by the Saṅgha for one offense...

[etc] ...this is a sending back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassanā*)’—having transformed this according to its function, it should be construed as: ‘He was sent back by means of the sending back to the beginning.’”

Alternatively, by forming a compound with the subsequent member through the method of non-elided (alutta) compounding—namely, “sending back to the beginning” (*mūlāya paṭikassanā* is *mūlāyapaṭikassanā*)—the construction should be joined as follows:

“The Sangha consents to that sending back to the beginning of the monk so-and-so, who was sent back by the Sangha on account of several unconfessed offenses committed in the interim. For it has been said accordingly:

In that very context, it is also permissible to connect [the phrase] "or rather, the sending back to the beginning is agreeable to the Saṅgha" with the subsequent clause by way of the singular (paccatta-vasena).
Regarding the statement, "By one granting that,

having first sent [the offender] back to the beginning, the probation (parivāsa) should afterwards be granted," here [it refers to] that probation consisting of both the suspension (odhāna) and the concurrent (samodhāna).

The meaning is that, having first sent that bhikkhu back to the beginning (*mūlāya paṭikassitvā*) by means of the tooth [of the offense], and having drawn him back on the day of the beginning, a *samodhāna-parivāsa* (concurrent probation) should be granted for his intervening offense.
How so? As it says in the *Vimativinodanī*: "Regarding the bhikkhu Udāyī, because of one intervening offense...
[omission] ...having sent him back to the beginning"—here, it is because of one intervening offense which served as the cause.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: “Having sent the bhikkhu Udāyī back to the beginning (mūlāya paṭikassitvā), having drawn him back on the day of the original offense (mūladivase), let the Saṅgha grant him a *samodhānaparivāsa* for that intervening offense.
Regarding the statement “he should be dismissed after having been made to confess [the offense] according to the doctrine of the Elder Mahāsumma,” the meaning is:
having made his incurability known to the Saṅgha by that very means, he should be dismissed by way of separating him from the group of those who possess a sense of shame (*lajjīgaṇa*).
The Discussion on the Combination of *Odhāna* and *Samodhāna* Parivāsa is finished.
244. The Discussion on the Combination by Value (*Aggha-samodhāna*):

"Combination by value" (*aggha-samodhāna*) means combination according to value, according to worth, or according to the number of offenses committed; [this applies] when many offenses have been incurred.
Among the offenses, those which have been concealed for a longer time are combined according to their value;

then, based on the calculation of the number of nights [concealed], probation (parivāsa) is granted for the remaining offenses that were concealed for a shorter time. This is called "combination by value" (agghasamodhāna).
"A hundred offenses" refers to a hundred offenses committed on a single day by way of bodily contact and so forth. "One thousand" [refers to a thousand].
“There are a thousand offenses. This should be construed with the phrase “having concealed them for a hundred nights. Regarding this, the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā* states:

“What is called ‘aggregation by value’ (agghasamodhāna) is that which should be assigned when one has committed several offenses on the basis of the same category (*sabhāgavatthu*) and they have been concealed for many nights;
the other [type] is by way of offenses on different bases (*nānāvatthu*). This is the distinction between these two.”
The Discussion on the Combination of Penances is finished.

246. In this Discussion on the Change of Sex: if the female sex-organ of a certain bhikkhu should appear, must he again take preceptors and undergo ordination again? Is it [the same as] bhikkhu-ordination?

When there is a question as to whether the calculation of the rains-residence (vassa) should be made starting from that [previous] point or starting from this one, he says "If... and so forth in order to avoid that [objection].
Anticipating the objection that "if this were the case, that bhikkhunī would have to live right in the midst of the bhikkhus," he says "It is unbecoming" and so forth.
If this were the case, [one must consider] the offenses committed at the time she became a bhikkhu.

Reflecting on the question, "How should this be done?", he said: "Those offenses that lead to confession," and so forth. In this context, "shared" with the bhikkhus by the bhikkhunīs refers to offenses such as acting as a go-between (*sañcaritta*);

"unshared" refers to offenses such as the emission of semen (*sukkavissaṭṭhi*). Granted that, by virtue of the Blessed One’s permission, one who has changed their gender is freed from unshared offenses;
however, when they return again to their original gender...
In order to avoid the suspicion that "an offense might arise again," the words "again, in his natural characteristics" and so forth were stated.
Now, to establish this meaning by means of the canonical text (Pāḷi), he said "And this has been said," etc.

Its meaning should be understood according to the method explained in the commentaries on the first Pārājika; however, since this section consists of a discussion on emerging from a grave offense, that very discussion is now being related here.
247. In this context, "an offense concealed that is common to nuns" refers to an offense such as acting as a go-between (*sañcaritta*);
here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). "To one who is undergoing probation" (*parivasantassa*) is a genitive of disregard.

Only the *mānatta* penance for a half-month must be given; probation (*parivāsa*) need not be granted again, because in her status as a nun she was not subject to probation—this is the intended meaning. *Mānatta*.

*Carantassa* (of one who is practicing) is a genitive used in the sense of disregard; it refers to the practice already established during the six-night *mānatta*, and the *pakkha-mānatta* must be given again.
Therefore he will say, “If [he has] practiced *mānatta*,” and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “when the unwholesome result has been exhausted,” this is said with reference to the disappearance of the male faculty (*purisindriya*). The establishment of the female faculty (*itthindriya*)...
However, it is only wholesome-resultant. For it is said in the Commentary: "Both are lost through unwholesome [states] and regained through wholesome [states].
Only the *mānatta* penance for six nights should be given; neither the *parivāsa* probation nor the *mānatta* penance for a fortnight should be given.
Having said, "But this is the distinction," he spoke the words beginning with "If" in order to show that distinction. There is no granting of probation (*parivāsa*);
rather, only the six-night penance (*mānatta*) is to be granted. Why? Because it was concealed during the time she was a nun.

For an offense concealed during the time one is a monk is subject to probation, but not one concealed during the time one is a nun; this is the distinction between these two cases. [The penance is] the fortnight-long *mānatta*.

“*Carantiyā*” (for one who is practicing) is a term of address used in disregard [of formal status]; the meaning is that she has already practiced the *mānatta* penance for half a month. For he will say later, “*Ciṇṇamānattāya*,” etc.
“For one practicing the six-night *mānatta*,” etc., is exactly according to the method already stated.
This concludes the discussion on the determination of the *parivāsa* probation.
Now, because a *saṅghādisesa* offense is a grave offense that leaves a remainder and is curable, it is like this:
suppose a person afflicted by disease is unable to do anything for his own benefit or happiness;
then a compassionate physician, impelled by compassion, treats him, restores him from his illness, and produces well-being and happiness.
Thus, a person who has committed a *saṅghādisesa* offense is unable to clear the path to heaven and liberation because it constitutes a transgression of the Teacher’s command and acts as an obstacle.
Therefore, the Blessed One, who is possessed of great compassion and whose mind is stirred by great pity,

establishes such a person in the bliss of heaven and liberation after effecting their emergence from the offense through numerous methods— this being the intention of the Blessed One, which those who know his purpose recognize.
The masters of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*), having elucidated the meaning of the Blessed One’s word through numerous reasons, provide a method for those desiring purification;

likewise do the masters of the sub-commentaries (*ṭīkācariya*) and others. When such a method has been provided, the wise, being able to attend to it with wise reflection (*yoniso manasikāra*), practice according to the instruction;
those who are unable, however, grasp the meaning otherwise and do not practice according to the instruction.
As they practice, their disciples and others follow in their footsteps and do the same. Therefore, those who practice according to the instructions—
having reconciled the Blessed One’s words from beginning to end, having properly weighed the words of the commentaries and sub-commentaries,
and having understood the Blessed One’s intention as it truly is— should apply themselves to the task of emerging from grave offenses.

Therefore, when monks come into the presence of a Vinaya-expert with the thought, "We shall effect the rehabilitation from a grave offense," the Vinaya-expert must ask, "What offense have you committed?
When he replies, "I have committed a *saṅghādisesa*," he should ask, "Which *saṅghādisesa*?
and when he replies, "This one named so-and-so," [the expert should recognize] the volition of desire to emit semen in the case of an emission of semen (*sukkavissaṭṭhi*).

The three factors are: the preparatory effort, and the emission. The five factors for bodily contact are: a human female, the perception of her as a female, lust for bodily contact, the exertion by means of that lust, and the actual occurrence of grasping the hand or similar acts. The five factors for indecent speech are:

a human female, the perception of her as a female, lust for the delight in indecent speech, the making of a suggestive allusion by means of that lust, and the understanding [of the meaning] at that moment.
There are five factors: a human woman who desires one’s own pleasure; the perception that she is a woman; lust for the service of satisfying one’s own desire;
the speaking of praise because of that lust; and knowing [the matter] at that very moment. These are the five factors. Regarding acting as a go-between:
the fact that those with whom one enters into such mediation are of the human species; their being fit to be spoken to; and the acts of accepting, investigating, and reporting back.

There are five factors: [the hut] being one of those such as "plastered on both sides" (ullitta) in the case of building a hut; the occurrence of the lower measurement; the site not having been designated;

the exceeding of the measurement; it being for one's own use; and its being a dwelling-house—these are the six factors regarding the seven types beginning with "endowed with measurement" (pamāṇayutta).
In the case of building a vihāra, there are those same six factors. Regarding the fault of ill-will, [the factor is] that the person who accuses is one who is fully ordained (upasampanna).

The five factors are: (1) the admission of the charge; (2) the perception that it is pure regarding that [charge]; (3) the groundlessness of the offense with which one accuses by way of view (*diṭṭhi*) and so forth;
(4) the accusation in the presence of the other with the intention of causing them to fall away; and (5) the other’s understanding of it at that very moment.
Regarding a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) belonging to one category, taking up some part or mere semblance of another category: the preceding [factors apply].

There are five [factors] and six factors. Regarding schism in the Saṅgha, there are four factors: striving for a schism, being admonished by means of a formal act (dhammakamma), the conclusion of the formal proclamation (kammavācā), and non-renunciation. Regarding those who follow the schism, there are four factors:
just as there was striving in that case, so here there is following; these are the four factors. Regarding those who are difficult to admonish, just as...
In that case, there are four factors: exerting oneself [to avoid it], and likewise, here, making it something that should not be spoken of.
Regarding the factors for one who corrupts a family, just as there was exertion in that case, so here there are four factors:
bringing about [the offense] through consent and so forth. Having thus cleared these factors, if there is a fulfillment of all factors, it should be called a *saṅghādisesa*. If not, this is not...

Having said, "It is a *saṅghādisesa* offense, or one of the other offenses such as a *thullaccaya*," he should say, "This is not an offense leading to rehabilitation; this is an offense leading to confession.
Therefore, confess it in the presence of a suitable monk," and thus cause her to confess.
However, if the shadow of a non-offense appears, he should say, "It is no offense," and dismiss her. But if the shadow of a *saṅghādisesa* offense appears...
If it is evident, one should ask, "Having committed this offense, did you conceal it or not?
When he replies, "I did not conceal it," he should be told, "In that case, you are not eligible for *parivāsa*; you are only eligible for *mānatta*.
But when he replies, "I concealed it," one should ask, "Did you conceal it by means of one of the ten modes, or by some other mode? Having asked this—
When it is said, "by one of ten reasons," it should be stated: "Even so, he is worthy of the *mānatta* penance, not worthy of *parivāsa*.
