Then, if he says, "by another reason," even in that case, one should ask: "Did you conceal [the offense] while knowing its status as an offense, or did you conceal it without knowing?
And when he replies, "I concealed it without knowing its status as an offense," [one should state]: "The status of having committed an offense..."
Having asked, "Did you conceal it intentionally, or did you conceal it having forgotten?
and being told, "I concealed it having forgotten," and having further asked, "Did you conceal it while being uncertain as to whether you had committed an offense, or were you certain?
and being told, "I was uncertain," one should say: "You are not eligible for probation; you are only eligible for the trial period (mānatta)."

Now, when one says, "I conceal it knowing," or when one says, "I conceal it remembering," or when one says, "I conceal it being free from doubt," he should be told, "You are worthy of probation. For this has been stated in the Samuccayakkhandhaka:
"He speaks thus: 'Friends, regarding this offense which was concealed knowingly, the granting of probation for that offense is in accordance with the Dhamma.'"
Because it is in accordance with the Dhamma, it takes root. But that offense, friend, which was concealed unknowingly—for such an offense, the granting of probation is contrary to the Dhamma;
because it is contrary to the Dhamma, it does not take root. Regarding a single offense, friend, a bhikkhu is worthy of the *mānatta* penance.
And he says this: “As for that offense which was concealed while being remembered, the granting of probation for that offense is in accordance with the Dhamma.”
Because it is in accordance with the Dhamma, it takes root. But as for this offense that was concealed while being unrepentant, the granting of probation for that offense is non-Dhamma;
because it is not in accordance with the Dhamma, it does not take root. "Friends, a bhikkhu is worthy of the *mānatta* penance for one offense," and he says:
"Friends, as for this offense that was concealed when free from doubt, it is in accordance with the Dhamma..."
“The granting of probation for an offense is valid because it is in accordance with the Dhamma.
But, friends, as for that offense which was concealed while one was in doubt, the granting of probation for that offense is invalid because it is not in accordance with the Dhamma.
For a single offense, friend, a bhikkhu is worthy of the *mānatta* discipline.”

Having thus made clear his status as one deserving probation (*parivāsāraha*), [the preceptor] reflects: "This monk is deserving of probation; among the three types of probation, which type of probation does he deserve?

Then, having asked, "Monk, how many offenses did you conceal? and having been told, "One offense," or "I concealed two, three, or more than that many offenses," [he asks again]: "For how many days did you conceal the offense?"
Having asked him, if he says, "I conceal it for only one day," or "I conceal it for two days, three days, or more than that," he should be told:
"For as many days as you concealed it, for so many days shall you undergo probation. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"For as many days as a monk knowingly conceals [an offense], for that many days must he undergo probation against his will."

Then, having understood, "This bhikkhu knows the limit of his offense; therefore, he is worthy of probation for what has been concealed," the formal act (kammavācā) appropriate to that should be performed.

And herein, the inquiry regarding the limit of the offense is solely for the purpose of performing the formal act, whereas the inquiry regarding the limit of the nights [is for the purpose of determining the duration of the probation].
However, it serves both that purpose and to demonstrate that [the *suddhanta-parivāsa*] is not suitable for that end.
For it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "That is twofold: the minor *suddhanta* and the major *suddhanta*.
And both of these should be granted to one who does not know, or does not remember, the delimitation of the nights—whether in their entirety or in part—or to one who is in doubt regarding them."
"But whether he knows the limit of his offenses—thinking, 'I have committed this many offenses'—or not, that is no reason," [he said].
Then, the sitting place of that bhikkhu must be known. For there are two kinds of sitting places:
the place where one may sit without having laid aside the duties, and the place where one may sit after having laid aside the duties.

In that regard, in a monastery with few bhikkhus, the interior of the monastery—delimited by the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*)—is the place where one may sit without having laid aside the formal observances (*vatta*) when staying in a location occupied by bhikkhus of like standing.

Beyond the precinct boundary, having descended from the main road, a place concealed by thickets or mounds is the place where one must sit after having laid aside the formal observances. For it has been said:

In the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "If there is a monastery with few monks where like-minded monks reside, one should perform the delimitation of the night right there in the monastery without setting aside the duties (*vatta*).

If it is not possible to clear [the area], then having set aside the duties according to the method already stated, at the time of dawn, together with one monk, one should enter the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*) according to the method stated in the commentary on the *mānatta*."

“Having passed by the main road, having gone off into a secluded place, and having sat down, one should undertake the duties in the manner already described even before dawn, and then announce the probation (*parivāsa*) to that bhikkhu. And [as stated] in the commentary on the *mānatta*:
“If it is a monastery with few bhikkhus, and like-minded bhikkhus are residing there, one should do so without relinquishing the duties.”
The nights should be counted within the monastery itself. If it is not possible to clear [the count], then having laid down the duties in the manner already described,
at the time of dawn, together with four or five bhikkhus, one should go beyond two *leḍḍupāta*s from the enclosure of an enclosed monastery,
or from the place where an enclosure would be required for an unenclosed one, and having stepped off from the main road—
This was said with reference to the statement: "One should sit in a place concealed by a thicket or a fence.
In that context, "the monastery has few monks" means that in a monastery where there are many monks, various monks are departing and various monks are arriving;
therefore, because it is difficult to clear up the causes for the interruption of the night-vow or the breaking of the observance, [one should sit in such a place].

It has been said. For it will be stated later: "Then it is not possible to clear [the offense]. "Like-minded bhikkhus are residing" was said because one who wishes to announce the conduct while reporting it in the presence of hostile, unlike-minded bhikkhus intends to make it known; therefore it was said. For it is stated in the Commentary:
"Therefore, it should be reported in the presence of one who is like-minded and free from enmity. But as for one who is unlike-minded, having heard [it]..."

"Even in the presence of such a preceptor, one should not report [the matter]," it is therefore to be understood that it is permissible to perform [the duties] outside [the monastery], without undertaking the formal conduct (*vatta*) in a residence where those of a different class dwell.
"In the monastery itself" means within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*). For he will say: "But if it is not possible... having crossed the precinct boundary."
"The taking up of the nights must be performed" means that the counting of nights must be carried out; for it is said in the *Mānatta-vaṇṇanā*: "The nights are to be counted.

Now, "if it is not possible to purify [the offense]" means that, either because the monastery has many monks or because it is a dwelling place for those of a different class, one is unable to purify even the causes for breaking the night-interruption or the duties. "Having laid down the duty" means...
Having set aside the duties of probation (*parivāsavatta*). "At the time of dawn" (*paccūsasamaye*) means during the final watch of the night, prior to the rising of the sun.
For it will be said: "Before dawn, having undertaken the duties in the manner described, the probation of that bhikkhu must be announced.
"Together with one bhikkhu" means [he should stay] without [another], for the purpose of being released from the interruption of the night caused by living apart (*vippavāsa*).

This was stated for the purpose of releasing one from the breach of the duties defined as going from a residence with monks to a non-residence without monks while being a regular (pakatatta) monk. For it has been said:
"Monks, a monk who is on probation must not go from a residence with monks to a non-residence without monks, except in the company of a regular monk or except in the event of obstacles."

"By the method stated in the commentary on the *mānatta* [penance]" means by the method stated thus: "having passed two *leḍḍu*-throws beyond the enclosure of an enclosed monastery, or beyond the place suitable for an enclosure in the case of an unenclosed one. If this is so, this presentation of the method is inconsistent;
for the *upacāra-sīmā* (proximate boundary) exists only at the enclosure itself or the place suitable for an enclosure. Why, then, is it [stated] there...?

In that [previous] case, it was stated as "crossing over two *leḍḍupāta*s from the boundary of the precincts" (*upacārasīma*); however, here it is stated as "crossing over the boundary of the precincts" itself. This is true;
nevertheless, because the sound of monks reciting and so forth can still be heard within the monastery, crossing over a very great distance was stated there.
But here, even the mere act of crossing beyond the boundary of the precincts is considered "crossing," and thus it is stated accordingly. This is the opinion of those who know the Buddha’s teaching.
For this is what the Aṭṭhakathācariyas [have said]. Thus it is stated in the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā:

"Although the passage beginning 'the enclosure of an enclosed monastery' does not exist in the Pāḷi, it is nevertheless stated that one should proceed exactly in that manner according to the word of the Aṭṭhakathācariyas."

In the commentary on the *mānatta*, the phrase "together with four or five bhikkhus" is stated for the purpose of releasing one from the interruption of the night caused by wandering with a group smaller than that.
The phrase "having passed two *leḍḍupāta*s," etc., is stated for the purpose of relinquishing the range of hearing and the range of sight of other bhikkhus.

For this very reason, the commentator of the *ṭīkā* said: "The phrase 'having passed two *leḍḍupāta*s' is intended to relinquish the range of hearing the sound of recitation and so forth of the bhikkhus in the monastery."
It is said: “‘Having stepped down from the main road’—this is for the purpose of relinquishing the range of hearing for monks who have set out on the path;

‘or by a thicket,’ etc., is for the purpose of relinquishing the range of sight. Therefore, the two types of places mentioned above are suitable as sitting places for monks who are practicing the *mānatta* penance while residing there. And among those, if [the residence] is within the monastery itself...
Having sat down, he remains there; it must be announced to all the bhikkhus who have entered the precinct boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*).

If he is outside the precinct boundary, it must be announced to those who have seen his form or heard his voice. It must certainly be announced even to those within twelve *hattha* [of distance] whom he has neither seen nor heard.
For it is said in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*: "For one who remains having set aside his duties, [it is to be announced] to those who have entered the precinct boundary..."

"There is no requirement to report everything; one should report what has been seen and heard. One should also report what has not been seen or heard if it is within twelve handspans [of the boundary].
This is stated to be the characteristic for one who dwells having set aside this duty.
Furthermore, for one who dwells without having set aside this duty, [the rule applies] only to the enclosure of the night within the monastery."

This is stated because it is mentioned in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that for one who has deposited [the bowl] and is staying [there], the undertaking of the duties (*vattasamādāna*) occurs once one has crossed the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*).
Now, for those standing inside the boundary (*sīmā*), the entire precinct constitutes the precinct; however, for those standing outside the precinct, it is merely twelve cubits (*dvādasahattha*).
For this very reason, if the community’s acquisitions, such as meals for recitation (*uddesabhatta*), are [received] inside the boundary...

It arises; it belongs to the Saṅgha residing within the boundary (*sīma*). If [the bowl] is outside the boundary, it belongs to those monks who have received it within twelve cubits (*dvādasahattha*);
therefore, this meaning is understood even by way of the precinct (*upacāra*). For thus it is said in the Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā:
"Having observed the presence means having observed [it] within the precinct of twelve cubits; for those who have not relinquished their duty, [it belongs to] the precinct-boundary (*upacārasīmā*)."
It is stated: "Having observed their state of arrival, their communal living and so forth should be understood.
Thus, for those who dwell in the vicinity while maintaining their observances (*vatta*), it is dwelling within the monastery itself;

whereas for those who dwell in the vicinity while having abandoned their observances, it is dwelling beyond two *leḍḍu-pāta* (the distance of two stone-throw) from the monastery—so it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā* and other commentaries.
Because it has come down in the treatises (*pakaraṇa*), the method of the Tathāgata is known as the "method found in the treatises. Now, however,
teachers [have adopted this] because it is extremely difficult to avoid the fault of breaking the observance of the night for one who has not laid aside his duties,

and because it is troublesome for one who has laid aside his duties to go outside the boundary (*sīma*) every day at dawn, and because there is the possibility of encountering dangers such as wild beasts and reptiles.
While attending solely to the perfection of the characteristics by way of avoiding the breaking of the night and the violation of the duties,
even those who have been assigned the duties perform both the probationary residence (*parivāsa*) and the penance (*mānatta*) within the monastery itself.
Some teachers [recommend] a dwelling hall for regular monks (*pakatatta*) in a suitable place outside the boundary of the precincts (*upacārasīma*).
Having had a bed prepared for the bhikkhus undergoing probation, and having had it constructed with a roof covering it on all sides, enclosed, provided with door-fastenings, and well-secured,
and having had that area surrounded by a fence, one should go there at evening time,
have the attendant novices and others turn back, and [enter] during either the first watch or the middle watch, when the sound has ceased from all around.
Having had the regular bhikkhus lie down in the hall, and having had the probationer bhikkhus undertake the duties and announce them, [the teacher] has them lie down on their respective couches;
then, at the time of the last watch of the night, he has them rise, and when dawn has arisen, he has them announce it and causes them to conclude the duties.
This method is called the "Teacher’s Method" because it is not found in the formal treatises (pakaraṇa) but was composed according to the opinion of the teachers.
This method, although not explicitly set forth in the texts according to the literal word, is nonetheless beautiful and praiseworthy when it is investigated by those who are modest,

gentle, learned, desirous of training, and knowledgeable in the Vinaya, as they avoid the faults regarding the breaking of the night and the distinctions of the duties in accordance with the sequence of the texts.
Therefore, it is appropriate to call it the "method of conformity" (*anulomanaya*).
But is it not the case that the Commentary states that only those who have not relinquished their duties may dwell within the monastery?

Then why do those who have relinquished their duties also dwell there? True; however, because there are few monks there, and because it is a dwelling place for monks of similar standing, they are able to avoid the faults of interrupting the night-vow or breaking the duties; therefore, throughout the entire day and night...
It has been stated that one may reside [in a monastery] without relinquishing the duties; however, here, because it is impossible to do so in that manner,

the teachers— considering that one who relinquishes the duties during the day and undertakes them at night is able to avoid faults such as the interruption of the observance (ratticcheda) due to the non-arrival of incoming monks and the occurrence of a break in the continuity of the recitation (saddachijjana)— deem this to be entirely consistent with that [practice].
It should be understood that they act in this way.

Let it be so; for those dwelling within the outer boundary (bahi-upacāra-sīmā), the Commentary states only that they sit in a concealed place, and not that they perform the distribution of voting tickets (sālākamma) or the preparation of couches (mañca) and so forth. If so, why do they perform these [other] acts? True.

Nevertheless, the formal distribution of voting tickets (*sālākaraṇa*) by those monks in their natural state (*pakatatta*) is for the purpose of avoiding the faults of breaking the night’s stay and violating the rules of conduct for monks under probation (*pārivāsika*) when separated from monks in their natural state;
this accords with the textual passage stating: "Upāli, there are three ways in which the night of a monk under probation is broken: staying together, being separated, and failing to announce.
The preparation of beds is for the purpose of avoiding the fault of breaking the night’s stay and violating the rules of conduct while staying together.
This accords with both the previously cited passage and the textual reading stated thus: "Monks, a monk who is on probation must not live under the same roof as a regular monk in an inhabited area;
he must not live under the same roof as a regular monk in a non-inhabited area;
he must not live under the same roof as a regular monk, whether in an inhabited or a non-inhabited area. By the word "etcetera," [it refers to] the evening time.

It includes going and so forth. Although in the commentary (aṭṭhakathā) only going at dawn is mentioned among these, going in the evening is for the purpose of dispelling dangers because the night journey is full of many risks;
thus, the statement that "one must indeed go for the sake of being released from obstacles" accords with the reading of the commentary.
[It also includes] causing the attendant novice monks and others to turn back.
This is for the purpose of removing the suspicion that one might share a sleeping place with one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*);
it accords with the wording of the *Mātikā* which states: "Whatever monk should share a sleeping place with one who is not fully ordained, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

Having had the regular monks (*pakatatta-bhikkhus*) lie down in the hall during the first watch or the middle watch—at a time when the sound [of voices] is cut off from all sides—for the sake of the monks undergoing probation (*pārivāsika-bhikkhus*).

The undertaking of the duties (*vatta*) is for the purpose of avoiding the hearing of the voices of other bhikkhus; that is for the purpose of avoiding the fault of not reporting [the time] and the fault of the breaking of the night.
This conforms to the reading regarding the breaking of the night as previously stated.
But surely, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, the undertaking of the duties is said to occur only before dawn; so why [does it say], "during the first watch and the middle watch"?

Is it stated thus? This is not a fault; for from the rising of the dawn yesterday until the rising of the dawn today constitutes one night-and-day, and that which is within the rising of the dawn today is called "inside" (anto).
From the rising of the dawn today onwards, the subsequent time is called "outside" (bahi) the dawn.

Therefore, even the undertaking of the duties performed during the first and middle watches of the night is indeed considered "done within the dawn," because it was done prior to the breaking of the dawn.

If one were to lie down without having undertaken the duties (*vatta*), then due to falling asleep, one might fail to perceive the time of sunrise and thus exceed the period for undertaking the duties.
Therefore, it is proper according to the tradition to lie down only after first undertaking the duties;
this also accords with the reading of the Commentary which states: "Having undertaken the duties in the manner described, before dawn itself."

"Let it be so; even though this is the case, why is it said 'having caused [the other] to announce' (*ārocāpetvā*)? Is it not true that the duty was already announced at the very moment it was undertaken within the boundary of the hall (*māḷakasīmā*)?
True, it was announced. However, this bhikkhu had set aside his daytime duties and was sitting down;
now he has undertaken them again. Therefore, although it was announced within the boundary of the hall, it must be announced once more. This too [is to be done] "before dawn."
The reading conforms to the statement: “Having undertaken the duties in the manner already described, the probation of that bhikkhu should be announced.
Now, why was it said, “having had them lie down on their respective couches”?

For surely, even if they were lying on each other’s couches, would they not—by lying outside the *pakatattasālā* (the hall of regular members) and beyond the place where water falls from the roof—be subject to the fault of severing the bond of co-residence?

"Is it only with those who have been released from probation? No, it should not be viewed in this way. For it is not only when one who is on probation (*pārivāsika*) lies down under the same roof as bhikkhus who are in good standing (*pakatatta*) that the interruption of the night of co-residence (*sahavāsa-ratti-ccheda*) occurs; rather, it also occurs between two persons who are both on probation themselves.
And this has been stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "If two who are on probation were to live together, they would [each] regard the other's transgression..."
“Having understood [this], they might become disrespectful or remorseful, or they might commit a more serious offense, or they might fall away from the faith;

therefore, sleeping together with them is prohibited in every respect. Regarding the statement, “Having woken them up during the last watch of the night and having had the dawn announced, they cause the duties (vatta) to be relinquished”:
here, the relinquishing of the duties occurs even before the dawn has actually risen.
If an interruption of the night occurs while [the observance] is being performed, that night does not count toward the tally;
therefore, one should consult the determination regarding the dawn discussed in the first section and ensure the state of sunrise is properly understood. It is said:
"Having had it announced, one should have the duty (vatta) relinquished. Why has it been announced? Is it not already at the very time of undertaking [the observance]?

"Is it announced? "It is true. Nevertheless, at the time of undertaking the duties of one on probation (*pārivāsika-vatta*), when some monks who have been announced depart at the time of the formal depositing [of the bowl and robes] and others arrive, there may thus be a shifting of the assembly (*parisā-saṅkamana*).
And that being the case, since there is the presence of newly arrived [monks], it must be announced; however, if there is no newly arrived monk, [it need not be].
There is no duty to announce [the offense]. Even so, because there is no fault in announcing it, a further announcement is rendered appropriate.
However, during the period of practicing the *mānatta* penance, even though the undertaking has already been announced, it must certainly be announced again when the penance is relinquished.
Why? Because it occurs on a different day. For it is said: "It should be announced every day. Even so, at the time of the evening undertaking—
If it is argued that there is no need for the duty of announcing when the bowl is set down because he will announce it [later], we say no.
At the time of undertaking the practice, those monks may come or they may not come; how could he possibly announce it to those who have not arrived?
Furthermore, if it were not announced, the night would be cut short. Therefore, on that day, once the dawn has risen, from the moment the bowl is set down...
It is our opinion that one should not report [a matter] immediately; rather, it should be grasped after having investigated it more thoroughly.

Thus, by means of the method found in the treatises or the method of teachers who follow the treatises, a Vinaya-expert—one who is learned, possessed of shame and gentleness, and a bearer of the Vinaya—establishing the command of the Perfectly Enlightened One for the sake of those gentle monks who desire purity, [should act].

Having thoroughly investigated for the sake of purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*), the rules for the probationer (*parivāsa*) and the duties of the one acting under instruction (*ānattacarana*) should be explained.
At this point, in order to provide skillful guidance regarding the discourse on probation and so forth for conscientious monks, the method of various opinions is stated:
some monks say that when constructing a hall for regular monks (*pakatatta-sāla*), one should designate a pillar in the middle of that hall as the boundary marker (*nimitta*).

Then, having marked out a space measuring twelve cubits, it should be prepared in such a way that when the monk who is undergoing probation lies down on his bed as arranged, his neck is above that space.
They say, "When this is done, it is well done," and they do so. Some [say], "The waist of the monk lying on the bed..."
They say and do that "it is above the designated area; when it is made in such a way as it should be designated, it is well-made.
However, that statement is found neither in the Canon nor in the commentaries or sub-commentaries; it is merely their own fabrication.
Their underlying intention might be this: "But one may sit down after leaving a twelve-cubit radius around [the seat]..."
The statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "It is permissible"; the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

"Then, having entered the twelve-fathom precinct, if one goes away while the [other] is still unaware, there is indeed a breaking of the night, but there is no breach of the rule (*vatta*)"; and the statement in the *Ṭīkā*:

"Even for those who have not seen or heard [of the danger], it should be reported to those within the twelve-fathom precinct. [And also: "Even for those who have not seen or heard [of the danger], to those within the twelve-fathom precinct..."
And there is the statement from the *Vajirabuddhi-Ṭīkā*: "It should be reported, 'This is the characteristic of one who dwells having set aside this duty'";
and the statement from the *Vajirabuddhi-Ṭīkā* which says: "'Having observed their presence' means having observed them within the twelve-cubit precinct;
having observed that those who have not set aside their duties have arrived within the precinct boundary, their co-residency and so forth should be understood."
Having observed this and grasped the meaning inappropriately, some maintain that the measurement must be exactly twelve cubits in every respect;

neither less nor more is permitted. Therefore, according to the method already stated, whether it be the neck or the waist of a monk lying down in a space of exactly twelve cubits measured from the central pillar, such being the case, within that space of twelve cubits—
If one is a *pārivāsika* (probationary) bhikkhu, then neither from living together nor from living apart do the faults of interrupting the night or breaking the observance arise.

In this regard, an investigation into what is appropriate and inappropriate should be conducted as follows. Regarding the aforementioned readings, the intended meaning (*adhippāya*) of the first reading is this:
if a regular (*pakatatta*) bhikkhu is sitting on the ground and a *pārivāsika* bhikkhu wishes to sit on a seat, [the following applies].
It is permissible for one to sit having left a twelve-cubit zone of proximity from the place where a regular (pakatatta) bhikkhu is sitting, but not within those twelve cubits.
By this, it is shown that when both are sitting on the ground, it is permissible even within twelve cubits;
however, if one sits outside the area of twelve cubits, it is permissible to sit even on a seat.

Therefore he said: “‘Not sitting on the ground’ means that while the regular monk is sitting on the natural ground, the other [the probationer] must not sit on anything higher, even if it be merely a layer of grass or a sandy surface.
However, it is permissible to sit provided one leaves a twelve-cubit space around him.
Thus, this [passage] indicates the place where the probationer may sit when the regular monk is sitting on the natural ground.
The reading does not indicate the place for laying out the bed or the place for lying down;
having failed to examine that entire passage in its complete sequence from beginning to end, they grasp the meaning improperly based on a mere fragment through mere conjecture.
However, this is the intended meaning of the second passage: having undertaken the formal observance (*vatta*) in a concealed place outside the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīmā*).

When a bhikkhu is seated, if another bhikkhu enters within a twelve-fathom radius of his seat and passes by while that seated bhikkhu is unaware of it, there is a breaking of the night for the bhikkhu undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*), but there is no breach of the formal observance (*vatta*).
Why is there a breaking of the night? Because he has entered the precincts. Why is there no breach of the formal observance?

"Because of not knowing. By this, it is shown that the precinct (*upacāra*) outside the boundary of the monastery grounds (*upacārasīmā*) measures twelve cubits (*dvādasahattha*) and constitutes the field for the announcement.
Therefore he said: "One should sit in a place concealed by a thicket or a fence;
before dawn, having undertaken the observance (*vatta*) according to the method stated, one should make the announcement. If another monk [is present] for some business..."
If he comes to that place, and if the [monk] sees him or hears his voice, it must be reported.
For one who does not report it, there is both a breach of the night and a breach of the duty (*vattabhedo*).

But if, having entered the twelve-cubit vicinity, he goes away while [the other] is still unaware, there is indeed a breach of the night, but there is no breach of the duty. Thus, this reading also illustrates the field for reporting.
It should be understood that it is not merely a lamp for placing the bed and so forth.

However, this is the intended meaning of the third reading: when the question arises whether one should announce [the arrival] only to those monks who have come to the place where the duties are undertaken within the outer boundary (bahi-upacāra-sīmā), and who have seen the forms or heard the sounds, [the answer is that it must be announced] even to those who have neither seen nor heard [them], provided they are within twelve cubits (dvādasahattha).

"It should be announced" means it should be reported. By this, he shows that for those who have neither seen nor heard [the offense], it should be announced only to those within twelve cubits, not to those beyond twelve cubits;

however, for those who have seen or heard [of the offense], it must indeed be announced to those within twelve cubits, as well as to those beyond twelve cubits, and even to those situated in the sky or elsewhere. Therefore he said: "This..."

In this regard, the Elder’s intention is as follows: for one who has laid aside the duties (*vatta*) and is living in retreat, there is no requirement to announce [the offense] to all those who have come within the vicinity;
rather, it should be announced to those who have seen the form or heard the sound. Even for those not seen or heard, it should be announced if they are within twelve *hattha* (cubits).
This is the characteristic of one who lives in retreat having laid aside the duties.
Thus, this reading also indicates the characteristic of what is to be announced, and not the laying out of a bed and so forth.
The intention of the fourth reading is also similar to that of the third reading.
However, the intention of the fifth reading is as follows: regarding the phrase "having observed the state of existence" (*atthibhāvaṃ sallakkhetvā*) in this passage of the commentary...
For monks who have laid down their formal duties (*nikkhittavatta*), having observed the presence of other monks within a twelve-cubit radius of their own sitting place,

and for those who have not laid down their duties, having observed the arrival of other monks within the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*), they should understand [the offense as] "living together" (*sahavāsa*) and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), living apart (*vippavāsa*), failure to inform (*anārocanā*), and wandering with an incomplete group (*ūnegaṇecaraṇa*) are included.
He includes [them]. And because he lived having informed the group and observed the presence of the bhikkhus, therefore—
since the observance was undertaken outside the precinct boundary for those who had relinquished their duties— he,
having observed the presence of other bhikkhus within twelve cubits of his own sitting place as the precinct, [includes] those who have not relinquished their duties within the monastery.
Having entered the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīmā*), one should understand that the causes for breaking the proper conduct (*vatta*) consist of:

[failing to] inform others of the arrival of other bhikkhus, staying apart from those with whom one normally dwells, and wandering about alone in a group (*ūnegaṇecaraṇa*). For it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*):
"And since he lived only after having informed the group and observed the presence of the bhikkhus, there was no fault of wandering alone in a group or of staying apart (*vippavāsa*) for him."

"or not. Thus, this reading indicates only the absence of fault because one has stayed after announcing the duty (*vatta*) even when the regular monks have departed and having observed the presence of other monks; it does not refer to the arrangement of beds and so forth.
Therefore, by grasping the intention of these readings in an improper manner, [the claim] that "the measurement is twelve cubits everywhere" [is refuted].
They wandered about conceiving [notions], and their disciples, sub-disciples, and others, following their example, did exactly the same; thus, that was not the standard.
How so? That which they measured as twelve cubits, having made the pillar in the middle of the hall of regular monks the mark, was not the standard.
For neither co-residence nor separation from the pillar or the hall is prescribed.
Rather, it must be with a regular (pakatatta) bhikkhu. For it is said in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
"In that context, 'living together' refers to living in one place with a regular bhikkhu according to the method beginning with 'under one roof'; 'separation' refers to living alone.
For the placing of a bhikkhu's neck within twelve cubits of that [place] constitutes such [separation].
Or they say it is the placing [of the body] on the hip; that too is not authoritative.

For when a monk is staying outside the boundary of the precincts (*upacārasīmā*), his entire body must be placed within the twelve-cubit precinct of the regular monks (*pakatattabhikkhu*), not merely a single part of it.
Now, their intention might be this: "If the entire body is included within a space of twelve cubits, there would be co-residence;
if it is excluded from that space, there would be separation. Therefore, let half be inside and half be outside.
This arises from wrong knowledge (*micchāñāṇa*). For the fault of co-residence was not stated by means of the twelve-cubit measure; rather—
He [should stay] in a sheltered place with one other. For this was said by the Blessed One in the *Pārivāsikakkhandhaka*:
“Monks, a monk who is on probation must not live in a sheltered residence together with a regular monk; he must not live in an unsheltered residence together with a regular monk;
he must not live in either a sheltered or an unsheltered residence together with a regular monk.”
It is also stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "In 'a dwelling with a single roof-cover,' etc., a 'dwelling' (*āvāsa*) is a resting place constructed for the purpose of residing.
A 'non-dwelling' (*anāvāsa*) is a shrine room (*cetiyaghara*), a Bodhi-tree house, a refuse heap, a woodshed, a water-shed, a privy, or a gateway—such things as these.
By the third word, both of these are included; in any one of these..."
In the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "One who has been suspended (*ukkhitaka*) is not permitted to dwell in a space that is covered by a single roof and delimited by the area where water falls;
however, one on probation (*pārivāsika*) is not permitted [to dwell] within the same residence. In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated:
"[The dwelling] is prohibited by the falling of water without distinction. In the *Kurundi*, it says: "In these many places bound by roofs of five colors..."
It is stated that "for one who is on probation and for one who has been suspended, lying down together with a regular monk (pakatatta) in the same water-pitcher is prohibited.
Therefore, it is not permitted even if they are in different immediate precincts, provided they are under the same roof.

However, if in this case a regular monk who was ordained that very day enters first and lies down, and a probationer—even if he has been on probation for sixty years—enters afterwards and knowingly lies down, [he incurs an offense].

There is both a breach of the night and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for violating the rule; however, for one who does not know, there is only a breach of the night, not the offense of wrong-doing for violating the rule.

But if, after he has first lain down, a regular monk (pakatatta) enters later and lies down, and the one on probation knows [of this], there is both a breach of the night and an offense of wrong-doing for violating the rule. If he does not know, there is only a breach of the night, not [the offense].

Regarding the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to the breaking of the enclosure: therefore, it should be understood that even in a hall or a monastery, as soon as one is released from the point where water falls from the roof-covering, the fault of living together no longer exists.
However, some [hold that] by rotating a wheel with a twelve-cubit length of staff from the middle pillar all around—
They draw a line on the outside; when it is thus drawn, that outer line measures seventy-two cubits from the entrance.
Then, having measured that area with a twelve-cubit measuring-stick and divided it, it consists of exactly six parts.
When one bed is assigned to each of those six parts within the boundary, there are exactly six bed-locations.
Therefore, they say that in a single circular enclosure (*vaṭṭamaṇḍala*), only six monks may reside simultaneously, neither before nor after the others, and not more than that.
But why do they act in this way? Because, according to the method previously stated, it has been taken as the rule that "the measurement everywhere is exactly twelve cubits.
Such, it is said, is their intention: [regarding] one on probation (*pārivāsika*)...
For a regular (pakatatta) bhikkhu, sleeping within twelve cubits of one another constitutes living together;

sleeping outside that distance constitutes living apart—and the same applies to each other. However, for those who act in this manner, even their own intention is not fulfilled, let alone the intention of the Blessed One.
How so? The intention of those [monks] is: "Let the monk who is on probation and the regular monks stand within a space of twelve cubits from one another.
However, when the boundary is being marked by taking the central pillar as the sign, the outer line all around is exactly twelve cubits from the pillar itself, not from the regular monks.
For they stand outside the pillar at a distance of one *ratana*, two *ratanas*, and so forth;
even from the outside, the line itself is only twelve cubits (*hattha*) from the pillar, not the monk lying upon it.
For he is both inside and outside the line by a measure of two *ratanas* or three *ratanas*. Even for each other, the boundary is only six parts, which is twelve cubits for each other.
There is [a bed], but neither a bed designated above that limit nor a monk lying upon it [is considered to be within].
For a bed stands having crossed the boundary by only one *ratana* or two *ratanas*;
likewise, monks while lying down do not lie strictly above the boundary, but lie having either crossed or not reached the boundary by even a span or a *ratana*.
Therefore, those bhikkhus undergoing probation (pārivāsika) do not even reach twelve cubits from regular bhikkhus (pakatatta), nor do they stand at a distance of one another;
they remain less than that. Consequently, their own purpose is not accomplished.

However, the Blessed One’s intention was this: if, because the monastery possesses the requisite factors such as having few bhikkhus and so forth, the formal act of suspension (vatta) is not imposed, [then the probation is valid].
If he remains only within the interior of the monastery, then a regular bhikkhu must not dwell under the same roof.
If he should sleep inside the area where water falls from the roof—whether in such a dwelling or in a non-dwelling—that is called "dwelling together," and there is a breaking of the night;
this meaning is to be made clear by the aforementioned Canon and Commentary.
Two [monks] should not dwell in a residence with a single roof-covering. If they should so dwell, for the senior monk there is only the breaking of the night;

for the junior monk there is both the breaking of the night and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for violating the proper conduct. If they are of equal standing in seniority, for one who does not know [the rule], there is only the breaking of the night;
for one who knows, there is both. This is the meaning: "Upāli, there are three ways in which the night of a monk on probation is broken."

“Living together, living apart, and not announcing [one’s offense]”—and also: “Monks, a monk undergoing probation must not live in a residence under one roof with another monk who is senior to him in standing and is also undergoing probation.
And regarding the phrase “with one senior in standing”: ... for if two monks undergoing probation were to live together, they might learn of each other’s transgressions and become disrespectful.
This should be explained by these passages from the Canon and the Commentary: “Or, having become remorseful, they might commit an even more serious offense or fall away [from the faith];
therefore, sleeping together with them is prohibited in every respect.

Furthermore, even when living apart, one who is on probation (pārivāsika) must not stay in a monastery devoid of monks; nor may he stay in a monastery devoid of monks without a regular monk (pakatatta).
One must not go to that residence; the Blessed One’s intention is that one should sit within the twelve-fathom precinct surrounding the place where monks dwell outside the boundary.
This is the meaning: "Monks, a monk on probation must not [go] from a residence with monks to a residence without monks..."
"One should go [only] with a regular monk (*pakatatta*), except in cases of obstruction," and so forth; "There are three, Upāli...
[omission] ...non-announcement (*anārocanā*)," and "There are four, Upāli, for a monk undergoing the *mānatta* penance that constitute a break in the night:
living together, living apart, non-announcement, and wandering alone in a small group," and "Living apart means staying by oneself alone," and since this...

“Having informed the community and having observed the presence of the monks, he may dwell; thus, for him, there is neither the fault of wandering with an incomplete group nor the fault of being separated from his companions.
And: “‘Having observed their presence’ means having observed them within a twelve-fathom precinct;
it should be understood that co-residence and so forth are established by observing whether they have come within the precinct boundary of those who have not relinquished their duties.”
This should be clarified by the readings from the Pāḷi, the Aṭṭhakathā, and the Vajirabuddhi-Ṭīkā as they have come down to us;
therefore, for one residing within a monastery, there is no separation (vippavāsa) regardless of where one stays within the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā).
Likewise, for one residing outside the precinct boundary, there is no separation provided one stays within twelve cubits (dvādasahattha) of the limit where the monks are seated.

Regarding the phrase "there is no separation": during the period of *parivāsa*, because of the statement "together with one bhikkhu," it is permissible to dwell within a distance of twelve *hattha* (within arm's reach) even when only one bhikkhu is present;

and during the period of practicing *mānatta*, because of the statement "together with four or five bhikkhus," it is likewise permissible to dwell within that same distance even when four or five bhikkhus are present.
It should be understood that there is no "separation" (vippavāsa).

However, from the moment one has undertaken the duty (vatta) and informed those bhikkhus, even if those bhikkhus depart for some business, there is no separation according to the method of the commentary (aṭṭhakathā) as previously stated. Likewise...

For it is said in the *Vimativinodanī*: “By the statement ‘he too goes before dawn for some business,’ it is shown that when the announcement has been made, even if all the bhikkhus have gone outside the monastery, there is neither the fault of wandering in a group smaller than a *gaṇa* nor the fault of being separated from one’s companions, because they are living together due to the announcement.
Therefore he says, ‘And this... and so forth. However, others [say]:

The teachers say: "Even at a place for undertaking duties outside the boundary, the enclosure of the fence must be constructed by regular monks (*pakatatta-bhikkhu*) alone, not by monks subject to legal procedures (*kammāraha-bhikkhu*).
Just as in the world a prison and such are to be built by those who inflict punishment, and not by those who deserve punishment, so it is here.
This [view] is not seen in the *Aṭṭhakathā* and other commentaries; for there is no mention of an enclosure of a fence.
It was made for the purpose of punishment; rather, it was for the purpose of abandoning the range of sight. For thus it is said in the *Sāratthadīpanī*:
"In a place concealed by a thicket or a fence, for the purpose of abandoning the range of sight.
Likewise, in the *Vimativinodanī* as well: "'By a thicket,' and so forth, is for the purpose of abandoning the range of sight. Hereafter—
The granting of the *parivāsa* (probation) and the granting of the *mānatta* (penance) should be understood according to the method explained in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
However, where there is anything to be doubted, we shall explain it for the purpose of dispelling that doubt.
Some monks say thus: "Even though a monk who is on *parivāsa* is senior [in ordination], when the duties (*vatta*) have been undertaken..."
He stands in the position of the youngest. For it is said:
"But where they serve food after having made [the monks] sit down, there the novices should sit down according to seniority, and the monks as the youngest of the Saṅgha.

Therefore, at the time of the announcement and so forth, one should say "I, Venerable Sir," and not "I, friend. In this regard, the following investigation should be made: those who are on probation and so forth...
The monks stand in the position of juniors by virtue of sharing in the limits of beds and the limits of seats, not solely because they have become junior.
For it was said by the Blessed One: “I allow, monks, for monks who are on probation (pārivāsika), five things according to seniority:
the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, the rainy-season robe (vassikasāṭika), the distribution of food (oṇojana), and the meal. And in the Commentary it says: “A regular monk (pakatatta)…”
Regarding the commentary on this passage, “Upon seeing a bhikkhu, one must rise from one’s seat; a bhikkhu of normal status (pakatatta) should be invited to sit”:
the words “must rise” and “should be invited” mean that even upon seeing one who has been ordained on that very day, one must certainly rise;
and having risen, one should not go behind his back thinking, “I was made to rise while sitting comfortably by him,” [but rather say], “This...
"One should invite them thus: 'Teacher, this is the seat; please sit here. In this very passage, the specific form of address "Teacher" (ācariya) is stated, and not elsewhere.

If even one who is senior in age were required to speak only as "Venerable Sir" (bhante), then here too it would have been said, "Venerable Sir, this is the seat"; however, it was not so stated. Therefore, that [specific] address does not apply to them.
This should be understood according to its essential meaning. However, in this section on the compendium of the Vinaya (*Vinayasaṅgahappakaraṇa*), it is stated:
"When announcing [the matter], if the other person is younger, one should say 'Friend' (*āvuso*); if they are older, one should say 'Venerable Sir' (*bhante*).
Furthermore, because it was previously stated [in the text] that "[together] with one bhikkhu," this refers to that bhikkhu who is the recipient and is of normal status (*pakatatta*).
It should be understood that this was said with a specific underlying intention (*sandhāya*).
However, many monks, having seated a monk on probation in the midst of the Saṅgha, having had him request the proper conduct (*vatta*),

and having had him undertake it at the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*), did not have him perform the announcement (*ārocana*) and instead made him depart from the midst of the Saṅgha to the edge of the assembly.
Having had him sit down there and having had him announce [his name], they cause him to relinquish his duties (*vatta*).
And their intention in doing so is this: "This monk, even though he is senior by virtue of his standing, is one who has not yet undertaken his duties;

therefore, at the time of the formal request, at the time of hearing the *kammavācā*, and at the time of undertaking the duties, he is worthy of sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha regarding his duties."
However, having undertaken the *navakattāniya* (the practice of sitting on a new mat), he is therefore not entitled to sit in the midst of the Saṅgha;
because he shares only in the limit of his seat, he is entitled to sit only at the limit of the assembly. This should be considered as follows:
when this bhikkhu sits in the midst of the Saṅgha, he does not sit having taken a seat according to seniority, but rather by virtue of being subject to formal legal acts (*kamma*).
Without taking a seat, he remained sitting in the squatting posture with his hands raised in *añjali*.

Furthermore, one who is subject to formal legal action (*kamma-āraha*) must be placed right in the midst of the Saṅgha and not outside; therefore, it cannot be said at that time that "he is not worthy of sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha.
Moreover, because the acts of requesting leave to depart, announcing the matter, and depositing the requisites have not yet been completed, [he remains within].

Because it would be impossible to maintain the Saṅgha of bhikkhus who are sitting very closely pressed against one another, and because there would be interference by the corners of robes, feet, backs, and so forth, it appears as if an act of disrespect were being shown.
Furthermore, the act of announcing [the offense] and the laying down of the formal act (vattanikkhipana) must be performed right in the midst of the Saṅgha;
one who performs them while sitting at the edge [of the assembly] contradicts the Aṭṭhakathā. For it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā:
“Having undertaken the duty, one must announce it right there to the Saṅgha...
[and so on] ...having announced it, if one wishes to lay it aside, it should be laid aside in the midst of the Saṅgha in the very manner already described. Why?

Because by having the announcement made at the very place where the undertaking occurred, and by having it laid aside right there, he causes the person to depart once all duties have been completed, and makes him sit down in his own seat.
"Obtained in accordance with the rule" is our position.
Likewise, at the time of announcing the observance in the evening, they first cause the most senior among the many *pārivāsikas* to undertake the observance and announce it;
then, in successive order, they cause the youngest to undertake and announce it last of all. At the time of setting aside [the bowl] in the morning...

But having first had the more junior monk announce [the number], they cause it to be set aside; then, in successive order, they have the more senior monks announce until all have been announced last of all. This might be their intention:
when there are ten regular monks and ten monks who are on probation, then, once the more senior one has first undertaken [the counting] and announced it, for him—
The announcement is heard by the remaining nineteen monks for the first [announcement], eighteen for the second, and seventeen for the third;
thus, decreasing in this sequence, the announcement for the very youngest monk is heard by ten regular (pakatatta) monks, because the others are not of regular status.
Then, at the time of the laying down [of the robe], the very youngest monk, having announced it to the ten monks previously announced by himself...
He deposits it; then, in reverse order, the second [monk] deposits it for eleven, and the third for twelve.
Thus, increasing in succession, the eldest of all, having announced it to the nineteen monks previously announced by himself, deposits it.
In this way, the depositing occurs according to the proper sequence. However, when the eldest of all has first deposited it...
Since those nine monks previously announced by himself were not yet included among those who had been assigned at that time, there was no depositing [of the robe] in their presence;
the same applies to the others. However, for some of them it would be too little, and for others too much;
therefore, following the method already stated, it should be deposited gradually, starting from the very first group of novices.
However, in the case of those venerable ones who speak thus, the monks who are *pakatattā* (in good standing) alone must be informed, not those who are *apakatattā* (of bad standing).
The formal act (*vatta*) must be relinquished in the presence of those who have already been informed, not in the presence of those who have not been informed.
But in this way, it is not only the *pakatattā* monks who need to be informed; rather, even those who are *apakatattā* [must be informed], if...
Because it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: "If two pārivāsikas see each other at the place where they have gone, both must inform the other.
Therefore, even if the matter has already been reported previously, one must still report it in the presence of those [monks] and deposit the period;
"if that monk has departed on some business, one should deposit it with whoever one sees first."
Because it is stated, "Having informed him, it should be deposited," therefore there is no fault even if one does not do so [in that specific manner],
since it has been informed to all. Some monks, thinking, "This is an announcement made only to a regular monk (pakatatta)," undertake the duties according to seniority in the evening,
and having announced [their intention], enter their own sleeping quarters to attend to the guarding of the door, the cleaning of the bed, and so forth.

Those who do so do not hear what has been announced to others. Furthermore, some, having themselves announced it in the morning and deposited it, go out for almsround and other purposes without waiting for the announcement or the depositing by others;
for those acting in this way, the mutual announcement among those on probation becomes precarious because there is the possibility that it may not have been heard by some.
Because it is found in the *pakaraṇas*. Not only in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, but also in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā* it is stated:
"If two *pārivāsikas* see each other at the place where they have gone, both must inform one another;
for it is said without distinction that 'it must be informed by the newcomer,' and 'it must be informed to the newcomer.'"
Likewise, some regular bhikkhus, having departed from the hall of the regular bhikkhus in the evening for the purpose of undertaking their duties, go near their respective beds;

while there, by way of moving about restlessly—arranging their own beds, setting out their requisites, and engaging in conversation and talk with one another—they do not hear the announcement of the duties for those on probation, nor do they attend to it. Some [do this] in the morning...

At the time of laying down the formal observances (*vatta-nikkhipana*), even when those monks undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*) are performing the announcement of the observances and the laying down of the observances, they do not hear them because they have fallen asleep.
Since there is the possibility that some among those performing these acts have not heard [the announcement], the announcement of the observances remains risky (*sāsaṅka*).
"Let it be risky; even if there is the possibility that those who hear [it] have not heard [it], for the announcers..."

If it is asked, "What fault is there since the observance (vatta) is fulfilled by the correct announcement?"—even though the observance is fulfilled because the announcers have announced correctly, one would be released only from the dukkaṭa offense for breaking the observance, not from the interruption of the night. For it is said in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
"If, even while making the effort, he is unable to reach [the bhikkhus] or to announce [the time], there is only the interruption of the night, but no dukkaṭa for breaking the observance."
Furthermore, other bhikkhus, having undertaken their duties, lay down at night;
due to the state of sleep, they hear the sound of humans, they hear the sound of drums and the like, and they hear the sound of vehicles such as carts and boats.
Because of that sound, they become apprehensive, thinking, "Is this [noise] from the bhikkhus? For that reason, they imagine there has been a breach of the night-vow. Why? Because: "And this..."
Having heard their sound of parasols, or their coughing, or their sneezing, one knows they have arrived;
having gone [to them], it must be announced. Even if one finds out after they have already departed, one must still follow them and announce it.

For it is said: "For one who is unable to reach them, there is only the breaking of the night [of the observance]; there is no offense of wrong-doing for the breach of the rule. Thus they should be informed.

— "Venerable sirs, do not think thus: this passage was not spoken with reference to those standing outside the formal boundary (*sīmā*), but rather with reference to those standing within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*).
For it is stated in that very same place: 'Even those who, without entering the interior of the monastery, go after having entered the precinct boundary.
Even there, because the status of being a guest (*āgantuka*) is recognized, there is a break in the night (*ratticcheda*); therefore, by the mere hearing of the word 'distant'..."
There is no interruption of the night; one who knows from his very seat, "This is the sound of the monks;
this is the sound of the drums, gongs, and so forth played by the monks; this is the sound of the carts and boats driven by the monks," is indeed one who effects the breaking of the night.
Therefore it was said: "The venerable Elder Karavīkatissa stated that the mere discernment, 'This is a recluse,' is the criterion."
Even seeing a crowd of people walking at a distance during the day, those who speculate, "Are these perhaps monks? and thus imagine it to be a breach of the night-vow, are mistaken;
that too is not a valid reason. Why? Because there is no definitive determination that they are "monks. For it is said in the Commentary:
"Even one traveling by boat on rivers and so forth, or standing on the opposite bank, or traveling through the air, or [those seen] on mountains, plains, in forests, and so forth..."

"Even if seeing a monk standing at a distance, if there is the discernment that 'this is a monk,' one should inform him by going by boat or other means, or by making a loud noise, or by pursuing him quickly. Thus, even upon merely seeing a monk, the very discernment that "this is a monk" is the criterion.
However, in the case of one who is not a monk, it matters whether such a discernment exists or not.
Or what need is there to say more? However, many bhikkhus, being attached to this seeing of forms and hearing of sounds, think:
"If it were morning, those two might occur; therefore, the duties must be laid aside even before the time when people depart or make noise.
Thinking thus, they lay aside the duties while the dawn has not yet risen. That is improper, because it constitutes a breach of the night-period.
But when the holder of the Vinaya is asked, "How many offenses do you have? For how long did you conceal them? For how long have you concealed them?", he replies:
"Venerable sir, I do not know the limit of my offenses; I do not know the limit of the nights; I do not remember the limit of my offenses;
I do not remember the limit of the nights; I am uncertain regarding the limit of my offenses."
When it is said, "He is doubtful at the end of the night," one should recognize that "this bhikkhu is worthy of the *suddhanta-parivāsa*.
Since that too is twofold— namely, the *cūḷa-suddhanta* and the *mahā-suddhanta*— then for the purpose of making known which of these this bhikkhu is worthy of,
one should count either in direct order starting from the date of full ordination (*upasampadā*), or in reverse order starting from the day the [period] was announced.
Or, having asked, "For how long have you been pure by means of confession, disclosure, and so forth?
and being told, "Yes, venerable sir, for this much time I have been pure," [the Sangha] should recognize, "This bhikkhu knows the limit of a certain number of nights;
therefore, he deserves the *cūḷasuddhanta* (minor purification). Having thus determined, they should exclude the period of his purity and establish the limit according to the period of his impurity.
Having performed this, the *cūḷasuddhantaparivāsa* (minor probation) should be granted. This [probation] ascends upwards and descends downwards as well.

However, when questioned either in direct order or in reverse order, if he says, "I do not know, I do not remember, and I am in doubt regarding the entire extent of the night," then [the Saṅgha should consider]: "This bhikkhu [regarding] the entire extent of the night..."

Having understood that "he does not know [the offense], therefore he is worthy of a *mahāsuddhanta* (great purification) probation," one should grant him a *mahāsuddhanta* probation, setting a limit for the period of time from his full ordination (*upasampadā*) down to the undertaking of the proper conduct (*vatta*).

However, the manner of their ascending and descending durations has already been stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). From this point onward, the procedure should also be understood according to the method presented in the Commentary.
Now, however, many bhikkhus, without investigating whether "this one is a minor Suddhantāraha" or "this one is a major Suddhantāraha," [proceed] during the formal act (kammavācā):
"he does not know the limit of the offense, he does not know the limit of the night;
he does not remember the limit of the offense, he does not remember the limit of the night; he is doubtful regarding the limit of the offense, he is doubtful regarding the limit of the night."
Taking only the non-specific statement into account, they think, "Having received the *suddhantaparivāsa* by means of this formal act (*kammavācā*),
and having observed it for either five days or ten days, there is liberation from indefinite offenses that were concealed for an indefinite number of nights";
thus, after observing [the probation] for either five days or ten days, they undertake the *mānatta*.
If they were to beg [for absolution] in this way, those bhikkhus, even if they lived in seclusion for a thousand times, would not be released from the offense. Why?
Because it contradicts both the Canon (Pāḷi) and the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). For it is said in the Canon:
"For as long as he knowingly conceals it, for that long must that bhikkhu live out his probation against his will. By one who has completed his probation..."
“A bhikkhu must undergo the *mānatta* discipline for more than six days.
Once the *mānatta* has been observed, that bhikkhu is to be rehabilitated (*abbheta*) wherever there is a Saṅgha of at least twenty bhikkhus.

Therefore, one who has not completed the probationary period (*parivāsa*) for the number of days the offense was concealed is not called “one deserving *mānatta*”; for one who does not deserve *mānatta*, the granting of *mānatta* is invalid. [Only] when the *mānatta* has been observed...

"He is not worthy of rehabilitation; for one unworthy of rehabilitation, rehabilitation does not take effect; a bhikkhu who has not been rehabilitated is not released from his offense and is not restored to his original status"—this is the Blessed One’s intended meaning here.
In the *Cūḷasuddhanta* commentary, however, it says: "While living together with him [the one undergoing probation], for as long a time as he..."
If it is said, "He knows his purification; having removed that much, he must remain on probation for the remainder, whether one month or two months," or if in the *Mahāsuddhanta* it is stated,
"Having taken that [period], one must count the nights from the day it was committed until the day of full ordination (*upasampadā*) and remain on probation," therefore,
one becomes worthy of the *mānatta* discipline only while remaining on probation for the duration of the concealed nights.
"He does not remain for even five days, ten days, or a full fortnight"—this is the intention of the commentators of the Aṭṭhakathā.

For that very reason, it is improper to grant *suddhanta-parivāsa* (probation from the beginning) to monks who are modest, amiable, and desirous of training, and who dwell having purified their offense at all times through confession, announcement, and so forth; [it is improper] for those who purify their offense through confession, announcement, and so forth...

It should be understood that it is appropriate to give [the robe] to those residing in the countryside and others who have lived there for a long time due to negligence after having failed to resolve [the offense].
Here too, the remaining analysis should be understood according to the method stated in the Aṭṭhakathā.
Furthermore, the Vinaya-holder [should ask]: "Friend, what offense have you committed? For how many nights has it been concealed?"
Being questioned, he said: "Venerable sir, having committed an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa), I concealed it for a full fortnight.

Having requested a fortnight’s probation from the Saṅgha and having been granted that fortnight’s probation by the Saṅgha, while still observing the rules of conduct and not having relinquished them, I committed another offense entailing suspension in the interim and concealed it for five days."

When this was said, [the teacher], having understood: "This bhikkhu deserves a probation that combines [the periods]; he is deserving of three combined probations, including one where the concealment is combined," said:
"In that case, bhikkhu, you deserve to be sent back to the beginning.

Having sent him back to the beginning, and treating the days already spent on probation as if they were not spent, [he imposed the probation] for the five days concealed during the interval for the offense concealed at the root.
Having combined the days, the combination of the periods of concealment (*odhāna-samodhāna*) should be granted.
From this point onward, the statements regarding the combinations of the periods of concealment are to be understood according to the method already explained in the *Pāḷi* and the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Furthermore, when questioned by the holder of the Vinaya: "Venerable sir, I have committed several offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (*saṅghādisesa*),"

When it is said, "There are many offenses concealed for one day... [and so on] ... there are many offenses concealed for ten days," having understood that "this monk is worthy of a combined probation according to the highest value," a combined probation (*samodhānaparivāsa*) should be granted according to the value of those offenses which were concealed for the longest period.
Regarding this, they say: "Those offenses which were concealed for the longest period..."

When it is said, "A simultaneous probation (samodhānaparivāsa) should be granted according to their combined value," if that is so, how is it to be applied in cases such as "concealed for a fortnight" (pakkhappaṭicchanna) or "concealed for a month" (māsappaṭicchanna)? In those cases too, one should say:
"Those offenses which were concealed for a fortnight, and those offenses which were concealed for a month.
If this is so, does it not result in a contradiction with the Canon (Pāḷi)? For in the Canon, [the probation] ends with "concealed for ten days" (dasāhappaṭicchanna).
Is it then the case that only this offense is shown, and not those concealed for a fortnight, a month, and so forth? True;
however, such a presentation in the Pāḷi is merely an illustration of the method (*naya*). For it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā:
"Having said 'concealed for a fortnight' regarding [an offense] concealed for fifteen days, the application (*yojanā*) should be made... and so on up to sixty years."
"Or, having stated 'concealed for more than sixty years' or even more than that, the application [of the rule] should be made.
The Elder Mahāpaduma also said: "This so-called Samuccayakkhandhaka is like the duration of the Buddhas' lives;
as for an offense, whether it be concealed or unconcealed, or concealed for an equal, less, or greater number of years..."

"Or rather, the only authority here is the capacity of the one who holds the Vinaya to compose the *kammavācā*"; therefore, one should not feel remorse regarding the performance of the *kammavācā* for those whose offenses have been concealed for a period of time.
Let it be so; even in this case, when a *kammavācā* has been performed by setting a limit for the concealment of the offense, [the validity of the act] extends beyond that point.

"How can one know that there is no offense? [The answer is: Now, monks who desire training perform the confession, announcement, and settlement of legal issues (desanā-rocana-vikaraṇa) even daily, or on a day-by-day basis such as every second or third day.
Even when they are unable to do so due to being occupied with duties, they do not let the Uposatha day pass by.
Even if it passes because of illness or other such reasons, they recognize the fact that it has passed; therefore, regarding the state of its having passed:
If there were an excess, one should perform the formal act (*kammavācā*) by increasing the duration according to the number of months concealed,

such as those concealed for a fortnight or those concealed for a month; however, since there is no excess beyond that limit, it should be understood that performing the formal act with a limit of a fortnight is in accordance with the proper method.

"Let it be so; nevertheless, regarding what was said—'many offenses concealed for one day... many offenses concealed for a fortnight'—how could I know that these were the very offenses concealed by me in this same sequence?
And since I did not know them, [the rule states]: 'And as for that offense, friend, which was concealed through ignorance...'"
Does this entail: "The granting of probation for that offense is illegitimate; because it is illegitimate, it does not take effect"?
It does not entail this. For in that case, one conceals [the offense] while being unaware of having committed it;

therefore, because the state of "perceiving it as an offense" (āpattisaññitā) mentioned in the phrase "there is an offense and he perceives it as such" is absent, it is indeed unconcealed. Thus, for what is unconcealed...

The granting of probation for an offense is contrary to the Dhamma. However, in this case, if one does not know the duration of the concealment itself—thinking, "I have concealed it for so many nights"—then even while there is such ignorance, the granting of probation is valid.
And for that very reason, in the *suddhantaparivāsa* (probation based on a pure end), [it is said]:
"He does not know the limit of the offense; he does not know the limit of the nights; [he does not know] the limit of the offense..."
"...he does not remember [the offense], he does not remember the limit of the night, he is doubtful regarding the limit of the offense, he is doubtful regarding the limit of the night"—
since it is stated that the granting of *parivāsa* occurs even when there is ignorance, non-remembrance, or doubt concerning the limit of the night, therefore,
even if one does not know the time of concealment as it truly was, [thinking] "many offenses concealed for one day...pe... many..."
In the phrase "offenses concealed for a fortnight," it should be understood that because there is no absence of those [days] not included [in the period], the designation is indeed valid.

Furthermore, they might say: "When it is stated, 'many offenses concealed for one day'... up to ... 'many offenses concealed for a fortnight,' among those days there are both offenses that have been concealed and those that have not."
Are all those offenses—whether unconcealed, whether concealed for a long time, whether concealed for a short time, whether single, or whether numerous—included by this very term?
They are indeed included. No doubt should be entertained here; for it has been said in the Commentary: "But in another case of emergence from an offense..."
This is the characteristic: if one performs a legal act of the Vinaya (vinayakamma) regarding an unconcealed offense as being “concealed,” his offense is cleared.

If one performs a legal act of the Vinaya regarding a concealed offense as being “unconcealed,” it is not cleared. Even for one who treats an offense that was concealed for a short time as having been “concealed for a long time,” it is cleared; [but] for one who treats an offense concealed for a long time...

If one says, “It was concealed not long ago,” the offense is not cleared. Even if one says, “It was many [offenses],” after having committed a single offense, it is cleared because there cannot be “many” without a single one.
However, if one has committed many offenses and says, “I committed one,” it is not cleared. Therefore, by these words, for all concealed offenses—
It should be understood that because they are subsumed under those [offenses], emergence from them is possible.
However, when questioned by a Vinaya-expert, he says: "Venerable sir, I have committed several *saṅghādisesa* offenses:
one emission of semen, one bodily contact, one lewd speech, one act of self-indulgence, and one..."

When it is said: "There is one case of misconduct (sañcaritta), one of building a small hut (kuṭikāra), one of building a large monastery (vihārakāra), one of malicious injury (duṭṭhadosa), one of a legal matter pertaining to something else (aññabhāgiya),
one of causing a schism in the Saṅgha (saṅghabheda), one of siding with those who cause a schism (bhedānuvattaka), one of being difficult to correct (dubbaca),

and one of corrupting families (kuladūsaka)," and it is understood that "this bhikkhu is worthy of a probation (parivāsa) consisting of a combination of these mixed offenses," then the probation is to be granted according to the method handed down in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).
It should be granted. Here it is asked: what is the difference between *agghasamodhāna* (combination by value) and *missakasamodhāna* (combined mixture)?

What is the distinction? It is said: *agghasamodhāna-parivāsa* is granted according to the value of that concealed offense when offenses concealed for a short time are combined with an offense concealed for a long time; whereas *missakasamodhāna-parivāsa*...
Having combined offenses with various bases, the [probation] is granted according to their mixture; this is the distinction between these two.

Alternatively, the masters (ācariyā) say that "valuation by combination" (agghasamodhāna) occurs through the combination of offenses with similar bases, while the other [type] concerns those with dissimilar bases.
For this very reason, the Venerable Master Vajirabuddhi said: "Valuation by combination means [the combination of] offenses with similar bases..."
"For one who has committed many offenses, after setting aside the offense concealed for many nights, [the probation] should be granted;
the other [probation] is by way of the various bases [of the offenses]. This is the distinction between these two.
Now, suppose there are offenses concealed for a long time and offenses not concealed for a long time that belong to different bases.
"For one who is undergoing [the offense], what probation should be granted: a combination by value (*agghasamodhāna*), or a combination of mixed types (*missakasamodhāna*), or both?

What is meant here? If one were to grant a combination by value, he would be restored from offenses of a similar nature that were concealed for a long time as well as those not concealed for a long time—both those concealed for a long time and those not concealed for a long time.

And not for those based on dissimilar matters.
