Furthermore, if one were to grant a combined probation (*missakasamodhāna*), the offender would be restored from the offenses concealed at the same time that are based on dissimilar matters, but not from those concealed at different times or those based on similar matters;
yet if one were to grant both of these simultaneously, there is no such rule in the Canon stating, "Two periods of probation should be granted in a single formal act."

Is it not stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*? It is said: For all these disciplinary acts (*vinayakamma*), such as probation (*parivāsa*) and so forth, it is indeed permissible to perform them by way of the subject matter (*vatthu*), the clan (*gotta*), the name (*nāma*), or the offense (*āpatti*).
In this context, "emission of semen" (*sukkavissaṭṭhi*) is both the subject matter and the clan; "Saṅghādisesa" is both the name and the offense.

In this context, by the expression “emission of semen, bodily contact,” etc., as well as by the expression “of various bases,” both the *vatthu* (the basis) and the *gotta* (the category/type) are included;
and by the expression “an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*)” as well as by the expression “offenses,” both the name and the actual offense are included.
Therefore, when the probation (*parivāsa*) is granted according to the total value [of the offenses], [one says]: “I...”
By the very statement, "Venerable Sir, I have committed several *saṅghādisesa* offenses," etc.,
it should be understood that one is purified from all offenses— whether concealed for a long time or not long concealed, whether they share the same basis (*vatthu*) or have different bases—
because the basis, the clan, the name, and the offense itself have been grasped [in that confession]. For this has been stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*:

"And herein, it is indeed permissible to perform the formal act (*kammavācā*) by joining together—either according to the basis, the clan, the name, or the offense—in the manner previously stated, saying either: 'I have committed offenses entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*) of various bases,' or simply: 'I have committed offenses entailing suspension.
This is the combined mixture. And in this section on the compendium of the Vinaya:
Having said that, [he continued]: "Therefore, we shall not present a separate *kammavācā* here;

for since it is possible to emerge from even those offenses belonging to different bases by means of the very *kammavācā* previously presented as common to all offenses, that same *kammavācā* is sufficient here."
If this is so, and the difference between the two need not be stated by the Elder Ācariya Vajirabuddhi, then why was it stated? [The answer is:

Among the three types of *samodhānaparivāsa* (combined probation), the *odhānasamodhāna* must be granted at the very time of the *odhūnana* (shaking off) for the purpose of a *mūlāyapaṭikassanā* (sending back to the beginning).
However, the *agghasamodhāna* and the *missakasamodhāna* parivāsas must be granted separately. When these have been granted in this manner...
This was stated for the purpose of showing the mere possibility of a distinction within the thought, "What is the difference?
However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, in order to show the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) of formal acts such as probation (*parivāsa*), it says, "Or by way of the basis (*vatthu*)," and so forth;
therefore, by way of that characteristic alone, emergence from offenses is possible even when they share the same basis. And for that very reason, in the Vinaya commentary named *Sāratthadīpanī*:
It should be understood that no distinction is stated in this Vinaya commentary titled *Vimativinodanī*.

If that were so, then even in the case of a combined formal act (*kammavācā*) for mixed offenses, there would be the possibility of rehabilitation from both long-concealed and recently concealed offenses.
For in that case as well, [one might say]: "Venerable sirs, I am guilty of numerous *saṅghādisesa* offenses..."
One might say, "I have committed offenses belonging to various bases," or "one [offense] of emission of semen... up to ... one [offense] of corrupting families.

This being so, since it would be possible to enumerate them by way of their bases, classes, names, and specific offenses—such as saying "many" or "Saṅghādisesa offenses"—would it not then be possible to be rehabilitated from both long-concealed and recently concealed offenses?
But it should not be viewed in this way. For the enumeration of the articles (vatthu) and so forth is for the purpose of including all offenses.
Even when they are included in this manner, because the period of concealment has not been stated, it is not known that "one must undergo probation for such a length of time.
When that is not known, there is no probation according to that measure; and in its absence, there is no emergence from the offense.

This is not possible; therefore, it should be understood that by means of a formal act (*kammavācā*) involving a combined and simultaneous procedure for mixed offenses, restoration from both long-concealed and short-concealed offenses is not possible.
The discussion on the determination of the probation (*parivāsa*) is concluded.
The Discussion on the Determination of the *Mānatta* (Probation).

In the discussion concerning *mānatta*, there are four kinds of *mānatta*: *appaṭicchanna-mānatta* (probation for an unconcealed offense), *paṭicchanna-mānatta* (probation for a concealed offense), *pakkha-mānatta* (fortnightly probation), and *samodhāna-mānatta* (combined probation).
In this regard, a monk who, having committed a *saṅghādisesa* offense...
If one confesses that very day and does not conceal it for even a single night,

then the *mānatta* penance granted to him without first granting *parivāsa* is called "unconcealed *mānatta*. However, if one who has committed an offense does not confess it on that day but conceals it for one night or more through ten modes of concealment,
then *parivāsa* must be granted there according to the number of days concealed.

The *mānatta* given to one who has completed his *parivāsa* is called "concealed *mānatta*. The *mānatta* given for exactly a fortnight to a nun who has committed an offense—whether concealed or unconcealed—is called "fortnightly *mānatta*.
However, when a monk, having completed his *parivāsa* for a concealed offense, [commits another] while still not having fulfilled his duties...

Having committed [an offense], he does not conceal it; having been sent back to the beginning for that, when the days already spent in probation are counted as days not yet spent because of the lack of concealment, the *mānatta* (penance) given without first granting the *samodhānaparivāsa* (probation for simultaneous offenses) is called *samodhānamānatta*.

This same principle applies during the period when he is eligible for *mānatta*, during the period of practicing *mānatta*, and during the period when he is eligible for rehabilitation (*abbhāna*). Among those, there are three types of *mānatta*.
They are not stated here because they are easily understood according to the method explained in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. The *pakkhamānatta* will follow later.

However, as for the *parivāsa* and *mānatta* [penances], because they are unstable for a worldling (*puthujjana*), there is a possibility of them changing depending on whether one is a householder or otherwise;
since it must be suspected regarding whether they should be granted again or not, they are shown in the *Pāḷi* in many ways.
These have been stated in detail. Among them, in order to dispel the doubts of the bhikkhus, he said "If anyone... and so forth, showing a portion of that detail.
Therein, "he goes astray" (*vibbhamati*) means he wanders about having become deformed; the meaning is that he returns to the lower state and becomes a householder.
"He becomes a novice" (*sāmaṇero hoti*) means that having abandoned the status of one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*), he enters the status of a novice (*sāmaṇera*). Therein...
One becomes a householder either by the fact of having committed a *pārājika* offense, or by renouncing the training through such statements as, "Regard me as a householder.
Among these, because one is incapable of receiving ordination again due to the first [case], probation does not take effect again;
however, because one is capable of receiving ordination again due to the second, it is said: "If he is ordained again. As for the other...
By virtue of having committed a *pārājika* offense, one is no longer a novice (*sāmaṇera*). Why? Because the going for refuge and so forth have been destroyed.

For it is said in the *Vimativinodanī*: "Because even for those who are fully ordained, the status of a novice—including the going for refuge and so forth—is destroyed by an offense equal to a *pārājika*, the assignment of lodgings ceases, and it should be understood that they no longer receive gains from the Saṅgha."

However, having become a householder, one must again obtain the mere status of a novice (*sāmaṇera*). Yet, if one has performed a renunciation of the training by saying, “Regard me as a novice,” and so forth, the status of a novice may indeed exist;
and if there is a desire to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) once more after that, the status of a fully ordained monk may also exist.
This applies even after one has performed a renunciation of the training by saying, “Regard me as a householder,” and so forth.
Even though he had returned to the state of a householder, he again went forth as a novice (sāmaṇera) and became a novice.
Since it was possible for him to receive full ordination (upasampadā) once more thereafter, it is said that "he received full ordination again.

Even though their probation (parivāsa) regarding their status as monks was not yet completed, because they had reached the state of householders and novices, the probation did not continue; for the Blessed One has prescribed probation only for those who are fully ordained.

The meaning is "because it has been prescribed. This being so, one might ask: "If he is ordained again, should the probation (*parivāsa*) be granted again? To this he says, "If he is ordained again," and so forth.
The meaning of that is: whether it be that renegade (*vibbhantaka*) or that novice (*sāmaṇera*), he returns to the state of being fully ordained; [regarding] the previous...
The granting of probation given previously when he was a bhikkhu is indeed the granting of probation now.
That probation which was granted previously when he was a bhikkhu is well-granted; it is not ill-granted.
Whatever period has been spent in probation is indeed well-spent; it is not ill-spent. Therefore, the remainder...
"The time must be spent" means this: having previously, during the period of being a bhikkhu,
taken a probation for an offense concealed for a fortnight and having spent only ten days of that probation, one should— having left the order while the probation was still uncompleted,
either as a novice or having been re-ordained— spend the remaining five days of the probation and thus complete it.

The same principle applies to those who are subject to the *mānatta* penance and others. Regarding those who are insane and so forth, it is stated that "the probation (*parivāsa*) does not take effect" because they were unaware of their offense at that time.
Since all three types of suspended monks (*ukkhepaka*) are excluded from the community by virtue of the formal act (*kamma*), there is no co-residence with them;
therefore, it is stated that "the probation of those who have been suspended does not take effect."

"If he is restored again" means that by means of the suspension of the *ukkhepanīyakamma* (act of suspension), he is reintegrated into the state of being a fellow member of the community (*samānasamvāsaka*).
As for the passage beginning "If the female characteristic appears in any bhikkhu," the meaning is easily understood according to the method explained in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
However, as for what was said—"the *mānatta* penance for a fortnight will follow later"—[it refers to the following].
In this regard, it should be understood as follows: *pakkhamānatta* is the *mānatta* penance to be given to a nun.
That, moreover, must be granted for exactly half a month, whether the offense was concealed or unconcealed. For it has been said:
"A nun who has committed a heavy offense (*garudhamma*) must undergo *mānatta* for a fortnight before both Saṅghas. And that [penance] by the nuns...
Having cleared one's own boundary, or if unable to clear the monastery boundary, one should clear the fragmented boundary;
having convened a quorum of four members at the very least, it should be given. If there is a single offense, it is by way of that one;
if there are two, three, or many, whether they share the same basis or have different bases.
Or rather, according to each of those [cases], one should apply the construction by taking whichever one desires from among the basis, the clan, the name, and the offense.
Herein, this is a mere indication of the beginning by way of a single offense:
that nun who has committed it, having approached the community of nuns, having arranged her upper robe over one shoulder, and having bowed at the feet of the senior nuns, should squat down...
Having sat down and extended her hands in reverential salutation, she should speak thus: “Venerable lady, I have committed one offense of going between villages;
venerable lady, I request a half-month *mānatta* penance for that one offense of going between villages.
After she has been made to request this three times, the Saṅgha should be informed by a competent and capable bhikkhunī: “May the Saṅgha listen to me...”
Venerable sirs, this bhikkhunī named so-and-so has committed one offense of going between villages;

she now requests from the Saṅgha a half-month’s *mānatta* discipline for that one offense of going between villages. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant a half-month’s *mānatta* discipline for that one offense of going between villages to the bhikkhunī named so-and-so. This...
The motion: "Let the noble Saṅgha hear me... [as before] ...and for a second time... and for a third time I speak this matter.
Let the noble Saṅgha hear me... [as before] ...let her speak. The Saṅgha has granted the fortnight’s *mānatta* penance to the nun so-and-so for one offense committed within a village boundary.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this."

At the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), having undertaken the observance and announced it to the Saṅgha in the same manner as described in the account of the *mānatta* penance for a bhikkhu,
she who wishes to dwell having laid down that observance must likewise lay it down in the midst of the Saṅgha,
or in the presence of one or two bhikkhunīs when other bhikkhunīs have departed, in the manner already stated. But for another...
Having informed an incoming bhikkhunī, it should be deposited; from the moment of its deposition, it remains in the status of one who is *pakatatta* (in good standing).
However, for a bhikkhunī who has undertaken [the probation] again and is waiting for dawn to rise, it is not permitted to stay in the presence of bhikkhunīs alone.
For it is said: "The *mānatta* penance must be undergone before both Saṅghas. Therefore, by her teachers and preceptors—
Having gone to the monastery, one should speak to a senior elder, a Dhamma-preacher, or a monk who stands on the side of those who provide assistance, saying:
"There is a legal procedure (vinayakamma) to be performed for a certain bhikkhunī; therefore, noble sirs, please send four monks.
It is not permissible for them not to provide assistance; they should say, "We shall send them. [This applies] by means of four regular (pakatatta) bhikkhunīs.

Having taken the bhikkhunī who is undergoing the *mānatta* penance and deposited her within the boundary before sunrise, one should depart from the vicinity of the village (*gāmūpacāra*) by two *leḍḍu-pāta*s, leave the path, and sit in a place concealed by thickets, walls, and so forth;
one must also pass two *leḍḍu-pāta*s beyond the vicinity of the monastery (*vihārūpacāra*). Four regular (*pakatatta*) bhikkhus should also go there, and having arrived—
However, one should not sit in the same place as the bhikkhunīs; rather, having stepped back, one should sit in a place nearby.

In the *Kurundi* and *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "For the sake of self-protection, one should go after taking with one's own party one or two experienced female lay followers (*upāsikā*) from among the bhikkhunīs, or one or two male lay followers (*upāsaka*) from among the bhikkhus. This is also stated in the *Kurundi* itself.
And it is stated that "it is permissible to leave the vicinity of both the nuns' quarters and the monastery," but it is not stated [to leave] "the village.
Now, while the nuns and the monks are thus seated, that nun, having undertaken the observance by saying, "I undertake the *mānatta* penance;
I undertake the duty (*vatta*)," should first announce this to the Saṅgha of nuns as follows:
“Venerable ladies, I committed one offense of going between villages.

I requested from the Saṅgha a half-month’s *mānatta* penance for that one offense of going between villages, and the Saṅgha granted me a half-month’s *mānatta* penance for that one offense of going between villages.
I am now practicing the *mānatta* penance; I am aware of it, venerable ladies. May the Saṅgha remember me as one who is aware.”
Then, having gone into the presence of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he should announce thus: "Venerable sirs, I have committed an offense...
[as before] ...I acknowledge it, venerable sirs; may the Saṅgha remember me as one who acknowledges it.
Here too, it is permissible to announce it in whatever language one knows. Having announced it, he should sit down in the very presence of the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs.
From the time it has been announced, it is permissible for the bhikkhunīs to go.
If there is danger and the bhikkhunīs expect to return to that very place, they must remain there. If another bhikkhu or bhikkhunī comes to that place, she who sees them must inform them.
If she does not inform them, there is both a breach of the night-period and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the violation of the rule.

If she enters the vicinity while still unaware [of the danger] and then departs, there is only a breach of the night-residence rule (*ratticcheda*), but no offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for breaking the duty.

If the nuns wish to go earlier in order to perform their duties toward their preceptors and others, they should leave one nun behind to protect against the offenses of spending the night apart, leaving the group, or crossing the boundary of a village;
when dawn has risen, that nun should deposit her duties in the presence of the one left behind.
By this method, the *mānatta* penance must be observed for fifteen nights in their entirety.
However, one who has not relinquished the formal duties (*anikkhittavatta*) must conduct themselves properly according to the procedure set forth in the *Pārivāsikakkhandhaka*.
This, however, is the distinction: regarding the instruction that "it should be announced to a visitor," as many [monks] as there may be—whether before the meal or after the meal—[must be informed].
If monks or nuns come to that village, it must be announced to everyone.

For one who does not announce it, there is both the violation of the night-period (*ratticcheda*) and the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for breaking the rule. Even if a monk enters the vicinity of that village during the night and departs, the night-period is indeed violated;
however, due to the factor of ignorance, one is exempt from the offense of breaking the rule.
In the *Kurundi* and other [commentaries], however, it is stated: "It should be announced in the same manner as for monks who have not laid aside their duties (*anikkhittavatta*).
This appears more appropriate because the duties of one undergoing probation (*pārivāsika-vatta*) and so forth are delimited by the ritual boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*).
It should be announced on the Uposatha day; it should be announced at the Pavāraṇā ceremony; and it should be announced daily to four monks and four nuns.
It must be announced. If the alms-round for the monks succeeds in that village, they should go right there.
If it does not succeed, they should wander elsewhere and then come back there to show themselves before departing;
or they should make an appointment outside the village, saying, "He will see us at such-and-such a place. By her, the place of appointment—

Having gone there, it should be announced; if she is not seen at the appointed place, having gone to the monastery, it should be announced. It should be announced to all the bhikkhus in the monastery.
If it is not possible to announce it to everyone, one should stand outside the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*) and send forth bhikkhunīs;
it should be announced to the four bhikkhus brought by them. If the monastery is distant or dangerous, [the same procedure applies].
One must go taking both laymen and laywomen with one. However, if she lives alone, she incurs the offense of staying apart during the night;
therefore, a regular bhikkhunī should be appointed and given to her so that they may dwell under one roof.
Having thus practiced the *mānatta* penance without interruption, her restoration (*abbhāna*) is to be performed before a community of twenty bhikkhunīs in the manner already described.

It should be performed thus: "If, while practicing the *mānatta*, she commits an intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*), she should be sent back to the beginning and the *mānatta* for that offense should be granted"—this is stated in the *Kurundi*.
This is what is called the "fortnightly *mānatta*" (*pakkhamānatta*).
Furthermore, although this fortnightly *mānatta* appears in the *Samantapāsādikā* as a Vinaya decision independent of the canonical text (*pāḷimutta*), in this [work]...
This was not raised by the Teacher in the *Vinayasaṅgahappakaraṇa*. However, this may be the Teacher’s intention:
that this probation for a fortnight (*pakkhamānatta*) was prescribed separately by the Blessed One specifically with reference to nuns alone and is not common to monks;
and since at this time the community of nuns does not exist, [it is omitted] for the sake of the brevity of the text.
"This too, and other such matters, should be looked upon with equanimity. Furthermore, even though the community of bhikkhunīs was not present, [they thought]:
"The community of bhikkhus will know the training rules (vatta) that must be undertaken by the bhikkhunīs.
For bhikkhunīs are of a weak nature and timid; they establish the Blessed One’s command and undertake such a training rule that is difficult and hard to accomplish."

Thinking, "They have undertaken [the training]; how much more so, then, should we? and thus reflecting and establishing themselves in the Blessed One’s command, they will undertake the duties such as the *parivāsa* probation;
considering this, even though it was not explicitly mentioned by the Teacher, it has been set forth here in this work, the *Vinayālaṅkāra*.
Therefore, by those monks who carry out the Teacher’s instruction and are endowed with faith, devotion, reverence, and the like toward the Perfectly Enlightened One...
One should train correctly. The sections following this are to be understood according to the method presented in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
The discussion on the determination of the *mānatta* penance is finished. 248.
In the discussion on the duties of one undergoing probation (*pārivāsika-vatta-kathā*), "one who is junior to a probationer" (*navakataraṃ pārivāsikaṃ*) means a probationer who is junior to oneself.

For when a *pārivāsika* (one undergoing probation) sets aside another *pārivāsika* who is junior to himself, all others—even those deserving of sending back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha*), those deserving of the trial period (*mānattāraha*), those undergoing the trial period (*mānattacārika*), and those deserving of rehabilitation (*abbhānāraha*)—remain in the very position of a regular monk (*pakatatta*). Therefore he said:
"even including those deserving of sending back to the beginning, etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [the other categories are included].
He includes those who deserve the *mānatta* penance, those undergoing the *mānatta* penance, and those deserving rehabilitation.
For they [the probationers] stand in the very place of the regular monks (*pakatatta*), and the regular monks stand in the place of those probationers.

"A foot-washing stand" refers to a piece of wood, a plank, or similar object upon which one stands while washing the feet. "Foot-scrubbers" refers to pebbles, gravel, and so forth; with these, one rubs the feet.
"By this" means by foot-stroking with pebbles, gravel, and so forth. For it was said by the Blessed One:
"Monks, I allow three kinds of foot-strokers: pebbles, gravel, and sea-foam.
"Also for one who consents to his co-residents" means for one who consents to the salutation and other services performed by his co-residents. "They perform the duty" refers to this much alone.
Because it has been so stated, it is not permissible for the co-resident disciples (saddhivihārika) and others to perform such acts as prostration toward him.
When he says, "Do not ask me for permission to enter the village," it is permissible to enter the village even without asking permission.

"Whosoever is senior" refers to whichever monk among those undergoing probation (pārivāsika) is senior. "Having consented to one who is junior" refers to one who is junior to the monk undergoing probation.

"To undertake the salutation and so forth. The phrase "when the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* is being performed" refers also to the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* performed by those who have not attended the *saṅgha* on the invitation day (*pavāraṇā-divasa*), such as those whose rains-residence (*vassa*) has been interrupted, when the *saṅgha* is performing the invitation ceremony.
"In that very place" means in the junior position within the *saṅgha*. "One should invite according to one's own *pāḷi*" means according to one's own seniority (*vassa*).
The invitation (pavāraṇā) should be performed according to the sequence of the bowls; however, the meaning is that it is not to be done when all [the monks] have already invited.

"Offering" (oṇojana) means giving away; furthermore, that giving away should be performed for the sake of the following day and so forth only by one who has himself accepted what was brought by the monk on probation (pārivāsika).
If he gives it away without having accepted it himself, he does not obtain [the merit].
It is said. "If he does not take [it] and does not relinquish it" means: if on the previous day he does not take it for himself, or having taken it, does not relinquish it.
"Catussālabhatta" is the meal being served in succession in the dining hall. "Standing within arm's reach" means:
"Standing within the reach of the donor's hand" means, in the sense of being at the place where the receiving is appropriate; this is the intended meaning.
"Even when food is served from a large vessel" means even when food is given after having been placed in large bowls for rice and other such containers.

From here on, the duties of one on probation (*pārivāsika*) should be understood according to the method presented in the Canon (*pāḷi*). However, the meaning therein is easily understood according to the method presented in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Because it is so, we shall speak only regarding the points that are difficult to understand.
Regarding the statement, "A novice (sāmaṇera) should not be attended upon," he says "another," etc., in order to show the two kinds of novices.

Regarding the statement, "Nuns should not be exhorted," [it refers to one] who, even when commanded by one who has received formal authorization, [does not do so] with respect to the heavy rules (garudhamma) or others...

"One does not obtain [the right] to exhort" means that he says, "The responsibility must be undertaken by a capable bhikkhu. The connection is that the bhikkhunīs who have arrived should be addressed.
"Subject to admonition" means one who possesses fault. "The position of seniority should not be given" means the place of preeminence should not be granted.
To the question "What is it?", he says: "By the reciter of the Pātimokkha," and so forth.
“Dust-covered ground” (*rajohatabhūmi*) means that the ground is struck and afflicted by dust; the sense is “ground strewn with dust.

“Requisites” (*paccaya*) is said with reference to the gains belonging to the rainy-season residence (*vassāvāsika*). “Standing on one side” means standing behind the monks, setting aside the formal textual recitation (*pāḷi*).
“He does not obtain a lodging” means he does not obtain it through the allocation by the rainy-season retreat (*vassagga*) because he shares only the limits of the bedding.

It would be so. Since it is stated without distinction that "it should be announced to a newcomer, and it should be announced to a newcomer," if two *pārivāsikas* see each other at the place where they have gone, both must announce [their status] to one another.
Just as there is no further requirement to announce it again to a monk who has arrived at the monastery after having been announced to outside, [so too here].
They say that even for one who has gone to another dwelling, there is no further need to announce [the offense] there if it was already announced previously.
"Without distinction" means without making a distinction between one who is on probation (*pārivāsika*) and one who has been suspended (*ukkhitaka*).

"Obstructed" (*obaddha*) means hindered. "Living together" (*sahavāsa*) refers specifically to lying down with a monk of the aforementioned type; it does not refer to the performance of other postures. The rest here is easy to understand.
“More blameworthy” (*pāpiṭṭhatara*) refers to an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*), stated here by way of its maximum degree.

However, from the perspective of the prohibitions regarding matchmaking (*sañcaritta*) and so forth, offenses such as the emission of semen (*sukkavissaṭṭhi*) are merely worldly transgressions (*lokavajja*). Even among those, offenses such as causing a schism in the Saṅgha (*saṅghabheda*) are indeed more blameworthy. Regarding the term *kamma*:

by the phrase “the formal act of one undergoing probation” (*pārivāsikakammavācā*), the meaning of the word *kammavācā* is also established as “speech that constitutes a formal act” (*kammabhūtā vācā kammavācā*).
It should be understood that [the term] means "accomplished. Regarding the word *savacanīya*, here the prefix *sa-* expresses the sense of "being" (*santi*);
thus, the meaning should be seen as "an action that proceeds by one's own word.
The intention is that one should not perform an action that proceeds by one's own command, such as saying, "Do not depart," or "Come into the presence of those who uphold the Vinaya."
For when someone has spoken thus, it is not permissible to pass by with disregard; the command of the Buddha and the Saṅgha would then be transgressed.
"A ground covered in dust" is a description of a particular leaf-hut (*paṇṇasālā*). "Requisites" refers to the robe for the rainy-season residence (*vassāvāsika-cīvara*).

"He does not obtain a dwelling" means he does not obtain one by means of the distribution according to the length of residence (*vassagga*). "The practice that is never-failing" (*apaṇṇaka-paṭipadā*) is the practice that is not deficient.
Regarding the phrase "even if he exerts himself": here, even one who does not exert himself is included once he has recognized that [the object] is beyond his reach.

"In general" means by way of the commonality of those who are *pārivāsika* (under probation) and *ukkhitaka* (suspended). "In places covered with five kinds of roofing materials" means in places roofed over with five types of coverings.
"Obstructed" (*obaddha*) means bound up with activities such as rising [to meet others], etc.; the meaning is "afflicted. Or, on a couch...
In the phrase "or on a seat," the word *vā* has the sense of inclusion (*samuccaya*).
By this, it is indicated that it is not permissible to sit even on long seats such as wooden planks, leather mats, and so forth.

"There is no offense of wrong-doing for breaking the duty" shows that there is no *dukkaṭa* offense even when one knows that an elder is breaking his duty. "Having caused him to relinquish the duty"—this also refers specifically to the probationary period (*parivāsa*) and so forth.
This was said with specific intent (*sandhāya*), not regarding all other types of formal acts (*kamma*).
They say: "He does not obtain a dwelling because he shares in the limits of the bedding; he also does not receive [the recitation of] the *uddesa* and so forth.

Because of the statement, "Even one who has been ordained that very day is considered a regular member (*pakatatta*)," it is permissible for him to dwell together with those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*). "Of equal years" (*samavassa*)...
By this, he illustrates that for two people lying down one after the other, there is the occurrence of both a breach of the rule and an offense.

"Each his own junior" means a junior such as one on probation (*pārivāsika*) and so forth. Having first received probation in the midst of the Saṅgha and then relinquished the observances, it is permissible for even a single person to again undertake or relinquish them in the presence of another; however, regarding the penance (*mānatta*), it is not permissible to relinquish it.

It is permissible. Some say it should not be undertaken because of the fault of wandering with an incomplete group (*ūnegaṇecaraṇa*). In the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, it is stated in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*: "Just as it is permissible to deposit the first undertaken observance in the presence of one person, so too is it permissible to undertake it.
This is the observance here which is called the "ninety-four observances of one undergoing probation" (*pārivāsikavatta*) in the *Pārivāsikakkhandhaka* of the canonical scriptures (*pāḷi*).
In the *Samantapāsādikā* as well, after providing a commentary on this much of the text, it says: "The discussion on the duties of one undergoing probation (*pārivāsika-vatta-kathā*) is finished.

However, in this work, the *Vinayasaṅgaha*, immediately after the rule "one should not walk up and down while another is walking up and down on the ground" (*na chamāyaṃ caṅkamante caṅkame caṅkamitabbaṃ*), and without including the rules beginning with "If, monks, there is a fourth person who is one undergoing probation" (*pārivāsikacatuttho ce, bhikkhave*), etc., [the author proceeds].

Having taken up the rules first promulgated, beginning with “Monks, a monk who is on probation must not consent [to certain acts],” and having provided a commentary on those rules, the sequence was stated differently as “this is the duty of one on probation.
This does not accord with either the Canon (Pāḷi) or the Commentary; however, this may have been the intention of the Teacher:
—The passages beginning with “If, monks, a fourth [monk] who is on probation... and so forth do not constitute duties to be undertaken by monks on probation;
rather, they are a demonstration of what should and should not be done by the monks performing the formal act (kamma).
Therefore, these should not be included among the duties of one on probation. The passage beginning with “Monks, a monk on probation must not consent... and so forth...

However, these are indeed the duties that must be properly observed by bhikkhus undergoing probation; therefore, it should be understood that these very duties pertaining to probationers are to be inserted here.

Furthermore, we have first shown the meaning of the duties prescribed first according to the sequence found in the Pāḷi, the Aṭṭhakathā, and the Ṭīkā, and subsequently the meaning of the items prescribed later has been stated later.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Ornament of the Discourse on the Determination of Emergence from Grave Offenses," in the *Vinayālaṅkāra*,
which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
33. Discussion on the Determination of Valid and Invalid Acts (Kammākammavinicchayakathā) 249.

Having thus concluded the discussion on the determination of emergence from grave offenses (*garukāpatti*), he now spoke the words beginning with “As for ‘valid and invalid acts’ (*kammākamma*) here,” in order to explain the discussion on the determination of valid and invalid acts.
In that context, it is performed by a concordant Saṅgha (*samaggena saṅghena*).

*Taṃti*-kamma refers to the fourfold legal procedure (*vinayakamma*) beginning with the motion (*apalokana*). The same method applies to the other [term] as well. The prefix *a-* has the sense of "increase" (*vuddhi*);

thus, an action that has not reached increase is *akamma*. *Kamma* and *akamma* are like fault and non-fault (*vajja-avajja*), or like fruit and non-fruit (*phala-aphala*). In this context, *kamma* refers to the two types of procedure: the motion (*apalokana*) and the resolution (*ñatti*). *Akamma*...

The two formal acts consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) and a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*). Alternatively, among these four, "formal act" (*kamma*) refers to a light procedure, while "non-formal act" (*akamma*) refers to a grave procedure.
Regarding "formal act that is a non-formal act" (*kammākamma*), the analysis should be understood as follows—this is the construction.
In this context, the particle *pana* is used in the sense of an alternative position; it refers to the section concerning the analysis of the emergence from grave offenses.
The meaning is: "another section concerning the discussion on the determination of what is a formal act and what is not a formal act should be understood," or "it is by me that this is being stated.
Regarding the phrase "the four formal acts" (*cattāri kammāni*): here, "four" (*cattāri*) is an indication of limitation.

By this, he shows that there are exactly four formal acts of the Vinaya, neither fewer nor more. "Formal acts" (*kammāni*) is an indication of the formal acts thus delimited. These are the "act of notification" (*apalokanakamma*), and so forth.
This is the explanation of the enumeration of the delimited formal acts (*paricchinnakamma*). In this context, *apalokana* means that one is informed (*apalokīyate*) or requested (*āyācīyate*);

the prefix *apa-* combined with the root *lok-* has the sense of requesting, and the suffix *-ana* expresses the abstract state (*bhāva*). An act to be performed by way of such an announcement is an *apalokanakamma*.
It is an act to be performed with the consent of the Saṅgha after having informed the Saṅgha residing within the boundary (*sīmaṭṭhaka*). A motion (*ñatti*) is an act of making known to the Saṅgha.
The meaning is "making known. An act to be performed by means of a motion (*ñatti*) is a *ñattikamma*; it is an act to be performed by a pure motion alone, without an announcement (*anussāvana*).
The second [member] completes the pair; because this act has a motion as its second part, it is a *ñattidutiya*.
Being both that *ñattidutiya* and an act, it is a *ñattidutiyakamma*. [This refers to] one motion and one announcement.
The action to be performed. That which has a motion as its fourth constituent is a "motion-and-fourth" (ñatticatuttha) action;
it is a motion-and-fourth action because this action consists of a motion as its fourth part. It is an action to be performed with one motion and three proclamations.
Thus he will say: "A procedure by way of intimation (apalokanakamma) is that which is carried out after purifying the Saṅgha consisting of those within the boundary," and so forth.

Having thus enumerated the four formal acts (*kamma*), and having asked about the causes of failure for those four acts according to the method presented in the *Kammavagga* of the *Parivāra*, he spoke the following in order to provide the answer: "In how many ways do these four formal acts fail?
They fail in five ways," and so forth. Therein, "from the basis" (*vatthuto*) means from the basis that serves as the cause for the disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*).

"From the motion (*ñatti*) and from the proclamation (*anussāvana*": these two refer specifically to the formal act of the *kammavācā*. "From the boundary (*sīmā*": from the established boundary that serves as the location for performing the formal act.

"From the assembly (*parisā*": from the Saṅgha of officiating members who are eligible to receive the formal act and whose consent is required. Indeed, these five alone are the causes of failure for all disciplinary acts (*vinayakamma*).
Then, in order to explain in detail—according to the method of the Pāḷi—the basis that constitutes a failure of the legal act (*kamma*), he said:
"A legal act that ought to be performed in the presence [of the accused] is performed in their absence; this is an illegal act (*adhamma-kamma*) because it is defective in its basis," and so forth.

Therein, by performing otherwise than these three—namely, that which ought to be performed in the presence, that which ought to be performed with questioning, and that which ought to be performed with admission—a *sativinaya* (settlement by recollection) [is likewise rendered invalid].
The resolution through past insanity, the verdict of further penalty, the act of censure, the act of demotion, the act of banishment, the act of reconciliation,
the act of suspension, sending back to the beginning, the trial period, rehabilitation, and full ordination—
by performing one of these thirteen formal acts upon someone who deserves another; and by performing the observance day ceremony or the invitation ceremony [upon one who is ineligible].
On the first day, by performing the formal act of full ordination for these thirteen types of persons: a eunuch, one living in communion through theft, one who has gone over to another sect,
an animal, a matricide, a patricide, a murderer of an arahant, one who sheds the blood of a Buddha, a schismatic, a defiler of nuns, a hermaphrodite,
and one who has previously committed an offense involving the defeat category, provided he is under twenty years of age.
Thus, these thirty-one actions constitute an illegal action (*adhammakamma*) that is defective in its basis (*vatthuvipanna*).

Ten reasons—five from the motion (*ñatti*) and five from the proclamation (*anussāvana*)—are obtained only within the formal act of recitation (*kammavācā*). Eleven reasons are obtained by way of the authorization of the boundary (*sīmāsammuti*).
Twelve reasons pertain to the assembly (*parisā*), namely those counted as the fourfold, fivefold, tenfold, and twentyfold groups.
In each of the four types of Saṅghas, [the validity of the act] is obtained by way of three kinds of Saṅghas—namely, those consisting of the *kamma-vatthu*, the *chandārahā*, and the *sammukhībhūtā*.

Having thus shown the causes for the failure of the formal act (*kamma*), he further said, "In a formal act to be performed by a quorum of four," and so forth, in order to show the specific designations for the monks seated in the Saṅghas of four members and so on. This is indeed easy to understand.

250. Following that, in order to show briefly the scope of the four types of formal acts (*kamma*), he said: “To how many bases does a *apalokana-kamma* proceed? and so forth. That too is easily understood. 251.
Then, desiring to explain those same formal acts as they function within those bases in detail, he said:
“This, first of all, is the method of the text (*pāḷinaya*). But here follows the exposition (*vinicchayakathā*) starting from the beginning. Regarding that exposition:

In response to the question, "Among the four types of formal acts (kamma), which one is called an act of notification (apalokanakamma)? he said, beginning with "An act of notification," in order to demonstrate it.
Therein, "having cleared the Saṅgha within the boundary" means having cleared the Saṅgha residing within the great boundary known as the "non-separation" (avippavāsa) boundary.
For there is no need to clear the Saṅgha when it has assembled within a broken boundary; rather, [it refers to] that which is reckoned as the non-separation boundary.
However, because a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) is extensive and because it is a dwelling place for many monks, it must be cleared for the sake of achieving unanimity (*samagga*).
Regarding the phrase "having brought the consent (*chanda*) of those entitled to give consent":

this refers to those monks who, having completed a quorum of four or more within that boundary and remaining without leaving hand-contact (*hatthapāsa*), [bring the consent] of other regular monks (*pakatatta-bhikkhu*) who have not come within their hand-contact.
Having brought the consent (chanda). For it is said: "In a formal act (kamma) to be performed by a quorum of four, there are four monks who are regular members (pakatatta) and eligible for the act;
the remainder, being regular members, are entitled to give their consent.

By the approval of the harmonious Saṅgha means that because consent has been brought, all the monks—whether they have come within arm's reach or not—are indeed in harmony; therefore, [it is said] "of the harmonious Saṅgha."

"By means of *anumati* (consent). "Having announced three times" means that without reciting the formal ritual formula (*kammavācā*) beginning with "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs," one announces three times, saying, "It is pleasing to the Saṅgha;
for a second time... for a third time it is pleasing to the Saṅgha. The construction is:

"The formal act (*kamma*) to be performed [in this manner] is called an act of intimation (*apalokanakamma*). "In the very manner stated" means in the very manner stated regarding the act of intimation.
By this, he extends the application of these two points: "having cleared the Saṅgha within the boundary" and "having brought the consent of those entitled to give consent.
The same method applies to the others as well.
In that regard, with reference to the objection—namely, which of the other formal acts (kamma) should be performed by means of the other formal acts—he says:
“*Tatra*,” etc. Let it be so; since this being the case, all formal acts (*kamma*) would have to be performed without distinction as if they were other [types of acts], he says:
“But the *ñattidutiyakamma* (formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation),” and so forth. Herein, the word “but” (*pana*) indicates a specific distinction;
the meaning is that there is indeed a distinction in the *ñattidutiyakamma*. The sections following this are easy to understand. It is precisely excluded in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).

The connection with the *ajjhāhāra* (supplying of words). Having considered the objection that "if this were so, there would be a corruption of the ritual action (*kammakopa*) even when there are omissions of syllables and the like," he says, "But if... and so forth.

In that context, "omission of syllables" refers to the dropping of sounds such as the *su*-kāra, *ṇā*-kāra, or *tu*-kāra in phrases such as "suṇātu me. "Omission of words" refers to the dropping of inflected words such as "suṇātu."
[This refers to] speaking. However, he will explain the phrase "ill-spoken word" later.
Now, showing the purpose of repeating [the action] again and again, he said: "This is a strengthening of an unshakable kamma;
in the case of a shakable kamma, it remains as a kamma. Therein, "this" refers to this action performed repeatedly. "In an unshakable kamma" means...

"In a case that is unshakeable, fit for its purpose, and where the preliminary work has been done" means it becomes a firm action, just as a load that should be tied with one rope is tied with a second, third, and so on.
"In a case that is shakeable" refers to a preliminary action that is defective—such as being deficient in syllables—and thus unfit for its purpose.
"Having become an action, it persists" means that when [the formula] is recited again and again, those [defects]...
Because it has been purified of such faults as missing syllables, it remains as a completely pure action (*parisuddhakamma*).

In the expression "in an unshakable action" (*akuppakamme*) or "in a shakable action" (*kuppakamme*), the locative case is used in the sense of a characteristic defined by its state (*bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇatthe*).

When there exists an earlier performed action that is unshakable, this subsequently repeated action becomes a strengthening action (*daḷhikamma*); [likewise] when the earlier performed action is shakable...
"When this [act] exists, the action that has been performed again and again remains as an unshakable, stable, and perfectly pure act.
Relying on this reading, the excellent teachers perform the *upasampadā* ceremony for even a single person many times.
But why do those monks [do so] for their own teachers and preceptors—who are modest, amiable, learned, and desirous of training?

"Do they take up the training in the presence [of others]? "They do not reject the training they have received from their own preceptors and teachers to take up another; rather, they double or triple it together with that very same training.
"Even so, would they do this only while lacking faith in the previous training, and not while having faith in it? "Not while lacking faith."
Even though those bhikkhus have faith, they perform [the rites] again and again because, through reasoning and through scripture, they do not see any danger but see only the benefit.
How do they see the benefit through reasoning? Just as in the world, people do not see any danger in repeatedly consecrating even a king who has already been consecrated;
rather, by means of the power of the consecration and such reasons as the attainment of royal majesty, they see only the benefit.

Furthermore, they do not see the danger in performing [the consecration] again and again; rather, even while performing the auspicious consecration ceremony for a shrine or an image that has completed its purpose—
reciting such words of the Blessed One as "Through many births in saṃsāra"— they fail to perceive the disadvantage in repetition,
but instead perceive only the benefits such as increased power and majesty, and thus they continue to perform it over and over.

In the same way, when monks—failing to perceive any disadvantage in repeating the formal act (*kammavācā*) for a monk whose higher ordination (*upasampadā*) has already been performed—perform the act again even though one of the five factors such as the subject matter (*vatthu*) of the prior act is incomplete, there arises a failure of the act (*kammakopa*).

Conversely, if the factors are complete in the act now being performed, there arises the perfection of the act (*kammassa sampatti*); and even if the perfection of the act had already occurred previously, [it remains so].
And they perform it while seeing the benefit consisting in its becoming more firm and stable. How do they see the benefit from the perspective of the tradition (*āgama*)?

Because, according to the method of characteristic observation, it is stated in the readings of the aforementioned *Parivāra-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Vinaya-saṅgaha* that for the purpose of purifying a wrongly uttered word, there must be a repeated recitation;
and because of [the mention of] the remaining faults of the formal announcements (*ñatti*) and the faults of the proclamations (*anusāvana*).
The purification of the defects regarding the failure of the site, the failure of the boundary, and the failure of the assembly has also been shown.
For that very reason, this latter reading was also stated by the Teacher; its meaning has already been explained above.
Thus, even though there may be the occurrence of frustration due to actions performed previously, one attains from the tradition the benefit known as success through the action performed now.
It should be understood as "passing by.

However, some teachers say that this reading—"it is permissible to speak again and again"—was stated with reference to the necessity of speaking at the very time of performing the first formal act (*kamma*) for the purpose of correcting what was wrongly uttered, and not with reference to a long period of time. This [is their view].
This statement has not appeared in the *Aṭṭhakathā* nor has it been analyzed in the *Ṭīkā*s and other commentaries;

it is merely their own opinion, and therefore it should not be accepted. Furthermore, even if one speaks repeatedly at that moment, speaking after that time is of great fruit and great benefit. For at that time, by speaking repeatedly, the faults of the motion (*ñatti*) and the proclamation (*anussāvana*) are avoided.
If one speaks well during the final recitation, one may be able to purify [the act] of the defects of failure regarding the site, failure regarding the boundary, and failure regarding the assembly.
For at that moment, it is that very same site, that very same boundary, and that very same assembly; therefore, those defects cannot be purified by repeated speaking.
However, if one performs it at a later time because the person was previously less than twenty years of age, [it can be purified].
Although there was previously a failure of the site, now that he has reached twenty years of age, there is perfection of the site;

although there was previously a failure of the boundary due to the mixing of boundaries and so forth, now, because it has been thoroughly purified to ensure the absence of such faults, there is perfection of the boundary;
and although there was previously a failure of the assembly due to factional proceedings and the like, now, because it has been thoroughly purified to ensure the absence of such faults—

When there is perfection of the assembly, it should be understood that because one is able to perform [the recitation] after having thus purified the five failures and accomplished the five successes,
the recitation at a later time is of great fruit and great benefit, even compared to the repeated recitation at the initial time.
If this were so, would one be young with respect to the training of full ordination (*upasampadā-sikkhā*)? One would not.
Why? Because one is established by that very [training] without having abandoned the ancient training.

Even so, if one stands by virtue of the success of previously performed deeds, one might not be young because of being established by that [success]. However, if the previous deeds have not been successful, now—
If one remains in the state of full ordination (*upasampadā*) by means of the very act of the ritual (*katakamma*), why would one not be a junior (*dahara*)?

Such being the case, one would indeed be a junior. Being thus a junior, by counting the years of the previous training and receiving salutations and so forth according to seniority, would one not be highly blameworthy?
[This refers to] the non-existence of the previous training in relation to the subsequent training.
One who knows the state of having received full ordination (*upasampadā*) as it truly is, and acts accordingly, is blameworthy;
however, one who does not know this, thinking "he remains within the previous training [of the novice]," and acts accordingly, should be understood as blameless. If it is asked how this is known:

"There is no offense for one who perceives a person under twenty years of age as being full [twenty]"; here, although there is no offense for the one performing the ordination, [the fault lies elsewhere].
However, that person remains unordained. But if, after ten years have passed, he ordains another, and by releasing him the quorum for the *gaṇa* is fulfilled, then that [other] is properly ordained.
And as long as he does not know [this], there is neither an obstacle to heaven nor an obstacle to liberation for him.
But having known it, he must be ordained again; thus it is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*.

It is understood thus: because of the failure of the basis (*vatthu*), due to the subversion of the formal act (*kamma-kopa*), it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that for a person who has not been fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) at a time when it was appropriate to become a preceptor (*upajjhāya*), there occurs the state of having become fully ordained through a subsequent ordination.

By this same method, [the same applies] due to the subversion of the boundary (*sīma*), the subversion of the assembly (*parisa*), the subversion of the motion (*ñatti*), and the subversion of the proclamation (*anussāvana*), all resulting from the subversion of the formal act.
Even a person who was previously unordained may, at a later time when they have reached maturity,
be ordained again by performing the formal act of ordination (*upasampadā-kamma-vācā*) after having cleared away the five faults of failure (*vipatti-dosa*).
That person should be understood as one who, although unordained during the time of the previous procedure, becomes ordained during the time of the subsequent procedure.
However, some monks, having renounced their former training, took up a new training;
yet those monks, by virtue of that new training, became as if young again. Acting in this way is exceedingly distinguished in merit:
seeing a monk who is junior to himself, one desires to attend upon that person and wishes to make that person senior to oneself.
One who desires to make oneself young may act out of reverence for the Dhamma; however, if one desires to become endowed with training, one should act in this way.
For that which is called "training" is accomplished only when one is possessed of the five factors, and purity of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*) alone is the cause.
Therefore, if the previous training has not been established, there is no need to renounce it.

She herself has fallen away. While remaining established in the previous training, if one who merely desires to disrobe were to perform the renunciation—not desiring to become a bhikkhu—he would simply make pure the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla).
Therefore, the renunciation of the ancient training appears inappropriate. Having thus renounced the ancient training...
It appears more appropriate to perform the training again and again rather than undertaking new training.

Why? Because when one takes up new training after renouncing previous training, even though the former training—which would have had to be renounced—is no longer present due to the successful completion of the subsequent training, nevertheless, [the fault remains] because of the successful performance of the new training.
There is no fault; even one who has reached youth is indeed suitable.
If both the former act and the latter act are successful, then in that case the renunciation of the former training is purposeless.
Even one established in the latter training is unsuitable because he has reached youth. But if, however—
Only the former action succeeds, not the latter action; this being so, even the ancient training established in the past has fallen through its renunciation.
Furthermore, the subsequent training does not succeed because of the involvement in one of the five failures of the latter action;
therefore, due to both the falling away from the former training and the non-attainment of the subsequent training.
Because it is abandoned on both sides, it is indeed improper.

However, when one undertakes a new training without renouncing the ancient training, even if the former act is completed while the latter act is not yet completed, one remains established in the former training;
likewise, even if the former act is incomplete while the latter act is completed, one is established in the later training.

Thus it is. Even though both the preceding and the subsequent pairs of training rules are complete in five factors, that bhikkhu remains established precisely in the former training, which has become more firm and stable through the subsequent practice.
Therefore, it should be understood that rather than renouncing the former training to take up a new one, it is more appropriate to repeatedly take up the new training without renouncing the former.
However, other teachers, disregarding the doctrine of those teachers who perform this [rite] again and again, speak in many ways with undesirable arguments.
How so? Some elders say: "What do these monks think when they perform it in this way?
Do they think, 'We shall re-establish a monk who has fallen into a *pārājika* offense back into the training'? They...
Seeing the elder monks repeatedly reciting the formal act (*kammavācā*), some elders thought, "For what reason are these monks doing this?
and said this. However, other elders thought, "Why do these monks perform it again and again?
Just as a thunderbolt (*asani*) brings about the end of life for beings with only a single strike, so too [should it be for] the Blessed One's..."

Thinking, "The formal act (kammavācā), being an authoritative command, accomplishes the ritual when recited once, not many times," they said this, even though they were reciting it again and again for the sake of completing the ritual.
However, seeing many monks performing it repeatedly, others spoke thus:
"These monks are acting in this way because they do not trust the training given by their teachers and preceptors."
"These recluses are offenders against the virtues of their teachers and preceptors," they said, thinking that "they are doing it again and again without having faith in the previous training.
However, other elders said, "It should have been stated repeatedly even at the very time of reciting the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma-vācā*)."
"...not at a later time. The reason for this has already been stated below. Others have said:

"It is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that [the motion] must be recited again and again only during the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*), and not during a formal act consisting of a motion and a single proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*);
yet these monks perform it again and again during the ordination formal act (*upasampadakammavācā*), which consists of a motion and three proclamations. This..."
"it does not agree with the commentary," they spoke while taking that [passage] as being of explicit meaning (*nītattha*) alone.
However, according to this method, it shows that among all four types of formal acts (*kamma*), the act must be performed again and again.

For while he specifically mentions the confusion of formal acts regarding the *ñattidutiyakamma*, it should be understood that the necessity of performing it repeatedly applies to all of them. Precisely for that reason, regarding the *ñatticatutthakamma* formula:
The fact that a person who was previously unordained must be ordained later at the very place where [others] were ordained is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of those things to be done by way of questioning, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) here includes those things to be done by way of acknowledgment and so forth. In that context:
"To do what should be done with questioning, yet does it without questioning" means that what ought to be done after having asked, having reproached, and having reminded, he does without asking,

without reproaching, and without reminding. "To do what should be done with admission, yet does it without admission" means that what ought to be done by establishing an admission and acting according to the admission given,
he does so without an admission— by force, against one who has not made an admission and is merely lamenting.
He performs [the act]. "Worthy of a verdict of mindfulness" (*sativinayāraho*) refers to one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), such as the Elder Dabba Mallaputta.

"Worthy of a verdict of past insanity" (*amūḷhavinayāraho*) refers to one who is insane, such as the monk Gagga. "Worthy of a formal act of further penalty" (*tassapāpiyasikākammāraho*) refers to one whose evil is excessive, such as the monk Upavāḷa.
"Worthy of a formal act of censure" (*tajjanīyakammāraho*) refers to one who causes quarrels, such as the eunuch or the monk Lohitaka.
"Of one deserving the act of reconciliation" means of one who repeatedly commits offenses, such as the bhikkhu Seyyasaka.

"Of one deserving the act of banishment" means of one who corrupts families, such as the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasu. "Of one deserving the act of reconciliation with the laity" means of one who corrupts laypeople by birth and so forth, such as the bhikkhu Sudhamma.
"Of one deserving the act of suspension" means of one who [conceals] an offense, such as the bhikkhu Channa.
For one who does not see his offense, who does not confess it, and who does not relinquish wrong view—such as the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha.
"Worthy of probation" means one who has committed a concealed *saṅghādisesa* offense. "Worthy of being sent back to the beginning" means one who has committed an intermediate offense.
"Worthy of the trial period" (*mānatta*) means one who has committed an unconcealed *saṅghādisesa* offense. "Worthy of rehabilitation" means one who has completed the trial period.
"A monk. "He confers full ordination" means he performs the formal act of ordination (*upasampadakamma*).
"He performs the Uposatha on a non-Uposatha day" means he performs the Uposatha on a day that is not the Uposatha day.
A "Uposatha day" refers to a day of reconciliation for a split Saṅgha during the remaining eleven months, excluding the month of Kattika.
And having set aside that threefold Uposatha day— namely, the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and as previously mentioned—
the one who performs the Uposatha on any other day is said to "perform the Uposatha on a non-Uposatha day.
For instance, when those disputing over minor matters such as bowls, robes, and so forth, suspend either the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā, then in that case...
When a legal case has been decided, they are not permitted to perform an *upasatha* for concord in the interim, thinking, "We have become united.
If they were to do so, it would be considered that the *upasatha* was performed on a day when no *upasatha* was due.
"He performs the *pavāraṇā* without a *pavāraṇā* day" means he performs the *pavāraṇā* on a day other than the *pavāraṇā* day. As for the *pavāraṇā* day, it occurs once in the month of Kattika.
Setting aside the day for the reconciliation of a split Saṅgha, the day postponed [for that purpose], and the two full-moon days—
these being the four types of invitation days— if one invites on any other day,
it is called "inviting when there is no [proper] invitation. Here too, when a minor dispute has been settled, one should not perform the invitation for the sake of formal reconciliation.
They obtain [it]. "By those who perform it, the invitation (pavāraṇā) is considered performed even without a formal invitation (appavāraṇāyā)"—this is the reading of the Aṭṭhakathā.
"For a monk who is insane, the authorization for the insane (ummattakasammuti), having been requested by the insane one, may be granted even in his absence;
even if he is not seated there, it is not invalidated because there is no fixed rule [regarding presence]. However, when it is granted in his absence, there is an absence of fault..."
In order to show this, it is said: "What is done in the absence [of the person] is well-done.

However, ordination by messenger cannot be performed in the presence [of the person], because of the possibility of differences in the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*). Actions such as overturning the bowl are permitted even when [the person] has merely been removed from hand-contact.
Regarding "in the presence of the Saṅgha" and so forth: as many monks as are entitled to participate in the formal act must have arrived.
The consent of those entitled to give consent has been obtained; those present do not protest—this is "presence before the Saṅgha" (*saṅghasammukhatā*).

By whatever Dhamma, by whatever Vinaya, and by whatever teaching of the Teacher the Saṅgha performs the formal act—this is "presence of the Dhamma" (*dhammasammukhatā*) and "presence of the Vinaya" (*vinayasammukhatā*).
In this context, "Dhamma" means the factual basis; "Vinaya" means both the formal accusation and the reminder.

The "Teaching of the Teacher" consists of both the perfection of the motion (*ñatti*) and the perfection of the proclamation (*anussāvana*). "Presence before the person" (*puggalasammukhatā*) means the presence of the one before whom the Saṅgha performs the formal act.
Because the month of Kattika is the month of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), it is said, "excluding the month of Kattika.
The phrase "and the day set aside by postponement" refers to the fourteenth or fifteenth day of the dark fortnight.
It is stated [in the *Sāratthadīpanī*]: "The phrase 'two full-moon days' is said with reference to those who have entered the rains retreat at the beginning and at the end.

Regarding the statement, "'Except for the month of Kattika,' he says this because it is not permissible to perform the Uposatha after having released the *sāmaggī-pavāraṇā* (unification invitation) in the month of Kattika when the unity of the Saṅgha has been established following the setting aside of the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā; however, if they [the monks] are in different boundaries (*nānāsīmā*)..."
If those who have performed the *pavāraṇā* separately for the Great *Pavāraṇā* achieve unity within the month of Kattika, they must perform only a unity *Uposatha*;
a *pavāraṇā* is not to be performed, because a second *pavāraṇā* is not prescribed for those who have already performed one in that same year.
The phrase "it is a day of unity" is said with reference to the performance of unity on a day other than the regular *Uposatha* day. However, if [the unity is achieved] on the fourteenth day...
If the Saṅgha achieves formal unity on the fifteenth day, then that is not a day for the *sāmaggī-uposatha*; it is simply a *cātuddasī* or *pannarasī* uposatha day.
The same principle applies to the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) mentioned above.

Furthermore, there is the "day set aside by postponement," which refers to a day such as the fourteenth of the dark fortnight that has been set aside because the Saṅgha is troubled by quarrelsome persons, or due to some other business, or because the invitation ceremony has already been performed.
"And two full-moon days": this refers to the two full-moon days of the former Kattika and the latter Kattika.

"This is fourfold" means that when one combines the invitation on the fourteenth day (*cātuddasī-pavāraṇa*) with the invitation by concord (*sāmaggī-pavāraṇa*) and the two full-moon days, it becomes fourfold;
and this is stated according to the normal practice (*pakati-cāritta*). However, when such a condition exists for both...
"The full moon day, the two preceding fourteenth days, and the fifteenth day immediately following the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight—

these three days as well are Pavāraṇā days. Thus it is stated in the *Vimativinodanī* that, having set aside these seven types of Pavāraṇā days, it is not permissible to perform the Pavāraṇā on any other day.

Having thus shown the determination regarding failure of the subject matter (*vatthu*), he now speaks the passage beginning with “But in the case of failure due to the motion (*ñatti*)” in order to show the determination regarding failure of the motion and the determination regarding failure of the proclamation (*anussāvana*).
Therein, regarding the fifth failure of the motion—“or he puts forward the motion afterwards”—the commentary on this states:
“having performed the formal act of proclamation (*anussāvana-kamma*); that is, the first proclamation.
Having announced it with “This is the motion,” and having stated the entire motion immediately after the proclamation, the intention is that one says “This is the motion” at the conclusion.
In the commentary on the failure of the fourth proclamation,
the phrase “yvāyanti” is intended to mean the various distinctions of phonetic syllables (*byañjana*).
Regarding the phrase "the division of phonemes (byañjana) is tenfold," it should be construed here as: "the division of phonemes is tenfold, in ten ways.
To the question "By what is this division [made]? he says: "by means of the cognition of phonemes (byañjanabuddhi).
Phoneme-cognition is the cognition that generates the syllables designated as 'phonemes' because they manifest the intended meaning; [it is] by means of that phoneme-cognition.
The meaning is: "by means of the very distinction of the consciousness that originates the syllable. Or, as stated in the *Vimativinodanī*:
"Or, when it is spoken by making a conjunct [consonant] follow, this too is heavy"—this is the construction.
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it says: "A syllable to be pronounced with the points of articulation (*ṭhāna*) and the organs of speech (*karaṇa*) made relaxed is 'relaxed' (*sithila*)."
Those same [consonants] should be pronounced firmly and without slackness; such a syllable is "firm" (*dhanita*).
Long is two *mātrās* in duration; short is one *mātrā*. Thus, there is a tenfold division according to the perception of consonants (*byañjanabuddhi*) by way of the "slack" (*sithila*) and so forth;
for all syllables are indeed a tenfold division of the consciousness that produces the syllable, according to the perception of consonants by way of the "slack" and so on. All syllables...
"Those [sounds] produced by mind (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*) are *byañjana* (phonemes) according to their intended meaning and expression.
That which has a conjunct (*saṃyoga*) following it is *saṃyogapara*. That which does not have a conjunct following it is *asaṃyogapara*;

for instance, in the phrase ‘āyasmato buddharakkhitatherassa yassa na khamati,’ the *ta*-kāra and *na*-kāra together are *asaṃyogapara*. The ‘instruments’ (*karaṇa*) are the throat and so forth. Thus much was said.

Furthermore, in the *Vimativinodanī*: “In that context, among terms such as ‘āyasmato,’ consonants such as the letter *s* and the letter *m*, when separated by vowels, are called ‘conjunction’ (*saṃyoga*).
A vowel such as *a* followed by such a conjunction is termed ‘followed by a conjunction’ (*saṃyogapara*). ‘Short’ (*rassa*) refers to a word devoid of consonants such as *a*.
‘Not followed by a conjunction’ (*asaṃyogapara*) refers to [words] such as ‘yassa na khamati. Regarding the letter *s*:
This was stated with reference to a word accompanied by consonants beginning with the letter *n*.

Even one who, instead of changing the letter *t* to *th* and saying “*suṇātu me*” and so forth, says “*suṇāṭu me*” and so forth—making it lax across different consonant groups (*vagga*) without applying the appropriate substitute (*ādesa*)—commits a fault of mispronunciation (*durutta*).
For instance, when one should say “*saccikatthaparamatthena*,” if one says “*saccikaṭṭhaparamaṭṭhena*,” [it is likewise faulty].

Where it should be called *atthakathā*, it is sometimes called *aṭṭhakathā*; it is appropriate to use such forms seen in the usage of the Pāli commentaries (*pāḷiaṭṭhakathā*) and similar works, and nothing other than that.
Therefore, he said: “Without destroying the tradition (*paveṇi*) that has come down in succession,” and so forth.
In cases such as “*dīgha* should be used where *rassa* [is expected],” when it should be “*bhikkhūnaṃ*,”...
When one should say "a bhikkhu" or "in many," one may say "in many"; when one should say "it is not pleasing," one may say "it does not please";
or when one should say "desirous of full ordination," one may say "seeking full ordination"—in such corresponding instances, it is permissible to substitute long for short and short for long vowels;
however, when one should say "nāga" (elephant), one must not say "naga."

It is stated: "One should not speak inappropriately in such instances—for example, saying 'sagho' when one should say 'saṅgho,' or 'tiso' when one should say 'tisso,' or 'yācantī' when one should say 'yācati.
However, it should be understood that both grammatical connection (*sambandha*) and word-formation (*vavatthāna*) are permissible in all cases.
The remaining points should be properly observed according to the method explained in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

253. Furthermore, the determination regarding the failure of boundaries (*sīmavipatti*) has been explained in its entirety in the preceding discussion on boundaries; therefore, it should be understood according to the method stated therein. Regarding the discussion on the failure of the assembly (*parisavipatti*):
"in a quorum of four" (*catuvaggakaraṇe*) means that which is to be performed by a Saṅgha consisting of a quorum of four.

"Not excluded" (*anissāritā*) means not cast out from the community either by the suspension of the Uposatha or by the state of being a separate resident through difference of doctrine. For in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*)...

Because it is stated, “Of one who is ‘not fully admitted’ (apakatatta) means of one who has been suspended (ukkhitaka) or of one for whom the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā has been set aside,” it should be understood that a monk for whom the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā has been set aside is indeed “not fully admitted.
Regarding those of pure virtue, those who have not committed a Pārājika offense are intended.
However, in the case of formal acts such as probation (parivāsa), even those who have committed grave offenses should be understood as being “not fully admitted.”
The remaining cases... [etc. "...are those who are entitled to give their consent" is said with reference to those standing at a distance of one arm's reach;

however, those standing without having left that distance are not entitled to give consent. Even they, when exceeding the fourfold assembly and so forth, become entitled to give consent only after leaving the distance of one arm's reach.
Therefore, consent or formal purity must be given by one who stands having left the distance of one arm's reach from the Saṅgha.
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, however, it says: "Those who have not been suspended and have not committed a *pārājika* offense are 'of natural status' (*pakatatta*);
thus it says, 'those of natural status who have not been suspended,' and so forth. In that context, 'not expelled' is a synonym for the preceding term.
'Pure in virtue' means they have not committed a *pārājika*. 'Neither their consent nor their purity goes [to them]' refers to when three or two [monks] are sitting."
The intention is that even if the consent and purity (*chandapārisuddhi*) of one or two individuals has been brought forward, it is as if it were not brought forward at all.

Thus, both the success and failure of all four types of formal acts (*kamma*) are recorded in the Canon (*Pāḷi*) and the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), and have been analyzed by the authors of the Sub-commentaries (*Ṭīkā*);
therefore, the four formal acts should be performed exactly according to the method stated in the Commentary.
Not by the method already stated. For it is said in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
