"The Dhamma and the Vinaya were spoken by the Buddha;
that which was understood in exactly the same way by his sons [the disciples];"
Therefore, since those masters of intelligence in former times composed commentaries (aṭṭhakathā),
whatever has been stated in those commentaries— therefore [it is accepted].
"Having set aside that writing on negligence,
for those who possess reverence for all the trainings,
it is because this [teaching] is the standard for the wise in this world."

For in this section on formal acts (*kammavagga*), the place for performing the four types of formal acts—beginning with the act of notification (*apalokanakamma*)—is stated to be exclusively a "bound boundary" (*baddhasīmā*) that is exempt from the eleven defects of boundaries;
it is not a "non-bound informal boundary" (*abaddha-upacārasīmā*), because of the statement: "Formal acts fail due to eleven modes regarding the boundary.
Indeed, those eleven defects do not exist therein. In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) as well, it says: "The act of notification..."
"Having purified the Saṅgha residing within the boundary, having brought the consent of those entitled to give it,

and having announced it three times with the approval of the harmonious Saṅgha, the formal act (kamma) is to be performed"— thus it is stated that even for a *apalokana-kamma* (an act by announcement),

the state of being to be performed occurs only within a *baddha-sīmā* (a formally established boundary), not within an *upacāra-sīmā* (a functional or informal boundary). For in the latter case, neither the purification of the Saṅgha residing within the boundary nor [the bringing of consent from] those entitled to give it [is required].

There is indeed the necessity that the Saṅgha’s gain must be given to those who have entered and re-entered within the boundary; therefore, this is also the position of those teachers who hold that "the formal act of the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā,

which consists of a motion (*ñattikamma*), may be performed even in a monastery outside a fixed boundary," as well as the position of those who hold that "the formal act of the offering of the Kaṭhina,
which consists of a motion followed by a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), must be performed only within the functional boundary (*upacārasīmā*)."
It should be understood that even the assertions of teachers may contradict the Canon (Pāḷi) and the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā).
Whatever needs to be said on this matter has already been stated in the commentary on the *Uposatha-pavāraṇa-kathā* and the commentary on the *Kathina-kathā*;
those who desire [clarity] should examine those passages thoroughly and dispel their doubts.

Nowadays, by virtue of their familiarity with the scribes, all the bhikkhus recite with great enthusiasm at the commencement of the taking of refuge and the formal ritual (kammavācā) the *Mahānāmakkāra* passage written at the beginning of all books; however,
that passage is neither included within the taking of refuge, nor included within the formal ritual, nor even included within the preliminary procedure (*pubbakaraṇa*) for the formal ritual.
Even if that [formula] is not recited, there is no loss of the going for refuge or of the formal ritual (kammavācā); nor is there any increase by its being recited.
Therefore, the masters of the manuals do not provide an explanation of that long formula of homage at the beginning of the going for refuge, nor at the beginning of the ritual;
however, one who does explain it [would explain] the words: "of the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
Although the meaning of these words— “the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One”— should be explained in detail,
as it is in works such as the *Visuddhimagga*, the *Samantapāsādikā*, and the *Sāratthadīpanī*, nevertheless, because they function to illuminate the qualities of the Blessed One exactly as they are,
all teachers recite them three times at the beginning of every treatise for the sake of auspiciousness.

Furthermore, while reciting, one should speak with a well-rounded phrasing and syllables befitting a recluse, without losing the perfection of the place and organ of articulation for the letters *na*, *mo*, and so forth, and by attending to the distinctions of softness, hardness, length, and shortness;
it should not be with a sound that is overly protracted, resembling the sound of singing. For this was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, [one should not recite] with a protracted [sound]..."
“The Dhamma should be sung with the melody of a song; whoever should sing it [otherwise], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
“One mora is called short, two morae are called long;
three morae should be known as a protracted (pluta), and a syllable is half a mora.”
Based on the phonetic rules (*saddalakkhaṇa*) stated by the masters of grammatical treatises (*saddappakaraṇācariya*), when a short vowel such as *o* occurs in sounds like *mo*,
it is pronounced with a duration of one and a half morae (*matta*) by combining one mora for the short vowel and half a mora for the consonant *ma*.
When a long vowel such as *ā* occurs in sounds like *na*, it is pronounced with a duration of two morae by combining two morae for the long vowel and half a mora for the consonant *na*.
It is uttered making a duration of two and a half *mātrās* as its measure, and not more than that. But is it not said:
"A *pluta* is to be known as three *mātrās*"? True; however, that [three-mātrā duration] is found only in cases such as calling from a distance, and not elsewhere. For it is stated in the *Kārikā*:
"In calling from a distance, in singing, and likewise in weeping;..."
“A single *matta* is said to be the duration of a blink; all these [moments] are not to be grasped here.

But for how long a time is one *matta* to be understood? The teachers say it is for the duration of the closing and opening of an eye. However, some teachers say it is by the measure of the time it takes to snap the fingers. For it was said by the Elder Ācariya Dhammasenāpati:
“The measure of a single *matta*, they say, is the closing and opening of an eye.”
"...they say it is even by the measure of a finger-snap.
Thus, according to the statement of the masters of the science of grammar (saddasatthācariyā), in the place of a pure short vowel there is a measure of one mora (matta);
in the place of a short vowel with a consonant, a measure of one and a half morae; in the place of a pure long vowel, a measure of two morae; and in the place of a long vowel with a consonant—
It is recited after observing a duration of two and a half measures (mātrās).

However, nowadays, monks, exerting great effort in their delivery of the *mahānāma-kāra-bhaṇana*, recite by projecting the tone such that at short syllables (*rassa*) they take about two measures, and at long syllables (*dīgha*) they take about four or five measures; this is improper.
It appears as if so. Others, having recited during the first round and reached the final phrase "of the Perfectly Enlightened One," do not stop there;

instead, they recite again "Homage to him" (*namo tassa*), pause at the letter *sa*, rest for a short while, and then begin the second round starting from "of the Blessed One" (*bhagavato*) and continue until the end, where they stop. During the third round...
However, they place [the formulas] at the very end, starting from the beginning. Many praise those who speak in this way, yet such a procedure is found neither in the Pāḷi nor in the Aṭṭhakathā.

Just as when the *ñatticatuttha-kamma* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) is being performed, the three proclamations—identical in both sound and meaning—are made so that they do not overlap or become confused with one another.

Thus, when the Mahānāma-kārapāṭha is recited three times, the three sections—from the beginning until the end—must be established as being identical in both sound and meaning, rendered free from confusion.
Regarding this, some say: "Just as for one traveling with speed, even after reaching the place where one ought to stop..."

He is unable to stand still suddenly; having gone only a single step, he stops. Likewise, for one reciting from the beginning, because of the great exertion, he is unable to stop even when the conclusion is reached;
yet, after reciting only two words, "Namo tassa," he is able to stop.
This being so, why is he able to do so during the second and third rounds? It is because, at that time, he has rested slightly during the second round.
"Having found relief, one is able [to recite]. In this way, those venerable ones bring distress upon themselves.

For it was not prescribed by the Blessed One, nor established by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma, that "when reciting the Mahānāmakāra, it must be recited with great effort on the first occasion. This being so, just as when the Pātimokkha-reciter...

When reciting the Pātimokkha, one should take as the measure of one's own memory the extent to which the monks who hear the Pātimokkha can hear it until the very end, and thus the Pātimokkha should be recited; likewise,
when pronouncing the formal act (kammavācā), it should be done according to the hearing capacity of the monks seated within the boundary (sīmāmaṇḍala) until the conclusion.
"One should speak after taking the measure of one's own breath," so it is said.

However, other teachers say that when there are words ending in the vowel *o*—such as *mo*-kāra and others—one should cause the sound of imitation to follow for two or three times with an additional syllable from other words;
having heard such a way of speaking from those teachers, [one should practice accordingly].
Other bhikkhus or householders who have become well-versed [in the tradition] do not hold the *kammavācā* (formal ritual proclamation) of other teachers in high regard;
they consider that through such a *kammavācā*, ordination (*upasampadā*) cannot be obtained.
However, it is only the disciples and grand-disciples of those teachers who speak in such a manner, and not other teachers. Those ancient teachers, however—

Having heard a sound that is endowed with melody—though devoid of any imitative noise—and which seems coherent even to those listening, being exceedingly delightful, they follow the example of what they have seen and think, "We shall do likewise.
For there is nothing stated in either the Vinaya or the treatises on grammar (saddasattha) to the effect that it should be spoken in such a manner; therefore, this matter ought to be investigated.
However, many bhikkhus— failing to understand the legal rulings (vinicchaya) set forth in the Vinaya such as "the lax and the tight,
the long and the short," etc., and failing to understand the linguistic rulings made in the treatises on grammar (saddasattha) such as "in these five groups," etc.—
and thus having received no instruction from the elders who were learned in the Tipiṭaka and experts in the Vinaya, [proceeded to confer] ordination here and there...
Accepting only the words of the monks who were composing [the work], and being ignorant of what was to be rejected and what was to be adopted,
they heard the recitation of the great elders— who had previously come from foreign lands, who were meritorious and endowed with eloquence—
and while recording it exactly as seen and heard, they established it without even consulting the opinion of those excellent elders.
Gradually, the wise should laugh at those who explain improper talk, saying:
"In this place they make a sound like that of a tigress; in this place they make a sound like that of a bird;
in this place they scatter betel-leaf powder; in this place they speak while leaning toward the south; in this place..."
Having said such things as, "They speak while leaning to the left," or "They speak while displaying graceful gestures at this spot," and believing those very words,
they sit at the foot of trees, in auspicious caves, and so forth; training themselves in those very utterances and reciting the ritual formulas (kammavācā) accordingly,
they say, "I am skilled in ritual formulas," and having thus convinced the foolish people, [they act] for each of them...

They recite the formal ritual (kammavācā) for those seeking full ordination; these monks should be regarded as transgressing the Blessed One’s command and causing the Dispensation (sāsana) to decline.
Furthermore, other monks dwelling in village residences and the like, not attending upon the wise, [neglect] even the perfection of the subject matter (vatthusampatti).

Many, not knowing as they truly are the failure of the site, nor the success or failure regarding the motion, the proclamation, the boundary, or the assembly, establish numerous disciples and perform the going-forth and full ordination, thereby increasing their following;
yet these very people cause the Blessed One’s dispensation to decline. Therefore, those who carry out the command of the Blessed One—being modest, pure, and learned—[should act accordingly].
Virtuous monks who desire training should not become companions, supporters, or those who share in the same communal life with such monks.
Now, the monks— “One should speak that which ends in ‘ca’,
that which ends in ‘sa’, and that which is equal to that which ends in ‘ta’;”
"Ending in the letter *ṇa*, ending in the letter *la*, speak as if ending in the letter *na*.

Relying on this verse, even in the formula for going for refuge, they recite the text "I go to the Buddha for refuge" as "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī," and likewise in the ritual proclamation (*kammavācā*),
they recite the text beginning with "He should first be made to take the preceptor" [in the same manner].

They recite: “First, one should have [the candidate] take a preceptor,” and so forth. Here, the reason should be considered both from the standpoint of logic (*yutti*) and from the standpoint of scripture (*āgama*).
In this regard, here is the consideration of logic: regarding the statement, “One should pronounce what ends in *ca*, what ends in *sa*, and what is equal to what ends in *ta*”:

here, the letter *ca* is produced in the palate (*tāluja*), while the letter *ta* is produced in the teeth (*dantaja*); thus, these letters are not identical even in terms of their place of articulation (*ṭhāna*). The letter *ca* has the middle of the tongue as its instrument of production (*karaṇa*).
The letter *ta* is produced at the tip of the tongue; thus, they are dissimilar even in terms of their place of articulation (*karaṇa*).
The letter *ca* belongs to the second group (*vagga*), while the letter *ta* belongs to the fourth group; thus, they are dissimilar even in terms of their group (*vagga*).

Due to the nature of conjunct consonants (*saṃyogakkhara*), the preceding vowel does not receive its own audible manifestation and instead attains a specific modification of the vowel; for this very reason, the teachers who compose the treatises on grammar [state this].
They say: "When followed by a conjunct consonant, there is shortness," and they also say: "The *e*-vowel and *o*-vowel preceding a conjunct must be stated as being only short.

This being so, how can a syllable that has received its phonetic realization through a conjunct consonant consisting of [sounds] with a different place of articulation (*asamānaṭṭhānika*), a different mode of articulation (*asamānakaraṇa*), and a different class (*asamānavagga*)—be [treated] by another [consonant] that likewise has a different place of articulation, a different mode of articulation, and a different class?
They would acquire the same sound through the conjunction of vowels.

Furthermore, these letters are not only in different positions, have different points of articulation (*karaṇa*), and belong to different classes (*vagga*), but they are also not proximate in position, not proximate in point of articulation, and not proximate in class.
Just as for those playing the lute, a string-sound that is distant from another distant string-sound is not concordant.
In this way, since a distant-positioned consonant functions as a distant-maker, how could a distant-positioned distant-maker be of identical pronunciation? Furthermore,
because the consonants of the groups (vaggakkharā) occur without mutual confusion and without identical pronunciation, when the rule "or at the end of a group,
within a group" applies and the *niggahita* is changed to the final letter of a group, [this occurs] when another group follows.

It does not reach the end of the other class; for by the rule, "In the [consonant] classes, the third and first [consonants] are the voiced and unvoiced [respectively]," when creating a doubling of dissimilar [sounds], there is no doubling of the other class within the other class.
And if the phoneme *ca* were of identical pronunciation with the phoneme *ta*, then what would be the purpose of writing the phoneme *ca*?
In all cases, one should have written only the form ending in the letter *ta*; however, not having written it thus, [the text shows] according to usage:
at places where there is a doubling of a similar first syllable, as in "kacco kaccāyano"; at places where there is a doubling of a dissimilar [first syllable], as in "vaccho vacchāyano";
at places where there is a doubling of a similar third syllable, as in "majjaṃ sammajjaṃ"; and at places where there is a doubling of a dissimilar [third syllable].

In the case of "upajjhā upajjhāyo," the doubling of two identical syllables is written only when they share the same position, the same function, belong to the same class (*vagga*), and have the same number of vowels, but not otherwise.

Therefore, in accordance with the usage, in places where the letter *c* or the letter *j* occurs, one must speak according to the pronunciation of their own respective classes (*sakavagga*), and not according to the pronunciation of other classes.
However, in the case of the letter *s*, because the letter *s* shares the same position as the letter *t*...

Furthermore, because they share the same place of articulation (*samānakaraṇa*), and because non-group consonants (*avaggakkhara*) are common to the group consonants (*vaggakkhara*), and because there is no separate recitation for non-group consonants as there is for group consonants, it would be appropriate to pronounce the letter *ta* in place of the letter *sa*.
For the letter *sa* is produced by the teeth (*dantaja*), and the letter *ta* is likewise; the letter *sa* is produced by the tip of the tongue (*jivhaggakaraṇa*), and the letter *ta* is likewise.
Therefore, it is logical that there is a similarity of sound (*samānasutibhāva*) among syllables that occupy the same position and perform the same function.

By this same method, even when [syllables] ending in *ñ* and *l* are spoken of as ending in *n*, one should understand that there is a dissimilarity of sound between those ending in *ñ* and *n*, whereas there is a similarity of sound between those ending in *l* and *n*. This is the investigation of the underlying logic here.
The investigation of the Āgamas, however, should be conducted as follows:
“That which ends in *ca* and that which ends in *sa* should be stated as being equal to those ending in *ta*;
that which ends in *ña* and that which ends in *la* should be stated as being equal to those ending in *na*.”

From where does this verse originate? From where has it come? By whom was it composed? In this regard, "from where does it originate" means it originates from the Blessed One, or from the Elders who compiled the Dhamma, or from the teachers of the commentaries. "From where has it come" means it is found in the Vinaya, or in the Sutta, or in the Abhidhamma;
that is, it is found in the Canon (Pāḷi), or in the commentary, or in the sub-commentaries (Ṭīkā) and so forth. "By whom was it composed"?
By the Venerable Elder Mahākaccāyana, the author of the *Netti*, *Nirutti*, *Peṭaka*, and *Upadesa* treatises;
or by the teacher Vajirabuddhi, the author of the *Mukhamattadīpanī*; or by the teacher Buddhapiya, the author of the *Padarūpasiddhi*;
or by the teacher Aggavaṃsa, the author of the *Saddanīti*; or by other Great Elders who were authors of grammatical treatises.

Or was it caused [to be composed]? Since such an inquiry regarding its source exists, it is not known whether this verse originated from the Blessed One himself, or from the Elders who compiled the Dhamma, or from the teachers of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*).

For it cannot be said that it "is found in the Vinaya, or in the Sutta, or in the Abhidhamma, or in the Canon (*pāḷi*), or in the commentary, or in the sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*). [It was composed] by grammarians such as the teacher Kaccāyana and others.
Nor is it seen to have been composed by teachers. This being so, this statement would fall into the state of being unauthoritative (*appaṭihīrakata*).
However, we have reflected thus: it is said that in the Rāmañña country, words ending in the letter *ca* or the letter *ña* do not exist in their own language;
for that very reason, when the monks of the Rāmañña country pronounce the reading "sacca," they say "satca."
They say: those who recite the reading as "pañcaṅga" say "pancaṅga.

Therefore, since those bhikkhus were unable to recite it according to the reading with the suffixes -ca and -ña—which do not exist in their own [vernacular] domain—they must have had this verse composed in accordance with their own language.
Even so, in the Maramma language, there is no distinction between words ending in -ca and words ending in -ña.
Because it appears as something distinct due to its extreme specificity, the bhikkhus of the Maramma country, following that popular saying,

are not entitled to say "I go for refuge to the Buddha," or "the first [candidate] should be made to take the upasampadā," or "the cause-condition (hetu-paccaya) is the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya).
Even among those of the Rāmañña country, although [such a distinction] does not exist separately in their own language...
A word ending in *ca* or *ña* should be spoken in accordance with the vernacular (*sakabhāsā*) at the time of speaking that vernacular as ending in *ta* or *na*;
however, at the time of speaking the Māgadhī language, since the separate usage of words ending in *ca* or *ña* is observed in the Māgadhī language,
they should be spoken according to the Māgadhī language by way of their being heard separately as ending in *ca* or *ña*.
It is our opinion that these matters should be explained exactly according to the text. This concludes the consideration of the tradition (*āgama*) in this context.
Regarding the teaching of the Conqueror, I have delivered this discourse;
let the wise disciples of the Conqueror consider what is appropriate and what is inappropriate.
"Having reflected upon what is appropriate and what is inappropriate,
let them retain that which is appropriate and abandon that which is inappropriate, being free from the fault of pride.
(254) Having thus shown the success and failure of the four types of action, [the author now] explains their bases and classifications.
Showing this, he said: "The act of seeking permission (*apalokanakamma*) goes to five grounds," and so forth.
In that regard, the detailed analysis should be understood according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. We shall demonstrate only the meaning of the words not [already] explained.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Even if it were a novice at present," even speaking dispraise of the Buddha and others, or regarding what is unallowable as being allowable, and so on—
Even the act of illuminating [the view] falls within the very category of failure in view; for that reason, he will say, "He must be made to relinquish that adherence.
The same principle applies to monks as well. One who holds wrong view is one who grasps the intention of the Buddha’s word in a perverted manner;
it is such a person who is described as "one possessed of an extreme-grasping view. Some, however, [regard] eternalism and annihilationism...
If they say, "He was possessed of some other [wrong] view," that is not correct.

This is because it was stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) above that the grasping at eternalism or annihilationism is the reason for the removal of the novice’s emblem (*liṅganāsanā*), and because here the intention is specifically the removal by means of disciplinary action (*daṇḍakamma*).
"Physical intimacy" (*kāyasambhogasāmaggī*) refers to things such as accepting a shared bed. "Gentle" (*sorata*) means one who delights in what is wholesome (*subhe rato*).
"Very well-restrained" (*suṭṭhu orato*) means "well-restrained" (*sorato*). "Of humble conduct" (*nivātavuttī*) means one who lives in a lowly manner.

It should be given even to such a person—that is, it must indeed be given to one who does not desist from censuring and so forth, even though they do not possess a boisterous nature and the like, and even though they have not been questioned, have not given their consent, and have not had a charge of an offense brought against them, provided that they have confessed the offense. To one who desists...
However, it should not be granted to one who is seeking forgiveness. "Granting the brahma-daṇḍa" means granting a harsh punishment, a severe penalty.
For when a formal act such as *tajjanīya* (reproof) has been performed, there is no prohibition against providing instruction and admonition;
however, once the brahma-daṇḍa has been granted, even those acts such as *tajjanīya* that were previously permitted are no longer allowed to be performed. "Neither... [and so forth].
Because even mere conversation, such as saying "you may speak," is prohibited by the word "not" in the passage beginning with those words;
for upon seeing him, the monks do not even turn their necks to look at him, since that punishment was prescribed precisely for the purpose of making him avoid [the community] and subdue his pride.
For this very reason, even though he had been subjected to formal acts of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) and so forth, the Elder Channa did not fear [to speak].
When the Brahma-daṇḍa was imposed, [the monk] fell down in a swoon, thinking, "I have been completely cast out by the Saṅgha.

However, it should be understood that for one who, knowing [the decree], continues to associate with the one subject to the Brahma-daṇḍa without avoiding him, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the imposition of the Brahma-daṇḍa being rendered meaningless. "By him" means by the one subject to the Brahma-daṇḍa. Just as in the case of those against whom formal acts such as the act of censure (tajjanīya-kamma) have been performed.

In the same way, one who wishes to propitiate the Saṅgha even more than that must conduct oneself properly; and this has indeed been shown explicitly by the words, "gentle and humble in conduct," and so forth.
Therefore he said: "For one who conducts himself properly and asks for forgiveness, the Brahma-punishment (brahmadaṇḍa) should be lifted.
*Paṭisaṅkhā* means having reflected, having examined with wisdom.
The connection is: "That which was authorized by the Blessed One as an act not to be saluted.

Having shown the general manner in which it was authorized by saying, "To perform a disciplinary act against that bhikkhu," one should understand that the passage beginning with "Then indeed" is cited from the Canon to show the specific manner in which it was authorized.
"This is the occasion for this act of seeking permission (apalokanakamma)."
This is the locus for the occurrence of the commonality of the *apalokana-kamma* (act of seeking permission).
Although it does not exist by way of specific distinction, it is expressed as if dependent on a qualification in order to show its non-occurrence elsewhere.
By the statement, "The *kamma* itself is the characteristic," all remaining [acts] included under *osāraṇā* and so forth are included by way of the characteristic common to the *apalokana-kamma*.
The etymological derivation is shown as: "That which has action itself as its characteristic is 'action-characteristic' (*kammalakkhaṇa*).

This should be understood as the place of completion for the remaining actions mentioned, just as the aggregates, bases, and so forth are the place of completion for the remaining aggregates and bases mentioned.
For this very reason, he will say: "But here, there is also a determination of the characteristic of action that is not included in the canonical text," and so on.
It should be understood that just as it is here, so too the characteristic of an act (*kammalakkhaṇa*) is stated for the subsequent formal acts such as the *ñattikamma* (act by motion) and others.
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is said: "The characteristic of the act is the act itself; thus, it is 'the characteristic of an act.

Like the acts of reinstatement (*osāraṇa*), banishment (*nissāraṇa*), and the bowl-act (*bhaṇḍukamma*), it does not receive another name while being an act; rather, it is characterized specifically as an act, hence it is called 'the characteristic of an act.'"
Thus it is said. However, in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, it is stated:

"The meaning is that this act of notification (*apalokanakamma*) proceeds on the grounds that 'this is the occasion for an act of notification. A 'characteristic of an act' (*kammalakkhaṇa*) is a characteristic that is an act itself.
Like the acts of reinstatement (*osāraṇa*), banishment (*nissāraṇa*), and the bowl-act (*bhaṇḍukamma*), it does not receive another name while being an act; it is simply an act."
"Having performed [the act], it is characterized [as such]; thus, the characteristic of the action (kamma-lakkhaṇa) is like the decisive support (upanissaya).

For all specific conditions, being free from the characteristics of the root-condition (hetu-paccaya) and so forth, are included therein"—so it is said. "The performance of that" refers to the procedure for performing an unworthy act.
By the words "he should not be saluted," it should be understood that he shows that there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who salutes him.

For one who disregards and transgresses a formal authorization of the Saṅgha—knowing that what has been done by the Saṅgha is a formal agreement (katikā)—there is indeed an offense, as if trampling [something precious].

255. Furthermore, this applies even to the community of monks; because it was taken merely as an illustration of an act of non-worship, the characteristic of a formal act (kamma) is indeed applicable to the community of monks as well. The place where voting sticks are distributed is called the *salākagga*.
The places for serving rice gruel and solid food are called *yāgagga* and *bhattagga*.

For in these places as well, the entire Saṅgha has assembled just as on the Uposatha day; thus, the formal act (*kamma*) is not a "fractional act" (*vaggakamma*), and even those who later object, saying, "We did not know this," do not do so.

However, they do object when [an act] is performed within a partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*). This is because regarding the requisites belonging to the Saṅgha, such as robes that have not been cut off...
When those seeking permission to give [the robe] must do so, they should perform the act only after obtaining the consent of everyone within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*).

However, if there is a person of a different faction who obstructs the legitimate permission-seeking, it is permissible to perform the act by means of having that person go outside the precinct boundary or by entering a fragmented boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*).
It is with reference to this that it is said: "He performs the act of permission-seeking."
He shows it in general terms; then, in order to show that *apalokana-kamma* (act of seeking permission) in its specific form, he says:
"If the robe has not been cut," and so forth. If the robe must indeed be given only after seeking permission, why then is there the authorization (*sammuti*) for the distributor of trifles?
To this he replies: "But by the distributor of trifles," and so forth. "A *nāḷi* or half a *nāḷi*" means [the amount] day by day, having sought permission.
This is the demonstration of the measure of what should be given. By this, it is shown that one should seek permission for the mere amount necessary for subsistence, and not for more.
The phrase "on a single day only," and so forth, demonstrates the limit of what should be given within the span of ten or twenty days on just one day.
By this, it is shown that it is not permissible to seek permission in such ways as "for as long as life lasts" or "until recovery from illness."
"Debt-obstruction" (*iṇapalibodha*) refers to the connection that "it is permissible to give the property used for the debt.

Furthermore, in the case of one who is obstructed by creditors, being modest, virtuous, and helpful to the Dispensation, the monks should give only a moderate amount of allowable goods (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*) after obtaining his consent;
however, they must not give a great debt such as a thousand or a hundred thousand. For such a person, by virtue of the practice of alms-gathering (*bhikkhācariyavatta*), [the debt is cleared].
All the bhikkhus, having searched for such a bhikkhu, must give [the robe].
Regarding the phrase "a canopy or a railing" (*chattaṃ vā vedikaṃ vā*): here, "railing" (*vedikā*) refers to a square mound built above the *cetiya*.
"Canopy" (*chatta*) refers to the pinnacle mound constructed by displaying rings above that; so it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
"From an offering placed near a cetiya" means from goods set aside by stewards (*kappiyakāraka*) after they have been applied toward the maintenance or the expansion of the cetiya.

"Even with what belongs to the Saṅgha" means not only from what has arisen there, but also from goods given to the Saṅgha by donors for the sake of the four requisites; it is not permitted to use them to provide a communal meal (*saṅghabhatta*), even by those giving a great almsgiving (*mahādāna*).
The intention is that it is not permissible to have it prepared like a meal for the Saṅgha (saṅghabhatta).
Because it is stated, "It is pleasing to consume it as one likes," one may take either a small or a large amount sufficient for one's own consumption;
however, one does not receive permission to take more than that.
“On the Uposatha day” is merely an illustration; it is well performed even if done on any other day whatsoever.
When performing it, one should make an agreement (*katikā*) such as: “Whatever belongs to the Saṅgha within the boundary of this monastery...
I find it agreeable to use [it] at will. Likewise, two or three [monks] should say: “It is agreeable to the Venerable Ones.”
In this context, the distinction lies solely in the statement. "Of those too" means of the trees. "That same agreement" means that no separate agreement should be made.
"Of those" refers to the trees; the connection is that "the Saṅgha is the owner. "In the former monastery" means in the monastery where an agreement had previously been made for use as one pleases.
"Having built and maintaining the courtyards" means [those courtyards] where, if they were not protected, fruits and flowers [would be lost].
"Trees are destroyed"—this was said with reference to such a situation; the intended meaning is that in such a place, no formal agreement (*katikā*) may be established for the Saṅgha.

However, those trees which were planted by individuals and tended from the very beginning must be enjoyed by those planters themselves after they have given a tenth part [to the Saṅgha]. "By them" means by those who have tended them.
*Tattha* means in that monastery. *Mūle* and so forth mean at the initial time; the meaning is "previously.
*Dīghā katikā* means an agreement for use as one pleases over an unlimited period of time. *Nikkukkuccena* means without having any remorse (*kukkucca*) thinking, "This has not been divided.
*Tanti khīyanamattameva* means that there is no fault for those who eat much because of that very act of complaining, provided it is their own [share].

Because only that which is the measure for personal use is permitted to be taken, the intention is that even when [the food] is being exhausted, one may take and eat as much as is sufficient for oneself.
It is said that one should not say, "Take [some]," because if one were to say that, they might think it was given by that very monk himself;
based on that, there would arise wrong livelihood. Therefore he said, "Having searched through," and so forth. "A half-portion" means...
One should give a half-share from one’s own portion to a single bhikkhu,
having freed oneself by saying, "The Saṅgha has authorized me to give this much," and speaking in such a way that they may have confidence in the Saṅgha itself.

"Without expectation" means that even when giving one's own belongings to persons authorized for such gifts— such as those who are ill, travelers, or lords— one must do so without expecting anything in return.
It should be given. However, it is not permissible to give to persons who have not been authorized, even if one does not expect anything in return.

Only that which belongs to the Saṅgha should be caused to be given according to the agreement. Even regarding what belongs to oneself, if the providers of requisites and others take it out of their own trust, one should not prevent them;
rather, one should remain silent, thinking, "This is allowable as already obtained. This is exactly as stated previously: "An angry..."
Indeed, the reason for remaining silent has already been stated previously in the passage beginning, "for he might even cut down trees.
Even though no harm was done by them, it is appropriate to remain silent out of compassion; however, it is not appropriate to say, "Take [it]," and so forth.

Because it is a valuable article... [etc. ...it should not be given, since living trees take the place of a monastery garden and the timber has not yet reached the stage of being a household construction material.
It is said: “You must take everything; it is not permissible to give [anything back]. “Having made an unmade dwelling” means having constructed a lodging that did not previously exist.
“At the time of maintenance” means when the fruiting season has arrived. “At the time of beginning maintenance” means at the time one has started to maintain it. 256.
“In the classification of the bases for a formal act consisting of a motion” means in the classification of the bases for a formal act (*ñattikamma*) consisting of a motion.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Ornament of the Discussion on the Determination of Valid and Invalid Acts," in the *Vinayālaṅkāra*,
which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
34. Discussion on the Determination of Miscellaneous Matters (Pakiṇṇakavinicchayakathā).

Having thus explained the discussion on the determination of what is action and what is not action, he now said, “Now the discussion on miscellaneous matters (pakiṇṇaka) should be understood,” etc., in order to explain the discussion on the determination of miscellaneous matters.
In that context, that which is scattered (kiṇṇa) in various ways (pakārena) is “miscellaneous” (pakiṇṇa), such as [the rules regarding] sleeping during the day.
Discourses that do not proceed separately but occur together within a single section by way of being treated as a group— such as the discourse on communal meals (*gaṇabhojana*) and so forth—
are called *pakiṇṇaka* (miscellaneous), by virtue of the suffix *-ka* having the sense of the word itself (*sakatthe*).
Herein, this is the matrix of the miscellaneous (*pakiṇṇakamātikā*):
The discourse on eating in a group, and eating in succession;
eating without having asked permission, and then [receiving] rag-robes;
and [receiving] uncut robes; a painted design, and eating prepared food.
Reciting and causing others to recite, as well as those separated by three years;
the long seat, attending the sick, and praising death;
throwing oneself down, and likewise sitting without having first inspected [the spot].
The piercing with stones for the sake of a gift, likewise the whitewashing of a wall;
the acquisition of a family through wrong view, and the gift of a cowherd;
the soliciting of what is righteous, and the discarding of excrement and so forth.
Bathing, rubbing the body with wood, wearing cosmetics and the like;
long hair, mirrors and such, dancing and so forth, cutting off limbs and the like;
the alms-bowl, all types of rag-robes, water-strainers, and nakedness.
Perfumed flowers, scented water, a mirror, and a single vessel;
a cloth for the head, a foot-rubber, a fan, and a parasol;
nails and hair, a waist-band, and lower and upper garments.
The tooth-stick made of wood, climbing trees, and likewise the "desire-constructed" Lokāyata doctrines;
garlic that has been spat out; things not to be stepped over and so forth; those who are not to be saluted and those who are to be saluted.
The discourse on performing salutations, and also the discourse on chairs and such;
high seats and large couches, and the use of palaces;
sandals and likewise vehicles, robes and torn robes.
Improper robes, the distribution of robes,
the staff and the *kaṭhina* cloth, as well as the householder’s robe;
the six robes, dyeing and so forth, and extra robes.
The eight excellent seats, the illegal formal act,
the motion, the gift of faith, and even the inner and outer robes;
the depositing of the robe, and likewise the sewing of the robe with a needle.
The barber’s tenth part, provisions for the journey, and even a portion of the land;
the five medicines used in combination, the second being fat and radish;
flour, astringent, leaf, fruit, lac, and salt.
Powder for non-human afflictions, collyrium, and eye-salve;
fumigation, nasal treatment, oil-preparation, sudation, and bloodletting;
foot-unguent, glandular disease, poison, and house-given medicine.
The case of Duṭṭhagahaṇika, jaundice, and skin disease;
a body with excessive secretions, as well as salt and sour gruel;
the discussion on internal fermentation and so forth, and the acceptance of what has been formally received.
Then there is the discourse on the one whose talk has been silenced, the acceptance of alms before the meal,
the forest-dweller, the pond-dweller, and likewise the one who has not performed the formal acts (*akatakappa*).
There is also the discourse on rice-gruel, the discourse on sugar, and the Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*).
And the discourse on benefits is included in the miscellaneous section. Regarding the discourse on eating in a group (gaṇabhojana):
herein, a "group" (gaṇa) is that which is to be counted or numbered; it refers to any collection whatsoever, but in this context, it refers to a group consisting of at least four members.
This is what is intended. They eat food; the act of eating is designated as the state of consuming.

"Group meal" (*gaṇabhojana*) means the eating of a group; [the offense occurs] in that regard. Regarding the phrase "there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for a group meal," here the locative case is used in the sense of a causal source (*janakahetu*).

"Except at the proper time" (*aññatra samayā*) means setting aside the seven kinds of occasions, such as being ill, and so forth. [This refers to] the formal announcement (*viññatti*) of this training rule.
Since the offense of eating in a group was prescribed in the context of the rule regarding eating after having made a request, it would have been clear from the basis of the matter itself;
therefore, without mentioning that, the word-commentary defines "eating in a group" by way of the invitation itself, stating: "Eating in a group means where... [etc.
...those who have been invited eat. However, some training rules may also correspond to the basis of the matter; thus, in the word-commentary—
Thinking that "group-meals" might occur in the manner already described, some might harbor such a doubt; therefore, to prevent this, it is said: "A group-meal arises in two ways.

Regarding the phrase "taking together," it should be understood that they are said to be "taking together" when they stand without being more than twelve *hatthas* apart from one another. [For example: "Give us all four our meal."

From the statement, "or they may request [it]," and from the preceding statement, "having requested thus: 'You give a meal for one bhikkhu, you [give] for two,'" it should be understood that even for one who consents to a request made by another for their own sake, there is indeed *gaṇabhojana* (eating in a group).
In the phrase "it arises from such a request," this means that when there is a request, for one who counts [the people].
If they eat together as one group, there is an offense under this training rule; if they eat separately, the offense should be understood to arise from requesting fine foods, such as rice with broth.
Regarding the phrase "having mentioned the names of the five kinds of food," they say: "Even if it is said, 'Take food,' it still constitutes eating in a group.
[As stated] below in the case concerning traveling on a journey and the case concerning boarding a boat: "'Right here...'"

"In the three *gaṇṭhipada* (commentaries on difficult points), it is stated: 'Because they did not accept [the food] when told, "Venerable sirs, please eat," out of fear of wrongdoing (*kukkucca*), therefore, even when told, "Please eat," it still constitutes a group meal (*gaṇabhojana*).

Furthermore, because it is stated, "He invites [them] by mentioning the names of the five kinds of staple foods," [it is understood that one says] either, "Eat rice," or, "Eat the meal."*"*" *Note: This sentence fragment appears to be a commentary explaining the specific application of the rule regarding group meals.*"
Or rather, it constitutes a *gaṇabhojana* (group meal) only when the name of the food is actually mentioned, and not otherwise.
Even in the case of the words, "Venerable sir, please eat right here," it must be understood that they invite [the monks] by specifically saying "rice" or "boiled rice.
Because they were invited as a group, those monks, out of a sense of propriety (*apakataññutā*), felt apprehensive and did not accept; this is our [position].
Having investigated, one should accept that which is more appropriate. In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it is stated:
"Because it is said 'by whatever synonym,' even by a general name such as 'Take food,' it constitutes a group meal (*gaṇabhojana*).
Furthermore, regarding the anxiety felt over the statement in the Canon—'Eat right here'—made in contexts such as traveling on a journey, that too [is included]."
It should be understood that [the action] is performed precisely because it is stated by mentioning names such as "rice" and so forth.
Regarding the statement in the *Kurundi*: "he arranges," this means he distributes [the material] into five sections and so on.
"He strikes" means that having cut [the material] with the wind, he strikes it with his hand or with a stick. "He makes thread" means he spins thread. "He twists" means [on] the stick...
Or he rolls it up in his hand. They say: "The making of a brand-new robe is what is meant here by 'robe-making'; needlework on an old robe is not called 'robe-making.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated with reference to a robe being made after cutting off a border-strip and adding it as a supplement: "'He sets it aside' means one end..."
He places it on the robe by means of binding. "He sews what has returned" means he turns back its second edge and sews it after it has been beaten.
"He binds an incoming patch" means, while making it adhere to the robe, he repeatedly binds it here and there with thread.
"He presses" means having taken it according to measure, he presses it with a stick or similar object. "He makes the thread."

One winds the thread by means of its triple-strand nature and so forth. "He winds" means that he makes the multi-stranded thread into a single unity by winding it with his hand or with a spindle-stick (*cakkadaṇḍa*).
"He performs a turning" means that he makes a turning-stick (*parivattanadaṇḍayantaka*).
Into this [stick], having inserted a ball of thread and placed it in a bamboo tube or similar vessel, one causes it to revolve; then, starting from the end of the thread...
"...pulling [it]," it is said. In the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, it is stated: "They do not sew the visiting cloth with a false thread and leave it there.
Rather, they touch it with their hands so that, with the wind blowing, it becomes a single layer. 'Rolls' means it turns back.
'Reverses' means he turns the thread back for the sake of easy grasping by those who are taking up the thread; [he does this] to the cloth..."

It is said: "The one intended here is the maker of a new robe, not the other; and [the phrase] *paṭṭaparivattanaṃ* refers to the turning over of the border-cloth for the sake of easy sewing by those who are sewing.
Regarding *animantitacatutthaṃ*: that group of four monks (*bhikkhucatukka*) which has a fourth member who was not invited is called *animantitacatutthaṃ*.
The same applies to the remaining cases. Therefore he said, "of five groups of four," because of the statement, "when the fourth has arrived, they do not wait."
"If no one else comes, and those four sitting there cannot sustain themselves [with the meal], it is not permissible," they say.
It is called "an improper invitation" because it constitutes an invitation that gives rise to the offense of eating in a group (*gaṇabhojana*).
"Having made them enter" means having had them sit down. "The group is split" intends to mean that the group does not incur the offense.

In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it is stated: “‘Having caused to enter’ means having joined them with those [invited monks]. ‘The group is split’ means that it is no longer a Saṅgha that has been invited.
This is because of the correlation with the canonical text: “Where four bhikkhus... eat... [and so forth]. Regarding the others, however—
"It is said: 'He becomes one who completes the quorum. "Without distinction" means by a term common to all, without specifying "whether he is ill or making robes.
"Therefore" means because of that lack of specification.
"When they have accepted and departed": here, at the moment of accepting an improper invitation, there is also an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding the preliminary action.

It should be understood that there is no offense; however, regarding the instigation through intimation, at the moment of the intimation itself, an *dukkaṭa* offense occurs under the other training rules.
Regarding the phrase "when they have eaten and departed": here, it is also permissible to take [the food] even when they have arrived, provided the act of eating is finished.
And "those things which were not taken together with them" refers to those foods for which there was no confusion regarding the meal.
They were not taken together by those monks because they were taken later by one [monk]. "O Great Elder" is said with reference to the monks.
"Accept the invitation" means: receive the meal offered as an invitation. "Those which" refers to the groats and so forth;
they were not taken together by those monks because they were taken later by one. [This was done] by the wise distributor of meals.
By the words "it must be [accepted]... it must be released," it is shown that when an improper invitation is accepted by the meal-designator, it is as if accepted by everyone;
furthermore, for those who take [the food] together, there is the offense of eating in a group (*gaṇabhojana*).
Because of the fear that the messenger, having arrived at the door, might say again, "Take the meal," it is stated, "without standing at the village gate. In that regard:
"Having gone there" means having gone to the presence of those standing here and there in the middle of the streets and so forth.
The same rule applies even when food is being given after being set down at the door of a house for the sake of the bhikkhus. However, when it is said, "Turn back," it is permissible to turn back;
for the phrase "turn back" is separated [from the following], and since it is subsequently said, "Take the meal," it is therefore permissible.
The Discussion on Successive Feasting (Paramparabhojanakathā) 2.
In this discussion on successive feasting, "successive feasting" (*paramparabhojana*) refers to the act of eating from one person after another. What is that?
It is the practice of eating from another person, setting aside the meal for which one was first invited. This is successive feasting.
Because it does not arise from either a formal request (*viññatti*) or an invitation (*nimantana*), like a meal for a group (*gaṇabhojana*), he said, "But as for eating in succession," and so forth.

The word *pana* indicates a specific distinction. Since that food becomes non-existent only by way of the act of assigning it [to others], the assignment was set aside by means of a supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*), and only the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) as originally formulated was established.

In the *Parivāra*, however, because even the permission regarding the act of formal assignment (*vikappanā*) is treated as being similar to a subsequent rule (*anupaññatti*), it is stated that there are "four subsequent rules.

By subsequently stating the method as explained in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other texts, one establishes that only formal assignment in the absence of the person concerned (*parammukhā-vikappana*) is valid, since this accords with the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
Some, however, [argue] that at that time, having placed [the object] near himself, [the Buddha did so] because there was no one else present.
The Elder did not perform an assignment in the presence [of the recipient], nor was an assignment in the presence specifically mentioned by the Blessed One;
nevertheless, they say that an assignment in the presence is also permissible. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*:
"If a bhikkhu says to one of five fellow practitioners, 'I give my expected meal to you,' or 'I assign it to you'..."
"Whether in the presence of the person saying, 'I give this to so-and-so,' or 'I dedicate this to so-and-so,' or whether in their absence,
if one consumes even a single grain of rice obtained from a family invited later— without having first dedicated the initial invitation—
it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Thus it is said.

When one is invited with five kinds of food, if one does not designate [the meal] out of order from whichever meal one was first invited, but instead takes the food of each subsequent person, it is called "successive eating" (*paramparabhojana*). Therefore, it is said:
"But if the original invitation is below and the later ones are above, starting from that which is above..."
“There is an offense for one who eats. When one inserts the hand inside and takes [the food] from the very bottom, even that which remains in the middle has entered the hand;
therefore he said: “But when the hand... [as before] ...or in whatever way one eats, there is no offense.
Because the milk and the essence remain on top, unmixed with the solid food, he said: “Milk or...”
It is said: "There is no offense for one drinking [it] as a juice.
Regarding the term "great lay follower" (*mahā-upāsaka*), it refers to the master of a household.

In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, the statement "there is an offense" appears to contradict the statement "it is permissible" found in the *Kuruṇḍī*. The intended meaning of both is clarified in the *Mahāpaccarī*, as stated in the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada*.
“They all invite” means they invite by way of an improper invitation. For it is said:
“‘Successive eating’ (paramparabhojana) means that one who has been invited to eat any one of the five kinds of cooked food, sets that aside and eats another of the five kinds of cooked food;
this is called ‘successive eating. Thus, even though he is on his almsround...
Regarding the first case, it is stated: "If one eats food obtained after wandering for alms, there is an offense.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is said: "This was stated with reference to milk or broth that stands above the rice, being mixed with the five kinds of soft foods.
Since these are not [considered] 'food,' there is no offense even if one drinks them out of order. Therefore, he said: 'By one who is eating,' and so forth."

It has been stated [thus]. However, in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, it says: “In this regard, according to the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), there is an offense for one who eats a meal received later after having invited monks...
‘There is an offense for one who eats a meal obtained by wandering for alms.
Furthermore, according to the *Khandhaka* of the Canon (*pāḷi*), it says: ‘We ate after wandering for alms early in the morning.’”
And because of the statement: “Monks, one should not consume another’s rice-gruel unless invited;

whoever should so consume it, he is to be dealt with according to the rule,” whether [the food] was announced after being invited or not invited, for a monk who has already accepted an invitation, any other food belonging to another that is different from the food of his first invitation constitutes the offense of *paramparabhojana* (successive eating).
"He prepares it. It is permissible to use what belongs to himself, or what has been received from the Saṅgha or a group, or what belongs to one who is not a householder;
however, because it was first fixed by invitation, even what belongs to others, such as regular meals (niccabhatta) and so forth, is permissible," it is said.
The Discussion on Not Asking for Permission.
3. Regarding the discussion on not asking for permission: "By ordinary speech" means that here, whatever can be heard by one standing within twelve cubits is called "ordinary speech.
"He should ask permission" means he should ask with such words as, "I am going to the house of so-and-so," or "I am undertaking a journey. The rest here is as follows.

This is quite clear. Accepting an invitation to one of the five kinds of cooked food, entering another house from a family home without having asked a monk who is present, failing to pass the midday mealtime, and the absence of either a proper occasion or an emergency—these are the five factors here.
Thus much is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*; in the *Vimativinodanī*... [text continues].

However, because it is stated that "there is no need to announce [the offense] after having searched," if one who ought not to be sought is seen in a place suitable for approaching, even if he stands beyond the range of hearing ordinary speech, one must approach him and ask for permission.
Therefore, he said: "Furthermore... whatever one sees, that person should be asked for permission," and so forth. In the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*):

And here, because only those who frequent the interior gardens and so forth are mentioned, there is an offense even for one who crosses from the monastery to the village street without a permitted reason, but not merely for one who crosses the vicinity of a house. As for what is stated in the Pāḷi—“for one entering the vicinity of another’s house...
[etc. ...he steps over the first threshold”—that refers to one who has already entered the village.

This was said with a specific intention; nevertheless, even for one who, without entering the vicinity of another’s house, goes by way of the middle of the street, stands facing the door of whichever house he desires, and looks at people as he passes by, there is indeed a *pācittiya* offense.
Regarding this, some say: "For one passing through the street, there are offenses corresponding to the number of houses [passed]. Others [say otherwise].
"But rather, it is 'according to the number of those families for whose sake he has gone. The five factors here are: accepting an invitation to any one of the five kinds of cooked food;
not asking an existing monk [for permission]; going from the house of a supporter to another house;
failing to pass the midday mealtime; and the absence of a valid occasion. This also applies to entering a village at an improper time.

“‘The precinct of an unenclosed village is to be understood in the same manner as described under the taking of what is not given’—by this, it is shown that here ‘the precinct’ refers to the second stone’s throw.

The rest here is self-evident. However, the three factors here are: entering a village at an improper time without having asked permission from a monk present, the absence of any authorized reason, and the act of entering the village at an improper time.”
The Discourse on the Rag-robe (Paṃsukūlakathā) 4.
In this discourse on the rag-robe, "unbroken body" means a fresh, moist body. By the word "fresh," the same meaning already stated is further clarified through a different synonym as "moist body.
"Dissimilar body" refers to a woman's body. Because it is a dissimilar body, one should not remain too close; thus he said:

“On the head,” and so forth. “It is allowable” means that even with regard to a body of a different gender, it is allowable to perform the procedure prescribed for oneself and to take hold of the cloth.
Some, however, say: “Although there is no offense under this training rule, for one who touches a female form, there is an *dukkaṭa*.
“Gone according to his karma” means [gone] from that state of existence as a *peta* to the state of being dead.
It shows [the state of the body]. "It is warm" (*abbhuṇheti*) indicates that the body possesses heat due to its proximity to death; for this very reason, he says "with a moist body" (*allasarīre*).

Even though it has reached the state of a corpse (*kuṇapa*), it is indeed "broken" (*bhinna*) because of its brokenness from the state of being moist. "In a dissimilar body" (*visabhāgasarīre*) refers to a female body.
The passage beginning with "on the head" (*sīse vā*) and so forth is stated with reference to the arising of a mental disturbance in a location below the neck and above the kneecaps.
"Whatever is done by one who does not touch [a woman] anywhere at all is indeed well-done.
For they say that even touching a dead body intentionally in any manner whatsoever constitutes the offense of *dukkaṭa* for touching what should not be touched; and that is indeed logical.

For the *dukkaṭa* that occurs regarding a female form such as the mind and so forth—which is not the basis for a *pārājika*—does not cease to apply when it concerns the body of a dead woman, which is the very basis for a *pārājika*."
This has been stated in the *Vimativinodanī*.
At this point, even though not explicitly mentioned by the Teacher, the discourse on rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*) should be understood through the common application of the term *paṃsukūla*.
For that [discourse] is introduced thus in the *Cīvarakkhandhaka*: "Now at that time, those monks who were receiving a robe from a householder..."

They accepted it; however, being scrupulous, they did not accept rag-robes, thinking, “Only one kind of robe has been permitted by the Blessed One, not two. They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“I allow you, monks, when accepting a robe from a householder, to also accept a rag-robe. Monks, I praise contentment with both of these.”

Regarding this, the Commentary states: “Therein, when they thought, ‘Only one robe was permitted by the Blessed One, not two,’ they understood the meaning of the phrase ‘with an itarītara robe’ to be ‘either one given by a householder or a rag from a dust heap.
In that context, however, ‘even with an itarītara’ means ‘with whatever [robe] it may be, whether of little value or of great value. Therefore, it is a dhutaṅga.”
Even for a monk who does not formally undertake [the practice], it is permissible to accept a robe from a householder simply by accepting a small amount of rag-robe material;
however, for one who maintains the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) of the rag-robe, a robe from a householder is not allowed.
This should be understood as being due to the formal undertaking: "I reject robes from householders; I undertake the ascetic practice of the rag-robe wearer."
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were traveling along a highway in the Kosala country.
Some of those bhikkhus entered a charnel ground for the sake of rag-robes, while others did not wait.
Those bhikkhus who entered the charnel ground obtained rag-robes; those bhikkhus who...
They did not come, and they said, “Friends, give us a share as well.
They replied, “Friends, we will not give you a share; why did you not come? They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, I allow that for those who do not come, a share need not be given against their will. In this context, “those who did not come” means until—
They were coming from the cemetery; they did not wait for them, but simply departed.
"Not unwillingly" means not out of a lack of desire to give; however, if they so wish, it should be given.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were traveling along a highway in the Kosala country.
They were there. Some monks entered the charnel ground for the sake of rag-robes; some monks remained behind.
Those monks who had entered the charnel ground for the sake of rag-robes obtained rag-robes.
Those monks who had remained behind said, "Friends, give us a share as well. They replied, "We do not..."
"Friends, we will give you your share; why did you not come down? They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
"Monks, I allow that for those who are waiting, a share may be given even against their will.
Now at that time, a number of monks were traveling along a highway in the Kosala country.
It happened that some monks entered the charnel ground first for the sake of rag-robes, while other monks entered later.
Those monks who had entered the charnel ground first obtained rag-robes;
those who entered later did not obtain any. They said, "Friends, we too..."
“Give us a share. They replied, “Friends, we will not give you a share;
why did you arrive so late? They reported this matter to the Blessed One. [The Blessed One said: “Monks, I allow that a share need not be given to those who arrive late against their will.”
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were traveling along a highway in the Kosala country.
They entered a charnel ground together for the purpose of seeking rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*). Some bhikkhus obtained rag-robes, while some bhikkhus did not obtain any.
Those bhikkhus who did not obtain any said, “For us too...”
“Friends, give us a share. They replied, “Friend, we will not give you a share;

why did you not receive one? They reported this matter to the Blessed One: “Monks, I allow that a share be given to those who have entered the rains residence together with equals, even if they do not wish for it.”
In that context, "they waited" means they remained in the vicinity. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Monks, I allow you to give a portion to those who are waiting, even if they are unwilling. "Vicinity" refers to the area near the charnel ground.

However, if people give [the remains] thinking, "Let those who have come here take them," or if they go away after making a sign, thinking, "Let those who arrive take them," then for those who have arrived...
It accrues to all of them. If she has been abandoned and they have gone their separate ways, he by whom she was taken is the owner.
"They entered the cemetery together" means either that they all entered simultaneously or that they entered in the same direction.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were traveling along a highway in the Kosala country.
They made a division and went to the charnel ground for the sake of rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*).
Some monks obtained rag-robes, while some monks did not obtain any. Those monks who did not obtain any said, "Friends, give us a share as well.
They replied, "Friends, we will not give you a share."
"Why did you not receive it? They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
"Monks, I allow that when those who have entered [the monastery] have made an agreement, a portion may be given to them even against their will. Therein, "having made an agreement" means:
having made an agreement outside [the monastery], thinking, "We shall all take whatever rag-robes are obtained after dividing them up. "Having discarded and gone" means...

They departed after discarding it without saying anything at all. By this, it is shown that when something is discarded with the words, "Let the monks take it," a share must indeed be given even against one's will;
however, when it is merely discarded and there is no prior agreement (*katikā*), if many enter together, the share must not be given against the will of the one who took it.
Those whose directions are the same—namely, those divided into the east and so forth—are called "similar" (*sadisa*).
He said: "They descended in one direction.

In the Discourse on the Robe that was Not Cut Off (Acchinnacīvarakathā), the "gradual discourse" (anupubbakathā) refers to a systematic exposition of the legal determination. Regarding the remaining requisites...
Because the lower robe and upper robe had already been taken by the co-residents (*saddhivihārika*), only the remaining items were left; thus he said, "having brought only the lower and upper robes.

It was stated, "The elders should not eat... [etc. ...until the co-residents have either arrived or not yet arrived," because they did not know whether the co-residents would come or not. "They receive for the sake of others" means their own robes.
Because they are giving it away while concealing it with a break-off from their own branch, they are permitted to break [the branches] even for their own sake.
Since there is the statement, "One should come having covered [the path] with grass or leaves," in such cases, the destruction of vegetation (*bhūtagāmapātabyatā*) is indeed permitted;
thus he says, "There is no offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for the destruction of vegetation. It is not [an offense] in their possession.
“Dukkaṭa”: there is no offense of wrong-doing even in wearing those banners of the heretics;
the connection is that they give them their robes. Because the robes were given by the elders themselves, it is said: “because he stands in the place of one whose robe has been stolen.
If he adopts their tenets, he is called one who has gone over to the faction of the heretics. Therefore it is said: “the tenet...”
Regarding the phrase "if he does not take it": by the rule, "If there is none, [taking] a robe belonging to the Saṅgha from a monastery...

[down to] ...there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," an offense of wrong-doing is stated for one who, having departed from the monastery entered upon the road, goes elsewhere to a place of his own choosing. And by this [rule], "the dwelling which he first enters," [an offense is stated] on the road.
It should be understood that even while staying in a monastery, if one goes about naked, it is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

If one asks, "If this is so, why was it not stated there?"—it is because there was no occasion for it. For in that context, by way of the connection: "I allow you, monks, for one whose robe has been stolen...
to request a robe," it is permitted to wear and wrap oneself in even a robe belonging to the Saṅgha.

By permitting, he said, "Having first taken whichever dwelling... one may wear it"; therefore, because there was no room for it [in that context], an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) was not mentioned.
"Monastery robe" means a robe used as a lodging. "With scraps of cloth" means with pieces of cotton rags. "On top of that" means on top of the floor-covering.
"By one who has gone abroad" means by one who has gone abroad without obtaining another robe. "In one place... it should be placed."
In this context, because it was brought having been taken with the remainder, and because it was set aside specifically for the purpose of communal use by the Saṅgha,
they say that even if it has been designated for one particular lodging, it is permissible to place it elsewhere.
"By means of use alone" means by using it when no other robe-cloth is obtained.
"Worn out through use" means worn out to such an extent that it is no longer possible to cover the body with that robe.
"By means of a transaction involving allowable goods" is stated for the purpose of releasing one from the offense of buying and selling.
The phrase "to one who asks for it" clarifies the meaning of this very term as "to one who causes it to be purchased or exchanged. For asking for it by means of one's own wealth is what is meant.

The intended meaning is that it is merely a change of name. He shows the proper conduct regarding the solicitation of those who have been invited by the Saṅgha with the words, "only the [stipulated] measure is permissible.
For when one has been invited by the Saṅgha, because it is common to all, it is not permissible to solicit for more than that.
"Whatever he invites" means whatever robe-material or other requisites he invites for, thinking, "I will give this. This refers to the act of soliciting.
"There is not" means that because it is being given without an explicit request (*viññatti*), the intention is: "What will he do after having requested it?

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of another," here too the words "for relatives who have invited [him]" continue to apply; thus he says, "to one's own relatives who have invited [him]," and so forth.

The four factors here are: the robe being of a type suitable for distribution, the absence of a [valid] occasion (*samaya*), the requesting of one who is not a relative, and the acquisition [of the robe] through that [request].
In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it is stated that "an invitation to the Dhamma" (*dhammanimantanā*) refers to an invitation consisting merely of the rules of conduct to be observed among recluses;
the meaning is that it is not an invitation made out of a desire to give. For this very reason, it says, "he shall request.
Indeed, what is called "requesting" (*viññatti*) occurs only from one who is unrelated and has not been previously invited.

By the statement, "One should come having covered [the ground] with grass or leaves," it is indicated that the destruction of living plants is permitted; thus he said, "nor by way of destroying living plants," and so forth.

Even one who first takes the outward signs with a pure mind but later adopts a different doctrine is still one who has gone over to another sect (a *titthiyapakkantaka*); thus he said, "even after putting on the robes, the doctrine must not be adopted."
"Whichever residence he first enters": here too, even when entering for the sake of a dwelling, robes, or other necessities, one must go after covering [the body] with grass or similar materials;
for it is stated as a general rule that "one must not come naked," which constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"With rags" means with pieces of discarded cloth. "By use alone" means by using [the robe] without having obtained another robe.
"Old through use" means that it has become worn out and unsuitable because, while being used, the robe has become tattered and frayed.
Regarding "for the sake of another," here too the phrase "for kinsmen who have invited him" continues to apply; thus he said, "for his own kinsmen who have invited him," and so forth.
But here, it refers to the case of one whose robe has been stolen or lost, [making it] for the sake of another who is neither a kinsman nor one who has invited him.
The meaning to be understood is that there is no offense for one who makes [the food] known while using a *nissaggiya* [robe];
otherwise, there would be no distinction from the phrase "for those who are relatives" or "for those who have invited [one]. For this very reason, he will say in the subsequent training rule:

"In the commentaries, however, it is stated that at the place where one is invited by a relative... only the proper measure is permitted; that does not agree with the Canon (Pāḷi). And: "But since this training rule..."
It was prescribed specifically regarding the matter of requesting for the sake of another; therefore, the phrase "for the sake of another" is not mentioned here.

Furthermore, the four factors in this case are: the robe being in a state suitable for assignment, the absence of a [permissible] occasion, the request made by one who is not a relative, and the acquisition [of the robe] through that [request].
“If an unrelated householder or householder’s wife should invite a monk to bring many robes for him, that monk may accept from them robes up to the limit of an inner and an outer robe;
if he should accept more than that, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
In this training rule regarding what is beyond that, the word *abhī* in the phrase *abhihaṭṭhum* means:
“Upasaggo” means “to take”; that is, “to seize,” as it is said. “Pavāreyya” means “he should cause to desire,” “he should arouse a wish or preference,” “he should speak,” or “he should invite.

Regarding the manner in which one who invites [another] to take what has been brought should speak—in order to show that mode of address, the word-commentary (padabhājana) for him is: “Take as much as you desire.”

It has been said. Alternatively, just as in the phrase “having seen renunciation as security,” the meaning is “having seen,” so too here, “he should invite by bringing” means “he should invite after having brought.

In that regard, there are two kinds of bringing: bringing by body and bringing by speech. For either by body one brings robes and so forth, places them at the feet [of the recipient], and says, “As much as...”
If one should invite [the donor] by saying, "Take as much as you wish," or if one should invite by saying with words,
"Our storehouse of cloth is full; take as much as you wish"—
both of these together are what is meant by the expression "should invite by bringing forth."
"Having the inner robe and the upper robe as the maximum" means that for this robe, the inner robe (*sāntara*) and the upper robe (*uttara*) are the limit;
what is meant is that together with the lower garment (*nivāsana*), the upper robe constitutes the highest allowable measure.
"From that, the robe may be accepted" means that from among the robes brought forward, only so much robe-cloth may be taken, and nothing beyond this; such is the meaning.
Since, however, it is only for a monk who possesses exactly three robes and whose entire set has not been lost that he must practice in this manner—
whereas for others it may be done differently— it is therefore stated in the word-commentary by way of the phrase "if the three are lost," etc., in order to show that distinction.
In this regard, the analysis is as follows: for one whose three robes are lost, two may be accepted;
having dressed in one and wrapped himself in another, he will seek another from a similar source. For one whose two are lost, one may be accepted.
If he normally goes about with only an inner and upper garment, two may be accepted; thus, by accepting just one, he remains equal [to the rule].
It will come to pass. For one who has lost one of the three, it should not be accepted. But for one who has lost one of the two, one may be accepted.
For one who has only one remaining, and that too is lost, two may be accepted.
