However, for a bhikkhunī, even when all five are lost, two may be accepted; when four are lost, one may be accepted; and when three are lost—
Nothing at all should be accepted, let alone two or one. For by whatever means one must remain with no more than an inner and outer robe;
beyond that, nothing is permitted—this is the characteristic here.
"I will bring the remainder" means: having made two robes, one will bring the rest again. "Not because it was cut off."

They give by virtue of qualities such as great learning (*bāhusacca*). Regarding the phrases "of relatives" and so forth, the meaning is that there is no offense for one who consents when relatives give, or when those invited (*pavārita*) give, or when one consents to [receiving] with one's own wealth.

However, in the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is said: "In the case of relatives or those who have invited one, even a large amount is normally permissible; however, in the case of those whose property has been confiscated, only the prescribed measure is permissible."

What was stated does not accord with the Pāḷi. However, because this training rule was laid down specifically regarding the instance of requesting for the sake of another, the phrase "for the sake of another" is not mentioned here.
The remainder is of plain meaning. Regarding the origin and other factors:

this too has six origins; it is an action (kiriya); it is not released by recognition (no-saññāvimokkha); it is without mental fault (acittaka); it is an offense of formal rule (paṇṇattivajja); and it consists of bodily and verbal action (kāyakamma-vacīkamma).
“Three minds, three feelings.
In the seventh [section], *paggāhikasāla* refers to the shop of cloth merchants; they also read it as *paggāhitasāla*.
The prefix *abhi-* indicates the absence of a specific meaning for it; therefore he said, “the meaning is ‘to take away’ (*harituṃ*). Regarding the word *vara-*...

Because it exists in the form of a wish, he said, "one may wish. In the phrase *daṭṭhu khemato*, the elision of the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*) should be understood as being for the sake of metrical composition (*gāthābandha*).
*Sāntara* means together with the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*). *Uttara* means the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).
*Assa cīvarassa* refers to the robe that is to be accepted. *Acchinnasabbacīvarena* means by one whose all three robes have been stolen.
"One whose robes are not cut off" means one for whom all robes have not been taken away; this is the meaning.

For when, at the time of being robbed, three robes are present and all of them remain uncut, he is called "one whose all robes are not cut off. It is for this very reason that it is said: "by one whose all robes are not cut off, by one who possesses the three robes. Regarding the term "by one who possesses the three robes":

This was stated with reference to the fact that the three robes were kept together at the time of the confiscation, but not with reference to the status of being a "three-robed one" (*tecīvarika*) in the Vinaya, nor with reference to the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) of being a three-robed one.
"One should proceed in this manner" means one should proceed according to the rule stated thus:
"That bhikkhu may accept a robe from him, provided it does not exceed the inner and outer robes. "By another" means...
"With all robes uncut": the meaning is that it applies to one for whom one or two of the three robes have not been cut.
"In another way as well" means in a manner other than the rule stated as "having the inner and outer robes as the maximum.
For one whose two of the three robes have not been cut, one [robe] may be accepted; when one [robe] has been cut, it must not be accepted.
For him, the acceptance of an inner and outer robe as the maximum is not possible. And this very meaning is clarified by the word-commentary (*padabhājana*).
Therefore he said: "in order to show that distinction.
However, some [hold that] because it is stated "by one who possesses three robes," one may use the three robes after having determined them as requisites-cloths (*parikkhāracoḷa*).
Some say that when that [robe] is lost, one is permitted to take many [others]; however, that should not be accepted.
For, by one who intends to show the meaning of the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), it was stated: "But because he has had all his robes taken away... [etc. ...in order to show that distinction.
And since such a meaning is not found in the word-commentary, therefore that [interpretation] must certainly not be accepted. As for what [is further said]:
In the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* it is stated: “For one who has determined his three robes, [if] the three are lost.
In this context, too, the inclusion of the term “determined” (*adhiṭṭhita*) should be understood as a mere description of the actual state;

however, it should not be taken to mean that the robe must have been determined by means of the formal determination of the triple-robe (*ticīvara*), because such a meaning is impossible according to both the Canon (*pāḷi*) and the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

Indeed, it cannot be understood that this training rule was prescribed solely for one who has already formally resolved (*adhiṭṭhita*) his robes by means of the resolution regarding the three robes (*ticīvarādhiṭṭhāna*).
For, since the previous training rule permitted a request from an unrelated person for one whose robes had been stolen,
the Blessed One— by permitting the acceptance of a request within the specific case of requesting without knowing the measure, even when exceeding the measure— [established this rule].

The training rule has been laid down; therefore, the notion that it is permissible for one who possesses the requisite robes (*parikkhāra-coḷika*) to accept even a great deal more is neither consistent with the Canon (*pāḷi*) nor does it accord with the Blessed One’s intention.
Regarding the statement, "He whose three [robes] are lost may accept two," this refers to one whose robe exceeds the triple set of robes (*ticīvara*).
It should be understood that if there is [a robe] kept elsewhere, it is permissible to accept it as well, because at that time it would otherwise be impossible to obtain that robe.

“He lives with only a single inner and outer robe” means that he lives either by virtue of the training rule concerning risky situations (*sāsaṅka-sikkhāpada*), or by virtue of the authorization for non-separation (*avippavāsa-sammuti*), or because he has not obtained a third robe.
It is said, “two are lost,” because of the context; therefore, it is said, “two are to be accepted.”
"One will be the same as one who consents to only one" means that when two of the three robes are lost,
he will be the same as one who consents to only one, because both abide in the state where the inner and outer robes are the maximum permitted.
"He who has only one" is said with reference to one whose remaining robe has been destroyed for some other reason.

Because it is said, “She gives [the food] thinking, ‘Let the remainder be yours alone,’” even after saying, “We will take what is appropriate in measure; we will bring the remainder,” and taking it, at the time of departure they say, “Let even the remainder be yours alone”; this is indeed permissible for those who have been invited (*pavārita*).

“For those who have been invited” means for those who have already been invited prior to the time of the interruption. It does not accord with the Canon because [the rule] states that one may accept no more than an inner and outer robe (*santaruttara-paramato*).

Because it is stated, "There is no offense for relatives or those who have invited one," this does not accord with the purpose of showing that there is no offense for accepting more than [the prescribed amount].
For there is no possibility of an offense at all for one who accepts only the inner and outer robes (*santaruttara*);

and the intention is that, since there would otherwise be the possibility of an offense due to the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), it is appropriate to show that there is no offense. However, some [hold] that "only the measure..."
They say that the phrase "it is allowable" is stated for the purpose of showing moderation (*sallekha*).
However, as for the passage beginning "because this... is not stated," the intended meaning here is as follows:

if it were said "for the sake of another," one would fall into the position that it is allowable to take even beyond the prescribed measure for the sake of others; and that [case] was already addressed in the context of the offense regarding soliciting for the sake of another.

When compared with the basis for its formulation, it does not accord; for it is not logical to state that there is no offense regarding the very same matter upon which the training rule was formulated.
However, in the three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, it is stated:
"Because this training rule functions by way of being dependent on one's own consent, it is said: 'for the sake of another.'"
It is stated that "there is no occasion [for it], therefore it was not mentioned. Here, since it is not stated "for the sake of another," one might ask:

is there an offense for one who solicits more than what is permitted from those invited by relatives for the sake of others? No, because in that case, non-offense is established by the preceding training rule itself.

[The factors are: being inferior to that [original amount], the cause of it being uncut and so forth, the solicitation of one who is not a relative, and the obtaining thereof through that [solicitation].
These are the four factors here.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: “In the text, ‘the shop for taking up cloth’ (*paggāhikasālā*) refers to a cloth shop.
For that is called a ‘shop for taking up cloth’ because it is a place where cloth is taken up by merchants. ‘Of this robe-cloth’ (*assa cīvarassa*) means of the robe-cloth that is to be accepted.”
"By one who possesses only three robes" (tecīvarikena): by this, he shows the absence of any other robe than the three that have been cut off, which might be kept in a monastery or elsewhere.
If such were available, it would not be permissible to ask for more; rather, having worn a temporary robe, one's own robe should be taken back.
For one who does not obtain even a temporary robe, [the rule permits] making a roof-covering with grass and leaves after clearing away vegetation.
Even making a request as if [one were] oneself is indeed permissible. "By another" means by one who does not have an unseized or complete robe.

The statement "two may be accepted" is said because of the governing context of "two are lost. It does not accord with the Canon because it does not agree with this canonical passage: "There is no offense in the case of relatives or those who have invited [one].
This is because [the rule] was stated specifically regarding the offense incurred in requesting more than that. "For the sake of another" means...
The phrase "it was not said" indicates this meaning: that there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya) for requesting more than that for the sake of another.
And as for that expiation, it would belong either to those for whose sake one requests, or to the requester himself;
yet it does not belong to those [for whom one requested], because they did not request it, nor does it belong to the requester, because he did not request it for his own sake.
Therefore, even when one causes [an object] to be made for the sake of another, an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) is not seen [to apply].

However, they say that because this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) operates by way of being dependent on one’s own approval, the phrase "for the sake of another" is not mentioned in the section on non-offenses (*anāpatti-vāra*);
and that appears reasonable, yet it should be accepted after careful investigation.
"Excessiveness regarding robes, the cause of having no [other] robes, requesting from one who is not a relative, and the acquisition through that—these are the four factors here.

Although this analysis of the training rule on excessiveness was not stated by the Teacher, we have included it because it pertains specifically to the section concerning those whose robes have been stolen;
for it applies during the periods of the training rule on requesting from one who is not a relative, namely at the time when one's robes have been stolen.

The Blessed One has stated that one may request [robes] from those who are unrelated; he has also stated, by means of a subsequent training rule, that one should take only a moderate amount of the robe-cloth given by them.
Therefore, this refers specifically to the case of one whose robe has been stolen.
This concludes the discussion on the determination of the theft of robes.
From here on, we shall explain the determination regarding the taking away of robes by way of commonality with theft. In this context, the phrase "I will give to you" means "I will give to you.
It is said that he gave [the items] thinking, "Carrying my bowl, robes, sandals, and rugs, he will set out on a journey with me.
Therefore he said, "He will set out on a journey through the countryside with me."
"Seizes by force" means he took it by means of physical compulsion; however, because he took it under the perception that it was his own, there is no *pārājika* offense.
An offense is prescribed because he took it after having caused [the owner] distress.
"He himself seizes; it is a *nissaggiya pācittiya*" refers to one who seizes a single robe or many robes tied together as one.
There is one offense for one who does not cut off [the robes] that are unfastened on one side and remain separate in many places;
and there are offenses according to the number of items for one who causes them to be brought, saying, "Bring the outer robe (saṅghāṭī)," or "Bring the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga).
Even for one who says, "Bring all those given by me," there are numerous offenses by that single utterance alone.
"Orders another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means: if one orders, "Take the robe," there is one offense of wrong-doing.

If the one ordered takes many, there is one offense of expiation (pācittiya). For one who says, "Take the outer cloak (saṅghāṭi), take the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga)," there is an offense of wrong-doing for every word.
For one who says, "Take all that was given by me," there are numerous offenses in a single utterance.
"Another requisite" refers to anything at all, even down to a needle, with the exception of the last robe that has reached the stage of being formally assigned (*vikappanupaga*).
Even in the case of needles placed inside a sheath, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for each item counted. It is the same when they are wrapped loosely.
However, according to the *Mahāpaccarī*, if they are tied up tightly, there is only one offense of wrong-doing. This also applies to those inserted into a needle-case.
The same method applies here. Having placed it in a bag, the same method applies to medicinal substances such as *tikaṭuka* and so forth, whether they are tied loosely or tied tightly.
"He gives it" means he gives it saying, "Venerable sir, this is suitable for you alone," or alternatively, "Friend, we will perform the duties of service for you;
we will receive the formal acceptance (*upajjhā*) from you; [we will listen to] the Dhamma..."

When he is told, "We gave you this robe-cloth thinking, 'He will master the Dhamma,' yet now you do not perform the proper duties, you do not take a preceptor, and you do not master the Dhamma," and he replies, "Venerable sir, I suppose you say this for the sake of the robe;
here, I give it to you," and thus he gives it; or else, when a young monk has gone away in some direction, [he says], "Bring him back."
If he says, “No,” and does not turn back, [the monks] should say, “Take his robe and block him. If he turns back in this way, it is well.
If he gives it, saying, “I suppose you are speaking for the sake of the bowl and robe; take them,” even in that case, he is giving it himself.
Or, seeing that he has gone away, [they may think], “We gave the bowl and robe thinking, ‘He will perform the duties for you.’”
If he says, "I am [your teacher]; you are now wandering about after having disrobed," and the other replies, "Take back your bowl and robes," and thus he gives them;
or if he says, "I give them only to one who receives the *upajjhāya*-ship from me, not to one who receives it elsewhere;
I give them only to one who performs the duties (*vatta*), not to one who does not; I give them only to one who masters the Dhamma..."
"I do not give to one who does not master it; I give only to one who does not disrobe, but I do not give to one who disrobes.
However, it is not permissible to give in this manner; for one who gives thus, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Yet, it is permissible to have [the robe] brought back.

One who takes back what was given after it had been relinquished must be dealt with according to the value of the goods. The rest here is self-evident. This is the decision extracted from the *Samantapāsādikā*.
Regarding the phrase *yampi tyāhaṃ*: here *yaṃ* is a word expressing a reason. Therefore, the connection here should be understood as follows:
“Because of that reason—namely, ‘he will set out on a journey through the countryside with me’—that I gave you a robe, friend, you do not act accordingly”;
thus, being angry and displeased, he took it back. Alternatively, *yaṃ* refers to the robe.

In this context, it should be connected as follows: "Thinking, 'He will set out on a journey through the countryside with me,' and 'I shall take back that robe which I gave to him,' he, being angry and displeased, took it away.
When one who has been commanded takes many, there is one *pācittiya* offense because the command "Take the robe" pertains to the single object of a robe.
There is only one *pācittiya*. Regarding the statement "for every utterance, there is a *dukkaṭa*," this refers to the *pācittiya*s according to the number of items taken away.
The phrase "many offenses for a single utterance" is said with reference to the *pācittiya* offense that must be incurred according to the number of items taken away;
however, the *dukkaṭa* that must be incurred for the command itself is only one.

By this [phrase], he refers to the statement: “There are *dukkaṭa* offenses according to the number of items. “In the same manner” extends by analogy both the multiplicity and the singularity of the offenses regarding robes that have been offered, whether loosely or tightly.
In cases such as “Friend, may I...,” even though it was spoken with the desire to take [the robe] for oneself, there is no offense because it was given by that very person.
“He will receive the *upajjhāya*-ship in our presence”: this indicates that the giving is valid even for a novice (*sāmaṇera*); therefore, although [this is not explicitly stated] in the Pāḷi...

It is stated, “having given a robe to a bhikkhu himself”; nevertheless, it should be understood that even if one gives it while [the recipient] is not yet fully ordained, there is still a *pācittiya* offense for one who takes it back once he has become fully ordained.
Here, the fact of his being fully ordained at the very moment of the taking back is the sole criterion.
“Gives” means he gives either out of pleasure or out of anger. “Restrain him” means prevent him. But thus...
Regarding the statement "it is not allowable to give": it should be understood that what has been given in this manner must not be used until one has formally resolved, "This belongs to him.
However, it is allowable to have it brought back; because such a gift is similar to a wage (*bhata*), it is allowable to have it brought back.
"Given after having relinquished" means: according to the method already stated, without giving it away and without being free from concern for it, [it is given] to that very person.

"Given. "He is to be dealt with according to the value of the goods": one who takes [the robe] without the perception that it is his own is to be dealt with for an offense after having the goods appraised.

The five factors here are: the robe being of the minimum size suitable for dedication (*vikappanupaga*), its having been given by oneself, the absence of the perception that it is one's own, the person being fully ordained (*upasampanna*), and the act of snatching away or causing it to be snatched away out of anger. This is the reading from the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, regarding the passage "Even though... he took it back," it should be construed by supplying the words:
"When I gave you that robe-cloth, I gave it with the perception that 'he would depart together with me,' not otherwise; yet, being angry, he took it back.
As for the single *dukkaṭa*: if one who has been commanded necessarily takes it back, [the offense occurs] at the moment of the command.
In this way, it is a *pācittiya*. If he does not take it away, then it should be understood as a *dukkaṭa* at that very moment. Regarding "many offenses by a single utterance":

if one who has been commanded takes [the robe] without obstruction, then at the very moment of the command, there are *pācittiya* offenses according to the number of objects (*vatthu*), because the offense is incurred at the very moment the action is performed; however, the robe is only *nissaggiya* once it has actually been taken away.
It occurs. If he does not take it back, it should be understood that there is only one *dukkaṭa* at the moment of the command.
In this way, the same principle should be known for other similar cases as well. "He will take up the preceptorship" indicates the giving [of the robe] to a novice;

by that, it also indicates the *pācittiya* offense even if one takes it back after having given it while he was a novice, once he has received full ordination. "Having personally given a robe to a bhikkhu..."
This was stated by way of the maximum limit. However, it is said that "it is permissible to have it brought back" because, when the legal action has not yet been performed, it is similar to a debt.
It is stated: "The five factors here are: the robe being the last one that has reached the stage of being allowable;
its having been given by oneself; the perception that it is one's own; the person being fully ordained; and either the taking away or causing to be taken away out of anger."
6. Discussion on the Paintings of Inspiration:
In this discussion on the paintings of inspiration, nothing is said in the *Sāratthadīpanī* because it is easily understood according to the method already stated in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated: "It is not permissible to say 'Do it,' because that would be a mere command."
Because it has been prohibited, it is permissible to speak to the gatekeeper by way of such expressions as, “Why do you not do [your duty]?
The phrase “a figure of a Jātaka” (jātakapakaraṇa) refers to any form whatsoever—whether female, male, or otherwise—that is connected with a Jātaka.
Since it is stated, “to have it made by others,” it is said that one does not even permit oneself to make an image of the Buddha.

The Discussion on Food Not Yet Fully Prepared (Vippakatabhojanakathā). 7. Regarding this discussion on food not yet fully prepared (*vippakata*), nothing is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, the *Vimativinodanī*, or the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*.
"First made" means "prepared"; "not yet finished" when prepared is "partially prepared" (*vippakata*). "Partially prepared" [is the term used].
"One who has left off eating" (*vippakatabhojana*) refers to a monk who, having first eaten, has not yet finished the task of eating.
The connection is that the monk must enter [the village] in this state. Regarding the statement "It is not even permitted to send him away empty-handed," the reason is given as:
"For he is indeed one who has left off eating," even if he has already drunk rice-gruel or chewed solid food.
Because he has not yet eaten his meal, his duty of eating is not finished.
"He is one who has been invited" means that since he is unable to eat after having risen from his seat once invited, he must be told [to wait] while water is not available near him;
the rest is easily understood.
The Discussion on One Teaching and Causing Another to Teach (Uddisantauddisāpanakathā) 8.

Regarding this discussion on one teaching and causing another to teach: "by one teaching" (*uddisantenā*) means by one giving the recitation, that is, by one causing [the other] to recite the text (*pāḷi*);

"by one causing to teach" (*uddisāpentenā*) means by one receiving the recitation, that is, by one causing [the other] to recite the text. By the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "even when speaking loudly" (*uccatarepi*),...
It groups [the cases] together under the same seat. The same principle applies here even for "a lower one.
9. Discussion on the Three-Year Interval:
In this discussion on the three-year interval, *tivassaṃ* means three years, or *tivassāni* means three years; [it refers to] those of three years.
“*Tivassantaraṃ*” means within three years; one who stands within three years is called “*tivassantaro*.

By that “*tivassantarena*,” the word *antara* expresses the sense of “in the middle,” and the suffix *-ṇa* is used in the sense of location (*ṭhitatthe*). Therefore, it is said in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*:
“*Tivassantarenā* means by one standing within the interval of three years. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, showing the actual form itself, it says: “*Tivassantaro*...”
He said, “Names,” and so forth. “All these” means all these three kinds of those who share a seat. The rest is easy to understand.
Regarding the discussion on long seats (dīghāsana):
in this discussion, “portable” refers to things suitable for being carried away, such as mats and the like; “non-portable” refers to [fixed] items.

A long seat (*dīghāsana*) is one that cannot be carried away by the wind, such as a stone seat or the like. Therefore, it is said in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: “A long seat is anything other than a bed or a chair that is sufficient for three people to sit together comfortably. Now, one might raise the objection: why is it stated that it must be “sufficient for three”? Is not even a seat sufficient for two people considered long? [The response to this objection follows:]... [text continues] ...it is because it is intended to include all types of long seats, such as those made of wood or bamboo. Furthermore, it is said that the rule regarding the long seat applies specifically to seats used for sitting; it does not apply to beds or couches, which are used for lying down. Thus, the definition of a long seat is established as being sufficient for three people to sit together comfortably.

This is the meaning intended here. *Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with the objection regarding the necessity of seating three people. The translation above reflects the full logical structure of the argument as presented in the commentary.*

Having intended this, he said: “I allow... pe ... this much is called a ‘long seat at the back’. For when there is a seat sufficient for two people that is not a long seat, it is permissible to sit together with those who share the same seat;

however, when a long seat is taken from the point where it is sufficient for three people onwards, it is permissible to sit together even with those who do not share the same seat. If this is so, [then] even with eunuchs and others...
Thinking, "It would be appropriate to sit together," and taking the censure to heart, he said: "I allow you, monks, excepting a paṇḍaka," and so forth.
In this regard, the meaning is easy to understand.
The Discussion on Attending the Sick.
11. In the discourse on attending to the sick, "fallen into" (*palipanno*) means submerged; the meaning is "besmeared. "Having lifted up" (*uccāretvā*) means having raised [the patient].

Regarding the term "one who has the same teacher" (*samānācariyako*): here they say, "Even if one teacher has one resident pupil (*antevāsiko*) and another attendant pupil (*saddhivihāriko*), these too are indeed 'those who have the same teacher' with respect to one another.
"He is unable to compound medicine" means he is incapable of preparing it.
The meaning is that he was unable to act accordingly when the physician said, "Having taken this and that medicine, you must mix it with this and give it.
"To clear away" (nīhātuṃ) means to remove; the meaning is to discard. In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it says:
"'He made a plaster on the ground' means that having washed the soiled spot on the ground where the sick person was lying, he smeared it with green grass."
The meaning is "she caused [it] to be done. It is said: "One who is unable to compound medicine is also unable to carry out the procedure prescribed by others.
Regarding the discourse on praising death (maraṇavaṇṇakathā): "Being desirous of death itself" means that their intention is to reach heaven upon the breaking up of this body.

In terms of meaning, they are indeed those who desire death. "Not knowing their state of desiring death" means not knowing their own state of desiring death, thinking, "Those with such an intention are called 'desirers of death'";

for it is not that they do not know the movement of their own minds. "By way of conventional usage" means by way of the preliminary conventional usage, at the moment of the volition that determines the intention to die.
The intention is that, due to the absence of compassion (*karuṇā*), it does not happen—as in the case of releasing a pig caught in a snare—out of a sense of pity (*kāruñña*).

The phrase "according to his lifespan" (*yathāyuka*) is stated by way of a synonym for the meaning already expressed as "according to the connection" (*yathānusandhi*); by "according to the connection," it is meant "according to the limit of the lifespan.
Alternatively, "according to the connection" means according to the continuous succession (*yathānuppabandha*), [lasting] as long as the continuum (*santāna*) exists in that particular existence.
It means that it proceeds without interruption; in other words, it persists for that long.
In the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: "By way of conventional usage" means by way of the preliminary conventional usage.

Because at the moment of the decisive volition of one intending death, there is an absence of compassion, it does not occur through pity—as in the case of releasing a boar caught in a snare—this is the intended meaning. "'According to its lifespan' (*yathāyu*)..."
"It is said that this very same meaning has been stated by way of another method according to the sequence [of the text]. However, in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, it is explained:
"'Being desirous of death' means that because they have the intention of reaching heaven through the breaking up of this body, they are in fact desirous of death in terms of their actual purpose.
'Those who have such an intention are called desirous of death'—thus [it shows] one's own state of being desirous of death."
"Those who have committed an offense while being unaware of it have fallen into a *pārājika*. For it is not said that they do not know the movement of their own minds.

'By way of conventional usage' means by way of conventional usage prior [to the final decision]; however, this does not apply once the decision has been reached, as it is not like releasing a pig caught in a snare.
'According to the sequence of connection' means without dying in the interim; such is what was stated."
Attapātanakathā 13.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the variation of case-endings" (*vibhattivyattayena*), it means by means of the transformation of case-endings (*vibhattivipariṇāmena*).

"The attainment of distinction" (*visesādhigamo*) refers to both concentration (*samādhi*) and insight (*vipassanā*). Because they are so exceedingly manifest, it is said, "it is seen as if it were already in the palm of one's hand. "He cuts off" (*upacchindati*)— [End of fragment]
He cuts off his food supply so that there may be no distraction from the attainment of distinction (*visesādhigama*).
"Attainment of distinction" refers to the acquisition of supramundane states (*lokuttaradhamma*). "Having declared" means having announced it. "He cuts it off;

it is not proper" means that noble ones announce the distinction they have attained only to fellow monks who possess a sense of shame (*lajjī*) when such a circumstance arises, and those monks [are] unsuitable...
The meaning is that they do not seek requisites through improper means; therefore, it is not permissible to cause remorse regarding the requisites sought by them and then cut off their food.
For, because they are of like status (*sabhāga*), one does not get to cut it off.
They indeed announce the field of what is allowable (*kappiya-khetta*). For that very reason, it is said: "For it is right to speak to fellow monks who are modest..."
"In the three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries it is stated: 'It is permissible'—this was said by way of showing the reason for [the rule] 'he interrupts [the meal], it is not permissible.
Alternatively, 'having declared the attainment of distinction' (*visesādhigama*) is said for the purpose of showing the state of having attained distinction;
and because the cutting off of food is permitted only by one who suspects an obstacle to attainment, [it is said] by one who has attained [distinction]."
In order to show that [this] should not be done, it was said: "Having announced his special attainment, he cuts off his food; this is not allowable.
To the objection, "But do the Noble Ones announce to others the special attainment they have themselves realized?", it was said:
"It is allowable to speak to fellow monks who are modest. This, in our view, is the more reasonable position here.
In the *Gaṇṭhipada* as well, this meaning has indeed been shown.

In the *Vimativinodanī* it is also stated: "By the change of case-endings means by the transformation of the grammatical case. ‘Attainment of distinction’ refers to both concentration (*samādhi*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
‘The attainment of distinction’ refers to the acquisition of supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*). ‘Having explained’ means having announced."

And this was said for the purpose of showing that a distinction has been attained. For monks who possess a sense of shame, having attained a distinction, must inevitably declare their attainment so that others may follow their example;
yet, even if they do not declare it because of a distinction they have attained, it is not permissible for them to cut off their food.
This is because the cutting off of food is intended solely to remove obstacles to attainment.
"Because it has been permitted, once that attainment is reached, it need not be performed at all. But is it proper to announce the attainment? To this he says:
'For [the Teacher] toward those who are like-minded,' and so forth. In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, it is said: "It appears as if already within hand's reach;
[the Teacher] cuts short [any hesitation] lest there be distraction on his part, having declared the specific attainment and [thereby receiving] the honor arising from it."
“Feeling ashamed, he stops eating because it has been declared [as such] to those of like standing; for they announce the allowable field,” so it is said.
14. In the discussion on sitting down without reflecting:
“without having reflected” means without having examined closely. Or, upwards...
“Or moving downward” means that they move upward or downward along the seated row in order to make room for those who arrive later.
“There is no need for examination” means there is no need for subsequent investigation by those who have arrived later.
He said, “in which no fold is seen,” meaning that if there were anything [else] below, the lower garment would gather into a fold.
And this reflection should be understood as applying only to what belongs to householders. In the *Vimativinodanī* as well, it is stated only thus:
“Regarding the statement ‘if anything [else] exists below, he takes the fold of the garment,’ it says ‘where no fold is seen.
And this reflection should be understood as applying only to what belongs to householders. In the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā* also, it says: “Without reflecting...”
"Without investigating. For when something exists in the lower part, a fold (vali) appears"—this much only.
In the discourse on the splitting of the rock by Davāya, the word *davā* signifies laughter (*hasa*). It is derived from the verbal root *vidh*, preceded by the prefix *paṭi*.
Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of rolling," he said: "With the intention of making it roll, a stone must not be rolled. Since the word *sila* denotes a stone, he said "not only...
and so forth, referring to the objection that "that very [stone] must not be pierced.
If this were so, it would not be permissible for the sake of anyone; therefore, he said "for the sake of a cetiya, etc. "Washing-stick" refers to a stick used for washing goods.
In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it is stated: “‘Washing the goods’ means washing robes; ‘washing-stick’ means a stick for washing robes.
This concludes the discussion on the plastering of the monastery grounds.

16. In the account concerning the lighting of a fire: "If he lights [it], it is a *pācittiya* offense" means that even if he applies fire to a dry place with this intention, for one who lights it with such an intent, it is indeed a *pācittiya*.

"An offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)" means that for one who applies fire to a dry place, or who applies fire without determining whether a dry place is "not dry," it is a *dukkaṭa*. The same principle applies even when the intention is for sport; if the intention is for sport... [the rule remains the same].
And it should be understood by way of the sound of crackling and the taste of flavor. *Paṭaggi* is a fire that serves as an opponent.
*Parittakaraṇaṃ* means making a protection. "Arising of its own accord" refers to that which arises through the mutual friction of bamboos and the like stirred by the wind.
"Without fuel" (*nirupādāno*) means devoid of combustible material. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: "Even with the intention of play..."
*Dukkaṭa* (an offense of wrong-doing) is said with reference to making fire upon dry grass and the like.

However, if one does so among wet things even with the intention of playing, it is indeed a *pācittiya* (an offense requiring expiation). *Paṭaggi* is a fire that is opposed to, or moves toward, [another fire];
its kindling even upon wet grass and the like is permitted. When kindling it, having seen a forest fire approaching from afar, [one should act].
Without setting it up all around the monastery at once, one should start from a single spot and gradually burn it all around the monastery;
having thus cleared an open space (abbhokāsa) all around the monastery so that even a great fire cannot reach it, a counter-fire (paṭaggi) should be set.
That [counter-fire] goes toward the forest fire, meets it, and unites with it.

"He attains Nibbāna together [with them]. 'The making of a protection' (parittakaraṇa) refers to the performance of guarding, such as cutting down trees and grass on all sides, digging moats, and so forth.
Therefore he said: 'the smoothening of the ground all around the grass huts,' and so on. However, in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, it is stated only as follows:
"'Protection' (paritta) means guarding; in order to demonstrate that, it was said: 'the smoothening of the ground all around,' and so on."
The Discourse on Families Acquired through Wrong View (Micchādiṭṭhikulābhatakathā). 17.
In this discourse on families acquired through wrong view, those who lack faith are called "faithless" (*assaddhā*); they are stingy among those faithless ones.
Families joined with wrong view are "families of wrong view" (*micchādiṭṭhikulāni*); this is a *tatiyātappurisa* compound with the middle term elided (*majjhelopa*).
“Families associated with the ten-based wrong view, which proceeds in the manner of ‘there is no gift’ and so forth;
among them”—this is the connection [with the phrase] “having received from families of wrong view.

Having examined the reason—namely, that for those who act without care there must be a cause for acting with care, and for those who give what is inferior there must be a cause for giving what is superior—one [should act accordingly].
"It is not fit to eat" means: "Without having investigated, one should neither eat it oneself nor give it to others.
To show the reason why this must be so, he said, "Even if it is mixed with poison," and so forth.

To show that it is not only almsfood [that is subject to this], he said, "And whatever else," and so forth. Regarding that, he stated the reason: "Even when the matter has not been concealed," and so forth.
Then he shows another [reason] with the words, "smeared with perfumes, turmeric, and so forth. There too, in order to show the cause, he says, "the locations of disease in the body," and so on.
The Story of the Gift of Gopaka.
18. In the story of the gift of the cowherd (*gopaka*): one who guards and protects what belongs to others is a cowherd;

the gift of such a person is a "cowherd’s gift" (*gopakadāna*), which refers to the gift that should be given to monks by gardeners and others. Regarding the phrase "having posted a notice" (*paṇṇaṃ āropetvā*):

it means having posted a notice stating, "Only so many trees [are permitted], and only this much [fruit] should be taken," which is to say, having written it down. "Having made a sign" (*nimittasaññaṃ katvā*)...
"Having made an agreement. "Children" refers to their children, grandchildren, and so forth; it includes all those who are cowherds.
In every case, when householders give to cowherds, one may take as much as the cowherds give.
However, since it is explained that in the case of what belongs to the Saṅgha, one must take only according to the established limit, it is said that "in meaning they are the same."

It has been stated [thus]. In the *Vimativinodanī* as well: "‘Having affixed a leaf’ means having affixed a leaf [with the instruction]: ‘Having protected so many trees, so much [fruit] is to be taken from them.
‘Having made a sign of recognition’ means having established a convention.
‘Children’—whosoever among their sons, grandsons, and others guard [the orchard], all of them are here called ‘children’. Thus it is said in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*.
However, it has been stated: "The phrase 'garden-keepers' should be understood in the sense of those who have been given leave [to take things].

Regarding the expression 'having understood the intention,' the conclusion here is that it is permissible to accept a gift from someone whose owners neither protect nor punish the monk receiving the gift;
yet even that is said to be 'not permissible if it belongs to the Saṅgha.'"
"In which" means in whichever residence. "Due to the absence of others" means due to the absence of other visiting monks. "Therein" means in such a residence.
"Having divided, they eat" means the intention is that they eat after having divided [the food] even for those visiting monks who have arrived.
"They properly provide for the four requisites" means by selling mango fruits and so forth, [they provide] for the four requisites, beginning with robes.

They bring [the goods] properly. "Given with a restriction for the sake of robes" means they were given with such a restriction as: "The fruits of these trees must be sold and applied solely toward robes; they must not be divided and consumed.
Even among those [goods], newcomers have no authority because, since they were given with a restriction for the purpose of using them as requisites, they have no authority to divide and consume them.
Regarding the phrase "one should not stand among them...": the intention here is that those who have arrived should divide [the fruit] and eat it according to the method explained below.

Regarding the phrase "one should abide by their agreement": this means either "one should not eat after having divided [it]," or "we shall take fruit from so many trees," or "we shall take so many fruits," or "for so many days..."
Whether they have made an agreement among themselves, saying, "We shall take [the requisites] inside," or "We shall not take anything at all," the incoming monks must remain [there].

This very point, which is indicated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* by the word "without authority" (*anissarā*), is shown in detail in the *Mahāpaccarī* by the passage beginning with "of the four requisites" (*catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ*). Regarding the phrase "only by way of use" (*paribhogavaseneva*), the word "only" (*eva*) here—
"Appropriated for an improper purpose" should be construed as "having divided that very [property] by way of personal use. Herein, "in this monastery" means in this kingdom.
"Requisites for lodgings" refers both to the lodging itself and to what has been set aside and designated for its sake.
"From the low end" means beginning with what is low; it is said, "starting from inferior lodgings. Even regarding lodgings, grass and such items constitute the low end.
The requisites for lodgings should also be disposed of, but only at the very lowest value.
By the phrase "having cut off the root and the basis, they must not be brought forward," what is meant? First, in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, this is stated:
"It is meant that not all lodgings are to be disposed of. Even when disposing of them at the lowest value...
The meaning stated here is that "the sites for lodgings (senāsana) must not be relinquished. This is our position.
Having investigated it, one should accept whatever seems correct.
It is permissible to perform worship of the Buddha with property belonging to the Dhamma, or to perform worship of the Dhamma with property belonging to the Buddha. However—
Is this appropriate? They say it is appropriate because of the statements: "Vāseṭṭha, 'the Dhamma-body' is indeed a designation for the Tathāgata," and "Vakkali, whoever sees the Dhamma sees me.
However, some [object] that if this were the case, it would contradict the statement: "Bhikkhus, whoever would attend upon me, let him attend upon the sick."
They say, "It would follow that it is proper to use what belongs to the Buddha to provide medicine even for the sick; therefore, it is not allowed.

That is not a valid reason. For by the statement, "Bhikkhus, whoever would attend upon me, he should attend upon the sick," neither the identity between oneself and the sick person nor the equality of the fruit of attending upon them is being asserted. This is the point here:
The meaning is: “Whoever would attend to me by carrying out my advice and instruction, he should attend to the sick;
one who follows my advice must attend to the sick. However, the meaning here should not be taken as implying that attending to the Blessed One and attending to the sick are exactly the same;
therefore, [the Buddha said]: “Ānanda, whatever Dhamma and Vinaya have been taught by me...”
Because of the statement, "He has been taught and established;

he shall be your teacher after my passing," and because it was said, "Now I alone advise and instruct you, but after I have attained final Nibbāna, these eighty-four thousand Buddhas will advise and instruct you," and because of the praise for a learned bhikkhu: "He who is learned... [the Buddha spoke thus].

Because it was said, "He is called your disciple, and he is the Buddha, Cunda," and because of the Tathāgata’s reverence for the Dhamma, it is our conviction that the former method alone is more highly praised.
In the *Vimativinodanī* as well: "'At which' means in whichever residence. 'Of others' means of other guests.
Even among those guests, the newcomers are not the masters" [referring to] the lodgings without interruption.
Because it was given by donors for the sake of robes during the *vasanta* season, or because it was assigned by the monks themselves, they have no authority to divide and consume it.
Even incoming monks who wish to do so must accept it for the sake of robes after entering that monastery during the rains retreat or other such times.
They must abide by their agreement, which is: "Without dividing all the fruits and produce, [they shall take] from these many trees..."
"Having divided the fruits, we shall consume them;

with other fruits and produce, we shall maintain the lodgings," or "We shall provide the requisites such as almsfood," or "Without dividing anything at all, we shall set it aside solely for the sake of the four requisites"—for those resident monks who thus properly set aside [the goods], the newcomers must abide by the agreement made by them. (From the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*)
The meaning is indeed indicated by the word “not subject to mastery” (anissarā);
it is shown in detail in the *Mahāpaccarī* by the passage beginning with “of the four conditions. Regarding the phrase “only by way of enjoyment,” the particle *eva* here is used out of place;
it should be construed as “having divided that very [matter] by way of enjoyment. “Therein” means in this monastery or in the kingdom. “The requisite of lodging” (senāsanapaccayaṃ).

And [it refers to] a lodging that has been set aside and designated for that purpose. To show again, by way of contrast, the meaning already stated in the phrase “having set aside one or two excellent lodgings,” it is said: “but having cut off the root of the site, it should not be brought [forward].
This means that having cut off the root of the site—which is the substance consisting of the lodging—one must not relinquish all the lodgings.

The meaning is as follows. However, some here say: “The meaning stated here is that even when distributing [the lodgings] starting from the inferior ones after setting aside one or two excellent lodgings, the grounds for the lodgings themselves must not be distributed.
That too is quite appropriate, because this meaning must necessarily be stated;
otherwise, some might think that even the actual sites (vatthu) should be distributed along with the buildings.
In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*: “Here, in this monastery, fear from foreign armies and the like has arrived.
Regarding ‘the cutting off of the root foundation’: because of the statement, ‘These [monks] are the masters of all lodgings,’ it is indicated that the others are not masters.
‘This very monk is the master’ means, it is said, that wherever he wishes, there he obtains his own authority; moreover, ‘a youth’...”
“They say: ‘With its basis’ means ‘together with the ground,’ this is what is stated.
Regarding the discourse on requesting protection from the righteous:
“‘Only as a debt’ is because there is no formal command [to that effect]. ‘Because of their lack of desire for his welfare’...”
“Having heard my word that ‘he is a thief,’ some will punish him, they will deprive him of life”—it is with such a perception [that one speaks].
By this, he shows that there is no fault even if someone is punished when “thief” is said impulsively, either out of mere fear or for the purpose of seizing requisites.
For the penalty for royal officers lies only in their pointing out [someone] as “this is a thief”; but for monks, [the penalty is different].

Furthermore, even if, based on a statement made by someone in the presence of a monastery attendant or others—such as, “So-and-so thief did such-and-such”—the king’s men inform the attendant and others and have them punished, the monk is not liable for the offense because he did not speak to the king’s men;
and it should be understood that those to whom he spoke did not themselves punish the thief. [If one says: “You [stole] what belongs to him...”
Regarding "he causes to take away": even if one who has been commanded causes another to take it away, there is no offense for the commander because the agreement (saṅketa) was not made with him.

"One who carries out his word" is said by way of formal courtesy. Even in the case of royal officers who do not carry out his word, if he speaks specifically addressing them, saying, "Have the requisites taken by this man brought here, and do not inflict punishment upon him," [there is no offense].
Even when the staff is taken, it is not merely the neck that is forbidden from being grasped;
rather, it is like the case where one has been commanded, "Steal such-and-such an article," and upon the arising of remorse, the act is subsequently prohibited.

Just as there is an offense for monks in accepting slaves and the like, so too there is a *dukkaṭa* offense in conducting a legal suit for their sake; thus he said, "A 'suitable lawsuit' is not permitted."

However, when a certain monk goes before judges for the sake of a field or similar property, even if a legal case is settled, it is not improper for all [monks] to accept that field or property, because it already belongs to the Saṅgha from the outset.
Nevertheless, offenses arise for the monks alone by virtue of their own initiative. Furthermore, regarding the request for protection for the sake of slaves and so forth—
"When asked by a layperson, it is indeed permissible for a monk to state that a suitable item has been acquired for the Saṅgha and to have a lay attendant or others carry out the transaction;
however, a monk may also personally carry out the transaction for a suitable item such as a monastery site," as stated in the *Vimativinodanī*.

In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, it is stated: "Regarding 'the neck,' it is merely the neck itself; there is no offense of defeat (*pārājika*). As for the instruction 'having had [it] made, it should be given back':
if it is a weapon, its edge must not be fashioned; however, it should be made known [as such] by some other means.
This concludes the discussion on the discarding of excrement and so forth.
20. In the eighth section on the disposal of excrement and so forth, regarding the disposal of excrement and such, there are these five factors:
the state of being excrement and so forth, not having asked for permission, a place for use, being beyond a wall or fence, and either disposing of it oneself or having it disposed of.
In the ninth section on disposal upon greenery, the phrase "of all" refers to both the monk and the nun. Herein...
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated only as much as this: "The field-keepers and those who guard the parks and so forth are indeed the owners.

However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: "In the eighth [offense], there are two factors: being within a wall or enclosure that is currently being used, and discarding excrement and so forth without having asked for permission.
In the ninth, because of the statement 'even a coconut with its top cut off,' [the offense applies] upon green crops..."
Throwing away is indeed prohibited. Therefore, he said, "where seeds have not been discarded," and so forth.
And where it is permissible to throw away, there it is certainly permissible even to void excrement and the like upon green vegetation. "Of all" refers to both monks and nuns—so it is stated.
However, in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, it is noted that the phrase "he throws away only after having informed the owner" does not appear in some manuscripts.
In some cases there is [an offense], for the mere state of existence [of the object] is sufficient, because the training rule applies regardless of whether an action was performed or not.

Here, the field-watchers and the garden-keepers are indeed the owners. If there is no agreement such as, "One must not discard refuse here in the Saṅgha’s field or garden," it is permissible for a bhikkhu to discard it because it belongs to the Saṅgha; however, it is not so for bhikkhunīs.
"For them [the robes] as well, it is permissible according to the method stated for those belonging to the community of bhikkhunīs, but not there for a bhikkhu.
Even so, it is said that they must be made only in a manner that is appropriate.
However, in the *Bhikkhuvibhaṅga*, in the commentary on the Sekhiya rules, regarding the phrase "not intentionally," it says: "For one going to a concealed place..."
If excrement or urine comes out suddenly, it is called "done unintentionally," and there is no offense. Regarding the phrase "not on green [vegetation]":
even if the root of a living tree that is visible in the earth moves, or a branch that is touching the ground moves, all of it is indeed reckoned as green;
however, it is permissible to sit on the trunk and drop it in a place that is not green.
If one is merely looking at a non-green area and it suddenly becomes green, and he remains standing in that place where it was sickly (or bare), it is permissible.

"Made on what is not green": even if, being unable to find a non-green spot, he makes it by placing a bundle of grass or a bundle of straw there, and later covers it over with green [grass], it is still permissible. "And here, by 'spittle,' nasal mucus is also included."
It is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "Not in water" refers specifically to water intended for consumption.
However, there is no offense regarding water that is not for consumption, such as water in a latrine, a cesspool, and so forth.

It is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that when it rains and there is a flood of water on all sides, it is permissible to leave even while looking for a place free of water; at such a time, [one may go] to a place without water.
It is stated: "If one does not obtain [water], it is permissible to do so. And in the *Vimativinodanī* commentary on that passage, it is said:

"In this context, since snivel is also included under 'saliva,' it should be understood that it is permissible to take away sugarcane refuse and the like by means of the mouth itself after making a mouthful of water, and to discard them in the water."
In this regard, there is a point to be considered by the wise: the Commentary states, "But there is no offense regarding water in a privy, the ocean, and so forth, when it is not fit for use.
This being the case, one might ask whether there is an offense or no offense regarding rivers, lakes, and the like.
Herein, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the ocean and so forth," rivers and lakes are also included; therefore, there is no offense.

Is this not so? It should not be viewed in that way. For if, in the phrase "the ocean and so forth" (*samuddādi*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) were to include rivers and lakes as well, then the commentators (*ṭīkācariyā*) would have said so;
yet they do not say it. Furthermore, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it would have stated merely "in water from latrines, the ocean, and so forth";
however, instead of saying that, it includes the qualifying causal phrase "in things unfit for use" (*aparibhogesu*).
By this it is known: "By the word 'etcetera' (ādi), only water from cesspools and the like, which are not for use, is included, and not water from rivers, lakes, and the like, which are for use.
And by that, water from latrines, the ocean, and so forth, because they are not for use, do not constitute an offense;
however, water from rivers, lakes, and so forth, because they are for use, do constitute an offense. But how [is it understood] that "[in those things] not for use"?
Should it be understood that this term possesses a causal meaning? Both through reasoning (*yutti*) and through scripture (*āgama*).
How through reasoning? Because of its non-deviant nature, as in the statement: "The waters of latrines, the ocean, and so forth, are both fit for use and unfit for use.
For a qualification is purposeful only when there is the possibility of deviation. How through scripture? For this has been said:
In the *Vinayavinicchaya*, the Elder Ācariya Buddhadatta states: "Because they are not for use (*aparibhogattā*). Therefore, by the word "etc.
(*ādi*), only waters that are not for use are included, not those that are for use. For this has been stated in the *Vinayavinicchaya-ṭīkā*:
"'In the water of latrines, the ocean, etc.'—here, by the word 'etc.', all water that is not for use is comprised."

For that very reason, he stated that those [waters] are unfit for use; therefore, it should be understood that it is not permissible for humans to discharge excrement, urine, or the like into waters such as those found in rivers, springs, lakes, ponds, and lotus pools that are intended for human use.
It is said in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "When it rains, there is a flood of water on all sides;
if one departs while merely looking for a place devoid of water, it is permissible. In such cases...

Since it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā that "it is permissible for one who cannot find a dry place at the proper time to do so," and because it accords with the Aṭṭhakathā that when traveling by boat or similar means on large rivers,
lakes, and so forth, if such circumstances arise, one may say, "Bring me to the bank," and even if it is impossible to reach the bank,
it is permissible to discharge [the water] into the water; there is no offense.
It is understood; it should be grasped after investigation.
Regarding the discussion on bathing and the felling of trees, etc.:
"In the case of bathing and the felling of trees, etc."—here, "in the manner of the eight-padded pattern" means in the shape of an eight-padded board, similar to a gambling board.
This is what is meant. "In the shape of the base of a betel-nut stand" means in the shape of the base of a spittoon.
In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it says: "In the pattern of an eight-square board means in the form of eight compartments on a gambling board.
'In the shape of the base of a betel-nut stand' means in the shape of the base of a spittoon. And this is said with reference to a circular support. Having raised up thorns..."
This is a designation for *katavaṭṭakapāla*. "Broad-handed" (*puthupāṇika*) refers to back-massage performed with the palms of the hands opened wide rather than being clenched into fists;
it is with reference to this very thing that "hand-massage" (*hatthaparikamma*) is said.
However, in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, it is stated: "Work to be done with a broad hand is 'broad-handed work' (*puthupāṇikamma*)."

Having thus shown what should and should not be done regarding bathing according to the Pāḷi, he now stated, "But here, this is the rule for bathing," etc., in order to show the procedure for bathing for monks who are bathing at a bathing place.

In that context, it was said [that one should not bathe where] because it brings lack of confidence to those who see [them], and because it is censurable as being like the work of laymen. Regarding the phrase "where":
“Or there, or... [as before] ... one must not descend. Since it is difficult to bathe with a bathing-cloth (*anudakasāṭaka*) when others are present, it is said:
“But having looked in all directions and ascertained that it is secluded. Even so, they might remain hidden by stumps, thickets, creepers, and so forth;
therefore he says: “A stump... [as before] ... having cleared the throat. The removal of the robe is done with the face turned upward.
"It may be necessary to hide oneself" means "having turned [the bowl] upside down... and removed [it]," as it was stated.
Then, with the words beginning "the waist-band," he states the rule for placing the waist-band. Then, addressing the objection—"If a bathing-cloth exists, one should descend after wearing it;
if it does not exist, what should be done?"—he says "if," and so forth. In that regard, previously [it was said] "by one who remains standing..."
Because the manner of one who is shameless has been prohibited by the words "one must not descend," this passage demonstrates the manner of one possessed of shame:
having sat down squatting at the water's edge and having removed his lower garment.
He says, "If there is a sloping place," and so forth, because if the woolly part or the smooth part were spread out, he might go elsewhere with it.

Regarding the question, "What should be done by one who is descending? it is said, "By one descending slowly," and so forth. Therein, "slowly" is stated in accordance with what was previously prohibited:
"One should not descend with speed. If one goes into water that is too deep, one's body may be shaken by being struck by the current, waves, wind, and so on;
if one sits in water that is too shallow, the body remains uncovered.
Regarding the statement "he may descend to the depth of his navel," it means he should not descend further than that.

Regarding the statement "having turned back without raising waves or making noise," it means he should turn back with his restlessness removed, neither stirring up waves by the movement of his hands and so forth nor making a sound.
To the question "What should be done after turning back? he says: "One should submerge oneself facing the direction from which one came."
The phrase "having offered while facing [the fire]" (*abhimukhena hutvā*) is a textual supplement (*pāṭhaseso*). Now, showing the fruit of that, he says "In this way," and so forth.

To the question of what should be done by one who is emerging from the water, he says "By one who is emerging," and so forth. The rest is easily understood. One should remain standing even after having put on the robe;
if one asks why, it is because the water has not yet reached the body; therefore, for a short time...
One should stand holding the edges of the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) with both hands and placing it in front.
Then, having ascertained whether the body is dry, one should put on the robe and proceed as desired. [This concludes] the discussion on sand and so forth.
22. In this story of Vaḷikā and others, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "hair-tassels and so forth," earrings and the like are included.
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: "A hanging thread (*palambakasutta*) is a thread worn hanging down in the manner of sacrificial ornaments. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated:

"By the word 'and so forth' in the phrase 'hair-tassels and so forth,' earrings and the like are included. A hanging thread (*palambakasutta*) refers to the form of threads and such worn by brahmins as sacrificial ornaments."
It is said [thus]. It is stated: "They circle as bracelets on the hands and feet. However, in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, it is written:
"'Kuṇḍala' refers to earrings and the like that hang down from the ears. It is further stated: "'Kāyūra' is the reading in the Pāli text;
'keyūra' and so forth is what has been cited by the teachers."
23. The Discourse on Long Hair.
In the *Sāratthadīpanī* commentary on this discourse, nothing is said. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it states: “‘Two finger-breadths’ (*dvaṅgule*) is the accusative plural;
the meaning is that it is not permitted to exceed the measure of two finger-breadths. And here, for one who has been two months...”
They say that even for one who does not know whether the length exceeds two finger-breadths, there are unintentional offenses (acittakāpatti) based on the counting of the hair and beard.
"With a comb" means with a comb made by binding together usīra, hīra, and so forth, and cutting them evenly.
"With oil-slime" means with oil mixed with resin. "Even for those whose heads are covered in dust and heated by the sun" refers to those whose heads are covered in dust and afflicted by the heat.
"With wet hands" means "with hands that are moist," so it is said.
Later, however, in the Pāḷi: "Now at that time, the group-of-six monks had their beards trimmed;
they let their beards grow long; they had them shaped like cow-hair; they had them made square; they had them shaped around the mouth."
They had them shaved half-way. They left the beard. They had hair removed from the private parts.
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying, "Just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures. They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
"Monks, one should not have a shave. One should not let the beard grow long. One should not have the hair of the head made like that of a cow."
"One should not have it made square; one should not have it made around the face; one should not have it made in the shape of two half-moons;
one should not leave a mustache; one should not have hair removed from the private parts; whoever should have it removed commits an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Thus it is said. In the *Aṭṭhakathā* as well: "'They have their beards trimmed' means they have their beards cut with a razor."
"Having their beard grown long" means they have it made long. "Sheep's wool" refers to a beard placed on the jaw after being made long like that of a sheep.
"Square" means four-cornered. "Around the mouth" refers to the removal of hair from the abdomen. "Half-moon" refers to the arrangement of a line of hair on the abdomen.
"There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" applies in all cases, including the arranging of the beard and so forth.
“It is an offense of wrong-doing,” it was said.
Again, in the Canon: “Now at that time, monks were having nose-hairs extracted using small pebbles and honey-scraps;
their noses became painful. ‘I allow you, monks, a pair of tweezers. Now at that time...”
The group-of-six monks had grey hair plucked out. People complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying, "They are just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One: "Monks, one must not have grey hair plucked out;

whoever should have it plucked out, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). It is further stated: "In the case of having the hairs of the nose plucked out with pebbles and so forth, there is an offense."
"It does not exist; however, tweezers are permitted for the purpose of protection," so it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā.

And regarding the rule, "Monks, one must not have grey hair removed," it is further stated: "In this context, if hair has grown on the eyebrows, the forehead, or the beard and stands there in a repulsive manner, it is permissible to have such hair removed, whether it be grey or not grey."

24. The Discourse on the Mirror, etc. In this discourse on the mirror, etc., a "mirror" (*ādāsa*) is a particular kind of vessel made of bronze, metal, or other materials for the purpose of people who are by nature fond of adornment seeing the reflection of their own faces.
A "water-bowl" (*udakapatta*) is a particular kind of vessel, such as a saucer or similar item, used for holding water.
“Bronze plates and so forth” refers to objects that, though not fashioned as mirrors, produce light due to their state of purity.

By the word “and so forth,” gold, silver, crystal, and the like are included. Regarding “sour gruel and so forth,” the word “and so forth” here includes liquids such as oil, honey, milk, and the like.
“Conditions for affliction” refers to conditions for a wound that has arisen in one’s own mouth. Therefore he said: “smooth skin...”
"Is there now a wound upon me? and so forth. It conditions life, thus it is the "life-conditioning formation" (*āyusaṅkhāra*). What is that? It is the personal existence (*attabhāva*).
Regarding the question, "Looking at that life-conditioning formation, in what manner should one look?", he says: "Am I now old, or am I not? The meaning of this is:
"Is my personal existence old, or is it not old?"—thus, by means of this mental attention under the heading of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
It is proper to look [at one’s reflection]. However, it is not proper to look out of attachment to oneself, thinking, “Does my physical form (attabhāva) look beautiful, or not?
As for the phrase “the face should not be smeared,” it means that the face should not be anointed with facial ointments that make the complexion of the skin clear and radiant.
"Should not be massaged" means one should not be massaged with various types of massage. "Should not be powdered" means one should not be smeared with face-powder.
"The face should not be marked with red arsenic" means that marks such as *tilaka* and the like should not be made with red arsenic.
Not only with red arsenic, but even with yellow orpiment and other such substances, those [marks] are likewise not permitted. Body ointments and the like are already well known.
25. Discussion on Dancing and the Like: In this discussion on dancing and the like, "good song" refers to a song associated with themes such as impermanence.
"By means of a fourfold rhythm" means by means of a complete mode of vocal delivery. The methods of delivery for the *taraṅgavatta* and other such rhythms are no longer in practice.
It is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, and in the *Vimativinodanī* as well: "A 'well-sung song' (*sādhugīta*) is a song associated with [themes such as] impermanence and so forth.
'By means of a fourfold turn' (*caturassena vattena*) means by means of a complete mode of recitation.

To show the common characteristic of all [rhythmic patterns], such as the 'wave-turn' (*taraṅgavatta*) and others, it is said: 'the characteristic of all...'. As many morae (*mattā*) as there are for a syllable..."
It is said: "When [the measure] is complete, speaking by adding even a slight excess is called 'speaking with distortion' (*vikārakathana*);
the meaning is that speaking without doing so is the defining characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*). However, in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, it is written:
"'Sādhugīta' means singing at the place of final Nibbāna. 'Dantagīta' is the vocal performance of those wishing to sing. Regarding *dantagīta*:
For the purpose of analysis, he said, “We shall sing,” and so forth. What is called the “four-cornered rhythm” (*caturassa-vatta*) is the rhythm of four-footed verses.

It is stated: “The methods of recitation such as the ‘wave-rhythm’ (*taraṅga-vatta*) and others have lost their practical application. [This concludes] the discussion on the cutting off of limbs and so forth.

26. Regarding the account of the cutting off of limbs and so forth, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “For one who cuts off his own sexual organ (*aṅgajāta*), there is a serious offense (*thullaccaya*); for one who cuts off anything other than that, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); and for one who cuts it off due to a medical affliction, there is no offense.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: “‘Sexual organ’ refers to the male characteristic devoid of seed. For when the seed is cut off...”
They say that one called an *opakkamika-paṇḍaka* (one who becomes a paṇḍaka through artificial means) is incapable [of the Path]. However, some say:
"At the very moment the seed is cut, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); when the male faculty and so forth have gradually disappeared, he is called a *paṇḍaka* and is incapable;
at that time, he should be expelled for the destruction of his gender. Or, regarding "causing such suffering": by means of blows with the fist and so forth.
“...for one who produces suffering for oneself,” it is said.

In the *Pattakathā* (28), regarding the phrase “a bowl-rest (*bhūmi-ādhāraka*),” this refers to a ring-shaped rest (*valaya-ādhāraka*). Regarding “a wooden rest and a staff-rest (*daṇḍa-ādhāraka*),” [it means] by means of a single piece of wood...
“With a support made of many sticks” means with a support made of many rods; however, one made of three rods is not permitted.
Regarding the statement “but having turned it upside down on the ground, it should be placed as a single unit,” they say here:
“When placing it, it is permissible to place the bowl so that one side touches the ground. “In a porch, a shed, and so forth.”

Regarding "of the front plastering, etc.": as for the phrase "having turned it over, it settles right there," the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries state that "having turned it over, on the third occasion it settles right there in the plaster. Regarding "around the perimeter" (*paribhaṇḍante*):

here, "perimeter" (*paribhaṇḍa*) refers to a thin layer of plaster applied for the purpose of strengthening the outer base of a house wall. [The term] "by means of thin plaster" (*tanukamiḍḍhikāya*)...
On a small stand. It is permissible to place it even on a stand made of wood.

For, from the statement, “I allow, monks, a stand,” they say that because the location for placing the stand is not restricted, it is permissible to place the bowl there on any part of the stand, such as the wooden base or elsewhere. [Regarding] “a bowl-shed”:

"In the *Gaṇṭhipada* it is stated: 'It is made by surrounding [the area] with bricks or the like, either circular or square, for the purpose of preventing bowls from passing through. *Ghaṭika* refers to the bolt fixed on top.
'It is permissible to use it temporarily' means that it is permissible to take it once, use it for food, and then discard it; this is the intended meaning."
*Ghaṭikaṭāha* means a potsherd. Regarding *pāḷiyaṃ abhuṃ me*: here, *bhū* is that which exists; thus, it is growth (*vaḍḍhi*). That which is not growth is *abhū*, meaning non-growth.
However, out of fear, that woman said, “*Abhuṃ*,” the meaning being, “I am ruined. *Chavasīsassa pattaṃ* means a bowl belonging to a corpse;
this genitive case expresses the relationship between the natural state and its transformation. Even though there is no actual difference [between the bowl and the corpse], [the genitive is used].
Or rather, this conventional expression [“the body of a stone statue”] occurs solely by way of metaphorical designation, as in such cases as “the body of a stone statue.
*Cabbetvā* means having eaten. *Taking a single mouthful of water* means lifting the bowl with the left hand alone and taking the mouthful with the mouth.
*With the soiled hand* means with the hand that has food remnants on it. *By this much* means by the mere act of taking a single mouthful.
"Having plucked out" means having extracted the flesh from there. Regarding all these cases, whether one knows the designation or not, it is indeed an offense—so it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.

However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: "Household refuse" (*gihivikaṭāni*) means things belonging to householders. In the Canon, it says "they are not to be touched," meaning they are not to be handled.
They are adorned. "Studded with forms" means studded with female forms and so forth. "A stand supported by the ground" refers to a bracelet-stand made of ivory and such materials.

Because the bowls placed upon this bracelet-stand do not roll away due to its suitability, it is said, "it is permissible to place three bowls. This term "ground-supported stand" is used with reference to its low height.

It was said: "In the case of those with a single wooden support and those with many stick-like supports" means: in those made with a single piece of wood as a support and those made with many sticks as supports;
these are higher and have the nature of falling along with the bowls, therefore it was said, "when they are well-secured.
"Like the edge of a lathe" refers to the edge of that lathe upon which one inserts the ink-pot and so forth and carves.
"Similar. Because the wooden support for such a bowl is not wide enough, even if placed [there], the bowl falls;

thus it is called "without a place" (*anokāsa*). "In the *ālindaka*, on the parapet, etc. means on the parapet in front of the porch, etc.; the meaning is "on a high base. "On the outer wall" means on the exterior wall of the palace, etc.
