"On a thin parapet" means on a railing (*vedikā*). In all cases, however, [the measurement] is from the span of a hand (*hatthappamāṇa*).
It is permissible to place it inside; however, on a stand, it is also permissible even outside of that.
Regarding the phrase "with another article," this refers to another article used as a support or burden.
Because it is stated "having tied it so that it hangs down," one should fasten the shoulder-strap of the bowl-bag in every way so that it does not slip from the place where it is attached.
It is permissible. Even though it has been tied, it is not permissible to place it on top; thus it is said, “those sitting on top [of the bowl] cover it and break it.
In that context, it is stated that “placing it there is permissible” because there is no suspicion of its being used as a seat. “Tied up” means either tied up or placed upon a tied-up umbrella.
“Whosoever” refers to anyone, whether carrying a full alms-bowl or an empty bowl. “To carry around” means day after day.

It is for the purpose of setting it aside for the sake of wandering for alms. However, if one does not obtain an alms-bowl, it is permissible to wander for alms on a single day, eat, and then discard [the bowl].
The same principle applies to leaf-cups and the like. “A bowl made from a corpse’s head” (*chavasīsassa patta*) means a bowl consisting of a corpse’s head;
this is a genitive case used to express the relationship between the material and its modification. “Having spat out” means having ejected [from the mouth]. “Receptacle” (*paṭiggahaṃ*)...

Because it is stated "having done so," it is permissible to take water with the hand that has been used for eating (the *ucchiṭṭha-hattha*), sprinkle it over the bowl, and wash the hand by means of rinsing and wiping.
For by this much alone, the hand is not said to have been washed after the bowl has been accepted as a vessel.
"Having taken a mouthful of water" means taking only water there with the hand that has been used for eating, without touching the bowl.
Having lifted it up and made a mouthful, or having lifted the bowl with the left hand alone, it is also permissible to take the mouthful with the mouth.
"Having rinsed it outside with water" means that it is also permissible to rinse a small amount of food from between two fingers and take it out.
Regarding "desiring to chew it back": here, even if one does not desire to chew it oneself, one may set aside what is fit for others to eat.
"He obtains it. "Having done it right there" means without removing it from its original position within the bowl itself.
"Having torn it out" means having peeled away that very flesh from there without leaving any remainder—so it is said.
In the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, however, it says: "'Of the porch-mushrooms and so forth' means of the mushrooms growing on the front porch and so forth. Having turned them over..."
Regarding the phrase "right there": here it is written that "having turned it over, on the third occasion it settles right there in the *miḍḍhikā*.
A *paribhaṇḍa* is called a thin layer of plaster applied for the sake of strengthening the outer base of a house;
here, [it is said] "the bowl breaks having been turned over," which means that because there is no suspicion of a breach in the foundation, one may place it in that spot.

"It is permissible," it is written. A bowl-stand (*pattamāḷa*) is constructed by encircling a circular or square base with bricks and the like to prevent the bowls from falling, and then covered over with a roof.
"A bowl-rim (*pattamaṇḍalikā*) or a bowl-receptacle (*pattapacchikā*) is made from black leaves and so forth," it is also written.
It is permissible to place [the bowl] on a support at the edge of the bed for the purpose of supporting the bowl.
Because it has been so stated. It is not permissible even on a bed or a support, because it is prohibited as a requisite for sitting.

Because it is close to the ground, it is permissible to hang it. Some say, "Based on the statement 'having hung it on the shoulder,' it is not permissible to place it on one's lap after hanging it from the forearm," but this is not correct.
This applies not only to "whose bowl it is," etc., if [it is held] by the hand...
It is stated with the understanding that there is a perception of a fracture even when a bowl is merely held, let alone when it is another part of the body;
however, this is stated in the *pāḷi* according to common parlance. A “bowl made of a jar-fragment” refers to a shallow vessel made from a piece of a jar.
The phrase “a bowl for a corpse’s head” is stated by way of conventional usage, such as “the body of a stone child” or “a stream of milk”; the meaning is that he has come to sit upon the couch.
"Pisācillikā" means "pisāca children," they say. "Dinnaka" means exactly what was given; "paṭiggahitaka" means exactly what was received. "Cabbetvā" means having chewed.
"Aṭṭhikaṇṭakāni" means bones and thorns. It is stated: "Whether one knows the designation for all these things or not, there is indeed an offense. Thus it is written.
29. The Discourse on All Rags from Refuse-Heaps, etc.
Regarding this discourse on all rags from refuse-heaps (*paṃsukūla*): it is called *paṃsukūla* because it arises or occurs in a state of being loathsome like dust (*paṃsu*).

One who has "all" of these is a "wearer of all rags from refuse-heaps" (*sabbapaṃsukūlika*); that is, one for whom every monastic requisite, such as the bowl and robes, is exclusively a rag from a refuse-heap.
The meaning is: "having made it, one should wear it with the virtue of wearing [rags].

With reference to the question, "Among the requisites of a recluse, which rag-robe (paṃsukūla) is permitted to be made and worn?", he said: "In this case, however, both robes and bedsteads and chairs are permitted as rags.
Therein, the robe is permitted both by way of the Vinaya and by way of undertaking the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga), whereas the bedstead and chair are permitted only by way of the Vinaya.

Regarding the question, "What kind of rag-robe (paṃsukūla) is not permissible? it is said: "But that which is fit for consumption, if given, may be accepted," meaning it must not be what is not given;
therefore, the intention is that such [ungiven] rag-robes are not permissible.

And here, by the term "fit for consumption" (ajjhoharaṇīya), he indicates both types of requisites by way of alms-food (piṇḍapāta), medicinal requisites for the sick (gilānapaccaya-bhesajja), and fermented urine (paakkhāra).
30. Discussion on the Water Strainer:
Regarding the "journey on the road," it is defined by its minimum extent as being one-and-a-half *yojanas* in length.
Even if one travels that distance without taking a water strainer, [one commits an offense] together with another monk who does not possess a water strainer.
If one has been asked for [an item] and does not give it, even though one possesses it, it is not permitted; it is indeed an offense.
Having authorized [the use of] a water-strainer with the words, "Monks, I authorize a water-strainer," they reported this matter to the Blessed One:
"It is not sufficient [to hold] a cloth. Because it was said, "Monks, I authorize a ladle-strainer," the ladle-strainer is considered small compared to the standard water-strainer.

It is understood. The method for a natural strainer (*pakatiparissāvana*) is not mentioned in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), but regarding the method for a ladle-strainer (*kaṭacchuparissāvana*), it is stated:
"A ladle-strainer is made by tying [the cloth] around three handles.
After mentioning the ladle-strainer, it further says: "The cloth was not sufficient. They reported this matter to the Blessed One."
—“I allow, monks, a water-vessel (dhamakaraṇa),” because it was said thus, it is understood that the water-vessel is smaller even than a ladle-strainer.
The method for making a water-vessel has already been explained below in the discussion on requisites.
“The monks were performing building work, but there was no strainer available. They reported this matter to the Blessed One.”
Because it is stated, “Monks, I allow a staff-strainer” (Cūḷavagga 259), it is understood that the staff-strainer is larger than the standard strainer (*pakatiparissāvana*).
Furthermore, because of the statement, “The staff-strainer was not sufficient; they reported this matter to the Blessed One:
‘Monks, I allow a filter-cloth’ (*ottharaka*),” [it is understood that the cloth is larger] than even the staff-strainer.
It is understood that the *ottharaka* (filtering cloth) is larger. Furthermore, the method for both of these water-strainers is indeed recorded in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
[End of] the Discourse on Nakedness.
31. Regarding the discussion on nakedness: "A naked person should not be saluted by one who is naked.
This means that a junior monk who is naked should neither salute nor pay homage to a senior monk who is naked.

Why? Because it was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, a naked person should not be saluted by one who is naked; whoever should so salute him incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Therefore, he should not be saluted.

The construction (*yojanā*). Here, however, in the case of the root *vad* in the sense of "salutation" and "praise," the suffix *ṇa* occurs because the root belongs to the *curādigaṇa*, and not because it has the sense of the causal (*hetu*). As it is said:
"With roots that are intransitive (*akammaka*), those *kicca*-suffixes occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*);
with roots that are transitive (*sakammaka*), they occur in the sense of the object (*kamma*), indicating what is worthy (*araha*) or honored (*sakkata*)."

According to the rule, it should be understood that the suffix *-tabba* occurs in the sense of the object (*kamma*). However, regarding the phrase "one should not pay homage with the body naked" (*na naggena abhivādetabba*), the construction here is simply: "a monk who is naked should not pay homage. But is it not said:
"Verbal roots that are intransitive [take the suffix] *ya* in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) when used in the neuter;
those ending in that [suffix] are generally used in the sense of the object (*kamma*). Those that are transitive take the three genders."

From the perspective of the word itself, since this verbal root (*dhātu*) is transitive, an object must be supplied and the grammatical gender must be established according to that object. Why, then, is the construction made with only this much? Because there is no desire to express the object.

For it has been said: “When there is no desire to express the object, the suffixes of the transitive verb denote the action itself (the abstract state), just as in the case of ‘cooking is done by Devadatta in the house.’”

Just as case endings, which consist of verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta-paccaya*), even when arising from transitive roots, express only the sense of the action (*bhāva*) without mentioning the object when there is no desire to express the object;

likewise, functional suffixes (*kicca-paccaya*), even when arising from transitive roots, express only the sense of the action without mentioning the object due to the absence of a desire to express the object. Therefore, the object is not brought forward (*anajjhāharita*).
It should be understood that the characteristic mark was not established according to the specific action, but rather according to the essential meaning.
For here, it should be known that the rule was established by taking the agent in a general sense, without considering that "this particular person is to be saluted.
However, regarding the statement "one who is naked should not be made to salute one who is naked," this refers to a naked monk who is senior in age.
The construction is: "A younger bhikkhu is not to be made to salute, nor to be made to pay homage.

For here, because the causative suffix (*kārita*) is seen as having the sense of the object-condition (*kamma-paccaya*), and because the verbal root (*dhātu*) is transitive, the younger bhikkhu becomes the agent of the root (*dhātukatta*), while the elder bhikkhu is the object of the root (*dhātukamma*).
Furthermore, in relation to the causative connection, the elder bhikkhu is the agent of the causative (*kāritakatta*).
The monk who has the work performed is younger. For it is said:
"It is considered 'kamma' because of its state of being connected with the causal action;
for otherwise [the term] would be untenable, since the causal action is primary."

Regarding the phrase "one should not cause [a junior] to pay homage while naked": here, the construction is that a senior monk who is naked should not be made to pay homage—that is, he should not be made to prostrate.

In this case as well, since there is no desire for a formal ritual procedure (*kammavācā*), it should be understood that the causal condition for the action exists precisely through the aforementioned method.
[Objection: But surely, when there is one who causes prostration, the act of being made to prostrate is indeed obtained; so then—

Why is it said, “Because there is no desire for the formal act (kammavācā)” [in the case of a non-human]? It is not so stated because of the absence of a desire for the procedure, based on the statement:
“The application of words follows the desire for the procedure. For this has been said by the ancient teachers:
“Even when a desire for the procedure exists, it may not come to pass; even when it does not exist, that [procedure] may come to pass.”
"It is like a girl with no belly, or the ocean as a water-pot. The other [terms] are also easy to understand.
They are called *paṭicchādiyo* because by means of them one conceals the various limbs (*aṅgamaṅgāni*).
The Discourse on Fragrant Flowers.

32. Regarding the discussion on perfumes and flowers: from the statement, "Having taken the scent of the perfume, it is permissible to place one's five fingers on the door," it is established that while it is permissible to accept the perfume when it is given, it is not permissible to smear it [on the body].
Now, however, after people have fed the bhikkhus and at the conclusion of the hand-washing, they give scented ointments for the purpose of rubbing the hands; as for that—
Having received [the ointment], some monks smear only their hands, while others smear their bodies and even their faces;
saying things such as, "How fragrant this is!", they display an appearance of extreme joy. Is this permissible or not?

Since it is stated that "it is permissible to apply the five-finger mark on the door," and this refers only to the fumigation of the door in the monastery, [the question arises] regarding the fumigation of the body.

Because it has not been stated [as permissible], and because it would contradict the statement, “Abstaining from wearing garlands, scents, ointments, and from the use of ornaments and finery,” it appears that this is not allowed;

however, this should be investigated further. From the statement, “Having taken flowers, one may deposit them in a corner of the monastery,” it is established that while it is permitted to take flowers when they have been given, it is not permitted to use them for adorning oneself or similar purposes.
Now, when fragrant flowers have been obtained by the bhikkhus, if they say things such as, "What a fragrant scent this flower has!
and, making a joyful expression, smell them—is that permitted or not permitted?

That too is permitted, because it was stated that they should be placed aside in the monastery itself, and because there is no mention of them being smelled and so forth; furthermore, this is because of the reading regarding garlands, perfumes, and the like.
It appears that [using it] in the direct order is not permissible; this should be investigated.
However, from the force of the statement "to set aside in one place," it is understood that it is permissible to perform such acts as worshipping a shrine or an image.
The Discussion on the Heated Footstool.
33. Regarding the discussion on the pouring-in of the foot-washing stand (*āsittakūpadhāna*), the phrase "with copper or silver" is stated with reference to the human custom of providing sustenance;
however, by means of the word "or" (*vā*) in the sense of an alternative, it includes "with gold or bullion," and so forth.
As for the phrase "because it has been rejected," this refers to the fact that the Blessed One rejected the pouring-in of the foot-washing stand in its general form.
It is not only a jewel casket that is not permitted, but also one made of wood. Here, the word "api" (also) has the sense of inclusion;
it includes those made of bamboo, palm leaves, rattan, and so forth. The Discussion on the Maḷorikā.

34. In the discourse on the *maḷorika* (waistband), it is said: “I allow you, monks, the *maḷorika*. This was permitted because a sick monk, while eating, was unable to support his bowl with his hand;
therefore, it was allowed. Previously, a support (*ādhāraka*) had been permitted for the purpose of protecting the bowl;
now, it is for the purpose of eating. It is called a *daṇḍādhāraka* because it is primarily a support for a staff.
It is called *maḷorika*. The connection is that the staff (*yaṭṭhi*)... and even the stools (*pīṭha*) and so forth are included right here by virtue of their commonality as supports (*ādhāraka*).
Regarding the support (*ādhāraka*), there are those that are pierced with holes and those that are not pierced;
among these, he asks which is appropriate, and says: "Because it falls under the category of a support... it is indeed permissible."

35. The Discussion on Eating from a Single Vessel, etc. In this discussion on eating from a single vessel, etc., "eating together" means eating simultaneously from one vessel at the same moment, not from different vessels.
Even regarding a single vessel, it must be at the same time; thus he says, "But if," and so forth. When that [other person] has departed...
Because he has departed, it is permissible for the other to eat the remainder. By this, he shows the state of not eating at the same moment.
In the phrases beginning with "for the other as well," "for the other" is a reciprocal expression; the meaning is: "for the other" [referring] to one who is other than the remaining eater.
By that, he refers specifically to the bhikkhu who went after taking the first portion. When that [first portion] is exhausted, because it is his turn, [he takes] the first...
Because the material already taken has been exhausted, it is permissible to take more. By this, he shows the state of not eating together.

One must not lie on the same bed even if there are different covers, because of the statement: "One must not lie on the same bed; whoever should so lie down incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
One must not lie on the same cover even if there are different beds. "Na... [The sentence is incomplete in the source].
Because of the statement, "They should lie down on a single covering," the meaning is even more so when there is oneness for both.
If this is so, one might wonder how there could be no offense in the absence of separate couches and separate coverings; considering this, he says, "But the demarcation," and so forth.
Furthermore, in the phrase "with a single covering and a single upper garment," this term *ekattharaṇapāvuraṇa* is not a *catthasamāsa* (a compound of four words).

[The questioner asks: "Is it so? Rather, it is an external-object compound (bāhiratthasamāsa)," he said, "those for whom there is one [thing that is] both a spread (*attharaṇa*) and a cloak (*pāvuraṇa*) are 'those having a single spread-and-cloak' (*ekattharaṇapāvuraṇā*).
This is an external-object compound consisting of three words with a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*). He asked, "What is this designation?
and replied, "This is a designation for those who lie down after spreading out one end and covering themselves with the other. Thus, this refers to those monks who lie down in such a manner.
The intended meaning is that the phrase "a single covering and upper garment" (*ekattharaṇapāvuraṇa*) is a designation. To the question "Of what [is this the end]?", he says:

"of portable [furniture]," and so forth. Regarding the discussion on the *celapaṭika*: in this discussion on the *celapaṭika*, *celapaṭika* means a cloth-spreading (*celasanthara*). But why was this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) laid down by the Blessed One?

What was the reason? "It is said that Prince Bodhi spread out the cloth rug with this intention: 'If I obtain a son, the Blessed One will step upon my cloth rug. However, he was incapable of obtaining a son; therefore, the Blessed One did not step upon it.
Had He stepped upon it, the prince, failing to obtain a son later on, would have fallen into the view: 'This one is not omniscient.'"
"This, first of all, is the reason why the Blessed One [prohibited] stepping on it.
Furthermore, since those monks who might step on it unknowingly would be held in contempt by householders, he laid down this training rule (sikkhāpada) to protect the monks from such contempt;
this is the reason for the promulgation of the training rule," so it is said in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, however, it is said: “The Blessed One remained silent; reflecting, ‘For what purpose has this great honor been performed by the prince?
he understood that it was done out of a longing for a son. For that prince was childless, and he had heard it said:
‘It is said that by performing service to the Buddhas, one obtains whatever is desired in the mind.’”
Having made the aspiration, "If I shall obtain a son, the Perfectly Enlightened One will step upon this hempen cloth;
if I shall not obtain one, he will not step upon it," he had it spread out.
Then the Blessed One, having reflected, "Will a son be born to him? saw that "one will not be born. It is said that previously, in a certain... [text continues]
While living in Dīpa, he who shared the same inclinations as his wife ate many fledglings. [The Buddha] understood:
"If this woman’s husband had been meritorious, she would have obtained a son; however, because they both committed an evil deed with a common intent, no son will be born to him.
But when the cloth was stepped upon, [the thought arose]: "This is an act of service toward the Buddhas."

"There is a worldly tradition that one obtains what has been prayed for; yet I have performed great meritorious service and do not obtain a son—this saying is empty," thus he might fall into a false conviction.
Furthermore, the non-Buddhist sectarians (titthiyā) would also criticize, saying, "There is nothing that these recluses (samaṇā) will not do;
they even wander about crushing their own undergarments. And at present, while they are treading upon them...
There are many bhikkhus who are knowers of others' minds; having recognized someone's capacity, they will approach them, and having recognized a lack of capacity, they will not approach them.
However, in the future, the supporting condition (*upanissaya*) will be weak, and they will not know the future.
Among those who do approach, if what was aspired to succeeds, that is well; if it does not succeed—
‘In the past, having performed services for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, they obtained whatever they desired; now they do not obtain it.
It is likely that those very bhikkhus were fulfillers of the practice, whereas these [present ones] are unable to fulfill the practice.
Thinking that people will become remorseful for these three reasons, the Blessed One, being unwilling to step forward, said:
"He remained silent. 'The Tathāgata has compassion for future generations'—this, however, was said by the Elder with reference to the third reason among those stated.
From the statement in the Pāḷi, "By one who is being asked, the rag-robe should be stepped upon," it follows that it must indeed be stepped upon only when one is being asked.

It is established that [the cloth] must not be stepped upon by one who has not been asked; furthermore, because of the statement "for the sake of auspiciousness" (*maṅgalatthāya*), it must be stepped upon by one who has been asked for the sake of auspiciousness, and not by one who has been asked for the sake of glory, beauty, and so forth.

Moreover, because of the statement "of householders" (*gihīnaṃ*) therein, the cloth-spread (*celasanthara*) of householders alone may be stepped upon, and not that of those who have gone forth. In the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), "whatever... [is said].
Because of the statement using the indefinite particle *vā*—“whether she be a woman who has lost her fetus or one who is heavily pregnant”—it is not only these two who are to be understood;

rather, by the phrase “or one whose fetus is established, or one who has given birth to a son,” and so forth, any auspicious women or even men are to be included. This is because it was stated, “in such places as these.”

It is established that it is not only in the aforementioned places, but also in similar auspicious locations, that it is permissible for anyone to step upon a cloth spread out when requested by householders for the sake of an auspicious ceremony;
this should be understood after careful investigation. For in the Pāḷi it is said: "Monks, I allow you to step upon a washed foot-cloth."

Because it is stated in general terms and because the *Aṭṭhakathā* says without qualification that "it is permissible to step upon it," it is established that a monk may step on a washed foot even if he is not asked;
however, since it is also said, "for the purpose of stepping with washed feet," it is not permissible to step on unwashed feet— one should accept this after careful consideration.
The Discourse on Foot-Scrubbers (Pādaghaṃsanīyakathā) 37.
In this discourse on foot-scrubbers, first, in order to show what is an improper foot-scrubber, it is said:
“A *kataka* is not allowed. When the question arises as to what a *kataka* is, it is stated: “A *kataka* is shaped like the pericarp of a lotus,” and so forth.
Why was it rejected? It is stated: "Because of devotion to luxury. Then, in order to show the permissible foot-scrubbers, he said:
"I allow you, monks, three kinds of foot-scrubbers," and so forth. The rest is easily understood.
The Discussion on the Fan.
38. In this discourse on the fan (*bījanī*), first, in order to show what constitutes an improper fan, it is said:
"A fan made with yak-tail hair is not permitted. Then, in order to show the six types of permissible fans, it is said:
"A mosquito-fan and so forth are permitted. In that context, the six permissible fans are: the mosquito-fan, the fan made of flax, the fan made of *usīra* grass, and the fan made of peacock feathers.
[The types of fans are] the *vidhūpana* and the palm-leaf fan (*tālavaṇṭa*). To show the distinction between them, he said:
"The *vidhūpana* is called a 'fan' (*bījanī*)," and so forth. Those made of *usīra* grass and peacock feathers are not mentioned because they are easily understood.
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: "'Fan' (*bījanī*) refers to a square fan; 'palm-leaf fan' (*tālavaṇṭa*) refers to a circular fan made from palm leaves and the like."
39. Discussion on the Parasol.
In this discussion on the parasol, "parasol" refers to three types of parasols: the white parasol, the palm-leaf parasol, and the leaf parasol.
Among these, the "white parasol" is a bright white parasol covered with cloth. The "palm-leaf parasol" is a parasol made from *vilīva* grass.
"A leaf umbrella" refers to one made from palm leaves or whatever other materials are available.

"Circularly bound and bound with strips" is stated for the purpose of showing the framework (*pañjara*) common to all three types of umbrellas; for they are indeed both circularly bound and bound with strips.
Furthermore, even a single-leaf umbrella made with a handle grown from that same tree is likewise [included].
The sixth [point] is as follows: “*Vilīvacchattaṃ* means a parasol made from *vilīva* bamboo. Regarding the phrase ‘made with a handle grown there’:
just as cowherds and others cut a palm leaf together with its stalk and use that very stalk as the handle for the parasol, it is with reference to this that it was said.
Thus it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, regarding “*vilīvacchattaṃ*... [the explanation continues].
It is made from bamboo tubes. "Arranged in circles" means: having placed a stick across long sticks in the shape of a ring and bound them with cords;
or having placed the long sticks straight both lengthwise and crosswise and bound them firmly;
or having arranged them crosswise and made them contractible by means of long handles, and then bound them crosswise with cords.
It is said that "made with a handle" means made together with palm leaves and so forth along with a handle.
However, here it is stated by way of the person who holds the umbrella; therefore, it is not permitted for a monk who is not ill to hold an umbrella.
The rest is easy to understand.
40. The Discourse on Nails.
Regarding the case that arose due to the condition of wearing long nails, it is stated: "Monks, long nails must not be worn;
whoever should wear them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Therefore, for one who wears them, there is an offense.
“They cut their nails with their own nails, they cut their nails with their mouths, and they rub them against walls;
thus their fingers become painful. When this matter was reported to the Blessed One, he said: “Monks, I allow a nail-cutter.
Because of this statement, it is permissible to carry a nail-cutter instrument. And as for the previous mention of “a nail-cutter that is curved,”...
"It is done so that [the nail] does not break; therefore, that is permissible," it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
"They fashion it with ridges for the sake of a firm grip when cutting the nails; therefore, that is permissible," it is said in the *Vimativinodanī*.
"By the measure of the flesh" means by the measure of the flesh at the tip of the finger. "Twenty-fold" refers to the twenty nails of the hands and feet.
They act according to what has been written. The rest is easy to understand.

Regarding the Discussion on Body Hair (*Lomakathā*): in this Discussion on Body Hair, it says, "They have the hair removed from the private parts. People criticized, complained, and spread it about, saying: 'Just as...'"
Regarding the case of householders who enjoy sensual pleasures, because of the statement, "Monks, [you should not... ...
it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" for one who causes hair to be removed, there is an offense for him who has it removed.

On account of this incident—namely, that a certain monk had a sore in his private parts and the medicinal ointment would not stay—the Buddha said: "Monks, I allow you, on account of illness, to have hair removed from the private parts."
There is no offense for one who has body hair removed from a congested area for the purpose of providing medicine as a condition for illness.
Regarding the statement, “Just like a goblin,” there is an offense on account of wearing [hair] because of the people’s reproach and the subsequent rule: “Monks, long nose-hair must not be worn;
whoever should wear it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). [The Buddha said: “I allow...”

“Monks, a pair of tweezers”: a pair of tweezers was permitted for the purpose of protection; therefore, it is permissible to have the hair of the nose removed with tweezers. “Grey hair” means white hair.
It is not permissible to have it pulled out because of the thought, “May the state of old age not come upon me.
“Having become hideous” means having become deformed. “Whether grey or not grey” means whether white or not white.
Or whether it is not white. It is permissible to have it taken up because it inspires confidence.

Regarding the discussion on the waistband (kāyabandhana): in the discussion on the waistband, "without a waistband" means without one that has been fastened; "by a bhikkhunī" is the remainder [of the phrase].

Alternatively, "without a waist-belt" (*akāyabandhanena*) means having not fastened a waist-belt; this is an instrumental expression used in the sense of a state of being (an *itthambhūta* construction), as in:
"With his head split open and blood flowing, he made [them] complain about the pickles. Therefore he said:
"By one who goes out without having fastened [it], wherever he remembers [to do so], there it should be fastened. As for "waist-belt," there are six kinds of waist-belts.
The *kalābu*, the *deḍḍubhaka*, the *muraja*, the *maddavīṇā*, the *paṭṭikā*, and the *sūkaranta*. Among these, the *kalābu* has many strings.
The *deḍḍubhaka* is shaped like the head of a water-snake. The *muraja* is made by wrapping it around in the shape of a drum-head.
The *maddavīṇā* is shaped like a *pāmaṅga* lute. Not even one of such types is permitted, let alone more.
There are many [types]. Therefore, there are four kinds of waistbands that are rejected and called "unallowable" (*akappiya*).
Two kinds of waistbands—namely, the *paṭṭika* and the *sūkaranta*—were permitted by the Blessed One and are called "allowable" (*kappiya*) waistbands.
For such a band, a plain woven strip or one woven from fish-bone fibers is suitable; all other varieties, such as those made of elephant-hair and so forth, are not.
It is not permitted. What is called a *sūkarantaka* (pig’s-tether) is shaped like a key-case;
however, a single-strand [cord] and a grape-vine waist-band conform to the *sūkarantaka*. Together with these two, there are eight types of waist-bands.

Regarding the statement, “Monks, I allow the *muraja* and the soft *vīṇā*,” this was permitted among the ten [types of waist-bands]; and herein, the *pāmaṅgadaśā* (the ten-fold grape-vine band) is one of the four...
It is not permitted above [the waist]. What is called *sobhaka* is a seam sewn after wrapping [the cloth] around.
What is called *guṇaka* is a seam sewn in the shape of a *mudiṅga* drum. For it is said that when sewn in this way, the inside becomes firm.

"At the edge of the cloth" (*pavananta*) refers to the border. In the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, however, it says: "What is called a *muddika-kāyabandhana* is prepared without making it square. The *pāmaṅgada-sā*..."
"Square. "In the shape of a drum" means by way of the manner of sewing a *saṅghāṭī* like a drum, or in the shape of a small head.

"The edge of the forest" means the boundary; it is also written as "the base of the fringe (*dasāmūla*). There is an offense in intentionally or unintentionally entering a village without a waistband. It is stated:

"It should be written that one must enter or turn back after fastening [the robe] from the place where it was worn."* *Note: This passage discusses the proper dimensions and methods of fastening for a monk's outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*) and the rules regarding its use when entering inhabited areas.*
The Discourse on the Undergarment and the Upper Robe (Nivāsanapārupanakathā) 42. Regarding the discourse on the undergarment and the upper robe:

"One should not wear a layperson’s garment such as that of an elephant’s trunk" means that here, what is called "an elephant’s trunk" refers to wearing [the cloth] draped from the base of the navel in the shape of an elephant’s trunk.
It is like the lower garment worn by the women of Coḷa. That called *macchavāḷaka* is worn by draping it so that it bites on one side and hangs down on the other.
That called *catukaṇṇaka* is worn by displaying four corners—two above and two below.
That called *tālavaṇṭaka* is a lower garment worn by draping a cloth in the shape of a palm-leaf fan. *Satavalika*.
The *nāma-dīghasāṭaka* is worn by repeatedly folding it up and tucking it into the waistband, or by wearing it so that folds appear continuously on the left and right sides.
However, if only one or two folds are visible starting from the knee, it is permissible.
"Wearing a *saṃvelliya*" means wearing it like a laborer or a mason, [tucking it] at the waist.
Having tied it, they wear it; thus, it is not permitted to wear it in that manner even for one who is ill or traveling on a journey.

Regarding the rule that one must not wear the dress of a householder—such as wearing white cloth and so forth—here, "whatever is the dress of a householder" includes the dress of wanderers (*paribbājaka*), the dress of those wearing a single robe (*ekasāṭaka*), the dress of drunkards (*soṇḍa*), the dress of palace attendants (*antepurika*), and the dress of high-ranking chiefs (*mahājeṭṭhaka*).
That which is worn like one entering a hut, the brahmin-style wearing, the *pāḷikāraka*-style wearing, and so forth—

all such ways of wearing [the robe] other than according to the characteristic of being perfectly circular are called "lay-style wearing. Therefore, it is just as the white-robed Aḍḍhapālaka Nigaṇṭhas wear their robes,
or as certain wanderers (*paribbājaka*) expose their chests and place the cloak upon both shoulders.
They arrange it as follows: just as people wearing only a single garment (ekasāṭaka) cover their backs with one end of the cloth they are wrapped in and place both corners on both shoulders;

or just as drunkards and the like, having encircled their necks with a cloth, let both ends hang down over the chest or toss them onto the back; or just as women of the inner apartments [wear a cloth] only as large as the pupil of the eye.
Having shown [the way], they put on their upper robes with the head covered;
just as Mahājeṭṭhā, having wrapped herself in a long cloth, covers her entire body with one end of it;
and just as farmers entering a field-hut wrap their cloth around themselves, tuck it under their armpits, and cover their bodies with one end of it. Just so...
And just as Brahmins, having tucked their lower garment between both armpits, drape it over their shoulders,
or just as a monk who is reciting the scriptures uncovers his left shoulder— already draped with the robe by wearing it over one shoulder—
and then places the robe upon his shoulder; in this manner, without so draping [the robe], all these and others should avoid such faults in the manner of draping.

One should wear the outer robe evenly all around without causing distortion. If one does not wear it in that manner, whether in a monastery or within a village, and makes any kind of distortion out of disrespect, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Discussion on the undergarment.
43. Regarding the discussion on carrying loads (*kājakathā*): "A shaven-headed woman" (*muṇḍaveṭhī*) refers to one who carries the attendants' requisites when a king goes somewhere;
this is the intended meaning. "A load carried by two poles" (*ubhatokāja*) is a burden that must be carried by being fastened to both sides, at the front and the back, of a single pole.
"A load carried by one pole" (*ekatokāja*) is a burden that must be carried by being fastened to only one side, at the back. "An intermediate load" (*antarākāja*).
Having fastened it in the middle, it is a load that must be carried by two people. Loads for the head and so forth are precisely those loads that must be carried by the head and so forth.
A "suspended load" (*olambaka*) is a load that must be carried by hanging it from the hand. Among these, only the "yoke-carrying" method (*ubhatokāja*) is not permitted; the others are permitted.
The Discussion on Tooth-sticks (*dantakaṭṭha-kathā*).

44. In the Discourse on the Tooth-stick, after demonstrating the five faults in not using a tooth-stick and the five benefits in using one, the Blessed One permitted the use of a tooth-stick for the monks. Therein, the "five faults" are:
it is detrimental to the eyes, the mouth becomes foul-smelling, the taste-carrying channels are not purified, and bile, phlegm, and food obstruct the throat.
"Bhattamassa nacchādetī" means that it is not beneficial for the eyes; it causes their deterioration.
"Nacchādetī" means it is not pleasing. The five benefits should be understood as the opposites of what has been stated.

Therefore, having prescribed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for chewing a tooth-stick that is too long and for chewing a tooth-stick that is excessively drying, [the Buddha] prescribed that it should be no more than eight finger-breadths in length, with four finger-breadths being the minimum.
The use of a tooth-stick is permitted. In this regard, "eight-finger-breadths at most" means that eight finger-breadths is the maximum length for this tooth-stick.
"Four finger-breadths at least" means that four finger-breadths is the minimum measurement for this tooth-stick.
"Excessively small" means too tiny. A tooth-stick of eight finger-breadths is called a large tooth-stick; one of four finger-breadths is a small tooth-stick.
The five, six, or seven-finger-width tooth-stick is called a medium tooth-stick. Therefore it was said: "by two kinds of water and three kinds of tooth-sticks.
Regarding the phrase "at most eight finger-widths," the Commentary states that this is "at most eight finger-widths by the human standard finger-width.
And here, "by the standard finger-width" should be understood as the natural finger-width; that is, by the natural finger-width of humans.
They say that a tooth-stick exceeding eight finger-breadths in length is not permitted; they chew one of exactly that size.
However, in the Commentary it is stated, "by the measure of the human finger," and not "by the natural finger.
Therefore, it refers to the finger-measure used by people when measuring houses and so forth, based on the carpenter’s cubit. By that [measure], for humans—
The meaning to be understood is that "at most eight finger-breadths" refers to the carpenter’s finger-breadth (*vaḍḍhakiaṅgula*), which serves as the standard measure (*pamāṇaṅgula*).
For it is said in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: "By 'the standard measure finger-breadth' is meant the carpenter’s finger-breadth. And in the *Vimativinodanī*:

"By 'the standard measure finger-breadth' is meant the carpenter’s finger-breadth; however, some say 'by the natural finger-breadth (*pakatiaṅgula*),' but that is [incorrect] because of the statement regarding the minimum of four finger-breadths."
"It is equal. For it is not possible to chew a tooth-stick measuring four finger-breadths without it getting stuck in the throat, measured by a natural finger.
45. The Discussion on Climbing Trees:
In the discussion on climbing trees, "a tree whose height is that of a man" means a *porisa* tree; [measured] with the hand raised upwards.
A tree-section measuring five cubits in height, equal to the size of a human body, is a "human-sized tree" (*porisa-rukkha*).

This is a designation for the whole based on its parts, as in the expression, "the ocean has been seen. They fall down, go forth, or proceed abundantly; thus they are "calamities" (*āpadā*), that is, dangers (*parissaya*).
A tree in which there is as much purpose as exists is a "tree with as-much-purpose-as-is-needed" (*yāvad-attha-rukkha*); here, the word *attha* means purpose.
It expresses purpose (*payojana*). The intended meaning is that as long as there is a need or purpose for the monk regarding that tree, he may climb it.
The rest is easy to understand.
The Discussion on Imposing One’s Will.

46. In the discourse on the imposition of consent (*chandāropana*), "consent" (*chanda*) refers to the Sanskrit language. "It should not be imposed" means it should not be placed upon the path of recitation.
"In one's own language" (*sakāya niruttiyā*) refers to the Māgadhī language. In that context, "Sanskrit" (*sakkaṭa*) means "made by those who dwell therein";
the meaning is that it was made by sages such as Aṣṭaka and Vāmadeva, who had stilled their evil. Alternatively, it means "to be honored" or "to be revered."
The meaning is that it should be honored by people seeking that goal, because the Pāli language brings benefit and happiness to human beings. It is called *bhāsā* because it is spoken (*bhāsīyati*).
Thus, "Pāli" is the compound of "Pāli" and "language" (*bhāsā*), meaning the Pāli language. It is "Sakā" because its etymology (*nirutti*) is contained within the three Vedas;

the meaning is that it is the word of the Blessed One (*sakā* = *bhagavato vacanaṃ*). It is "Māgadhikā" because it was born in Magadha; [it originated] in the kingdom of Magadha during the time of the first cosmic age (*ādikappa*).
The meaning is "born. *Utti* means "speech"; *nirutti* is speech brought forth—that is, it is spoken by being extracted from the Three Pitakas.
For this has been said by the ancients:
"That Magadhi is the root language;"
“Humans who speculate about the beginning,
as well as the Brahmas who speak from what they have heard,
and even the Fully Awakened Ones declare thus.”
The rest is easy to understand.
Regarding the Discourse on Lokāyata (47):

in this discourse on Lokāyata, "loka" refers to that in which merits and demerits, as well as their respective results, arise and are established; thus, it is the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*).
It is called *āyata* because they strive intensely (*ābhuso*) and exert energy (*vīriyaṃ karonti*) therein; thus it is *lokāyata*, meaning the world’s intense exertion.
Its sense is: "the place where beings intensely exert their energy. What is that? It is the teaching of the heretics (*titthiya-sattha*).
All of it is vomit; why? Because it has previously been consumed by birds and the like. All of this remaining food is not vomit, for no one [has consumed it].
Because it has never been enjoyed before. A white crow [is so called] because of the whiteness of its beak; a black crane [is so called] because of the blackness of its feet.

That which has no purpose (*attha*) therein is "meaningless" (*niratthaka*); a meaningless reason is a "meaningless cause" (*niratthakakāraṇa*). That which is connected with that is "connected with a meaningless cause.
It is a *tittha*, meaning a landing place or port, because people cross over there. Like a *tittha*...

A "ford" (*tittha*) refers to a doctrine; those who possess such a ford are "ford-makers" (*titthiya*), meaning those with perverted views. That wherein one instructs one's own disciples is a "teaching" (*sattha*);
the teaching of the ford-makers is the "ford-maker’s teaching" (*titthiyasattha*). Regarding the phrase "low arts (*tiracchānavijjā*) are not to be mastered":
here, "low arts" refers to any external sciences that are unbeneficial. They are "not to be mastered."
"One should not master it oneself" means one should not teach it to others. The rest is easy to understand.

Regarding the "Discourse on Throwing Away" (Khipitakathā): in this discourse, "thrown away" (*khipita*) means that which was thrown away. The verbal root is *khip*, meaning "to throw. Because it is characterized by the state of being [the action] itself (*bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇattā*).
*“Tasmiṃ khipite”* is a case-ending form. The phrase *“yasmiṃ kismiñci puggale”* (in whatever person) must be supplied because it functions as a qualifying subject.
*Jīvā* is derived from the verbal root *jīv*, meaning “to live” or “to sustain life,” with the case-ending elided. When a monk has insulted someone, the word *“jīvā”* (live!
should not be uttered; likewise, when a layperson insults a monk and says, *“Live on, venerable sir!”* (*jīvatha bhante*), [the monk should remain silent].
The construction is: "When [the word] *sati* [is present], it is permissible for a monk to say, 'May you live long'.

Regarding the term "vuccamāne" (being spoken), since the characteristic here denotes the object (*kamma*), one must supply the characteristic-bearing object (*lakkhaṇavantakamma*) "bhikkhusmiṃ" (in the monk), which stands in grammatical apposition with it as the object;
for example, how so? "While the cows were being milked, the man arrived. However, other teachers [explain] in such cases...
In these instances, they say that by supplying the word "when existing" (*santesu*), this very [word] is the characteristic phrase (*lakkhaṇapada*);

however, regarding the two phrases "when cows are being milked" (*gosu duyhamānāsu*), they state that the agent is established here through the modification of the base (*pakativikati*). This should be accepted after careful investigation. The Discussion on Garlic (*Lasuṇakathā*)
49. Regarding the discourse on garlic: in the Pāḷi it is stated, “garlic (lasuṇa) means that which is from Māgadha. However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it says:

“‘From Māgadha’ means born in the Magadha [country]. For here, only garlic grown in the kingdom of Magadha is intended by the term ‘garlic,’ and even that must be the bulbous garlic (bhaṇḍika-lasuṇa), not that which has one, two, or three seeds.
But in the Kurundi, without specifying the country of origin...”
It is said: "The so-called *māgadhaka* is the garlic from Bhaṇḍika. If one swallows two or three bulbs after combining them into a single mass, there is one *pācittiya*.
However, for one who breaks them apart and eats each individual bulb, there are *pācittiyas* according to the number of acts;
this is a *pācittiya* for a bhikkhunī, whereas for a bhikkhu it is a *dukkaṭa*.
The distinction between the onion (*palaṇḍuka*) and the others should be understood by way of their color or their core (*miñjā*). First, by way of color:
the so-called onion is pale yellow; the *bhañjanaka* is red in color; the *haritaka* is green in color.
As for the core, however, the onion has one core, the *bhañjanaka* has two, the *haritaka* has three, and the *cāpalasuṇa* (wild garlic) is coreless.

For it has only the mere sprout [of the seed]. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other texts, it is said: "The onion has three seeds, the bhañjanaka has two, and the green garlic has one. These onions and so forth are permissible by their very nature;

however, even the Magadhan variety is permissible when used as a seasoning for soups and the like. For that [Magadhan variety] is permissible when added to boiling bean soups and such, or to preparations of fish and meat.

It is stated that it is permissible to add [the spice] to oil and the like, or to jujube-sālava and the like, or to sour soups and the like, or to post-meal refreshments (uttaribhaṅga), or indeed anywhere at all—even into a bowl of rice-gruel.
"By its very nature" means without adding broth, condiments, or the like. "Jujube-sālava" refers to a preparation of solid food made by drying jujube fruits and grinding them into powder.
This is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
50. The Discussion on What Should Not Be Touched, etc.:
In this discussion on what should not be touched, etc., "ground prepared with plaster" (*paribhaṇḍakatabhūmi*) refers to ground made smooth with clay and colored black or otherwise.
“Reclining place” (*senāsana*) refers specifically to beds, chairs, and so forth.

“It is permissible to use it in that same way” means it is permissible to use it in the manner already enjoyed by other resident monks (*nevāsika*). Regarding this, it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* (Commentary):

“If the residents place them on the ground because they are not in need of them, there is no offense for them either. “The door as well,” etc., refers to the doors, windows, and so forth mentioned therein.

"Even if it has not been prepared (aparikammakatā), it must not be leaned against. Regarding 'in the hair' (lomesu): this means when [the hair] touches [the ground]," so it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
In the *Vimativinodanī* as well: "A ground that has been plastered (*paribhaṇḍakatabhūmi*) means a ground made smooth by black pigment and so forth.

Or, 'a lodging' (*senāsana*) means a bed, a chair, and so forth. By the phrase 'it is permissible to use it in that very way,' [it is meant that] by resident monks who have washed their feet and so forth..."
This shows that an offense is prescribed for one who intentionally uses a place for cleaning with unwashed feet and so forth;
because it is stated generally in the phrase “a door as well,” etc., doors, windows, and so on—even if they have not been treated (with plaster)—must not be leaned against.
It is said: “Even for one who leans against them unknowingly, there is an offense here according to the counting of body hairs. Thus it is stated in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*.
It is stated: "If resident monks place [an object] on the ground out of natural necessity, there is likewise no offense for them;

it is also written that doors, windows, and so forth, even if not yet finished with plastering, must not be leaned against. This concludes the discussion on those who are not to be saluted and those who are to be saluted.
51. Regarding the discourse on those not to be saluted and those to be saluted (*Avandiya-vandiya-kathā*):

here, in accordance with the *Senāsanakkhandhaka* of the canonical text (*pāḷi*), the author of this treatise has stated ten who are not to be saluted and three who are to be saluted; however, nothing further is stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) or sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*).

Therefore, the meaning should be understood according to the method presented here. In the *Parivāra-pāḷi*, however, within the *Upāli-pañcaka*, twenty-five [cases] are given by way of five groups of five.
Five are said to be not to be saluted, and five are said to be to be saluted. How so? “Venerable sir, how many, indeed, are those who are not to be saluted?
“Upāli, there are these five who are not to be saluted. Which five? One who has entered among the houses is not to be saluted;

one standing in the street is not to be saluted; one whose head is covered is not to be saluted; one who is not paying attention is not to be saluted; one who is asleep is not to be saluted. These, Upāli, are the five.”
They are not to be saluted. Furthermore, Upāli, there are five others who are not to be saluted. Which five? One drinking gruel is not to be saluted;

one at the head of the meal is not to be saluted; one who has turned away is not to be saluted; one who is distracted by something else is not to be saluted; one who is naked is not to be saluted. These, Upāli, are the five who are not to be saluted.
Furthermore, Upāli, there are five others who are not to be saluted. Which five? One who is eating is not to be saluted.
One who is eating is not to be saluted; one who is defecating is not to be saluted; one who is urinating is not to be saluted; one who has been suspended is not to be saluted.
These, Upāli, are the five who are not to be saluted. Furthermore, Upāli, there are another five who are not to be saluted. Which five?
One who was ordained later is not to be saluted by one who was ordained earlier; one who is not fully ordained is not to be saluted; one who belongs to a different community is not to be saluted.
One who speaks contrary to the Dhamma, though senior, is not to be saluted; women are not to be saluted; eunuchs are not to be saluted. These, Upāli, are the five who are not to be saluted.
Furthermore, Upāli, there are another five who are not to be saluted.

Which five? One on probation is not to be saluted; one deserving to be sent back to the beginning is not to be saluted; one deserving the *mānatta* penance is not to be saluted; one undergoing the *mānatta* penance is not to be saluted; one deserving rehabilitation is not to be saluted.
“...are not to be saluted. Upāli, these are the five who are not to be saluted.
“How many, Bhante, are those who are to be saluted? “Upāli, there are these five who are to be saluted. Which five?

One who was ordained earlier is to be saluted by one who was ordained later; one who belongs to a different community and is senior and speaks according to the Dhamma is to be saluted; and a teacher is to be saluted.”

“The preceptor is worthy of veneration; the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is worthy of veneration in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. These, Upāli, are the five who are worthy of veneration.
And in the commentary: “‘Has gone to darkness’ means he has entered into darkness. For when one venerates him, even his forehead [might strike] the legs of the bed or other such objects.”
He might strike back. "Not attending" means not attending to the salutation because he is preoccupied with his duties.
"Asleep" means one who has fallen into sleep. "One who has turned away" refers to an enemy, a hostile person, or an incompatible individual who stands on the side of an adversary;
such a person is not to be saluted. For if he were being saluted, he might even strike with his foot. "Intent on something else" means [intent] on another [matter].
"Reflecting. "Eating" means eating such things as flour cakes (*piṭṭhakhajjaka*). One who is voiding excrement or urine is not to be saluted because he has gone to an improper place.
"One who has been suspended" (*ukkhitaka*)—one who has been suspended by any of the three kinds of acts of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) is not to be saluted.
However, the four types of persons who have undergone acts such as censure (*tajjanīyakamma*) are to be saluted, and the *uposatha* and *pavāraṇā* ceremonies may be performed together with them.
Regarding those stated from the beginning as not to be saluted: for one who actually salutes both the naked person and the suspended monk, there is an offense.
However, for the others, salutation is prohibited on account of their being unsuitable and for the reasons mentioned in between.
Hereafter, even the ten types beginning with those ordained later are not to be saluted precisely because they constitute grounds for an offense. For one who salutes them...
"For indeed, there is an offense by rule alone. Thus, regarding these five sets of five, for one who pays homage to thirteen persons, there is no offense;

for paying homage to twelve, there is an offense. "The teacher is to be paid homage"—it is stated that this fivefold teacher consists of the teacher of going-forth, the teacher of full ordination, the teacher of dependence, the teacher of recitation, and the teacher of exhortation; this fivefold teacher is to be paid homage.

“‘By the reason stated in the intermediate [text]’ means: by the reason stated as ‘for one who bows down, the forehead might strike the legs of the bed, etc.’—so it is said in the *Sāratthadīpanī*. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: ‘In the case of the bed-legs and so forth, the forehead might strike [them];
thus, in the dark, having spread out a leather mat, for one who bends down to bow down, the forehead...”
Or [the head] strikes the eye or the bed and so forth. By this, having stated that there is no offense even for one who bows, he demonstrates that there is no total prohibition of bowing.
Thus it is in all cases where there is no prohibition by other Suttantas.
However, it is not permissible to bow to those who are naked and so forth. "Turning back from one side" (*ekato āvatto*) means turning away toward the side of faults and rebirth.
The meaning is "entered. Therefore he said, "standing among the faction of adversaries. Regarding "being venerated": it means being venerated by bowing down.

Since among those worthy of veneration, both the *uddesācariya* (teacher of recitation) and the *nissayācariya* (teacher of dependence) may be junior, it is stated that "only those who are senior are to be venerated" as the ones to be venerated.
In the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, it is also read as "ekāvatto."
"Angry" means, it is said, "overcome by anger. Some say "wearing a single cloth," meaning he stood having removed his upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).
All of that contradicts the text cited in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. For "single-folded" (*ekāvatta*) is what is cited;
therefore, that [other interpretation] should not be accepted. "Because of the reason stated in the interval" means because he was preoccupied with his duties, he was not paying attention.
It is stated [in the commentary] by way of the reasons mentioned in the passage beginning with, "one might strike one's forehead," and so forth.

In the *Dutiyagāthāsaṅgaṇika-aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary on the Second Collection of Verses), it says: "The ten persons who should not be saluted are the ten individuals mentioned in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*.
'And with the añjali-greeting' means that both the añjali-gesture and the respectful service (*sāmīcikamma*) should not be performed toward them."
The meaning is that they should not be shown the Khandhaka duties, such as asking for water or taking the fan, nor should one raise their joined palms (añjali) in greeting them.
Regarding the phrase "an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for ten," this means that for those same ten [monks], an offense of wrong-doing occurs for one who acts in this manner;
therefore, even the mere act of raising the joined palms should not be performed toward them.
“Venerable sir, when a junior bhikkhu is bowing at the feet of a senior bhikkhu, how many qualities should he establish within himself before bowing at his feet?
“Upāli, when a junior bhikkhu is bowing at the feet of a senior bhikkhu, he should bow at his feet after establishing five qualities within himself. Which five?”
What five? Upāli, when a junior monk is bowing at the feet of a senior monk, he should put his upper robe over one shoulder, raise his joined palms in salutation, and stroke the feet with both palms;
having established affection and reverence, the feet should be bowed to. Upāli, when a junior monk [is bowing at the feet] of a senior monk...
"By one who is bowing at the feet of a bhikkhu, the feet should be bowed to after having established these five qualities within oneself.
At this point, the method of bowing was explained by the Perfectly Enlightened One to the Venerable Upāli.
Regarding the phrase "having bowed with the fivefold prostration," the nature of those five is also stated here. How so? [It is said] regarding one who is senior...
When prostrating at the feet, both shoulders must be uncovered and then saluted; one should not salute while covering both shoulders with the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).
Rather, having arranged the *uttarāsaṅga* over one shoulder, one should salute.

By this, it is made clear that regarding the outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*), there is no fault whether it is arranged over one shoulder or not. [With] the hands joined together, radiant with the ten nails...
"One should pay homage with the hands raised in *añjali*, not merely by extending the palms of the hands, nor by extending the fists of the hands, and so forth.
And: "One should not pay homage merely by touching the corner of the robe with one hand;
rather, one should pay homage while stroking the feet with both palms of the hands. And: "By those paying homage in this manner..."
"Having set aside a corrupt mind and a lack of respect, one should pay homage; rather, having established affection and reverence, one's feet should be worshipped.
Thus was the method of homage explained. How is the specific form of the fivefold prostration described?
Herein, "having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder" is the first.
"Raising the hands in *añjali*" is one; "rubbing the feet with both palms" is one; "establishing affection" is one;
and "establishing reverence" is one—thus, the nature of the fivefold prostration (*pañcapatiṭṭhita*) is described.
Therefore it was said: "Having established these five qualities within oneself, the feet should be venerated. Thus, for the entire world...

It is appropriate to pay homage according to the method of veneration taught by the Lord of Dhamma— the one who brings about welfare and happiness— to the Venerable Thera Upāli, for the purpose of promoting great welfare and happiness through both physical prostration and mental prostration.
Now, however, the teachers are teaching the method of veneration to newly arrived youths and novices.
They do not train by taking this text as it was spoken; rather, they train by following the method transmitted through the lineage.

How so? If one is to stand and pay homage, one should place both soles of the feet evenly upon the ground, bring both palms together levelly, and, having placed them against the forehead, bow down facing the object of veneration.

“Worship them! This method accords with both this statement from the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*: “In this way, the Great Being, having bowed down toward the city of Bārāṇasī like a golden plantain tree, paid homage to his mother and father,” and with these words from the commentaries:
“Having raised his hands in a brilliant añjali joined by ten fingernails, he placed it upon his head,” and so forth. Here...
However, they state the formal procedure (*sarūpa*) as follows: [the hands] rest upon five points—the two palms of the feet, the two palms of the hands, and the forehead.
If you are paying homage while seated, first place both palms of the feet evenly on the ground, raise both knees evenly, and place both elbows evenly above the two knees.
Having made the two palms of the hands level and joined them in the gesture known as *añjali*, place them upon the forehead, which is considered the head, and pay homage.
Then, bowing down, place both knee-caps and both temples evenly upon the ground;
extend the two palms and set them level on the earth, with the head between the two.
"Having placed [the hands] upon the backs of the hands and resting them on the ground, pay homage.

Here, however, they describe the form of the five-pointed prostration by making the two soles of the feet one, likewise the two kneecaps one, the two elbows one, the two palms of the hands one, and the head one.
This method is not seen in the Pāḷi, the commentaries, or the sub-commentaries.
But when they have approached and are at the time of paying homage at the feet, some first touch their own heads with their hands and then, with those two hands,
massage the elders' kneecaps over the top of their robes. Others first touch the elders' kneecaps together with the robes and then, with those same two hands, [touch] their own heads.
They grasp [the feet]. Some merely touch them with their lips. This practice is not seen anywhere else.

However, when the monks of the Rāmañña country approach in this manner to pay homage, even if they do not see the elders' feet, they search for them, draw them out from beneath the robes, repeatedly rub the feet with their hands, roll them over with their heads, and kiss them.
Having licked [the feet], they pay homage as if they were seeing their own dear and beloved preceptor or teacher who had returned from a long absence.

That action appears to correspond to the text found in the *Parivāra-pāḷi*, which states: "The feet should be saluted by massaging them with both palms of the hands, while manifesting affection and reverence. Not all of them, however...
They see the canonical text (pāḷi) and act according to the tradition alone; therefore, for the benefit of all, we have extracted the method of the canonical text.

For the method of the canonical text is more authoritative than the method transmitted through tradition; therefore, it is our conviction that noble persons who revere the command of the Blessed One should cultivate the method of the canonical text, and this should be accepted after investigation.
55. The Discussion on Stools, etc.

Regarding this discussion on stools, etc.: "a square stool" means one that is perfectly square. "A foot eight finger-breadths is permissible" means that only one with feet measuring eight finger-breadths is permissible.
"Even one exceeding the measure is permissible" refers specifically to one that is perfectly square.
It has been stated. However, a chair that is elongated or square, even if it has seven or five legs, is not permitted if the legs are high.

A *bhaddapīṭha* (an auspicious chair) is one made of rattan in a square or other such shape; thus, it is called a "rattan-made chair. "Above the wooden plank" means below the wooden surface situated in the form of a crossbar (*aṭani*).
The word "above" (*upari*) is used with reference to the time when the leg is inserted after being positioned upwards.
It has been said. However, because it stands in a curved shape like the two hind legs of a sheep, it is called an "eḷakapādapīṭha" (a sheep’s footstool).
56. The Discussion on High and Large Beds and Seats.
In the discussion on high and large beds and seats, [the phrase] "beasts of prey" refers to attractive beasts of prey; [it means] "crowded with unallowable forms."
“An improper bed is a *pallaṅka*,” so it is stated in the *Sārasamāsa*. A “large woolen rug with long hair” (*mahākojava*) is a black woolen rug whose hair exceeds four finger-breadths in length.
Because of the statement, “It is said that its hairs exceed four finger-breadths,” they say that [a rug] with hair less than four finger-breadths is permissible.
A “woven, variegated woolen covering” (*uṇṇāmayattharaṇa*) is a woolen covering made variegated by means of cuttings from walls and so forth.

A *ghanapupphaka* is a woolen spread (*uṇṇāmayattharaṇa*), meaning a red woolen spread. A natural cotton mattress (*pakatitūlikā*) is a mattress filled with one of three types of stuffing known as tree-cotton, rattan-cotton, or silk-worm-cotton.

Regarding the terms *uddalomī* and *ekantalomī*, it is stated in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*: “*Uddalomī* is a woolen spread with hair on both sides; *ekantalomī* is a woolen spread with hair on one side.

However, in the *Sārasamāsa*, it says: “*Uddalomī*... [The text continues: “...is a woolen spread with hair on both sides. [Note: The provided source text for the *Sārasamāsa* excerpt appears incomplete.]
"Single-sided wool" (*ekatolika*) means "with hair on one side"; "double-sided wool" (*ubhatolika*) is what is meant by "both sides raised.

Regarding "made of silk and *kaṭṭissa*," the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla stated it means "made of silk and *kasaṭa*. "Pure silk" (*suddhakoseyya*) means free from any stitching with jewels. However, in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said here:
"With the exception of the mattress (*tūlikā*), all [bedspreads] such as the *gonaka* are stitched with jewels."
It is said, “they are not allowable. In this context, by the phrase “except for a mattress,” it is indicated that even a mattress that is not sewn with jewels is not allowable.

However, by the statement “those sewn with jewels are not allowable,” it should be understood that those which are sewn with jewels may be used as floor coverings or, as appropriate, placed upon beds and the like.
And here, having reached the method of the Vinaya, since one must stand firm in what is grave, the detailed exposition (vinicchaya) should be understood according to the very method stated herein.
However, others say that because the teaching of the Suttas was spoken with reference to householders as well, the statement “except for a mattress...
it is allowable” was made in order to include them.
“With antelope skins” means with the skins of the *ajina* deer. It is said that those skins are very fine;

therefore, they are sewn together by making double or triple layers. Hence it is called “an antelope-skin couch. It covers the upper part, thus it is an “upper covering” (*uttaracchada*), meaning a canopy;
and since a red canopy is intended here, he says “by a red canopy fastened above.”
"It is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* that 'the wearing of saffron robes dyed with redwood (ratta) is permitted, but those dyed with safflower (kusumbha) and so forth is not permitted.
A 'large pillow' (*mahā-upadhāna*) is a pillow that exceeds the prescribed measure. And here, although it is said in the *Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā*:
'Even two non-red [pillows] are indeed permitted; having obtained more than that, they should be given to others. If one is unable to give them,'..."
It is stated without distinction that "one may lie down after spreading [a rug] across the bed and providing an upper coverlet";
however, in the commentary on the Senāsanakkhandhaka, it says: "For one who is not ill, only two things are permitted—a pillow for the head and a pillow for the feet.
For one who is ill, having spread out bolsters and provided an upper coverlet..."
Since it is stated, “it is even permissible to lie down,” it should be understood that only one who is ill is permitted to lie down after spreading [the rug] crosswise on a bed.
Regarding the phrase “sitting leaning against,” this means “sitting with support. This much of the legal analysis (*vinicchaya*) has been recorded in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: “‘Forms of wild beasts’ refers to manufactured forms of wild beasts. ‘Exceeding four finger-breadths’...”

The distinction between *uddalomī* (with hair pointing upward) and *ekantalomī* (with hair on one side) is as follows: it is said that those [blankets] which are less than four finger-breadths [in length] fall under the category of *uddalomī* and so forth.
A "woven variegated woolen rug" (*vānacitro uṇṇāmayattharaṇo*) is a patterned woolen coverlet made by weaving various colored woolen threads in the manner of wall-patches and the like.

"Densely flowered" (*ghanapupphako*) means having thick coloration. An "ordinary cotton mattress" (*pakatitūlikā*) is a stuffed cushion filled with cotton (*tūla*). "Variations" (*vikatikā*) refers to...
Or, it is understood as being variegated with paintings in the form of lions and so forth.
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*: “*Uddalomī* is a woolen rug (*uṇṇāmayattharaṇa*) with the nap on both sides; *ekantalomī* is a woolen rug with the nap on one side only.
*Koseyyakaṭṭissamayaṃ* means woven by inserting golden threads between silk threads; indeed, it is said that the golden thread is called *kaṭṭissaṃ*.
And it is called *kasaṭa*. For this very reason, they say that the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla stated, “made of silk-cotton (*koseyya-kasaṭa*)”;
thus, “studded with jewels” means coated with gold. “Pure silk” means devoid of such jewel-studying.
Because the skins of the *ajina* deer are exceedingly fine, they are sewn after being made into double or triple layers; hence it is said, “a seam of antelope skin.”
"By a red canopy" means by a canopy that is entirely red. However, that which is multicolored, whether it be a woven design (*vānacitta*) or a painted design (*lepacitta*), is permissible.
The same principle applies to both red footstools (*ubhatolohitakūpadhāna*). As for the phrase "or variegated," this is stated because it is allowable in every respect;
it is not, however, because variegation is unallowable in the case of the two footstools. For the word "red" (*lohitaka*) does not apply to a variegated pattern.
It is permissible. Because by the very mention of "a canopy" (*paṭaliggahaṇena*), there is the implication that it includes even a painted rug (*cittaka-attharaṇa*).
However, the saffron robe (*kāsāva*) does not receive the designation "red-limbed" (*lohitaṅga*); therefore, it is permissible even for a canopy or for a rug with two pillows.
The phrase "if it is of the proper measure," etc., is intended to show that another kind of pillow which exceeds the proper measure is prohibited.
This was stated not for the purpose of showing that high and large beds are permitted, because it was not said so; however, that pillow is allowed for laypeople observing the Uposatha.
For at that time, only high and large beds were not permitted for them. Although in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* and other texts it is said:
"With the exception of the cotton-down mattress (*tūlikā*), all [beds] such as the *gonaka* and others, even if sewn with jewels..."
"It is not allowable," it is said; however, it should be understood that the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* alone is the authority regarding what is permissible and what is impermissible.
"Abhinissāya" means "relying upon. This concludes the discussion on the use of palaces.
Nothing is said regarding this in the *Pāsādaparibhogakathā*, the *Sāratthadīpanī*, or the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated: "‘Variegated with gold, silver, and so forth’ refers to monastic lodgings belonging to the Saṅgha.
As for personal property variegated with gold and so forth, it is not even permissible for a bhikkhu to accept it; for [it is said]: ‘By no one...’"
Because it was stated, “Gold and silver may be accepted by way of exchange,” for that very reason it is said here in the Commentary:

“Whether in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha or in a private dwelling. This is stated specifically regarding improper articles such as woolen blankets and the like, because there is no fault in a single bhikkhu taking them.
The Discussion on Footwear:
In this discussion on footwear, "the color of fresh aruṭṭha fruit" refers to the color of a newly harvested aruṭṭha fruit; some also say it is the color of a crow’s wing when wet with water.
"Sandals made of wool" refers to sandals made from blankets consisting of woolen hair, or sandals made directly from woolen hair itself.
“*Kāḷasīha* is a species of black-faced monkey. The rest here is easily understood from both the *Pāḷi* and the *Aṭṭhakathā*,” so it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: “*Addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇā* means having the color of a fresh *ariṭṭha* fruit;
they also say it has the color of a crow’s wing when wet. *Rajanaṃ* is said with reference to the color of the blue and other pigments smeared on top.”
Therefore it is said, “having wiped with a cloth. For when it is wiped in that manner, [the odor] disappears.

However, as for that which has acquired a black, red, or other color because it was dyed with black, red, and so forth in order to remove the bad smell from the hide—that cannot be removed by cloths and the like;
it remains the very nature of the hide. Therefore, it should be understood that this is permissible. *Khallakaṃ* means...
A covering for the heels is permissible merely as a fastening to be attached above the heels in order to prevent them from wearing away; it should not cover the entire surface.
By "variegated" is meant variegated strips in terms of their shape, not in terms of color, because they fall under the category of patches and the like that must be removed entirely.
Because they have faces resembling those of cats, great owls are called "bird-cats" (*pakkhibiḷāla*).
Their "hide" refers specifically to that with coarse hair. Regarding the phrase "sandals made of wool," sandals made of woolen blankets are included here.
As for the "black sīha," this is a species of black-faced monkey. It is stated: "The hide is not permitted" means it is not permitted to make a sitting mat or a rug;
however, its use as a floor-covering and so forth is indeed permitted.
In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, however, it says: “‘Migamātuka’ is his name, and ‘Vātamiga’ is also his name.
It is written: ‘The black lion, the black-faced monkey. ‘Skin is not permitted’: by whatever method skin will be permitted, that will become clear later.
It is stated: ‘Acceptance on account of one’s own private property is prohibited.’”

It has been stated: "Although the matter would have been settled by the words, 'Monks, no hide whatsoever should be worn,' the specific phrase 'no cow-hide' was spoken later out of fear that the permission— 'Monks, in all border regions I allow hides for spreading'— might be wrongly applied here as well."
