In the Discourse on Carriages (*Yānakathā*), regarding the passage, "Monks, I allow a handcart yoked with men," the completion of the sentence occurs for each term individually: "Monks, I allow [what is] yoked with men; monks, I allow a handcart."
Regarding the term *adhippetam* (intended), he said: “Whether it be a vehicle drawn by men with a woman as the driver... or even men [themselves], it is indeed permissible.
Regarding the phrase *pīṭhakasivikam*, the *Sāratthadīpanī* states: “*Pīṭhakasivikam* is a chair-carriage (*pīṭhakayānam*). *Paṭaṅkin* is a designation for a swing-cot (*andolikā*). [Alternatively:
“*Pīṭhakasivikam* is a chair-carriage made of wood-boards and so forth. *Paṭapotalikam* is a swing-cot. Every kind of vehicle, even including sandals (*upāhana*), [is included].”
"In the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated: 'It is permitted for one who is ill and unable to go.

57. Discussion on Robes (*Cīvarakathā*): In the discussion on robes, "worn-out" means those that have been washed once. "Removed from the weather" means removed from the weather over a long period of time.
"Of those with the cloth removed" means of rags (*pilotika*). "In the market" refers to a robe made from rags fallen from a shop.
"Effort must be made" means that a search must be undertaken. There is no limit here; even a hundred pieces of cloth are permitted.
All this is stated with reference to a monk who accepts [the gift]. "The bolt is sewn" means that having removed it from there...
The *Aṭṭhakathā* states: "An *allīyāpana-khaṇḍa* is a patch; *suttena saṃsibbitaṃ tunnaṃ* means sewn with thread; *ovaṭṭikaṃ* is making [the patch] rounded;
*kaṇḍupakaṃ* is called a *muddikā* (a small square patch); *daḷīkammaṃ* refers to a patch that is fixed by sewing it on without first removing [the old cloth].
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it says: "*Acchupeyyaṃ* means one should fix [it]."
"Hatavatthakānan" means of cloths that have become worn out. "Uddharitvā allīyāpanakhaṇḍan" is explained as "a piece of cloth for patching after removing a weak spot.
"Diguṇaṃ saṅghāṭin" means a double-layered outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*). "Ekacciyam" means a single-layered upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).
"Aggaḷaṃ ajjhāpessanti" means one should cause a piece of rag to be attached to a worn-out place.
The Discussion on Cut Cloths:
In this discussion on cut cloths, regarding the statement that "among the three robes, one should make [them] by cutting two or even one," it says here:
"Monks, I allow a cut outer robe (saṅghāṭi), a cut upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), and a cut inner robe (antaravāsaka)."
According to the wording, it must be made by cutting [the cloth] into five or seven pieces and so forth; the meaning is that it should not be made without cutting.
Regarding the statement, "If it is not sufficient, a visiting monk's cloth (āgantuka-paṭṭa) should be given":
here, if the cloth is not sufficient for the purpose of all three robes when made by cutting, two robes should be made from the cut portions, and one robe should be made from the uncut portion.
It should be made. When two robes have been cut and made up, if the garment is not sufficient, there are two robes that are uncut;
one robe must be cut. Even when one robe has been cut and made up, if the garment is not sufficient, the meaning is that in such a case, an incoming patch should be applied without cutting.
To establish this point by means of the Pāḷi:

He said, “For this has been stated,” and so forth. Therein, the phrase “I allow you to add even a further addition” means that if [the robes] cannot be made [to fit] in this way, one is permitted to add even a border for a guest.
This concludes the discussion on improper robes.

In the discourse on improper robes, the Blessed One prohibited these items—namely, nudity, a garment of kusa grass, a garment of wood-shavings, a blanket of human hair, a blanket of animal hair, a garment of owls’ wings, and a goatskin—because they constitute the formal undertakings of other sectarians and are grounds for a grave offense (thullaccaya).
Therein, "nudity" refers to the state of being naked or the state of being a naked ascetic (acelaka). "A garment of kusa grass" refers to [a robe] woven from kusa grass.
A garment made of bark (*katacīvara*). A garment of *vākacīra* is the bark-garment of ascetics.
A garment made of wood-slats (*phalakacīvara*) is a robe made by sewing together slats shaped like wooden boards. A hair-blanket (*kesakambala*) is a blanket made by weaving hair into a loom.
A yak-tail blanket (*vālakambala*) is a blanket made by weaving the tails of yaks. An owl-wing garment (*ulūkapakkhika*) is a covering made from the wings of the bird-owl.

“Antelope skin” (*ajinakkhipa*) refers to the hide of an antelope with its fur and hooves intact. Since these serve as the banners of the non-Buddhist sects and are well known for not being robes, they were not mentioned here by the Teacher.

However, because the *potthaka* (woven cloth) is not well known [as such], he spoke of it, and then described all the blue-colored garments and so forth as having an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) as their basis.
Because it was stated, “They should be given in the middle of a triple-layered robe (*tipaṭṭacīvara*),” the triple-layered robe [is implied].

It is established that it is permissible to keep [them]. This indicates that among many-layered robes such as the *tipaṭṭa* and others, one should make such pieces of cloth or rags (*paṭapilotika*) of unsuitable color [for formal use].
A *kañcuka* is a garment worn on the body after being fastened over the head.
Therefore he said: "It is permissible to tear it apart, dye it, and then use it. A *veṭhana* is a head-wrap. A *tirīṭa*...
A crown. To show its specific quality, he said, "But the tirīṭaka," and so forth.
Regarding the discussion on the distribution of robes:
in the discussion on the distribution of robes, it is said, "Bhikkhus, Ānanda is wise; bhikkhus, Ānanda has great wisdom."
For when someone will understand in detail the meaning of what has been spoken by me in brief,
they will indeed make a *kusim*, they will indeed make a half-*kusim*, they will indeed make a *maṇḍala*, they will indeed make a half-*maṇḍala*,
they will indeed make a *vivaṭṭa*, they will indeed make an *anuvivaṭṭa*, and they will indeed make a *gīveyyaka*.

From the statement: "They will call it 'Jaṅgheyyaka,' they will call it 'Bāhanta,' it will be cut short, rough-hewn with a knife, suitable for a recluse, and undesirable to one's enemies," [it follows from the words]:
"Do you see, Ānanda, how the Magadha territory is laid out in squares, laid out in rows, laid out with boundaries, and laid out with crossroads?"
Having heard the words spoken briefly by the Blessed One, the Venerable Ānanda arranged robes for many monks in accordance with the Blessed One’s intention.
In the same way, such robes should now also be arranged.
In this context, "plotted out" means divided like a square field; "lined out" means [measured] in length and breadth.
And it is long and bound by boundaries. "Bound by boundaries" means that between [the long stretches], it is bound by short boundaries.
"Laid out like a crossroads" (siṅghāṭakabaddha) means that in places where one boundary intersects another, it is "laid out like a crossroads";
the meaning is that its shape is like a quadrangle. "Yatra hi nāma" means "he who indeed. In phrases such as "kusimpi nāma," *kusi* refers to the length and breadth.
And "windward" and so forth is a designation for long strips of cloth. "Half-moon" (*aḍḍhakusī*) is the name for strips of cloth that are short in between.
"Circle" (*maṇḍala*) refers to the large circle on each individual panel of a five-panel robe.
"Half-circle" (*aḍḍhamaṇḍala*) refers to a small circle. "Swirl" (*vivaṭṭa*) is the middle panel sewn together by joining a circle and a half-circle.

"Anuvivaṭṭanti" refers to two strips [of cloth] on both sides of it. "Gīveyyakaṃ" is an additional strip sewn with another thread for the purpose of strengthening at the place where the neck is wrapped.
"Jaṅgheyyakaṃ" is a strip sewn in the same manner at the place reaching down to the shanks.
These are the names for the strips at the place of the neck and the place of the shanks. "Bāhantaṃ" means...
"Anuvivaṭṭānaṃ" means one section on each side outside [the main body]. Thus, this is explained by means of the five-section robe (*pañcakhaṇḍika-cīvara*).
Alternatively, "anuvivaṭṭāni" is a name for the four sections: two on one side of the *vivaṭṭa* (the central fold) and two on the other side.
"Bāhantaṃ" refers to a robe of the measure of a *suppa* (a winnowing-basket) that has been folded and placed over the arm by one wearing it.
"Both ends stand facing outward; this is their name. For this very method is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā," so it is recorded in the Aṭṭhakathā.
This concludes the Discussion on Sewing Robes.

In the discourse on sewing robes with a wooden board and a thimble: At that time, the monks were sewing robes by driving stakes into various places and binding them together; consequently, the robes became distorted.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One: "I allow you, monks, a wooden board and a cord for the wooden board; [use these] here and there."
"Having fastened it, one should sew the robe. They spread the *kathina* on uneven ground; the *kathina* breaks apart... [omission] ...
"Monks, the *kathina* must not be spread on uneven ground. Whoever should spread it there, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
They spread the *kathina* on the bare ground; the *kathina* becomes covered in dust. "I allow you, monks, a grass mat."
"It wears out within the period of the *kathina*. I allow you, monks, to attach a border along the length. The *kathina* is not sufficient.

I allow you, monks, having sewn it with a staff-like *kathina*, with strips, with slips, with a binding cord, and with a binding thread, to stitch the robe. The intermediate threads become uneven. I allow—"
“Monks, it is called ‘kaḷimbhaka’ because the threads are crooked. Monks, I allow ‘moghasuttaka’ (useless thread).
Now at that time, monks stepped on the kaṭhina cloth with unwashed feet, and the kaṭhina was defiled.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One: “Monks, the kaṭhina must not be stepped upon with unwashed feet.”
"Whoever should step upon it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Now at that time, the monks stepped on the kaṭhina with wet feet, and the kaṭhina was damaged.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One: "Monks, the kaṭhina must not be stepped upon with wet feet."
"Whoever should step upon it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Now at that time, monks stepped upon the kaṭhina cloth while wearing sandals, and the kaṭhina cloth was damaged.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One: "Monks, one should not step upon the kaṭhina cloth while wearing sandals. Whoever should step upon it..."
“There is an offense of wrong-doing.

Now at that time, the monks, while sewing robes, were receiving [the thread] with their fingers, and their fingers became painful. They reported this matter to the Blessed One: “I allow you, monks, to use a thimble.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks used various kinds of thimbles, including one made of gold.
[It was] made of silver. People criticized, grumbled, and complained, saying, "Just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One: "Monks, various kinds of precious objects should not be kept.
Whoever should keep them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Monks, I allow [objects] made of bone... up to ... made of conch-shell."
Now at that time, needles, knives, and cases were being lost. They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“I allow you, monks, a needle-case. The needle-cases became disorganized.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One: “I allow you, monks, a bag for the cases. A shoulder-strap...
"It does not exist... [as before] ...I allow you, monks, a shoulder-strap and a binding cord.
Now at that time, monks sewing robes in the open air were distressed by both cold and heat.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One: "I allow you, monks, a robe-stiffening hall and a robe-stiffening pavilion."
The kathina hall had a low foundation and was flooded by water. They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, I allow you to build it on a high foundation. The masonry collapsed. “Monks, I allow you to build up; I allow three kinds of masonry:
masonry of brick, masonry of stone, and masonry of wood. Those climbing up were distressed. “I allow…”
“Monks, there are three kinds of staircases: a brick staircase, a stone staircase, and a wooden staircase.
As they were ascending, they fell. ‘Monks, I allow a handrail. Grass and dust fell from the plastered hall.
‘Monks, I allow you to plaster it over and smear it, making it white-colored, black-colored, or treated with red ochre.”
"Garland-work, creeper-work, shark-tooth pattern, fivefold pleating, and robe-strings.
Now at that time, the monks, having sewn their robes, would depart just as they were, leaving the *kaṭhina* frame behind;
consequently, the robes were eaten by rats and termites. They reported this matter to the Blessed One: "I allow you, monks—"
Regarding "to roll up the *kathina*": the *kathina* cloth becomes torn.
"I allow you, monks, to roll up the *kathina* with a cow-hair brush. Regarding "the *kathina* slips off": "I allow you, monks, a binding cord.
Now at that time, monks would leave after hanging the *kathina* over walls or pillars; it would then fall down.
The *kathina* is torn. They reported this matter to the Blessed One: "I allow you, monks, to hang it on a doorpost or on a wall-bracket.
This is the reading found in the *Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka*. "'Kathina' refers to a ladder as well, or any one of the mats, screens, or reed-mats that are to be spread there. 'Kathina-rope'..."
By means of which, while sewing a double-layered robe, they obstruct the *kaṭhina* robe.
"The *kaṭhina* does not suffice" means that a *kaṭhina* made according to the measurement of a tall monk does not suffice when spread out for the robe of a short monk;

it remains only inside [the robe] and does not reach the border-strips (*daṇḍaka*)—this is the meaning. "A *kaṭhina* with border-strips" refers to one where, in its middle, there is a short [section].
The meaning is: "I authorize another ladder to be constructed according to the measure of a monk's [height].

*Bidalaka* means folding the edge of a straw mat back according to the measure of the staff-frame and doubling it over. *Salāka* refers to a wedge inserted between the two layers of a double-layered robe (*dupaṭṭacīvara*).
*Vinandhanarajju* refers to a binding rope for a small ladder together with a large ladder.
"To bind with a cord" (*vinandhituṃ rajjuṃ*): "A binding thread" (*vinandhanasuttakaṃ*) is a thread for binding a robe to a small ladder.
"Having bound the robe, one sews it" (*vinandhitvā cīvaraṃ sibbitun ti*): having bound the robe there with that thread, one sews it.
"They are uneven" (*visamā hontīti*): some are small and some are large. "A *kaḷimbhaka*" is a means of making a measurement known.
"Any [leaf] such as a palm leaf, etc. "A false thread" means making a mark on wood by carpenters using a turmeric thread, just as they do with a black thread.
"Receiving it with a finger" means receiving the needle-point with a finger. "A receptacle" means a finger-sheath.
"A workshop box" means any small container such as a bowl or a casket. "On a high base" means on a mound of earth.
The meaning is: "Having scattered [the earth], I authorize you to build a high foundation. "Having plastered over and having smeared over" means:
having shaken off the covering and made it a solid framework, one should smear it with clay both inside and out.
"With a cow-horn" means: having inserted bamboo or a wooden pole inside, one should roll it up together with that.
"Binding-cord" (*bandhanarajju*) and likewise "binding-cord for that which has been gathered together" (*saṃharitassa bandhanarajju*):

this is the reading in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. "In the direction of the wind, he makes a border" (*anuvātaṃ paribhaṇḍaṃ*): it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* that he makes [this] out of *kilañja* (grass mats) and so forth.
"Folding" (*bidalaka*): this is a designation for a specific action known as making double. Of what is there the making double? Of that *kilañja* and so forth by which a large *kaṭhina* [is made].
It is spread out for him. For that [cloth] should be gathered at the edges to the measurement of a staff-kathina and made double-layered.
A "receptacle" (*paṭiggaha*) is a finger-cuff. A "bowl" (*pāti*) is a particular kind of vessel made in the shape of a receptacle. "It is not approved" means it is not sufficient.
"To build with a low foundation" means to build with a low foundation all around the exterior wall.
"In order to pile [the robes]," according to the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
"Even a ladder" means a platform constructed by joining four poles together, made long and square to the measurement of the robe;
for here, having tied the corners of the robes evenly, they sew the robe as desired. Therein, it should be spread out.
On top of that ladder, it should be spread out for the purpose of supporting the robe.

Regarding the phrase "by which," etc., he says this because the compound *kathinarajju*—meaning "the binding-cord for the robe on the ladder designated as *kaṭhina*"—is a *majjhimapadalopi* (middle-term-elided) compound.
In that context, when one of two layers becomes excessive, folds (*valiyo*) arise there.
Therefore, for a double-layered robe (*dupaṭṭacīvara*), both layers should be made equal; the binding cord is to be understood as the "stiffening cord" (*kathinarajju*).
In the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated: "In the text, 'it wears out within the Kathina' means that the edge of the robe bound during the Kathina period wears out."
"Bidalaka" is a designation for a specific type of action known as "doubling. Of what is there doubling?

It is of that *kaṭhina* (ritual robe) which was spread out large by means of reeds and so forth. For that [robe] must be gathered together at the edges to the size of the *daṇḍakaṭhina* and then doubled;
otherwise, in the case of a small robe, when performing the application of the *anuvāta-paribhaṇḍa* and other such methods, [the doubling would not be possible].
There is no room for the hand. When there is a measuring-stick, once one has identified which of the two robes [is which], it is easy to discern what has been sewn and what has not been sewn.
When the *daṇḍakathina* (the wooden frame for sewing) is prepared, there is no need for many assistants. It is written: "Without shrinking, the robe becomes even;
the corners also become even. This is because it is stated that "the marking is done with a turmeric string."
"It is established that it is permissible to sew a robe with a turmeric thread. Regarding this, some hold the view that it is not allowable.
"A bowl" (*paṭiggaha*) means a finger-casket. "A dish" (*pāti*) has the shape of a bowl. "A bowl-bag" (*paṭiggahathavikā*) means a bag for a finger-casket;
thus it is stated in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*.
The Discourse on Householder Robes and Other Matters.
In this discourse on householder robes and other matters, it is said: "Monks, I allow a householder robe. Whoever wishes may be a wearer of rag-robes;
whoever wishes may accept a householder robe. Monks, I praise contentment with whatever is obtained."
From the words, "I praise [this]," it follows that a bhikkhu who has not undertaken the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) but wishes to wear rag-robes (paṃsukūla) must be one who wears rag-robes.
However, he who wishes to accept a householder’s robe-cloth given by laypeople must be one who accepts householder’s robe-cloth.
But for a bhikkhu who has undertaken the ascetic practice, [regarding] a householder’s robe-cloth...
"I reject [fine robes] and undertake the refuse-rag-wearer’s practice"—because he has thus resolved, it is not permissible for him to accept a robe from a householder.
"A robe from a householder" means a robe given by householders. "By whatever [means]" means by anything whatsoever, whether of little value or of great value.

“*Itarītarena* means ‘by this or that. Since the word *itara* expresses indefiniteness, when stated twice, it has the same meaning as the word ‘whatever’ (*yaṃkiñci*); thus it is said in the *Sāratthadīpanī*:
‘I allow, monks, a cloak; I allow, monks, a silk cloak (*koseyyapāvāra*).’”
From the statement, "Monks, I allow a *kojava*," it is also permissible to accept items such as a *pāvāra*.

In this context, a *pāvāra* is a woolen cloth made of cotton and other materials that still has the fleece attached. Regarding the allowance, "Monks, I allow a *kojava*," only a natural *kojava* is permitted here;
a large-backed *kojava* is not permitted. A *kojava* is made of wool and resembles a *pāvāra*. [A] "large-backed..."

In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: "A *kojava* is a four-finger-breadth flower-patterned rug, which has acquired the conventional designation ‘*mahāpiṭṭhiya*’ because it is to be spread upon the backs of elephants.

In the *Vimativinodanī* as well, it is stated: "*Mahāpiṭṭhiya-kojava* is a woolen covering that has acquired the conventional designation ‘*mahāpiṭṭhiya*’ because it is to be spread upon the backs of elephants. [This is also found] in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*.
However, it is said: "The so-called *mahāpiṭṭhiyaka-java* is a cloth with flowers [printed] more than four finger-breadths in size.
Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow woolen cloth (*kambala*)," even expensive woolen cloths such as the *aḍḍhakāsiya* are permitted.
Here, *kāsi* refers to a thousand [pieces of gold]; a *kāsiya* is one worth that amount. This, however, is five...
It is worth six hundred [coins], therefore he is called Aḍḍhakāsī.
Regarding the Discourse on the Six Robes: In the Discourse on the Six Robes, [it says]: "Monks, I allow you six kinds of robes: linen, cotton, silk..."

Based on the statement, "Kambala, sāṇa, and bhaṅga," it is permissible to use the six types of robes beginning with *khoma*, as well as the six types of secondary robes (*anulomacīvara*) beginning with *dukūla*.
In this context: "Khoma" refers to cloth woven from *khoma* fibers, such as a robe made of *khoma* silk.
"Kappāsika" refers to that which is woven from threads produced from cotton. "Koseyya" refers to [cloth] produced from threads generated by silkworms.
*Vāyitaṃ*: woven. *Kambalaṃ*: a robe made of wool. *Sāṇaṃ*: a robe made from *sāṇa* fibers. *Bhaṅgaṃ*:
a robe made from all types of flaxen threads (*khoma-sutta*) and so forth, or one made by mixing some of them together. Some say that *bhaṅga* is also made exclusively of hemp (*vāka*).
However, these six robes—*dukūla*, *paṭṭuṇṇa*, *somārapaṭa*, *cīnapaṭa*, *iddhija*, and *devadatta*—are included within these very same categories.
The "anulomas" (suitable counterparts) are not mentioned separately. For *dukūla* is a counterpart to *sāṇa* because it is made of flax (*vāka*).
*Paṭṭuṇṇa* is cloth produced in the region of *paṭṭuṇṇa*. Indeed, it is stated in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*: "A specific kind of silk from *paṭṭuṇṇa*.
*Somāra* and *cīna* cloths are fabrics produced in the regions of *somāra* and *cīna*, respectively. These three—*paṭṭuṇṇa* and the others—are counterparts to silk (*koseyya*).

[It is] because it is made from thread spun by insects. That which is born of supernormal power (*iddhija*) refers to the robes produced through the merit-based psychic power (*puññiddhi*) of "come-hither" monks (*ehibhikkhu*);
since that consists of one or another of the fabrics such as *khoma*, it conforms to those very [categories]. A robe given by deities is "deity-given.
This is like the cloth given to the Elder Anuruddha by the celestial maiden Jālinī, which was produced on the Wishing Tree (*kapparukkha*).
"In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: 'That too is a derivative (*anuloma*) of linen and so forth, because it possesses the nature of one or another among them.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: 'Linen (*khoma*) is a robe made of linen cloth woven from linen threads; they say that is made of flax (*vāka*).
That woven from cotton threads is 'cotton' (*kappāsika*). The others are likewise. 'Wool' (*kambala*) refers to [the wool] of sheep and so forth..."
A cloth woven with woolen thread. "Bhaṅga" refers to robes woven from all types of linen thread and so forth, or those woven by mixing some of them together;

some say that *bhaṅga* is made of cotton alone. *Dukūla*, *paṭṭuṇṇa*, *somārapaṭa*, *cīnapaṭa*, *iddhija*, and *devadatta*—these six types of robes are not mentioned separately because they are merely variations (*anuloma*) of these very same [categories].
Dukūla is the "anuloma" (corresponding type) of sāṇa because it is made of cotton. Regarding *paṭṭuṇṇa*, it is stated in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* that it is a specific kind of silk (*koseyya*).

*Somāra-paṭa* and *cīna-paṭa* are garments produced in the regions of Somanātha and China, respectively. The three types beginning with *paṭṭuṇṇa* are the "anuloma" of *koseyya* because they consist of threads spun by insects.
*Iddhija* refers to robes produced through the power of merit (*puññiddhi*) of those who have come as monks (*ehibhikkhus*).
"It is said that [robes] produced from wish-fulfilling trees (*kapparukkha*) and those given by deities— such as *khoma* cloth and others—
are suitable for all of them. This concludes the discussion on dyeing and related matters.
In this discourse on dyes, because of the statement: “Monks, I allow six dyes: root-dye, stem-dye, bark-dye, leaf-dye, flower-dye, and fruit-dye,” the robe should be dyed with one of these six dyes;
it should not be dyed with yellow myrobalan or pale clay. A robe dyed with that [dye]...
It becomes discolored. The appearance of the various dyes has already been explained below in the discussion on requisites.
In that context, "with chakaṇa" means with cow dung; "with pale clay" means with reddish-brown clay.
Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow you to boil dye in a small dye-pot," the robe should not be dyed in cold water; for by that [method], it would become discolored.
Dyed robes become foul-smelling. In this context, "cold water" refers to unboiled dye-water.
Because of the statement, “Monks, I allow you to tie on a support-ring,” it is permissible to tie on a support-ring.
In that regard, a "support-ring" (*uttarāḷumpa*) is a circular base; having placed it in the middle of the dye-pot, one surrounds that base with [the pot].
The meaning is: "I authorize [the use of] a stand for dyeing. For when it is made in this way, the dye does not overflow.
In that context, "having placed it in the middle of the dye-pot" means having placed it inside the dye-pot.
Thus, when the circular support is placed inside the dye-pot, water remains in the middle, while the dye-sediment stays outside the circular support, all around within the pot.
"In 'to throw in,' it means to throw in the dye-skin," so it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated:
"For when it has been done thus—having placed the dye-water inside the circular base and the skin on the outside—the separation is effected.
It does not float up because, being merely water, there is no emergence of froth. In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*... [text fragment ends]
However, it is said: "There is no offense regarding cow dung; it was prohibited because of its unsightly appearance. They say that saffron flowers are not permitted.

Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow you to give a small amount [of dye] either in water or on the back of the fingernail," one should determine whether the dye is properly cooked or not by doing so.
In that regard, "either in water or on the back of the fingernail" means: if...
When it is fully cooked, a small amount poured into a water bowl does not suddenly spill; even when poured onto the back of the fingernail, it remains there without flowing away.

Because of the statement, “Monks, I allow a dye-scoop and a staff-pot,” a scoop, a staff, and a pot are required for the purpose of protecting the cauldron at the time of observing the dye. In this context, "dye-scoop" (rajanuḷuṅka) means:

A dye-vat (*rajanauḷuṅkaṃ*). Regarding "a staff-pot" (*daṇḍakathālakaṃ*): the staff itself is the "staff-pot. Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow a dye-jar (*rajana-kolamba*) and a dye-pitcher (*rajana-ghaṭa*"), these too are required.
Therein, a "dye-jar" (*rajana-kolamba*) is a dye-basin (*rajana-kuṇḍaṃ*).
Therein, a "dye-basin" (*rajana-kuṇḍaṃ*) is a large pitcher for holding boiled dye. [Also] because of the statement, "Monks, I allow a dye-tub (*rajana-doṇikā*")..."
Because cloth may be crushed even while being carried on the shoulder or in the bowl, and because the robe may become torn,
a dye-vat should be desired for the purpose of protecting the robe. Because of the statement, “I allow, monks,
a grass mat,” a grass mat should be made for the purpose of protecting the robe from becoming soiled with dust when it is spread out on the bare ground.
“Monks, I allow a robe-pole and a robe-string,” because of this statement, when the robe is being eaten by termites and other insects on a grass mat,
the robe should be spread out on either a robe-pole or a robe-string; for if the robe is attached by its middle,
the dye will drip away from both sides.
“Monks, I allow you to tie it at the corners,” from this statement it should be tied at the corners;

for when the robe is being tied at the corners, [the dye] might leak out because the corner has become worn. “Monks, I allow a cord for the corners,” from this statement it must be tied with a cord for the corners;
for by tying it in this way, the dye will not leak out to one side. “I allow—”
Monks, it should be dyed in such a way that one can turn it over repeatedly, and one must not depart while the drops of dye have not ceased falling;
for as long as the dripping of the dye-liquid has not been cut off, one must not go elsewhere.
Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow you to immerse it in water," [one should immerse] the thick cloth in water.
It should be soaked. In this context, "stiff" means hardened due to being over-dyed. "To soak in water" means to place it in water and leave it there.
Once the dye has been extracted, that water should be discarded and the robe should be kneaded.
Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow you to beat it with the hand," a stiff robe should be beaten with the hand. "Not..."
"Monks, robes that have not been torn should be worn; whoever should wear them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Because of this statement, robes that have not been torn—that is, ivory-colored saffron robes—should not be worn.
In this context, "ivory-colored saffron robes" refers to those worn after being dyed one or two times so that they have the color of ivory.
The Discussion on Extra Robes:

In this discussion on extra robes, because of the statement, “Monks, an extra robe must not be kept; whoever should keep one shall be dealt with according to the rule,” it refers to an extra robe kept more than ten days after the robe-making ceremony (*kathina*) has been dismantled and the robes have been finished.

For one who keeps [it] beyond that limit, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow you to keep an extra robe for a maximum of ten days," it follows that:
even when the Kathina has been suspended, for one who keeps it within the ten-day interval;

for those who have had the Kathina spread, even when the Kathina has not been suspended, within the five-month interval; and for those who have not had the Kathina spread, even beyond that [five-month period], within the ten-day interval.
Within ten days, there is no offense regarding an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*).
Because of the statement, “Monks, I allow you to assign (*vikappeti*) an extra robe,” it is permissible to wear an extra robe after ten days once it has been assigned.
But how large a robe should be assigned? “Monks, I allow [a robe] eight finger-breadths in length by the Sugata’s finger-breadth.”
Because of the statement, "One may assign the lower robe (*pacchima-cīvara*) as being four finger-breadths wide," it is permissible to assign a robe that is, at the very minimum,
eight finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in width by the measure of a Sugata’s finger.
In this context, what is called a "Sugata’s finger" is three times the measure of a carpenter’s finger, which is the finger-measure of an average-sized man.

By the natural human finger-breadth, this is four and a half finger-breadths; therefore, in length, it is one cubit by the carpenter’s hand (or builder’s cubit), which is one and a half cubits by the natural hand;
in width, it is one span by the carpenter’s hand, which is one span plus six finger-breadths by the natural hand.
It is permissible to designate the last robe as such if it is of these dimensions, but not if it is smaller than that.
It is not permitted; however, it should be understood that what exceeds the standard measure is permitted. Regarding the Discussion on the Eight Privileges:
in the Discussion on the Eight Privileges, [it says], "Monks, I allow you: a rainy-season robe, food for newcomers, and food for those departing..."

Because of the statement, “Food for the sick, food for those attending the sick, medicine for the sick, regular rice-gruel, and a water-strainer for the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs,” it is permissible to accept these eight kinds of gifts.
In that regard, when monks have laid aside their robes and their bodies are being rained upon, their nakedness is impure, loathsome, and repulsive; therefore—
The rains-bathing cloth was permitted. A visiting monk may not be skilled regarding the streets or skilled regarding the alms-round;
he wanders for alms exhausted. Therefore, meals for visitors were permitted.
A departing monk, while seeking his own meal, might leave the caravan, or he might arrive at the wrong time at the place where he intends to go or where he wishes to stay.

He will become exhausted from traveling the road; therefore, there is the meal for those on a journey. For a sick monk who does not obtain suitable food, his illness will increase or he will pass away; therefore, there is the meal for the sick.
A monk attending the sick, while searching for his own meal, will bring out the meal for the sick only after the sun has risen high.

Therefore, there is the meal for those attending the sick. Because the illness of a sick monk who does not obtain suitable medicines will either increase or lead to his death, there is medicine for the sick.
Because yagu was permitted by the Blessed One while he was at Andhakavinda, seeing ten advantages, there is constant yagu.
Because the nakedness of women is impure, loathsome, and repulsive, the water-bathing cloth was therefore permitted for the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs.
The Discussion on the Sitting Mat, etc.

In the discussion concerning the sitting mat (*nisīdana*), because of the statement: “I allow you, monks, a sitting mat for the protection of the body, the protection of the robes, and the protection of the lodgings,” it is permissible to carry a sitting mat for the purpose of guarding the body and so forth against the discharge of impurities.
Its method of construction has already been explained below. “I allow you, monks, a rug (*paccattharaṇa*) as large as [required].”
Because of the statement, "He desires to make a spread as large as that," it is permissible to make even a large spread,

since a seat that is too small fails to protect the lodging. Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow a kaṇḍupaṭicchādi (itch-covering cloth) for one who has an affliction such as itch, boils, sores, or scabies."
When such ailments exist, it is permissible to have a "scraping cloth" (*kaṇḍupaṭicchādi*) for the purpose of protecting one's robes and other requisites.
Its measurement is exactly as stated below. Because of the statement, “Monks, I allow a face-wiping cloth,” a face-wiping cloth is permissible for the purpose of cleaning the face.
That too is exactly as stated below. [And because of the statement: “Monks, I allow a requisite-cloth (*parikkhāracoḷaka*).”
According to the words of the text, when the three robes are complete and there is need for items such as a water-strainer or a needle-case, it is permissible to have requisites-cloth.

"Monks, I allow you to determine the three robes, but not to assign them; the rain-bathing cloth may be determined for the four months of the rainy season, but after that, it must be assigned; the sitting mat may be determined, but not assigned."

One should perform both the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and the assignment (*vikappanā*) according to the method stated in the following words: "One may determine a bedspread but not assign it;
one may determine a kaṇḍupaṭicchādi (itch-cover) for as long as there is an illness, but after that, one must assign it;
one may determine a face-towel but not assign it; one may determine a requisite-cloth but not assign it."
This is the summary here; the detailed account, however, has already been stated above.
Regarding the discussion on illegal formal acts (*adhammakamma-kathā*):
in this discussion on illegal formal acts, the passage beginning with "Monks, [this is] not... [up to] an offense of wrong-doing" refers to the following: "At that time..."
The group of six bhikkhus performed an illegal formal act in the midst of the Saṅgha. They reported this matter to the Blessed One, who said: "Bhikkhus, an illegal formal act must not be performed;
whoever should perform one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
This was said with reference to the passage found in the Uposatha-kkhandhaka. The phrase "I allow... [and so on] ...to censure" is likewise found [there], as is the statement: "To the Blessed One..."
They reported this matter: "I allow you, monks, to protest when an illegitimate legal procedure (*adhammakamma*) is being carried out.
In this context, "they indeed carry it out" means that they carry out an illegitimate legal procedure even by trampling upon the established training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
"I allow... to protest"—when such an illegitimate legal procedure is being performed, [the monks] should, by means of the virtuous ones...
The meaning is that it should be protested against by saying, "That illegal act has not been performed by the monks;
it is a bad act and must be performed again," and it is not to be accepted through silence. Regarding the phrase "because of the statement":
this refers to the statement based on taking the earlier reading; and regarding the statement "an illegal act should not be performed," this refers to the statement based on taking the later reading.
The construction should be made in two ways: "And an illegal act being performed must be stopped by the monks.

Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "By those who stop it," etc., [it refers to]: "At that time, the well-behaved monks protested while an illegal act was being performed by the group-of-six monks; the group-of-six monks became resentful, they became..."
[The monks] provoked resentment, caused dissatisfaction, and threatened them with death. They reported this matter to the Blessed One:

"I allow you, monks, to disclose your view. But when they disclosed their view in the very presence of those [monks], the monks of the group-of-six became resentful, became dissatisfied, and threatened them with death. They reported this matter to the Blessed One.

They reported [the matter]. [The Buddha said: “I allow you, monks, to protest with four or five [monks], to reveal one’s view with two or three, and to resolve ‘this is not acceptable to me’ with one. This was said with reference to these passages.
Regarding the phrase “by way of speech,” this should be connected individually with the three recipients mentioned in the Canon and the three verbal actions.
The construction is: "All this was said for the sake of ensuring there is no distress, not because of the existence of an offense. How is it that there is the possibility of no distress?
Because it is impossible to carry out an act of censure (*niggahakamma*) against them, and because it prevents other forms of distress. Therefore, it is stated in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*:
"For the sake of their being free from distress means that the Saṅgha does not perform a formal act against the Saṅgha."
“Furthermore, there are many other calamities; therefore it was said. Regarding the discussion on the formal motion (*okāsakata-kathā*):
in this discussion on the formal motion, [the passage] beginning with “Monks, one who has not made a formal motion,” etc., [refers to] at that time the group of six monks (*chabbaggiyā*).
Monks were accusing a monk of an offense without having granted him leave. They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
"Monks, a monk should not be accused of an offense without having been granted leave. Whoever should accuse him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow you to accuse a monk of an offense after having had him grant leave, saying: 'Venerable sir, please grant me leave; I..."

This was said with reference to the reading: "desiring to say that. Regarding the intentions (*adhippāya*): the intention to cause one to fall away means desiring to cause [someone] to fall away from the Teaching.
The intention to revile means desiring to abuse or to insult another. The intention regarding formal acts (*kamma*) means desiring to perform a formal act such as censure (*tajjanīya*).
The intention regarding rehabilitation means desiring to cause [someone] to emerge from an offense. The intention regarding the suspension of the *uposatha* and *pavāraṇā* means...
"Desiring to suspend the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā. "With the intention of investigating" means desiring to examine.
"With the intention of preaching the Dhamma" means desiring to teach the Dhamma. Thus, the meaning is that there are many kinds of intentions among monks who reprove others.

"In the case of the first four intentions" refers to the intention to cause to fall away, the intention to abuse, the intention to perform a formal act (*kamma*), and the intention to cause to emerge.

For one who does not cause leave to be granted, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Even after having caused it to be granted, for one who reproves [the monk] in his presence, there are offenses of formal meeting (*saṅghādisesa*), expiation (*pācittiya*), and wrong-doing according to the circumstances;
however, if he reproves him in his absence, there is only an offense of wrong-doing. This is the summary of the meaning here. The rest is easy to understand.
Having stated, "The grounds for setting aside [the inquiry] must be known," he spoke the passage beginning with "Let the Sangha hear me" in order to show those grounds. For the investigator...
The construction is: "For one speaking with the intention of investigating, there is no *okāsakamma* (formal granting of leave).
For a preacher of the Dhamma who speaks without specifying [a particular person], there is no *okāsakamma*. However, if he speaks by specifying [a person], there is an offense;
therefore, it should be construed that "one must go after having pointed that out. The rest is easily understood.

The Discourse on the Misappropriation of What is Given in Faith (Saddhādeyyavinipātanakathā) 60. In this Discourse on the Misappropriation of What is Given in Faith: “Monks, when it is said, ‘[This is for] mother and father,’ what can we say?
Monks, I allow you to give to mother and father; however, monks, what is given in faith must not be misappropriated.”

Because of the statement, "Whoever should misappropriate it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," it is not permitted for one to misappropriate what has been given to a monk by donors out of faith and give it to householders.
Regarding the phrase, "And, monks, [what is] given in faith," here, one who gives it to other relatives indeed misappropriates it;
however, if one's mother and father, even if established in royalty, should request it, it ought to be given.
Because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is not permissible to give [robes] even to relatives such as brothers, sisters, and so forth.
For it was said by the Elder Ācariya Dhammasiri in the *Khuddasikkhā*:
“Robes offered out of faith must not be cast away;”
"It is not permitted for mothers, nor for fathers, nor even for other relatives.
In the commentary on the training rule concerning buying and selling as well, it says: "When one says to a mother or a father, 'Give this,' there is no formal request (*viññatti*);
when one says, 'Take this,' there is no misappropriation of what was given in faith (*saddhādeyyavinipātana*)."
"An invitation occurs when one says to a stranger, 'Give this'; there is a misappropriation of a gift of faith when one says, 'Take this.
When one engages in buying and selling by saying, 'Give this for that,' it is an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*). Thus it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
Therein, [the author] states: "Because the misappropriation of a gift of faith is possible in the case of other relatives, he also shows the state of its absence."
"Regarding the statement, 'But [the offense occurs] toward one's mother or father,' this is what is stated in the *Vimativinodanī*.
In the discussion on the *santaruttara* (upper and lower robes), the word *antara* denotes the middle. One who dwells by way of virtue is a *vāsaka*; [as for the phrase] 'within' (*antare*),"

What should have been called "the upper robe" (*vāsako*) and "the inner robe" (*antaravāsako*), is instead called simply "inner" (*antaro*) by means of an elided compound (*uttarapadalopī-samāsa*), as in the cases of "form-existence" (*rūpabhavo*) being called "form" (*rūpaṃ*), and so forth.
The word *uttara* signifies "upper. That which is fastened thoroughly is a "fastening" (*āsaṅgo*).

What should have been called "a fastening on the upper [robe]" (*uttare āsaṅgo*), is called simply "upper" (*uttaro*) according to the aforementioned method; thus, "inner" (*antaro*) and "upper" (*uttaro*) together form *antaruttarā*.
"One who goes about with the inner and upper [robes]" (*santaruttara*) is a *dvandva-bahubbīhi* compound where the first member is joined by the particle *saha*.
Alternatively, "one who goes about together with the inner and the upper" (*saha antarena ca uttarena ca*) is a *tipada-bahubbīhi* compound.
One should not enter a village having set aside the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*) and wearing only the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) and the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).
This is the meaning. In expressions such as “he saw the wanderer with the triple staff,” this instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa);

therefore, one should enter the village having dressed in the inner robe (antaravāsaka) properly covering the three circles, having fastened the waist-band (kāyabandhana), and having put on the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) and the outer cloak (saṅghāṭi) doubled up.

The Discussion on the Laying Aside of the Robe (Cīvaranikkhepakathā) 62. Regarding the discussion on the laying aside of the robe: *saṃharīyati* means "it is gathered," referring to the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*). The sixth case ending (*chaṭṭhī*) is used here in the sense of the object (*kammatthe*) in connection with the abstract state (*bhāvayoge*).
*Nikkhepāya* means "for the purpose of setting down"; it refers to going after having placed the outer robe in the monastery without taking it along. Five [offenses].
The meaning is that there are [valid] reasons. "Or he is ill" means he is ill and thus unable to go after taking [the food].
"Or there is a rain-season agreement" means an agreement has been made, thinking, "This is the rainy season.
"Or it is for one who has gone to the other side of a river" means one must eat after having crossed to the far bank of a river. "Or it is a dwelling protected by a bolt" means a bolt...

Even after giving, it should be given; or it is a well-guarded dwelling. "Or the kaṭhina has been spread" means that the kaṭhina has been spread in that monastery, because there is no possibility of practicing without having undertaken the kaṭhina for those for whom the kaṭhina has been spread. The rest is easy to understand.
However, the dwelling of one who lives in the forest is not well-guarded because, due to having few bhikkhus, it is a place where thieves and others frequent.
*Ca*. "In a vessel for storing goods" means in a vessel for storing goods such as robes and so forth. The rest is easy to understand.
Regarding the discussion on surgery and the application of lint:
in the discussion on surgery and the application of lint, concerning the phrase "either surgery or the application of lint," here [it refers to] by whatever means.

Surgical treatment (*satthakamma*) consists of cutting and so forth with a knife or similar instruments. Vaginal injection (*vatthikamma*) is the pressing of substances such as oil into the vagina by means of anything whatsoever.
Regarding this, the *Sāratthadīpanī* states: "The practice of cauterizing the vulva is permissible because there is no prohibition against it.
However, the *Vimativinodanī* explains: "Vaginal injection means that [substances] such as oil located in the vagina rise up into the interior of the body."
Thus it is said: "In this way, by crushing the bladder with the hand.

However, in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, it is stated: "Regarding 'in the narrow passage'—that is, in the anus of a monk or the urinary passage of a nun—it is permissible because there is no prohibition against inserting [the instrument] in the natural direction.
It is not permissible, however, in accordance with the practice of the Teacher’s bladder-treatment."
Why? Because it indicates that the prohibition is the ultimate limit of what ought to be prohibited. What is meant?
Although the use of a knife had already been prohibited previously, later—by stating, "Monks, [you should not... up to ...
there is a grave offense (thullaccaya)"—the prohibition of the use of a knife was reiterated twice. Therefore, two finger-breadths around the narrow part must be avoided.
This shows that there is nothing beyond the surgical operation [on the wound].
Furthermore—previously, the surgical operation was prohibited only for the wound itself; subsequently, even two finger-breadths around the wound were prohibited.
Therefore, it is established that this prohibition applies only to that [specific case] and not to others. Herein, "a knife" means one who carries a knife, or...
In passages such as "one should seek," it refers to everything by which one cuts. Therefore it is said, "with a thorn," and so forth.
However, it should be understood that the administration of caustic (khāru) is permitted here in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga* for the region of the thighs and the mouth;
some, however, alter the reading to "or surgical treatment" (*satthakamma*) and perform vaginal treatment (*vatthikamma*). What is meant by "vaginal"? The urethra (*agghikā*).
They explain the meaning as follows: "It is called *vatthikamma* because of cutting with that [instrument].
However, they should be refuted by showing the word-analysis for the phrase, "one should seek a knife-bearer for him.
It is said: "A *aṇḍavuḍḍhi* is a *vātaṇḍaka*; an *ādānavatti* is an *anāhavatti*. The remainder should be understood according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

The Discourse on One Formerly a Barber (Nahāpitapubbakathā). 64. Regarding the phrase "one formerly a barber" (*nahāpitapubbo*): it means one who was a barber in the past; that is, having been a barber previously, he has now become a monk.
By that monk who was formerly a barber. "Barber’s equipment" (*khurabhaṇḍa*) refers to the barber’s tools, such as razors and so forth.

This is an illustrative method (upalakkhaṇanaya), as in the case of such passages as “the prince who had obtained a sunshade. Furthermore, there is a twofold formal promulgation (paññatti): “Monks, one who has gone forth must not encourage [others] in what is improper;
whoever should so encourage them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). And monks, one who was formerly a barber must not carry a barber’s kit;
whoever should carry it, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Thus the rule is established in two ways.
Therefore, one who has gone forth—whether previously a barber or not—must not encourage others toward what is unallowable (*akappiya*).
Furthermore, a monk who was previously a barber must not carry a razor marked with his own name, nor razor equipment such as the razor case, the whetstone, or the razor pouch.
The remainder should be understood according to the method explained in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. [As stated] in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*:

However, it is said: "Because it was stated, 'Monks, one who has gone forth must not incite another to what is improper,' the intention is that this applies not only to the ten training rules, but also to whatever is improper for a monk."

65. Discussion on the Tenth Part (*Dasabhāgakathā*). In this discussion on the tenth part, "belonging to the Saṅgha" means seeds that are the property of the Saṅgha. "On land belonging to an individual" means on land that is the property of a specific person.
"Having given a share" means having given a tenth part, known as the root-share, to the owners of the land.
"Having given. "They should be enjoyed" means that the fruits of those seeds should be enjoyed by the planters;
the rest is easy to understand. This, it is said, was the ancient custom in Jambudīpa:
at the time of the first aeon, the people of the first aeon, having appointed the Bodhisatta as King Mahāsammata, [all went] from their own respective fields of rice and grain...
Having divided the growing rice-fruits into ten portions, they consumed them after giving one portion to King Mahāsammata, who was the lord of the earth.
This is stated because it was the custom of the people of Jambudīpa from that time onwards.
For this very reason, it is said in the Vinaya commentary named *Sāratthadīpanī*: "Having given the tenth part" means having given the tenth portion. Therefore he said:
“It has been said: ‘Having divided it into ten portions, one portion should be given to the owners of the land.

Regarding the discussion on provisions for a journey (pātheyya-kathā): in the discussion on provisions for a journey, [the passage] beginning with “I allow you, monks,” was spoken in the city of Bhaddiya by one who had made excessive use [of the property].
Having been requested by the merchant Meṇḍaka, [the Buddha] gave his consent; however, here first the five products of the cow were authorized with the words:
"I allow you, monks, the five products of the cow: milk, curd, buttermilk, fresh butter, and ghee.
Subsequently, after speaking in accordance with the merchant's request, he said, "Monks, there are wilderness paths," and so forth, in order to grant permission.
The remainder should be understood according to the method stated in the Aṭṭhakathā.

By stating, "If one does not obtain it in that way, it may be taken even by requesting from a place where one is not known or not invited," this shows that there is no fault regarding the condition of requesting (*viññatti-paccaya*) at such times.
However, because it is said, "On a road to be traveled in a single day, one should seek for the sake of a single meal," [the rule applies] from that point onward.

It is shown that requesting more than this is not permitted. By the words “If the journey is long,” etc., it is meant that if on a path that would normally take a month there is a wilderness that takes only seven days, one should seek only enough provisions for seven days;
beyond that, one need not seek them, because the remainder of the road is well-supplied with food and alms are easily obtained through wandering for alms and so forth.

67. The Discourse on the Great Authorities (*Mahāpadesakathā*). In this discourse on the great authorities, the term "great authorities" refers to four: two that are not rejected and two that are not authorized.

Demonstrating this, [the Buddha] said, "Monks, whatever... and so forth. Among those, even regarding the two that are not rejected, there are two types based on whether they conform to what is unallowable (*akappiya*) or conform to what is allowable (*kappiya*).
"Two; likewise even when not permitted.
In this context: "rubbing" means examining. *Paṭṭuṇṇa* is cloth produced in the region of Paṭṭana.
For it is said in the *Abhidhānakośa*: "Paṭṭuṇṇa is a specific kind of silk (*koseyya*). [Cloths] produced in the regions of China and Soma are [also included].
Cīnasomāra-paṭas: paṭṭuṇṇa and the other two are similar to silk (koseyya) because they consist of threads produced by insects.

That which is "produced by psychic power" (iddhimaya) refers to robes manifested through the merit-power of "Come, monk" (ehibhikkhu) [ordination]; since that is one of the types such as khoma, it is similar to those very same materials.
A robe given by deities is "deity-given" (devadattiya); it is produced from the wish-fulfilling tree (kapparukkha).
The cloth given to the Elder Anuruddha by the celestial maiden Jālinī is similar to that;
it too conforms to linen and the like, because it is of the same nature as one of those materials. The two cloths are mentioned by way of their names;
this is merely to show their specific forms, not to exclude others, since even *paṭṭuṇṇa* cloth is mentioned by its name. *Tumba* refers to three types of vessels.
“*Phalakatumbo* refers to gourds (*lābu*) and the like. *Udakatumbo* refers to a water-splashing hut.
A ‘thatch-umbrella’ is an umbrella made by weaving bamboo and reeds,” as stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
“‘Cooked food for the time being’ is said with reference to cooked items; however, raw items may be [accepted] from those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) in cold water.”

If the drink is given after being crushed and strained, it is indeed permissible even after the meal. And since this point was not stated explicitly in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, he said, "But in the *Kuruṇḍī*," and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "sugarcane juice is without sediment," this was mentioned in the discussion on what may be taken during the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*) by virtue of its commonality with what may be drunk;
however, it should be understood that it is actually only for a seven-day period (*sattāhakālika*). These are the four juices.
"Phala, patta, puppha, and ucchu-rasa are the four," as stated in the *Vimativinodanī*. Regarding the statement "two cloths by way of teaching":

these are the Chinese cloth (*cīnapaṭa*) and the Somāra cloth. "Three" means three including the *paṭṭuṇṇa* cloth. "Produced by psychic power" refers to that which arose for the "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*) candidates.
"The one belonging to Devadatta" was obtained by the Elder Anuruddha; so it is said in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*.
In the *Saṃsaṭṭhakathā*,
the statement beginning with “what is received on that very day is allowable at the proper time” and so forth is said with reference to all things of mixed flavor (*sambhinnarasa*).
For if a beverage were received together with an entire coconut fruit, even after the husk had been removed, [it would be considered mixed].
If the coconut husk is removed, it is permissible even at the wrong time.
If they give cold milk-rice with a lump of ghee placed on top, it is allowable to remove the ghee that is not mixed with the rice and consume it for seven days.
The same principle applies to solidified honey, molasses, and so forth. [Likewise regarding] almsfood adorned with cardamom, nutmeg, and other such items...
Those teeth, having been extracted and washed, may be used for as long as one lives;
the same principle applies to ginger and other such items when added to rice gruel, or to lac and madhuka when added to oil and other such substances.
Thus, whatever remains unmixed in flavor, even if received together with other things, becomes pure in that same way.
It is permissible to wash or chop [the fruit] and consume it according to the appropriate time for each.
However, if it has become mixed in flavor—that is, if it is blended—it is not permissible.

For when things of different time-periods are mixed in flavor with one another, even those of the "time-for-a-watch" (yāmakālika) period and so forth take on the specific nature of the "time-for-as-long-as-life" (yāvakālika) item. This applies to both types of "time-for-a-watch" items as well.

The seven-day [medicine] and so forth bring their own specific nature [to the other]. When a seven-day medicine is mixed with a lifetime medicine, it brings that lifetime medicine to its own specific nature;

therefore, a lifetime medicine received on that same day is allowable for seven days when combined with another lifetime medicine received on that same day or one received previously, and for six days when combined with one received two days prior... and so on.
It should be understood that what has been received for seven days is allowable on that very day.
For this very reason, it was not said, "Monks, a life-long medicine received on the same day as a seven-day medicine," but rather, "What is received is allowable for seven days.

Furthermore, regarding the passing of the time-period, the watch of the night, and the seven days, [the distinctions are made] by way of the training rules concerning eating at the wrong time, storing food, and medicines.

The offenses are to be understood [as follows]. Furthermore, among these four kinds of time-limited [medicines], only this pair—namely, that which is for as long as life lasts (*yāvakālika*) and that which is for a watch of the night (*yāmakālika*)—is both subject to storage within the monastery and subject to the fault of hoarding (*sannidhi*).

However, that which is for seven days (*sattāhakālika*) and that which is for as long as life lasts may be placed in an improper storehouse, and they do not produce the fault of hoarding. The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
The Discussion on the Five Medicines:

In this discussion on the five medicines, because of the statement, “Monks, I allow you to receive those five medicines at the proper time and consume them at the proper time,” even rice-gruel may be drunk by monks afflicted with an autumnal ailment.
Food rises up [as indigestion]; even when food has been eaten, it rises up. Because of that, they become emaciated, haggard, discolored, and jaundiced, with their limbs covered in visible veins.

For them, there might be a medicine, or something considered a medicine by the world, which would serve the purpose of nutriment for the world, yet no coarse food would be perceived. In this regard, there are these five medicines. Namely:
— Ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses: these medicines may be accepted at the proper time and consumed at the proper time.
In this context, "by means of an autumnal ailment" refers to a bile-related illness that arises during the autumn season.
For at that time, people are drenched by the rainwater and trampled by the mud, and from time to time the illness becomes severe.

"By that [process], their bile becomes located within the stomach (*koṭṭha*). 'And it should perform the function of food' means it should accomplish the purpose of food"—this is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

In the *Vimativinodanī*, it says: "'The bile becomes located within the stomach' means that the unbound bile (*abaddhapitta*), having spread throughout the exterior of the body, becomes located within the stomach; by that, the bile becomes deranged."
This is what is stated as the intended meaning (*adhippāya*).

In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, it is said: "Because a contradiction is shown later in the passage beginning with 'They become even more emaciated by both of these,' it should be understood that this was stated according to whatever was available, without regard for the formal cause (*nidāna*)."
If it is asked why it was not stated according to the specific occasion (*yathānidāna*), it is because the intention was to refer to other instances as well.
For even at the time of every Buddha, there was the consideration that ghee and so forth were to be used for seven days. Such was the Blessed One’s intention when he spoke those words.
For this very reason it was said: “It should serve the purpose of food, yet no coarse food should be discerned. Thus, having received [the medicine] at the proper time...
Regarding the phrase "to be consumed at the proper time," no specific limit for the time has been established here;

rather, how could there be such a limit when the Blessed One intended [the rule] to depend on other factors, stating that those medicinal roots and so forth, having been accepted, may be used "for as long as life lasts"?
As for the statement, "Monks, I allow you to accept those medicines at the proper time and consume them at the proper time," [it refers to the specific occasion of their initial acceptance].
It should be understood that this was said with the intention: "Having made a store, I allow you to consume it at the proper time on successive days.
Otherwise, given the excellence of the Blessed One, the arising of such thoughts as "this would be medicine" and so forth would not be possible.
Since permission for refined food is already established, these [allowances] were stated with regard to what is suitable and appropriate for a specific illness.
Why? Because it shows the attainment of a state such as emaciation, saying "to a greater degree.

If it is argued that just as "molasses" is spoken of in relation to sugarcane juice, so too "ghee" (*sappi*) should be spoken of in relation to butter (*navanīta*), and thus butter should not be mentioned separately—no, because the intention is to show a distinction.
Just as, even though [the meaning] is established by the mention of molasses, [a further term is used] subsequently...
It should be understood that sugarcane juice was permitted separately because it was placed in the category of molasses-water due to its general similarity to sugarcane;
likewise, fresh butter was permitted separately because of the intention to show a specific rule for it.

This specific rule for it, however, is to be understood by way of the commentary on the medicinal substances training rule (bhesajja-sikkhāpada). For it is said there: "Having boiled [the milk], ghee..."
“Having prepared it, if one wishes to consume it, it is permissible even if it has not been washed to cook it. In that regard, ghee is cooked;
it is not uncooked. Likewise with molasses. Fresh butter, however, is indeed uncooked,” and so forth.
This concludes the second discourse on medicine.

In the second discussion on medicines, because of the statement: “Monks, I allow you to accept those five kinds of medicine and consume them both at the proper time and at the improper time,” for those monks who accept those five kinds of medicine at the proper time and consume them at the proper time, even those ordinary, coarse foods—
“They do not even cover them, much less provide food for them. Afflicted by both that autumnal illness and this lack of food, they become even more emaciated.

In this context, since it has been permitted both at the proper time (*kāla*) and at the improper time (*vikāla*), it is allowable to consume [food] even at the improper time. Regarding that, “they do not cover”:
“They do not decay, nor are they able to alleviate wind-disease (*vātaroga*). ‘Glossy’ (*senesitāni*) means smooth.
‘By one who does not relish the meal’—this is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* as ‘by one for whom the meal is unpalatable.

However, in the *Ṭīkās*, it is stated only thus: ‘They do not please (*nacchādenti*) means they do not arouse a sense of taste (*ruci*). But in the *Mahāvibhaṅga*: ‘Those things which are for sick bhikkhus to take as medicine...’”
The medicines are as follows: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses.

Having accepted these, they may be used by keeping them in store for a maximum of seven days; for one who exceeds that limit, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).

From this statement, it should be understood that the status of these five medicines as "seven-day" items is established; however, in this particular context, it is stated by way of a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
The Discussion on Fat as Medicine.

In this discussion on fat as medicine: “Monks, I allow fats as medicines—namely, fish fat, crab fat, porpoise fat, pig fat, and donkey fat—when received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time.”

to use it for the enjoyment of oil. Monks, if one has received [food] at an improper time, cooked it at an improper time, and mixed it at an improper time, and should eat it, there is an offense of three *dukkaṭas*.
Monks, if one has received [food] at a proper time, cooked it at an improper time, and mixed it at an improper time, and should eat it, there is an offense of two [dukkatas].

“...of offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Monks, if what was received at the proper time is cooked at the proper time and mixed together at the improper time, and one should consume it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Monks, if what was received at the proper time is cooked at the proper time and mixed together at the proper time, and one should consume it, there is no offense.
In this context, regarding the phrases “received at the proper time,” and so forth:
The meaning is: having received [the medicine] before midday has passed, having cooked it, and having strained it.
Regarding the phrase "to use by way of oil-consumption," it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary): "to use it by way of the seven-day oil-consumption.
However, in the *Ṭīkās* (Sub-commentaries), it says: "Susukā is a species of fish found in the ocean; they also call it a *kumbhila*. *Saṃsaṭṭha*..."
"It has been strained. Regarding "use as oil," it is said that this refers to use for a period of seven days.
This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, was already given above in the discussion on the four times [for taking medicine].
The Discussion on Root Medicines.
In the Discourse on Root Medicines: “I allow you, monks, root medicines:
turmeric, ginger, *vaca*, *vacatta*, *ativisa*, *kaṭukarohiṇī*, *usīra*, and *bhaddamuttaka*;
or whatever other root medicines there may be that do not serve as edible food for the purpose of edible food, nor as soft food for the purpose of soft food.”
“They spread [the medicine]; having accepted them, one may keep them for as long as life lasts and consume them when there is a requisite reason.

For one who consumes them when there is no requisite reason, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). In this context, “white bark” means white *vacā* root. The rest has already been explained above.
This concludes the discussion on medicinal powders.

In the discussion on medicinal pastes (*piṭṭhabhesajja*), because of the statement, “Monks, I allow a grinding stone and a grinding bowl,” when there is need for root medicines that have been ground into powder, it is permissible to keep both a grinding stone and a grinding bowl.

In this context, “grinding stone and grinding bowl” refers to the stone used for grinding and the bowl used for grinding. One grinds upon the grinding stone until [the substance] is reduced to fine powder.
It is called *nisada* because roots, medicines, and so forth are ground upon it; thus, it is a grinding stone (*pisana-silā*).

It is called *nisada* because by means of it roots, medicines, and so forth are ground—that is, they are made into powder and dust. It is called *pota* because it is to be nourished (*posetabbo*), meaning a child (*dārako*);
or, because of its small size, it is like a young one (*poto*), thus it is a "little one. It is a *nisadapota* because it is both a *nisada* and a *pota*. [The term] *nipubbo-sada*...
The verbal root is *cuṇṇakaraṇa* (to powder).
Regarding the discussion on decoction medicines:
in the discussion on decoction medicines, [it says], "Monks, I allow decoction medicines: the decoction of *nimba*, the decoction of *kuṭaja*..."

The bitter decoction of *paṭolaka*, the bitter decoction of *phaggavaka*, the bitter decoction of *nattamālaka*, or whatever other bitter medicinal decoctions there may be that do not serve the purpose of a chewable food (*khādanīya*) among chewable foods, nor serve the purpose of a soft food (*bhojanīya*) among soft foods—having accepted these, one may keep them for as long as life lasts, and consume them when there is a suitable occasion;
when there is no suitable occasion, [one may consume them]... [if they have been kept].

Because of the statement, "For one who consumes [them], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," it is permissible to receive those bitter medicinal herbs (kasāva-bhesajja) and keep them for as long as life lasts, and to consume them when there is a suitable occasion.

In this context, *phaggu* refers to a species of creeper. *Nattamāla* refers to the *karañja* tree. Regarding the phrase "with bitters," the *Vimativinodanī* states: "With the extracts taken from the bark and other parts after they have been heated in water."
The Discussion on Leaf Medicines.
In this discussion on leaf medicines, it is said: "Monks, I allow leaf medicines:
neem leaves, *kuṭaja* leaves, *paṭola* leaves, *nattamāla* leaves, *phaggava* leaves, *sulasī* leaves, cotton-tree leaves, or whatever other [leaves] there may be."
"There are medicinal leaves which do not serve the purpose of a solid food (*khādanīya*) among solid foods, nor do they serve the purpose of a soft food (*bhojanīya*) among soft foods;
having accepted them, one may keep them for as long as life lasts and consume them when there is a suitable occasion.

For one who consumes them when no such occasion exists, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Because of this statement, [these are] those that do not serve the purpose of solid or soft food.
Having accepted those leaves as well, it is permissible to keep them for as long as one lives and to consume them when there is a suitable reason.
The meaning regarding the *acchavasaṇṭhī* and so forth should be understood in the same manner as stated in the commentary on the *nissaggiya* rules.

The determination of the medicinal roots and so forth has already been explained in the commentary on the *khuddaka* (minor) rules; therefore, we shall here describe only that which was not previously mentioned.
The Discussion on Fruit Medicines. In this discussion on fruit medicines, it is said: "I allow you, monks, fruit medicines:
*biḷaṅga*, long pepper, black pepper, yellow myrobalan, beleric myrobalan, emblic myrobalan, *goṭṭhaphala*, or whatever other fruits there may be."

Because of the statement: “Medicines that do not serve the purpose of solid food among solid foods, nor serve the purpose of soft food among soft foods, may be accepted and kept for as long as life lasts;

they may be consumed when there is a requisite condition, but for one who consumes them when no requisite condition exists, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” it follows that they do not serve the purpose of solid or soft food.
Having accepted those fruits, it is permissible to keep them for as long as one lives, and provided there is a suitable reason, it is also permissible to consume them.
Regarding the discussion on resinous medicines: in the discussion on resinous medicines, [the Buddha said], "Monks, I allow resinous medicines: asafoetida, asafoetida-resin, and asafoetida-leaf."

Curd, curd-skin, curd-foam, and *sajjula*— or whatever other medicinal substances there may be that do not serve the purpose of solid food among solid foods, nor serve the purpose of soft food among soft foods—
one may accept these to keep for as long as life lasts and consume them when a requisite condition exists; for one who consumes them when no requisite condition exists, [there is an offense].

Because of the statement, “there is an offense of wrong-doing,” it is permissible to accept those resin medicines and keep them for as long as one lives, and to consume them when there is a suitable occasion.
In this context, *hiṅgu*, *hiṅgujaṭu*, and *hiṅgusipāṭikā* belong to the same species as *hiṅgu*.
*Takataka*, *pattitaka*, and *takapaṇṇa* belong to the same species as lac (*lākha*).
In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*, however, it is said: “*Hiṅgujatu* is that produced by cooking the stalks, shoots, and sprouts of the *hiṅgu* tree.
*Hiṅgusipāṭikā* is that produced by cooking its roots and branches. *Takaṃ* is the water used for boiling the bark of that tree.
*Takapattī* is the water used for boiling its leaves. *Takapaṇṇī* is the water used for boiling its fruit. Alternatively, ‘*takaṃ*...”
"Lākha" means lac. "Takapatti" means a branch of the *kittima* (artificial) lac-tree. "Takapaṇṇī" means ripe lac; thus it is written.
Regarding the phrase "when there is a requisite condition," the state of being a requisite condition (*satipaccayatā*) here should be understood in two ways: by way of being ill and not being ill.

For in the section on non-offenses for the training rule concerning eating at the wrong time (*vikālabhojana*), the state of being a requisite condition is stated without distinction for all three types of medicines, such as those to be kept for a watch of the night (*yāmakālika*). In this Khandhaka...
“It is permitted, monks, for one who is ill, molasses; for one who is not ill, molasses-water. It is permitted, monks, for one who is ill, salt-vinegar;
for one who is not ill, that which is mixed with water. Since this has been said, it is established that “the conditionality [of food] is twofold, according to whether one is ill or not ill”;
otherwise, in the absence of a condition, one would incur the offense regarding molasses-water and the like, and from that—
This contradicts the Pāli. "For the purpose of food" means the function of food, or the meaning is "maintaining the activity of food.
"By means of using oil" means by means of using it for a period of seven days. "With flours" means with ground oils.
"Koṭṭhaphala" is the fruit of the *koṭṭha* tree; it is also written as "madanaphala," so it is said.
The Discourse on Saline Medicines. In the Discourse on Saline Medicines: "I allow you, monks, saline medicines:
sea salt, black salt, rock salt, sochal salt, and biḷa salt; or whatever other saline medicines there may be that are not among the foods to be chewed."
"Because of the statement: 'They distribute for the purpose of solid food (khādanīya), not for the purpose of soft food (bhojanīya) in the case of soft food;

having accepted them, one may keep them for as long as life lasts and consume them when there is a requisite condition; for one who consumes them when there is no requisite condition, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),' it follows that after accepting those salts, one may keep them for as long as life lasts, provided there is [a requisite condition]..."
It is permissible to consume these as requisites. Among them: *sāmudda* (sea salt) remains like sand on the seashore;
