*kāḷaloṇa* (black salt) is natural salt; *sindhava* (rock salt) is white in color and arises from a mountain;
*ubbhida* (soil salt) arises from the earth like a sprout; and *bila* (cave salt) is cooked together with various ingredients and is red in color.
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, however, it is stated: “*Ubbhidaṃ* means salt made of saline soil (*ūsarapaṃsu*).

In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it is stated: “*Ubbhidaṃ* is salt made of saline soil; *bila* is a specific kind of salt. The same is stated in the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā*. This concludes the discussion on powdered salt (*cuṇṇakathā*).

In the *Cuṇṇakathā*: “I allow you, monks, for one who has an itch, or a boil, or a discharge, or severe scabies, or a bodily affliction, or whose body is foul-smelling, medicinal powders; for one who is not ill, I allow charcoal powder, clay, and dye-boilings.
I allow you, monks, a mortar and pestle. Regarding the phrase “or whose body is foul-smelling,” this refers to certain people, such as horses and so forth.
The body has a smell like that of a corpse; for this, all types of powders—whether sirīsa, kusumbha, and so forth, or fragrant powders—are permissible.
"Chakaṇa" means cow dung. "Rajananippakka" means dye-sediment;
even ordinary powder, having been ground and moistened with water, is permitted for bathing, as this too is included within the category of "dye-sediment," according to the Aṭṭhakathā.
It has been stated [thus]. However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is said: "‘Chakaṇa’ means cow dung. ‘Ordinary powder’ (*pākatikacuṇṇa*) refers to unboiled alkaline powder;
by this, everything is permitted except for scented powder. In the *Vimativinodanī* as well, it is said: "'Chakaṇa' means cow dung.
'Ordinary powder' refers to unboiled alkaline powder, but scented powder is not permitted."
It has been stated. In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā* it is also said: “*Chakaṇa* means cow dung. ‘Ordinary powder’ (*pākatika-cuṇṇa*) refers to unboiled alkaline powder.
By this, they say that everything is permitted except for scented powders.
Because of the statement, “Monks, I allow a powder-sifter,” when there is a need for sick monks to sift medicinal powders, [it is permitted].
A powder-shaker is permitted. Because of the statement, “Monks, I allow a cloth-shaker,” when there is a need for fine powders, a cloth-shaker is permitted.
In the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated: “‘Powder-shaker’ means a strainer for powders ground in a mortar. In the *Vajirabuddhiṭīkā* as well, it is stated: “‘By shaking’ means by straining.”
The Discussion on Afflictions by Non-Human Beings:
In this discussion on afflictions by non-human beings, because of the statement, "Monks, I allow raw meat and raw blood in the case of an affliction by a non-human being," for whichever monk,
having eaten raw meat and drunk raw blood, that affliction by a non-human being [is cured].
It subsides; there is no offense for him. In that case, regarding the statement "he ate raw flesh and drank raw blood," it was not the monk who ate or drank;
rather, a non-human being, having eaten and drunk, departed. Therefore it is said:
"That affliction caused by a non-human being subsided for him."
The Discourse on Eye Salve (*Añjanakathā*). In this discourse on eye salve, because of the statement: "Monks, I allow eye salve:
black eye salve, liquid eye salve, ear-eye salve, red ochre, and lamp-black," when monks suffer from eye disease, eye salves and the like are permitted. Therein, "eye salve" means...
This is a comprehensive statement. *Kāḷañjana* is one type of collyrium (*añjana*).
*Rasañjana* is that made from various ingredients. *Sotañjana* is the collyrium produced in river currents and the like. *Geruka* refers to golden *geruka*.
*Kapalla* is the soot taken from the crest of a lamp flame—so it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, however, it says: "Golden *geruka*..."
"Gold, tin, and so forth," it is said. It is stated in the same way in the *Vimativinodanī* as well.
Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow sandalwood, tagara, kāḷānusāriya, tālīsa, and bhaddamuttaka," these sandalwoods and so forth are permitted when there is a need for ointments and powders.
In that context, "sandalwood" refers to red sandalwood and the like.
“Any kind of sandalwood. Tagara and so forth are well known; other things such as blue lotuses (*nīluppala*) are also certainly permissible.
‘With ointments and grinding-powders’ means with things that are to be ground together with the ointments. For there is no grinding-powder whatsoever that is not permissible.

Thus it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*); however, in the Sub-commentary (*Ṭīkā*), it says: “‘Ointment-grinding-powder’ refers to any kind of powdered substance that is to be ground for the purpose of an ointment.”
It has been stated [thus]. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is said: “‘Eye-salve and its application’ refers to the medicinal substance to be ground for the purpose of applying eye-salve.
Because of the statement, “Monks, I allow an eye-salve container,” a place for storing eye-salve is permitted.
“Monks, a luxurious eye-salve container must not be used; whoever should use one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Monks, I allow—”
According to the statement, “It may be made of bone, of ivory, of horn, of reed, of bamboo, of wood, of lac, of metal, or of conch-shell,” these are allowable.
In this context, “made of bone” refers to anything made of bone except human bone.
“Made of ivory” refers to anything made of all types of ivory, such as elephant tusks and so forth. As for “made of horn,” that which is unallowable is excluded.
There is no [prohibition] regarding those made of reeds and so forth;
they are exclusively permissible. Because of the statement, "I allow, monks, a lid," it is also allowable to have a lid for the ointment-box.
Because of the statement, "I allow, monks, having tied it with a string, to fasten it to the ointment-box," the lid [should be attached] with a string.

Having tied it, it should be fastened to the ointment-box. Because of the statement, “I allow you, monks, to sew it with thread,” it is permissible to sew it with an ointment-box thread so that it does not fall off.
Because of the statement, “I allow you, monks, an ointment-stick,” an ointment-stick is also permitted. “Monks, one should not carry an ointment-stick of high quality or of various kinds.”
Whoever should hold it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Because of the statement, "I allow, monks, [an ointment-stick] made of bone...

[etc. ...made of conch-shell," only these very ointment-sticks are permitted. Because of the statement, "I allow, monks, what serves as a substitute for a stick," even that which serves as a substitute for an ointment-stick is permitted.
In this context, "what serves as a substitute for a stick" refers to that wherein a stick [is inserted].
They pour it out; the meaning is that I allow that hollow tube or the bag.

Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow a bag for ointment," even a bag is permitted. Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow a shoulder-strap and a binding cord," a shoulder-strap is also allowed for the purpose of attaching the ointment bag to the shoulder.
A binding thread is also permissible. Regarding the discussion on the nose:
from the statement in the *Natthukathā*, "Monks, I allow oil for the head," [it follows that] for one suffering from heat in the head...
Oil is permitted on the head of a bhikkhu. Because of the statement, “I allow you, bhikkhus, nasal therapy,” when there is an ailment that cannot be cured otherwise, nasal therapy is permitted.
Because of the statement, “I allow you, bhikkhus, a nose-pick,” a nose-pick is permitted for the purpose of clearing the nose. “Bhikkhus, you should not use an elaborate nose-pick.”
"It should not be kept; whoever should keep it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Monks, I allow [nostril-cleaners] made of bone... pe... or made of conch-shell," because of this statement, only these [materials] are permitted for nasal cleaners.
"Monks, I allow twin nasal cleaners," because of this statement, if one pours the nasal medicine unevenly, [one should use] a twin nasal cleaner.
It should be kept. In this context, "a pair of nose-pipes" refers to a single nose-pipe made from those two tubes.
Regarding the discussion on the smoking tube (*dhūmanetta*): because of the statement in the discussion on the smoking tube, "Monks, I allow you to smoke," [it is used] with a pair of nose-pipes.
If it is not possible to endure [the illness], it is permissible to drink medicinal smoke.

Because of the statement, “Monks, I allow a smoking tube,” one should light that very wick and, for the purpose of drinking [the medicine], the smoke from the smoking tube should be inhaled even if it burns the throat.
“Monks, various elaborate smoking tubes must not be used; whoever should use one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).”
From the statement, "I allow, monks, [smoking tubes] made of bone... [and] made of conch-shell," it follows that these very materials are to be used for the smoking tubes (*dhūmanetta*).

From the statement, "I allow, monks, a lid," a bag for the smoking tube is also permitted for the purpose of preventing insects and other creatures from entering. From the statement, "I allow, monks, a double-layered bag,"...
When [the bag] is being rubbed on one side, a twin-strap bag is permissible.
Because of the statement, “Monks, I allow a shoulder-strap for binding,” a binding strap for a shoulder-strap is permissible for a smoke-tube bag.
The Discussion on Oil-Cooking.
In the *Telapākakathā* (The Discourse on Oil-Cooking), because of the statement, “Monks, I allow oil-cooking,” when there is an ailment of wind (*vātābādha*), oil-cooking is permitted.
In that context, regarding the phrase “Monks, I allow oil-cooking,” anything whatsoever into which medicinal ingredients have been added is entirely allowed.
“Monks, oil into which too much fermenting agent (*majja*) has been added must not be drunk; whoever should drink it, [would be guilty of an offense].”
It should be dealt with according to the rule. From the statement, "I allow you, monks, to drink such oil into which liquor has been put,

provided that in that oil-brewing the color, smell, or taste of the liquor is no longer discernible," it follows that one may drink such oil in which the color, smell, or taste of the liquor added to the oil-brewing is no longer perceived.
It should be drunk. In this context, "with too much marrow added" means with excessively added marrow;

the meaning is that they were prepared by adding a large amount of intoxicant. Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow you to resolve [the oil] as an ointment," when there is oil that cannot be drunk due to having too much intoxicant added, it is permissible to resolve it as an ointment. "Monks, I allow three..."
Regarding the statement, "There are three kinds of vessels: the iron vessel, the wooden vessel, and the fruit vessel," these three types of vessels used for cooking oil are permitted.
Discussion on the process of sweating (sedakamma).

In the discussion on fomentation therapy (*sedakamma*), because of the statement, “Monks, I allow fomentation therapy,” it is permissible to perform fomentation therapy when there is wind in the limbs.
In this context, “wind in the limbs” refers to wind in the hands or feet.

When one cannot endure [the condition], because of the statement, “Monks, I allow fomentation by means of materials (*sambhāraseda*)”, one should employ fomentation by means of materials when one cannot endure [the condition] through simple fomentation therapy.
It is permissible to do so. In this context, "decoction of various ingredients" refers to a decoction made from various kinds of leaves.

When one cannot tolerate [the standard application], because of the statement, "Monks, I allow a 'great decoction' (mahāseda)," it is permissible to prepare a great decoction when one is unable to endure the decoction of ingredients.
In that regard, "great decoction" means a large decoction; [it involves] a pit for the embers measuring a man's height.
The meaning is: having filled [the vessel] with sand, gravel, and so forth, and having covered it, one should spread various wind-dispelling leaves upon it;
then, lying down there with the body smeared with oil and turning over and over, I allow you to foment the body.
Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow fermented water (*bhaṅgodaka*) for those who cannot endure [the heat]," [this is permitted] when there is great sweating.
When it is not tolerable [to cure a wound], it is permissible to apply a decoction bath (*bhaṅgodaka*). In this context, "decoction bath" refers to water boiled with various medicinal leaves;
one should foment [the area] by repeatedly sprinkling it with both those leaves and the water.
Since it is stated, "Monks, I allow a water-tub," when it is not tolerable [otherwise], one may use a decoction bath.
It is permissible to construct a water-vat. In this context, "water-vat" means:
"I allow that one fill a tub or a trough with hot water and enter therein to perform sudation"—this is the meaning.
The Discussion on the Removal of Blood.
In the discourse on the extraction of blood, because of the statement, “Monks, I allow you to extract blood,” it is permissible to extract blood when there is a swelling.
In this context, “there is a swelling” means that wind has entered into each joint.
“To extract blood” means to extract blood with a lancet. It becomes unbearable; monks, I allow [the following].
"Having discharged blood, they shall cause it to enter [the wound] with a horn.
Regarding the discourse on foot-unguents:
from the statement in the discourse on foot-unguents, "Monks, I allow foot-unguents," when the feet have become cracked...
Foot ointment should be cooked. Since it is stated, "Monks, I allow you to prepare *pajja*," when one is unable to endure [the pain] due to foot ointment oil, *pajja* should be prepared.
In that context, "to prepare *pajja*" means that by means of various medicinal substances such as coconut and so forth, that which restores cracked feet to their natural state [is prepared].

The meaning is: having put [the ingredients] together, to prepare a foot-ointment; that is, to cook suitable medicinal herbs for the feet. Regarding the discussion on the affliction of boils (*gaṇḍābādhakathā*):
because of the statement in the discussion on the affliction of boils, "Monks, I allow surgical treatment (*satthakamma*) when there is an affliction of boils," [surgery is permitted].
A surgical procedure should be performed. Because of the statement, “Monks, I allow castor-water,” when there is need, castor-water should be given.
Because of the statement, “Monks, I allow sesame paste,” when there is need, sesame paste should be given.
“Need for sesame paste” means need for ground sesame seeds. “I allow... [and so forth].
Because of the statement, "Monks, there is the *kabaḷikā*," when there is need for a *kabaḷikā*, a *kabaḷikā* should be given.

In this context, a *kabaḷikā* means placing a lump of honey into the opening of a wound. Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow a bandage for wounds (*vaṇabandhanacoḷa*)," when there is need for a bandage for wounds, a bandage for wounds should be given. "Monks, I allow... [and so forth].
According to the statement, "It should be sprinkled with crushed mustard," if the wound is moist, it should be sprinkled with crushed mustard.
Here, "with crushed mustard" means with ground mustard.
According to the statement, "I allow you, monks, to apply fumigation," if the wound has become dry, one may apply fumigation.
It is permissible. Because of the statement, “Monks, I allow you to cut [the flesh] with salt crystals,” if an overgrowth of flesh protrudes, it should be cut.
In this context, “overgrowth of flesh” refers to excess flesh that rises up like a stump.
“To cut with salt crystals” means to cut with brine. Because of the statement, “Monks, I allow wound-oil,” if...

A wound does not heal; therefore, wound-healing oil should be prepared. Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow a bandage and all wound-treatment," if the oil drips out, a bandage must be applied, and every form of wound-treatment should be performed.
In this context, "bandage" refers to a cloth for stopping the flow of oil. "All wound-treatment" refers to whatever [is required].
“There is such a thing as wound-treatment; I authorize it all,” is the meaning. The discussion regarding the great poison has already been stated above.

“Having taken it oneself”: this applies not only to one bitten by a snake, but whenever there is any other poisonous bite, it may be used after having taken it oneself; however, for other purposes, it is permissible only if it has been received [as an offering]. This is the discussion regarding the taking of poison.
In the *Visapītaka-kathā* (The Discussion on Poisoning), because of the statement, “Monks, I allow you to give dung to drink,” it is permissible to give dung to a monk who has drunk poison.

Because of the statement, “Monks, I allow that which one receives while performing [the act]; that itself constitutes the formal acceptance (*paṭiggaha*), and it need not be accepted again,” that very same thing is permissible.
However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary), it is stated that it should not be accepted again...
"It should be accepted" means: if it has reached the ground, it should be made to be accepted; however, it is permissible to take what has not yet reached [the ground].

Regarding the discussion on the affliction caused by what was given by a householder, from the statement in that discussion, "Monks, I allow you to drink cold gruel," [it follows] regarding the affliction caused by what was given by a householder...

It is permissible for a monk to drink cold gruel. In this context, "a disease given by the housewife" (*gharadinnakābādha*) refers to a disease arising from a potion used for subjugation (*vasīkaraṇa*).
However, in the *Ṭīkā*, it is stated: "A 'disease given by the housewife' is a malady produced by medicine administered by the housewife for the purpose of subjugation.
Therefore, it says: 'a disease arising from a potion for subjugation. And here, the word 'house' (*ghara*) refers to the housewife without distinction."

It is stated: "That which is currently occurring is intended. In the *Vimativinodanī* as well, it is stated: "'The ailment caused by what was given by the household' means an ailment arising from a love-potion medicine administered by the mistress of the house.
Regarding "cold mud," the meaning is: "I authorize [the use of] the clay clinging to the plowshare of one who is plowing, having mixed it with water, for him to drink."
The Discussion on Dysentery:
In the discussion on dysentery, based on the statement, “Monks, I allow you to give a meat-broth to drink,” it is permissible to give a meat-broth to a monk suffering from dysentery.
In this context, “one with dysentery” (*duṭṭhagahaṇika*) means one whose digestion has failed; [it refers to one] who suffers with difficulty.
The meaning is that excrement is coming out. "Amisakhāra" refers to the alkaline water that has dripped from the ashes after burning boiled rice with dried fish.
However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated: "Alkaline water that has dripped from those ashes means:
having placed those ashes in a strainer and poured water over them, the alkaline water that has dripped down from beneath those ashes."
The Discourse on the Affliction of Jaundice:

Regarding this discourse on the affliction of jaundice, because of the statement, “Monks, I allow you to give a decoction of harītakī with urine to drink,” it is permissible to give a decoction of harītakī with urine to a monk afflicted by jaundice. In that context, “a decoction of harītakī with urine” means:
Harītakī treated with cow’s urine.
Regarding the discussion on skin diseases:

according to the statement in the discussion on skin diseases, “Monks, I allow you to apply fragrant ointments,” it is permissible for a monk suffering from a skin disease to apply fragrant ointments.

**Discourse on a Body with Excessive Humors** Regarding the discourse on a body with excessive humors: from the statement, "Monks, I allow you to drink a purgative," it is permissible for a monk whose body has excessive humors to drink a purgative.
In this context, "one whose body has excessive humors" refers to one whose bodily humors (doṣa) are aggravated. [The text continues: "with clear gruel..."
If there is need for clear rice-gruel, it is permissible to drink clear rice-gruel because of the statement:
"I allow you, monks, clear rice-gruel. In this context, "clear rice-gruel" refers to rice-water decoction (*taṇḍulodakamaṇḍa*).

If there is need for unseasoned broth, it is permissible to drink unseasoned broth because of the statement: "I allow you, monks, unseasoned broth. In this context, "unseasoned broth" refers to that which is not greasy.
“Mung bean boiled water. However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī* and the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated:

And in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated: “‘With kaṭākaṭa’ means with bean-soup made by boiling mung beans and straining them without stirring.

Regarding the *paṭicchādanīya* (concealment-gruel), there is a need for it; because of the statement, “Monks, I allow *paṭicchādanīya*,” it is permissible to consume *paṭicchādanīya*. In that context, “with *paṭicchādanīya*” refers to meat broth.
The Discourse on Brine with Salt (*Loṇasovīrakakathā*): In the *Loṇasovīrakakathā*, because of the statement, “Monks, I allow brine with salt for one who is ill;
for one who is not ill, I allow it when mixed with water to be consumed as a drink,” a monk who is ill may drink brine with salt.
One who is not ill should consume it after mixing it with water; and because of the statement "by way of consuming as a drink," this is permitted even at the improper time.
In that regard, "salt-vinegar" (*loṇasovīraka*) is a single medicinal substance prepared from all flavors.
It is said that one making it [uses] the decoctions of *harītakī*, *āmalaka*, and *vibhītaka*, all types of grain, and all vegetables, as well as the seven kinds of grain.
Having added boiled rice, plantain fruits and all other fruits, the shoots of vetasa, ketakī, and date palms and all such shoots, pieces of fish and meat,
and various medicinal substances such as honey, molasses, rock salt, sea salt, and pungent spices,
they smear the mouth of the jar and leave it for one, two, or three years; when that has fully matured, it becomes the color of rose-apple juice.

For those suffering from wind-disorders, coughs, skin diseases, jaundice, facial discoloration, and the like, as well as for those who have eaten rich, oily foods, there is no other medicine that so effectively digests the meal as this subsequent drink (uttarapāna).
This is permitted for monks even after the midday meal; for the sick, it is exactly as prescribed before.
However, for those who are not sick, it is permissible only when mixed with water for the purpose of drinking.
In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, however, it is stated: "Because it is said 'by means of consuming as a drink,' salted sour gruel (*loṇasovīraka*) is [permissible] for the watch-period (*yāmakālika*).
In the *Vimativinodanī*, however, it says: "The connection is 'it is allowable by means of consuming as a drink.

But because it is stated thus, some say that salted sour gruel is for the watch-period; others, however, say: 'For the sick it is just as usual, but for those who are not sick it must be mixed with water.'"
Because it was stated [in that way], it is said: "Like sugar, it is for seven days. However, in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, it says:

"The status of being a condition for mindfulness was stated without distinction. In this Khandhaka, it is stated: 'Monks, I allow sugar for the sick, sugar-water for those not sick, salt-vinegar for the sick, and water-mixed [vinegar] for those not sick. Therefore, it is established..."
“It has been said: ‘The conditionality of mindfulness is twofold, by way of being ill and not being ill. Regarding the discussion on being ill within the rainy-season retreat and so forth:

Tathāgatas, though they already know, ask; though they already know...

"Or we shall lay down a training rule.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, where is this rice-gruel?
Then the Venerable Ānanda reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him, saying: "This is unbecoming..."
Ānanda, this is unbecoming, unsuitable, unworthy of a recluse, improper, and not to be done.
How indeed, Ānanda, could you intend such abundance? Whatever, Ānanda, is stored inside is improper;

"Ānanda, this will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... Having rebuked him and given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:

Whoever should consume it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Bhikkhus, if it has been stored indoors and cooked indoors by oneself... "
If it were cooked [by others], and he were to consume it, there is an offense of three *dukkaṭas*.
If, monks, it was stored inside, cooked inside, and cooked by others, and he were to consume it, there is an offense of two *dukkaṭas*.
If, monks, it was stored inside, cooked outside, and cooked by himself, and he were to consume it, there is an offense of two [dukkaṭas].
Regarding offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*): Monks, if food has been stored outside and cooked inside, and it is cooked by oneself—if one should consume it, there is an offense of two wrong-doings.

Monks, if food has been stored inside and cooked outside, and it is cooked by others—if one should consume it, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Monks, if food has been stored outside and cooked inside, and it is cooked by others...

If he should consume that which was cooked [inside], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Monks, if it was stored outside, cooked outside, and cooked by himself, and he should consume it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Monks, if it was stored outside, cooked outside, and cooked by others, and he should consume it, there is no offense. From this statement, regarding [food] sufficient for a shared meal...
It should be understood that when these three factors are present—being stayed in the place, being cooked there, and being cooked by oneself after having been ordained—there are three offenses;
when two are present, there are two offenses; and when one factor is present, there is one offense.
“Dwelling inside” means dwelling in an unallowable hut. “Cooked by oneself”: herein, it is not permitted for a bhikkhu to cook any kind of foodstuff himself.
Even if they throw green ginger leaves, galangal, or salt into his hot rice gruel, he must not stir it;
however, it is permitted to stir it with the intention, “I am extinguishing the gruel.”
Even after receiving rice that has already been boiled, it is not permissible to cover it [and re-cook it]. However, if people give it while covering it, it is permissible.
It is also permissible to cover it [with the thought], "Let the rice not go cold.
Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow you to cook it again," it is permissible to cook again what was previously cooked by those who were not yet ordained. For it is said:
In the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is said: “But in the case of milk, sour gruel, and so forth, once they have been boiled, it is permissible to apply fire [to them again], because re-cooking is permitted.

Because of the statement, “Monks, I allow you to store [food] inside,” it is permissible to store rice and other grains inside during times of famine. Because of the statement, “Monks, I allow you to cook inside...”

During a time of famine, it is permissible to cook inside [the monastery]. Because of the statement, “I allow you, monks, to cook for yourselves,” during a time of famine, it is permissible even to cook by oneself.
Because of the statement, “I allow you, monks, what is grown inside, cooked inside, and cooked by oneself,” during a time of famine, all three are permissible.
The Discussion on What is Taken Up and Received.

In this discussion on what is taken up and received, it is said: "Monks, I allow that wherever one sees fresh fruit or hard food and there is no attendant for allowable things (kappiyakāraka), one may take it oneself, carry it away, and having seen an attendant for allowable things, set it down upon the ground."
Because of the statement, “Monks, I allow you to accept what has been taken up [by another] so as to consume it,” it is permissible to consume it after having done so;
there is no offense. This concludes the discussion on what is brought from that place.
Then, regarding the statement in the *Tato-nīhaṭaka-kathā*: “Monks, accept it; monks, consume it.

I allow you, monks, to consume what has been brought out from that [gift], provided it is not leftover (*anatiritta*), by a monk who has finished eating and is no longer invited,” this refers to food brought out from the gift at which the monks have been invited to eat; such food may be consumed by a monk who has finished his meal and is no longer invited.
It may be eaten; there is no offense under the training rule regarding being invited to eat. For it is said in the Commentary:
"Regarding 'brought out from there,' it means brought out from wherever they are invited to eat.
This concludes the discussion on what was received before the meal.
In the discourse on receiving food before the meal, because of the statement: “Receive it, monks; consume it, monks;

I allow you, monks, to consume what was received before the meal, provided it has not been made ‘leftover’ by one who has finished eating and refused further food,” a monk who has received and set aside food before the meal may consume it without having made it ‘leftover,’ even if he has already finished his meal and refused further food.
It is permissible to eat; there is no offense under the training rule concerning one who has already finished eating (*pavārita*).
In the *Vanaṭṭhapokkharaṭṭhakathā*:
"Now at that time, the Venerable Sāriputta suffered from a bodily ailment of burning heat..."
There was. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached the Venerable Sāriputta;
having approached, he said this to the Venerable Sāriputta: “Friend Sāriputta, what brings relief to your bodily affliction of burning heat?
“By means of lotus roots and stalks, friend,” [he replied]. … [and so on] … Then, for the Venerable Sāriputta—
When he had consumed the lotus roots and stalks, the affliction of bodily fever subsided... [as before] ... "Accept them, monks;

consume them. I allow you, monks, for one who has finished eating and is invited to stop, to consume lotuses growing in a forest or in a pond that have not been left over. Because of this statement, [one may eat] lotuses growing in a forest or in a pond by one who has finished eating and is invited to stop.
It is permissible for a bhikkhu to consume [it]; there is no offense under the training rule concerning being invited to eat.
In this context, "grown in a forest" and "grown in a pond" means that which is produced both in a forest and in a lotus thicket. This concludes the discussion on what has not been made allowable.

In the *Akatakappakathā*, it is stated: “Monks, I allow you to consume fruit that is seedless, from which the seeds have been removed, and for which the *akatakappa* (the ritual preparation) has not been performed.

Because of this statement, it is permissible to consume fruit that is either naturally seedless or from which the seeds have been extracted, even without performing the *samaṇakappa* (ascetic’s preparation) by means of fire, a knife, or the fingernails.
In this context, “seedless” refers to young fruit whose seeds have not yet produced a sprout.

It does not produce [new fruit]. Regarding "fruit from which the seed has been extracted": this refers to mangoes, jackfruits, and the like, which are to be consumed after the seed has been extracted and removed.
When no one is available to perform the *kappa*-act (the ritual preparation), it is permissible to consume those fruits even without such a preparation. This concludes the discussion on rice gruel.
In the Discourse on Gruel: “There are these ten benefits, brahmin, of gruel. What ten? One who gives gruel gives life;
gives beauty; gives happiness; gives strength; gives eloquence.
When gruel is drunk, it wards off hunger, dispels thirst, harmonizes the wind, cleanses the bladder, and digests any remaining undigested food. These, brahmin, are the ten...”
These are the ten benefits of rice porridge:
"Whoever gives rice porridge at the proper time and with respect to those who are self-restrained and live on what is given by others..."
He bestows upon him eight states:
longevity, beauty, happiness, and strength;
and from that, inspired eloquence arises within him.
It dispels hunger and thirst, and it balances the bodily humors;
it cleanses the bladder and digests food.
This medicine was praised by the Sugata.
Therefore, indeed, a person who desires happiness, whether seeking human pleasures or aspiring to divine joys, ought always to give rice-gruel.

—“I allow, monks, rice-gruel and honey-balls,” because of this statement, it is permissible to accept both rice-gruel and honey-balls.
Regarding the words “of those who long for” and “who desire” in the verse of thanksgiving, they are connected with the phrase “it is indeed sufficient to give.
However, if there is a reading “of those longing and desiring,” that very one should be accepted.

whoever should so consume it is to be dealt with according to the rule. Because of this statement, one who consumes it in such a manner incurs an offense under the training rule concerning eating in succession (*paramparabhojana*). “Rice-gruel” (*bhojjayāgu*) refers to that which generates an invitation. “Is to be dealt with according to the rule” means he is to be dealt with for eating in succession.
In the *Guḷakathā* (The Discourse on Sugar), because of the statement, “Monks, I allow sugar for one who is ill,

and sugar-water for one who is not ill,” it is permissible for a monk who is ill to eat a lump of sugar even at an improper time (*vikāla*). However, one who is not ill [may consume] that which is mixed with water.

Having prepared it, it is permissible to consume it by using it as sugar-water. Regarding this, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “‘For one who is ill, sugar’: the meaning is that I allow sugar after the meal for one who is ill with such a disease.
Because it is said, “with such a disease,” [it refers to] the kind of disease with which sugar must be consumed by one who is ill; with that kind of disease...
It appears as if it were said, "by one who is ill with such-and-such a disease";

this should be understood after careful investigation. Among these various discourses, whatever is not found in the treatises that are to be commented upon has been extracted by us from the Canon (Pāḷi) and the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) for the benefit of well-behaved bhikkhus, and [presented] according to the words of the masters of the Ṭīkās.
Having been set down after being adorned, let the wise, free from doubt, investigate it.
67. The section beginning with "Whatever, monks...
is called the Discourse on the Great Authorities (*Mahāpadesakathā*). In that context, they are so called because great matters (*mahante atthe*) are demonstrated by means of them.

*Mahāpadesā*: they are called *mahāpadesā* because great matters (*attha*) are seen or made known therein; or alternatively, they are called *mahāpadesā* because they are the locus (*padesa*), that is, the sphere of occurrence, for great matters.
What are they? They are these very four recitations (*pāṭha*) or meanings (*attha*).
Therefore it was said: "These four *mahāpadesā*," and so forth. In this context, the "Elders who compiled the Dhamma" refers to Mahākassapa and the others.
“Having taken the sutta” means: having taken and considering the sutta beginning with “excepting the juice of grain and fruit,” etc.
“Seven grains” refers to: “Rice, paddy, kudrūsa, wheat, varaka, barley, and kaṅgu—these are the seven grains; nīvāra and the rest are their varieties.”

The seven grains have been mentioned. "All other vegetables" refers to mung beans, black gram, and so forth. "Eight drinks" refers to mango drink, rose-apple drink, coconut drink, plantain drink, lotus-root drink, grape drink, honey drink, and *phārusaka* fruit drink.
"By this method" means by the method of conforming to the Sutta; for it is said in the Commentary: "Conformity to the Sutta consists of the four Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*).
"Without regard for the Canon or the Commentary" means that [the meaning] has already come down as of explicit meaning (*nītattha*) within the Canon itself.
"Having taken up. "Others as well" means others besides those previously mentioned.

By this, he shows that what are called the "Great Authorities" (mahāpadesa) are not merely those already stated, but rather many various kinds revealed through the power of the knowledge of one who is a bearer of the Vinaya (vinayadhara). This is the discourse on the benefits (ānisamsa-kathā).

68. Regarding the discourse on the benefits (*ānisaṃsa*): one who upholds the Vinaya is a "Vinaya-holder" (*vinayadhara*), namely, a monk skilled in the mastery of the Vinaya through training, recitation, attention, investigation, and acting in accordance with it. Those for whom the mastery of the Vinaya is their root are "those rooted in the mastery of the Vinaya.
Who are they? They are the five benefits. These are the benefits to be obtained by making the mastery of the Vinaya itself the root or the cause.
The meaning is: "not making another study, or practice and so forth, the root. Alternatively, *pariyatti* means mastery;
mastery of the Vinaya is *vinayapariyatti*. Those for which this is the root are *vinayapariyattimūlakā*;
the meaning is that the benefits arise because they have the mastery of the Vinaya as their cause. With the words beginning "Which ones," [the text] explains those five benefits and so forth.

Having asked about the specific nature [of the five benefits] and having answered with the words "one's own" and so forth, he says "For it has been said" (*vuttañhetaṃ*) and so on in order to support that statement with the canonical text (*pāḷi*).

Having thus shown the specific nature of the five benefits, he now asks "How is it for him? and so forth, and answers with "In this case, a certain person" (*idhekacco*) and so forth, in order to show those very same benefits in detail.
Therein, "the state of one's own aggregate of virtue being well-guarded" (*attano sīlakkhandhasuguttabhāvo*) means...
It is precisely by way of the state of committing an offense and not otherwise that there is an offense;

thus, having shown the cause for committing an offense, he said, "One who commits an offense commits it in six ways," etc., in order to show the non-committing [of an offense] through the absence of those [causes].
Therein—“One commits an offense intentionally;”...
“He conceals his offense;
he goes upon a wrong path—
it is such a person who is called ‘shameless.’”
One who does not feel shame or dread of blame because of the characteristics of a shameless person described above is called *alajjī*;
the state of being such is *alajjitā*. That which lacks knowledge is *aññāṇa*; the state of being such is *aññāṇatā*. The state of having done what is improper is *kukkucca*;
one who is affected by that is *kukkuccapakata*; the state of being such is *kukkuccapakatatā*. That which is allowable is *kappiya*; that which is not allowable is *akappiya*.

Regarding that which is unallowable (*akappiya*), one who has the perception that it is allowable is "one with the perception of the allowable" (*kappiyasaññī*); the state of being such is "the state of having the perception of the allowable" (*kappiyasaññitā*).
The other [terms] should be understood by way of their opposites. In these five instances, there is the elision of the letter *y*;

therefore, they should be construed as "he incurs an offense through lack of shame" (*alajjitāya āpattiṃ āpajjati*), and so forth. And this is an ablative expression used in the sense of a cause (*hetvattha*). "He remembers" is *sati*.
*Samussana* means confusion. Confusion of mindfulness is *satisammoso*; therefore, it is "from confusion of mindfulness" (*satisammosā*).
Here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the cause (*hetvatthe*). Now, in order to show those causes in detail, he says "How... and so forth.
That is to be understood by following the method [of analysis]. "Ariṭṭho" refers to the monk Ariṭṭha; "Kaṇṭako" refers to the novice Kaṇṭaka; from Vesālī...
Those born in Vesālī are the Vesālikas; they are the sons of the Vajjis, thus "Vajjiputtas. Being both Vesālikas and Vajjiputtas, they are called "Vesālika-Vajjiputtas.

Ariṭḍha the bhikkhu and Kaṇṭaka the novice are the "Ariṭḍha-bhikkhu-Kaṇṭaka-sāmaṇera-Vesālika-Vajjiputtakas. Encouragement by others, ignorance, and the overcoming of doubt are "encouragement-by-others-ignorance-and-overcoming-of-doubt. Who are they?
"Vādā. Those for whom these are primary are those characterized by misrepresentation, ignorance, doubt, wavering, and so forth. They are called "vādā" because they argue by means of these;
thus, "those for whom misrepresentation, ignorance, doubt, wavering, and so forth are the arguments" (parūpahāra-...-vādā). Who are they? They are the proponents of false views. Ariṭṭha...
and the sons [of the Buddha], as well as those whose arguments consist of misrepresentation... and the Mahāsaṅghikas and others who are enemies of the Dispensation.
The term "names" (nāma) should be construed according to the rules of collective compounds (*samuccaya-dvandva*). The remainder is easily understood.
The discussion on the benefits (*ānisamsa*) is concluded.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Vinayālaṅkāra*, which is a commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*.
The Thirty-fourth Chapter, titled "The Ornament of the Discourse on the Analysis of Miscellaneous Matters.
Explanation of the Concluding Discourse.

In the first verse of the *Nigamagāthā*, the construction is as follows: "Requested by King Parakkamabāhu, who desires the endurance of the True Dhamma and illuminates the Dispensation, I, he [the author], composed this *Vinayasaṅgaha*.

In the second and third verses: "In that delightful and charming place, adorned with a hundred palaces—adorned with a hundred palaces, strewn with various groves of trees, and a dwelling for those delighted in meditation—for those who delight in meditation..."
The construction is as follows: "While dwelling—residing—in the Jeta Grove, known by the name Jetavana, a monastery that serves as a resort for monks and is endowed with cool water;

or rather, while I, that very same person, was dwelling there, I composed this compendium of the Vinaya, which is beneficial, being a source of welfare for yogis, and essential, being possessed of the core meaning."
By this composition of verses, whatever merit has been accomplished by me, and whatever other merit distinct from this composition has been produced by me—
by this meritorious deed, in my second existence, rejoicing in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, delighting in virtue, conduct, and good qualities,
and unattached to the five sensual pleasures, may I become a son of the gods, foremost among the foremost.
Having attained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) in his final existence, and having seen the Lord of the World, the Protector,
who is devoted to the welfare of all beings— the one named Metteyya, the bull among sages, the best of sages—
and having heard the teaching of the True Dharma from that steadfast one, he will realize the supreme fruit of Arhatship and receive the Dispensation of the Victor.
"May I shine and may I cause others to shine"—this is the explicit interpretation (*pākaṭayojanā*).
However, when this interpretation is accepted, the wise do not accept the statement of the excellent teacher (*ācariyavara*). How so?

For here, having become a son of the gods in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in his second existence from this one and having attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), [he attains it] in his final existence.
The teacher’s aspiration—that one might attain the fruit of Arhatship after hearing the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One Metteyya—is improper.
For a stream-enterer has no rebirth-linking beyond seven existences;
and even in a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand existences among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, [there is no such rebirth for one who has entered the stream].

The time for his rebirth has not yet arrived. Furthermore, if one were to say, "Having been reborn in the Brahma-world in the interim, he will become a human being at the time of the Blessed One Metteyya," this too is not tenable. For there is no further rebirth in the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) for noble ones who have gone to the Brahma-world.
Indeed, it is stated in the *Yamaka-pakaraṇa* of the Abhidhamma: "For one who has passed away from the form realm..."
“Only seven underlying tendencies (anusaya) underlie one being reborn in the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu).
Now, if one were to say, “He could attain the supreme fruit (aggaphala) while remaining in the Brahma-world itself,” that is not seen to be the case according to the Teacher’s word;

for since it was said, “May I beautify the Conqueror’s Dispensation (sāsana),” only his state as a monk (bhikkhu) is seen there. Indeed, it is one who has become a monk who beautifies the Dispensation.
He is able. And in the *Abhidhammatthavibhāvanī*:
“May I see and honor him who, with a pure mind, illuminates his teaching at that time—Sāriputta, my venerable teacher.”

It was stated precisely with reference to one who has become a bhikkhu. Furthermore, if one were to say, "Having been a long-lived terrestrial deva in the interim, he would then become a human," even in that case, an noble person (ariyapuggala) who was a disciple of one Buddha could not again become a disciple of another Buddha;
however, the teacher [in question] was a master of the entire scriptural tradition (pariyatti), an author of numerous treatises, and [a teacher] of many...

He was the teacher of the teachers of those elders who composed the treatises; therefore, these verses were not placed here alone, but were also placed at the conclusion of the Vinaya commentary named the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
Consequently, one should investigate this, considering that there must be a specific reason for it.

Alternatively, by this... [as before] ...having become a son of the gods, he first attains the aforementioned fruit—the benefit characterized by non-attachment to the five sensual pleasures—delighting in the virtues of joyous conduct and behavior among the Tāvatiṃsa gods; then, in his final existence... [as before] ...he shall shine.
This is the construction. Alternatively, by this... [as before] ...having become unattached to the five sensual pleasures, in his final existence... [as before].

The construction is as follows: having heard the teaching of the True Dhamma, they shall attain the first fruit, the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), and thereafter, having realized the supreme fruit, the fruit of arhatship (arahattaphala), they shall cause the Conqueror’s dispensation to shine.
Just as the Elder Aññāta-Koṇḍañña attained the fruit of stream-entry after hearing the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma in the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*.
Having attained it, and subsequently having realized the fruit of Arhatship, he adorned the teaching of the Victor; such is the meaning.
Other methods as well, which accord with the words of the Elder, should be considered by the wise.
The commentary on the concluding discourse is finished.
Concluding Statement:
In the delightful land of Jambudīpa, within the realm of Maramma,
there stands a city named Ratana, situated in the district of Tambadīpa.
In that city of jewels— which was the lamp of the Conqueror’s teaching,
a mine of many gems, an abode for virtuous people,
and adorned with golden palaces— there lived a king who was the lord of many provinces.
Known by the names Sirīsudhammarāja and Mahādhipati,
this king of great majesty ruled according to the Dhamma;
the king had the Great Cetiya with its jeweled crest constructed.
In those days, in the great forest, there was a mountain named Tiriya;
it was the dwelling place of those who lived in the ancient forest, a place worthy of spiritual cultivation.
It was free from the eighteen defects and endowed with the five factors.
Having reached the characteristics of the forest and adorned by the established boundaries,
the Great Elder dwelling on that mountain was well-known as "The Ornament of the Tipiṭaka," having received his formal designation on two occasions.
Venerated and beloved by those three kings,
skilled in the scriptures and a practitioner of the path—
such as I am, having been requested by modest and virtuous bhikkhus;
For the benefit of the Dispensation, I have composed this *Vinayālaṅkāra*,
which increases virtue, assists those who possess a sense of shame,
provides a thorough commentary on the *Vinayasaṅgaha*, and is practiced by the virtuous.
When the ears of the Victor’s Dispensation were pierced by the destruction of its form,
and when the Kali Age had arrived— characterized by forms that are empty of their own essence—
this commentary was completed by me for the sake of the Dispensation.
Having gained victory twice over two golden monasteries,
through this meritorious deed and other wholesome actions,
when I pass away from here and come into my second existence:
In the region of the Himalayas, on Mount Gandhamādana,
near the Maṇiguhā cave and the Mañjūsaka tree,
there I shall become an excellent earth-deva of exceedingly long life.
Endowed with wisdom and energy, a devotee of the Buddha’s teaching,
as long as the dispensation endures,
may I, with a joyful heart, perform the worship of the cetiyas, the worship of the Bodhi tree, and the worship of the Saṅgha.
I would perform services for the bhikkhus who are practicing the path;
I would dispel the doubts of those devoted to the study of the scriptures;
and I would be a companion to the kings who uphold the Dispensation.
May I be capable of restraining those who seek to suppress the Dispensation.
But when the Dispensation has vanished, may I constantly perform worship at Mañjūsā, Rukkhuttama, Nandamūla, and Pabbhāra.
But when Paccekabuddhas of great renown arise,
then I would perform service for them throughout the entire aeon.
With that very same physical form, I would remain until the appearance of a Buddha.
Remaining among human beings during the appearance of a Buddha,
having gone forth into the teaching of the Blessed One Metteyya and having satisfied that Conqueror, may I receive the supreme prophecy.
Having received the prophecy and fulfilled all the perfections,
I shall become a Buddha in the future time, together with the world of gods.
The *Vinayālaṅkāra-ṭīkā* is completed.
